Feature: Chinese language learning opens doors to study, careers for Indonesian youth
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
19:48:57 CST
20:48:57 KST

JAKARTA, Nov. 2 (Xinhua) -- The 2026 Indonesia HSK study in China and career expo was held in Jakarta on Sunday, bringing together 21 Chinese universities, including Peking University and Tsinghua University, and attracting about 3,000 Indonesian students, Chinese language learners and parents seeking information on study opportunities in China.
Among the crowds at the exhibition was Calysta Jacqueline Wijaya, a 16-year-old Indonesian high school student who was exploring admission requirements at Chinese universities. Though only in her first year of high school, Calysta has already been learning Chinese for 11 years.
"I want to study pharmacy in China," Calysta told Xinhua, noting that she hopes to bring professional knowledge back to Indonesia to help more people.
Calysta is now working to improve her score on the Chinese Proficiency Test, or HSK, as she prepares to apply to Chinese universities.
Her classmate, Richard Dharma Hungnata, shares a similar aspiration. Having studied Chinese since his first year of primary school, the 15-year-old can already communicate fluently in the language.
Previous visits to Beijing, Shanghai and other Chinese cities have left him deeply impressed by China's development.
With a strong interest in mathematics and physics, Richard hopes to study engineering at a Chinese university. He plans to take the HSK exam after his second year of high school, aiming for a higher score to strengthen his university applications.
Their Chinese teacher, Zheng Wenting, who also heads a Mandarin education center in Indonesia, has witnessed growing enthusiasm for the language.
Zheng told Xinhua that more Indonesian parents have become interested in having their children learn Chinese in recent years, while an increasing number of students are aspiring to study in China. Reflecting this trend, enrollment at her institution has grown from about 50 students per intake a decade ago to nearly 500 today.
From learning Chinese characters and pinyin in primary school to exploring university programs and future careers, Chinese language education is becoming an integral part of the educational journey for a growing number of Indonesian youth.
Yet language proficiency offers more than a gateway to university admission.
At the booth of the Beijing-based China University of Petroleum, Dexter Godwin, an Indonesian graduate who earned his degree in petroleum engineering from the university in 2025, was attending the expo to share his university experiences with prospective applicants.
After learning online about the university's strengths in petroleum engineering, Dexter decided to pursue his studies in China.
During his four years there, he not only acquired professional knowledge but also learned Chinese.
He has since secured a job at an oil company operating in Indonesia, successfully embarking on his professional career.
"I feel fortunate to have studied at China University of Petroleum for four years and to be able to put what I learned into practice," Dexter said, adding that he had benefited greatly from his academic training and the support of his teachers.
As cooperation between China and Indonesia continues to expand in trade, infrastructure, energy and other sectors, young professionals equipped with both Chinese language proficiency and specialized skills are finding broader career opportunities.
According to Chinese Testing International Co., Ltd., since the HSK exam was introduced in Indonesia in 2001, the country has established 56 test centers and recorded more than 300,000 test takers cumulatively. Indonesia ranked fourth worldwide in the number of HSK test takers in 2026.
Liu Xiaolong, deputy general manager of Chinese Testing International Co., Ltd., said Chinese language learning, studying in China and career development are becoming increasingly interconnected.
As bilateral cooperation expands across various fields, young professionals with both Chinese language skills and specialized knowledge are increasingly sought after in the job market, he added.
Chen Wu, education counselor at the Chinese Embassy in Indonesia, said youth exchanges are a vital force in sustaining the friendship between the two countries, adding that China welcomes more young Indonesians to deepen their understanding of China through educational experiences. ■

Economic Watch: Chinese central bank shifts policy rate anchor to overnight
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
19:48:57 CST
20:48:57 KST

BEIJING, Nov. 2 (Xinhua) -- China's central bank on Monday changed its main policy rate from the seven-day reverse repo rate to the overnight reverse repo rate as it conducted 541 billion yuan (about 80.6 billion U.S. dollars) of overnight reverse repos.
The People's Bank of China (PBOC) conducted this operation at an interest rate of 1.25 percent through fixed-rate, quantity-based bidding. It was the first operation under a revised mechanism announced late last month.
An overnight reverse repo is a transaction in which the central bank purchases securities from financial institutions with an agreement to sell them back the next day. The operation provides liquidity to the financial system.
Under the revised mechanism, the PBOC will now conduct overnight reverse repo operations every working day, with overnight operations becoming its main open market instrument.
Other tools previously priced relative to the seven-day reverse repo rate, such as temporary repo and reverse repo operations, will instead be linked to the overnight reverse repo rate, with existing spreads unchanged.
Analysts said the adjustment marks another step toward strengthening price-based monetary policy regulation, with a shorter-term main policy rate and more consistent benchmarks across policy tools.
The change is in line with the PBOC's emphasis on paying less attention to quantitative targets and giving greater weight to interest rates and other price-based tools, according to analysts.
PBOC Governor Pan Gongsheng said at a forum in October that the central bank would consider shifting the tenor of its main open market operations to overnight at an appropriate time to improve the precision of interest rate regulation. The overnight repo rate would then become its principal policy rate.
Pan said the PBOC will continue to assess and refine its monetary policy framework and give greater weight to interest rate-based regulation.
Zhang Xu, an analyst at Everbright Securities, said establishing the overnight rate as the main policy rate would provide a clear benchmark for the market, reduce irrational interest rate fluctuations, and improve the transmission of monetary policy signals.
Wang Jian, an analyst at Guosen Securities, said the adjustment goes beyond simply shortening the tenor of the operations from seven days to overnight.
It will help streamline the transmission of policy rate changes via money market rates to borrowing costs in the real economy, allowing interest rates to respond more promptly to funding supply and demand while facilitating a steadier shift from quantity-based to price-based monetary policy regulation, Wang explained.
Dong Ximiao, chief economist at Merchants Union Consumer Finance, said conducting overnight reverse repo operations every working day would help reduce disruptions to policy rate signals during tax payment periods and at month-ends.
The operations would also shorten the transmission chain from the policy rate to money market rates, bond yields and lending rates, thus improving the efficiency of monetary policy regulation, Dong said. ■

ULAN BATOR, Nov. 2 (Xinhua) -- A bear attacked and killed 63 sheep and goats belonging to a herder in western Mongolia, local media reported on Monday, citing the Ministry of Environment and Climate Change.
The incident occurred in Bugat soum (an administrative subdivision) last Friday. Hunters later shot and killed the bear as it attempted to flee, the ministry said.
Bear sightings in and around residential areas across Mongolia have been reported over recent months, prompting authorities to urge the public to remain vigilant and take precautions to reduce the risk of encounters.
Earlier in October, a man in his 40s was killed and a woman in her 50s was seriously injured in a bear attack in Ulan Bator, the capital of Mongolia. In a separate incident last week, a 35-year-old herder was injured in a bear attack in the northern province of Darkhan-Uul.
Experts say encounters between bears and livestock, as well as bear sightings in residential areas, have become increasingly common over recent years.
They attribute the trend to several factors, including climate change, food shortage in bears' natural habitats and the overexploitation of natural resources. ■

China Focus: China mulls amendments to Criminal Procedure Law to better protect rights
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
19:48:21 CST
20:48:21 KST

BEIJING, Nov. 2 (Xinhua) -- China's top legislature on Monday began deliberating a draft amendment to the Criminal Procedure Law aimed at better punishing crimes while further protecting the rights of participants in criminal proceedings.
The 55-article draft amendment was submitted for its first reading at a bimonthly session of the Standing Committee of the National People's Congress (NPC), which runs from Monday through Friday.
The draft stipulates strengthened presumption-of-innocence protections, refined rules on the use of detention and other compulsory measures against criminal suspects and defendants, and provisions regarding foreign-related criminal proceedings.
It also includes stronger protections for victims and lawyers involved, as well as juvenile participants in relevant proceedings -- as victims, suspects, defendants or witnesses.
Moreover, the draft covers the sealing up, seizure, freezing, and handling of property involved in criminal cases.
The draft stresses a criminal procedure system with a focus on court proceedings to ensure that court hearings are fully functional and play a substantive role in criminal justice, so that courts, procuratorates and police agencies divide responsibilities, cooperate, and act as a mutual check on one another.
China's current Criminal Procedure Law was adopted in 1979 and amended in 1996, 2012 and 2018.
A report to the NPC Standing Committee session on the draft said further changes are needed because serious violent crimes and the share of offenders receiving heavy sentences have declined for years in China, while minor crimes are rising. Also, some offenses have moved online and become international, requiring stronger cross-border judicial cooperation.
Amendments to the Criminal Procedure Law aim to further regulate the exercise of judicial power through a comprehensive and efficient institutional framework, enhance judicial credibility and strengthen the public's perception of the rule of law, the report said.
China is believed to be one of the safest countries in the world, among the nations with the lowest rates of crime and homicide.
According to China's police authority, criminal cases nationwide fell by 12.8 percent in 2025, reaching the lowest level this century. Meanwhile, Gallup's 2025 Global Safety Report ranked China as the third-safest place globally and fourth in the law and order index.
The findings also echo the international perception. More international travelers are experiencing that sense of security firsthand as visa-free access expands, travel services improve and urban support systems are strengthened.
Behind this safe environment lie China's long-term efforts to ensure public security through a well-established legal framework, community-based governance, modern technology and rapid police response. ■

Iran says it can reopen Hormuz in two days if US meets conditions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
11:48:15 UTC
20:48:15 KST

Foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said the timeline shortened from the seven days first proposed in September was “another indication of Iran’s good-faith approach” but that “everything depends” on Washington.
Iran said on Monday it was ready to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days if the US accepted its conditions, having proposed a seven-day timeline when it first put the idea to Washington through Qatar in September.
"The possibility of implementing this plan in two days is another indication of Iran's good-faith approach," foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said.
"We have stated that, if Iran's demands are met, it would be possible to restore security to the Strait of Hormuz and resume the negotiating process within a short period," he added.
Baghaei said that an exchange of messages was ongoing with the US via mediators and that "everything depends" on the US side accepting Iran's demands. "Only then can we discuss the subsequent stages," he explained.
Tehran's conditions include ending the war on all fronts, unfreezing Iranian assets abroad, lifting sanctions on its oil sector, and ending the US naval blockade of Iranian ports.
Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi set out further requirements in an Al Jazeera interview released on Sunday, saying Washington must also accept a new transit route through the strait agreed between Iran and Oman, reduce US troop numbers in the region, and remove sanctions imposed since August.
Washington has rolled out a fresh wave of measures from August onwards, which it described as the "economic asphyxiation" of Iran.
Since the Iran war broke out in late February, Tehran has claimed it maintained control over Hormuz, regularly targeting vessels that attempt to cross without its authorisation. Meanwhile, the US imposed a naval blockade on Iranian ports.
Diplomatic activity speeds up
The diplomatic activity comes as both Washington and Tel Aviv have intensified military threats. On Saturday, Trump said he still had to "take care" of one or two targets, including Pickaxe mountain in central Iran, a site Washington suspects houses nuclear infrastructure, which Tehran denies.
Baghaei warned at Monday's briefing that "any act of aggression against Iran, any military attack against Iran, by whatever means, will be met with a powerful, immediate and comprehensive response from us."
Iran's deputy foreign minister Kazem Gharibabadi travelled to Doha on Monday to help draft a preliminary agreement, with Qatar acting as mediator.
China said it was sending its special envoy Zhai Jun to Iran, Oman and Saudi Arabia to press all sides to halt the fighting. President Xi Jinping said the Middle East and Gulf must not become an arena for great-power competition. Beijing and Muscat jointly called on Washington and Tehran to return to the "Islamabad memorandum of understanding," Chinese state media reported.
Officials in Tehran continued to set red lines. Deputy parliament speaker Ali Nikzad said Iran would not enter nuclear negotiations under pressure, and that previous talks had produced only broken promises.
Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, said on Saturday that the US would need to meet Iran's conditions before talks could begin. Rezaei said he had received a letter from US Vice President JD Vance but had not yet replied.
US military command CENTCOM rejected Iranian claims that its strikes had targeted only military objectives. CENTCOM said on X that Iran had deliberately hit residential areas, civilian centres and civilian sailors in international waters, and that its attacks had killed at least 20 people.
Anwar Gargash, adviser to the UAE president, told the Manama Dialogue conference in Bahrain that Abu Dhabi did not want a prolonged crisis with Iran but acknowledged that trust had been lost. "This damage was not caused by us. Rather, following Iran's attack on us, trust was damaged," he said.
The diplomatic activity falls ahead of US midterm elections on Tuesday, in which economic pressures linked to the Iran war have increased the likelihood of Republican losses in Congress.
The announcement of results on Wednesday coincides with the anniversary of the 1979 seizure of the US embassy in Tehran, during which 52 US diplomats were held for over a year. Tehran-organised demonstrations against the US are expected across the country, while billboards depicting Trump behind prison bars have been erected in Tehran in recent days.
Trump said on Sunday evening that he and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had held "very good" talks the previous day and discussed Iran, without elaborating. Netanyahu's office has not commented on the meeting.
Since Israeli voters went to the polls last Tuesday, Netanyahu has spoken publicly only about the vote. Results remain inconclusive, with preliminary assessments suggesting he may not secure a coalition, although no alternative government has taken shape.

Russia halts chemical exports after Ukraine hits its rocket fuel plants
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
11:48:12 UTC
20:48:12 KST

- Russia banned exports of benzene, toluene, xylenes and phenol outside the Eurasian Economic Union for three months to keep domestic plants supplied.
- The ban follows a series of Ukrainian strikes on Russian chemical and propellant plants, though Moscow has not linked the two.
Russia has banned exports of benzene, toluene, xylenes and phenol for three months, saying it needs to keep its own factories supplied with the industrial chemicals, the government announced on Nov. 2.
The ban, signed by Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin, covers coal-derived and petroleum benzene, toluene, ortho-xylene, para-xylene and phenol shipped outside the Eurasian Economic Union, the Russia-led trade bloc that includes Belarus, Kazakhstan, Armenia and Kyrgyzstan. Transit shipments, humanitarian aid and supplies for Russian operations on the Arctic archipelago of Svalbard are exempt. The government did not say what caused the supply problem or how large it is.
In its announcement, the government listed civilian uses for the chemicals, including paints and coatings for the automotive, aviation, shipbuilding and rail industries, food packaging, flooring, cable insulation and medicine. All six are also basic feedstocks for the wider chemical industry. Toluene, for example, is the raw material for TNT, the standard military explosive used in artillery shells and bombs.
Russia’s government has not linked the export ban to the war. It follows months of Ukrainian drone and missile strikes on Russian chemical, refining and propellant plants, many of which Ukraine’s General Staff says feed missile and rocket production.
Over the past two weeks alone, Ukraine reported hitting the Tolyattikauchuk synthetic rubber plant in Samara region for the third time this year, as well as the Voronezhsintezkauchuk rubber plant, both of which Kyiv says produce rubbers used in solid rocket propellant for tactical and ballistic missiles. On the night of Oct. 31, Ukrainian drones and Neptune missiles struck the Kamensky Combine in Rostov region, which makes solid propellant for Uragan, Smerch and Tornado-S rocket launchers, and President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed the strike the next day. Earlier in October, Ukraine said it hit the AVISMA plant in Perm region and a chemical plant in Tver region that makes a fuel component for Kh-55 and Kh-101 cruise missiles.
Much of Russia’s petroleum benzene, toluene and xylene comes from oil refineries and petrochemical complexes, including Rosneft’s Ryazan refinery, Slavneft-YANOS in Yaroslavl, the Moscow refinery, Sibur’s ZapSibNeftekhim in Tobolsk and Uralorgsintez in Perm region. Ukraine has also struck Russian refineries repeatedly this year, and Moscow has banned gasoline exports since the spring and restricted diesel exports, with the gasoline ban now extended to Jan. 31, 2027.

Prague, Kraków and Istanbul: These are the best European cities for solo travellers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
11:46:26 UTC
20:46:26 KST

A new ranking for solo travel has evaluated the most visited European cities by looking at things like accommodation costs and the perception of safety.
Solo travel seems to be constantly on the rise, but making the decision to take that first trip alone isn’t an easy one.
After you’ve decided to take the plunge, you then need to pick a destination, and some places are undoubtedly better suited to single guests.
Thinking about heading abroad by yourself this year? Then you might just want to take a look at the newly released Solo Travel Index by Radical Storage.
Created by analysing the 48 most visited cities in Europe against 11 factors, the index evaluates things like the average daily spend per person, the safety score from Numbeo as well as the number of hostels – a mainstay of solo travel.
Each factor was rated between one and 10 based on how the city compared with the others, and the 11 scores were then averaged to create an overall result.
The best cities for solo travel in Europe
After all that number crunching, Czechia’s capital Prague came out on top, with a mid-range day priced at €134.33 for accommodation, food, transport and entertainment, and with the eighth-highest safety score on the list.
Second place went to Kraków in Poland, the second-cheapest city in the ranking, while Istanbul in Türkiye came third thanks to its hostel dorm bed prices, which were the lowest of any city looked at.
Gdansk in Poland also made the cut, ranking fifth overall. Alongside Poland, both Portugal and Spain had two entries in the top 10 each, with Lisbon (fourth) and Porto (seventh) in the former and Seville (eighth) and Barcelona (ninth) in the latter.
The top 10 European cities for solo travel
- Prague, Czechia
- Kraków, Poland
- Istanbul, Türkiye
- Lisbon, Portugal
- Gdansk, Poland
- Berlin, Germany
- Porto, Portugal
- Seville, Spain
- Barcelona, Spain
- Riga, Latvia
The worst cities for solo travel in Europe
On the flip side, Zürich was named the worst city in Europe for solo travel due to its high prices, with accommodation coming in at €168.13 a day, the highest in the study, while it also has the second highest food costs and third highest transport costs.
Reykjavík in Iceland came second from last, quickly followed by Venice. Again, both cities were held back by their higher prices, which affect solo travellers who will not be splitting accommodation costs.
According to Radical Storage, a day in the bottom 10 worst-ranked cities costs an average of €252 per day, nearly €100 more than the top 10, where the average is €153.
The bottom 10 European cities for solo travellers
- Zürich, Switzerland
- Reykjavík, Iceland
- Venice, Italy
- Aarhus, Denmark
- Cologne, Germany
- Geneva, Switzerland
- Frankfurt, Germany
- Nice, France
- Marseille, France
- Dublin, Ireland

Swiss president insists arms contracts must be respected amid US delivery delays
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
11:45:25 UTC
20:45:25 KST

Beyza Binnur Donmez
02 November 2026•Update: 02 November 2026
Swiss President Guy Parmelin on Monday stressed that international arms procurement contracts must be honored, raising concerns over lengthy delays in military equipment deliveries from the US.
Responding to an Anadolu question during a press briefing for foreign journalists in Bern, Parmelin said Switzerland’s defense purchases from the US have traditionally involved dealing with the American government rather than directly with manufacturers.
“In the end, it’s the government, and that complicates the situation,” he said, referring to arrangements involving new fighter jets.
Parmelin emphasized that Switzerland expects suppliers to fulfill their contractual obligations, citing delays involving the Patriot air defense system.
“When you pay and you buy, you sign a contract, you expect the contract to be respected and to receive your delivery,” he said.
Asked whether the procurement difficulties signaled a loss of confidence in the US, Parmelin stopped short of confirming such a shift.
“Without saying that trust has disappeared, this is something extremely delicate when it comes to your personal security, the security of your country,” he said, referring to equipment facing delivery delays of five to seven years.
He said Switzerland, as a neutral country outside military alliances, must strengthen its domestic defense industry and logistical capabilities while diversifying arms purchases and expanding cooperation with neighboring European countries.
Parmelin stressed that such cooperation must respect Switzerland’s neutrality obligations under the Hague Conventions.
“Therefore, we cannot do just anything. We have commitments; we have contracts with various countries to purchase arms. These contracts must be respected,” he said.
In late October, Switzerland said it was considering buying military equipment directly from US defense companies instead of relying on Washington as an intermediary.
Under the US Foreign Military Sales program, Switzerland purchases American military equipment through the US government, leaving buyers with limited options to resolve pricing disputes or seek compensation for delayed deliveries.
Urs Loher, head of the Federal Office for Defense Procurement (Armasuisse), told Swiss daily Neue Zurcher Zeitung that certain components of the Patriot air defense system might be purchased directly from manufacturers, while acquiring advanced fighter jets such as the F-35 through this route would not be feasible.
The proposed shift comes as Switzerland faces a five- to seven-year delay in receiving its Patriot missile systems, with Washington prioritizing deliveries to Germany.
Switzerland has already paid more than 1 billion Swiss francs (over $1.2 billion) in advance for the systems.
Swiss authorities have also assessed an alternative air defense system, with the Federal Council expected to make the final decision.

‘I have two days until the food in my fridge runs out’: Thousands of Russian emigrants left scrambling after Serbia shuts down Alta Bank, freezing their savings
On October 30, Serbia’s Central Bank revoked the license of Alta, one of the few local banks where Russians could relatively easily open an account. Clients’ accounts were frozen. Many had kept money there from selling property in Russia, while others received their salaries through Alta accounts. Authorities promised to return up to 50,000 euros for lost deposits. What will happen to the rest of the money remains unclear. Meduza spoke with affected Russians, including entrepreneurs who used Alta accounts for their businesses, about how the bank’s closure will affect their lives.
‘We went to the ATM, but it wasn’t working. A branch employee announced that it wouldn’t open. The app wouldn’t load.’
Anton, an IT specialist, whose family kept money from the sale of an apartment in an Alta account
We moved to Serbia as a family. My wife moved first, last year, for work; then our child started school, and I only moved this year. My wife works in IT, and I was in IT too, but I haven’t found anything and I’m still unemployed.
The Alta account belonged to my wife. She opened it back in the summer of last year because the bank made it easy for Russians to open accounts there. The bank was accommodating with foreign transfers, and the money from the sale of our Russian apartment was sitting in Kazakhstan.
The apartment was in the Moscow region. We sold it in 2023, when we decided we would be leaving Russia. The sale was legal, but we didn’t want to explain why the money ended up in Kazakhstan. When we transferred it there, the process of receiving it took a long time, so we decided not to repeat it here.
When we opened the account, we asked whether we would need any documents on the origin of the money for transfers from the Kazakh account. We were told that for transfers of up to 10,000 euros a month, no documents were required. So we decided not to draw any extra attention and just send the money over gradually.
We made our last transfer to Alta on October 26. We didn’t have any plans for the money yet. We had thought about buying property [in Serbia], but we couldn’t afford it without a mortgage, so we decided to hold off for now.
We had about 70,000 euros in the account. That was only part of our savings. Another part was already in a different bank in Serbia, and a third part remained in Kazakhstan.
In the morning, my wife woke up, read the news about the license revocation on Threads, and we quickly got dressed and went to the ATM. It wasn’t working. Then we went to the branch. We stood there for half an hour, and an employee came out and announced that the branch would not open that day. The app wouldn’t load either. So we couldn’t transfer or withdraw any money.
Of course we were very upset, and at first there was even panic. But then we calmed down: this wasn’t our last money, and we have a card from another bank with funds for everyday life. We then looked for information online and found out that the insured deposit amount is 50,000 euros. That covers more than half of our money, which gave us a bit of peace of mind.
While we stood in line at the branch, everyone was sharing news they had read. There were people in line whose situation was far scarier than ours: they had all their money in Alta. After talking in chats, we found people in the same boat and agreed to share information. On Monday, several people are going to consult with lawyers, and they promised to share the results with everyone.
We’re waiting for Monday, when the Deposit Insurance Agency will publish the full procedure for returning funds up to 50,000 euros: where to go, what to submit, and so on. After that, we’ll figure out how to file a lawsuit as part of the bankruptcy proceedings.
Hi, I’m Katya.
I’ve been running Meduza’s crowdfunding since 2021. Today, supporting Meduza is a crime in Russia. You can be sent to prison just for donating. We’re still able to do our work thanks to thousands of our Russian readers who now live abroad. But even they’re no longer safe.
Imagine you’ve left Russia, but then your mom becomes seriously ill. It could be your last chance to see her, so of course you go home. At the border, you’re interrogated. Officers hack into your phone and search for any trace that you’ve donated to Meduza.
The Kremlin is counting on that fear, and it’s working. People are afraid to donate. I’m afraid for our supporters, because any one of them could end up in prison. And I’m afraid for Meduza. Without crowdfunding, we simply can’t continue. So if you live outside Russia and don’t have to worry that donating to Meduza could keep you from going home to your family, I’m asking for your help. Please support our work.
‘The day before the bank closed, I picked up a complete set of documents for opening a sole proprietor account’
Dmitry, a private entrepreneur in the arts, used Alta to register as a sole proprietor
My wife and I have lived in Serbia for a year and a half. We left Russia in 2022. We wanted to leave right away, but we needed the mobilization to give us that final push.
I became an Alta client as soon as I had the energy to deal with things like bank cards, about six months after arriving. The options for non-residents are limited: the [state-owned] Banka Poštanska štedionica and Alta. The latter turned out to be more modern, with a decent app. I used the account for everyday card payments, online purchases, and to get a bank statement for my residence permit application.
The day before the bank closed, I picked up a complete set of documents after opening a business account, which is mandatory in Serbia for running a sole proprietorship.
I found out about the license revocation in the morning from a message from an acquaintance, then started reading Serbian channels. My reaction was a kind of giddy hysteria, something like, “well, the barn’s already burned down, might as well let the house go too.” After the bureaucratic adventures with visas and residence permits in three different countries, this feels like an annoying inconvenience, nothing more.
At the time the license was revoked, I had about 100 euros in the account, so we weren’t hit too hard in that sense. Our main monthly budget is in cash. We have no savings: basically everything I earn goes straight to current expenses.
Then I started digging deeper into the context. And if what people are writing is to be believed, Alta was closely tied to the SNS. After [former President Aleksandar] Vučić‘s defeat, people tried to move money out of Serbia. If anything, this feels more like good news to me, because I’m used to the state seizing or shutting down good businesses, and here it seems to have happened the other way around. After living under the Russian regime, this is very unusual.
I don’t have access to my funds right now. I tried to pay by card, but the payment didn’t go through. I haven’t contacted the bank. Everywhere it says you have to wait for information about which bank will pay out deposits. There’s no point going to the ATMs: for non-residents, all transactions went through the teller. You couldn’t withdraw or deposit money at the ATM.
I had hoped that the whole quest of registering the company was over and that getting my residence permit would be finished any day now. We applied for the residence permit on the basis of opening the sole proprietorship, and the last step in setting everything up was opening an account for the legal entity. Two state organizations were waiting to work with me and needed my business account. Now it’s unclear where else I’ll be able to open an account. I hope that having a residence permit will at least expand my options a little.
I’m not too worried about the procedure for getting the money back, since the amount in the account is small. For now we’re just waiting. There’s been no information from the bank. What do I plan to do next? Live. We’ll manage, it’s just a bank. The main inconvenience is where and how to open a business account to keep running the sole proprietorship legally. But there are a lot of us in this situation, so something will work out.
‘My Serbian card was the only way I could withdraw money from PayPal’
Artem, a photography teacher living in Montenegro, used Alta to withdraw earnings from PayPal
I’ve been living in Montenegro for three years now. I used to be a photojournalist. Now I teach photography online, give lectures, and do consultations. My daughter goes to school here.
I opened the account at Alta because PayPal doesn’t work properly in Montenegro, and I receive payments for my work through it. As it turned out, the Serbian card wasn’t just my main option: it was the only way I had to turn my PayPal money into cash and pay for things here. Now I don’t have that option anymore.
Before that, I had a card from Uzbekistan’s Kapitalbank, which really helped me out abroad. It closed for technical reasons, and I can no longer reinstate it. That’s when I opened an account at Alta.
Actually, it had been time for me to switch accounts for a while already. I’d heard that Russians now need a Serbian residence permit to open an account at a Serbian bank, and mine is Montenegrin. So formally, I no longer qualified as a client and should have moved on this a bit earlier. But I certainly couldn’t have imagined that a bank could just slam shut like this in a single day, without warning.
My saving grace is that I don’t have any savings: I basically live paycheck to paycheck. So I didn’t have any substantial amounts sitting in Alta. But that doesn’t mean there’s no problem. My money isn’t in the bank, it’s on PayPal, and now I just can’t use it.
If I had known in advance that the bank would close, I would have at least withdrawn a few hundred euros to have money for everyday expenses: paying for my daughter’s school lunches, going to the store, paying for Serbian language classes. Now I’ll have to borrow from friends for all of that.
The problem isn’t just cash, either: I still need to pay by card sometimes. For example, I won’t be able to buy a plane ticket at all now. There are some vague options left, like transferring money through Russia in rubles and then getting cash at local exchange offices. But I don’t just need cash!
I think there are other Russians in Montenegro who used Alta cards too. And a lot of them are probably in a much worse position than me right now, since some people had large sums in the bank. As I understand it, they’re supposed to get their money back, but that involves certain complications and delays. If someone lives in Montenegro like I do, they might have to travel to Serbia to get it.
This isn’t my first year in emigration, and I’m used to things like this. But banks in other countries where I’ve had accounts have never closed this suddenly before. The only comparison I can make is the 1998 default in Russia. Back then the dollar rose several times over in a short period, prices jumped sharply, and it was a shock. But even then we roughly understood that something was going to happen. The only question was how badly things would crash. This time it was a complete surprise.
I can only guess why this happened. It seems to me that there could be political reasons behind the bank’s closure, maybe its ties to Russian structures. But these are purely amateur guesses on my part. I’m a photographer. I don’t understand any of this.
My plan now is to look for other ways to get money, other payment systems, and open new accounts. There’s Revolut, cryptocurrencies, and some other options. In Montenegro, in theory, I can open a bank account completely legally. But the problem is that I still won’t be able to work with PayPal the way I used to. For now I’m in limbo. I have two days, until the food in my fridge runs out, to find a way to get money.
I think if this situation had happened to me three years ago, or during the hardest period of my emigration — about a year and a half after leaving Russia — I would have had a panic attack. I just wouldn’t have known what to do, and the whole thing would have been very hard. But now, no, my reaction is more like, well, that’s kind of funny.
Over four years of emigration I’ve built up some experience, and I’m confident I’ll find other ways to get money.
‘I sold property, the money arrived in my account, and then this happened’
Boris, who moved to Serbia in the summer of 2026, kept money from selling an apartment in Russia at Alta
I’m part of the recent wave of emigration. I moved to Serbia at the end of summer. You remember what that period was like: rumors of a new mobilization round, severe internet restrictions in Russia, and concerns about physical safety in major cities. That’s what mainly drove the move.
Almost all of my acquaintances who moved this summer and fall ran into the same problem: nobody wants to open accounts for Russians. Banka Poštanska used to open accounts, but it stopped, and I didn’t make it in time. There were literally only a few options left, including Alta. I chose it because the terms were better and the bank agreed to open an account fairly quickly.
But the account wasn’t opened on the first try either. It didn’t work out in Belgrade itself, and we were turned down in the suburbs too. It worked on the second or third attempt. That’s just how it is in Serbia: one day you show up and they might open an account, another day you show up and they won’t. It all depends on the employee and the branch.
I didn’t pay any bribes: I showed a lease agreement and the “white card,” a document registering a foreigner’s place of residence. These things are fairly easy to get. I moved, rented an apartment, got the lease, and that was enough for the bank.
But the real problem is that almost all the banks don’t want to open accounts for Russians, even those who have a Serbian residence permit. As I understand it, this has to do with their cooperation with the European financial system. Serbian banks have the right to choose their own clients, and it turns out that nobody wants you as a client, even if you want to deposit a decent amount of money, simply because you have the wrong citizenship. It’s a pretty discriminatory thing.
I opened the Alta account in August and started the process of moving my assets out of Russia. I sold some property, and the money had literally just arrived in the account not long before. I hadn’t even had time to do anything with it yet, and then this situation happened.
Alta was my main account in Serbia. I used it for everyday expenses alongside cash. Right now, let’s just say I’m not left with nothing, but I urgently need to register other cards and figure out how to transfer money to them, since you can’t pay cash everywhere. You need some form of non-cash payment regardless.
The problem is that the amount in the account is higher than the 50,000-euro insurance limit. I only found out that this limit even existed on the day the bank closed. Right now I’m sitting in chats, trying to figure things out, and cooperating with other affected people. There’s still a lot of uncertainty.
I found out about the license revocation from a friend. He forwarded me a message from a Serbian public page and wrote, “Hey, didn’t you have money in there?” And I said, “Damn, yeah.” My first reaction was anxiety, shock, denial. It was a real black swan event. Then I started reading what other people were writing. In the “Guide from Oleg”, a separate thread was set up right away to discuss the situation. A chat also appeared for depositors who had more than the insured amount in their accounts, and people there are now looking for lawyers.
After the news broke, I didn’t even try to withdraw or transfer money. People in the chats were writing that it was pointless: nothing works because the bank has already been banned from carrying out transactions. There’s no access to funds right now. In fact, all I have left is cash. If I’m careful, it will last about a week. If I’m not careful, about three days. I had planned some purchases to furnish the apartment, and I wanted to buy myself a new laptop for work. Now all of that will have to be postponed, for obvious reasons.
Right now I’m trying to transfer money from Russia through cryptocurrency, but that has its own risks too. Some of my friends have had their Russian bank accounts blocked over similar transactions, because crypto transfers are often used in shady schemes.
Before, I could more or less get money out of Russia through SWIFT. It somehow worked even from sanctioned banks. But now I don’t have a proper Serbian account, so I have to deal with cryptocurrency instead. Even if it’s a gray area, I still need to live somehow. I need money to get by.
What to do next about the money in Alta is still unclear. Everyone in Serbia is off until Monday. You won’t get any answers from anyone over the weekend. So we’re waiting for Monday, worrying, feeling anxious. If there are collective lawsuits, I’ll definitely join one. But as I understand it, the first step will be getting the insurance payout, up to 50,000 euros. After that, we’ll have to figure out what to do with the remaining amount.
I read that the insurance payouts might go through Banka Poštanska. I’m afraid there will be some kind of collapse there. I happened to walk past that bank before the election once, when, as far as I remember, it was handing out government payments to Serbs of 6,000 dinars apiece. The lines were unbelievable.
I assume things could be even worse now. Government payouts are one thing. A bankrupt bank is another altogether. It might take dozens of hours in these lines. But the plan is: first collect the insured amount, then deal with the rest.
Honestly, I have no idea at all why this collapse happened in the first place. I don’t know the bank’s history very well either. But it really bothers me that the Serbian regulator made such an abrupt decision, when, it would seem, nothing hinted at it beforehand.
The bank was operating normally, people were coming in, depositing money, opening accounts. Did the Serbian regulator miss the moment when the bank started having serious problems? They should have taken action while the bank could still be saved. But instead, they just say, all of a sudden: that’s it. It’s screwed, pardon my language.
The National Bank of Serbia has revoked the operating license of Alta A.D., Belgrade
At today’s meeting, the Executive Board of the National Bank of Serbia decided to revoke the operating license of Alta A.D., Belgrade. The Deposit Insurance Agency will be appointed liquidator by court decision.
The Executive Council noted that the license revocation was preceded by supervisory measures aimed at improving the bank’s liquidity. It found that the bank’s financial position had significantly worsened over the preceding period, that there was a risk of further deterioration in its financial position or liquidity, and that depositors’ interests were therefore at risk.
Given that the conditions for revoking the bank’s operating license had been met, the National Bank of Serbia made the above decision in accordance with the Law on Banks in order to protect depositors’ interests and preserve the stability of the financial system.
The Deposit Insurance Agency will ensure, within seven business days, the payout of insured amounts and depositor access to funds in accordance with the Law on Deposit Insurance.
What worries me isn’t just the situation with the bank itself, but also the attitude toward Russian émigrés in Serbia. I saw on Twitter how some Serbs were mocking Russians who came to the closed Alta branches and stood in line there.
You understand, when many migrants arrive in any country, it always provokes a reaction of irritation. Housing prices go up [because of high demand from migrants], and people start hearing a foreign language on the streets. Many newcomers don’t want to integrate into the local culture. You can feel that resentment toward Russians is growing in Serbian society.
I haven’t lived here long, but I talk to Russian friends who moved here earlier. And based on what they tell me, and my own impressions, this tension is growing.
This spills over into various posts online too. Today one Serbian public page posted something like: “Ha ha ha, look, the Russians are standing in line.” But the comments were very mixed. Some people joined in the mockery, while others defended the Russians. Someone wrote: “I’m Russian myself, put yourself in my shoes. I’m in another country, and I can’t even get a bank to open an account for me.”
There’s this kind of political discussion happening, an exchange of opinions, both good and not so good. For now we’re just waiting for Monday. First we need to understand how to get the insured amount, and then figure out what to do with the rest of the money.
‘We used the bank for everyday operations: receiving payments from clients, paying taxes and office rent, and employee salaries’
Olga (name changed), an entrepreneur, used Alta to manage her own business’s accounts
I’ve lived in Serbia since 2023. My partners and I founded a company here. We immediately opened Alta accounts for the company and the partners. Later we hired a few employees, and they got Alta accounts too. There was an option to open an account at Banka Poštanska, but our accountant recommended Alta because of its more convenient service.
We used the bank for ordinary operations: receiving payments from our clients, paying taxes and office rent, employee salaries and their associated taxes, utility bills, and fees for subcontractors.
I found out about the license revocation on the morning of October 31 and was scared at first. I imagined how much effort it would take to go through another bureaucratic cycle. I didn’t try to withdraw or transfer money after the news came out, and I didn’t contact the bank either.
In our case, things aren’t so critical. We made all our payments this month, there’s only a small amount left in the company account, and we’re not expecting any incoming payments in the next week. There’s a bit of time to get oriented. I now plan to open new accounts for the company and for myself as soon as possible, and then request a refund of the money.
‘Right now there’s panic and hysteria in all the chats’
Apollinaria, director of the human rights foundation “Freedom and Law,” helps Russians whose money has been frozen in Alta accounts
I’ve worked in human rights for many years and have lived in Serbia for a long time. So the situation Russians are facing right now isn’t foreign to me. I understand very well what people in this position are going through. Several of my own friends have become hostages to this situation, among others.
Some people had sole proprietorship accounts at Alta, others had all their savings there, money from selling apartments and cars in Russia. Some now have 50,000, 100,000, or 180,000 euros frozen. That’s simply an enormous amount of money. People were planning to live on it for a while or to buy property, and now that possibility is gone.
For example, I saw a story in the chats about people who had 180,000 euros in the bank. They were supposed to close on an apartment purchase next Wednesday. You can imagine the state these people are in right now. It’s everything you’ve saved over your whole life: a sold apartment, a sold car. And when you’ll get it back is completely unclear.
Or another story: a young woman received her salary on an Alta card, and now all her money is blocked. She has 3,000 dinars left in cash, which is less than 30 euros. It’s a tragedy for everyone, but everyone’s is different.
Alta was the only bank that opened accounts for Russians without employment contracts, lease agreements, or other paperwork. People went there not because they wanted to, but because they had no choice.
There’s one other bank, API Bank, formerly VTB. It opens accounts, but everything there is very expensive. A lot of people don’t want to go there for security reasons, because that bank has a direct connection to Russia. Now people find themselves in a situation where they not only can’t get their money, but also don’t know where to open a new account.
I believe responsibility for what happened lies with Vučić‘s former government. The bank was probably used for corrupt purposes, to move and launder money. And when the new government came in, it thought first and foremost about its own priorities, not about the Russians who had opened accounts there.
Russians are also an affected party here. Just like Serbian citizens, we paid taxes and lived here. Yes, we’re not citizens, but we’re honest people, residents of this country. We want to understand what’s going to happen to our money.
Right now there’s panic and hysteria in all the chats. The first thing I recommend is to calm down, not panic, and not take hasty action under the influence of emotion. We all remember the 2008 crisis, when a lot of people lost everything. The Great Depression is worth remembering too.
I understand how serious the current situation is, but right now it’s very important not to do anything rash. Have a glass of wine, a shot of rakija. That’s just my personal suggestion. Calm down a little, and then act. For our part, we [activists] have started preparing appeals to government agencies.
I just finished drafting a letter to the National Bank of Serbia, which we prepared together with lawyers from Kovcheg. The project’s head, Anastasia Burakova, helped a great deal. We cite Serbian law and ask that measures be taken so that Russians can exercise their right to open accounts at other banks.
The next step will be a petition. In it, we plan to address not only the National Bank of Serbia, but also the new government, students, the Finance Ministry, and other government bodies. We have several main demands. First, we want precise deadlines for returning the funds, tied to a specific date.
Second, we want a detailed explanation of the procedure for returning funds to sole proprietors and individuals who are not Serbian citizens, because right now people have no idea what to do, in what order to apply, or what documents to submit. We want official clarification and guarantees on payment timelines.
Our third demand is for urgent action to ensure that Russians can open accounts at other Serbian banks, because right now many people simply can’t continue their normal lives and work.
I’m afraid that when the Deposit Insurance Agency starts making payments, Russians won’t be first in line. Alta had a lot of Serbian depositors and registered businesses. At best, we’ll end up second. That’s why it’s important for us to get official answers.
We’re not planning simply to sit and wait. The main thing right now is for people to know what to do and when they’ll be able to get their money back.

Delivery of First British Type 31 Frigate Delayed by Two Years Until 2028
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
11:43:14 UTC
20:43:14 KST

The first Type 31 frigate, HMS Venturer, is scheduled to be handed over to the UK Royal Navy in 2028.
Navy Lookout reported this.
The ship will be handed over to the Navy two years later than originally planned at the time of its launch.
Sir Nick Hine, Babcock’s Chief Executive Marine, said the company is working to reduce the schedule delay across the entire program to build five frigates.
He estimated that the delay could reach approximately two years. At the same time, the company hopes to minimize the impact of the first ship’s construction delay on subsequent deliveries across the program.
Hine cited the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic, the United Kingdom’s withdrawal from the European Union and Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine among the main causes of the delays. These events drove up the cost of energy resources, labor, and components, and complicated supply chains.
Additional problems arose during the construction of the first two ships — HMS Venturer and HMS Active. Design changes, disruptions to the construction sequence, and the need to redo some work resulted in significant additional costs for the company.
In May 2026, Babcock announced a £140 million write-off to cover the costs of rectifying defects.
According to Navy Lookout, Babcock’s total losses under the Type 31 frigate construction contract have exceeded £300 million. Meanwhile, the company’s management notes that accelerating construction under the program’s current funding arrangements will be difficult without additional investment.
The United Kingdom originally planned to commission the first Type 31 frigate back in 2023. However, the schedule was revised in 2020: the ship was due to be launched in 2023, handed over to the Royal Navy in 2025 and commissioned in 2027.
During the construction of HMS Venturer, it was decided to keep the ship in the assembly hall for longer to install as much equipment as possible before launch. The vessel was moved out of the assembly hall on May 27, 2025, and launched on June 14 that year – approximately 15 months later than the schedule approved in 2020.
In October 2026, the UK Ministry of Defence told Parliament that HMS Venturer was expected to be handed over to the Navy by the end of the decade, without specifying an exact date. Meanwhile, shipbuilder Babcock is now targeting 2028, a delay of about two years from the previous schedule.
While the delay to the Type 31 program is estimated at approximately two years, the British Type 26 frigate construction program has also encountered serious difficulties.
Construction of the lead ship in the class, HMS Glasgow, began on July 20, 2017. It was originally scheduled to be handed over to the Navy in the mid-2020s, but the ship is now expected to achieve initial operational readiness only in October 2028.
After its launch in late 2022, HMS Glasgow was moved to a dry dock at BAE Systems’ Scotstoun facility, where fitting-out work is still underway. As of November 2026, the frigate has not yet been handed over to the Royal Navy.

Six in seven journalist murders go unpunished,  UNESCO reports
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
11:42:49 UTC
20:42:49 KST

Six in seven journalist murders go unpunished, UNESCO reports
Global impunity for journalist killings has risen for the first time in more than a decade, while the growing use of drones is an emerging threat for reporters in conflict zones, according to the latest report from UN cultural organization UNESCO.
“Journalists are increasingly paying with their lives for reporting from the frontlines of war and far too often those responsible for their killings are not held accountable,” said Director-General Khaled El-Enany.
UNESCO first began measuring the proportion of journalist killings that go unpunished in 2012. The rate reached 86 per cent in 2024-2025, up one per cent from the previous two-year period.
A confirmed total of 189 journalists and other media workers lost their lives in 2024-2025, or 20 per cent more than during the previous biennium and the highest number since 2014-2015.
More than two thirds, 127, were killed in conflict zones, accounting for 67 per cent of the death toll.
Paying the ultimate price
The findings come in the Director-General’s Report on the Safety of Journalists and the Danger of Impunity, which is published every two years to mark the International Day to End Impunity for Crimes against Journalists, observed on 2 November.
“Over the past year, at least 34 journalists paid the ultimate price. Six of every seven such killings go unpunished. In conflict settings, the rate of impunity is close to 100 per cent,” UN Secretary-General António Guterres said in his message for the Day.
“This is a heinous affront to the victims and their loved ones, as well as all of us who depend on journalists to remain informed and engaged.”
‘A global scourge’
Killings were recorded across all regions of the world during the 2024-2025 biennium, representing “a global scourge”, the report said.
The highest number of verified cases were in the Arab States (97) followed by Latin American and the Caribbean (37), Asia-Pacific (34), Central and Eastern Europe (14), Africa (6) and Western Europe and North America (1).
The State of Palestine had the highest number of killings in both years, at 30 and 32, respectively.
New technologies, growing risks
The report also identified what UNESCO called “a disturbing new threat” – the growing use of drones to kill journalists. During 2024-2025, drone strikes killed 50 journalists, or 40 per cent of all those killed in conflict zones.
It documented seven incidents in which several journalists were targeted and killed in a single attack, including strikes on media workplaces and temporary reporting centres. Fifteen journalists were reportedly killed while wearing press vests or in vehicles clearly marked ‘Press’.
“I reiterate my call for the respect of UN Security Council Resolution 2222 unanimously adopted in 2015 on the protection of journalists, media professionals and associated personnel as civilians in situations of conflict, a status reaffirmed in the Pact for the Future,” said Mr. El-Enany.
Progress is possible
The report also highlighted progress, as impunity in non-conflict countries has continued to decline. The rate has fallen from 94 per cent in 2012 to 77 per cent in 2026, or one percentage point per year.
The number of journalist killings in non-conflict zones, 85, is also the lowest in 18 years.
“This demonstrates that when governments invest in investigations, prosecutions and protections for journalists, progress is possible,” UNESCO said.
Women journalists under fire
The agency noted, however, that women journalists continue to face particular risks, both in war zones and online. Thirteen out of the 14 women killed in 2024-2035 were in countries experiencing armed conflict.
Furthermore, a 2025 study by UN Women and the International Center for Journalists found that 75 per cent of women journalists had experienced online or offline abuse and harassment. More than 40 per cent reported offline violence linked to online attacks, up from 20 per cent in a 2020 UNESCO survey.
“Across the world, journalists continue to pay an outrageous price for telling the truth,” the UN Secretary-General said.
“On this International Day to End Impunity for Crimes against Journalists, we demand justice. When journalists are targeted and their reporting is extinguished, it makes victims of us all.”

Washington is reportedly planning to resume Russian natural gas shipments to Europe via Ukraine as part of negotiations to reach an energy cease-fire between Russia and Ukraine, according to a recent report by The Wall Street Journal.
US, European and Ukrainian officials reportedly told The Wall Street Journal that US President Donald Trump's representatives, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, proposed using an American intermediary for Russian natural gas sales during visits to Moscow and Kyiv in September.
The alleged proposal would circumvent European sanctions and allow Russian natural gas to return to the European market, presenting a potentially lucrative opportunity for US investors.
The report said negotiators viewed regaining access to the European natural gas market as a major incentive to persuade Russian President Vladimir Putin to agree to a broader cease-fire with Kyiv.
A White House official reportedly proposed holding the funds in a secure escrow account in a third country to prevent Moscow from using the revenue generated to finance the ongoing war, the report said.
The alleged proposal would involve reactivating the Soviet-era pipeline network that connected the Urengoy natural gas fields in Siberia to Europe via Ukrainian territory.
This push conflicts with current EU regulations mandating that all Russian natural gas imports be phased out by the end of next year.
Before the war, Russia accounted for 45% of Europe's natural gas supplies, but this figure fell to 11%. The resulting gap has been largely filled by US liquefied natural gas (LNG), which accounts for 30% of Europe's consumption.

====================================================================================================

Precious metals continue to plunge for 2nd consecutive month
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
11:39:40 UTC
20:39:40 KST

Burhan Sansarlioglu and Emir Yildirim
02 November 2026•Update: 02 November 2026
Precious metal prices continued to plummet for the second consecutive month as oil prices climbed, the US dollar strengthened and fears of a global economic slowdown kept investors away from commodities.
Since the outbreak of the US-Israeli war with Iran at the end of February, commodity prices have seen sharp volatility, affecting gold, silver, platinum and palladium.
Gold started 2026 strongly at $4,313 per ounce, reaching a record high of $5,600 in January and finishing the first month of the year with a 12.4% increase, while it peaked at $5,263 in February.
Escalating tensions in the Middle East led to an 11.32% sell-off in March, marking the sharpest monthly drop in gold since the 2008 financial crisis, followed by an 11.7% plunge in June, leading to a 7.1% total loss for the first half of the year.
Gold rebounded 10% in August, but ongoing uncertainties led to a drop of 6.6% in September and 6.8% in October, closing the month at $3,876 per ounce. It was the first time gold had dipped below $4,000 since July.
Silver followed a similar path, starting the year at $71 per ounce and hitting a record of $121.7 in January, followed by an increase of 12.6%, then a drop of 19.9% in March, 1.9% in April, a slight rebound of 2.2% in May and a decline of 22% in June, ending the first half down 17.3%.
Like gold, silver also rebounded in August but fell 7.6% in September and dropped 18.8% in October, ending the month at $49.1 per ounce. It dipped below $50 for the first time since November 2025.
The situation for industrial precious metals was even worse, as platinum lost 24.4% by the end of June despite having hit a record of $2,923.3 in January, followed by an 8.5% rise in February and a 17.2% decline in March to $1,960.1. Platinum closed July with a 6.1% gain and August with an 8.9% increase.
Platinum dipped 4.6% in September and 16.2% in October, closing the month at $1,434.
Palladium followed suit, surging as high as $1,788.7 in February before losing 24.2% in the first half and dropping 19.1% in October to $980. It dipped below $1,000 for the first time since June 2025.
Zafer Ergezen, a futures and commodity markets expert, told Anadolu that high oil prices reinforced expectations of sustained inflation, driving up interest rates and prompting investors to flock to cash instead.
"Investors are shifting towards risk-free returns and moving away from riskier instruments," he said, noting that the strengthening of the dollar and selling driven by the need for cash affected gold the most despite central bank purchases.
He noted that the situation for silver was somewhat worse, while high oil prices reinforced expectations of higher inflation and led to forecasts of a global growth slowdown, prompting the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank to revise their growth forecasts.
"Silver is more used in industrial applications than gold, so a slowdown in silver demand is expected, and we're seeing a steeper decline in silver than gold," he said. "If oil prices fall towards the end of the war, silver may even outperform gold but high oil prices lead to selling pressure on silver."
"The outlook for platinum and palladium is more negative because these metals are generally used much more extensively in industrial applications, so concerns over a slowdown in global growth impact these metals more," he added.
Ergezen said that rising demand for electric vehicles (EVs) continued to cause a decline in demand for platinum and palladium, but the supply side for both commodities remained strong. A recovery in the two industrial metals may not be likely any time soon as long as inflation and oil prices remain elevated.
He added that these two metals may recover less strongly than silver, even if the war ends and oil prices fall.

====================================================================================================

COP31 explained: Why the Türkiye climate summit matters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
11:38:12 UTC
20:38:12 KST

From 9 to 20 November, governments, scientists, activists, corporate lobbyists, diplomats, Indigenous Peoples and communities affected by climate change will gather in Antalya, Türkiye, for COP31, the annual UN climate conference.
COP31 comes after a year in which the climate crisis has become even harder to ignore. In September 2026, the United Nations acknowledged for the first time that the world is set to overshoot its target of limiting global warming to 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels within the next few years. The warning came as global temperatures continued to soar with the last two months setting global heat records.
The science is undeniable; the legal obligations irrefutable; and the human rights stakes unfathomable. Human activities, particularly the extraction and burning of coal, oil and gas, are heating the planet and intensifying threats to human rights. Governments cannot portray climate inaction as a neutral position. Climate inaction, and worse, governmental provision of tax, political, and regulatory support to the fossil fuel industry, are deliberate choices made in the face of overwhelming evidence, with devastating consequences for people and their rights. By acting together and placing justice at the centre of climate action, governments can still limit further harm and build a fairer future.
What is a COP meeting?
COP stands for Conference of the Parties. It is the main decision-making forum of the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change, or UNFCCC, the international treaty agreed in 1992 and the parent treaty of the 2015 Paris Agreement.
COP meetings bring almost every country together to negotiate collective action, based on historical responsibility and capacity, on reducing greenhouse gas emissions, adapting to climate change and supporting countries and communities experiencing loss and damage.
This year’s unusual leadership arrangement gives both Türkiye and Australia significant responsibility as co-hosts. Türkiye will host COP31 and Australia will lead the official negotiations. Both countries must demonstrate credible climate leadership and not hide behind each other to deflect attention from their lack of action. Türkiye’s continuing reliance on coal and pursuit of fossil gas risk locking it into a high-emissions pathway. Australia must confront the contradiction between leading global climate negotiations and continuing to support fossil fuel extraction and use.
Pre-COP31 spotlight on the Pacific
Official pre-COP meetings and leaders’ events already took place in Fiji and Tuvalu from 5 to 8 October, bringing Pacific leadership and priorities into the run up to the main summit. Amnesty International has documented how climate change is already harming human rights in Tuvalu, Kiribati and other Pacific Island countries. In Tuvalu, Kiribati and across the region, rising seas, extreme heat, drought and saltwater intrusion threaten people’s rights to water, food, health, housing, culture and a safe future.
Students from the Pacific took the fight against climate change to the world’s top court, leading the International Court of Justice to issue a landmark Advisory Opinion in July 2025, which made it clear that governments have a legal obligation to protect human rights from climate change impacts.
After more than 30 years of climate negotiations, governments can no longer hide behind promises of future action. The science is settled, the solutions are available and the resources exist. Continued delay is a political choice, one that protects fossil fuel interests while Pacific communities lose land, livelihoods, rights and cultural heritage.
As President of Negotiations, Australia must ensure that Pacific demands become concrete COP31 outcomes. It cannot credibly claim climate leadership abroad while expanding fossil fuel projects at home that deepen the harms to Indigenous People, Pacific neighbours and other frontline communities. Australia must end this contradiction by ending fossil fuel expansion, accelerating a just transition and securing far greater support for communities facing irreversible loss and damage.
Why is COP31 so important?
Every COP matters, but the window for preventing escalating and irreversible harm is closing rapidly. In October 2026, the UN Environment Programme warned that the world needs to cut carbon emissions by nearly a fifth in the next four years, and by close to half within a decade, to avoid overshooting climate targets by a disastrous margin. The higher and longer the overshoot, the greater the danger to people, ecosystems and economies. The harm caused cannot be undone.
Overshooting 1.5°C cannot become an excuse for resignation. Every fraction of a degree matters to human and planetary life. Governments must cut emissions urgently through a just and equitable phase out of fossil fuels, protect affected communities and prevent warming from reaching even more dangerous levels.
Yet many major economies continue to approve new fossil fuel production and prolong dependence on coal, oil and gas, including through subsidies, tax breaks, and other support. In many contexts, the fossil fuel industry is a powerful actor, shaping politics and legislation domestically and overseas. Meanwhile, climate science is being undermined and the social solidarity needed to drive action is being deliberately fractured by authoritarian state and corporate forces. The result is a vicious cycle of disinformation, regulatory sabotage, coercive diplomacy and fossil fuel lock-in. It lays bare a widening gap between what science tells us is necessary and what human rights law obligates governments to do one hand, and what governments are willing to do on the other hand.
Discover how the world’s slide into authoritarian practices is accelerating the climate crisis in this op-ed:
How is climate change affecting human rights?
Everyone has the right to live in a clean, healthy and sustainable environment. Climate change also threatens the rights to life, food, water, health, housing, culture and an adequate standard of living.
In 2026, unprecedented climate-related disasters worldwide and itshuman consequences were visible across the world:
- A catastrophic glacier collapse in the Himalayas unleashed flooding across Nepal and Tibet with more than 1400 people killed.
- Severe flooding affected Mozambique, Eswatini, South Africa and Zimbabwe early in the year, killing more than 200 people, destroying homes, damaging health facilities and schools, and devastating farmland and livelihoods.
- Record-breaking heatwaves and drought killed tens of thousands and fuelled severe wildfires across the world, including in Türkiye, Indonesia, Europe, North Africa and Canada. These led to significant damage and evacuations.
The human cost of climate breakdown is impossible to ignore any longer.
Why must fossil fuels be phased out?
We know that humans’ burning of fossil fuels is the main source of greenhouse gases that become concentrated in our atmosphere. These gases trap the sun’s heat, leading to a long-term rise in the planet’s average temperature and causing shifts in weather patterns as well as rising sea levels that will wipe out small island states and much low-lying coastal land.
Therefore, to protect human rights now and in the future, and prevent even greater harm, governments must deliver a full, fast, fair and funded phase-out of fossil fuels.
There are many alternatives to fossil fuels, like wind and solar power, that will enable us to reduce our dependency on fossil fuels. The global push towards electrification using renewable energy is essential, but the transition must respect human rights and not reproduce the abuses and inequalities of the fossil fuel economy.
What must governments agree at COP31?
Amnesty International is calling on governments to advance three priorities:
- Stop the climate crisis at its source: End fossil fuel expansion and accelerate a full, fast, fair, funded and human rights-compliant transition away from coal, oil and gas, with the states the most responsible for historical emissions moving furthest and fastest.Renewable energy is cheaper than fossil fuels; governments must stop supporting their allies in the fossil fuel industry with taxpayer funded subsidies.
- Support communities through the transition: Make the Just Transition Mechanism. a body established at COP30 that aims to coordinate international cooperation for just transition initiatives, operational, properly funded and accountable, with Indigenous Peoples, workers and affected communities directly involved in decisions.
- Scale up climate finance: High-income, high-emitting countries must tax major polluters and substantially increase grants-based climate finance to support a just fossil fuel phase-out, adaptation, loss and damage, and the protection of forests and other critical carbon-storing ecosystems. This support must uphold human rights and avoid pushing lower-income countries deeper into debt.
Justice demands that those most responsible for heating the planet, and those with the greatest capacity to act, do and pay their fair share.
Read more on how the climate crisis cannot be solved behind closed doors in this joint op-ed from Directors for Amnesty International in Brazil, Türkiye and Australia:
Spotlight on Türkiye
In September, the Turkish authorities launched a nationwide operation targeting LGBTI+ organizations, activists and human rights defenders. Homes, venues and offices were raided, more than 100 people were detained, dozens of whom were subsequently remanded in pretrial detention and over 1000 social media accounts belonging to activists, journalists and human rights organisations were blocked or restricted, including that of Amnesty International Türkiye. In October, in another serious escalation, authorities raided and seized control of a major opposition television channel in a significant blow to press freedom.
This is not an isolated attack or one confined to a single community. It is part of a sustained crackdown with arbitrary restrictions on peaceful assembly, association and expression over the last decade. Environmental defenders, journalists, women’s rights activists, political opponents and LGBTI+ communities may be targeted in different ways, but the effect is the same: dissent is silenced, divisions are stoked, and fear spreads – making it harder for people to hold their government accountable for climate action or any other human rights issue.
For the vital negotiations about protecting our shared future to be effective and equitable at COP31, Türkiye must end its crackdown on human rights and those who defend them.
Why is protecting civic space important for a UN summit like COP?
UN climate conferences remain among the few global spaces where almost all states come together alongside Indigenous Peoples, civil society representatives in all their diversity and communities campaigning for climate justice. Fossil fuel lobbyists will be there too – as they are in almost all forums where climate change is discussed. Protecting civic space at COP is essential to overcoming fossil fuel obstruction and securing effective climate action. As it is, the scales are tipped in favour of industry. Any erosion in protections for civil society at COP will tip the scales further.
Around the world, governments and corporations have criminalised protest and subjected environmental human rights defenders to intimidation, surveillance, detention and violence. Authoritarian attacks on environmental human rights defenders, women, LGBTI+ people and other marginalised communities are not separate political projects. They divide societies, weaken collective action and protect entrenched power while fossil fuel production continues.
Yet people continue to resist as documented by Amnesty International in its new briefing, ‘Protecting our Future: Environmental Human Rights Defenders Powering Just Transitions’.
There can be no climate justice without the freedom to demand it.
