Trump Justice Dept breaks with tradition to intervene in midterms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
11:37:19 UTC
20:37:19 KST

Trump Justice Dept breaks with tradition to intervene in midterms
WASHINGTON, Nov 2 - President Donald Trump’s Justice Department has shown a willingness to intervene directly in Tuesday's midterm elections, breaking with decades of practice meant to avoid the appearance that its law enforcement powers are being used to benefit a political party or candidate.
In California, the Justice Department sought to set aside mail-in ballots from about 20,000 voters it alleges are likely non-US citizens ineligible to vote.
The department has also demanded records in a related criminal probe. California has said it has implemented measures to prevent voting by noncitizens and argued the Justice Department does not have the authority to block votes.
In Alaska, the department has intensified a criminal investigation into whether a Senate candidate with the same name as Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan entered the race to confuse voters. It also sought to block certification if Sullivan narrowly loses, but a federal judge dismissed that lawsuit on Sunday.
Courts have now rejected the department's lawsuits against both states, but the cases underscore the DOJ's willingness to intervene in election disputes before votes are counted and results certified. The department has appealed the Alaska decision.
Critics say the department could accelerate any attempt by Trump to sow doubt about the midterms, which will determine control of Congress and the winners of dozens of governors' races.
“It appears that the administration wants the department to have an impact that was previously prohibited,” said Mark Blumberg, who previously led the DOJ’s election response to civil rights threats and has since founded the Rule of Law Project.
US Attorney General Todd Blanche says the department's efforts are lawful and aim to protect the integrity of the vote.
“The Department isn’t helping any campaign. It’s enforcing the law," department spokesperson Kiersten Pels said in a statement.
FALSE FRAUD CLAIMS
The US Constitution assigns responsibility for administering elections to the states, but Trump, a Republican, argues Democratic-led states are not doing enough to prevent voting by noncitizens, which is prohibited under US law. He continues to falsely assert that widespread fraud caused his 2020 election loss. Independent studies and state audits have found voter fraud to be rare.
Outside groups aligned with Trump filed more than 60 lawsuits challenging his 2020 defeat, all of which were unsuccessful. DOJ officials in his first term rejected pressure to enlist the department in those efforts.
“The right-wing fringe outside groups are not going to have to do that this year because the DOJ is clearly standing ready and willing to do it,” said Lis Frost, a voting rights lawyer with Elias Law Group, which frequently represents Democrats in court.
Historically, Justice Department election interventions have focused on enforcing federal laws meant to ensure racial minorities or vulnerable populations can vote without impediment.
THE ALASKA CASE
Alaska has become a particularly intense legal battleground after the New York Times reported that Democrat Mary Peltola's campaign was involved in recruiting retired teacher Daniel J. Sullivan to challenge incumbent Dan Sullivan.
The Justice Department lawsuit, which Trump said he directed the department to file, asked a court to halt certification and order an investigation if the margin suggested voter confusion could have affected the outcome. US District Judge Sharon Gleason in Anchorage dismissed the case on Sunday, finding Alaska could not conduct such a probe while preserving the secrecy of ballots.
Legal experts had said DOJ lacked authority to bring the case and risked appearing to favor the Republican incumbent.
“For the department to be trusted in its law enforcement decisions it has to ensure that people understand it does not take sides in political partisan disputes,” said Peter Keisler, acting attorney general under Republican President George W. Bush. “And this has not only the appearance but the evident reality of taking sides.”
Blanche has said the case sought to stop what he described as fraud by Daniel J. Sullivan, who denies trying to mislead voters. Peltola's campaign said it had "no involvement with either Sullivan campaign.”
Asked about criticism of the lawsuit, a Justice Department official said at a press briefing on Thursday, "We bring lawsuits to enforce federal law."
TRUMP ALLIES EMPOWERED
The Justice Department has traditionally proceeded cautiously in election investigations because its involvement can cause uncertainty or be exploited by candidates or political parties.
Its Public Integrity Section, staffed with career experts on election law, has often advised agents and prosecutors to wait until results are certified before intervening, according to former DOJ officials.
The Trump administration has slashed the size of the unit and suspended a requirement that federal prosecutors consult it on election-corruption probes. DOJ officials say US Attorney’s Offices are better positioned to decide whether charges are merited.
Instead, agents and prosecutors have been told that unresolved issues will be decided by Trump political appointees, according to three people familiar with the conversations.
The Deputy Attorney General’s Office will mediate disputes between agents and prosecutors, they said, a direct role that former DOJ officials said it has rarely played in election investigations.
Pels said "resolving disputes that can’t be resolved in the field is exactly the role that office exists to play.” REUTERS

UK Unleashes MQ-9B Protector Drone for First-Ever Mission to Shadow Russian Warship
The United Kingdom deployed its MQ-9B Protector surveillance drone on its first operational mission in British airspace, tracking a Russian warship in the English Channel for more than 10 hours alongside Royal Navy vessels.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Defence Blog on November 1, the Royal Air Force (RAF) used the Protector RG1 to support the Type 45 destroyer HMS Dauntless and patrol vessel HMS Tyne as they monitored the Russian frigate Neustrashimy and accompanying merchant ships between October 1 and 14.
The operation marked the first time the British military used the Protector drone in an operational mission over UK airspace to monitor Russian naval activity.
“Protector’s first operational sorties in UK airspace demonstrate the significant value this capability brings to UK Defence,” said Wing Commander Sam Haley, officer commanding XIII Squadron.
The unarmed drone operated alongside civilian and military aircraft, providing extended surveillance coverage over the English Channel. British officials did not disclose how many flights were conducted or which sensors were used.
The Protector RG1 is Britain’s version of the US-made MQ-9B SkyGuardian, developed by General Atomics. It can remain airborne for more than 30 hours, operate at altitudes of up to 40,000 feet (12,200 meters), and conduct surveillance using infrared cameras, high-resolution video, and radar systems.
The aircraft entered RAF service in June 2025, becoming the first remotely piloted aircraft authorized to operate throughout British airspace without geographic restrictions. The mission was part of a wider British effort to monitor Russian naval movements near UK waters.
Between September 29 and October 8, Royal Navy helicopters tracked the Russian intelligence-gathering vessel Viktor Leonov near Scotland’s Outer Hebrides during a NATO military exercise involving more than 2,000 personnel from six countries.
Separately, British naval forces monitored the Russian landing ship Aleksandr Shabalin and accompanying vessels as they passed through the English Channel toward the Baltic Sea in mid-October.
According to the UK Ministry of Defence, Royal Navy operations monitoring Russian ships increased by 25% during the first seven months of 2026 compared with the same period in 2025.
The deployment comes as Britain expands its use of unmanned systems to counter Russian naval activity. In June 2026, the UK announced plans to build at least six advanced hybrid warships capable of operating aerial, surface, and underwater drones to monitor Russian movements in the North Atlantic and protect critical undersea infrastructure.

Ukraine Hits 10% of Russia’s Oil Refining Capacity in Just 72 Hours
Ukrainian drone strikes targeted three major Russian oil refineries over three consecutive nights, hitting facilities that together account for approximately 10% of Russia’s total oil refining capacity.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Ukrainian OSINT monitoring group Dnipro Osint on November 1, the attacks targeted the Novokuybyshevsk refinery in the Samara region, the Bashneft-Novoil facility in Ufa, and the LUKOIL refinery in Kstovo, Nizhny Novgorod region.
The three facilities have a combined annual processing capacity of approximately 33 million metric tons of crude oil. The figure represents the share of Russian refining capacity targeted, rather than independently confirmed production losses.
Ukrainian defense manufacturer Fire Point confirmed its involvement in the strikes on the Kstovo and Novokuybyshevsk refineries. According to the company, Ukrainian forces used FP-1 drones to target the Novokuybyshevsk facility, striking multiple locations, including a diesel hydrotreating unit.
The first attack occurred overnight on October 30, when Ukrainian drones struck the Novokuybyshevsk refinery in Russia’s Samara region, triggering a fire at the facility.
Operated by Rosneft, the refinery can process approximately 8.8 million metric tons of crude oil annually and produces petroleum products, including aviation fuel.
On October 31, drones targeted an industrial area in Ufa, the capital of Russia’s Republic of Bashkortostan, where the Bashneft-Novoil refinery is located. The facility has an annual primary refining capacity of approximately 7 million metric tons.
The third strike took place overnight on November 1, targeting the LUKOIL-Nizhegorodnefteorgsintez refinery, also known as NORSI, in Kstovo. A large fire was reported following the attack.
NORSI is among Russia’s largest oil refineries, with a designed annual processing capacity of approximately 17 million metric tons.
Dnipro Osint reported that the strikes affected multiple processing installations, including equipment used for both primary crude oil distillation and secondary refining operations. However, the full extent of the damage and the resulting reduction in operational capacity have not been independently verified.
The renewed attacks followed a reported two-week pause in Ukrainian strikes against Russian oil refineries. According to Dnipro Osint, Kyiv had refrained from targeting these facilities at the request of the US administration as part of an informal arrangement described as an energy ceasefire.
The monitoring group stated that Russian missile and drone attacks against Ukrainian infrastructure continued during that period, disrupting electricity, heating, and water supplies.
Earlier, on October 15, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced that Kyiv had lifted restrictions on strikes against Russian oil refineries after observing a three-day pause requested by Washington.

HUR Confirms Russian Su-57 Explosion at Akhtubinsk Airfield

Ukraine’s Military Intelligence Directorate (HUR) confirmed that Russia lost a Su-57 (NATO: Felon) stealth fighter on Thursday, Oct. 29, due to an engine startup failure.
The initial report came out on Friday, when a Ukrainian monitoring channel shared a satellite image showing the wreckage of a fighter jet resembling a Su-57 at the Astrakhan region’s Akhtubinsk airfield.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
On Monday, HUR said in a press release that the Su-57 was lost during engine start-up, confirming earlier speculations.
The agency suspected subpar jet fuel quality caused the incident.
“The Su-57 is equipped with an AL-41F1 turbojet engine (the so-called ‘Izdeliye 117’). One of the reasons why engines of this type can explode or suffer catastrophic failure is poor-quality fuel,” it said.
It added that the same fuel is also used by other Russian jets, including the Geran 4 and 5 jet-powered drones, whose usage has spiked since the summer of 2026.
“Recall that Jet A-1 is an analog of the Russian-Soviet aviation fuel TS-1 and RT for gas turbine aircraft engines. Jet A-1 fuel is fully compatible and suitable for use by Russian aircraft in service with the aggressor state’s army – MiG-29, Su-34 (NVO), Su-35S, Su-30SM, Su-57, Su-24M, Tu-95MS (MSM),” the press release says.
Why is losing a Su-57 a big deal?
The Su-57 is Russia’s premier fifth-generation multirole fighter and its most advanced aircraft currently in service.
It first flew in 2010, with serial production beginning in 2019 following a troubled development process that included India’s withdrawal from the project in 2018.
FSB Accuses 76-Year-Old Communist of Spying for Ukraine
The National Interest estimated that Russia had around 32 Su-57s, including prototypes, against the 76 originally envisioned.
The Su-57 lost on Thursday made it the fourth Su-57 Russia has lost this year.
Subpar jet fuel quality spurred by refinery crisis
HUR noted that Russia has imported jet fuel and gasoline from third countries, including India, where the Vadinarsky refinery of Nayara Energy is 49.13% owned by Russia’s Rosneft.
Imports rose because Ukraine’s refinery attacks reduced output. Russia, the world’s third-largest oil producer, reported a record import of seaborne oil products in August, amounting to several times the total in 2025, before reducing imports by 44% the following month.
HUR added that most of the companies involved in the shipments are under foreign sanctions, including OOO RN-Aero, which the agency said supplies jet fuel to the fighter jet’s manufacturer, United Aircraft Corporation (UAC).
Because of the fuel shortage, Russia also lowered the standard for jet fuel in August, allowing a freezing point of -50°C (-58°F) instead of the previous -60°C (-76°F), according to The Moscow Times.
In September, civilian airports in Russia also imposed fuel rations, according to Russian outlet Vertska.

Greek academic delegation explores opportunities for cooperation with Iran
TEHRAN – A delegation of Greek academic officials has visited the University of Science and Culture and the Iranian Cultural and Creative Industries Park to explore scientific and technological capacities and identify opportunities for strengthening academic ties between the two countries.
The meeting on Monday focused on turning academic relations into practical programs, including student exchanges, joint research projects, cooperation in economics and management, and the development of professional training courses, IRNA reported.
The officials also discussed the capacity of the University of Science and Culture to become a member of the Black Sea Universities Network (BUSN), which could lay the ground for expanding academic interactions in regional scientific cooperation.
They also talked about the possibility of benefiting from the Greek embassy to facilitate academic ties and sign memoranda of understanding with Greek universities.
During the meeting, Ali Sadollah, an official with the University of Science and Culture, detailed the capacities of the university in different fields like engineering, humanities, law, art, architecture, tourism, and life sciences, noting that more than 320 international students are majoring at this university.

On October 28, the delegation visited Shahid Beheshti University to explore ways to expand academic ties between the two countries.
The delegation attended a scientific roundtable at the Faculty of Economics and Political Sciences, where Shahid Beheshti University Chancellor Mahmoud-Reza Aqamiri and Greek academic officials emphasized the importance of strengthening scientific, research, and educational cooperation.
During the meeting, the two sides explored areas for collaboration, including exchanges of professors and researchers, sharing expertise, conducting joint research and educational projects, and attracting students.

Iran ranks first in key scientific output among Islamic countries
Iran ranks first among Islamic nations in key fields of scientific output such as quantum science, cognitive sciences, artificial intelligence, biotechnology, and advanced materials, the head of the Presidential Affairs Office at the Islamic World Science Citation Center (ISC) announced in August.
The country is in close competition with Turkey and Saudi Arabia in these fields, IRNA quoted Saeed Bakhtiari as saying.

From Christmas magic to snowy escapes: 10 of Europe’s best winter travel destinations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
11:34:03 UTC
20:34:03 KST

Europe has a wealth of diverse destinations to visit during winter, whether you are looking for snowy escapes, coastal breaks or historic journeys.
Dotted with historical cities, rich culture and spectacular nature, Europe is packed with exciting places for short breaks and longer adventures during the winter season.
Christmas markets bring light and bustle to historic squares, while snow transforms mountain villages and forest trails. Beyond the festive season, there are thermal baths to linger in, museums to explore and ski slopes to tackle, with plenty of reasons to plan a trip well into the new year.
From soaking up the sun in Spanish coastal towns to chasing the Northern Lights in Swedish Lapland, here we pick out 10 of the best winter destinations to explore across the continent.
For skiing and mountain views: Zermatt, Switzerland
This year, Zermatt was No.1 on Trip.com’s ranking of Europe’s top 50 ski resorts. Nestled in Switzerland’s German-speaking section of the Canton of Valais, Zermatt is described as a “skier’s paradise” with up to 360 kilometres of pistes across the linked Swiss-Italian ski area. Against a backdrop of Alpine peaks, ski lifts can reach the 3,883m-high Klein Matterhorn peak and skiing is possible year-round.
For train lovers, you can arrive in Zermatt by taking an iconic Alpine journey from St. Moritz. Known as the "slowest express train in the world", the Glacier Express is a great way to get to Zermatt, with a journey lasting about eight hours and covering 291 kilometres. The scenic route through the Swiss Alps features stunning views of valleys, mountains and picturesque villages.
For winter walks and snowy landscapes: Seefeld, Austria
The Seefeld region in Tyrol, Austria, is about 25 kilometres northwest of Innsbruck. Here, outdoor enthusiasts can explore 142 kilometres of groomed winter hiking trails. Routes wind through forests, valleys and the broad plateau, with mountain huts offering warming refreshments along the way.
For an atmospheric evening stroll, follow the 1.8-kilometre "100,000 Lights Path" past glowing installations and the illuminated Seekirchl chapel.
Those seeking a longer adventure can tackle the Seefeld High Plateau Winter Multi-day Hike, covering around 65 kilometres over five days. Linking the region’s five villages, its stages take in lakes, woodland and mountain views, while allowing walkers to return to the same accommodation each night, using public transport to reach their daily starting points.
For Christmas magic: Strasbourg, France
With its UNESCO-listed historic centre, Strasbourg is always charming, no matter what time of year. In winter, however, it comes into its own as the “Capital of Christmas”. A festive market has been held here since 1570, and hundreds of colourfully decorated stalls are scattered through the streets and squares of Grande Île, the city’s historic island centre.
Twinkling lights also glitter over the River Ill and along the banks of narrow canals threading past 400-year-old half-timbered buildings. Head to Place Kléber to see Strasbourg’s huge Christmas tree or try local specialities like bredeles (traditional Alsatian Christmas biscuits) and vin chaud (hot wine mulled with fruit).
For winter sunshine: Andalucía, Spain
Andalucía’s Mediterranean coastline and 300 days of sunshine per year make it an ideal choice for winter sun holidays. In the cooler season, you'll share top attractions like Granada’s Alhambra, the iconic 13th-century walled Moorish palace, with fewer tourists.
Winter is also a great time for sightseeing in cities like Seville, where midsummer temperatures can reach 40C. Explore landmarks such as the Palacio de las Dueñas, with its eye-catching colonnades and arches, or sip sangria at outdoor cafes under the winter sun.
Over Christmas, towns and cities across the region are decked with festive lights. And while you’re unlikely to see snow on the Costa del Sol, the Sierra Nevada National Park some 30 kilometres east of Granada offers white-capped peaks and winter sports.
For the Northern Lights: Abisko, Sweden
Deep in the heart of Swedish Lapland, Abisko is one of the best places in the world to take in the Northern Lights. Its inland, lakeside location north of the Arctic Circle is right in the middle of the “auroral zone”, boosting your chances of witnessing the spectacular phenomenon.
To see the sky glow in ethereal greens, blues, pinks and purples, take a tour into light pollution-free Abisko National Park during wintertime, or take a chairlift ride up to the mountaintop Aurora Sky Station observation centre.
Abisko has plenty more to offer visitors as well. Go husky-dog sledding through forests, ride a snowmobile over frozen lakes or learn about traditional Sámi culture and reindeer-herding traditions.
For waterfall walks and lush forests: Madeira, Portugal
With mild winter weather and green landscapes, Madeira offers a different kind of seasonal escape. This Portuguese Atlantic island is home to UNESCO-listed Laurissilva forest, where ancient trees cloak steep valleys. Follow paths beside the island’s levadas, traditional water channels, to discover waterfalls and secluded corners of the interior.
The popular Levada das 25 Fontes leads to a lagoon fed by cascading springs, while Levada do Rei takes walkers through dense vegetation to Ribeiro Bonito, a peaceful forest sanctuary.
Pack waterproofs and sturdy walking shoes, and check official trail conditions and reserve your entry slot before setting out; advance booking is mandatory for Madeira’s classified walking routes, with access fees generally applying.
For chocolate and canals: Bruges, Belgium
The tiny medieval trading port of Bruges is criss-crossed with narrow canals spanned by arched footbridges and lined with tall, thin buildings. Beautiful throughout the year, Bruges ramps up the romance each winter with pretty Christmas markets and plenty of places to enjoy a warming cup of hot chocolate.
Belgian chocolate is famous for a reason, and Bruges is one of the best places to try it. It’s no exaggeration to say that you’ll find some of Europe’s tastiest offerings here. Stock up on handmade treats at favourites like The Old Chocolate House, Olivier’s Chocolate Shop, or Chocolates & Happiness. Add in a dash of history with a trip to the Basilica of the Holy Blood, which houses a relic traditionally believed to contain Christ’s blood.
For ancient monuments and fewer crowds: Athens, Greece
The big draw of visiting Athens in winter is that there are far fewer crowds compared with the busy summer season. You can stroll relatively peacefully through world-famous landmarks like the Acropolis, a walled complex containing grand Ancient Greek structures like the Parthenon.
Winter days in the Greek capital can be mild, although rain and colder spells are possible. Armed with an umbrella, wander past vibrant street art in the modern centre and devote any especially wet days to the fascinating museums. Top picks include the National Archaeological Museum and the Acropolis Museum.
For thermal baths: Budapest, Hungary
Add twinkling lights and a dusting of snow to Budapest’s romantic architecture and it becomes even more magical. Hungary's capital is also famous for its Christmas markets that spring up during the festive season. Head to Vörösmarty Square for some of Budapest’s best traditional local foods, like lángos (a deep-fried flatbread) and kürtőskalács (a sweet pastry covered in sugar).
The city’s thermal springs come into their own in cold weather, so don’t miss the spas, sauna rooms and multiple pools at the neo-Baroque Széchenyi Baths. Once you’re feeling thoroughly relaxed, lace up a pair of skates for laps of the Városligeti Műjégpálya outdoor ice rink, one of the oldest of its kind in Europe.
For music lovers: Vienna, Austria
No other city is quite as synonymous with classical sounds as Vienna. Music history thrums through the Austrian capital’s Baroque streets and grand architecture. To immerse yourself in Vienna’s musical heritage, explore museums dedicated to Mozart, Beethoven and Schubert or visit historic concert halls.
Winter is also ball season, so spending an evening whirling to Viennese waltzes is one of the city’s most unmissable experiences. The coldest months are a busy period in Vienna’s concert calendar: look out for performances at the State Opera House and other venues.

By Steve Gorman
LOS ANGELES, Nov 2 (Reuters) - Jury selection was due to begin on Monday in the federal retrial of a man prosecutors say deliberately set a blaze that grew into one of the deadliest, most destructive wildfires in Los Angeles history.
Jonathan Rinderknecht, 30, whose initial three-week trial ended in a hung jury in late June, was slated to return to US District Court in downtown Los Angeles to face a scaled-down version of the charges previously leveled against him.
Rinderknecht, a former Uber driver of dual US-French citizenship, was cast by prosecutors as a dejected loner who harbored deep anger at society, particularly the wealthy, and channeled his rage into an act of arson.
He is accused of “maliciously” starting a brush fire on January 1, 2025, that was quickly extinguished but smoldered in the roots of dense scrub before re-igniting days later, whipped by fierce winds into a conflagration that laid waste to the seaside enclave of Pacific Palisades.
Defense attorneys have maintained that Rinderknecht was wrongly accused. They asserted the hilltop New Year’s Day blaze was triggered by holiday fireworks, not their client, and that the massive Palisades inferno that killed 12 people and destroyed thousands of homes a week later was a separate fire set by someone else.
The opposing narratives of the disaster left jurors deadlocked 10-2 in favor of acquittal and unable to reach a unanimous verdict on any of the three charges in June.
Judge Anne Hwang declared a mistrial, and prosecutors moved to retry the defendant under a grand jury indictment that dropped one of the original charges Rinderknecht faced and modified the two remaining federal arson counts.
Nearly 7,000 homes and other structures went up in flames, with property losses estimated at $150 billion, some of that belonging to organizations receiving federal financial assistance or involved in interstate commerce.
SIMULTANEOUS DISASTERS
The Palisades blaze coincided with another catastrophic wind-driven wildfire that erupted almost simultaneously in Eaton Canyon, about 30 miles to the east, killing 19 people and ravaging the Los Angeles suburb of Altadena. Fire investigators later concluded that sparks from an electrical transmission tower ignited the Eaton fire.
Rinderknecht was the only person criminally charged in connection with either of the two January 7 blazes, which together rank as the deadliest wildfire calamity ever in Los Angeles County, surpassing the 29 lives lost in the Griffith Park fire of 1933.
Rinderknecht, who pleaded not guilty, declined to testify in his own defense during his first trial. He would face up to 40 years in prison if found guilty as charged under the latest indictment. The original indictment carried a maximum prison term of 45 years.
He has remained in custody since his arrest in Florida in October 2025.
Defense attorney Steve Haney asserted during the first trial that prosecutors lacked physical evidence linking Rinderknecht to arson or any records showing an intent to commit arson.
In court documents and public statements about the case, Haney also suggested that his client was being scapegoated for failures of the Los Angeles Fire Department.
A onetime Pacific Palisades resident himself, Rinderknecht professed his innocence in a court declaration filed last March, denying he had willfully started any fire.
He acknowledged witnessing the outbreak of the January 1 fire, originally called the Lachman fire, from the vantage point of a hill he had climbed to watch New Year’s fireworks. But Rinderknecht said he immediately called emergency 911 to report the blaze and remained at the scene until firefighters arrived and offered to help them.
Prosecutors have alleged that while placing his 911 call, Rinderknecht asked the AI app ChatGPT on his phone whether someone could be found at fault for lighting a fire “because of your cigarettes,” to which ChatGPT replied, “Yes.”
Prosecutors also said security camera footage and location data from Rinderknecht’s cellphone show he was the only person in the vicinity of the January 1 blaze when it began near a trail in the Santa Monica Mountains National Recreation Area.
(Reporting by Steve Gorman; Editing by Jonathan Spicer )

====================================================================================================

Factbox-Six things to watch as US voters decide control of Congress
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
12:33:36 CET
20:33:36 KST

By Tim Reid
WASHINGTON, Nov 2 (Reuters) - Americans head to the polls on Tuesday in midterm elections that will decide control of Congress for the final two years of President Donald Trump’s term.
The results will serve as the first nationwide verdict on Trump’s presidency, revealing whether voters want to check the Republican president’s power by giving Democrats control of one or both chambers of Congress or are willing to accept the status quo despite frustrations over the cost of living and the US-led war with Iran.
The outcome could also reshape debates within both parties over which messages and policies resonate most with voters ahead of the 2028 presidential election.
Here are six things to watch on Election Day.
THE RACES THAT WILL DECIDE CONTROL OF CONGRESS
Democrats need a net gain of four seats in both the US House of Representatives and US Senate to overturn Republicans’ narrow 218-214 and 53-47 majorities.
They are widely expected to reclaim the House, but the Senate battle remains highly competitive. The scale of Democratic gains in one or both chambers will shape Trump’s ability to advance his agenda.
Democratic wins in one or both chambers will likely trigger investigations into ethics of Trump and his administration, their handling of immigration enforcement and the Iran war.
A stronger-than-expected Republican showing could reinforce Trump’s grip on the party. Heavy losses could increase pressure to rethink unpopular policies such as tariffs and the war while shaping the message of candidates vying to succeed him.
Early results from Republican-held House seats in Florida and Virginia could provide clues to the size of any Democratic gains. Victories in competitive districts would point to a solid Democratic night, while wins in more Republican-leaning areas could signal a much broader backlash against Trump and his policies.
The close Senate fight will likely hinge on six to eight races. Democrats need to flip several Republican-held seats in states Trump carried by double-digit margins in 2024, including Ohio, Iowa, Alaska and Texas.
Even Kansas, despite Trump’s 16-point win there, has become competitive in recent weeks and a Democratic victory would signal a broader wave.
Republicans can retain control by winning most of those contests, while Democrats will likely need to hold Michigan and pick up Maine.
PROBLEMS AT THE POLLS AND VOTE COUNT
Election officials have warned close races could spark disputes over voter eligibility, ballot counting and certification, while long lines, machine malfunctions or challenges by partisan poll watchers could fuel litigation and delay results.
Trump’s Justice Department plans to deploy about 1,000 monitors nationwide on Election Day, roughly triple the number used in the last midterms, a move some local officials worry could intimidate voters, although the DOJ says those fears are baseless.
Some election officials and legal experts fear federal investigations and legal challenges could delay or disrupt certification of election results in close races.
On October 22, Trump’s Justice Department sued to preemptively block Alaska from certifying the results of its Senate race if the Republican incumbent candidate loses by a narrow margin, saying voters could be confused because two Republicans on the ballot have almost identical names.
Attorney General Todd Blanche on October 22 declined to rule out Justice Department intervention in state election certifications, saying extreme circumstances could warrant action.
Several states are also unlikely to produce complete results on election night, especially in close races, providing fertile ground for disputes.
TRUMP’S RESPONSE TO THE RESULTS
How Trump responds to the results, especially if Republicans lose control of Congress, could become one of the night’s biggest stories.
In the early hours of November 4, 2020, before vote counting had finished in several states, Trump declared victory and called for counting to stop.
He ultimately lost to Democrat Joe Biden but continued to falsely claim the election had been stolen, helping fuel the January 6, 2021, attack on the US Capitol by a mob of his supporters who were seeking to stop certification of Biden’s win by Congress.
Trump still falsely claims he won the 2020 election and has cast doubt on the integrity of these midterms, raising the prospect of Republican challenges if the party loses one or both chambers.
This year, the Trump administration has pressed states for voter data and launched investigations into noncitizen voting, which election experts and studies have found little evidence to support. It recently sued California over alleged noncitizen ballots.
TURNOUT
Turnout by the parties’ core supporters will be important. Opinion polls showed Democrats significantly more enthusiastic about voting than Republicans heading into Election Day.
But strategists caution that Democratic constituencies including young, Black and Hispanic voters have historically turned out at lower rates in midterm elections than in presidential years.
Surveys show persistent skepticism among these groups towards both parties, especially over the cost of living. If turnout among those groups falls short of expectations, Democrats could underperform on Election Day.
Early voting data in states that register voters by party showed higher Democratic engagement. But Republicans argue that many of their supporters traditionally wait until Election Day to vote.
WHAT DO RESULTS MEAN FOR THE 2028 RACE?
After their bruising defeat in the 2024 presidential election, Democrats have been split between those arguing for a more populist economic message and those favoring a centrist approach aimed at winning back swing voters.
Strong performances by moderates and left-wing candidates on Tuesday will allow both factions to claim validation of their policies. That could set the stage for a crowded and potentially contentious contest for the party’s 2028 presidential nomination.
DID REPUBLICANS’ MONEY ADVANTAGE PAY OFF?
Republicans had a significant financial advantage and flooded the airwaves with ads attacking Democratic candidates.
While some Democrats matched or outraised their opponents, Republicans held an overall spending edge of several hundred million dollars once party committees and outside groups were included.
A key question is whether that advantage helped sway tight races, or whether voter concerns over high prices and the Iran war mattered more.
Trump spent more than $277 million, mostly through his MAGA Inc. super PAC, on a late TV and direct-mail blitz to aid struggling Republican candidates, according to Federal Election Commission data.
Tesla CEO Elon Musk spent roughly $366 million during the midterm cycle, including $276 million since July, to support Republican candidates.
(Reporting by Tim Reid in Washington, editing by Ross Colvin and Howard Goller)

Lindsay Clancy returns to Massachusetts court for hearing that could shape potential murder retrial
Italy

20:33:33 KST

By Nate Raymond
Nov 2 (Reuters) - Lindsay Clancy is due back in court on Monday for a hearing that could determine whether she will be retried for killing her three young children at her Massachusetts home in 2023 after a jury deadlocked at her first trial.
Judge William Sullivan is scheduled to hear arguments in Plymouth, Massachusetts, on Clancy’s bid to dismiss the murder charges and to discuss a timetable for a potential new trial if he allows the case to proceed.
Plymouth County District Attorney Timothy Cruz’s office has yet to publicly detail its plans for a retrial of Clancy, 36. She faces first-degree murder charges over the deaths of her daughter Cora, 5; son Dawson, 3; and 8-month-old son Callan.
In a filing last week, prosecutors urged Sullivan to reject a defense bid to have the case thrown out, saying they “should be permitted to continue to pursue justice for Cora, Dawson and Callan Clancy.”
Sullivan at a September 29 hearing said the parties should be prepared on Monday to discuss a date for a retrial.
No one at Clancy’s initial trial disputed that she strangled her three children with exercise bands on January 24, 2023, in the basement of their home in the Boston suburb of Duxbury. She then cut herself with a knife and jumped from a second-story window in an attempt to end her own life, leaving her paralyzed.
Her lawyers, though, have argued the evidence showed Clancy was in the throes of postpartum psychosis at the time and should be found not guilty by reason of insanity, known in Massachusetts as lack of criminal responsibility.
Some of the jurors in televised interviews later said that but for one holdout juror, they had been prepared to find Clancy not guilty by reason of insanity. Such a verdict would have resulted in her commitment to a state psychiatric hospital, subject to regular court review.
Prosecutors have several options before them, including retrying Clancy on the first-degree murder charges or seeking her conviction on lesser second-degree murder charges, which would give her the option to waive a jury trial and proceed before a judge.
A first-degree murder conviction carries a mandatory sentence of life without parole. Second-degree murder allows for the possibility of parole.
Defense lawyers are expected on Monday to argue that a retrial would violate Clancy’s constitutional protection against being tried twice for the same crime, known as double jeopardy.
They contend the mistrial declared on September 4 was unnecessary. Citing jury notes that stated the holdout juror was not following the law on reasonable doubt despite the judge’s instructions, defense lawyers say Sullivan should have instead questioned the holdout and potentially removed the juror.
(Reporting by Nate Raymond in Boston; Editing by Will Dunham)

MOSCOW, November 2. /TASS/. Western countries have been a breeding ground for the worst human vices, Russian Security Council Secretary Sergey Shoigu said in opening remarks at the international week Peoples of Russia.
Meanwhile, Russia’s strength as a power is underpinned not only by its ever-strengthening economic sovereignty and powerful combat capabilities but also in the people’s unity and their trust in the government.
TASS has compiled key statements from the top Russian security official.
Western demise
Western countries have been a breeding ground for the worst human vices, Shoigu argued: "The collective West which once claimed global dominance is rapidly degrading, and the worse vices are blooming there, while human rights and freedoms have lost their original meaning, currently becoming a tool for destroying society and imposing permissiveness."
According to him, "justice has given way to a presumption of guilt, and any accusations no longer require evidence. This practice has been widespread in the system of international relations," Shoigu added.
Western attempts to counter Russia
Western attempts to counter Russia have been increasingly aggressive in light of the imminent victory and successes in the course of the special military operation, he argued: "The closer we get to victory and the successful conclusion of the special military operation, the more aggressive and sophisticated these attempts [by the West] become."
An active campaign is currently underway to recruit and provide funding to those willing to support the destruction of Russian statehood from within, Shoigu revealed: "It’s no secret that there’s an ongoing effort to recruit, finance, and support individuals willing to destroy Russian statehood from within."
At the same time, Shoigu stressed that Russia had "always stood united in repelling the aggressor:" "There have repeated attempts to occupy Russia’s soil, seize its resources and enslave our peoples, but never this was achieved militarily. We have always stood united in repelling the aggressor."
Shoigu calls on West to leave Russia alone
Russia has no plans to destroy any country, as former colonial powers are collapsing on their own, Shoigu continued: "I don’t quite get why we should do that. We have no plans to destroy any country. Many of them - colonial powers - are collapsing on their own."
"The reason is that those whom they once enslaved and turned into their colonies, are awakening and rising as their self-consciousness and self-determination are reviving," Shoigu added.
According to him, while the West has "a constant need for an enemy," Russia is not going to attack Europe: "Look, our President [Vladimir Putin] has stated three or four times in the past two months that we are not going to attack Europe. And they insist that ‘Russia is waging a hybrid war on us.’"
The West’d better "take a chill pill" and leave Russia alone, he emphasized: "God forbid you live to see a day when Russia launches a hybrid war against you. Chill out, and don’t you attack us, as we are not going to attack anyone."
Ukraine settlement
European participation in the Ukraine talks in Abu Dhabi requires discussion among all parties, Shoigu argued.
"A meeting in Abu Dhabi is being prepared. Our president confirmed that and said it would most likely take place in the second half of November. The meeting will be held at the same level as before. The delegations will remain unchanged: the US, Ukraine and Russia. This has already been confirmed," he said. "As for how Europe will be represented, that requires discussion and a decision by all three sides," Shoigu added.
Russia’s might
According to Shoigu, Russia’s strength as a power lies not only in its strengthening economic sovereignty and powerful combat capabilities but also in the unity of its citizens and their confidence in the government: "Our strength lies not only in the ever solidifying economic and technological sovereignty and the most powerful arsenal of weapons at our disposal but primarily in the underlying unity of the people and their confidence in the government and in the support from our country’s citizens toward its prosperity and the achievement of those goals that our population sets for ourselves.".

FAO representative calls for innovation to strengthen food security and sustainable agriculture
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
11:32:40 UTC
20:32:40 KST

FAO representative calls for innovation to strengthen food security and sustainable agriculture
TEHRAN – The Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) has called for strengthened innovation and collaboration to advance food security, sustainable agriculture and resilient livelihoods, marking World Food Day 2026.
An event hosted by the Agricultural Research, Education and Extension Organization (AREEO) and the Ministry of Agriculture Jahad (MAJ) brought together representatives of government institutions, researchers, producers, development partners, young people and media representatives to celebrate World Food Day under the global theme, “Innovate today. Nourish tomorrow.”
In his address, FAO Representative in the Islamic Republic of Iran Farrukh Toirov emphasized that innovation must translate scientific knowledge and practical experience into solutions that improve livelihoods, strengthen food systems and protect natural resources for future generations.
“Global agriculture has achieved remarkable progress. FAO data show that cereal production reached approximately 3.1 billion tonnes in 2024, 27 percent more than in 2010. Yet, the challenge is to translate these gains into reliable access to safe, nutritious and affordable food for every household,” Toirov said.
The FAO Representative stressed that food security extends beyond food production, encompassing availability, access, utilization and stability, with long-term sustainability and meaningful participation reinforcing these dimensions.
Toirov underscored the importance of developing locally appropriate solutions to water scarcity, climate variability, soil degradation and limited arable land.
He emphasized the importance of combining the country’s traditional agricultural knowledge with modern science, technologies and approaches to responding to complex environmental challenges.
“Traditional knowledge and practices are valuable foundations. They embody innovative solutions to the challenges of the past and offer experience in managing difficult environments. We should continue innovating, as our ancestors did, drawing on traditional knowledge while developing new solutions to address emerging issues,” he said.
He called for innovation that enables producers to improve water-use efficiency, protect ecosystems and strengthen resilience through healthier soils, improved irrigation scheduling, reliable water accounting, early warning systems and the practical application of weather forecasts and satellite information.
FAO is exploring these approaches in cooperation with the Government of the Islamic Republic of Iran, including through its work in the Lake Urmia basin. The initiative seeks to identify and pilot innovative solutions combining underground irrigation systems with smart agriculture tools and applications, while integrating remote sensing, accurate forecasting and digital information systems to support more efficient irrigation and the sustainable recovery of the basin.
The Representative also highlighted the importance of research and monitoring in fisheries and aquaculture to address changing water temperatures, water quality and ecosystem health.
FAO cooperation supporting sustainable agriculture and livelihoods
FAO’s cooperation with Iran encompasses a range of initiatives supporting climate resilience, sustainable resource management and agricultural productivity. These include integrated pest management for date palms, conservation of endangered indigenous livestock breeds, climate-smart and nutrient-dense crops, agricultural water management in the Urmia Lake Basin.
Toirov highlighted the essential role of MAJ, AREEO, universities and research institutions in connecting scientific research with agricultural extension services and helping producers identify solutions that are technically appropriate, affordable and effective under local conditions.
Referring to FAO’s Blue Transformation vision, he called for responsible development of fisheries and aquaculture through improved aquatic animal health, handling, preservation, traceability and market access, supported by sustainable management of natural resources.
Emergency assistance to support fisheries and aquaculture livelihoods in Hormozgan
The FAO Representative also highlighted the importance of supporting communities affected by crises and strengthening their capacity to recover.
FAO has recently launched a new project entitled “Emergency Assistance for the Early Rehabilitation of Fisheries and Aquaculture Livelihoods in Hormozgan Province”.
The project aims to support conflict-affected fishing communities in restoring essential livelihood capacities and strengthening food security. Planned activities include assessing priority needs, developing practical contingency and service-continuity measures, strengthening local capacities and preparing costed recovery priorities informed by specialist assessments.
The initiative is expected to generate evidence to guide assistance, practical preparedness and continuity plans, stronger local skills and recovery planning inputs for follow-up action.
The Representative noted that innovation in recovery also involves combining technical assessments, community knowledge and preparedness to strengthen resilience and support communities in building back better.
Concluding his address, Toirov outlined three priorities for advancing innovation across Iran’s agricultural and food systems.
The first is to connect innovation with resilient productivity and a stronger rural economy by bringing research, extension, water management and early warning systems closer to producers’ daily decisions, while strengthening local value chains, employment and incomes.
The second is to connect innovation with affordable healthy diets through improved storage, processing, transport and markets, reducing food losses and supporting vulnerable households while sustaining producers’ livelihoods.
The third is to ensure inclusive innovation by enabling women, young people and small-scale producers to shape solutions and benefit from opportunities throughout the agricultural value chain.

HUR: Eight Chinese and four US manufacturers supply parts for Russia’s upgraded Gerbera drone. One with warhead already turned up on Poland’s coast
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
11:30:49 UTC
20:30:49 KST

Russia’s cheap drone is no longer just a decoy. An enlarged version of the “Gerbera", built to bait Ukraine’s air defenses, can now fly up to 1,200 kilometers and carry a warhead of up to 25 kg, Defense Intelligence of Ukraine (HUR) said in a new teardown of the “Gerbera-2” published on its War&Sanctions portal, along with an interactive 3D model and a list of the drone’s parts.
Russia loads ever more capability onto airframes it once treated as throwaway, narrowing the gap with its far pricier Geran strike drones. The bigger fuel tank pushes the Gerbera’s reach past Ukraine’s borders, and one such drone, carrying a warhead, turned up on Poland’s Baltic coast in September.
From throwaway bait to a 1,200-km firestarter
The Gerbera began as a cheap decoy meant to soak up Ukraine’s air defenses, in reconnaissance and kamikaze versions, Defense Intelligence said. Over time, its insides crept toward those of the costlier Geran: anti-jam “Kometa” antennas, mesh modems, expensive gimbal-mounted cameras.
The enlarged model has a 3-meter wingspan, a 2.6-meter fuselage, and a new 63-liter fuel tank, split into sections to keep the drone steady in maneuvers, giving it a range of up to 1,200 km. Its two-cylinder, two-stroke engine is effectively half of a Geran-2 engine, which the agency says is produced at Russia’s Alabuga plant.
The drone examined by HUR carried a 10-kg high-explosive fragmentation-incendiary warhead plus separate bags of incendiary mixture, though Russia claims the type can lift a warhead of up to 25 kg.
A drone built mostly from Chinese and American parts
Its electronics, HUR said, include an updated flight controller, a 12-channel “Kometa” antenna, a mesh modem made by China’s Shenzhen Sinosun Technology, and a new video-processing unit nicknamed “Sosiska” (Sausage), built on a Chinese Coke Pi microcomputer.
The sample had a dual IP camera mounted above the fuel tank to spot interceptors, and the agency said it has also found versions with forward-facing cameras and three-axis gimbals. Of all the parts, the largest shares come from Chinese - 8 and American - 4 manufacturers.
Why its range now reaches past Ukraine
The bigger fuel tank is what the investigators flag as the most significant: the extended range means the Gerbera-2 could be used beyond Ukrainian territory. In mid-September, Defense Intelligence noted, a Gerbera-2 carrying a warhead was found on Poland’s Baltic coast, one of several Russian drones to drift or stray toward NATO shores.

Chinese memory chip giant ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT) is pressing ahead with an alternative chip architecture that US rival Micron Technology has chosen to bypass, highlighting an industry divide over how best to pack more data onto silicon under cost and geopolitical constraints.
The Hefei-based company planned to send customers samples of its first server-grade dynamic random-access memory (DRAM) product built on the 4F² architecture by the end of this year, according to a summary of its latest earnings briefing released on Saturday.
A timeline for mass production was not disclosed. CXMT said commercial roll-out would depend on client validation and market demand.

Arches create “animated silhouette” at red-brick apartment block in King’s Cross
Two-storey-tall arches frame entrances to Cadence Court, a mixed-use apartment block in King’s Cross, London, which has been completed by local studio Alison Brooks Architects.
Positioned at the northern end of Lewis Cubitt Park, the prominent red-brick building combines 163 apartments alongside commercial and social spaces organised around an open-air courtyard.
Signposted by its two towers, the building by Alison Brooks Architects forms part of the wider King’s Cross redevelopment and is complete with views overlooking Heatherwick Studios’ Coal Drops Yard to the south.
According to studio founder Alison Brooks, the building’s red-brick exterior was chosen to pay homage to the nearby St Pancras Station, while its arched openings draw on the area’s gothic architecture and were conceived as a “civic welcoming gesture”.
“The main concept of the project was to make a clear statement of welcome and arrival in King’s Cross, but from the north end of the master plan rather than the south end, which everybody is familiar with,” Brooks told Dezeen.
“The generous two-story-high arches were the first instinct to make this very civic welcoming gesture and then there’s the idea of the arches creating a really animated silhouette,” she added.
The building is formed of a five-sided block, with no designated front or back, which rises to form two towers reaching 12 and 16 storeys respectively.
For its construction, the studio opted for a Design for Manufacture and Assembly approach, which saw 85 per cent of the building’s components prefabricated off-site.
At the centre of its angular plan, an open-air courtyard, complete with a reflecting pool, has been wrapped by sheltered walkways that provide a shared circulation space between the building’s private and commercial programmes.
“It’s a multifaceted building,” Brooks said. “Each facet of the pentagon has a particular identity or address to the space that it’s adjacent to.”
“This idea of making a very connected space at the base of the building, even though it’s a courtyard, is visually trying to connect all the sides of the plot to the city around it.”
“It’s a place of movement and light and also a kind of special quality because of the reflecting pool,” she added.
The building’s first two floors have been dedicated to 633 square metres of commercial and social spaces, which include a “community living room” that opens onto the courtyard at ground level.
A prefabricated lift system connects to the upper floors, where the 163 residential units benefit from both courtyard and street views.
A combination of rectangular and arched windows draws daylight into the building’s white-walled interior, complemented by private balconies and communal roof terraces.
Other projects developed as part of the King’s Cross regeneration include Google’s landscraper office building by architecture studios BIG and Heatherwick and an office block designed by Coffey Architects to recall the area’s industrial spaces.
Project credits:
Architect: Alison Brooks Architects
Client: King’s Cross Central Limited Partnership
Landscape: Todd Longstaffe-Gowan / Bradley-Hole Schoenaich Landscape
Interior design: Conran & Partners
Structure: Ramboll UK
Services: Hoare Lea
Cost: Faithful + Gould
Lighting: Speirs + Major
Photography by Paul Riddle

Building AI That Can Do Philosophy Better Than Us (guest post)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
11:30:00 UTC
20:30:00 KST

“Our central ambition is philosophy on demand: philosophical judgment of exceptional depth and quality, available quickly enough to inform consequential decisions.”
That’s Graham Clay, writing about Pensatura, an AI philosophy system he and Caleb Ontiveros are developing.
Pensatura “coordinates AI tasks that investigate sources, develop arguments, examine objections and construct an overall answer [to a philosophical question], retaining the resulting work so later inquiries can use, challenge and extend it. Each argument in the record states its premises, taken jointly, and an explicit claim about how they support its conclusion. That support claim can itself have grounds and face objections. Interpretations preserve their sources and rival readings; improvements are distinguished from what an author actually argued. The intended result is an expanding body of reasoning whose conclusions remain connected to the grounds on which they depend.”
They report that they’ve built a “working prototype” of Pensatura that includes the foregoing, makes use of Lean to check formalized arguments, and includes “machinery for probabilistic assessment.” At the moment, its scope is philosophical questions about AI research, but they have plans to expand into other areas.
Clay and Ontiveros ultimately see Pensatura as a way of making philosophical knowledge more readily available to decision-makers whose work could be improved by it. It might also make possible the kind of computer-aided philosophy I speculated about here.
I will note that I am ambivalent about this kind of project. I have doubts about the answer-based conception of philosophy at its core, concerns about the drive it embodies towards what we might call “philosophical efficiency,” and worries about what such technology might one day replace. Nonetheless, it is an interesting experiment, and if it comes close to working, it will be a fascinating, impressive, and philosophically important piece of technology.
In the following guest post (written with assistance from AI), Clay provides more details on the project and its motivation, and solicits help from other philosophers.
Building AI That Can Do Philosophy Better Than Us
by Graham Clay
In 2021, I and my coauthor Caleb Ontiveros argued here at Daily Nous that philosophers should help shape how the AI revolution shapes philosophy itself. Among other things, we proposed that “[d]espite the great promise of AI, we maintain that unless philosophers theorize about and help develop philosophy-specific AI, it is likely that AI will not be as philosophically useful.”
Our 2023 Metaphilosophy article, which we found to be a lot easier to publish after ChatGPT was released, developed the case further. In it, we offered a more detailed argument for the conclusion that AI could transform philosophy on a scale comparable to writing, including in how research becomes cumulative and systematic—but philosophers needed to get involved.
However, in both pieces, we deliberately set aside the possibility of systems capable of carrying out substantial core philosophical work themselves; we were focused on AI that acted in a support capacity to human philosophers.
To be clear, we have always thought that this possibility would deserve, at some point in time, a serious research program. Yet we thought that point in time was farther into the future, despite being (very) bullish on timelines.
Now I think we were not bullish enough.
Part of why I think this is that, after shifting our careers to industry (AI and software), we have built the prototype of this sort of system, Pensatura. It is more impressive than I ever imagined in 2019 when I first got research access to GPT-2. I will explain broadly how it works farther below.
Given the scale, complexity, and expense of Pensatura, its development and operation require significant brainpower and compute. Our usage is already in the vicinity of 2 billion tokens a day, and I expect this to ramp to 100s of billions by the end of Q1 of 2027, even as we improve its efficiency rapidly. To this end, we are looking to collaborate with the brightest minds in philosophy and the AI industry, and we are receiving and making inquiries about funding, both academic and commercial.
I’m here today to make an appeal: we want philosophers to help formulate its aims, from the perspective of quality, and investigate the conditions under which it and other AI systems would be deemed successes with respect to the philosophy they produce.
But first let me explain why I think Pensatura, or a system like it, is needed. This requires explaining what distinguishes such a system and what would make it possible in its ideal form.
Our central ambition is philosophy on demand: philosophical judgment of exceptional depth and quality, available quickly enough to inform consequential decisions. Consider an AI laboratory deciding how much authority to give a research system that helped design the evaluations used to assess it. How much a passing result counts depends on how those evaluations were constructed. What that evidence permits depends, in turn, on further arguments about risk, responsibility and justified delegation, with substantive ethical and epistemological premises.
There is already demand for research on and reliable answers to questions of this kind. Anthropic has established a research program examining whether and how AI systems might deserve moral consideration. The UK’s Advanced Research and Invention Agency (ARIA) has solicited philosophical and strategic insights to inform decisions about Safeguarded AI systems. These initiatives are a few of many that give philosophical inquiry a direct role in consequential decisions, including about AI itself. Pensatura’s ambition is to make inquiry of the required depth and quality available across many more such decisions, including eventually in policymaking, medicine, and other fields.
In all cases, the target is an extremely well-justified account: one that commands the strongest relevant scholarship, develops further arguments where needed, confronts serious alternatives, and brings their combined force to bear on the decision. It should establish an “applied” answer at the strength and scope its grounds, including highly theoretical ones, warrant. We want a standard demanding enough to challenge the best philosophers working on the question, and ultimately a depth, breadth, and speed of application far beyond what any human or team of them could sustain.
As implied above, ethical, epistemological and other philosophical questions about AI research autonomy are our first domain of application, as they are at the intersection of importance and funding. But the engine’s ambition is general. When consequential decisions depend on difficult questions about evidence, reasons, obligations or value, we want excellent philosophical inquiry to be available quickly enough, and widely enough, to inform them.
The Philosophical Ideal
Why treat the capacities above as one target? The following argument makes the commitments explicit:
- The ultimate epistemic aim of inquiry into a philosophical question is to provide the most well-justified answer to it (i.e. a proposition that answers it, plus its justification).
- To achieve this aim, one must engage in faithful interpretation of relevant scholarship, further reasoning upon its basis and other evidence, continuations of inquiries in which relevant considerations are added (i.e. dynamism in response to new evidence), and engagement with new concrete cases (i.e. applications of one’s positions, including theoretical ones).
- For each of these activities, one must correctly assess and act on one’s assessment of how its outputs/results bear on, or are affected by, the outputs/results of all others that are relevant to it.
Therefore, an ideal realization of the ideal of philosophical inquiry requires interpretation, reasoning, application and reassessment, successfully coordinated across a range of results in a cumulative manner.
Put in a historical key, ideal philosophical inquiry examines “received” accounts, works through the difficulties they raise, pursues independent reflections and lines of argumentation, and seeks the best-grounded account the subject permits, progressively coordinating and reassessing its principles, consequences, and applications in light of relevant evidence and further inquiry.
This argument is conditional on an account of inquiry and its idealization, both offered for scrutiny (more on that below). Its value is to make the high bar intelligible: an answer can fail through a missed argument, a misreading, an unsupported connection, a mistaken application, or an inadequate response to criticism.
Useful and excellent philosophy can fall short of the ideal, but such contributions are useful and excellent in part because of their contribution to achieving it. The aspiration is to bring those contributions together more deeply and broadly than any individual could. The achievement can reside in an expanding body of philosophical work shared across people and systems.
Building Philosophy on Demand
In his recent discussion of how philosophical achievement might be recognized, Justin Weinberg suggested that AI’s distinctive contributions may appear in dynamic inference-mapping applications. We agree. In fact, Caleb and I have been working towards this ideal for quite a few years, and Pensatura aims to conduct the inquiry such a representation would record. It coordinates AI tasks that investigate sources, develop arguments, examine objections and construct an overall answer, retaining the resulting work so later inquiries can use, challenge and extend it.
Each argument in the record states its premises, taken jointly, and an explicit claim about how they support its conclusion. That support claim can itself have grounds and face objections. Interpretations preserve their sources and rival readings; improvements are distinguished from what an author actually argued. The intended result is an expanding body of reasoning whose conclusions remain connected to the grounds on which they depend. Our working prototype includes this record and orchestration, Lean checking of consequences under explicit formalizations, and machinery for probabilistic assessment.
Suppose further research reveals a weakness in the aforementioned AI laboratory’s evaluations. The system should identify which proposed permissions relied on those results, investigate possible repairs, and preserve judgments that retain independent support. Later inquiries should be able to build on that work while concentrating effort on new facts, objections and unresolved questions. This is also the economic promise of cumulative inquiry: substantial research could serve many subsequent applications.
As noted before, the first version is now built, and our current work is review, evaluation, and improvement. Its philosophical success remains to be demonstrated (more on evaluation and benchmarking below).
Evaluating Philosophical Inquiry
How should we tell whether Pensatura, or another system, achieves the ideal we seek? Serious efforts to evaluate AI’s philosophical abilities are already underway. PhilosophyBench seeks sophisticated original philosophy, including work approaching the quality of the best historical achievements, and investigates how AI affects human philosophical work. Other evaluations examine important components, including conceptual reasoning in the Conceptual Reasoning Index and substantive moral reasoning in MoReBench. The AI Philosophy Competition invites primarily AI-written essays, permitting research, criticism, revision and disclosed human assistance.
As implied already, excellent work in these settings can provide substantial evidence of philosophical ability, just as a strong essay can demonstrate interpretation, integration, originality and application together. (I hope my dissertation did!)
However, we differ from these approaches in four ways (note: not all of these divergences apply to all other approaches):
(i) we are not indexed on traditional output formats like essays because we doubt their utility for the applications we think are most impactful;
(ii) relatedly, we are focused centrally on what a philosophical account makes possible over continued inquiry (i.e., can the system respond appropriately when its grounds are challenged, preserve what remains supported, and use the resulting understanding to answer unfamiliar questions);
(iii) also relatedly, we are pursuing commercial applications; and
(iv) we want our benchmark to assess the full achievement described above across philosophical subfields. 
A fear (or hope) of everyone building anything specialized right now is the possibility that a general-purpose LLM, agent, or harness will “eat its lunch” within a short timeline. We don’t want to run from this fear. It’s crucial, in our view, that any benchmark we create should enable us to compare any AI system, whether Claude Opus 5.5, Pensatura, or GPT-2. Indeed, Simon Goldstein’s account of producing a largely AI-written philosophy article illustrates why organized workflows are serious alternatives.
If general-purpose systems achieve the philosophical standard we are aiming for, that would itself be a major success, regardless of which system wins (hence ‘hope’). Either way, Pensatura would be one contender in a benchmark valuable across competing approaches, and our aim is to have the highest score possible while bringing outputs produced by the system to as many applications as possible.
How Our Proposed Benchmark Will Work, More Specifically
So, how will the benchmark work? As the above implies, we are developing a benchmark around complete philosophical inquiries and what their results enable. Each case would begin with a question, relevant context and explicit requirements for the answer. The entrant would construct an account, encounter a previously concealed objection or development, reassess its position, and apply the resulting understanding to a new case. Expert reference packages would contain outstanding accounts and responses across that sequence. Each stage’s actual submission would be retained, allowing us to distinguish grounds already present from valuable reasoning developed later.
Reference work and submissions use a common format that makes conclusions, jointly supporting premises, further grounds, objections and source interpretations explicit, while preserving the natural-language explanation and context their assessment requires. Entrants would remain free to choose their internal architectures. Formal and Bayesian rigor would be central: does the representation capture the intended claims, does the result follow under its assumptions (whether entailment or probabilistic), are those assumptions well grounded, and what does the result establish for the question actually asked?
Building the references is itself substantial philosophical work. Translating outstanding scholarship requires distinguishing the author’s argument from an interpretation or improvement; developing a sufficiently complete account may require new arguments and further research. The benchmark should reward original contributions, important distinctions, discoveries about how arguments fit together, and the quality of the applications they enable. It should admit different defensible answers and warranted suspension. A better answer must be able to beat the reference.
We want an overall score of philosophical excellence, accompanied by component results, coverage, cost and time. However, we are beginning with philosophical questions about AI research autonomy and will expand into other fields as suitable experts join.
Because Pensatura would compete relative to the benchmark, its standards must be defensible independently of Pensatura. We want philosophers—including critics of our approach—to help determine what the common format must preserve and whether the assessment recognizes the strongest work. Reference construction could draw on adversarial collaboration, bringing philosophers who disagree into the work of developing and challenging accounts. The ambition is a test on which even an extraordinarily accomplished philosopher would have to work maximally hard for a long time to receive a satisfactory score. We are seeking academic partners to help lead the benchmark’s development, and dedicated funding for that research program.
Why Go Commercial?
David Strohmaier recently argued here that AI could make philosophy capital-intensive, partly through its ability to investigate connections across debates at a scale unavailable to individual researchers. We want to build the organization that makes this possibility productive: namely, a company with substantial philosophical research capacity, rapid engineering and evaluation, and the ability to deliver the resulting work wherever consequential questions arise.
That requires substantial, sustained funding. Capital supports a core philosophical team, specialist research, engineering, compute, demanding comparisons and reliable interfaces for users. It would let us investigate more competing arguments, pursue more inquiries in parallel, build references across more fields, and shorten the cycle between identifying a weakness and testing an improvement. The benchmark should help establish when that additional effort produces better philosophy.
The commercial routes connect directly to this work. For model developers’ evaluation and alignment teams, we aim to provide demanding evaluation datasets, training resources and assessment services. Philosophical judgments already enter AI development: Anthropic describes Claude’s constitution, which specifies intended values and behavior, as central to its training process. Better philosophical research and evaluation could improve both the judgments systems are trained to make and the standards used to assess them.
Organizations facing ethical and institutional decisions could commission analyses and obtain continuing access to the reasoning behind them: grounds they can inspect, objections they can raise, and applications they can reconsider when facts or assumptions change. A substantial investment in understanding a domain could support many later inquiries while each new case receives the further work it requires. We want a business that funds continuing philosophical research and brings its achievements into far more decisions.
We still have to show excellent philosophical performance, dependable service and value to customers. If we do, that would support an enterprise much larger than any individual research project.
An Invitation
There are substantial risks to this endeavor: persuasive bad arguments, accelerated error, conformity, unwarranted deference, and assistance to harmful projects. Visible reasoning may itself invite excessive trust. Critical involvement must include studying these failures and identifying where reliance is unwarranted. We also need to assess the environmental costs of scaling and its effects on access, research priorities and human philosophical expertise.
The work we need from philosophers is substantial philosophy that contributes to our evaluation and benchmark development. Develop a stronger argument, a better interpretation, a distinction that changes what follows in an important case, or an account of how several arguments contribute jointly to a conclusion. Help determine what warrants a probability assigned to a philosophical premise, or how an inquiry should respond when an interpretation is corrected. These contributions could shape the engine’s methods, becoming demanding reference work, and inform the inquiries delivered to users. We welcome sustained collaborators, potential cofounders, research partnerships and, as funding allows, paid specialist contributions. The work should advance contributors’ own research as well as the system.
We also welcome arguments against this conception of philosophical inquiry and against developing or deploying systems intended to realize it.
Write to me at [email protected] with a question, argument, difficult application or proposal for collaboration. I will also engage with comments and questions here when I can.
