Want to Sign With a Hollywood Agent? Start Making Fun of AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
11:30:00 UTC
20:30:00 KST

“Hi there!” says an AI avatar of a clean-cut man dressed casually in a denim shirt, with a mostly empty bookcase in the background. “I’m Clark from Marlow & Finch. To get us started, why don’t you tell me a bit about yourself?”
The real human on the other end of the call—Graham Raabe, in glasses and ball cap—is more than ready to dive in. “Happy to, and happy to be here,” he tells his AI job interviewer. “I’m Chick Bongo. I’ve spent about 10 years in sales. Really good at managing badger margin, spent quite a bit of time with sprocket moss, particularly proud of my goosebuckle.”
“Managing badger margin sounds like a serious skill,” the unfazed bot replies. “And that goosebuckle experience is impressive.” Raabe continues to answer Clark’s boilerplate questions with complete nonsense, the fake interviewer echoing most of it in mechanical tones of approval and amazement. When the interviewer inquires what kind of salary range “Chick Bongo” has in mind, Raabe replies, “Six hundred.” Clark interprets this to mean $600,000, calling it a “bold number,” but adds that he admires the “confidence” in the ask.
Raabe isn’t really after a new gig. Actually, in addition to his job as manager of a sales team in the fintech space, he is among a crop of comedians who have recently blown up online—and secured talent representation—by figuring out inventive ways to troll and satirize AI. Absurd, rapid-fire exchanges with agents like Clark have become Raabe’s signature comic routine, one that has doubled his Instagram audience from around 50,000 to more than 100,000 followers over the past two months.
Raabe tells WIRED that he’s been pursuing stand-up comedy and screenwriting as hobbies for the better part of a decade, and trained in improv and sketch at the renowned Upright Citizens Brigade theater. It wasn’t until May of this year, he says, that he started experimenting with office humor videos on Instagram and TikTok.
“I actually didn't start with any AI-adjacent content,” Raabe says. “It was primarily more of a down-the-middle, workplace comedy play, and I was just encouraged by the results and the feedback that I got.”
Raabe has a knack for clever linguistic play, and one of his earlier bits involved substitutions for stock or cliché phrases you might hear in a meeting: instead of “the ball is in your court,” he suggests in one clip, try “the hawk is on your glove” or “that’s your microwave beeping” or “the decision goblin lives at your address.”
Then Raabe started using AI bots to “quiz” him on this type of corporate jargon—his chatbot challenged him, for example, to come up with a euphemism for explaining that his team walked into a meeting unprepared. (“We brought forks to a soup party” was his twist on the phrase.)
Finally, Raabe hit upon the bizarro AI interviewer format. Though he’s never personally endured a bot screening for employment, he was aware of the trend and saw potential in the interview agents from the AI research lab Tavus. (“Screen thousands,” the tool’s marketing copy reads. ”Miss nothing.”) The Tavus bots, Raabe found, could be customized to deliver the conversational rhythms and escalation he needed for a video sketch, and he launched a popular series called “How to Fail Your AI Interview,” in which he derails calls with the avatars with digressive tactics—claiming to have known the bot in college, for example, or insisting on “icebreakers” before the interview begins.
“Most of my comedy is to play off straight men, and AI is the ultimate straight man to improv against,” Raabe explains.
The concept quickly took off, with commenters sharing their own frustrating experiences in real AI interview scenarios. It was around when he began this transition into AI comedy that he gained representation at Dulcedo Management, a talent agency with clients throughout North America, including influencers, models, athletes, and creators. That placed him in a comedy cohort with creators Matt Husk (@husk.irl) and Sam Wassef (@ahh.gpt), two other content creators whose viral AI trolling led to agent deals despite—or perhaps in some way because of—entertainment studios rapidly integrating the tech into production workflows.
Alex Melendez, associate director of gaming and entertainment at Dulcedo, tells WIRED that the company came across Raabe when he had fewer than 10,000 followers and were instantly taken with his sharp timing and original, well-executed premises. As for the AI interview videos, he says that Raabe is mining rich territory.
“There's something inherently funny about the contradiction surrounding AI right now,” Melendez explains. “We're constantly hearing about how it's going to transform industries and replace jobs, and then you see it struggle with something incredibly basic. That disconnect creates a lot of comedic opportunity.” He feels that Raabe and others “are giving audiences a way to laugh at something that can otherwise feel intimidating or overwhelming,” and that the rapid evolution of AI means a steady flow of new material.
“Every development brings another moment that makes people stop and think, ‘What is actually happening?’” Melendez says. “Comedy has always been a way to make sense of cultural shifts, and AI is no exception.”
And though AI may be the butt of these jokes, many tech developers and companies seem to be all for it. “I've gotten multiple DMs from people who are product managers at companies that build AI video avatars like this,” Raabe says. “They've told me that they love to see people having fun with the tools, and occasionally I've gotten messages from product managers who are like, ‘Thanks for pointing out that particular skill gap because now we know how to fix it.’”
Likewise, the surreal and wildly viral dialogues between Matt Husk and OpenAI’s ChatGPT have exposed the weaknesses of the LLM, forcing the company to acknowledge these shortcomings. In his videos, Husk (as he is known across his social media accounts) typically asks the chatbot for some kind of help, with his theoretical problems ranging from drowning in quicksand to simple challenges like counting to a hundred. Without fail, the chatbot cheerfully botches the job, and it tends to gaslight Husk about getting the answer wrong if he presses it to admit fault.
Husk’s content has earned him some 2 million followers combined across Instagram, TikTok, and YouTube, as well as a deal with the talent agency Unicorn, where he’s represented by Ali Fischbein, founder of the production company Lil Fish Comedy. (Fischbein declined to comment for this article.) And as with Raabe, Husk’s rise as a social media star has coincided with a role as pressure-tester for his favored product.
In April, on the tech podcast Mostly Human, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman was prompted to react to a Husk video in which he used ChatGPT as a stopwatch and found that it measured a span of a few seconds as lasting “around 10 minutes.” Altman laughed at the glitch, claiming that it was a “known issue,” and predicted that it would be another year before the voice model could set an accurate timer.
Not everyone in this scene is examining areas where AI might be improved, however. Sam Wassef, who has more than 860,000 followers as @ahh.gpt on Instagram, instead embodies a humanoid parody of a chatbot, delivering a pitch-perfect impression of the inanities and non sequiturs you’ve come to expect from these pioneering models, often while guzzling water by the gallon. Wassef’s shorts featuring this blathering character make up a mysterious countdown—he is a third of the way through a planned run of a hundred posts—and have expanded to cinematic scope. One of the latest videos sees him prattle on about the bright future of AI as the camera gradually reveals that he is standing alone in the center of a barren mall among dark, empty storefronts.
Wassef is signed with talent managers Mikayla Haycock and Adam Loria at Night Media, who declined to comment for this article. Their involvement is more evidence that the entertainment world is looking for people with inventive angles on the AI zeitgeist, which, as Melendez says, is an indicator that they can apply the same comedic skill set to other topics and platforms. The ultimate goal for a client like Raabe, Husk, or Wassef, he explains, “is for audiences to become invested” in them as a performer, not just “the format or trend” that gave them their start. The name of the game is growth and longevity regardless of where public discourse may go next.
“Virality can open the door,” he says, “but it's the talent behind it that builds a lasting career.”

Bulgarian paper Capital headlines with "Iliana Iotova has been elected president – her victory seals the new status quo". She ran against Andrey Gyurov, who was backed by Bulgaria's pro-Western parties. As a reminder, she was the president's vice president for nine years, before he resigned and was elected PM. The liberal and pro-Western paper writes that now, Radev and his ruling party have consolidated their control over the three branches of government – the National Assembly, the government and the presidency, which had previously acted as a political counterbalance. Now, the only remaining counterbalance to the government is the justice system. The paper says that the elections have also deepened divisions within Bulgarians and called into question the country's direction after Communism and the choice between Russia and Western allies.
Dnevnik looks at who exactly Iotova is: Bulgaria's first woman president. She has already spent many years at the political top, always supported by the Communists and later Socialists. After the fall of one of the country's most prominent Communist leaders in 1996 and during the post-Communist transition, she was the head of the Bulgarian Socialist Party's press centre. She then took part in national politics, with stints as an MEP, vice president and now president.
In Belarus, human rights groups warn of a dangerous practice. Radio Free Europe writes that at least 22 political prisoners are being held in psychiatric hospitals and not traditional prisons. Locking up critics of the government in psychiatric facilities has long been a method used in Soviet countries. Human rights defenders and doctors say that the method "has found a modern resurgence" in Belarus. The prisoners have to undergo compulsory psychiatric treatment that has no predetermined end date. That means the prisoners are out of the conventional prison system and they cannot benefit from amnesties, for instance, and other basic rights.
In Germany, the Eagle's Nest, one of the last structural relics of Adolf Hitler's dictatorship, burned down in a suspected arson attack last month. Now, the burning question is: should it be rebuilt? The Guardian writes that with a far-right resurgence in Germany, experts there are divided as to whether the Eagle's Nest retreat is best restored or left as a ruin. Its architecture is intended to overwhelm and intimidate and combined with its history, it's a big tourist attraction: more than 300,000 tourists used to go there per year. But after the efforts of more than 200 firefighters, the tourist attraction is closed indefinitely. If it is reconstructed for a new generation of visitors, The Guardian says those in charge should try to mitigate the risk of creating a shrine for neo-Nazis.
Finally, Halloween is over, but one costume is still making the headlines: Heidi Klum's severed hand. Vogue France called it "her most disgusting ever" – the best Halloween compliment!

First Asian hornet nest in Poland eliminated but experts warn more to appear next year
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
11:28:14 UTC
20:28:14 KST

Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!
Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.
Poland’s first-ever nest of Asian hornets, an invasive species seen as a particular threat because it preys on honeybees, has been eliminated. But scientists who have studied the colony say that it is likely more will be found next year.
Since arriving in France in 2004, Asian hornets have gradually spread to other European countries.
The first confirmed nest to be found in Poland was sighted in a tree in the village of Wielka Wieś near Kraków in mid-October, with individual hornets also being spotted at the apiary of the city’s AGH University of Science and Technology.
The nest was removed last week and sent to be studied by a team of scientists at Wrocław University of Environmental and Life Sciences, reports the Polish Press Agency (PAP).
Paweł Migdał, from the university’s faculty of biology and animal science, told PAP that the nest was “fairly large” considering the Polish climate, containing around 1,000 workers and several dozen queens and males.
The scientists’ assessment of the nest revealed that it contained eggs and larvae, indicating that the hornets inhabiting it were still feeding, he added.
“I think we’ll find more of these nests,” Migdał told PAP. “They’re often built in the treetops, which means they’re invisible until the leaves fall in the autumn.”
Young queens had already left the nest to establish new ones after overwintering, and have greater chances of surviving the longer and warmer the Polish autumn is, he explained. They seek shelter in warm, dry places, such as underground or in storage areas.
With queens measuring 30mm and males about 24mm, Asian hornets, also known as the yellow-legged hornet, are smaller than the European variety, and no more dangerous to humans than European hornets or wasps.
The major concern over their arrival relates to their tendency to seek out beehives and prey on honeybees.
“Besides killing honeybees, their presence also causes bees in apiaries to stop working,” explained Migdał. “With the European hornet, the bees recognise the threat but, in a sense, continue working. However, the yellow-legged hornet presents a completely new threat to them.”
The number of bee colonies in Poland has risen 54% over the last decade to reach two million, thanks in part to a state programme supporting beekeepers.
Bees' value to the ecosystem as pollinators is estimated to be worth 5bn zloty (€1.1bn) https://t.co/ElISOc2o2T
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 30, 2022
The scale of the species’ invasiveness is shown by the fact that it releases an average of 150 young queens from its nest, and sometimes even 500 – each of which can potentially create its own nest – while European hornets release just 50, Migdał pointed out.
The location of the first nest found in Poland surprised scientists as the closest previously known was in Opava, around 150 km away in the Czech Republic. The hornets therefore probably travelled in a vehicle, although Migdał noted a potential concern that other populations might be found between the two sites.

Trump could launch nuclear strike on Iran within days, commentator claims
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

20:26:26 KST

US commentator Tucker Carlson claimed late Sunday that the Trump administration could be days away from launching a nuclear strike on Iran, alleging that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is pressuring President Donald Trump to authorize an attack on a suspected nuclear site in central Iran.
In a lengthy post on the US social media company X, Carlson identified the potential target as Pickaxe Mountain, where Israeli intelligence allegedly believes Iran has resumed its nuclear enrichment program.
Carlson is a conservative political commentator and former Fox News host whose program, Tucker Carlson Tonight, aired from 2016 to 2023.
He now hosts an independent political show on X, where he regularly comments on US foreign policy and international affairs.
Carlson claimed conventional US weapons could not penetrate the estimated 300 feet of solid granite protecting underground tunnels at the site, leaving a nuclear strike as the only military option.
“Bibi (Netanyahu) calls Trump about it every day,” Carlson quoted an unnamed informed observer as saying.
Carlson argued that Netanyahu’s political survival is driving his push for further military action. He claimed Netanyahu needs Trump’s intervention to secure a 61-seat majority in the Knesset following the latest election results, warning that otherwise he could lose power and face investigations and possible imprisonment.
He also alleged that Netanyahu has been pressing senior US officials, including Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and US Central Command chief Adm. Brad Cooper, to resume major combat operations.
Carlson also claimed that Secretary of State Marco Rubio and CIA Director John Ratcliffe were following Netanyahu’s lead.
He further said former President Barack Obama had also opposed the Iran peace agreement being drafted in Doha.
Fears of regional escalation
Carlson said US allies in the Middle East were increasingly concerned about renewed fighting. He claimed Netanyahu secretly traveled to Abu Dhabi on Sept. 27 to persuade the UAE to support a final attack on Iran, but Emirati officials refused.
Warning of the economic consequences, Carlson said eight months of conflict had severely affected Gulf economies, as well as global energy and fertilizer markets. He claimed 11 of the world’s approximately 850 oil supertankers were badly damaged in the Strait of Hormuz in October alone.
He also warned that a nuclear explosion at Pickaxe Mountain could contaminate the Gulf and threaten the water supply of around 100 million people.
Carlson argued that a US nuclear strike could establish a dangerous precedent, potentially encouraging Russia to use nuclear weapons against Ukraine, triggering renewed nuclear tensions between India and Pakistan, and prompting North Korea to attack Seoul.
READ: Israeli Democrats leader warns Netanyahu could use new attack on Iran to stay in power
“After the first nuclear strike, World War Three is inevitable. That war would be short and final,” he wrote.
He further alleged that the Trump administration had quietly revised US nuclear doctrine since February to make the first use of so-called “battlefield nukes” easier and more likely.
Vance, Witkoff urge Trump to pursue diplomacy
Carlson said Trump could decide by Nov. 7 whether to authorize the use of nuclear weapons, adding that Vice President JD Vance and special envoy Steve Witkoff were urging him to pursue a diplomatic agreement with Tehran.
Although acknowledging that negotiations would be difficult, Carlson said people who had spoken with Iranian decision-makers believed there was a consensus that further conflict would benefit no one and that an agreement was worth pursuing.
He concluded by warning that the consequences of a nuclear strike would extend far beyond Iran, arguing that the international public had been excluded from decisions that could threaten millions of lives.
“Now would be the time for them to speak up,” Carlson wrote.
US could strike remaining Iranian nuclear sites ‘within 10 minutes’
Carlson’s claims follow Trump’s remarks to reporters at his Mar-a-Lago estate in Florida on Saturday that one or two Iranian nuclear facilities remained potential targets and that the US could strike them within 10 minutes.
Trump specifically mentioned Pickaxe Mountain, saying he had military plans for the area, but did not indicate that a nuclear strike had been authorized.
“You probably could look at Pickaxe Mountain, you have to take care of that. We can do that all very quickly,” he added.
In an Oct. 16 interview with Newsmax, he explicitly ruled out using nuclear weapons against Iran.
Separately, Axios reported that Trump and Netanyahu held a tense phone call on Saturday, citing Israeli and US sources. According to the report, Netanyahu is pushing for renewed military action immediately after Tuesday’s US midterm elections, while Trump prefers to allow diplomatic negotiations to continue.
A White House official said the administration does not comment on sensitive military plans, adding that Trump is keeping all options open to prevent Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon.
Secretary of State Rubio has also said no final decision has been made on resuming strikes.
Iran, meanwhile, denies any nuclear activity at the Pickaxe Mountain complex. Its supreme leader has warned Washington and Tel Aviv against launching further attacks.

Argentina courts AI data centres with no regulation and tax breaks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
11:25:46 UTC
20:25:46 KST

Argentina’s president, Javier Milei, is courting AI data centre investment in Patagonia, promising light regulation and tax breaks.
Argentina's cool southern region of Patagonia is becoming a hotspot for data centres, and the country's president is on a mission to lure them in.
While some communities in the US and Europe push back against data centres, Argentina’s government is making the opposite pitch. President Javier Milei says his country will not regulate AI, and he is offering a corporate tax cut to large projects in the sector, though the Senate has yet to approve it.
Patagonia’s appeal is practical: plenty of empty land, cool air, strong winds, and gas from the Vaca Muerta shale formation to cool and power the data centres.
Like his ally, US President Donald Trump, Milei frequently posts AI-generated images on social media. He has also proposed creating "nonhuman corporations" run entirely by AI agents.
"We are not going to regulate artificial intelligence," Milei told the US Chamber of Commerce in Washington last month. "We are going to leave it free."
Visitor logs obtained by The Associated Press show a steady stream of tech figures meeting with Milei and his aides in recent months, from venture capitalist Peter Thiel to representatives of OpenAI, Amazon, Google, Oracle and data centre companies.
Foreign Ministry records show that data centre developer Crusoe, which helped build OpenAI’s flagship campus in Texas, sought talks this year with Argentine energy officials about US government-backed investments.
“In densely populated parts of the US and Europe, there’s a lot of fighting over access to the grid and who should get the electricity," said Marta Zlotkowska, head of international development at Green Capital.
The Polish renewable energy company plans to build a $3 billion (€2.7 billion) data centre in Patagonia that would be leased to big tech firms for AI computing, though it has yet to secure a customer.
"We compared potential locations for the project around the world and Argentina — well, Patagonia — came out on top in every category," she said.
Patagonia’s AI promise
To win over companies wary of Argentina’s chronic economic instability, Milei is pushing an incentive scheme that would slash the corporate income tax rate to 15% from 25% for projects of at least $1 billion (€892 million) in AI and other emerging industries. The measure is awaiting Senate approval.
The payoff for Argentines remains unclear. Data centres employ relatively few people. Milei’s proposed incentives don’t require companies to reserve computing capacity for local consumption or to disclose their energy and water use.
"We’re not talking about data centres designed to strengthen Argentine technological sovereignty," said Alan Rocha Varsanyi, a researcher at Observatorio Petrolero Sur, an Argentine environmental group. "The computing capacity will be exported wherever OpenAI or the other companies need it."
Blueprints, not yet bulldozers
For all Milei’s hype, Argentina lags in the race to become a regional data centre hub, as its neighbours tout cheap land, renewable power and expanding fibre-optic connections to US tech giants.
Milei insists his calls for unfettered AI give Argentina an edge at a time when the European Union and a growing number of US states have adopted new regulations. Critics warn he is pushing to deploy AI in Argentina without safeguards against risks ranging from mass surveillance to cyberattacks.
"Without rules, Argentina will become a laboratory — like when companies go to developing countries to test strange drugs they can’t test in major developed countries," said Nicolás Wolovick, a computer science professor at the National University of Córdoba.
Milei may hear similar concerns next week when Pope Leo XIV, who has warned of AI’s threats to humanity, visits Argentina on his Latin American tour.
Even some in Milei’s own government acknowledge that his anti-regulation stance complicates efforts to build a clear legal framework, with one senior official not authorised to brief media saying companies are waiting for Argentina to settle rules on training AI with copyrighted works and sending personal data abroad.
Servers and sheep
In remote ranching outposts across the treeless plateau of Chubut province, life revolves around tending flocks on steppes and shearing sheep in sheds. With the wool industry in decline after decades of drought, overgrazing and soaring production costs, some ranchers are betting on a different kind of shed — filled not with fleece but with blinking racks of servers.
"Sheep farmers are looking very hard at what alternatives can be found to bring in more income," said Francisco Sáenz, an agricultural engineer and fourth-generation sheep farmer.
His family is among 14 landowners who have leased a combined 130,000 hectares (about 321,000 acres) to Green Capital for its planned data centre. The ranchers expect to keep grazing sheep alongside their colossal future neighbour.
Construction isn’t expected to begin until around 2028. If operated continuously at its projected peak demand, the finished campus would use about 2.7 times as much electricity in a year as the entire city of Buenos Aires consumed in 2025, according to an AP calculation.
Green Capital promises to generate all its own electricity from wind turbines, solar farms and gas-fired generators rather than strain Argentina’s congested grid. Provincial officials are counting on the project to deliver billions of dollars in investment, highly skilled jobs and a market for surplus wind power.
But some residents of Trelew, a dust-blown city near the proposed site, say they have no way to judge those assurances. Environmental studies are still underway, permits are pending and the company hasn’t specified how much water the project would need or how much of its power would come from gas.
"There’s just so little information," said Cristina Gibón, 46, who fears the environmental toll of data centres. "Maybe we’ll have water until we’re old. But afterwards, our children will still be here, and they won’t have those resources."
Worries like hers are feeding a wider backlash against Milei's courtship of Big Tech. In Trelew, a small group of residents has rallied online and in the main square under the banner "Trelew Free of Data Centres".
In Congress, where lawmakers recently accused Milei of selling off the country at a hearing on billionaire Peter Thiel’s interests in Argentina, the opposition has forced the president to gut a bill easing restrictions on foreign land ownership and has stalled his plan to let AI agents control companies.
Back on his family’s farm, Sáenz sees a familiar Argentine reflex.
"Whenever a foreign company wants to make a major investment in Argentina, there’s a lot of criticism. Many people’s first reaction is to say, 'No, they’re terrible people coming from the outside to take our resources,'" he said.
"I’m not saying big companies are the best thing ever. I’m just saying that when I look at other countries, I see stable economies."

Supermarket freezers in Belgium and Sweden hit by suspected cyber-attack
- Published
Dozens of supermarkets in Belgium and Sweden have been hit by a suspected cyber-attack affecting its refrigerators and freezers.
Around 40 Delhaize supermarkets and 15 Carrefour stores were affected in Belgium, while several ICA and Coop shops in Sweden were hit. Thirteen SuperValu shops have also been impacted in Ireland.
Thousands of euros worth of food has had to be thrown away, according to local media reports, with one ICA store in Sweden saying temperatures for its freezers had been set to 50 C (122F).
It is not clear who is behind the attack, which follows a similar incident last month that affected hundreds of French supermarkets.
Delhaize, one of Belgium's biggest supermarket chains, told Belgian media a "computer incident" had occurred overnight at 40 shops.
Carrefour, a French-owned supermarket, said it was "currently analysing" the incident at 15 of its Belgian stores.
Meanwhile, a spokesperson for ICA in Sweden confirmed the incident had affected a "small number of ICA stores operating outside ICA's central network".
"ICA is currently supporting the affected stores in managing the situation," they said.
One of the IVA branches located in Sjöbo, southern Sweden, wrote on social media: "Our refrigerators and freezers have been hacked overnight and they have set the temperature to 50 degrees."
The store was closed earlier but has now reopened to customers.
Seven out of the 800 Coop stores in Sweden are also affected but the "situation is currently contained and under control", the company told the BBC.

Egypt, Saint Catherine's Monastery to resolve status dispute
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
11:24:21 UTC
20:24:21 KST

Breadcrumb
Egypt, Saint Catherine's Monastery move to resolve months-long status dispute
A legal dispute between the Egyptian government and Saint Catherine's Monastery is drawing to a close after the two sides agreed on the terms of a possible settlement.
News of the settlement emerged on 24 October, when Archbishop Symeon of Saint Catherine's Monastery sent a letter to the Egyptian Foreign Ministry, expressing his intention to sign the settlement agreement.
The expected settlement would end months of uncertainty over the monastery's legal status and a potential strain in relations between Egypt and Greece, with the religious assets of the monastery, its administration and heritage being globally famed as belonging to the Greek Orthodox monastic tradition.
Greek Foreign Minister George Gerapetritis described the breakthrough as a "historic day" for Hellenism and Orthodoxy, in general.
"The beacon of Orthodoxy, the Holy Monastery of Saint Catherine of Mount Sinai, is acquiring a solid legal foundation through the agreement between the Monastery and the Egyptian State," the Greek minister said in a statement on October 24.
He also described the agreement as the "embodiment of a profound strategic relationship" with Egypt, referring to the expansion of this relationship across all fields.
Inside the draft settlement
The Egyptian Foreign Ministry has welcomed approval by Archbishop Symeon to sign a contract to end the legal dispute.
Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty reaffirmed Egypt's centuries-old commitment to safeguarding the monastery and ensuring that its spiritual and religious standing remains intact, according to a statement by the Egyptian Foreign Ministry on October 24.
While full details of the agreement have not been officially released, statements by Archbishop Symeon and reports in the Greek press indicate that the deal strikes a balance between Egyptian sovereign law and the monastery's historical autonomy.
Egypt is expected to recognise the monastery's right to govern its internal affairs, including the admission of monks and the election of its archbishop and its administration.
The monastery, its churches, chapels and pilgrimage sites would remain dedicated to Orthodox Christian worship, with only the monastery's monks entitled to possess and use them freely and in perpetuity, according to reports in the Greek press.
The monastery would, meanwhile, commit to retaining the site's designated religious use and be required to obtain permits from Egyptian archaeological authorities for work on its premises.
The monastery could also seek leases for agricultural land that an Egyptian appeals court had previously ruled belonged to the Egyptian state.
The proposed agreement would also require Egypt to protect the monks' way of life, amid concerns that increased tourism could disrupt the monastery's daily routine.
The possible agreement, Egyptian observers said, is a win-win for Egypt and the monastery.
Mustafa Waziri, former head of the Supreme Council of Antiquities, the executive arm of the Egyptian Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities, said the proposed settlement serves the interests of the monastery as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
"It also serves the interests of the monks of the monastery," he told The New Arab.
Waziri added that the proposed settlement protects Egyptian state properties, while preserving the spiritual and historical status of the monastery.
"Settling the dispute in such a peaceful manner nips tensions between Cairo and Athens in the bud," Waziri said.
Legal ambiguity
Founded in the 6th century, Saint Catherine's Monastery is the oldest Christian house of worship still in use for its initial function.
Standing at the foot of Mount Horeb where the Old Testament records Moses receiving the Tablets of the Law, the monastery's walls and buildings are of great significance to studies of Byzantine architecture. It houses outstanding collections of early Christian manuscripts and icons.
The legal status of the monastery remained uncertain for a millennium and a half. In recent years, however, disputes with the Egyptian government over this status seeped into local courtrooms.
In 2015, South Sinai authorities launched legal proceedings, disputing the monastery's ownership and use of dozens of plots of land around the monastery.
In 2024, South Sinai authorities and the archbishop of the monastery agreed on a draft settlement, but this settlement has yet to be formally signed, according to Greek media.
In 2025, the Ismailia Appeals Court upheld state ownership of the plots of land referred to above, while recognizing the right of the monastery's monks to use the site and its religious and archaeological areas.
This legal stalemate eventually drew high-level involvement from Egypt and Greece, becoming a central topic of discussions between the Egyptian president and the Greek prime minister and the foreign ministers of the two countries.
Diplomatic stakes
No specific date has been set for signing the deal between the Egyptian government and Archbishop Symeon.
Nonetheless, the archbishop, who was elected as the monastery's abbot almost a year ago, is expected to sign such a deal once he recovers from his illness and resumes his duties.
The deal reportedly enjoys explicit support from the Ecumenical Patriarchates of Constantinople, Jerusalem and Alexandria, as well as the Orthodox Churches of Greece and Cyprus.
In a statement, Archbishop Symeon said this backing gave him and the Sinai Brotherhood the support needed to proceed with the signing in the near future.
The breakthrough comes at a critical moment for relations between Egypt and Greece, as both Eastern Mediterranean nations join forces against the latest ratification of a controversial maritime boundary delimitation deal between Turkey and Libya by the eastern Libya parliament, specialists in Cairo said.
The deal, initially signed by the western Libya government and Ankara in 2019, is viewed by Cairo and Athens as violating their Eastern Mediterranean rights and encroaching on their territories.
The two capitals have already protested the latest move by the eastern Libya parliament, which was a major focus of discussions between the Egyptian and Turkish foreign ministers in Ankara earlier in October.
Some Greeks accuse their government of giving up rights to Saint Catherine's Monastery to secure continued Egyptian presence in the Greek camp in the showdown with Turkey over Eastern Mediterranean rights.
In Egypt, the potential deal is seen as an important move for clearing the air between Cairo and Athens at an important time for their relations.
Ambassador Rakha Ahmed, a former assistant to the Egyptian foreign minister, said Egypt and Greece agree on several key portfolios.
"Cooperation on these portfolios, I believe, shouldn't encounter political roadblocks," Ambassador Ahmed told TNA.
"The legal dispute over the status of the monastery could have strained ties between the two countries, but Egypt has succeeded in containing the issue quickly," he added.

Bulgarian Olympic Committee President Vesela Lecheva has officially announced that she will run for president of the International Shooting Sport Federation (ISSF), BTA reports.
The former world champion and Olympic silver medallist in rifle shooting faces three other candidates: current ISSF President Luciano Rossi, European Shooting Confederation President Alexander Ratner and Ukraine’s Konstantin Pivovarov.

Supermarket cyberattacks spread across Europe as hackers turn freezers into ovens
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
11:24:10 UTC
20:24:10 KST

Supermarket chains in at least three European countries reported unusual disruptions Monday after refrigerators and freezers at dozens of stores malfunctioned overnight, apparently as a result of a cyberattack.
Retail giant Ahold Delhaize initially reported an "IT incident" in which temperatures in refrigeration systems at dozens of its supermarkets in Belgium and Luxembourg suddenly rose overnight. Swedish supermarket chains ICA and Coop also reported sharp temperature increases in freezers at several of their stores.
Ahold Delhaize later confirmed that the incident was a cyberattack, while at least one ICA store in Sweden also attributed the disruption to hackers. Sweden's National Cybersecurity Center confirmed that it was involved in the investigation.
One affected ICA store reported that hackers had set the temperature of its refrigerators and freezers to 50 degrees Celsius (122 degrees Fahrenheit), mirroring a cyberattack that struck hundreds of supermarkets in France three weeks earlier.
Coop, a Swedish consumer-owned retail group, told the newspaper Aftonbladet that six of its stores had experienced similar incidents.
The reports from Belgium, Luxembourg and Sweden come after an unprecedented cyberattack on French supermarkets last month, when hackers remotely manipulated refrigeration systems, driving temperatures in freezers and cold-storage rooms to at least 50 degrees Celsius.
The attack spoiled vast quantities of fresh and frozen food, forcing retailers to discard tons of products and causing estimated losses of tens of millions of euros.
French authorities did not publicly identify those responsible for the sabotage. However, the attack came amid growing European concerns about possible Russian hybrid operations, including cyberattacks, in retaliation for European support for Ukraine. No evidence publicly linking Russia to the supermarket incidents has been established.
Hundreds of French supermarkets targeted
The attack in France occurred overnight Oct. 11-12, when unidentified hackers gained remote access to software controlling temperatures in refrigerators, freezers and cold-storage rooms used by major French supermarket chains.
The attackers changed the settings remotely, causing temperatures to rise, in many cases to 50 degrees Celsius.
The heating was timed to occur between 11 p.m. and 4 a.m., when stores were closed and employees were generally absent.
When the first workers arrived the following morning, they discovered refrigeration units that were warm and, in some cases, extremely hot. Food stored inside had spoiled, and some equipment had partially melted.
Retailers were forced to discard enormous quantities of food that no longer met health and safety requirements. Fires also broke out in several cases.
French reports at the time said more than 400 supermarket locations had been affected. The reported figures included at least 300 Intermarché and Netto stores, nearly 100 Coopérative U outlets, approximately 80 Carrefour supermarkets, about 30 Monoprix stores and several locations belonging to the E.Leclerc group.
The figures reflected initial reports across the different chains and were not necessarily a count of confirmed, directly affected stores. Les Mousquetaires, the retail group behind Intermarché and Netto, separately confirmed that approximately 150 of its stores had been directly affected.
The Paris prosecutor's office announced a preliminary investigation into the cyberattack.
French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu's office said he was personally monitoring developments and that France was coordinating its response with European partners.
Danish refrigeration systems under scrutiny
According to sources familiar with the matter, the attack in France targeted refrigeration control systems manufactured by the Danish company Danfoss.
In recent months, the company disclosed several critical security vulnerabilities affecting software packages used in its refrigeration systems.
On Sept. 18, Danfoss reported a vulnerability that could allow attackers to gain read-and-write access to internal system variables, as well as upload and execute unauthorized computer code.
It has not been publicly established whether that particular vulnerability was exploited in the French attack.
On the day the French cyberattack became public, Danfoss said it was "aware of incidents in France affecting a limited number of refrigeration management systems."
The company said the affected units had been operating with outdated firmware, the embedded software that controls the equipment.
Danfoss said it had long recommended that customers update supported systems to the latest firmware and replace older-generation equipment with current products.
The company also recently noted that hackers had breached or attempted to breach refrigeration systems at supermarkets in Russia and Israel in 2022. Those stores were using outdated versions of Danfoss refrigeration controllers.
The incidents have highlighted the security risks associated with commercial refrigeration systems that can be monitored and controlled remotely.
Although such systems allow retailers to manage temperatures and equipment more efficiently, remote connectivity can also provide attackers with a way to manipulate machinery if security weaknesses are left unaddressed.
Suspected cyberattack on US military supermarkets
The severe disruptions caused by the French attack also recalled similar incidents reported in late August at at least six U.S. military commissaries, grocery stores located on military installations where service members and other authorized shoppers buy food.
Beginning Aug. 26, several military bases across the United States reported refrigeration failures.
At Fort Huachuca in Arizona, all the freezers at the base commissary reportedly switched to defrost mode overnight, causing frozen and refrigerated food to spoil.
Other military commissaries restricted sales, with some temporarily offering only shelf-stable products.
The U.S. Defense Department confirmed at the time that it was aware of a "possible refrigeration disruption" affecting the military commissary network but declined to speculate about the cause.
Investigative units from the Army and Air Force, including the cybercrime unit of the Army Criminal Investigation Division, opened an inquiry.
Last week, Reuters reported that the Pentagon suspected the refrigeration failures at the military bases were caused by a cyberattack.
U.S. military officials told the news agency that American cyber investigators were cooperating with French law enforcement authorities in their investigation.

Republicans, Democrats set midterm closing arguments as Michigan endorsement roils Senate race

Republicans, Democrats set midterm closing arguments as Michigan endorsement roils Senate race
DETROIT/WASHINGTON Nov 2 - Democrats sought on Monday to contain a rift in Michigan's US Senate race after one of their own crossed party lines to endorse the Republican candidate, as both parties made final pitches before midterm elections that will decide control of Congress
US Representative Haley Stevens, who lost the Michigan Democrats' Senate primary to Abdul El-Sayed in a bitterly contested race, publicly backed Republican candidate Mike Rogers and appeared with him at a Detroit church, threatening to worsen divisions in a state viewed as crucial to Democratic hopes of retaking the US Senate.
The unexpected move lifted the mood of President Donald Trump's Republicans before Tuesday's midterms even as a federal judge dismissed a US Justice Department lawsuit seeking to block certification of election results in Alaska if Republican incumbent Senator Dan S. Sullivan narrowly loses in the battleground state.
In Michigan, Stevens' decision to endorse Republican Rogers surprised party leaders, with some members, such as Representative Debbie Dingell, saying that it created a "distraction" for Democrats.
Stevens said in a video posted to social media: "I don't belong in Abdul's campaign."
MICHIGAN RIFT
Stevens' endorsement of Rogers came on the day she was scheduled to appear with El-Sayed in a show of party unity. But the planned event unraveled after Stevens called on El-Sayed to condemn an outside group's ad that she said blames Israel for high grocery prices.
"That ad was very painful," Stevens told CNN on Sunday night. "There are so many Democrats who want to vote for our Democratic nominee, and they're just being told, 'Hey, this is a party you don't belong in, or this is a campaign you don't belong in.'"
El-Sayed's campaign recently asked Stevens to skip his events through Election Day so as "not to distract from the central issues of the campaign," a person familiar with the matter said.
Republicans sought to capitalize on Stevens' move. "When you see a party, and at least a sliver of the party, veering off into the virulent hate that they have been spewing toward a group of people, it gets dangerous," Rogers said.
El-Sayed, an Egyptian-American Muslim born in Michigan, has been targeted by Trump and other Republicans who have repeatedly questioned his loyalty to the United States and baselessly called him a terrorist sympathizer whose election would invite attacks on Americans. El-Sayed has called questions about his loyalty to the United States “shameful.”
The attacks fit a broader pattern of inflammatory rhetoric from some Republicans targeting Arab Americans, Muslims and transgender people and portraying Democrats as communists and dangerous radicals ahead of the midterms.
Stevens' mother, Maria Marcotte, said her daughter decided to endorse Rogers because of what she described as dangerous political rhetoric from El-Sayed, pointing in part to his past appearances with Hasan Piker, a left-wing streamer who has been criticized for his comments about Israel and American Jews.
"She's really reached a point where she felt like her constituents, the people that she cares about, and the people she knows and loves are scared and frightened by some rhetoric that's coming out," Marcotte said in an interview with Reuters from the porch of her home in Birmingham, a northern Detroit suburb.
A spokesperson for El-Sayed's campaign said it raised $1.2 million in the four hours after Stevens endorsed Rogers, making it the campaign's second-best fundraising day since the Democratic primary election in August.
A New York Times/Siena poll released and partly conducted on Sunday showed El-Sayed with a 53% to 42% lead over Rogers.
A number of Stevens' congressional staff resigned over the endorsement, according to reports from CNN and the Hill, while some voters expressed disdain.
"Haley Stevens is a traitor," said Pamela Johnson, 72, after casting her ballot for El-Sayed in Warren, a Detroit suburb.
ALASKA INTERVENTION FALTERS
Also on Sunday, the Trump administration's attempt to intervene in Alaska's Senate race faltered when a federal judge dismissed the US Justice Department's lawsuit seeking to block certification of the results if Republican incumbent Senator Dan S. Sullivan narrowly loses.
The Justice Department argued voters may be confused by the presence of a challenger named Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. on the same ballot.
The issue has roiled the campaign over the last several days after the New York Times reported that Democrat Mary Peltola's campaign was involved in recruiting Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. into the race as a spoiler.
The senator said on Sunday he would accept the results of Tuesday's election even as the Trump administration presses a criminal investigation into the issue.
Peltola has denied involvement, and Sullivan Jr. has denied coordinating with Peltola's campaign.
"I think it's great that it got thrown out," said Aileena Bird, a 24-year-old resident of Wasilla, Alaska, who said she voted for Peltola. "I think that more should be done to fight against what Trump has been doing in trying to suppress the voters." REUTERS

President Volodymyr Zelensky voiced readiness to meet with Russia's President Vladimir Putin in Turkey to discuss peace talks, in an interview with CNN Turk published on Nov. 1.
A meeting between the leaders is essential, said Zelensky, adding that Turkey can be a practical and realistic mediator of future talks between Moscow and Kyiv.
The comments come ahead of expected technical-level talks between Ukraine, Russia, and the U.S. in Abu Dhabi later in November.
Kyiv hopes the discussions could pave the way for an eventual leaders' summit — likely involving U.S. President Donald Trump — which it sees as crucial for resolving territorial issues.
The Kremlin has long avoided a face-to-face meeting between Zelensky and Putin, proposing a phone call instead, the Kyiv Independent has learned.
Ukraine's president met with Recep Tayyip Erdogan, his Turkish counterpart, in Istanbul on Oct. 31 to discuss bilateral relations and security in the Black Sea.
Turkey has carefully balanced its relationship with both Kyiv and Moscow, maintaining economic ties with Russia while providing arms to Ukraine.
Ankara played a central role in establishing the Black Sea Grain Initiative in 2022, enabling the safe maritime export of grain before Moscow exited the deal a year later. Turkey has also hosted three rounds of peace talks between Ukrainian and Russian delegations in 2025.
Zelensky's comments come amid Washington's efforts to revive peace talks, which have effectively stalled earlier this year as Russia demands that Kyiv cede Donbas, a partially occupied and strategically important region in Ukraine's east.
In the interview, Zelensky said the upcoming technical talks would focus on the possibility of a partial energy and maritime ceasefire, as well as exchanges of captives.
The leaders' summit would then tackle a path toward a full ceasefire and security guarantees, he said.
The president rejected the possibility of formally recognizing occupied territories as part of Russia and said a ceasefire should be established along the current front lines as a first step toward further talks.

Ebola cases, AI math breakthrough and the dangers of making daylight saving time permanent
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
11:20:49 UTC
20:20:49 KST

Happy Monday, listeners! And happy November. For Scientific American’s Science Quickly, I’m Rachel Feltman. You’re listening to our weekly science news roundup.
We’ll start with an update on the ongoing Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Last Tuesday, data from the country’s Ministry of Health confirmed more than 10,000 cases since May. And nearly half of those people have died.
This is the fastest known Ebola outbreak in history. For context, the deadliest outbreak on record, which occurred in West Africa between 2014 and 2016, resulted in 28,000 cases and 11,000 deaths. But that outbreak lasted more than two years, and the current outbreak in the DRC was declared less than 200 days ago. And the difference in their trajectories is striking. On day 187 of the current outbreak, the official case count was 10,060. On day 186 of the West Africa outbreak, just 544 cases had been recorded.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
There are a few factors making this outbreak tough to manage. The first is the actual species of Ebola-causing virus fueling the outbreak. Of the six known species in this genus, four cause the kind of severe hemorrhagic fever you probably think of when you hear the word “Ebola.” The West African epidemic was caused by one of those four viruses, which is somewhat confusingly now called the Ebola virus but used to be called the Zaire virus, and which has the highest fatality rate of the four. Fortunately, an extremely effective vaccine was developed and deployed to help end that epidemic.
This latest outbreak is caused by a different species: the Bundibugyo virus. It’s much less common, having only caused two other known outbreaks in the past.
Another factor in the outbreak’s breakneck growth is that the DRC is really struggling to track cases and administer care. The Associated Press reports that at least half of all deaths have been in people who were never admitted to treatment centers. And contact tracing isn’t going well, either. An outbreak is considered under control when 95% of all new cases come from contact with previously known and recorded cases. But at present, something like 80% of new cases are emerging from unknown sources.
In other words, there are still lots of people out transmitting the disease that haven’t yet been identified by contact tracers. Distrust of the government and, by extension, of health workers is also a huge issue, with many reportedly believing the outbreak is a hoax. Last month a nurse was killed and another health care worker was severely injured as they attempted to respond to reports of Ebola.
However there is some good news, which is that clinical trials are ongoing to find a good vaccine candidate. Last Monday the first participant was vaccinated. The clinical trial is called Tumaini, which means “hope” in Swahili. The trial is made up of people who have recently been in close contact with individuals now confirmed to have the Bundibugyo virus. The first vaccine up for testing is the one tailored to prevent the Ebola virus, but several Bundibugyo-specific inoculations are currently in development and will be tested as well.
Now let’s get into some news about artificial intelligence. Just a few weeks after dropping hundreds of AI-generated math breakthroughs on a field that’s already in crisis, OpenAI is piling on more. Here to tell us more about this shake-up is artificial intelligence and technology reporter Peter Hall. He’s currently working as an editorial fellow at Scientific American. Thanks so much for coming on to chat, Peter.
Peter Hall: Good to meet you and good to talk with you.
Feltman: So could you give our listeners a little bit of backstory for how this has been heating up?
Hall: Yeah. So over the past few months OpenAI and Anthropic, as well as other players, have really been trying to flex the ability of their models by, um, proving or disproving famous math conjectures.
And last week OpenAI introduced these three results across math, physics and theoretical computer science that are quite big. And Anthropic also released the same result, almost at the same time on the same day.
Feltman: And so, to give our listeners a little bit of context, what kinds of problems are we talking about and what does this process usually look like, you know, when human mathematicians are involved?
Hall: So there’s a huge collection of problems that mathematicians have conjectured or guessed over decades of research. For the proofs from last week, these centered around problems related to Millennium Prize Problems, which are these group of seven problems that the Clay Mathematics Institute published in 2000 as a collection of problems that have existed across math and physics and computer science that are so noteworthy and so important and so difficult that they would get a million-dollar prize for a solution to them.
Feltman: So is there any controversy about whether what OpenAI and Anthropic are presenting are actually solutions to these problems, that they’re solved?
Hall: Right. So that’s the other side of the coin is that, usually, you know, math research is published in journals or on preprint servers or in conferences. It’s discussed among mathematicians.
These don’t really follow the same blueprint there. These are just kind of, like, put in GitHub repos as just a collection of AI-generated text and programming that they claim not only shows that the result is true but also has verified it in a programming language called Lean, which is meant specifically for mathematics.
So definitely the aspect of, like, how intelligible these results are and what kind of insights people are gaining from them has been a huge point of controversy—and you know, who gets the credit when a model is just outputting a bunch of ideas that we don’t really know exactly what they’re building off of.
Feltman: It’s like when that monkey took a selfie, except I had more respect for both the monkey and the photographer than I unfortunately do for a lot of AI companies. Well, what are the potential benefits to the mathematics community of these proofs being out there? You know, are there any upsides?
Hall: You know with previous drops, there has been efforts from the communities to go through the proof, really, you know, with a very fine-tooth comb and turn it into something that is expository and something that we can look at the techniques for and really understand some sort of mathematical insight for it.
You know, the hope is that solutions like these and the proof steps, even if they’re not written the best right now, can at some point down the line be turned into something that is useful. Like, you know, I can use the ideas from this to solve some other problem that I’ve seen elsewhere in my research.
Feltman: Well thank you so much for coming on to talk through this with us.
Hall: Of course. Thank you.
Feltman: Now for some research on an extremely timely subject: daylight saving time. DST just ended for those of us in the United States—not counting several territories, including Puerto Rico, and the exempt states Hawaii and Arizona,minus the Navajo Nation, which does still observe DST. Complicated, right? And it’s not like “springing forward” and “falling back” are much fun to deal with, either. Research suggests that shifting our clocks back and forth by an hour takes a toll on the body and the mind.
So it’s not surprising that this practice is pretty unpopular, and you might have celebrated when the House of Representatives passed the Sunshine Protection Act in July. That bill, which has yet to clear the Senate, would make DST permanent and therefore “preserve” an hour of afternoon sunlight as we head deeper into fall. Last week President Donald Trump blasted the Senate for failing to take a vote in time to implement permanent DST this year, claiming in a social media post that literally no one wanted to change their clocks. While that’s characteristically hyperbolic, recent survey data does suggest that almost half of U.S. adults are opposed to all the falling and springing.
But according to a new analysis published in Current Biology, making DST permanent could have serious, dangerous consequences for school-age children. Researchers at the University of Washington who study how school start times impact adolescent health decided to quantify exactly how many more trips to school would happen in darkness if we switched to year-round DST. They found that the Sunshine Protection Act would lead to more than two billion dark morning commutes for children. They also confirmed that fatal morning crashes involving kids aged five to 18 are more likely to occur if the sun has yet to rise. So those additional dark commutes really do pose a risk.
The researchers aren’t arguing in favor of continuing to swap our clocks back and forth; in fact, they point out that while permanent DST would be the worst-case scenario for dark school commutes, our current system creates twice as many dark mornings as would occur under permanent standard time.
Listen: I’m as bummed out by an afternoon sunset as anyone else. But as long as we can get rid of the twice-a-year upheaval, I’m personally good with whatever. And keeping kids safe as they wait for the bus—or, even better, as they walk or bike to school, because we love a pedestrian-friendly commute—seems pretty worthwhile to me.
That’s all for this week’s science news roundup. We’ll be back on Wednesday to talk about how soybeans quietly swept the nation and on Friday we’re going to talk about how AI swept everywhere.

Marielle Issa and Aaron Shattuck fact-check our show. Our theme music was composed by Dominic Smith. Subscribe to Scientific American for more up-to-date and in-depth science news.
For Scientific American, this is Rachel Feltman. Have a great week!

Hackers attack supermarket fridges in Belgium, Sweden and Luxembourg
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
11:19:32 UTC
20:19:32 KST

An employee cleans freezers that are out of power at an ICA supermarket in Stockholm, on Nov. 2, 2026. | TT News Agency photo by Fredrik Sandberg via AFP/Getty Images
Refrigerators in dozens of supermarkets across Belgium, Sweden and Luxembourg were out of service on Monday, local news outlets reported, in what appears to be a repeat of cyberattacks that hit French supermarkets last month.
Several store managers told local media that refrigerator temperatures suddenly spiked to up to 50 degrees Celsius. This mirrors the French incidents, in which attackers mid October appeared to remotely manipulate the fridges’ defrosting mechanisms so that they overheated.
It's not confirmed that the attacks are connected or used the same software vulnerabilities that hit French chains last month.
Advertisement
Belgian media reported on Monday morning that temperatures in supermarket refrigerators had suddenly spiked, leading them to throw food away.
Supermarket chain Delhaize alerted its store managers early on Monday morning of problems with refrigerators, and Belgian broadcaster RTBF cited a store manager as saying that the problems were due to a cyberattack like those in France. Dutch media reported that Delhaize stores in Luxembourg are also affected.
A spokesperson for the company said it is aware of an "IT incident affecting the refrigeration systems in a number of Delhaize stores."
A spokesperson for Colruyt, which operates Spar stores in Belgium, said in a statement that fridges in “around five” Spar stores have been affected. “We are currently doing everything we can to resolve the issue,” they said, adding that no Colruyt stores have been affected. Fifteen Belgian Carrefour stores are reportedly also affected.
A spokesperson for the Centre for Cybersecurity Belgium said the agency is "closely" following the incident.
Stores in Sweden have also been hit. A spokesperson for supermarket chain ICA confirmed an “incident overnight affecting a small number of ICA stores operating outside ICA’s central network” which affected its fridges and freezers. Swedish media also reported that Coop stores have been hit.
French supermarkets were hit with a wave of similar incidents mid October, when attackers hit refrigerators by Danfoss, a Danish manufacturer of store fridges. The attacks in France triggered a response from the country’s prime minister and its cybersecurity agency.
Danfoss did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Will renewed conflict derail Ethiopia's economic growth?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
11:19:00 UTC
20:19:00 KST

Will renewed conflict derail Ethiopia's economic growth?
November 2, 2026
Ethiopia's economy is growing strongly. The International Monetary Fund (IMF) forecasts real growth of 9.2% for the 2025–26 fiscal year. But renewed fighting in the north, high reconstruction costs and climate-related crop problems are threatening the country's economic recovery.
London-based financial analyst Abdulmenan Mohammed warns of the consequences of further escalation. "If there is a major conflict [...] the current economic growth will not be sustainable," he told DW.
The costly legacy of the Tigray war
The war that raged in Tigray and other parts of Ethiopia between 2020 and 2022 inflicted extensive damage. Infrastructure was destroyed, businesses lost production capacity and agricultural land could no longer be cultivated in some areas.
A World Bank-backed damage and needs assessment puts the damage caused by several conflicts in Ethiopia between November 2020 and December 2021 at more than $22.6 billion (€20.2 billion). Economic losses amounted to around $6 billion. The estimated bill for reconstruction and economic recovery stands at approximately $19.7 billion, which covers the total funding needed, not annual costs or damage caused by the current escalation.
A reconstruction plan covered the period from 2023 to 2028. However, it remains uncertain whether the work can be fully funded and completed within that timeframe.
Financial analyst Abdulmenan Mohammed believes the economic consequences of the Tigray war were even more severe. In addition to the direct destruction, he points to lost economic output, high inflation and foreign currency shortages at the time. International trade conditions also deteriorated: in 2022, Ethiopia lost its benefits under the US African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA), which had allowed certain African exports to enter the US market duty-free.
Growth despite the crisis
Following the Pretoria peace agreement in November 2022, the economy began to recover. According to the IMF, it grew by 7.2% in 2022–23 and 8.1% in 2023–24. The organization puts growth at 9.2% for 2024–25 and forecasts a further 9.2% for 2025–26. Agriculture, mining and electricity generation are among the main drivers.
This does not contradict the economic damage caused by the war. Gross domestic product (GDP) measures the total economic output of a country. If major sectors outside conflict-affected areas continue to expand, the overall economy can grow even while individual regions are still suffering the consequences of violence.
However, high growth rates do not mean that the country's economic problems have been resolved. Reconstruction remains a major challenge, inflation continues to put pressure on households and the government has to service its debt. In late 2023, Ethiopia defaulted after missing an interest payment on a Eurobond. Reforms supported by an IMF program launched in 2024 are intended to address structural weaknesses in the economy.
More military spending, less money for development
A renewed escalation could put additional pressure on public finances. The government would have to spend more on military personnel, equipment and logistics. At the same time, economic activity and, consequently, tax revenues could decline in the affected regions.
"A substantial share of government resources would be tied up in military spending that would otherwise be available for infrastructure, education and social services," warned Abdulmenan Mohammed. The extent of this impact would depend on the scale and duration of any renewed conflict.
A prolonged war could also prompt businesses to postpone investments. International lenders and donors might become more cautious, while the government would need additional funds for security and humanitarian assistance. This could leave less money available for roads, energy infrastructure and other development projects.
Inflation and foreign currency shortages
The IMF forecasts an average inflation rate of 11.7% for 2025–26. Prices are therefore expected to continue rising, although at a slower pace than in previous years.
Abdulmenan Mohammed expects a further escalation to intensify inflationary pressures. "If the conflict escalates further, inflation is likely to rise," he said. To finance additional spending, the government might resort to more domestic borrowing. This could crowd out private businesses by making it harder for them to access credit and finance investments.
The military also needs foreign currency to purchase equipment from abroad. If this demand increases, fewer foreign exchange reserves could be available to private businesses for imports. This would put further pressure on the birr exchange rate and drive up the cost of imported goods, fuel and industrial inputs.
The extent of these effects on the BRICS member state would also depend on export earnings, monetary policy and developments in international markets. A new surge in inflation is therefore a risk, but not an inevitable consequence of the escalation. A combination of rising prices and uncertain incomes would be particularly difficult for poorer households.
Agriculture and tourism particularly vulnerable
Abdulmenan Mohammed sees agriculture, as well as the tourism and hospitality sectors, as particularly vulnerable. "Agriculture is especially exposed because much of the fighting takes place in rural areas where farmers work," he said.
Insecurity around farmland, disrupted transport routes and shortages of agricultural inputs can undermine production. At the same time, parts of the country are experiencing insufficient rainfall and poor harvest prospects. Failed harvests reduce farmers' incomes, while lower food supplies can push prices even higher.
Tourism is also highly sensitive to security risks. Travel advisories and reports of fighting can deter visitors, reducing revenues for hotels and tour operators.
Could neighboring countries benefit from the crisis?
When making investment decisions, international investors consider not only market size but also political stability, security and the reliability of state institutions. A further escalation could therefore delay investment decisions or prompt companies to consider alternative locations.
However, there is currently no concrete evidence that companies are already withdrawing investments from Ethiopia because of the fighting and relocating them to neighboring countries such as Kenya. Abdulmenan Mohammed also sees no demonstrable economic advantage for Kenya at this stage. Beyond security, factors such as tax administration, public services and governance also play a decisive role.
This article was originally published in German.

Kremlin Downplays Prospect of Resuming Gas Shipments to Europe via Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
11:17:44 UTC
20:17:44 KST

Russia is unlikely to resume natural gas deliveries to Europe via Ukrainian pipelines anytime soon, the Kremlin said Monday, downplaying reports that the option was being discussed as part of a proposed winter energy ceasefire.
The Wall Street Journal reported earlier that the Trump administration suggested the idea during talks in September as an incentive for Moscow to halt strikes on Ukraine’s energy grid. According to U.S. and European officials, advocates of the plan argued it would also allow Ukraine to collect transit fees while helping lower European heating costs.
Under the proposal, Russian gas would be sold through a U.S. intermediary to navigate European sanctions, with proceeds placed in an offshore escrow account to prevent Moscow from using the funds to finance its war effort.
“Frankly, the situation on the ground speaks all too clearly to the fact that those kinds of plans are impossible to implement right now,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters during a daily briefing. “But as for what the future holds, we’ll see.”
Peskov said any renewal of gas shipments through Ukraine would “depend on the willingness of buyers, the willingness of sellers and the capacity of sellers.”
He noted that, while the European energy market remains a “premium one,” countries in the Global South have demonstrated themselves as “centers of economic growth,” meaning that their consumption of oil and gas will only increase in the coming years, with Moscow poised to supply all of their energy needs.
Russian gas shipments to Europe by pipeline have largely stopped since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, and Brussels has committed to ending all imports of Russian oil and gas by the end of 2027.
According to the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis, a U.S.-based think tank, the EU imported 6.9 billion cubic meters of Russian gas in the first three months of 2026, a 16% increase from the first quarter of last year and the highest volume since 2022.
Still, Russia now accounts for just 11% of Europe’s natural gas consumption, down from 45% on the eve of the 2022 invasion of Ukraine.
AFP contributed reporting.

Blackout leaves over 50,000 without power on Spain's La Palma amid torrential rain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
11:16:11 UTC
20:16:11 KST

Alyssa Mcmurtry
02 November 2026•Update: 02 November 2026
A blackout left more than 50,000 customers without electricity on Spain's Canary Island of La Palma early Monday as torrential rain battered the island, authorities said.
Power had been restored to about 75% of those affected by midmorning, roughly four and a half hours after the outage began, according to national grid operator Red Electrica.
The Canary Islands government said the island lost electricity at 6.42 am local time (0642GMT).
A lightning strike hit an electrical substation around 4 am, sparking a fire that knocked out medium- and low-voltage lines. Although service was initially restored, a subsequent failure at the Los Guinchos power plant triggered the island-wide outage. The cause of the disconnection remained unclear.
The island's port, airport, General Hospital and Hospital de Dolores continued operating on backup power.
The regional government issued its highest rainfall alert for eastern La Palma at 2 am.
Emergency officials said the area recorded 62 millimeters (2.4 inches) of rain in one hour and 138 millimeters (5.4 inches) over 12 hours.
Firefighters also responded to a storm-related house fire, while landslides were reported, though they were less severe than anticipated, according to Spanish broadcaster Cadena SER.
An orange alert for heavy rainfall remained in effect until Tuesday morning.
The Canary Islands were unaffected by the April 2025 blackout that left mainland Spain and Portugal without electricity for around 10 hours.
A European expert panel concluded in March that the earlier outage resulted from multiple factors, including failures in voltage control that caused generators to disconnect in succession.

Jaguar designs Knightsbridge flagship to be "physical expression" of Type 01 electric car

Jaguar designs Knightsbridge flagship to be “physical expression” of Type 01 electric car
British car brand Jaguar has redesigned its flagship store in Knightsbridge, London, which is the only place in the world where the public can see the recently unveiled Type 01 electric car.
Jaguar overhauled itp show in central London to align its aesthetic with its latest electric car, which was created as the first car in a new era for the brand. It aimed for the flagship store to be a clear departure from the traditional car showroom.
“[We wanted] to create a physical expression of the new Jaguar,” said Jaguar Land Rover spatial brand design team senior manager Nick Rolls, whose team was responsible for overhauling the store.
“Rather than a traditional showroom, we wanted to design a destination where architecture, culture, hospitality and craftsmanship come together – and London felt like a natural home for that vision,” he continued.
“The space has been purpose-designed from the ground up to embody the brand’s new identity – it gave us the opportunity to truly rethink what a Jaguar destination could be outside traditional conventions.”
The showroom has space for two cars to be displayed, one of which is currently the Type 01, with the showroom being the only place in the world where it is on display to the public.
However, the majority of the ground floor of the space is occupied by a restaurant.
Named Café Eighty-One, the restaurant by Michelin-starred chef Michael O’Hare was finished in rich red fabric.
Upholstered benches run around the space, while a series of booths line the front facade of the showroom.
“Food is one of the most universal forms of connection,” said Rolls. “We wanted Café Eighty-One to be a welcoming space where people could spend time, meet friends or discover something new.
“It’s designed to be a destination in its own right, helping make Jaguar at Knightsbridge part of London’s cultural and hospitality landscape,” he continued.
According to Rolls, the extensive use of red was a nod to the surrounding brick architecture in central London.
“Jaguar’s design philosophy is exuberant modernism, so colour plays an important role in creating emotion, atmosphere and a sense of occasion,” he said.
“The rich reds within Café Eighty-One were inspired by London’s iconic red-brick architecture, which is so prevalent throughout Knightsbridge and the surrounding neighbourhoods,” he continued. “It was a way of connecting the interior to its setting while creating a warm, vibrant environment that feels distinctly London.”
Through the rest of the spaces, the materials and colours were chosen to directly evoke the interiors of the Type 01 electric car.
“The relationship is deliberate,” said Rolls. “The interiors share the same emphasis on materiality, craftsmanship and bold, contemporary form that defines Type 01.”
“Materials such as travertine, tactile textiles and warm brass reference the vehicle’s interior, while the use of sculptural shapes, carefully composed lighting and strong geometric forms reflects the same creative philosophy behind the car,” he continued.
While the public restaurant and showroom space are on the ground floor, a lower level contains more private spaces for sales, meetings and for discussions about customisation.
One of these, called the Design Vault, was entirely finished in rich navy blues.
Overall, Rolls hopes that the revamped space will help people understand the current, major rethink that the brand is embarking on.
“I hope people leave with a deeper understanding of Jaguar,” he concluded.
“Every element of the destination has been designed to reflect craftsmanship, creativity and bold design. We want people to feel a genuine connection to the brand and to see Jaguar through a new lens.”
The creation of the showroom follows the launch of Jaguar’s second electric car earlier this year, the Type 01. The car is the production version of the much-discussed Type 00 concept car, which drew much attention in 2024 when it was unveiled following a rebrand for the car company, which was described as a “complete reset”.
