====================================================================================================

Will Europe defend the ICC or remain Washington’s supplicant?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
11:14:44 UTC
20:14:44 KST

The US government has done what even the harshest critics of the International Criminal Court (ICC) might once have considered unthinkable.
Last month, Washington placed the Court itself on its sanctions list, extending a campaign that had already targeted 13 of its officials. Europe has condemned the move. The question is whether it intends to do anything more.
The immediate dispute concerns the ICC's investigation of alleged crimes committed in Gaza and its November 2024 arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defence Minister Yoav Gallant.
Washington also objects to the Court's investigation of alleged crimes by American personnel in Afghanistan.
The US argues that the ICC cannot exercise authority over nationals of countries that have not accepted its jurisdiction.
But Article 12 of the Rome Statute permits jurisdiction over crimes committed on the territory of a state party, regardless of the accused person's nationality.
Palestine is a state party. There is a legal disagreement here, but the answer cannot be to punish the judges for adjudicating it.
ICC judge Kimberly Prost has described how American sanctions led to the cancellation of credit cards and her Amazon and Google accounts, leaving everyday activities unexpectedly difficult.
Such measures do not merely inconvenience judicial officers; they enlist banks and technology companies in a campaign that can isolate individuals from essential services.
When judges become financially untouchable because of the cases before them, the principle of judicial independence has suffered a serious injury.
The October 9 designation carries the same threat to the institution as a whole.
American persons and businesses are generally barred from dealings involving blocked parties, and assets subject to American jurisdiction may be frozen.
Washington has issued licences permitting many routine ICC operations to continue until 7 April 2027, with other exemptions covering certain services.
That temporary permission is not security. It means an international court must plan its finances, contracts and technology around deadlines and exceptions set by a government hostile to its work.
Speak out, speak loud
Europe's response has been eloquent but hesitant: leaders declared their support for the Court at their October 15-16 meeting and urged Washington to reverse course.
On October 23, the European Commission advised EU businesses to continue serving the ICC, pointing in particular to European payment infrastructure.
Yet the Commission still favours diplomacy and has not activated the principal legal instrument available to resist the extraterritorial effects of American sanctions.
Assurances of solidarity are less persuasive when the institutions asked to provide banking and technological services remain anxious about American retaliation.
The hesitation is harder to justify because all 27 EU member states are parties to the Rome Statute.
Under Article 86, they have undertaken to cooperate fully with the Court in investigating and prosecuting crimes within its jurisdiction.
That provision does not specifically command activation of the Blocking Statute, but it gives the European debate a legal dimension that diplomatic statements obscure.
States committed by treaty to supporting the Court cannot treat the erosion of its operational independence as someone else's problem.
That instrument is the European Union's Blocking Statute, Council Regulation 2271/96.
Adopted in 1996 in response to American measures involving Cuba, Iran and Libya, it reflects a straightforward proposition: Washington cannot assume that its sanctions policy automatically governs lawful commercial activity in Europe.
The regulation is not a declaration of sympathy. It creates obligations intended to prevent European economic operators from becoming instruments of a foreign government's extraterritorial policy.
Where the regulation's annex lists specified American measures, European companies are prohibited from complying with their requirements, subject to authorised exceptions.
They may seek damages caused by the application of those measures, while foreign court judgments based on them cannot be enforced in the EU.
Affected operators also have reporting obligations.
The Commission must amend the annex to cover ICC sanctions; the existing statute does not automatically protect the Court. That is the decision Europe has been reluctant to take.
The Dutch bank ABN AMRO, which handles the ICC's finances, faces potential American penalties if it continues providing banking services after the temporary sanctions exemption expires in April 2027.
Its extensive American operations expose it to considerable financial and regulatory risks.
Although the bank has not announced that it is terminating its relationship with the Court, the uncertainty places it in an increasingly difficult position.
Activating the EU Blocking Statute could prohibit the bank from withdrawing its services merely to comply with the specified American sanctions, although it would not eliminate the risk of American retaliation.
The consequences are already evident in the insurance sector. On October 1, the ICC and the French insurance giant AXA terminated their contractual relationship by mutual agreement.
AXA had provided health insurance services to the Court. According to the Financial Times, the company cited concerns about the extraterritorial application of American sanctions.
Months of discussions reportedly failed to produce an arrangement that would adequately protect the parties without European blocking legislation. The ICC subsequently arranged coverage with another insurer whose identity has not been disclosed.
An international criminal court operating on European soil should not have its access to ordinary banking and insurance services determined by Washington's political objections to its judicial decisions.
Calls for action are also coming from within the EU itself. Fifty-eight members of the European Parliament wrote to Commission President Ursula von der Leyen after the latest sanctions, urging deployment of the Blocking Statute.
Parliament has also pressed for such protection in earlier resolutions.
These representatives understand the implications of allowing an external power to determine whether an institution headquartered on European soil can obtain ordinary commercial services.
Can Europe take on the US?
Legitimate doubts remain about how much the statute can accomplish.
When Europe updated it in 2018 to counter renewed American sanctions on Iran, companies with substantial American exposure still feared exclusion from United States markets and financial networks.
A European legal prohibition does not erase those risks. Nor does it necessarily persuade a multinational bank to sacrifice its American business.
The Commission is right to consider the costs, but an imperfect remedy is not an excuse for refusing to use it.
Activation should therefore be accompanied by practical protection. The EU should secure reliable euro-denominated payment channels, work with banks and insurers prepared to serve the Court, and reduce dependence on vulnerable American technology infrastructure.
It should enforce the regulation consistently and provide clear guidance on the scope of permissible conduct and available exemptions.
If European businesses are expected to resist extraterritorial pressure, governments must do more than congratulate them for their courage while leaving them to absorb the losses.
The alternative is an extraordinary form of institutional dependence. European leaders speak incessantly about strategic autonomy and the rules-based international order.
They regulate powerful American technology companies, defend the sovereignty of European markets and claim an independent voice in world affairs.
Yet, when sanctions reach a court in The Hague, they seem content to ask Washington to reconsider. The issue is no longer a shortage of legal instruments; it is whether the political will exists to deploy them.
Europe's credibility is also on trial. Its governments have strongly supported the ICC's investigation of Russian conduct in Ukraine and the warrant against Vladimir Putin.
That support should not evaporate when the Court examines allegations involving Israeli leaders or American personnel.
The allegations must be tested according to evidence and law, not the identity of the accused or the diplomatic influence of their governments.
If international criminal justice is welcomed against adversaries but obstructed when allies are implicated, the promise of equal accountability becomes difficult to defend.
This inconsistency is not lost on countries across Africa, Asia and Latin America, where complaints about selective international justice have circulated for decades.
Many governments joined the Rome Statute on the understanding that the gravest crimes would be examined without political privilege.
A European refusal to protect the Court when Washington objects would reinforce the belief that universal principles carry an unwritten exception for powerful Western states.
No amount of rhetoric about human rights can easily repair the damage done by visible double standards.
The Commission should amend the Blocking Statute's annex to cover the relevant ICC sanctions and use the months before the American operational licence expires to put real safeguards in place.
It should also make it clear that disagreement with the Court is not a licence to interfere with its independence. Europe need not approve every ICC decision to defend the institution's right to make decisions free of economic intimidation.
Will Europe finally exercise the legal authority it claims to possess, or continue as a supplicant of Washington, requesting permission to uphold principles it says are non-negotiable?
The answer will matter to judges in The Hague and to victims awaiting justice in places far beyond Europe.
It will also reveal whether European strategic autonomy is a serious commitment or merely a phrase repeated whenever exercising it would be inconvenient.

U.S. executive becoming first laywoman to head Vatican ministry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02

20:13:14 KST

U.S. executive starting key job as first laywoman to head Vatican ministry
Maria Montserrat Alvarado, a 39-year-old U.S. media executive, becomes the new head of Vatican communications this week, the first laywoman to head a Vatican "ministry."
The Mexican American will also be the first non-Italian to lead a vast department overseeing all of the Vatican's television, radio and print operations, as well as its press office.
Analysts say the appointment of a professional woman to the key post signals that Pope Leo views women differently from his predecessors at the Vatican, where nuns have tended to be the women holding senior positions.
Her appointment, announced in June, came as a surprise even to Alvarado.
"I didn't apply, I wasn't chosen" through a standard application process, she said in a television interview with U.S. Catholic media outlet EWTN News, where she has served as president and chief operating officer since 2023.
It was "an appointment from the Holy Father," U.S.-born Pope Leo XIV said of the new role for Alvarado, who uses the name "Montse."
EWTN News is the news division of the Eternal Word Television Network, the largest Catholic television network in the United States, which was founded by a nun and has established itself as a touchstone for conservative Catholics.
It hasn't always had a warm relationship with the Vatican.
Certain programs on the network developed a reputation for their criticism of Leo's Argentine predecessor, Pope Francis, a reform-minded pontiff who angered some within the Church's conservative wing, particularly in the U.S.
In 2021, Francis appeared to call them out on it, bemoaning a "major Catholic television channel that is constantly criticizing the pope."
"I may personally deserve attacks and insults because I am a sinner, but the Church does not deserve this; it is the work of the devil," he said.
Alvarado was a presenter for EWTN at that time.
Alvarado's background
Born in Mexico, Alvarado arrived in the U.S. as a child and grew up in Miami before moving to Washington to pursue her studies.
For 14 years, Alvarado worked at the Becket Fund for Religious Liberty, a nonprofit law firm that defends religious freedom.
At the helm of EWTN News since 2023, she oversaw international media platforms that produced content in seven languages across television, print, radio, digital media, and social networks.
Alvarado hadn't planned on a career in media and communications, telling EWTN that her "great ambition had always been to get married and have children."
She was married, but is now divorced, and the union has since been annulled by the Church.
Alvarado succeeds 70-year-old Paolo Ruffini, who was appointed by Pope Francis in 2018 and was the first layperson to lead a dicastery, the Vatican term for a ministry.
"This is a woman who has been chosen for her skills and her qualities," Lucetta Scaraffia, the founder of the Vatican's women's magazine Women Church World and a professor of history at Rome's La Sapienza University, told AFP.
As the first non-Italian to occupy the post, Alvarado "will have another way of dealing with things" and a "much more international" outlook, Scaraffia said.
"She is a highly accomplished communications manager" who "has built this career for herself," and her appointment signals that "the pope has a different attitude toward women," she said.
"Until now, the women chosen for important positions were highly obedient nuns -- they weren't really chosen for their merits," Scaraffia said.

Supermarket freezers across Europe hit by second suspected cyber-attack
Unknown

2026-11-02
11:12:36 UTC
20:12:36 KST

Supermarket chains in Sweden, Belgium and Luxembourg have said the temperatures of their refrigerators and freezers in dozens of stores rose overnight, prompting fears of a cyber-attack similar to one that caused millions of euros of food losses in France.
Sweden’s Coop chain told the daily Aftonbladet on Monday that six of its stores had been affected, while ICA said it was “aware that a limited number of stores were affected by an incident overnight which impacted their refrigeration and freezer systems”.
The Dutch retailer Ahold Delhaize, which last month reported a cybersecurity incident to police in the Netherlands, said an “IT incident” had hit fridges and freezers in dozens of its supermarkets in Belgium and Luxembourg.
A company spokesperson, Sarah De Meester, said the supermarket chain had established that temperatures in the cooling systems had increased, adding that the incident was being investigated.
Belgium’s Le Soir newspaper reported that dozens of stores and supermarkets were affected, including five Spar outlets, multiple Shop & Go convenience stores attached to Q8 service stations, and a number of smaller Proxy Delhaize minimarkets.
“We started mobilising technicians at 1am,” Stephan Moelans, the chief executive of Sabcobel, which specialises in refrigeration system installations, told the paper. “We spent all night and morning disconnecting the affected installations from the grid.”
French police said in October that hackers had seized control of cooling units at up to 700 supermarkets in a large-scale attack that led to heavy losses of chilled and frozen foods and underlined the vulnerability of internet-connected systems.
Hackers had remotely overridden the settings on thousands of freezers, fridges and chiller cabinets, pushing them from as low as -27C to well over 50C. The Intermarché, Coopérative U, Carrefour, Leclerc and Monoprix chains were among those affected.
Stores had to discard vast quantities of fresh meat, dairy and frozen products, with many suffering losses ranging from tens of thousands of euros to more than €130,000 (£109,000). Two stores in Alsace reported a combined loss of €270,000.
Most supermarket cold aisles are connected to the internet to allow remote maintenance and alerts for system failures. In the French attack, the hackers pirated controllers mostly supplied by the Danish company Danfoss.
They disabled alarm systems before adjusting the thermostats or extending the defrost programme by hours. Danfoss said it had identified security flaws last year and had “long recommended” customers install updates.
The Paris prosecutor’s office has opened a formal investigatiion into the French attack, saying damage included “food losses and fires”, and the prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, instructed France’s national cybersecurity agency, ANSSI, to investigate.
ANSSI subsequently confirmed that supermarkets using controllers from two other companies were also targeted in the attack.

Lindsay Clancy returns to Massachusetts court for hearing that could shape potential murder retrial

Lindsay Clancy returns to Massachusetts court for hearing that could shape potential murder retrial
Nov 2 - Lindsay Clancy is due back in court on Monday for a hearing that could determine whether she will be retried for killing her three young children at her Massachusetts home in 2023 after a jury deadlocked at her first trial.
Judge William Sullivan is scheduled to hear arguments in Plymouth, Massachusetts, on Clancy's bid to dismiss the murder charges and to discuss a timetable for a potential new trial if he allows the case to proceed.
Plymouth County District Attorney Timothy Cruz's office has yet to publicly detail its plans for a retrial of Clancy, 36. She faces first-degree murder charges over the deaths of her daughter Cora, 5; son Dawson, 3; and 8-month-old son Callan.
In a filing last week, prosecutors urged Sullivan to reject a defense bid to have the case thrown out, saying they "should be permitted to continue to pursue justice for Cora, Dawson and Callan Clancy."
Sullivan at a September 29 hearing said the parties should be prepared on Monday to discuss a date for a retrial.
No one at Clancy's initial trial disputed that she strangled her three children with exercise bands on January 24, 2023, in the basement of their home in the Boston suburb of Duxbury. She then cut herself with a knife and jumped from a second-story window in an attempt to end her own life, leaving her paralyzed.
Her lawyers, though, have argued the evidence showed Clancy was in the throes of postpartum psychosis at the time and should be found not guilty by reason of insanity, known in Massachusetts as lack of criminal responsibility.
Some of the jurors in televised interviews later said that but for one holdout juror, they had been prepared to find Clancy not guilty by reason of insanity. Such a verdict would have resulted in her commitment to a state psychiatric hospital, subject to regular court review.
Prosecutors have several options before them, including retrying Clancy on the first-degree murder charges or seeking her conviction on lesser second-degree murder charges, which would give her the option to waive a jury trial and proceed before a judge.
A first-degree murder conviction carries a mandatory sentence of life without parole. Second-degree murder allows for the possibility of parole.
Defense lawyers are expected on Monday to argue that a retrial would violate Clancy's constitutional protection against being tried twice for the same crime, known as double jeopardy.
They contend the mistrial declared on September 4 was unnecessary. Citing jury notes that stated the holdout juror was not following the law on reasonable doubt despite the judge's instructions, defense lawyers say Sullivan should have instead questioned the holdout and potentially removed the juror. Six things to watch as US voters decide control of Congress
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
11:12:12 UTC
20:12:12 KST

Six things to watch as US voters decide control of Congress
WASHINGTON, Nov 2 - Americans head to the polls on Tuesday in midterm elections that will decide control of Congress for the final two years of President Donald Trump's term.
The results will serve as the first nationwide verdict on Trump's presidency, revealing whether voters want to check the Republican president's power by giving Democrats control of one or both chambers of Congress or are willing to accept the status quo despite frustrations over the cost of living and the US-led war with Iran.
The outcome could also reshape debates within both parties over which messages and policies resonate most with voters ahead of the 2028 presidential election.
Here are six things to watch on Election Day.
THE RACES THAT WILL DECIDE CONTROL OF CONGRESS
Democrats need a net gain of four seats in both the US House of Representatives and US Senate to overturn Republicans' narrow 218-214 and 53-47 majorities.
They are widely expected to reclaim the House, but the Senate battle remains highly competitive. The scale of Democratic gains in one or both chambers will shape Trump's ability to advance his agenda.
Democratic wins in one or both chambers will likely trigger investigations into ethics of Trump and his administration, their handling of immigration enforcement and the Iran war.
A stronger-than-expected Republican showing could reinforce Trump's grip on the party. Heavy losses could increase pressure to rethink unpopular policies such as tariffs and the war while shaping the message of candidates vying to succeed him.
Early results from Republican-held House seats in Florida and Virginia could provide clues to the size of any Democratic gains. Victories in competitive districts would point to a solid Democratic night, while wins in more Republican-leaning areas could signal a much broader backlash against Trump and his policies.
The close Senate fight will likely hinge on six to eight races. Democrats need to flip several Republican-held seats in states Trump carried by double-digit margins in 2024, including Ohio, Iowa, Alaska and Texas.
Even Kansas, despite Trump's 16-point win there, has become competitive in recent weeks and a Democratic victory would signal a broader wave.
Republicans can retain control by winning most of those contests, while Democrats will likely need to hold Michigan and pick up Maine.
PROBLEMS AT THE POLLS AND VOTE COUNT
Election officials have warned close races could spark disputes over voter eligibility, ballot counting and certification, while long lines, machine malfunctions or challenges by partisan poll watchers could fuel litigation and delay results.
Trump's Justice Department plans to deploy about 1,000 monitors nationwide on Election Day, roughly triple the number used in the last midterms, a move some local officials worry could intimidate voters, although the DOJ says those fears are baseless.
Some election officials and legal experts fear federal investigations and legal challenges could delay or disrupt certification of election results in close races.
On October 22, Trump's Justice Department sued to preemptively block Alaska from certifying the results of its Senate race if the Republican incumbent candidate loses by a narrow margin, saying voters could be confused because two Republicans on the ballot have almost identical names.
Attorney General Todd Blanche on October 22 declined to rule out Justice Department intervention in state election certifications, saying extreme circumstances could warrant action.
Several states are also unlikely to produce complete results on election night, especially in close races, providing fertile ground for disputes.
TRUMP'S RESPONSE TO THE RESULTS
How Trump responds to the results, especially if Republicans lose control of Congress, could become one of the night's biggest stories.
In the early hours of November 4, 2020, before vote counting had finished in several states, Trump declared victory and called for counting to stop.
He ultimately lost to Democrat Joe Biden but continued to falsely claim the election had been stolen, helping fuel the January 6, 2021, attack on the US Capitol by a mob of his supporters who were seeking to stop certification of Biden's win by Congress.
Trump still falsely claims he won the 2020 election and has cast doubt on the integrity of these midterms, raising the prospect of Republican challenges if the party loses one or both chambers.
This year, the Trump administration has pressed states for voter data and launched investigations into noncitizen voting, which election experts and studies have found little evidence to support. It recently sued California over alleged noncitizen ballots.
TURNOUT
Turnout by the parties' core supporters will be important. Opinion polls showed Democrats significantly more enthusiastic about voting than Republicans heading into Election Day.
But strategists caution that Democratic constituencies including young, Black and Hispanic voters have historically turned out at lower rates in midterm elections than in presidential years.
Surveys show persistent skepticism among these groups towards both parties, especially over the cost of living. If turnout among those groups falls short of expectations, Democrats could underperform on Election Day.
Early voting data in states that register voters by party showed higher Democratic engagement. But Republicans argue that many of their supporters traditionally wait until Election Day to vote.
WHAT DO RESULTS MEAN FOR THE 2028 RACE?
After their bruising defeat in the 2024 presidential election, Democrats have been split between those arguing for a more populist economic message and those favoring a centrist approach aimed at winning back swing voters.
Strong performances by moderates and left-wing candidates on Tuesday will allow both factions to claim validation of their policies. That could set the stage for a crowded and potentially contentious contest for the party's 2028 presidential nomination.
DID REPUBLICANS' MONEY ADVANTAGE PAY OFF?
Republicans had a significant financial advantage and flooded the airwaves with ads attacking Democratic candidates.
While some Democrats matched or outraised their opponents, Republicans held an overall spending edge of several hundred million dollars once party committees and outside groups were included.
A key question is whether that advantage helped sway tight races, or whether voter concerns over high prices and the Iran war mattered more.
Trump spent more than $277 million, mostly through his MAGA Inc. super PAC, on a late TV and direct-mail blitz to aid struggling Republican candidates, according to Federal Election Commission data.
Tesla CEO Elon Musk spent roughly $366 million during the midterm cycle, including $276 million since July, to support Republican candidates. REUTERS

Hackers send fake nuclear threat alert to Ukraine emergency app
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
11:11:28 UTC
20:11:28 KST

Unknown hackers have targeted Ukraine’s nationwide emergency alert mobile app, sending residents in Kyiv a warning that they were at risk of an imminent nuclear strike.
The app reported a high possibility of nuclear radiation late on Sunday. It also wrongly warned of a chemical threat to the Ukrainian capital and street-to-street fighting. The messages were written in English with spelling mistakes, as well as in Ukrainian.
Many residents ignored the alerts, which began shortly before 11pm local time, assuming that the app had been compromised. Others were scared. “I was briefly terrified,” one woman, Nina, said. “I lay on my bed and wondered what was coming.”
A message written in Russian also claimed Ukraine was about to be hit by Oreshnik missiles, which can carry nuclear warheads. The Kremlin has used the ballistic weapon three times before, hitting the Kyiv region, and the cities of Dnipro and Lviv.
In a post on Sunday, the Ukrainian emergency app said “unauthorised parties” had interfered with its operation. The channel had been temporarily suspended, it said, warning users not to click on links in “suspicious notifications”.
It was unclear on Monday who might have carried out the cyber-raid, or why. Russian officials claimed hackers had also sent fake emergency alerts there after gaining access to the app of the ministry for emergencies, based in Moscow.
One of their posts mentioned the hacking group Hitcore. Mash, a Russian Telegram channel with links to the security services, said it had spoken to representatives of Hitcore and that they had claimed responsibility for the attack. The report could not be verified.
The fake nuclear threats to Ukraine came as Russia resumed its attacks on the southern city of Kherson, just hours after the end of a ceasefire during which hundreds of people were evacuated from the nearby Kremlin-controlled town of Oleshky.
Kherson’s military administration said a Russian drone hit a hospital at 7.40am. Video footage showed wrecked rooms, with windows blown out, doors broken, and debris on the street. Nobody was hurt, officials said.
There is evidence that the Russian army used the six-day ceasefire, which the White House said was brokered by the first lady, Melania Trump, to strengthen its positions in Oleskhy and to rotate in new troops. Bodies of dead civilians were also removed from a hospital morgue.
Footage shared with Sky News showed Russian soldiers deploying heavy military equipment and delivering ammunition. They carried large bags into burned out houses and buildings and disappeared into basements, the broadcaster reported.
Armoured vehicles were spotted moving around Oleshky’s streets. The occupied city is 3 miles from Kherson, on the opposite bank of the Dnipro River. Before last week’s truce, resupply was difficult because of the threat from Ukrainian kamikaze drones.
According to the commander of Ukraine’s 34th Separate Marine Brigade, Dmitry Pulinets, Russian soldiers were previously unable to drive in the city, “neither during the day, nor at night, nor in bad weather”.
“Now they have this opportunity. And for the last few days this movement has been happening constantly,” he told Sky News.
The ceasefire expired at 11pm on Sunday. Both sides hailed the local pause in the fighting – the most significant since 2022 – as a success. Ukraine’s ombudsman, Dmytro Lubinets, who visited Oleshky to coordinate the mission, said it could be repeated on other parts of the frontline.
However, Vladimir Putin’s spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said on Monday there were no plans for another truce elsewhere. He said it was “standard practice” for army units to regroup in “such circumstances” and added that he assumed Ukraine’s armed forces had “done the same”.

Alarms and card machines at risk as a million UK lines yet to make digital switch
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
11:11:16 UTC
20:11:16 KST

Businesses face soaring costs and disrupted services if they delay, as Brussels pushes for copper networks to be retired across the EU by 2035.
Openreach has warned that fewer than 100 days remain before the UK’s old analogue phone network is permanently switched off on 31 January 2027.
The BT Group network operator said about one million copper-based lines were still active, including 300,000 at business premises and that failure to migrate these systems to digital alternatives "poses severe operational, safety, and compliance risks".
It is not only home phones that rely on the network. Card payment terminals, lift emergency phones, fire alarm panels, security systems and door entry units could also stop working if they are not moved to digital services in time.
"Businesses and organisations that delay action are making things harder for themselves," said James Lilley, Openreach’s director of All-IP.
"We are urging businesses to act now, audit their remaining analogue services, and work with their communications provider on a migration plan today."
What happens to those who don’t switch?
Openreach doubled rental prices for legacy lines on 1 October, and further rises are planned from February. Customers who have not switched by the deadline may be moved automatically to a temporary, last-resort service that allows only essential calls. The company said this would be significantly more expensive than digital alternatives.
Households that want to keep a landline will not lose it. Instead, the phone will plug into a broadband router and work over the internet.
Those with a phone line but no broadband are a shrinking group, according to the UK regulator Ofcom. BT raised line rental for its landline-only customers by £1 (€1.20) a month from 31 March this year with a guarantee of no further increases for 12 months, while call charges remained the same.
Ofcom said it would monitor BT’s prices for these customers.
Many people have already given up the landline altogether. Ofcom found that just over a million households switched to a broadband-only service in the year ending in July 2025.
In Europe Norway and Spain have already shut down their copper networks and the EU wants to make it mandatory everywhere by 31 December 2035, with only limited exceptions.
Member states would have to submit national plans by 2029 to phase out copper between 2030 and 2035, with safeguards including clear communication about switch-off dates and service continuity.

Syria, Iraq stir hope despite memories of war with resumption of Shiite pilgrimages- analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
11:09:44 UTC
20:09:44 KST

DAMASCUS — Syria and Iraq are discussing the restoration of organized Shiite pilgrimages to the Sayyida Zaynab shrine near Damascus, following high-level talks on October 28. The prospect has raised hopes of reviving businesses that once depended on religious tourism, while reopening painful questions about the role of Iran-backed armed groups during Syria’s civil war.
For more stories from The Media Line go to themedialine.org
The discussions took place during Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Faleh al-Zaidi’s visit to Damascus, where he met Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa. The two leaders proposed establishing a committee to arrange visits and ensure pilgrims’ safety, but no timetable or final agreement has been announced.
For Ali al-Hassan, who has kept his shop opposite the shrine closed since the fall of Bashar al-Assad’s government in December 2024, the possibility of renewed tourism offers hope of recovering his livelihood.
“I used to sell perfumes and fabrics that pilgrims would take home as gifts for their families,” al-Hassan told The Media Line. “Visitors came from Iraq, Iran, Lebanon, and several other countries, and they were all Shiites.”
The shrine, traditionally believed to contain the tomb of Zaynab, a granddaughter of the Prophet Muhammad, is among the most important pilgrimage destinations for Shiite Muslims. Before Assad’s overthrow, thousands of visitors supported a local economy of hotels, restaurants, shops, and transportation services.
Although small groups have continued visiting since the change of government, organized religious tourism has declined sharply, leaving many businesses closed and hotels largely empty.
The prospect of renewed activity has also revived concerns among Syrians who remember the involvement of Iran-backed armed groups in the country's civil war.
A diplomatic opening
Al-Zaidi's October 28 trip was the first visit by an Iraqi prime minister since Assad’s overthrow.
During his stay, he visited the Sayyida Zaynab shrine and the Umayyad Mosque in Damascus, accompanied by Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani.
The Iraqi prime minister’s office announced that he had donated $10 million from his personal funds, allocating $5 million to each religious site.
The gesture carried religious and diplomatic significance. The Sayyida Zaynab shrine is revered by Shiite Muslims, while the Umayyad Mosque is among the most important historic sites in Sunni Islamic tradition.
Al-Sharaa had previously told Iraq’s Dijlah television channel that Shiite religious sites remained accessible and that Syria was preparing to receive Iraqi delegations. He attributed delays to security problems following the former government's collapse.
Protecting worshippers remains a concern. In January 2025, Syrian authorities announced that they had thwarted an Islamic State plot to bomb the Sayyida Zaynab shrine, arresting four suspects.
Memories of war complicate the return
During Syria’s civil war, Iran-backed Iraqi and Lebanese armed groups fought alongside Assad’s forces, frequently invoking the defense of Shiite shrines to justify their intervention.
Their activities extended beyond protecting religious sites to military campaigns against opposition-held areas. Forces supporting the former government have faced documented allegations of killings, displacement, sieges, and other abuses.
In Idlib province, political activist Bilal al-Khalaf told The Media Line that Iraqi armed factions had contributed to civilian suffering and the destruction of residential neighborhoods.
He argued that those responsible for wartime crimes should face investigation and prosecution, but ordinary Shiite worshippers should not be held accountable for the actions of armed groups.
“Pilgrims should not be held responsible for the actions of armed groups, just as victims should not be asked to forget their memories or give up their right to justice,” he said.
Religious rituals raise local concerns
Not all concerns about the return of pilgrims are tied to the armed conflict.
Nawfal al-Ahmad, who has lived in Sayyida Zaynab for 40 years, recalled how large religious processions previously blocked streets, disrupted traffic, and interfered with residents’ daily activities.
He was particularly troubled by public performances of tatbir, a mourning ritual practiced by some Shiite Muslims that involves striking the head with sharp instruments to draw blood.
The practice commemorates the suffering associated with Imam Hussein ibn Ali, who was killed at the Battle of Karbala in 680. It remains controversial within Shiite Islam, and some prominent religious authorities oppose it because of the physical harm involved.
“These practices were disturbing, and they disappeared after Assad’s fall. But now, with delegations potentially being allowed to return, we hope they will perform their rituals in an orderly manner and without bloody scenes,” al-Ahmad told The Media Line.
He stressed that he did not oppose pilgrimages themselves but wanted ceremonies conducted without disrupting neighborhood life.
Objections have also emerged within Syrian religious circles.
In a statement issued Friday following al-Zaidi’s visit, the Forum of Levantine Preachers, known in Arabic as Multaqa Duat al-Sham, warned against allowing armed factions associated with abuses during the civil war to reestablish themselves under the cover of religious tourism.
The forum called for preventing individuals implicated in violence or sectarian incitement from exploiting religious gatherings to regain influence. It also urged respect for religious sanctities and restrictions on rhetoric that could inflame sectarian hostility.
Syrian official promises protection, oversight
Ahmad Anwar al-Alabi, who spoke as an official responsible for religious endowments at Syria’s Ministry of Awqaf, said the government regarded access to religious shrines as a legitimate right protected by freedom of worship.
He explained that authorities were considering organized groups and designated visiting periods, with security coordinated through the Interior Ministry and other relevant agencies.
“The objective is not to impose restrictions on religious practices, but to ensure that visits take place in an organized manner that respects the sanctity of the site and Syrian laws,” al-Alabi told The Media Line.
He rejected the possibility of religious gatherings being exploited for military or political purposes.
“A visit to the Sayyida Zaynab shrine is purely religious. It is not an entry point for military activity, displays of armed force, or political mobilization,” he said.
Al-Alabi said the arrangements should prohibit weapons, displays supporting armed organizations, and activities likely to inflame sectarian divisions.
He also stressed that religious affiliation or nationality should not be grounds for suspicion. Responsibility for wartime crimes, he said, must be established individually through evidence and legal procedures.
Economic recovery and regional relations
The pilgrimage initiative forms part of broader efforts by Damascus and Baghdad to rebuild relations following Assad’s overthrow.
During al-Zaidi’s visit, the governments also discussed trade, investment, border security, and rehabilitating the Kirkuk-Baniyas oil pipeline, which could give Iraq another route for exporting oil through Syria to the Mediterranean.
Religious tourism could help revive the economy around Sayyida Zaynab, where hundreds of families have depended directly or indirectly on businesses serving pilgrims.
But before larger groups return, the two governments must finalize arrangements that protect visitors and residents while addressing concerns that armed factions could exploit the reopening.
Al-Hassan, meanwhile, is considering reopening the shop that supported him for more than two decades. For now, its doors remain closed.

Trump's Gaza plan stalls as Israel's political deadlock deepens
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
11:08:43 UTC
20:08:43 KST

Negotiations over the future of the Gaza Strip have reached a standstill, even as Washington continues pressing for implementation of U.S. President Donald Trump's plan to end the war. Sources familiar with the talks describe a significant diplomatic impasse, with no meaningful progress toward the next phase of the American framework. Meanwhile, Hamas remains armed and is attempting to rebuild its ranks, while the IDF continues targeting the terrorist organization's operatives.
The situation has been further complicated by the political deadlock following Israel's October 27 election. With no clear parliamentary majority and no certainty over the formation of a stable government, Israel's political leadership faces significant obstacles to establishing a long-term policy for Gaza.
That uncertainty directly affects decisions about advancing the American plan. While Washington wants to see progress, Israeli officials still do not know what the country's governing policy toward Gaza will look like in the coming months.
Israeli security officials also believe Hamas is preparing an international public relations campaign focused on the humanitarian consequences of the approaching winter. According to sources familiar with the assessments, the terrorist organization is expected to highlight weather-related damage, inadequate infrastructure and shortages of warm clothing and essential supplies for Gaza residents.
Israeli officials assess that Hamas intends to use the humanitarian situation to increase international pressure on Israel, hoping that criticism will lead to a suspension of targeted strikes or at least a reduction in their frequency.
The sensitivity surrounding Israeli military operations has already affected the pace of strikes in Gaza. In August, amid diplomatic tensions with Washington and statements by the Gaza Board of Peace concerning targeted strikes in central Gaza, the IDF's Southern Command was required to obtain approval from the highest military and political levels before carrying out certain targeted killings.
That policy remained in effect for several weeks and led to a reduction in the pace of aerial operations against Hamas terrorists.
Major change planned in management of Rafah pilot
Despite the diplomatic stalemate, preparations are advancing for one of the central components of the American plan: the "Green Rafah" pilot project.
Over the past month, the IDF has concentrated efforts in the Tel al-Sultan neighborhood of Rafah, sealing underground tunnels in the area. The objective is to neutralize the underground infrastructure ahead of the pilot's expected launch in the near future.
However, a significant change is approaching in the project's management. In recent months, an Israeli project management company signed an agreement with the Gaza Board of Peace, the international body responsible for overseeing parts of the Strip's reconstruction. Under the agreement, the company will assume responsibility for managing the tunnel-sealing project on the board's behalf.
The IDF is expected to withdraw from the civilian management and execution of the project, transferring responsibility to a dedicated administration operating under the Board of Peace and American management.
The company has already completed its logistical preparations at Kerem Shalom, including arrangements at a concrete plant that will support the work. Within the next two weeks, it is expected to formally take over management of the project from the IDF.
As part of the transition, contracts with construction companies and concrete suppliers will be transferred to the new administration. Responsibility for delivering materials, locating underground tunnels and conducting drilling operations is also expected to shift to the civilian management team.
The arrangement is intended to move a central element of the reconstruction preparations out of the IDF's direct civilian management structure, even as the military continues its security operations in the area.
IDF continues targeting Hamas terrorists
While preparations for the civilian pilot proceed, IDF military operations in Gaza have not stopped.
Southern Command forces continue operating against Hamas terrorists who, according to the military, are attempting to restore the organization's capabilities and advance plans for attacks.
Several members of Hamas' military wing were killed in Israeli strikes over the past week, including Nukhba operatives and terrorists who participated in the October 7, 2023, invasion of Israel.
The IDF maintains that the Hamas terrorists targeted throughout the war, particularly in recent weeks, were involved in rebuilding the organization's military capabilities and planning attacks against Israeli troops and civilians, in what the military describes as systematic violations of the ceasefire.
The military also emphasizes that Southern Command forces remain deployed in accordance with the agreement and that operations to eliminate threats will continue.
The developments highlight the growing gap between Washington's diplomatic objectives and the situation on the ground. The United States is pressing to advance the next stage of Trump's plan, transfer responsibility for civilian projects and launch the pilot program in Rafah.
Yet Hamas continues to retain its military capabilities, the IDF continues carrying out targeted strikes and the central question of disarming the terrorist organization remains unresolved.
Above these obstacles hangs Israel's political uncertainty, which complicates decisions about the Strip's future and the extent to which Jerusalem can commit to the American framework.
For now, despite sustained US pressure and preparations on the ground, there is no indication of a significant breakthrough that would allow the diplomatic process to move forward.

Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02

20:08:01 KST

Strengthening academic and scientific cooperation to understand the evolution of past trade and economic investments and to more effectively define future priorities and initiatives that address new challenges—at the regional and global levels—for economic activities, trade, and investment flows between Italy, Turkey, Europe, and the broader Mediterranean region. This was the focus of the Italian-Turkish scientific symposium, held today at the Palazzo di Venezia in Istanbul at the initiative of the Italian Embassy in Turkey, with the participation of the Italian Historical Institute for the Modern and Contemporary Ages (ISIEMC) and the Turkish Academy of Sciences (TUB). “Trade agreements, the modernization of the customs union between the European Union and Turkey, and the dynamics of trade—which today make us Ankara’s leading Mediterranean partner and second-largest European partner—are issues of the utmost relevance to us, as is the possibility of ‘triangular partnerships’ with other regions of the world, starting with Africa. Gaining a deeper understanding of these issues is essential for developing new tools and projects to reinforce the unique nature of these centuries-old relations.” This was stated by the Italian Ambassador to Turkey, Giuseppe Manzo, as he opened the day’s proceedings, which—in the presence of approximately 150 academics, researchers, and entrepreneurs—were led by the director of ISIEMC, Gaetano Sabatini, who explained the system of Ottoman “capitulations.” Speaking on behalf of the Turkish Academy of Sciences, Ismail Koyuncu confirmed Tuba’s support for the new phase of scientific cooperation between Italy and Turkey. Among the other presentations at the conference—which took place as part of the embassy’s “Ideha26” promotional program and to mark the 170th anniversary of diplomatic relations between Italy and Turkey —were those by Giampaolo Conte of Roma Tre University, who explored the presence of the Italian financial sector in Turkey; Alessandro Albanese of the University for Foreigners of Perugia, who discussed economic relations between Turkey and the European Community in the 1960s; by Ebru Boyar of MRTU University in Ankara, who presented the case of an Italian family that published a major newspaper in Turkey in the early 20th century; and finally, by Lelio Iapadre of the United Nations University in Bruges, who spoke about Italy and Turkey in the European Union.

Two-thirds of funding pledged for Africa's Ebola response has yet to be disbursed, the head of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) warned Monday, calling for urgent action to contain the rapidly spreading outbreak.
International partners committed approximately $2.9 billion in cash and in-kind assistance to the response, according to figures released by Africa CDC in September.
"This outbreak reminds us that health security is shared. For the first time, Ebola has reached three African regions. Yet, two-thirds of the pledged response funds are still pending," Africa CDC Director-General Jean Kaseya wrote on US social media platform X.
The current outbreak of the Bundibugyo virus strain has affected four African countries: the Democratic Republic of Congo, Uganda, Kenya and Nigeria.
In Congo, the death toll surpassed 5,000 from more than 10,000 confirmed cases, according to government figures released Saturday.
"Every day of delay puts more families and frontline health workers at risk," Kaseya warned.
He said Africa CDC was working closely with African leaders to ensure safe access for health teams, particularly in conflict-affected areas.
"We must act now, together, to stop the spread," he added.

Accused arsonist in Los Angeles' deadly Palisades fire returns for federal retrial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
11:07:09 UTC

Accused arsonist in Los Angeles' deadly Palisades fire returns for federal retrial
LOS ANGELES, Nov 2 - Jury selection was due to begin on Monday in the federal retrial of a man prosecutors say deliberately set a blaze that grew into one of the deadliest, most destructive wildfires in Los Angeles history.
Jonathan Rinderknecht, 30, whose initial three-week trial ended in a hung jury in late June, was slated to return to US District Court in downtown Los Angeles to face a scaled-down version of the charges previously leveled against him.
Rinderknecht, a former Uber driver of dual US-French citizenship, was cast by prosecutors as a dejected loner who harbored deep anger at society, particularly the wealthy, and channeled his rage into an act of arson.
He is accused of "maliciously" starting a brush fire on January 1, 2025, that was quickly extinguished but smoldered in the roots of dense scrub before re-igniting days later, whipped by fierce winds into a conflagration that laid waste to the seaside enclave of Pacific Palisades.
Defense attorneys have maintained that Rinderknecht was wrongly accused. They asserted the hilltop New Year's Day blaze was triggered by holiday fireworks, not their client, and that the massive Palisades inferno that killed 12 people and destroyed thousands of homes a week later was a separate fire set by someone else.
The opposing narratives of the disaster left jurors deadlocked 10-2 in favor of acquittal and unable to reach a unanimous verdict on any of the three charges in June.
Judge Anne Hwang declared a mistrial, and prosecutors moved to retry the defendant under a grand jury indictment that dropped one of the original charges Rinderknecht faced and modified the two remaining federal arson counts.
Nearly 7,000 homes and other structures went up in flames, with property losses estimated at $150 billion, some of that belonging to organizations receiving federal financial assistance or involved in interstate commerce.
SIMULTANEOUS DISASTERS
The Palisades blaze coincided with another catastrophic wind-driven wildfire that erupted almost simultaneously in Eaton Canyon, about 30 miles to the east, killing 19 people and ravaging the Los Angeles suburb of Altadena. Fire investigators later concluded that sparks from an electrical transmission tower ignited the Eaton fire.
Rinderknecht was the only person criminally charged in connection with either of the two January 7 blazes, which together rank as the deadliest wildfire calamity ever in Los Angeles County, surpassing the 29 lives lost in the Griffith Park fire of 1933.
Rinderknecht, who pleaded not guilty, declined to testify in his own defense during his first trial. He would face up to 40 years in prison if found guilty as charged under the latest indictment. The original indictment carried a maximum prison term of 45 years.
He has remained in custody since his arrest in Florida in October 2025.
Defense attorney Steve Haney asserted during the first trial that prosecutors lacked physical evidence linking Rinderknecht to arson or any records showing an intent to commit arson.
In court documents and public statements about the case, Haney also suggested that his client was being scapegoated for failures of the Los Angeles Fire Department.
A onetime Pacific Palisades resident himself, Rinderknecht professed his innocence in a court declaration filed last March, denying he had willfully started any fire.
He acknowledged witnessing the outbreak of the January 1 fire, originally called the Lachman fire, from the vantage point of a hill he had climbed to watch New Year's fireworks. But Rinderknecht said he immediately called emergency 911 to report the blaze and remained at the scene until firefighters arrived and offered to help them.
Prosecutors have alleged that while placing his 911 call, Rinderknecht asked the AI app ChatGPT on his phone whether someone could be found at fault for lighting a fire "because of your cigarettes," to which ChatGPT replied, "Yes."
Prosecutors also said security camera footage and location data from Rinderknecht's cellphone show he was the only person in the vicinity of the January 1 blaze when it began near a trail in the Santa Monica Mountains National Recreation Area. REUTERS

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Fuel surcharges on international flights by Taiwan-based airlines will rise for the fifth time this year, bringing them closer to April’s record levels, the Civil Aviation Administration said Monday.
Oil prices have swung sharply this year following the US war in Iran. In April, the CAA raised surcharges to record highs of US$45 (NT$1,465) for short-haul flights and US$117 for long-haul flights. The CAA announces rates in US dollars.
Short-haul routes cover much of Asia, excluding India and the Middle East, and long-haul routes cover the rest of the world, including Europe and the Americas.
Rates fell in June and July before climbing for four straight months. The most recent change takes effect Sunday.
Taiwan’s surcharges float with the state-owned CPC Corp.’s posted international aviation fuel price. Whenever the price exceeds US$50 per barrel, short-haul surcharges rise by US$2.5 and long-haul surcharges by US$6.5 for every US$10 increase. Surcharges have applied throughout the year as prices have stayed above US$50 every month this year.

Europe could face colder weather as polar vortex weakens
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
11:00:54 UTC
20:00:54 KST

The stratospheric polar vortex over the northern hemisphere is facing the prospect of an unusually early weakening. Forecast models suggest it could weaken significantly over the next 10 days, when it would typically be strengthening.
A major sudden stratospheric warming (SSW) event is possible. This could influence weather patterns in the following weeks, increasing the likelihood of persistent areas of high pressure across the mid-latitudes and colder conditions weeks later.
The polar vortex is a large area of low pressure and cold air high above the Arctic. It weakens during the summer before strengthening during autumn and into winter. Its strong anticlockwise circulation helps contain the coldest air near the pole, although disturbances can allow colder air to spill southwards into the mid-latitudes.
An SSW event occurs when temperatures high in the stratosphere rise rapidly, often by as much as 50C in just a few days. This is associated with a dramatic weakening, or even reversal, of the strong westerly winds surrounding the polar vortex, disrupting its circulation. The earliest recorded major SSW, occurred on 28 November 1968, after records began 1958. Current forecast models strongly favour a significant weakening of the vortex, but a complete reversal of the winds required for a major SSW remains uncertain.
Such a development would mark a notable early-season disruption, with potential implications for weather patterns into early winter. The likelihood of colder, more settled conditions across northern Europe could increase, although a spell of severe cold appears unlikely over the next two to three weeks.
Meanwhile, an area of low pressure that deepened in the Mediterranean Sea last week is expected to bring heavy rain and strong winds to central and southern Italy on Monday, prompting warnings being issued for these areas. More than 100mm of rain is forecast to fall in just 24 hours across higher ground in southern Italy.
The system is expected to move eastwards across the Ionian Sea, before making its way to Greece, which is still recovering from exceptionally wet and unsettled weather last week.

Spoiler candidates are nothing new in US politics. It’s clear why Trump is targeting Peltola | Petala Ironcloud
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
11:00:42 UTC
20:00:42 KST

Days before Alaskans get to vote, the federal government is already trying to overturn the result.
Last week, at Donald Trump’s behest, the justice department sued to block the certification of Alaska’s US Senate race, if the Republican incumbent narrowly loses; a judge dismissed that suit on Sunday, though the administration said it planned to appeal. On Wednesday, Trump demanded that Mary Peltola, the Alaska Native Democrat whom polls favor to win, be removed from the ballot and prosecuted. Piling on, Alaska’s Republican governor has since ordered an investigation into Peltola’s campaign.
A New York Times investigation reported that operatives working with Peltola’s campaign helped recruit the other Sullivan, a retired teacher from Petersburg, to split the incumbent’s vote. Peltola and her campaign have denied this.
Whatever your reaction to the tactic, it’s generally legal in Alaska, where the state supreme court refused to remove the other Sullivan from the ballot.
In 2020, Trump’s allies pushed Kanye West on to ballots in states including Vermont, Arkansas and Wisconsin to take away votes from Democrats. Again, in 2024, Trump allies worked to get Jill Stein and Cornel West on ballots in swing states, and Trump praised both from a rally stage because each “takes 100%” from Democrats.
Not one federal lawyer intervened. What’s different in Alaska is not the tactic. It’s that the federal government has decided to police it in one race, before a single vote is counted.
The pretext falls flat. In Ohio, the Libertarian candidate Bill Redpath is being promoted by Democrat-affiliated groups, as Republicans have spent more than $1.58m boosting Gregory Levy, a progressive candidate. At the same time in Iowa, Democratic-aligned Pacs have deployed hundreds of thousands of dollars to promote a Libertarian candidate, Thomas Raymond Laehn, whose presence on the ballot could eat into the Republican candidate Ashley Hinson’s already slim polling lead.
That last example is the very same tactic, used by the same party, against the same kind of target: a Republican in a tight race. The justice department hasn’t touched this. It has sued in only one state, the one where an Alaska Native woman is favored to win.
The Democratic candidate Peggy Flanagan in Minnesota, a member of the White Earth Band of Ojibwe, is experiencing similarly heightened scrutiny in her US Senate campaign.
On 21 October, the Wall Street Journal reported that Flanagan had inflated her credentials by claiming Phi Beta Kappa membership. WSJ’s perusal didn’t hold up. Phi Beta Kappa’s associate secretary and chief operating officer, Amber Fox, confirmed to CBS News that Flanagan was inducted in 2002. WSJ eventually corrected the story.
Political scientists have shown how doubts about electability follow women of color. Primary voters may personally agree with their positions, yet withhold support because they fear other voters, especially general-election swing voters, won’t back the candidates. Local party chairs share these doubts too.
Researchers at Rutgers’ Center for American Women and Politics have also found that Native American women in politics, among other women of color, carry heightened stress and perform additional emotional labor because of their intersecting identities, though Native women remain among the least studied groups in the field.
Peltola and Flanagan are testing these entrenched doubts in majority-white statewide races, and the scrutiny lands right as they do.
Peltola has also weathered two major New York Times investigations in five weeks, one into her treatment of staff and one into the ballot scheme, and her lead has held.
No Native American woman has ever served in the US Senate. This year, two are within reach of it, and both have spent the final weeks of their campaigns fending off scrutiny, one from a major newspaper that appears to have gotten the story wrong, the other from a federal government that has singled out her race alone.
Why Alaska? The simplest answer is arithmetic. Republicans hold the Senate 53-47, and Alaska is one of only a small handful of toss-ups that will decide if Trump can keep his majority for the last two years of his presidency. It’s a state he has carried three times, but a majority of likely voters now disapprove of him.
Alaska Native voters complicate the picture even more deeply. In 2024, the North Slope and North-west Arctic district, where Alaska Native voters are a majority, gave Trump half its vote in the presidential race and Peltola 55% in that year’s House race. Many of the voters Washington now claims to be protecting chose both.
But the method matters more than the motive. A justice department that will sue to pre-empt a state’s certification, on behalf of one candidate, before a single ballot is counted, is testing the limits of a power the constitution leaves to states.
If it works in Alaska, what stops it from working in 2028, in any state that is close enough to matter? That it is being tried first on an Alaska Native woman, in a state far from Washington’s attention, should ring alarm bells for far more people than the Native voters it targets first.
I’m an enrolled member of the Fort Peck Assiniboine and Sioux Tribes, and on Tuesday I will vote in New York, not Alaska.
But I’ve watched this race the way many Native people have: as a test of whether Washington will truly let us win on the same terms as everyone else. My great-great-great-great-grandfather, Mahpiya Maza, also known as Chief Iron Cloud, signed the 1868 Treaty of Fort Laramie, which guaranteed Black Hills to the Sioux, a promise the federal government broke within a decade.
It was a harbinger Native people know well, and it’s one we recall when the government tries to rewrite the rules after the fact. What is now happening in Alaska looks familiar.
- Petala Ironcloud is a Lakota-Dakota investigative journalist and writer based in New York City

Who funded the midterms? Inside US elections’ historic bipartisan spending
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
11:00:40 UTC
20:00:40 KST

The upcoming midterm elections will be the most expensive elections ever conducted in the US. And more of the money is “dark” than ever before, meaning it’s impossible to get a full picture of who is spending gargantuan sums to influence races that could provide a critical check on Donald Trump’s second term.
The elections have also shown how money in politics is being reshaped, with the increasingly powerful role played by big donors from the tech industry as well as the growing concentration of spending among a few powerful individuals and corporations.
The impact of the rise of megadonors such as Tesla founder Elon Musk, and an increase in dark money among the very top donors, on this year’s electoral outcome is hard to quantify.
But signs of massive spending are everywhere. Ad industry tracker AdImpact predicts $11.6bn in ad spending this cycle, surpassing the $11.2bn spent in the 2024 presidential election. OpenSecrets, a nonpartisan research group tracking money in politics, pegs total spending in the midterms as on track to reach $11.9bn.
The top 40 donors are giving more than ever before: $2.4bn by mid-October, seven times the amount the top 40 in 2014 gave, adjusted for inflation, according to a new analysis from the nonpartisan, pro-campaign finance reform institute the Brennan Center for Justice. But the significant difference since then is that those top donors now give more to Republicans, and by a larger differential. In 2014, the top 40 gave to Democrats two to one, but this year the top 40 gave to Republicans three to one over Democrats.
Spending from Super Pacs, which can accept unlimited amounts of money to spend in elections, hit the $2bn mark by the end of September, which is 51% higher than the last midterm cycle, adjusted for inflation, according to the Brennan Center analysis.
And the New York Times counted at least $1bn that has already been spent by dark money groups by the end of August. “Dark money” is composed of organizations like 501(c)4 non-profits, which are groups that are not required to disclose their donors at all, since they are not supposed to have political activity as their primary purpose. (Those rules are often flouted in spirit, if not in practice.) This dark money spending is increasingly widespread in even lower-profile races across the country, and during primary contests. The Brennan Center’s recent number crunching estimated that dark money groups account for an unprecedented 29% share of the top 40 donors and that $699m is largely untraceable.
The landmark 2010 supreme court ruling Citizens United changed American campaign finance forever by allowing corporations and labor unions to spend unlimited sums on political expenditures. But rules against Super Pacs working closely with campaigns and candidates meant to counter the risk of corruption inherent in unlimited independent election spending are continually flouted and rarely enforced. Trump himself has repeatedly referred to the Super Pac Maga Inc as being under his personal control and subject to his decision-making, which is against campaign finance law.
Democrats are poised to regain control of the House and possibly the Senate, even as Republicans heavily outspent them, with polls showing minimal results from deluges of attack ads in competitive races. Exact figures for the disparity are hard to pin down, and are changing constantly. For example, on Friday, with only days until the election, the former New York City mayor Michael Bloomberg dropped another $36m for Democratic candidates on top of the $80m he already committed. But best estimates show a steep Republican advantage in Senate race spending, and a narrower one in House races.
The surge in spending is a warning sign for elections ahead, Brennan’s Ian Vandewalker said: “We’ve long had a system of limits and disclosures, but that’s increasingly going away.” Vanderwalker points to trends like new very wealthy industries like AI and cryptocurrency that have burst onto the scene, donating heavily to both parties, “clearly hoping for light or no regulation from the government, which is only going to increase”, and megadonors like Musk whose major spending “looks like a business investment”.
Bought by billionaires
Elon Musk’s ideological and personal business interests are well-documented, but other top megadonors fly below the radar. George Soros is one of the rare top 40 individual donors who give primarily to Democrats. Billionaires such as Wall Street’s Jeffrey Yass and the Uihlein family (owners of shipping giant Uline) are longtime Republican mega givers, focused on school choice and traditional ultraconservative causes, respectively. Combined, the two families gave at least $260m in the 2026 cycle.
Other megadonors include AI tycoons Marc Andreessen and Ben Horowitz, whose giving focuses on deregulation, advancing the crypto industry and electing pro-AI candidates. Israeli American businesswoman Miriam Adelson gave $67m this cycle and is known for advocating for far-right pro-Israel policies from the US government and exerting significant influence on Trump’s US-Israel policies.
Musk alone has given $483m so far in the midterms, a figure double what Soros gave to Democrats in 2022. The richest person in the world has been focused on trying to help Republicans keep a Senate majority, particularly in a close Texas race. Musk’s business empire and personal fortunes have been aided by his close relationship with the Republican candidate Ken Paxton.
New rules, new industries
A June supreme court decision allowing political parties to spend more in coordination with the candidates they support has helped the GOP inject big money from wealthy donors into small but crucial races, where Democrats enjoyed an advantage from raising more directly from smaller donors. Prior to the ruling, national party committees could only spend from $130,600 to $4,071,800 in coordination with an individual Senate candidate, and from $65,300 to $130,600 in coordination with an individual House candidate. But the court scrapped those limits. The shift means Republican committees have been able to raise more than $48m, dwarfing the $4m additional Democrats added, furthering the influence of big pocketbooks on smaller races that used to benefit from more grassroots local giving.
The past decade has also seen a major shift in the industries that influence elections with major spending. Labor, favoring Democrats, used to account for 14% of the top 40 midterm donors – now, it doesn’t even rank in the top 40, according to Brennan. Traditional finance interest giving has also declined in influence–from almost half of the top 40 donors in 2014 to only 15% this year.
New industries like crypto and artificial intelligence, and megadonors associated with them, are crowding out those traditional industries, as the scale of the big money gets bigger. Even the real estate industry, a longtime steady bipartisan giver, has seen its contributions relatively dwarfed by this new money.
The share of top donors giving to both parties has vastly increased this year, by more than 100 times the levels seen in 2022 and 2018. Strikingly, that means that in this election cycle, the bipartisan big spenders – largely cryptocurrency, online gambling, AI and pro-Israel interests – gave almost as much to both parties as the top donors giving to only Democrats.
All of this cash has resulted in record amounts of advertisement spending, but with unclear results. Some polling shows very little movement in Senate races in Alaska, Georgia, Maine, Michigan, North Carolina, Ohio and Texas before and after a GOP ad blitz this fall.
And all of this money doesn’t even account for growing informal influence campaigns – campaign or Pac payments to online social media political influencers are rarely tracked or disclosed. Campaigns can pay through middlemen companies, and the influencers are not required by law to tell their audiences if they are being paid to support a candidate.
Although it’s unknown how exactly the exorbitant spending affected 2026 votes, the bigger shifts cannot be ignored, says Vanderwalker – and serve as a warning for the 2028 election. It’s easier than ever for politicians to rely on one single megarich donor, he said: “In a democracy, it’s supposed to be one person, one vote, and the more one person can influence, the less egalitarian our system becomes.”
