Prediction market bettors are the new political pundits. Why are we listening to them? | Judith Levine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
11:00:40 UTC
20:00:40 KST

Online betting is a bit like Donald Trump.
The prediction markets – platforms where users bet on whether events will occur – pretend to be populist, pushing the nabobs aside and representing the “wisdom of the crowd”. “This data is bottom-up, not elites-driven,” a Kalshi spokesperson told Reuters. But in fact, the markets are controlled by a few, skillful traders.
Their users are led to believe they can strike it rich. But like gamblers everywhere, most of them lose most of the time, while enriching the casino and bankrolling the winner’s takings.
The markets pretend honesty and transparency, but they open the door to fraud and insider trading.
Like opinion polls, they affect voters’ expectations of the outcomes of elections but make them no smarter about whom to vote for.
Fundamentally, the assumptions projected by the prediction markets are Trumpian. The companies suggest that their results are improved by the financial stake customers have in them.
“Prediction markets are a way to see what people are saying when there’s money on the line,” said the Kalshi spokesperson. When money talks, in other words, its message is more authentic and valuable than mere political speech.
The prediction markets made a better collective call on the 2024 elections than conventional polls and pundits, particularly in the swing states. But why?
The authors of a much-cited 2025 study from Vanderbilt University infer that their results – that Polymarket was more accurate than polls – were “in alignment with research on the ‘Wisdom of Crowds’ theory, which suggests a large group of people are often accurate in predicting outcomes, even if they are not necessarily experts or closely aligned with the issue at hand”.
But more recent analyses suggest that the betting masses are not so wise after all. A new working paper from scholars at the London Business School and Yale University looked at publicly available trading data from Polymarket. Whereas almost every wagerer’s outcomes were no better than chance, they discovered, the “accuracy comes from a minority of persistently skilled traders, around 3% of accounts”. The crowd “generates most of the volume but little of the information”.
The crowd also furnishes most of the cash but reaps little of it. Analyzing 1.6m Polymarket accounts, or “wallets”, traded since November 2022, the Wall Street Journal found: “Casual traders are bleeding cash while a small number of sophisticated pros – including trading firms with access to vast streams of data – eat their lunch.”
What skills do these pros employ? They react quickly to public and financial news, say the London and Yale authors. They gather poll data and buy access to big data streams, which can cost $200,000 annually. They analyze the data using “algorithms to predict price movements and manage risk”, says the Journal, “faster than any human”.
Operating at scale and speed, with commensurate information and discipline, the pros can make tens of thousands of trades a day. And the more they trade, the more they earn.
In the Journal’s analysis, three-quarters of the profits went to 0.1% of the accounts. Of at least 2.3 million accounts on Polymarket’s site, just 2,000 netted a total of almost half a billion dollars.
Meanwhile, the median Polymarket user placed 46 trades across 10 active trading days in 2026, according to Pew Research. And because the few have the skills to trade against the mistakes of the many, the losses of the many bankroll the profits of the few.
The traders steering the prediction markets are not PhD pollsters and PBS talking heads. But they are elites nonetheless – the same elites who dominate Wall Street and make economic policy, whichever party is in office.
If it were a simply a matter of some people’s money squandered or increased, the problems of the traders would remain with the traders. But the press and the public are listening to them more and more. “Prediction market odds shift voters’ expectations substantially,” a study funded by the Brennan Center found.
The same features that rig the markets in favor of the few can distort what we think we know about coming elections. Explained CoinMarketCal, a newsletter serving crypto traders: “A market price reflects trades, liquidity, and available capital, not a representative poll. A well-funded trader can move a thin contract without any change in voter sentiment.”
And it’s not just expectations that prediction markets influence. They can also change voter behavior. “Elections have the property that what one believes is going to happen can actually affect what happens if a candidate is thought to be losing momentum or the campaign is flagging,” the Barnard College economics professor Rajiv Sethi told NPR.
Gaming on votes is not new, and its history is thick with corruption. Tammany Hall, New York’s Progressive Era Democratic party machine, kept a war chest for electoral wagers and publicized them vigorously to boost political momentum. In the 1904 presidential elections, the New York Times accused the Republicans of finagling the betting odds to help Teddy Roosevelt.
The corruption has simply moved online. There’s two-bit graft like the trick the expelled Republican representative George Santos pulled in 2023: he bought Kalshi contracts on whether he would attend the State of the Union address, posted on social media that he would, then stayed home and earned $18,000 on the bet. “There was absolutely no intent to deceive any person,” the compulsive liar’s lawyer protested.
While prediction market participation by elected officials and candidates constitutes illegal insider trading, the law did not stop aides this spring from betting on their own candidates. Polymarket has investigated dozens of cases of potential fraud related to the midterms. But with millions of trades moving both in the country and offshore, it may be impossible for companies to keep up with the fraudsters.
Especially not under an administration stinking of corruption and a presidential family deeply engaged in the crypto and prediction markets.
Donald Trump Jr’s venture firm 1789 Capital has invested half a billion dollars in Polymarket. On the day after Daddy’s 2025 inauguration, Kalshi announced it was “beyond excited” that Junior had joined the exchange as a paid adviser.
Trump Sr, who made $1.4bn on crypto in 2025 and has vowed to make the US the “crypto capital of the world”, declared in May that prediction markets also “will thrive” under his presidency.
There is overwhelming popular, bipartisan opposition to betting on politics and elections. Half the states ban it to some degree. But federal regulation is unlikely any time soon. Before Michael Selig was appointed to chair of the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, which regulates online prediction and crypto markets, he was a corporate lawyer for prediction markets and crypto.
Without government oversight or publicly traded stocks, it is even hard to evaluate election betting sites as businesses.
Estimates of trading volume on the midterms range widely. The Anti-Corruption Data Collective, the New York Times’s source, says it has surpassed $220m in 2026, up from $92.4m in the 2024 election cycle. Meanwhile, CNN quotes spokespeople for the two biggest platforms, Kalshi and Polymarket, who claim a total of $1.4bn for the upcoming midterms.
But the house doesn’t profit directly from the bets; users determine the prices and the odds. Revenue comes from trading fees and money earned on the funds sitting in the companies’ coffers between buys and payouts. Increasingly, media, financial and tech companies, including CNN, Fox, Dow Jones and Palantir, are striking deals to use the data.
Kalshi was recently valued at $22bn and Polymarket at $9bn. This could be a bubble that will burst, as artificial intelligence’s appears to be doing.
Some condemn the prediction markets as inherently morally and psychologically harmful. On this, I’m agnostic. A casino on your phone makes betting easier, but it does not turn every user into a fiend. And while the psychological profile of these online bettors – young, male, impulsive, irrationally optimistic, overly self-confident – makes them unnerving as pundits, if the question is whether Zimbabwe’s cricketers will beat Afghanistan’s or the US will confirm the existence of aliens, my feeling is, let the people bet.
But democracy is not cricket. These markets commodify a politics already gravely corrupted by money and gamify a discourse ever thinner on content or nuance. They should be banned.
- Judith Levine is a frequent contributor to the Guardian. Her Substack is Today in Fascism

What can Democrats actually do if they win Congress?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
11:00:38 UTC
20:00:38 KST

If Democrats win back the US House of Representatives or the Senate in the midterm elections on Tuesday, the final two years of Donald Trump’s presidency will look markedly different from the first half. But what would the Democrats’ actually be able to do with either – or both – chambers of Congress in their control?
What can Democrats do if they win the House?
If Democrats take the House, Republicans would lose their ability to pass legislation through that chamber without Democratic support. A Democratic majority could launch investigations into the administration, demand documents and testimony, and subject senior officials to sustained congressional scrutiny. They might come under pressure from their support base to impeach Trump for a third time.
What can Democrats do if they win the Senate?
The Senate confirms cabinet officials, ambassadors and federal judges, including supreme court nominees. A Democratic majority could block or delay many of Trump’s appointments, and force the White House to negotiate over legislation.
What if Republicans win?
Even if Republicans retain one or both chambers, a reduced majority could make governing more difficult, particularly when legislation requires near-unanimous support from the party’s own members.
What will Democrats investigate if they win?
Political reporter Joseph Gedeon laid out the most consequential investigations Democrats could launch if they take back Congress. Here are a few of the investigations:
- The family business: Robert Garcia, the top Democrat on the House oversight committee, has ranked Trump family corruption first on his list of priorities, while Representative Jamie Raskin has requested information on the business dealings of Trump son-in-law Jared Kushner and son Donald Trump Jr.
- Epstein and the emails: Thanks to a tag-team effort by Representatives Ro Khanna and Thomas Massie, the Department of Justice was forced to release millions of files related to Jeffrey Epstein last year. But off the bat, the justice department blew the legally mandated deadline to disclose the files. Then it released only about 3.5m pages of the 6m in its possession; it said it had deemed the rest duplicates. And there has been bipartisan consternation about heavy redactions in some places, and the apparently accidental disclosure of the names of victims in other places. The justice department is now facing a lawsuit from journalist Katie Phang over many of these issues. Even under a Republican-controlled Congress, the oversight committee under its GOP chair, James Comer, has been a rare spot of bipartisan comity, with members of both sides routinely (but not always) acting in concert to subpoena witnesses and hold them in contempt when they don’t cooperate. Expect that to continue in any new Democratic Congress.
- The Pentagon and the war: Jason Crow, a Colorado congressman who sits on the armed services and intelligence committees and co-chairs the House end corruption caucus, says he will start with the Pentagon, citing reports of defense money steered toward companies linked to the Trump family.
- Impeachment: House minority leader Hakeem Jeffries says Democrats have ruled nothing out regarding impeachment this time around, while the Republican House majority leader, Steve Scalise, predicts an attempt on “Day 1”.
What did the Democrats do last time they flipped the House under Trump?
In 2018, halfway through Trump’s first term, the Democrats flipped the House of Representatives in a sweeping blue wave. House committees quickly launched dozens of inquiries into his businesses, his handling of the Russia probes and possible conflicts of interest.
Just over a year after the 2018 midterms, after months of leftwing calls for impeachment, the House voted mostly on party lines to impeach Trump.
Democrats had accused Trump of pursuing a scheme to cheat in the upcoming presidential election by pressuring Ukraine to manufacture bad news about Joe Biden and then blocking congressional oversight. Trump was later acquitted in the Republican-controlled Senate on both articles of impeachment.
In 2021, Trump was impeached – and acquitted – a second time for inciting the January 6 attack on the US Capitol.

NEW DELHI, Nov. 2 (Xinhua) -- Over 20 flights were cancelled in the southern Indian states of Tamil Nadu and neighboring Andhra Pradesh on Monday in the wake of severe cyclonic storm Murasu, officials said.
Amid heavy downpour, at least 11 flights were cancelled at Chennai airport in Tamil Nadu, while 10 flights were cancelled at Vijayawada International Airport in Andhra Pradesh.
Reports said the flight cancellations have affected passengers traveling to and from Chennai and Vijayawada. Passengers have been advised to check their flight status with the airline before proceeding to the airports.
According to officials, the deep depression over the Bay of Bengal has intensified into severe cyclonic storm Murasu.
According to the India Meteorological Department (IMD), Murasu over West Central and adjoining Southwest Bay of Bengal moved west-northwestwards and lay centered at about 120 km east-southeast of Nellore, Andhra Pradesh and 160 km northeast of Chennai.
The IMD said Murasu is very likely to move northwestwards and cross the south Andhra Pradesh coast with wind speed of 100 to 110 kmph gusting to 120 kmph between Nellore and Narsapur during midnight, where it is likely to make landfall in the early hours of Tuesday.
The fishermen have been advised not to venture into the Southeast Bay of Bengal and into the Southwest Bay of Bengal until Wednesday.
Thousands of people have been evacuated along the eastern coast.
Prakhar Jain, a senior official of Andhra Pradesh State Disaster Management Authority, told local media that around 2,000 people have been evacuated and the process is underway.
In view of the forecast of heavy rain, the administrations of Tamil Nadu's Chennai and Tiruvallur have declared a holiday for all schools and colleges on Monday. The IMD has issued an orange alert for six districts and a yellow alert for five districts in Telangana, warning of adverse weather conditions.
Authorities in Odisha have expedited the evacuation of people from vulnerable areas on Monday in the wake of Murasu.
The new cyclone comes days after Andhra Pradesh and Odisha were battered by cyclone Arnab.
In Odisha, the death toll from cyclone Arnab rose to six on Sunday, while 10 people remained missing. ■

====================================================================================================

Scientists link wildfire smoke during pregnancy to higher autism risk
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
11:00:10 UTC
20:00:10 KST

Pregnant women living in areas with higher levels of microscopic soot and ash from wildfires may be more likely to have a child later diagnosed with autism, according to a nationwide study of nearly 900,000 births in the United States. The research, published in JAMA Pediatrics, indicates that exposure to wildfire smoke during the middle and later stages of pregnancy is associated with an elevated risk of autism spectrum disorder, though no meaningful link was found for attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). As wildfires grow more frequent and intense, the findings point to the potential benefits of helping expectant mothers reduce their exposure to smoke-filled air.
Wildfire smoke is a complex mixture of gases and fine particulate matter, often referred to as PM2.5 because the individual airborne particles measure 2.5 micrometers or smaller in diameter. That is less than one-thirtieth the width of a human hair, making the particles small enough to bypass the body’s upper airways, penetrate deep into the lungs, and enter the bloodstream. In this study, researchers examined how prenatal exposure to these particles relates to two common neurodevelopmental conditions that begin in early childhood. Autism spectrum disorder is a condition characterized by differences in social communication, sensory processing, and repetitive behaviors, whereas ADHD involves persistent difficulties with sustaining attention, impulse control, and hyperactivity.
Rising temperatures, prolonged droughts, and human land use have caused wildfires to burn larger areas and produce heavier plumes of smoke across North America. Studies show that fine particles generated by wildfires tend to be more toxic than particles from other sources because of their distinct chemical makeup, smaller particle size, and frequent co-occurrence with high heat.
Once inhaled by a pregnant woman, these microscopic pollutants may affect fetal development through several biological pathways. The authors of a 2021 review argued that fine particles can cross the placenta and trigger brain inflammation and oxidative stress, an imbalance between cell-damaging molecules and the body’s ability to neutralize them, potentially disrupting how neurons and their supporting cells grow and function.
Brain imaging research has linked prenatal fine particle exposure to differences in newborn brain development, with a study of newborn brain imaging finding that higher prenatal exposure to general fine particulate matter was associated with reduced myelin, the protective fatty coating that insulates nerve fibers. Even so, epidemiological evidence linking air pollution to specific childhood diagnoses has been mixed. For instance, a 2020 meta-analysis of childhood studies found no consistent relationship between general particulate air pollution and an increased risk of ADHD. Only two prior studies had specifically investigated prenatal wildfire smoke and autism, both limited to California, and they reached differing conclusions about whether risk increases during the third trimester or only under extreme smoke conditions in areas with otherwise clean air.
“Wildfire smoke is an increasingly important public health concern, and its effects extend well beyond the communities where fires occur,” study lead author Stefania Papatheodorou, an associate professor of epidemiology in the Department of Biostatistics and Epidemiology at the Rutgers School of Public Health, told PsyPost. “Smoke can travel long distances, exposing pregnant individuals hundreds or even thousands of miles away. Although previous research has linked prenatal air pollution exposure with autism, much less was known about wildfire-related pollution specifically. We wanted to examine whether exposure to wildfire smoke during pregnancy was associated with subsequent autism diagnoses in a large national population.”
To examine how wildfire smoke relates to early brain development on a national scale, Papatheodorou and her colleagues analyzed health records from the U.S. Medicaid Analytic Extract database, which covers more than 40 percent of births nationwide. Their cohort included 893,212 mother-child pairs with pregnancies conceived on or after January 1, 2007, and delivered through 2014. To ensure accurate tracking of prenatal health and location, the researchers restricted the sample to women aged 12 to 55 who remained continuously enrolled in Medicaid from three months before pregnancy through one month after delivery and who had the same residential zip code at the start of pregnancy and at delivery.
On average, mothers in the study were about 25 years old, and the children were roughly evenly split between boys (50.6 percent, or 452,218 children) and girls (49.4 percent, or 440,994 children). Based on Medicaid enrollment records, 40.6 percent of the mothers were White, 30.5 percent were Black, 21.3 percent were Hispanic or Latino, 4.1 percent were Asian or Other Pacific Islander, and 3.5 percent were of unknown race or ethnicity. The researchers followed the children’s medical records through the end of 2018, resulting in an average follow-up period of 6.3 years for children diagnosed with autism and 7.1 years for those diagnosed with ADHD. Diagnoses were identified using validated algorithms that scan medical billing claims for specific diagnostic codes and age criteria.
“An important strength is the inclusion of a large population of Medicaid-insured families, who are often underrepresented in research,” Papatheodorou said. “Understanding environmental risks in these populations is essential to developing public health responses that serve all families.”
To estimate wildfire smoke levels where each mother lived, the team used a previously validated machine-learning framework that mapped daily concentrations of fine particulate matter across every square kilometer of the contiguous United States. The system subtracted background pollution from total particle levels that incorporated fire emissions, isolating the specific fraction of fine particulate matter originating from wildfires and aggregating those levels weekly for each mother’s zip code.
The researchers then used statistical survival models, which track how much time passes before a diagnosis occurs. They combined these with distributed lag models, a technique for estimating how exposure during each week of pregnancy relates to later risk, to evaluate how cumulative and weekly smoke levels across the first 33 weeks of pregnancy related to a child’s likelihood of being diagnosed with autism or ADHD. They stopped the primary prenatal tracking window at 33 weeks so that the analysis could cover most of pregnancy while still including many babies born prematurely.
Because air pollution levels and medical diagnosis rates vary across communities, the statistical models accounted for a wide range of individual and neighborhood factors. At the individual level, the authors adjusted for maternal age, race and ethnicity, number of previous births, season of conception, prenatal folic acid prescriptions, smoking, alcohol or substance abuse, and poor nutrition. They also controlled for average outdoor temperature during pregnancy, non-wildfire background particle pollution, and local socioeconomic measures, including zip-code median household income, high school graduation rates, population density, urban or rural status, county obesity rates, and distance to the nearest hospital.
Across the entire cohort of 893,212 children, 8,357 were diagnosed with autism and 22,302 were diagnosed with ADHD during the follow-up period, meaning the share of children diagnosed by age 8 (the cumulative incidence) was 1.9 percent for autism and 10.4 percent for ADHD. Depending on the year, wildfire smoke accounted for between 4.4 percent and 7.5 percent of the total fine particulate matter in the air. Pregnancy-long averages for wildfire-specific particles were relatively low at 0.55 micrograms per cubic meter of air, compared with about 9.4 micrograms per cubic meter from non-wildfire sources.
The researchers found that an interquartile range increase in cumulative wildfire fine particulate matter across pregnancy, defined as an increase of 0.75 micrograms per cubic meter (the spread between the 25th and 75th percentiles of exposure), was associated with a 30 percent relative increase in the risk of an autism diagnosis (a hazard ratio of 1.30, with the plausible range running from a 7 percent to a 59 percent increase). The relationship was not strictly linear, as risk estimates rose across low and moderate smoke levels before leveling off at the highest concentrations.
“This describes a relative difference in the rate of diagnosis during follow-up,” Papatheodorou explained. “Even a moderate association can matter at the population level when an exposure affects many pregnancies, but translating this result into an absolute increase in risk requires additional information.”
“One notable finding was that the association with autism was apparent in a national cohort rather than a population selected for proximity to major wildfires,” she added. “This reinforces the importance of considering transported smoke and cumulative exposure during pregnancy, rather than focusing only on people living near a fire.”
In contrast, the same increase in prenatal wildfire smoke exposure showed no meaningful association with ADHD, yielding a relative risk increase of just 3 percent that was not statistically significant (a hazard ratio of 1.03, with a plausible range from a 9 percent decrease to a 17 percent increase). Non-wildfire background particle pollution was associated with a smaller, 10 percent relative increase in autism risk (and was not associated with ADHD). When the team examined the timing of exposure week by week, they observed a gradual increase in risk from early to late pregnancy for both outcomes, with the strongest estimates for autism appearing during mid-to-late gestation, particularly after approximately week 15. The authors suggest this window may matter because late fetal development involves rapid brain growth, the formation of connections between neurons, and the maturation of neural circuits.
“We also did not observe a clear association with ADHD,” Papatheodorou noted. “That difference raises questions about whether the findings reflect differences in biological pathways, susceptibility, exposure timing, or how these conditions are identified, questions that require further investigation.”
When the researchers broke the data down by the child’s sex, the overall pregnancy-wide risk estimate for autism was 31 percent higher for both boys and girls, though the estimate for girls was less precise and its plausible range (from a 12 percent decrease to a 98 percent increase) included the possibility of no effect. In week-by-week analyses, boys showed elevated risk across most of gestation while increases among girls appeared mainly in mid-to-late pregnancy.
Autism estimates were elevated across all racial and ethnic groups, while regional analyses suggested higher but imprecise estimates in the South for both conditions, though the ranges overlapped with other regions. The authors noted that regional variation could reflect differences in fire behavior and smoke composition, climate and co-occurring heat, background pollution, socioeconomic factors, health care access, and local diagnostic practices.
The results also held up across sensitivity tests that extended the pregnancy window to 37 weeks or restricted the analysis to children diagnosed after age 5. To test how vulnerable the findings were to unmeasured confounding (hidden factors not captured in the data that might be related to both smoke exposure and autism), the authors calculated that such a factor would need to be linked to both higher wildfire smoke exposure and autism by a risk ratio of at least 1.92 each, conditional on the measured covariates, to fully explain away the observed association.
These findings align in part with other research linking airborne pollutants to neurological and psychiatric outcomes, including a study using genetic data to estimate long-term pollution exposure that connected particulate components like black carbon, rather than direct prenatal wildfire smoke, to higher risks of both autism and attention disorders, the latter sitting in some tension with the new study’s null ADHD finding. Focusing specifically on smoke, a study of pediatric emergency visits found that higher wildfire smoke exposure was associated with more emergency department visits for youth psychiatric crises such as anxiety, depression, and schizophrenia, suggesting that smoke exposure may carry short-term mental health risks for children as well.
At the same time, the lack of an association with clinical ADHD diagnoses partly echoes a study of school-age children that examined general industrial and traffic air pollution rather than wildfire smoke. That earlier investigation found that prenatal air pollution exposure was associated with modestly higher teacher-reported ADHD symptom scores, particularly in boys, even though it was not linked to a higher rate of formal clinical ADHD diagnoses.
“Our findings suggest that wildfire smoke exposure during pregnancy may have implications for children’s longer-term neurodevelopment, in addition to its better-known effects on respiratory and cardiovascular health,” Papatheodorou told PsyPost. “We observed an association with autism diagnoses, but our study does not establish that wildfire smoke causes autism. The broader message is that protecting people from wildfire smoke matters even far from an active fire. This is a public health challenge that requires cleaner indoor air, accessible information, and support for families—not a responsibility that should fall entirely on pregnant individuals.”
As with all research, there are some caveats to consider when interpreting these findings. Because smoke levels were assigned to each mother’s residential zip code, which was confirmed only at the start and end of pregnancy, the data could not capture moves in between, how much time pregnant women spent outdoors, or whether they used indoor air filters during smoky days. According to the authors, the leveling off of risk estimates at the highest smoke levels could reflect behavioral adaptations during severe smoke events, exposure misclassification, less precise estimates at the upper end of exposure, or selection related to early pregnancy loss. In line with that last possibility, higher wildfire smoke exposure early in pregnancy has been linked to pregnancy loss in a 2025 study of Colorado pregnancies led by one of the same authors.
“The most important caveat is that this was an observational study,” Papatheodorou cautioned. “We identified an association, and other factors may have contributed to the findings despite our efforts to account for them. Our exposure estimates represent outdoor pollution where participants lived, rather than the amount of smoke each individual actually inhaled.”
“We also identified autism through health care records, so access to evaluation and diagnostic services can influence which children receive a recorded diagnosis,” she added. “Autism has a complex, multifactorial basis. These findings should not be interpreted as identifying a single cause.”
There are also a few limitations related to the study population and time frame. Families who left the Medicaid program before their children were old enough to be evaluated could have been missed, though statistical weighting suggested that loss to follow-up did not skew the results. In addition, the pregnancies in this cohort occurred between 2007 and 2014 among low-income Medicaid beneficiaries, meaning the findings may not automatically generalize to higher-income populations or reflect the potentially heavier wildfire smoke conditions seen in more recent years. The authors noted that future studies using more recent birth cohorts are needed to test whether these associations persist under contemporary smoke conditions, as well as to evaluate the combined effects of wildfire smoke and other environmental and social stressors.
“Our next steps are to explore whether associations with wildfire smoke differ across autism subtypes and extend this work to other neurodevelopmental outcomes,” Papatheodorou said. “We also plan to examine how environmental and social conditions may shape susceptibility. Our long-term goal is to translate these findings into prevention by identifying when reducing exposure matters most, which populations need additional support, and which strategies effectively protect pregnant people and their children.”
“Our findings add to the reasons to take wildfire smoke seriously as a widespread environmental exposure,” she added. “They also underscore the need for further research to confirm the association and better understand the processes underlying it.”
The study, “Prenatal Exposure to Wildfire PM2.5 and Risk of ASD and ADHD in Children Enrolled in Medicaid,” was authored by Stefania Papatheodorou, Hayon Michelle Choi, Krista F. Huybrechts, Sonia Hernandez-Diaz, Yang Liu, Danlu Zhang, Matthew Shupler, Michael Leung, Wanyu Huang, Xinye Qiu, Yaguang Wei, Christopher J. McDougle, Evgenia Papatheodorou, Joel D. Schwartz, Brent A. Coull, Marc G. Weisskopf, and Antonella Zanobetti.

Brick bathhouse by Kengo Kuma nears completion in Copenhagen

Brick bathhouse by Kengo Kuma nears completion in Copenhagen
Pyramidal towers frame pools at the Kai Water Culture House by Japanese studio Kengo Kuma & Associates, which is nearing completion in Copenhagen.
Set to open on the city’s harbour in December, the 5,800-square-metre aquatic centre will contain ten indoor and outdoor pools, alongside wellness facilities and cultural spaces.
Kengo Kuma & Associates was commissioned alongside Danish firms Cornelius Vöge, Søren Jensen and Vilhelm Lauritzen Architects to realise the new cultural and recreational facility on the city’s artificial island of Christiansholm – known locally as Papirøen, or Paper Island.
Photos revealed ahead of the opening show the facility’s five staggered buildings perched atop a glazed base and fronted by a wooden pier that provides direct access to the sea.
“The Water Culture House is a significant new landmark on Copenhagen’s waterfront,” Kengo Kuma & Associates lead architect Yuki Ikeguchi said. “It is part of the story of the city and the harbour’s transformation from an industrial to a cultural harbour.”
“As the cultural cornerstone of Papirøen, the house is a gathering place with water and community as its focal point, embraced by a public harbour bath,” Ikeguchi added.
Constructed from 300,000 handmade bricks, the tapered volumes are punctuated by triangular and square openings that filter dappled light into the indoor pools.
“The bricks are arranged in a staggered, stepped pattern, giving the building its distinctive texture and sculptural character,” Vilhelm Lauritzen Architects said.
“A total of 403 windows of varying sizes act as viewing apertures, framing the surroundings and creating captivating experiences of natural light as it shifts throughout the day,” it added.
The tallest of the five volumes, dubbed the Culture Tower, houses the centre’s cultural programmes, which include a third-floor events space. Meanwhile, the other four towers each house lofty indoor pools.
Nestled between the five brick volumes on the first floor is an outdoor pool, framed by the building’s sloped facades, and an open-air Onsen – a Japanese-style hot spring – that overlooks the harbour.
The Kai Water Culture House is set to open to the public on 5 December, with its wooden pier slated for completion early next year.
The facility sits among a wider redevelopment of Copenhagen’s Paper Island led by Danish studio COBE. Recent projects on the island include a 20,000-square-metre apartment complex informed by the area’s 300-year-old warehouses.
Photography by Rasmus Hjortshøj

My Journey to the Center of America’s Political Spam Text Hell
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

My Journey to the Center of America's Political Spam Text Hell
I've gotten nearly 2,000 campaign fundraising texts that were meant for someone else. I tried to find out why—and uncovered a labyrinth of politicians, data brokers, and shady tactics.
Just as my kid is nodding off for the night, it arrives: a ding. It’s Nancy Pelosi, texting to tell me that if I don’t donate $5 immediately, American democracy will basically collapse. A few minutes later, it’s Cory Booker, with an urgent request. Don’t even get me started on James Talarico.
Sometimes I’m driving, or making dinner, or trying to focus on my work, and another three messages arrive. Barack Obama NEEDS me. There’s a critical deadline approaching. A generous donor has offered an 800 percent match. Everything is at stake.
As I was writing that last paragraph, I got a message from Angus, a cat belonging to Sam Forstag, a Democratic congressional candidate in Montana. Angus needed me to know that Sam was out there working to flip Montana’s First Congressional District, taking on his Republican opponent and the wealthy special interests backing him.
I’m not sure what Angus expected me to do about it.
Political fundraising texts are a fact of American life. They’re intrusive, melodramatic, and relentless.
This year alone, I’ve received 725.
In the first 20 days of October, more than 190 arrived—nearly 10 a day.
On October 14, I got 21.
The strangest part is that most of these messages aren’t meant for me.
They’re meant for a family member who I’ll call John, for privacy reasons. John lives in California and has made small donations to Democrats. I live in New York and have made no political donations at all. We have different names, phone numbers, and bank accounts—a distinction that has apparently proven difficult for a substantial portion of the American political fundraising industry.
For years, I diligently opted out. I’ve replied “STOP” 49 times since 2021, by my phone’s count. Sometimes “Stop2End,” when that was the magic word. In November 2025, I told Jon Ossoff’s campaign some version of “stop.” It did not stop. Since then, I’ve received 13 more texts boosting his campaign, from nine different numbers.
When the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee texted to inform me that Bill Clinton, Barack Obama, and Joe Biden were calling me personally to action, I replied “eat shit.” That didn’t work either.
Exhausted, I decided this month to figure out what the hell was going on. Why did so many campaigns have my number? Why did they think it belonged to someone else? And why wouldn’t they fucking stop?
For starters, I downloaded my Messages history and pulled out the political texts I’ve received in recent years. Since March 2022, I’ve gotten 1,735, from 812 different phone numbers. By any measure, this is simply too many texts—nearly none of which were meant for me.
James Carville had written 27 times, soliciting money for at least a dozen political organizations. Ken Burns wanted help electing Jacky Rosen, then Roy Cooper, then Sherrod Brown. On April 2, 2025, the day after Cory Booker finished his 25-hour Senate floor speech, I received the same first-person appeal from “Cory” three times in less than two hours, sent by three different fundraising operations.
The thing is that John—the person these campaigns had me confused with—isn’t a particularly big donor. Federal Election Commission records show roughly 160 contributions since 2017, totaling about $1,700. The median gift was $6. This year, John donated six times, for a total of $51.
In the same period, my phone received 725 fundraising texts literally begging for his money.
The Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee alone sent 60 of them—22 in the first 20 days of October—from 28 different numbers. My relative had given it $5, once, in 2020. The DCCC sent another 41 messages; it had received $8. House Majority PAC, which has never received a dime from John that I could find, kept offering to multiply contributions by as much as 900 percent.
I understand the logic of these messages on some level. They are cheap, and the strategy isn’t all that different from how a lot of scams work—spray out messages and pray someone will bite. You don’t need many people to respond for it to pay off. What I couldn’t understand, though, was how I’d gotten wrapped up in all of this. I didn’t have to look far for the answer.
Almost every text contained a link that, after a few redirects, led to ActBlue, the platform Democrats use to process donations. Helpfully, many of those links carried tracking codes—strings of letters and numbers identifying the fundraising appeal, the message being sent, and sometimes where the campaign got the recipient’s contact information.
An October DCCC link, for instance, contained acq_sms.p2p_fr_2026.10.13_b1_dccc_rent_4mtch_st. Squint a little and you can make out abbreviations for acquisition (“acq”), peer-to-peer fundraising (“p2p_fr”), and a rented list (“dccc_rent”). But one word kept appearing in these strings across messages from otherwise unrelated campaigns: Sterling.
Sterling Data Company is a relatively small firm that uses AI to help Democrats find people likely to give them money. In 2022, Forbes reported that Sterling had assembled a database of roughly 30 million political donors, with hundreds of details about some of them, including what cars they drove and what they watched on Netflix. Sterling says it uses that information to predict who might donate to a particular candidate.
Sterling appears to get much of its information from other data brokers, combining details about people’s age, location, politics, and donation histories into voter profiles that campaigns can buy or rent.
Of the 725 texts I’d received this year, nearly half contained tracking codes that appeared to reference Sterling. They came from dozens of PACs and campaigns, including the DCCC, DSCC, James Talarico, and Mark Kelly.
FEC records show that a Biden joint fundraising committee paid Sterling about $1.87 million for donor lists over four months beginning in November 2023. Around the same time, a text from the committee reached my phone with a code containing strl2b.
The DSCC’s first reported payment to Sterling came on November 22, 2023—the very day I received one of its texts tagged STL2. According to FEC data, the committee has continued paying Sterling, including roughly $250,000 this summer, which preceded another wave of Sterling-tagged texts.
Those recent texts all appeared to link back to a common platform. Dozens of campaigns had their own web addresses, but I could see that they used nearly identical software and tracking codes, often ending in tier1. Sterling’s own website advertises something it calls “Tier 1 contact data intelligence,” though I couldn’t establish whether the two were connected or who ran the system. Still, the breadcrumbs were leading me to suspect that, at some point, a Sterling database mixup had lumped John together with my phone number.
“High-frequency solicitation is a necessary evil,” Martin Kurucz, Sterling’s CEO, tells me when I ask about all of this. “Few people give, so every campaign chases the same donors, and texting at scale works too well to skip.”
Kurucz declined to discuss Sterling’s proprietary data but confirmed that the company handles the texting itself and can rent the same record to multiple campaigns. Sterling limits how often individuals can be contacted, he said, though he didn’t specify what those limits are.
“No contact database is perfect,” Kurucz says. Even matches made with moderate confidence are generally accurate enough to be worth using, he says. Wrong numbers tend to drop out of circulation because the recipients don’t engage.
Kurucz wouldn’t confirm that Sterling has caused the deluge of misdirected text messages my way, but he also didn’t deny it. Instead he offered some advice for making them stop: Don’t respond at all.
I found that there’s another way out: lawsuits. At least two people have successfully gotten a settlement out of Democratic organizations over apparently misdirected campaign texts, which presumably included never being contacted again.
That seems like a lot of work, though. Meanwhile neither of those lawsuits established how the wrong names got attached to their numbers. I still don’t know for sure how mine got mixed up with John’s. But the outcome is the same: The DSCC now texts me more often than my mother. Replying “eat shit” another hundred times won’t change that.

Why a Top House Democrat Now Supports Impeaching Trump and Hegseth
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

When the top Democrat on the House Armed Services Committee was asked by TIME in May about the prospect of impeaching President Donald Trump, he declined to commit, warning that every impeachment he had witnessed during his decades in Congress had left its target politically stronger. Five months later, Rep. Adam Smith of Washington is prepared to take that risk.
With Democrats hoping to reclaim control of the House in Tuesday's midterm elections, Smith says that he now supports impeaching Trump and is inclined to also back proceedings against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, making him one of the most senior Democrats to endorse such a course.
"Trump has become beyond dangerous. He is just completely out of control in what he says and how he is governing," Smith told TIME in an interview a week before the election. "I think we have to try, even if it doesn't succeed."
Smith's endorsement is particularly significant because he would be in line to chair the Armed Services Committee if Democrats win the House, putting him at the center of investigations into the Pentagon's handling of the war with Iran, its approach to Ukraine, and military operations in Latin America.
His position comes as Democrats prepare for the possibility of reclaiming congressional power with little agreement over how aggressively to confront the President. Interviews with more than two dozen Democrats reveal a party broadly convinced that Trump has engaged in conduct warranting impeachment, but deeply divided over whether another attempt to remove him would be an effective use of its authority. Trump's two previous impeachments ended in Senate acquittals, and even a Democratic victory this week is unlikely to produce anything approaching the two-thirds majority required for conviction.
Smith, who has served in the House since 1996, noted previously that he was one of the few House members to have sat through three impeachments. "Every single time the person impeached got stronger after they were impeached than before," Smith told TIME in May, arguing that Democrats needed to consider what another impeachment could realistically achieve rather than pursue it simply to demonstrate their willingness to confront Trump. "I want to make sure that if we're going down that road it's going to help defeat Trump and his poisonous ideology," he said at the time.
Since then, he says, Trump's increasingly conciliatory posture toward Russian President Vladimir Putin, his decisions involving American support for Ukraine, and his public rhetoric have convinced him that the President's continued tenure presents an extraordinary danger. "The Ukraine stuff definitely had a profound impact," Smith says. "When I saw how close he was getting to Putin and shutting off support for Ukraine, being more pro-Putin. I mean, that's a big part of it." He also cites Trump's increasingly "unhinged speeches," including remarks about rising gasoline prices amid the war in the Middle East.
Smith’s willingness to embrace impeachment puts him at odds with more cautious Democrats who want the party to prioritize addressing the economic concerns that have dominated the campaign, while establishing an investigative record that might ultimately lead to impeachment. He acknowledges the formidable obstacles to removing Trump but argues that the political environment has changed since the President's first term. "I don't think it will be viewed as negatively or as partisan as in the previous two efforts, just because the public is waking up to the con game that Trump put on," he says now. "The impeachable offenses have been obvious for a long time.”
Other senior House Democrats are less certain that pursuing impeachment would accomplish much, even if they share Smith's assessment of Trump's conduct. Rep. Jamie Raskin of Maryland, who led the House managers during Trump's second impeachment trial in 2021, says he has "little doubt that the president has committed multiple impeachable offenses," citing what he describes as unconstitutional military action and abuses of congressional spending authority. But he draws a distinction between establishing grounds for impeachment and deciding whether another trial would be the best use of Congress's time and political capital.
"The question of whether he committed impeachable offenses and whether we are going to pursue impeachment are two different issues," Raskin tells TIME.
Trump was impeached in 2019 over his dealings with Ukraine and again in 2021 over his role in the Jan. 6 attack on the Capitol. Both proceedings ended in acquittal, although seven Republican senators voted to convict him in the second trial. While some Democrats regarded those efforts as necessary to establish a historical and constitutional record, another impeachment could consume months of congressional attention, galvanize Trump's supporters, and leave voters questioning what the party had accomplished with its new majority.
Sen. Adam Schiff of California, who led the prosecution during Trump's first impeachment trial, says Democrats should avoid reaching conclusions before knowing the composition of the next Congress and what investigations might uncover. "There's no question he's been engaging in conduct that is very likely impeachable," Schiff told TIME. "The question is, is it viable?"
Schiff disputes the notion that the earlier impeachment efforts strengthened Trump politically, but argues that Democrats should concentrate initially on investigating corruption that has affected Americans' finances. "Our primary focus ought to be on corruption that has raised the cost of living for people," he says.
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries has similarly declined to commit to impeachment, saying Democrats "haven't ruled anything in, and we haven't ruled anything out." He has indicated that investigations should help determine whether the House pursues that course.
Some Democrats are looking toward members of Trump's Cabinet, particularly Hegseth, as potentially more viable targets, reasoning that Republicans who would never vote to remove the President might be more willing to turn against a defense secretary whose leadership has drawn criticism from within their own party. "There are Republicans who would support impeaching Hegseth who might not support doing it to Trump," Smith says.
The Defense Secretary has faced mounting scrutiny over his handling of the Iran war, the removal of senior military officers, and the Pentagon's relationship with Congress. Some Republicans have publicly expressed frustration with his leadership and the department's failure to provide adequate information about the war's objectives, costs, and duration. A push to impeach him has already taken shape in the Republican-controlled House, although Trump has defended Hegseth, calling him a "great warrior" and dismissing Democratic efforts to remove him.
Raskin says that impeaching a Cabinet secretary would be less likely to consume Congress's agenda or raise the same concerns about overturning the result of a presidential election. "The question of cabinet officers is a little bit easier because it doesn't necessarily consume all of the policy oxygen in Congress," he says.
However, impeaching Hegseth would require a majority in the House, and removing him would still require a two-thirds vote in the Senate. Republicans who have criticized his performance have not necessarily indicated any willingness to support impeachment. But the growing unease over the administration's military decisions, particularly the conduct and costs of the war with Iran, could offer Democrats an opening that does not exist with Trump.
Rep. Jason Crow of Colorado, a member of the Armed Services Committee who served as a House manager during Trump's first impeachment trial, says lawmakers have been preparing for extensive investigations into the Pentagon regardless of the election's outcome. He cites the removal of senior military officers, alleged misuse of defense funds, threats against NATO, possible troop withdrawals from Europe, and the administration's handling of the Iran war as areas demanding scrutiny. But Crow stops short of endorsing impeachment as the preferred course. "Impeachment is only one tool that Congress has," he told TIME.
"If the goal is to get Pete Hegseth out of the Department of Defense to stop corruption, to erect some guardrails against this runaway, reckless administration, and to protect the country against the increased erratic and dangerous behavior of Donald Trump, then we have to look post-November what the Congress looks like," Crow says. "Maybe impeachment is part of that. I wouldn't hesitate to use that if that's the right one."
