The self-making world
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

Listen to this essay
29 minute listen
The French naturalist Jean-Baptiste Lamarck was 65 when his great treatise on the transformation of life was published. With Philosophie zoologique (1809), translated a century later as Zoological Philosophy, Lamarck intended to establish an entirely new science, one built on the idea that all living beings are constantly transforming themselves, from the tiniest microbes to the most complex mammals, gaining new forms and new abilities. It wasn’t the bodily structures of organisms that determined their ways of life, Lamarck said, but just the opposite: their ways of life in response to their circumstances gave rise to their changing bodily forms. ‘Can there be any consideration in natural history more important,’ he demanded, ‘or deserving of greater attention, than the one I have just set forth?’ (My translation.)
But if you’ve heard anything at all about Lamarck, it’s probably how wrong he was about one animal in particular, the giraffe, and how this giraffe fiasco epitomises his wrongness about everything. Lamarck suggested that, by stretching to reach leaves in high tree branches, giraffes slightly elongated their necks, creating tiny changes that were then handed down to their offspring, accumulating over many generations to produce the long necks we see today. Around the turn of the 20th century, Lamarck’s giraffe idea became a laughing stock when biologists roundly rejected the notion that bodily changes undergone in the course of an individual lifetime could be inherited in the next generation.
It wasn’t only his ideas about long-necked mammals that came under attack. Lamarck’s interest in giraffes was just a passing mention in the midst of his voluminous writings, which set out a revolutionary, field-founding theory: organisms, he claimed, transform themselves and, in doing so, they remake the world. That idea has drawn scorn for more than two centuries.
Though Lamarck is often overlooked, his science was foundational to modern biology and informed the theory of evolution that Charles Darwin later developed. Darwin followed Lamarck in believing in the agency of living beings to transform themselves and their environment. But most people don’t know about Lamarck’s influence on Darwin because, around the turn of the 20th century, Darwin’s followers expurgated every trace of Lamarckism from their neo-Darwinist version of evolution, rendering living beings the objects of random variation and outside forces. For the neo-Darwinists, living things played no direct role in the evolutionary process. Evolution happened through random genetic variation and external environmental pressures. For Darwin’s followers, organisms were just as passive as they had been for the creationists, who saw them as products of divine will.
Throughout the history of modern biology, most powerful figures in science and politics have ridiculed and repressed Lamarck’s radical idea that organisms have agency in the evolutionary process. In mainstream biology today, a neo-Darwinian view of living things as passive still largely dominates, though research in several areas has been challenging its reign.
This is the story of how Lamarck’s radical idea was cast aside by mainstream science, and why it was overlooked for so long. It is also the story of a surprising reversal: in recent decades, some biologists have begun turning back toward Lamarck’s view of life.
While many people think of giraffes when they hear Lamarck’s name, few know that he coined the word ‘biology’, in 1802. He needed a name to designate a new science he thought should exist: a science of all living beings, and only living beings. At the time, there was no such field. There were broader sciences, such as natural history, which included inanimate things like rocks, rivers and mountains; and there were narrower sciences, such as botany or zoology, which covered subsets of the living world. But Lamarck thought there should be a science of life. At the heart of his new science, he developed the first theory of what we now call ‘evolution’, although he didn’t call it that. He simply referred to ‘change’.
Lamarck lived and worked in the Jardin des plantes (Garden of Plants) in Paris from 1788 until his death, aged 85, in 1829. His life was tumultuous, to say the least. He lived through the French Revolution, then under Napoleon, then during the Bourbon Restoration. He survived the Reign of Terror, as well as the withering disdain of Napoleon and his circle of scientific advisors, and the return of the monarchy; he also outlived three wives and four of his eight children. In the last decade of his life, he was blind and frail but carried on working with the help of his daughter Rosalie. At the end of his long career, he had identified and named more than 6,000 species, and for more than two decades had taught a legendary course in the Garden of Plants, drawing students from all over the world. The course grew so famous that even fictional characters attended it, such as the lovelorn young Amaury, hero of Sainte-Beuve’s autobiographical novel Volupté: The Sensual Man (1834).
By daring to usurp God’s monopoly on Creation and reassign it to mortal beings, Lamarck provoked the ire of the mighty and powerful. He wrote that life originated in spontaneous generation, brought about by natural forces such as electricity and heat acting upon inanimate matter. This led to the emergence of the simplest organisms: single-celled protozoa and algae. From that point, a property intrinsic to living matter exerted itself, a tendency to complexify, which Lamarck named ‘the power of life’. As organisms grew more complex, another cause of transformation came into play: their responsiveness to the environment. In the simplest beings, this responsiveness was rudimentary – an irritability or sensitivity, and reflexive reaction. But in birds and mammals, Lamarck argued, it rose to the level of ‘acts of will’, through which creatures could form ‘habits’ and ‘ways of life’ in response to their circumstances. By means of these behaviours, they directed their inner fluids toward the limbs and organs they used most. (Darwin would later propose a similar idea. In 1868, he suggested that parts of the body threw off particles of inheritance, called ‘gemmules’, which were modified by an animal’s behaviours and could carry the modifications into its offspring.)
He imagined the simplest animals might reveal to him the foundation of animal life
Not only did living beings create and transform themselves, according to Lamarck’s picture of things, they also made and re-made the inanimate world. Plants played the primary role in this process, he thought, because they could invent themselves out of just sunlight, air and water. He described experiments to confirm this miraculous capacity. For instance, carve a hollow into the side of a turnip and suspend the vegetable in a window by its root, Houdini-style: nothing up its sleeves! Keep the hollow filled with water, and you’ll see that the turnip will grow a whole flowering plant. It has created itself literally from thin air. Plants, by bringing together the primitive elements into combinations, originated the cosmic relay chain, then handed off their work to animals. By eating, digesting and engaging in their other functions and behaviours, animals produced more elaborate compounds, and so they shared with plants the defining ability of all living beings to build, compose and create.
Having begun his career in botany, in 1793 Lamarck was obliged to move, reluctantly, into zoology. This was in the midst of the Revolution, during the transitional moment when the main botanical garden in Paris – the King’s Garden – became the republican Garden of Plants under the auspices of a new National Museum of Natural History. The committee in charge of this transformation did not assign Lamarck to a chair in botany as he wanted, but instead to the lowliest chair in zoology: the Professorship of Insects and Worms. He would later tell his students that he’d been, at first, disappointed: if he couldn’t carry on studying botany, then why not charismatic megafauna, like lions? But then he’d had two hopeful thoughts. First, his assigned creatures constituted nine-tenths of the animal world, so he hadn’t been relegated to an unimportant corner of zoology. And, second, he imagined the simplest animals might reveal to him the foundation of animal life. Contemplating his insects and his worms with this faint gleam of hope, he created a new taxonomic category, ‘invertebrates’, and set to work studying them.
The invertebrates, he told his students in 1800, ‘conduct us insensibly toward the inconceivable limit of animalisation’, toward those beings ‘barely endowed with animality’ with whom ‘nature perhaps began’. For Lamarck, this essence of animal life was the power of generation and regeneration: the ability to produce living matter, including new bodily tissues and new organisms. The simplest animals had the most widespread generative faculties. For instance, the Genevan naturalist Abraham Trembley had shown that, if you cut up polyps (freshwater hydras) into lots of pieces, they regenerate an entire animal from each part. Other invertebrates, too, had incredible powers of generation. Insects could metamorphose. Crustaceans could grow new legs. Sea stars, new rays. Snails, a new head. The invertebrates far outnumber the vertebrates, Lamarck explained, thanks to this generative ability. Their number is unknowably vast because of the ‘infinite smallness’ of the smallest among them. These animals display a ‘frightening fecundity’, he wrote; it seems that ‘matter animalises itself from every direction.’ Lamarck marvelled at the tiny coral polyps that were identified as the chief producers of the great calcareous mountain chains and enormous banks of chalk found all over Earth. These minuscule animals create islands, fill bays and gulfs, clog ports and ‘completely transform the coastlines’.
The invertebrates became the basis of Lamarck’s idea that living organisms held a monopoly on creative agency. Religious faith, Lamarck acknowledged, could be a consolation for a ‘good man who persuades himself of it’ but was ‘absolutely foreign’ to his own study of living nature. Souls were not physically knowable, whereas the dynamic, creative action of living beings was everywhere apparent. Life, to Lamarck, now became the manifest capacity to create in the face of all nature’s forces of destruction.
The incessant creative activity of each organism was far from solitary. Living beings collaborated as they worked to form the world and fend off destruction, and Lamarck took a great interest in this collaborative action. For instance, one spring day in 1798, having brought his family to a country house he briefly owned outside Paris, he noticed a swallow’s nest in one of the windows. Shortly afterwards, a local child destroyed the nest, leaving the pair of swallows homeless just as the female was about to lay her eggs. Immediately, 10 or 12 other swallows gathered around the wreckage. The birds were so agitated and noisy that at first Lamarck assumed they were quarrelling, but he soon realised it was just the opposite. They had organised themselves to rebuild the nest collaboratively. He watched in amazement as some remained by the construction site while others came and went with twigs. Swallows generally take eight to 12 days to build their nest, Lamarck observed, but these worked so diligently that they finished it the following morning.
The seal used its hind limbs as a paddle when swimming. They hadn’t become a fin because the seal also used them for seizing prey
As evidence of animals’ power of creation and self-transformation, Lamarck cited many examples in which the increased use of a body part had apparently developed and shaped it: the webbed feet of water birds from pushing against the water; the hooked talons of eagles from clasping branches; shorebirds’ long, skinny legs and necks. Lamarck reckoned that shorebirds dislike the water yet have to wade out to catch their prey. Sinking into the mud, they stretch their legs in distaste, straining to keep their body above water, and craning their necks. This behaviour over many generations resulted in stilt-like legs and snaky necks.
When a seal arrived in the menagerie of the natural history museum in June 1809, Lamarck watched the animal with fascination. Its obvious kinship with land mammals confirmed his idea that all mammals, and indeed all life, had originated in the water. He noticed that the seal used its hind limbs as a paddle when swimming. Yet the legs hadn’t fully joined together to become a fin because the seal also used them for seizing prey. The distinctive combination of uses for the hind limbs had produced a structure that could work either like a paddle or like a hand.
Lamarck had set Aristotle’s ancient Scale of Nature not just in motion but in a great commotion. For two millennia, since the time of Aristotle, natural philosophers had imagined every being ranked from simplest to most complex in a fixed, unchanging order. Each form of life had its appointed place in the hierarchy. But now Lamarck announced that, rather than being arrayed along the Scale of Nature, living beings were themselves ever making and remaking the order of life by their own incessant activity, and in many directions at once.
Lamarck’s idea of self-making and world-making organisms gained him powerful enemies. His nemesis was the palaeontologist Georges Cuvier, a favourite of Napoleon. Cuvier was a devout Lutheran who categorically rejected the idea that living forms changed over time and instead upheld the fixity of species. His central anatomical principle, the principle of correlation of parts, was an assertion of rational design: he claimed that one could infer all the parts of a creature from any single part because they all implied one another by rational necessity. Cuvier also insisted that animals’ habits and behaviours followed from their structures – they behaved as they were designed to behave – whereas Lamarck said it was just the opposite: animal structures resulted from their habits and behaviours. This same commitment to fixity shaped how Cuvier read the fossil record.
Cuvier believed in extinctions and was a leading figure in establishing their reality. But he assumed that creatures went extinct because catastrophes, like floods and fires, eliminated them, and then those creatures were replaced by newly created ones. This idea supported the doctrine of special creation: that God had created each species for its place in nature. Cuvier’s science was perfectly suited to Napoleon’s purposes. It was a scientific doctrine of revolutionary change that was also profoundly conservative, each revolution imposed from the outside, each a return to the same ultimate authority, and the whole thing guaranteed by Napoleon’s own scientific experts rather than the Church. Cuvier’s science was cutting-edge, but at the same time, it bolstered an authoritarian order. It was emphatically not the science of the materialist, atheist revolutionaries; but nor was it the older science of the Catholic Church. Cuvier translated the authority of religion into science – a powerful modern concoction.
Rather than consolidating power, Lamarck’s theory distributed it throughout the living world
It’s no surprise, then, that Napoleon loathed Lamarck, who challenged Cuvier’s model of science. This hatred was dramatically apparent on a freezing day in November 1809 when the members of the National Institute stood shivering as they awaited the emperor in a salon of the Tuileries Palace to present their new works. We have the story from the astronomer François Arago, who was present as a new member of the Institute at the age of 23. Standing near young Arago was Lamarck, 65 and frail, holding a copy of his Philosophie zoologique. Napoleon at last entered the room and marched up to Arago as he would to a new conscript, fixing him with a stare and barking: ‘You’re very young! What’s your name?’ Before Arago could answer, his neighbour on the right, eager to be noticed, replied: ‘His name is Arago!’ Napoleon: ‘What science do you cultivate?’ Arago’s left-hand neighbour piped up with: ‘He cultivates astronomy!’ While Arago ruefully reflected that Napoleon must take him for a mute or an imbecile, the emperor turned to Lamarck, who presented his magnum opus. Growling that he was accepting it only ‘out of consideration for your white hair’, Napoleon snatched the book and, without looking at it, thrust it into the hands of an aide, while Lamarck, with tears of humiliation rolling down his cheeks, tried to explain what was in it.
Had Napoleon known what was in the book, he would certainly have liked it even less. Rather than consolidating power, Lamarck’s theory distributed it throughout the living world.
After Lamarck died, Cuvier emerged as the victor who wrote the history, quite literally. While director of the National Institute, he wrote Lamarck’s official ‘eulogy’, which is surely the nastiest eulogy ever written, dismissing Lamarck’s theory as poetry rather than science. This set the tone for assessments of Lamarck’s ideas for a long time to come.
Following Cuvier, many others ridiculed Lamarck’s science. Because it emerged in the midst of the French Revolution and replaced God with the creative agency of living organisms, it smelled to contemporaries of atheism, revolution and regicide. These ill odours promised trouble not only for Lamarck and Lamarckism but for evolutionary theory more generally.
Darwin struggled over his relations with Lamarck. He drew, importantly, on Lamarck’s theory in formulating his own, but he also insisted on the distinctness of the two. As he wrote to his geologist friend Charles Lyell in 1863, he knew that an association with Lamarckism would be ‘very injurious’ to his theory’s reputation. Still, Darwin did retain various forms of agency within the evolving organism, including Lamarck’s principle that animal behaviours produced heritable effects on their bodies, which Darwin called ‘the inherited effects of use and disuse’. Natural selection, he believed, worked in conjunction with these other factors. But after Darwin died, his followers around the turn of the 20th century eliminated all traces of Lamarckism from their neo-Darwinist theory, rendering organisms as passive as they had been at the hands of Cuvier’s divine creator. The eradication of Lamarckism became the defining feature of neo-Darwinism.
A founding figure in this movement was the German biologist August Weismann. In the 1880s, he began to draw a sharp distinction between somatic (body) cells and germ (reproductive) cells. He said that no changes taking place in the somatic cells could ever be transmitted to the germ cells. This is the so-called Weismann barrier, eliminating the possibility of ‘inheritance of acquired characters’. In a rather cruel series of experiments, Weismann chopped the tails off several generations of mice in order to show that their offspring had perfectly healthy tails. He himself acknowledged that this result had no real bearing on Lamarck’s theory: neither Lamarck nor Darwin had ever claimed that amputations were inherited, only internally generated changes. But Weismann reckoned it would defeat popular belief in the inheritance of acquired characteristics. The mouse-tail experiments remain rhetorically powerful, and still appear in biology textbooks today.
Weismann emphasised that his approach to science rested on the assumption of a divine presence behind the whole process. He assured his readers that his biology didn’t just leave room for a ‘Universal Cause’ but actually demanded one. He wrote of a ‘Final Cause’ operating ‘behind’ the mechanism of the universe. All agency lay with this remote, divine presence and none with the evolving, mortal beings themselves. Therefore, Weismann said his science was ‘absolutely opposed’ to materialism.
There’s a eugenic logic in the idea that living beings are the passive objects of genetic programming and outside forces
The ‘Weismann barrier’ – the exclusion of Lamarckian inheritance – became the central principle of neo-Darwinism. After the identification of the structure of the DNA molecule in 1953, Francis Crick restated the Weismann barrier as the ‘central dogma of molecular biology’: DNA transcription runs only in one direction, from DNA through RNA to protein, never in the reverse, from which Crick drew the implication that acquired characteristics could never be inherited. Nothing a living being did could make a difference to the machinery of inheritance.
Denying the agency of organisms has not been a purely intellectual mistake. It has had implications reaching far beyond the debates of scientists. For one thing, there’s a eugenic logic built into the idea that living beings, including humans, are the passive objects of genetic programming and outside forces. Essentially all the neo-Darwinists of the early through middle decades of the 20th century were fervent eugenicists. Crick is an example. ‘Let us take up this whole question of eugenics,’ he exhorted his colleagues at a London conference in 1963. ‘I do not see why people should have the right to have children,’ he observed. He mused that it would be a fairly simple matter for a government to sterilise the whole population by putting some chemical in the food supply and then reverse the effect only for those people ‘licensed to bear children’. These were not fringe views; eugenic theories and programmes were mainstream in neo-Darwinist biology for much of the 20th century, and some still linger today.
Additionally, the idea of the fundamental passivity of organisms has helped inform two centuries of environmental destruction, as it has encouraged people to regard the living world as raw material to manipulate and exploit for economic and imperial gain. Lamarck, who witnessed the Industrial Revolution firsthand, warned of this in his last work. He pointed out deforestation and its consequences, and he lamented that people were selfish and shortsighted, waging wars and plundering nature for riches, annihilating their own means of conservation. He concluded despairingly: ‘It looks as if man were destined to exterminate himself after making the globe uninhabitable.’
From the start, Lamarck’s science of self-making, world-creating living beings antagonised the powerful. In contrast, the dominant tradition in evolutionary biology from the end of the 19th century, largely abiding still today, renders living organisms as the objects of external forces, posing no threat to gods or monarchs or other worldly powers. Evolutionary science became the reductive account of an essentially passive living world. By this standard, Lamarck’s vision of a world continually in the making, shaped by its own mortal inhabitants, wasn’t even wrong: it just wasn’t science. But science, like living beings, is always changing. Evolutionary biology today is full of exhilarating unrest.
Lamarck’s ideas have been making a comeback in several areas of biology. For instance, the study of epigenetic inheritance – involving structures outside the DNA that influence gene expression – has demonstrated, throughout every kind of organism, that characteristics acquired in an individual lifetime can indeed be inherited. Many of the examples that scientists have been finding involve the responses of various kinds of animals to climate change. An example is the spiny chromis, a slender damselfish inhabiting the coral reefs of the Pacific. In 2015, marine biologists showed that its metabolism responds to the higher water temperatures brought on by climate change by transforming in myriad ways, and that these changes are inherited from generation to generation. The spiny chromis isn’t alone. In 2020, scientists found that the reef-building coral that provides the damselfish’s home also responds to changing ocean temperatures and salinity with epigenetic changes that it passes on to its offspring.
German evolutionary geneticists have found that wild guinea pigs subjected to heat-stress show heritable alterations in their livers, which play a crucial role in metabolic regulation; and biologists in the United States and Kenya have shown that the metabolisms of baboons also heritably change in response to differences in their food supply. In fact, it seems increasingly apparent that all kinds of living beings respond to their changing environments with heritable epigenetic transformations. These might provide means of rapid adaptation that precedes, and perhaps shapes, slower genetic changes.
Bird nests, beaver dams, termite mounds – the evidence of organisms creating their own environments is ubiquitous
Another area of current interest is the role of animal behaviour in directing natural selection. Martha Muñoz, an ecologist and evolutionary biologist at Yale University in Connecticut, studies a kind of lizard in the Dominican Republic called the anole, which is closely related to the iguana. Muñoz has shown that, as these lizards moved from the coast up into the mountains, reaching as high as 3,000 metres, they adapted to the much colder temperatures by being ‘behaviourally nimble’, for example, by basking on the sun-drenched boulders. Rather than showing physiological differences that would give them greater cold tolerance, they have rapidly evolved shorter legs and flatter skulls, enabling them to hide from predators in the crevices of the rock. ‘Far from being passive vessels at the mercy of their circumstances,’ Muñoz told the journal Science in 2022, ‘organisms can influence evolution directly.’ Her research confirms that ‘behaviour is one of the major architects of evolution’ and that ‘organisms can influence natural selection.’
The theory of ‘niche construction’ offers another example. The central principle of this theory is that organisms contribute to shaping their environments, creating the ecological niches that exert selective pressures on them. Bird nests, beaver dams, termite mounds, worm and mole burrows, spiderwebs, beehives – the evidence of organisms creating their own environments is ubiquitous. John Odling-Smee, the scholar who coined the term ‘niche construction’, wrote in 2024 that biologists should rethink what the theory of evolution should be about: not just natural selection acting upon organisms in given environments but ‘the coevolution of organisms with their environments’.
Neo-Darwinism, with its passive model of living beings, has been teetering on its throne. One current movement, known as the extended evolutionary synthesis, seeks to widen the evolutionary picture beyond the neo-Darwinist focus on random genetic variation and natural selection, in part by including behavioural and even cultural elements. Many animals have something like what we call culture in humans, and this includes cultural forms that are inherited and passed down. Lamarck knew this. He wrote that intelligent animals – birds and mammals – could create new habits and ways of life that would be maintained over generations. There is overwhelming and definitive evidence that all kinds of animals – birds, primates, whales, fish, insects – learn from one another and have cultural traditions that are handed down from generation to generation. Communication and social learning make a crucial difference to survival and reproduction, and therefore to evolution. Animals communicate vitally important things to one another including information about food, predators, songs, migration routes and where to find a mate. To give just one example, humpback whales develop different approaches to hunting from one community to another – one in the Northeast Pacific, another in the Gulf of Maine – and teach these to their offspring.
These innovative humpback whales, along with the nimble mountain lizards of the Dominican Republic and legions of other living things – all of them, in fact – exemplify what Lamarck knew and mainstream evolutionary biology has long denied. Living beings are active, self-making, and world-making. They are creators, even the humblest of them. The implication, deeply unpopular with autocrats from Napoleon onward, can be a source of hope: neither creativity nor transformative power can ultimately be controlled or monopolised.

Born in Israel, barred from IDF service: 43 young people fight to enlist
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
10:59:14 UTC
19:59:14 KST

Rain Arfon, Moliv Vicente, Mariel Aya Ay and John Ray Dalisay are still waiting to receive their military draft notices. The four 20-year-olds finished high school some time ago, but unlike their former classmates, they know that their draft notices, if they ever arrive, will come only after a prolonged struggle.
Born in Israel to parents who arrived from the Philippines as migrant workers, the young men and women petitioned Israel's Supreme Court, sitting as the High Court of Justice, late last year alongside approximately 40 others in similar circumstances. They had one request: to enlist in the Israel Defense Forces.
Last month, the state finally presented its position in response to the petition, but it offered little hope. According to the State Attorney's Office, whose position also reflects those of the Defense Ministry and the Population and Immigration Authority, the matter must be decided by the country's political leadership. That means waiting until a new government is formed.
"At this time, given the election period we are in, the sensitivity of the issue and the absence of a serving interior minister, it is appropriate for the matter to be brought before senior policymakers only after a new government is formed," the state wrote in its response to the petition.
"These are individuals residing in Israel illegally who are not entitled to any legal status in the country and who seek to enlist in the IDF without first having their civil status in Israel regularized."
Last month, John Ray and Moliv expressed their fears of another postponement in an interview on the "Behind the Uniform" podcast.
"It's really close to the elections. We don't know what will happen by then. We just hope they'll address our situation," Moliv said, referring to the proximity of the deadline for the state's response to Election Day.
The repeated delays have become particularly painful amid the war and the severe shortage of combat troops on the front lines.
"In these months, we could already have completed basic training and moved forward, taken part in something," John Ray said in frustration. "Right now, we're just waiting, and it's a waste of time. There are enough people in our situation to form an entire company."
At the same time, Ray stressed that despite the prolonged wait, his motivation to serve remains strong.
"I don't know why it keeps getting postponed, but people shouldn't think that because we've been rejected so many times, we're losing our spirit," he said. "On the contrary, every postponement gives me more determination, strength and motivation to keep fighting for this goal.
"I know that ultimately I have to fulfill my dream of enlisting in the military. It's important. We're three years into the war, we're dealing with a shortage of soldiers and reservists are being called up for endless rounds of duty."
Speaking to ynet and its parent newspaper Yedioth Ahronoth, John Ray expressed further frustration over the state's response.
"It's a waste of time. It's simply frustrating," he said. "By the time a government is formed and starts functioning, a great deal more time will have passed.
"Our enlistment is highly relevant to the current situation. I had hoped to enlist back in March.
"It feels like they're passing the responsibility to someone else, as though nobody wants to deal with the issue, so they're dumping it on the next government while time keeps passing.
"It's hard for me to understand. In our case, both sides stand to benefit, and the decision to postpone the response yet again is frustrating. We were afraid of another delay, but we hoped it wouldn't happen."
In previous years, young people born in Israel to migrant worker parents were granted legal status under various government decisions. However, those born in Israel approximately 20 years ago were not given the same opportunity to obtain citizenship or regularize their residency status.
As a result, young men and women who graduated from Israeli high schools in recent years have been left living in the country without recognized legal status or a clear future.
Throughout the outgoing government's term, these young people repeatedly tried to resolve their status in Israel, but their efforts were unsuccessful.
Those failures led to the current petition, filed by attorneys Zari Hazan, Meital Lupolianski and Dror Strum on behalf of 43 young men and women.
This time, the petitioners chose to approach the Defense Ministry rather than the Interior Ministry.
Their legal argument rests primarily on a provision of the Defense Service Law that they contend authorizes military recruitment regardless of citizenship. The law refers to those eligible for service as including "permanent residents and persons ordinarily residing" in Israel.
However, the state's response makes clear that under current IDF recruitment policy, people whose legal status in Israel has not been regularized are excluded from military service. Recruitment is limited to Israeli citizens and permanent residents with officially recognized status.

Retired officer: Russian mass strikes unlikely to break Ukrainian resolve
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
10:59:00 UTC
19:59:00 KST

Retired officer: Russian mass strikes unlikely to break Ukrainian resolve
Russia's attack on a passenger train in Dnipro was a war crime, but such strikes rarely break a population's will to resist, said retired Estonian Brig. Gen. Alar Laneman.
Last week, Russian forces struck a train standing at Dnipro Railway Station Thursday morning, killing at least 14 people and injuring at least as many more, according to Ukrainian authorities.
Speaking on ETV's "Ukraina stuudio," Laneman, a retired brigadier general in the Estonian Defense Forces (EDF), said Russia was pursuing a calculated strategy to undermine Ukraine's will, often laying the groundwork for attacks with disinformation campaigns portraying civilian infrastructure as legitimate military targets.
These campaigns will claim, for example, that "'Ukraine is planning a provocation by attacking one of its own cities, villages or critical facilities,'" he explained. "Then the attack happens, and 'See`Ukraine did it.'"
Before the Dnipro strike, Russian messaging had accused Ukraine of using its railways to transport troops, equipment and weapons, but the target, Laneman stressed, was clearly a passenger train.
He said it was a textbook war crime, and evidently intended to shock and mentally wear down the population. "And then hope that the Ukrainian public will pressure the government into surrendering or something," he added. "We've seen this throughout the war."
Russia 'resourceful' in exploiting opportunities
Laneman also acknowledged that Ukraine also lacks the resources to defend all civilian infrastructure against Russian missiles and attack drones, adding that it is particularly difficult to protect because railways and other civilian facilities aren't normally expected to be deliberate targets. Even so, history suggests such tactics rarely work.
"As a rule, these [mass attacks] don't have the effect of breaking a population's resolve to resist," he said. "They simply don't have that effect."
Commenting on the situation in Oleshky, Laneman said it was positive that an agreed ceasefire there had held during the evacuation of residents, although Russia may have used the pause to move additional troops into the area.
"Russia is very, very resourceful when it comes to exploiting any opportunity, and it would be strange if they didn't," he said.

The Sudanese army said Monday that a group of Rapid Support Forces (RSF) members had defected and surrendered to its troops in Damazin, the capital of southeastern Blue Nile state.
The army’s 4th Infantry Division said in a statement that the group surrendered to its forces in Damazin but did not disclose how many members were involved.
The army said the development was the latest in increasing defections from the paramilitary group amid fighting in Blue Nile state.
The group’s commander, Jado Mohammed Hamed Shawqar, provided information concerning the management of military operations in Damazin, according to the statement.
The army said Shawqar also gave information about “Ethiopian support” to the RSF and the participation of foreign mercenaries in the fighting.
There was no immediate comment from the RSF on the army’s statement.
The RSF has seen several defections among its field and political figures in recent months, including political adviser Fares Al-Nour, commander Maj. Gen. Al-Nour Ahmed Adam, known as Al-Nour Al-Qubba, and field commander Ali Rizkallah, known as Al-Savana.
On Aug. 13, the Sudanese army announced that a force comprising 21 commanders and 270 personnel had joined its ranks. Another group of four commanders and 318 members, led by Lt. Col. Musa Ali Ahmed, defected on Aug. 19.
The announcement came a day after the Sudanese government said it had filed complaints against Ethiopia with the UN Security Council and the African Union Peace and Security Council, accusing Addis Ababa of hosting the RSF and allowing drone attacks from its territory on civilian facilities and power stations in Sudan.
There was no immediate comment from Ethiopia on the accusations.
Sudan’s humanitarian crisis has continued to worsen amid the war between the army and the RSF, which erupted in April 2023 over disagreements concerning the integration of the country’s military forces.
The conflict has killed tens of thousands of people and displaced around 13 million, according to UN and international estimates.

Mexican Grand Prix, told Sky.
                                    
"Keeping 12 feels like a new starting point—a chance to rebuild
and try to repeat what I've achieved.
                                    
"It's a way to stay focused for the coming year.
                                    
"I'm starting to realize what I've achieved.
                                    
"The final lap was truly emotional; I eased off the pace
completely because I had tears in my eyes—I was struggling to
even see the track.
                                    
"It was an incredibly moving experience, and it still is now.
                                    
"It's an amazing moment, especially being able to share it with
my family, my team, and my friends".
                                    
The Bologna native thanked Mercedes for helping him stay
grounded.
                                    
"One thing I've been taught is to try to stay true to
yourself—no matter how much success you achieve, where you
happen to be, or how fast you're moving," he said.
                                    
"It's crucial to always keep your feet on the ground and take
the time to enjoy these moments.
                                    
"There's also a fantastic group of people here who play a vital
role in helping me do that. A special thanks goes to them, too.
                                    
"People mostly see us out on the track and don't see everything
that goes on behind the scenes, but I can guarantee that the
work these guys do is incredible".
                                    
He also spoke about being lifted onto the shoulders of two of
the sport's all-time greats, Max Verstappen and Lewis Hamilton,
on Sunday's podium.
                                    
"I'll have it (the photo) framed and put it up on the wall at
home," he said.
                                    
"It was incredible. These are the kinds of moments that stay
with you for the rest of your life".
                                    
Antonelli said the moment he realized he could actually win the
title was when he came from the back of the grid to win the
Italian Grand Prix at Monza in September.
                                    
"It has been an incredible season," he continued.
                                    
"We have been very consistent.
                                    
"Now we will try to finish on a high note: there are still some
races left, and it would be great to wrap things up with some
strong results, looking ahead to 2027."
He also said Ayrton Senna was his model.
                                    
"Ayrton will always remain a source of inspiration—not just as a
driver, but as a person, too," he said.
                                    
"This year, I've often gone back and watched many of his
interviews to get a better sense of how he approached races and
the season as a whole.
                                    
"Along with my family, he will always be a point of reference
for me".

Kazakhstan's population increases by over 133,000 in 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
10:55:46 UTC
19:55:46 KST

Kazakhstan's population increases by over 133,000 in 2026
Kazakhstan's population continues to grow, reaching 20,633,529 as of October 1, 2026, an increase of 133,707 since the beginning of the year, Qazinform News Agency reports, citing the Bureau of National Statistics.
The population grew by 28,710 over August and September, up from 20,604,819 on August 1.
Natural population growth accounted for most of the increase, with births exceeding deaths by 128,303 since the beginning of the year. Net migration contributed another 5,404 people.
Population growth was largely concentrated in urban areas, where the number of residents rose by 169,048 to 13,254,158 as of October 1. Meanwhile, the rural population declined by 35,341 to 7,379,371.
Migration was a key factor behind this gap. Despite natural population growth, rural areas recorded a net migration loss of 84,850 people, while urban areas gained 90,254 residents through migration.
Astana recorded the largest population increase among Kazakhstan's three major cities, adding 67,974 residents since the beginning of the year. As of October 1, the capital's population stood at 1,707,150, up from approximately 1.69 million on August 1.
Almaty remained Kazakhstan's largest city, with a population of 2,392,105, an increase of 44,002 since the beginning of the year. Shymkent's population grew by 26,693 to 1,320,743.
Among the regions, Turkistan remained the most populous, with 2,141,409 residents, despite a decline of 7,796 since the start of the year. Meanwhile, Almaty region saw its population rise by 21,890 to 1,618,422.
Population declines were also reported in Zhambyl, Karaganda, Kyzylorda, Kostanay, and several other regions, while Ulytau region remained the least populated, with 217,046 residents.
Earlier, Qazinform News Agency reported that nearly 2.9 million people aged 60 and over live in Kazakhstan.

Kazakhstan and Azerbaijan advance Caspian Bridge ferry system and intermodal terminal projects
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Kazakhstan and Azerbaijan advance Caspian Bridge ferry system and intermodal terminal projects
Nurlan Zhakupov, Chairman of the Management Board of Samruk-Kazyna JSC, held a meeting with senior representatives of AZCON Holding, Azerbaijan’s state-owned holding company, Qazinform News Agency cites the press service of Samruk-Kazyna.
The meeting focused on opportunities to strengthen economic ties between Kazakhstan and Azerbaijan, with particular attention to joint initiatives in the transport, logistics and maritime sectors.
As part of the meeting, the sides signed two documents aimed at further developing transport and logistics connectivity between the two countries.
The first agreement establishes a framework for cooperation between Samruk-Kazyna JSC and AZCON Holding on the development of a new trans-Caspian ferry system, known as Caspian Bridge. The document sets out the key principles and areas of collaboration for preparing and implementing the project.
The second document, a Term Sheet signed by Kazakhstan Temir Zholy JSC and Azerbaijan Railways CJSC, outlines the principal terms for establishing an intermodal freight terminal and creating a joint venture.
The initiative is intended to expand container and other freight transportation between the two countries, with a particular focus on the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route (TITR).
The agreements mark a further step towards strengthening Kazakhstan-Azerbaijan cooperation and developing transport infrastructure and logistics opportunities across the Caspian region.

Five months without losing positions and 1,700 targets hit: the week's results at the front
Kyiv • UNN
Ukrainian units are holding back Russian forces in several directions. The "Rarog" Brigade hit 1,700 targets, while the 32nd Brigade has held its positions for five months.
Throughout the week, Ukrainian units continued to hold back Russian forces in several sectors of the front, maintain defensive positions, and inflict losses on the enemy. The results included 1,700 targets hit by operators of the "Rarog" Brigade over seven days and five months of holding positions by the 32nd Separate Mechanized Brigade without enemy advances. This was reported by the General Staff of Ukraine, UNN writes.
Details
In the Pokrovsk sector, the 32nd Separate Mechanized Steel Brigade destroys an average of about 110 Russian servicemen every week. To ensure logistics on the front line, soldiers are increasingly using unmanned ground vehicles. The brigade was also among the first in this sector to begin using strike ground robots.
In the Oleksandrivskyi sector, paratroopers of the 79th Separate Tavria Air Assault Brigade are conducting offensive operations and destroying the enemy.
In the Prydniprovske sector, marines of the 34th Separate "Borysfen" Brigade are taking part in demining Kherson and the surrounding areas, as well as escorting civilians into dangerous areas so that they can collect belongings from their homes. During the ceasefire related to the humanitarian mission in Oleshky, the military helped journalists from various countries cover the situation. In addition, the brigade controls the coastal and island zones.
In Kharkiv region, the 113th Separate Territorial Defense Brigade and the 11th Border Guard Detachment are holding their positions and thwarting attempts by Russian forces to infiltrate Ukrainian defensive lines.
The General Staff separately highlighted the work of air defense units. Servicemembers of the 1020th and 1021st Anti-Aircraft Missile and Artillery Brigades of the Air Force are protecting designated facilities, while personnel of the 302nd Anti-Aircraft Missile Kharkiv Brigade are shooting down Russian drones in the northern sector.
Each of these results means cities saved, positions held, and the lives of comrades-in-arms preserved

Less playtime, more revenue: Roblox’s $1.6 billion paradox
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
10:55:31 UTC
19:55:31 KST

Less playtime, more revenue: Roblox’s $1.6 billion paradox
Roblox users spent less time playing, and fewer paid for purchases than a year earlier. Yet quarterly revenue rose 16% to nearly $1.6 billion, Qazinform News Agency reports.
The company’s October 29 shareholder letter shows how those trends can coexist.
Users spent nearly 34 billion hours on Roblox between July and September 2026. The platform averaged 138 million daily active users.
Together, those figures suggest roughly two hours and 40 minutes per daily active user. That estimate uses the company’s rounded figures across the quarter’s 92 days.
The scale remains enormous, but activity fell compared with the same period in 2025. Total hours declined 15%, while the daily audience shrank 9%.
Compared with the previous quarter, however, both measures recovered. Hours increased 17%, and daily active users rose 12%.
Why revenue rose while sales fell
Roblox recorded $1.572 billion in quarterly revenue, compared with $1.360 billion a year earlier.
Its bookings moved in the opposite direction, falling 12% to $1.697 billion. This measure tracks sales activity, mostly purchases of the platform’s virtual currency, Robux.
The difference comes partly from when Roblox records those purchases as revenue.
A virtual currency purchase counts toward bookings first. Roblox then recognizes much of that money as revenue over time.
That means earlier purchases can support today’s revenue even when current sales decline. Revenue and bookings are separate measures and cannot be added together.
Fewer paying users, higher spending per payer
Roblox averaged 30 million paying users each month, down 16% year over year. However, average bookings per monthly paying user increased 5%.
The company is also adjusting how it recommends games.
“In Q2’26, we began optimizing our Recommended for You (RFY) algorithm for long-term retention,” Roblox said.
Roblox said its Plus subscribers averaged twice the playtime of users without the subscription. They also spent seven times as much Robux.
Those comparisons describe subscriber behavior; they do not establish that subscribing caused higher spending.
The company also plans to introduce skippable video advertisements before gameplay.
Billion-dollar revenue, but still a loss
Roblox’s revenue growth did not produce a net profit. The company reported a $230 million quarterly loss, compared with $258 million a year earlier.
Developer Exchange expenses totaled $403 million. Through that program, eligible creators exchange earned Robux for real money.
Earlier, Qazinform News Agency explored how Roblox’s “Grow a Garden” became popular among children in Kazakhstan.

Prosecutors raise reward for arrest of “Bolle Jos” to €2m
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
10:53:54 UTC

Prosecutors raise reward for arrest of “Bolle Jos” to €2m
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Dutch prosecutors have raised the reward for the capture of the convicted drugs baron Jos Leijdekkers, nicknamed “Bolle Jos” or “Chubby Jos”, to €2 million.
The tenfold increase is an attempt to raise the pressure on the 35-year-old, who is believed to be hiding out in Sierra Leone, where Dutch authorities say he is in a relationship with the daughter of president Julius Maada Bio.
Leijdekkers is the most wanted fugitive on Europol’s list of top criminals after Dutch and Belgian courts sentenced him to a total of 103 years in prison in absentia. The reward is the largest of its kind ever offered by the Netherlands.
Two years ago was found guilty in Rotterdam of transporting nearly seven tonnes of cocaine in six shipments, an armed robbery in Finland and ordering an assassination. He has denied all involvement in drug trafficking through his lawyers.
The prosecution service said information leading to his arrest would be handled in strict confidence and not shared with other police forces or the authorities in the west African country.
Dutch justice minister David van Weel said last month that the European Union had withheld €18 million in budget aid to Sierra Leone because of its continued refusal to hand over Leijdekkers.
But the country’s leaders said the payments had been delayed because of “procedural issues” and had nothing to do with the row over Leijdekkers’ extradition.
Earlier Sierra Leone said the Dutch pressure in the case was “scandalous” and accused Van Weel of engaging in “neo-colonialism”.
Chief minister David Moinina Sengeh said: “Hand on heart, our security intelligence does not know where Leijdekkers is. If they know, show the pictures.”

French school protests resume on smaller scale after holiday break
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
10:53:39 UTC
19:53:39 KST

French school protests resume on smaller scale after holiday break
French students back from autumn holidays blocked some high schools on Monday, determined to revive last month's protest movement despite a handful of concessions from the government during the break. Blockades took place in several cities across France, including Paris, Marseille and Rennes.
French high school student protests resumed on Monday on a much smaller scale than in past weeks as pupils returned from a two-week break, with youngsters trying to blockade a few high schools in Paris, Marseille and Rennes, French media reported.
By 08:30 GMT some 41 high schools – about 1 percent of those nationwide – were blockaded, the Education Ministry said.
In the southern city of Marseille, several garbage bins were stacked in front of the entrance to one high school on Monday morning.
"We've resumed the movement because we were supposedly given answers, but... it's clearly not enough," 16-year-old Meriem told AFP, perched on one of the dumpsters.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Hundreds of France's more than 3,000 high schools were blockaded in the weeks prior to the break. The protests, which began in the Paris suburbs in September, have spread across France and broadened beyond education to focus on the cost of living, drawing in trade unionists and activists and sometimes turning violent.
Read more'We're fed up': Paris students rise up in a movement that shows no sign of slowing
A wave of so-called "Gen Z" protests has swept across European countries including Germany, Italy, Belgium and Albania, driven by grievances including the cost of living, the poor state of schools and perceived corruption.
Last month French protests degenerated into violent clashes with the police and outright riots in several cities, with shops looted, in a test for President Emmanuel Macron's minority government.
"In terms of blockades – or rather, attempted blockades – the phenomenon is very marginal. We're talking about just a handful of units, a few individual schools," Education Minister Edouard Geffray told radio station France Inter on Monday morning.
He said protests are allowed but preventing access to schools is illegal.
Police officers were present, TV footage showed, though not in full anti-riot gear.
Students want the renovation of aging schools, more teachers, more university places and the end of a university admissions system they see as socially unfair.
Read moreWhat France's student protesters want – and what the government is offering
Geffray offered last week to cap class sizes at 28, dedicate €4 billion ($4.47 billion) to renovating schools, create 15,000 new places for students in higher education and a new admission system by 2028.
But high school student representatives said the offers were not enough and that they would keep protesting.
(FRANCE 24 with Reuters and AFP)

Help Ukrainian soldiers survive the cold: Latvia launches winter clothing donation campaign
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
10:53:03 UTC
19:53:03 KST

The Latvian charity organization "Tavi draugi" and the state-owned postal company "Latvijas Pasts" are organizing their seventh knitted clothing donation campaign to support Ukrainian soldiers, running from November until the end of March next year.
Residents are encouraged to donate knitted socks, hats, scarves and gloves, which are urgently needed on the front lines and in military hospitals. The recommended sock sizes range from 37 to 45, while neutral, inconspicuous colors are preferred for all knitted items.
The organizers explain that Latvijas Pasts will deliver donated knitted items to the charity Tavi draugi free of charge. The organization will then gradually transport the donations to Ukraine according to requests from Ukrainian soldiers.
Donations can be sent through Latvijas Pasts' blue parcel lockers across Latvia or handed in at the company's customer service locations during opening hours.
To send knitted items free of charge using a parcel locker, donors must register their shipment at mans.pasts.lv, select domestic shipping within Latvia and choose a parcel locker as both the sending and receiving method. The designated receiving parcel locker is "Mārupe, Ziemeļu iela 10, Lidosta Rīga, Mārupes pag., Mārupes nov., LV-1044".
After entering the sender's and recipient's details, including a telephone number, donors must enter the discount code "TAVIDRAUGI" in the promotional code field and click "Apply". Once the total shipping cost is reduced to zero euros, they should select the "Pay" button to complete the process.
The generated shipping label must be printed and attached to the parcel. If donors cannot print it themselves, they can do so at a parcel locker by entering the shipment number or scanning the barcode. 
Parcels can be deposited at any Latvijas Pasts parcel locker.
 The maximum parcel dimensions are 39 × 38 × 58 centimeters, and the weight must not exceed 31.5 kilograms.
When handing in donations at a customer service location, the parcel must be labeled: Campaign "TAVIDRAUGI", Ziemeļu iela 10, Mārupes novads, LV-1000.
Knitted items can also be handed over to a postal worker if the customer already receives other postal or payment services at home. However, the "Postman at Home" service cannot be requested solely for the purpose of donating items.
The campaign organizers also note that, as the cold season begins, Ukrainian soldiers are requesting additional supplies, including chemical hand warmers, thermal underwear, tea, cold and flu medication, and other essential items to help them stay warm.
Since the beginning of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Tavi draugi and Latvijas Pasts have delivered tens of thousands of kilograms of knitted items donated by Latvian residents to Ukraine.

Denmark seeks EU approval to introduce social media age limit of 15
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
10:52:22 UTC
19:52:22 KST

Denmark’s government will ask the European Commission to let it introduce a minimum age of 15 for access to social media while negotiations on common EU rules continue.
The move follows a report by Danish newspaper Politiken that the Commission will not approve new national laws restricting access to social platforms for 12 months. The announcement could delay Denmark’s planned age limit, which was due to take effect on July 1, 2027.
Minister for Digitalization Christina Egelund, a member of the Moderates party, criticized the Commission’s position in a written response to Danish news agency Ritzau.
“I am disappointed and bewildered by the EU Commission’s announcement. It is not reasonable that the Commission creates a vacuum where the protection of children and young people is lower than it could have been,” she said.
The government has agreed on a national age limit of 15 with Venstre, Denmark’s Liberal Party, and the Conservative People’s Party. Under the plan, a bill would be presented at the beginning of 2027 and take effect that July.
Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, a Social Democrat, has described the agreement as a historic step concerning children’s access to platforms such as TikTok and Snapchat.
But Christel Schaldemose, a Danish Social Democrat in the European Parliament, told Politiken that the Commission’s announcement could mean the age limit cannot be introduced for another three years.
Schaldemose was the European Parliament’s chief negotiator on the Digital Services Act, the EU law regulating online platforms. She believes the Commission is holding back national measures because it has proposed common rules to protect children online.
That proposal must be negotiated between the European Parliament and EU member states.
Egelund supports common European rules but says Denmark should be allowed to act while that work continues.
“It will take a long time before the new rules have an effect in reality, and we have already waited for the Commission for a year since 25 member states called on the Commission to act in the Jutland Declaration during the Danish EU presidency,” she said.
The minister said she was prepared to withdraw the Danish law once common EU rules took effect. Until then, she wants member states to be able to introduce their own measures.
“I will pursue this further and discuss both with the Commission and with the other member states that are also being held back in the fight to protect children and young people online,” she said.
Egelund did not say whether the government still expected the Danish age limit to take effect on July 1, 2027.

Two men holding hands punched in suspected hate crime
Two men walking hand in hand in Roskilde were punched in the face early Sunday after a group of men approached and asked whether they were homosexual, police said.
Central and West Zealand Police described the attack as unprovoked and said they were treating it as a hate crime.
One man from the group punched both men with a clenched fist. One of the victims fell to the ground after being struck. The group then left the scene.
The attack took place on Jernbanegade in Roskilde, west of Copenhagen. Police received the report at 4:37 a.m.
A hate crime involves a criminal offense committed with a discriminatory motive, such as attacking someone because of their sexual orientation. Such a motive can lead to a harsher sentence.
Police described the attacker as light-skinned and of average build, wearing a black shirt, black trousers and black shoes.
Investigators are seeking witnesses and obtaining surveillance footage from cameras in the area.
Support for Denmark’s largest left wing party falls to its lowest since 2022
A new poll shows the governing party losing support after disputes over student grants and its choice of a political adviser.
Denmark’s Socialist People’s Party, a left-wing party known as SF, has fallen to 9.4% in a Voxmeter poll for Danish news agency Ritzau.
It is the party’s lowest result with the polling institute since December 2022. SF won 11.6% of the vote in the March 24 election, becoming the second-largest party in the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament.
The latest poll places it fifth, behind the center-left Social Democrats, the right-wing Danish People’s Party, the economically liberal Liberal Alliance and the center-right Conservative People’s Party.
SF has faced pressure over a government proposal to end SU, Denmark’s state student grants, for students living with their parents.
The cuts form part of the government’s budget proposal. SF accepted the measure as part of a compromise, despite its record of defending the grants.
Party leader Pia Olsen Dyhr has said “it is no secret that this is not something we came up with”.
Olsen Dyhr, who is minister for economic and interior affairs, previously faced scrutiny after hiring a special adviser who had been accused of harassment several years earlier. The adviser left shortly afterward.
Last week, Signe Munk stepped down as minister for cities, rural areas and transport because of stress. Fellow SF member Karina Lorentzen Dehnhardt replaced her.
Venstre, Denmark’s center-right Liberal Party, has 6.5% support in the same poll.
The party expelled lawmaker Preben Bang Henriksen last week after he refused to promise that he would follow the party line in future votes. Before that, Søren Gade left parliament because he could no longer identify with the policies set out by Venstre leader Troels Lund Poulsen.
Voxmeter conducted telephone and online interviews with a representative sample of 1,007 people over 18 between October 26 and November 2. The maximum margin of error for individual parties is plus or minus 2.5 percentage points.
Supermarket refrigeration systems targeted in three European Countries
Supermarkets in Sweden, Belgium and Luxembourg have reported incidents affecting their refrigeration systems, with one Swedish store saying hackers set the temperature to 50 degrees.
Several Ica stores and six Coop stores in Sweden were affected, according to Swedish newspaper Aftonbladet. In Belgium and Luxembourg, Dutch supermarket group Ahold Delhaize confirmed that someone had tampered with its cooling systems’ temperature settings, Reuters reported.
An Ica store in Sjöbo said on Facebook that its equipment had been hacked and staff were throwing away goods.
“We are incredibly sorry, and we are working on throwing everything out and getting it up and running again,” the store wrote.

That attack involved thermostats made by Danish company Danfoss. The company told Danish news agency Ritzau at the time that “a limited number” of systems had been affected.
The reports do not establish whether Danfoss equipment was involved in the latest incidents. The total number of stores affected remains unknown, as does who is responsible.

New EU handling fee applies to non-EU online orders even if purchased before November 1
Danish shoppers who ordered goods from outside the EU before November 1 could still face a new handling fee that took effect Sunday.
The Danish Customs Agency says the fee depends on when a package is declared to customs, not when the order was placed.
Customs declarations typically take place when packages arrive in the EU, meaning purchases made shortly before November 1 may still be affected.
The new EU handling fee is 2 euros, approximately 15 DKK, per item category in a package, regardless of its total value.
Items sharing the same customs commodity code count as one category.
For example, three cotton T-shirts would incur a single 2-euro fee, while a cotton T-shirt and denim jeans would count as two categories, costing 4 euros.
The charge comes on top of a temporary EU customs duty introduced this summer.
That duty amounts to 3 euros per item category for packages worth less than 150 euros.
The measures follow a sharp increase in low-value goods arriving from online retailers outside the EU, particularly China.
In 2025, the Danish Customs Agency recorded 68 million item entries in packages valued below 150 euros.
An analysis found that more than 90 percent of packages entering Denmark contained Chinese goods.
Customs Agency Director Christian Lützen previously described the growth as “a major problem across the EU countries,” arguing that the duty could encourage consumers to shop with Danish businesses.
Chinese online marketplaces Shein and Temu rank among Denmark’s 10 most-used online stores, according to a survey by Dansk Erhverv, the Danish Chamber of Commerce.
Both platforms have faced criticism over product quality and potentially illegal chemicals.

AI ceiling sensors help reduce patient falls by 47 percent in North Jutland hospitals
Seven hospital departments in Denmark’s North Jutland Region have recorded 47 percent fewer patient falls after introducing an AI-powered monitoring system.
The technology uses ceiling-mounted sensors to detect when patients are at risk of falling and alert healthcare staff.
According to the region, the time taken for staff to reach patients after a fall has also decreased by 35 percent.
At the Department of Geriatric Medicine at Regionshospital Nordjylland in Hjørring, the system has been in use for three years.
Head nurse Dorte Nielsen said the sensors have made a difference when caring for older, frail patients, particularly during night shifts with limited staff.
Previously, patients who fell could remain on the floor for extended periods before being discovered, especially if they were unable to call for help.
“Previously, you could not know whether the patient had been lying on the floor for two hours,” Nielsen said.
Before the system was introduced, staff took an average of 10.48 minutes to reach a patient after a fall. That figure has since fallen to 1.53 minutes.
When sensors detect a potential fall, staff receive an alert identifying the patient’s room.
If a fall occurs, the system records a 30-second animated reconstruction that staff can review to assess how the patient landed.
Nielsen said this helps determine whether a doctor should be called or medical scans are necessary.
The system also indicates whether staff are present in a room without identifying individuals or their number.
Nielsen emphasized that protecting privacy remains important so neither patients nor employees feel monitored.
FaceTime while driving costs woman conditional loss of licence in Denmark
A Danish court has ruled that using a correctly mounted phone can still lead to the conditional loss of a driving licence if it distracts the driver from traffic.
A 46-year-old woman has been given a conditional driving ban after using FaceTime while driving on a motorway near Copenhagen.
Although her phone was correctly mounted in the car, Glostrup District Court found that the video call distracted her to such an extent that she failed to pay sufficient attention to the traffic around her.
The case highlights an important distinction for motorists in Denmark: using a mounted or hands-free phone while driving may be legal, but drivers can still be penalised if using it causes dangerous or inattentive driving.
The woman was stopped by police on Motorring 3, Copenhagen’s western ring motorway, in Glostrup on January 13.
Before she was stopped, she had failed to react appropriately to vehicles trying to merge onto the motorway. Several motorists had to brake or accelerate to enter the traffic.
Police found that her attention had been directed towards her phone rather than the road ahead.
Glostrup District Court ruled on Wednesday that she had disregarded essential road-safety considerations.
In addition to the conditional loss of her driving licence, she was fined DKK 2,500.
She must now pass both a new theory test and a practical driving test to retain her licence, according to the prosecution service at Copenhagen Vestegn Police.
“The case emphasises how important it is to keep your focus on traffic when driving a car – even if the phone is correctly mounted,” assistant prosecutor Sabrina Berggren said.
Although the woman was not holding the phone, the FaceTime conversation affected her driving and therefore road safety, Berggren said.
Hands-free does not mean distraction-free
The Danish Road Safety Council (Rådet for Sikker Trafik) also warns motorists that hands-free calls can be distracting.
Jakob Bøving Arendt, CEO of the council, said in a written comment to Ritzau that inattention is one of the major causes of deaths on Danish roads.
Although using a hands-free phone while driving is legal, the council recommends limiting its use because conversations can reduce a driver’s mental attention, he said.

Temu drops sharply in popularity among Danish online shoppers
The Chinese-owned shopping platform has fallen from third to tenth place among Denmark’s most-used online stores, while second-hand marketplace Vinted is gaining ground.
Temu has lost significant ground among online shoppers in Denmark over the past year.
In the third quarter of 2025, the Chinese-owned platform was the third most popular online store among Danish consumers. A year later, it has fallen to tenth place, according to the latest E-commerce Tracker from the Confederation of Danish Industry (DI).
The quarterly survey, conducted by research company Epinion, asks Danish consumers where they made their most recent online purchase.
Mie Bilberg, chief consultant for e-commerce at DI, says new customs rules may help explain Temu’s decline.
Previously, Danish consumers could order very cheap products directly from China without paying customs duty on low-value packages. That advantage has now been reduced.
“You used to be able to order a pack of hair elastics directly from China and have it delivered to your home in Næstved for just a few kroner,” Bilberg said.
When extra charges are added, she said, buying the same product from a Danish retailer such as supermarket chain Føtex can become more attractive.
“It is a step towards European webshops being able to compete on more equal terms with the Chinese ones,” she said.
Under the new rules, packages worth less than 150 euros are subject to a customs charge of three euros. Many such shipments were previously exempt. From November 1, an additional handling fee of two euros will also apply.
Second-hand shopping gains ground
While Temu is losing popularity, second-hand marketplace Vinted remains Denmark’s second most-used online shopping platform.
Bilberg said the result reflects a broader shift towards buying used goods.
“This aligns with the trend we are seeing both in Denmark and globally, where consumers are buying more second-hand,” she said.
Consumers are increasingly concerned about climate, looking for unique products and trying to make their money go further as everyday expenses remain high, she added.
German fashion retailer Zalando remains the most-used online store among Danish consumers.
Danish health and beauty retailer Matas has moved into third place, replacing Temu.
