Belgian prime minister offers resignation amid budget deadlock
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
10:49:56 UTC
19:49:56 KST

Melike Pala
02 November 2026•Update: 02 November 2026
Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever submitted his resignation to King Philippe on Monday after his five-party coalition failed to agree on the 2027 budget, but the monarch deferred a decision and announced consultations with coalition leaders.
"The King is holding his decision in suspense and will begin consultations with the presidents of the majority parties tomorrow," the Royal Palace said in a statement posted on US social media platform X.
De Wever met the monarch at the Royal Palace in Brussels for more than 90 minutes amid tensions over efforts to address a €10 billion ($11 billion) budget shortfall, according to public broadcaster VRT.
Negotiations have been deadlocked for weeks, with disagreements reportedly centered on the Flemish socialist Vooruit party and the Francophone center-right Reformist Movement (MR).
De Wever had ruled out entering the new year with a provisional budget, which would allow the government to continue operating under the previous year's spending framework.
Under Belgium's constitutional system, the king can decline to accept a prime minister's resignation or keep it under consideration to give coalition partners more time to reach an agreement.
Alternatively, he could accept it, leaving the government in a caretaker capacity with limited powers until a new political arrangement is reached.
The latest standoff follows a similar crisis in late 2025, when the federal government sought to identify around €10 billion in savings.
At the time, De Wever requested a 50-day extension from the king rather than offering to resign.
The coalition eventually reached an agreement on Nov. 24, securing €9.2 billion in savings.

fala’s porto house pairs striped marble with playful geometric forms and sculptural interiors

Unknown Publisher

fala’s porto house pairs striped marble with playful geometric forms and sculptural interiors
an oversized window disguises two floors, while three distinct columns and colorful details challenge the rules of a compact home in portugal.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
FALA ATELIER FITS A HOUSE INTO A SKEWED PORTO PLOT
On a compact plot in Porto, Portugal, fala atelier has completed a house that makes an unusually generous amount of room for geometry. Named House Around a Column, the 120-square-meter residence occupies a site of just 60 square meters, surrounded on all sides by neighboring buildings. Its black-and-white marble facade immediately stands out, with an oversized window and colorful geometric accents offering the first clues to what unfolds inside. Rather than attempting to disguise the constraints of its location, the Portuguese architecture studio turns them into the starting point for a carefully orchestrated series of spatial and visual surprises.
The site itself is anything but straightforward. Its irregular outline presented the architects with the challenge of fitting a functional residence into a distorted footprint. Instead of imposing a conventional rectangular arrangement, fala takes the plot’s longest wall as its principal reference, developing a set of geometric rules that organizes the interior. A continuous circulation route follows this boundary and connects the house’s different levels. Within an otherwise tightly contained volume, the resulting arrangement emphasizes vertical movement, allowing the architecture to make use of height where horizontal space is limited.
THREE GEOMETRIC COLUMNS SHAPE THE DOUBLE-HEIGHT INTERIOR
The ground floor accommodates the house’s secondary functions, while the main living area occupies the first floor. Here, a single uninterrupted room extends between two large windows, creating a sense of openness within the compact structure. Above it, an angular opening in the ceiling, reminiscent of an Ellsworth Kelly composition, introduces a double-height void. Two staircases, each with a distinct character, continue the circulation towards the rooftop. Together, these elements establish a sequence of spatial connections that gives the residence a more complex interior than its modest footprint might suggest.
Three columns, one circular, one hexagonal, and one square, punctuate this vertical arrangement, introducing different geometries into the same architectural composition. In the main living space, a triangular kitchen, a striped floor, and an isolated column form an unlikely but carefully considered ensemble. Unusual handrails and whimsical pieces of furniture add further layers to the interior, where almost every element seems to have been given its own particular shape. The apparent playfulness, however, follows a precise spatial logic, allowing fala to reconcile its collection of forms within a relatively small area.
COLORFUL DETAILS TRANSFORMS THE HOUSE’S FACADES
Facing the street, the house presents a graphic composition of black-and-white marble stripes, interrupted by a window that appears almost too large for the building. Its proportions are deliberate: two openings belonging to different floors are visually combined into a single figure, concealing the division between the levels. The facade becomes an exercise in manipulating scale and perception, allowing the architects to give the compact residence a distinctive presence within the dense urban setting. The contrast between the marble pattern and the oversized opening makes the exterior as geometrically deliberate as the rooms behind it
Color introduces another layer of architectural mischief. A pink circle, a yellow triangle, and a green square serve as a handle, handrail, and shutter, respectively, transforming familiar functional elements into abstract shapes. At the opposite end of the house, the narrow rear facade follows a similar graphic logic. Two windows sit beneath a striped cornice, while a hovering semicircular handrail gives the elevation the faint appearance of a mischievous face. With its calculated geometries and unexpected details, fala’s House Around a Column demonstrates how a constrained urban plot can accommodate an architecture that is precise without feeling entirely serious.
project info:
name: House Around a Column (fala 143)
architects: fala atelier | @fala.atelier
location: Porto, Portugal

Russia Suffers Bloodiest Month of War as 54,400 Troops Killed or Severely Wounded in October
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
10:49:09 UTC
19:49:09 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia Suffers Bloodiest Month of War as 54,400 Troops Killed or Severely Wounded in October
October delivered a devastating blow to Russia’s war effort, as Moscow suffered record battlefield losses while Ukrainian forces reversed its territorial gains, reclaiming more land than Russian troops managed to seize.
Russia suffered its heaviest monthly military losses since launching its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, with 54,400 Russian troops killed or severely wounded in October 2026, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced on November 1.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Zelenskyy, October marked a record month for Russian military losses, with October 21 setting a new single-day record of 2,250 Russian troops killed or severely wounded.
Despite continued Russian offensive operations, Ukrainian forces also reclaimed more territory than Russia managed to capture during the month.
Ukraine’s Defense Forces liberated 96.2 square kilometers (37.1 square miles) of Ukrainian territory in October, exceeding Russian territorial gains by 10.4 square kilometers (4 square miles), Zelenskyy said.
“We continue to reclaim what is ours,” the Ukrainian president stated, thanking Ukrainian troops and military units for their efforts. The record losses came as Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces (USF) reported their highest monthly results since the beginning of the full-scale invasion.
According to USF commander Robert “Madyar” Brovdi on November 1, Ukrainian drone units struck 64,807 Russian targets throughout October, averaging 2,091 targets per day—approximately one every 41 seconds.
The units also reported 16,796 Russian personnel casualties during the month, their highest monthly figure to date. This represented a 24.71% increase compared with September and a 52.55% increase compared with August.
On October 24 alone, the Unmanned Systems Forces reported 701 Russian personnel casualties, their highest daily total for the month.
Throughout October, Ukrainian drone operators conducted 255,605 combat missions, including approximately 151,500 strike missions and 104,000 reconnaissance flights. Nearly 70% of the reported Russian personnel casualties inflicted by these units occurred along the Dobropillia-Pokrovsk, Oleksandrivka, and Huliaipole sectors of the front.
Brovdi emphasized that the figures cover only the Unmanned Systems Forces and do not include results achieved by other Ukrainian military formations.
Zelenskyy stressed that Russia could end its mounting losses by agreeing to a ceasefire and pursuing diplomatic negotiations. “Russia is losing. We are holding our positions, liberating territory, and ensuring that every day of war costs the aggressor as much as possible,” he said.
Earlier on November 1, Zelenskyy also confirmed that Ukrainian forces had struck a Russian Pantsir-S2 air defense system and an S-400 Triumph command vehicle, with the targeted equipment valued at approximately $70 million. The operation was carried out by Ukraine’s Security Service (SBU) and other Defense Forces units.

Citizenship for money: former top official of the State Migration Service Pimakhova sentenced to 9 years in prison
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
12:48:30 EET
19:48:30 KST

Citizenship for money: former top official of the State Migration Service Pimakhova sentenced to 9 years in prison
Kyiv • UNN
Dina Pimakhova was sentenced to 9 years in prison for bribes of $1,800 and $30,000. The court also banned her from holding government positions for three years.
The High Anti-Corruption Court (HACC) sentenced former First Deputy Head of the State Migration Service of Ukraine Dina Pimakhova to nine years in prison for taking bribes to arrange documents for foreigners. UNN reports this, citing the Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor's Office.
Details
On Monday, November 2, a panel of judges of the High Anti-Corruption Court announced a guilty verdict against former First Deputy Head of the State Migration Service of Ukraine Dina Pimakhova. The court found her guilty of criminal offenses under Part 4 of Article 368 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine, concerning soliciting and receiving an undue advantage on an especially large scale.
In addition to her main punishment, Pimakhova was also barred for three years from holding positions specified by law involving the performance of functions of the state and local self-government, with the exception of elected positions.
What the former SMS official was tried for
According to the investigation, the corruption episodes that formed the basis for the criminal prosecution of Pimakhova took place in 2017, when she was serving as First Deputy Head of the State Migration Service.
In particular, in June 2017, during a meeting with an acquaintance, the official, according to the prosecution, requested $1,800 for assisting in arranging documents for the legal stay in Ukraine of a Vietnamese citizen. The matter concerned obtaining a temporary residence permit valid for one year, with the possibility of subsequently extending it for up to three years. The investigation established that Pimakhova received the specified amount.
Later, according to law enforcement officials, she offered to arrange for an Iranian citizen to obtain Ukrainian citizenship, even though he did not have the necessary legal grounds to acquire it. For assisting with the expedited processing of citizenship, the official requested an additional $30,000.
How Ukrainian citizenship was planned to be arranged
The investigation paid particular attention to the mechanism by which the foreigner was supposed to obtain a Ukrainian passport.
According to the prosecution, Pimakhova proposed using the procedure for acquiring Ukrainian citizenship by territorial origin. To this end, it was allegedly planned to create fictitious grounds that would allow the foreigner to confirm family ties with Ukrainian citizens. In particular, the scheme involved falsifying DNA test results that were supposed to certify nonexistent family ties. These documents could subsequently be used when applying to a court to establish the legal fact of kinship.
A favorable court decision was supposed to serve as the basis for subsequently formalizing Ukrainian citizenship and obtaining an internal passport and a passport for travel abroad. However, the scheme could not be fully implemented because information about the law enforcement agencies' operational measures was disclosed.
NABU special operation and conflict with the SBU
The Pimakhova case gained wide publicity as early as the end of 2017 because of a conflict between Ukrainian law enforcement agencies. At the time, the National Anti-Corruption Bureau was conducting an undercover special operation aimed at exposing a possible corruption scheme in the State Migration Service.
According to the detectives' plan, the operational measures were intended to help identify officials involved in illegally arranging Ukrainian documents for foreigners in exchange for monetary compensation. To document possible corrupt actions, NABU used an agent who contacted Pimakhova and discussed arranging the documents.
At the same time, on September 26, 2017, the official herself approached the Security Service of Ukraine with a statement alleging that NABU representatives had provoked her into taking a bribe. At the end of November, SBU officers detained the anti-corruption bureau's agent during operational measures. After that, NABU stated that the special operation had been disrupted and accused the SBU and the Prosecutor General's Office at the time of interfering in the investigation.
Instead, the State Migration Service claimed that NABU officers had attempted to provoke Pimakhova into accepting an undue advantage.
The events caused a public confrontation between law enforcement agencies and called into question the prospects for the investigation. Subsequently, the criminal proceedings concerning possible provocation of a bribe by NABU detectives were repeatedly closed due to the absence of elements of a crime. The relevant decision was finally made in April 2021. Its legality was upheld by the Appeals Chamber of the HACC.
The investigation and trial lasted for years
Following the events of 2017, the investigation concerning Pimakhova continued.
In March 2018, the Cabinet of Ministers dismissed her from the position of First Deputy Head of the State Migration Service. On December 19, 2019, NABU detectives notified the former official of suspicion. That same month, the High Anti-Corruption Court imposed a preventive measure on her in the form of nighttime house arrest. In June 2020, it was replaced with a personal recognizance obligation.
In December 2020, law enforcement officers completed the pretrial investigation and opened the materials for the defense to review. On June 30, 2021, the indictment was submitted to the High Anti-Corruption Court.
The trial on the merits began in August 2021 and lasted for more than five years. In May 2026, the court completed Pimakhova's questioning, which had lasted for more than three weeks. On October 28, the former official delivered her closing statement, after which the judges retired to the deliberation room to reach a decision.
What Pimakhova stated in her defense
Throughout the trial, the former official denied her guilt and insisted that she had not committed any corruption-related offenses. According to her, she had acted exclusively within the scope of her official powers and could not independently make decisions regarding the processing of documents for foreigners or the granting of Ukrainian citizenship.
Pimakhova also claimed that the NABU agent who established personal contact with her had persistently offered to help her process the documents and had raised the issue of monetary compensation. She explained her conduct during her communication with the agent by saying that she wanted to establish his true intentions.
In her closing statement on October 28, 2026, Pimakhova once again denied the charges. In addition, she spoke about a recent search of her home conducted by employees of the National Police's Department of Internal Security. According to the former official, the law enforcement officers who conducted the search allegedly already knew in advance about a possible guilty verdict in her case.

Japan launches new national agency to boost disaster response
Japan is one of the most disaster-prone places on earth, but it has never had an agency dedicated to dealing with disasters
Japan on Monday launched a new national agency focused on disaster management with the goal of making the country better prepared should there be a megaquake along the Pacific coast or in Tokyo, or an eruption of Mount Fuji.
More than 350 workers at the National Disaster Management Agency will oversee preparedness, emergency response and reconstruction efforts.
The agency is not being created in anticipation of any specific calamity, but rather is meant to fill a gap amid worries about whether the nation is prepared for a crisis along the lines of the 2011 quake and tsunami in northern Japan, which killed nearly 20,000 people, and the subsequent Fukushima nuclear disaster.

Newborn among 15 killed as Myanmar military strikes maternity clinic and school, sources say
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
11:46:45 CET
19:46:45 KST

BANGKOK, Nov 2 (Reuters) - A newborn baby was among at least 15 people killed in Myanmar military strikes at multiple locations over the weekend, including a maternity clinic and a school, an ethnic armed group, an aid worker and rights monitors said on Monday.
The bombings come as the military-backed government, attempting to rebuild diplomatic ties after years of isolation, escalates its campaign to retake territory lost to resistance groups that now control large areas of the country.
A spokesperson for the military-backed government did not immediately respond to requests for comment. It has previously said it is waging a legitimate campaign against “terrorists.”
On Sunday, airstrikes hit four townships in western Rakhine state, where fighting has been fierce in recent weeks as the Arakan Army, which controls most of the state, has neared the capital, Sittwe.
The strikes hit a bridge in Kyauktaw, locations in Kyaukpyu and Pauktaw, and a makeshift clinic and maternity ward in Arakan Army-held Mrauk-U, killing at least 12 people and wounding 32, an Arakan Army spokesperson and an aid worker said.
The week-old baby girl, who has a surviving twin, was due to return home the following day but was “crushed and killed when the building collapsed from the blast,” said Mrauk-U-based aid worker Wai Hun Aung.
Four other people, including healthcare workers, also died, he said.
A day earlier, an airstrike on Loikaw, in Kayah state near the Thai border, hit a school during classes, killing three students and wounding five, the Karenni Human Rights Group (KnHRG) said on Monday.
Thai fighter jets have been carrying out air patrols as the conflict has spilled over the border, damaging homes and injuring at least one person on the Thai side, Thailand’s government said.
Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul said his government has urged Myanmar to exercise caution to ensure the situation does not affect Thailand.
A Y-12 transport aircraft and a fighter jet dropped more than 20 bombs on the Loikaw school, according to KnHRG and Banyar Khun Aung, secretary of the Karenni Interim Executive Council, who said there were no military movements or clashes in the area.
“Targeting a school where young children are learning and repeatedly bombing is an inhumane act that amounts to a war crime,” he said.
CIVIL WAR DISPLACES MORE THAN 3.5 MILLION
Myanmar has been in turmoil since the military ousted Aung San Suu Kyi’s elected government in a 2021 coup, triggering a civil war that the United Nations estimates has killed 100,000 people and displaced more than 3.5 million.
Coup leader turned president Min Aung Hlaing’s military has received support from China, India and Russia. His administration has gained increasing international recognition in recent months, including secret talks with US officials as the Trump administration reverses years of isolation.
But his forces are struggling to dislodge opposition groups and increasingly rely on airstrikes, powered by jet fuel obtained mostly from Iran in shipments disguised with sham paperwork, Reuters reported earlier this year.
United Nations investigators accused Myanmar’s military in August of deliberate aerial attacks on civilian buildings including schools and hospitals.
Myanmar’s foreign ministry said in response to the UN allegations that the military “exercises maximum restraint to avoid civilian harm.”
The weekend attacks follow a deadly wave of strikes a month earlier in Rakhine’s Kyauktaw and Ponnagyun townships that killed at least 58 people at camps for internally displaced civilians, drawing fierce international condemnation.

Argentina’s austerity-hit economy reels towards recession, testing Milei ahead of 2027 vote
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
11:46:42 CET
19:46:42 KST

By Nicolás Misculin
BUENOS AIRES, Nov 2 (Reuters) - At a family-owned factory in Buenos Aires, a machine used to wrap packets of colored socks sits silent.
Eseka still produces nearly 3 million items a month at the factory, including underwear and swimwear for its Cocot and Dufour brands. But like many local businesses, it is struggling to stay afloat. Since President Javier Milei took office nearly three years ago, sales have fallen around 40%, battered by weak consumer demand and competition from cheaper imports as the government has lifted trade restrictions.
That matters in Argentina, where household consumption accounts for about two-thirds of gross domestic product, making any sustained pullback in spending a drag on the broader economy.
Economists says the economy likely slipped into a recession in the third quarter, a test of voter patience a year ahead of the October 2027 presidential election, when Milei is widely expected to run for a second term.
Some 32,300 businesses — roughly 6% of the total companies in Argentina — closed in the period from when Milei took power in December 2023 through to July, according to think-tank Fundar.
“The situation is critical,” said Ricardo Kuchikian, who owns Eseka with his brother Gustavo. The firm posted losses last year and shed about 30% of its workforce, according to the brothers. Over half of the circular knitting machines in the sock factory stand idle.
“Consumption has fallen very sharply over the past three years,” Kuchikian said.
In the first nine months of the year consumption in Argentina fell 2.7% compared with the same period in 2025, according to market research firm Scentia, which tracks sales across supermarkets, small retailers and e-commerce platforms.
While Milei’s radical austerity measures have slowed inflation to 30% from a sky-high 200% and brought other macroeconomic imbalances under control, their benefits have yet to reach much of the broader public. The share of Argentines living beneath the poverty line has risen to nearly a third of the population, after falling to an eight-year low in 2025.
To boot, Argentina likely dipped into recession in the third quarter, economists say, driven by austerity and tight monetary policy. A slight rebound is forecast in 2027.
Economic activity is forecast to have contracted for a second consecutive quarter in the July-September period, meeting the common definition of a recession. Official data for the quarter will be released in November.
“Argentina’s economy is technically in a moderate recession,” said Ricardo Delgado, head of consultancy Analytica. GDP already fell 0.6% in the second quarter from the first, and Delgado forecasts a further contraction of around 1.5% for the third quarter.
According to a recent survey by consultancy Giacobbe y Asociados, Milei’s approval rating slipped slightly in October to 36% while disapproval rose to 56%.
To be sure, not all of the economy is suffering. Energy, mining and agriculture have emerged as the winners under Milei’s model, driven by exports and investment in Argentina’s vast shale oil and gas reserves, as well as rising global demand for minerals such as lithium.
But the strength of these export-oriented sectors has so far not offset the slump in other industries tied to the domestic market. Textiles, auto manufacturing, retail and construction have all remained under pressure as consumers continue to feel the squeeze.
Analytica’s Delgado said he expected that two-track economy to continue with “ups and downs” in 2027, warning that household finances were unlikely to improve meaningfully before the election.
Milei has ruled out changes to his economic plan, dismissing as “colossal stupidity” claims that people were unable to make ends meet.
‘AGGRESSIVE COMPETITION’
Investors have cheered Milei’s easing of strict import restrictions, capital and currency controls and other regulations that long weighed on business in Argentina. But for many local firms, the shift has brought a painful adjustment, exposing them to cheaper imported goods just as domestic demand weakens.
Official data from August showed manufacturing fell 3.2% year-on-year, retail and wholesale trade dropped 3.5%, and construction declined 2.5%, according to Argentina’s INDEC statistics agency.
“Since the end of 2023, I think sales have fallen 40%,” said Martin Abigador, director of Dakuba, another family-owned business that distributes fabrics.
His company has been unable to offset what he described as “aggressive competition” from foreign imports, mainly from China.
Back at the sock factory, Kuchikian feared that if Milei’s policies continue “national industry could disappear.”
A spokesperson for the government defended the uneven pace of the recovery, saying that growth never occurs uniformly across sectors.
“This is the economic program the president believes in, and he is not going to change it,” the spokesperson said.
(Reporting by Nicolas Misculin; Writing by Lucinda Elliott; Editing by Anthony Esposito and Rosalba O’Brien)

THE HAGUE, Nov 2 (Reuters) - Dutch prosecutors are offering a record €2 million ($2.2 million) reward for information leading to the arrest of convicted cocaine kingpin Jos Leijdekkers, one of Europe’s most-wanted fugitives, the authorities said on Monday.
Leijdekkers is a Dutch national who has been living in Sierra Leone for the past years, the Dutch prosecution service said. Prosecutors have demanded his extradition, but Sierra Leone has refused to cooperate, prompting the European Union to cut some aid to the West African country.
The reward, the highest bounty ever offered by the Dutch authorities, is available to any person who provides the crucial tip leading to Leijdekkers’ arrest, prosecutors said in a statement. According to police, Leijdekkers also goes by the name of Omar Sherrif in Sierra Leone.
The 35-year-old was sentenced in absentia to 24 years in prison by a Dutch court last year for smuggling more than 7 metric tons of cocaine and is also the subject of several ongoing police investigations in the Netherlands. In neighbouring Belgium a court sentenced him to 79 years in prison.
Dutch authorities estimate Leijdekkers has made tens of millions of euros from cocaine smuggling. He is also suspected of money laundering and involvement in the use of extreme violence, they said.

UK to unveil migrant settlement overhaul after months of debate
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
11:46:33 CET
19:46:33 KST

By Sam Tabahriti
LONDON, Nov 2 (Reuters) - Interior minister Shabana Mahmood will on Monday set out reforms to how migrants can settle in Britain, in a bid to balance voter demands for lower immigration with business warnings that tough rules could deter workers who the country still needs.
The reforms are the government’s latest attempt to toughen the rules after the number of arrivals surged following Britain’s departure from the European Union, with post-Brexit immigration policies leading to an influx of healthcare workers and students from around the world.
Despite dropping in the opinion polls since the governing Labour Party elected Andy Burnham as prime minister, Nigel Farage’s populist Reform UK party has been a major factor in driving the push for stricter migration controls.
Under current rules, most migrants can apply for indefinite leave to remain after five years in Britain, enabling them to claim some welfare benefits. Mahmood proposed replacing that with an “earned settlement” system, making 10 years the standard route to permanent residency and requiring some lower-paid workers, including care workers, to wait up to 15 years.
Speaking before Mahmood’s announcement later on Monday, junior business minister Chris McDonald said immigration levels had become unsustainable under the previous government that was led by the Conservatives.
“The plan around immigration is about controlling borders, but it’s also about ensuring that we invest in the young people in our country, so that they can get these jobs, so we don’t have to bring people in from overseas too,” he told Sky News.
MIGRATION FALLING, QUESTIONS REMAIN
The government argues the changes are needed because around 350,000 lower-skilled workers and their dependants who arrived after Brexit are expected to become eligible for settlement in the coming years.
Net migration in Britain fell sharply last year, with official figures showing it almost halved to 171,000 from 331,000 a year earlier, extending a steep decline from a record 944,000 in 2023.
Burnham last week backed the principle that settlement should be “a right to be earned” but the prime minister has also routinely praised foreign care workers after his late father was given support in a care home.
Owners of UK care homes, unions and some Labour lawmakers have said the care system will struggle to operate if international workers are deterred from moving to Britain.
Media reports have suggested Mahmood could soften some elements of the original proposals, potentially exempting care workers already in Britain or offering them a quicker route to settlement.
A cross-party parliamentary committee last year warned that the government did not have a full understanding of how skilled worker visas were affecting different sectors of the economy.
(Reporting by Sam Tabahriti; editing by Andrew Heavens)

As peacekeepers leave Western Sahara, refugees yearn to end a half-century wait
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
11:46:03 CET
19:46:03 KST

TINDOUF, Algeria, Nov 2 (Reuters) - At 51, Binina Mohamed is as old as the conflict that drove her from the Western Sahara region into a refugee camp in southern Algeria, where she has spent her life among tens of thousands of others facing a similar fate.
The confrontation over her native land, often described as Africa’s longest-running territorial dispute, was brought back into focus this weekend by a UN Security Council spat that led to the end of a decades-old peacekeeping mission there.
The Western Sahara conflict pits Morocco, which considers the territory its own, against the Algeria-backed Polisario Front, a political and military organisation that has been seeking a separate state there since the departure of former colonial power Spain in 1976. Peacekeepers have watched over the territory since 1991, when the UN brokered a ceasefire ending years of guerrilla warfare between the two sides.
Thousands of Sahrawis fled hostilities to the Tindouf area in southwestern Algeria, where the Polisario administers five refugee camps.
During a rare visit to the region for foreign media outlets, organised by the Polisario, Mohamed described how her daughters, now in their twenties and thirties, had never visited the region where she was from.
“I do not want them to reach the age of 50 without seeing their homeland,” she told Reuters.
One of her daughters, Safia Al-Saleh, 33, said she hoped her own two children would have a different future.
“I want my children and my grandchildren to study and grow up in their own country, not to grow up like us here, as refugees, with nothing,” she said.
DIPLOMACY IN DEADLOCK
The uncertainty facing refugees such as Mohamed has become a central point of contention in the latest diplomatic battle over Western Sahara.
The dispute heated up last year when the UN Security Council backed Rabat’s plan to give the region autonomy under Moroccan sovereignty as the “most feasible” way to resolve the conflict.
After abstaining last year, Russia this year vetoed a US-drafted resolution that would have reaffirmed that position. When a competing Russian resolution was defeated, it left the UN mission without a renewal of its mandate.
In a speech at the council, Algeria’s UN envoy defended the Polisario’s stance and highlighted a decline in aid and the suffering of refugees in the camps.
Morocco’s envoy in turn said the harsh conditions in the camps were the responsibility of Algeria, a longtime Russian ally, which he accused of denying the refugees their right to return home. He urged Algiers to allow the UN to register the refugees, saying other nationalities were present there.
Algeria and the Polisario say over 160,000 live in the Tindouf refugee camps. UNHCR says it provides assistance to an estimated 90,000 of the “most vulnerable” refugees there.
Morocco disputes both numbers, citing a lack of a UN census, and accuses the Polisario and Algeria of using Sahrawis as political pawns, which Algiers denies.
As the dispute grinds on, Mohamed’s family described daily problems in the camp, including access to water and the harsh climate.
More than 80% of the camps’ residents rely on humanitarian assistance to meet basic food needs, the World Food Programme said in a statement earlier this year.
Another of Mohamed’s daughters, Aisha Salem, a 24-year-old fighter with the Polisario Front, said she wanted a different future for the next generation: “We don’t want to live the way our grandparents did, through displacement and deprivation,” she said.
Mohamed echoed the sentiment. “We want stability. We are tired of being refugees,” she said. “The one who has no land has no life.”
(Reporting by Abdelaziz Boumzar; Writing by Dina Sakr; Editing by Alexander Dziadosz and William Maclean)

Spanish authorities have identified 66 of the 69 people killed in last week’s high-speed train crash near Urda in central Spain, the regional high court said Monday.
Families have been notified in 60 cases involving 36 men and 24 women, according to a Sunday night update from the center coordinating the identification effort.

Another victim was Julieta Gallego, a 24-year-old long jumper, broadcaster Cadena SER reported.
More than 60 specialists have worked in Toledo since Wednesday to carry out autopsies and identify the dead using fingerprints and DNA.
 
- Investigation into collision
The crash occurred Wednesday when a Renfe high-speed train struck the rear of a stationary Iryo train near the town of Urda in Toledo province. Transport Minister Oscar Puente said a failure in the automatic train protection system had brought trains to a halt before a controller authorized the Renfe train to resume normal speed.

Russians Claim New Ka-52 Helicopter Tactic: Shooting Down Drones with S-8 Rockets
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
10:44:03 UTC
19:44:03 KST

Russian military forces have begun using modified S-8 unguided aircraft rockets to intercept aerial targets.
Footage showing the weapon’s use was published on the SMOTRIM platform.
The modernized S-8VC rockets are deployed from Ka-52M attack helicopters equipped with specialized B8V10-UV launch modules.
The key feature of this modification is the incorporation of a proximity fuze, which detonates the warhead near the target without requiring a direct hit.
Target acquisition and tracking are carried out using an electro-optical targeting system featuring both daytime and nighttime imaging channels.
Російські гелікоптери Ка-52 озброїли ракетами С-8ВЦ з повітряним підривом для перехоплення БпЛА.
Джерело: СМОТРИМ https://t.co/uDgu6zdx5F
— Владислав (@Vladislav110528) November 2, 2026
The S-8 family of 80 mm unguided aircraft rockets was originally developed in the Soviet Union in the late 1960s by the OKB-16 design bureau.
The rockets were designed to replace the obsolete 57 mm S-5 rockets and entered service with Soviet military aviation in the 1970s for engaging ground targets.
Structurally, the rocket consists of a warhead with a fuze, a solid-propellant rocket motor, and a folding fin assembly that deploys after the rocket exits the launch pod.
The S-8VC version was specifically developed to counter aerial targets by creating a cloud of fragmentation elements along the flight path of an unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV).
The munition has an 80 mm caliber and an operational range of several kilometers.
Previously, Ka-52 helicopter crews used the onboard cannon and modified 9K121 Vikhr guided missiles to intercept aerial targets.

Switzerland holds national conference on dangers of the 'manosphere'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
10:41:42 UTC
19:41:42 KST

Switzerland holds national conference on dangers of the ‘manosphere’
A recent study shows that in Switzerland, one in five men subscribe to a concept of masculinity based on domination. A national conference in Bern on Monday aims to gain a better understanding of the phenomenon.
The findings of the study published in June by the University of Zurich and the mencare/männer.ch association show that 20% of the men surveyed and 7% of the women surveyed subscribe to the idea of masculinity based on domination. The “M-factor”, as measured in the study, refers to a set of attitudes encompassing various restrictive conceptions of masculinity and gender relations.
More
One in three Swiss young men believes in ‘dominant male’
The concept is associated with claims of male superiority, a propensity for violence, misogyny, contempt for sexual minorities and a rejection of equality. The phenomenon particularly affects young men. Half of men aged 18 to 24 are concerned about the growing marginalisation of “real men” in society. And nearly one in three men in this age group belongs to the group with the highest scores.
“A young person in the process of forming their identity will be affected, destabilised and influenced by this worldview,” says Gilles Crettenand, head of mencare/männer.ch in French-speaking Switzerland, in an interview with Keystone-ATS news agency.
A national conference
To tackle this phenomenon, Switzerland is seeking to coordinate its efforts. A national conference entitled “Beware the Manosphere!”, aimed at specialists and networking, took place on Monday in Bern. It was opened by minister Beat Jans, head of the Federal Department of Justice and Police, alongside parliamentarians (Zurich) and Nathalie Fontanet (Geneva).
The aim of the conference is to create a shared knowledge base and to disseminate information that will enable a better understanding of the scope and dynamics of male-centred violence and radicalisation. To this end, practitioners, experts and representatives from the government, the cantons and municipalities will exchange their experiences and knowledge by pooling their expertise. National collaboration is essential, emphasises Crettenand.
“Changing social gender norms involves many factors. We need to work on all levels simultaneously,” he notes. He highlights the various areas of focus: prevention and health promotion (particularly in schools) and security (in collaboration with the police). “These areas are complementary, so we need to forge links and develop a network of expertise,” adds Crettenand.
Tools to prevent abuse
The Men and Masculinities Centre of Expertise also organises training courses for professionals in the health, social care, education and security sectors. The canton of Zurich has been very active in this area. Geneva and the French-speaking cantons are beginning to allocate funds for action programmes, such as in Vaud, for example.
He emphasises the need to inform and train parents and teachers, as well as those directly affected including pupils, both girls and boys. “The more we equip them with the tools to analyse information – through critical thinking, and by developing psychosocial and interpersonal skills – the less vulnerable they will be to this kind of language, behaviour and subsequent misconduct,” argues Crettenand.
Crettenand is delighted that interventions in schools aimed at young people are becoming increasingly common. “We need to roll out this action plan in as many cantons as possible, because that is the only way it will be truly effective,” he concludes.

Swiss president says Bern turns to trade diversification amid growing global economic uncertainty
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
10:41:13 UTC
19:41:13 KST

Beyza Binnur Donmez
02 November 2026•Update: 02 November 2026
Switzerland is pursuing a strategy of trade diversification to reduce economic dependencies and safeguard its prosperity amid growing global uncertainty and trade tensions, President Guy Parmelin said Monday.
"Trade relationships are being challenged. Economic dependencies are increasingly being used as a tool of power," Parmelin told foreign journalists at a press briefing in Bern.
Warning that the international economic order is "under pressure," he stressed that Switzerland’s reliance on foreign markets makes isolationism untenable.
"Our prosperity depends largely on international trade," he said. "Therefore, isolationism is not an option for Switzerland. Nor is inaction. Diversification is our answer."
Parmelin highlighted recent diplomatic and trade initiatives involving India, Thailand, Vietnam, and China, including an enhanced free trade agreement signed with Beijing last Friday.
He also pointed to Switzerland’s agreement with the countries of the South American trade bloc Mercosur, covering a market of around 270 million people.
However, he emphasized that expanding into new markets would not come at the expense of traditional partners.
Bern is opening new doors, while maintaining relationships with its main traditional markets in Europe and the US remains a "priority," according to the president.
"We do not want to reduce our trade with Europe or the United States. We want to increase our trade with the entire world," he said.
Parmelin added that trade tensions with Washington had demonstrated the need to defend Swiss interests while maintaining dialogue.
"Those who have several strong partners are less vulnerable," he explained.
Underlining that "cooperation is better than confrontation" and "common rules are better than the law of the jungle," the president said this is why Bern remains committed to "open, fair, and rules-based" global trade.

Michigan's early voters shrug off Stevens' flip to Republicans
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
10:40:47 UTC
19:40:47 KST

Breadcrumb
Michigan's early voters shrug off Haley Stevens' 'shocking' endorsement of Republican
Two days before election day for the US midterms, a last-minute endorsement by Michigan Democratic Representative Haley Stevens for Republican Mike Rogers for Senate has largely served to energise support for her former primary opponent Abdul El-Sayed.
El-Sayed has seen a surge in fundraising, while Stevens has been banished from her own party, possibly ending her political career. This could be a watershed moment for Democrats, who, if they are successful in Michigan on Tuesday, would show that they no longer need the support of their party's establishment to win.
"I think she overestimated her capacity and underestimated what the reaction would be," James Zogby, veteran pollster and president of the Arab American Institute, told The New Arab. "I think this will have little effect on the race."
Stevens' endorsement follows her criticism of a political ad for El-Sayed unaffiliated with his campaign. It depicts an American family struggling to afford groceries because US tax money has gone to Israel. After she asked him to condemn it, he said he didn’t agree with the contents of the ad.
She nevertheless broke with his campaign, a decision he appeared to welcome. Instead of attending a party unity event with El-Sayed, she attended a Sunday church service with Rogers, essentially cementing her public endorsement of a man she had until recently repeatedly condemned for his policies.
On Sunday, the last day of early voting in Michigan, the turnout was high at Dearborn’s Ford Community and Performing Arts Center–and so were hopes–two days ahead of an election that could usher in the country’s first Muslim American senator.
Long lines wove throughout the venue, as people of all ages and backgrounds, including local politicians, who had an air of both celebration and urgency, cast their ballots. According to local media, at least two-thirds of Michiganders have voted early.
As the day wore on, word spread of Stevens’ endorsement of Rogers. The news only seemed to give people the resolve to get out the vote.
"It's a huge election right now, without saying too much. If you're watching the news, a lot of people are coming out. We have two big candidates–we have Abdul El-Sayed, and we have Mike Rogers. That’s causing a lot of controversy right now," Wesam Tanana, an election volunteer, told TNA.
"This is the biggest turnout I've seen in the last 20 years I've been coming here volunteering. There are a lot of things on the ballot–like high gas prices, high rent, and what Michiganders want. I think that’s the big battle right now," he said.
"I think candidates finally realise the importance of the Arab and Muslim votes. Democrats are now campaigning here to win back the Arab American and Muslim bloc. I think this community is done with sitting out an election," Mohammed Mawla, a member of the Dearborn Heights School Board, told TNA.
"We've just seen Haley Stevens endorse the Republican candidate, which is shocking because this is not only an attack on Abdul El-Sayed. This is an attack on a Democratic US majority," he said.
"It shows we've really dodged a bullet with having her as the Democratic nominee," he said.
As of Sunday night, El-Sayed had seen $1.2 million in donations following the news of Stevens' endorsement of Rogers. As for Stevens, by the end of the day, the majority of her staff had resigned and Democratic Party leaders, including Chuck Schumer, described her move as a "betrayal".
Stevens has long been a thorn in the side of progressive Democrats. In 2022, with the help of AIPAC and affiliated pro-Israel groups, she won the Democratic primary against veteran House member Andy Levin, a popular Jewish politician who had criticised Netanyahu. Many progressives saw her loss to El-Sayed as vindication for the 2022 race.

Nuclear strike on Iran? Trump and Netanyahu beat drums of war

Nuclear strike on Iran? Tucker Carlson gives stark warning as Trump and Netanyahu beat war drums
Fears of a renewed US-Israeli military assault on Iran have intensified following fresh threats from President Donald Trump, reports of military preparations and claims that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is pressing Washington to launch strikes after Tuesday's US midterm elections.
The warnings come despite diplomatic efforts led by Qatar and regional mediators to bring Washington and Tehran back to negotiations and prevent another war.
Conservative American commentator Tucker Carlson claimed on Monday that the Trump administration could be days away from launching a nuclear strike against Iran under pressure from Netanyahu.
In a post on X, Carlson identified the potential target as Pickaxe Mountain, near the Natanz nuclear facility in Isfahan province.
Carlson claimed Israeli intelligence believes Iran has resumed uranium enrichment at the site, allegedly protected by 90 metres of solid granite.
He argued that conventional US weapons could not penetrate the underground tunnels, leaving a nuclear strike as the only military option.
Quoting an unnamed observer, Carlson said Netanyahu was calling Trump daily about the issue.
Carlson also alleged that Washington had quietly revised its nuclear doctrine since February to make tactical nuclear weapons easier to deploy.
He claimed Trump could decide whether to use nuclear weapons by 7 November, although Vice President JD Vance and US envoy Steve Witkoff reportedly favour diplomacy.
The allegations remain unverified, with no official confirmation that Washington is considering a nuclear strike.
Under pressure from Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu, the Trump administration may be within days of launching a nuclear strike on Iran. The target would be Pickax Mountain in central Iran, where Israeli intelligence claims the Iranian government has restarted its nuclear enrichment program. No conventional weapon in the American arsenal can penetrate 300 feet of solid granite to destroy the tunnels where enrichment is supposedly taking place. The only military option is a nuclear strike. Netanyahu has been pushing hard for one. “Bibi calls Trump about it every day,” says an informed observer. Netanyahu is cornered and desperate. After last week’s election results, he can’t form a government unless Trump intervenes directly in Israeli politics and brokers a deal with other parties that gives Netanyahu 61 seats in the Knesset. Otherwise, he is out as prime minister and on his way to ignominy, investigations and possibly jail. Netanyahu must stay close to Trump. He needs this war. To that end, he’s applied maximum pressure to his closest allies in the administration, including Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth and CENTCOM commander Brad Cooper. Both oppose a negotiated settlement to the war they’ve so grievously mismanaged; both are pushing to restart major combat operations. Secretary of State Marco Rubio and CIA director John Ratcliffe are also following Netanyahu’s lead, as are leaders of the Democratic Party. In a recent meeting on the subject, former president Barack Obama said he opposes the current Iran peace deal being drafted in Doha. The rest of America’s longtime allies in the Middle East are terrified by the prospect of more war. On September 27th, Netanyahu flew secretly to Abu Dhabi to enlist the UAE in his lobbying effort for a final attack on Iran. The Emiratis refused. After eight months of conflict, Gulf economies are teetering. So are global energy and fertilizer markets. They won’t recover soon. Globally, there are a total of about 850 supertankers used to transport oil from producers to the rest of the world. In October alone, 11 of them were badly damaged in Hormuz. At this pace, a global depression is imminent. A nuclear strike would radically accelerate the destruction. Fallout from a ground explosion at Pickax Mountain would contaminate the Persian Gulf, poisoning the water supply for 100 million people. And those are just some of the immediate consequences for the region. The rest of the world is every bit as exposed. No country other than the United States has ever used a nuclear weapon in war. Some would like to. An American nuclear attack on Iran would set a new precedent. The Russians have already told at least two other governments that an American nuclear strike on Iran would free them to use nuclear weapons against Ukraine. Pakistan and India would be tempted to do the same against each other, as would North Korea against Seoul. After the first nuclear strike, World War Three is inevitable. That war would be short and final. We’ve been sleepwalking toward this moment for months. Since February, the administration has quietly rewritten America’s nuclear doctrine to make first use of so-called “battlefield nukes” easier and therefore more likely. No one in Washington in either party seems bothered by this. Now we’re on the brink of it. Close observers say Trump is likely to decide by next weekend whether or not to use nuclear weapons. That would be November 7, six days from now. To his credit, he’s hesitating. At the moment, Trump is listening to his vice president, JD Vance, and to his envoy and friend Steve Witkoff, both of whom argue a deal with Iran can be made. They’re right, though it won’t be simple. The Iranians are famously frustrating to negotiate with under any circumstances, and elements of that government have become more radical since Ayatollah Ali Khamenei and his family were killed in February. After decades of isolation, even relatively moderate Iranian leaders seem confused by how decisions are made in the West. (There is a widespread belief in Tehran, for example, that the United States government controls Israel.) But overall, people who have spoken to decision-makers in Iran say there is consensus there that more war is bad for everyone and a deal is worth making. One group that hasn’t been consulted so far is the global population — the hundreds of millions of people who will be killed along with their children if Trump is pushed by Netanyahu into launching a nuclear strike next week. Now would be the time for them to speak up.

Israel's Channel 12 similarly reported that Trump wanted Israel to avoid interfering in Qatar-mediated talks.
Trump later described their conversation as "a very good talk".
US and Israeli military preparations
In addition, Israeli broadcaster Kan reported that the US had transferred 10 military cargo aircraft to Israeli airbases in the Naqab (Negev) desert, although Washington has not confirmed the movements.
Kan also reported that Washington had moved a Patriot missile defence system from Texas to reinforce Gulf defences.
Israeli newspaper Yedioth Ahronoth reported that Israel had completed preparations for renewed military operations, with the final decision resting with Trump.
Axios reported that a possible week-long offensive could target Iranian leadership, nuclear facilities, energy sites and infrastructure.

"Pronunciation respelling"
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
10:38:40 UTC
19:38:40 KST

"Pronunciation respelling"
« previous post |
In a comment on yesterday's post ktschwarz informed us that
"Pronunciation respelling" is Wikipedia's name for things like "KUV-uh-nuhnt"; I don't know if it's used more widely.
I've somehow managed to fail to learn that term, though of course I was familiar with the practice.
The Wikipedia article explains further that
A pronunciation respelling is a regular phonetic respelling of a word that has a standard spelling but whose pronunciation according to that spelling may be ambiguous, which is used to indicate the pronunciation of that word. Pronunciation respellings are sometimes seen in word dictionaries.
The term should not be confused with pronunciation spelling which is an ad hoc spelling of a word that has no standard spelling. Most of these are nonce words though some have achieved a certain amount of standardization, e.g., the informal use of the word gonna to represent an informal pronunciation of going to.
The OED calls its current version "Simple Text Respell", discussed further here.
Early versions of pronunciation respelling seem to have relied heavily on diacritics, as illustrated in "The Synopsis of Words Differently Pronounced by Different Orthoepists" in Noah Webster's American Dictionary of 1841.
For some information about the history of various variant types, see here. Both the practice and the term have been around for a long time, though it's not yet clear to me when (the various versions of) the term came into use.

New disruption of refrigerators in supermarkets across Europe — cyberattack is suspected
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
12:38:04 EET
19:38:04 KST

New disruption of refrigerators in supermarkets across Europe — cyberattack is suspected
Kyiv • UNN
The temperature of refrigerators and freezers suddenly changed in dozens of stores in Belgium and Sweden. The retail chains are investigating an IT incident.
Supermarkets in Belgium and Sweden reported sudden changes in the temperatures of their refrigerators and freezers on Monday, November 2, raising concerns about a cyberattack similar to those that recently occurred in France. UNN reports this, citing Bloomberg.
Details
Delhaize, which is owned by Dutch retailer Ahold Delhaize, confirmed that an "IT incident" occurred at approximately 40 of its stores in Belgium on Sunday evening, November 1, affecting refrigeration systems, Belgian news agency Belga reports. A small number of Carrefour Belgium and Spar supermarkets also reported a similar problem, Belga reports.
Several ICA and Coop supermarkets in Sweden are experiencing higher freezer temperatures, according to a report in the newspaper Aftonbladet. Freezer temperatures rose to 50°C, Ica Kvantum in Sjöbo, Sweden, said on its Facebook page, adding that it suspected a hack. Two more ICA stores are also reporting problems, and Coop has six affected stores in the central part of the country, Aftonbladet reports.
"We are aware that a limited number of stores were affected by an incident that occurred overnight and impacted refrigeration and freezer systems. ICA is currently supporting these stores in resolving the situation. We will provide further information when we can," an ICA Sverige spokesperson said by email to Bloomberg on Monday, November 2. The spokesperson did not confirm a cyberattack.
ICA owns approximately one-third of the Swedish grocery market, while Coop has about 17%.
These incidents raise concerns about a repeat of the disruptions that occurred in France last month, when 700 stores were affected by cyberattacks that disabled refrigeration systems and forced stores to throw away products. The affected companies included Intermarché, Coopérative U and Carrefour SA. No group has publicly claimed responsibility for the hack.
Last month, a cyberattack caused several days of service disruptions and empty shelves at Ahold Delhaize stores in the Netherlands. The company has still not reported what exactly caused the problem.
In the United States, the Pentagon said last week that it was investigating a malfunction involving freezers used to store food at several military facilities.

Iliana Iotova and Kiril Valchev: Bulgaria’s new President and Vice President
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
10:37:33 UTC
19:37:33 KST

Author
Diana Tsankova
News
Iliana Iotova and Kiril Valchev: Bulgaria’s new President and Vice President
Monday 2 November 2026 10:45
Monday, 2 November 2026, 10:45
Iliana Iotova and Kiril Valchev
PHOTO BTA
Font size
Iliana Iotova will continue to serve as Bulgaria’s president for the next five years, retaining her position as head of state and Commander-in-Chief of the country's armed forces.
In the presidential runoff held on November 1, 2016, she secured nearly 58% of the votes, defeating her opponent, former caretaker Prime Minister Andrey Gurov, who received just over 39% of the vote.
- Iliana Iotova is Bulgaria’s 7th president and first woman elected to the post
- Andrey Gyurov: We accept the results, surprising as they may be
Iliana Iotova took over as head of the presidential institution on January 23 this year, following Rumen Radev’s early departure from his second term as head of state to assume the role of prime minister.
On the eve of presidential election runoff, Iliana Iotova addressed voters with the following message: “Bulgaria is greater than any political party or any politician. It is our common home. I want this home to be a place of peace for our children, where they can grow up feeling secure and with a future ahead of them. I also want Bulgaria to have its own strong and confident voice in Europe. The choice is ours, and that is why we must vote.”
Her message resonated with the majority of Bulgarian voters, who have grown weary of the cycle of elections over the past five years.
Iliana Iotova
PHOTO BGNES
Biography of Bulgaria’s seventh President
President Iliana Iotova graduated from the Alphonse de Lamartine French Language High School in Sofia and earned a degree in Bulgarian Philology from Sofia University “St. Kliment Ohridski.” She subsequently specialized at France’s National School of Administration and the Centre for European Studies in Strasbourg.
She worked as a reporter, editor, news presenter and Director of News and Current Affairs at the Bulgarian National Television, where she worked from 1990 to 1997. She subsequently headed the press office of the Bulgarian Socialist Party and held various senior positions until her election as vice president. From 2005 to 2007, she served as a Member of Parliament, before becoming a Member of the European Parliament in June 2007, a position she held for three terms as part of the Group of the Progressive Alliance of Socialists and Democrats.
Iliana Iotova is fluent in French and has good command of Russian and English. She is married and has one son.
Kiril Valchev will be Iliana Iotova’s Vice President when she takes office on January 22, 2027. The longtime journalist and current Director-General of the Bulgarian News Agency (BTA) will serve a five-year term as Vice President.
Kiril Valchev
PHOTO BGNES
Biography of Vice President Kiril Valchev
Kiril Valchev graduated from the National High School of Ancient Languages and Cultures “St. Constantine-Cyril the Philosopher” and holds a Master’s degree in Law from the Faculty of Law at Sofia University “St. Kliment Ohridski.” For many years, he hosted current affairs programmes on Darik Radio and also gained journalistic experience at Deutsche Welle and the BBC.
Between 2000 and 2004, he worked as a part-time assistant professor in civil law at Sofia University. Since 2005, he has been a managing partner at a law firm specialising in media and intellectual property. Valchev was elected Director-General of the Bulgarian News Agency (BTA) in 2021 and is currently serving his second term. He has visited all 193 United Nations member states and every continent.
PHOTO BGNES
Messages from the President and Vice President fоllowing the November 1 еlection
In her first statement as President-elect, Iliana Iotova thanked everyone who had supported her on her path to the presidency.
“We ran a positive campaign and did not allow ourselves to make a single attack against our opponents. We did not allow hate speech, confrontation or division to become part of our campaign, even for a second. We spoke to Bulgarian citizens about the issues that matter in their everyday lives - incomes, peace and the challenges they face - and they understood our message. I still cannot understand who misled Mr Gurov into pursuing such an extremely aggressive campaign against our presidential ticket. With their votes, people sent a clear message: ‘This is not the way. This is unacceptable in Bulgarian elections!’ They placed their trust in a political approach where good decisions are made through dialogue, discussion, the pursuit of solutions, and cooperation and coordination with other institutions.”
PHOTO BTA
For his part, newly elected Vice President Kiril Valchev noted that twice as many voters had backed the election of Bulgaria’s first female president in the second round.
''I would like to extend my special thanks to Bulgarians around the world who cast their votes. They will be my primary focus. Another important responsibility I will have as Vice President will be to ensure that our country is better represented around the world. I will serve as another guarantor within the Presidency of Bulgaria’s place in Europe, where it has been for 14 centuries, as well as of democracy in our country. We will pay particular attention to young people. We will invite them to the Presidency to hear their ideas about Bulgaria’s future, because the most important goal is to bring as many people as possible together around the cause of Bulgaria. We must ensure that our children stay in Bulgaria and that those who have left come back'', Vice President-elect Kiril Valchev said.

Netherlands offers €2m bounty for capture of cocaine kingpin Jos Leijdekkers
THE HAGUE – Dutch prosecutors are offering a record €2 million (S$2.9 million) reward for information leading to the arrest of convicted cocaine kingpin Jos Leijdekkers, one of Europe’s most-wanted fugitives, the authorities said on Nov 2.
He is a Dutch who has been living in Sierra Leone for the past years, the Dutch prosecution service said.
Prosecutors have demanded his extradition, but Sierra Leone has refused to cooperate, prompting the European Union to cut some aid to the West African country.
The reward, the highest bounty ever offered by the Dutch authorities, is available to any person who provides the crucial tip leading to his arrest, prosecutors said in a statement.
They said Leijdekkers, who is known in the Netherlands as Bolle Jos or Chubby Jos, is a key player in international cocaine trafficking. According to police, he also goes by the name of Omar Sherrif in Sierra Leone.
The 35-year-old was sentenced in absentia to 24 years in prison by a Dutch court in 2025 for smuggling more than 7 metric tonnes of cocaine and is also the subject of several ongoing police investigations in the Netherlands.
In neighbouring Belgium, a court sentenced him to 79 years in prison.
The Dutch authorities estimate Leijdekkers has made tens of millions of euros from cocaine smuggling. He is also suspected of money laundering and involvement in the use of extreme violence, they said. REUTERS

UK to unveil migrant settlement overhaul after months of debate

Unknown Publisher

UK to unveil migrant settlement overhaul after months of debate
LONDON, Nov 2 - Interior minister Shabana Mahmood will on Monday set out reforms to how migrants can settle in Britain, in a bid to balance voter demands for lower immigration with business warnings that tough rules could deter workers who the country still needs.
The reforms are the government's latest attempt to toughen the rules after the number of arrivals surged following Britain's departure from the European Union, with post-Brexit immigration policies leading to an influx of healthcare workers and students from around the world.
Despite dropping in the opinion polls since the governing Labour Party elected Andy Burnham as prime minister, Nigel Farage's populist Reform UK party has been a major factor in driving the push for stricter migration controls.
Under current rules, most migrants can apply for indefinite leave to remain after five years in Britain, enabling them to claim some welfare benefits. Mahmood proposed replacing that with an "earned settlement" system, making 10 years the standard route to permanent residency and requiring some lower-paid workers, including care workers, to wait up to 15 years.
Speaking before Mahmood's announcement later on Monday, junior business minister Chris McDonald said immigration levels had become unsustainable under the previous government that was led by the Conservatives.
"The plan around immigration is about controlling borders, but it's also about ensuring that we invest in the young people in our country, so that they can get these jobs, so we don't have to bring people in from overseas too," he told Sky News.
MIGRATION FALLING, QUESTIONS REMAIN
The government argues the changes are needed because around 350,000 lower-skilled workers and their dependants who arrived after Brexit are expected to become eligible for settlement in the coming years.
Net migration in Britain fell sharply last year, with official figures showing it almost halved to 171,000 from 331,000 a year earlier, extending a steep decline from a record 944,000 in 2023.
Burnham last week backed the principle that settlement should be "a right to be earned" but the prime minister has also routinely praised foreign care workers after his late father was given support in a care home.
Owners of UK care homes, unions and some Labour lawmakers have said the care system will struggle to operate if international workers are deterred from moving to Britain.
Media reports have suggested Mahmood could soften some elements of the original proposals, potentially exempting care workers already in Britain or offering them a quicker route to settlement.
A cross-party parliamentary committee last year warned that the government did not have a full understanding of how skilled worker visas were affecting different sectors of the economy. REUTERS

Breadcrumb
Democrats, Trump hold final rallies before pivotal US midterm elections
Democrats teed up final get-out-the-vote rallies Monday on the eve of US midterm elections where they expect to win at least partial control of Congress and impose political constraints on President Donald Trump for the first time in two years.
Rallies—including by star Democratic Senate candidates James Talarico in Texas and Adam Hamilton in Kansas—were capping a campaign of breathtaking tension and bitterness.
For his closing argument, Trump chose a speech in Washington at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool—a landmark that has become synonymous with the 80-year-old president's obsessive, controversial drive to redevelop the US capital.
"We're going to win," he said on Sunday.
Polls, however, show that Democrats are near certain to take the majority from Republicans in the House of Representatives and have a real shot at winning the currently Republican Senate.
Even winning just the House would mean Democrats have voting power over the federal budget and would lead powerful committees able to investigate alleged corruption under Trump, the Epstein files and other explosive issues.
The loss of total Republican dominance would push Trump into unfamiliar and uncomfortable territory: a lame-duck period beset with high inflation at home, the sputtering war against Iran and hostile Democratic investigations into his activities in Washington.
But a decade into the Trump era, Democrats remain wary about predictions of victory.
"Nauseously optimistic," Democratic Senator Raphael Warnock told CNN to describe the mood.
Scorched earth
Democrats are facing late internal divisions, with left-wing candidates challenging at times with the party's establishment.
In a startling display of infighting on Sunday, Democratic congresswoman Haley Stevens in Michigan endorsed Republican candidate Mike Rogers against left-wing progressive candidate Abdul El-Sayed in her state's key Senate race.
Trump was quick to praise Stevens for her "bravery", posting on his Truth Social platform that "Haley said what few people are willing to say."
Stevens, who lost a bruising primary to El-Sayed in August despite being backed by the Democratic establishment, struggled to explain her decision in an interview with CNN.
"It's just where I was at the end of the night and earlier this morning," she said.
Trump's Republicans have fought a political scorched-earth campaign, painting Democrats as communists and openly branding El-Sayed, who is Muslim, as a terrorist.
Addressing a crowd in Iowa on Sunday, Trump said Democrats are "extreme and dangerous radicals" who will "steal your wealth" and let in migrants to "ransack, rape and plunder."
But polls show Americans heavily souring on Trump's wrecking-ball act.
An NBC News poll released on Sunday showed 60 percent disapprove of his performance, particularly over high prices exacerbated by his now eight-month-long war against Iran.
While the House seems highly likely to turn Democratic, the battle for the Senate is up in the air.
Only a third of the Senate's 100 seats are being contested in these midterms, and few of the races were seen as favorable to Democrats.
However, with surprisingly strong challenges in deeply Republican states, pollsters now say the odds of a Democratic flip are at minimum even.
The final New York Times/Siena poll released Sunday evening showed Democratic candidates leading in all seven seats viewed as most competitive, though five remained within the margin of error.
A Democratic Senate would be able to shut down Trump's lifetime appointments to courts—including the Supreme Court.
While Tuesday is election day, early voting has already seen a record 54 million people cast ballots around the country.
The midterms have seen about $11 billion spent on advertising, with large chunks coming from individual mega-donors.
Elon Musk, a close Trump ally who led the so-called DOGE effort in dismantling entire government departments, has given a staggering nearly half-billion dollars to help get Republicans elected.

Eurozone manufacturing growth remains solid in October despite supply pressures
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
10:30:31 UTC
19:30:31 KST

Gokhan Ergocun
02 November 2026•Update: 02 November 2026
Manufacturing output across the eurozone expanded solidly in October, although supply chain bottlenecks and cost pressures intensified, according to survey data published on Monday.
The headline seasonally adjusted S&P Global Eurozone Manufacturing Purchasing Managers' Index stood at 52.7 in October, down slightly from 52.9 in September.
The reading remained comfortably above the 50 no-change mark, signaling expansion across the single-currency area for the ninth straight month.
Six of the eight surveyed eurozone countries registered manufacturing growth, while France and Italy were the only member states to record contractions.
Factory production levels increased for the 10th consecutive month, though the rate of expansion moderated to a four-month low amid a slowdown in total new order growth.
In contrast, export business rose at the sharpest rate in just over 4.5 years.
Goods producers added staff for the third consecutive month, while backlogs of work increased at the joint-fastest pace since May 2022.
Firms stockpiled inputs to the greatest extent since December 2022 to protect against supply disruptions, as vendor delivery delays worsened to the greatest degree since June.
Input price inflation surged to a five-month high, driven by higher energy prices and raw material shortages.
In response, manufacturers raised their selling prices sharply, maintaining the pace of price increases seen in September.
While companies remained optimistic about output growth over the next 12 months, positive sentiment slipped below the survey's historical average.
