Canadian minister stops short of endorsing EU carbon tax as energy alliance deepens
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
10:30:18 UTC
19:30:18 KST

The Canadian climate Minister's reluctance to openly commit to cooperation with the EU on its climate policy stems from the fact that Ottawa is effectively seeking an exemption from the bloc's carbon border tax, according to a December 2025 internal document seen by Euronews.
Canadian Climate and Environment Minister Julia Dabrusin has defended industrial carbon pricing as a tool to cut CO2 emissions and protect businesses from unfair competition, but stopped short of explicitly endorsing the European Union's carbon border tax.
"Industrial carbon pricing is important in a low-carbon economy, which is where the world is going. But these are conversations for us to have (...) those are conversations that are still to be had," Dabrusin told Euronews.
Opposition to the EU's carbon border tax — the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) — could expose potential limits to a budding energy alliance between Brussels and Ottawa, as the transatlantic partners embark on a new path of cooperation, hailed at the Montreal summit on 29-30 October.
But when asked whether Canada would back CBAM — which came into effect in January 2026 and imposes a carbon cost on certain imports to protect European producers from competitors operating under weaker climate rules — Minister Dabrusin offered no explicit endorsement.
Dabrusin's reluctance to commit to cooperation with the EU on its climate policy stems from the fact that Ottawa is effectively seeking an exemption from the bloc's carbon border tax, according to a December 2025 internal document seen by Euronews.
"Canada continues to seek a practical agreement with the EU to reduce CBAM's administrative burden for Canadian exporters, and the Prime Minister's Personal Representative to the European Union is fully engaged," the internal document from Canada's trade and foreign affairs ministries reads.
At the closing press conference on 30 October, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said that "a series of trade issues that had been bubbling along" had been discussed, but stopped short of sharing details.
"We are working together to find common solutions (on CBAM and other trade issues)," Carney told reporters on 30 October.
Carney has been attempting to diversify Canadian trade away from its heavy dependence on Washington, making access to the EU market increasingly important.
However, the Canadian document identifies CBAM as a potential obstacle to expanding exports to Europe, particularly in aluminium, steel, critical minerals and hydrogen.
"Canadian exports are not exempt from CBAM and exporters will face carbon charges and complex administrative requirements that could create market access risks and potential competitiveness challenges in the EU market," the document reads.
Lobbying for an exemption
Canada does not qualify for an exemption, despite its existing carbon-pricing policies and close trade relationship with the EU under the Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA), according to the document.
Nonetheless, Ottawa wants Brussels to recognise its domestic carbon-pricing system as sufficiently comparable to the EU's to reduce the administrative and financial burden on Canadian businesses.
Although the legal obligation falls on EU importers, critics argue that such requirements and costs are likely to be passed on to exporters through commercial agreements.
Stephanie Kusie, the Canadian Conservatives' shadow minister for international trade, also raised concerns about how the EU's CBAM could affect businesses.
"Canada is facing an EU carbon tariff in the coming months that could affect $3 billion in Canadian exports. Instead of fixing the issue, the PM has spent months distracting Canadians with talk of the EU," said Kusie.
Between 2021 and 2024, Canadian exports of goods covered by the EU's carbon border mechanism averaged C$28 billion a year, representing 7.4% of Canada's exports to the bloc, according to the document.
Minister Dabrusin said the Canadian government supports industrial carbon pricing, which it has had in place for years and intends to strengthen.
Dabrusin argued that industrial carbon pricing was among the most effective ways to reduce emissions while keeping businesses competitive in a global economy shifting towards lower-carbon production.
However, despite having its own industrial carbon-pricing system, Canada is not exempt from the EU's carbon border levy. Under the bloc's rules, a full exemption is linked to participation in, or a connection with, the EU Emissions Trading System — a condition Canada does not currently meet.
Moreover, the EU's carbon price is significantly higher than Canada's domestic carbon price trajectory.
Battle of semantics over EU-Canada relations
The EU-Canada summit took place as the EU seeks to build a network of trusted economic partners amid souring relations with the United States, which have become more uncertain under Donald Trump's administration.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney told the EU-Canada summit that Ottawa aims to become an associate member by June next year.
However, divergences over the nature of this renewed relationship have been voiced by several member states, led by Germany, particularly over the definition of associate membership. EU leaders agreed to define the concept by the 2027 summit.
Dabrusin told Euronews that, for Canada, delivering on substance rather than semantics was important.
"The main thing for us is deepening the relationship with the EU (...) The conversations we had today underlined how much we have in common in terms of interests and values, and these are things we can build on as we launch the Alliance for the Future," Minister Dabrusin said.

Many London architecture firms not paying London Living Wage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
10:30:00 UTC
19:30:00 KST

Many London architecture firms not paying London Living Wage
The majority of the London-based studios in The Pay 100‘s fifth annual salary survey are not paying Part I architectural assistants the London Living Wage, as required by the Royal Institute of British Architects (RIBA).
An engineering firm has topped the leaderboard for the average salaries for UK architects, according to a survey conducted by the anonymous group The Pay 100.
Engineering firm tops architect salary leaderboard
Published over the weekend, the survey provides rough figures only based on the mean figures submitted by respondents. This year’s data collected the annual salary of 127 firms in the UK and the mean number of hours of unpaid overtime per week.
Topping the leaderboard with the highest average annual salary for architects with less than five years’ experience is BakerHicks, an engineering and design firm, which paid £72,000.
Second on the list is London studio Hopkins Architects at £63,700, and joint third at £56,300 are London practices Samuel Chisholm Studio and Thomas Alexander Design.
The survey also presented figures for Part I and Part II architectural assistants. Transport for London had the highest wage for Part II roles at £44,000, followed by Foster + Partners at £42,000.
Majority of London firms not paying London Living Wage
The results for Part I roles included salaries from 30 studios, 21 of which were based in Greater London.
Only the top four studios on the leaderboard – Haworth Tompkins, Allford Hall Monaghan Morris, Studio McW and Studio PDP – paid more than the London Living Wage of £32,136, which RIBA declared a requirement for relevant offices.
Twelve of the 30 studios were paying Part I roles less than the £29,328 UK Living Wage.
Low wages “a threat to the future of the profession”
Alongside its survey data, The Pay 100 wrote an open letter to RIBA, asking it to take action on the financial wellbeing of those working in the architecture industry and to ensure the long-term future of the profession.
“Our aim has always been to create tangible financial incentives for employers to improve pay, empower employees to make informed career decisions, and encourage a healthier, more sustainable profession,” said The Pay 100 in the letter.
“We recognise that architecture practices operate within a highly competitive market, often under significant financial pressure themselves,” it continued. “Nevertheless, the commercial challenges facing practices should not prevent the profession from addressing the deteriorating conditions experienced by many employees.”
“Poor financial conditions for staff are not merely an employment issue; they are a threat to the long-term health, resilience and future of the profession.”
It went on to set out two courses of action it called for RIBA to take: establishing “meaningful minimum salaries” for RIBA chartered practices, and taking full ownership of The Pay 100 and its annual salary survey.
The Pay 100 said a framework of minimum salary levels should be established across different architecture roles, increasing year-on-year in line with inflation.
“A profession cannot sustainably advocate for the value of its services while leaving the financial conditions of its workforce to market pressures alone,” it said. “The RIBA should take a leading role in addressing this imbalance.”
After five years of aiming to improve pay transparency with its annual surveys, The Pay 100 wants RIBA to take ownership of the survey and commit resources to it, developing it into an industry-wide initiative.
“We believe that improving pay transparency across UK architecture should be a core responsibility of the profession’s leading membership body,” said The Pay 100.
“Under the RIBA’s stewardship, the survey could benefit from significantly greater reach, sustained institutional support and broader participation across the profession,” it continued.
“This would provide a foundation for more comprehensive salary data, stronger engagement between employers and employees, and meaningful progress towards better financial conditions throughout the industry.”
The Pay 100 ended its letter by asking for a public response from RIBA by 1 December

Bolivia declares national emergency over El Niño as drought hits over 78,000 families
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
10:29:09 UTC
19:29:09 KST

Drought is already affecting more than 78,000 families in seven regions of the country.
Grappling with both flooding and drought, Bolivia has declared a national emergency over El Niño.
Bolivian President Rodrigo Paz declared a state of emergency on 31 October to free up resources for dealing with the impacts of the weather phenomenon.
The measure will make it possible to mobilise financial and human resources, as well as to coordinate the work of national institutions with international cooperation in order to assist the affected areas.
"Unlike in other years, when we waited for this blow from the environment to arrive, we have taken a decision, with international cooperation and national efforts, to pool financial and human resources to deal with this phenomenon", Paz explained in a message to the population.
More than 78,000 families affected by drought
The situation is already particularly worrying in the regions suffering from water shortages. According to data from the Vice Ministry of Civil Defence, at least 78,200 families have been affected by the drought in seven of the country’s nine departments. The affected regions are La Paz, Oruro, Potosí, Cochabamba, Chuquisaca, Tarija and Santa Cruz. In addition, 63 communities have declared a drought, while others are preparing for possible flooding.
The president has warned that the country could face a combination of extreme events, with a lack of rainfall in some areas and intense rain in others. "This will be a phenomenon that will hit very hard, with both drought and flooding," said the head of state, who called on public administrations and citizens to work together to limit the damage.
A decree to anticipate extreme events
The emergency decree covers the risks associated with El Niño during the 2026-2027 period, among them droughts, floods, frosts, hailstorms, forest fires and river overflows. The declaration of emergency is intended to facilitate a coordinated response between the different levels of government and to strengthen support for the most vulnerable communities.
El Niño is a natural climate phenomenon linked to warming of the waters of the equatorial Pacific, which disrupts rainfall and temperature patterns in different parts of the world. In Bolivia it can cause periods of drought and episodes of intense rainfall, with consequences for the population, agriculture and livestock.

Why is Narva's C1 Estonian exam pass rate half the national average?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
10:28:00 UTC
19:28:00 KST

Why is Narva's C1 Estonian exam pass rate half the national average?
Only 14.9 percent of candidates passed September's C1 Estonian exam in the eastern border town of Narva, compared with 29.3 percent nationwide.
Teachers pointed to limited practice, exam format and study materials — though the exam board said the pass rate was typical.
The Council of Europe's official Common European Framework (CEF) global scale described C1 as "Effective Operational Proficiency" or "Advanced." It is the second highest on the CEF scale after C2.
In the third quarter of this year, 358 people across Estonia took the C1-level Estonian language exam, with 105 achieving the required result. Of 67 candidates in Narva, which is largely Russian-speaking, just 10 passed the C1 exam.
However, Maiki Udam, head of the Department of Education Quality at the Education and Youth Board (Harno), emphasized that a pass rate of around 30 percent had been typical for the C1 exam down the years. C1 pass rates could not be compared with lower levels, she added: the higher the required level, the more difficult the exam and so the smaller the proportion who passed.
According to Narva College lecturer Inguna Joandi, transitioning from B2 (the next level down from C1, or upper intermediate) to C1 did not simply mean learning more grammar or new words. What changed was the range of topics a person had to be able to discuss, and the depth of those discussions.
"C1 requires a very broad outlook. A person must be familiar with what is happening in Estonia, what the different points of view are and how events in the world are interpreted. They must be able to express their thoughts in Estonian," Joandi explained.
Darja Berestova, head of the B-Lingua language school in Narva, described the transition from B2 to C1 as a major leap. For a start, much depended on the individual's B2 result: someone who scraped a pass with 61 percent was unlikely to pass C1 come the following spring; a result over 80 percent offered considerably brighter prospects, however. Berestova estimated that preparing properly for C1 might require 200–250 contact hours.
In Narva, learners sometimes have to create their own language environment
One difficulty both teachers highlighted was the limited opportunity to use Estonian outside lessons, for instance at home. Berestova said everyday practice might not be sufficient to reach C1, and in Narva people often had to actively seek out chances to communicate in Estonian. She compared the situation with Tartu and Viljandi, where she said there were more opportunities.
Joandi, however, believed the lack of a language environment could not be used as an excuse not to use the language. If suitable opportunities were scarce, learners should seek them out themselves, including via the broadcast media.
"In Narva, people often say that there is no Estonian-language environment here. So in that case a person has to create one for themselves. There is television and radio. In every institution, you can find someone who speaks Estonian. You simply have to cross that barrier and start speaking Estonian with them," Joandi advised. Newspaper articles, radio, lectures and other materials also helped, she said.
Memorized texts not enough to pass the exam
According to the teachers, another obstacle might be that candidates prepared too narrowly, learning typical expressions and texts but being unable to adapt them to different situations. Joandi said this could happen particularly if a person lacked the ability to produce a coherent text even in their native tongue.
"These texts may be structurally correct, but the exam assesses how well a person can cope independently in a specific situation. If they speak only in memorized phrases and cannot freely explain their thoughts, that is a problem," Joandi continued. She added she considered the first component of the oral exam, a presentation on an assigned topic, among the most difficult — some candidates talked about themselves or their work, when the task required public speaking.
Berestova also said candidates struggled with the need to use language flexibly. Beyond grammar and vocabulary, they required phraseology and functions, colloquial expressions and an awareness of linguistic nuance.
Udam meanwhile said writing and speaking were often the most difficult parts of the exam, because candidates had to produce their own texts rather than rely on input material provided.
Berestova said there were too few practical sample tasks in Harno's public online environment, meaning teachers often had to create exam-format tasks themselves. She would have liked at least eight to 10 recent past papers to be made publicly available, so learners could practice the structure and timing as well as individual skills.
Joandi agreed more materials could have been available, but pointed out that study material generally was plentiful. Harno's Udam explained that sample materials were meant to introduce task types and difficulty, not replicate the exam, and that older samples did not lose value because Estonian did not change so quickly.
From 2027, candidates would have to pay for their third and subsequent exam attempts. Udam said this could reduce the number of people taking the exam every three months without significant improvement.
One student learned Estonian mostly on her own, passed C1 on the second attempt
For all the structural explanations, individual cases showed what was possible, including aspects of self-learning and with a clear motivating reason. The experience of Narva College student Anastasiia Vorobiova demonstrated that attaining C1 did not necessarily require years at an Estonian-language school. She moved to Estonia from Ukraine around four years ago, began learning Estonian after arriving, and had studied it for just over three years. A qualified teacher, she realized she needed a C1 certificate to be able to work in Estonia.
After a B1 course and exam, she pressed on, but largely independently — using for instance the Videoõps YouTube channel, textbooks and grammar materials, reading books from the simpler to more complex as time went on, and borrowing Estonian translations of English-language books from Narva Library.
Despite all this Anastasiia did not pass C1 on her first outing. Grammar alone was not enough at C1, she confirmed: a candidate had to be able to express their thoughts freely and speak on a wide range of topics. She prepared for the second attempt at Narva College, and benefited from the language buddy program thanks to which she found an Estonian conversation partner. These two spoke Estonian with each other once a week, bringing her more practice and developing her grammar. Most of Anastasiia's vocabulary was derived independently, however, through literature, film and video clips. She also said she found the listening task hardest — following a longer lecture, concentrating, taking notes and recapping it afterwards.
Anastasiia said she did not regard her certificate as a sign that her language learning was over. "Don't learn a language just for the exam. It's important to understand why you need it and to have an interest in the language," was her advice to other learners.

Russia seizes Ukrainian hotels on Sea of Azov coast and sells holidays at them

Russia seizes Ukrainian hotels on Sea of Azov coast and sells holidays at them
The Russian occupation authorities have declared at least 521 hotels and holiday resorts on Ukraine's Sea of Azov coast "ownerless", with at least 77 of them already under the control of Russian businesses.
Source: a Reuters video investigation published on 2 November
Details: The journalists analysed orders issued by the occupation authorities, company and property registers and tourism development plans, as well as hundreds of photographs and videos.
Under the procedure described by Reuters, in 2022 owners were given just three days to personally present their property documents and passport to the occupation administration. Otherwise, the property was officially registered as "ownerless". The owners included Ukrainians who had fled because of the invasion and were unable to return.
At least 20 resort properties included on these lists have come under the control of a Russian state entity.
Examples include the Admiral and Perlyna Tavrii hotels in Kyrylivka. The Ukrainian owners of Perlyna Tavrii told Reuters that they had not handed over management of the hotel to the occupation authorities or anyone else, nor had they authorised its operation.
According to Russian corporate registers, the company operating the hotel was owned between 2023 and 2025 by the son of Yevgeny Balitsky, the Moscow-appointed head of the occupied part of Zaporizhzhia Oblast.
The hotels are being advertised through new Russian websites, social media and bloggers. Among the offerings of one Russian tour operator, Reuters identified ten hotels that had previously been included on lists of "ownerless" properties.
At the same time, some of the properties remain closed. When the journalists attempted to book a room at the Admiral in July, they were told that the hotel had not opened for the 2026 summer season.
Background:
- On 22 October, a CIR investigation reported on Russia's financial control over the occupied territories.
- Occupation administrations are linking eligibility for certain social benefits to accounts with Russia's Promsvyazbank.

Rome prosecutors open new investigation into Pasolini's murder
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
11:27:25 CET
19:27:25 KST

The Rome Public Prosecutor's Office
has opened a new investigation into the murder of filmmaker Pier
Paolo Pasolini, who was brutally killed in the seaside Rome
district of Ostia on the night between November 1 and 2, 1975.
                                    
The case has been reopened after a lawyer, Stefano Maccioni,
filed a petition saying that recently discovered archive footage
and other evidence shows that the rent boy who initially took
the rap was not alone on the night of the murder.
                                    
The death of the 53-year-old iconic poet, novelist, director and
leftist political commentator remains a mystery.
                                    
A 17-year-old, Pino Pelosi, confessed to murdering Pasolini the
day after his death and was found guilty in 1976, but several
years later retracted his confession, saying he was pressured
into making it.
                                    
Pelosi was released on parole in 1983 and died of cancer aged 58
in 2017.
                                    
The initial ruling said Pelosi was not alone when Pasolini was
killed but a subsequent decision by an appeals court upholding
the conviction did not confirm the role of any accomplices and
that is sentence was later ratified by the supreme Court of
Cassation.
                                    
"We trust that the Public Prosecutor's Office in Rome will
finally be able to provide the answers we have been seeking for
far too many years," said Maccioni, who previously represented
one of the victim's cousins, Guido Mazzon, and is now working on
behalf of the Lazio Journalists Guild, filmmaker David Grieco,
and writer Giovanni Giovannetti.
                                    
"At the same time, we urge all those who have chosen to remain
silent about what they knowe until now, to come forward and
speak".
                                    
Previous petitions to reopen the investigation filed in 2016 and
2023 were rejected by the Prosecutor's Office.

As peacekeepers leave Western Sahara, refugees yearn to end a half-century wait
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
10:27:05 UTC
19:27:05 KST

As peacekeepers leave Western Sahara, refugees yearn to end a half-century wait
TINDOUF, Algeria, Nov 2 - At 51, Binina Mohamed is as old as the conflict that drove her from the Western Sahara region into a refugee camp in southern Algeria, where she has spent her life among tens of thousands of others facing a similar fate.
The confrontation over her native land, often described as Africa's longest-running territorial dispute, was brought back into focus this weekend by a UN Security Council spat that led to the end of a decades-old peacekeeping mission there.
The Western Sahara conflict pits Morocco, which considers the territory its own, against the Algeria-backed Polisario Front, a political and military organisation that has been seeking a separate state there since the departure of former colonial power Spain in 1976. Peacekeepers have watched over the territory since 1991, when the UN brokered a ceasefire ending years of guerrilla warfare between the two sides.
Thousands of Sahrawis fled hostilities to the Tindouf area in southwestern Algeria, where the Polisario administers five refugee camps.
During a rare visit to the region for foreign media outlets, organised by the Polisario, Mohamed described how her daughters, now in their twenties and thirties, had never visited the region where she was from.
"I do not want them to reach the age of 50 without seeing their homeland," she told Reuters.
One of her daughters, Safia Al-Saleh, 33, said she hoped her own two children would have a different future.
"I want my children and my grandchildren to study and grow up in their own country, not to grow up like us here, as refugees, with nothing," she said.
DIPLOMACY IN DEADLOCK
The uncertainty facing refugees such as Mohamed has become a central point of contention in the latest diplomatic battle over Western Sahara.
The dispute heated up last year when the UN Security Council backed Rabat's plan to give the region autonomy under Moroccan sovereignty as the "most feasible" way to resolve the conflict.
After abstaining last year, Russia this year vetoed a US-drafted resolution that would have reaffirmed that position. When a competing Russian resolution was defeated, it left the UN mission without a renewal of its mandate.
In a speech at the council, Algeria's UN envoy defended the Polisario's stance and highlighted a decline in aid and the suffering of refugees in the camps.
Morocco's envoy in turn said the harsh conditions in the camps were the responsibility of Algeria, a longtime Russian ally, which he accused of denying the refugees their right to return home. He urged Algiers to allow the UN to register the refugees, saying other nationalities were present there.
Algeria and the Polisario say over 160,000 live in the Tindouf refugee camps. UNHCR says it provides assistance to an estimated 90,000 of the "most vulnerable" refugees there.
Morocco disputes both numbers, citing a lack of a UN census, and accuses the Polisario and Algeria of using Sahrawis as political pawns, which Algiers denies.
As the dispute grinds on, Mohamed's family described daily problems in the camp, including access to water and the harsh climate.
More than 80% of the camps' residents rely on humanitarian assistance to meet basic food needs, the World Food Programme said in a statement earlier this year.
Another of Mohamed's daughters, Aisha Salem, a 24-year-old fighter with the Polisario Front, said she wanted a different future for the next generation: "We don’t want to live the way our grandparents did, through displacement and deprivation," she said.
Mohamed echoed the sentiment. "We want stability. We are tired of being refugees," she said. "The one who has no land has no life." REUTERS

Ethiopia's rebel Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) claimed Monday that its fighters killed 500 soldiers and wounded 800 others during clashes with federal government forces and allied militias in the country's northern Tigray region.
The rebel group said the casualties occurred during fighting Saturday near the historic city of Aksum, where its forces launched a counteroffensive against Ethiopian troops and fighters from the allied Tigray Peace Forces (TPF).

FSB Reports Interception of More Booby-Trapped FPV Goggles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
10:26:04 UTC
19:26:04 KST

The press service of Russia’s State Security Service (FSB) reported on Monday, Nov. 2, that it had intercepted a consignment of booby-trapped first-person view (FPV) drone pilots’ googles. According to their account, an unnamed number of goggles were purportedly donated by volunteers to military units engaged in Russia’s “special military operation” – President Vladimir Putin’s term for his war on Ukraine.
In what appears to be a repeat of the February 2025 scheme, which was attributed to Ukraine’s Main Intelligence Directorate (HUR), the goggles were found to contain improvised explosive devices (IEDs) containing plastic explosives intended to function when the operator switched on the goggles while wearing them.
According to the FSB the plan was detected when a Russian serviceman in the Volgograd region became suspicious of two sets of goggles he had received in the post, and, remembering warnings issued after last year’s attack, handed them over to the FSB who x-rayed them. This showed that the cooling fans in the equipment had been removed and replaced with IEDs.
The FSB then published a video of the devices being dealt with using a “demining robot,” before issuing a general warning and attempting to track down more devices originating from the source. From the images posted by the FSB, the goggles seemed to be the same or a similar model of goggles used in the earlier attack – the Chinese made Skyzone Cobra X v4 FPV googles.
Russia Launched 36 Ballistic Missiles, 1,940 Drones in the Last Week
How the plot was engineered
As in the 2025 attacks this plan followed much the same structure according to the FSB account.
It said that Ukrainian intelligence officers, posing as patriots, used anonymous Telegram accounts to establish contact with and offered support to representatives of legitimate Russian volunteer organizations. Having identified an ongoing need for drones and FPV goggles they offered to supply the goggles directly to individual servicemen asking for the targeted soldiers to post “video messages of gratitude” on social media.
The FSB said, “As a result of the measures taken, security agencies in various regions of the Russian Federation seized a batch of similar IEDs camouflaged inside FPV goggles, transmitted by the enemy through the Russian Post.”
In issuing its general warning, the FSB emphasized that the “perpetrators” “acted covertly, did not disclose their personal information, phone numbers, or place of work, and refused to switch to the Max messenger app.”
It added that it was searching for those who sent the IEDs and further warned that “The Ukrainian special services’ persistent focus on ‘committing terrorist attacks’ against Russian military personnel,” and called on “ volunteers, charitable organizations, and individuals of the need to obtain humanitarian aid from verified sources only and to ensure they [donations] are screened for explosive devices and toxic substances.”
It followed this with a description of how “various items can be disguise IEDs. For example, IEDs disguised as perfume sets, power banks, music speakers, gift figurines, church utensils, auto parts, paving slabs, and heated shoe insoles,” saying these were examples of devices that have previously been defused.
The investigative Department of the FSB in the Volgograd region said it has opened a criminal case under those parts of Russia’s criminal code relating to the illegal trafficking in explosives or explosive devices, the illegal manufacture of explosives, manufacture, alteration or repair of explosive devices and preparation for a terrorist act.

A major cyberattack on Belgian supermarket 40 Delhaize, Carrefour and Spa and other supermarket chain stores has taken place, with €100,000 worth of food thrown away.
Dozens of Belgian supermarkets have been hit by a cyber attack that saw their refrigerators turned up to 70 degrees Celsius, resulting in €100,000 worth of food being thrown away, according to Belgian media reports on Monday.
Some 40 Delhaize supermarkets, 15 Carrefour stores, and five Spar locations have reportedly been impacted. Butchery group De Laet en Van Haver also said that their fridges were affected.
"We have identified an IT incident affecting the refrigeration systems in several dozen stores. We immediately took the necessary measures to keep our stores operational," a spokesperson from Delhaize told Euronews.
Cybercriminals carried out the attack between Sunday night and Monday morning, skyrocketing refrigerator temperatures.
Problems reportedly also occurred at a number of stores of the Swedish supermarket chain ICA last night.
It follows a similar attack in France just weeks ago, on 12 October, when hundreds of French supermarkets belonging to the Intermarché and Coopérative U chains fell victim to a cyberattack targeting their refrigeration systems.
Stephan Moelans, CEO of refrigeration installer Sabcobel, told the Belga news outlet that the Belgian attack involves exactly the same mechanism as the previous French cyberattack.
"Over the past few weeks, we've been working very hard to protect our customers' fridges against this vulnerability," Moelans said.
The refrigeration executive said a software update alone is not enough to address the vulnerability, with physical modifications required instead.
"That requires investment. The simplest solution is to manage the fridges over a secure internet connection. Most of our customers switched to that after the attack in France."
Sabcobel know of around twenty affected units, out of the hundreds it manages across Belgium.
This is a developing story that our journalists are updating.
Euronews has reached out to Carrefour and Spa for comment.

Sudan files complaints against Ethiopia with UN over deadly drone spree
One-way drone attacks have killed or wounded 484 civilians since February, Khartoum says.
Sudan has lodged a complaint against Ethiopia with both the United Nations Security Council and the African Union’s Peace and Security Council after a series of deadly drone attacks this year.
In a statement late on Sunday, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs accused the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) paramilitary group of using Ethiopian territory to launch “brazen aggression” against “civilian sites and power stations” in Sudan, resulting in hundreds of casualties and disruptions to essential services.
The string of incidents “places Ethiopia before international law”, the ministry added.
Sudan’s military has repeatedly accused Ethiopia of aiding the RSF, which it has been fighting in a civil war since April 2023. Ethiopia, meanwhile, has accused the Sudanese military of backing rebels linked to the Tigray People’s Liberation Front, a charge Khartoum denied.
The ministry’s statement came alongside a report from Sudan’s army-led Transitional Sovereignty Council that alleged 70 assaults from February 15 to October 27 involving 187 one-way attack drones.
The attacks killed or wounded 484 civilians and killed 176 Sudanese soldiers, the report said, with another 200 soldiers wounded.
“Since February 2026, armed drones have taken off from Ethiopian soil … to strike Sudanese cities and civilians,” the report said.
The report identified launch sites at Asosa Airport in western Ethiopia, the Kurmuk-Gizen border area and Bahir Dar airbase in northwestern Ethiopia’s Amhara region.
Last month saw 28 attacks carried out by 97 drones, the report said.
It cited an October 9 attack on displaced families in Wad el-Mahi, located in Sudan’s Blue Nile region near the Ethiopian border, which it said killed 30 civilians – 26 women and four children – and wounded 100.
A spokesman for UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said on Saturday that he was “appalled” by the impact of drone strikes in Sudan, days after another strike on a market in RSF-controlled territory in Darfur killed more than 100 people.
The secretary-general “strongly condemns the escalating drone attacks in Sudan by the parties to the conflict and the catastrophic toll these attacks are inflicting on civilians”, the spokesman said, adding that the strikes constitute violations of international humanitarian law.

Belgian Prime Minister prepares to resign after budget talks collapse
Kyiv • UNN

Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever is meeting King Philippe on Monday to tender his resignation amid the threat of the collapse of his coalition government over attempts to reduce the budget deficit by €10 billion. Politico reports, according to UNN.
Details
Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever will meet King Philippe on Monday to offer his resignation. This comes amid the threat of the collapse of the five-party coalition, whose members cannot agree on reducing the budget deficit by €10 billion.
Over the weekend, government representatives tried to reach an agreement on next year's budget. However, the negotiations ended unsuccessfully on Monday morning. Tuesday was considered the unofficial deadline for concluding a deal, as the budget must receive parliamentary approval by the end of the year.
During the negotiations, De Wever sought to demonstrate to financial markets that Belgium is fulfilling its obligations to the European Union. In 2025, the country's budget deficit stood at 5.2% of GDP, and next year it is forecast to rise even further.
The prime minister had previously ruled out starting the new year with a temporary budget that would allow the government to continue spending in accordance with last year's budget.
The main disagreements during the negotiations arose between the Flemish socialists from the Vooruit party and the French-speaking center-right Reformist Movement (MR).
The socialists insisted on raising taxes for citizens with the highest incomes. In contrast, MR representatives rejected this proposal and opposed a broader reform of the value-added tax.
"There were still too many taxes on the table," said Reformist Movement Deputy Prime Minister David Clarinval after the negotiations ended. At the same time, he did not rule out resuming the talks as early as Monday.
Budget negotiations in Belgium also dragged on last year. In November, De Wever asked King Philippe to extend the deadline for reaching an agreement. The monarch granted the government an additional 50 days.
If snap elections are held in Belgium, support for radical political forces may grow. According to polls, the far-right Vlaams Belang party and the far-left Workers' Party (PTB-PVDA) are showing strong results.

Jailed PKK founder Ocalan moved to new section of Turkish island prison
Improving prison conditions for Abdullah Ocalan has been a key Kurdish demand in push to end PKK-Turkiye conflict.
Turkiye has moved the jailed founder of the Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK), Abdullah Ocalan, to a newly-built section of the island prison where he has been held for 27 years, pro-Kurdish legislators said as they urged Ankara to speed up the stalled peace process.
Mithat Sancar, a member of the Peoples’ Equality and Democracy Party (DEM) delegation that regularly visits Ocalan, confirmed the transfer on Saturday in an interview with the Kurdish television channel Medya Haber TV.
He said the move “necessitates an acceleration of the (peace) process”, which he said had been paused for two months. “The process cannot proceed with unilateral expectations and demands,” he said.
Fellow DEM politician Pervin Buldan said on Sunday that Ocalan himself had announced the transfer, but played down its significance.
“This new facility is part of the prison; it is not somewhere outside the prison,” she said, according to the AFP news agency. “The question of status cannot be defined solely by Mr Ocalan having moved to this location.”
Erbil-based broadcaster Kurdistan24 described the facility as a new house built for Ocalan on Imrali island. It said the move was seen as part of preparations to give him a more active role in the peace process. Better prison conditions for Ocalan have been a key Kurdish demand.
The PKK was founded in 1978 by Ocalan and others, initially fighting for an independent Kurdish state, before shifting its demands to autonomy and greater rights for Turkiye’s Kurds, who make up an estimated 15 to 20 percent of the population. The group launched an armed campaign against the Turkish state in 1984 and is designated a “terrorist” organisation by Turkiye, the United States and the European Union.
The conflict has killed more than 40,000 people. Ocalan has been held on Imrali, in the Sea of Marmara, since his capture in 1999.
In February last year, Ocalan called on the PKK to disband and disarm and the group announced its dissolution that May. Turkiye’s parliament adopted a law offering limited amnesty for PKK fighters in August and the PKK leadership has repeatedly demanded Ocalan’s release as part of the process.

Estonia expels Russian national over ties with Russian secret services
The Estonian Internal Security Service (KAPO) has deported Russian citizen Leonid Karabeshkin from the country and imposed a Schengen entry ban on him due to his ties with Russian secret services.
Source: KAPO; European Pravda; Estonian public broadcaster ERR; Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna
Details: Estonian police reported that the goal of the deportation is to prevent and counter activities that threaten the security of Estonia and Europe.
KAPO spokesperson Marta Tuul told ERR that Karabeshkin had ties with Russian secret services and individuals acting in their interests.

Details: Police added that the Russian national maintained contacts with Sergei Rekeda and Sergei Rudnov. The latter is under British and Ukrainian sanctions.
Karabeshkin also cooperated with CIRP – the Russian Centre for International and Regional Policy – in whose events individuals associated with Russia's Federal Security Service (FSB) participated.
Media reports show that Karabeshkin worked in Estonia at the private higher education institution Euroacademy, where he engaged in teaching and research activities.
Tsahkna, commenting on the deportation of the Russian citizen, emphasised that Estonia "will not turn a blind eye" to threats to its security or the security of Europe.
Quote from Tsahkna: "Those with links to Russian intelligence services and hostile influence networks have no place exploiting our openness. One such individual has now been expelled from Estonia and barred from entering the Schengen area. Rightly so. We will not tolerate activities that undermine our security."

Oil prices fell on Monday morning as talks in Qatar revived hopes of reopening the Strait of Hormuz, but US President Donald Trump kept the threat of fresh strikes alive and Israel's Benjamin Netanyahu reportedly urged him to hit Iran straight after Tuesday's midterm elections.
Oil started the week on the back foot, with Brent crude, the global benchmark, trading at around $108.5 a barrel on Monday morning, down roughly 2.8% from its Friday close, as Iranian negotiators held talks in Qatar on a plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz.
The US benchmark West Texas Intermediate also fell 3% to under $100 a barrel.
However, there were few signs of a breakthrough behind the market move.
US President Donald Trump kept military options open, while Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu reportedly pressed him to strike Iran as soon as Americans had voted in Tuesday's midterm elections.
Shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow waterway between Iran and Oman that normally carries around a fifth of the world's oil, has been heavily disrupted since the war began in late February.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said over the weekend, in an interview posted on Telegram, that the plan under discussion could see the strait reopened in as little as two days, provided Washington met a series of conditions.
Araghchi added that Tehran was not holding direct talks with the US, and that the outcome would depend on how Washington answered Iran's questions.
Iranian officials have previously demanded an end to the US naval blockade of Iran's ports, the lifting of sanctions on its oil exports and a halt to fighting on all regional fronts.
Mixed signals from Washington
Speaking to reporters at a Halloween party at his Mar-a-Lago resort in Florida on Saturday night, Trump said the negotiations were "going fine", though he described the Iranians as "not very reliable".
"We're not in that much of a hurry from the standpoint that we've knocked out their navy, we've knocked out their air force,” Trump said. However, he added that the US still had "to take care of, I would say, one or two sites", which could be done "in 10 minutes".
Asked whether he expected to return to war this week, Trump replied: "Let’s say I did. Would I tell you?"
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio also said on Saturday that no decision had been made on resuming military action.
Last week, the Wall Street Journal reported that US Vice President JD Vance had written to Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, at Trump's direction to revive peace talks.
Trump denied this, saying the outreach concerned medical supplies Iran needed.
Benjamin Netanyahu urged Trump in a phone call on Saturday to resume strikes immediately after the midterms, news site Axios reported, while Trump wants to give diplomacy more time.
Trump described the call as "very good".
Netanyahu is also fighting for his political future as his bloc won 53 of the 120 seats in the Knesset, Israel's parliament, in the 27 October election, short of the 61 needed for a majority, while the opposition bloc led by former army chief Gadi Eisenkot took 48.
Netanyahu's Likud party has claimed, without evidence, that the vote was stolen.
A war premium is still priced in
Goldman Sachs said in an investor note on Monday that a geopolitical risk premium of around $27 a barrel "now explains most of October's crude price rally", which briefly took Brent to $118.
The bank raised its forecast for Brent at the end of this year to $105 a barrel from $90, saying markets were putting more weight on the risk of escalation after the US midterms.
Supply risks also remain.
The UK Maritime Trade Operations centre, which monitors shipping in the region, said on Sunday it had received a report of a projectile hitting a vessel in the Strait of Hormuz.
On Friday, Iran had also reported multiple strikes against ships, signalling that tensions in the maritime chokepoint have not eased.

Algerian troops arrive in Niger in first foreign deployment since 1973
An Algerian army convoy has arrived in Niger in Algeria's first foreign troop deployment since it sent forces to support Egypt during the 1973 war with Israel.
Niger, like other countries in West Africa's Sahel region, is battling insurgents linked to al Qaeda and Islamic State.
Algeria, which shares a border with Niger, has traditionally regarded stability in the Sahel-Sahara as an important regional security priority.
Energy is an important focus for Algeria in Niger, where Algerian state-run oil and gas firm Sonatrach has investments.
One major project, the Trans-Saharan Gas Pipeline with Niger and Nigeria, aims to deliver African gas to Europe and other international markets.
Reuters spoke to 10 people who said the first Algerian military convoy had reached Arlit, a uranium mining town in the country's northwest.
Algeria has said the decision to deploy troops was taken to protect the country's energy and economic interests, without disclosing the size of the force or the timetable for their arrival.
Military officers have ruled Niger, which has uranium, oil and gold resources, since the July 2023 coup that ousted President Mohamed Bazoum, which Algeria initially opposed.
The deployment is a sign that relations between Algiers and Niamey have improved since last year, when Niger recalled its ambassador from Algeria, after Mali accused Algeria of shooting down one of its drones near the border.

No plans to destroy countries as colonial powers crumble — top Russian security official
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
10:19:49 UTC
19:19:49 KST

MOSCOW, November 2. /TASS/. Moscow has no plans to destroy any countries, as former colonial powers are falling apart on their own, Russian Security Council Secretary Sergey Shoigu said.
"I don’t quite get why we should do that. We have no plans to destroy any countries. Many of them - colonial powers - are collapsing on their own," he said on the sidelines of the Peoples of Russia International Week.
"The reason is that those whom they once enslaved and turned into their colonies, are awakening and rising as their self-consciousness and self-determination are reviving," Shoigu added.
"An old man in Vietnam told me: ‘You know, I’m from the generation that still remembers and that was told about portable French guillotines in Vietnam.’ This is, in fact, what those countries brought to the colonies they ruled and sought to use for decades and centuries," he noted. "Our goal is different. The goal is to make sure that our country remains united and indivisible for decades and centuries and for us to respect and understand each other," the top Russian security official said.
According to Shoigu, this policy does not always receive support in the West because "they have a constant need for an enemy."
Peoples of Russia International Week
The Peoples of Russia International Week, organized in accordance with President Vladimir Putin’s order, is being held to coincide with People’s Unity Day, celebrated on November 4. The event is coordinated by the office of the Russian Security Council. The focus of discussions is on national unity, historical memory, the continuity of generations, service to the country and responsibility for its future, and the promotion of strong families.
The Peoples of Russia International Week brings together government officials, members of international organizations, the business community, academic and expert circles, cultural figures and public organizations from Russia, as well as about 50 delegates from 35 countries, including those considered unfriendly.
TASS is a strategic information partner of the event.

Palantir AI tech unused or little used by 29 NHS trusts said to be benefiting from it
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
10:19:46 UTC
19:19:46 KST

More than two dozen hospital trusts the NHS claims have benefited from Palantir’s medical data platform are not using all or most of the AI-powered technology, the Guardian can reveal.
The 29 hospital trusts that NHS England publicly lists as “realising benefits” from the controversial £330m federated data platform (FDP) have said the system is not live or they are not using any of its applications. The apparent gap between the NHS claim and the trusts’ understanding was described as “very misleading” by one senior health official.
It comes as the health secretary, Yvette Cooper, faces calls from MPs and campaigners to axe the US tech firm’s contract to deliver the flagship government AI system, which aims to connect scattered medical files, speed up hospital discharges and improve surgery scheduling among other potentially life-saving improvements.
Palantir’s UK and Europe chief executive, Louis Mosley, said ending its contract would be “putting politics above patients” and accused critics of “Palantir Derangement Syndrome”. The company has contracts to supply AI to the Israeli military and Donald Trump’s homeland security crackdown, while its billionaire founder, Peter Thiel, has questioned democracy, said tech companies can “unilaterally change the world” and called technology an “incredible alternative to politics”.
NHS England has previously faced scrutiny over how it has used data to defend the Palantir contract, which began in 2024. It claims 117,539 more operations were carried out by trusts using the FDP in a year, but this summer it conceded it could not prove cause and effect, and the Office for Statistics Regulation (OSR) watchdog ran an investigation. Asked about the claim of NHS Trusts “realising benefits”, the OSR said it will now be “taking this forward under our casework function”.
The contrast between the number of hospitals the NHS claims realise benefits from Palantir’s technology and the statements of the hospitals themselves emerged from more than 100 freedom of information requests. NHS England states on its website that 137 trusts are “live” with the FDP, but of those described as “realising benefits”, 29 responded that they were either not using the system or its apps.
Epsom and St Helier said it was “not using FDP at the moment”, Kent and Medway said the trust “has been focused on other priorities … the FDP is not currently live”, Mersey Care said they had “not yet gone live with the FDP”, Nottingham University Hospitals said “no implementation timeline has been agreed”, and University Hospitals of North Midlands said: “FDP is not live. We do not intend to roll it out in the future.”
Chi Onwurah, chair of the Commons science and technology committee, said: “If many NHS trusts don’t see the value of the FDP, serious questions need to be asked about whether the hype surrounding Palantir’s products matches reality.”
She called on the government to activate the 2027 break clause in Palantir’s contract and launch an open competition for a UK-owned and based supplier to handle patient records. The Commons health select committee is also calling for ministers to pull Palantir’s deal.
The FOIs were obtained by Medact, a medical charity campaigning for Palantir to be ejected from the NHS, and shared with the Guardian. Medact spokesperson Dr Rhiannon Mihranian Osborne said: “Our NHS institutions are meant to work in the interests of public trust and evidence-based healthcare, not use creative accounting to justify a deeply controversial contract. There is no good reason for the government to continue this failing project. We now have to ask, if ministers are using these flawed claims to make their decision, are they being misled?”
Asked to respond, NHS England insisted nearly 140 trusts “have now reported benefits from the wide range of tools available on the platform, helping staff join up and improve care for patients, and work more efficiently.”
It has previously said that its list of hospital trusts reporting benefits includes those using the tools for back office data analysis and submission rather than to support patient care. It is understood trusts that say they do not use the FDP may use a small part of its functionality to help calculate treatment costs. For example, Torbay and South Devon NHS Foundation Trust said it is “not currently operationally using the FDP” but NHS England records it as “live” because infrastructure is in place “to support data submission, rather than active operational use of FDP apps.”
Palantir has been hitting back against criticism of its deal and last month hired Labour’s former deputy leader and member of the House of Lords Tom Watson as a full-time senior lobbyist. Watson this week has been posting videos on X aiming to debunk “myths” about Palantir, including concerns that public services will become “locked in” to its systems. He rebutted criticism from the Green party leader Zack Polanski, who said it was “beyond ridiculous” that Lord Watson was a life peer.
Watson and Mosley have also been writing directly to critical MPs in letters that have counted the times they have spoken out against the company, which one recipient, Labour’s Clive Lewis, described as “very Big Brother”.
Marc Farr, chair of the NHS Chief Data and Analytics Officers Network, said: “I am concerned to hear that there are 29 trusts reported as receiving benefits but when asked are not actually using the tool. It is great that a number of trusts that have adopted the FDP are benefiting from this nationally funded programme, but it is crucial for public support … that benefits are reported accurately, transparently and in a way that can be properly verified.”
A Palantir spokesperson said: “Palantir software is helping to deliver better care, with trusts using it recording 117,000 additional operations, a 14.3% reduction in discharge delays for long stay patients and a 5.6% improvement in the number of people finding out whether or not they have cancer within 28 days.”

Russia plans to delay Defense Ministry pay for the first time amid budget gap - report
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
12:19:30 EET
19:19:30 KST

Russia plans to delay Defense Ministry pay for the first time amid budget gap - report
Kyiv • UNN
Russia’s Defense Ministry plans to defer December salaries until January, except for participants in Russia’s war in Ukraine. The budget deficit could rise to 3.2% of GDP.
Russia’s Ministry of Defense plans for the first time to postpone December salary payments until January, while the Russian government is preparing for a sharp increase in the budget deficit by the end of the year. Bloomberg reported this, UNN writes.
Details
According to a draft order by Russia’s Ministry of Defense, salaries for each December, starting in 2026, will be paid the following January. Previously, a provision stipulated that December payments had to be made by the end of the year. A similar practice existed in the Soviet Union.
Monthly salaries for December will be transferred between January 11 and 21. The order does not apply to service members taking part in the Russian Federation’s war in Ukraine, who will continue to receive their December payments by December 25, the publication writes.
"This change could help the government manage cash flows by shifting a significant portion of spending into the next financial period. December usually accounts for a disproportionately large share of annual government spending, which has risen sharply during the war," the publication notes.
In the fifth year of Russia’s war against Ukraine, Moscow’s plans to reduce the budget deficit, as noted, were undermined by another escalation of the conflict following the failure of earlier US-backed attempts to reach a peace settlement.
Russia’s government spending is expected to exceed the initial plan by approximately 10% this year, reaching 48.5 trillion rubles ($602 billion). The full-year deficit is projected to increase to 7.3 trillion rubles, or 3.2% of gross domestic product, from approximately 2.2% in September.
The overspending reflects an increase in war-related expenditures, the publication writes. Russia’s latest budget plans also point to increased military spending in the coming years, which "indicates that President Vladimir Putin is preparing for a prolonged confrontation," the publication states.
According to official forecasts, military spending will decline only slightly, to 16.6 trillion rubles in 2028 and 16.3 trillion rubles in 2029, after reaching an expected record level of 17.1 trillion rubles next year.
According to the explanatory note to the draft budget, payments to Russian service members will account for between 9% and 10.4% of total defense spending over the next three years.
In September, Putin increased the authorized strength of Russia’s armed forces to 2,441,630 personnel, including 1,550,500 service members. Since 2022, the authorized number of service members has increased by more than half a million people.

“We need to adapt to new challenges and find new answers to new questions and new threats,” he said, adding that Italy and Türkiye were well positioned to do so.

He also highlighted longstanding bilateral ties as the two countries mark 170 years of diplomatic relations. Italy is Türkiye’s leading trading partner in the Mediterranean and its second-largest in Europe, he said.
The ambassador pointed to educational and cultural exchanges, noting that Turkish students form Italy’s second-largest international student community. Italian scholars and Turkish archaeologists are also working together on 15 missions.
Manzo voiced support for reforming the UN Security Council to make it “more transparent and democratic”, recalling a book he received from Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan bearing the phrase “The world is bigger than five”.
He also highlighted cooperation in space exploration, including joint satellite projects and Türkiye’s first astronaut travelling to space alongside Italian astronauts.
‘I felt at home’
Reflecting on his first months in Ankara, Manzo praised Turkish hospitality and said he had immediately felt welcomed.
“I felt at home,” he said.
Originally from Naples, the ambassador said his Mediterranean background helped him connect with Turkish culture. He described Ankara as his home and praised Istanbul’s historical ties with Italy.
Manzo concluded by extending his best wishes to the Turkish people on the occasion of Republic Day.

The survey collected 1,436 valid responses from Taipei residents aged 20 and older, with a 95% confidence level and a margin of error of ±2.9 percentage points.

As aid situation worsens, displaced Sudanese worry about warnings of famine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
10:16:58 UTC
19:16:58 KST

As aid situation worsens, displaced Sudanese worry about warnings of famine
Sudan’s displaced people now face a mounting food crisis, with warnings of famine.
The sound of gunfire forced 50-year-old Aisha Adam to flee her home in the al-Kalakla neighbourhood of Khartoum days after war erupted in Sudan between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) on April 15, 2023.
She went to the neighbouring city of Omdurman, but fighting followed her and in May 2023, Adam had to find a new refuge. It brought her to a camp for internally displaced people (IDPs) in Port Sudan, on the country’s Red Sea coast, where she lives with her orphaned grandson and nephew.
“Amid the clashes, I left with my grandson for the bus station, intending to travel to Wad Madani in Gezira state, south of Khartoum. But I found a bus heading to Port Sudan and boarded it, even though all I knew about the city was that it was safe,” she told Al Jazeera.
The fighting between the SAF and the RSF has killed as many as 200,000 people, according to aid workers. The war has also displaced 13 million people and led to famine in parts of the country.
After Adam was forced to move to Port Sudan, she initially stayed at a shelter for IDPs in the centre of the city. In June, she and others were relocated to a displacement centre on the outskirts of the city.
Accommodation was allocated according to household size. Adam was given a tent to share with the two children under her care, and shared a boundary with two other families.
“At the first shelter, I received some assistance from organisations, other agencies and even ordinary people. But things are different here. The aid we receive has decreased significantly, so I had to try to find work to avoid starving to death,” she said.
Adam’s struggle to feed the two children comes as Sudan faces deepening food shortages. In a joint statement released on October 27, the United States Department of State warned of the deterioration in food availability and the risk of famine in the coming months.
“Sudan is experiencing an alarming deterioration in its food security. The risk of famine in the coming months, as warned by the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification, needs urgent action,” the statement said.
Fatima is experiencing the real-life consequences highlighted in the report, as finding food becomes a daily struggle. Humanitarian assistance over the past six months has been limited, and she recalls receiving aid on only three occasions. Once, she received 550,000 Sudanese pounds ($59.13) in cash. Another time, she was given 12kg of flour. At the last distribution, she received personal hygiene supplies for women.
“I have no choice but to work. There is no one I can rely on. My two sons are missing, and I do not know where they are, while my other son died before the war began,” she said.
Adam leaves her accommodation early in the morning and heads to a nearby market, where she makes and sells zalabia, a traditional Sudanese fried pastry, alongside tea and coffee. Some days she makes a profit; on others, she loses money.
“I do not know how to calculate my profit. But as soon as I finish selling the zalabia, I go to buy the ingredients … for the next day: 3kg of flour for 21,000 pounds ($2.25), 2 litres of oil for 22,000 pounds ($2.36) and three bags of charcoal for 9,000 pounds ($0.97),” she told Al Jazeera.
Adam says the money left after buying these supplies is often insufficient to provide a meal for herself and the two children in her care. A kilogramme of lentils, one of the cheapest food items available to her, costs 16,000 pounds ($1.72). Meat is no longer on her shopping list, and her diet now consists mainly of lentils and rice.
“Fortunately, aid organisations have been providing water for the past five days. Before that, I used to buy 18 litres for 1,500 pounds ($0.16). Sometimes I did not have the money and had to borrow it,” she said.
Adam says her priority is to keep her small business running. It helps her put food on the table while helping her cope with the pain of not knowing what happened to her two missing sons.
“The important thing is that we eat, even if it is only lentils and water, with nothing else. But my greatest fear is that we will fall ill, because we have no money for treatment,” she said.
Her struggle reflects the wider food crisis facing millions in Sudan. On October 22, 2026, the World Food Programme (WFP) announced that funding shortages had forced it to cut monthly food assistance to displaced people, affecting about 900,000 people.
Meanwhile, some 19.5 million people across the country face acute hunger, including five million experiencing emergency levels of food shortages. The risk of famine persists in several hunger hotspots, particularly in Greater Darfur and Greater Kordofan, the WFP says.
Esraa Mohammed, supervisor of the al-Suraiha 8 IDP camp in al-Obeid, says displaced families are facing severe shortages of humanitarian assistance and lack even the most basic necessities.
“We have 450 registered displaced people in the camp, in addition to 40 newly arrived people who have not yet been added to the official records,” she told Al Jazeera. “Most arrive wearing torn clothes after their journeys, with nothing to protect them from the sun or rain, and without even a single meal.”
Mohammed says some organisations provide food assistance, including about 400ml of cooking oil per person and 250gm of peas per person. Another organisation distributes lentils, flour, oil and salt.
But these supplies are insufficient to sustain her family for a month, forcing her and other displaced Sudanese to look for casual work to make ends meet. Sometimes they find work; at other times, they go to bed without food.
“There are 100 children in the camp, 30 of whom are suffering from severe acute malnutrition. They also urgently need clothes to protect them from harsh weather conditions and cover their small bodies,” she said.
Mohammed added that some displaced people arriving from South Kordofan had told her they were forced to eat tree leaves while fleeing their homes because they feared being killed by the RSF, following reports of civilians being murdered, detained or raped by fighters from the group.
Ahmed Ismail, an expert on the United Nations and NGOs, describes the humanitarian situation in Sudan as extremely serious, with the basic needs of the population far exceeding the support being provided.
“Sudan is facing a complex crisis involving famine, displacement, the collapse of health services, the destruction of livelihoods and serious violations against civilians,” he told Al Jazeera.
Humanitarian monitoring had indicated an increase in civilian deaths, including those linked to difficulties accessing food, healthcare and shelter, as well as casualties from attacks and violations, including drone strikes.
“When assistance declines, the most vulnerable families are deprived of food and medicine, increasing the risk of death among children, women and older people, particularly in conflict and displacement areas,” Ismail said.
Continued reductions in aid, alongside escalating violations and restrictions on humanitarian access, could turn the crisis into an even wider catastrophe, he warned.
“Denying the severity of conditions in some areas did not change the reality of the suffering experienced by civilians,” he said.

The demonstrations featured drone ships from firms including US-based Maritime Tactical Systems and STR8 in cooperation with Taichung-based Thunder Tiger, as well as underwater robots from New Taipei’s AwareOcean and Singapore’s BeeX, per the Liberty Times.
STR8 Industries’ Ghostwake is said to be among the fastest known drone boats, with its lunge burst and navigation capabilities. It has a mast system that can be raised or lowered and can remain operational for up to seven days in open seas.
AwareOcean says its Delphin uses sonar and high-definition imaging for underwater surveys. Singapore’s BeeX presented its hovering underwater carrier, which can perform underwater inspections for up to eight hours, per BeeX.

The ceasefire enabled a humanitarian mission to the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky and for hundreds of stranded citizens to leave.
Russia resumed attacks on Ukraine's Kherson region on Monday, after the end of a local ceasefire in the area, the longest truce in the war between the neighbours since 2022, Kyiv said.
A rare pause in fighting, brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump, ended on Sunday after starting on Tuesday.
The ceasefire enabled a humanitarian mission to the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky and for hundreds of stranded citizens to leave.
It was the longest pause in fighting between the neighbours in the full-scale invasion, now in its fifth year, which has killed hundreds of thousands and displaced millions.
"At around 8:00 am this morning, Russian occupiers attacked a car with a drone in the Korabelny city district" of Kherson, local authorities said in a statement, adding that a 62-year-old woman and 73-year-old man were wounded and hospitalised.
Russia refused a Ukrainian offer to extend the truce, a senior Ukrainian figure told the AFP news agency on Sunday.
Kherson's regional governor Oleksandr Prokudin had warned local people to be particularly vigilant when the ceasefire ended.
Ukraine's military alleged Russia used the pause in fighting to "fortify its positions".
Russian attacks also killed one person in Izium, a city in the country's north-eastern Kharkiv region, the local governor there said.
US-mediated talks between Russia and Ukraine are set to resume this month.
The Kremlin has repeatedly rejected calls for a wider ceasefire and said it intends to press on with its full-scale offensive to seize the rest of eastern Ukraine.
App hack
The fresh wave of strikes on Kherson come a day after Ukraine said its air raid alert system had been compromised, after baseless alerts of a radiation threat appeared on the app.
"Hi! A nuclear alert is about to go off all across Ukraine! Don't worry, the Oreshnik is on its way," one of the fake warnings in Russian said.
Several regional governors also warned that the system had been hacked and advised residents that there was no imminent threat.
By midnight local time the national alert system was operating normally, the State Emergency Service said in a statement.
"We once again urge citizens not to click on links from unknown sources and not to spread unverified information," the agency said.
And hours later, Russia also announced its emergency warnings app came under a "massive cyberattack" on Monday, in an apparent exchange of blows as their longest truce came to an end.
Moscow's emergencies ministry said hackers posted "false information" on the app, which is designed to warn the public of incoming drone attacks and other threats.

Number of journalists killed worldwide rises by 20% compared to previous years — UNESCO
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
10:13:04 UTC
19:13:04 KST

PARIS, November 2. /TASS/. A total of 189 journalists were killed in connection with their professional activities in 2024-2025, up 20% from 2022-2023, according to a report by the UNESCO Director General on the safety of journalists and the risk of impunity for crimes against them.
Of the deaths recorded in the report, 127 occurred in combat zones. The document noted that 40% of these journalists were killed by drone strikes. The highest number of journalists were killed in Palestine: 62, followed by Mexico: 17, and Sudan: 14. According to UNESCO, the conflict in Ukraine claimed the lives of 12 media workers during the period in question.
"Local and international war reporters face increased safety risks, especially due to direct exposure to crossfire as well as deliberate targeting even far away from the frontline. In conflict zones, groups of journalists totalling 36 were reportedly killed in temporary field media houses and workplaces in four countries. In one instance, a single attack led to the killing of nine journalists," the report said.
Over the past 20 years, UNESCO has recorded the deaths of 1,600 journalists, yet only 14% of these cases have been investigated. Meanwhile, according to the document, the proportion of unresolved investigations in countries without armed conflict has fallen from 94% in 2012 to 77% in 2026.
"Nevertheless, the commitment to press freedom is more urgent than ever, as it remains under severe threat in both conflict and non-conflict settings, and journalists continue to pay a heavy price," UNESCO Director General Khaled El-Enany emphasized.

No sign of deal on budget ahead of crucial week in parliament
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Budget talks between the coalition and opposition parties at the weekend have failed to produce an agreement, meaning the plans will go before parliament this week without majority support.
The coalition parties D66, CDA and VVD had hoped to strike a deal with the opposition before the plans are debated this week, but were unable to find a breakthrough despite speaking to three different combinations.
Prime minister Rob Jetten said at his weekly press conference last Friday that he still wanted to come up with an agreement that balanced the demands of left and right-wing parties, while the opposition groups have repeatedly urged him to pick a side.
Jetten appeared to be close to securing the support of the left-wing parties Pro and Volt in September after agreeing to abandon €6 billion of welfare spending cuts. But the cabinet is unprepared to meet the two parties’ other demands to raise wealth taxes to make up the shortfall.
Pro leader Jesse Klaver said after meeting Jetten and other coalition leaders in the Catshuis, the prime minister’s official residence, that “there is no political will to work with us”.
“That’s because the cabinet has chosen to give more money to those with the largest fortunes,” Klaver added.
Abortion and surrogacy
Pro and Volt are the only combination that can offer the three coalition parties the votes they need for a majority in both houses of parliament. Jetten also held a video conference with the leaders of three right-wing parties – the farmers’ party BBB, JA21 and the orthodox Protestant SGP.
The parties have drawn up a laundry list of issues where they want the cabinet to make concessions or block legislation, including reforms to facilitate late-term abortions and surrogacy, which the Bible-belt SGP opposes.
The farmers want agriculture minister Jaimi van Essen to scrap his plans to reduce nitrogen pollution by putting up low-emission zones around protected nature areas and offering buyouts to livestock farmers, but none of the coalition parties are prepared to go back to the drawing board.
The three parties said in a statement that they saw “opportunities to talk further”, but there were no signs of a significant shift in their direction. Jetten said on Friday that it was “not sensible” to make the budget vote dependent on non-financial issues.
A third potential route to a majority in the lower house, via the minor parties ChristenUnie and 50Plus, along with the far-right splinter group of former PVV MPs led by Gidi Markuszower, also seemed doomed after ChristenUnie leader Mirjam Bikker came away from talks saying the process was “not going well”.
“We’re doing things we should have sorted out in August,” Bikker said. “And that’s frustrating”.
Jetten warned at his press conference that opposition parties were jeopardising vital measures to ease the cost of living, such as an extension to the discount on fuel duty, if they voted down next year’s budget.
MPs are due to debate the budget measures on Wednesday, with the votes due to take place on November 12.
