Argentina's austerity-hit economy reels towards recession, testing Milei ahead of 2027 vote
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
10:12:23 UTC
19:12:23 KST

Argentina's austerity-hit economy reels towards recession, testing Milei ahead of 2027 vote
BUENOS AIRES, Nov 2 - At a family-owned factory in Buenos Aires, a machine used to wrap packets of colored socks sits silent.
Eseka still produces nearly 3 million items a month at the factory, including underwear and swimwear for its Cocot and Dufour brands. But like many local businesses, it is struggling to stay afloat. Since President Javier Milei took office nearly three years ago, sales have fallen around 40%, battered by weak consumer demand and competition from cheaper imports as the government has lifted trade restrictions.
That matters in Argentina, where household consumption accounts for about two-thirds of gross domestic product, making any sustained pullback in spending a drag on the broader economy.
Economists says the economy likely slipped into a recession in the third quarter, a test of voter patience a year ahead of the October 2027 presidential election, when Milei is widely expected to run for a second term.
Some 32,300 businesses — roughly 6% of the total companies in Argentina — closed in the period from when Milei took power in December 2023 through to July, according to think-tank Fundar.
"The situation is critical," said Ricardo Kuchikian, who owns Eseka with his brother Gustavo. The firm posted losses last year and shed about 30% of its workforce, according to the brothers. Over half of the circular knitting machines in the sock factory stand idle.
"Consumption has fallen very sharply over the past three years," Kuchikian said.
In the first nine months of the year consumption in Argentina fell 2.7% compared with the same period in 2025, according to market research firm Scentia, which tracks sales across supermarkets, small retailers and e-commerce platforms.
While Milei's radical austerity measures have slowed inflation to 30% from a sky-high 200% and brought other macroeconomic imbalances under control, their benefits have yet to reach much of the broader public. The share of Argentines living beneath the poverty line has risen to nearly a third of the population, after falling to an eight-year low in 2025.
To boot, Argentina likely dipped into recession in the third quarter, economists say, driven by austerity and tight monetary policy. A slight rebound is forecast in 2027.
Economic activity is forecast to have contracted for a second consecutive quarter in the July-September period, meeting the common definition of a recession. Official data for the quarter will be released in November.
“Argentina’s economy is technically in a moderate recession,” said Ricardo Delgado, head of consultancy Analytica. GDP already fell 0.6% in the second quarter from the first, and Delgado forecasts a further contraction of around 1.5% for the third quarter.
According to a recent survey by consultancy Giacobbe y Asociados, Milei’s approval rating slipped slightly in October to 36% while disapproval rose to 56%.
To be sure, not all of the economy is suffering. Energy, mining and agriculture have emerged as the winners under Milei’s model, driven by exports and investment in Argentina’s vast shale oil and gas reserves, as well as rising global demand for minerals such as lithium.
But the strength of these export-oriented sectors has so far not offset the slump in other industries tied to the domestic market. Textiles, auto manufacturing, retail and construction have all remained under pressure as consumers continue to feel the squeeze.
Analytica's Delgado said he expected that two-track economy to continue with "ups and downs" in 2027, warning that household finances were unlikely to improve meaningfully before the election.
Milei has ruled out changes to his economic plan, dismissing as "colossal stupidity" claims that people were unable to make ends meet.
'AGGRESSIVE COMPETITION'
Investors have cheered Milei’s easing of strict import restrictions, capital and currency controls and other regulations that long weighed on business in Argentina. But for many local firms, the shift has brought a painful adjustment, exposing them to cheaper imported goods just as domestic demand weakens.
Official data from August showed manufacturing fell 3.2% year-on-year, retail and wholesale trade dropped 3.5%, and construction declined 2.5%, according to Argentina’s INDEC statistics agency.
“Since the end of 2023, I think sales have fallen 40%,” said Martin Abigador, director of Dakuba, another family-owned business that distributes fabrics.
His company has been unable to offset what he described as "aggressive competition" from foreign imports, mainly from China.
Back at the sock factory, Kuchikian feared that if Milei's policies continue "national industry could disappear.”
A spokesperson for the government defended the uneven pace of the recovery, saying that growth never occurs uniformly across sectors.
"This is the economic program the president believes in, and he is not going to change it," the spokesperson said. REUTERS

President Xi and President Steinmeier noted that as the world’s second and third largest economies, China and Germany should shoulder the responsibility for safeguarding world peace and development and striving for a more just and equitable global governance system. Both sides spoke highly of the fruitful outcomes of China-Germany relations, and agreed to uphold mutual respect and equality, expand mutually beneficial cooperation, deepen people-to-people exchanges, and properly handle differences through dialogue and consultation, so as to usher in a new chapter of China-Germany all-round strategic partnership.

The two presidents’ visits to China have sent out a positive message of strengthening communication and coordination, deepening open cooperation, and supporting multilateralism and free trade, and set a sound example for the growth of China-EU relations. China will work with various parities to focus on cooperation and mutual benefits, and inject more certainty to the stability and prosperity in today’s world.
Shenzhen TV: Could you share the background of the 11th Lancang-Mekong Cooperation (LMC) Foreign Ministers’ Meeting? As the host, what are China’s expectations for the event?
Mao Ning: This year marks the 10th anniversary of the first LMC Leaders’ Meeting. Over the past decade, with the concerted efforts of all countries, LMC has grown from strength to strength, becoming a stellar example of regional cooperation brimming with vitality and potential. Solid progress has been made in building a community with a shared future between China and the five Mekong countries bilaterally and multilaterally. The Lancang-Mekong Innovation Corridor has become a new highlight. Faster headway is being made in boosting regional power connectivity. The LMC Special Fund has provided support for over 1,000 small and smart projects. The Lancang-Mekong Sweet Spring Action and the Hundred, Thousand, Ten Thousand Action Plan on Lancang-Mekong Agricultural Cooperation, among others, have delivered real results. The Lancang-Mekong Visa has facilitated people-to-people exchanges among the six countries.
As the century-defining transformation unfolds at an accelerating pace, LMC’s role in promoting openness and development and safeguarding peace and tranquility is becoming even more pronounced. China hopes to take the upcoming Foreign Ministers’ Meeting as an opportunity to work with the five Mekong countries to take stock of past experience, plan future cooperation, discuss in particular the blueprint for LMC 2.0, explore new mechanisms for openness and cooperation, build more platforms for industrial innovation, and make greater progress in law enforcement and security cooperation, so as to inject strong impetus into building a Lancang-Mekong community with a shared future of peace, prosperity and sustainable development.
People’s Daily: On October 31 Beijing time, the Committee on Disarmament and International Security (First Committee) of the 81st session of the UN General Assembly adopted the resolution “Promoting international cooperation on peaceful uses in the context of international security” tabled by China. Could you share more details?
Mao Ning: We welcome the adoption by the First Committee of the resolution “Promoting international cooperation on peaceful uses in the context of international security.” The resolution calls for efforts to coordinate both development and security, strengthen the role of the UN, and safeguard developing countries’ lawful rights to peaceful uses of technology. The resolution urges all countries to take concrete actions to promote international cooperation on peaceful uses, and avoid maintaining restrictions incompatible with their international obligations. The resolution also decides to continue consideration of the relevant issue at the UN General Assembly.
This is the fourth time for China to submit the resolution on peaceful uses of technology to the UN General Assembly since 2021, which has received broad support from the international community. Acting on the resolution is an important step for China to implement the Global Security Initiative. We will work with various parties to promote the full and effective implementation of the resolution and make sure that progress in technology will further contribute to peace and development for humanity.
Global Times: The Spokesperson said a few days ago that China will send special envoys to the Middle East, the Gulf region, the Red Sea and the Horn of Africa. Can you share more details?
Mao Ning: To deliver on the initiatives and propositions put forward by President Xi Jinping on promoting peace and security in the Middle East and the four principles on the constructive participation of relevant parties in the resolution of African hotspot issues, Special Envoy of the Chinese Government on the Middle East Issue Zhai Jun will visit Iran, Oman and Saudi Arabia in early and mid-November; Special Representative of the Chinese Government on African Affairs Liu Xianfa will visit Ethiopia, Djibouti and Egypt in early and mid-November; and Special Envoy for the Horn of Africa Affairs of the Foreign Ministry Hu Changchun will visit Eritrea in early November. These shuttle diplomacy visits in this period of time by Chinese special envoys and special representative are aimed at promoting peace talks, easing tensions, and playing a constructive role for upholding regional peace and stability.

China Focus: UN official says world can learn from China's urban renewal experience
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
18:10:49 CST
19:10:49 KST

FUZHOU, Nov. 2 (Xinhua) -- Valuable lessons for global urban development can be drawn from China's people-centered approach to urban renewal, Anacláudia Rossbach, United Nations under-secretary-general and executive director of UN-Habitat, said during the Global Observance of World Cities Day in China's Fuzhou.
Under the theme "Regenerating the City: Adequate Housing for All," the activities in Fuzhou, capital of east China's Fujian Province, brought together city leaders, planners and other stakeholders to discuss global housing challenges from Oct. 31 to Nov. 2.
UN-Habitat's World Cities Report 2026 estimates that up to 3.4 billion people lack access to secure, safe and adequate housing, including more than 1 billion people living in informal settlements and slums. Rossbach called for scaling up inclusive urban regeneration efforts to address this crisis.
Describing China's urban transformation experience as "fantastic," Rossbach said the country's approach to urban development offers valuable lessons, particularly in its growing emphasis on people-centered, neighborhood-level solutions.
Rossbach also pointed to China's efforts to balance cultural heritage preservation with modernization. "In Chinese cities, they all work together in a very balanced way," she noted.
This approach is reflected in Jingdezhen, China's "porcelain capital." Located in Jiangxi Province in the country's east, it was among five cities honored with the fourth-cycle Global Award for Sustainable Development in Cities (Shanghai Award).
Jingdezhen has combined the preservation of its centuries-old ceramic heritage with inclusive neighborhood renewal, improvements to older residential areas and expanded public services. The Jingdezhen Handicraft Porcelain Industry Sites, notably, were added to the UNESCO World Heritage List in July 2026.
China has set a target of renovating 1,500 old streets and factory compounds from 2026 to 2030, bringing in new industries and business models to inject fresh momentum into urban development.
During her visit to Fuzhou, Rossbach toured a regenerated old town quarter where historic buildings have been preserved and new buildings have been designed in traditional architectural styles. She was impressed by the bustling street life and the local application of the "proximity" concept, which clusters services, commercial outlets and public transport links for residents' convenience.
Rossbach also highlighted China's attention to vulnerable groups in urban renewal, such as children, older people and persons with disabilities. She recalled seeing elderly residents practicing tai chi and children playing in public spaces during an earlier visit to Beijing.
Under the national urban renewal plan (2026-2030) released earlier this year, China aims to launch renovations of 115,000 old urban residential compounds, retrofit or install 575,000 residential elevators, and build or upgrade 50,000 hectares of urban green space.
"The solution is not just building houses. It's not enough. This is the main lesson that we learned from China. You have to create the conditions for people to live together," said the UN-Habitat chief.
Adequate housing, she explained, involves not only affordability and accessibility but also good connectivity to urban infrastructure, cultural adequacy and climate resilience.
"We learned from many examples, including here in Fuzhou, how important it is to work with communities to understand what their vision for the city is, what their aspirations and expectations are, so that they can be reflected in city planning and housing policies," Rossbach added.
The three-day event was jointly organized by China's Ministry of Housing and Urban-Rural Development, the Fujian provincial government and UN-Habitat. ■

China Focus: China's draft law calls for fair, equitable global anti-corruption governance system
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
18:10:42 CST
19:10:42 KST

BEIJING, Nov. 2 (Xinhua) -- China's top legislature began deliberating a draft law on combating cross-border corruption, which includes a provision on promoting the building of a fair and equitable global anti-corruption governance system.
The draft was submitted for its second reading at a session of the Standing Committee of the National People's Congress, which runs through Friday.
The draft further elaborates on the legislative purpose and enriches the principles guiding efforts to combat cross-border corruption.
It also stipulates that such efforts must be conducted in strict accordance with the Constitution and laws, follow statutory procedures, and respect and protect human rights.
The draft law was first submitted for deliberation in late August. The formulation of the law is an important step by China to put in place a systematic and comprehensive foreign-related legal framework for anti-corruption, according to the top legislature.
Structured into six chapters and 47 articles, the draft sets out the principles, scope and key positions underpinning China's efforts to combat cross-border corruption.
The revised draft also sets out provisions on the use of information technology by authorities in combating cross-border corruption.
It requires relevant authorities and their staff to keep confidential any state secrets, work-related confidential information, trade secrets, personal privacy and personal information obtained during supervision and investigations.
It also requires Chinese companies operating across borders to set up integrity and compliance departments or appoint dedicated staff, based on their size, business scope and risk prevention and control.
The draft states that efforts to combat cross-border corruption should leave no area beyond oversight, leave no ground unturned and show zero tolerance for corruption.
They should also address both the symptoms and root causes of corruption through a systematic approach, while actively participating in global anti-corruption governance.
China has stepped up international cooperation in combating corruption in recent years. Since the launch of Operation Sky Net in 2015, China has brought back 14,048 fugitives from more than 120 countries and regions and recovered 66.62 billion yuan (about 9.92 billion U.S. dollars) in illicit assets by the end of 2024, according to official data.
In 2025, China deepened international anti-corruption cooperation and investigated 505 cross-border corruption cases. A total of 963 fugitives were repatriated to the country in 2025.
The draft law also helps to regulate the development of cross-border businesses and build a world-class business environment aligned with market principles, the rule of law and international standards.
China is a major trading partner for more than 160 countries and regions, and its total trade in goods has ranked first in the world for eight consecutive years. By the end of 2025, Chinese investors had established more than 50,000 overseas enterprises across 190 countries and regions. ■

The draft is now under its third reading at the ongoing session of the Standing Committee of the National People's Congress, the country's top legislature, which runs through Friday.
The draft also clarifies jurisdictional provisions and aligns them with other relevant laws.
Following its second reading in June, which added protections for older people, people with disabilities and other groups, the latest draft authorizes procuratorates to bring public-interest litigation in cases involving the building of accessible environments.
The system of procuratorial public interest litigation was launched on a trial basis in 2015 and formally introduced nationwide in 2017.
Its remit has gradually expanded from environmental protection and food and drug safety to areas such as child protection, workplace safety, data privacy and combating telecom fraud. ■

Ryanair eyes cost cuts as it faces a €2 billion rise in its fuel bill next year
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
10:10:34 UTC
19:10:34 KST

One of Europe's biggest airlines saw its first-half profit fall 15% as higher fuel costs and lower fares outweighed passenger growth.
Ryanair reported a net profit of €2.15 billion for the period between April and September 2026, the first half of its financial year ending March 2027.
The result was 15% below the same period last year.
This came as unhedged jet fuel prices doubled while fares also fell, although passenger numbers increased. The airline is reviewing costs as it prepares for a further rise in its fuel bill next year.
On a per-share basis, the Irish airline's first-half diluted earnings fell 14% to €2.05 per share. In the same period, revenue rose 3% to €10.08bn and passenger numbers grew by 6% to 125.8 million, but fares fell by 4%.
Ryanair said the Middle East conflict had made consumers more hesitant and led them to book later as operating costs increased by 10% to €7.69 billion.
The results reflect only part of the rise in fuel prices as Ryanair has hedged 80% of its fuel needs for the year ending March 2027, using financial contracts to lock in prices in advance.
This has helped protect its earnings, but the price of the remaining 20% doubled.
A €2 billion fuel bill increase
According to Ryanair, its fuel bill could rise by around €2 billion in the financial year ending March 2028, based on current forward prices.
"Unless there is a swift resolution of the Middle East conflict, we expect jet-fuel prices to remain elevated well into 2027," CEO Michael O'Leary said.
O'Leary warned that cheaper fuel hedges would expire ahead of summer 2027, leaving European airlines facing much higher bills.
He also previously warned that European airfares could rise by up to 20% in 2027 in an exclusive interview with Euronews in late October.
However, Ryanair expects higher fares and cuts in competitors' capacity to fall short of fully covering its extra fuel costs.
To address the elevated costs, Ryanair is reviewing possible cost-cutting measures, including temporary pay freezes, lower crew-to-passenger ratios and greater use of AI across operations and support teams.
The airline also announced an €800 million share buyback programme, starting in February 2027 and expected to run for around 10 months, subject to market conditions.
Demand for October–December remains strong, with fares running modestly above last year, but late bookings make the outlook harder to predict.
Ryanair said it was too early to give a full-year profit forecast, citing uncertainty over conflicts, fuel prices, the wider economy and European air traffic control disruptions.
In September, Ryanair announced it would reduce its winter schedule to limit exposure to unhedged fuel costs, cutting its full-year passenger target from 216 million to 214 million.
Ryanair's share price was up by 2% in Dublin in early trading on Monday.

The draft amendment was submitted for third reading at a session of the Standing Committee of the National People's Congress, which runs through Friday.
The draft proposes adding provisions on "enhancing water security safeguards" and "accelerating the development of a national water network that is systematic and complete, safe and reliable, intensive and efficient, green and smart, with smooth circulation and orderly regulation."

In addition, the draft includes provisions to encourage public participation in protecting and conserving water resources and preventing and controlling water-related disasters. ■

China Focus: Yellow River, China's mother river, runs clearer after decades of conservation
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
18:10:02 CST
19:10:02 KST

ZHENGZHOU, Nov. 2 (Xinhua) -- The Hukou Waterfall on the Yellow River, once depicted on China's fourth-series 50-yuan banknotes as a torrent of muddy, turbulent water, now presents a markedly different scene, with its cascading waters running clear.
Photographer Lyu Guiming, known for documenting the waterfall in Jixian County, Shanxi Province, since 1999, has witnessed the change.
"Over the past decade, clear cascades at the waterfall have been my main photographic subject," Lyu said. "The contrast with the old scenes is striking."
The changing waterscape reflects decades of efforts to protect and manage the Yellow River, China's second-longest river, which flows 5,464 km from its source in the highlands of Qinghai Province through nine provinces and autonomous regions, crossing deserts and loess lands before emptying into the Bohai Sea in Shandong Province, east China.
In 1946, under the leadership of the Communist Party of China, an agency for people's Yellow River management was established on the river's banks in Heze, Shandong Province.
Because Henan Province was frequently affected by flooding on the river, the Yellow River Conservancy Commission (YRCC) later moved its headquarters to Zhengzhou in December 1953.
Thanks to 80 years of conservation efforts, the river, once prone to devastating floods, heavy sedimentation and shifting channels, now has cleaner waters and more sustainable water use.
Historical records show that before the founding of the People's Republic of China in 1949, the river's lower reaches experienced more than 1,500 dyke breaches and overflows and changed course 26 times. Sediment was a persistent challenge, giving rise to the old saying that half of a bowl of Yellow River water is sand.
Wei Xiangyang, the commission's chief engineer, outlined progress in flood control, a central part of river management.
Dykes built to withstand major floods now stretch 1,371 km in total along the lower reaches. Forty flood-control reservoirs on the river and its tributaries have a combined flood-control capacity of 19 billion cubic meters.
Over the past eight decades, these infrastructure projects have helped avoid an estimated 10.09 trillion yuan (around 1.5 trillion U.S. dollars) in economic losses from floods, Wei said.
Efforts to curb soil erosion have also produced substantial results. Zhu Xiaoyong, director of the commission's soil and water conservation bureau, presented data showing that 290,500 square km of land affected by soil erosion across the river basin have been rehabilitated. Soil and water conservation measures have kept about 24.7 billion tonnes of sediment from entering the river.
The Yellow River spans multiple regions and forms an integrated ecosystem that requires coordinated cross-regional management.
"After years of research, we have developed a reservoir operation approach that stores clean water while discharging sediment," said Zhang Jinliang, chief scientist of Yellow River Engineering Consulting Co., Ltd. "Precision water-sediment regulation marks a shift from passive response to proactive action in managing the river."
Water allocation has also achieved better coordination. Since a unified water-management system covering all provincial-level regions along the river was introduced in 1999, the Yellow River has flowed uninterrupted for 27 consecutive years.
Over the years, more efficient water use has helped expand irrigated farmland in the river basin to 132 million mu (8.8 million hectares). The basin and downstream irrigation areas produce roughly 89.5 billion kilograms of grain annually, or 13.3 percent of China's national grain output.
YRCC figures also show that water quality in the Yellow River Basin has markedly improved. The proportion of monitoring sections graded Class I to III, indicating good water quality, rose from 59.1 percent in 2016 to 93.2 percent in 2025.
The changes are also visible in communities along the river. Lyu's photographs documenting the Hukou Waterfall's shifting waterscape have helped boost local tourism. His widely shared photos have helped turn tourism into a pillar industry in a county that was once impoverished.
"The Yellow River ecosystem forms an integrated whole," he said. "From headwater conservation in the upper reaches and soil and water conservation in the middle reaches to wetland restoration in the lower reaches, green has become a defining feature of high-quality development in the Yellow River Basin." ■

Singapore-Mercosur trade pact takes effect with Argentina
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
18:09:57 CST
19:09:57 KST

SINGAPORE, Nov. 2 (Xinhua) -- The Mercosur (Southern Common Market)-Singapore Free Trade Agreement entered into force between Singapore and Argentina on Sunday, completing its implementation with all four founding Mercosur member states, Singapore's Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry and the Argentinian Embassy in Singapore have said.
The agreement had previously taken effect with Paraguay, Uruguay and Brazil, marking a milestone in Singapore's economic engagement with Latin America, the duo said in a statement on Sunday.
The agreement covers trade in goods and services, investment, government procurement, digital trade, intellectual property and economic cooperation.
Under the pact, Mercosur will eliminate import tariffs on about 96 percent of products over up to 15 years, with around 25 percent of tariff lines receiving immediate duty-free access. It also establishes common rules of origin and more transparent customs procedures.
"Argentina's position as a major agricultural and food producer supports Singapore's efforts to diversify food import sources and strengthen food resilience. There are also opportunities in sectors such as energy, infrastructure, logistics, technology and services," said the statement. ■

Ukraine can buy 500 Patriot missiles, but they may arrive only in years. One estimate says they’d last about three months
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
10:09:30 UTC
19:09:30 KST

Kyiv says it cannot wait years for the 500 Patriot interceptors the US cleared for sale on 30 October. Deliveries may start only in a few years, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy wrote just after midnight, asking partners to send missiles from their own stocks this winter.
The timing is the problem. Since 14 October, Russia had launched more than 100 ballistic missiles at Kyiv and Kyiv Oblast, Zelenskyy said on 27 October. Meanwhile, the US is delaying PAC-3s, the Patriot missile built mainly to stop ballistic missiles, while older PAC-2s keep arriving, an anonymous NATO source told Radio Svoboda on 29 October.
What Washington approved
The State Department approved a possible sale of 500 PAC-3 MSE missiles with spare parts, worth an estimated $2.1 billion. It is not a signed contract, and no delivery date was given. Ukraine, the buyer, would pay with Canadian, German, and Norwegian contributions through the JUMPSTART program, plus funds from an EU loan.
Ukraine wants partners’ Patriot interceptors now. Europe can hand them over only with US approval, Ukraine’s president says
Ukraine had asked Washington for a winter package of 100 interceptors a month, Zelenskyy wrote. He first put that figure to European allies in July. Five hundred PAC-3s could have been a very effective defense package this winter, he added. He proposed that partners send missiles from existing stocks in winter 2026–2027. They would refill their arsenals later from production that, in his words, Ukraine and its partners have contracted and paid for. He called this entirely realistic.
Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty’s senior Washington correspondent Alex Raufoglu, citing his own sources, wrote that deliveries of the new missiles are not expected until after 2030.
Just over three months of cover
Five hundred missiles would not last long anyway, Ukrainian military outlet Defense Express estimated. Building one PAC-3 MSE takes about 24 months, it wrote. It put Ukraine’s need at about 150 anti-ballistic interceptors a month, noting estimates as high as 350. Used very sparingly, 500 would cover just over three months of ballistic attacks.
“Above all, we do not have enough missiles for Patriots”—Zelenskyy after 100+ ballistic missiles
For this winter, the outlet pointed to Poland and Germany, which have sent PAC-3 MSEs before, though in tens rather than hundreds. It named Japan, which it called the only country to have set up its own production of them.
In April, Ukrainian Patriot crews were already rationing missiles mid-attack.

Snow and rain forecast across Kazakhstan on November 3–5
Kazhydromet has released its weather forecast for Kazakhstan for November 3–5, 2026, Qazinform News Agency reports.
Most of Kazakhstan is expected to remain dry under the influence of a high-pressure system. However, an approaching northwestern cyclone will bring rain to western regions on November 4–5, with heavy downpours possible in some areas.

Qarmet targets 4 million tons of steel output in 2026
Kazakhstan’s President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev has visited the converter plant of Qarmet, a key facility in the company’s steelmaking operations, Qazinform News Agency reports, citing the Akorda press service.
During the visit, the President was briefed on the steel production process, which begins with molten iron supplied from a blast furnace. The iron is then converted into steel before being sent to continuous casting machines and subsequently to rolling mills for further processing.
In 2024, Qarmet carried out major overhauls of converters No.1 and No. 2, replacing their bodies entirely and installing more advanced structures. The modernization is expected to expand the company’s product range, increase steel production volumes and improve equipment reliability. The company is also continuing efforts to switch several technological processes to natural gas.
Qarmet Chairman of the Board of Directors Andrey Lavrentyev briefed the Head of State on the company’s improving production performance and the implementation of its investment program.
By the end of 2026, Qarmet plans to produce 4 million tons of steel, 3.6 million tons of coal concentrate and 3.9 million tons of iron ore concentrate.
Since the company began operations, its total investment has exceeded $2.7 billion. The funds have been allocated to modernizing existing facilities and developing new production capacities.
Qarmet is Kazakhstan’s largest mining and metallurgical company, operating a fully integrated production cycle. It is also the only integrated mining and metallurgical complex in Central Asia with its own coal, iron ore and energy resources.
The company employs approximately 35,000 people, including more than 14,000 workers at its metallurgical plant in Temirtau.

Albert Heijn sister chain hit as fridge hacks spread in Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
10:06:50 UTC
19:06:50 KST

Albert Heijn sister chain hit as fridge hacks spread in Europe
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Hackers managed to tamper with fridges and freezers at supermarkets in Belgium, Luxembourg and Sweden overnight, including at least 40 branches of Albert Heijn’s sister chain Delhaize, weeks after a similar attack hit hundreds of supermarkets in France.
A Delhaize spokesperson confirmed the hack on Monday morning, newspaper HLN reported, and said shops in both Flanders and Wallonia had been hit.
Delhaize is calling it an “IT incident”. Carrefour said 15 of its Belgian stores had also been hit, Colruyt said five independently run Spar stores had similar problems, and butcher chain De Laet & Van Haver also reported a sudden rise in temperatures.
Delhaize told broadcaster NOS that some of its branches in Luxembourg had also been hit, but did not say how many. The company said it had immediately disconnected the refrigeration systems from the internet.
Some reports showed that fridge temperatures had risen by up to 70°, while RTL Info reported increases to around 15°, mainly in freezers. Store managers got a text message from Delhaize at around 4am warning them of the problem, and some stores brought in refrigerated lorries to save their stock.
Swedish stores hit
In Sweden, supermarket group Ica said a “limited number” of its stores had been affected overnight, and Coop told news agency TT that six of its stores in central Sweden had problems with their refrigeration. One Ica store in southern Sweden said on social media that its fridges and freezers had been set to 50°.
French attack
One month ago on the night of October 11, hackers raised the temperature of refrigeration systems at hundreds of French supermarkets, including Intermarché, E.Leclerc and Coopérative U stores, to 50°, destroying fresh and frozen food.
The stores all used equipment from Danish manufacturer Danfoss, which told news agency AFP that most of the affected systems were outdated and no longer received security updates.
It is not yet clear whether the stores hit on Monday use Danfoss systems. In October, RTL Z found that 57 refrigeration systems in the Netherlands could be hacked the same way.
Delhaize and Albert Heijn are both owned by Zaandam-based Ahold Delhaize, which reported a cyberattack to Dutch police in October after shutting down several IT systems. Delhaize told NOS it was investigating whether that attack was linked to Monday’s hack.

Kremlin says it assumes that the Ukrainian army used the Oleshky ceasefire to regroup in line with 'normal practice'
MOSCOW, Nov 2 - The Kremlin said on Monday that it assumed that the Ukrainian army used a local ceasefire last week in and around the Russian-held southern town of Oleshky to regroup, something it called normal practice, but said it had no specific information on whether Russian forces had done the same.
Ukraine's General Staff on Monday accused Russian forces of using the ceasefire to strengthen their military positions, saying they had rotated units, fortified positions, expanded anti—drone measures along roads, and increased logistics activity, including deliveries of ammunition.
Asked about the Ukrainian allegation, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters on a conference call:
"Such questions are best directed to our Ministry of Defence. But in this case, it is safe to assume that the Ukrainian armed forces also used this period to regroup and so on. This is standard practice in such situations. But I am not familiar with the specifics (regarding Russian forces)."
He also said that no similar local ceasefires modelled on Oleshky, which allowed humanitarian aid to be delivered and residents to be evacuated, were planned for now. REUTERS

Kamala Harris is back on the campaign trail – and insists she hasn’t decided on 2028
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
10:00:38 UTC
19:00:38 KST

Two years on from her devastating presidential election defeat, Kamala Harris was greeted like a rockstar as she took the stage before a rapt audience at Georgia’s Clark Atlanta University.
When a politician is greeted by a friendly crowd, they often hear chants of their name. But at Clark, an historically-Black college (HBCU), students instead delivered a school spirit chant for the Atlanta University Center, celebrating an HBCU alumna – and the country’s first female and first Black vice-president – as one of their own.
Harris is “big sister general”, said Sanaiya Archer, a sophomore at Spelman College in Atlanta. “I’m able to see myself in her. Not that I personally relate to her, but she went to an HBCU, she’s an HBCU alum, I’m at an HBCU. And it’s just amazing to see a Black woman that I can see anywhere else in my life on a presidential scale.”
That scale has yet to reach the Oval Office. In 2024, following the reluctant withdrawal of Joe Biden, Harris launched a 107-day campaign for the White House which again brought to the US tantalizingly close to electing its first female president. She lost.
Donald Trump’s return left Democrats reeling – again. Even as it contests this week’s midterm elections, the party has yet to settle on who could lead it back into power, and how.
Harris, forced by Biden’s late exit to conduct the shortest presidential campaign in modern US history, has not yet ruled out another run for the Democratic nomination. But is a figure so closely associated with the party’s past really the person to manifest a more successful future?
At Clark on Thursday, she was treated like a returning hero. “I’ve come here to remind you, don’t ever let anybody take your power from you,” Harris said. “Don’t ever let anybody tell you who you are. You tell them who you are!”
She was aware, she stressed, of how her loss affected some of the young Black women before her. “You know, we’ve been spending the last year and a half, so many of us, going through a range of emotions,” Harris said. “You cried. I heard you. Anger, depression, sadness, frustration, a sense of – of helplessness and powerlessness, folks feeling like, ‘I’m watching all this happen, but I can’t do anything about it’.”
“Well,” she said, “that moment has passed”.
Harris has spent the last month recultivating relationships, appearing in front of the friendliest of audiences on behalf of Democratic candidates around the country.
In Mississippi earlier this month, Harris appeared at a high school rally in Columbus and took part in a rural healthcare roundtable in Clarksdale, campaigning for Scott Colom, the Democratic challenger of US Republican senator Cindy Hyde-Smith. Polls point to a surprisingly close contest in a historically-Republican state.
Similarly, Nevada’s Democratic attorney general Aaron Ford is now in a toss-up race for the state’s governorship against Republican incumbent Joe Lombardo. Harris met with unionized culinary workers in Las Vegas in October.
Harris has also campaigned for Democratic gubernatorial nominee David Crowley in Wisconsin, and the party’s New Hampshire Senate nominee Chris Pappas. She returned to Michigan – a state which Trump flipped in 2024 – in September to campaign for Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic senate candidate.
After dozens of trips to Georgia as vice-president, and having all but rented an apartment in Atlanta while campaigning for president, Harris returned to the state last week to campaign alongside Democratic senator Jon Ossoff – who has also been mooted as a potential 2028 contender.
Ossoff is popular in his state, confident on stage, and widely expected to retain his Senate seat by a convincing margin. But even he looked a little awkward when walking out after Harris had instead been erroneously announced too early, leaving a roomful of Democrats momentarily disappointed.
“Let me be really blunt,” Ossoff said, dissecting Trump’s obsession with voting results from the 2020 election in the county that covers the core of Atlanta. “Why Fulton county? It’s the same reason he’s obsessed with Philly. It’s the same reason he’s obsessed with Detroit. It’s because for this committed, lifelong racist, the fact that Black voters were instrumental to his defeat is even more offensive than the defeat itself.”
Voter turnout has been surging in Georgia – particularly in Black communities, and Atlanta’s politically potent purple suburbs. Early voting set a record on the last day of open polls before Election Day, with about 2.8m votes cast: turnout of 37% so far.
Harris, who has been channelling Black anger and anxiety on the campaign trail for others, has been pushed back on questions about her own political ambitions, even while shoring up relationships in swing states on the road. Speaking to actress Keke Palmer on a podcast earlier this month, she swatted away a question about another run for president.
“Oh, girl, come on!,” Harris replied. “I haven’t decided. I haven’t decided yet. I will. I promise you. But the midterms, the midterms, the midterms. ’28 doesn’t matter if we don’t do ’26 right: what’s right in front of us.”
While Harris had to navigate a short runway in 2024, the last two years have offered the former vice-president an opportunity to redefine herself and offer a new vision for a Democratic party that faltered. She has tried to do that, at times – while opting to lay low, at others.
At a fundraising dinner in Atlanta for Fulton county Democrats on Friday evening, Harris reinforced themes she has returned to over the last year; that the country cannot simply be repaired after Trump’s departure, but must be fundamentally changed for the better.
Trump, whom she dubbed the “decorator in chief”, is leading “an administration that is stone cold corrupt”, Harris said, recounting highlights from his second presidency – from the offer of checks from tariff revenue to a teleprompter handler who profited on prediction markets with wagers on the president’s next words. “This is the most callous, corrupt presidential administration in America’s history.”
Democrats must not squander power if they recapture it, she said.
“It is the job of the Democratic party to be ready to match the resolve of the people with the resolve to govern. And to be candid, that’s going to require a certain kind of ruthlessness,” Harris said. “Not ruthlessness in the sense of cruelty, because that’s not who we are. But in our willingness to use our power to deliver on our commitments.
“And we must be uncompromising to deliver actual relief. We must be impatient with injustice. We must be intolerant of cronyism and corruption. And we must be intolerant of the status quo, because it’s ain’t working for a whole lot of people.
“Our party cannot no longer let process stand in the way of progress, because … the American people cannot afford to wait for that time.”
At Clark, at least, the bright-eyed students of the AUC who waited for a glimpse of Harris outside the hall like theater fans seeking autographs seem to want her to run.
Carington Hill and Naomi Blakey are two first-year students at Clark who attended Harris’s address. “We just turned 18,” Blakey said. “We were just talking about how when voting came and the election ended, how we were upset about how he won.”
Blakey wants Harris to run again, she said. “Because me and my friends weren’t ready … I didn’t get to vote. And I feel like my vote could have made a difference, and it could have not, but still, I wanted to.”
Hill also wants Harris to run again, but expressed apprehension about the public’s appetite for a Black woman in charge. “We’re not progressive enough,” she said. “I feel like all their biases would come back and we would vote for the bad person in a way again.”
“Well, not we” she added, pointing at her friend and herself. “But other people would vote for that bad person again. You know what I mean?”

It’s time to block reckless AI IPOs and tax billionaires | Naomi Klein and Ilana Glazer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
10:00:38 UTC
19:00:38 KST

America is a divided country in crisis. Despite the sunny economic forecast coming from the Trump administration, millions of Americans are struggling to find and keep jobs, getting crushed under the rising cost of living, and losing health insurance when they need it the most.
Meanwhile, via corporate consolidation and political corruption, the billionaire class is getting richer faster than ever before: a 40% increase in wealth in just the last two years. Today, the combined wealth of nearly 3,000 global billionaires equals one-fifth of the entire world’s yearly output. Nearly 1,000 billionaires live and do business in the United States.
The tools of their domination are tax loopholes, corporate mergers and, in the tech world where many of these billionaires exist, IPOs. When a company goes public, its founders and investors win the capitalist lottery. And instead of paying their fair share of taxes and redistributing resources back into society, most turn around and fund even more corporate consolidation and political corruption to extend their dominion.
Elon Musk became an instant trillionaire when SpaceX went public earlier this year, on the backs of workers’ pensions – and is bankrolling the Republican midterm campaigns with a small percentage of his egregious gains. Oracle’s Larry Ellison – currently seventh on the Forbes billionaires list – backed the Paramount-Warner Brothers merger that is destroying the film industry and the livelihoods of the Americans who labor in it. Google’s Sergey Brin spent $100m opposing California’s Prop 40, a one-time wealth tax that would put the funds toward healthcare and other public services.
To pay for essential services, we must tax billionaires, and pass legislation to do so starting in California and New York, but that is clearly not enough. We cannot allow more billionaires – or trillionaires – to be made in this country, further expanding the inequality chasm that’s turning a dignified life into a luxury in this country. We must also block the impending tech IPOs and preserve what’s left of our economy and our society.
The Trump administration and tech investors have positioned IPOs as market success stories: when a company goes public, US investors could gain from their valuations. But regular Americans also shoulder a company’s risks – and risk their own futures when that stock ends up in their retirement accounts without consent.
Problems with a private company or its products become problems for everyone invested in that company once it goes public, whether they’ve made the choice or not. And when the speculative investment bubble pops – such as with the 2008 crisis – regular people end up holding the bag.
It’s no secret that the AI companies Anthropic and OpenAI are intending to go public in the near future. Both of these players also had major security flaws exposed recently, and openly acknowledge mind-bogglingly huge amounts of debt. If these companies are allowed to go public, their cofounders and investors – some of whom are already billionaires – will rise to whole new strata of private wealth.
Americans, meanwhile, will be financially crushed if the technologies fail or if these companies prove unable to make good on their extravagant financial promises. Already, the 10 most valuable public companies are in tech, which means the country’s economy depends on the stability of a single industry, one with an undeniable history of bubbles, crashes and, in extreme cases like Theranos, outright fraud.
June’s highly contentious SpaceX IPO already carries great risk for regular investors. If more speculative tech companies with staggering risk profiles are allowed to follow suit, the results will become too much for the market to bear.
If and when the AI bubble bursts, it will take all of us with it, investors or not. Recessions level lives indiscriminately, and globally. The one exception will be the billionaires, who will have sufficient resources to walk away from the wreckage relatively unscathed.
We cannot let the billionaire class take these kinds of risks with our future. To stop these reckless IPOs we must stand together, take collective action, and push for real change. We must find legal and legislative avenues to stop the new tech IPOs from minting new billionaires and transferring the AI industry’s enormous risks onto us.
The first step is passing wealth taxes on billionaires to keep them in check. Today, let’s send a message to the billionaires that Americans will not lie down and let them bulldoze working people and the environment on their way to the bank. Tax the billionaires. Block the IPOs.
- Naomi Klein is a Guardian US columnist and contributing writer. She is the professor of climate justice and co-director of the Centre for Climate Justice at the University of British Columbia. Her latest book is End Times Fascism: And the Fight for the Living World, co-written with Astra Taylor
- Ilana Glazer is a comedian and video-podcaster who co-created the comedy series Broad City, wrote and starred in the movie Babes, made her Broadway debut last year in Goodnight, and Good Luck and, now, hosts the comedy and socio-political video-podcast, It’s Open With Ilana Glazer

‘They assume the man next to me is the owner’: four women doing business in Africa in their own way
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
10:00:37 UTC
19:00:37 KST

Africa is thought to have a higher proportion of female entrepreneurs than any other continent and yet many still struggle to access financing. Four business leaders from Nigeria, Uganda, Kenya and Malawi tell us about the inspiration behind their success – and the challenges women still face.
Ifedolapo Runsewe, Nigeria: giving waste tyres a new life
On the outskirts of Ibadan in south-west Nigeria, thousands of discarded tyres are fuelling an industrial experiment.
They arrive at Freee Recycle’s factory where they are sorted, shredded and reduced to rubber granules. Some will become playground surfaces. Others will be turned into gym flooring, paving blocks and interlocking tiles.
Ifedolapo Runsewe, the company’s founder, is building an industrial recycling business in a sector where women rarely own factories or lead manufacturing operations.
In Nigeria, women own about 40% of small businesses, but 56% of female entrepreneurs’ last loan applications were denied, compared with 17% for men, according to the World Bank. In capital-heavy fields such as recycling, this financing gap may prevent female entrepreneurs becoming factory owners.
Runsewe has made that leap. She has built a factory that turns one of Nigeria’s most intransigent waste problems into products. The factory employs about 62 people, collecting tyres from four states in Nigeria: Oyo, Lagos, Osun and Kwara.
Nigeria produces millions of waste tyres each year. Many end up in dumps or are burned to recover scrap metal, releasing hazardous pollutants.
“Burning tyres releases a complex mix of toxic chemicals – it’s not just pollution, it’s a direct public health threat,” says Oladele Ogunseitan, a presidential chair at the University of California, Irvine.
After more than 12 years in banking, Runsewe became interested in tyre recycling after seeing first-hand the impact of burning tyres. What convinced her there was a business opportunity was the fact that almost every part of a tyre can be recovered and reused. She started Freee Recycle in 2020.
The challenge has been to convince people that waste can be a business.
Recycling tyres requires substantial capital. Turning the recovered rubber into finished products requires another layer of machinery, expertise and investment. And unlike collecting waste, manufacturing depends on finding customers willing to buy what comes out of the recycling process.
“People view recycling as more of an informal, small-scale activity rather than a serious business capable of generating substantial returns,” she says. “And that is absolutely not true.”
Early on, she encountered another obstacle: the assumption that an industrial recycling business was a man’s domain.
“I’d go into banks and boardrooms, and investors would assume the man next to me is the owner. As soon as I spoke, the question came up: why should we give a woman millions, hundreds of millions?”
Yet she does not want her business reduced to a story about gender. “I don’t think organisations choose to work with us because we’re female-owned,” she says. “They see a brand that is good, transparent, credible and ethical.”
Freee Recycle has secured partnerships with organisations including Michelin, Save the Children and the International Committee of the Red Cross. And she is looking into expanding beyond tyres. “There are plans to set up what would be the first in Nigeria dedicated to recycling aerosols, like insecticide cans and spray containers,” she says.
Through the company’s Freee art residency programme, launched in 2025, discarded tyres have been transformed into large-scale artworks inspired by African history and culture, including the Bata drum, Ikom monoliths and Benin bronze traditions.
The symbolism is deliberate: materials that would otherwise be thrown away are being given another life.
 
Valentine Benjamin
Kyokushaba Shine, Uganda: building solar-powered irrigation systems
As a little girl, Kyokushaba Shine would watch her mother get up before dawn, labouring hard all day to tend to the acres of onions she had planted near their house in Kabale, southern Uganda.
Often her mother’s harvests – the family’s only source of income – would fail. A lack of water or degraded soil could leave them with almost no yield, making it difficult to put enough food on the table.
Now, as a water engineer and entrepreneur, Kyokushaba, 31, has made it her mission to help farmers like her mother.
“I started my company with the goal of designing small and affordable irrigation systems for smallholder farmers. When I started the business in February 2025, I had neither staff nor capital, but I had a goal in mind and I wanted to work towards it,” she says.
In just over a year, Kyokushaba says Winta Engineering Solutions has installed 30 water systems across Uganda, most of them solar powered, and more than 10 of them for female farmers. Her business employs a team of people, 80% of them women.
The goal, Kyokushaba says, is relatively simple: ensure farmers have reliable access to water using mostly solar-powered pumps, then combine this with modern irrigation technology, such as drip irrigation, that allows water to be used more efficiently. Winta Engineering Solutions designs and installs the equipment, digging boreholes where needed and providing farmers with training on how to operate and maintain the systems.
Kyokushaba has started collaborating with local microfinance providers, connecting them with farmers, who are offered loans of about 5m Ugandan shillings (about £1,000), a sum most do not have readily available, but can usually repay within two years.
She also runs educational programmes that address bigger challenges, including the impact of the climate crisis and soil degradation on farmers’ ability to produce food.
“Farmers want results fast, so they use fertilisers to increase their yields quickly, but sometimes that means they don’t protect the health of their soil,” says Kyokushaba. “It’s not enough to have sufficient water if the soil is degraded, and that’s why we have started working on awareness campaigns.”
There is one other issue that matters deeply to Kyokushaba: creating opportunities for women in a sector still largely dominated by men.
“As a woman, you can show up in spaces where men are trying to push you out, and where men are trying to set the agenda. This needs to change,” she says.
She is also driven by personal reasons. “I have a five-year-old daughter, and it’s just me and her. I want her to see and know that she can do anything she puts her mind to. I want her to know that she’s strong, that women and girls are strong.”
 
Stefanie Glinski
Wawira Njiru, Kenya: feeding 700,000 schoolchildren a day
From a young age, Wawira Njiru knew she wanted to help people at home in Kenya, but it was not until she was at university abroad that her path to feeding the nation’s schoolchildren began.
While studying for a degree in nutrition in Australia, she raised A$1,200 (£630) and decided to build a small makeshift kitchen in her home town of Ruiru, 12 miles (20km) from Nairobi. In 2012, it started providing 25 children with one school meal every day.
“Teachers said food was the biggest need. Kids were fainting. One teacher said they used to keep packs of glucose in the staff room for when a child faints. I thought that was insane. Why don’t we just feed them?”
Food4Education was born, and nearly 15 years later it has 209 kitchens which feed more than 700,000 children daily. Food is distributed using a fleet of motorbikes and trucks.
For an operation cooking for hundreds of thousands of children, the emissions could be huge. But the flagship kitchen in Nairobi, which feeds about 60,000 children, runs on solar and steam.
Kitchens have been transitioning to use eco-briquettes made in Kenya from sawdust and agricultural waste, including leaves. “If we were to cook for every child in Kenya using firewood, it would be equivalent to 1.1m acres [0.45 hectares] of forest being cut down. That’s about three times the size of London,” says Njiru.
The amount of food waste is small, running at about 2%, because a digital platform verifies who is eating before the next day’s food is produced.
In early 2026, there was a mango crisis in Murang’a county when hot weather meant there was a surplus of the fruit and 5,000 farmers were left with produce they could not sell. “The governor reached out and asked if we could absorb the mangoes,” says Njiru. “We bought 1.3m mangoes over a couple of weeks and distributed them to schoolchildren.” The farmers were paid, children were fed and there was minimal waste.
About 80% of everything Food4Education buys comes from local smallholder farmers. “We make sure we’re aligning what we eat with what’s being grown. When there are more beans, we serve more beans. When there’s more of a certain type of lentil, we serve that,” says Njiru.
She says the organisation now has a huge amount of buying power, given that it buys about 130 tonnes of food a day.
Food4Education, with 6,000 employees, is mostly powered by women. Njiru noticed that men were reluctant to work in kitchens when she started out. “I’ll never forget the man who once told me he’d rather be jobless than work in a kitchen,” she says. Having a predominantly female workforce has affected how the organisation runs, she believes. “I think women want to get things done. I’m not saying men don’t, but it’s very innate to women to focus on what needs to be done and not be paralysed by a big challenge.”
Njiru gets emotional when she talks about the impact on their livelihoods. “I meet women and they say, ‘I was able to build my first home’ or ‘I was able to save up to send my child to university’. Now they’re independent and can take care of themselves.”
 
Sarah Johnson
Chifuno Stevens, Malawi: turning peanut shells into fuel
When Chifuno Stevens looks at Dedza town, a bustling district in Malawi’s central region, she sees a landscape caught between natural beauty and severe environmental threat.
For years, household waste from the town has been dumped haphazardly across Dedza mountain. At the same time, a heavy reliance on firewood and conventional wood charcoal has rapidly stripped the mountain of its trees.
Deeply concerned by the ecological damage, Stevens, 35, decided to step in.
“I started the organisation in September 2020 to address two massive challenges: poor waste management and rapid deforestation,” she says. “Many households rely on charcoal and firewood for cooking, which puts enormous pressure on our forests. Meanwhile, agricultural waste is discarded and left to rot. I wanted to find a practical way to address both problems while creating economic opportunities for local women.”
Six years later, what began as a community awareness initiative has blossomed into the Chifuno Changa Green Initiative (CCGI), a women-led enterprise that fuses environmental conservation with economic empowerment.
The initiative works directly with 18 local women from the Dauya Ladies Environmental Group.
The enterprise’s core activity revolves around producing and selling eco-friendly charcoal briquettes made from agricultural waste, specifically peanut shells. By converting discarded shells into a clean-burning alternative, CCGI provides families with a viable fuel source that actively reduces the pressure on endangered local forests.
The business has also found creative ways to integrate into the local economy, partnering with its sister business, Dedza Pottery. The pottery workshop uses CCGI’s briquettes as a supplementary fuel when energy supplies fall short.
To build long-term economic resilience, Stevens has expanded the group’s operations beyond green energy. Since early 2026, CCGI has provided sewing classes for its members, enabling them to make and sell reusable tote bags using vibrant local kitenge fabric.
She has also begun offering tours of the briquette workshop to tourists, enabling them to interact with the artisans and have a go at making the briquettes themselves.
“Some people are hesitant to try charcoal briquettes because they are unfamiliar with them,” she says. “We have found that people need to experience using them to trust their benefits, so we are working to carry out more live demonstrations to build that confidence.”
Keeping the products affordable for low-income consumers while trying to grow the business is a delicate balancing act, says Stevens.
“As a woman leading an organisation, I want to ensure that business growth translates into meaningful and sustainable income opportunities for the women involved,” she says. “My ultimate aim is for CCGI to become a financially sustainable business rather than one that depends entirely on external aid.”
Securing a reliable, year-round supply of peanut shells remains a constant puzzle, compounded by a pressing need to invest in specialised equipment to make production processes more efficient. Like many small enterprises, systemic barriers to accessing finance have at times restricted CCGI’s capacity to scale up and meet growing demand.
Despite the uphill battle against these economic and environmental challenges, Stevens’s mission remains unchanged.
“I remain deeply committed to this work because I firmly believe that protecting the environment and creating economic opportunities for women must go hand in hand,” she says. “That is the ultimate key to unlocking a sustainable future.”
 
Kenneth Zindondo

In brief
- Australian novelist Craig Silvey has been sentenced to seven months in jail.

Award-winning young adult novelist Craig Silvey was jailed on Monday for seven months after pleading guilty to distributing and possessing child exploitation material.
The 44-year-old was found with numerous sexually explicit photos and videos of children and adults on his laptop and mobile phone when police raided his Fremantle home, the District Court of Western Australia heard.
Silvey, a father of three, also engaged in an online conversation with another user on a pornography website, where his handle was Jimmy, Jimmy, Jimmy.
In the chat, Silvey described himself as a "Fremantle guy" before telling the user "you sound amazing ... we have very similar interests, would love to chat more; do you have Signal or Session?"
The pair moved to an encrypted messaging app, where he said he was "extremely open-minded and obsessed with taboos" and preferred boys aged five-plus before adding that "eight was the perfect age".

"I want to make out with little ones," the author said in one message.
"I haven't had any experience, I'm sad to say.
"I'm a bit obsessed."
Silvey, who has been shortlisted for the Miles Franklin Literary Award and the International Dublin Literary Award, also wrote he was "drooling" over a sexually explicit photo of a naked man and boy together.
Silvey 'betrayed the trust of thousands of people', judge says
Prosecutor Daniel Harrop said a generation of children, particularly vulnerable children grappling with questions of gender identity and sexuality, had found safety in Silvey's books and his offending had shattered it.
Judge Hayley Cormann said it was very serious and very disturbing offending.
"This offending involves children, and it is destructive, and it is devastating," she said.
"Your communication was open, it was assertive, and it was unmistakable.
"You did this as a means to engage with others, and ultimately as a means to sexually satisfy yourself as part of your fantasies."
Silvey's lawyer claimed the writer didn't have a sexual interest in children and his behaviour was an escape from the pressures of his life.
But Judge Cormann rejected this, saying his crimes were repulsive and degrading and the consequences of his abuse would have a long-lasting impact on his victims.
"You acknowledge you have devastated and betrayed the trust of thousands of people, and you have let an entire community down," she said.
"For the victims of this type of offending, it is real, and they are traumatised."
The bestselling author pleaded guilty in January. He is best known for his 2009 coming‑of‑age novel Jasper Jones, considered a modern Australian classic and adapted into a feature film and several stage productions.
He has also been widely recognised for other books, including Rhubarb and Honeybee — which won the Australian Indie Book Award in 2021 — and the children's novel Runt, which was also made into a film.
Publishers Allen & Unwin and Fremantle Press, which released Rhubarb, stopped promoting his books after Silvey was charged and most of his titles were removed from reading lists across the country.
Two charges of producing and possessing further child exploitation material were dropped in May.
Silvey was made eligible for parole.

Hundreds of Mundane AI Apps Are Hiding Sexually Abusive Deepfake Features
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

At first glance, the self-proclaimed “pet portrait” app Viefur appears to be just another AI slop generator. Using digital coins sold in the app—around $4 will buy 130 coins—pet photos can be turned into an “anthropomorphic portrait,” with the critter dressed in “human clothing” and inserted into bizarre scenes. Think a hamster wearing beach shorts, sunglasses, and lounging in a swimming pool or a Hawaiian shirt-wearing cat, drinking from a coconut.
All of this is cover for what appears to be the app’s true purpose: creating sexually abusive deepfake images.
A WIRED investigation found the app is part of a network of more than 400 connected domains and apps that, like Viefur, often claim to be everyday services—such as language tuition or AI workout coaches. When accessed under certain conditions, however, apps in the network stealthily load a web interface allowing the generation of explicit AI sexual images and videos using photos users upload. The apps include AI scenes such as “bedroom rape” and “threatening knife,” where a man holds a knife to a woman’s neck.
The network was discovered hiding in plain sight, by multiple researchers, after they investigated links from thousands of video ads containing explicit deepfake content that were published on Meta’s Facebook and Instagram. As WIRED has reported in recent months, hundreds of these ads contained AI generated child sexual abuse material, including images of real children and a member of a European royal family. The ads reached tens of thousands of people and have prompted investigations from regulators around the world.
In each case, the ads linked out to the deceptive apps in Apple and Google’s app stores—allowing people to generate explicit images and make payments using Apple and Google Pay. The network behind the nudify apps appears to have been publishing them for around a year, at times publishing dozens per week. This is despite Google, Apple, and Meta saying they enforce their policies that do not allow harmful deepfake content on their platforms.
The apps and domains investigated by WIRED appear to be run by Chinese developers and a Hong Kong registered entity called KeLing Technology Limited, according to a review of web domains and how the services operate. Email addresses linked to the entity, apps, and related services, did not respond to multiple requests for comment from WIRED, but after being contacted, they appeared to erase public connections between KeLing Technology Limited and the deepfake tools.
“This is an organized, commercially run operation: One operator behind hundreds of disposable apps and domains, cloaked to pass App Store review and pushed through tens of thousands of Meta ads under fake payer names,” says Paul Bouchaud, a lead researcher at the nonprofit AI Forensics, who investigated the network. “They don’t expect enforcement to catch up, and so far it hasn’t.”
Hidden Behavior
Download one of the apps in the deepfake network and you may see exactly what was advertised—such as an app to create AI pet pictures. But behind the scenes, researchers found, the apps are quietly making determinations about whether to show the benign content or load a web interface showing explicit deepfakes.
“Each time the application is downloaded, there is a call to the server with some information, such as where the user is coming from, the language, some unique identifier, and then the server replies whether or not to show the explicit or the non-explicit version of it,” explains Bouchaud, who reverse engineered the apps’ and associated websites’ code. They say there’s no clear list of reasons why one user may be shown the explicit version of an app, but one trigger appears to be downloading it after clicking an associated ad on Meta’s platforms.
Websites linked to the apps have revealed the network’s secrets and the scale that it operates on. Opening one of the apps’ websites will likely show an entirely black screen and no content. The only noticeable change is that the URL updates to include the word “risk.” But the websites host the hidden explicit deepfake layer that can be loaded in each app.
This web interface contains dozens of pornography deepfake video and image templates—with users able to upload images of people to be added to the sexual scenes. The interface allows the purchase of “diamonds” to generate images and links to other social media accounts where users can contact the developers with questions or complaints.
Also hidden in the websites’ code are details about the entire network. A JavaScript bundle that can easily be unpicked, researchers say, contains a list of all the domains and apps that have been created by the developers—including app package details, encryption keys, Facebook advertising trackers, and more.
“They contained this giant configuration list of other domains with different encryption keys,” says Maël Le Touz, a staff threat researcher at security firm Infoblox, who identified almost 500 linked domains. “They run the same code and they all reference one another.”
Bouchard’s analysis of when domains were registered found that the apps started to appear toward the end of 2025, with a spike during the spring of this year. At one point, around 30 nudify apps-websites were being registered each week, the researcher says, with 27 live on Google’s Play Store in September. These apps had been downloaded more than 350,000 times collectively and many were rated suitable for all age groups, Bouchard’s research says.
One of the most popular apps, called DiffAI, was created in December 2025 and has been downloaded more than 100,000 times from the Play Store. A user review on Google’s Play Store stated: “This app contains templates for creating CSAM and other types of pornographic material. It performs no age verification.”
DiffAI was removed from the Play Store shortly before WIRED contacted Google about the network. Google did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment, though it had removed the majority of the apps ahead of being contacted. (Portions of the deepfake network were reported on by Danish journalists in September.)
Similarly, Apple removed 19 apps from its App Store, including pet photo app Viefur, after WIRED asked the company about the activity and shared associated domains. “We designed the App Store to be a safe and trusted place for our users, and nudification apps and other pornographic content are strictly prohibited,” says Apple spokesperson Adam Dema.
“We review every app before it’s published, and these apps complied with our rules when we reviewed them,” Dema says. “After approval, their developers changed the website the app pulls its content from, replacing what we approved with pornographic content, and promoted it through pornographic ads hosted on a third-party platform.” The company says it has suspended tens of thousands of apps for using these “bait-and-switch” tactics over the last year and recently updated its app store rules to further restrict “nudify” tools.
Chinese Origins
Central to the “nudify” network appears to be a host of Chinese developers whose identities seem to have been intentionally hidden. “It’s using exclusive Chinese hosting, the code is written in Chinese and has a lot of comments in Chinese,” Le Touz says, noting explicit videos in ads posted to Meta’s platforms promoting the apps contained watermarks from Chinese-language video editing software.
The apps and domains across the network have often used generic privacy policies, free email addresses from Gmail or Outlook, and obscure developer names as part of their alleged efforts to hide their connections. Ads for the apps posted on Meta’s platforms have also used apparently false names—such as Draftmondcreldbro Duhustepre and Swaldmungsha Glasirdcroldshold—and pages with no followers. Since the start of this year, Bouchaud’s research has found tens of thousands of explicit deepfake ads linked to the network—often using similar language in their advertising copy—on Meta’s platforms.
“These ads violate not just one, but several of Meta’s policies,” says Katie Paul, the director of the Tech Transparency Project, who first uncovered the ads showing deepfake explicit depictions of minors. “There is no question about what you are seeing, what the app is advertising,” she says. Paul says tech companies need to answer questions about where money generated from the apps goes and how those behind the nudification apps and services constantly seem to bypass their content moderation and safety systems.
KeLing Technology Limited appears to be a significant part of the operation. While the company’s website is little more than a shell, its name was listed as the contact details of the first website registered in the network. This website’s brand name also appeared as part of the contact details within the explicit deepfake template that was used in the apps. Bouchaud also identified an administration login page linked to the explicit deepfake interface that mentions “Keling.” And email addresses using the company’s domain appeared on at least one app that have been removed from app stores.
Towards the end of September, a notification sent to users of the explicit deepfake interface announced that a new AI model could be used—the model was called Veyra, with a tagline in the apps of “More real. More natural. More wild.” The homepage of a website called Veyra AI listed its contact email as a KeLing Technology address.
When WIRED contacted KeLing email addresses, plus some of those listed in apps privacy policies, we received no response. However, after WIRED reached out, someone renamed some of the associated online social media channels, removed KeLing email addresses from the AI Veyra website, and removed the KeLing Technology Limited address from the first registered website.
Meta says it banned KeLing Technology Limited from advertising in 2025 after it failed to “comply with a cease and desist letter.” (Meta declined to share the letter with WIRED citing legal reasons.) “We have strict rules against promoting nudify apps and work aggressively to keep this material off our services,” a Meta spokesperson says. Meta says that while KeLing Technology Limited has continued to try and advertise through other ways, it takes action against the ads when it becomes aware of them.
After WIRED shared the 400-plus domains with Meta, the spokesperson said they had shared more than 3,000 associated ads linked to them, two-thirds of which it had already removed from its systems. Meta later told WIRED it has taken action against 11,600 ad accounts, more than 4,700 business pages, 5,200 users, and 15,000 pages linked to the domains, blocking 209 apps from advertising on its platforms.
“The criminals behind them take increasingly deceptive steps to evade detection—hiding behind fake names and identities, running ads that look benign, and sometimes linking to Google's and Apple's app stores, with the ads' true intent revealed only after a click,” the spokesperson says.
As WIRED finished reporting this story, similar ads and apps continued to be published on the tech platforms.
