10 Candidates Who Could Make History in the Midterms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

The Nov. 3 midterm elections are already groundbreaking.
It’s the most expensive election cycle in U.S. history in terms of political ad spending, with more than $11 billion expected to be spent, according to analysis firm AdImpact. States have redrawn congressional maps between censuses at a rate the National Conference of State Legislatures says has not been seen since the 1800s, as parties try to secure victories. And Donald Trump has an historically low approval rating for a President heading into the midterms.
This election is also set to see massive turnover on Capitol Hill, with dozens of members of Congress resigning, retiring, or seeking other office.
Depending on the results, it could see a number of identity barriers broken, too. A record 26 women are vying for Governor posts across the country, according to Rutgers University's Center for American Women and Politics. A handful of candidates for Congress could also become national historic firsts if they win.
Here’s who to watch out for.
First Black Speaker of the House?
Rep. Joseph Rainey of South Carolina is believed to be the first Black American elected to the U.S. House in 1870. He also was the first Black American to preside over the House of Representatives—albeit temporarily—during a debate on an appropriations bill providing for the management of Native American reservations in 1874.
But no Black person has served as Speaker of the House. That could change if an anticipated blue wave in November gives Democrats the majority. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries has broad support in the New York congressional district he represents and is on track for re-election in a race against Republican opponent Lewis Mizrahi that is widely considered uncompetitive. Jeffries, who served in Congress for nearly 14 years, was elected unopposed in 2022 as House Democratic Leader, succeeding Speaker Emerita Nancy Pelosi and making him the first Black leader of a major political party in Congress. But the path to the speakership isn’t guaranteed, as the center-left Jeffries may have to unite an ideologically fractious Democratic caucus.
First Muslim Senator?
Michigan Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, a former local public health director and podcaster who has never held elected public office, could become the first Muslim U.S. Senator if he beats Republican candidate Mike Rogers. El-Sayed leads, according to public opinion polling, though Michigan electoral results can be unpredictable.
El-Sayed has run on a progressive platform, including advocating for Medicare for All and ending U.S. military funding to Israel, which has ruffled some moderate and Jewish Democrats. His identity has also become a campaign target for Republicans: Rogers and Donald Trump have tried to link El-Sayed and his family to the transnational extremist group Muslim Brotherhood, and El-Sayed has been pressured to reaffirm his commitment to the Constitution over his faith, which defenders have said reflects the Islamophobia he faces.
“I'm not running to be the first Muslim anything,” El-Sayed told CNN in August. “I just want to be a really, really great senator for my state.”
First openly gay male Senator?
The first openly LGBT person elected to the U.S. Senate was Sen. Tammy Baldwin (D, Wis.), who was elected in 2012, but Chris Pappas, a Democratic House member who has represented New Hampshire's 1st congressional district since 2019, could become the first out gay man serving in the U.S. Senate. Pappas, 46, married his partner, lawyer Vann Bentley, in 2023. He is also a vocal LGBT rights advocate in Congress. “I’m not thinking much about history right now,” Pappas told the New York Times in an interview. “I’m really thinking every day about the struggles of New Hampshire.”
Pappas is running against Republican nominee John E. Sununu, a former U.S. Senator seeking to reclaim his seat from retiring Sen. Jeanne Shaheen. Pappas leads in public opinion polling. While Republicans have largely not made Pappas’ sexuality a focus of their political campaigns, the GOP has alleged that Pappas failed to disclose a relationship with a corporate lobbyist.
First Korean-American governor?
Cyndi Munson, a Democrat, was the first Asian-American woman elected to Oklahoma’s state legislature and currently serves as the lower chamber’s minority leader. She now aims to replace the term-limited Republican Gov. Kevin Stitt and become the first Korean-American governor in the U.S., though a recent poll shows her Trump-backed opponent, Republican former state senator Mike Mazzei, leading.
First Black female governors?
Keisha Lance Bottoms is the Democratic nominee running against Republican billionaire Rick Jackson to replace the term-limited Georgia Republican Gov. Brian Kemp. Polls have been mixed and most forecasters have rated the race a toss-up.
If Bottoms wins, she would not only become the state’s first Black and first female governor; she could also become one of the U.S.’s first Black female governors, an honor she might share with Minnesota gubernatorial candidate Lisa Demuth. Bottoms told ABC News in October that the potential milestone is “much more personal” for her. “My family goes back at least five generations in Georgia,” she said. “I’m a descendant of slaves on both sides.” Stacey Abrams, the former minority leader of Georgia’s state House, previously tried to become the first Black female governor, but fell short in the 2018 and 2022 elections.
Bottoms was the mayor of Atlanta from 2018 to 2022, presiding during the COVID-19 pandemic, and shocked the state’s political establishment when she said she would not seek re-election. She has faced criticism from Jackson and others for walking away from the job. She since served in the Biden Administration in various roles, including as a senior adviser and leading the White House Office of Public Engagement.
In Minnesota, whoever wins the race for governor will break the state’s glass ceiling, as no woman has ever been elected to lead the state. Senator Amy Klobuchar is the Democratic nominee, while Republicans nominated Demuth, a state representative since 2018 and speaker of the state House since 2025.
“I look forward to serving—if given the opportunity, your trust in me—as the first female governor here in the state of Minnesota and the first Black woman to serve as governor of any state in the United States,” Demuth said in her mid-October debate with Klobuchar. Polls, however, show voters leaning toward Klobuchar, as Demuth faces stiff political headwinds from being associated with Trump, who has frequently attacked Minnesota.
First Native American female governors?
In 2018, Deb Haaland made history as one of the first Native American women, alongside Sharice Davids, to be elected to Congress. Haaland is a member of the Laguna Pueblo, a federally recognized tribe in New Mexico that has existed longer than the U.S. has. As a congresswoman, she focused on environmental justice, climate change, and missing and murdered indigenous women. In 2021, Haaland became the Biden Administration’s Interior Secretary. Haaland is now running to become governor of New Mexico, and she could potentially make history again, this time as one of the first Native American women to lead any state.
But to do so, Haaland, a Democrat, must defeat her Republican opponent Gregg Hull, who was formerly the mayor of Rio Rancho. So far, polls show Haaland leading.
In Alaska, Bernadette Wilson, who is of Aleut heritage, is a Republican candidate for governor. Wilson, a conservative activist and former radio host, has the backing of President Trump, but veteran Sen. Lisa Murkowski, a moderate Alaska Republican, and her father, former Gov. Frank Murkowski, both endorsed Wilson’s Democratic opponent, Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, whom Wilson trails in the polls. Forecasters, however, rate the race as a toss-up.
First Native American female Senators?
At least four Native American men have served in the U.S. Senate, but no Native American woman ever has—yet.
When Yup'ik Alaska Native Mary Peltola was first elected to the U.S. House in an August 2022 special election to replace the late Representative Don Young, she became the first Alaska Native member of Congress and the first woman to represent Alaska in the chamber. If she beats incumbent Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan—and polls show her slightly leading—she could become the first Alaska Native Senator as well as one of the first Native American women in the Senate.
In Minnesota, Democratic Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan is running for the Senate and could also become one of the first Native American women in the chamber. That is, if Flanagan—a member of the White Earth Band of Ojibwe, the largest federally recognized tribe in Minnesota—beats GOP nominee and political newcomer Michele Tafoya. Polls show Flanagan leading.
“I’m not running to make history, but it’s about damn time there was a Native American woman serving in the United States Senate,” Flanagan said on the campaign trail in October. “And she might as well be from White Earth.”

DRC: Restrictive measures obstruct care for sexual violence survivors in North Kivu
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

Goma – The de facto authorities in North Kivu province, eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) – the FNR1, formerly AFC/M23 – have been imposing harmful restrictions related to seeking care for sexual violence for months. These policies obstruct people from accessing this essential care and put them at greater risk, says Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF). 
MSF acknowledges the commitments made by the FNR leadership in early October to address these issues. So far these corrective measures have not been implemented. Restrictive measures remain in place. We urge the FNR to immediately implement the agreements made to guarantee safe, confidential access to care.
Since the beginning of 2026, the authorities overseeing health services in North Kivu have introduced or proposed measures for healthcare workers, health facilities, and humanitarian organisations that raise serious concerns about medical confidentiality, medical ethics, victim and survivor protection, and access to healthcare.
These measures include pressuring health workers to reduce victim and survivor numbers by narrowing the definition of sexual violence, for example, by limiting recognition of sexual violence to people presenting with visible signs of injury; requiring intrusive and medically unnecessary physical examinations to prove violence or assault; requiring victims and survivors to report to the police before seeking care; and restricting eligibility for care to people who present within 72 hours of the assault.
The de facto authorities have also instructed organisations and health providers, including MSF, to use documentation that requires intrusive, stigmatising, and non-essential questioning that is irrelevant to treatment — including victims and survivors’ names, addresses, and details of alleged perpetrators. This undermines patient confidentiality, puts victims and survivors at further risk, and goes against international medical ethical standards. Patients – particularly women – report being questioned or threatened against seeking care at humanitarian-supported clinics.
Healthcare workers and health partners have told MSF they have been threatened with suspension or even imprisonment if they do not comply with the new measures. These threats are already deterring some healthcare workers from providing essential care to victims and survivors of sexual violence, and, in some cases, causing them to stop their work altogether out of fear. This further reduces people’s already limited access to care.
MSF is already seeing the impact of these measures, with consultations for victims and survivors of sexual violence falling sharply. In several health centres MSF supports in North Kivu, dozens of entries relating to these consultations were erased from records, drastically reducing the official number of reported cases. Some centres have also stopped recording cases altogether, or have reported very few for several months.
Reviewing data from some of the health facilities we support in North Kivu, 41 per cent less people had sought this care in August 2026, when comparing to January 2026. Other facilities we support in North Kivu also saw significant declines, from providing care to around 80 victims and survivors per month in 2025 to as few as nine per month in 2026. Communities also report growing fear about accessing services.
A drop in reported cases does not mean sexual violence is decreasing. It simply means survivors face barriers to safe and confidential care.
Akke Boere, MSF director of operations
“Making the crisis less visible does not make the underlying violence disappear,” says Akke Boere, MSF director of operations. “A drop in reported cases does not mean sexual violence is decreasing. It simply means survivors face barriers to safe and confidential care.”
“The priority must be to remove barriers to care, strengthen protection and access to justice, and address the conditions that allow sexual violence to persist,” says Boere. “The current restrictive measures are not the way to achieve this — they only further harm survivors.”
MSF has maintained regular dialogue with the de facto authorities, including with their leadership. While these exchanges have resulted in commitments to address the issue, the harmful and restrictive measures have continued.
“MSF calls for immediate action from the FNR to ensure that care for survivors of sexual violence is protected, confidential, accessible, and focused on health needs,” says Boere. “Official guidance must be issued to health authorities to ensure healthcare workers are no longer subjected to pressure, and activities must be overseen in a way that preserves confidentiality and does not intimidate or harm survivors or health workers.”
At the same time, MSF emphasises that access to healthcare should never depend on reporting to the authorities or pursuing legal action. While accountability for perpetrators is essential, making care conditional on reporting risks deterring victims and survivors from seeking urgent treatment and potentially exposes them to further harm.
About MSF's response to sexual violence in eastern DRC
Sexual violence in eastern DRC is a longstanding crisis, driven by decades of armed conflict, the actions of all parties to the conflict, weak justice and protection systems, social normalisation, and harmful gender norms. MSF currently provides medical care across 16 projects in North Kivu, South Kivu, and Ituri provinces, and remains one of the few organisations providing immediate care to victims and survivors in many areas.
In 2024, nearly 45,000 victims and survivors received care in MSF-supported facilities across DRC; this rose to 53,000 in 2025. In the first half of 2026, MSF teams treated over 19,400 people for sexual violence in North Kivu alone.

Russia exports half of traditional volume in October due to blocked Black Sea
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
12:00:00 EET
19:00:00 KST

Russia exports half of traditional volume in October due to blocked Black Sea
Having harvested a record crop, Russia is unable to export it: 2026 figures are close to the results of 2025 (over 144 million tonnes are projected), while exports have dropped significantly.
Source: Russian publication pravda.ru
Details: In 2025, Russia harvested 141.2 million tonnes of grain, including 91.1 million tonnes of wheat. Currently, Russia has harvested 135 million tonnes of grain.
Arkadiy Zlochevsky, President of the Russian Grain Union, said that October shipment volumes are expected to reach three million tonnes.
"This is half of the usual autumn figures (over 6 million tonnes) and significantly lower than the figures for October of last year (5.6 million tonnes), when the export potential was lower than the current one," the publication states.
In attempts to overcome export stagnation due to transportation problems in the Black Sea, the Russian Ministry of Agriculture is considering new routes. However, each of them is associated with serious infrastructural and economic barriers.
The ministry considers the use of the Northern Sea Route possible, but for now, it has been recognised as economically unviable. Its implementation requires a specialised icebreaker fleet, appropriate port infrastructure and expensive insurance.
The reorientation of some flows towards the Baltic is already underway with the support of Russian Railways and traders, but these volumes are not capable of compensating for the overall decline in exports, the Russian department noted.
Meanwhile, China's potential as a main buyer is limited. The main obstacle is China's ban on the import of winter wheat, Russia's main crop, which accounts for two-thirds to three-quarters of the entire harvest, the publication notes.
"The situation with overflowing grain storage facilities and falling prices due to surpluses poses a threat to the long-term stability of the industry. Redirecting logistics from the South to the East or North is not a simple technical solution, as transportation costs directly affect the competitiveness of grain in foreign markets," the publication notes.
If the current logistics model is not adjusted promptly, without certainty in the possibility of selling products, Russian agrarians may reduce sowing volumes.
"In the absence of effective mechanisms for moving grain from regions to ports, high yields lead to the accumulation of surpluses and a drop in domestic prices, which threatens the profitability of all agricultural production," the publication states.
Background:
- Russian grain exports, which bring about US$15 billion annually into Russia's economy, have turned out to be almost completely paralysed due to Ukrainian strikes on ports in the Azov and Black Seas.
- Russian grain exporters are trying to find new supply routes: the ports of the Azov-Black Sea basin are blocked, and exporting through the Baltic ports is too expensive.
- Russia began using the Arctic port of Murmansk for the first time to export grain from Stavropol Krai amid problems with grain exports through the Black Sea.
- The Russian port of Novorossiysk resumed grain shipments for export, but volumes remain significantly lower than last year's, and overall Russian grain export shipments through ports have dropped fourfold.
- Grain-laden vessels began moving through the Kerch Strait from the Azov Sea after a three-month suspension of transport amid Ukrainian drone attacks.
- The Ukrainian Ministry of Agrarian Policy was verifying reports on the resumption of vessel movements carrying Russian grain through the Azov and Black Seas.

Press review: Moscow and Kiev positive on Alyoshki truce as Lavrov attends G20 in US
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

MOSCOW, November 2. /TASS/. Russia and Ukraine conclude their Alyoshki ceasefire, while Russia’s top diplomat Sergey Lavrov takes part in the G20 Foreign Ministers’ Meeting in Atlanta. Meanwhile, a power struggle over control of Poland’s Constitutional Court breaks out. These stories topped Monday’s newspaper headlines in Russia.
Izvestia: Moscow, Kiev positive about results of Alyoshki ceasefire
The mission in Alyoshki has "successfully concluded," Russian ombudswoman Yana Lantratova said. Humanitarian aid was delivered to Alyoshki residents, and those who chose to leave the dangerous town did so. They have already been accommodated in south Russia’s Krasnodar Region, with some receiving medical assistance. The evacuees said many of them literally ate grass and lived under incessant Ukrainian aerial attacks for days over the past few days. The humanitarian ceasefire officially ended at 11:59 p.m. Moscow time (8:59 p.m. GMT) on November 1, but Lantratova did not rule out organizing new missions to help those remaining in the town leave. Washington, Kiev and Moscow have acknowledged the success of the campaign. It could create a positive backdrop for reviving trilateral peace talks, experts say.
"Our troops have accomplished all tasks as part of the humanitarian operation. The Ukrainian army was only required to keep quiet and not to open fire," military expert Viktor Litovkin told Izvestia. It was the Ukrainian army that blockaded the town by mining all roads leading to it with drones, which ultimately created a challenging humanitarian situation there, he recalled.
US First Lady Melania Trump, who mediated the ceasefire agreement, was satisfied with the results of the mission and expressed hope that it would help resolve the Ukraine conflict and "become the starting point for lasting peace."
The localized ceasefire in Alyoshki could pave the way for further humanitarian operations, Denis Denisov, an expert at the Financial University under the Russian Government, argued. According to him, another humanitarian ceasefire under international monitoring could take place at the Zaporozhye Nuclear Power Plant (ZNPP), which would help establish a safe zone for personnel rotation and reduce nuclear risks.
In the event of victory in the November 3 congressional election, US President Donald Trump could show greater interest in targeted humanitarian initiatives, researcher at the Institute of CIS Countries Alexander Dudchak told Izvestia.
The successful completion of the Alyoshki operation will create a positive backdrop for reviving trilateral talks between Moscow, Kiev and Washington, experts argue. However, the humanitarian and political tracks between Russia and Ukraine obviously run in parallel, so one should not expect any automatic progress in the peace process. Kremlin Aide Yury Ushakov stressed earlier that the upcoming round of talks in Abu Dhabi following a lengthy pause will be "a trial meeting."
Vedomosti: Russia’s top diplomat attends G20 Foreign Ministers’ meeting in US
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov’s visit to the United States for the G20 Foreign Ministers’ Meeting in Atlanta showed that Washington and Moscow have been making little headway on Ukraine and have yet to tackle key issues. However, the positive sign is that America is still trying to act as a mediator, Pavel Koshkin, a senior researcher at the US and Canadian Studies Institute of the Russian Academy of Sciences, told Vedomosti. According to him, this is reflected in more constructive remarks from US Secretary of State Marco Rubio. "Against this background, Patriot supplies to Ukraine have been approved, but this should be considered in the context of long-term allied obligations. They are also trying to involve Russia in the diplomatic orbit," the expert noted. In the US understanding, Russia will remain a threat anyway, he explained, but the approach to relations with it is that risks must be reduced. The other issues, including the diesel deal announced by Trump on his Truth Social media platform on October 9, are linked to whether the Ukraine crisis will be resolved, the expert pointed out.
In this context, it cannot be said that Lavrov’s trip was related exclusively to bilateral relations between Russia and the United States, as the agenda was centered around issues facing the G20.
"However, Ukraine remains a key issue for the two countries. And no progress is in sight here. And it will be difficult for the Trump administration to pursue a constructive policy course in the next two years. In other words, the bilateral agenda remains hostage to the Ukraine crisis," Koshkin concluded. The difficulties in relations between Europe and the US do not alter the fact that Washington will have to take Brussels’ opinion on Ukraine into account, he added.
Among other things, Lavrov held talks with Rubio on the sidelines of the G20 meeting, the Russian foreign minister said at a news conference on October 30. The two top diplomats discussed "bilateral relations and interaction at multilateral venues, including the UN, the G20 and the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation, which is set to hold a summit in China’s Shenzhen in November soon," Lavrov said. While in Atlanta, he also held talks with his Japanese counterpart, Toshimistu Motegi, marking the first meeting with a top Japanese diplomat in several years.
Lavrov arrived in Atlanta for the G20 Foreign Ministers’ Meeting on October 30. The two-day meeting that concluded on October 31 became a key event ahead of the G20 Leaders’ Summit scheduled to be held in Miami in mid-December.
Media: Potential outcome of political crisis around Constitutional Court in Poland
On Friday night, Poland came to the brink of a coup as a dispute broke out between Prime Minister Donald Tusk and President Karol Nawrocki, supported by the Law and Justice (PiS) party, over control of the Constitutional Tribunal, the republic’s supreme constitutional court.
Last weekend, Nawrocki held consultations with political forces, but a way out of the crisis is still not on the horizon as the conflicting sides continued to accuse each other of attempting a coup and abusing power. Lawyers are at a crossroads as the current situation extends beyond the existing laws, and neither solution has any legal basis. The key paradox is that the body tasked with resolving disputes is at the epicenter of the dispute.
Many Poles view the developments as a power struggle between politicians who have gone too far. "What is happening is living proof of how a serious state can start morphing into a banana republic sooner than anyone expected," Rossiyskaya Gazeta quoted Polish lawyer Marcin Matczak as saying. "All it takes is for politicians from the two most influential forces to decide that a violent confrontation could earn them more brownie points politically than compliance with laws," he argued. "The whole situation reflects a deeply divided society and a weak political class," the newspaper Fakt reported. According to it, "the current Polish political elites care neither about the state, nor about democracy, or about citizens."
The current situation around the Constitutional Tribunal reflects a long-standing conflict in Poland between the liberals, led by Tusk, and the country’s national-conservatives, led by PiS leader Jaroslaw Kaczynski, Dmitry Bunevich, an advisor to the director of the Russian Institute for Strategic Studies, explained to Vedomosti. Both Tusk and Nawrocki are using this conflict to rally their respective electorates ahead of the upcoming elections to Sejm, scheduled for next fall. While Nawrocki has managed to strengthen his position as the leader of the right-wing camp, a snap election is unlikely; and Tusk holds a majority in the Sejm and has no interest in such a scenario, Bunevich argued.
Tusk sought to demonstrate his strength, relying, among other things, on verdicts by European courts, Stanislav Kuvaldin, researcher at the European Union Research Sector at the Russian Academy of Sciences’ Primakov Institute of World Economy and International Relations (IMEMO RAS), said. Tusk’s actions have led to the unification of right-wing forces, including those that previously had strained relations with one another, in Poland. In this light, Nawrocki is indeed strengthening his position as he has emerged as a leader of the right-wing camp - a significant development ahead of the elections due to take place a year from now, the expert told Vedomosti. According to Kuvaldin, protests may also continue, and even if an overhauled Tribunal begins its work, half of the political parties and a large segment of Polish society will simply refuse to recognize its legitimacy.
Kommersant: OPEC+ moves to keep oil output targets steady for fourth consecutive month
The seven OPEC+ countries once again put adjustments to their output policy on hold, agreeing to leave their December targets unchanged at the levels set in September. Despite rising production and exports through the Strait of Hormuz, the core oil-producing countries, including Russia, continue to produce below their assigned quotas. The alliance may resume output increases in the spring of 2027, provided its forecast of growing crude demand proves accurate.
At a meeting on November 1, the seven OPEC+ countries agreed to keep their December output quotas unchanged at the levels set in September, according to the organization’s decision. As a result, production levels have remained unchanged for four consecutive months. The OPEC+ producers raised their collective oil production quotas by 188,000 barrels per day (bpd) between June and September.
The decision to maintain current oil output levels was largely expected in a situation where supply volumes remain below the established limits and the market is paying less attention to OPEC+ decisions than to how the conflict in the Middle East evolves, Open Oil Market Director General Sergey Teryoshkin told Kommersant. According to him, the current level of quotas will likely remain unchanged until the end of 2026, and future decisions will depend on when and how the Middle East conflict is resolved.
OPEC+ may resume easing its output curbs next spring, before the peak season begins, if incoming data support its forecast for oil demand in 2026-2027, Andrey Polishchuk, senior oil and gas industry analyst at Euler, argued. OPEC expects global oil consumption to increase by 200,000 bpd in 2026 and by as much as 2.6 million bpd in 2027.
Media: Binance hack sends Bitcoin plunging
The Binance hack and a record $6.3 billion heist sent Bitcoin prices tumbling to $76,000. The crypto firm was hacked after its infrastructure was compromised, experts said. This means that Russian crypto custodians will have to implement multi-layered security measures, including cold wallets, key distribution and multi-signature protocols, to safeguard client funds when full-scale trading opens on the Russian cryptocurrency market. Such security measures will require significant investment from market players, meaning only a few of them will be able to build robust infrastructure.
A major decline in Bitcoin prices began on the night of October 29 after reports of the Binance hack emerged. Binance reported a heist of about $6.3 billion. "That could potentially be the largest heist ever in the history of cryptocurrencies," Shard, a Russian platform for assessing digital asset risks, noted. The downturn was further fueled by a massive outflow from ETFs that reached $643 million on October 30.
The Binance hack shows that "neither the scale of the company nor its billions of dollars’ worth of investment in security guarantees complete protection for its assets," Alexander Peresichan, CEO of Tehnobit Systems, told Kommersant.
Should the withdrawal of funds remain blocked longer than the stated period, the risk of a large-scale client exodus will increase, Managing Director of the Investment Business Development Department at Sberbank Roman Kozhura warned in an interview with Vedomosti.
The incident will likely prompt further scrutiny of the safety of Binance’s internal systems by the US Department of Justice and the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN), Kirill Komalenkov, director for strategic communications at Bitbanker, argued.

Israeli man allegedly brutally murders wife with an axe in front of their four children
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
09:59:49 UTC
18:59:49 KST

A 43-year-old woman was found dead in Petah Tikva on Sunday night shortly after midnight, according to police and emergency medical responders. After receiving reports of a violent incident, emergency personnel discovered the woman with severe wounds, no pulse, and not breathing, and ultimately pronounced her dead at the scene.
Police are still investigating the incident as of press time; however, the woman was allegedly beaten with an axe in her apartment in front of her four children, the oldest of whom is 12 years old. Her husband was found a few hundred meters from the crime scene, having apparently taken his own life.
Initial police investigations indicated that the couple had no history of domestic violence, and neighbors were shocked by the news.
The issue of femicide has plagued multiple sectors of Israeli society for several years, although it largely fell out of the mainstream news cycle with the outbreak of the Israel-Hamas war in 2023. Nevertheless, Israeli activists and researchers have continued to document and battle the pattern of violence toward and murder of women.
'This murder could have been prevented'
"While politicians are busy playing musical chairs, a murderer has taken a woman's life with an axe in front of her children," said Tal Hochman, head of the Israel Women's Network (IWN). "The most devastating part is that this murder could have been prevented; violence against women never begins with murder."
According to the IWN, 17 women have been murdered in 2026 in cases of gender-based violence, and the main suspect in 80% of those cases is a spouse or ex-spouse.
What is more, according to a 2025 IWN report, in over one-third of femicide cases, welfare services or police were aware of domestic violence in the home before the murder happened. In a few cases, welfare services were even aware that the suspect was unstable before the murder.
The Michal Sela Forum, an Israeli non-profit dedicated to combating domestic violence, also issued a statement pointing out that the latest murder was the fourth case of femicide since the beginning of October, and that 2026 has seen a total of 25 people killed in domestic settings, including four men and four children.
"The murder of women in their own homes is merely the tip of the iceberg," the Michal Sela Forum said in its statement on Monday. "We must not accept a reality in which women are murdered in their own homes—sometimes even before the eyes of their children."
'The murder of women is not an inevitable fate'
Rivka Neuman, who chairs the Women's Status Advancement Division at the Women's International Zionist Organization (WIZO), noted that, behind the statistics, "lie lives cut short, families shattered, and children left orphaned at a young age—bearing the weight of lifelong trauma."
"The murder of women is not an inevitable fate," Neuman added. "We must not wait for the next victim before taking action."
Alon Hachmon contributed to this report.

US Senate midterm poll results published by The New York Times and Siena University on Sunday indicate that Republicans trail the Democrats in most battleground states.
The survey shows that Texas is ready to flip Democratic. If accurate, that means that Texas is primed to elect a Democrat to the Senate for the first time in nearly forty years.
Kansas, which is in a similar situation, has not elected a democrat since 1932.
The polls point to a major shift in the political landscape of the US and signal that a significant blow is underway for the Trump administration, which has benefited from a Senate majority in Congress since the 2024 elections.
In order to win a majority in the Senate, the Democratic Party must hold all of its seats and flip at least four of the seats currently held by Republicans.
Democrats lead in key states for majority control of Senate
There are seven "battleground states" - closely contested states determined by narrow voting margins where candidates from either party could secure the win.
Democrats lead in five Republican strongholds, according to the NYT poll.
Those leads are significant in Kansas, Maine, Ohio, and Texas. Meanwhile, Democrats lead narrowly in Alaska, while a sixth Republican state, Iowa, shows an extremely tight race.
Dissatisfaction with Trump administration a major factor in electorate shift
The results reflect dissatisfaction with the incumbent administration. US President Donald Trump's approval rating has recently been polled at 32%, slightly higher than his all-time low.
A Washington Post-ABC News-Ipsos poll released last month found that 52% of Americans strongly disapproved of Trump, with mounting economic fallout from the war with Iran being a central issue.
The president has been campaigning consistently in the run-up to the November third midterm elections, with recent rallies having been held in Florida, Kansas, and Iowa.
At one of the rallies, Trump said Democrats left the US in a "dark age" but "we quickly turned it into the golden age of America" during his administration.

INTERVIEW – Israeli war damaged 22.5% of Lebanon’s agricultural land: Minister
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
09:59:09 UTC
18:59:09 KST

Israel’s war on Lebanon damaged around 22.5% of the country’s agricultural land, affecting approximately 56,000 hectares directly, Lebanese Agriculture Minister Nizar Hani said.
“Around 52,000 hectares of the affected land are located in the south and Nabatieh governorates, while another 4,000 hectares are in the eastern Baalbek-Hermel governorate,” Hani told Anadolu in an interview.
He said the damage caused by the Israeli war extended beyond farmland and crops to cattle, sheep and goats, as well as beekeeping.
“Lebanon lost more than 30,000 beehives and around 70% of the livestock in southern Lebanon as a result of the war,” Hani said.
Large areas planted with olive trees and tobacco were also damaged, he said, noting that southern Lebanon is a major agricultural production region that accounts for around 70% of the country’s citrus output and 90% of its banana production.
Those crops are consumed locally and exported to neighboring markets, including Syria, Jordan and Iraq.
Clashes along the Lebanese-Israeli border began on Oct. 8, 2023, between Hezbollah and Israel against the backdrop of the Gaza war before expanding in September 2024 into a broader Israeli military campaign.
A ceasefire was reached on Nov. 27, 2024, but Israeli attacks have continued across Lebanon.
“Israel used white phosphorus during the war and sprayed areas near the border, particularly forested land, with glyphosate herbicide,” Hani said.
The minister said tests conducted by Lebanese authorities through the end of 2025 on soil, crops, forest areas and water produced results that remained within what he described as “under control” levels.
“Winter rainfall has helped reduce some of the effects of the substances,” he said.
However, the latest round of fighting, which began in March 2026, and Israel’s continued occupation of several areas prevented specialist teams from accessing some locations to conduct new tests.
“The Agriculture Ministry plans to collect and test new samples as soon as access becomes possible to assess the environmental and agricultural impact,” Hani said.
The fighting widened again on March 2 against the backdrop of the US-Israeli war on Iran, developing into a second major confrontation.
By mid-October, the conflict had killed 4,389 people and wounded 12,424 others.
Despite a US-sponsored framework agreement reached in June between Beirut and Tel Aviv providing for a gradual Israeli withdrawal and deployment of the Lebanese army, Israel has continued attacks and maintains control of areas inside Lebanese territory.
The Lebanese minister said around 24,000 hectares of olive-growing land in southern Lebanon were directly affected by the Israeli war.
“Another 750 hectares were taken out of agricultural production after Israeli forces bulldozed farmland and uprooted and took olive trees,” he added.
Hani said his ministry has begun this year’s olive pressing season and collected around 20 samples last week from mills near areas still under Israeli occupation.
“The available results showed no risks associated with consuming olive oil and olives produced in the tested areas of southern Lebanon,” he said.
Assessments remain incomplete, however, because teams are still unable to reach other areas.
“Lebanon faced significant pressure on food markets when the latest fighting began in March, coinciding with the start of the local agricultural production season,” Hani said.
At the time, Lebanon continued to rely on imports of some crops from neighboring countries, particularly Jordan, Syria and Egypt.
“Regional disruptions affected supply chains and increased pressure on markets during March,” he added.
Conditions began to improve in April as domestic production rose and the country entered its main fruit and vegetable production season.
“Lebanon can produce most of its fruit and vegetable needs during the summer, significantly reducing its dependence on imports,” Hani said.
He noted that earlier assessments by the UN World Food Program (WFP) and the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), in cooperation with the Lebanese Agriculture Ministry, had warned of food security risks between April and July 2026.
Those estimates suggested around 1.2 million people living in Lebanon could face difficulties securing adequate food and would require support.
“Despite the war and losses, the agricultural season continued,” Hani said.
“Agriculture accounts for around 9% of Lebanon’s gross domestic product, rising to roughly 13% when related food industries are included,” he added.
Hani described Syria as a “strategic and essential partner” for Lebanon because of their shared land border and commercial ties.
“Cooperation between Beirut and Damascus includes efforts to combat cross-border diseases affecting livestock, including foot-and-mouth disease,” he said.
The two countries are developing joint programs and mechanisms to reduce the risk of disease transmission.
Syria is also Lebanon’s closest foreign market for agricultural products. Lebanon exports several crops, including grapes, avocados and custard apples to Syria and imports vegetables and some fruits during the winter.
Syria additionally serves as a major land corridor for Lebanese agricultural exports to Jordan, Iraq and Gulf countries.
“Egypt receives large quantities of Lebanese apples by sea, while most other agricultural exports travel overland through Syria,” Hani said.
The minister said the reopening of the Saudi market to Lebanese agricultural products over the past year has provided important support to the sector, particularly with the resumption of overland transport to Gulf countries.
“Exports of several Lebanese agricultural products increased between 20% and 40% in the third quarter of this year compared with the same period last year,” he said, attributing the improvement partly to restored land transportation routes.
Lebanese exports to Saudi Arabia had faced restrictions since 2021 after millions of Captagon pills were discovered hidden in a shipment of pomegranates from Lebanon. The restrictions were later expanded to other Lebanese products.
Saudi Arabia lifted the ban on Lebanese products last June after nearly five years, allowing maritime exports to resume.
The land transport route through the Masnaa border crossing with Syria was reopened in August alongside tighter export controls and anti-smuggling measures, including advanced inspection systems for trucks and goods.
Hani called Türkiye a major supporter to Lebanon, saying a joint agricultural agreement between the two countries is nearly ready for signing.
He said he had met Turkish Agriculture and Forestry Minister Ibrahim Yumaklı and that Beirut had requested Ankara’s support in several areas related to agricultural development.
The minister also highlighted the role of Turkish Ambassador to Lebanon Murat Lutem in strengthening bilateral relations and advancing cooperation.
Agricultural cooperation between the two countries in recent years has included the provision of seedlings and agricultural supplies, as well as exchanges of expertise drawing on Türkiye’s experience in agriculture and forest management.
Cooperation has also extended to fighting forest fires, with Turkish aircraft assisting Lebanese Civil Defense and army teams in firefighting operations on several occasions.
“Cooperation is reciprocal,” Hani said, noting Lebanon’s support for Türkiye following earthquakes and major forest fires in recent years.
Despite extensive losses to agricultural land, livestock and crops, Hani said increased domestic production and the recovery of foreign markets had helped Lebanon’s agricultural sector absorb part of the pressure caused by the war.

Ukraine Strikes Russian Pantsir-S2 and S-400 Air Defense Systems Worth $70 Million

Ukraine Strikes Russian Pantsir-S2 and S-400 Air Defense Systems Worth $70 Million
Ukrainian forces struck a Russian Pantsir-S2 air defense system and an S-400 Triumph command vehicle, causing an estimated $70 million in losses to Russia’s air defense capabilities, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed on November 1.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Zelenskyy’s official statement on November 1, the strikes targeted a modernized Pantsir-S2 short-range surface-to-air missile and gun system, along with a command-and-control vehicle belonging to Russia’s S-400 Triumph long-range air defense system.
The Pantsir-S2 is designed to intercept aircraft, helicopters, drones, and incoming missiles at short distances. It is commonly deployed to protect military installations and larger air defense systems against aerial threats.
The S-400 Triumph, meanwhile, is one of Russia’s primary long-range air defense platforms, designed to engage aircraft and missiles. Its command vehicles coordinate radar information and direct engagements across the system’s components.
Zelenskyy estimated the combined value of the two targeted air defense assets at approximately $70 million. The extent of damage to each system was not specified.
The Ukrainian president credited the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) and other units of the Defense Forces for the operation.
The announcement also followed a separate Ukrainian long-range strike against the Kamensky Combine, a Russian defense industry facility in the Rostov region involved in missile and rocket propellant production.
During the overnight attack on October 31, Ukrainian forces used Neptune missiles and attack drones to target the industrial complex, according to Ukraine’s General Staff.
The facility produces components associated with ammunition for Russia’s Uragan, Smerch, and Tornado-S multiple-launch rocket systems. Ukrainian military officials reported that the strike ignited a warehouse containing finished products and damaged four production workshops.
Zelenskyy confirmed the attack on the Kamensky Combine on November 1, identifying the facility as part of Russia’s defense-industrial infrastructure supporting missile production.

Germany is not ruling out relinquishing its hosting rights for World Ice Hockey Championship over Russia's participation
Kyiv • UNN
The German Ice Hockey Federation does not rule out boycotting the World Championship following the CAS decision to allow Russia to participate. They are also considering giving up their hosting rights.
Germany is not ruling out a boycott or even relinquishing its hosting rights for the Ice Hockey World Championship following the decision by the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS), which allowed Russia to participate. This was stated by the president of the German Ice Hockey Federation (DEB), Frank H. Lutz, on MagentaTV, reports UNN.
Details
Lutz does not rule out a boycott of the World Championship.
"Of course, there is also a risk that countries will say: "We cannot participate in the tournament under these circumstances." I certainly hope not. But there have already been indications of this in the past. For example, in Latvia, competing against Russian teams is prohibited by law. We would have to consider what this would mean for a tournament such as the World Championship. I very much hope that this will not lead to a boycott, because it benefits no one, especially the athletes. But, of course, this cannot be completely ruled out," Lutz said.
Lutz also left open the worst-case scenario of relinquishing the hosting rights, although only as a last resort.
"I do not want to be pessimistic. Nor do I want to call the staging of the World Championship into question. But, of course, we, as the DEB (German Ice Hockey Federation), must also consider the option of withdrawing from hosting this World Championship. Because we cannot take on a financial risk that we can no longer manage. I believe that we will find a solution. I am very, very optimistic about this. But, of course, this is also something that can reasonably be expected of us," said the head of the German Ice Hockey Federation.

FPCE writes to PM Modi, lists 5 key changes to RERA to strengthen homebuyer protection
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
09:56:30 UTC
18:56:30 KST

NEW DELHI: The Forum for People's Collective Efforts (FPCE), which spearheaded the movement for the Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act, has written to Prime Minister 
Narendra Modi
 seeking changes to the law to strengthen homebuyer protection.
In its letter, FPCE has called for separating the promotion and development of the real estate sector from the legal framework meant to protect homebuyers.
It has also sought the re-enactment of RERA as a dedicated Real Estate Homebuyer Protection Act, with consumer protection at its core.
The organisation has made five key recommendations:
- Separate real estate development from homebuyer protection: Keep the promotion and development of the real estate sector separate from the law designed to protect homebuyers.
- Re-enact RERA: Bring in a dedicated Real Estate Homebuyer Protection Act that places the interests of homebuyers at its centre.
- Shift administration to a consumer protection ministry: Entrust the law's administration to a ministry whose primary mandate is consumer protection, such as the Department of Consumer Affairs.
- Ensure accountability: Introduce an effective accountability framework for real estate regulatory authorities.
- Prepare a time-bound action plan: Direct the ministry of housing and urban affairs to examine FPCE's report and draw up an action plan with clear timelines.

Robots strut their stuff, race up sacred China mountain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Robots strut their stuff, race up sacred China mountain, some carrying eggs and watermelons
Dozens of robots took on more than 3,000 steps up one of China's most famous peaks Monday, many carrying eggs and watermelons in a race organizers billed as a test of real-world machine endurance, state media showed.
For hundreds of years, Mount Tai -- the tallest peak in China's eastern Shandong province -- was an important pilgrimage for Chinese emperors, and it features prominently in Chinese mythology.
But the rugged terrain would prove a stern test for some competitors. One humanoid robot wearing a bandana collapsed in a heap on the cobbled route before engineers rushed in to repair it, while another tumbled down a flight of stairs and came to rest beside a rubbish bin.
The UNESCO World Heritage site hosted technologies of the future as part of a new World Mountain Robot Challenge, footage from state broadcaster CCTV showed.
Over a 2.4-mile course with more than 1,970 feet of ascent, robots and their engineers from around 90 teams were tasked with either completing the route as fast as possible or transporting fragile goods such as fresh eggs and watermelons to the summit.
A canine robot made by Beijing Lingyi Technology -- a subsidiary of industry giant Unitree -- completed the course in 43 minutes, 41 seconds, to win the four-legged speed category.
Most tourists take at least two hours to complete the route, according to CCTV.
The fastest humanoid robot -- belonging to Beijing-based team Zhishen Lingyue -- completed a shorter race course in 27 minutes and 26 seconds.
Organizers called Mount Tai's rocky terrain a "natural extreme testing ground" that could help train robots for real-world use, local media reported.
The race, organized by the state-run China Media Group, featured cash prizes for winners in several categories, including the fastest robots and the best load-carrying four-legged machine.

Temperature soars at Swedish grocery store freezers, one store blames hackers
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
10:52:43 CET
18:52:43 KST

STOCKHOLM/BRUSSELS, Nov 2 (Reuters) - Ahold Delhaize and Colruyt said on Monday that an IT incident overnight hit fridges and freezers in dozens of stores in Belgium and Luxembourg, while Swedish grocers ICA and Coop reported similar temperature spikes, with one store blaming a cyberattack.
The incidents follow an attack in France last month, in which police said hackers seized control of cooling units at hundreds of supermarkets, raising temperatures as high as 50 degrees Celsius (122 degrees Fahrenheit) and causing fires and food losses.
Ahold also reported a cybersecurity incident to Dutch police last month after it detected suspicious activity in its infrastructure.
On Monday, the Delhaize supermarket chain realised there were temperature increases in the cooling systems, Delhaize spokesperson Sarah De Meester said. The company is investigating the incident.
Stephan Moelans, the CEO of Belgian refrigeration company Sabcobel, which operates Delhaize’s systems, told the Belga news agency that the incident was a cyberattack, in which the units’ evaporators were switched to defrost mode. Moelans’ office declined to comment when contacted by Reuters.
A spokesperson for Colruyt Group, which operates Spar stores in Belgium under a franchise system, said five shops had their fridge systems attacked.
From refrigerators and heating systems to security cameras and alarm networks, an expanding range of devices once largely mechanical can now be monitored and controlled remotely, creating new opportunities for cybercriminals.
Authorities have not indicated who could have been behind last month’s incidents. There were no claims of responsibility.
SWEDISH STORES ALSO AFFECTED
The head of Sweden’s national cybersecurity centre, John Billow, told Reuters it was working on several incidents regarding refrigeration systems in grocery stores around Sweden.
One Swedish ICA store said on social media that the temperature of its refrigerators and freezers had been “hacked” overnight and set to 50 degrees Celsius. It said later that the store had since opened.
At an ICA Baronen store in Stockholm, a notice said all the shop’s freezers were broken due to a cyberattack. The store’s sales manager said the attack happened at 2 a.m. (0100 GMT) and was noticed at 5.30 a.m..
“We are aware that a limited number of stores were affected by an incident overnight, which impacted their refrigeration and freezer systems,” a spokesperson at privately held ICA said in an email.
Privately held grocery retail group Coop told Swedish daily Aftonbladet that six of its stores had been affected by similar incidents. It did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
“We have in recent weeks… identified that we have quite a lot of exposed operational technology devices in Sweden that we have been clear about the necessity to update or patch,” the cybersecurity centre’s Billow said.
An Estonian supermarket chain was also affected, with temperatures set to 50 degrees, technology supplier Kitman Coldtech told public broadcaster ERR.
“This is very fresh, it happened this morning,” Kitman CEO Jann Mutso told ERR. He declined to name the affected grocery chain.
(Reporting by Anna Ringstrom, Louise Rasmussen and Johan Ahlander in Stockholm; Inti Landauro in Brussels; editing by Terje Solsvik, Kirsten Donovan)

By Florence Loeve
PARIS, Nov 2 (Reuters) - The head of the European Space Agency will meet officials in the United Arab Emirates this week as Europe seeks new partners and aims to reduce its reliance on the United States for space exploration.
The rise of Elon Musk’s SpaceX has laid bare Europe’s reliance on American space technology.
“Number one, we should strengthen our capability, become a stronger player in the global ecosystem, but one that uses its strength to still work with other partners,” Josef Aschbacher, director general of the ESA, told Reuters. He will attend meetings in Dubai and Abu Dhabi.
“We realised that in exploration, Europe is very exposed to the United States,” Aschbacher added, saying that European political leaders had told him that the region needed “more autonomy and more strength”.
COOPERATION WITH NASA WEAKENED
The ESA’s decades-long cooperation with US space agency NASA has weakened after Washington scaled back or halted common projects, including the Lunar Gateway programme to deploy a space station in lunar orbit and the Mars Sample Return mission.
About 5% of the ESA’s budget is linked to cooperation with the US, Aschbacher said. Europe also relies on US providers to send its astronauts into space.
Aschbacher said that over the longer-term the ESA hopes to sign a framework agreement with the UAE, which launched the Arab world’s first mission to Mars in 2020.
The UAE operates several satellites, and sent two of its nationals into space through its astronaut programme, but cannot yet organise launches on its own and does not own an independent satellite navigation system like the EU’s Galileo or the US Global Positioning System (GPS).
Discussions between ESA and the UAE include a possible lunar rover launch and the potential participation of an Emirati astronaut in the EPIC programme, which would fly a crew to the International Space Station aboard a SpaceX spacecraft.
Aschbacher will visit a joint venture between Franco-American startup Loft Orbital and Abu Dhabi-backed Marlan Space to develop a satellite constellation, after France and the UAE agreed to deepen a strategic defence agreement between the two countries.
Asked if the UAE could invest in projects in collaboration with the ESA, Aschbacher declined to discuss ongoing talks. He said in September that Europe would need €10 billion ($11.2 billion) over the next 10 years to strengthen its autonomy in space.
Aschbacher said the funding gap may be discussed with the UAE but he added that the ESA first needs European governments to agree on their own level of funding.
“Once this decision is made, we will look into international cooperation,” he said.

BRUSSELS, Nov 2 (Reuters) - Belgium’s King Philippe urged Prime Minister Bart De Wever on Monday to find a compromise over next year’s budget, with his government on the brink of collapse following the failure of another round of late-night negotiations.
De Wever had offered his resignation in a meeting with the king on Monday morning.
The king will weigh De Wever’s offer, but will also hold talks with the leaders of the other coalition parties from Tuesday, the Royal Palace said in a statement.
“In light of the large geopolitical uncertainty and severe economic challenges, the country can’t afford a long political crisis,” it said.
The government has been arguing for months about €10 billion ($11.2 billion) in budget cuts and tax increases De Wever says are needed to keep state finances in check.
A coalition deadline to reach an agreement on next year’s budget had been set for Tuesday.
Like other European countries, including France and Italy, Belgium is struggling to balance ballooning national debt with demands from protesters for greater spending to improve services, such as education. Demonstrators have clashed with police in countries including France, Spain, Italy and Belgium in recent weeks.
Without an agreement the Belgian government could only work with a limited budget next year, allowing it to spend one-twelfth of this year’s budget per month.
The crisis coincides with heightened stress on financial markets, where interest rates have risen sharply on government bonds of Belgium, France and other European countries seen to have weak government finances.
The European Commission forecast in May that Belgium’s debt-to-gross domestic product ratio would be 110.5% this year, behind only Greece, Italy and France among euro zone countries, with a projected general government deficit of 5.2% of GDP.
Belgium’s 10-year benchmark bonds were trading at a yield of 4.36% on Monday morning, against 4.92% for France and 3.30% for Germany.
Four months ago, Belgian 10-year yields were at 3.48%.
De Wever has repeatedly warned of an “interest snowball” without budget cuts, where Belgium would need to take on new loans to be able to pay interest on existing debt.
In months of talks, De Wever’s Flemish nationalist N-VA and the liberal MR have not been able to compromise with their socialist and centrist coalition partners.
The N-VA and MR have pushed for cuts in spending including on healthcare, while their partners demand higher wealth taxes to bring in more resources.
The king will meet De Wever again on Friday. If the king ultimately accepts the prime minister’s resignation, he could ask other parties to form a coalition or could call for fresh elections.

Nowak’s stepmother, Katie Nowak, said: “I do feel that we have been failed multiple times. I fear that we may have been manipulated in our darkest hours. And I fear that some decisions were made to try and protect the police and their reputation rather than help us as a family.”
The student was murdered by Vickrum Digwa, who stabbed him as he walked home from a night out in Southampton in December 2025. Nowak was handcuffed by police officers while bleeding to death after Digwa, who was eventually jailed for life, had falsely accused him of racial abuse.
In police bodyworn camera footage that prompted a public outcry, Nowak was heard repeatedly saying: “I’ve been stabbed,” to which an officer replied: “Don’t think you have, mate.”

Hampshire and Isle of Wight chief constable, Alexis Boon, told ITV News: “I am incredibly sorry that in his final moments, when he needed us most, we failed him. I recognise that, for Henry’s family, this has been about more than the circumstances of one night. They have rightly raised serious concerns about the police response and their treatment throughout the investigation and since. No family should ever find themselves in this position.”
Nowak’s family revealed that the IOPC had said in April: “No [Hampshire police] officers would be subject to conduct or criminal investigation. This was because there were no concerns identified in relation to officer actions.” Less than two months later, Hampshire and Isle of Wight constabulary was forced to apologise for its actions.
The police watchdog’s director of engagement, Derrick Campbell, told ITV News: “The IOPC is committed to establishing the full circumstances of this case, including whether any of the officers involved should face disciplinary proceedings, and providing Henry’s family with answers to the questions they rightly have about how the police treated Henry in the way they did on that terrible night, and why.”

Second-pillar fund withdrawers can start saving again this month
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
09:49:00 UTC
18:49:00 KST

Second-pillar fund withdrawers can start saving again this month
People who withdrew their second-pillar pension savings following reforms can, five years on, start contributing again from this month, and experts urge them to do so.
Estonia's pension system rests on three pillars: the state-funded first pillar, the previously mandatory funded second paid from social tax and gross salary, and the voluntary third (private pensions plan).
Second-pillar contributions became voluntary in 2021, and about a third of savers withdrew their funds following the changes, with the first major wave in September that year.
Applications to resume contributions can be submitted and were open from November 1. Those who left in the first wave can begin making contributions in May 2027; the rule is that five years must elapse between leaving the pillar and restarting .
Commenting on how things have developed since 2021, Heidi Reinson, a researcher in economic behavior at the University of Tartu, said: "There were more people who had no other savings, such as a third pension pillar or other financial reserves. Among them were many people who had high-interest payday loans hanging over their heads, as well as large families. But what is perhaps most interesting is that trust in the state, the financial sector and the media was much lower among those who left the second pillar."
A third of the withdrawn money went on loan repayments, while nearly a fifth went straight into consumption. On the latter, Reinson recalled anecdotal stories of televisions bought at the Ülemiste mall which were too large to fit into taxis.
A year after the reforms, half the money was sitting in people's current accounts.
Pension fund assets currently total €8 billion, but without the withdrawals they would amount to €11 billion. Age Petter, head of Swedbank Investment Funds, noted someone earning the average salary had accumulated just over €8,000 by 2021 — but would now have seen that grow to around €20,000 had they not withdrawn.
Investor Kristjan Liivamägi said the state adds €80 for every €40 a person contributes. "If we take the average Estonian earning a gross salary of €2,000 a month, then two percent of their salary goes into their second pension pillar. That's about €40. The state adds another €80 from social tax," he said. A 45-year-old on that salary would accumulate around €63,000 by retirement, assuming no salary growth and returns of about 7 percent a year.
Reinson warned of a longer-term consequence: a wealth gap between savers and non-savers. "People regret not having saved, and then that wave of regret will be even stronger. Then you see that your colleague, who has been earning the same average salary as you, is in a much better position when they retire," she added.

====================================================================================================

Why India is taking a different route in the global chip race
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
09:48:38 UTC
18:48:38 KST

India is pouring billions into semiconductors – just not where you might expect
India is plowing billions into becoming a global chipmaking hub, while smartly taking a route different from that of industry giants racing to produce the most advanced processors powering the AI boom.
The South Asian country already has a substantial presence in semiconductor design. Now, New Delhi wants to establish a domestic manufacturing industry and become a reliable global supplier.
That ambition was on display at the Semicon India event in New Delhi in September, when Prime Minister Narendra Modi pitched India as an alternative manufacturing destination amid growing demand and concerns over global chip production bottlenecks and supply uncertainties.
“The world needs new and trusted locations for chip manufacturing and India is preparing itself for this,” Modi told the conference.
A month earlier, in his Independence Day address, Modi had made semiconductor development an important component of the wider Make-in-India manufacturing push. “Chips are indispensable; without them, the world would come to a standstill,” he noted.
The initiative comes as artificial intelligence, data centers, electric vehicles, and expanding electronics production drive demand for semiconductors. But India’s strategy is not to immediately challenge the industry’s technological leaders on their own terms.
“I believe this is one of the smartest and most far-sighted choices India has made,” the co-founder and CMO of chip startup Indiesemic, Jinal Shah, told RT in emailed comments. Indiesemic is based in Ahmedabad, the capital of Modi’s home state Gujarat.
Why India is betting on older chips
While manufacturers such as Taiwan’s TSMC and South Korea’s Samsung compete to produce ever-smaller processors, including 2-nanometer chips used in high-performance computing and AI, India is initially concentrating on established technologies known as mature nodes.
These chips, ranging from 28 to 180 nanometers, may not be at the cutting edge of technology, but are essential to automobiles, industrial machinery, telecommunications, household appliances, and electricity networks.
Even the AI boom needs them. Because data centers cannot work without power-management chips, networking components, and other such chips.
Mature-node technologies account for nearly 70% of global chip production by volume, said Neil Shah, the co-founder and vice-president of research at the think tank Counterpoint Research. Starting with mature-node fabrication, specialized semiconductors, and conventional chip assembly and testing is “the only commercially rational entry point for India,” Shah told RT.
A leading-edge 3-nanometer fabrication plant can cost more than $15 billion to construct, according to Indian government think tank NITI Aayog. Making them also requires specialized equipment and expertise accumulated over decades – the latter especially is why the US has found it difficult to quickly replicate TSMC’s manufacturing success.
Pursuing 2-nanometer production is “simply too expensive,” the secretary at India’s Electronics and Information Technology Ministry, S. Krishnan, recently admitted.
Although eclipsed by the AI chips, mature-node chips are a high-growth market. Industry researcher TrendForce reported in June that rising demand for power-related semiconductors, including those used in AI infrastructure, was tightening manufacturing capacity and could sustain price increases into 2027.
India designs chips for the world. Why doesn’t it make them
India is hardly a newcomer to the semiconductor business. The country accounts for nearly a fifth of the global chip-design workforce and hosts major research and development centers for companies such as Intel, Qualcomm, and Texas Instruments.
Indian engineers contribute to the development of sophisticated chips used around the world. Yet, much of the actual manufacturing takes place overseas.
Imports currently meet an estimated 90%-95% of India’s semiconductor demand, according to NITI Aayog. The think tank projects that the country’s chip market will grow to more than $200 billion by 2035, driven by electronics, automobiles, telecommunications, and digital infrastructure.
Getting into chip fabrication gives India two opportunities: reducing the dependence on imported chips for its expanding domestic industries, and supplying overseas markets looking for alternative manufacturing locations.
Bridging the gap: From designing chips to making them
India’s first semiconductor mission resulted in 12 approved manufacturing projects involving more than $17 billion in planned investment. These include a silicon fabrication plant, two specialized semiconductor facilities, and nine assembly, testing, and packaging units.
Five of the nine units have already begun commercial production, including those operated by US memory-chip maker Micron and Indian companies Kaynes Semicon, CG Semi, CDIL Semiconductor, and Suchi Semicon. Modi inaugurated commercial production lines at CDIL in Punjab and Suchi Semicon in Gujarat during the September industry event.
However, these units largely focus on assembly, packaging and testing rather than manufacturing integrated circuits directly on silicon wafers. Building that capability is the next major step.
The Semicon 2.0 program, backed by $13.5 billion, is intended to build an industry around such factories, extending support to equipment manufacturers, specialized chemicals, raw materials, chip design, research, and workforce development.
“India currently relies almost entirely on foreign nations for these foundational raw materials and machinery,” the director of the Sudeet Foundation, Raghava Srinivasan Balakrishnan, told RT.
Indian conglomerate Tata Group is building an $11 billion fabrication plant in Dholera, Gujarat, with Taiwan’s Powerchip Semiconductor Manufacturing Corporation. Commercial production is targeted for mid-2028, initially using 55-nanometer and 90-nanometer technology before moving to 28 nanometers.
At the September conference, US-based Applied Materials announced plans to invest $5 billion in India over the next decade, including in research, domestic supply chains, and workforce development.
The government is also trying to help Indian companies move from designing chips to developing commercially viable products of their own.
Centralized access to professional design tools and infrastructure “significantly lowers the initial capex barriers,” technology policy researcher Pranay Kotasthane wrote in August, welcoming the support for chip-design startups.
Could India eventually make advanced chips?
New Delhi’s ambitions don’t stop at mature-node manufacturing.
In a roadmap released in May, NITI Aayog proposed building a semiconductor value chain worth $120 billion-$150 billion by 2035, with India becoming one of the world’s top three destinations for outsourced semiconductor assembly, testing, and advanced packaging.
The roadmap identifies advanced packaging as an opportunity. Combining different chips into increasingly sophisticated packages can improve performance without relying entirely on the race to make transistors smaller.
”Instead of chasing the global wafer race from behind, India should define its own pathway,” the report says.
The NITI Aayog also recommends building strength in specialized analog semiconductors and materials, such as silicon carbide and gallium nitride, which are important for electric vehicles, renewable energy, and industrial power systems.
India is not abandoning the ambition of making cutting-edge processors altogether, but just being pragmatic by going for the low-hanging fruit first.
Getting to the top of the hill will require experience in operating commercial wafer fabrication plants, developing a skilled workforce, and building a domestic network of equipment and materials suppliers.
For now, the country is seeking to establish itself in parts of the semiconductor industry where demand is already substantial and its existing strengths offer it a clear commercial edge.

The social policies pursued between 2020 and June 2026 have improved protection for vulnerable groups, but have also created fiscal risks that affect the state budget as a whole. Prada champions the human touch and not AI slop for their new Christmas campaign
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
09:45:25 UTC
18:45:25 KST

Prada's new advertising feels like a direct response to those still indulging in a tech that is threatening human creativity and livelihoods. Their ‘Drawing Prada: Animated By Hand’ campaign shows that the "not-made-by-AI" approach has become a major selling point.
As generative AI continues to pollute the internet and advertising, certain luxury houses are betting on human craft when it comes to their Christmas marketing.
Call it "effort signaling" all you want; their efforts are to be applauded at a time when cost-cutting initiatives result in mediocre and bar-lowering slop.
One luxury brand choosing to celebrate human creativity this year is Italian fashion house Prada, which has swapped AI-generated dross for traditional, hand-drawn illustration for their new Christmas campaign.
Combining live-action footage with hand-drawn characters, the ‘Drawing Prada: Animated By Hand’ campaign has enlisted veteran animator John Pomeroy to lead a team of artists to bring animated characters and environment to life.
“That sense of touch expresses a fundamental notion of humanity, and a connection with craft that always lies at the very heart of Prada’s approach to creation,” according to a press release.
The campaign, developed under the creative direction of Miuccia Prada and Raf Simons, with Ferdinando Verderi overseeing campaign creative direction, sees each frame drawn by hand and the live-action scenes photographed by Glen Luchford.
Check out the campaign below, which features a cast of celebrity ambassadors including Sadie Sink, Maya Hawke, Chen Haoyu, Luther Ford and Kelvin Harrison Jr.:
Best known for his work at Disney, Pomeroy has contributed to iconic films including the Oscar-nominated Winnie the Pooh and Tigger Too (1974), The Rescuers (1977), Pete’s Dragon (1977) and The Fox and the Hound (1981).
After his departure from Disney, he established independent animation studio Don Bluth Productions, creating films like The Secret of NIMH and The Land Before Time.
He later returned to Disney, where he worked on films such as Pocahontas, Fantasia 2000, Atlantis: The Lost Empire and Treasure Planet. He later worked as an animator on films like Curious George, several Tom and Jerry films, and Space Jam: A New Legacy.
In a behind-the-scenes film accompanying the campaign, Pomeroy explained his commitment to traditional technique.
“I learnt my craft with pencil and paper, through traditional, analogue drawing. We’ve remained faithful to that approach and want to pass it on to future generations,” said Pomeroy.
“There’s a very distinct and purposeful reason to do hand-drawn animation, and that’s to see that there’s value in it and that hand-drawn and handcrafted work is still alive in the world today.”
Prada's ad comes at a time when other brands aren't caring as much. Their 2026 campaign feels like a direct response to those still indulging in a tech which is threatening human creativity and livelihoods.
Unlike Coca-Cola and their AI-generated Christmas advertisements, which faced criticism in both 2024 and 2025 (since the brand did not learn from their mistake the first time around), certain companies are starting to understand how fed up potential consumers are with AI.
More and more people have grown wary of the pervasive tech and there is a growing backlash towards the rise of AI – leading younger, digital-savvy generations to appreciate the value of human creativity while older generations embrace the traditional crafts in a bid to push back against soulless imagery.
Moreover, the "not-made-by-AI" approach has become a massive selling point, and Prada have understood the value of delivering an antidote. Their new campaign has sparked enthusiasm online, with users commenting: "Love it when ads go AI free, much respects to the artists"; "Now this, THIS is how you make an ad"; "Normally not interested in Prada, but I'm reading "Animated by Hand" and I'm in"; and "Such a breath of fresh air seeing something with soul again".
It goes to show that something as simple as hand-drawn illustration can still create enthusiasm.
Your move Coca-Cola. Let's see if a multi-billion company can be bothered to pay real animators this year or if they'll churn out yet another deeply derivative campaign based on the works of artists, used without permission.

Hackers raised freezer temperature at Estonian supermarket chain to +50°C
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
