Hackers raised freezer temperature at Estonian supermarket chain to +50°C
An Estonian supermarket chain has been hit by a cyber attack which saw attackers access a computer controlling refrigeration, and setting a freezer to 50 degrees above zero.
Jann Mutso, CEO of Kitman Coldtech, which makes the affected tech, said one of its clients was attacked, adding that other Estonian clients have also been hit. The methods match similar attacks seen in France and the Netherlands last month.
Mutso declined to tell ERR which store's cooling system had been the victim, and said due to a swift response no wide-ranging damage was caused by the sudden temperature spike.
"One of our clients was attacked," Mutso said, describing the victim as a "large chain store". He continued: "More has happened. I don't know exactly yet, but other clients in Estonia have also been attacked, not only ours. This is very fresh, it happened this morning."
The attackers gained access to the control computer of an older type of Danfoss refrigeration system and raised its temperature to 50 degrees above zero, much as had happened in the incidents in France and the Netherlands recently.
"The signature is the same, but I can't comment further yet," Mutso said.
Mutso said it is normal in large food stores for refrigeration systems to be digital and connected to the network, but that the current attack had sought specific security holes. Supermarkets are tackling the issue, he said.
"All the store chains have started fighting this and have updated their controllers, but there are also places where the controllers are old and not updated, and it is those which are being targeted now," he continued.
He said he the current incident was responded to within 10 minutes of being reported, meaning no damage was caused. However, disrupting digital systems can directly impact on food safety and cause significant damage, Mutso added.
According to information on Kitman Coldtech's website, its clients include four major supermarket chains in Estonia: Selver, Rimi, Coop and Lidl.

Saudi-led coalition intercepts a missile as fighting rages in Yemen’s al-Jawf
Houthi-affiliated media report that seven people were wounded in strikes on the city of Hodeidah.
The Saudi-led coalition in Yemen says air defences intercepted a Houthi missile, while fighting continues to rage along key fronts between the armed group and forces loyal to the internationally recognised Yemeni government.
Defences “intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile” targeting Saudi Arabia’s southern region, said coalition spokesman Major General Turki al-Maliki in a statement on Monday.
Earlier, he said defences destroyed a drone launched toward the southern region on Sunday evening.
Also on Monday, the Saudi Civil Defence authority issued and then lifted alerts warning of “potential danger” in the city of Abha, as well as the provinces of Khamis Mushait, Taif and Najran.
The authority warned residents against “filming, publishing or sharing information” related to missile and drone attacks.
In Yemen, a media outlet affiliated with the Houthi armed group, also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God), reported that seven people were wounded in Saudi-led coalition air strikes on Hodeidah on the Red Sea coast.
Four people were wounded in the attacks on Ras Isa port dock, while three others suffered injuries in a strike on an oil company site in the governorate’s Bajil district, Houthi media reported.
There was no comment on the reports from the Saudi-led coalition.
Humanitarian crisis
The latest clashes come as Yemeni government forces keep up their campaign to regain positions from the Iran-aligned Houthis in the strategic northern governorate of al-Jawf.
Yemeni army spokesman Colonel Majed Abdullah al-Nazili said on Sunday evening that government forces conducted 1,272 “targeting operations” against Houthi fighters, fortifications and weapons supplies over 24 hours.
Operations are ongoing in al-Jawf, neighbouring Marib and al-Bayda to the south, added al-Nazili. Government forces killed roughly 500 Houthi fighters and destroyed or disabled nearly 170 vehicles, equipment or heavy weaponry.
Al Jazeera could not independently verify the claims.
In southwest Yemen, the Houthis continue to besiege the city of Taiz, blocking the entry of food, fuel and medical supplies, in what authorities warn is a mounting humanitarian crisis.
Taiz Governor Nabil Shamsan has called for urgent help for the city’s deteriorating health facilities. He said 120 health centres have stopped operating and another 66 are close to shutting down since the Houthis cut off supply routes to the city in early October.
Nour al-Din al-Mansouri, a member of the committee facilitating the work of the Taiz Siege Affairs Office, told Al Jazeera that at least 23 trucks were damaged or overturned in the past two weeks while seeking alternative routes to Taiz.
The city is Yemen’s third-largest and home to about one million of the country’s roughly 43 million people.
Full-scale fighting reignited in Yemen in September, when the Houthis made crucial gains that tightened their grip on the Red Sea coast.
Yemen’s internationally recognised government launched a campaign called Operation Dawn of Yemen last month to regain Houthi-held sites and restore government control over other territories held by the group, which seized the capital Sanaa in 2014.

18:43:55 KST

EU energy ministers want to shield households and businesses from a harsh winter pricing, as the massive geopolitical shock in the Middle East has sent European gas prices surging past a four-year high of €97 per megawatt-hour.
EU energy ministers met energy on October 29 and confronted a painful reality: despite massive efforts to wean the bloc off Russian fuel, the EU remains entirely at the mercy of the next global supply disruption.
Why? Before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, it supplied around 45% of the EU’s gas imports, compared with just 12% in 2025. To replace it, Europe has turned to more expensive liquefied natural gas (LNG) from countries such as the US. Meanwhile, the conflict in the Middle East (with the closure of the Strait of Hormuz) is pushing prices higher as Europe competes with Asian countries for alternative imports.
To provide immediate relief to consumers this winter, member states intend to lower utility bills by reducing electricity network charges and cutting state-imposed taxes on power. Additionally, the plan introduces incentives for households and businesses to shift high-energy activities to cheaper, off-peak hours. To secure physical supplies, the plan also mandates stricter coordination of emergency gas stockpiles across member states to prevent regional shortages as temperatures drop.
Can these measures be enough? Are energy bills reaching a breaking point for households? Our poll is anonymous and takes only a few seconds to complete. Kyiv refuted reports of the threat of an epidemic of cholera, dysentery, and hepatitis A
Kyiv • UNN
No outbreaks of cholera, dysentery, or hepatitis A have been recorded in the capital. Epidemiological risks are assessed as low, and the water is tested daily.
Reports of a threat of an epidemic of cholera, dysentery, and hepatitis A in Kyiv do not correspond to the actual epidemiological situation. As of November 1, no outbreaks of dangerous infectious diseases had been recorded in the capital. This was reported by the Kyiv City Center for Disease Control and Prevention of the Ministry of Health, UNN writes.
Details
Experts explained that assessing potential epidemiological risks is part of regular preventive work and does not mean that an outbreak or epidemic is being forecast.
The center also stressed that power outages and temporary interruptions in water supply in themselves do not indicate a deterioration in the epidemiological situation.
According to experts, short-term interruptions in water supply caused by the de-energization of pumping stations are promptly resolved. At the same time, the quality of drinking water in the capital is checked in laboratories every day.
Epidemiologists continue to constantly monitor infectious disease incidence and water safety. Currently, epidemiological risks in Kyiv are assessed as low.

Dutch MP proposes law banning 'harmful addictive design features' on all digital platforms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
09:43:04 UTC
18:43:04 KST

MP Barbara Kathmann tabled a proposal in the Dutch Parliament to end addictive design features such as endless scrolling, autoplay and manipulative algorithms for all online services including social media, gaming, dating apps and streaming platforms.
A Dutch MP has proposed a new law banning "the most harmful addictive design features" on digital services, such as infinitive scrolling, autoplay videos, push notifications and manipulative algorithms.
Barbara Kathmann, an MP from the Dutch Parliament’s main opposition party, the centre-left Progressief Nederland (PRO), submitted the proposal on Monday 2 November, saying the ban "protects both children and adults".
BigTech platforms are facing mounting global pushback over concerns that their services are designed in harmful ways that encourage addiction and other destructive behaviours. Meta, TikTok and SnapChat, among others, have all been brought to court in recent years by rights groups.
Kathmann is working with parliamentarians across Europe in Germany, France, Belgium, Luxembourg, Austria, Italy, and Portugal, who want to regulate digital platforms and address their alleged harmfully designed services.
"People need to regain control over their own time and attention. Manipulative tricks online can have a major impact on our mental and physical health, brain development and attention span, now and for future generations," said Kathmann.
"The Netherlands must therefore show leadership now and be the first in the world to ban addictive design. We can only stand up to Big Tech’s manipulative tricks if we protect everyone."
The proposed law would subject digital platforms to a "fairness by design" duty of care, requiring them to prove their online services are not addictive and instead make sure their features are designed to be "fair and non-manipulative".
'Addictive algorithms manipulate our minds'
This is not the first time a Dutch politician has submitted a proposal on the topic.
In 2023, a report by Dutch MEP Kim van Sparrentak, also from PRO, was adopted by the European Parliament calling for the European Commission to put forward a proposal for an addictive design ban.
She backed today’s proposal in the Dutch Parliament saying, "With this law, the Netherlands is taking the lead in Europe, and we can finally build a safe and non-addictive internet.
"No self-discipline can beat Big Tech’s addictive tricks. Every day that we fail to take action, we let addictive algorithms manipulate our minds and in the long run our democracies, as they keep offering the most extreme content to keep us hooked.
"And Europe is failing to take action. Companies like Meta are filling their pockets with money earned by exploiting your attention and the way you are wired, whilst the tech lobby is sharpening its knives to water down the rules."
The Commission is due to table a proposal this November under its Digital Fairness Act, with a EU-wide addictive design ban a key measure among several others aimed at enhancing consumer protections in Europe.
The Act is complemented by other EU legislation in the pipeline, such as the EU Kids Act, which aims to protect children online by shifting the burden of responsibility from parents to digital platforms, requiring them to make their services safe by design.
The EU Digital Services Act, which has been in force since 2022, combines several measures requiring very large online platforms (VLOPS) such as Meta and very large online search engines (VLOSEs) like Google to detect, remove and prevent illegal content, hate speech and dangerous products.

US Reportedly Seeks to Restore Russian Gas Supplies to Europe Through Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
09:42:00 UTC
18:42:00 KST

The administration of US President Donald Trump is pushing to restore Russian natural gas supplies to Europe through Ukraine, potentially reversing Kyiv’s decision to end Russian gas transit nearly two years ago.
The proposal was discussed during negotiations in September as part of a potential “energy ceasefire” ahead of winter, The Wall Street Journal (WSJ) reported on Nov. 2, citing US, European and Ukrainian officials.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
It would involve selling Russian gas through a US intermediary, allowing the arrangement to circumvent European sanctions while creating lucrative investment opportunities for American companies.
Under the plan outlined by Trump’s special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, Russia’s revenues from gas sales would be deposited into an escrow account in a third country to prevent Moscow from using the money to finance its war against Ukraine.
Washington is also considering reopening the Nord Stream pipeline system as part of a broader deal to end the war, according to WSJ sources.
The proposal faces significant political resistance in Europe, where governments have spent years reducing their dependence on Russian energy following Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
How Russian gas flowed through Ukraine
Ukraine was historically one of the main transit routes for Russian natural gas exports to Europe. Its extensive Soviet-era pipeline network connected Russian gas fields in Siberia with European markets, supplying countries across Central and Western Europe.
Ukraine, Russia Hit by Hackers Sending Fake Nuclear Attack Alerts
The network included major pipelines such as Bratstvo (Brotherhood) and Soyuz (Union), which carried gas through Ukraine toward Slovakia and other European destinations. Gas also moved through southern Ukraine and Moldova toward the Balkans and Türkiye.
Even after Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, Ukraine continued transporting Russian gas to European customers under a five-year transit agreement signed by Naftogaz and Russia’s Gazprom in December 2019.
In 2024, the final full year of the arrangement, approximately 42 million cubic meters of Russian gas flowed through Ukraine daily, equivalent to around 15 billion cubic meters annually, according to S&P Global.
Slovakia, Austria, Moldova and other European markets continued receiving supplies through the network.
Transit ended at 7 a.m. Kyiv time on Jan. 1, 2025, when the agreement expired. Kyiv refused to negotiate a new arrangement with Moscow, arguing that continuing to facilitate Russian gas exports would generate revenue for the Kremlin while Russia continued its war against Ukraine.
The Gas Transmission System Operator of Ukraine confirmed that the Ukrainian gas transmission system had switched to operating without Russian transit. The decision also cost Ukraine an important source of revenue from transit fees.
Russian oil still flows through Ukraine
The end of Russian gas transit did not mean that all Russian energy exports through Ukraine stopped.
Russian crude oil continued to move through the country via the southern branch of the Soviet-era Druzhba (Friendship) pipeline, which supplies refineries in Hungary and Slovakia.
Both countries have maintained their reliance on Russian oil and benefit from exemptions under EU sanctions.
Ukraine transported approximately 9.73 million metric tons of Russian crude through Druzhba in 2025, according to Ukrainian energy consultancy ExPro.
Slovakia received nearly 4.9 million tons, while Hungary received approximately 4.35 million tons.
The volumes were 14% lower than in 2024, partly because the Czech Republic stopped importing Russian oil through the pipeline in March 2025.
Druzhba also became the focus of a major dispute between Kyiv, Budapest and Bratislava in early 2026.
Russian oil deliveries to Hungary and Slovakia were suspended on Jan. 27 after a Russian strike damaged infrastructure linked to the Druzhba pipeline near Brody in western Ukraine, according to Kyiv.
The disruption triggered a diplomatic dispute, with Hungary and Slovakia stepping up pressure on Zelensky over the halted supplies.
Budapest and Bratislava accused Kyiv of deliberately delaying the restoration of deliveries, while Ukraine maintained that the pipeline had been damaged by Russian attacks and required extensive repairs.
The dispute escalated further as the EU pushed for an independent inspection of the damaged pipeline.
Ukraine announced in April that repairs had been completed. Russian oil transit resumed on April 23, with Hungary and Slovakia receiving renewed supplies through the pipeline.
Kyiv’s announcement also came amid efforts to unblock a €90 billion EU loan for Ukraine that Budapest had been blocking.
The dispute demonstrated how dependent some European countries remain on Russian energy despite the EU’s broader efforts to reduce that dependence.
Europe resists a return to Russian gas
European officials and EU leadership remain skeptical of Washington’s proposal, pointing to the bloc’s commitment to phase out Russian natural gas imports.
The EU has spent years diversifying its energy supplies, increasing imports of liquefied natural gas (LNG) and pipeline gas from alternative suppliers.
In February 2026, the EU adopted new legislation to phase out Russian gas imports. The restrictions began taking effect in March, with transitional exemptions for certain existing contracts.
The EU’s target is to end Russian gas imports by September 2027, with a limited possible extension for some long-term contracts.
One WSJ source compared the prospect of resuming Russian gas purchases to former British Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain’s decision to sacrifice Czechoslovakia in pursuit of an agreement with Adolf Hitler.
European opposition could nevertheless face pressure as the continent prepares for winter.
Washington reportedly believes that soaring energy prices, LNG supply shortages linked to the conflict in the Middle East and relatively low gas storage levels could make European governments less resistant to the proposal.
The administration is reportedly presenting renewed Russian gas exports as a way to lower energy prices, generate investment opportunities for US companies and provide Moscow with an economic incentive to negotiate an end to the war.
Washington also eyes Nord Stream
The Trump administration is also considering the possibility of restoring gas supplies through the Nord Stream pipeline system, which connects Russia directly to Germany under the Baltic Sea.
The first Nord Stream pipeline began operating in 2011, allowing Russia to bypass traditional transit countries, including Ukraine, and deliver gas directly to Germany.
Nord Stream 1 halted deliveries in August 2022, while Nord Stream 2, completed in 2021, never entered commercial operation. Both pipelines were badly damaged in underwater explosions in September 2022, as documented by the United Nations.
One senior US official told WSJ that former German Chancellor Angela Merkel’s mistake was promoting the pipeline project without first securing a broader security agreement with Russia.
The official suggested that energy cooperation should have been part of a wider arrangement addressing Moscow’s security concerns.
Restarting Nord Stream would require overcoming substantial technical, regulatory and political obstacles. The pipeline network running through Ukraine, by contrast, could reportedly resume operations much more quickly.
Kremlin rejects energy truce
The Kremlin has previously rejected the idea of an energy ceasefire with Ukraine.
Russian presidential spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Moscow needed “peace, not a truce.”

US Justice Department escalates legal fight over California noncitizen voter list
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
09:41:39 UTC
18:41:39 KST

Gizem Nisa Demir
02 November 2026•Update: 02 November 2026
- Justice Department urges federal judge to consider contempt proceedings against immigrant rights group after it publishes findings challenging accuracy of government's data
The US Justice Department on Sunday defended a list of more than 20,000 people it alleges are noncitizens registered to vote in California, accusing an immigrant rights group of violating a court order by questioning the list’s accuracy.
PBS News reported on Sunday that the dispute follows a Friday ruling by US District Court Chief Judge James Boasberg, who granted the Coalition for Humane Immigrant Rights (CHIRLA) access to the federal data while prohibiting the disclosure of names and restricting its use to arguments concerning the group's legal standing.
In the US, noncitizens generally cannot vote in federal or state elections, including California state elections. 
However, San Francisco allows eligible noncitizen parents and legal guardians of children in the city's public school system to vote in local school board elections under a city ordinance. This means that the presence of a noncitizen on a voter registration list does not, by itself, establish that the person registered illegally.
In court filings Saturday, CHIRLA's attorneys said their analysis found that more than 40% of the people on the federal list did not appear in California's voter registration records.
They also identified 22 people who were likely naturalized US citizens and said the list included thousands of other people who appeared to be US citizens.
The Justice Department argued Sunday that the analysis violated Boasberg's order because it was unrelated to the group's legal standing. It also suggested referring the matter for an investigation into possible criminal contempt of court.
"The report's political grandstanding about alleged inaccuracies that purportedly impact California voters generally, or comparisons between the government's list and the full 'California voter file,' has no relevance to whether the particular plaintiffs in this case have standing," the department said.
University of California rejects allegations
Alberto Lammers, a spokesman for the University of California, Los Angeles' Voting Rights Project, which conducted the analysis, rejected the allegations.
"Plaintiffs' counsel and their experts fully complied with the court's orders," he said.
In a separate case, the Justice Department appealed a ruling by US District Court Judge Trina L. Thompson that barred federal officials from ordering California election offices to remove suspected noncitizens from voter rolls, separate their ballots or threaten legal action.
A hearing was scheduled for Monday.
The Trump administration has faced several legal setbacks over its efforts to challenge alleged noncitizen voter registrations.
A California federal judge previously rejected its demand to separate ballots cast by suspected noncitizens, warning that last-minute orders could "wreak havoc" on the state's election. Two appellate judges upheld the decision.
California election officials say the federal list contains numerous errors and that there is insufficient time to complete the legally required removal process. The administration, however, maintains that the list was compiled by comparing state voter registration records with federal citizenship data.
The Justice Department has also subpoenaed several California election offices and warned officials of possible criminal charges for knowingly allowing noncitizens to vote.

MOSCOW, November 2. /TASS/. Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB) has reported the seizure of a mined batch of FPV drone goggles intended for the Russian military in the special military operation zone as humanitarian aid.
TASS has compiled key details about the report.
Terror plots
- The FSB thwarted a series of sabotage and terrorist attacks using improvised explosive devices concealed inside FPV drone goggles intended for delivery to the Russian military in the special military operation zone, which were plotted by Ukrainian special services.
- Acting on instructions from military counterintelligence, a Russian serviceman in the Volgograd Region brought two FPV goggles he had received from a volunteer to the FSB for inspection.
- Explosive ordnance specialists established that Ukrainian special services had planted improvised explosive devices in the FPV goggles instead of cooling solutions.
- As a result of the measures taken, a batch of similar improvised explosives camouflaged as FPV goggles, sent into the country via the Russian Post, has been confiscated across Russia, the FSB said.
- The explosive devices would have detonated when the FPV glasses were switched on, potentially killing servicemen, the FSB specified.
- Posing as pseudo-patriots, agents of Ukrainian special services established communication with representatives of Russian humanitarian organizations and charity foundations, using anonymous accounts on the Telegram messenger, to arrange supplies to Russian Defense Ministry units, the FSB noted.
- During these exchanges, the FSB continued, they refused to share their names, phone numbers and job information or switch to the Max messenger for calls as they communicated with volunteers to arrange the delivery of FPV goggles with homemade explosive devices, while demanding video feedback with words of gratitude from Russian fighters.
- According to the enemy’s plans, volunteers were supposed to later deliver the FPV goggles laden with improvised explosive devices to Russian drone operators taking part in combat operations against Ukrainian troops, the FSB said.
Probe
- The FSB’s investigative department in the Volgograd Region has opened a criminal case.
- Efforts to identify those responsible for the shipment are underway.
Call to volunteers
- The FSB has called on volunteer organizations to accept humanitarian aid only from reliable sources and inspect it for explosives.
- Ukrainian special services can use various items to disguise homemade explosive devices, the FSB warned.
- The agency recalled that improvised explosive devices disguised as perfume sets, power banks, music speakers, miniature souvenir statues, church utensils, car components, paving slabs and even heated insoles have previously been neutralized.

The Middle East and Gulf region should not become a battleground for great-power rivalry and Beijing is willing to work with Arab nations to achieve lasting peace, President Xi Jinping told Oman's sultan on Monday.
China has traditionally played a low-key diplomatic role in the Middle East but has stepped up efforts to try to help end tensions amid the US-Israeli war on Iran, which has snarled the Strait of Hormuz and driven up global energy and shipping costs.
Xi told Omani Sultan Haitham bin Tariq al-Said that the world is undergoing profound changes.
"The Middle East Gulf region should not become an arena for great-power rivalry and geopolitical conflict. Peace and stability in the region require joint nurturing and protection by all parties," Xi said, according to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.
China has consistently been committed to stopping the war and hopes to contribute "wisdom and solutions to resolving the region's security dilemmas", he added.
It is willing to strengthen communication and coordination with Arab countries, including the Gulf Cooperation Council states, to work together toward restoring peace and achieving lasting stability and security, Xi said.
In a 20-point joint statement, both sides said they agree that normal and safe navigation should resume in the Strait of Hormuz. The countries also called for the US and Iran to pursue peaceful options, return to the agreement struck in June aimed at ending the conflict and restart dialogue.
The ministry said later on Monday that Zhai Jun, its special envoy to the Middle East, would visit Iran, Oman and Saudi Arabia this month.
Haitham arrived in Beijing on Sunday for a two-day visit, the first by an Omani head of state since the countries established ties in 1978.

"The prosperity of nations requires an environment defined by security, peace, respect for state sovereignty, and adherence to international law – an environment where disputes are resolved through peaceful means."
He also said Oman was open to entering into a preferential bilateral trade and investment agreement with China.
"We are confident that such an agreement would open new avenues for trade and investment, facilitate and enhance commercial and investment exchanges between our two nations," Haitham said.
China is Oman's largest trade partner, with tourism and business links boosted by direct flights between Beijing and Muscat since November.
Oman, which exports crude oil and energy products to China, has also been looking to further develop its renewable energy supply chains and digital commerce.
Their joint statement said the countries have agreed to deepen practical cooperation in the oil and natural gas sector, as well as expand cooperation in new energy fields such as solar photovoltaics, wind power, power transmission and transformation, and energy storage.
The Omani leader, who was welcomed on the tarmac in Beijing by People's Bank of China governor Pan Gongsheng, also emphasised cooperation between investment and financial institutions. (Reuters)

Russia’s economy is losing momentum: production is declining, and regions are becoming dependent on subsidies
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
11:37:43 EET
18:37:43 KST

Russia’s economy is losing momentum: production is declining, and regions are becoming dependent on subsidies
Kyiv • UNN
Russia’s Ministry of Economic Development forecasts a 0.2% decline in industrial production in 2026. Sixty-five regions depend on assistance from the federal center, while the metallurgical industry has lost 5.2%.
The Russian economy is showing increasingly pronounced signs of crisis: for the first time in five years, Russia’s Ministry of Economic Development is forecasting a decline in industrial production at the end of the year. The shift to a wartime economy did not meet the Kremlin’s expectations — production, regional revenues and domestic demand are declining. This was reported by the Foreign Intelligence Service, UNN writes.
Russia’s Ministry of Economic Development officially recorded an industrial downturn for the first time in the past five years. At the end of 2026, a decline of 0.2% is expected instead of the projected growth of 0.6%. Over the first eight months of the current year, the indicator remained at zero, while in August it fell by 0.8% year-on-year. This negative trend was a direct consequence of the Kremlin’s shift of the Russian economy to a "wartime footing
It is noted that the key factor was the contraction of domestic demand caused by high inflation, currency fluctuations and expensive borrowing. At the same time, amid the economic crisis, production at defense-industry enterprises is also being curtailed due to cuts in the state defense order — enterprises that, according to Moscow’s promises and calculations, were supposed to support the overall situation in the country.
The industries most affected were those directly dependent on consumer activity and lending: the automotive industry, construction, agriculture and the chemical industry. The decline in revenues is turning regions into subsidized ones, further undermining the population’s purchasing power. As of today, 65 constituent entities of the Russian Federation are unable to sustain themselves without assistance from the center and are subsidized, while only 24 remain donor regions.
Overall, Russia’s metallurgical industry has lost 5.2% of its total output, chemical enterprises 3%, garment production 4.2%, elevator production has fallen by 20%, and freight railway car production by 30%. Petroleum product production has been declining for the third consecutive month, while oil production could fall by the end of the year to its lowest level in the past 17 years.

Swiss satellite set to improve solar storm forecasts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
09:36:14 UTC
18:36:14 KST

Swiss satellite set to improve solar storm forecasts
Swiss Federal Institute of Technology ETH Zurich is developing a new satellite to study solar storms. From 2030, the research satellite called Ethos is set to help forecast space weather more accurately, the university announced on Monday.
Powerful solar flares heat up the upper atmosphere and cause it to expand. As a result, satellites in low Earth orbit enter denser layers of air and are slowed down more significantly. They lose altitude and may deviate from their calculated trajectory.
This increases the risk of colliding with other satellites or space debris. However, according to the university, it has so far only been possible to predict the extent to which the atmosphere reacts to solar activity with a degree of uncertainty.
Ethos is designed to investigate these relationships in greater detail. The small satellite, weighing around 25 to 30 kilograms, will be equipped with several scientific instruments for this purpose. Among other things, these will measure the energy emitted by the Sun, as well as X-ray and extreme ultraviolet radiation during solar flares.
+ Strong solar storm brings Northern Lights in Switzerland
Other instruments will monitor changes in the ionosphere – an electrically charged layer of the Earth’s upper atmosphere – and determine the satellite’s orbit with high precision.
Data series for climate research
The combination of these measurements is intended to show how fluctuations in solar activity alter the ionosphere and, as a result, change the density of the upper atmosphere and the drag experienced by satellites. The data could help to improve space weather forecasting and provide satellite operators with early warning of potential orbital changes.
The satellite is also intended to support the long-term observation of solar radiation. Several existing measurement missions are expected to reach the end of their operational lifetimes around 2030. ‘Ethos’ is designed to help ensure that the measurement series continue without interruption. According to ETH Zurich, the data are also significant for climate research.
The mission is being developed by ETH Zurich in collaboration with the Davos Physical-Meteorological Observatory, the University of Bern and the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology in Lausanne (EPFL). The research institutions are developing the scientific instruments, whilst the satellite itself is to be supplied by a commercial provider.

Nuclear radiation in Russia, Ukraine? No, just hacked warning alerts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
09:35:46 UTC
18:35:46 KST

Nuclear radiation in Russia, Ukraine? No, just hacked warning alerts
Warnings startle people in Ukraine, but authorities say they cleared up the confusion in under an hour.
Ukraine and Russia have accused each other of hacking into systems used to send out emergency alerts to citizens, raising fears of a new escalation of digital and psychological warfare tactics.
The systems’ apps sent out radiation alerts on Sunday and Monday to civilians before officials issued public clarifications.
The fake threats began on the same day as a localised ceasefire in the Russian-occupied Kherson region came to an end on Sunday. The truce, which the United States said was brokered by first lady Melania Trump, is the longest so far in Russia’s more than four-year war on Ukraine. The ceasefire lasted for six days, during which humanitarian aid and evacuations were allowed in the Russian-occupied town of Olekshy.
Al Jazeera’s Audrey Macalpine, reporting from Kyiv, said many people in Ukraine now expect renewed fighting along the front lines.
Here’s what we know about the fake notifications:
What happened?
Ukraine’s Air Force said late on Sunday that users of its Air Alert app, which warns people of incoming air attacks, received fake warnings of nuclear and chemical threats to areas in and around Kyiv.
Users were also warned of potential street combat and told that Russia’s hypersonic Oreshnik missile had been deployed.
“The air alert app appears to have been subjected to enemy influence,” the Ukrainian Air Force said on Telegram.
“There is no radiation threat! Stay calm and follow our updates on our channel.”
Ukraine’s Center for Strategic Communications blamed Russia. In a post on X, the agency pointed to the use of the Russian language in one of the fake messages. The Ukrainian government said a separate app created for the capital city was working normally.
The fake alerts came just after 10pm (20:00 GMT), startling a lot of people, Macalpine reported.
“Even the speakers here in the centre of the city rang out warnings of these attacks,” she said. “But most people here understood within at least half an hour that this was some kind of hacking attack.”
Hours later on Monday morning, similar announcements came from Russia’s Ministry of Civil Defence, Emergencies and Disaster Relief, which said its warnings app came under a “massive cyberattack” and wrongly warned users of imminent drone attacks. The ministry did not name any suspects but said the alerts spread “false information”.
Media reports said the hackers warned Russians that “nuclear warheads mounted on P1-Suns [Ukrainian drones] had been launched on all regions” of the country. The alerts also instructed people to “urgently” stock up on food for three weeks and to hide.
Has this happened before?
This appears to be the first time either Ukraine’s or Russia’s official alert apps have been hacked.
However, cyberwarfare has long been a major part of the countries’ previous confrontations.
Russian hackers have attacked Ukraine’s election systems in the past and in January 2022 attacked Ukrainian government and banking sites. Cyberwarfare tactics have only intensified since February 2022 when Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine. In late 2023, the Russian hacker group Sandworm took the private telecommunications network Kyivstar offline, disrupting notifications for days.
Ukrainian groups have also launched multiple cyberattacks on Russia.
The country’s volunteer-based IT Army of Ukraine was founded in the wake of Russia’s invasion specifically to engage in cyberwarfare against Russia and has reportedly targeted the Moscow Stock Exchange, Russia’s power grids and several government websites. In 2022, the Reuters news agency reported Ukrainian attackers used facial recognition software to scan the faces of dead Russian combatants and notified their families of their deaths.
Why is the threat of nuclear radiation in Ukraine significant?
Ukraine is particularly vulnerable because it has already suffered one nuclear disaster and it remains at risk due to fighting around another major nuclear plant.
In April 1986, the Chornobyl nuclear power plant, located in the then-Ukrainian Soviet Republic, exploded, releasing radioactive material. Scores of people died from the explosion itself, but thousands later developed severe health issues as a result, including thyroid cancer. Radiation was detected as far away as Sweden. It’s regarded as one of the two worst nuclear accidents in history along with the 2011 Fukushima disaster in Japan. Chornobyl remains a ghost town after its inhabitants were evacuated.
Ongoing fighting in the Ukrainian region of Zaporizhia has raised fears that the tragic story could repeat itself. Russia partly controls the region, including Enerhodar, where the Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant, Europe’s largest nuclear energy facility, is located.
Both sides have repeatedly launched attacks on each other’s positions with Russia targeting the Ukrainian-held provincial capital, Zaporizhzhia, and Ukraine targeting Russian-held areas, including Enerhodar.
Last week, the International Atomic Energy Agency, the United Nations nuclear watchdog, said a welder working at the Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant was killed in a drone attack. The head of the agency, Rafael Grossi, called for “maximum military restraint” from both sides.

"Not the time for Russia to return" — Finnish politicians condemn sports court ruling
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
11:32:35 EET
18:32:35 KST

Finnish politicians have roundly condemned the decision, handed down by the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) on Friday, which allows Russian teams to return to ice hockey’s international tournaments.
Finland's sports minister Mika Poutala (CD) told Yle on Monday that Russia's return to international sports is not welcome, adding he had discussed the issue with his Swedish counterpart, Jakob Forssmed.
"At least with Sweden, we clearly share a common view on this: that it's not the time for Russia to return to ice hockey, or to sports in general — especially not under its national colours," Poutala said.
According to the CAS ruling, Russia can once again compete in men's and women's world championships as well as in the world juniors.
The verdict overturned an exclusion handed down by the International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF) after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
In its ruling, CAS said there was insufficient evidence to support the security concerns that IIHF had raised as a reason for Russia's exclusion.
In response, an IIHF statement noted that the federation "maintains that its decisions were necessary to protect the safety and security of all participants and safeguard the integrity of its competitions".
Ball in Finland's court
The decision puts particular focus on next year's men's world championship tournament in Germany, as Ukraine has also qualified.
Finland is committed to abiding by CAS decisions, meaning in practice that the Finnish team is set to also take part in the tournament. Finland are currently reigning world champions, having secured the title in dramatic fashion against this year's hosts Switzerland in May.
However, Poutala noted on Monday that Finland can decide otherwise, with the Finnish Ice Hockey Association ultimately responsible for making that call.
There is a growing swell of support among Finnish politicians for Finland to withdraw from the tournament.
Foreign Minister Elina Valtonen (NCP) wrote on social media platform X on Sunday that "Russian athletes will have no business coming to Finland next year" if the war in Ukraine continues.
"I intend to advance the necessary measures in the coming days," Valtonen added in her post.
Speaker of Parliament Jussi Halla-aho (Finns) also shared his opinion in a social media post, writing on Facebook that Finland should skip the tournament if Russia is permitted to take part.
Finnish President Alexander Stubb meanwhile told Yle's Ykkösaamu programme on Saturday morning that he disagrees with the CAS decision.

Temperature soars at Swedish grocery store freezers, one store blames hackers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
09:32:13 UTC
18:32:13 KST

European supermarkets hit by new fridge cyber attack
STOCKHOLM/BRUSSELS, Nov 2 - Ahold Delhaize and Colruyt said on Monday that an IT incident overnight hit fridges and freezers in dozens of stores in Belgium and Luxembourg, while Swedish grocers ICA and Coop reported similar temperature spikes, with one store blaming a cyberattack.
The incidents follow an attack in France last month, in which police said hackers seized control of cooling units at hundreds of supermarkets, raising temperatures as high as 50 degrees Celsius (122 degrees Fahrenheit) and causing fires and food losses.
Ahold also reported a cybersecurity incident to Dutch police last month after it detected suspicious activity in its infrastructure.
On Monday, the Delhaize supermarket chain realised there were temperature increases in the cooling systems, Delhaize spokesperson Sarah De Meester said. The company is investigating the incident.
Stephan Moelans, the CEO of Belgian refrigeration company Sabcobel, which operates Delhaize's systems, told the Belga news agency that the incident was a cyberattack, in which the units' evaporators were switched to defrost mode. Moelans' office declined to comment when contacted by Reuters.
A spokesperson for Colruyt Group, which operates Spar stores in Belgium under a franchise system, said five shops had their fridge systems attacked.
From refrigerators and heating systems to security cameras and alarm networks, an expanding range of devices once largely mechanical can now be monitored and controlled remotely, creating new opportunities for cybercriminals.
Authorities have not indicated who could have been behind last month's incidents. There were no claims of responsibility.
SWEDISH STORES ALSO AFFECTED
The head of Sweden's national cybersecurity centre, John Billow, told Reuters it was working on several incidents regarding refrigeration systems in grocery stores around Sweden.
One Swedish ICA store said on social media that the temperature of its refrigerators and freezers had been "hacked" overnight and set to 50 degrees Celsius. It said later that the store had since opened.
At an ICA Baronen store in Stockholm, a notice said all the shop's freezers were broken due to a cyberattack. The store's sales manager said the attack happened at 2 a.m. (0100 GMT) and was noticed at 5.30 a.m..
"We are aware that a limited number of stores were affected by an incident overnight, which impacted their refrigeration and freezer systems," a spokesperson at privately held ICA said in an email.
Privately held grocery retail group Coop told Swedish daily Aftonbladet that six of its stores had been affected by similar incidents. It did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
"We have in recent weeks... identified that we have quite a lot of exposed operational technology devices in Sweden that we have been clear about the necessity to update or patch," the cybersecurity centre's Billow said.
An Estonian supermarket chain was also affected, with temperatures set to 50 degrees, technology supplier Kitman Coldtech told public broadcaster ERR.
"This is very fresh, it happened this morning," Kitman CEO Jann Mutso told ERR. He declined to name the affected grocery chain. REUTERS

Ryanair CEO warns fares could rise by up to 20% in 2027 as fuel bill jumps by $2.2 billion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
09:27:47 UTC
18:27:47 KST

Ryanair CEO Michael O'Leary told CNBC Monday that European airfares are set to rise "significantly," growing by as much as 20% next year as fuel hedges expire.
The budget air carrier's profit fell 15% to 2.15 billion euros ($2.3 billion) in the first fiscal half of the year, as the price of its 20% unhedged jet fuel doubled.
"So we're facing 2027 where we have much higher oil prices... I think they're going to get passed on in significantly higher airfares," O'Leary told CNBC's Steve Sedgwick on Monday.
"The market customers have been insulated for the last 12 months... but those hedges are rolling off. There's still no resolution in the Middle East. Jet oil today is $170 a barrel. I mean, this is a very significant cost cliff we're all facing next year. I believe you're going to see airfares rise next year across Europe by 10%, maybe even 20%," O'Leary added.
Ryanair said it doesn't expect an increase in short-haul airfares to fully offset an estimated 2-billion-euro increase in fuel charges next year. It is therefore launching a cost review, which will include lowering crew rations, a potential temporary pay freeze and the use of AI to drive further efficiencies.
Ryanair's Irish-listed shares initially edged higher in early Monday trading before paring gains to trade below the flatline. The stock has fallen over 22% this year.
The airline said in September it would cut its full-year traffic target from 216 million passengers to 214 million passengers in a bid to reduce its exposure to unhedged fuel during the winter. It's now expecting winter traffic between November and March to remain broadly flat year-on-year.
"I think you're seeing even this winter, all of the airlines across Europe, even Ryanair, for the first time in many years, we cut our winter capacity," O'Leary said. We'll only be flat this winter over the prior year, because it makes no sense for us to be growing capacity if we're buying unhedged oil at $170 a barrel."
Ryanair hedged 80% of its jet fuel at $67 per barrel for the year, which it said gave it an advantage over its competitors as its earnings remained insulated from volatile oil prices. The carrier added that it has hedged at least 25% of its 2028 jet fuel prices at $95 per barrel.
Earnings remain 'hostage' to oil prices
The share price reaction on Monday says more about investors' expectations than the numbers alone, according to Adam Vetesse, market analyst at eToro.
"Investors appear to have already priced in the hit from unhedged fuel and softer summer fares, leaving room for relief that the quarter landed exactly where consensus had predicted," Vetesse said.
"Near-term earnings remain hostage to oil prices and close-in bookings, but the market's early bounce suggests investors are willing to give Ryanair the benefit of the doubt that its cost advantage will matter more than the fuel spike once the dust settles," he added.
Ryanair also noted in Monday's announcement that it held 2.6 billion euros in cash as of 30 September, even after repaying 1.3 billion euros in debt.
"You know we've paid off all of our debt this year, so we have effectively zero debt. We have 650 aircraft on the balance sheet. We're significantly cash positive," O'Leary told CNBC, adding that the challenge facing all airlines is the volatility in oil prices, lack of hedging, and higher financing costs.
"So you see, some of our competitors are doing sale and leasebacks to generate cash. They're just mortgaging their futures; they're Ponzi schemes."

Sweden’s Military Reserves Shrink Despite Plans to Expand Army
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
09:27:43 UTC
18:27:43 KST

Sweden’s pool of trained military reservists is shrinking because more people are leaving the reserve than are joining it.
According to a government proposal on military staffing reported by Swedish broadcaster SVT, the decline is mainly due to a lack of refresher training.
Under current rules, people are removed from the military reserve if they have not served or completed refresher training in the past ten years.
The Swedish government acknowledges that in recent years, the number of trained military reservists has been declining faster than new personnel can be added. The situation is expected to worsen as the government establishes new military units.
According to the government report SOU 2025:86, Sweden may need at least 100,000 trained reservists by 2035. Meanwhile, the number of conscripts serving in combat units is planned to increase to 51,000.
To address the problem, the government proposes scrapping the 10-year limit and keeping people in the military reserve until the end of the year in which they turn 47, even if they have not completed refresher training.
However, returning these reservists to combat units would require mandatory refresher training. A shortage of professional officers and training resources remains a major challenge.
According to the Swedish Armed Forces’ 2027 budget document, the country plans to train 12,000 conscripts annually from 2032.
However, further recruitment increases could make it harder to organize refresher training for reservists because of competition for instructors and training resources.
On October 22, the parliamentary Defense Committee approved the proposed changes. A parliamentary vote is scheduled for 4 November, with the new rules set to take effect on 1 January 2027.
Sweden also considered in 2025 allowing retired officers up to the age of 70 to return to service to address personnel shortages.
In August 2026, the Swedish military leadership presented a plan to reorganize the army by 2040. It includes creating one army corps, three divisions, territorial forces, and a reserve force.

Russia eyes Pantsir-S1 air defense sale to Azerbaijan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
09:26:46 UTC
18:26:46 KST

- Russia’s arms export chief Dmitry Shugaev said he expects Moscow and Baku to eventually agree on Pantsir-S1 air defense sales to Azerbaijan.
- He also said Russia will help Azerbaijan build and modernize repair facilities for its Russian-made armored vehicles under a newly signed program.
Russia expects to reach a deal to sell Pantsir-S1 air defense systems to Azerbaijan, the head of Russia’s arms export regulator said, in a sign that military trade between Moscow and Baku is picking up again after a year-long diplomatic rupture.
Dmitry Shugaev, director of the Federal Service for Military-Technical Cooperation, said on Russian state military channel Zvezda on Nov. 1 that the Pantsir-S1 is in high demand among foreign customers and that he believes Russia and Azerbaijan will agree on a sale after some time. He did not say how many systems Baku might buy, what a deal would be worth or whether formal negotiations have started. Azerbaijan has not commented.
In the same interview, Shugaev said the two countries have signed a program under which Russia will help build and modernize facilities for repairing the armored vehicles already in Azerbaijani service, TASS reported. Azerbaijan bought large numbers of Russian armor in the 2000s and 2010s, including about 100 T-90S tanks and roughly as many BMP-3 infantry fighting vehicles and BTR-80A armored personnel carriers.
The Pantsir-S1 is a short-range air defense system that carries both surface-to-air missiles and twin 30 mm cannons on a single truck. It is built to protect bases, cities and longer-range air defense batteries from aircraft, helicopters, cruise missiles and drones, and the export version can engage targets at ranges of up to 20 km (12 miles) and altitudes of up to 15 km (about 49,000 feet). Russia has sold it to more than a dozen countries.
Relations between Moscow and Baku collapsed after Russian air defenses brought down an Azerbaijan Airlines Embraer E190 over the Caucasus on Dec. 25, 2024. The jet crashed near Aktau, Kazakhstan, killing 38 of the 67 people on board. Azerbaijan demanded that Russia accept responsibility and threatened international legal action, and President Ilham Aliyev skipped Russia’s Victory Day celebrations in May 2025.
Vladimir Putin acknowledged in October 2025 that a malfunction in Russian air defenses caused the crash and promised compensation. In April 2026, the two countries’ foreign ministries said they had settled all issues related to the crash, including compensation, and pledged to develop their “allied” cooperation.
Azerbaijan has relied mainly on Turkey and Israel for modern weapons in recent years. On Sept. 30, at the ADEX 2026 exhibition in Baku, it signed Turkish defense contracts worth more than $500 million, covering 14 Hürkuş-II trainer aircraft, Baykar’s Mızrak loitering munition and Antidot system, and Roketsan’s Barbaros coastal defense system, along with a memorandum on Aselsan’s ALP-100 radar. In October, Israeli outlet Globes reported that Azerbaijan is the unnamed customer behind a $235 million Elbit Systems order for PULS rocket launchers and EXTRA-MR rockets.
Those deals came as Ankara and Baku traded public criticism this fall over Azerbaijan’s ties with Israel, a religious dispute and credit for the 2020 Karabakh war, OC Media reported, though the two governments have continued signing defense agreements.
Oryx, an open-source project that counts only losses backed by photo or video evidence, has documented at least 54 Russian Pantsir systems lost in the war against Ukraine since the full-scale invasion began in February 2022, 53 of them Pantsir-S1s and one an upgraded Pantsir-S1M. Ukraine’s SBU security service has made the system a priority target for its long-range drone units, since Pantsirs are among Russia’s main defenses against those drones.

TPLF claims 500 Ethiopian soldiers killed in fresh clashes in Tigray
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
11:43:16 UTC
20:43:16 KST

Ethiopia's Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) has claimed that its fighters killed 500 soldiers and wounded 800 others in clashes with federal government’s army and allied forces in the country's northern Tigray region.
The group said the casualties occurred during fighting on Saturday near the historic city of Aksum, where its forces launched a counteroffensive against Ethiopian troops and members of the allied Tigray Peace Forces (TPF).
The figures were reported by the TPLF-affiliated Dimtsi Weyane television station. They could not be independently verified, and the Ethiopian government has not commented on the claims.
TPLF reports heavy casualties and territorial gains
According to Dimtsi Weyane, the fighting took place in the Daero Hafash and May Tmqet areas of Naeder district. The broadcaster said 500 combatants, including two regiment commanders, were killed, while another 800 were seriously wounded.
Government troops had advanced from Aksum and Mahbere Dego before encountering resistance from TPLF rebels, the report said.
The group also claimed to have captured territory and seized weapons, ammunition, food supplies and medical equipment.
It accused federal forces of using artillery and drones during the operations and said telephone and internet services had been disrupted in the area.
Renewed fighting raises fears of wider regional conflict
The latest claims follow weeks of clashes between federal forces and TPLF rebels, raising concerns that Ethiopia could face another large-scale conflict in Tigray.
Government troops and allied forces captured several towns, including the regional capital, Mekelle, in early October. TPLF fighters have since continued to launch counterattacks.
The renewed violence has also sharpened tensions between Ethiopia and neighbouring Eritrea. Addis Ababa has accused Asmara of supporting armed groups operating in Tigray, allegations that Eritrea has rejected.
Sudan has separately accused Ethiopia of allowing 70 drone attacks to be launched from its territory between February and October, claiming the strikes killed or wounded hundreds of civilians and soldiers.
Sudanese authorities have also accused Addis Ababa of supporting the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), which has been fighting Sudan's army since 2023.
The escalation threatens to deepen instability across a region still grappling with the consequences of the 2020-2022 Tigray war, which displaced millions of people and caused widespread humanitarian suffering.

Russian strikes increase Ukraine&apos;s need for foreign aid - Bloomberg
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
11:25:12 EET
18:25:12 KST

Russian strikes increase Ukraine's need for foreign aid - Bloomberg
Kyiv • UNN
The intensification of Russia's attacks is increasing Ukraine's need for Western financing. The NBU forecasts a 0.4% decline in GDP in 2026.
Against the backdrop of intensified Russian strikes on Ukrainian infrastructure, Ukraine’s need for foreign financial assistance is growing, while the continuation of the war through 2027 will increasingly depend on the stability of Western funding. This is stated in a report by Bloomberg Economics, UNN writes.
Details
Russian forces have intensified strikes on Ukrainian business infrastructure, energy facilities, and the civilian transport network, using drones and missiles. According to analysts, this could lead to a contraction of the Ukrainian economy in 2026.
Last week, the National Bank of Ukraine significantly downgraded its forecast for GDP dynamics in 2026. Instead of the previously expected growth of 1.8%, the regulator now forecasts a 0.4% contraction of the economy.
If the forecast comes true, this will be Ukraine’s first economic downturn since 2022, when the country’s GDP fell by more than 30% following Russia’s full-scale invasion.
Despite the resilience of the Ukrainian economy during five years of full-scale war, the intensification of Russian attacks on energy, industrial, and export infrastructure is increasing the country’s need for external support.
At the same time, maintaining the level of international assistance is becoming more difficult due to war fatigue and political changes in European countries.
The European Union, Ukraine’s largest donor, has allocated more than $100 billion to support Ukraine’s wartime needs in 2026–2027. However, according to Kyiv’s estimates, these funds may be insufficient due to rising costs amid the continuation of the war.
Last month, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that Ukraine would need €70 billion ($78 billion) in 2027 to finance its defense.
Bloomberg Economics identifies political uncertainty in key European states as an additional risk to continued support for Ukraine. In particular, the presidential election in France and parliamentary elections in Italy and Poland could complicate decision-making on future assistance.

Israel’s Defense Ministry signs a 15-year deal worth over $190 million to establish a training center for the IDF’s new artillery system
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
09:25:10 UTC
18:25:10 KST

- i24NEWS
- Israel
- Defense News
- Israel invests over $190 million in training for new artillery systems
Israel invests over $190 million in training for new artillery systems
“The agreement we signed is significant news for strengthening the power and readiness of the IDF"
Israel’s Defense Ministry has signed a 15-year agreement with Elbit Systems to build and support a training center for artillery crews preparing to operate the IDF’s next generation of howitzers and rocket launchers.
The deal, worth more than $190 million, or approximately NIS 600 million, will provide simulators, classrooms and other training infrastructure for soldiers and commanders using the SIGMA self-propelled howitzer and PULS rocket launcher system.
The project comes as the Artillery Corps prepares for the platforms’ full entry into operational service. According to the ministry, the facility is intended to shorten qualification courses and improve proficiency while reducing the expense and wear associated with training on operational equipment.
Driving and mission simulators will form part of the training program. Elbit will also provide instruction, maintenance and logistical support throughout the agreement.
The ministry’s Defense Procurement Directorate negotiated the contract through its Land Procurement Unit, working with the IDF Ground Forces.
Zeev Landau, the ministry’s deputy director general and head of the procurement directorate, said the investment would strengthen military readiness while supporting Israeli industry. He said combining simulation technology with long-term support would help artillery crews make fuller use of the new systems’ capabilities.
Boaz Cohen, executive vice president and general manager of Elbit Systems Land, said the training program was designed to deliver efficient instruction and maintain the Artillery Corps’ readiness. "Elbit, as a partner to the needs of the defense establishment and the IDF, has developed for the Ground Forces one of the world’s most advanced training and instruction arrays."

Israel's Beilinson Hospital preforms break-through robotic lung transplant, doctors say patient is recovering faster than expected
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
09:25:07 UTC
18:25:07 KST

Beilinson performs groundbreaking robotic lung transplant in bid to ease recovery
The team rehearsed the procedure in a dedicated simulation and planned ventilation, monitoring, circulation management and emergency responses
Beilinson Hospital in Petah Tikva has performed a lung transplant using a surgical robot, joining a small group of medical centers worldwide offering the procedure, according to the hospital.
Surgeons used the da Vinci system to connect the donor lung to the patient’s blood vessels and airway through small incisions, avoiding the extensive chest opening and rib spreading associated with conventional surgery.
The operation, performed last month, could mark a significant change in how selected patients undergo transplantation. Doctors at Beilinson hope the approach will reduce postoperative pain and help patients breathe, cough and clear secretions more easily during recovery.
Dr. Yuri Peisakhovich, the hospital’s director of thoracic surgery, led the operation and described it as a turning point for lung transplantation in Israel. He said the team aims to make robotic transplantation without a large chest opening standard practice within five years.
According to Beilinson, approximately 20 robotic lung transplants have been performed worldwide, with the first carried out in Spain three years ago.
Extensive preparation
The operation required coordination among dozens of specialists, including surgeons, anesthesiologists, nurses, heart-lung machine operators, pulmonologists, intensive care teams and tissue-typing laboratory staff.
Dr. Shai Fine, director of anesthesiology and operating rooms, said the robotic equipment presented particular challenges because its arms restrict immediate access to the patient.
The team rehearsed the procedure in a dedicated simulation and planned ventilation, monitoring, circulation management and emergency responses. The patient was also connected to a heart-lung machine in advance as a precaution, Fine said.
The robotic transplant followed another minimally invasive lung transplant at Beilinson about a month earlier. In that operation, surgeons used two small incisions—one above the abdomen and another in the chest—in place of a large conventional incision.
The hospital said that experience helped prepare the team for the robotic procedure.
Encouraging early recovery
Dr. Dan Gurfiel, director of the hospital’s cardiac and thoracic surgery intensive care unit, said reducing postoperative pain was a central reason for pursuing the robotic approach.
He reported that the patient’s recovery exceeded the team’s expectations, with almost no pain medication needed beyond paracetamol. According to Gurfiel, the patient also spent less time in intensive care and in the hospital overall.
The account reflects the experience of this patient; the hospital did not provide comparative outcome data.
Dr. Osnat Livne-Straichman, director of Beilinson’s Institute of Pulmonary Diseases and Allergy, said the hospital’s experience performing more than 1,000 lung transplants helped make the procedure possible. She credited the multidisciplinary team with bringing the technique to eligible patients in Israel.

Ukrainian Drones Hit Major Oil Transport Hub in Samara Region
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
09:24:24 UTC
18:24:24 KST

Ukrainian drones struck one of Europe’s largest oil transport hubs in Russia’s Samara region, independent media reported Monday, as local authorities confirmed the overnight attack in the southern region without detailing any damage or casualties.
Samara region Governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev said early Monday that air defense systems were repelling an air barrage and urged residents not to post photos or videos online.
Samara’s Kurumoch International Airport temporarily suspended flights for two hours during the air raid alert.
The exiled news outlet Astra said it used eyewitness photos of a smoke cloud in Samara to identify at least one targeted facility as Transneft’s linear production and dispatch station. NASA satellite imagery also showed a large, black plume of smoke rising in the area where the site is located, directly southeast of the regional capital.
The Transneft station spans 216 hectares (534 acres) and has 71 storage tanks with a total capacity of 1.6 million cubic meters. It receives crude from Western Siberia, the republic of Tatarstan, the Orenburg region and Kazakhstan via four pipelines before routing it toward two refineries and the Druzhba export pipeline.
Monday’s attack marks the fifth drone strike on the Transneft production and dispatch station after reported strikes on Oct. 2, 7, 10 and 11.
It also came as Russia’s Emergency Situations Ministry said a major cyberattack targeted the app it uses to send people warnings about incoming air attacks. Ukraine reported a similar cyberattack on its air raid alert system, which it said sent out false messages about a radiation threat.
Russia’s Defense Ministry said it intercepted 212 Ukrainian drones across Russia and annexed Crimea between Sunday evening and Monday morning. Authorities in the Belgorod, Voronezh and Rostov regions reported minor damage and injuries.
In an interview with state TV channel Vesti on Sunday, Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak, who oversees Russia’s energy sector, said Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries were adding to global fuel market imbalances and affecting prices.
That same day, Nizhny Novgorod region Governor Gleb Nikitin said a large-scale Ukrainian drone caused “significant damage” to an industrial facility. He did not identify the site that was hit. The region is home to the NORSI oil refinery, one of Russia’s largest.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky also said Sunday that his armed forces had hit the Kamensky plant in Russia’s Rostov region, which he said was involved in the manufacture of Russian missiles.
Despite U.S. attempts earlier this month to introduce an energy ceasefire in the war, which is now approaching its fifth year, Russia and Ukraine have continued to target power grid infrastructure, as well as oil refineries and other facilities.
Reuters contributed reporting.

German MPs and ministers warned iPhones have been targeted by spyware
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
09:23:40 UTC
18:23:40 KST

Those affected have been told to treat their phones as compromised, but it is not yet known who is behind the attack or how many people were hit.
Germany’s digital minister, Karsten Wildberger, has confirmed that members of the Bundestag and the federal government received warnings from Apple that their iPhones may have been targeted by spyware.
Speaking on ARD’s Bericht aus Berlin on Sunday, Wildberger said there had been "a notification from Apple that certain devices may have been compromised with so-called spyware".
According to a letter from the Federal Office for Information Security (BSI) seen by Wildberger, the alerts began reaching the affected phones on 29 October. They warned that Apple had detected an attack using "mercenary spyware".
Wildberger said the BSI had "reacted super quickly" and written to everyone affected about what to do. He did not say how many politicians had received the alerts, or who they were.
According to Wildberger, the BSI advised those affected to assume - as a precaution - that their device may have been compromised, because the alerts do not show whether an attack succeeded.
Euronews has contacted the BSI for comment.
What is an Apple threat notification?
Apple sends threat notifications when it believes that a user has been individually targeted by mercenary spyware, which it describes as "vastly more sophisticated than regular cybercriminal activity".
Apple says Mercenary spyware is harder to detect and prevent, but the vast majority of users will never be targeted.
The warnings appear on the iPhone’s lock screen and in its settings, and are also sent by email.
According to the BSI, spyware of this kind can give attackers access to messages, including those sent on encrypted apps, as well as to calls, contacts, calendars and location data. It can also switch on a phone’s microphone and camera.
Neither Apple nor the German authorities have said who may be behind the attack.

NATO fears Trump clampdown in case of midterms defeat – Politico
NATO is worried that Donald Trump could significantly reduce US involvement in the bloc if the Republican Party loses the midterms on November 3, Politico has reported, citing European officials and diplomats.
Officials in the military bloc are “bracing for a worst-case scenario” as a result of the vote on Tuesday, the outlet said in an article on Sunday.
If a victory for the Democrats blocks Trump from legislating domestically, he may decide to go after NATO to rally his MAGA base, diplomats told the outlet.
The US could withdraw thousands more troops from Europe, cut American funding for the bloc, or limit the NATO-backed PURL arms-buying scheme for Ukraine, they suggested.
Trump “could be very pissed off” after the midterms, if so, “he’ll be very harsh,” one diplomat reportedly warned.
When addressed for comment by Politico, White House Assistant Press Secretary Olivia Wales insisted that “Trump has done more for NATO than anyone else,” including persuading member states to boost defense spending to 5% of GDP by 2035, increasing the US militarily presence in Greenland, and undertaking diplomatic efforts to resolve the Ukraine conflict.
“The president will never settle for the West’s managed decline and will continue to unapologetically advance our interests at home and abroad,” she said.
However, Wales stressed that Trump “remains firm that our NATO allies should have been there for the US” during the war with Iran.
After the bloc’s members in spring refused to join the US-Israeli campaign against the Islamic Republic and countries such as Spain and Italy barred the Pentagon from using bases on their territory for attacks, Trump said he was “never swayed by NATO. I always knew they were a paper tiger.” When asked if he could reconsider the American membership in the bloc, Trump said: “Oh yes, I would say [it’s] beyond reconsideration.”
Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said previously that the US and the rest of NATO members were “engaged in an unhealthy, traumatic relationship,” which required the attention of a therapist.
In a separate comment, Zakharova noted that the Trump administration “has stopped hiding its disappointment” with the organization. “NATO strategists should take a break and reflect in order to avoid making irresponsible decisions that could lead to a disaster — not just for the bloc, but for the entire world,” he warned.
Around a half of the 2,000 US soldiers stationed in Romania left the country last year, with some 5,000 American servicemen currently being in the process of withdrawing from Germany.
According to media reports, Trump wanted to order a pull-out of as many as 25,000 soldiers from Europe earlier this year, but Secretary of State Marco Rubio talked him out of it. American forces on the continent number around 80,000.
The NBC News average of national polls, published on Monday, suggested that 52% of Americans preferred a Democrat-controlled Congress as a result of the midterms, with 44% being in favor of a Republican one. Trump’s approval rating stands at 38% a day before the vote.
