Burnham declines to say net migration still too high as Mahmood prepares to unveil tougher settlement rules – UK politics live
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
09:22:16 UTC
18:22:16 KST

Foreign skilled workers eligible for ILR before end of decade set to contribute £115bn to economy, thinktank says
Shabana Mahmood has justified her proposal to make it harder for low-skilled workers, including care workers, to qualify for indefinite leave to remain (ILR) on the grounds that they will be a net burden on the taxpayer. In his statement (see 10.12am), Chris Philp referenced a claim she made in a speech in March when she said:
We have never, in the history of this country, had so much low-skilled migration in so little time. We estimate, based on findings from the migration advisory committee … That the lifetime cost to the taxpayer will be £10bn.
At the time, the Home Office published a document explaining how they arrived at the £10bn figure.
The IPPR, a left-leaning thinktank, has published a briefing today suggesting this figure is miseading because it does not present the full picture. It says:
The £10bn figure should be put in wider context. New IPPR analysis suggests that, as a whole, the estimated net lifetime fiscal contribution of all skilled workers (including health and care workers) who were expected to settle in 2026-30, along with their adult dependants, is roughly £115bn. This follows the same approach as the Home Office in calculating the £10 billion net cost for care workers and adult dependants (see methodology below for more details). The risk of deterring skilled workers who make a significant fiscal contribution should therefore be an important consideration for the final set of proposals.
Both the Home Office and the IPPR are using from a report published by the migration advisory committee (MAC), The Fiscal Impact of Immigration: Static and Dynamic Estimates for the UK. It was published in December last year and it focuses in particular on people who came to the UK in 2022/23 on skilled worker (SW) visas, and on people with health and care worker (H&C) worker visas. The report contains figures supportive of both sides of this argument.
It says that, for most categories of foreign worker visas, the people who receive them will make a net contribution to the economy over the course of their lifetimes. The only exceptions are dependant children, and adult dependants of people on H&C visas.
These calculations involve working out whether the amount that people will contribute in taxes over the course of a lifetime will outweigh the amount they will cost due to benefits claimed or healthcare consumed (or education costs, if they are children). To work this out, economists need to make assumptions about how much people will earn, when they will retire, and how long they will live.
This chart illustrates the pattern. It shows how the 2022 H&C main applicants (ie, not dependants) are expected to contribute for the next 30 years, before they start becoming a net burden.
But the MAC does say that care workers (a subset of H&C workers) will be a net burden. It says:
The H&C workers are less fiscally positive compared to UK residents of the same age (though much better than the median) – but there is still the additional benefit to the fiscal balance of having more younger workers than the UK average. We can split this group of main applicants into those who came as care workers and those who came in other health and care occupations (mainly nurses and doctors). For care workers, the lifetime contribution is estimated to be -£36,000, whilst for the other occupations it is +£166,000. Care workers are therefore fiscally negative over their lifetimes and broadly similar to the UK median for the age group.
The report also makes the point that most UK residents will, over the course of their lifetimes, end up being a net burden. But it says “because our tax system is strongly progressive, the upper end of the income distribution contribute much more than the median”. This means that, even though the average Briton using the median definition is a net cost, the average Briton using the mean definiton puts in enough to keep the system going. These figures illustrate this point.
Andy Burnham is now on his way to the Commonwealth summit in Antigua. The government plane that is taking him left from Stansted early this morning, but it went to Manchester first, where it stopped to pick up the PM. He is now en route to the Caribbean, where he will arrive this evening after a refuelling stop in Canada.
Tories and Reform UK accuse Mahmood of surrendering to 'open-borders Labour left'
Chris Philp, the shadow home secretary, is already ridiculing the indefinite leave to remain (ILR) announcement coming this afternoon. In a post on social media, he claimed that she was surrendering to “the open-borders Labour left”.
Later today the government will announce their u-turn on ILR, or Indefinite Leave to Remain.
It’s clear Shabana Mahmood has been forced to surrender to Angela Rayner and the open-borders Labour left. She will now allow hundreds of thousands of low-wage and no-wage migrants to stay in the UK forever and claim benefits.
By Mahmood’s own admission in a speech this March, letting low wage care workers alone stay forever will cost taxpayers £10 billion and be an “affront”. Now it looks like she’s about to do exactly that. After talking tough all year, Mahmood appears to have capitulated control of immigration policy to Angela Rayner - and Mahmood’s position is looking increasingly untenable
The Conservative plan is a ten year route to ILR, only for high wage workers. No more low wage workers should be allowed in, and those already here should be required to leave when their temporary work visa expires
Nigel Farage, whose Reform UK party wants to get rid of ILR completely, has made a similar argument in his own social media post.
The Labour Party is at war with itself over Indefinite Leave to Remain (ILR), with Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood losing a fight to the far left of her own party. Tomorrow, she’s expected to cave on plans to even tinker with the ILR numbers. Angela Rayner emerges victorious, with her defence of the Tory-era policies hinging on “fair play” towards foreign nationals.
But what about fair play towards the British public? Doesn’t that count for anything anymore? Villages, towns, suburbs, and cities have to deal with the weight and strain of all this. Not only are ordinary Brits never consulted, but this current cabinet doesn’t even have an electoral mandate. It is rightly infuriating to most people who increasingly want net negative migration into Britain.
‘Was I not enough?’: care worker barred from meeting home secretary tells his story
Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, is due to meet some union leaders today to discuss with them her plans for indefinite leave to remain. Andrea Egan, who as Unison general secretary has many members working in the care sector, has been particularly critical of the original proposal to make foreign care workers wait 15 years for ILR. Recently she condemned Mahmood for refusing to let her bring a care worker to a meeting they were due to have about the plans.
That care worker was a Nigerian called Kolade. Aamna Mohdin has interviewed him, and he explained what he wanted to tell Mahmood.
For Kolade, the row encapsulates what he believes is missing from the immigration debate: the voices of those whose lives could be upended by its policies. He has watched politicians dismiss care work as low-skilled and portray migrant workers as a burden on the British economy.
“I was just going to tell her that is not correct,” he said. “We are not a burden to the British state. We are also contributing as much as we can, supporting British families.
“She talked about fairness to the British people. I was going to tell her that caring for British families is our own little way to show that we are contributing, and that we have earned our rights to stay in this country, a place we’re currently calling home.”
Burnham declines to say net migration still too high as Mahmood prepares to unveil tougher settlement rules
Good morning. Often these days, when the government has a big announcement and just before the relevant minister starts to give the details in a statement to MPs, Lindsay Hoyle, the Commons speaker, erupts with fury and rants and raves at the Treasury bench about how all the main points have already been leaked to the media, in contravention of the ministerial code.
Not today. Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, will this afternoon unveil the final version of her plans to make foreign workers wait longer before they can apply for indefinite leave to remain, and we know relatively little about what she will say. The original plans were unveiled last November and they would require most workers to wait 10 years, not five, for ILR, with care workers having to wait 15 years. They would also apply to foreign workers already here, not just new arrivals. These proposals were hugely controversial, and Andy Burnham himself was among the ministers arguing that care workers should be treated more kindly.
As Jessica Elgot and Chris Osuh report in our overnight story, there has been some sort of climbdown in relation to care workers.
But it also seems to be the case that the broad thrust of the plan is being retained and that ILR rules are being toughened in a way that will affect hundreds of thousands of people.
The detail, which is coming after 3.30pm, will be crucial; so will the reaction of Labour MPs. When Mahmood announced these plans last autumn, some government backbenchers were horrified. But mostly public condemnation was muted. At the time Reform UK had a lead of more than 10 points over Labour in the polls and Mahmood – who was arguing that net migration was too high and that low-skilled foreign workers ended up being a burden on the taxpayer (a key Reform UK claim, although one contested by experts) – was pushing at an open door.
Now the situation is very different. The electoral threat from Nigel Farage has receded quite a lot. And net migration is falling like a stone. Here are the figures from last week’s OBR report.
To implement the ILR changes, Mahmood does not need primary legislation and that means there will be no chance for potential Labour rebels to amend the plans in the Commons. But it has been reported that more than 100 MPs are queasy about what is being planned.
And Andy Burnham himself has accepted that the context has changed. We won’t hear from him until much later, because he is spending most of the day on a flight to the Commonwealth summit. But, in an interview for an ITV documentary being broadcast tomorrow, he declined to say that net migration was too high. When Keir Starmer was PM, he regularly did say this, and that he wanted immigration to fall “significantly”. Burnham told ITV small boat crossing numbers were “too high, for certain”. However, asked about legal migration, he replied:
It’s come right down. And I think when you have planned migration, it’s difficult to say is it too high or too low, because it’s got to be, if you like, following gaps in the economy.
Burnham said legal migration had “come right down”. He declined to be drawn on whether it had to come down further.
This means that Mahmood will today be defending plans drawn up in response to a problem that some might argue no longer exists. However, speaking in the Commons last November, Mahmood argued she had to do something about the “so-called Boriswave, specifically the cohort of lower-qualified workers who – along with their dependants – entered the country through the health and care visa” because some of them were “never expected to be net economic contributors”, making “more stringent” controls needed.
Here is the agenda for the day.
11.30am: Downing Street holds a lobby briefing.
12.30pm: Danny Kruger, Reform UK’s head of government preparations, gives a speech to the Policy Exchange thinktank.
2.30pm: Angela Rayner, the housing secretary, takes questions in the Commons.
After 3.30pm:Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, gives her statement on the changes to indefinite leave to remain rules.
Evening: Andy Burnham arrives in Antigua for the Commonwealth summit.
Also, at some point today Labour will give an update on how many power-sharing agreements at council level with Greens will continue, in the light of Labour HQ saying recently Labour councillors should only continue to work with local Green parties willing to disown the “Zionism is racism” motion passed at the Green conference.

Belgian government crisis looms as budget talks collapse

Belgian government crisis looms as budget talks collapse
BRUSSELS, Nov 2 - Belgium's King Philippe urged Prime Minister Bart De Wever on Monday to find a compromise over next year's budget, with his government on the brink of collapse following the failure of another round of late-night negotiations.
De Wever had offered his resignation in a meeting with the king on Monday morning.
The king will weigh De Wever's offer, but will also hold talks with the leaders of the other coalition parties from Tuesday, the Royal Palace said in a statement.
"In light of the large geopolitical uncertainty and severe economic challenges, the country can't afford a long political crisis," it said.
The government has been arguing for months about €10 billion ($11.2 billion) in budget cuts and tax increases De Wever says are needed to keep state finances in check.
A coalition deadline to reach an agreement on next year's budget had been set for Tuesday.
Like other European countries, including France and Italy, Belgium is struggling to balance ballooning national debt with demands from protesters for greater spending to improve services, such as education. Demonstrators have clashed with police in countries including France, Spain, Italy and Belgium in recent weeks.
Without an agreement the Belgian government could only work with a limited budget next year, allowing it to spend one-twelfth of this year's budget per month.
The crisis coincides with heightened stress on financial markets, where interest rates have risen sharply on government bonds of Belgium, France and other European countries seen to have weak government finances.
The European Commission forecast in May that Belgium's debt-to-gross domestic product ratio would be 110.5% this year, behind only Greece, Italy and France among euro zone countries, with a projected general government deficit of 5.2% of GDP.
Belgium's 10-year benchmark bonds were trading at a yield of 4.36% on Monday morning, against 4.92% for France and 3.30% for Germany.
Four months ago, Belgian 10-year yields were at 3.48%.
De Wever has repeatedly warned of an "interest snowball" without budget cuts, where Belgium would need to take on new loans to be able to pay interest on existing debt.
In months of talks, De Wever's Flemish nationalist N-VA and the liberal MR have not been able to compromise with their socialist and centrist coalition partners.
The N-VA and MR have pushed for cuts in spending including on healthcare, while their partners demand higher wealth taxes to bring in more resources.
The king will meet De Wever again on Friday. If the king ultimately accepts the prime minister's resignation, he could ask other parties to form a coalition or could call for fresh elections. REUTERS

Türkiye aims to foster 13 unicorn startups in 2027 strategy

Under the 2027 Presidential Annual Program, Türkiye plans to scale its venture capital investment volume to $1 billion annually, up from $500 million, while cultivating a total of 13 Turkish unicorns, known as “Turcorns.”
These goals aim to improve access to critical financing, boost domestic innovation capacity and strengthen Türkiye’s global tech competitiveness.
Ankara plans to launch new calls for proposals under an investment-based support program to facilitate the growth of early-stage high-tech firms.
Türkiye’s Scientific and Technological Research Council (TÜBİTAK) generated similar momentum, with its entrepreneurship support programs receiving 2,844 applications from January to September.
Meanwhile, efforts are underway to accelerate promotion of the Tech Visa program, which targets remote professionals, global investors and talent to integrate them into the domestic ecosystem.
The visa initiative received 634 tech startup applications, leading to 135 approvals and the establishment of some 60 new tech startups operating in the country.
At the same time, the Competitive Sectors Program, implemented under the EU’s Instrument for Pre-Accession Assistance, has already strengthened domestic research and digital infrastructure through 43 projects with a combined budget of $291.2 million during the IPA-II period.
Türkiye also expanded its presence in the Digital Europe Program, with some 118 institutions securing $16 million in funding across 21 projects, while the European Digital Innovation Hubs granted $8.4 million to some eight consortia.
Meanwhile, startups awarded a tech startup badge will have priority access to support, incentives and procurement, while their offerings will be integrated into the State Supply Office catalog to boost commercialization and branding efforts.
There will be venture capital fund calls, fund-of-funds mechanisms and co-investment instruments to ensure that tech startups can access the necessary capital.

Emergency power outages begin in some Ukrainian oblasts
Emergency power outages have been applied in certain oblasts of Ukraine on 2 November, with the most difficult power supply situation remaining in Kyiv and Dnipropetrovsk oblasts.
Source: Artem Nekrasov, First Deputy Minister of Energy
Details: The energy infrastructure of these two oblasts has sustained massive damage due to Russian strikes. Damage to equipment has restricted the transmission capacity of electricity to consumers, forcing power engineers to apply emergency outages.
The Ministry of Energy noted that the cause of emergency outages in certain regions is also a drop in voltage within the high-voltage grid. Previously posted schedules do not apply there. A return to them will be possible after the situation in the energy system stabilises.
Consumers are advised to check up-to-date information regarding outages on the official resources of distribution system operators.
Background: On the morning of 2 November, emergency power outages were introduced in Kyiv and Kyiv Oblast by order of state-owned electricity transmission operator Ukrenergo due to the Russian attacks.

Taoyuan Airport to begin north runway maintenance Tuesday
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
09:21:28 UTC
18:21:28 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taoyuan Airport will begin annual maintenance of its north runway on Tuesday, Taoyuan International Airport Corp. said Monday.
The work will focus on key sections of the runway and taxiways and be carried out between 1 a.m. and 6:30 a.m., during the airport’s routine overnight maintenance closure, the company said in a statement. The south runway will remain fully operational throughout the project.
Construction is scheduled for odd-numbered days in November, excluding weekends and public holidays. Airport officials will assess weather conditions and flight volumes before each workday and postpone construction if conditions are unfavorable or traffic is heavier than expected.
The airport operator has established a task force to coordinate the project and minimize operational disruptions. It has also held several coordination meetings with the Civil Aviation Administration’s Air Navigation and Weather Services, airlines, ground-handling companies, and construction contractors to review contingency plans and work arrangements.
The airport conducted an operational impact assessment using flight volumes during the National Day holiday period as a benchmark. Officials said the task force would maintain communication among all parties and coordinate construction in real time to ensure normal flight operations.
Taoyuan Airport surpassed 40 million passengers this year on Oct. 13, highlighting the importance of regular runway maintenance amid frequent aircraft movements. The airport operator said the work would ensure the runway is in optimal condition ahead of the Christmas and New Year holidays and the Lunar New Year travel peak.

Taiwan airlines to raise fuel surcharges
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
09:21:03 UTC
18:21:03 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Fuel surcharges on international flights operated by Taiwanese airlines will increase from Sunday, Nov. 8, following a rise in aviation fuel prices, the Civil Aviation Administration (CAA) said Monday.
The surcharge will rise from US$37.50 (NT$1,221.34) to US$40 for short-haul routes and from US$97.50 to US$104 for long-haul routes, the CAA said in a press release.
CPC Corp.’s reference price for international aviation fuel climbed from US$177.89 to US$183.09 per barrel, moving from the 15th to the 16th tier of the fuel surcharge adjustment mechanism, the CAA said.
The CAA and Taiwanese airlines agreed on the mechanism in 2005, linking passenger fuel surcharges to CPC’s published international aviation fuel price per barrel.
Under the system, no surcharge is imposed when the price is below US$40 per barrel. Once it reaches US$40 but remains below US$50, airlines charge US$5 for short-haul routes and US$13 for long-haul routes.
For every additional US$10 increase in the fuel price, the surcharge rises by US$2.50 for short-haul routes and US$6.50 for long-haul routes.
The CAA said it has asked airlines to disclose relevant background information, including the share of fuel costs in their overall operating expenses and how the surcharges are calculated, to address consumer concerns. Passengers can contact airlines directly or visit their official websites for more information.

Tartu's Christmas village takes shape ahead of First Advent opening
Tartu is once again transforming Town Hall Square for the holidays, with an outdoor ice rink, Christmas tree and festive pavilions set to open November 29.
Construction of the public ice rink began Monday, marking the start of preparations for Tartu Christmas City 2026. As in previous years, festivities will officially kick off on the first Sunday of Advent.
This year, the city's official Christmas tree will arrive from the Peipsiääre Municipality village of Välgi on November 17.
Its owners, Roman Gelokhov and his family, decided to donate the nearly 15-meter-tall spruce after growing concerned that frequent strong winds in the area made its proximity to their house dangerous.
"We were worried that the tree could eventually fall on the house one day," Gelokhov said. "When the opportunity came up to give our spruce a new life as Tartu's Christmas tree, we thought it was a wonderful solution."
The family regularly spends time at Town Hall Square during the holiday season, but this year's festivities will now be especially meaningful.
"It'll be something special to see a tree that was once part of our home now decorate Tartu and bring holiday cheer to thousands of people," Gelokhov added.
More info to come
Meanwhile, work on the Christmas village pavilions and other infrastructure is scheduled to begin November 23, with cafes and skating equipment arriving afterward.
The public ice rink, built around Tartu's iconic Kissing Students statue and fountain, will be among the main attractions.
During construction, visitors are asked to take care when crossing the square, as the ice rink site is fenced off and construction equipment moves around the area.
More details and event info for the Christmas village will be published online in the coming weeks.

Column: Regional public goods and the future of agrifood cooperation in the Greater Mekong Subregion
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
17:19:50 CST
18:19:50 KST

by Zhan Yifan
The six countries of the Greater Mekong Subregion (GMS) share more than a river: climate risks, market volatility, food-safety pressures and the hardships faced by smallholder farmers. In September, the 23rd Annual Meeting of the GMS Working Group on Agriculture brought together agriculture ministries and development partners in Bangkok under the theme "Regional Public Goods: Unlocking the Potential for the Sustainable Growth of the GMS Agrifood Sector." One question kept recurring: how can cooperation move beyond scattered pilot projects and deliver durable regional solutions?
A benefit becomes a regional public good when it crosses national borders, when regional coordination achieves more than any country could accomplish alone, and when no country is excluded from enjoying it. Agriculture is full of such public goods: shared water and soil health, interoperable digital traceability systems, electronic certification, climate early-warning systems and harmonized sanitary and phytosanitary arrangements. None can be built by one country alone, and the more countries participate, the greater their value.
One of the most rewarding aspects of the meeting was seeing countries with very different starting points advance a common agenda and learn from one another. Vietnam has made low-emission agriculture its vision, building on its one million hectares program for high-quality, low-emission rice production and aiming to cut emissions across all crops by at least 50 percent by 2050, compared with the 2030 baseline. Thailand is building practical trade foundations through its National Single Window, digital traceability and green lanes, arguing that regional systems should connect existing national platforms rather than build new ones. Laos is prioritizing digital sanitary and phytosanitary systems, while Cambodia is promoting inclusive digital public goods for smallholder farmers.
China's contribution to this shared agenda is rooted in its own practice. It has proposed making agriculture more technology-driven, eco-friendly, quality-focused and brand-oriented, and stands ready to share its experience.
On the ground, cooperation is already delivering results. The China-Laos Railway's Lancang-Mekong Express cold-chain train links Vientiane and Kunming in some 30 hours, reducing transport loss of Lao tropical fruits. China and Thailand mutually recognize each other's certifications: China recognizes Thailand's Good Agricultural Practice, while Thailand recognizes China's organic certification. This has shortened customs clearance times for Thai fruit by 40 percent and cut testing fees by 30 percent. With Myanmar, China has built a "rice-fish-duck" symbiosis demonstration zone that raises farmers' incomes while improving soil health. China has also proposed a GMS mutual recognition list for agrifood quality and safety, along with technical assistance on standards.
These approaches are not competing alternatives; they are complementary pieces of the same puzzle. The China-Thailand durian traceability pilot, which began as an Asian Development Bank-supported demonstration project and has since moved towards market-driven operation, shows that a tangible, industry-chain-driven initiative can deliver real regional benefits. The message is clear: regional public goods are most persuasive when they grow out of real industry chains and deliver visible benefits, with every country able to contribute and learn.
Yet enthusiasm for the concept outruns our ability to deliver. Four hurdles stand out: pilot projects often fade when funding ends; data remain fragmented; standardization takes time, trust and political will; and monitoring, reporting and verification, as well as certification remain too costly for smallholder farmers.
The way forward is to act pragmatically, step by step. Start where the value is visible. Begin with problems that affect everyone, such as congested border crossings and duplicate testing, and deliver quick results. Prioritize interoperability over new platforms: investing in connecting existing systems yields better returns than building new infrastructure. Design for sustainability from day one by embedding pilot projects in local institutions and settle funding and exit arrangements in advance. Make governance inclusive, so that smallholders, women and young people can participate and share in the benefits.
Regional public goods provide the GMS with a good framework for cooperation, but a framework alone does not guarantee results. The region has the aspirations, experience and mutual trust needed to turn this framework into shared facilities, data and benefits. China is willing to contribute its experience and learn from the diverse practices of its neighbors. On the banks of the Mekong, as in agriculture itself, what we build together goes further than what each of us can build alone.

17:19:45 CST
18:19:45 KST

BEIJING, Nov. 2 (Xinhua) -- China's top legislature on Monday began deliberating a draft amendment to the Law on Renewable Energy that would strengthen the management of renewable energy development and construction.
The draft was submitted for its first reading at the 25th session of the 14th National People's Congress Standing Committee, which runs from Monday to Friday this week.
Developing renewable energy is a key task for improving energy structure, ensuring energy security, building a strong energy nation and advancing ecological civilization.
Since the 18th National Congress of the Communist Party of China in 2012, China has made historic achievements and undergone historic transformation in renewable energy development, establishing the world's largest and fastest-growing renewable energy system.
The revised draft consists of 10 chapters and 76 articles. Major amendments include specifying the strengthening of Party leadership, improving legislative purposes and related requirements, enhancing resource surveys and development planning, and reinforcing management of renewable energy development and construction.
These amendments also cover bolstering renewable energy production and transmission management, improving market trading and pricing mechanisms, promoting consumption, advancing technological innovation and industrial development, strengthening safeguards and supervision, and refining legal liabilities.
The amendments also stipulate the implementation of the green electricity certificate system for renewable energy. China introduced the green electricity certificate system as a pilot program in 2017. In December 2023, China's National Energy Administration issued an initial batch of certificates.
Since the beginning of the 14th Five-Year Plan period (2021-2025), with rapid progress in building a unified national power market, the participation of new energy sources such as wind and solar power has accelerated, with more than half of new energy electricity now priced through the market.
Currently, China's power market is operating soundly. From January to September this year, market-traded electricity volume steadily increased, reaching 5,853.6 billion kilowatt-hours, up 18.9 percent year on year. ■

The value of total building approvals rose 13 percent to 19.02 billion Australian dollars (about 13.37 billion U.S. dollars), driven by a 45.9 percent increase in non-residential building approvals to 7.96 billion Australian dollars, statistics showed.

U.S. proposes resuming Russian gas sales to Europe through American intermediary, but European officials firmly reject idea, WSJ reports
The United States has proposed a plan to Vladimir Putin that would let Russia sell its natural gas to Europe through an American intermediary, bypassing European sanctions, sources told The Wall Street Journal.
Donald Trump’s special envoys, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, put forward the idea during trips to Moscow and Kyiv in September, the newspaper’s sources said. The White House wants Russia to funnel proceeds from gas sales into an escrow account in a third-country jurisdiction, preventing the Kremlin from using the money to finance the war.
American negotiators believe Russia’s return to the European natural gas market would give Putin a powerful incentive to agree to an energy truce in Ukraine. Gas supplies would also provide Kyiv with income from transit fees, and the sales could open profitable opportunities for American investors.
Trump’s negotiators tried to present the plan to European leaders as a way to lower energy prices ahead of winter, when Europe’s gas reserves fell to their lowest level for this time of year in several years, The Wall Street Journal reported.
Europe’s official position is that the EU will not resume buying Russian gas. The Trump administration expects that resistance to prove “less rigid than meets the eye.”
In private, however, European officials categorically reject the idea. One senior official from a Scandinavian country said resuming purchases of Russian gas would contradict everything Europeans stand for. Another senior official from a major European country compared the plan to former British Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain’s sacrifice of Czechoslovakia in his dealings with Hitler.
EU countries agreed in early 2026 to fully phase out Russian liquefied natural gas by January 1, 2027. Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said Russian companies would soon redirect part of their LNG supplies from Europe to “friendly” countries.
Senior Russian and American officials held talks in early October 2026 on bringing an American investor into the Nord Stream pipeline projects, Reuters reported. Russian presidential special representative Kirill Dmitriev and Jared Kushner took part in the discussions. A deal on American participation in the Nord Stream pipelines would let the United States profit from energy supplies to Europe after the war ends, Reuters noted.

====================================================================================================

Eisenkot's five bad choices, and how Netanyahu could benefit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
09:19:07 UTC
18:19:07 KST

Nearly a week after Israel's October 27 election, the political deadlock appears no closer to resolution. Gadi Eisenkot, chairman of the Yashar! party and the leading candidate to receive the first mandate to form a government, faces five possible paths forward. At least four of them are far from what the former IDF chief of staff had envisioned before the election.
Yet while Eisenkot faces difficult decisions, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu appears to have even fewer viable options for assembling a government, unless he can persuade elements of the rival bloc to join him. The paradox is that Eisenkot's attempts to break the deadlock could ultimately work in Netanyahu's favor.
It is no coincidence that Eisenkot opened a lengthy statement Saturday night with the words "At a historic crossroads." Whichever path he chooses, forming a government may require him to break at least one campaign promise, whether by establishing a minority coalition or entering an alliance with ultra-Orthodox lawmakers and possibly members of the Arab Ra'am party. Even if he succeeds, the compromises could carry a considerable political cost in a future election.
Option 1: A government with United Torah Judaism, and possibly Ra'am
This is perhaps the scenario Likud fears most, and the one favored by Eisenkot's associates. But it would require him and his allies to abandon a central campaign pledge: the vision of an "alliance of those who serve," built around parties committed to expanding military and national service.
If Eisenkot pursues this route, he would have to negotiate directly with United Torah Judaism (UTJ), the ultra-Orthodox party whose lawmakers oppose compulsory military service for the population they represent. Some of its members describe their political worldview as anti-Zionist. At the center of any negotiations would be one of Israel's most divisive issues since the October 7 massacre: military conscription.
Throughout the election campaign, Eisenkot and his political partners made the issue a central priority. The Yashar! leader established a clear principle that only parties willing to advance military and national service for all Israeli citizens would be eligible to join his government. It is highly doubtful that UTJ would accept that condition.
Such negotiations could become a political trap. Any concessions Eisenkot makes could find their way into the media and later be used against him by Netanyahu and Likud, particularly if Netanyahu temporarily distances himself from his traditional ultra-Orthodox partners. UTJ, meanwhile, has refused to commit to recommending any candidate during the consultations with President Isaac Herzog later this week.
Even an agreement with UTJ may not be sufficient. Eisenkot could also need Arab parties to abstain from a crucial parliamentary vote, or potentially require Ra'am's active support to assemble a viable majority.
Likud officials are concerned about precisely such an arrangement. "Our fear is that a government with Arabs and Haredim, even with Shas's six seats, could last an entire term," a senior Likud official told ynet in the past 24 hours.
Another obstacle would be Yisrael Beiteinu chairman Avigdor Lieberman, a senior member of Eisenkot's political bloc. Lieberman promised during the campaign that he would not sit in a government with ultra-Orthodox or Arab parties, and reiterated that position after the election.
Eisenkot could therefore force Lieberman into an uncomfortable choice: break his own campaign pledge to remove Netanyahu from power, or risk sending Israel back to the polls.
Option 2: A minority government relying on Arab parties
This scenario would require Eisenkot to negotiate with Arab parties despite having promised not to establish a government with them.
In the political climate following October 7, it is doubtful that large sections of the Israeli public, particularly voters who supported Naftali Bennett's Beyachad party or Lieberman's Yisrael Beiteinu, would readily accept a government dependent on Arab parliamentary support.
Even if Eisenkot pursued the arrangement, something his associates currently deny is under consideration, and persuaded his political partners to support it, the resulting government could be highly unstable and potentially short-lived.
Netanyahu could emerge as the political beneficiary. Voters who opposed him in the election but rejected an Eisenkot government relying on Arab parties might reconsider their allegiance in a subsequent vote.
The prime minister began campaigning against the possibility of a government backed by Arab parties on election night, following their unprecedented electoral success. His messages on X have largely been short and direct. "You must not form a government with them," he wrote Sunday.
For now, this is Eisenkot's least preferred scenario, and figures within his bloc give it little chance of succeeding.
One of its leading advocates is Democrats chairman Yair Golan, who argues that the broader anti-Netanyahu bloc commands 67 Knesset seats when the Arab parties are included. Golan says the opposition must rethink its approach and cooperate with them.
His preferred formula would bring Ra'am into the coalition while relying on outside parliamentary support from the Joint List.
Option 3: A unity government under Netanyahu, or a rotating premiership
Only days before the election, Eisenkot declared in a recorded interview that he would not serve under Netanyahu in any political arrangement. "If that happens, I will resign an hour later," he said.
Joining a Netanyahu-led government would carry enormous political risks, particularly among voters who backed Eisenkot and his partners specifically to bring the prime minister's tenure to an end.
The cautionary example is Benny Gantz, Eisenkot's former political partner, whose electoral standing suffered dramatically on two occasions after joining Netanyahu.
The first came during the COVID-19 pandemic, when Gantz entered a unity government in 2020. His Blue and White party subsequently fell from more than 30 Knesset seats to a single-digit result in the 2021 election.
The second came after the October 7 massacre, when Gantz joined Netanyahu's emergency government while enjoying strong public support. His polling numbers later collapsed from nearly 40 projected seats to below the electoral threshold, ultimately prompting him to withdraw shortly before the 2026 election.
"Be Rabin, not Gantz," veteran Arab lawmaker Ahmad Tibi urged Eisenkot after the election, an apparent warning about the political fate of those who enter unity arrangements with Netanyahu.
Eisenkot would not be the only leader facing a broken promise. All his political partners have pledged not to serve with Netanyahu, making it unclear who would follow Eisenkot into such an arrangement.
Lieberman has already rejected a unity government, just as he has ruled out both a minority government relying on Arab parties and a partnership with the ultra-Orthodox. Golan also categorically opposes unity with Netanyahu.
Yair Lapid and members of his faction would be expected to end their partnership with Bennett if such a government were formed, given Lapid's consistent opposition to serving alongside or under Netanyahu.
A unity deal could therefore fracture the anti-Netanyahu bloc or dismantle it entirely. Furthermore, Netanyahu could potentially bring down the government at a politically advantageous moment, leaving Eisenkot to bear much of the electoral damage, just as Gantz did.
Another unresolved question is whether Netanyahu wants such a government at all. A senior Likud official told ynet Saturday night that the chances were already slim because "the concessions are too great."
Nevertheless, ynet has learned that Netanyahu was asked in private conversations about the possibility of a rotating premiership in a unity government. "We are examining everything. I am not completely ruling out any option," he replied.
There may still be a limited political benefit for Eisenkot in attempting this route. If he offers unity and Netanyahu rejects it, Eisenkot could present himself to the public as the responsible leader who sought a compromise while his rival refused.
Option 4: Another election
If none of the first three scenarios materializes, Israel could once again face an election, despite President Isaac Herzog's repeated appeals to political leaders to avoid another vote.
The possibility of US President Donald Trump intervening to encourage a unity government has also been raised, particularly one that excludes National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir's Otzma Yehudit party.
Eisenkot himself has declared that "another election would be a mistake." Behind that statement lies a widely shared political assessment that Netanyahu's bloc could benefit from a second round.
The reasoning is straightforward. Over the coming weeks, Eisenkot may become embroiled in countless negotiations, political maneuvers and public disputes. To move closer to forming a government, he could be forced to compromise on his promises not to cooperate with the ultra-Orthodox, Arab parties or Netanyahu himself.
Even unsuccessful negotiations could provide material for a future Likud campaign, allowing Netanyahu to portray Eisenkot and his allies as politicians who abandoned their commitments when the opportunity to govern arose.
There is also uncertainty about whether the unusually high turnout recorded in the October election would be repeated. Israelis living abroad who traveled to vote might be less willing or able to make the journey again, while overall participation could also decline.
But Netanyahu's most immediate advantage would be simpler: he would remain prime minister while the political system struggled to form an alternative government.
For an incumbent facing the possibility of losing office, additional time can itself be a valuable political asset.
Option 5: Using the ‘clear parliamentary majority’ against Netanyahu
Even if Eisenkot cannot form a government, he may still have an opportunity to use the new Knesset's composition to advance key legislation before another election.
In a statement Saturday, Eisenkot pledged to make use of what he called the "clear parliamentary majority" opposed to Netanyahu.
That could mean establishing a state commission of inquiry into the October 7 massacre, repealing legislation associated with the government's judicial overhaul and potentially advancing a new military service framework, provided there is sufficient time and parliamentary support.
Eisenkot is currently working to secure recommendations from other parties ahead of Herzog's consultations, scheduled to begin Wednesday, November 4. Senior figures in the anti-Netanyahu bloc say it is particularly important that the Yashar! chairman receive the first opportunity to form a government.
One senior figure outside Eisenkot's party warned Sunday: "If the entire bloc does not recommend Eisenkot, all the judicial overhaul laws passed by the current coalition will take effect on January 1, 2027, as stipulated by law."
The warning refers to legislation concerning the attorney general's office, the Police Internal Investigations Department and changes to the composition of the Judicial Selection Committee.
Under the opposition bloc's plan, receiving the first mandate could help Eisenkot and his allies secure control of the Knesset's Arrangements Committee, which oversees parliamentary procedures during the formation of a new government.
The bloc hopes to use that position to advance two particularly consequential moves: replacing the Knesset speaker and overturning the judicial overhaul legislation before its scheduled implementation. Both would require sufficient parliamentary cooperation and votes.
Bennett's Beyachad party announced Sunday that it would recommend Eisenkot to Herzog as its candidate to form the next government. Figures in the anti-Netanyahu bloc also expect the Democrats to back him.
The remaining uncertainty concerns Lieberman, who has yet to publicly commit to a candidate and has not clarified his intentions even in private discussions among the opposition leaders.
That leaves Eisenkot approaching the presidential consultations with a considerable advantage in potential recommendations but no clear route to a governing coalition.
For Netanyahu, the situation is hardly ideal. His own parliamentary bloc lacks the numbers to form a government without new partners. Yet as long as Eisenkot cannot reconcile the conflicting demands of his allies, the prime minister could continue to benefit from the deadlock.
The immediate question is whether Eisenkot can turn the opposition's parliamentary strength into a workable government. If he cannot, the next battle may be over what the new Knesset can accomplish before Israel is drawn into another election.

Russians Unveil Filin Missile on Launch Platform for the First Time
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
09:18:15 UTC
18:18:15 KST

The first image has emerged showing Russia’s new Filin cruise missile mounted on a ground-based launcher with a solid-fuel booster.
Russian propagandist Yuri Podolyaka published the photo.
Russia reportedly began using the missile against Ukraine in late summer 2026.
A solid-fuel booster is mounted beneath the missile’s fuselage for launch. It provides the initial thrust needed to accelerate the missile and lift it into the air. The missile then switches to its own turbojet engine.
The engine is the Russian-made R500, manufactured by Reynolds LLC. It was previously identified in the S-71K Koverand and S-71M Monokhrom series of air-launched cruise missiles.
According to War&Sanctions, the missile is about 3.5 meters long, has a 3-meter wingspan, and a maximum launch weight of around 210 kg. Depending on the version, it carries either a 50 kg or 100 kg warhead.
The missile is designed to carry one of three warhead types: high-explosive fragmentation, penetrating, or thermobaric.
The missile’s airframe is made of composite materials, including carbon-fiber and fiberglass, which helps reduce its overall weight.
Some components are manufactured using 3D-printing technology. The missile features a straight wing, tail surfaces, and an upper air intake for its turbojet engine.
The missile can fly at altitudes up to 6 km and can also operate at extremely low altitudes.
According to its stated specifications, the Filin has a maximum speed of up to 800 km/h and an operational range of 600 to 1,200 km.
Militarnyi previously reported that Russia had developed a ground-based launch system for the S8000 BanderoL cruise missile.

Abdel Raouf Arnaout and Sahin Demir
02 November 2026•Update: 02 November 2026
Israel remained on the highest state of military alert on Monday, a day before the US midterm elections, amid concerns over a possible resumption of war with Iran, according to Israeli media.
Americans head to the polls Tuesday for midterm elections halfway through Republican President Donald Trump’s second term, with all 435 seats in the House of Representatives, 35 Senate seats and governorships in 36 states up for grabs, alongside thousands of local positions and ballot measures.
Trump has repeatedly pledged not to launch new strikes against Iran before the midterm elections, while suggesting that military operations could resume afterward, amid a continued US military buildup in the region and stalled diplomatic efforts.
According to Israeli media, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government has been pushing for renewed strikes against Iran, ostensibly aimed at overthrowing its government, although Israeli officials acknowledge that the final decision rests with the White House.
Israeli news website Walla reported Monday that the military remained on high alert amid US and Israeli concerns that Iran could launch a surprise attack, either directly or through allied groups, against American interests in the region or Israel.
The report said intelligence agencies fear Tehran could stage a large-scale military provocation that might influence the US midterm elections.
Walla said the Israeli military had intensified defensive and offensive preparations in recent weeks in coordination with US Central Command (CENTCOM) and the Pentagon.
Citing unnamed Israeli military officials, the website said security coordination between Israel and the US had reached its highest levels and that Israel would receive advance warning if Washington decided to attack Iran.
However, Israeli military assessments suggest that the likelihood of a US preemptive strike before the midterm elections remains low, as Trump prefers to exhaust diplomatic negotiations and pressure before resorting to military action, according to the report.
Walla also said that more than 3,000 US troops were stationed in Israel, noting that no unusual increase in American military aircraft arrivals had been recorded over the past week, unlike the periods preceding previous escalations.
The report added that Israeli officials believe Tehran is seeking to buy time in negotiations with Washington, while disagreements persist over Iran’s nuclear program and ballistic missiles.
Concerns over renewed war
Tensions between Washington and Tehran have persisted since the US and Israel launched a war against Iran in February, followed by a ceasefire in April and renewed confrontations between the US and Iran in July.
The developments come amid warnings that Netanyahu could seek to push Washington toward another military confrontation with Tehran.
In an article published Sunday, Haaretz military analyst Amos Harel warned that Netanyahu might resort to military and political escalation to remain in power, using the Iranian issue and pressures surrounding the US midterm elections.
Harel also warned against attempts by Netanyahu to persuade Washington to resume military operations despite lacking a domestic mandate to launch another war.
Israeli Channel 12 reported Sunday that Netanyahu had pressed Trump during a phone conversation to resume the war against Iran after the US midterm elections, while the American president preferred to give diplomacy another chance.
The heightened security alert also comes amid political uncertainty in Israel following last week’s parliamentary elections.
Netanyahu’s bloc secured 53 seats in the 120-member Knesset, compared with 48 for opposition parties led by former army chief Gadi Eisenkot and 19 for Arab parties.
No bloc secured the 61 seats required to form a government, leaving Israel facing a political deadlock.
The results have complicated efforts to form a governing coalition amid disagreements among opposition parties over whether to seek support from Arab parties.

Europe space chief heads to Gulf as bloc looks beyond US
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
09:17:06 UTC
18:17:06 KST

Europe space chief heads to Gulf as bloc looks beyond US
PARIS, Nov 2 - The head of the European Space Agency will meet officials in the United Arab Emirates this week as Europe seeks new partners and aims to reduce its reliance on the United States for space exploration.
The rise of Elon Musk's SpaceX has laid bare Europe's reliance on American space technology.
"Number one, we should strengthen our capability, become a stronger player in the global ecosystem, but one that uses its strength to still work with other partners," Josef Aschbacher, director general of the ESA, told Reuters. He will attend meetings in Dubai and Abu Dhabi.
"We realised that in exploration, Europe is very exposed to the United States," Aschbacher added, saying that European political leaders had told him that the region needed "more autonomy and more strength".
COOPERATION WITH NASA WEAKENED
The ESA's decades-long cooperation with US space agency NASA has weakened after Washington scaled back or halted common projects, including the Lunar Gateway programme to deploy a space station in lunar orbit and the Mars Sample Return mission.
About 5% of the ESA's budget is linked to cooperation with the US, Aschbacher said. Europe also relies on US providers to send its astronauts into space.
Aschbacher said that over the longer-term the ESA hopes to sign a framework agreement with the UAE, which launched the Arab world's first mission to Mars in 2020.
The UAE operates several satellites, and sent two of its nationals into space through its astronaut programme, but cannot yet organise launches on its own and does not own an independent satellite navigation system like the EU's Galileo or the US Global Positioning System (GPS).
Discussions between ESA and the UAE include a possible lunar rover launch and the potential participation of an Emirati astronaut in the EPIC programme, which would fly a crew to the International Space Station aboard a SpaceX spacecraft.
Aschbacher will visit a joint venture between Franco-American startup Loft Orbital and Abu Dhabi-backed Marlan Space to develop a satellite constellation, after France and the UAE agreed to deepen a strategic defence agreement between the two countries.
Asked if the UAE could invest in projects in collaboration with the ESA, Aschbacher declined to discuss ongoing talks. He said in September that Europe would need €10 billion ($11.2 billion) over the next 10 years to strengthen its autonomy in space.
Aschbacher said the funding gap may be discussed with the UAE but he added that the ESA first needs European governments to agree on their own level of funding.
"Once this decision is made, we will look into international cooperation," he said. REUTERS

Kiev plotted headset bombs targeting Russian drone operators – FSB (VIDEO)

Kiev plotted headset bombs targeting Russian drone operators – FSB (VIDEO)
Ukrainian intelligence agencies have attempted to provide Russian military supply chains with booby-trapped equipment into Russian military supply chains, exploiting volunteer organizations supplying troops, Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB) has warned.
The agency said on Monday that it had recently thwarted a series of attempted attacks on Russian drone operators involving first-person view (FPV) headsets rigged with explosives. It urged volunteer groups to scrutinize potential donors more carefully and outlined warning signs that could indicate a Ukrainian sabotage operation.
The alleged tactic resembles a high-profile Israeli intelligence operation in Lebanon in 2024, when thousands of booby-trapped pagers infiltrated Hezbollah’s supply chain and were subsequently detonated, killing and injuring members of the Lebanese militant group and others. The devices were supplied through a network involving a Taiwan-based manufacturer. The Ukrainian operation described by Russian security officials has been much smaller in scale.
Kiev claimed responsibility in early 2025 for supplying Russian troops with 80 explosive-rigged drone goggles. Ukraine’s military intelligence agency, HUR, was reportedly inspired by Mossad’s pager operation. Russian military-linked sources reported at the time that a batch of Skyzone Cobra X V4 goggles had been fitted with explosives, resulting in the injury of several servicemen.
In March, the FSB also reported intercepting a shipment of more than 500 booby-trapped electrically heated insoles. Both operations allegedly involved attempts to exploit established volunteer networks supplying Russian troops.
According to the FSB, the latest plot was uncovered after a Russian serviceman received an offer of suspicious drone headsets and contacted military counterintelligence. Specialists examined the equipment and confirmed that it contained explosives. A subsequent investigation identified several other suspicious donations allegedly linked to Ukraine, the agency said.
As with the devices attributed to HUR last year, explosives had allegedly been installed in place of the headsets’ cooling fans.
Ukrainian intelligence agencies, which reportedly received extensive CIA training following the 2014 armed coup in Kiev, have also been implicated in a series of targeted bomb assassinations, including attacks that killed civilians.
The FSB warned volunteer organizations that donors unwilling to disclose identifying information, including photographs or mobile phone numbers, should be treated with suspicion. It also identified requests for video confirmation that donated equipment had reached its recipients as a likely indication of a sabotage attempt.
Ukrainian operatives allegedly used psychological manipulation to gain the trust of volunteers. One woman involved in collecting aid said the person who sent her the booby-trapped equipment had claimed to prefer smaller volunteer groups because larger organizations were supposedly more susceptible to embezzlement.

Decades-long UN mission ends as Russia criticizes US stance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
09:15:07 UTC
18:15:07 KST

Decades-long UN mission ends as Russia criticizes US stance
The UN’s peacekeeping mission in the disputed territory of Western Sahara has ended after 35 years following a Security Council standoff over a US proposal that Russia said would deny the region’s people the right to decide their future.
The mandate of the UN Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara (MINURSO) expired on October 31. Moscow expressed regret over the outcome, having vetoed Washington’s proposed overhaul and unsuccessfully sought an extension of the existing mandate.
“Russia was unable to support the intention of depriving Western Sahrawis of the right to vote,” Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said on Sunday, accusing Washington of trying to “artificially accelerate the settlement process.”
Morocco governs most of Western Sahara, a former Spanish colony it annexed in 1975 following Spain’s decision to withdraw. The Algeria-backed Polisario Front seeks independence for the territory.
MINURSO was established alongside a UN-brokered ceasefire in 1991 to organize a referendum offering independence or integration with Morocco. Disputes over voter eligibility prevented the vote, and Polisario resumed hostilities in 2020.
The US draft would have extended the mission for a year, removed the referendum reference from its name, and made Morocco’s plan for autonomy under its sovereignty the sole negotiating basis. It received 11 votes in favor. Russia’s proposal to preserve the existing mandate secured only three, with Washington opposed and 11 members abstaining.
During Friday’s Security Council meeting, Russian UN Ambassador Vassily Nebenzia said the council “cannot automatically predetermine issues of sovereignty,” arguing that Washington’s recognition of Moroccan sovereignty over Western Sahara undermined its impartiality.
Washington recognized Moroccan sovereignty over Western Sahara in 2020 under President Donald Trump as part of a deal involving Rabat’s normalization of relations with Israel.
US Ambassador Mike Waltz defended changing a mission whose referendum had never materialized. “We will not lend our vote to business as usual,” he said. The UK and France criticized Russia’s veto.
Moroccan Foreign Minister Nasser Bourita said Rabat had anticipated Moscow’s opposition and made no attempt to change it. “We have not gone back 35 years; we have turned the page,” he told broadcaster 2M on Saturday, according to Morocco World News. He said Morocco remained committed to the ceasefire. The Royal Cabinet welcomed the outcome and called for the territory’s removal from the council’s agenda.
Algeria, which supports independence for Western Sahara, said it deeply regretted the non-renewal, blaming the US draft’s “excessive bias” toward Morocco. Its Foreign Ministry said making Morocco’s autonomy plan the sole basis for negotiations “emptied the right to self-determination of its substance.”
Polisario representative Sidi Omar thanked Russia for blocking a text he said would “torpedo the foundations of the UN peace process,” Reuters reported. In a separate statement on Sunday, the movement said Morocco and its allies bore “full responsibility” for weakening MINURSO’s mandate and for any consequences arising from the mission’s closure.
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres warned of escalating hostilities on Sunday and said the mission’s departure did not extinguish the Sahrawis’ right to self-determination.

U.S. HADES Reconnaissance Aircraft Prototype Makes First Flight
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
09:09:41 UTC
18:09:41 KST

The first HADES reconnaissance aircraft prototype completed its maiden flight as part of the U.S. Army’s effort to modernize its aerial intelligence capabilities.
The U.S. Army announced the milestone in an official press release.
The aircraft made its first flight on September 11, after successfully completing pre-flight readiness checks.
The flight was prepared and conducted by the U.S. Army’s Fixed Wing Project Office in cooperation with Sierra Nevada Corporation, the program’s lead systems integrator.
Before the flight, engineers and test pilots modified the aircraft’s structure, integrated specialized equipment, and carried out preliminary airworthiness checks.
The successful completion of the maiden flight paves the way for the next phase of the program: integrating and flight-testing reconnaissance systems.
The military plans to evaluate the aircraft’s intelligence-gathering capabilities in various operational environments, including its signals intelligence (SIGINT) systems.
The results will be used to assess the performance, compatibility, and readiness of the onboard systems for subsequent operational demonstrations.
HADES (High Accuracy Detection and Exploitation System) is an advanced airborne intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance (ISR) system being developed for the U.S. Army.
It is designed to replace the Army’s turboprop reconnaissance aircraft and provide greater range, speed, operating altitude, and payload capacity.
The jet-powered Bombardier Global 6500 was selected as the basis for the HADES program. It offers significantly better flight performance than the U.S. Army’s previous reconnaissance aircraft.
According to Bombardier, the standard Global 6500 can remain airborne for up to 18 hours, enabling long-duration reconnaissance missions far from its home airbases.
In January 2024, the U.S. Army began procuring Bombardier Global 6500 business jets to develop its new HADES airborne reconnaissance system.
Before that, the U.S. military tested the ARTEMIS and ARES reconnaissance platforms, based on the Bombardier Challenger 650 and Global 6500 aircraft, respectively.
ARTEMIS aircraft were repeatedly deployed to monitor Russian military activity near Ukraine. In August, the U.S.ARTEMIS II conducted a reconnaissance mission over the Black Sea, south of occupied Crimea.

Live Updates: Iran says "ball is in the U.S. court" on deal to end war as Trump keeps his intentions veiled
What to know about the Iran war today:
- Mediators continue pushing for a deal between the U.S. and Iran to end the eight-month war sparked by U.S. and Israeli strikes on the Islamic Republic. Three consecutive days of indirect, closed-door negotiations led by Qatar have yielded no apparent breakthrough, with Iran saying Monday that "the ball is in the U.S. court."
- President Trump has kept his intentions on Iran ambiguous, saying Saturday that the U.S. still has targets to "take care of," and then telling a radio network on Sunday that the war will soon be over "one way or the other … either they'll make a deal, or we'll just end it."
- Mr. Trump told reporters he had a "very good talk" Sunday with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, discussing the Iran war. Sources quoted by Axios said the president wants to let negotiations play out, while Netanyahu is pushing to resume strikes on Iran.
Iran says the "ball is in the U.S. court" on any prospective peace deal
Iran's foreign ministry spokesperson said Monday that the next move in the standoff with the United States is for President Trump to make.
"The ball is in the U.S. court, because our demands have been stated very clearly and transparently, and Iran's demands are reasonable and logical," Esmaeil Baqaei told journalists in Tehran.
Baqaei said ongoing negotiations, which have been brokered by Qatar, Pakistan and other mediators, were centered around the a seven-day proposal that Iran originally presented to the U.S. side in September, which calls for frozen Iranian assets to be released, the U.S. naval blockade to be lifted and an end to fighting on all fronts, in exchange for the phased reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and further negotiations on other topics.
President Trump rejected the initial proposal, but both sides have since exchanged revisions, and Mr. Trump has said repeatedly in recent weeks that he just needs to make a decision on whether to launch new attacks on Iran, or to make a deal to end the war.
Speaking Sunday to a radio network ahead of a campaign rally in Iowa, Mr. Trump said he would finish with the war soon, "one way or the other."
"Either they'll make a deal, or we'll just end it," he said, without offering any further context.
Netanyahu reportedly pushes for new U.S. strikes on Iran
President Trump told reporters Sunday that he'd spoken with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Saturday and had a "very good talk with him."
Mr. Trump gave no details but said the two had discussed the war in Iran.
According to sources cited by Axios, Netanyahu pushed for Mr. Trump to strike Iran but the president wants to let the negotiations play out.
The U.S. and Iran both engaged in indirect talks via mediators led by Qatar who are pushing to strike a deal between both sides before the conflict escalated.
Mr. Trump has repeatedly hinted he is considering resuming attacks on Iran after the midterm elections.
Push for U.S.-Iran deal shadowed by threats to resume fighting
Qatari mediators are leading indirect talks aimed at reaching a deal between the U.S. and Iran, but the closed door negotiations have been punctuated by exchanges of threats between the leaders of both countries.
Iranian negotiators are in Qatar for talks on a proposal that could reopen the Strait of Hormuz soon, according to Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, who added the outcome depends on answers provided by the United States.
On Saturday, President Trump said the U.S. still had to "take care of" one or two more potential targets in Iran, citing a suspected nuclear complex at Pickaxe Mountain. On Sunday he reiterated the threat, saying he may have to give Tehran "the hammer" at some unspecified time.
Meanwhile, Iran's Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei warned on Saturday there would be no "geographical limitations" should the fighting with the U.S. resume, adding that there is a "vast theatre" to inflict damage.
Both sides have previously acknowledged that indirect talks are underway but consistently exchange threats.
CBS/AFP

The United Arab Emirates' presidential adviser said Sunday that his country hopes a diplomatic breakthrough in Qatar-led mediations is possible, but that they are also preparing for the possibility of escalation.

"We don't really want to see another round of confrontation in the region," Gargash told the audience. But he added that his country and the region are braced for the "the worst," referring to the resumption of active hostilities.
The UAE was consistently targeted by Tehran in the opening weeks of the war in retribution for U.S. strikes on Iran, disrupting tourism and daily life, and effectively throwing the security landscape of the region into question.

Britain's UKMTO maritime agency said "the master of a merchant vessel has relayed a mayday call... stating that another vessel has been struck by an unknown projectile" in the strait.
Earlier, Qatar's state news agency said a Qatari gas tanker had been attacked on Friday with "unidentified objects" while transiting Gulf waters. None of the crew members onboard the vessel were injured, and there was no environmental impact from the attack, the report said.

Stroopwafel wars: supermarkets slash prices to 34 cents a pack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
09:09:00 UTC
18:09:00 KST

Stroopwafel wars: supermarkets slash prices to 34 cents a pack
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Dutch supermarkets are locked in a price war over stroopwafels, with discount chain Dirk now selling a pack of 12 for 34 cents, Het Parool reports.
That works out at just over 2.8 cents a biscuit, which makes it one of the few food items actually getting cheaper.
Meanwhile, tourists are paying around €13 for a single stroopwafel in central Amsterdam.
In mid-October a pack of Bakker Joop stroopwafels cost 42 cents at Jumbo and 38 cents at Dirk. Albert Heijn was charging 42 cents for a pack of its own brand.
All three have since cut further. Jumbo and Albert Heijn are now at 36 cents, although Albert Heijn’s packs hold only 10 biscuits. That leaves its customers paying the most per waffle, at 3.6 cents each.
Retail expert Paul Moers told the paper that the supermarkets make nothing on the deals, they are so-called “lost leaders” that bring people into the shops, who then inevitably buy other things.
The holdout
Not every chain has joined in. Frisian supermarket Poiesz still charges €1.15 for the same Bakker Joop pack, which earned Moers’ “respect”.
He expects the prices could drop by a few more cents, since the chains are already making heavy losses. Eventually, he said, “the joke will wear off” and the supermarkets will move on to another product.
In Gouda, the stroopwafel’s home town, bakers are unbothered. “It’s comparing apples and oranges,” said Mike van den Berg of Berg’s Bakery and Van Vliet Siroopwafels. “As a baker you have to believe in your product.”
Moers had a final word on the bargain biscuits. They contain no butter, he said, which “says something about how blandening of Dutch taste”.

Hypersonica raises a hundred million for deep strike
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
09:08:43 GMT
18:08:43 KST

Hypersonica, the British-German company developing hypersonic deep-strike systems for Europe, has raised €100 million in a Series B round co-led by Lightspeed and General Catalyst, money it will put into accelerating development, increasing its testing cadence and expanding operations across Europe, according to the company.
Existing investors including Plural and 201 Ventures continued their participation in the round, which the company says is expected to support the creation of hundreds of highly skilled engineering and manufacturing jobs across the United Kingdom and Germany.
Co-founders Dr Philipp Kerth, the chief executive, and Dr Marc Ewenz, the chief technology officer, said: “The debate about whether Europe needs hypersonic deep-strike capability is over. Governments have recognised the requirement and begun funding programmes. The challenge now is delivery. Europe needs credible hypersonic long-range capability, and more value for every pound and euro it spends.
“We have shown that next-generation hypersonic systems can be developed in Europe faster and more affordably than conventional wisdom suggests. And we’re proud to be backed by investors who share our conviction that Europe should be able to develop and produce advanced strategic capabilities itself.
“Series B marks our transition from demonstration to delivery. This funding will accelerate development, increase testing cadence, support European reindustrialisation and help ensure Europe has access to sovereign capability developed and produced in Europe.”
Alexander Schmitt, a partner at Lightspeed, said: “Hypersonica is redefining how advanced defence capability gets built. The team pairs deep technical expertise with exceptional speed of execution, and the strength of our support reflects our confidence in both the technology and their ability to deliver.”
Jeannette zu Fürstenberg, president and managing director at General Catalyst, said: “Strategic autonomy begins with the ability to build critical technologies at speed, at scale and at a fraction of the cost of traditional systems. That is exactly what Philipp, Marc, and the Hypersonica team are doing. They combine the ambition to tackle one of Europe’s most critical capability gaps with the engineering excellence to actually solve it. As Europe invests in its security and resilience, it will be companies like Hypersonica that play a defining role in translating ambition into real capability.”
The company tested its HS-1 prototype in February, reaching speeds above Mach 6 over a range exceeding three hundred kilometres and becoming the first privately funded European defence company to achieve that. It says the development model behind the flight reduces costs by more than eighty per cent against conventional approaches, and that it has since expanded its engineering team, deepened engagement with governments and strengthened partnerships across the European defence industrial base.
Government money has started moving in the same direction, and the Defence Investment Plan allocates an initial £770 million over four years to the United Kingdom-German Deep Precision Strike programme under the Trinity House Agreement, and a NATO-led multinational initiative announced in July envisages £37 billion of investment in deep precision strike over the next decade.
Long-range conventional strike has been the most visible European capability gap since the war in Ukraine began. Britain and France hold Storm Shadow and SCALP, air-launched weapons with ranges in the low hundreds of kilometres, and the ground-launched systems that would reach further were removed from European arsenals by the Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty. Filling the gap has so far meant buying American, which brings export control conditions with it.
The company stresses that it develops, owns and controls its technology in Europe and that its systems are free of the International Traffic in Arms Regulations, the American export regime that gives Washington a say over where a weapon containing United States components can go and how it can be used. European governments have pushed harder on that point since 2022.
Hypersonic weapons travel above Mach 5 and manoeuvre during flight, so they follow nothing like the predictable arc of a ballistic missile and are considerably harder for existing defences to engage. Russia and China have both fielded systems of this kind, and the European Long-range Strike Approach brings together France, Germany, Italy, Poland, Britain, the Netherlands and Sweden on a parallel effort.
Hypersonica aims to deliver hypersonic deep-strike systems by 2029, and it raised €23.3 million in a Series A round led by Plural in February, announced alongside the HS-1 flight. The company operates from Munich and London.

Loading on Russian Railways network down 1.4% in October — operator

MOSCOW, November 2. /TASS/. Loading on the Russian Railwayus network in October amounted to 95.6 mln metric tons, down by 1.4% compared to the same period last year, the holding company said.
The rise in loading was provided by Kuybyshevskaya (+22.1%), Trans-Baikal (+13.9%), Oktyabrskaya (+5.6%), Far Eastern (+5.1%) and Gorkovskaya (+4.7%) railways, the Russian Railways said.
An increase is noted in shipment of metallurgical freight, including ferrous metals (+8.7%), non-ferrous ore (+9.8%), coke (+21.1%), and scrap metal (+22.5%). Railway shipments of cement (+9%) and chemicals (+9.4%) increased as well.
"The freight turnover continued growing in October (+2.5%) amid the negative overall dynamics of shipments associated with external factors, which reflects the ongoing reorientation of cargo flows and increasing transportation distance," Russian Railways said.
Loading in January - October 2026 totaled 920 mln metric tons and dropped by 0.8% year on year.
