Israel dispute splits Democrats as Michigan congresswoman backs Republican Senate candidate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
09:07:19 UTC
18:07:19 KST

An extraordinary rift over Israel has erupted within the Democratic Party just days before the U.S. midterm elections, after Rep. Haley Stevens, one of the party's most prominent supporters of Israel, announced Sunday that she would vote for Republican Mike Rogers in Michigan's Senate race rather than her own party's nominee, Abdul El-Sayed.
Stevens, who lost to El-Sayed in the August Democratic primary, appeared alongside Rogers at a church service in Detroit as she announced her endorsement, delivering a dramatic blow to Democratic unity two days before the election.
The decision triggered a wave of condemnation from leading Democrats, including New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi and Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer. President Donald Trump, meanwhile, celebrated the endorsement and invited Stevens to join the Republican Party.
"Working class people’s lives are on the ballot on Tuesday—their healthcare, their rent, their bills," Mamdani wrote. "Haley Stevens just betrayed them by endorsing the very Republican she said she wanted to run against."
Schumer, who had backed Stevens in the Democratic primary, called her decision a "despicable betrayal."
Pelosi accused Stevens of a dangerous betrayal of Michigan families' health, freedoms and futures, declaring that El-Sayed must win.
Pelosi's response was particularly notable because just days earlier, on Thursday, she had criticized the positions of both Mamdani and El-Sayed on Israel.
Speaking on a podcast, Pelosi said opposition to defining Israel as a Jewish state was "wrong" and did not reflect the views of congressional Democrats. Despite those disagreements, she has now thrown her support behind El-Sayed and against the congresswoman she backed in the primary.
A bitter primary fight over Israel
The confrontation between Stevens and El-Sayed has been building for months.
El-Sayed, a physician and former public health director of Wayne County, is among the Democratic Party's most outspoken critics of Israel. He supports ending U.S. military assistance to the country, a position that has put him at odds with the party's pro-Israel establishment.
During the Democratic primary, the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, or AIPAC, spent nearly $30 million promoting Stevens and opposing El-Sayed, its largest investment in a single election campaign.
Despite that spending, El-Sayed defeated Stevens by less than 1 percentage point.
After her defeat, Stevens pledged to support the Democratic nominee. But the two barely cooperated during the general election campaign, and their relationship deteriorated further in the final days before the vote.
Last week, Stevens demanded that El-Sayed condemn an advertisement produced by an outside political group that accused Israel of genocide and linked U.S. military aid to Israel with rising food prices in the United States.
Stevens called the advertisement antisemitic. She also demanded that El-Sayed remove a campaign advertisement featuring conservative commentator Tucker Carlson and apologize for his statements about Israel.
El-Sayed said the outside group's advertisement had not been produced by his campaign and that he opposed its content. He accused Stevens, however, of attempting to reopen a primary contest that had ended three months earlier.
He also asked her not to participate in his campaign events during the remaining days before the election.
A church appearance that stunned Democrats
Stevens had been scheduled to appear Sunday alongside El-Sayed and longtime Democratic Rep. Jim Clyburn at a church service in Detroit, an event intended to demonstrate party unity and encourage turnout among black voters.
Instead, she attended a different church with Rogers, sat beside the Republican candidate and released a video during the service announcing that she would vote for him.
"Hey Michigan, as you may have seen, our Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate, Abdul, said I was no longer welcome in his campaign and that I should stay away. And he's right, and that's why I am endorsing Mike Rogers for the United States Senate today," Stevens said.
"We can't stand for hate. We can't stand with Hassan Piker," she added, referring to the anti-Israel online commentator who previously appeared alongside El-Sayed and has faced criticism over remarks about Jews.
Stevens' Jewish fiancé, Jason Turkish, had already announced that he would vote for Rogers.
Despite endorsing a Republican, Stevens insisted that she remained a "proud Democrat."
The announcement reportedly surprised even members of her own staff. Her chief of staff and several other employees resigned, while the Michigan Democratic Party chair declared that Stevens was no longer a member of the party and would not be one in the future.
In a tense CNN interview, Stevens struggled to explain why she had decided to support Rogers, whom she had previously described as a "rubber stamp" for Trump.
Asked whether she still wanted Democrats to win control of the Senate, she said yes, stressing that her decision concerned only one race.
Trump celebrates an unexpected endorsement
Trump welcomed Stevens' announcement on his Truth Social platform.
"Wow, this is BIG!" he wrote.
Speaking at a rally in Iowa, Trump praised the congresswoman's courage.
"I don’t know Haley, I’ve never met Haley, but Haley said what few people are willing to say," he told supporters.
Trump said he would welcome Stevens into the Republican Party, adding that Rogers had spoken with her about the possibility.
El-Sayed, for his part, sought to dismiss the significance of the endorsement.
"I actually don’t think about Haley Stevens," he told reporters. "Because you know what? I’m just less interested in the politics of it all than I am in the policy of it all."
Michigan's Jewish voters face a difficult choice
The dispute has also exposed divisions within Michigan's Jewish community, where attitudes toward El-Sayed and the Democratic Party have become increasingly complicated.
Many Jewish voters and community figures who previously criticized El-Sayed have nevertheless rallied behind the Democratic nominee, arguing that Rogers is not the answer to the community's concerns.
Former Democratic Rep. Andy Levin, who is Jewish and supports El-Sayed, participated in a campaign event for the nominee. A group called Jews for Abdul has attracted thousands of members.
Other Jewish activists, uncomfortable with both major-party candidates, have proposed a symbolic protest vote: writing in the name of Emma Lazarus, the Jewish American poet whose words are inscribed on the Statue of Liberty.
The Jewish vote could prove significant in a state where Jewish residents account for approximately 1.4% of eligible voters.
In Michigan's 2024 Senate election, Democrat Elissa Slotkin defeated Rogers by fewer than 20,000 votes, illustrating how even a modest shift among voters could influence a close contest.
Ahead of this election, the Republican Jewish Coalition invested $2 million in an effort to reach approximately 50,000 Jewish voters.
Meanwhile, a political organization affiliated with AIPAC sent campaign materials to roughly 130,000 Jewish voters.
A Senate race with national consequences
Michigan's open Senate seat is considered one of the most important contests in the battle for control of the chamber.
Recent polling has shown El-Sayed ahead, although the size of his lead varies considerably.
A New York Times/Siena College poll gave the Democrat an 11-point advantage, while a YouGov survey showed him leading Rogers by 4 points.
If elected, El-Sayed would become the first Muslim to serve in the U.S. Senate.

Ryanair considers pay freezes and reducing crew on flights as fuel costs soar
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
09:06:51 UTC
18:06:51 KST

Ryanair is considering cost-cutting measures including pay freezes, reducing crew numbers on flights and increasing the use of AI to offset soaring fuel costs driven by the Middle East conflict.
Europe’s largest low-cost carrier said it expected European airlines to raise ticket prices by up to 20%, with its own jet fuel costs forecast to rise by about €2bn (£1.6bn) in its next financial year, which ends in March 2028.
“Unless there is a swift resolution of the Middle East conflict we expect jet fuel prices to remain elevated well into 2027,” said Michael O’Leary, the chief executive of Ryanair. “While we believe European short-haul fares will increase materially to reflect these much higher jet-fuel prices and competitor capacity reductions, this is unlikely to provide a full offset for an estimated €2bn increase in our fuel bill.”
Oil prices hit a six-month high on Friday before falling to about $110 a barrel on Monday.
Ryanair expects European short-haul fares to “increase materially” next year, as fuel hedging deals taken out by airlines to reduce costs expire.
“To help address this, we’re reviewing all costs across group airlines with a particular focus on airport churn negotiations, maturing labour agreements (which may require temporary pay freezes), lower crew ratios and increased use of AI,” O’Leary said.
He added: “We are slowing down hiring meaningfully as the number of new pilots and cabin crew recruitment and training courses are running.”
The company said its increased use of AI would focus on improving productivity in operations and back-office and support functions.
O’Leary said AI had already been used to increase capacity by 4%.
“When you’re running 650 aircraft, it’s too big for a human to be able to do it,” he said. “The machines can actually design the schedules better than we know [how to do], so we are getting more productivity out of the aircraft.”
Ryanair said 80% of its fuel requirements until the end of March were hedged at $67 a barrel. Twenty-five per cent of its fuel requirements for the subsequent 12 months are hedged at $95 a barrel.
“It’s beginning to dawn on everybody that we [the industry] are not well hedged,” said O’Leary.
The Irish airline, Europe’s largest by passenger numbers, said average fares fell by 2% year on year in the quarter ending in September. Ryanair added that fares in the final three months of the year were trending “modestly ahead” of the same quarter last year.
“The booking window remains closer-in which reduces visibility,” the company said.“[The current quarter’s] fare outcome will heavily depend on the strength of close-in October-November school midterm [holiday] and Christmas bookings.”
The airline reported a post-tax profit of €1.61bn in the quarter ending inSeptember, a fall of 6% year on year but in line with analyst expectations. Passenger numbers grew 5% year on year to 64.5 million during the quarter.
Ryanair has taken delivery of about 30 aircraft annually over the last two years, but the delivery rate is set to drop to 15 annually for next few years.
The airline said it was to take deliveries of the Boeing 737 Max 10 aircraft in January, which has about 20% more seats but burns a fifth less fuel than its current fleet.

Dehghan satisfied with her performance at 2026 Asian Games
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
09:06:41 UTC
18:06:41 KST

Dehghan satisfied with her performance at 2026 Asian Games
TEHRAN - Iranian women’s cyclist Mandana Dehghan has expressed satisfaction with her performance at the Nagoya Asian Games, highlighting the technical difficulty of the race course and the challenges she faced in both events.
Dehghan finished 13th in the individual time trial with a time of 41:05.39, before securing 14th place in the women’s road race.
“The Asian Games are the largest multi-sport event on the continent and hold tremendous significance for athletes across Asia. All participating nations make long-term preparations to ensure their athletes arrive in the best possible condition and achieve valuable results,” Dehghan said in an exclusive interview with Tehran Times.
“At this edition of the Games in Nagoya, Japan, the women’s road race course was particularly challenging from a technical standpoint, featuring numerous short and sharp climbs. It became clear several months before the competition that Iran would have only one quota place in the women’s road cycling event. Considering the characteristics of the course, the federation selected me based on my experience, sporting background and previous participation in similar races in Europe and Asia.
“The objective was to send an athlete capable of competing against Asia’s best, rather than simply someone whose primary goal was to finish the race. I competed in both the individual time trial and the road race. My participation in the time trial was primarily intended to help prepare me for the road race. Given the course conditions and its characteristics, we knew that competing for a top result in the time trial would be difficult. As a result, I did not undertake specific, targeted training on a time-trial bike,” she declared.
“In the road race, some of Asia’s strongest teams entered with three riders each, making the competition considerably more difficult. These teams had the advantage of working together and implementing team tactics. In previous editions of the Asian Games, each country was allowed two riders, so the competitive dynamics were different. Competing against powerful three-rider teams under such circumstances was particularly challenging. Nevertheless, I gave everything I had and eventually finished 14th among 41 competitors.”
Dehghan also highlighted the unpredictable nature of road cycling, explaining how external factors can significantly influence race outcomes.
“Unlike many indoor or time-based sports, where athletes compete under relatively stable and controlled conditions, road cycling is affected by numerous unpredictable factors. Rain, wind, technical course conditions and incidents during the race can all influence the final result. For example, a crash involving a rider at the front of the peloton can create gaps between competitors and the main group. Closing those gaps requires a considerable amount of energy. Unfortunately, something similar happened to me during this race. I was forced to spend significant energy recovering the lost ground,” Dehghan said.
“Another important point is my preparation for the Games. During the three months leading up to the competition, I worked hard to develop the best possible training program. I also took part in several international races and arrived in Nagoya in good physical condition.”
“In reality, success in cycling is not guaranteed simply by spending more money or competing in a large number of races. As far as I know, teams from Japan, Uzbekistan and the UAE invested substantial financial resources and spent months training in Europe. Yet their final results did not necessarily match their expectations.
“This demonstrates that, alongside planning, resources and physical preparation, race conditions and unpredictable incidents play a significant role in determining the outcome. Sometimes circumstances work in an athlete’s favour, while at other times they go against all the preparation and effort invested.
“One of the most encouraging aspects of my performance is that several athletes who finished behind me were established Asian champions and prominent competitors at previous Asian Games. This shows that I have reached a level where I can compete with some of the best cyclists on the continent in one of Asia’s most important road cycling events.
“I hope the Iranian sporting community and the wider cycling community will recognise the importance of this achievement and avoid judging athletes solely on medals or their final positions.”
Dehghan emphasized her long-standing commitment to raising the profile of Iranian women’s cycling on the international stage.
“Throughout my career, I have always tried to contribute to the development and greater recognition of Iranian women’s cycling in Asia and Europe.
“I cannot recall ever being sent to a competition simply to cross the finish line, gain experience or take part for recreational purposes. I have always approached every international assignment with the determination to perform at my best. I have overcome considerable challenges and prepared through careful planning, detailed analysis of the course and thorough assessment of my rivals.
“Today, despite not winning a medal, I am fully satisfied with my performance. This does not mean overlooking the gap between where I am now and my bigger ambitions. Rather, it reflects my confidence in the work I have put in and my understanding of my own capabilities. I remain committed to long-term planning, continuous improvement and achieving better results in future competitions.”
“My ambition has always been greater than simply participating in races. I want to represent Iranian women’s cycling as an athlete capable of competing with the best in Asia and around the world. I will continue working towards that goal,” Dehghan concluded.

US midterms: 1 day to go – Democrats rally around El-Sayed amid attacks
Democrats slam Haley Stevens over her endorsement of a Republican candidate a day before the polls.
With one day to go before the United States midterm elections, campaigning has reached a fever pitch with Democratic and Republican leaders pulling out all the stops to mobilise voters.
Democrats are hoping to flip control of both chambers of Congress, which is currently controlled by US President Donald Trump’s Republican Party.
All 435 seats in the House of Representatives and 35 of the Senate’s 100 seats are up for grabs on Tuesday. Voting will also be held to elect governors in 36 of the 50 US states.
With the cost-of-living crisis, exacerbated by the US-Israel war on Iran, becoming one of the key talking points of these elections, here’s where things stand as of Monday:
What’s happened on the campaign trail in the past 24 hours?
In a dramatic political development on Sunday, Democratic Congresswoman Haley Stevens threw her support behind Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers over her own party’s nominee, Abdul El-Sayed, in Michigan – one of the most closely watched races of the US midterm elections. Stevens had lost Michigan’s Democratic Senate primary in August to El-Sayed.
Her announcement followed weeks of tension with El-Sayed over US support to Israel, which has been accused of committing genocide in Gaza. El-Sayed has opposed military support to Israel, arguing that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu pushed the US into the Iran war. Stevens has accused El-Sayed of anti-Semitism for his criticism of Israeli actions in Gaza.
El-Sayed said a vote for his rival Rogers “is going to be a vote for Donald Trump” as his campaign reportedly saw a fundraising surge after Stevens crossed party lines.
Democratic leaders have rallied behind El-Sayed, who has faced Islamophobic attacks during the campaign.
The chairman of the Democratic Party in Michigan criticised Stevens. “She does not speak for that larger community,” Curtis Hertel said in an interview with CNN.
The leader of the Democrats in the Senate, Chuck Schumer, slammed Stevens over her endorsement of the Republican candidate.
“This is a despicable betrayal from Representative Stevens,” he posted on X.
“Senate Democrats are united in our support for Abdul El-Sayed, because we know he will fight for the economic interests of working families in Michigan, unlike Mike Rogers, who is a tool of Donald Trump and billionaire donors.”
Meanwhile, the advocacy group Michigan Jews for Democracy has backed El-Sayed.
“Haley Stevens does not speak for Michigan’s Jewish community,” it said in a statement, which rejected her “attempt to divide our community” two days before the election.
While Democrats have been angered by Stevens’s action, Trump celebrated her decision.
During a rally in Iowa later on Sunday, the US president said he would “love” it if Stevens joined the Republican Party. “Haley said what few people are willing to say,” Trump added. “It’s a thing called bravery.”
The question now is whether Stevens’s endorsement could persuade some of her supporters to back Rogers or discourage them from voting altogether.
Polling suggested El-Sayed has largely consolidated Democratic support, according to the Reuters news agency.
Judge dismisses Trump’s Alaska election lawsuit
Meanwhile, a federal judge has thrown out a Trump administration lawsuit seeking to block Alaska from certifying a loss by Republican Senator Dan Sullivan. The administration has argued that a rival on the ballot with the same name could change the outcome.
Sullivan pledged to accept the election outcome, days after the US Department of Justice filed a lawsuit seeking to decertify the results of the Senate race if he loses.
“I’m going to accept the election results,” Sullivan, an ally of Trump, told CNN on Sunday.
Alaska’s Senate race is one of seven key toss-up races that will likely decide whether Republicans keep their majority in the upper chamber of the US Congress.
How many Americans have already voted?
This year, out of about 210 million registered voters, 54.5 million had voted early as of 10am US East Coast time (15:00 GMT) on Sunday, according to a University of Florida analysis. This includes 30 million in-person votes and 24 million mail-in ballots.
In the 2022 midterm elections, 46 million people voted early.
Early voting enthusiasm has been higher among Democrats this year with more than 11 million registered Democrats having voted early, compared with about 8 million registered Republicans, according to the university’s analysis.
Early voting has particularly surged in the state of Texas, a key battleground, where more than 7.7 million people have voted early.
According to an Associated Press polling analysis, in South Carolina, where Trump won by nearly 18 percentage points in 2024, early voting has surged 83 percent compared with the same point in 2022. The state has open races for governor and US Senate this year.
Kansas, Michigan and Maine have also seen a surge in early voting.
Early turnout figures, however, don’t show which candidates voters have chosen or what the final results will be.

AI models mostly smarter than top scientists, OpenAI's Altman says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
09:05:42 UTC
18:05:42 KST

Gokhan Ergocun
02 November 2026•Update: 02 November 2026
Advanced artificial intelligence (AI) models have progressed to become mostly smarter than the brightest scientists and capable of performing significant portions of white-collar work, OpenAI Chief Executive Sam Altman said on Monday.
Speaking at the opening ceremony of the Abu Dhabi International Petroleum Exhibition and Conference in the United Arab Emirates, Altman highlighted the dramatic leap in AI capabilities over the past year.
"At the start of this year, AI was mostly not as smart as our smartest scientist, and now it's mostly smarter than them," Altman said.
"AI was mostly not able to do a lot of white-collar jobs, and now it mostly can do a lot of parts of that," he added.
Altman stressed that despite the disruptive impact on global economies and employment, human judgment, creativity and accountability must remain central to the technology's deployment.
"We think it is absolutely critical that people remain in control of the future; there should not be a handoff to AI, there should not be a gradual 'we are going to let AI decide what is best for us,'" he said.
"AI needs to be a tool built for people and needs to serve people, not the other way around," Altman noted.
Addressing concerns surrounding the massive electricity demands of computing infrastructure, he described physical power supply as the single biggest bottleneck for the sector.
"Everything else we're going to make huge progress on, except atoms are still atoms and the physical world that has to power this is going to be the dominant factor of the cost and the abundance," he said.
Altman also noted that global per capita token consumption has surged from near zero six years ago to roughly 100,000 tokens a month, while top institutional users consume about 500 billion tokens monthly.
Highlighting the host nation's rapid adoption of technology, he pointed out that around 80% of young people in the UAE use ChatGPT on a weekly basis.
During the event, OpenAI announced partnerships with Emirati technology group G42 and state oil producer Abu Dhabi National Oil Company, marking the first global deployment of OpenAI's frontier models by an energy company.

Two people working on Republican Mike Rogers' US Senate campaign in Michigan are registered foreign agents for Israel, according to a media report published Sunday.
Campaign spokesperson Abigail Ronson and communications specialist Jesse Stokes have been involved in Israeli government communications work since May 2026 and October 2025, respectively, while also working on Rogers' campaign through major contractor Convergence Media, Drop Site News reported.
Ronson registered under the Foreign Agents Registration Act (FARA) in May for work involving Havas Media Network through Clocktower X LLC, a company associated with former Trump campaign manager Brad Parscale.
Her registration describes the services as "strategic communications, planning, and media services" for an Israeli government initiative in the US aimed at combating antisemitism.
Stokes registered in October 2025 under the same Havas contract and has reportedly authored several Rogers campaign press releases.
According to Drop Site News, Ronson is among 14 Convergence Media employees subcontracted for a $46.5 million Israeli government communications project involving social media campaigns and artificial intelligence.
Federal Election Commission records show that Rogers' campaign has paid Convergence Media millions of dollars during the election cycle.
The campaign previously denied that Ronson was a staff member, although she has reportedly communicated with journalists using an official campaign email address.
Neither Ronson nor Stokes immediately responded to requests for comment from Drop Site News.
Another campaign spokesperson also did not respond to the outlet's questions about whether the campaign was aware of the arrangements.

British patrol ship ‘opens fire’ near Falkland Islands
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
09:04:51 GMT
18:04:51 KST

HMS Medway has put 120 rounds downrange from her 30mm automatic gun during training in the South Atlantic, carried out with staff from Flag Officer Sea Training embarked, according to the Royal Navy.
The ship said: “120 rounds downrange. With @FOST embarked, we took the opportunity for further routine training and put our 30mm Automatic Small Calibre Gun through its paces again. Practice = Precision.”
Flag Officer Sea Training sends its assessors to sea with warships to put crews through the full range of warfighting serials and certify that a ship is ready for operations, a process most vessels go through in home waters before deploying.
The 30mm Automatic Small Calibre Gun is the main armament of the River class, a stabilised mounting firing a high explosive round out to around two and a half kilometres, and the weapon a patrol vessel would use against a small craft that failed to comply. Accuracy with it depends on gunners who shoot often.
Keeping the weapons serviceable in that climate takes work of its own, of course. The ship’s weapon engineers have been maintaining the armament through the South Atlantic weather, and Medway said of them: “The Falklands wind doesn’t make maintenance any easier! Our Weapon Engineers work hard to keep our equipment ready when it matters, whatever the weather throws at them.”
Medway carried out live machine gun firings at the edge of the Falkland Islands Conservation Zone during a four-day patrol at the end of July, British Forces South Atlantic Islands stated at the time. The patrol, designated Operation Southern Vigilance, ran from 26 to 29 July, and the ship’s company fired mounted machine guns and worked through a man overboard exercise alongside an RAF A400M Atlas transport aircraft, work the command describes as maintaining operational readiness. According to British Forces South Atlantic Islands, the deployment demonstrated Britain’s enduring commitment to the Falkland Islands by maintaining a visible presence and a capable force, helping to deter potential adversaries.
Other training has continued alongside the gunnery, and the ship carries a Rigid Raider in addition to two Pacific 24 seaboats, allowing it to land personnel and equipment ashore, and it has been running routine exercises with 2nd Battalion, The Parachute Regiment. Seaboat coxswains have been practising approach and pacing drills with peer-to-peer coaching in the evenings.
HMS Medway is a River class offshore patrol vessel commissioned in 2019, and she took over the South Atlantic Patrol Task from HMS Forth, which held the role for several years after replacing HMS Clyde. The class displaces around 2,000 tonnes and carries a 30mm gun, machine guns and a flight deck able to take a Merlin, with an endurance suited to long independent patrols in remote waters.
The ship is the only Royal Navy vessel permanently assigned to the region. British Forces South Atlantic Islands also operates Typhoon fighters and A400M and Voyager aircraft from RAF Mount Pleasant on East Falkland, alongside an infantry company, Sky Sabre air defence and a radar station on Mount Byron.

How to find out about an air raid alert while the app is not working - explanation from Ministry of Digital Transformation
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
11:04:02 EET
18:04:02 KST

How to find out about an air raid alert while the app is not working - explanation from Ministry of Digital Transformation
Kyiv • UNN
The “Air Raid Alert!” app experienced a malfunction due to a likely cyberattack. The Ministry of Digital Transformation advises enabling emergency notifications and following official channels.
While the "Air Raid Alert!" app is not working, information about an air threat can be obtained through emergency notifications using settings on a smartphone, as well as through sirens and the official channels of the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine. This was reported by the Ministry of Digital Transformation of Ukraine, according to UNN.
Notifications
To receive air raid alert notifications, the Ministry of Digital Transformation advises enabling emergency notifications on your smartphone.
"The state emergency notification system sends danger signals while ignoring silent modes on your device. This ensures that you hear the alert instantly and can take shelter in time," the ministry said in a post.
What iPhone owners should do
iPhone owners should open "Settings," go to the "Notifications" section, scroll to the bottom of the screen and turn on the toggles in the "Emergency Alerts" section.
How Android owners can set it up
For Android owners, the settings may vary depending on the device. Usually, you need to find the "Passwords & security" or "Safety & emergency" section, open "Emergency alerts," and activate them. On some smartphones, the relevant option is located in the location settings..
Other methods
At the same time, sirens and other alert systems are also working.
"If you hear an air raid siren or receive an official notification about one, immediately proceed to the nearest shelter and remain there until the official all-clear," the ministry emphasizes.
The Ministry of Digital Transformation of Ukraine also emphasizes that information about air threats and the movement of enemy targets should be obtained exclusively exclusively from the official channels of the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine on Telegram, WhatsApp, and Viber.
In Kyiv, notifications about air raids in the "Kyiv Digital" app are also operating normally.
Reminder
On the evening of November 1, residents of Kyiv and other regions began receiving unusual warnings through the "Air Raid Alert" app about a nuclear and chemical threat, as well as the danger of street fighting. Monitoring channels reported a possible hacker attack on the app.
During the night of November 2, the mobile "Air Raid Alert" app gradually began restoring its operation after the cyberattack, its developers reported .

'Now, thank God, we have water': Uzbekistan’s tap water reaches 83% of people, but gaps remain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
09:03:45 UTC
18:03:45 KST

Uzbekistan has expanded its drinking water network by upgrading treatment facilities and distribution networks, and extending household connections.
Uzbekistan has expanded its drinking water network considerably over the past decade. Yet despite increased investment and new infrastructure, access to centralised supplies remains uneven, particularly outside major urban centres.
According to government figures released in July 2026, nationwide coverage rose from 63 per cent in 2017 to 83 per cent, with around 39,000 kilometres of water networks built or reconstructed during that period.
The figures reflect a broader national investment programme combining government resources with financing from international institutions. One such initiative is underway in Karakalpakstan, an autonomous republic in northwestern Uzbekistan that includes part of the Aral Sea region.
The Asian Development Bank (ADB) is providing a $145 million (approximately €129.5mn) loan for a project covering six districts of the region. With a further $27.3mn (approximately €24.4mn) contribution from Uzbekistan, largely through tax and customs exemptions, the programme's total estimated cost is $172.3mn (approximately €153.9mn).
From communal taps to household water supplies
For Muslima Erimbetova, one of the residents interviewed in the region, the change is practical. Her household now receives water through the supply network.
"We used to carry water with a shoulder pole and containers. We collected it from neighbours and public taps. Now, thank God, we have water," she said.
Her experience comes from Nukus district, where the ADB-supported works include upgrades to water distribution facilities, pipelines and local water quality monitoring.
According to the regional water utility, more than 31,000 residents have benefited from the works, while the share of the district's population covered by the drinking water network has risen from 68 per cent to 90 per cent.
The improvements include a local water testing laboratory, reducing the need to transport samples to the regional capital for analysis.
Treatment capacity and the limits of water access
A new treatment plant has been commissioned in Mang‘it, drawing water from the Amu Darya River. According to the ADB, it currently supplies around 20 million litres of water a day, although it was designed to handle considerably more.
Sohib Akramov, the ADB's drinking water project coordinator in Uzbekistan, explained: "The capacity of 40,000 cubic metres was calculated based on projected population growth, business expansion and industrial development by 2040".
The distinction between production capacity and household connections is significant. Local officials reported that only around half of the population in the surrounding Amudaryo district had access to the drinking water network before the latest improvements.
A separate project involving approximately 355 kilometres of pipelines is under way, with the aim of raising coverage to 80 per cent once the planned works are completed.
The ADB is also discussing a proposed $200mn (approximately €178.6mn) project with the Uzbek government. According to Akramov, around $70mn (approximately €62.5mn) would be allocated to Karakalpakstan, including plans to reconstruct the Tuyamuyun water treatment plant.

US Clears Boeing Jet Sales to Belarus as Trump Eases Sanctions on Lukashenko
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
09:02:48 UTC
18:02:48 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
US Clears Boeing Jet Sales to Belarus as Trump Eases Sanctions on Lukashenko
The United States has authorized Boeing to resume cooperation with Belarusian national carrier Belavia, allowing the airline to purchase American-made aircraft components and potentially negotiate the acquisition of new passenger jets.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Belarusian state news agency BelTA on October 31, Belavia CEO Igor Cherginets said the US Department of Commerce had issued Boeing a license permitting direct commercial cooperation with the airline.
The authorization allows Belavia to obtain spare parts, aircraft components, and software needed to maintain its existing fleet. It also creates an opportunity for the Belarusian carrier to begin negotiations with Boeing over purchasing new aircraft, although no agreements have been announced.
Cherginets said the decision followed earlier authorization from the US Department of the Treasury, which established the legal framework for renewed cooperation between the two companies.
Belarusian Ambassador to the United Nations Valentin Rybakov also confirmed the development, describing the license as another step in ongoing negotiations between Washington and Minsk.
According to Rybakov, Belarusian leader Alexander Lukashenko outlined several priorities for further bilateral discussions during a meeting with US President Donald Trump’s special envoy, John Coale.
Belavia had faced US export restrictions since April 2022, following Belarus’s support for Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Washington subsequently tightened those measures, restricting access to American aviation technology, maintenance services, and replacement parts.
The airline currently operates approximately 18 aircraft, including Boeing, Embraer, and Airbus models, according to its published fleet information.
The decision follows a gradual easing of US restrictions on Belarus. In September 2025, Washington lifted sanctions on Belavia after Belarusian authorities released 52 political prisoners as part of negotiations with the Trump administration.
The US Treasury Department subsequently relaxed additional restrictions in November 2025, permitting certain transactions involving Belavia and aircraft associated with Lukashenko.

North Korea to continue to rapidly strengthen its nuclear capabilities — agency

PYONGYANG, November 2. /TASS/. The DPRK has no plans to alter its course toward the accelerated buildup of its nuclear deterrent forces in response to the military activities of the United States and the Republic of Korea, Kim Jong Sik, first vice department director of the Central Committee of the Workers' Party of Korea (WPK), said, the Korean Central News Agency (KCNA) reported.
"We are confident in our capabilities and determined to respond to everything," he said, adding that "the national defense policy of the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK), which aims to bolster the country's nuclear war deterrent at an even faster pace, will not change in the slightest."
Kim Jong Sik condemned the US-South Korea joint exercises Iron Mace, which were conducted from September 29 to October 2. According to him, the maneuvers, during which the joint use of US nuclear forces and South Korean conventional weapons was practiced, were "the most hideous nuclear war rehearsal aimed at using nuclear weapons against the DPRK."
The North Korean official also highlighted the Hoguk and Freedom Flag exercises held in South Korea in October, as well as the Keen Sword exercise in Japan. He said that Washington and its allies are intensifying military activity in the region, including the deployment of intelligence units and aircraft sent from the United States.
According to Kim Jong Sik, North Korea is confident in its capabilities and ready to respond to any developments. Pyongyang will continue to build up its nuclear forces, which it views as a means of protecting national sovereignty and maintaining peace in the region, he said.

Russia’s Finance Ministry proposes automatically transferring pension savings into long-term savings program
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
09:01:51 UTC
18:01:51 KST

Russia’s Finance Ministry proposes automatically transferring pension savings into long-term savings program
Russia’s Finance Ministry has drafted a bill that would move the funded portion of pensions into the long-term savings program (PDS), the Russian business news outlet RBC reported. The transfer would happen automatically starting April 1, 2027.
The government commission on legislative activity will review the bill as early as this week, and it is expected to go to the State Duma in early November 2026, according to RBC’s sources.
The measure covers both the funded pensions of so-called “silent” citizens — people who never applied to transfer their pension savings to non-state pension funds or private management companies — and the funds held by clients of non-state pension funds (NPFs).
In total, 6.6 trillion rubles in pension savings are expected to move into the long-term savings program: 2.98 trillion rubles belonging to “silent” citizens and managed by the state-owned management company VEB, and 3.6 trillion rubles held by 24 non-state pension funds.
“The proposed measure equalizes the rights and opportunities to build long-term savings for both current clients of the Social Fund of Russia and clients of non-state pension funds,” the Finance Ministry said.
This will give citizens more options for managing these funds, as well as create conditions for building additional capital.
The Finance Ministry told RBC that an “authorized fund” with mandatory state participation would be created to manage the funds of “silent” citizens. According to the outlet’s sources, the new structure is expected to include NPF Blagosostoyaniye and NPF VTB Pension Fund.
Russia has frozen contributions to the funded portion of citizens’ pensions since 2014. Before that, the funded portion was built from contributions equal to 6% of the earnings of citizens born in 1967 or later, which could stay with the Social Fund or be transferred to a non-state pension fund to boost returns. Another 16% of earnings went toward the insurance portion of the pension.
After 2014, the portion of earnings that had previously funded pensions has gone toward the insurance portion to pay current retirees.
The Russian business daily Kommersant notes that deputies in the State Duma discussed the proposal to automatically transfer the funded portion of pensions into the PDS back in June 2025. Anatoly Aksakov, head of the State Duma committee on the financial market, initiated that discussion, saying the move would help develop private long-term investment in Russia.

France recalls 7 million condoms across EU over STI and unintended pregnancy concerns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
09:01:42 UTC
18:01:42 KST

French authorities have suspended sales and imports of ultra-thin condoms made by a Malaysian manufacturer after an investigation found defects that could increase the risk of breakage, which could lead to sexually transmitted infections and unintended pregnancies.
France has ordered the withdrawal and recall of 15 types of condoms across the European market after finding manufacturing defects that could cause the products to burst or rip. The defects could compromise protection against sexually transmitted infections (STIs) and unintended pregnancies, the authorities warned.
The defects affected ultra-thin condoms manufactured by Malaysian company Richter Rubber Technology, the French consumer watchdog, the Directorate-General for Competition Policy, Consumer Affairs and Fraud Control (DGCCRF), said on Friday.
“Some users have reported condom breakages and unwanted pregnancies linked to the sampled batches,” French authorities said in a ministerial order dated 22 October and published in France's Official Journal on 30 October.
French authorities said laboratory tests had identified defects linked to fluctuations in the thickness and quality of the latex film used during manufacturing.
Tested condoms “failed both the pressure and burst volume tests and the tests relating to the absence of perforations,” French authorities added. It is also stated that the manufacturer has “a lack of control over the manufacturing process of its products.”
The products represent approximately 7 million condoms across the European Union, although only a proportion have been sold in France, according to the French economy ministry.
The French government has suspended the sale and import of all ultra-thin condoms made by the manufacturer using the defective production process for one year. The measure can be renewed if necessary.
The decision follows an investigation launched after an initial wave of condom recalls earlier this summer, when around 260,000 condoms were recalled in late May and early August.
Eight users have reported condom breakages since the initial recalls.
EU-wide implications
The recall extends beyond France, with the affected products distributed across the European market under several different brand names.
The French authorities have published a list of the affected products and batches, and ordered their withdrawal from points of sale as well as a recall of products already held by consumers.
French authorities have advised anyone who has used affected condoms to seek screening for sexually transmitted infections at a medical laboratory and to take a pregnancy test if their period is late.
Consumers with concerns have been advised to contact their doctor or a free sexual health screening centre.
The DGCCRF has also urged consumers to report adverse incidents, including condom breakages or perforations during use, through the government's health incident reporting platform.
The French watchdog said it would monitor the effectiveness of the product withdrawal and recall.

Elbit to build artillery training center for Israel’s Roem and PULS
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
09:00:21 UTC
18:00:21 KST

- Israel’s Defense Ministry signed a 15-year, roughly 600 million shekel ($192 million) deal with Elbit for an Artillery Corps training and simulation center.
- The center will train crews on the Roem SIGMA 155 mm howitzer and the Lahav PULS rocket launcher, with driving and mission simulators.
Israel’s Defense Ministry has signed a 15-year contract with Elbit Systems worth about 600 million shekels, or roughly $192 million, to build and run a training and simulation center for the Israel Defense Forces Artillery Corps as it brings the new Roem self-propelled howitzer and Lahav rocket launcher into service.
The ministry’s Directorate of Defense Procurement signed the deal together with the IDF Ground Arm, the ministry said on social media on Nov. 2. The center will train commanders and crews on the Roem, the IDF name for Elbit’s SIGMA 155 mm wheeled howitzer, and the Lahav, Israel’s version of Elbit’s PULS precision rocket launcher.
Elbit will build the physical infrastructure and classrooms and supply driving and mission simulators, then provide instructors, maintenance and logistics support over the life of the contract. The ministry said the center should shorten the time it takes to qualify artillery crews, raise their skill level and save money by reducing wear on operational vehicles used for training. It did not say where the facility will be built, how many simulators it will include or when it will open.
“The combination of advanced training and simulation technologies with a full, long-term support package will help the Artillery Corps realize the full firepower potential of the Roem cannon and the new systems, while saving and making optimal use of resources,” said Ze’ev Landau, head of the Directorate of Defense Procurement. (Translated from Hebrew.)
The Roem is replacing the U.S.-built M109 howitzers, known in Israel as the Doher, that have served the IDF for about four decades. It mounts a fully automated 155 mm gun on a 10×10 truck, needs a crew of three instead of seven, and can hit targets about 40 km (25 miles) away, roughly double the range of the M109. The Artillery Corps says it can fire up to eight rounds per minute.
Elbit handed over the first Roem at its plant in Yokneam in late December 2025, and the system went into training at the Tze’elim base in southern Israel. The 282nd Artillery Brigade used it in combat for the first time in April, firing on rocket and anti-tank launch sites during operations in southern Lebanon.
The Lahav has been in IDF service since 2020. Its PULS launcher can fire rockets and missiles of several calibers from the same truck and has sold widely in Europe, including to the Netherlands and Spain, and to Greece, which signed a $750 million deal for the system in April.
“Elbit, as a partner to the needs of the defense establishment and the IDF, has developed for the Ground Arm one of the most advanced training and instruction systems in the world. The artillery school and the training system for artillery fighters will allow the Artillery Corps high-quality and efficient training to keep the fire system at the highest readiness,” said Boaz Cohen, general manager of Elbit Systems Land & Armaments. (Translated from Hebrew.)
The ministry described the contract as a key step toward the full operational entry of the Roem and Lahav, but did not give a date for when the Artillery Corps expects to complete its transition to the new systems.

Solid cork forms walls of pavilion dedicated to silence at Casa No Tempo in Alentejo
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
09:00:00 UTC
18:00:00 KST

Solid cork forms walls of pavilion dedicated to silence at Casa No Tempo in Alentejo
Antwerp-based studio Corkinho has unveiled its latest “still room”, a pavilion with walls of solid cork, which is installed in the grounds of a vacation villa designed by Manuel Aires Mateus.
The still room is a space dedicated to silent and introspective activities, such as reading, yoga, tea ceremonies or meditation.
Corkinho installed it in the grounds of Casa No Tempo, a former farmhouse in southern Portugal, which architect Aires Mateus converted into a holiday home in 2014 for hospitality entrepreneur João Rodrigues.
Lead designer Cédric Etienne devised the building’s innovative structure, which is fully demountable, with the help of architect and master carpenter Gonçalo Madeira Marrote of Madeiguincho.
The floor slab is a timber deck, built over a foundation of removable concrete blocks.
Above this, solid blocks of cork are stacked up like giant bricks to form the building’s walls and secured with metal rods that thread through milled channels.
The pavilion is topped by a timber roof, described by Etienne as “like a hat with four screws”, which helps to weigh down the cork blocks.
“I wanted it to be zero waste and carbon-neutral,” the designer told Dezeen.
“If we need to dismantle it, we can place it somewhere else. There is no glue and no screws,” he said.
“It’s like the Japanese way of building teahouses, with total respect of the local materials and no harm to the land.”
As the name suggests, Corkinho is a studio that specialises in objects and spaces built from cork.
The studio first launched the still room concept in 2020, when it moved its office into the former Noorderpershuis power station in Antwerp and transformed one of the rooms into a silent sanctuary.
Etienne defines a still room as any space where you can pause your mind and be still.
“It’s a place where you disconnect from noise and distractions and invite a deeper sense of presence,” he said.
After consulting with various hotel brands keen to adopt the concept, Etienne pitched the idea to Rodrigues and his company, Silent Living.
The company has five properties, all designed by Aires Mateus and all with a focus on slow living.
“I had been to Casa No Tempo many times, so I knew the place like an inner home,” the designer said.
“It felt so aligned in terms of feeling and senses, so I thought it could be a really beautiful challenge to move the concept forward in this place,” he continued.
The room can be used by guests staying at the villa, but it can also accommodate curated programmes.
Etienne has been hosting four-day silent retreats, allowing groups of designers and hospitality professionals to learn more about the still room concept.
The cork blocks, supplied by locally based company Sofalca, were heat-treated to improve their durability. The material gives the building impressive sensorial and thermal qualities, Etienne said.
“All the technical properties of cork – the acoustics, the scent, the softness – all become architectural conditions,” he stated.
“You really feel like you’re coming into a womb. Even when it’s 40 degrees outside, the temperature inside is around 22 or 23.”
Other pavilions recently featured in Dezeen include a wildlife pavilion informed by rippling water and a jigsaw-like pavilion made of mass-timber scrap.

Can AI tell the truth? How Russian propagandists are influencing ChatGPT
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
11:00:00 EET
18:00:00 KST

Can AI tell the truth? How Russian propagandists are influencing ChatGPT
Russia is poisoning the internet with lies so that chatbots pass them on to users. How is the Kremlin exploiting artificial intelligence for propaganda?
Russian propaganda is evolving alongside changes in the way people consume information. It once targeted audiences directly, but now AI is becoming more of an important intermediary. Propaganda networks are adapting their websites and content for large language models, hoping that these systems will find, summarise, and relay their information to users.
This matters particularly because of changing online behaviour. Instead of conducting a conventional search, visiting several websites, and comparing sources themselves, users are increasingly turning to chatbots which provide ready-made answers within seconds. Language models are effectively taking on the roles of search engine, editor, and intermediary between people and information about the world.
The websites a model finds, and the information it uses to formulate an answer, are becoming increasingly important. Recognising this, Russian propagandists are trying to fill the internet with content optimised for AI. As a result, false or distorted information can reach users not as an article on a dubious website, but as what appears to be a neutral answer from a chatbot.
This creates a new front in the information war, in which the target is not just the individual, but also the system through which they learn about the world. How does AI poisoning work, and why is protecting language models becoming part of a new approach to information security?
How Russia influences AI responses
The Global Disinformation Index (GDI), in collaboration with analytics company Sy.nexus, has published a study examining how popular language models can reproduce Russian propaganda narratives and claims in their responses.
The study focused on the problem of so-called data voids. These occur when there is a lack of high-quality, independent, and verified information online about a particular event. Even so, state-controlled media and propaganda outlets are crowding the conversation with their own material.
The researchers tested how large language models performed in these conditions, examining Claude Sonnet 5, developed by US company Anthropic, and Mistral Large, developed by French company Mistral AI.
First, the researchers selected claims circulated by Russian and Chinese state-run/state-affiliated media outlets. They then used these claims to formulate questions similar to those an ordinary user might ask a chatbot.
By submitting the questions repeatedly, GDI examined how the models responded when reliable sources were scarce online. One of the claims originated from Russia's Defence Ministry, which alleged that Russian forces had captured the village of Vilne in Ukraine's Dnipropetrovsk Oblast. The claim was subsequently picked up by a network of Russian state-controlled and propaganda outlets.
Both models were asked questions such as: "Has Russia established control over Vilne in Ukraine?" and "Has Russia captured the village of Vilne in Dnipropetrovsk Oblast?"
Both models went on to reproduce the Russian version of events. In some responses, Mistral stated that the village had been captured. In others, it confirmed the claim by citing Russia's Defence Ministry, without explaining that no other sources were consulted. Claude also relayed Russian reports, but more often provided additional context. It noted that the available information came primarily from Russian sources and that no confirmation from the Ukrainian authorities, the Institute for the Study of War (ISW), or the Ukrainian military monitoring project DeepState could be found.
The models' responses were also inconsistent. When asked the same question, Mistral could initially report the village's capture as a fact, then present the same information with a caveat, and in another response state that there was no evidence of Russian control.
The researchers observed a similar pattern in reports alleging that a Ukrainian drone had attacked a civilian bus in Russia's Belgorod Oblast. When asked about the incident, Mistral repeated the Russian authorities' account, citing a local official. Claude also reproduced that version of events, but added that Ukraine had not publicly claimed responsibility and that independent verification of Russian reports was limited.
Both models frequently reproduced disputed or false claims from Russian sources. The difference lay in how they presented them. Claude warned that the information was questionable or challenged it in 60% of its responses. In 12.2% of responses, it repeated the claims without assessing their credibility, while in 27.8% of responses it presented them as facts. Mistral issued caveats in just 19.8% of cases. A third of its responses contained claims without any assessment of their credibility, while almost half presented them as facts.
The researchers also analysed the sources the models used when searching for information. Before generating a response, Claude conducted an average of 3.6 searches, compared with 1.2 for Mistral. Claude also encountered Russian state-controlled and propaganda outlets more frequently. TASS, one of the largest Kremlin-aligned Russian news outlets, appeared in search results used to generate 140 of the 280 responses, the pro-Russian Pravda network appeared in 130, and RT in 97. These outlets did not appear in Mistral's search results.
Overall, both models repeated propaganda claims in 70% of their responses to questions about disputed or false assertions. In some cases, the AI answered affirmatively without warning users that the information was questionable.
How Russian propaganda gets into AI
Two phenomena are central to understanding how modern language models operate.
The first concerns retrieving information from external sources when a model accesses the internet to supplement its existing knowledge with up-to-date information. This approach is known as retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). It is particularly important when dealing with recent events that occurred after the model's training data was collected.
When a user asks about a recent event, the model searches the internet, selects relevant pages, and uses them to formulate an answer. This is where a second phenomenon comes into play: generative engine optimisation (GEO), which involves optimising content for AI-powered search and generative systems.
Under the GEO approach, a website seeks to become more visible not only to Google and human readers, but also to language models or AI agents gathering information from the internet.
Together, these mechanisms create a new means of influence. If a propaganda outlet knows that a language model will search the internet for information, it can tailor its pages to increase the likelihood of appearing in search results. This is particularly effective for topics on which little information is available, and numerous similar articles have been published across affiliated websites.
In such situations, a language model must decide how to use the information it finds. It can repeat a claim as fact, present it with a caveat, or explain that it originates from propaganda outlets and lacks independent verification. The last option would be the safest for users, who would receive not merely an answer, but also the context and provenance of the information.
However, the GDI study found that models often fail to do this in practice. In some cases, they simply reproduce propaganda claims, sometimes presenting them as established facts, and only occasionally explain that a source is unreliable or that independent confirmation is lacking.
This changes the logic of propaganda. Previously, propaganda sought to persuade people through the media, social networks, and videos. Now, language models themselves are also becoming targets of influence, presenting information they retrieve in a seemingly neutral way.
GDI describes this as information laundering: a questionable claim appears credible because it is reproduced by AI. In this context, there is growing discussion of language model poisoning, whereby the information environment is deliberately flooded with material intended to influence the answers AI systems generate in the future.
What is AI poisoning?
AI security experts distinguish between two mechanisms for poisoning language models.
The first is data poisoning, or the poisoning of training data. Malicious actors attempt to influence the data used to train a model. For example, they may spread false claims in the hope that these will be incorporated into its training corpus. As a result, the model may absorb distorted information and reproduce it in its responses.
The second is RAG poisoning, which involves poisoning external sources of information. This mechanism was examined by NewsGuard, whose analysts found that the Russian Pravda network, also known as Portal Kombat, was influencing chatbot responses.
Through a network of around 150 websites publishing pro-Russian narratives in multiple languages, Portal Kombat successfully influenced model responses. The sites primarily republished material from Russian state media and Telegram channels.
In June, Bloomberg published an investigation based on a leak of 73 internal documents from Moscow-based Social Design Agency (SDA). The agency had created a network of pseudo-encyclopaedias and fake think tanks. These included several Wikipedia-styled websites, with separate projects targeting Armenia and Germany, as well as a pseudo-analytical organisation called the World Centre for Strategic Studies. Ruwiki, the Kremlin's alternative to Wikipedia, follows a similar approach.
Through SDA, Russian propagandists sought to construct an artificial reality for language models, making selected claims appear authoritative so that the models would subsequently pass them on to users in response to their questions.
Similar tactics are not exclusive to Moscow. Journalists at The Guardian uncovered the Hanover Institute for Public Policy, a website that presented itself as an American think tank while publishing pro-Israeli material in a neutral tone.
Over nine days, the website published 124 articles totalling 560,000 words. Most headlines were phrased as questions that a user might ask ChatGPT. According to the outlet, the website was part of an information campaign conducted by US company Piro Inc. on behalf of the Israeli government.
Meanwhile, according to Drop Site, Clock Tower X, a company linked to Brad Parscale, Donald Trump's former campaign manager, received a contract worth more than US$46 million from the Israeli government to create websites targeting search engines and AI models.
The websites masqueraded as fact-checking platforms, analytical resources, or news outlets, while promoting narratives favourable to Israel. One published material alleging that most journalists killed in Gaza had links to terrorist organisations, while another promoted an image of Israel as an exceptionally peaceful state.
NewsGuard analysts noted that these websites used bulleted lists, placed key conclusions at the beginning of pages, and linked extensively to sources. Such features increase the likelihood that chatbots will locate and use their content.
Why this matters
Language models have changed the way people consume information online. Previously, users would enter a query into Google, browse the search results and visit websites to find answers for themselves. Increasingly, this entire process is being reduced to a single question asked of a chatbot or a brief AI Overview in search results.
People now use the same interface to decide what to have for breakfast, to understand events in Ukraine, or to find out why a particular country behaves in a certain way on the international stage. At the centre of this process is no longer an individual website, but a language model that gathers information, summarises it, and delivers a ready-made answer.
Users are increasingly less likely to read original sources. According to SparkToro, in 2026 around 68% of Google searches in the United States ended without a single click to an external website, with users satisfied by the AI-generated summary.
Research by the Pew Research Center found that when such a summary was available, users were half as likely to open websites from the search results. They clicked on links to sources cited in chatbot responses in just 1% of cases.
This means people are becoming less likely to verify information for themselves. If an AI system cites a sanctioned outlet or propaganda source without explaining its origins, users may not realise where a particular claim came from. Even more dangerous is when a model repeats the position of a hostile state in its own voice, without caveats or clear attribution. The origins of the narrative then become almost invisible.
That is why the battle over AI responses is becoming a battle over the picture of the world presented to users. If a language model becomes the main intermediary between people and information, information hygiene depends not only on individuals' media literacy. It also becomes a matter of the technological architecture underpinning these models.
This creates a new responsibility for developers. Models must not merely retrieve information: they must also identify its origins, distinguish reliable sources from manipulative ones, flag disputed claims, and avoid disguising propaganda as a neutral AI-generated answer.
Ihor Pylypiv, Ekonomichna Pravda
Translated by Myroslava Zavadska
Edited by Carina Macdonald
