Ukraine and Russia say emergency air-raid warning systems hit by cyber-hacks – Europe live
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
08:59:58 UTC
17:59:58 KST

In Kyiv, residents received a succession of unusual alerts late on Sunday night over the period of roughly an hour.
Typically, people can receive several alerts a day warning of incoming Russian drones or missiles; locals after four years of living in a warzone are used to their phones going off, often followed by sirens in the street.
But these messages warned of radically different threats- a nuclear radiation warning, a chemical attack and even an incident of street fighting in Kyiv.
One of the messages was also transmitted in Russian, a clear tell that something was potentially off.
The messages sent out were:
22:47: “Radiation threat. Radiation threat declared in Kyiv.”
22:48: “Hi! There will be a nuclear alert across Ukraine. Don’t worry, it’s Oreshnik flying” [This message was written in Russia]
22:49: “Chemical threat. There is a threat of a chemical attack on Kyiv. Don’t go outside.”
22:49: “Street fighting threat. Street fighting is taking place in Kyiv. Don’t go outside.”
23:53: An all clear is sent out
Ukrainian authorities within the hour had publicised messages on Telegram saying they believed the app system had been compromised.
The air raid alert channel said “unauthorised parties” had interfered with the system, which had been temporarily taken off line. It urged users to not click on links in “suspicious notifications”.
The Air Force wrote on Telegram: “The Air Alarm application has probably been subjected to hostile interference. There is no radiation threat! Stay calm and follow our updates on our channel.”
Russia resumes attacks, with fortified positions, after Oleshky ceasefire
Luke Harding
The fake nuclear threats to Ukraine came as Russia resumed its attacks on the southern city of Kherson, just hours after the end of a ceasefire during which hundreds of people were evacuated from the nearby Kremlin-controlled town of Oleshky.
Kherson’s military administration said a Russian drone hit a hospital at 7.40am. Video footage showed wrecked rooms, with windows blown out, doors broken, and debris on the street. Nobody was hurt, officials said.
There is evidence that the Russian army used the six-day ceasefire to strengthen its positions in Oleskhy and to rotate in new troops. Bodies of dead civilians were also removed from a hospital morgue.
Footage shared with Sky News showed Russian soldiers deploying heavy military equipment and delivering ammunition. They carried large bags into burned out houses and buildings and disappeared into basements, the broadcaster reported.
Armoured vehicles were spotted moving around Oleshky’s streets. The occupied city is 3 miles from Kherson, on the opposite bank of the Dnipro River. Before last week’s truce, resupply was difficult because of the threat from Ukrainian kamikaze drones.
According to the commander of Ukraine’s 34th Separate Marine Brigade, Dmitry Pulinets, Russian soldiers were previously unable to drive in the city, “neither during the day, nor at night, nor in bad weather”.
“Now they have this opportunity. And for the last few days this movement has been happening constantly,” he told Sky News.
The ceasefire expired at 11pm on Sunday. Both sides hailed the local pause in the fighting – the most significant since 2022 – as a success. Ukraine’s ombudsman, Dmytro Lubinets, who visited Oleshky to coordinate the mission, said it could be repeated on other parts of the frontline.
However, Vladimir Putin’s spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said on Monday there were no plans for another truce elsewhere. He said it was “standard practice” for army units to regroup in “such circumstances” and added that he assumed Ukraine’s armed forces had “done the same”.
'I was briefly terrified'- Kyiv residents on fake nuclear warning
Luke Harding
My colleague, Luke Harding in Kyiv, has also filed this dispatch from the Ukrainian capital where residents received those fake alerts last night, saying they were at risk of an imminent nuclear strike.
Many residents ignored the alerts, which began shortly before 11pm local time, assuming that the app had been compromised.
Others were scared. “I was briefly terrified,” one woman, Nina, said. “I lay on my bed and wondered what was coming.”
The app reported a high possibility of nuclear radiation late on Sunday. It also wrongly warned of a chemical threat to the Ukrainian capital and street-to-street fighting. The messages were written in English with spelling mistakes, as well as in Ukrainian.
A message written in Russian also claimed Ukraine was about to be hit by Oreshnik missiles, which can carry nuclear warheads. The Kremlin has used the ballistic weapon three times before, hitting the Kyiv region, and the cities of Dnipro and Lviv.
It was unclear on Monday who might have carried out the cyber-raid, or why. Russian officials claimed hackers had also sent fake emergency alerts there after gaining access to the app of the ministry for emergencies, based in Moscow.
One of their posts mentioned the hacking group Hitcore. Mash, a Russian Telegram channel with links to the security services, said it had spoken to representatives of Hitcore and that they had claimed responsibility for the attack. The report could not be verified.
My colleague, Jon Henley, is covering this latest wave of supermarket fridge cyber-attacks.
He notes that in the France attacks last month, hackers had remotely overridden the settings on thousands of freezers, fridges and chiller cabinets, pushing them from as low as -27C to well over 50C.
Stores had to discard vast quantities of fresh meat, dairy and frozen products, with many suffering losses ranging from tens of thousands of euros to more than €130,000 (£109,000). Two stores in Alsace reported a combined loss of €270,000.
The Intermarché, Coopérative U, Carrefour, Leclerc and Monoprix chains were among those affected.
Most supermarket cold aisles are connected to the internet to allow remote maintenance and alerts for system failures.
In the French attack, the hackers pirated controllers mostly supplied by the Danish company Danfoss. They disabled alarm systems before adjusting the thermostats or extending the defrost programme by hours.
More supermarket fridge hacks reported in Sweden, Belgium and Luxembourg
Another hacking threat has appeared to resurface again: Supermarket operators across Sweden, Belgium and Luxembourg are reporting that the temperatures in their freezers were raised overnight, leading to huge quantities of spoiled food and other damage.
We saw this sort of attack affect French supermarkets en masse last month – where the fridges and freezers in hundreds of supermarchés were hacked and had their internal temperatures raised.
That led to in-store fires and a loss for supermarkets like Carrefour estimated to be in the hundreds of millions.
This morning, Ahold Delhaize, the Dutch multinational company which operates the Delhaize chain in Belgium and Luxembourg said dozens of its stores had been hit be an “IT incident’. Last month it had also reported hacks in its Albert Heijn stores in the Netherlands. It also operates supermarket chains in Greece( Alfa-Beta Vasilopoulos), Romania (Mega Image) and Serbia (Maxi).
Colruyt, which operates Spar stores in Belgium has also said five shops had their fridge systems attacked.
Swedish supermarkets ICA and Coop have also reported incidents. ICA said the freezer temperature at one store had been set to 50C, similar to the France hacks.
Russian emergency ministry app hacked hours after Ukraine attack
In Russia, authorities said this morning that hackers had gained access to the Emergency Ministry’s mobile app and sent out “fake information”.
The Emergency Ministry said it had to take the app offline temporarily but reassured residents that the wider alert system – SMS texts, broadcasts, street sirens and loudspeakers – was still in operation.
The Russian ministry didn’t say who was to blame for the attack. But Ukrainian media reported claims from Ukrainian cyber group Atesh that they were responsible for sending messages, which also contained nuclear threats.
One of the messages reportedly told residents, there was “a risk of getting lively” and warned them to “stock up urgently on food for three weeks and hide”.
Belgian king 'considering' PM's resignation offer, criticises budget stall
An update in now on the Belgian PM, who’s just left the royal palace where he had a 90minute meeting with the king to offer his resignation.
The palace says that the King is “considering his decision and will consult with the party leaders of the various coalition partners starting tomorrow.”
Prime Minister Bart De Wever had offered his resignation to the king this morning after failing to pass a budget and coalition party talks breaking down last night.
The king admonished the lack of accord between politicians in the current environment of “great geopolitical uncertainty”. His statement reads:
The king regrets that no agreement has been reached on a credible budget aligned with current challenges.
In a context of great geopolitical uncertainty and significant economic challenges, the country cannot afford a prolonged political crisis.
'Disinformation as much a part of war as bombs and bullets'
Frances Mao
Back to the cyber warfare we saw last night in the app hacking in Ukraine, and then Russia.
As I noted earlier, this was direct attack on a core channel of communications between Ukrainian authorities and citizens; this app is embedded in everyday life in a war zone.
And while the full impact of the hack is still unclear – how many Ukrainians were deceived and believed the warnings for example - residents nonetheless have described how alarming it was getting a message on their phone warning of potential nuclear warfare.
Cyber-warfare expert Don Smith, from IT security firm Sophos, says these sorts of attacks are aimed at grounding down people’s mental toughness.
Disinformation is as much a part of war as bombs and bullets. Targeted information attacks could aim to impact the mental resilience of the people of Ukraine.
Their resilience is a key part of their ability to defend against the Russian military.
However he noted the ameaturish nature of this attack. One of the message sent out, in Russian, was almost jokey and casual in tone, reading: “Hi! There will be a nuclear alert across Ukraine. Don’t worry, it’s Oreshnik flying”, a reference to Russia’s hypersonic missiles which can pretzel and outpace most interceptors.
Usually the best information warfare is not obvious or explicit, where this very clearly is. It could indicate desperation from Russia.
Belgian PM meeting with King to tender resignation
Belgium’s prime minister Bart De Wever is handing in his resignation this morning following failed attempts to pass a budget, local media are reporting.
De Wever has been trying to get budget cuts through, and failed in late-night coalition talks yesterday to secure a compromise.
He arrived at the Royal Palace in Brussels this morning to meet with King Philippe, Belgian media say.
However they report he may be instructed to try and secure a deal again, by a certain deadline.
In Kyiv, residents received a succession of unusual alerts late on Sunday night over the period of roughly an hour.
Typically, people can receive several alerts a day warning of incoming Russian drones or missiles; locals after four years of living in a warzone are used to their phones going off, often followed by sirens in the street.
But these messages warned of radically different threats- a nuclear radiation warning, a chemical attack and even an incident of street fighting in Kyiv.
One of the messages was also transmitted in Russian, a clear tell that something was potentially off.
The messages sent out were:
22:47: “Radiation threat. Radiation threat declared in Kyiv.”
22:48: “Hi! There will be a nuclear alert across Ukraine. Don’t worry, it’s Oreshnik flying” [This message was written in Russia]
22:49: “Chemical threat. There is a threat of a chemical attack on Kyiv. Don’t go outside.”
22:49: “Street fighting threat. Street fighting is taking place in Kyiv. Don’t go outside.”
23:53: An all clear is sent out
Ukrainian authorities within the hour had publicised messages on Telegram saying they believed the app system had been compromised.
The air raid alert channel said “unauthorised parties” had interfered with the system, which had been temporarily taken off line. It urged users to not click on links in “suspicious notifications”.
The Air Force wrote on Telegram: “The Air Alarm application has probably been subjected to hostile interference. There is no radiation threat! Stay calm and follow our updates on our channel.”
Good morning and welcome to our live coverage of key events in Europe.
Ukraine and Russia have reported corresponding cyber-hacks on their app warning systems overnight.
These are the mobile apps which send alerts and air-raid warnings, alerting citizens to when missiles and drones are incoming (and thus advising residents to seek shelter or go down to a bunker).
This appears to be the first breach of the app, on such a scale, during the war so far; directly immobilising one of the most important channels of communication authorities have to help advise citizens.
In the Ukraine hack, the app started spewing out alarming fake messages late on Sunday night – warning residents of a nuclear radiation threat in the capital Kyiv, a chemical attack, street fighting and also incoming Oreshnik hypersonic missiles, which Ukraine lacks interceptors for.
Ukraine’s Air Force issued clarification within the hour on Telegram, urging people to remain calm and disregard the messages, one of which was written in Russian.
Some hours later, Russian authorities said its warning app had been hacked and had to be taken offline. A Ukrainian hacker group has claimed to have sent fake alerts warning of nuclear warheads to users inside Russia.
Amid the cyber warfare overnight, both sides also carried out strikes, targeting energy sites like oil refineries. Strikes have been reported in Zaporizhzhia and Odesa.

For US Democrats, climate policy is now about energy bills
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
08:59:00 UTC
17:59:00 KST

For US Democrats, climate policy is now about energy bills
November 2, 2026
President Donald Trump's administration has gutted US climate policy. Yet even as wildfires, record heat waves and flooding hit communities across the country, Democrats are keeping quiet about global warming on the midterm campaign trail.
Instead, candidates are packaging climate policy as an affordability issue, stressing how Americans are struggling to afford gas, groceries and to insure their homes against climate-fueled weather extremes.
Take Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico in Texas, who represents the party's best chance at winning the race in the Republican stronghold in nearly 40 years. Though he makes some mention of climate change on his campaign's "energy and environment" page, that is not his focus.
His pledges center around lowering energy costs, providing emergency relief for spiking utility bills, making data centers pay for their own grid upgrades and growing energy sector jobs.
This aligns with analysis from nonprofit news organization Inside Climate News showing that the Democrats have dramatically reduced mentions of climate change in their press releases and campaign messaging.
"We've entered an interesting space where climate policy doesn't need to be called climate policy to be climate policy," Max Frankel, executive director of the SEEC Institute, a nonprofit that helps guide climate policy in Congress, told DW.
What would a Democratic win mean for climate policy?
Most forecasts project Democrats winning the House and a narrow majority in the Senate in the November 3 election. But without control of the White House, passing any legislation will be difficult and almost any climate policy will have to be a bipartisan endeavor, say analysts.
Given that and the Democrats' messaging-shift to affordability over climate, few experts expect a fully resurrected Inflation Reduction Act. Introduced under the Democrats to create incentives for building clean energy projects, the legislation was largely decimated by President Trump's major tax law.
But Democrats may try to bring back some climate-friendly IRA provisions, particularly measures aimed at lowering household energy costs, analysts told DW. Those include incentives for home energy-efficiency upgrades and appliances like heat pumps to replace oil and gas heaters that typically help bring down household energy bills.
Politicians could also expand an IRA manufacturing tax credit for solar, batteries, and critical minerals that largely survived. One bipartisan bill proposes extending it to include nuclear fusion components.
"It's not going to be anything at the scale of the IRA," Adrian Deveny, founder of Climate Vision, a policy firm dedicated to decarbonization, told DW. "It's like singles and doubles as opposed to a home run, which is still worth doing."
A first bipartisan test over building infrastructure
In a rare area of agreement between the parties, some Democrats and Republicans are already backing a reform bill they're hoping to pass before a new Congress is sworn in January.
If enacted, the bill could make it significantly easier to build major infrastructure projects in the US, including long-distance transmission lines that carry electricity between regions but that currently take years to build because of complex permitting rules.
"The biggest beneficiary of building more transmission will be wind and solar power, because the best and cheapest way to generate wind and solar energy tends to be far away from cities," said David Spence, a political scientist at the University of Texas who researches the politics of energy regulation. "And so, they need transmission to get their product to market."
But environmental groups say the bill could also speed up the approval of fossil fuel projects.
If Democrats win big in the midterms there might be some "peeling off their support for that bill because they think they can do better in the next Congress," said Spence.
Looking to the 2028 presidential elections
Major new federal climate legislation is a long shot before the 2028 presidential election. And afterwards it would likely require Democrats winning the White House, the Senate and the House. While no 2028 platforms have been released yet, policy experts expect a few ideas to feature prominently.
One is data centers. Opposition to the energy-guzzling infrastructure being built en masse to power the AI boom is mounting across the country. Half of Americans are now against data centers being built close to their homes, according to a pollfrom news outlet Politico.
"I'm sure every candidate is going to have a platform with a focus on data center constraints on some level, as a way to address affordability," Deveny, who led negotiations on the IRA, said. "And that's the entry point for climate policy."
There are several ideas currently circulating — including a proposal by Democrats Bernie Sanders and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez to pause data center construction — as well as ending tax breaks for data centers and imposing new taxes on their electricity use.
Democrats may also seek to restore the IRA's clean energy tax incentives. This year, more than 150 legislators co-sponsored the so-called Energy Bills Relief Act designed to reinstate IRA clean energy tax incentives, reform how transmission permits are granted, and make data centers pay for the grid upgrades they need. The bill is unlikely to pass anytime soon but offers a window into what Democrats might support.
"By far, the biggest consensus — to the extent there's anything remotely resembling a consensus — is restoring a lot of the clean energy tax incentives from the IRA," Deveny said. "Not everybody supports that but it is a highly supported idea amongst most congressional Democrats."
Support for other proposals include a new federal program to help insurers cover climate-driven disasters and bring down hefty premiums, as well as so-called climate superfunds. This would require fossil fuel companies to contribute to the costs of damage caused by extreme weather and adapting to the risks of climate change.
Vermont and New York both passed legislation to create funds, although a federal judge blocked New York's.
The 2028 presidential race is expected to begin a few weeks after the midterms end, bringing a fresh round of policy ideas and debates. A new president typically gets to drive the legislative agenda in the beginning of their term if their party also wins Congress.
"As long as the consensus is that clean energy is the cheaper source of energy, and it's going to provide stability over the long term for high energy costs — there's a million ways you can propose solutions through that lens," Deveny said. 
Edited by: Jennifer Collins

French school protests resume on smaller scale as students return from break
Italy
Unknown Publisher

09:58:40 CET
17:58:40 KST

PARIS, Nov 2 (Reuters) - French high school student protests resumed on Monday on a much smaller scale than in past weeks as pupils returned from a two-week break, with youngsters trying to blockade a few high schools in Paris, Marseille and Rennes, French media reported.
Hundreds of France’s more than 3,000 high schools were blockaded in the weeks prior to the break. The protests, which began in the Paris suburbs in September, have spread across France and broadened beyond education to focus on the cost of living, drawing in trade unionists and activists and sometimes turning violent.
A wave of so-called “Gen Z” protests has swept across European countries including Germany, Italy, Belgium and Albania, driven by grievances including the cost of living, the poor state of schools and perceived corruption
Last month French protests degenerated into violent clashes with the police and outright riots in several cities, with shops looted, in a test for President Emmanuel Macron’s minority government.
“In terms of blockades—or rather, attempted blockades—the phenomenon is very marginal. We’re talking about just a handful of units, a few individual schools,” Education Minister Edouard Geffray told radio station France Inter on Monday morning.
He said protests are allowed but preventing access to schools is illegal.
Police officers were present, TV footage showed, though not in full anti-riot gear.
Students want the renovation of aging schools, more teachers, more university places and the end of a university admissions system they see as socially unfair.
Geffray offered last week to cap class sizes at 28, dedicate €4 billion ($4.47 billion) to renovating schools, create 15,000 new places for students in higher education and a new admission system by 2028. High school student representatives said the offers were not enough and they would keep protesting.
($1 = 0.8948 euros)

Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever pictured ahead of a meeting at the Egmont Palace, in Brussels, on Oct. 23, 2026. | Belga photo by Benoit Doppagne via AFP/Getty Images
BRUSSELS— Belgium’s King Philippe is considering Prime Minister Bart De Wever’s resignation after the premier offered to step down following failed attempts by his coalition government to agree to plug a €10 billion budget gap.
In an 11th-hour attempt to reach a deal for next year’s budget, top officials from De Wever’s five-party government gathered over the weekend, but left without an agreement early Monday morning. Tuesday was widely seen as the unofficial deadline to strike a deal, as the budget still has to pass through parliament before the end of the year.
As part of the talks, De Wever wanted to show financial markets that Belgium is on track to meet its European obligations. Belgium had a deficit of 5.2 % of GDP in 2025, which is expected to rise further next year.
Advertisement
After De Wever offered his resignation Monday morning, the palace said the king was “postponing his decision” and “will begin consultations tomorrow with the party leaders of the various coalition partners.” It added that the king “is appealing to everyone’s sense of responsibility and urges all stakeholders to prioritize the general interest and a spirit of compromise.”
The prime minister is expected to meet the king again on Friday.
De Wever had ruled out starting the new year with a temporary budget, which would let the government continue with the same budget as last year’s.
Budget talks have been ongoing for weeks, with tensions emerging mostly between the Flemish socialists of Forward and the Francophone center-right Reformist Movement.
The former asked for more contributions from the highest incomes, through taxes, while the latter ruled that out and pushed back against a wider reform of value-added tax.
There were still “far too many taxes on the table,” David Clarinval, deputy prime minister for the Reformist Movement, told reporters when talks broke up. He didn’t rule out discussions resuming today.
Advertisement
Last November, Belgium’s budget talks also went into extra time. On this occasion, De Wever did not tender his resignation, but requested an extension to budget talks from King Philippe. The king granted him an additional 50 days to reach an agreement.
If Belgium is on track for snap elections, the country could lean toward extreme parties, with both the far-right Vlaams Belang and the far-left Workers Party performing well in the polls.

PROFILE – Kimi Antonelli: Formula 1’s youngest world champion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
08:56:53 UTC
17:56:53 KST

- Five consecutive victories in China, Japan, Miami, Canada and Monaco helped Antonelli build an early advantage in the championship race
Mercedes driver Kimi Antonelli became the youngest world champion in Formula One history Sunday, winning the title in only his second season after replacing seven-time champion Lewis Hamilton.
The Italian secured his maiden championship by finishing third behind Max Verstappen and Hamilton at the Mexico City Grand Prix, putting the title beyond the reach of his rivals with four rounds remaining.
The result lifted Antonelli to 380 points, giving him an unassailable 121-point advantage over Hamilton, his nearest rival, with a maximum of 100 points still available.
Aged 20 years and two months, Antonelli broke the record set by Sebastian Vettel, who was 23 when he won the 2010 championship.
He also became the first Italian to claim the drivers’ crown since Alberto Ascari in 1953, ending a 73-year wait.
 
From Bologna to Hamilton’s Mercedes seat
Born in Bologna on Aug. 25, 2006, Antonelli began karting at an early age under the guidance of his father, Marco, a sportscar driver and team owner.
Mercedes recruited him to its junior program in 2019, when he was 12.
Antonelli won the Italian and German Formula 4 championships in 2022 before claiming the Formula Regional Middle East and European titles the following year.
Mercedes then allowed him to bypass Formula 3 and move directly into Formula 2 in 2024. He finished sixth, winning races at Silverstone and the Hungaroring.
The team made an even bolder decision for 2025, selecting the 18-year-old to replace Hamilton after the seven-time world champion left Mercedes for Ferrari.
Antonelli stepped into one of the most closely scrutinized seats in motorsport after just one season in Formula 2.
Although he did not win a race, he finished seventh in his rookie season with three podiums and became the youngest driver to lead a Grand Prix and record a fastest lap.
 
Second-season breakthrough
Antonelli opened the 2026 season by finishing second behind Mercedes teammate George Russell at the Australian Grand Prix on March 8.
One week later in China, he became Formula One’s youngest Grand Prix polesitter before converting pole position into his maiden victory. The result also made him the sport’s second-youngest race winner behind Verstappen.
Victory at the third round in Japan on March 29 made Antonelli the youngest driver to lead the world championship.
He then won in Miami, Canada and Monaco, extending his run to five consecutive victories.
His Monaco performance was particularly dominant. 
Antonelli became the race’s youngest winner and completed his first career Grand Slam by taking pole position, recording the fastest lap and leading every lap.
His momentum was interrupted by mechanical problems. An electrical failure forced him to retire while running second in Barcelona, while another car problem and a time penalty left him without Grand Prix points in Britain, reducing his championship lead over Russell to 25 points.
Antonelli responded by winning in Belgium on July 19, holding off Charles Leclerc after a safety-car restart and a late challenge. Podiums in Hungary and the Netherlands helped him rebuild his advantage.
His defining performance came at the Italian Grand Prix at Monza on Sept. 6, where a power-unit change left him 19th on the grid.
Antonelli charged through the field and overtook Russell in the closing laps, becoming the first Italian to win his home Grand Prix since Ludovico Scarfiotti in 1966.
Mercedes team principal Toto Wolff called it an “amazing drive” and said “there was nothing that would have stopped him.”
“Even starting P19, I believed that this might be possible,” Antonelli said after what he described as the most special victory of his career.
A week later, Antonelli won the Spanish Grand Prix in Madrid to extend his championship lead to 81 points.
He remained on the podium in Bahrain and Singapore before taking his ninth victory in Austin on Oct. 25. 
The result increased his advantage over Russell to 123 points, leaving him within two points of securing the championship before Mexico.
 
Handling the title pressure
Antonelli acknowledged feeling the pressure before the decisive race.
“I’ve been a bit more tense this weekend than usual,” he said after qualifying, adding that it had been difficult to keep his emotions under control.
He nevertheless completed the task by finishing third Sunday, becoming world champion seven years after joining the Mercedes junior program.
“We did it! And I wouldn’t be here without Mercedes and without my family,” Antonelli said after the race. “I’m speechless, I’m trying to process what’s just happened.”
Even before he secured the title, his performances had earned praise from the two British drivers who remained his only mathematical rivals.
“The reality is my teammate has done a better job than me this year,” Russell said in September. “He deserves to be leading.”
Hamilton, whose Mercedes seat Antonelli inherited, also praised him after the Monaco Grand Prix in June.
“Kimi’s doing an incredible job, just delivering weekend in, weekend out,” Hamilton said. “It’s great to see.”
The title gave Mercedes its first drivers’ championship since Hamilton’s final crown in 2020.
It also vindicated the team’s decision to accelerate Antonelli’s career: a driver promoted to Formula One at 18 became its youngest champion in only his second season.

Outside parties broke into Air Alert, Ukraine’s main air raid warning app, late on 1 November and pushed false threat warnings to users’ phones, the app’s developers confirmed. Ukraine’s Air Force said there was no radiation threat and that the app had likely come under enemy influence. The developers suspended the app overnight and then began restoring it.
The fake leaned on a fear Russia keeps feeding. Russia has fired the Oreshnik, its intermediate-range ballistic missile, at Ukraine three times. The most recent strike came on 24 May near Bila Tserkva, a day after Ukraine warned of a possible strike with Kyiv among likely targets. In September, a Russian lawmaker threatened a fourth launch.
What users received
Around 22:45, the app began sending alerts about chemical and radiation threats and street fighting in Kyiv. Some messages were in Russian. They warned of an Oreshnik strike and carried a link to a Telegram channel.
Shortly after 23:00, the Air Force urged Ukrainians to stay calm and follow its own channel for updates.
The app’s team said outside parties had interfered with the app without authorization. It had disabled push notifications and temporarily suspended the app. The team added that the app stores no personal data, so users face no threat. It urged them not to open links from suspicious notifications.
Before 02:00 on 2 November, the developers said they were gradually bringing the app back after the cyberattack. The map again shows yellow and red danger levels, which cover drone attacks and massive drone or missile attacks, and push alerts are working. The display of targets on the map remains suspended.
Sirens kept working
Meanwhile, sirens and other warning systems kept working, Ukraine’s Digital Transformation Ministry said. It advised people to turn on emergency alerts on their phones and to rely only on official Air Force channels. In the capital, alerts in the Kyiv Digital city app worked normally, the ministry added. Ajax Systems built the app in 2022 at the initiative of IT company Stfalcon, with the ministry’s support.

Italy considers Türkiye a crucial partner in European security and seeks closer cooperation on regional stability, NATO and international initiatives, Italian Ambassador to Türkiye Giuseppe Manzo told Anadolu in an exclusive interview.
"We really believe that Türkiye has a crucial role in our security," Manzo said, emphasizing the importance of European security within the broader NATO framework.
"I think it's fair to say that we both want more Europe in NATO," he added.
The ambassador said strengthening political cooperation on regional security was among his priorities, highlighting the NATO summit, the 4+4 meeting and COP31 as opportunities for closer coordination.
He also pointed to shared concerns about threats facing NATO's eastern and southern flanks.
"We need to adapt to new challenges and find new answers to new questions and new threats," he said.
"I think Italy and Türkiye are very well equipped to do this."
Manzo said the countries' geographical positions -- Italy in the Mediterranean and Türkiye at the crossroads of Europe and Asia -- offered opportunities to develop new approaches to regional and international challenges.
"By nature, we are well positioned to develop new answers and new tools to address both old problems and new challenges," he said.
 
Trade, cultural ties and international cooperation
The ambassador highlighted the countries' longstanding relationship as they mark 170 years of diplomatic ties.
He described Italy as Türkiye's leading trading partner in the Mediterranean and its second-largest in Europe.
Manzo also emphasized educational and cultural exchanges, noting that Turkish students make up the second-largest international student community in Italy.
He pointed to archaeological cooperation, with Italian scholars and Turkish archaeologists working together on 15 missions.
On international governance, Manzo voiced support for reforming the UN Security Council to make it "more transparent and democratic."
He recalled receiving a book from Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan containing the phrase "The world is bigger than five," describing the message as relevant to discussions on reforming international institutions.
The ambassador also highlighted cooperation in space exploration, including joint satellite projects and Türkiye's first astronaut traveling to space alongside Italian astronauts.
 
'I felt at home'

Japan tracks Chinese destroyers and supply ships near Okinawa
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
08:53:11 UTC
17:53:11 KST

- Japan tracked a Chinese Luyang III destroyer and Fuyu-class support ship heading into the East China Sea through the Miyako Strait on Nov. 1.
- A second Luyang III destroyer and a Fuchi-class supply ship sailed the opposite way into the Pacific on Nov. 2, watched by Japanese P-1 and P-3C aircraft.
Japan tracked four Chinese navy ships moving through the Miyako Strait between Okinawa and Miyako Island over two days, with one destroyer pair heading back into the East China Sea and another heading out into the Pacific, the Joint Staff of Japan’s Defense Ministry said in a post on Nov. 2.
On Nov. 1, a Luyang III-class guided-missile destroyer and a Fuyu-class fast combat support ship sailed northwest through the strait toward the East China Sea. On Nov. 2, a second Luyang III-class destroyer and a Fuchi-class replenishment ship sailed southeast through the same waters toward the Pacific. The Joint Staff did not give the ships’ hull numbers or say where either group was going.
The Japan Maritime Self-Defense Force watched both transits from the air. A P-1 maritime patrol aircraft from Fleet Air Wing 1 at Kanoya, in Kagoshima Prefecture, and a P-3C Orion from Fleet Air Wing 5 at Naha, on Okinawa, carried out surveillance and intelligence gathering, the Joint Staff said.
The Luyang III, known in China as the Type 052D, is the Chinese navy’s most numerous modern air defense destroyer, armed with vertical-launch cells for surface-to-air, anti-ship and land-attack missiles. The Fuyu class, or Type 901, is China’s largest class of replenishment ship, built to keep aircraft carrier groups supplied with fuel and ammunition at sea. The smaller Fuchi class, or Type 903, is the navy’s standard fleet oiler and supply ship. Pairing a destroyer with a supply ship lets the warship stay at sea for longer deployments beyond China’s coastal waters.
The Miyako Strait, about 250 km (155 miles) wide, lies within Japan’s exclusive economic zone but is an international waterway that foreign warships may legally transit. It is one of the main routes the Chinese navy uses to reach the western Pacific from its bases on the East China Sea.
Chinese traffic through the strait has been heavy in recent weeks. The aircraft carrier Liaoning and three destroyers sailed through it into the Pacific on Oct. 14 and carried out flight operations south of Ishigaki Island. On Oct. 27, the Type 055 destroyer Lhasa, the Type 052D destroyer Xining, the frigate Yancheng and the supply ship Hoh Xil Lake also transited the strait, and Chinese Y-9 surveillance aircraft crossed the gap between Okinawa and Miyako on several days in late October, prompting Japanese fighter scrambles. The activity coincided with Keen Sword, a large U.S.-Japan military exercise that ran from Oct. 19 to 29.

Põltsamaa school hires security amid ongoing student disruptions
Põltsamaa Basic School is bringing in security patrols and equipping staff with panic buttons after repeated disruptions by a small group of students.
The school's Põltsamaa campus has 603 students, but a small handful of sixth- and seventh-graders has been causing ongoing problems with their conduct, said principal Henry Kallaste.
"They skip school, and when they do show up, they disrupt classes, run through the halls and kick trash cans," Kallaste said. This in turn distracts other students, even leaving some classmates frightened.
The final straw, he said, was when the students in question broke into the school building one evening.
Starting Monday, the school and municipality will bring in security guards and give staff panic buttons to summon security when needed. The goal, Kallaste explained, is to allow students to learn and teachers to teach in peace, while giving parents confidence that their children are safe.
Mayor Taavi Aas said the municipality had contacted police, but patrols are not always readily available in smaller towns. For now, Põltsamaa Municipality has hired private security through the end of the year, at a cost of a few thousand euros a month.
"It's not prohibitively expensive, but of course it will depend on how often staff use the panic buttons and how many calls security responds to," he added.
Mayor: Current measures 'don't work on everyone'
Aas said officials are continuing to work with the students to change their behavior, but the process can be a lengthy one, particularly for kids under 14. Seeking a court order for placement in a secure educational facility is a multi-step process requiring extensive evidence, he explained.
The municipal mayor added that the situation in Põltsamaa reflects a broader nationwide problem, arguing that a sense of impunity among kids under 14 can breed trouble in other municipalities as well.
"The only measures we can use to guide them are persuasion, talking to them and social programs," Aas said. "Unfortunately, that doesn't work on everyone."
He argued that some sort of disciplinary measure should be easier to impose, warning that delays in the current process allow disruptive behavior to continue and affect others.

WSJ: US pushes to resume Russian gas supplies to Europe via Ukraine
The United States is supporting the swift resumption of Russian natural gas supplies to Europe via pipelines running through Ukraine as part of negotiations aimed at reaching an energy ceasefire ahead of the approaching winter.
Source: The Wall Street Journal, citing its own sources among US and European officials
Details: The idea, put forward by US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff during trips to Moscow and Kyiv in September, would involve selling Russian gas through a US intermediary to circumvent European sanctions – and could offer a lucrative opportunity for US investors, according to people involved in the discussions.
The WSJ noted that the issue has become particularly relevant since Ukraine resumed strikes on Russian oil refineries. US officials also believe that Russia's return to the European market would serve as an incentive for Kremlin leader Vladimir Putin to agree to a deal and would provide Kyiv with revenue from transit fees.
White House officials have proposed that Russia deposit the proceeds from gas sales to Europe into an account in a third country so that the Kremlin could not use the money to finance the war.
The WSJ reported that they had sought to persuade the EU to support the proposal, even though under current EU legislation all purchases of Russian natural gas must be completely phased out by the end of 2027.
European officials cited by the newspaper indicated that the EU broadly rejects the idea of allowing Russian gas to return to its markets.
The US, for its part, is now considering the possible resumption of Nord Stream pipeline operations as a potentially important element of a broader agreement – not only to end the war in Ukraine but also to resolve longstanding disputes between Russia and America's European allies.
Earlier reports indicated that the US had proposed that European countries unfreeze some Russian sovereign assets blocked following the start of Russia's full-scale war against Ukraine and transfer them to a financial vehicle under Washington's control in an effort to revive peace negotiations.
Background: On 9 October, US President Donald Trump said he had spoken with Russian leader Vladimir Putin and reached an agreement with him on supplying Russian diesel fuel to US and global markets.

IDF ends controversial Hebron operation after days of terror probe, forced evacuations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
08:49:48 UTC
17:49:48 KST

The IDF on Monday announced it is exiting the Hebron neighborhood it has occupied since last weekend.
The Jerusalem Post reported on Thursday that this might occur as early as this past weekend.
None of this was certain, and the situation was highly dynamic, since, to date, pre-elections, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu rejected the clear recommendation from IDF Chief of Staff Lt.-Gen. Eyal Zamir to leave the area and allow the at least 2,000 evacuated Palestinians to return to their homes.
But there was some increased expectation that Netanyahu might show more flexibility to IDF recommendations now that the election has passed and he feels in a stronger political position than expected.
The IDF occupied the area in response to last Friday morning’s deadly Hamas terrorist attack and noted that the terrorists were connected to a broader Hamas clan in the neighborhood in question, though the IDF never presented concrete evidence of how most of the 2,000 evacuees could be connected to any specific crime.
IDF recommended return of evacuated Palestinians last week
Already by Sunday-Monday of last week, the IDF was recommending that it allow the evacuated Palestinians to return, saying that it had inspected all of the relevant areas, and there was no clear military reason to remain.
The forced evacuations from Hebron appear to be different from other recent incidents.
Although in early 2025, Israel cleared areas of Jenin, Tulkarm, and Nur al-Shams in the West Bank, evacuating close to 40,000 Palestinians, those areas had experienced well-documented mass terror incidents dating back to early 2022.
The IDF carried out multiple temporary evacuations at that time and even sent in the Palestinian Authority to fight large and organized terror groups before undertaking the mass evacuation and destroying several structures in those areas.
In contrast, this time, the IDF provided little information about the offenses of the 2,000 evacuated Palestinians, other than to say that they were familially connected to the Hamas-linked Gaza clan.
While during the 2015-2016 stabbing intifada and in earlier years, Hebron had been one of the most violent and unstable areas – and there have been some terror incidents emanating from Hebron over the past three years of war – generally, it has not been one of the leading problem spots.
In addition, the IDF said it destroyed illegally built structures that could make security operations harder to carry out. However, the military was extremely vague about what those operations were and why entire buildings needed to be destroyed to carry them out.
Pressed about how many of the 2,000 hamula (“clan”) members have records linking them to terror (or at a minimum, to rock throwing), multiple IDF sources did not appear to have any specific information on the topic.
Rather, the operation seemed to be motivated by public statements made by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defense Minister Israel Katz about clearing or destroying the neighborhood of the two men involved in the terror incident on Friday – apparently a collective punishment measure.
While Israel has placed closures on terror-emanating areas in the past, it has not carried out mass evacuations and building demolitions to such an extent without a specific connection to those being impacted.
Meanwhile, Adalah petitioned the High Court of Justice last Thursday on behalf of Hebron’s municipality and seven residents, seeking to halt what it described as forced evacuations and demolitions during an IDF operation, and secure the return of residents ordered out of their homes.
The petition asks for an immediate order barring further evacuations and the demolition of homes, businesses and other civilian buildings while the case is considered. It also seeks safe passage for medical teams, emergency vehicles and municipal workers, arguing that sweeping movement restrictions are cutting residents off from essential services.
Petition alleges troops seized homes, demolished civilian infrastructure
According to the petition, troops ordered families in the Ein Deir Baha and al-Jalda neighborhoods of western Hebron to leave their homes around 12:30-1 a.m. on the night of October 23-24. Orders were announced over loudspeakers, leaving residents insufficient time to prepare, the petitioners said.
Residents were told they could not return until further notice, without being given a timetable or conditions for their return, the petition alleges. It says some families spent the night outside and some residents were unable to take their vehicles with them.
Municipal figures cited in the petition put the number of families affected by the operation at 780, which could reach much higher than the original 2,000 estimate, up to 4,969 people, which itself was up from 488 families and 3,171 people earlier.
The petition alleges that troops took over some homes and turned them into military positions, while demolishing civilian buildings and requiring traders to remove goods from their businesses at short notice.
It says restrictions also affect residents who remain at home, hindering access to medical treatment and the movement of ambulances and emergency vehicles. According to the municipality’s figures cited in the filing, blocked access routes had prevented rubbish collection and left approximately 1,200 tons of waste accumulating across the city by Wednesday.
Adalah argues that the scale and open-ended nature of the evacuations violate international humanitarian law. Article 49 of the Fourth Geneva Convention permits temporary evacuation where civilian safety or imperative military reasons require it, and requires evacuees to be returned once hostilities in the area have ended.
The petitioners contend that no specific justification has been provided for evacuations on this scale. They argue that barring residents’ return indefinitely, while damaging or taking over their homes, risks making their displacement lasting.
They also invoke the convention’s prohibition on destroying property unless military operations make it absolutely necessary, arguing that a general reference to security needs cannot justify demolitions across residential neighborhoods.
The petition further alleges collective punishment, citing both the measures imposed on residents and statements by Israeli officials presenting the operation as a means of exacting a price for the shooting. The convention prohibits punishing protected civilians for offenses they did not personally commit.
Adalah said it approached the authorities on Sunday and sent a reminder the following day, but had received no substantive response by the time it filed the petition.
The case names the defense minister, the head of IDF Central Command, the military advocate-general and the attorney-general as respondents. Alongside an urgent hearing, the petitioners seek immediate protection against further evacuations and demolitions, followed by orders lifting the challenged restrictions and ensuring residents’ safe return.
Already on Sunday, the Association for Civil Rights in Israel (ACRI) demanded that displaced residents be allowed to return, movement restrictions be lifted, and demolitions carried out as punishment be halted. It also requested the orders authorizing the measures already taken.
It argued that public statements by ministers indicated a punitive purpose, including Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich’s description of demolitions as serving as deterrence and as exacting a price for the attack.
“No attack, however grave, gives the military license to punish an entire city,” ACRI executive director Noa Sattath said.
In an initial decision last Friday, Justice Gila Canfy Steinitz directed the state to respond and said she expected it to refrain from changing the existing situation or demolishing additional buildings, pending a further decision.

Anthrax outbreak kills hippos in DR Congo’s Virunga National Park
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
08:49:32 UTC
17:49:32 KST

Anthrax outbreak kills hippos in DR Congo’s Virunga National Park
Drought and conflict compound the threat to wildlife in eastern DR Congo.
Vitshumbi, DR Congo – While the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) continues to grapple with the deadliest Ebola outbreak in its history, another disease is taking a heavy toll on wildlife in Virunga National Park in the country’s east.
Over the past four weeks, hippopotamus carcasses have been discovered in the Semuliki River, west of Africa’s oldest national park, raising concern among communities living along its banks.
“It was in mid-September that we began to notice the mass deaths of hippos in the Semuliki River. We have started to fear this situation, which is unfolding whilst we are in the midst of the Ebola outbreak,” Michael Kambale, a resident of the Vitshumbi enclave, about 100 kilometres (62 miles) north of Goma, the capital of North Kivu province, told Al Jazeera.
Following laboratory tests, Virunga National Park confirmed that anthrax, caused by the bacterium Bacillus anthracis, was responsible for the wildlife deaths.
According to park officials, 28 hippos died over approximately one month.
“This disease can be transmitted to humans through contact with a dead or sick animal or by consuming its meat,” Virunga National Park said in a press release sent to Al Jazeera.
Anthrax threatens wildlife and local communities
Joel Mbusa Mapoli, an expert in ecology and veterinary medicine, said the deaths represented a significant loss for Virunga National Park and called for urgent action to contain the outbreak.
He explained that hippos act as ecosystem engineers, altering nutrient flows and the ecological conditions of their habitats.
Virunga National Park said it was focusing on surveillance, the safe management of carcasses and reducing risks to wildlife and local communities.
“Teams are monitoring the affected area, recording new cases of mortality and coordinating the safe handling and disposal of carcasses,” the park said.
“People living in the affected area and its surroundings are being informed about the outbreak; they are advised not to touch, skin or consume animals found dead, and to report any carcasses or suspected cases to the relevant authorities,” the park added.
Founded in 1925, Virunga is Africa’s oldest national park and is renowned for its biodiversity.
Conflict puts conservation at risk
Olivier Ndoole Bahemuke, a Congolese environmental activist and head of Alerte Congolaise pour l’environnement et les droits de l’homme, a nonprofit organisation operating in the DRC, said the armed conflict that has persisted in the country for nearly three decades had fuelled poaching and deforestation.
The park says it has lost control of a significant part of its territory over the past four years because of the ongoing conflict between the Congolese army and M23 fighters.
The M23 armed group says it is helping protect the area from poachers and other potential human threats.
Drought and recurring anthrax outbreaks
Park officials said anthrax outbreaks had previously been observed among hippos and other wild animals in the ecosystem during periods of drought.
According to Mapoli, several factors contribute to recurring anthrax outbreaks in Virunga National Park. These include the persistence of the bacterium in the environment, deteriorating ecological and climatic conditions, the concentration of animals around aquatic habitats and difficulties in monitoring wildlife health.
“When vegetation becomes scarce, herbivores may graze closer to the ground and congregate around the few remaining grazing areas and water points, thereby increasing their exposure to contaminated soil,” Virunga National Park said in a statement sent to Al Jazeera, adding that the situation was being monitored “closely”.
The park’s February 2026 census estimated the hippo population at more than 2,700, distributed across 171 groups.
In 2025, an anthrax outbreak killed 65 hippos in Virunga National Park, according to the park’s February 2026 population update. Park staff mobilised excavators to retrieve the carcasses from the water.
According to park officials, anthrax can survive for decades in the soil in the form of spores.
Protecting hippos means protecting the ecosystem
Mapoli said the response to anthrax should combine conservation measures with public health interventions, in line with the One Health principle, an approach that recognises the links between human, animal and environmental health.
He called for stronger epidemiological surveillance, better protection for local communities, proper management of animal carcasses and greater collaboration among state, non-state and para-state bodies.
“The hippopotamus is one of the flagship species of the Virunga ecosystems. Its disappearance could lead to a major disruption of aquatic ecosystems, as these animals play a role in the exchange of matter between terrestrial and aquatic environments,” he told Al Jazeera.

Most Flemings opting for cremation, significant differences with Brussels and Wallonia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
08:48:32 UTC
17:48:32 KST

More and more people are being cremated after their death: in Flanders, the cremation rate has risen above 80 per cent for the first time this year. As a result visits to the cemetery on 1 November, All Saints’ Day, increasingly take on a different form. In Brussels and Wallonia, people are still far more often opting for burial.
Most Flemings opting for cremation, significant differences with Brussels and Wallonia
“The number of cremations is rising for various reasons,” says Tom Wustenberghs, chair of the Flemish Association of Crematoria. “On the one hand, there is the practical aspect: a cremation offers the bereaved or the funeral director flexibility when planning the funeral. Cremations are also increasingly taking place well ahead of the ceremony,” he notes.
In addition, there is the matter of aftercare. “For most people who opt for a cremation, the ashes are subsequently scattered. Usually in a garden of rest, but they can also be scattered at sea or, for example, in the River Scheldt in a biodegradable urn. In such cases, there is no longer a physical grave that needs to be maintained afterwards,” explains Wustenberghs.
Cost can also be a factor, but whether cremation is always cheaper than a burial “depends on individual choices”. “The most recent studies I’ve seen on this estimate the cost of a funeral at around 6,500 euros, whether it’s a burial or a cremation. In the case of a cremation, this includes the costs of the funeral director, collection and preparation, the coffin and the urn, the cremation itself, and the ceremony, excluding catering.”
Major differences with Brussels
There are major differences between the regions. Whilst 81 per cent of people in Flanders now opt for cremation, the figure in Brussels is 63 per cent. However, the figures for Brussels are not entirely accurate. Anyone living in Brussels, but who is cremated in Flanders will, in fact, be counted in the Flemish figures.
According to Wustenberghs, the difference in Brussels can be explained by the large number of different religious communities. “According to Islamic rules, it is forbidden to cremate a body,” says Mustapha Ouriaghli, a Muslim funeral director from Schaarbeek in Brussels.
“Nevertheless, we are also seeing many changes here. The first generation, who moved to Brussels in the 1960s, often still opted for repatriation and a burial in their country of origin,” he explains. “But with the second and third generations, it’s completely different. Since the coronavirus pandemic, we’ve really seen a shift in that regard.”
"People are much more likely to choose to be buried in a Muslim plot here in Belgium, so that their families can easily pay their respects afterwards. As a result, the demand for plots is also increasing. Not every municipality in Brussels is doing enough to anticipate these growing needs," says Ouriaghli.
Even lower in Wallonia
In Wallonia, the ‘cremation rate’ (the number of cremations as a proportion of the total number of deaths) is even lower. “Wallonia is a lot more traditional in that respect,” explains Wustenberghs. “But the distance to the crematorium, which is greater in Wallonia, also plays a role.”
“In any case, we are seeing that cremation is chosen much more frequently in cities. In Ghent and Antwerp, the cremation rate is sometimes higher than 90 per cent,” he says. “In Limburg and West Flanders, however, it is somewhat lower. And in Wallonia, too, the number of cremations is particularly lower in rural areas.”

Türkiye seeks stronger South Korea partnership in energy, tech, logistics: President Erdogan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
08:48:06 UTC
17:48:06 KST

Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan has identified South Korea as a potential key partner in Türkiye’s planned second nuclear power plant in Sinop on the country's Black Sea coast.
In an interview with Yonhap News Agency ahead of his state visit to Seoul this week, Erdogan said the visit aims to strengthen political dialogue and reinvigorate economic ties between the two countries.
"We regard the Republic of Korea as a great potential collaborator on this initiative," Erdogan said.
South Korea and Türkiye signed a memorandum of understanding on nuclear energy cooperation during South Korean President Lee Jae Myung's state visit to Türkiye last year. The agreement provides for cooperation in reactor technology, site assessment, licensing, financing and business models.
According to Erdogan, Türkiye has since conducted extensive preliminary feasibility studies with South Korea's state-run Korea Electric Power Corp. (KEPCO) and continues to assess the project's technical and economic viability.
"We attach considerable importance to the negotiations we are holding with Korea on this topic. We are well aware of our Korean friends' experience with nuclear energy," he said.
However, Erdogan stressed that Ankara's final decision would depend on several considerations, including electricity generation costs, financing arrangements and the project's potential contribution to the Turkish economy.
"We are taking into account our contacts with other countries and examining all possible choices in light of our national interests," he said.
 
Broader cooperation in technology and defense
Beyond nuclear energy, Erdogan expressed optimism about expanding cooperation in semiconductors, robotics, artificial intelligence (AI), defense and other advanced technologies.
"Our goal is to transform these prospects into tangible initiatives, facilitate business opportunities for our companies, and enhance reciprocal investments," he said.
The Turkish president also welcomed South Korea's interest in Türkiye’s PD170 turbodiesel aircraft engine, highlighting opportunities for deeper defense industry cooperation in unmanned aerial vehicles, engine technologies and electronic systems.
He encouraged South Korean companies to increase their investments in Türkiye and establish closer partnerships with Turkish businesses, particularly in joint production and technology development.
"With its strong manufacturing infrastructure, skilled workforce and strategic location, Türkiye offers significant opportunities for Korean investors," Erdogan said.
"By combining the Republic of Korea's expertise in technology and innovation with Türkiye's manufacturing strength, we can achieve far greater success."
As examples of successful bilateral economic cooperation, Erdogan cited Hyundai Motor Group's longstanding automotive manufacturing operations in Türkiye and South Korean steelmaker POSCO's investments in the country's steel industry.
He also welcomed Hyundai's launch of electric vehicle production at its plant in Izmit.
 
Türkiye seeks Korean investment in transport and logistics
Erdogan also called for greater South Korean involvement in Türkiye’s transport and logistics infrastructure projects, pointing to mounting risks to global energy markets and international trade routes, including disruptions affecting the Strait of Hormuz.
"The current crisis has once again demonstrated just how vital it is to develop reliable alternative routes for international trade," he said.
He highlighted Türkiye’s efforts to strengthen transport and logistics connections between Asia and Europe, including plans to revive the historic Hejaz Railway, and said Ankara wanted greater participation from South Korean companies in regional infrastructure investments.
"We would like to see greater participation by Korean companies in Türkiye's regional transport and logistics investments," Erdogan said, adding that his government was ready to support South Korean firms interested in investing in the country.
 
Erdogan calls for more balanced bilateral trade
On broader economic relations, Erdogan urged the two countries to address what he described as a significant imbalance in bilateral trade.
Türkiye exported approximately $1.14 billion worth of goods to South Korea in 2025, while its imports from the country reached $10.26 billion.
"We have set a target of $15 billion in bilateral trade volume. As we work toward this goal, we prioritize developing a more balanced trade structure, expanding investment and encouraging greater collaboration in production," he said.
Erdogan emphasized that increasing trade should go hand in hand with expanding reciprocal investment and strengthening industrial partnerships.
 
'Forged in blood': Erdogan highlights historic ties
Looking beyond economic and strategic cooperation, Erdogan stressed the importance of the longstanding friendship between the two countries, describing their relationship as one "forged in blood."
"The bonds of brotherhood and mutual trust that have been passed down through generations are at the center of our relationships. It is our responsibility to pass this treasured legacy on to future generations in an even stronger form," he said.
"I believe that our visit will pave the way for concrete steps to further advance cooperation between our two countries."
South Korea and Türkiye are set to mark the 70th anniversary of the establishment of diplomatic relations in 2027, providing an opportunity to further strengthen their longstanding political, economic and cultural ties.

- Students want better schools, more teachers, more university places and fairer admissions; Minister Edouard Geffray offered €4 billion and 15,000 new places, but students said it was not enough.
AI generated
PARIS – French high school student protests resumed on Nov 2 on a much smaller scale than in past weeks as they returned from a two-week break, with youngsters trying to blockade a few high schools in Paris, Marseille and Rennes, French media reported.
Hundreds of more than 3,000 high schools in France were blockaded in the weeks prior to the break. The protests, which began in the Paris suburbs in September, have spread across the country and broadened beyond education to focus on the cost of living, drawing in trade unionists and activists and sometimes turning violent.
A wave of so-called “Gen Z” protests has swept across European countries, including Germany, Italy, Belgium and Albania, driven by grievances including the cost of living, the poor state of schools and perceived corruption.
In October, French protests degenerated into violent clashes with the police and outright riots in several cities, with shops looted, in a test for President Emmanuel Macron’s minority government.
“In terms of blockades – or rather, attempted blockades – the phenomenon is very marginal. We’re talking about just a handful of units, a few individual schools,” Education Minister Edouard Geffray told radio station France Inter on the morning of Nov 2.
He said protests are allowed but preventing access to schools is illegal.
Police officers were present, TV footage showed, though not in full anti-riot gear.
Students want the renovation of ageing schools, more teachers, more university places and the end of a university admissions system they see as socially unfair.
Geffray offered last week to cap class sizes at 28, dedicate €4 billion (S$5.73 billion) to renovating schools, create 15,000 new places for students in higher education and a new admission system by 2028. High school student representatives said the offers were not enough and they would keep protesting. REUTERS

US midterms: Polls show Democrats ahead in battle for Congress
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
08:46:31 UTC
17:46:31 KST

- Economy, cost of living emerges as leading voter concerns, followed by health care, war with Iran
Democrats lead Republicans in national polling ahead of Tuesday's US midterm elections, with new surveys showing the party gaining ground in several closely contested Senate races as voters express dissatisfaction with President Donald Trump's handling of the economy.
With all 435 House of Representatives seats and 35 Senate seats on the ballot, the elections will determine whether Republicans retain control of Congress for the remaining two years of Trump's second term.
A RealClearPolling average of surveys conducted through Oct. 30 shows Democrats leading Republicans 52% to 43.1% on the generic congressional ballot, an 8.9-percentage-point advantage.
An NBC News survey conducted Oct. 28-30 found Democrats ahead 52% to 45%, while an Emerson College poll conducted Oct. 24-26 put the gap at 10 points.
The generic ballot measures nationwide preferences for congressional candidates rather than support in individual districts, meaning a national lead does not necessarily translate into a corresponding number of House seats.
 
House: Democrats lead nationally
Republicans currently control the House, where 218 seats are needed for a majority.
The nonpartisan Cook Political Report's latest ratings, updated Friday, place 222 districts in categories favoring Democrats and 195 favoring Republicans, with another 18 classified as toss-ups.
Of the 18 toss-up districts, 14 are currently held by Republicans and four by Democrats.
Cook shifted another 12 House races toward Democrats on Oct. 30, including Republican-held districts in Colorado and Pennsylvania, reflecting changes in its assessment of the electoral landscape.
Among the closely watched contests are California's 22nd District, where Republican Rep. David Valadao faces Democrat Randy Villegas; New York's 17th, where Republican Rep. Mike Lawler faces Democrat Cait Conley; and Texas' 15th, where Republican Rep. Monica De La Cruz faces Democrat Bobby Pulido.
Republicans are also contesting Democratic-held seats in Florida, North Carolina and Texas, where redistricting has altered the electoral landscape.
However, district-level polling remains uneven, and the national figures offer only a broad indication of the environment in which individual races are being fought.
 
Senate: Democrats gain ground in battlegrounds
The battle for the Senate is more complicated.
Republicans hold 53 seats, compared with 47 held by Democrats and two independents who caucus with them.
Democrats need a net gain of four seats to secure a majority.
A 50-50 split would leave Republicans in control because Vice President JD Vance can cast tie-breaking votes.
The latest New York Times/Siena University polls, conducted from Oct. 23-Nov. 1, show Democratic candidates ahead in six of seven key Senate battlegrounds and effectively tied with Republicans in the seventh.
Five of those Democratic leads are in Republican-held states, including Texas and Kansas, which have not elected Democratic senators since 1988 and 1932, respectively.
In Michigan, the only Democratic-held seat among the seven surveyed, Abdul El-Sayed leads Republican Mike Rogers 53% to 42%, an 11-point advantage.
In Texas, Democrat James Talarico leads Republican Ken Paxton 50% to 43%, while in Maine, Democratic challenger Troy Jackson has 51% support against Republican Sen. Susan Collins' 45%.
Former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown leads Republican Sen. Jon Husted 49% to 44% in Ohio, while Democrat Adam Hamilton leads Republican incumbent Roger Marshall by the same margin in Kansas.
The contests are tighter in Alaska and Iowa.
In Alaska, Democrat Mary Peltola leads Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan 48% to 46%, while Iowa Democrat Josh Turek is effectively tied with Republican Ashley Hinson, 48% to 47%.
The surveys show Democrats improving their position since September in six of the seven states.
Maine shifted from a three-point Republican lead in September to a six-point Democratic advantage, while Michigan's Democratic lead widened from five to 11 points.
Kansas moved from a tie to a five-point Democratic lead, while Alaska was the only state where Democrats lost ground, with their advantage narrowing from seven points to approximately one point.
The surveys did not include North Carolina, another Republican-held seat where recent polling has consistently shown Democrat Roy Cooper leading Republican Michael Whatley.
The latest findings are not uniform across pollsters, and several battleground contests remain close in broader polling averages.
 
Trump's approval and voter priorities
The New York Times/Siena surveys found that just 38% of likely voters across the seven battleground states approved of Trump's job performance.
Democratic candidates also led among independent voters in every state surveyed, while respondents expressed greater trust in Democrats on the cost of living, foreign wars and protecting the interests of ordinary people.
Across the seven states, Democratic candidates held a nine-point advantage over Republicans on handling the cost of living.
The findings are consistent with broader national dissatisfaction.
An Associated Press-NORC survey conducted on Oct. 8-12 found that 36% of voters approved of Trump's job performance, while 64% disapproved.
The economy and cost of living emerged as the leading election concerns, cited as important voting issues by 85% and 84% of respondents, respectively.
Health care followed at 69%, while 64% identified the war with Iran as an important issue.
The survey also found that 47% of voters wanted Democrats to control the House, compared with 38% who preferred Republicans. For the Senate, the figures were 46% and 38%, respectively.
 
What the polls cannot predict
Despite Democrats' polling advantage, uncertainties surrounding turnout and survey accuracy could affect the results.
The New York Times/Siena polls, which surveyed between 610 and 1,215 likely voters in each state, had margins of sampling error ranging from 3.3 to 4.8 percentage points.
They also found that voters who made their decisions during the preceding month favored Republicans by nine points, indicating that late shifts in support could matter.
Polling errors can arise from inaccurate turnout assumptions, difficulties reaching certain demographic groups and systematic biases shared by multiple surveys.
The surveys also found that Democrats' support among some key demographic groups had strengthened since September, although polling has historically struggled to accurately measure white working-class voters.
With several Senate contests separated by only a few percentage points, small differences between polling estimates and actual voting patterns could change the balance of power in Congress.

Strong exports supporting China's auto sector despite sluggish domestic demand: Fitch
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
08:45:11 UTC
17:45:11 KST

Tuba Ongun
02 November 2026•Update: 02 November 2026
Robust exports are supporting China's car industry against weak domestic demand, though regulatory shifts and squeezed profitability will limit the 2027 outlook, Fitch Ratings said Monday.
The credit rating agency projected local passenger-car retail volume to drop about 20% in 2026, before a mild low-single-digit recovery next year as product upgrades and accelerated new-energy vehicle (NEV) purchases ahead of the tax-rebate expiration assist demand.
Domestic passenger-car retail deliveries dropped 24.5% year-on-year in the third quarter of 2026, while wholesale deliveries decreased 5.8%, according to the report.
Artificial intelligence (AI) adoption and NEV market penetration reached 65.8% as demand for internal combustion engine models stayed suppressed, it added.
Exports remained the primary growth driver for the country's automotive sector, it said.
Passenger-car exports surged 72% from a year ago to a record 2.7 million units in the third quarter of this year, with NEVs representing 59% of total overseas deliveries, the rating agency reported.
Fitch expected auto deliveries overseas to remain strong over the next one or two quarters as carmakers accelerate shipments prior to regulatory adjustments.
Export growth is projected to decelerate significantly next year owing to potential EU import quotas on Chinese-built hybrids starting in late 2026 and a reduction in China's NEV export VAT rebate to 9% from 13% beginning April 2027, the agency indicated.
Rising demand from emerging economies and expanding European manufacturing capacity are projected to cushion the negative impact, it added.
The industry's financial margins remain fragile, with operating profit across China's auto manufacturing declining 23% on an annual basis from January to September, Fitch reported.
The industry's operating margin shrank to 3.3% during the nine-month span and fell to 1.4% in September, the report showed.

Russian citizen expelled to 'prevent activities' that 'threaten' Estonia
A Russian citizen was expelled from Estonia on Monday who had links to the Russian security services, Estonia's Internal Security Service (KAPO) said. Between 2022 and 2024 he worked for ERR's Russian-language radio service.
Kapo said it had recommended that Russian citizen Leonid Karabeshkin (Estonian spelling: Karabeškin) be sent out of Estonia and banned him from entering the Schengen area.
It posted the statement on X along with a video of a man being escorted by two police officers to the Russian border at Koidula in south Estonia.
"The aim of the expulsion is to prevent and counter activities that threaten the security of Estonia and Europe more broadly," KAPO wrote.

Links to Russian intellegence
Kapo spokesperson Marta Tuul told ERR that Karabeshkin had connections with Russian intelligence services and people working on their behalf.
"He regularly traveled to Russia and met with them there. Several of them have been sanctioned by the European Union and Ukraine for carrying out Russia's hostile influence activities. And he is linked to influence networks such as CIRP, RuBaltic and Regnum, as well as individuals associated with them," she said.
"In the case of Regnum, we are talking about Sergei Rekeda and also Sergei Rudnov. The latter is also on the United Kingdom's and Ukraine's sanctions lists. CIRP is the Center for International and Regional Policy of Russia, and he worked there as a project manager, while several people with FSB backgrounds have participated in events organized by the center," Tuul explained.
Minister of Foreign Affairs Margus Tsahkna (Eesti 200) said Estonia will not turn a blind eye to threats to our security or that of Europe.
"Those with links to Russian intelligence services and hostile influence networks have no place exploiting our openness. One such individual has now been expelled from Estonia and barred from entering the Schengen area. Rightly so. We will not tolerate activities that undermine our security," he said.
