Karabeshkin worked at ERR
Karabeshkin worked as a foreign news reporter for Estonian Public Broadcasting's (ERR) Russian-language radio news from 2022 to 2024.
The employment contract was terminated by mutual agreement, although not because of the circumstances that came to light on Monday. Both before and after his employment, he occasionally appeared as a guest to comment on foreign affairs in Russian-language radio and television programs.
ERR Management Board Chairman Erik Roose said that, in light of Monday's news, ERR has conducted an initial rapid assessment, as the news is unpleasant and requires more thorough analysis.
"There were no suspicions concerning Karabeshkin when he was hired. During his employment, the editorial team also saw no signs of such attitudes or influence activities that would have been reflected in the content. Otherwise, we would have acted immediately and terminated his employment contract. We will continue discussing with editorial managers what lessons can be learned from this," Roose said.
Asked whether Karabeshkin's influence activities were in any way reflected in his work at ERR, KAPO's Tuul said probably not.
"However, it did give him an opportunity to gain access to people he was interested in," she said.
Tuul said Karabeshkin had contacts with Russian intelligence services and shared information with them about the Russian-speaking population living in Estonia. Asked what specific activities by Karabeshkin led to his expulsion from Estonia, Tuul replied that such matters are assessed as a whole, rather than on the basis of a single incident. "This was systematic activity."
Karabeshkin is also a political scientist and was a former lecturer at the now-defunct private university Euroacademy in Tallinn from 2006-2020. His specialization was international relations, Russian foreign policy, and political processes in the former Soviet Union.

"The Federal Security Service thwarted a series of sabotage and terrorist attacks using improvised explosive devices concealed inside FPV drone goggles intended for delivery to the Russian military in the special military operation zone, which were plotted by Ukrainian special services," the FSB said.
According to the agency, acting on instructions from military counterintelligence, a Russian serviceman in the Volgograd Region brought two FPV goggles he had received from a volunteer to the FSB for inspection. Explosive ordnance specialists established that Ukrainian special services had planted improvised explosive devices in the FPV goggles instead of cooling solutions. "As a result of the measures taken, a batch of similar improvised explosives camouflaged as FPV goggles, sent into the country via the Russian Post, has been confiscated across Russia," the FSB said.
The explosive devices would have detonated when the FPV glasses were switched on, potentially killing servicemen, the FSB added.
"Posing as pseudo-patriots, agents of Ukrainian special services established communication with representatives of Russian humanitarian organizations and charity foundations, using anonymous accounts on the Telegram messenger," to arrange supplies to Russian Defense Ministry units, the FSB continued. During these exchanges, they refused to share their names, phone numbers and job information or switch to the Max messenger for calls as they communicated with volunteers to arrange the delivery of FPV goggles with homemade explosive devices, while demanding video feedback with words of gratitude from Russian fighters, the FSB said.
According to the enemy’s plans, volunteers were supposed to later deliver the FPV goggles laden with improvised explosive devices to Russian drone operators taking part in combat operations against Ukrainian troops, the FSB noted.
A criminal case has been opened, and efforts to identify those responsible for the shipment are underway, the FSB concluded.

The Ukrainian Defense Forces’ drones attacked the Samara oil pumping and dispatch station in Russia’s Samara Region.
Exilenova+ shared footage showing a fire at the facility.
The attack took place overnight on November 2, 2026. An air raid alert was issued in the region at 11:19 p.m. on November 1 (Kyiv time). About an hour later, Russia imposed flight restrictions at Kurumoch Airport near Samara. The drone alert was lifted at 06:56 a.m.
The attack sparked a fire at the facility. NASA’s FIRMS satellite monitoring service detected a thermal anomaly in the area of the station at 04:13 a.m.
The Samara Linear Production and Dispatch Station (LPDS) is a major hub in Russia’s Transneft oil pipeline network. It is used to receive, store, blend, and pump crude oil.
Major pipelines deliver oil to the facility from Tatarstan, Western Siberia, and other Russian oil-producing regions. The station also blends crude oil with different sulfur contents to produce Urals, Russia’s main export-grade crude oil.
The previous attack on the station took place on October 11, 2026. In total, the facility was attacked at least four times in October – on October 2, 7, 10, and 11.
Previous attacks destroyed four RVSPK-50,000 storage tanks, which had a combined capacity of up to 170,000 tonnes of oil.

A satellite built for Rassvet, Russia’s answer to Starlink, burned up on 30 October, Ukrainian defense outlet Defense Express reported. It is the network’s second loss since launches began in March. A third stricken satellite may have been saved, though sources disagree.
On 5 February, Ukraine and SpaceX blocked the Starlink terminals Russian troops had used without permission. Officially, Rassvet is a commercial internet service. If it works, though, Russian forces could get satellite links that Kyiv has no US company to ask to switch off. The EU’s 21st sanctions package targeted Rassvet in July but left its operator, Bureau 1440, off the list.
A satellite that apparently never maneuvered
Satellite No. 17 went up on 19 July aboard a Soyuz-2.1b rocket with 15 others. It apparently never fired its engine, Defense Express wrote. After 103 days, residual air drag pulled it low enough to burn.
No. 23 was sinking too. On 20 October, at 220 km, Bureau 1440 managed to start lifting it, and it keeps climbing, Defense Express said. Space analyst Anatoly Zak’s launch page still lists it among satellites expected to fall, citing the Aerospace Corporation. Public tracking data from 1 November put it at about 316 km, marked active.
Slow, but working
Of the 30 satellites in orbit, 26 have reached about 500 km, Defense Express said. The outlet described that as a staging altitude before a joint climb to the planned 800 km. Russian telecom outlet ComNews offered another reading in July: Bureau 1440 had likely lowered the working orbit to 514 km. The company’s press office did not answer ComNews.
Russia is building Starlink no foreign company can switch off. Ukraine names 49 firms behind it, and 23 face no sanctions from Kyiv’s allies at all
The first loss followed the same pattern. Satellite No. 4, from the March batch, fell in early June without ever raising its orbit.
The serial satellites are already in test use. At a Moscow tech forum on 7 October, Bureau 1440 showed a video call over Rassvet to Adygea, a Russian republic, according to ComNews. Its first such demo, in 2023, ran on test satellites.
Flat objects on Russian Molniya-2 drones were reported as Rassvet terminals. Serhii “Flash” Beskrestnov, an adviser to Ukraine’s president, rejected that, and Defense Express concluded they are probably not.

Russia’s new Filin cruise missile caught on camera
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
08:37:36 UTC
17:37:36 KST

- A photo shows Russia’s new Filin cruise missile on a ground launcher with a solid-fuel booster that launches it before its turbojet takes over.
- Ukraine’s HUR says the Filin has a claimed 1,200 km range, 50 or 100 kg warheads and the same R500 engine as Russia’s S-71 missiles.
A photo of Russia’s new Filin cruise missile sitting on a ground launcher with a solid-fuel booster strapped under its fuselage has surfaced for the first time, Ukrainian defense outlet Militarnyi reported, showing how Russia gets the low-cost missile into the air.
The booster fires first to accelerate the missile off the launcher and into flight, then drops away while the Filin’s own small turbojet engine takes over for the cruise to its target. The photo does not show where or when it was taken, or what type of vehicle or rail carries the launcher.
Russia began using the Filin against Ukraine in late summer 2026, Ukraine’s military intelligence agency HUR said in October, when it published an interactive 3D model of the missile and a breakdown of its parts on its War&Sanctions portal. HUR said the missile is built by NPO Molniya, part of the state-owned Tactical Missiles Corporation, and continues a push by Russian industry toward cheap, jet-powered, ground-launched strike weapons.
The Filin is small for a cruise missile. Its composite carbon-fiber and fiberglass fuselage is 3.5 m (11.5 feet) long, with a 3 m (10-foot) wingspan, and some parts are 3D-printed. Russia claims it can fly at up to 800 km/h (500 mph) and reach targets up to 1,200 km (745 miles) away, at altitudes from just above the ground to 6 km (about 20,000 feet). HUR said versions exist with 50 kg (110-pound) and 100 kg (220-pound) warheads, a fraction of the payload of Russia’s larger cruise missiles such as the Kh-101. Those performance figures come from Russian sources and have not been independently confirmed.
The engine is a Russian-made R500 from a company called Reynolds, according to HUR. The same engine was previously found in Russia’s air-launched S-71K Kover and S-71M Monochrome cruise missiles. HUR also said the Filin’s onboard electronics are made by PLAZ, a company involved in producing the Harpiya drone, a modified version of the Geran-2 long-range attack drone, and that the missile contains electronic components made in the United States and China.
That combination of a jet engine, a ground launcher and a small warhead puts the Filin between Russia’s Geran attack drones, which are slower and use propellers, and its full-size cruise missiles, which cost far more. Ukrainian outlet Defense Express has suggested the Filin may be the 800 km/h jet-powered drone that Ukrainian sources reported Russia using earlier this year.
Russia has been fielding several new low-cost strike weapons in recent months. Ukrainian officials have also identified the air-launched S8000 Banderol cruise missile and jet-powered versions of the Geran, and a small, previously unseen Russian cruise missile came down almost intact in Odesa region on Oct. 27.

Researchers find way to optimize biodiesel by mixing rapeseed, linseed oil
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
08:37:09 UTC
17:37:09 KST

TOMSK, November 2. /TASS/. Scientists have found a way to optimize the properties of biodiesel by blending rapeseed, linseed, and safflower oils in a ratio of 90%, 5%, and 5%, respectively, making it possible to produce fuel with target characteristics without chemical additives and reduces logistics costs by 10-15% compared to imported raw materials, the Russian Ministry of Education and Science told TASS.
One of the main obstacles to the commercial application of biodiesel is the influence of the raw material fatty acid composition on its properties: low-temperature performance, oxidative stability, specific heat of combustion, and viscosity. Scientists consider the pre-blending of vegetable oils prior to transesterification to be a promising approach as combining raw materials with complementary fatty acid profiles helps neutralize limitations and improve properties. However, the choice of oils is often dictated by regional availability and cost rather than properties optimization.
"Scientists from Tomsk Polytechnic University, together with colleagues, have proposed an approach that allows optimizing the physicochemical properties of oil-based biodiesel fuel and, in the long term, creating a cost-effective strategy for producing biodiesel with specified characteristics without chemical additives," the ministry noted.
The comprehensive predictive model proposed by the scientists is adapted to raw materials common in regions with a temperate continental climate, specifically rapeseed, flax, and safflower, said Vladlena Chobotova, a research engineer at the Heat and Mass Transfer Laboratory,. This approach transforms the pre-blending of oils from a simple logistical measure into a precise tool for tailoring biofuel properties to the EN 14214 standard without chemical additives.
The scientists selected unrefined rapeseed, linseed, and safflower oils as raw materials due to their inherent properties, regional availability, and lower cost compared to refined counterparts. The properties of rapeseed oil allow for obtaining biodiesel with a high cetane number and oxidation capacity, linseed oil helps reduce viscosity, and safflower oil yields fuel with properties intermediate between rapeseed and linseed. Methanol and potassium hydroxide were used as the alcohol and alkaline catalysts, respectively.
In the course of their research, the scientists developed eight predictive models that link raw material composition to fuel properties. Their accuracy was confirmed by statistical verification. It was also established that blending rapeseed, linseed, and safflower oils before transesterification alters the fatty acid composition almost linearly. The yield of methyl esters was 96.8-99.2%, which complies with the EN 14214 standard. Minor fatty acids significantly affect viscosity and low-temperature properties. The optimal ratio is 90% rapeseed, 5% linseed, and 5% safflower. The algorithm can be integrated into automated raw material management systems to adjust the formulation during price and quality fluctuations. The results obtained showed that using regionally available oils reduces logistics costs by 10-15% compared to imported raw materials. At the same time, the proposed optimization model can be easily adapted to other regional oil combinations, making it promising for localized and cost-effective biodiesel production.

Long road from Russian occupation: Stories of Oleshky residents
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
10:35:30 EET
17:35:30 KST

Journalists representing Ukrainian and foreign media outlets spent several hours waiting for citizens who had spent over a day traveling to Ukraine from the temporarily occupied town of Oleshky in Kherson region. As stipulated by the humanitarian mission plan, they traveled from their hometown by bus to Anapa (Russia), then by plane to Belarus, and from there once again by bus to a meeting point in Chernihiv region.
Everything was prepared at the site for the arrival—tents set up by the State Emergency Service (SES), the Ukrainian Red Cross Society (URCS), and charitable foundations, alongside volunteers, hot food, warm blankets, and pet food.
The first vehicle to enter the site was an SES truck, from which the barking, whining, and meowing of animals could be heard. Volunteers immediately transferred the animals, frightened and exhausted by the long journey, into a URCS truck.
"There are approximately 70 animals here. All of them will undergo rehabilitation," a volunteer from the UAnimals animal and environmental protection organization reported.
After some time, buses and an extended convoy of ambulances arrived at the site. People stepped out of the buses exclaiming, "Glory to Ukraine!", "My dears!", "We are finally home." Many wept—both men and women. Someone immediately expressed concern for their German Shepherd, checking how it endured the trip before walking over to the URCS truck. Another evacuee recounted how, while still in Oleshky, they managed to coordinate with volunteers to successfully transport dogs across the river using a drone that flew over to Mykolaiv.
Volunteers, medical personnel, and psychologists immediately began assisting the evacuees.
"We took only personal belongings, documents, and photo albums containing our entire lives. And I took my apartment keys... We have nowhere to go..." an elderly woman recounted.
Meanwhile, 72-year-old Ms. Olya, following the mandatory rehabilitation provided to all evacuees, will travel to her children in Odesa.
Every arriving individual holds a distinct story. Nearly all remain uncertain of what lies ahead, and all of them are still mentally rooted in Oleshky.
"I was left alone; my husband passed away, and my son was killed last year. I have a brother living in Vinnytsia region who is inviting me to stay. There is a family house where no one currently lives. It is difficult, but I ultimately decided to leave Oleshky. I said goodbye to my men, so to speak, because I do not know when I will be able to return to visit them at the cemetery," shared another distinguished elderly lady.
The woman noted that food conditions in Oleshky had deteriorated severely since May.
"The younger ones rode bicycles or walked to Radensk. I did not go. Even if they offered me a million, I wouldn't go. I am no longer at an age where I can ride a bicycle," the interlocutor stated.
According to her, they had recently been receiving humanitarian aid drops: "Our people dropped humanitarian aid from large drones. They called those drones 'Baba Yaga'... You do not leave the house at night—blackouts were always enforced—but you hear something drop, and in the morning you check: humanitarian aid, canned goods, stewed meat, grains, pasta... As for vegetables, we grew small amounts ourselves. But crops only grew for those who had access to water and generators."
When asked what she desired most at that moment, she replied: "Sweets. Really, really delicious ones."
An elderly man joined the conversation: "In September, I rode a bicycle 20 kilometers to get food. I hadn't ridden a bike in five years. I am already 79. It took me two hours to get there. I bought 30 to 40 kilograms of provisions. I couldn't ride back loaded like that, so I walked back from Radensk to Oleshky on foot, pushing a bicycle laden with food... It took me six hours of walking. That is how one had to survive."
He added: "And you had to walk with extreme caution because many areas are mined. I nearly lost my life there seven days ago... I was walking home, already very close, when a drone crashed into a lighting pole just a few meters from me. It fell. Smoke filled the air. Breathing was difficult. For a minute, I couldn't see anything... By some miracle, those flying concrete shards from the shattered pole missed me... That was the final straw: I realized I could no longer live there and decided to leave."
Mikhailo Paliy was met upon his return by his family—his wife and two daughters.
"We lived under Russian occupation for two years. Two years ago, when I was 14, my mother, my sister, and I left Oleshky, while my father stayed behind. We evacuated through Russian filtration checkpoints. We were subjected to a four-hour interrogation solely because we lacked Russian documents," Liza Paliy recounted.
When asked how she planned to welcome her father at home in Kyiv, Liza responded: "We bought salo and cooked borscht so he could eat proper, normal food."
"We sincerely hope these humanitarian missions will continue, and that people will be given the opportunity to leave occupied territories safely, without fear or interrogations at Russian checkpoints," the young woman emphasized.
Liza harbors a dream—to visit Crimea. In 2014, the family planned a trip to the peninsula, but the Russian occupation disrupted those plans. The dream remains undiminished. She firmly believes that following the de-occupation of Ukrainian territories, she will certainly travel to Crimea—passing through our Oleshky.

MC HotDog released the song “The Tenants Downstairs” in August 2023. Its lyrics tell the story of a person who, while falling from a building, witnesses the troubled lives of other residents below.
The song was distributed through Hit FM, YouTube, and Spotify, prompting listeners to point out similarities to Zhu's comic “Jumping from a Building” (跳樓), Storm Media reported. The comic appeared in Zhu's 2004 collection “Nothing New Happening.”
MC HotDog subsequently removed the song and its unreleased music video in September 2023, issuing a public apology in which he said he and his company had made a serious mistake. He also apologized to Zhu for releasing the song without obtaining authorization and said he would be more careful about verifying the sources of material used in future songwriting.
However, the two sides failed to reach a licensing agreement, and MC HotDog later released another song titled “Upstairs Landlord,” according to Storm Media. Believing he had been mocked, Zhu decided to pursue civil and criminal complaints.
In its civil ruling, the court found substantial similarities between the song and Zhu's comic, per ETtoday. Both works focused on a protagonist's changing state of mind and included plot elements involving domestic violence between a married couple, depression, unemployment, and a man wearing women's clothing.
The court said that although the lyrics incorporated some new ideas, they retained the comic's core elements and distinctive characteristics. On Monday, prosecutors indicted the rapper under the Copyright Act for allegedly adapting Zhu's work without authorization and making it available online.

“The Enhanced Trade Partnership between the UK and Taiwan sets a precedent for Japan to follow,” one of the sources said. The framework leaves room for future agreements tailored to specific regions or industries, “minimizes political sensitivity” and gives Tokyo some protection if China retaliates, they said, adding that the pact could be signed by year’s end.
A draft agreement includes five areas of cooperation: economic resilience and innovation, industry cooperation on disaster risk reduction, digital trade, trade facilitation, and sustainability, per Nikkei Asia.
Jasmine Lee, a corporate analyst, said, “Collectively, strategic deals with Britain and Japan, both prominent members of the Group of Seven, create momentum and space for Taiwan to navigate pressures from China and [US President Donald] Trump's tariff war, and capitalize on Taiwanese tech leverage on the world stage.”
Katsuya Yamamoto of the Sasakawa Peace Foundation think tank said that Japan has traditionally been reluctant to establish a formal, broader economic framework with Taiwan, partly out of concern for its relations with China. “However, the strategic and economic environment has changed considerably.”
Yamamoto pointed out that “economic security has become a major policy priority, and both Japan and Taiwan share an interest in strengthening the resilience of critical supply chains, particularly in advanced technologies and semiconductors.” “It would be a natural step toward building a more resilient, diversified, and secure economic order in the Indo-Pacific,” he added.
Yamamoto said that a bilateral trade agreement “could serve both practical economic purposes and a broader strategic objective by deepening cooperation among like-minded economies and reducing excessive dependence on any single market or supply chain.”
David Parker, managing partner at corporate advisory firm Kameido Group, said, “There is no question that Japan and Japanese leaders view Taiwan as a critical economic security partner.”
“This reflects both complementary capabilities as well as growing alignment in their respective strategic interests and approaches to economic security,” he added.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — A Ministry of National Defense report found no wrongdoing in the budgeting process for the military's procurement of long shelf-life bottled water under the 2025 special budget for strengthening national defense resilience.
Taiwan's military initially proposed spending NT$800 million (US$26.1 million) to purchase bottled water with a shelf life of five to seven years. KMT Legislator Ma Wen-chun (馬文君) opposed the proposal, questioning the estimated price of NT$120 per bottle.
Although the military initially defended its cost estimate, it conducted a new evaluation following widespread criticism, lowering the estimated unit price to NT$35 in July 2026, per Liberty Times. Ma subsequently called on the military to provide a detailed review of the procurement process, along with follow-up studies on the shelf life and quality of the bottled water, per UDN.
In its follow-up report, the military explained that the initial cost estimate was based on import prices for similar products sold in Japan, Norway and the US, per China Times.
During its revised evaluation, the military lowered the estimated unit price to NT$60 after identifying domestic suppliers. It then reduced the estimate further to NT$35 through a competitive bidding process.
The report found no irregularities in the procurement process. However, it thanked lawmakers for their oversight, which helped reduce the initial cost estimate by more than 70%.
Ma commented that the MND had initially refused to back down on the budget item, saying the controversy highlighted problems with the ministry's approach to budget allocation, per FTNN.
The KMT legislative caucus also commented on the report, saying its oversight had helped prevent unnecessary spending, per TVBS. The caucus stressed that although the party supports increased defense spending, individual budget items and procurement procedures should remain subject to scrutiny.

Four Chinese research vessels probe Taiwan’s undersea cables
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
08:32:35 UTC
17:32:35 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Four Chinese research vessels spotted near Taiwan since May may have been collecting intelligence on international undersea cables, Japan’s Yomiuri Shimbun reported.
An analysis by Taiwan-based geospatial data firm ingeniSPACE found that the four survey ships stopped or slowed in waters where cables linking Taiwan with other countries are laid.
One Taiwanese official called the findings “reasonable” and consistent with authorities’ understanding of the situation. Another official told the newspaper they could not rule out the possibility that Chinese vessels were gathering information on undersea cables.
The vessels are the Xiang Yang Hong 22, which belongs to China’s Ministry of Natural Resources; the Tongji and Jia Geng, operated by universities in Shanghai and Fujian; and the Mushanzi, identified through an automatic identification system, the analysis showed.
The Xiang Yang Hong 22 slowed down, stopped, and changed course irregularly in waters north of Taiwan, according to the analysis. The Jia Geng displayed similar behavior in waters off the east coast, the Mushanzi in the Bashi Channel to the south, and the Tongji repeatedly sailed around Taiwan, stopping and slowing down several times.
China has a track record of using research vessels to gather intelligence. In August, the Xiang Yang Hong 03 was seen operating over key undersea cables and deep-sea areas within Taiwan’s and Japan’s exclusive economic zones. The Wall Street Journal reported Sunday that China is sending a growing number of survey ships to waters east and south of Taiwan to collect data that could aid a potential invasion.
Motohiro Tsuchiya, a national security professor at Keio University, told the Japanese newspaper that the recent Chinese vessels may be studying not only the locations of the cables but also the seabed terrain, depth, and ocean currents around them with the goal of cable sabotage.
The findings come as Taiwan continues to face frequent cable disruptions. In the past four years, an average of seven to eight submarine cable incidents occurred annually in Taiwan’s coastal waters, according to the Ministry of Digital Affairs.
The risks extend beyond Taiwan. Experts say cables connecting the US with Taiwan, Japan, and the Philippines are among the most vulnerable to Chinese gray-zone activities and maritime pressure.
Jason Wang, ingeniSPACE’s chief operating officer, said China has been “deploying gray-zone tactics in a wide area along the First Island Chain in anticipation of a contingency,” adding that Chinese ships had been seen engaging in similar activities in waters near Japan and the Philippines.
Chisako Masuo, a professor of international relations at Kyushu University, said China might be looking to disrupt Japanese society and cut communications between Japan and the US by severing undersea cables off Japan’s Pacific coast.
The disruptive actions previously directed at Taiwan could potentially be deployed against Japan in the future, she added.

Association calls for minimum standards for childcare centres
In many places, playgroups can be run by people without teaching qualifications or in accordance with standardised safety requirements. Playgroup leaders now want to change this by introducing binding legal requirements.
In many cantons, there have so far been no legal requirements for playgroups and childcare centres, as the Swiss Association of Playgroup Leaders (SSLV) noted on Monday. This relates to safety plans, staff-to-child ratios and the pedagogical qualifications of staff.
The association criticised the fact that playgroups could often be set up without having to provide any evidence of compliance. Yet, according to the SSLV, studies show that qualified early intervention has a significant impact on later success at school. The SSLV therefore believes that voluntary guidelines are no longer sufficient to alleviate this pressure.

Latvia spent a total of 30.114 million euros from its contingency fund during the first nine months of this year, representing 34.1% of the amount initially allocated in the 2026 state budget and 29.9% after taking into account the budget reallocation made in September, according to information published by the Fiscal Discipline Council (FDP).
Of this amount, 2.975 million euros was spent in the first quarter, 6.239 million euros in the second quarter and 20.9 million euros in the third quarter.
During the first nine months of 2026, a total of 90 funding requests from government institutions were approved under the contingency fund programme, including 20 in the first quarter, 25 in the second quarter and 45 in the third quarter.
The largest allocations during the nine-month period included 9.04 million euros for five requests submitted by the Ministry of Welfare, 6.405 million euros for three requests from the Ministry of Health and 2.994 million euros for 11 requests from the Ministry of Agriculture.
Meanwhile, 2.368 million euros was allocated to 13 requests from the Ministry of Transport, 1.915 million euros to five requests from the Ministry of Education and Science, 1.914 million eurosto four requests from the Ministry of Culture, 1.747 million euros to nine requests from the Ministry of Finance and 1.526 million euros to nine requests from the Ministry of the Interior.
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs received 865,100 euros for ten requests,
 while 252,400 euos was allocated to seven requests from the Ministry of Smart Administration and Regional Development. The Ministry of Defence received 236,900 euros for two requests, the Ministry of Climate and Energy received 49,300 euros for one request, and the Ministry of Justice received 46,300 euros for three requests.
In addition,  503,400 euros was allocated to six requests from the Cabinet of Ministers during the first nine months of the year. The State Audit Office received 168,400 euros for one request, while the Central Election Commission was allocated 83,000 euros for one request.
The 2026 state budget initially earmarked 88.3 million euros for the programme "Funds for Unforeseen Events", which was 21.4 million euros less than in 2025. However, in September, a decision was made to reallocate 12.3 million euros from the budget programmes and subprogrammes of ministries and other central government institutions to the contingency fund.
Funding under the "Funds for Unforeseen Events" programme is allocated to measures of particular national importance,
 expenses not covered by existing state budget appropriations, disaster and natural calamity response measures, compensation for resulting damage, and other unforeseen circumstances.
Requests for funding must be submitted by the ministry responsible for the relevant sector.

What's the EU's plan to cut your energy bill? Ask the Euronews AI chatbot
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
08:30:57 UTC
17:30:57 KST

EU energy ministers discussed measures to ease winter energy costs as the Strait of Hormuz remains closed, driving energy bills higher. But what do they include? Ask the Euronews AI chatbot.
At the EU Council energy meeting in Luxembourg on October 29, ministers discussed strengthening the bloc’s energy security, affordability, and resilience to limit the Middle East war's effect on European energy bills.
Europe meets 57% of its energy needs through imported fossil fuels. This leaves the bloc highly vulnerable to global market shocks and price swings when gas supply conditions shift, such as rising demand or conflict-related shipping constraints.
Wholesale gas prices on the Dutch Title Transfer Facility (TTF) rose from about €28 per megawatt-hour (€/MWh) in January to almost €104 at the end of October. Europe's energy regulator, ACER, estimated that the Middle East crisis added €18-€33 billion to the bloc’s gas import costs for the same volume, pushing overall inflation to 3.8% in September.
Ministers negotiated cutting electricity costs and taxes for winter, ensuring electricity excise taxes are no higher than natural gas excise taxes. They backed maximising existing grids, strengthening interconnection between member states, increasing investment in domestic clean energy, and diversifying supplies. The EU’s adopted approach must always be grounded in coordination and solidarity among member states.
These measures build on the EU’s efforts to strengthen energy resilience since Russia’s war in Ukraine began and on its latest plan, AccelerateEU, proposed in April to expand clean energy, diversify supplies, and speed the clean-energy transition.
They also complement national measures, with governments spending €17.9 billion on short-term relief this year, including energy vouchers, price caps, and excise-duty cuts.

Merve Berker
02 November 2026•Update: 02 November 2026
Democratic candidates are leading in five Republican-held US Senate races and are effectively tied in another ahead of the midterm elections, according to the latest New York Times/Siena University polls released Sunday.
The surveys, conducted across seven battleground states, found Democrats ahead in Texas, Kansas, Maine, Ohio, and Alaska, while the race in Iowa remains virtually tied.
In Michigan, the only Democratic-held Senate seat included in the surveys, Democrat Abdul El-Sayed leads Republican Mike Rogers by 11 percentage points.
According to The New York Times, Democrats need to defend their existing Senate seats and flip at least four Republican-held seats to secure a majority.
In Texas, Democratic state legislator James Talarico leads Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton 50% to 43%, despite the state not electing a Democratic senator since 1988.
In Kansas, which has not elected a Democratic senator since 1932, Democrat Adam Hamilton leads Republican Senator Roger Marshall 49% to 44%.
Former Democratic Senator Sherrod Brown also leads Republican Senator Jon Husted 49% to 44% in Ohio.
In Maine, Democratic former state senator Troy Jackson leads Republican Senator Susan Collins 51% to 45%.
Meanwhile, Democrat Mary Peltola holds a narrow 48% to 46% advantage over Republican Senator Dan Sullivan in Alaska, while Democrat Josh Turek is effectively tied with Republican Ashley Hinson in Iowa.
The polls also revealed widespread dissatisfaction with President Donald Trump's handling of the economy, with only 38% of likely voters across the seven states approving of his job performance.
Democrats held a nine-point advantage over Republicans on handling the cost of living, leading on the issue in every state surveyed.
Democratic candidates also led among independent voters across all seven states, while the surveys indicated renewed support from younger and Latino voters.
However, voters who made their decisions during the past month favored Republicans by nine percentage points.
The polls showed Democratic candidates improving their positions in six states compared with September, while losing ground only in Alaska.
The surveys interviewed between 610 and 1,215 voters per state from Oct. 23 to Nov. 1.
Margins of sampling error among likely voters ranged from 3.3 percentage points in Texas to 4.8 points in Alaska.

The Apec moment Hong Kong needs to seize
Hong Kong’s future value might lie less in its connectivity alone than in making different institutional systems work together
3-MIN READ3-MIN
 Listen
Cheng Xianyue is a member of the Chinese Association of Hong Kong and Macau Studies. 
The first Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) forum finance ministers’ meeting to be held in Hong Kong focused on openness, cooperation and resilience. These themes go to the heart of a question confronting the city: as globalisation becomes more difficult and the rules and security boundaries governing international markets grow more complex, what can Hong Kong still offer cross-border commerce?
Globalisation is not over. Capital still seeks opportunities overseas, while technology, energy, raw materials and supply chains cannot simply retreat behind national borders. Yet geopolitics, industrial policy, technology controls, data governance and financial security increasingly shape investment decisions.
For decades, globalisation was largely about lowering costs and reducing barriers. Its next phase could be defined by a different challenge: how to keep cross-border transactions moving when borders matter again.

Thousands evacuated as India braces for second cyclone in a week
Cyclone Murasu expected to hit coast near Ongole late on Monday with wind speeds of 100-110km/h, Meteorological Department says.
Authorities in India’s southern state of Andhra Pradesh have begun evacuating residents from low-lying coastal areas as Cyclone Murasu bears down on a region still recovering from a deadly cyclone last week.
About 2,000 people had been evacuated by Monday, Prakhar Jain, managing director of the Andhra Pradesh State Disaster Management Authority, told the Reuters news agency. “We are planning to evacuate some 30,000 people,” he said.
The India Meteorological Department (IMD) said the cyclone was likely to cross the south Andhra Pradesh coast between Nellore and Narsapur near the town of Ongole from 11:30pm (18:00 GMT) on Monday to 4am on Tuesday (22:30 GMT on Monday).
“It is very likely to … cross south Andhra Pradesh coast as a severe cyclonic storm with wind speeds of around 100 to 110 kilometres per hour [60 to 70 miles per hour],” IMD said, projecting gusts of 120km/h (75mph).
Chief Minister N Chandrababu Naidu directed officials to prepare for the cyclone. He said estimates suggested that 6,000 to 8,000 electrical poles could be damaged, posing a “severe threat to power supply”.
Deputy Chief Minister Pawan Kalyan wrote on X that the cyclone was set to have a severe impact on Nellore, Prakasam, Bapatla and Krishna districts.
Six National Disaster Response Force (NDRF) teams and seven State Disaster Response Force teams have been deployed in advance, Jain said, according to the IANS news agency. Three of the NDRF teams were sent from neighbouring Tamil Nadu, the ANI news agency reported.
In Nellore district, Collector Himanshu Shukla urged fishermen not to go to sea and ordered officials in coastal areas to remain at their posts.
Schools have been closed in Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu and Odisha with rain expected to continue over parts of Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Odisha and Chhattisgarh until Wednesday even as the storm weakens, according to ETV Bharat.
Murasu is expected to be less intense than Cyclone Arnab, which struck the same coastline on Wednesday, killing six people and destroying dozens of homes and crops.

Bitcoin remains stable after Binance’s record hack
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
10:28:28 EET
17:28:28 KST

Bitcoin remains stable after Binance’s record hack
Kyiv • UNN
Bitcoin changed little after the Binance hack, despite the theft of $6.3 billion in assets. Traders consider the incident an operational shock.
After last week’s record cyber theft at the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, traders who had prepared for the worst instead watched bitcoin perform an unexpected "feat": defying gravity. Bloomberg reports, writes UNN.
Details
The original cryptocurrency was little changed on Monday, November 2, trading at around $78,000 at 8 a.m. London time. It was down about 5% from Thursday’s high, before Binance reported a hack in which $6.3 billion worth of assets were stolen. The token’s resilience is largely attributed to Binance’s swift response, as the exchange pledged from the outset to cover all losses, the publication notes.
"Bitcoin’s ability to hold its position over the weekend is essentially a vote of confidence in Binance’s statements," said Caroline Moron, co-founder of Orbit Markets. "The market is clearly convinced that Binance has sufficient funds to cover the losses."
Bitcoin was already under pressure last week because of a sell-off in risk assets, so its relative resilience highlights how differently traders view this incident compared with the last major disaster to hit one of the largest cryptocurrency exchanges. During the collapse of FTX, the second-largest exchange, in 2022, bitcoin fell 19% in three days, as the company led by former billionaire Sam Bankman-Fried went from a liquidity shortfall to bankruptcy.
Sean McNulty, a derivatives trader at market maker AQC Tech, said one reason bitcoin is holding up better this time is that Binance is buying back tokens to compensate users for their losses. But, he said, the overall mood remains anxious.
"People see this as just the tip of the iceberg and expect more hacks, given the capabilities of AI," McNulty said, referring to the use of artificial intelligence in cyberattacks this year. "If Binance, the world’s largest exchange, can be hacked, then no one will be safe."
As a sign of broader concern, demand is growing for short-term protection against a decline in bitcoin. According to data based on options on the cryptocurrency derivatives platform Deribit, the one-day put delta skew—a measure of how much more traders are paying for protection against a significant decline than for a bet on a comparable rise—increased by about 1 percentage point over 24 hours to 6.37 points.
Kelly Ye, head of research at trading firm Talos, said traders are reacting to the hack differently than they did to the FTX collapse, which was linked to fraud.
"The market viewed this as an operational shock rather than a systemic one," Ye said, noting that the depth of Binance’s order book fell by 25–30%, but buyers returned within a few hours. "This is a completely different picture compared with 2022, when trust in the market had completely evaporated," she said.
U.S. midterm elections on Tuesday, November 3, could have a greater short-term impact on cryptocurrency markets. A change in party control of Congress "could have significant implications for how cryptocurrency market-structure legislation develops," said Jeff Ko, chief analyst at ViaBTC.
Until last week, the largest cryptocurrency-related hack had been the 2025 hack of the Bybit exchange, which resulted in losses of about $1.5 billion. The Federal Bureau of Investigation linked the Binance and Bybit hacks to the North Korean hacker group TraderTraitor.
As with Binance, the Bybit hack initially had little impact on bitcoin. However, losses increased in the following days, causing the cryptocurrency to fall by about 14% in the week after the February 21 attack.
Regarding the latest hack, Ye noted that traders best able to detect market disruptions as they occur had spread their risks across several exchanges.
"For institutional investors, the lesson is simple: no single platform is a safe place to store risks or analyze prices," she said.

====================================================================================================

China's draft financial law seeks to strengthen protection for consumers, investors
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
16:27:25 CST
17:27:25 KST

BEIJING, Nov. 2 (Xinhua) -- China's top legislature has started deliberating the draft financial law, which includes better protections for financial consumers and investors, as well as new provisions regulating online marketing of financial products and services.
The draft was submitted for its second reading at a session of the Standing Committee of the National People's Congress, which runs through Friday.
The proposed law is designed to serve as a foundational, comprehensive and overarching piece of legislation for China's financial sector, providing guidance and a regulatory framework for the country's financial legal system.
To strengthen the protection of financial consumers and investors, the revised draft stipulates that providers of financial products and services must establish fair and reasonable transaction terms. They must not use standard-form clauses to unfairly restrict consumer or investor rights, reduce or exempt themselves from liability, or impose additional responsibilities on consumers and investors.
It also requires entities marketing financial products and services to strengthen customer suitability management, obtain relevant customer information in accordance with regulations, accurately explain their offerings, fully disclose risks, and ensure that products and services are appropriate for customers' circumstances.
The revised draft also introduces targeted provisions to tighten oversight of online marketing activities involving financial products and services.
Under the proposed provisions, the online provision or marketing of financial products and services must comply with relevant laws, administrative regulations and rules issued by financial regulators under the State Council, including specific requirements governing online financial activities.
Financial products and services offered through non-public issuance must not be advertised or publicly solicited via the internet or other channels, including through disguised forms of public solicitation.
The revised draft also adds provisions emphasizing a market-oriented and law-based approach to financial development and promoting the development of international financial centers.
Additional provisions further seek to address the regulation of asset management businesses and cross-border financial activities. ■

====================================================================================================

Retirement does not increase loneliness among older Australians: study
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
16:27:21 CST
17:27:21 KST

MELBOURNE, Nov. 2 (Xinhua) -- Retirement does not make older Australians lonelier, with a new study finding no measurable difference to loneliness before or after leaving the workforce.
Researchers led by Australia's Monash University tracked 7,434 Australians aged 55 to 75 over nearly two decades, using data from the Household, Income and Labor Dynamics in Australia Survey. The study challenged the assumption that retirement leads to isolation, according to a university statement released Monday.
The team followed the same Australians for nearly two decades, and found that their loneliness did not change in the three years before or after retirement.
The study found that about 17.5 percent of older adults reported high levels of loneliness. The findings were consistent across demographic and socioeconomic groups, including people with different incomes, wealth levels and occupational backgrounds.
Loneliness tended to increase continuously from the late 60s, suggesting that aging, rather than the transition out of work, was associated with rising loneliness, according to the researchers, noting that efforts to address loneliness should focus on social connection throughout later life, including support for people experiencing major life events such as losing a spouse. ■

WELLINGTON, Nov. 2 (Xinhua) -- More than 913,000 people have cast their votes in the first seven days of advance voting for New Zealand's 2026 general election scheduled for Nov. 7, exceeding the number recorded at the same stage of the 2023 election.
A total of 913,762 votes were cast between Oct. 26 and Nov. 1, compared with 712,192 during the equivalent period in 2023, the Electoral Commission noted on Monday.

About 600 voting places will be open each day this week ahead of the election day when more than 2,300 voting places will operate nationwide, according to the commission.
Prime Minister Christopher Luxon's center-right National Party is seeking a second term after taking office in 2023, while Labor, led by former Prime Minister Chris Hipkins, is campaigning to return to power amid public concerns over the cost of living, economic growth, jobs and public services.
New Zealand citizens or permanent residents aged 18 or above, who have lived in New Zealand continuously for 12 months or more at some time in their life, are eligible to vote in the election, the commission said, noting that official election results are scheduled to be declared on Nov. 27. ■

Erdogan seeks $15B trade target and deeper strategic ties on South Korea visit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
08:25:09 UTC
17:25:09 KST

Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan has outlined an ambitious agenda for expanding Türkiye’s strategic partnership with South Korea, setting a $15 billion bilateral trade target and identifying nuclear energy, defence industry, advanced technology and transport infrastructure as key areas for cooperation.
In an interview with South Korea’s Yonhap News Agency ahead of his state visit to Seoul, Erdogan said the two countries should build on their historic ties, rooted in the Korean War, and turn their longstanding friendship into stronger economic and technological partnerships.
The visit comes ahead of the 70th anniversary of diplomatic relations between Türkiye and South Korea next year. Erdogan said strengthening political dialogue, increasing investment and expanding industrial cooperation would be central to the discussions.
Nuclear energy and trade at the centre of talks
Erdogan described South Korea as a strong potential partner for Türkiye’s planned Sinop Nuclear Power Plant, saying discussions with the Korean side had advanced following a memorandum of understanding signed last year.
Türkiye has conducted preliminary feasibility work with Korea Electric Power Corporation (KEPCO), while assessments continue on technical and economic conditions and the project’s investment model.
The president said the final decision would depend on electricity generation costs, financing arrangements and the project’s wider benefits for the Turkish economy.
On trade, he pointed to a significant imbalance between the two countries. Türkiye exported approximately $1.14 billion worth of goods to South Korea in 2025, while imports reached $10.26 billion.
Erdogan said Ankara wanted to narrow the gap and make trade more balanced and sustainable, with opportunities for Korean investment in automotive manufacturing, batteries, semiconductors, robotics, biotechnology, medical equipment and renewable energy.
He cited Hyundai’s automotive operations and POSCO’s steel investments in Türkiye as examples of existing cooperation, adding that the launch of electric vehicle production at Hyundai’s facility in Izmit was welcome.
Defence cooperation gains momentum
The Turkish president also highlighted opportunities to expand defence industry cooperation, particularly in unmanned aerial vehicles and engine technologies.
He welcomed South Korea’s reported interest in the PD170 engine, developed by Turkish Engine Industries (TEI), a subsidiary of Turkish Aerospace Industries. The engine is used in Türkiye’s ANKA and AKSUNGUR unmanned aircraft.
Erdogan described the interest as recognition of the progress Turkish engineers have made and said the two countries could extend their existing defence cooperation into unmanned systems, engines, electronic systems, and advanced engineering.
He also pointed to the Altay main battle tank as an example of the countries’ previous cooperation in the defence sector.
Erdogan calls for joint role in Gaza reconstruction
Turning to Gaza, Erdogan said the ceasefire agreement was an important step but had not brought life back to normal for Palestinians, who continue to face severe humanitarian conditions.
He called for obstacles to aid deliveries to be removed and reconstruction to accelerate, stressing the need to rebuild hospitals, schools and homes and restore water and electricity infrastructure.
Erdogan welcomed South Korean President Lee Jae-myung’s statements on Gaza and support for humanitarian assistance. He said Türkiye’s experience in humanitarian aid, construction and infrastructure could complement South Korea’s strengths in technology, engineering and financing.
The two countries could cooperate on rebuilding health facilities, schools and housing, as well as restoring energy and water networks, he said.
However, Erdogan stressed that Palestinians must determine Gaza’s future and rejected any reconstruction plan that would force them from their homeland.
He reiterated Türkiye’s position that lasting peace requires an independent and sovereign Palestinian state based on the 1967 borders, with East Jerusalem as its capital.
Regional security and transport corridors
Erdogan also addressed tensions involving Yemen and Saudi Arabia, condemning attacks targeting civilians and airports and expressing Türkiye’s support for Saudi Arabia’s sovereignty, territorial integrity and security.
He said Ankara was working to advance the Mecca Agreement, including through its approval process in the Turkish parliament and efforts to strengthen institutional cooperation and joint defence capabilities.
On Yemen, Erdogan called for an end to the fighting and a political settlement involving all parties, while emphasising the need to preserve the country’s sovereignty and territorial integrity.
The president also highlighted the strategic importance of Türkiye’s transport links as disruptions affect shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab al Mandab.
He said the risks to global energy and trade routes underscored the need for reliable alternative corridors, pointing to Türkiye’s efforts to connect railways, roads, ports and logistics centres into an integrated transport network.
Among the projects he outlined was the revival of the historic Hejaz Railway, built during the reign of Ottoman Sultan Abdulhamid II. Türkiye is pursuing work with Syria and Jordan, while agreements with Saudi Arabia on railway and logistics cooperation are also part of the wider effort to strengthen connections between the Gulf, Türkiye and Europe.
Erdogan additionally cited the Middle Corridor, which crosses the Caspian Sea, and the Development Road project linking Iraq’s Grand Faw Port to Türkiye as complementary routes that could expand regional trade and reduce transport times and costs.
He said South Korean companies could contribute through railway infrastructure, signalling, communications systems, logistics centres and intelligent transport technologies, adding that Ankara was ready to support Korean firms investing and creating jobs in Türkiye.

European allies are concerned that a defeat for the Republican Party in the midterm elections could intensify US President Donald Trump’s critical stance toward NATO, reports Politico.
Five diplomats from the alliance, speaking on condition of anonymity, told Politico that the primary concern is that Trump—facing domestic constraints due to a lack of support in Congress—might seek to leave a lasting mark on foreign policy in his capacity as Commander-in-Chief. This could mean the withdrawal of thousands more troops from Europe.
A high-ranking European defense official noted that presidents nearing the end of their terms often exhibit frustration and engage in foreign policy adventurism. In contrast, attacks on NATO appear to be a consistent element of Trump’s worldview. Olivia Wales, an assistant to the White House Press Secretary, told Politico that President Trump has done far more for NATO than anyone else. She pointed to his success in securing an agreement to increase defense spending to 5% of GDP, the expansion of the US military presence in Greenland, and his efforts to put an end to Russian aggression in Ukraine. 
Wales emphasized that Trump maintains the view that NATO allies should have come to his aid in a war with Iran.
 She added that the President will never accept the decline of the West and will continue to defend American interests—both at home and abroad—without making any compromises.
It is expected that the Democrats will win a majority in the House of Representatives in the midterm elections and could potentially shift the balance of power in the Senate; meanwhile, President Trump’s approval ratings have fallen to an all-time low.
Concerns among officials highlight the growing transatlantic tension, which has intensified following the US’s temporary suspension of Starlink services for Ukrainians, as well as Trump’s attempts to curry favor with Russian dictator Vladimir Putin just weeks before the elections. An intensification of criticism from the American side could deal a further blow to NATO, especially given that Russia is stepping up its sabotage campaigns and hybrid warfare in Europe. One NATO diplomat remarked that Trump could become very angry, and if that happens, his tone is likely to turn very sharp.
At the heart of these concerns is a reassessment of the deployment of US forces in Europe, which is expected in December. If Trump finds himself unable to influence domestic legislation, he might seek to significantly increase the number of troops withdrawn from Europe—a move intended to energize his MAGA movement.
Oana Lungescu, a former NATO official and associate fellow at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI)—a British think tank—suggested that Trump might also choose to link the American military presence in Europe to a US-proposed peace plan for Ukraine. 
She noted the risk that all these issues—the review of US force levels, Ukraine, and the European security architecture—could, to some extent, be perceived as part of a broader deal with Putin,
 creating a highly dangerous situation for Europe.
Trump has also indicated that he might reduce U.S. contributions to the alliance’s funding, curtail NATO-led arms procurement schemes for Ukraine, and potentially strengthen ties with Russia. A significant Republican defeat in the midterm elections could lead to major changes at the Pentagon, which in turn would affect plans currently being developed within the institution. US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth has become highly unpopular in Congress, largely due to his refusal to provide regular budgetary and operational reports. This has fueled speculation that Hegseth could lose his position following a Republican electoral defeat—partly because a Democrat-led Congress might launch investigations into the dismissal of generals and admirals without valid cause.
If Hegseth remains in office, the Pentagon could experience a transitional period, which might result in the decision regarding the withdrawal of US troops from Europe being delayed by several months.

Dutch campaigners accuse Philip Morris of heated tobacco fraud

Dutch campaigners accuse Philip Morris of heated tobacco fraud
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
A criminal complaint is being filed against Phillip Morris for fraud and forgery. A Dutch anti-smoking foundation says it has falsely presented heated tobacco as less harmful than smoking, and broken the ban on advertising tobacco in the Netherlands.
Stichting Rookpreventie Jeugd, a foundation that campaigns against youth smoking, said on Monday it would hand the complaint to the public prosecution service (OM) in mid-November.
The foundation, chaired by former lung specialist Wanda de Kanter, says Philip Morris backs its claims mainly with its own studies and leaves out worrying findings from independent research. It also accuses the company of illegally promoting heated tobacco through specialist shops.
Cancer charity KWF, the lung and heart foundations, the Antoni van Leeuwenhoek cancer institute and the lung doctors’ association NVALT have pledged to back the complaint.
“Since fines from regulators and settlements with bereaved relatives have not stopped Philip Morris from committing new violations, it is now up to criminal law,” lawyer Sjoerd Lopik said in a statement.
In June, doctors and health groups complained to the advertising watchdog about a Philip Morris campaign that used an AI tool to help people object to tougher EU tobacco rules. The Reclame Code Commissie later ruled that the campaign breached the advertising ban.
The foundation’s previous criminal complaint against tobacco makers, filed in 2016, did not lead to a prosecution. A court ruled that regulating the industry was a matter for the government. The foundation says the new complaint is based on breaches of existing law.

A prominent Michigan Democrat endorsed Republican Mike Rogers on Sunday, giving President Donald Trump's Republicans an unexpected boost in a critical US Senate race two days before midterm elections that will decide control of Congress.
US Representative Haley Stevens, who lost the Michigan Democrats' Senate primary to Abdul El-Sayed in a bitterly contested race, publicly backed Rogers and appeared with him at a Detroit church, threatening to worsen divisions in a state viewed as crucial to Democratic hopes of retaking the US Senate.

"I don't belong in Abdul's campaign," Stevens said in a video posted to social media.

Hours later at a political rally in Iowa, Trump invited Stevens to join the Republican Party. He told reporters beforehand that he would reach out to her to thank her for the endorsement, which he called "a smart thing to do because El-Sayed would destroy our country".
Thirty-five Senate seats and all 435 House of Representatives seats are on the ballot on Tuesday. Republicans hold narrow majorities in both chambers. Polls show Democrats are favoured to win a majority of the House and are locked in a tight battle for control of the Senate, where the outcome likely will rest with a handful of states, including Michigan and Alaska.
If Democrats take control of the House or Senate, they could block Trump's legislative agenda for his final two years in office and launch investigations of an administration that has so far faced largely compliant Republican majorities. The White House has been preparing to implement portions of Trump's agenda without the aid of Congress, including its tariff pressure on trading partners.
Michigan rift

"That ad was very painful," Stevens told CNN on Sunday night. "There are so many Democrats who want to vote for our Democratic nominee, and they're just being told, 'Hey, this is a party you don't belong in, or this is a campaign you don't belong in.'"
El-Sayed's campaign recently asked Stevens to skip his events through Election Day so as "not to distract from the central issues of the campaign", a person familiar with the matter said.
Republicans sought to capitalise on Stevens' move. "This is courage in politics in America today," Rogers said. "When you see a party, and at least a sliver of the party, veering off into the virulent hate that they have been spewing toward a group of people, it gets dangerous."
Later on Sunday at the Iowa rally, Trump repeated false claims that El-Sayed is a "jihadist" – attacks that fit a broader pattern of inflammatory rhetoric from Trump and other Republicans targeting Arab Americans and Muslims.

Europe seeks Central Asia's critical minerals as producers push for local processing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
08:19:13 UTC
17:19:13 KST

At a forum in Tashkent, participants examined technology transfer, financing and transport routes. A recent German-Kazakh industrial roadmap and preliminary financing terms with a French bank illustrate the different stages of cooperation.
European demand for critical minerals is prompting discussions with Central Asian producers over investment in mining and processing. While European industries are looking for alternative sources of supply, countries such as Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan want foreign investment and technology to develop their own manufacturing capabilities.
These different priorities were discussed at the International Mining and Metals Forum, held in Tashkent, where industry representatives examined opportunities for commercial cooperation.
"Brussels expects not just agreements. It expects development of clear investment partnerships with countries like Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan in the broadest sense," said Marat Terterov, founder of the Brussels Energy Club, an independent non-profit organisation that brings together energy experts, policymakers and industry representatives.
Terterov also pointed to the need for investment in mineral processing, industrial supply chains and transport infrastructure, including the Middle Corridor linking Central Asia to European markets.
Europe's search for alternative suppliers
The EU identifies materials including lithium and tungsten as critical because of their economic importance and supply risks.
Germany is among the European economies seeking to diversify its sources.
"In Germany we need a lot of critical minerals because we invest in renewable energies, we invest in electric cars, we invest in high technology," Matthias Vollert, Germany's ambassador to Uzbekistan, told Euronews.
In a joint declaration issued on 29 September, Germany and Kazakhstan endorsed a 2026–2028 roadmap covering industrial cooperation, mineral extraction and processing, as well as increased production of higher-value goods in Kazakhstan.
German company HMS Bergbau AG is also pursuing a lithium extraction and processing project in eastern Kazakhstan. The potential investment could reach $500mn (approximately €449mn), subject to confirmation of commercially viable reserves. The project remains in the exploration and development phase.
Uzbekistan seeks greater value from mineral processing
Uzbekistan is pursuing a similar industrial approach, seeking to develop the domestic processing of minerals rather than relying primarily on exports of raw materials and concentrates.
The Uzbekistan Technological Metals Complex (TMK) is a state-owned industrial company established in 2024 to develop the country's mineral processing industry. It works with materials including tungsten and molybdenum, producing industrial products such as tungsten oxide and carbide, as well as molybdenum bars and briquettes.
"The main reason is making value. So in every step, in every stage we are making the value and then exporting," said Timur Khikmatullaev, TMK's Special Representative for Global Integration.
According to Khikmatullaev, Germany was the company's first export market. TMK also reports exports to Belgium, the Netherlands, Türkiye, the United States, Canada, South Korea and Japan.
According to shipment records published by 52wmb, a commercial trade-data platform, TMK exported molybdenum products to Belgium and the Netherlands, as well as tungsten oxide to the Netherlands, in August 2026.
European technology and financing
Alongside its existing exports, TMK is seeking investment and manufacturing expertise to expand production within Uzbekistan.
In September, the company held a roadshow in Berlin, bringing together representatives of around 20 German companies and international financial institutions.
Discussions covered supplies of critical minerals, technology transfer and participation in new manufacturing projects. TMK presented a portfolio of more than 140 proposed investment projects, with a combined estimated value of $4.2bn (approximately €3.77bn), according to the company.
On 16 October, TMK and France's Société Générale signed a preliminary term sheet for pre-export financing.
The discussions follow a mandate agreement signed in June to arrange €50mn in financing intended to support production capacity and export operations. A final loan agreement has not yet been announced.
International mining partnerships beyond Europe
Cooperation in Uzbekistan's mining sector also extends beyond European investors.
AzerGold, Azerbaijan's state-owned mining company, established its first foreign subsidiary in Uzbekistan in October. The company is seeking permits to begin an 18-month exploration programme at the Akba gold deposit in the Kashkadarya region.
"If the results are going to be positive, we plan to establish the joint venture and then to develop the deposit," Ilyas Ismayilli, General Director of AzerGold Uzbekistan, told Euronews.
Separately, AzerGold is working towards a trilateral joint venture with Uzbekgeologorazvedka JSC and the Azerbaijan–Uzbekistan Investment Company to explore gold and rare earth minerals in the Navoi region. The partners signed a preliminary agreement in July, but the venture has yet to be formally established.

Skater Niina Petrõkina sets PB to take silver in Canada
Estonian figure skater Niina Petrõkina set a new personal best and finished second at the Grand Prix stage in Kelowna, British Columbia.
The reigning and two-time European champion placed third after the short program. She had had planned to open her free skate with a quadruple salchow — a jump she has landed well in training in Canada — but opted instead for a clean triple. Her other jumps landed well too, and her step sequence and spins were graded level four.
This brought her a score of 143.83 for the free skate, just below the PB she set at this year's European Championships, where she took gold with 145.53. Her combined total of 221.07 improved on the 216.14 she recorded in January, however, giving a new PB across both programs.
This is her second career Grand Prix medal, after third place at the US stage last season.
The result was also a great birthday present for Petrõkina's coach, Svetlana Varnavskaja.
Mao Shimad (Japan), the four-time junior world champion who turned 18 recently, won her first senior Grand Prix title, scoring 153.33 in the free skate for a combined 235.44.
American Isabeau Levito came third.

Ukrainian drones attack Russia’s Samara region, reportedly striking Europe’s largest oil storage facility
Ukrainian drones struck Russia’s Samara region overnight on November 2. Regional authorities had not officially commented on the strikes by the time of publication, but Samara’s airport suspended operations for two hours because of the drone threat.
Ukrainian monitoring channels and Astra, an independent Telegram channel, cited photos and videos from eyewitnesses in reporting that the drones, according to preliminary reports, struck the Samara Linear Production and Dispatch Station (LPDS) near the settlement of Prosvet.
The Samara LPDS is the largest tank farm in Europe, part of a network operated by Transneft. Four pipelines carrying oil from Western Siberia, Tatarstan, the Orenburg region, and Kazakhstan connect to the station.
Ukrainian military drones struck the Samara LPDS several times in October, causing fires and damaging storage tanks.

US Warns of Possible Mass-Casualty Terror Attack in Moscow
The US Embassy in Russia warned of a possible mass-casualty terrorist attack at a major cultural site in Moscow on October 31, prompting Russian security services to launch a response after receiving intelligence from Washington.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to a security alert issued by the US Embassy on October 31, the potential threat concerned the Tsaritsyno Museum-Reserve, a historic palace and park complex in southern Moscow.
The embassy urged American citizens to avoid the museum and surrounding area on October 31, warning that an incident involving a large number of casualties could occur. US officials also confirmed that Washington was coordinating its response with the relevant Russian authorities.
Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB) subsequently acknowledged receiving information from the United States about preparations for a possible terrorist attack in Moscow. The FSB said the intelligence had been transmitted through established communication channels between the two countries and that appropriate security measures were being taken.
The warning coincided with two concerts scheduled at the Tsaritsyno complex on October 31, including performances at the Bread House at 5 p.m. and Bazhenov Hall at 6 p.m.
Russian Telegram channel Baza reported that the museum grounds had subsequently been closed to incoming visitors, with people permitted only to leave the park. Law enforcement personnel were reportedly deployed across the site.
However, museum administrators initially stated that they had received no information about a security threat and that the complex continued operating normally.
The US Embassy advised American nationals in Moscow to remain vigilant, avoid large gatherings, monitor local news, keep mobile phones charged, and carry identification documents.
The embassy also recommended reviewing personal security plans and registering with the Smart Traveler Enrollment Program (STEP) to receive emergency notifications.
The warning follows a previous terrorist attack in the Moscow region in March 2024, when gunmen attacked the Crocus City Hall concert venue, killing more than 140 people. The Islamic State claimed responsibility for that attack.

Prime Minister Bart De Wever offers resignation to King Filip
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
08:16:09 UTC
17:16:09 KST

As many Belgians enjoy a long holiday weekend at the start of the Flemish half-term, Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever (Flemish nationalist N-VA) is tendering his resignation to the King on Monday morning. The federal leader was unable to reach an agreement with his coalition partners on the budget.
Prime Minister Bart De Wever offers King Filip his resignation
Budget talks among the partners of the 5-way government have broken down for the time being at least: how did it come to this?
Prime Minister Bart De Wever (N-VA) is tendering his resignation to the King, as he was unable to reach an agreement on the budget. This is now officially a “political crisis”, concludes VRT NEWS political journalist Bart Verhulst. Does this also spell the end of the government? And what happens next?
Prime Minister Bart De Wever has been unable to reach an agreement on the budget with his coalition partners Flemish socialist Vooruit, Flemish Christian democrat CD&V, Francophone liberal MR and Francophone centrist Les Engagés. Negotiators parted ways again last night without a deal.
In substance, the deadlock centres mainly on a single issue. “It’s at a standstill because socialist Vooruit wants people with the ‘strongest shoulders’ to make greater efforts, as do centrist Les Engagés and Christian democrat CD&V. On the other hand, you have Flemish nationalist N-VA and conservative liberal MR – a classic left-right divide, in other words,” analyses Verhulst.
MR Deputy Prime Minister David Clarinval voiced opposition to “too much taxation, while according to Foreign Minister Maxime Prévot (Les Engagés), listing all the sticking points would take “an eternity”.
Prime Minister De Wever subsequently concluded that reaching an agreement was (for the time being) impossible and announced that he would tender his resignation to King Filip. A “dramatic turn of events”, concludes Verhulst. “If this isn’t a political crisis, then I don’t know what is.”
What happens next?
King Filip sees Prime Minister De Wever at the Palace at 9.30 am to discuss the deadlock. “Either the King accepts the resignation, in which case the government will fall, or the King will take time to consider the resignation and give De Wever more time, as he did last year,” says Verhulst. In principle, a new majority could also be found without the need for new elections.
A move in a well-versed Belgian political playbook
A year ago, the De Wever government found itself in much the same situation. Back then, too, the search for 10 billion euros proved fruitless. Although Prime Minister Bart De Wever (N-VA) did not tender his resignation in early November 2025, he did ask the King to extend the deadline. He was granted an extra 50 days. “That was a kind of leverage at the time. Now the word ‘resignation’ is being used explicitly,” explains Verhulst.
On 24 November 2025, an agreement was finally reached to make savings of 9.2 billion euros. Will they manage to reach an agreement this time around as well?
“In principle, they could meet again as early as late this morning, for a final attempt to reach a deal tonight and be able to go to parliament tomorrow. Or we’re heading for something far worse.” In any case, De Wever is determined to avoid the so-called ‘twelfths’ at all costs.
A budget with so called twelfths involves mirroring expenditure and income from this year’s budget each month next year.
