China's President Xi Jinping on Monday called for joint efforts to maintain peace and stability in the Middle East, warning against turning the Gulf region into an arena for major-power rivalry and geopolitical conflicts, according to state media.
 
Xi made the remarks during talks with Oman's Sultan Haitham bin Tariq at Beijing's Great Hall of the People, Xinhua News reported.
 
Xi said the Middle East and Gulf regions should “not become a wrestling ground for major-country rivalry and geopolitical conflicts,” stressing that regional peace and stability require joint efforts by all parties.
 
He added that China was willing to strengthen communication and coordination with Arab and Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) countries, including Oman, to help restore regional peace and achieve lasting stability.
 
In a joint statement issued following the talks, China and Oman called for disputes to be resolved through political and diplomatic means and urged the US and Iran to pursue a peaceful path, achieve a ceasefire and prevent a broader war.
 
The two sides urged Washington and Tehran to return to the Islamabad memorandum of understanding and resume dialogue and negotiations as soon as possible, with the aim of reaching a comprehensive agreement that also addresses Iran’s nuclear program, according to the Omani Foreign Ministry.
 
They also stressed the need to restore normal and safe navigation through the Strait of Hormuz and agreed to remain in contact over developments concerning the strategic waterway, the statement said.
 
Oman expressed support for Chinese initiatives aimed at promoting peace and stability in the Middle East and said it hoped Beijing would play a greater role in achieving lasting regional security.
 
China, for its part, praised Oman’s longstanding efforts to reduce regional tensions, build mutual trust and promote peace, highlighting Muscat’s role in Gulf and Middle East issues.
 
On Yemen, the two countries urged the parties to prioritize the interests of the Yemeni people, resolve differences through dialogue and consultation, and resume the political process as soon as possible while respecting Yemen’s independence, unity and territorial integrity.
 
Haitham's visit marks the first by an Omani sultan to China since diplomatic relations between the two countries were established 48 years ago.
 
It comes amid the ongoing US-Iran conflict that began in February following US-Israeli military strikes against Tehran.
 
‘Higher level’ in bilateral ties
 
On bilateral relations, Xi called for strengthening the strategic partnership with Oman to a “higher level,” saying the two countries share a longstanding friendship and increasingly strong political trust.
 
The joint statement said the two sides agreed to deepen coordination between China’s Belt and Road Initiative and Oman Vision 2040 and expand cooperation in energy, investment, finance, artificial intelligence and other advanced technologies.
 
They agreed to deepen oil and natural gas cooperation while expanding work in renewable energy, including solar and wind power, electricity transmission and energy storage.
 
The two countries also agreed to strengthen cooperation in artificial intelligence, digital infrastructure, space and investment, as well as military, security and judicial fields.
 
They also said a local-currency swap agreement would be used to deepen financial cooperation and facilitate bilateral trade and investment.
 
Haitham said China had become Oman’s largest trading partner, with direct investments by Chinese companies in partnership with the Oman Investment Authority exceeding 33 billion yuan ($4.6 billion) in recent years.
 
He also expressed Oman’s willingness to conclude a preferential bilateral trade and investment agreement with China.
 
The two countries also called for accelerating negotiations on a China-GCC free trade agreement and agreed to maintain communication on holding the second China-Arab and China-GCC summits in China at an appropriate time.
 
Following the talks, the two leaders witnessed the signing of an agreement and 14 memorandums of understanding and cooperation protocols covering areas including satellite navigation, supply chains, green development, local-currency exchange, digital payments and digital currency.

Andrew's mom in Lviv suddenly needs money for a new washing machine, and Andrew has been living in Canada for five years now. So it's no surprise he started wondering about how to send money to Ukraine from Canada without overpaying on fees or waiting a week. There are plenty of options, but he needs something reliable and fast. And most importantly, his mom has to be able to pick up the money on the other end. So let's walk through it with Andrew as the example.
Where does the money go, and when can mom receive it?
Let's take Meest Canada, since that's who Andrew uses. They send the transfer in US dollars to PrivatBank, and the money shows up in the bank the next business day. That makes it a fast option and an easy one to understand. If Andrew sends it on Monday, his mom can receive it at the bank on Tuesday. If he sends it on Friday, she can receive it on Monday, because only business days count.
That's pretty much what the best way to send money to Ukraine looks like: one bank, one currency and no surprises. You just send the transfer, and the recipient can receive the money at a branch or in the app. And the money will wait at the bank for up to 30 business days. For more detailed information, look at https://ca.meest.com/services/service/sending-money-to-ukraine.
How much does sending money to Ukraine cost?
The commission depends on the amount. It's the same all across Canada, so it doesn't matter whether Andrew lives in Toronto or Vancouver. Up to $100, the commission is $6. From $101 to $200, it's $10, and from $201 to $500, it's $12. For bigger amounts, it goes up to $16-22, and above $1,000 it's 2%.
So for sending money to Ukraine for $300, Andrew will pay $12. Clear pricing is more useful than hunting for the cheapest option: you can see the total before you even go to the office.
What do you need to bring to send money?
Andrew walks into a Meest office to do a money transfer to Ukraine from Canada. He fills out a quick form with his address and phone number, then shows an ID with his date of birth. It sounds like a lot, but it's a secure setup, and the ID part is just there because of anti-money laundering rules. The one thing to get right is his mom's name. It has to match her passport exactly, so he asks her to snap a photo of that page.
When he's done, he gets a 6-digit control number and a receipt. He sends the number to his mom, along with the amount and his last name, and keeps the receipt. Most people get stuck on little things, like a wrong letter in a name or an ID left at home. So before he heads out, Andrew skims the terms and conditions and checks everything one more time. No surprises that way.
How does Mom get the money: at the bank or on her phone?
This is probably the nicest part, because there are two methods for getting the money. The first is at a bank branch. Mom brings her passport or her PrivatBank card, gives them the transfer number, the sender's name, the amount and the currency, and gets her cash. If she doesn't have a card yet, the bank can open one for free if she wants. With it, she can receive transfers online, at ATMs and by phone.
If she lives in a small town, it's a good idea to call the branch first and ask if they have enough cash on hand. Sometimes they don't have a large sum, and the payout can be delayed.
The second way is online, on her phone:
- Open Privat24
- Go to the "Service" menu
- Choose "International transfers"
- Pick Meest and enter the transfer number
Andrew's mom went with the app. She says it beats standing in line. So that's the whole process, an easy way to send money from Canada to Ukraine: a form, a number and a bank. You can explain the whole thing to your mom over the phone. By the way, Meest Canada has other services too, so you can send not only money but also parcels, pretty much anywhere in the world.

Ukraine’s and Russia’s ombudsmen agree to keep working on regular humanitarian missions after the Oleshky evacuation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
08:13:26 UTC
17:13:26 KST

Ukraine’s and Russia’s human rights commissioners have agreed to keep working on regular humanitarian missions after the evacuation from occupied Oleshky, Ukrainian ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said on 31 October. A day later, the ceasefire that made the evacuation possible ended.
Without a new truce, the people left behind are back where they were. In July, the Institute for the Study of War concluded that Russia was effectively blockading Oleshky, which lies across the Dnipro from Ukrainian-held Kherson. In May, journalist Zarina Zabrisky said the existing route out, through occupied Crimea, Russia, and Belarus, did not work: only three of 20 people who recently tried it got through.
Oleshky as a first step
Lubinets wrote that he and Russian ombudsman Yana Lantratova had agreed to continue work on regular missions. He said Oleshky should be the first step, since people living near the front line need constant support.
Lantratova claimed the same day that the sides had agreed to hold regular missions.
The truce had been coordinated by US First Lady Melania Trump. On 1 November, Lubinets said both sides had kept their commitments. He added that the two were working through the possibilities of continuing such steps.
Who stayed behind
On 30 October, Lubinets wrote that some buses were heading to Ukraine and others to Russia. About 700 to 1,000 people may remain in Oleshky, The Insider correspondent Tatiana Popova estimated on 31 October. Many feared a provocation or did not want to leave their homes.
Meanwhile, Ukrainian troops used the truce to evacuate 167 civilians, 22 of them children, from Ukrainian-held riverside settlements that came under daily Russian shelling, Ukraine’s General Staff reported on 1 November.
Bodies moved to Henichesk
On 1 November, Ukrainian journalist Oleh Baturin wrote that Henichesk residents had told him dozens of civilians’ bodies were brought there from Oleshky. Volunteer Kseniia Arkhipova confirmed it, he said. By her data, 47 bodies had been kept in the basements of Oleshky’s hospital since May.
How these people died remains unknown. In September, Tetiana Hasanenko, head of Oleshky’s Ukrainian military administration in exile, said more than 100 bodies lay in the basement of the hospital, which had had no electricity for four years.

Will France's political turmoil pave the way for the far-right in 2027?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
08:12:22 UTC
17:12:22 KST

Emmanuel Macron swept to power in 2017, defeating far-right candidate Marine Le Pen in a landslide victory that was widely hailed as a triumph of his newly established centrist movement over France's political extremes.
Five years later, Macron defeated Le Pen again in the second round of the 2022 presidential election, securing a second term despite the far-right leader's growing popularity.
But France faces a different political landscape ahead of the 2027 presidential election.
Macron is constitutionally barred from seeking a third consecutive term, and his centrist movement has no clear successor.
His presidency has faced mounting criticism over France's growing debt and rising living costs, amid deepening political polarisation and growing support for parties on both the far right and far left.
The latest wave of demonstrations, including high school students protesting against poor conditions in their schools and wider protests over economic pressures, has added to the political uncertainty. Both the far right and far left are seeking to capitalise on the unrest ahead of the election.
“I would say the political impact of those protests, and especially if they're associated with violence, is likely to benefit Marine Le Pen,” François Gemenne, a political scientist at Sciences Po in Paris and the University of Liege in Belgium, tells TRT World.
Violence accompanying demonstrations across France has damaged or looted thousands of businesses, intensifying criticism of Macron's government over its ability to maintain public order.
Can Le Pen capitalise on the unrest?
The unrest has raised questions about the French government's ability to contain violence accompanying demonstrations, with security forces facing scrutiny over their response.
Against this backdrop, Le Pen “doesn't have much to do to gain in polls because every time the situation appears chaotic, people will turn to the political party that represents order,” Gemenne says, referring to the National Rally's emphasis on security and its anti-immigration policies.
“For better or worse at the moment, Marine Le Pen represents order, which means that a lot of moderate voters, especially from the center right, are likely to vote for the extreme right because they will become convinced that the situation is desperate.
“And understanding goes that desperate situations call for desperate measures like a Le Pen presidency,” he says.
France's history offers examples of political upheaval followed by the rise of leaders promising stability.
A decade after the French Revolution of 1789, Napoleon Bonaparte seized power in a coup in 1799, presenting himself as a figure capable of restoring order after years of political unrest. He crowned himself emperor in 1804.
The Revolution of 1848, which established the short-lived Second Republic, was similarly followed by a conservative backlash. Louis-Napoleon Bonaparte, Napoleon's nephew, was elected president before seizing power in 1851 and proclaiming himself emperor the following year.
“The far-right could be seen as a ‘Parti de l'Ordre’, evoking memories of 1848 after the riots and the failed new revolution in May 1848,” Jean-Sylvestre Mongrenier, a French professor of history and geography and a geopolitics researcher at the Thomas More Institute, tells TRT World.
However, Mongrenier believes Le Pen cannot capitalise on the unrest alone.
He says different factions of the right and far right would need to unite, or at least establish a common political platform, to convince voters they could govern effectively and restore law and order.
“In my opinion, many electors are ready for that,” he says.
Is centrism at a dead end?
As protests continue across France, Macron's government has backed legislation that could make people who knowingly participate in violent groups financially liable for damage caused during demonstrations.
The French Senate approved the proposal on October 28, with provisions allowing liability of up to €10,000. The bill still requires approval from the National Assembly.
But the legislation has drawn criticism over provisions that could hold individuals financially responsible for damage they did not personally cause.
The controversy has increased political pressure on Macron. His centrist alliance lost its parliamentary majority in the snap election he called in 2024, leaving successive governments struggling to govern without a majority.
Against this backdrop, Macron and his minority government appear “weaker than ever at the moment,” Gemenne says.
He says potential centrist presidential candidates, including former prime ministers Gabriel Attal and Édouard Philippe, also appear “weak”.
“A lot of their voters are now turning towards the extreme right because they're afraid that those candidates will be too weak.”
With the political centre struggling, attention has turned to a possible second-round presidential contest between the far right and Jean-Luc Melenchon, the left-wing leader who has publicly supported the demonstrations.
“Such a situation is not in the favor of the political center, quiet, appeased and pragmatic, what we call the ‘cercle de la raison’,” Mongrenier says.
If tensions continue to escalate, Macron's allies might instead become “The Dead Centrist Society”, he adds.
Gemenne believes a contest between the far right and far left could leave moderate voters searching for an alternative.
“If you look at the polls at the moment, there is a real possibility of a showdown between the far right and the far left, with the far right almost sure to win in that case, which is the reason why a lot of moderate voters, both from the left and the right, are hoping to rally around a moderate candidate to avoid the showdown between the far right and the far left,” Gemenne says.
One possible alternative, he suggests, is Christine Lagarde, the French economist who previously headed the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and currently serves as president of the European Central Bank (ECB).
On October 29, Lagarde announced that she would step down on February 7, 2027, before her term expires in October.
She said she wanted “to have the freedom of speech, the freedom of expression and the freedom to engage on matters that are not monetary policy matters”.
“I’m interested in the truth, and I see the truth being very often damaged, contradicted by misrepresentation,” she said.
Her announcement has prompted questions about whether she could play a greater role in French political debate, although she has previously ruled out running in the presidential election.
Lagarde's economic credentials and experience in international institutions could make her an influential moderate voice at a time when France's political centre is struggling.
However, Macron also entered politics with a background in investment banking, and his economic policies have faced sustained criticism amid France's financial difficulties.
Gemenne believes Lagarde would nevertheless offer voters a different profile.
“She's a woman and she's more senior.”
Can Le Pen become France’s Meloni?
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, the longtime leader of the far-right Brothers of Italy party, has adopted a more pragmatic approach towards European institutions since taking office in 2022, while maintaining a hardline stance on immigration.
Her political trajectory raises the question of whether Le Pen could follow a similar path, presenting herself as a more acceptable choice to moderate voters and France's political establishment without abandoning the National Rally's far-right identity.
Le Pen also faces legal challenges. In July 2026, an appeals court upheld her conviction for embezzling European Parliament funds to pay party staff but shortened her electoral disqualification, allowing her to contest the 2027 presidential election.
Le Pen subsequently announced her candidacy and said she would challenge the conviction before France's highest court.
Despite these challenges, Gemenne says Le Pen's appeal partly rests on the perception that she could follow Meloni's example.
Many voters want to believe that “Le Pen will be like Meloni and so that it will not be as disastrous as the media are saying,” he says.
Meloni's rise has offered Le Pen an example of how a far-right party can broaden its electoral appeal and establish working relationships with European leaders after entering government.
Her experience could therefore strengthen Le Pen's efforts to convince French voters that a National Rally government would not necessarily bring the political upheaval its opponents predict.
Both leaders have sought to broaden their parties' appeal beyond their traditional support bases, although their political circumstances and paths to power differ.
Gemenne, however, remains sceptical that the National Rally has fundamentally changed.
“Time and time again the National Rally keeps trying to convince voters that it has changed, that it is no longer the same party as before,” he says.
“But time after time they proved that they're still the same extreme right party than they were before.”

Facing Chinese pressure, Taiwan says it must be master of its own maritime information
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
09:12:09 CET
17:12:09 KST

By Fabian Hamacher
TAINAN, Taiwan, Nov 2 (Reuters) - Taiwan must be the master of its own maritime information and conduct its own ocean surveys given the island’s fate rests on protecting its waters, the minister in charge of the Coast Guard said on Monday.
Taiwan has complained of a stepped up harassment campaign by China to assert sovereignty and jurisdiction claims over its waters using both Coast Guard and scientific research ships. China recognises no sovereignty claims by Taiwan.
Speaking at a sea drone forum in the southern city of Tainan, Kuan Bi-ling, head of Taiwan’s Ocean Affairs Council, which runs the Coast Guard, said Taiwan’s resources, energy, and the transport of supplies all depend on the ocean.
“Taiwan also sits on one of the most important shipping routes in the global supply chain. Therefore, protecting these waters concerns not only the daily lives of Taiwan’s people but also global economic development,” she said.
However, Taiwan faces many challenges, “including the threat of grey-zone harassment”, Kuan added, referring to China’s activities which stop short of outright combat but are designed to pressure and wear out Taiwan’s forces.
To counter those risks, the Coast Guard needs more equipment and more comprehensive intelligence to spot threats earlier and respond more effectively, she said.
“We maintain that Taiwan’s ocean must be surveyed by ourselves, and that we must master our own information.”
China on Saturday said it had sent another Coast Guard patrol in the waters off Taiwan’s east coast.
Taiwan has reported several incidents this year of Chinese research ships sailing near the island too.
China’s military also operates around Taiwan on an almost daily basis.
Taiwan’s democratically elected government says China has no jurisdiction over any of its waters and that it is in breach of international law by trying to prove otherwise with its patrols.
Taiwan also says China has been harassing merchant shipping with radio messages in waters that are not under Chinese jurisdiction.
China has never renounced the use of force to bring Taiwan under its control, but says it would prefer “peaceful reunification”.
(Reporting by Fabian Hamacher; Writing by Ben BlanchardEditing by Shri Navaratnam)

Energy workers were carrying out repairs, and the outages were expected to be lifted once the grid stabilized.

Residents were advised to stock up on water, with no estimate yet available for when supplies would be restored.

How the president’s party has fared in every US midterm election since 1946
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
08:05:03 UTC
17:05:03 KST

How the president’s party has fared in every US midterm election since 1946
Only twice in the past 20 midterms has the president’s party gained House seats. Polls suggest 2026 won’t be the third.
On Tuesday, Americans head to the polls for the United States midterm elections, held halfway through a president’s four-year term. Voters will choose all 435 members of the US House of Representatives and 35 of the Senate’s 100 seats. The voting will decide which party controls Congress for the next two years.
Although the president’s name won’t appear on the ballot, the vote is widely seen as a verdict on the presidency, and the president’s party almost always pays the price.
In 18 of the 20 midterms held from 1946 to 2022, voters took House seats away from the party in control of the White House. The average loss was 26 seats. Only Bill Clinton’s Democrats in 1998 and George W Bush’s Republicans in 2002 bucked the trend.
Political scientists call this the “presidential penalty”, or the “midterm penalty”. The president’s party tends to lose seats simply because it holds power as voters use the midterms to put a check on the White House.
The House: 18 losses in 20 midterms
The chart below shows how many House seats the president’s party has won or lost in each midterm since 1946 from Harry S Truman to Joe Biden.
Democratic presidents have suffered the biggest midterm defeats since 1946. On average, their party has lost about 29 House seats in a midterm, compared with about 23 under Republican presidents.
The largest loss came in 2010, two years after Barack Obama became the first African American elected president, when Democrats lost 64 House seats and Republicans took control of the chamber. The Democrats under Truman lost 56 seats in 1946, and under Clinton, they lost 54 in 1994, each time losing control of the House.
The worst Republican defeats came under Dwight D Eisenhower when the party lost 50 seats in 1958 and Gerald Ford when it lost 48 in 1974. Donald Trump’s first midterm in 2018 cost Republicans 42 seats and control of the House.
Big losses often cost the president’s party its majority. In seven of the 20 midterms since 1946 (1946, 1954, 1994, 2006, 2010, 2018 and 2022), the House changed hands.
The Senate: 13 losses in 20 midterms
The president’s party has lost Senate seats in 13 of the 20 midterms since 1946 but lost control of the chamber in only six: 1946, 1954, 1986, 1994, 2006 and 2014.
Unlike the House of Representatives, where every seat is up for election every two years, only about a third of the Senate’s 100 seats are contested in each cycle because senators serve six-year terms and their elections are staggered. That means which states are voting can matter as much as the national mood.
Eisenhower’s Republicans suffered the biggest Senate loss in the period, giving up 13 seats in 1958. Truman’s Democrats lost 12 in 1946, and Obama’s Democrats lost nine in 2014, handing control of the chamber to Republicans.
At times, the two chambers have moved in opposite directions. In 1982, Ronald Reagan’s Republicans lost 26 House seats but gained one in the Senate. In 2018, Trump’s Republicans lost the House but added a Senate seat, and in 2022, Biden’s Democrats lost the House while gaining one seat in the Senate.
These split results show that a backlash against the president does not land evenly across Congress. A party can hold its ground on a favourable Senate map while losing competitive House districts.
What does it mean to lose the House or Senate?
Losing seats and losing control are not the same thing. Lyndon Johnson’s Democrats lost 47 House seats in 1966 but kept their majority. Twenty years later, Reagan’s Republicans lost only four House seats but lost the Senate after an eight-seat setback.
Control of the chambers decides who sets the agenda and passes legislation. A bill must pass both chambers before it reaches the president for his approval or veto, so an opposition majority in either can block the president’s plans.
A House majority can also mean a party is able to launch investigations and impeach a president while a Senate majority can reject the president’s nominees, including federal judges, who serve for life.
This year, Democrats need to gain three seats to win the House and four to win the Senate. A 50-50 split in the Senate would leave Republicans in control because Vice President JD Vance may cast tie-breaking votes.

UN warns of irreversible damage to glaciers from global warming
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
08:04:16 UTC
17:04:16 KST

UN warns of irreversible damage to glaciers from global warming
Two United Nation reports published on Monday warn that global warming exceeding 1.5 degrees Celsius will have “irreversible” consequences for the Earth’s glaciers, sea ice and frozen surfaces. They call for action to be taken “as quickly as possible”.
Exceeding the 1.5-degree threshold of global warming compared with pre-industrial levels – the most ambitious target of the Paris Agreement in 2015 – “will lead to significant – and often irreversible – consequences within the cryosphere and the polar oceans”, that is to say, “the regions of the planet characterised by the presence of snow, ice and frozen ground”, states one of the reports.
This will lead to melting glaciers and sea ice, thawing permafrost, and an accelerated rise in sea levels. The repercussions will be manifold and will increase the risk of flooding, economic and ecological damage, as well as water shortages and hazards in mountainous areas.
Some impacts are already visible, such as the loss of 20% of Switzerland’s glacial mass, the report highlights. And even though the 1.5-degree target remains relevant, it is already “too high” for the cryosphere, whose “safe temperature” is closer to 1 degree, or even lower.
‘Very slow’ recovery
Global warming has already reached 1.37 degrees compared with pre-industrial levels. And according to the European Copernicus network, the 1.5-degree threshold could be exceeded by around 2030.
“To limit […] the damage caused by ice loss in the polar and mountainous regions of the globe […] temperatures must be brought well below 1.5 degrees as quickly as possible”, explains James Kirkham, lead author of one of the reports, published a week before COP31, where countries are due to discuss measures to tackle global warming.
+ Swiss glaciers lost 20% of their volume in five years
“Every additional fraction of a degree and every year spent above this threshold will lead to more devastating consequences,” he insists.
Scientists are particularly warning of the risks of crossing certain tipping points. They stress that, even if global warming is brought back below 1.5 degrees, “recovery will be very slow”.
Thus, in the case of the ice caps, bringing global warming back below the average threshold of 1.5 degrees “will not, however, undo the consequences of the warming experienced during the period when the threshold was exceeded”, warns Chen Zhao, a glaciologist specialising in Antarctica and a contributor to the reports.
‘Glimpses of hope’
Nevertheless, a few “glimpses of hope” remain: some glaciers could partially recover if global warming quickly falls back below an average threshold of 1.5 degrees, or even 1 degree. Arctic sea ice could also benefit.
“But, unfortunately, the timeline for this recovery is far from linear compared to that of the decline. It could take several decades, or even centuries,” explained Matthew England, an oceanographer and climatologist at the University of New South Wales.
The second report shows that a temperature rise exceeding 2.8 degrees Celsius, which were to persist into the next century, would have significant consequences. Sea levels could thus rise by up to 5 cm per year by 2150, compared with the current rate of 0.45 cm. The thawing of permafrost could also release as much CO₂ each year as the United States – the world’s second-largest polluter – currently emits.
‘Tsunami from the mountains’
A worst-case scenario that is not so unlikely: according to a recent UN report, even if countries met their climate commitments, the world is heading for warming of around 2.6 degrees Celsius by 2100.
“A temporary overshoot of 1.5 degrees does not mean that the Paris Agreement’s targets are irrelevant. On the contrary, it makes them even more urgent,” notes Mr Kirkham. And “sufficient and immediate political ambition”, particularly in terms of reducing fossil fuel use, “can still significantly reduce the damage to the cryosphere and its consequences” for people and the planet.
“The decisions taken over the next few years will determine the extent of the damage,” emphasises Gunjan Silwal, a Nepalese glacier researcher, in a statement, pointing out that “the tragedy in Nepal is just a foretaste”.
This “mountain tsunami”, caused by the collapse of a glacier and a section of a mountain peak in the north of the country – which scientists attribute to global warming – left more than 1,500 people dead and 5,000 missing in August.

The award‑winning author Craig Silvey sent multiple messages about his sexual desire for young boys and was caught with explicit images of children and adults.
The young adult novelist was jailed on Monday for seven months after pleading guilty to distributing and possessing child exploitation material earlier this year.
The 44-year-old was found with numerous category one photos and videos on his laptop and mobile phone when police raided his Fremantle home, the Western Australian district court heard.
Silvey, a father of three, also engaged in an online conversation with another user on a pornography website, where his handle was Jimmy, Jimmy, Jimmy.
In the chat, Silvey described himself as a “Fremantle guy” before telling the user: “You sound amazing … we have very similar interests, would love to chat more; do you have Signal or Session?”
The pair moved to an encrypted messaging app, where he said he was “extremely open-minded and obsessed with taboos” and preferred boys older than five before adding that “eight was the perfect age”.
“I want to make out with little ones,” the author said in one message.
Silvey, who has been shortlisted for the Miles Franklin Literary Award and the International Dublin Literary Award, also wrote he was “drooling” over a sexually explicit photo of a naked man and boy together.
Judge Hayley Cormann said it was very serious and very disturbing offending.
“This offending involves children and it is destructive and it is devastating,” she said.
The popular author is best known for his 2009 coming‑of‑age novel Jasper Jones, considered a modern Australian classic and adapted into a feature film and several stage productions.

Russia is using new "Gerbera" with extended range of up to 1,200 km - DIU
Kyiv • UNN
The Defence Intelligence of Ukraine revealed the specifications of the “Gerbera-2,” with a range of up to 1,200 km and a warhead of up to 25 kg. The drone consists predominantly of Chinese components.
The aggressor country is using a larger, extended-range version of the Gerbera UAV, capable of carrying a warhead weighing up to 25 kilograms. The Main Directorate of Intelligence of the Ministry of Defence of Ukraine published information about the components and electronics of the Gerbera-2 unmanned aerial vehicle, reports UNN.
The enemy is using a larger, extended-range version of the Gerbera UAV, capable of carrying a warhead weighing up to 25 kg
Details
The HUR of the Ministry of Defence of Ukraine published an interactive 3D model, information about the components, and the electronic component base of the Gerbera-2 UAV on the War&Sanctions portal.
"The enemy has significantly upgraded the Gerbera unmanned aircraft, which were initially developed as decoys to overload air defence systems. The first versions had the 'Reconnaissance' and 'Kamikaze' modifications, but remained relatively simple and inexpensive aircraft. Gradually, their 'filling' began to approach the equipment of significantly more expensive Geran-type UAVs: Kometa systems, mesh modems, and costly cameras on gimbal mounts. Recently, the enemy began using an enlarged version of the Gerbera. The new model has a wingspan of 3 m and a fuselage length of 2.6 m. Thanks to a new fuel tank with a capacity of 63 litres, the UAV can cover a distance of up to 1,200 km," the intelligence service explains.
According to the available information, to maintain the aircraft's stability during manoeuvres, the tank is divided into separate sections internally. The two-cylinder, two-stroke engine is effectively half of the engine from the Geran-2, production of which has been localised in Alabuga.
"The sample examined used an OFZBCh-10 high-explosive fragmentation incendiary warhead weighing 10 kg, as well as separate bags containing an incendiary mixture. According to the characteristics stated by the enemy, the UAV can carry a warhead weighing up to 25 kg. The electronics of the Gerbera-2 consist of an updated flight controller, a 12-channel Kometa, a mesh modem manufactured by Shenzhen Sinosun Technology Co., Ltd (PRC), and a new video-processing unit called 'Sosiska', built on a Chinese Coke Pi microcomputer," the post states.
In addition, the sample examined had a dual IP camera mounted on the fuselage above the fuel tank and intended to detect interceptors. It was also found that versions exist with forward-facing IP cameras and cameras mounted on three-axis gimbals.
"The new Gerbera contains the largest number of components from Chinese (8) and American (4) manufacturers. The UAV's operational range, increased by means of the large fuel tank, indicates that the area of its use may extend beyond the territory of Ukraine. It was precisely a Gerbera-2 with a warhead that was discovered in mid-September on Poland's Baltic coast. The HUR of the Ministry of Defence of Ukraine continues its systematic work to examine weapons samples used by the enemy and to inform the world about new threats," the post says.

The Defence Forces of Ukraine struck the Energia plant and facilities in Oryol, Donetsk, and Tolyatti. The strikes complicate the production of missiles and drones.

Memo to King Charles: if the Dutch king can apologise for slavery, why can’t you? | Raoul de Jong
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
08:00:36 UTC
17:00:36 KST

Dear King Charles,
You are currently on a Caribbean royal tour through the Bahamas, Guyana, and Antigua and Barbuda. I understand that during this tour you will not issue a formal apology for Britain’s role in the transatlantic slave trade, or address the role your own family played in it. You will instead express your “sorrow”, and this will make it easier for politicians to also dodge the question. Whether that is Kemi Badenoch calling an apology a “navel-gazing distraction”, or the prime minister, Andy Burnham, saying he would support an apology, while flatly opposing reparations.
Coincidentally, I’m also in the middle of a world tour for the English translation of my book, Jaguarman, a novel about how my enslaved Surinamese ancestors survived 300 years of hell on Earth. I travelled from Ghana to Indonesia to New York, when I was asked to respond to you, as soon as possible. That’s how it often goes in this strange story, I’ve noticed: people like you get centuries to find the right words, while we must scramble to respond to your actions. But, yes, I do have something to say.
Three years ago your Dutch counterpart, King Willem-Alexander, stood before an audience of people of colour, many of them my friends. Dressed up like kings and queens, they listened solemnly as he did what you will not and apologised for the role of the Dutch state in enslaving our ancestors, and for the failure of his own family, the house of Orange-Nassau, to act against it. Slavery was “a crime against humanity”, he said, “and the stadholders and kings of the house of Orange-Nassau did nothing to stop it”.
It was a moment that people on whose shoulders I stand had fought for for centuries, often at the risk of their health or even their lives. Willem-Alexander’s speech was directed at people of colour such as me. But I felt that the apology was perhaps even more important for the rest of the population.
It happened in 2023, on 1 July, the day the Netherlands commemorates the abolition of slavery, a celebration called Keti Koti. In the Netherlands, many institutions tend only to invite writers such as me to speak on this one particular day, so as Willem-Alexander was addressing the nation, I was somewhere else, in a small library, in front of an audience of mostly white people, giving my own lecture about what they could learn from my Black ancestors.
We from the colonial diaspora already know the true history of our mother country. We already know what the powers that govern us are capable of. We know the darkness they can create. And we also know that it is possible to come through that darkness. To me, the apology was most important for all these other people who thought my history had nothing to do with them. For those who had never considered that there might be something to learn from the people who gave me this life.
You know the truth, Willem-Alexander knows it, I know it, but many of your subjects do not. The truth is my ancestors were kidnapped. Chained. Trafficked across the ocean. Sold. Torn from one another. Turned into property. Brainwashed. Silenced. Mocked. Cursed. But the fire inside us was never extinguished. Despite the plantations. Despite the Atlantic. Despite the slave forts. That is why I am alive.
That is not a small thing. It is enormous. That’s why the people receiving Willem-Alexander’s apology were dressed up like kings and queens. They know what a huge gift it is to be alive, and how important it is to take care of what you have been given. They know that they have not been put on this earth in order to wither. They have been put on this earth to blossom. And even if all your freedom is taken away from you by other people, you can find ways to flourish, because the spark of life itself is on our side.
Its fire will keep burning, your majesty, whether you apologise or not. The true heroes in this history were rarely born as royalty. But, of course, being born as royalty doesn’t prevent you from doing the right thing. You cannot stop the truth from coming out. But you can choose whether history remembers you as someone who stood in its way, or someone who stood with it.
- Raoul de Jong is a Dutch novelist

Alain Werner: A life spent fighting impunity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
08:00:00 UTC
17:00:00 KST

Alain Werner: A life spent fighting impunity
For nearly 25 years, the Geneva lawyer Alain Werner has helped victims of war crimes seek justice. He continues this fight as director of the non-governmental organisation Civitas Maxima, even as international justice comes under mounting strain.
How does someone end up documenting war crimes in order to bring their perpetrators before the courts? Almost by chance, according to Alain Werner, director of the Geneva-based NGO Civitas Maxima.
“I don’t know whether I had much freedom in choosing to study law,” the lawyer replies, weighing his words carefully. With a father who specialised in international arbitration, a mother who worked as a prison chaplain and a grandfather who was a judge, the call of the law was hard to resist.
“In the end, I embarked on a career that was legal enough to please my dad and human enough to please my mum,” Werner says with a smile, adding that he was “a good boy”.
“But the immense stroke of luck I had was that I started studying law at the University of Geneva in 1993, just as our field was being revived,” he adds. Now approaching 54, his eyes still light up when he talks about that period.
International justice on the rise
That year, the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia had just been established. The tribunal for Rwanda followed a year later.
“After stalling for around 50 years from the end of the Nuremberg trials to the fall of the Berlin Wall, international justice suddenly exploded,” Werner says. As a law student, he attended a seminar given by Robert Roth, a professor who would later become a judge at the Special Tribunal for Lebanon. After qualifying as a lawyer, Werner headed to New York and the prestigious Columbia University. There he encountered another leading figure in the field he would eventually enter: the American lawyer Reed Brody — known as the “dictator hunter” — at the international human rights organisation Human Rights Watch.
“He was a star to me. We would try to catch his eye from the lecture hall, hoping to work with him, but he barely looked at us. He already had his teams,” Werner jokes. At the time, he could not have imagined that they would later work together for several years on the trial of former Chadian dictator Hissène Habré.
As he recounts his story, Werner makes frequent references to friends and colleagues he admires, places he has visited and historical events, punctuating them with legal details. He speaks at a dizzying pace. Mid-sentence, he apologises, stops, goes back, then leaps forward again; his animated body language as he shifts in his chair seems to mirror the movements of his mind.
He completed his studies in New York in 2003, a year after the International Criminal Court (ICC) was established in The Hague. “I remember thinking: ‘If progress continues at this pace, in 20 years we’ll have won: impunity will no longer be the rule, but the exception,’” he says with conviction.
Charles Taylor’s trial
Back in Switzerland, Werner was eager to leave again as soon as possible. In 2003, the Swiss government sent him on a mission to Freetown, the capital of Sierra Leone, as an expert at the Special Court for Sierra Leone. The country was just emerging from a bloody civil war. Werner would stay for three years.
“An incredible stroke of luck!” he exclaims. Werner, a modest man, invokes luck repeatedly during our conversation, almost obscuring the enormous amount of work he must have done to establish himself in the select circle of international criminal justice.
In 2006, an event changed the course of his career. The former Liberian president, Charles Taylor, was arrested in Nigeria and transferred to Freetown. He was accused of supporting rebels from neighbouring Liberia who belonged to the Revolutionary United Front (RUF), a group responsible for unimaginable atrocities in Sierra Leone. Taylor would become the first former head of state to be convicted by an international court since the Nuremberg trials.
“Nobody had ever thought this time would come,” Werner recalls. He was one of the few lawyers in the prosecutor’s office familiar with the crimes committed by the RUF. He was asked to stay on and help establish the link between those atrocities and Taylor. What followed were months of travelling across West Africa in search of repentant fighters who had received orders from the deposed president.
“I spent all of 2008 in hearings in The Hague,” he says. “We heard around 100 witnesses, about 30 of them insiders. It was an extraordinary experience.”
See our profile of the director of the Geneva Appeal:
More
An advocate for the laws of war in a world that no longer believes in them
Working with victims
In 2009, his friend, British lawyer Karim Khan – who would become ICC prosecutor in 2021 before being removed from office in 2026 – invited Werner to join him in Phnom Penh, Cambodia. Together, they would represent around 30 victims in the first trial of a senior Khmer Rouge official. Werner was not paid, but accepted without hesitation.
“I had dreamed of playing a more direct role alongside victims,” he says. Unlike in the Taylor trial, where they could only testify, victims of the Khmer Rouge had the opportunity to join proceedings as civil parties. Werner represented a group of relatives of detainees who had been tortured and then executed at the S-21 detention centre, where between 12,000 and 20,000 people were killed between 1975 and 1979.
Werner’s voice falters as he admits that he was “slapped in the face” by the realisation of how raw their pain remained, and how urgently they still needed justice, 30 years after the events. “Perhaps that was what cemented my allegiance to victims,” he adds, once again weighing his words carefully.
Although he has chosen never to defend perpetrators, the lawyer is wary of being labelled a “hero”.
“I have always had enormous respect and admiration for defence lawyers,” he stresses. They do “a much more difficult job” and, he knows, receive far less recognition from the general public.
As a teenager, Werner saw his stepfather, the Geneva banker Robert Leclerc, convicted in a fraud case following a highly publicised trial. At the time, he regarded the family’s lead lawyer, a prominent criminal defence specialist, as a kind of “Zorro, fighting everyone alone, the ultimate shield against the machinery of justice”. “Out of loyalty to my family history, I should have tried to become a leading criminal defence lawyer in Geneva,” he adds. Today, dressed in an elegant light-grey suit, he retains only the uniform – without the tie.
Justice under pressure
When Werner founded Civitas Maxima in 2012, he set out to contribute, on his own scale, to a fairer system of international justice, without “blind spots” that allow certain leaders to escape justice for political reasons. He acknowledges that this ambition is now “completely against the prevailing winds”.
Werner watches with bitterness as the ICC comes under pressure. The court has been targeted by Donald Trump’s administration, which objects to its arrest warrants for Israeli leaders, including the prime minister. Some of its officials have already been sanctioned. Washington is now threatening to expand those measures and has pledged to dismantle the ICC “brick by brick”, while pressuring states to withdraw from it.
“I would never have thought the situation would become so catastrophic,” Werner sighs. But while he condemns the political attacks on the ICC, he also takes a critical view of the court’s record. It has an annual budget of around €200 million.
“The ICC has spent more than €2 billion to secure ten convictions in almost 25 years. The vast majority of those convicted have been rebels, all of them Africans,” he laments.
Werner is convinced that “the fight must now be taken to the national level”. This means strengthening specialised war crimes units and expanding the use of universal jurisdiction, which allows states to prosecute perpetrators of the most serious crimes even when those crimes were committed abroad.
See also: International Geneva is home to several NGOs working to combat impunity:
More
The Swiss NGOs that use universal jurisdiction to bring war criminals to justice
Fighting impunity
After 14 years at the helm of Civitas Maxima, whose annual budget has now reached CHF 2.5 million, Werner can point to several successes. The painstaking evidence-gathering carried out day after day by his team of around 20 people has helped bring several individuals involved in civil wars to justice.
Among them is the former Liberian rebel commander Alieu Kosiah, convicted of war crimes by Switzerland’s Federal Criminal Court in Bellinzona in 2021. It was the first trial of its kind before a non-military court in Switzerland. In 2023, he was convicted on appeal of crimes against humanity, another Swiss first.
Four other criminal convictions in France and the United States add to the record, along with “a dozen arrests or arrest warrants”, Werner says, proud of how far the work has come. Other cases are under way elsewhere in the world, he says, but for now they remain confidential.
Confronted with the retreat of international courts and a growing climate of impunity, Werner, who is the father of two young daughters, refuses to give in to pessimism.
“The worse things get, the more we have a duty to resist,” he insists. “What is at stake is whether our children and future generations will still believe that these crimes – which are so serious and affect us all – must be punished.”

How the Swiss were encouraged to save
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
08:00:00 UTC
17:00:00 KST

How the Swiss were encouraged to save
“Feed your savings now or starve in old age” and similarly blunt aphorisms were printed on cards issued to Swiss schoolchildren in 1946 in an attempt to motivate them to start saving. Adults were also encouraged, by various means, to set money aside for the future.
Swissinfo regularly publishes articles from the Swiss National Museum’s blog External linkdedicated to historical topics. The articles are always written in German and usually also in French and English.
Until well into the 20th century, people largely had to fend for themselves if they fell on hard times. Substantial outside help was rare. Consequently, it seemed advisable to encourage the less well-off sections of society to set money aside for just such an eventuality. From 1800, charitable institutions began setting up small regional savings banks with the aim of fostering a culture of industriousness and thrift among the lower classes and of “providing them with the means to safely store their hard-earned, meagre savings while also earning interest”, as stated in the articles of association of one such organisation, the Ersparniskasse des Kantons Zug, in 1840. Cantonal banks and Raiffeisen credit unions later also picked up on the idea, increasingly offering attractive terms for savings. There were even small collection offices known as ‘Einnehmereien’ in smaller communes. Their sole purpose was to receive savings deposits on behalf of the banks, and they were generally run on a voluntary basis by teachers, clergymen or the local mayors.
At times, the attractive interest rates made savings accounts so popular that limits had to be placed on the amount which each individual could deposit. Bourgeois society’s eagerness to encourage a steady flow of savings deposits was not entirely selfless. It was hoped that if the poorer classes had more reserves to fall back on this would ease the strain on the rudimentary system of relief initiated by the churches, local authorities and rich private individuals whenever someone was in need. In other words, encouraging saving was seen as a means of helping people to help themselves. Ultimately, the abundant flow of savings deposits also allowed banks to issue credit on a wider scale, for example granting loans to farmers or businesses to enable them to procure capital goods such as seeds, livestock or machinery in the belief that this would, in turn, spur economic progress.
Small incentives
Money boxesExternal link were the most obvious symbol of setting money aside for a rainy day, and they became commonplace in Switzerland from 1900 onwards. These mostly oval-shaped, metal containers were handed out by banks to customers who expressed an interested in saving. However, the bank itself retained the key. To access their stash of coins and notes once the little box was full, people had to take it along to a branch to be opened at the counter. The cashier would then bag up the money and credit it to their savings account. If anyone asked to make a withdrawal, it was not unusual for the person behind the counter to enquire into their precise reasons for doing so – creating a kind of additional social hurdle that boosted the practice of saving. The money boxes were not originally aimed primarily at children. Instead, their conspicuous presence in the home was to serve as a reminder to adults of the importance of saving. In an era where addictions to alcohol and gambling were rife, the little money box was a good way of enabling part of a person’s wages to be stored away safely out of reach at an early stage.
Children were to be given additional motivation to get into the savings habit through a school savings bank scheme known as the Schulsparkasse. Pupils could buy colourful savings stamps from their teacher for 20 centimes each. These were then stuck onto a personal savings card, visible to all the other children, thereby generating a not unwelcome competitive pressure. When all the spaces on the card had been filled, the teacher took it to the bank along with the money collected. The amount on the card was then recorded in that child’s savings booklet. There were similar schemes for adults in the form of Sparvereine. These savings associations based on mutual motivation were popular throughout Switzerland, but especially so in the Basel area.
Nest eggs take a back seat
A pivotal change that emerged in the mid-20th century was to fundamentally transform the nature of saving. At the socio-political level, the very notion of building up a nest egg, which had previously been strongly propagated, suffered a setback with the introduction of Old Age and Survivors’ Insurance (OASI) in 1948 and the subsequent gradual move towards making health insurance and other forms of insurance compulsory. Voluntarily setting money aside for a rainy day was replaced by government-mandated saving in the form of binding premium payments. Since then, these compulsory insurance schemes and other social security benefits have ensured that people generally no longer fall into dire material hardship, even in old age or when faced with reversals in life such as illness or unemployment. Nevertheless, the idea of personal savings has remained important, although the focus has shifted more towards using that money to acquire long-desired consumer goods, pay for education and training or realise the dream of becoming a homeowner.
As a result, the idea of teachers attempting to instil a savings habit by means of the school savings banks began to lose ground in the second half of the 20th century. Those in charge increasingly struggled to see the real-world benefits of this laborious process of saving in small amounts. Instead of relying on schools or parents to impart financial knowledge, banks henceforth turned directly to young people themselves. In its 1948 annual report, Zürcher Kantonalbank confirmed that young adults were “particularly susceptible to the temptation to spend impulsively”, arguing that this was why they needed a special savings book for this age category. Interest tables purporting to show the large sums that could be accumulated even by saving small amounts, attractive terms and conditions, and trite slogans like “Save today, secure tomorrow” were used to encourage young people to take a sensible approach to money. While the plastic money boxes handed out from the 1970s still served the original purpose, the fact that they could now easily be smashed open with targeted hammer blows or even came with the key to open them diminished their standing as symbols of a steely determination to save.Balancing our income and expenses remains highly challenging for most of us, no matter what age we are. That’s why the money we manage to save usually isn’t sufficient for us to realise all our dreams. Just think of Mani Matter’s Sidi Abdel Assar vo El HamaExternal link: “If only I’d started saving sooner!”
Matthias Wiesmann is an economic historian and corporate archivist at Zurich Cantonal Bank.

Eight architecture and design events in November from Dezeen Events Guide

Eight architecture and design events in November from Dezeen Events Guide
Miami art week, Design Doha Biennial, Dubai Design Week and the Dezeen Awards 2026 party are among the key architecture, design and art events featured in Dezeen Events Guide this November.
Other events taking place during the month include Collectible New York, Cairo Design Week, Irish Design Week and BDNY.
Dubai Design Week
3 to 8 November, UAE
Dubai Design Week celebrates its 12th edition in 2026, returning with a programme of fairs, exhibitions, installations, talks and markets.
The festival’s headline event Downtown Design takes place from 4 to 8 November in the city’s design district and welcomes brands such as Trika Arabia, Bottega Living, Biscuit, Alain Ellouz Paris and 1971 – Design Space.
Other events in the lineup include the competition-winning Urban Commissions installation by Dubai-based NAO Architects and the In Other Words group exhibition.
Design Doha Biennial
5 November 2026 to 31 Janaury 2027, Qatar
The second edition of the Design Doha Biennial celebrates design, architecture and craft from the Middle East, North Africa, and South Asia (MENASA) region.
The festival programme features exhibitions, talks, installations, awards and other pop-up events, including the latest edition of Arab Design Now, which showcases projects from 81 participants.
Collectible New York
6 to 8 November, USA
Taking place at 210 East 86th Street, annual design fair Collectible New York presents works and talks from global designers and galleries.
Spotlighting contemporary pieces, the fair is separated into four categories: the Main exhibition, Fashion, Bespoke and New Garde.
The event follows Collectible’s Brussels edition, which took place earlier this year in March.
Irish Design Week
7 to 14 November, Ireland
2026 marks the fifth edition of Irish Design Week, which takes place at multiple venues across Ireland, including the Royal Irish Academy of Music.
The festival celebrates regional design, architecture and craft through exhibitions, summits, open studios, workshops, awards and talks.
BDNY
8 to 8 November, USA
Returning to the Javits Center in New York City, the exhibition and talks series at this year’s Boutique Design New York (BDNY) follows the theme Designed to Be Remembered.
The showcase highlights furniture, textiles and lighting, focusing on “unforgettable” materials and small details, with more than 700 brands taking part in the fair.
Dezeen Awards 2026 party
16 November, UK
This year’s Dezeen Awards party takes place in London‘s Royal Opera House, where the winners of 49 project categories will be announced, as well as the architecture, interiors and design projects of the year, six Designers of the Year and the Regional Showcases.
The event celebrates the work of the designers and architects with refreshments and music. The dress code is dress to impress!
Cairo Design Week
19 to 28 November, Egypt
There are three districts participating in the 2026 edition of Cairo Design Week: Heliopolis, Zamalek and Downtown.
The design week spotlights Egyptian creativity, from its contemporary design to the capital‘s historic architecture.
The festival programme includes exhibitions, installations, tours of often-private properties and talks.
Miami art week
30 November to 6 December, USA
Dezeen Events Guide will launch its annual guide to Miami art week, accompanied by an interactive map to help you navigate the city.
The week-long festival takes place across Miami, with fairs, exhibitions, talks, pop-ups, open showrooms, tours and parties spanning Miami Beach and Miami Design District.
Two of the largest events include the Design Miami and Art Basel Miami Beach fairs, running from 1 to 6 December and 4 to 6 December, respectively.
Check out last year’s guide to Miami art week here.

Drones attack Samara oil pumping station in Russia – media
That is according to the Telegram channel Astra, Ukrinform reports.
"The Samara LPDS near the settlement of Prosvet was likely attacked: black smoke is rising from the direction of one of Europe's largest tank farms," the report said.
The Samara LPDS is a major critical infrastructure facility in Russia's main oil pipeline transportation system, located in the Samara region. Local authorities have not officially reported an attack on the facility, but residents confirmed hearing explosions and seeing a column of smoke rising from the direction of the station.
Overnight, Samara Region Governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev reported a drone attack without specifying the locations: "An attack by the Ukrainian Armed Forces on our territory is being repelled. Air defense systems and mobile fire groups are operating."
A photograph sent to Astra by readers also shows smoke rising from the direction of the Samara Linear Production and Dispatch Station. The image was verified by an Astra OSINT analyst, who established that it was taken from the New Bridge in Samara.
The facility is one of Europe's largest tank farms. The station has 71 storage tanks with a total capacity of more than 1.6 million cubic meters of oil.
The facility has been attacked several times before in October. Strikes and large-scale fires were recorded on October 2, 7, 10 and 11, 2026. In particular, the destruction of four RVS-50000 storage tanks and a major fire at the station were confirmed on October 7.

Trump could launch nuclear strike on Iran within days, commentator claims
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
07:57:31 UTC
16:57:31 KST

US commentator Tucker Carlson claimed late Sunday that the Trump administration could be days away from launching a nuclear strike on Iran, alleging that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is pressuring President Donald Trump to authorize an attack on a suspected nuclear site in central Iran.
In a lengthy post on the US social media company X, Carlson identified the potential target as Pickaxe Mountain, where Israeli intelligence allegedly believes Iran has resumed its nuclear enrichment program.
Carlson is a conservative political commentator and former Fox News host whose program, Tucker Carlson Tonight, aired from 2016 to 2023.
He now hosts an independent political show on X, where he regularly comments on US foreign policy and international affairs.
Carlson claimed conventional US weapons could not penetrate the estimated 300 feet of solid granite protecting underground tunnels at the site, leaving a nuclear strike as the only military option.
"Bibi (Netanyahu) calls Trump about it every day," Carlson quoted an unnamed informed observer as saying.
Carlson argued that Netanyahu's political survival is driving his push for further military action. He claimed Netanyahu needs Trump's intervention to secure a 61-seat majority in the Knesset following the latest election results, warning that otherwise he could lose power and face investigations and possible imprisonment.
He also alleged that Netanyahu has been pressing senior US officials, including Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and US Central Command chief Adm. Brad Cooper, to resume major combat operations.
Carlson also claimed that Secretary of State Marco Rubio and CIA Director John Ratcliffe were following Netanyahu's lead. 
He further said former President Barack Obama had also opposed the Iran peace agreement being drafted in Doha.
 
Fears of regional escalation
Carlson said US allies in the Middle East were increasingly concerned about renewed fighting. He claimed Netanyahu secretly traveled to Abu Dhabi on Sept. 27 to persuade the UAE to support a final attack on Iran, but Emirati officials refused.
Warning of the economic consequences, Carlson said eight months of conflict had severely affected Gulf economies, as well as global energy and fertilizer markets. He claimed 11 of the world's approximately 850 oil supertankers were badly damaged in the Strait of Hormuz in October alone.
He also warned that a nuclear explosion at Pickaxe Mountain could contaminate the Gulf and threaten the water supply of around 100 million people.
Carlson argued that a US nuclear strike could establish a dangerous precedent, potentially encouraging Russia to use nuclear weapons against Ukraine, triggering renewed nuclear tensions between India and Pakistan, and prompting North Korea to attack Seoul.
"After the first nuclear strike, World War Three is inevitable. That war would be short and final," he wrote.
He further alleged that the Trump administration had quietly revised US nuclear doctrine since February to make the first use of so-called "battlefield nukes" easier and more likely.
 
Vance, Witkoff urge Trump to pursue diplomacy
Carlson said Trump could decide by Nov. 7 whether to authorize the use of nuclear weapons, adding that Vice President JD Vance and special envoy Steve Witkoff were urging him to pursue a diplomatic agreement with Tehran.
Although acknowledging that negotiations would be difficult, Carlson said people who had spoken with Iranian decision-makers believed there was a consensus that further conflict would benefit no one and that an agreement was worth pursuing.
He concluded by warning that the consequences of a nuclear strike would extend far beyond Iran, arguing that the international public had been excluded from decisions that could threaten millions of lives.
"Now would be the time for them to speak up," Carlson wrote.
 
US could strike remaining Iranian nuclear sites 'within 10 minutes'
Carlson's claims follow Trump's remarks to reporters at his Mar-a-Lago estate in Florida on Saturday that one or two Iranian nuclear facilities remained potential targets and that the US could strike them within 10 minutes.
Trump specifically mentioned Pickaxe Mountain, saying he had military plans for the area, but did not indicate that a nuclear strike had been authorized. 
"You probably could look at Pickaxe Mountain, you have to take care of that. We can do that all very quickly," he added.
In an Oct. 16 interview with Newsmax, he explicitly ruled out using nuclear weapons against Iran.
Separately, Axios reported that Trump and Netanyahu held a tense phone call on Saturday, citing Israeli and US sources. According to the report, Netanyahu is pushing for renewed military action immediately after Tuesday's US midterm elections, while Trump prefers to allow diplomatic negotiations to continue.
A White House official said the administration does not comment on sensitive military plans, adding that Trump is keeping all options open to prevent Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon. 
Secretary of State Rubio has also said no final decision has been made on resuming strikes.
Iran, meanwhile, denies any nuclear activity at the Pickaxe Mountain complex. Its supreme leader has warned Washington and Tel Aviv against launching further attacks.

Xi Jinping warns against great-power conflict in the Gulf as China, Oman eye trade pact
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02

16:52:37 KST

The Middle East and Gulf region should not become a battleground for great-power rivalry, and China is willing to work with Arab nations to achieve lasting peace, Chinese President Xi Jinping told Oman's sultan on Monday.
China has traditionally played a low-key diplomatic role in the Middle East, but has stepped up efforts to try to help end tensions amid the US-Israeli war on Iran, which has snarled the Strait of Hormuz and driven up global energy and shipping costs.
Xi told Omani Sultan Haitham bin Tariq al-Said that the world is undergoing "profound changes unseen in a century."
"The Middle East Gulf region should not become an arena for great-power rivalry and geopolitical conflict. Peace and stability in the region require joint nurturing and protection by all parties," Xi said, according to China's Foreign Ministry.
China has consistently been committed to stopping the war, and hopes to contribute "wisdom and solutions to resolving the region's security dilemmas," he added.
China is willing to strengthen communication and coordination with Arab countries, including the Gulf Cooperation Council states, to work together toward restoring peace and achieving lasting stability and security, Xi said.
Last week, China's Foreign Ministry said the country will soon be dispatching its special envoys to the Middle East to promote engagement and de-escalation.
First China trip
Haitham arrived in Beijing on Sunday for a two-day visit, the first by an Omani head of state since the countries established ties in 1978.
Haitham told Xi his government had deep appreciation for China's positions on key issues concerning the region, Omani state media reported.
"We believe that development and stability are inextricably linked," he said.
"The prosperity of nations requires an environment defined by security, peace, respect for state sovereignty, and adherence to international law - an environment where disputes are resolved through peaceful means."
New avenues for trade, investment with Oman, China
He also said Oman was open to entering into a preferential bilateral trade and investment agreement with China.
"We are confident that such an agreement would open new avenues for trade and investment, facilitate and enhance commercial and investment exchanges between our two nations," Haitham said.
China is Oman's largest trade partner, with tourism and business links boosted by direct flights between Beijing and Muscat since November last year.
Oman, which exports crude oil and energy products to China, has also been looking to further develop its renewable energy supply chains and digital commerce.
The Omani leader, who was welcomed on the tarmac in Beijing by People's Bank of China Governor Pan Gongsheng, also emphasized cooperation between investment and financial institutions.
