NATO pushes faster counter-drone defenses and AI-enabled targeting as threats evolve
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
07:52:32 UTC
16:52:32 KST

NATO is reshaping how it develops military technology as alliance leaders warn that cheap drones, artificial intelligence, and rapidly evolving battlefield threats are compressing timelines for innovation from decades to months.
The effort was on display at NATO FUSE, held in Latvia on October 29-30, where NATO's Allied Command Transformation brought together three major initiatives: the Digital Backbone eXperimentation (DiBaX), the Layered Counter-UAS Initiative (LCI-X), and Next Generation Targeting (NGT).
The event brought together military organizations, operators, and industry to test concepts and gather data on what works under realistic conditions rather than serving as a procurement exercise.
Speaking to Defense & Tech by The Jerusalem Post right before the Operation NATO FUSE drills in Latvia, Maj.-Gen. Arnoud Stallmann said repeated drone incursions and lessons emerging from modern conflicts have forced the alliance to rethink both its defenses and how quickly it adopts technology.
According to Stallmann, more than 30 countries and over 100 companies are now participating in the drills in Latvia. D&T understands that while Israeli companies have participated in prior NATO events, none participated in Operation NATO FUSE.
"What we see nowadays is that the incursions into Poland last September were the start," said Stallmann, who is the assistant chief of staff for multi-domain capability at NATO. "We see it all the time in our nations on the eastern flank, with drones entering our airspace."
But the challenge extends beyond just drones.
"Simultaneously, we have a task to build a backbone; we recognized a problem that the whole targeting process in general is very labor intensive,” Stallmann said, adding that NATO commanders have identified key gaps in connectivity, digital infrastructure, and next-generation targeting that must be urgently addressed.
"It’s a sprint," he said, pointing to funding already allocated this year and next year.
Modernization push
At the same time, NATO is confronting a strategic environment in which allied territory can no longer be assumed safe from direct threats. Small drones have emerged as a low-cost means of surveillance, disruption, and attack, creating pressure for defensive systems that are both scalable and affordable.
"We really need to find other solutions," Stallmann said, emphasizing the importance of developing lower-cost intercept options rather than relying on expensive air defense assets such as fighter aircraft or missile interceptors designed to defeat larger threats.
Stallmann explained that NATO’s current focus is on building a layered and interoperable network capable of protecting key areas while sharing data across borders and domains. And that requirement places command-and-control at the center of NATO's modernization effort.
The alliance is exploring a framework in which national and industry-developed systems can plug into a common command architecture – a concept such as a mosaic of interoperable capabilities connecting air, land, and cross-border operations.
But cross-border coordination remains one of the most complex challenges facing NATO's command structure, making data sharing and interoperability critical requirements for future systems.
That challenge sits at the center of NATO's modernization push. DiBaX serves as a test environment where NATO, allied operators, and industry evaluate connected technologies against operational problems. NATO describes its developing digital backbone as an integrated layer of software, data networks, and infrastructure designed to allow forces to connect, share data, and operate together.
This year's DiBaX experiments focused on resilient command-and-control, maintaining communications when networks are disrupted, and accelerating decision-making through the integration of data, sensors, and artificial intelligence. The event also hosted both counter-UAS and targeting experimentation.
Drone threat
To address the drone threat, NATO is advancing the Layered Counter-UAS Initiative, or LCI-X, a campaign of operational experimentation designed to test, integrate, and scale counter-drone capabilities across the alliance. According to NATO, the initiative moves progressively from testing individual systems to integrating connected counter-UAS cells and linking them with NATO command-and-control networks.
LCI-X has been running through a series of dedicated C-UAS events conducted in Finland and Latvia over the past year. The campaign is intended to connect sensors, effectors, and command-and-control systems while providing industry with direct operator feedback.
The alliance is deliberately avoiding commitment to a single technology path.
"We are looking wider than just what we have in our own stock," Stallmann said, adding, "We're not advocating that we have a total solution, but we have a layered C-UAS solution.”
Next-generation targeting
NATO's targeting effort is advancing in parallel. The Next Generation Targeting initiative aims to create a federated framework that integrates national data through modular AI and data-management tools while retaining human authority over engagement decisions.
Stallmann explained that the goal is to reduce information-to-decision timelines and improve sensor-to-shooter coordination across land, sea, air, space, and cyberspace domains.
NATO says NGT is intended to complement existing command-and-control systems through federated data sharing and AI-assisted analysis. One objective cited by the program is reducing information-to-decision latency by more than 50%, while keeping human operators in control of engagement decisions.
For Stallmann, the broader challenge is institutional rather than technological. For much of his career, Stallmann said military modernization followed a predictable path of incremental improvements, but the rise of AI and autonomous systems has altered that dynamic.
"During my first 20 years as an operator, I was seeing incremental improvements and developments. Once in a while, you get a new airplane or platform and there's a leap. But in the digital age, and with what’s going on in AI, decision-advantage needs to go faster than that of the enemy."
‘Ramping up speed’
According to Stallmann, NATO must also adopt capabilities faster than traditional procurement timelines allow.
"We have our innovation hubs, but we need to ramp up our speed, and we need to not introduce weapons systems that take 20 years. We need to adopt quicker and innovate quicker, because the enemy is doing that too."
Stallmann explained that NATO understands that it cannot rely solely on existing inventories to solve emerging challenges.
Lessons from Ukraine have demonstrated that the pace at which drone technology evolves creates the need for military organizations to adapt much more quickly than traditional procurement systems allow. Prior to his current position in NATO, Stallmann led the Directorate for Ukraine, with all Dutch efforts to support Ukraine, such as deliveries of platforms and training, combined in his team.
Stallmann described the current experimentation exercises not as an endpoint but as the beginning of a continuous process of adaptation driven by operational feedback from ongoing conflicts, particularly Ukraine.
"The character of war is changing, and we need to adapt to that new character of war," he said.
The same mindset is driving NATO investments beyond drones and digital networking. Stallmann said that the alliance is also examining emerging technologies such as quantum computing and quantum-resistant systems, which he described as a potential game changer approaching the horizon.
For NATO's transformation leaders, the broader objective is cultural as much as technical. The alliance must learn to field new capabilities at a pace measured in months and years rather than decades. And FUSE might just be the critical part of a broader effort to move technologies from experimentation into operational capability.
"This is not only the end point. It's the start of a learning curve; learn fast and we are going to continue," Stallmann said. "This is the beginning of a never-ending cycle."

Albert Camus' classic existential novel 'The Stranger' receives a sleek, stunning cinematic update
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
07:52:28 UTC
16:52:28 KST

The Stranger, directed by François Ozon, just opened in theaters, and it’s an interesting, atmospheric adaptation of Albert Camus novel that intelligently updates the story with a 21st-century sensibility.
First and foremost, it is cinematic, combining Ozon’s storytelling skill with stunning black-and-white visuals. The novel, one of the most important works of existentialist literature, is told from its anti-hero’s emotionally detached, even numb, point of view.
Its protagonist wrestles with questions of how to act in a godless universe where everything is absurd and meaningless, and makes a shocking choice to commit a murder that apparently means nothing to him.
Ozon decides to expand on the novel’s story by situating its anti-hero, Meursault, firmly in a vividly depicted time and place and deepening the roles of the people around him, since dramatizing his inner life would make for a bleak, one-note movie.
Most importantly, he brings the late 1930s/early 1940s Algiers to life and shows the culture clash between the formal, Francophone community (the so-called “pieds-noirs”) and the indigenous population, some of which is shown to still be traditional and some of which is modernizing.
Camus' original work sometimes seen as detached from Arab Algerian population
Camus, born and raised in the French community in Algeria, had a complex relationship to the place and to the French colonials there. He was politically active in trying to help the Algerians obtain rights and independence but also rejected the terrorism of some factions and felt that a compromise allowing French residents to continue living there was possible.
His grandparents moved to Algeria, and he was the second generation born there, so his roots in the country ran deep. In recent decades, the fact that the Arab characters in the book, including the murder victim, are not named came under criticism and was seen as evidence of the colonialist French community’s detachment from the Arab population.
The film opens with a montage detailing life in colonialist Algeria, and much of the movie features atmospheric street scenes that make it clear that the French community there is only part of the picture. As the film focuses on Meursault (Benjamin Voisin, Lost Illusions), much of it is wordless, especially the first half.
He is a handsome clerk in his late 20s in a commercial office who lives alone in a tiny apartment in Algiers. One morning, he receives a telegram informing him of his mother’s death in a government-run old-age facility in a rural area.
He is emotionless as he is given two days off from work and goes to the facility to observe the mourning ritual and attend her funeral. He is not interested in his mother’s friends and what they have to say, or in a man who calls himself her fiancé and grieves for her.
A relationship without meaning
Back in Algiers, he meets Marie (Rebecca Marder, A Radiant Girl), a typist who used to work at his company, and they spend the day together at the beach and the movies, drifting into a sexual relationship. When she asks him if he loves her, he says he doesn’t; that love means nothing to him.
As is not uncommon, she still hangs around him, and when she asks if he wants to marry her, he says he will if she wants to, because it makes no difference to him.
So, the dream of love and having a family means nothing to him, although he clearly enjoys sex. This may make him not unlike many commitment-phobic, taciturn guys. But where he differs becomes clear in his relationship with his volatile neighbor, Raymond (Pierre Lottin), who may or may not be a pimp.
He has beaten his Arab girlfriend, Djemila (Hajar Bouzaouit), whom he suspects of cheating on him, and wants to lure her back to see him again so he can insult her one more time. But he needs Meursault’s help to write her a letter.
Meursault complies, not sympathizing with either Raymond or his mistress, in a storyline that demonstrates how the colonials could take advantage of the impoverished indigenous population. A drunken, elderly neighbor (Denis Lavant) who beats his dog also latches on to Meursault, evoking the same indifference.
When Meursault commits the murder, seemingly on impulse, and is apprehended, he is as detached as he had been in all the previous scenes. He only shows real emotion, anger, when a priest comes to console him against his wishes.
The trial is the core of exploring the novel’s message, and the prosecutors spend more time on whether Meursault, who doesn’t deny his guilt, cared about his mother’s death than anything else, as his own lawyer knew they would.
Not caring about the loss of one’s mother is seen as a worse crime than taking the life of an Arab, and no one seems to think Meursault will pay a heavy price. In contrast to the book, the Arab characters have names, and the script is critical of the lack of concern for them on the part of the prosecutors and other characters.
While this may sound heavy, the movie is engrossing from start to finish and gets across the message about the exploitation of and disregard for the Arab population effectively.
My main criticism is that the film’s black-and-white cinematography and Voisin and Marder’s good looks combine to make some scenes seem like a perfume or cologne commercial, because we have seen so many similar images in such ads.
The adaptation will make you want to reread the novel. It will also make you think. It brings to mind a quote from Pauline Kael’s review of the great new wave classic Breathless by Jean-Luc Godard, also concerning a murder which evokes no feeling in the murderer, and which was doubtless influenced by The Stranger.
Kael wrote, “They just don’t give a damn. How do we connect with people who don’t give a damn? Well, is it really so difficult? Even if they weren’t all around us, they’d still be (to quote Double Indemnity) ‘closer than that.’”
The Stranger is a classic of modern French literature, and adapting it for the screen must have been daunting, but Ozon, an eclectic and often playful and original filmmaker who has made such movies as the Mystery Swimming Pool and the drama about sexual abuse by priests, By the Grace of God, is up to the task.

Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed faced pointed questions about his views on Israel during an interview on CBS's 60 Minutes on Monday, amid growing controversy over his stance and a closely watched race against Republican Mike Rogers.
During the interview with journalist Ross Douthat, El-Sayed addressed his criticism of US policy toward Israel. He argued that Washington has spent years declaring its support for a two-state solution while simultaneously providing military assistance to parties he claims are working to prevent the establishment of a Palestinian state.
El-Sayed also accused Israel of committing genocide in the Gaza Strip, an allegation Israel rejects and which his Republican opponent, Rogers, has also disputed.
The exchange on 60 Minutes drew particular attention ahead of Tuesday's midterm elections because of El-Sayed's previous statements about Israel and his ongoing confrontation with Rogers.
Rogers has said that he supports Israel's right to defend itself and exist as a Jewish state, and accused El-Sayed of refusing to recognize Israel's right to exist. As such, Douthat opted to directly ask El-Sayed, "Does Israel have a right to exist?"
In response, El-Sayed objected to repeatedly being questioned about Israel's right to exist when, he argued, no one asks him about Palestine's right to exist.
"Does Palestine have a right to exist?" Douthat asked.
"Yes," El-Sayed replied.
"And does Israel have a right to exist?" the interviewer continued.
"Yes, if there is a shared understanding..." El-Sayed began to answer, but Douthat interrupted, seeking clarification about the qualification.
"Just let me explain," El-Sayed said. "I believe that this is the problem with this debate. We start from where we sit rather than start from principles. I believe in equal rights to peace, dignity, and self-determination for Palestinians and Jewish Israelis alike."
El-Sayed addresses Israel's right to exist
He went on to clarify his position: "If the Palestinian people decide and the Israeli people decide that they want two states for two people, and they decide that on equal terms, I'm for it. If they decide that they want one state shared in a different way, I'm for that."
El-Sayed therefore answered affirmatively when asked whether Israel has a right to exist, but tied his response to an agreement between the two peoples. Unlike the traditional American position, he did not present the continued existence of two separate states as the only outcome he would support.
This was not the first time the Senate candidate had avoided giving a direct, unconditional answer to the question.
In an earlier CNN interview, when asked whether Israel had a right to exist, El-Sayed said Israel already exists and that he would not participate in what he described as a game of "gotcha" questions.
In the latest interview, El-Sayed also sought to emphasize his commitment to the security of Jews in the United States.
Asked whether he was doing enough to reassure Jewish voters in Michigan, he said that despite disagreements over Israel, he and the Jewish community agreed on many other issues.
He pledged to stand alongside American Jews in defending their rights and security.
Democratic divisions deepen as Stevens endorses Rogers
The remarks came amid growing political tensions in Michigan, where El-Sayed and Rogers are competing for the seat being vacated by retiring Democratic Sen. Gary Peters. The contest is considered one of the key races that could determine control of the Senate following Tuesday's elections.
Earlier on Sunday evening, another dramatic development unfolded in the state's election campaign when Democratic Rep. Haley Stevens, who lost to El-Sayed in the primary, appeared alongside his Republican opponent, Rogers, at a church in Detroit and announced her endorsement of him.
The move followed a heated dispute over a campaign advertisement produced by an independent political organization supporting El-Sayed, which drew a connection between the cost of living in the United States and American assistance to Israel.
Stevens condemned the advertisement as antisemitic, while El-Sayed clarified that his campaign had not been involved in producing it and that he disapproved of its content.
Stevens's decision to endorse the Republican candidate, rather than support her own party's nominee as previously planned, drew sharp criticism from senior Democrats.
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer condemned the move, calling it a disgraceful betrayal.
Despite the political turmoil, El-Sayed maintained a lead over his Republican opponent, Mike Rogers, in the polls.
According to the latest RealClearPolling polling average cited in the report, the Democratic candidate had 49.3% support compared with 45.4% for Rogers, a lead of approximately four percentage points.
The latest CNN poll showed a seven-point lead for El-Sayed, with 49% support compared with 42% for Rogers.
A YouGov poll conducted between October 26 and 29 also showed El-Sayed ahead, with 51% compared with 47% for Rogers.
However, all of these surveys were conducted before Stevens's dramatic announcement that she would endorse Rogers, meaning the impact of her decision on voters could not yet be assessed.
The election is scheduled for Tuesday, with the Michigan race considered one of the most important contests in the battle for control of the Senate.
US President Donald Trump, who supports Rogers, also attacked El-Sayed during the campaign, accusing him of having ties to the Muslim Brotherhood.
El-Sayed distanced himself from the organization and argued that Republican attacks against him were also directed at his Muslim identity.
Michigan is home to large Arab-American and Jewish communities, and positions on Israel, the Gaza war, and US military assistance have become central issues in the state's election campaign.
With voting set for Tuesday, the exchange on 60 Minutes once again highlighted the political dispute over how the United States should approach Israel and whether a Senate candidate can support the right to self-determination of both peoples without explicitly committing to a two-state solution.
At the same time, the public rift between El-Sayed and Stevens illustrated the depth of divisions within the Democratic Party over Israel, particularly in one of its most consequential races in the upcoming elections.

Court orders fraudulent 'rabbi,' wife to pay NIS 830,000 to woman in exploitation settlement
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
07:51:57 UTC
16:51:57 KST

A Petah Tikva court on Sunday approved a settlement requiring Shaul Elkariv, known as the “criminals’ rabbi,” and his wife, Tova, to pay NIS 830,000 (about $264,000) to Nechama Gabai, who had sued them for NIS 1.17 million (about $372,000). The court’s approval makes the settlement a binding judgment.
The agreement ends an unusual lawsuit alleging a long-running pattern of exploitation, intimidation, and financial control, during which hundreds of thousands of shekels were transferred to the couple.
According to the complaint, filed by attorneys Dov Weinroth and Osher Rubinger, Gabai, a mother of three struggling personally and financially, turned to Elkariv in 2021 after he was presented to her as a rabbi, a kabbalist (a practitioner of Jewish mysticism), and someone with spiritual powers who could help people in trouble.
Lawsuit alleged Elkariv took advantage of Gabai in order to take money
As their relationship grew closer, Gabai said, Elkariv became a central figure in her life, and she came to rely on his advice and follow his instructions on personal, family, and financial matters.
The lawsuit alleged that Elkariv took advantage of her trust and dependence on him to persuade her to transfer large sums of money to him and his wife.
Between February and March 2022, the lawsuit says Gabai transferred a total of NIS 745,467 to the couple. Most of the money came from the sale of an apartment as part of her divorce, and the rest came from government benefits she relied on to support herself and her children.
One of the most striking details in the lawsuit is how the transfers were made. According to Gabai, Elkariv went with her to the bank, told her what to do, and in some cases even introduced himself to bank employees as her father. When she expressed doubts about the transfers, the lawsuit alleged, he reassured her, claiming he had spoken with her divorce lawyer, who he said knew about the transfers and approved them.
The money was transferred in several installments, according to the lawsuit: some to the Elkarivs’ joint bank account, some to Tova Elkariv’s personal account, and some in cash. Gabai said Elkariv presented the transfers as a way to protect her assets and keep them safe.
According to the lawsuit, Gabai kept the transfers secret from her family for years. Her relatives found out only in late 2025, after she ran into financial trouble and asked them for help.
The lawsuit alleged that Gabai was afraid to ask Elkariv for the money back, in part because, she claimed, he had threatened to harm her family if they interfered in his affairs.
Elkariv reportedly promised to pay Gabai back, described funds paid as a loan
Transcripts of conversations between Gabai and her brother, and between her family members and Elkariv, were attached to the lawsuit. According to Gabai, Elkariv admitted in those conversations that he had received the money, promised to return it, and even said he planned to take out a loan to pay it back. The lawsuit further alleged that he asked the family to sign a document describing the money as a loan. Despite those alleged promises, the money had not been returned by the time the lawsuit was filed.
The lawsuit also cites an earlier case in which Elkariv sued Rabbi Shmuel Eliyahu and others for defamation over publications about him. In July 2024, the Tel Aviv District Court threw out that suit. The ruling examined testimony and publications about how Elkariv presented himself and allegations that he exploited women who came to him in distress. That case is separate from Gabai’s lawsuit.
Gabai sought the return of NIS 745,467, plus interest and inflation adjustments that brought the total to about NIS 970,000, as well as NIS 200,000 in additional damages for the alleged harm and the severity of Elkariv’s conduct. At her request, the court froze assets during the proceedings to secure her claim.
The parties ultimately settled, with the Elkarivs agreeing to pay Gabai NIS 830,000.

Polish energy and industry sectors must turn to saltwater
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
07:48:47 UTC
16:48:47 KST

As freshwater shortages become increasingly severe, the industrial use of seawater for cooling is gaining importance. In the future, it may also become necessary to use saline water from mining operations. In both cases, specialised valves and fittings designed to operate under extreme conditions are essential. Polish companies have been manufacturing such equipment for decades.
These products primarily include a wide range of valves and fittings incorporating bronze components, ensuring a long service life in contact with aggressive saline environments. Today, such solutions are used not only in the energy, petrochemical and shipbuilding industries, but also in data centres and server rooms.
“This is one of our key product groups, and one that we are continuously developing. We started with solutions for the shipbuilding industry, gradually expanding our product range and, consequently, broadening our customer base. As a result, for a quarter of a century we have been supplying specialised valves and fittings designed to operate in saline environments, primarily valves and butterfly valves. These now include not only products operating in an open/close mode, but also those capable of regulating the flow of process fluids,” emphasises Marek Felsztyński, President of the Management Board of Zetkama.
Different approaches to seawater cooling
Various seawater cooling solutions are available on the market.
In the case of server rooms, two cooling models are competing to become the preferred solution.
The first is an indirect cooling system.
“Seawater flows through a heat exchanger, cooling a separate, closed freshwater circuit connected to the server room. The seawater does not come into direct contact with the electronic equipment. In the second type of system, known as direct cooling, a sealed, nitrogen-filled capsule containing servers is submerged in the sea, with its casing acting as a heat exchanger. Cooling takes place through convection, without air conditioners or refrigeration units,” explains Robert Wojtynek.
Zetkama’s valves and fittings are primarily intended for use in the onshore and coastal sections of indirect cooling systems, including pumping stations, onshore heat exchangers and distribution manifolds.
In Scandinavia, an interesting example of seawater cooling technology is Google’s Hamina data centre in Finland, which has been operating since 2011.
“However, these are still isolated installations,” notes Robert Wojtynek.
“Realistically speaking, seawater cooling systems currently account for only a very small share of the global data centre market. For the vast majority of planned data centres, seawater cooling is not geographically feasible. This is not a matter of technological competition, but simply physical location. Nevertheless, we can reasonably assume that the share of such solutions will increase over time,” Wojtynek explains.
Dramatically low water levels in many European rivers may indeed encourage investors to consider the use of saline groundwater in the coming months and years.
“Before that happens, however, we are already seeing growing interest in moving away from conventional evaporative cooling towers towards closed-loop systems. This is an excellent way to achieve a significant reduction in annual water consumption,” says Felsztyński.
He adds:
“Another solution, also attractive from the perspective of a valve manufacturer, is changing the source of water. This applies to industry, the energy sector and data centres alike. Instead of rivers and deep wells, wastewater treatment plants could become the source of water.”
A challenge extending beyond Poland
According to data from Poland’s Supreme Audit Office (Najwyższa Izba Kontroli), between 2020 and 2023, mines in Silesia discharged as much as 469 million cubic metres of saline water into the Vistula River basin and 264.5 million cubic metres into the Oder River basin.
As the report’s authors emphasise, the average salinity of water discharged by mines is approximately 8 grams per litre. This means that rivers in Poland can sometimes be saltier than the Baltic Sea, whose average salinity is around 7 grams per litre.
Meanwhile, according to the European Union’s Joint Research Centre, salinisation affects approximately half of Europe’s continental river network. In 2% of cases, salinity levels significantly exceed international standards for the protection of aquatic life.
A direct consequence of increased salinity in the Oder River basin is the recurring proliferation of golden algae.
Scientists also warn that river salinisation may pose risks to agriculture and human consumption.
The use of saline water for irrigation, cooling and industrial production creates risks of corrosion, technical problems and secondary salinisation of soils and water resources [1].
Although using saline water in industrial cooling processes does not solve the underlying problem, it could significantly reduce the volume of saline discharges into rivers.
“This is also a very interesting technological and operational challenge. Zetkama has the necessary valves and fittings that could be used in implementing such projects,” says Robert Wojtynek.
There is little doubt that seawater or saline water from mining operations will be more expensive than the tap water currently available, partly because of the specialised valves and fittings required for desalination or direct use in industrial installations.
However, it is worth noting that in August this year, 625 of Poland’s 2,479 municipalities issued appeals and warnings calling for restrictions on water consumption.
Water shortages were reported in several regions, including the Kuyavian-Pomeranian, Masovian, Lublin and Łódź voivodeships [2].
Invaluable experience from the shipbuilding industry
For decades, the shipbuilding industry has operated in an environment where installations routinely come into contact with saltwater.
“Seawater is used, among other things, in cooling systems, ballast installations and fire protection systems. As a result, the industry has developed material and engineering solutions that can now serve as an important reference point for other sectors increasingly dealing with water of elevated salinity,” Robert Wojtynek explains.
In shipbuilding, particular attention is paid to the appropriate selection of materials for valves, butterfly valves, gate valves, bodies, seals, connections and actuating components.
Exposure to seawater and the marine atmosphere can affect both the external parts of valves and fittings and components that come into direct contact with the fluid.
Incorrect material selection can lead to corrosion of valve seats, discs, plugs or guiding elements, potentially compromising the proper functioning of the equipment.
Depending on operating conditions, materials with enhanced corrosion resistance are used, including copper and bronze alloys, as well as appropriately selected high-alloy steels, including superduplex stainless steel.
“The experience we have built over decades of cooperation with shipyards in designing, manufacturing and servicing solutions intended for saline environments now enables us to offer products for virtually any industry planning to use saltwater, regardless of its origin or the technological process in which it will be applied,” concludes Marek Felsztyński.
Zetkama, part of the Mangata Holding group, remains one of the leading manufacturers and suppliers of industrial valves and fittings in the Polish and international markets.
Sources:
[1] River salinisation in Europe – Poland among the hotspots, Wodne Sprawy

Virtual Reality series' production begins in Arkhangelsk

16:47:46 KST

ARKHANGELSK, November 2. /TASS/. Filming of the 15 Miles of Light Virtual Reality (VR) series, telling five stories of the northern seas, lighthouses and expeditions, began in the Arkhangelsk Region. The project's scripts, filed from different regions and even countries, were selected in a competition, the project's leader Tamara Statikova told TASS.
"Right now, the project is approaching the filming - we are looking forward to a few busy days at the theater, museum and educational venues in Arkhangelsk and Severodvinsk: the Arkhangelsk Viktor Panov Youth Theater, the Severodvinsk Drama Theater, the Arkhangelsk College of Culture and Art, and the Northern Maritime Museum. We are working closely with the Arkhangelsk branch of the Russian Theater Society, which supports the project and helps organize the filming process," the project's leader said.
Experts of the Northern Maritime Museum have selected five true stories about events that happened at lighthouses and at sea. "The Tragedy at the Lighthouse" is a story about how caretakers at the Zhuzhmuy Lighthouse in the White Sea died in the winter of 1873. "The Navigator of Polar Seas" tells about one of the most important professions on any ship - about those responsible for passage planning. The third topic, "Dead Man's Chest," offers a look at the history of a particular person through marine life and objects. "The Race for the Arctic. Georgy Sedov" invites the audience to speculate about the author of the expedition to the North Pole. "Why the Svyatogor Was Sunk" is a story about the most powerful icebreaker of the early 20th century.
Each of the five stories will be different from others. In one episode, the viewer will take the place of Georgy Sedov and will hear uncomfortable questions about his expedition. Another episode will be a film about a tragedy at the lighthouse: the viewer will see how the expert commission that arrived at the scene discovered the dead team. "It is important for us not just to retell historical events, but to find ways of telling stories so that the viewer could have a feeling of being inside the event," the project's leader added.
According to her, The 15 Miles of Light is also a training program for the regional film industry and an opportunity for local residents to gain new skills. "We want students to gain real production skills, learn modern technologies and try professions that are in demand in the film industry. One of important objectives that the project has is to train regional specialists, expand their competencies and create conditions for creative industries' development in the North," she said. "We hope the gained experience would not to remain inside one laboratory, we hope it will become the basis for new creative teams and projects in the Arkhangelsk Region."
The VR series will become part of the Northern Maritime Museum's permanent exhibition. Actors from the Arkhangelsk Lomonosov Drama Theater, the Viktor Panov Youth Theater, and the Severodvinsk Drama Theater will take part in the film's episodes.

Ukraine's Defence Intelligence reveals upgraded Gerbera drone with 1,200 km range
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
09:47:00 EET
16:47:00 KST

Ukraine's Defence Intelligence reveals upgraded Gerbera drone with 1,200 km range
Defence Intelligence of Ukraine (DIU) has released the specifications of Russia's Gerbera-2 drone, which can travel up to 1,200 km and carry a warhead weighing up to 25 kg.
Source: Defence Intelligence of Ukraine
Details: DIU has published an interactive 3D model of the drone on its War&Sanctions portal, along with information about its components and electronic component base.
DIU noted that the Russians initially developed Gerbera drones as simple and inexpensive decoys designed to overload air defence systems. The first versions came in the Reconnaissance and Kamikaze variants, but their equipment subsequently began to resemble that of the more expensive Geran-type UAVs. In particular, they began to be fitted with Kometa navigation systems, mesh modems and costly cameras mounted on gimbals.
"Recently, the enemy has begun using an upgraded version of the Gerbera. The new model has a wingspan of 3 m and a fuselage length of 2.6 m. Thanks to a new 63-litre fuel tank, the drone can travel up to 1,200 km. To maintain the aircraft's stability during manoeuvres, the tank is divided internally into separate sections," the report said.
DIU also reported that the drone is equipped with a two-cylinder two-stroke engine that is essentially half of the engine used in the Geran-2, production of which has been localised in Alabuga.
"The specimen examined was fitted with a 10 kg OFZBCh-10 high-explosive fragmentation incendiary warhead and separate bags containing an incendiary mixture," DIU noted.
Meanwhile, DIU said that, according to the specifications claimed by the Russians, the Gerbera-2 can carry a warhead weighing up to 25 kg.
"The Gerbera-2's electronics include an upgraded flight controller, a 12-channel Kometa system, a mesh modem manufactured by Shenzhen Sinosun Technology Co., Ltd (China), and a new Sosiska video processing unit based on the Chinese Coke Pi microcomputer," the report said.
According to Ukrainian intelligence, the specimen examined was also equipped with a dual IP camera mounted on the fuselage above the fuel tank to detect interceptor drones. Versions fitted with forward-facing IP cameras and cameras mounted on three-axis gimbals have also been identified.
DIU stressed that the new Gerbera contains more Chinese- and US-made components than those from any other countries – eight and four respectively.
"The UAV's increased operational range, made possible by its large fuel tank, indicates that the area in which it may be used could extend beyond Ukraine. It was a Gerbera-2 fitted with a warhead that was discovered on Poland's Baltic coast in mid-September," DIU emphasised.
Background: In May, P1-SUN interceptor drones made by the Ukrainian company SkyFall captured video for the first time of Russian Gerbera drones being destroyed while being used as carriers for FPV drones.

US: Nine killed in Florida jet crash
November 2, 2026
A private jet crashed in a residential area of Cresthaven in the US state of Florida's Palm Beach County on Sunday, killing all nine people on board.
The Learjet 60 business jet nose-dived into the south Florida neighborhood and exploded.
Videos circulating on social media, recorded by people from their vehicles, shows the plane making a loud whooshing sound as it rapidly descends to hit the side of a road and erupts into a large fireball.
The plane's descent in the footage resembled — as Florida Governor Ron DeSantis described — "a missile going down."
A thick plume of black and gray smoke is seen rising against houses, which were narrowly missed.
The crash left a crater on the road, with flames flickering around it.
What do we know about the Florida plane crash?
The plane had departed from Austin-Bergstrom International Airport in Texas and was bound for North Eleuthera Airport in the Bahamas, according to the Federal Aviation Administration.
It was heading east at 35,000 feet (about 10,660 meters) when the pilots reported turbulence, icing and precipitation. They requested to climb another 2,000 feet (about 610 meters).
Just moments after, the jet dived steeply, at 10,000 feet per minute initially and then at 20,000 feet per minute to reach up to 30,000 feet per minute — a speed exceeding the plane's design limits — as per air traffic control recording and flight tracking data.
Last words from the cockpit — 'We are out of time'
LiveATC, which provides live air traffic control broadcasts, captured the harrowing final moments of the crash in an audio recording from a Miami air traffic control center.
A person from the plane's cockpit is heard saying "Mayday, mayday, we are descending 10,000 feet per minute."
The person declares an "emergency" just seconds later, urgently reporting a descent of 20,000 feet per minute.
"We're going to crash into the ground" the voice from the cockpit says and then goes on to report that the descent was at 22,000 feet and the plane was banking 60 degrees.
A scream is heard before the final words from the cockpit — "We are out of time."
Investigation underway
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said that the crash occurred at 12.50 pm local time and described the incident as a "horrific tragedy."
The cause of the crash and the identities of those on board the plane were not immediately known.
The National Transportation Safety Board has launched a probe into the incident.
There are no immediate reports of anyone on the ground being injured or killed.
Palm Beach County Commissioner Joel Flores said at a press briefing that some 600 people were being evacuated from the area and relocated to two shelters.

RFK Jr is wrong about the Arab world
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
07:45:35 UTC
16:45:35 KST

RFK Jr is wrong about the Arab world
The challenges in knowledge production in Arab societies cannot be blamed on some kind of innate incompetence or a single political group.
At a recent campaign rally in Michigan, United States Secretary of Health Robert F Kennedy Jr made remarks that have caused much controversy. He alleged that Muslim Arabs do not produce science and literature and do not win major awards because of the influence of the Muslim Brotherhood.
This was not merely a hasty and inaccurate assessment of the knowledge production of a specific demographic. It was a statement that reflects racist attitudes and misconceptions about an entire region and an entire religion. It is also easily refutable.
There are plenty of Muslim Arab scientists, thinkers and writers who have made major contributions over the past century. Some of them are Nobel laureates, such as novelist Naguib Mahfouz, diplomat Mohamed ElBaradei, journalist Tawakkol Karman, and scientists Ahmed Zewail, Moungi Bawendi and Omar Yaghi. Many others have not received a Western award but have nevertheless contributed significantly to their own countries and the world.
The Arab world does face challenges in knowledge production, but this does not prove an inherent deficit in its people or the overwhelming influence of a certain political group. Rather, it reflects historical and institutional conditions that impact this process.
A changing history of knowledge
Human civilisations have not been equal in knowledge production across history. Some have witnessed scientific and intellectual flourishing while others have faced decline and turmoil.
Downturns have not occurred because populations had suddenly lost their mental capacities but because the political, economic, cultural and institutional conditions that allow knowledge to thrive change over time.
In the case of the Islamic civilisation, its centres – from Baghdad and Damascus to Cairo and Cordoba – experienced a vast scientific and intellectual movement involving scholars, translators, philosophers, physicians and mathematicians from diverse religious and linguistic backgrounds for centuries. This prosperity was not isolated from the world; it was built on the translation, critique, development and interaction with Greek, Syriac, Indian and other bodies of knowledge.
Meanwhile, parts of Europe experienced significant backwardness in scientific education and development. However, Europe was not a monolith, nor were those centuries a homogeneous dark period. It also witnessed varying intellectual, institutional and scientific developments across different regions and timeframes.
European conditions then gradually changed: Educational institutions and universities evolved, networks for book and knowledge circulation expanded, and European scientific traditions interacted with scientific knowledge transferred from the Islamic world and elsewhere.
No one can claim, based on these historical disparities, that Europeans are inherently incapable of producing science or that their religion or ethnic origins preclude them from innovation. Serious historical interpretation focuses on institutions, economics, education, political patronage and knowledge networks rather than claims that certain populations lack innate abilities.
The exact same principle must apply to Arabs and Muslims today. Since Europe was able to change the conditions of knowledge production, it is illogical to assume that the contemporary reality of Arab and Islamic societies reflects fixed limits in their scientific or literary capacities.
Science is universal and not the racial or religious property of anyone. Decline is not a genetic destiny for any people, and prosperity is not an eternal privilege.
Today’s challenges
Rejecting RFK Jr’s generalisations does not mean denying the challenges facing scientific research in many Arab countries. There are serious questions concerning research and development funding, university independence, education quality, freedom of research and expression, institutional stability, the ability to attract and retain scientists, and links between knowledge and the economy and production. However, these questions are the beginning of scientific analysis, not the end.
A society that does not provide a researcher with a suitable laboratory, does not grant universities sufficient independence, does not allocate the necessary resources for research and does not ensure the continuity of scientific institutions cannot expect results comparable to those of a society that invests sustainably in these areas.
Furthermore, wars, conflicts, displacement, brain drain and weak scientific cooperation can disrupt the accumulation of knowledge, even when a society possesses qualified human capital. The capacity for thought and innovation is one thing, and the ability to translate them into sustainable scientific production is another. Between the two lies an entire system of socioeconomic conditions, institutions and policies.
Blaming the challenges contemporary Arab societies face on a single political group – in RFK Jr’s case, the Muslim Brotherhood – and presenting this as a comprehensive explanation for the state of science and literature among hundreds of millions of people falls short of serious historical or social analysis.
Scientific production is influenced by a set of intersecting variables: state structure, economic policies, education quality, research expenditures, academic freedom, stability, international relations and the capacity for knowledge circulation.
Certain political movements or intellectual trends might impact educational policies or the cultural climate in specific contexts. However, proving this impact requires evidence and comparative analysis, which RFK Jr would likely fail to produce, should he be asked to do so.
Moving from critiquing an institution or political movement to issuing a judgement on Arabs or Muslims in general is a form of racism, hatred and Islamophobia because it transitions from analysis to generalisation, and from seeking causes to reproducing stereotypes.
A meaningful response to RFK Jr
The problem with RFK Jr’s statement is not merely its factual inaccuracy regarding awards and their superficiality, but the logic upon which it is based: transforming historical disparities in knowledge production into broad judgements about peoples.
His words hold symbolic, intellectual and political significance, reflecting a hostile Orientalist stance towards Arab-Islamic and even Eastern heritage.
A serious response to these statements requires more than merely recalling past glories or listing Arab and Muslim scientists and thinkers; it requires turning the discussion into a project for the future.
In the Arab world, we need more independent universities capable of research, equipped laboratories, sustainable funding, an environment that permits critique and experimentation, policies that retain scientific talent and institutions that link education with the economy and innovation.
We also need a documented, critical rereading of the history of sciences in Islamic civilisation – one that studies both achievements and failures and examines how scientific concepts emerged, evolved and were transferred between civilisations.
A civilisation does not regain its stature by repeating that its ancestors were great but by building the institutions that allow new generations to produce new knowledge.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

In fact, Iranians are the people who treat Jews with the greatest kindness."
The United States is the greatest threat to the non-proliferation regime.
In response to a question regarding Trump’s threat to attack Iran’s remaining nuclear facilities, Baghaei stated, "We certainly speak out, and we certainly document instances of gross human rights violations; however, experience has taught us that the world is all talk."
“We regret that the United Nations and the Agency’s Board of Governors remain silent in the face of such threats. The United States is, in truth, the greatest threat to the non-proliferation regime.”
‘Surrender’ has no place in Iranian nation’s lexicon
The spokesman for Iran’s Foreign Ministry further rejected remarks by US officials suggesting that Iranians would soon be forced to surrender, saying the word has no place in the Iranian nation’s vocabulary.
“What does this kind of language even mean? The word ‘surrender’ is simply not in our lexicon,” Baghaei emphasized.
Baghaei stressed that Iran had not been and would not be deceived because it was not its first experience in dealing with US officials.
He said Tehran judged Washington by its actions on the ground rather than its rhetoric.
He added that while Iran monitors various views and voices, the US government’s concrete action remained the decisive factor.
“Contradictory positions and double standards are, above all, indicative of deep confusion within their own governing structure,” the spokesperson emphasized.
Countries should not allow their territory to be used against Iran.
In response to claims made by Emirati official Anwar Gargash, the Foreign Ministry spokesperson emphasized, “It is not Iran that has destroyed trust; one cannot remedy a situation brought about by one’s own actions, and they must abandon the misguided approaches of the past.”
Iran cannot remain silent or fail to respond when the territory of regional states is used against it. Unfortunately, some of these countries not only failed to prevent this but actually encouraged it.
“Trust requires reciprocal action. We harbor no hostility toward any country in the region; we believe that regional nations should cooperate, and we expect them to ensure that their territory is not explo
American society is fed up with the parasitic behavior of the country's officials.
In response to US threats, he added, "Every act of deception involves two parties: the deceiver and the deceived. We will not be deceived; fully aware of what has transpired over the past two years, we take everything into account. While there may be differing voices within the US ruling establishment, American society itself is weary of the parasitic behavior of its officials. It is, therefore, not implausible that some within the US establishment might argue that America is squandering its wealth on a party whose only activity in our region is the commission of crimes.”
“Iran has remained mindful of these various perspectives, and it is the actual conduct of the United States that matters to us. These contradictory claims leave the international community bewildered: with whom, exactly, should one engage in the United States? Do all roads lead to Tel Aviv? This is a question that the United States must answer."
Iran rejects transfer of enriched uranium abroad
When asked about the possibility of uranium being removed from the country, Baghaei replied, "No."
Commenting on calls for Iran to withdraw from the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT), Baqaei said that, in light of developments over the past 15 years, the Iranian people have a legitimate question about why the other side continued to seek excuses despite Iran’s repeated efforts to demonstrate the peaceful nature of its nuclear program.
He pointed out that the opposing side has assassinated the martyred Leader of the Islamic Revolution, Ayatollah Seyed Ali Khamenei, who had issued a religious decree prohibiting the production and use of nuclear weapons.
Baqaei stressed that Iran’s nuclear program has always been and remains peaceful, adding that the other side’s persistent claims that Iran poses a threat have fueled the debate, as if those making such allegations are deliberately turning a blind eye to reality.
He acknowledged that the question of withdrawal from the NPT is a genuine issue under discussion, but emphasized that, at the decision-making level, Iran remains a member of the treaty and considers itself bound by its commitments.
Addressing claims made by the Kuwaiti government against Iranian nationals, the Foreign Ministry spokesperson said, "These accusations are categorically rejected. We call upon the Kuwaiti government to cease the harassment of its own citizens for expressing sympathy toward Iran. The allegations leveled against Iran are entirely baseless. We remain committed to the principle of good neighborliness."
Regarding the Foreign Ministry's plans to revive regional meetings, he noted, "Over the past year, we have utilized several significant opportunities, including the Shanghai Cooperation Organization summit. Recent developments have not caused us to lose sight of the importance of regional processes."

Soomaa farmers lose 150 cattle to wolves as court blocks hunting permit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
07:44:00 UTC
16:44:00 KST

Soomaa farmers lose 150 cattle to wolves as court blocks hunting permit
Farmers in Soomaa in southwest Estonia have been facing wolf attacks on livestock as well as bears destroying feed. Hunting permits were suspended soon after being issued.
While the Environmental Board issued hunting permits, following the attacks, courts suspended them within hours following a legal challenge. Wolf cull season starts in November in any case.
Farmer Tiit Soa, who raises cattle in Soomaa, told "Aktuaalne kaamera" he had never before seen wolf attacks on this scale, and even larger livestock like cows have not escaped the wolves. Soa says he has lost as many as 150 cattle, a quarter of his total herd, to wolf attacks.
The Environmental Board puts the number of cases of wolf attacks this year, up to October 30, at just one more than that – 151.
"The number of large predators needs to be brought under control, and common sense is needed," Soa said.
Soa estimates the economic loss resulting from the attacks to be around two hundred thousand euros. To qualify for compensation, however, owners must first have implemented all preventive measures, including the installation of electric fences.
However, as a boggy area, the natural conditions in Soomaa, a national park, are distinct, so much so that the large fluctuations in water levels make it almost impossible to install an electric fence which would meet the board's requirements, Soa said.
"The Environmental Board says you have to erect a fence. We built that fence, and the wolf came that very night and killed two calves straight away. The only thing that helps is physically standing guard over the herd, occasionally setting off fireworks rockets and driving around."
Soa has to effectively maintain guard on his livestock round the clock, which he said is starting to affect his health.
According to the Ministry of Climate, responsibility for the herd lies primarily with its owner.
"We must still focus on prevention, and if it is not possible to keep animals in a particular location, or if it is not possible to keep animals of a certain age there, then livestock farmers must also consider exactly where they keep their animals," said Aimar Rakko, head of hunting at the Ministry of Climate's forestry department.
Tanel Türna, head of the Environmental Board's hunting and aquatic wildlife department, suggested a change of tactics.
"Perhaps the same manpower being used to drive around the area could instead be directed towards gathering the calves together in the evenings. It certainly wouldn't be an easy undertaking, but it would produce results. The alternative is that these wolves will keep coming back for as long as they have the opportunity to get hold of something somewhere," Türna said.
Bears have also appeared in Soomaa this year and while they have not reportedly slaughtered livestock, they have instead raided hay bales, stored as animal fodder. The Environmental Board has issued 64 hunting permits, 26 of which have been suspended by a court at the request of the Eesti Suurkiskjad (Large Carnivores) NGO. The latest permits were suspended within two hours the Friday before last, October 23.
The same NGO has successfully appealed to the courts in the past to suspend large predator culls. The wolf cull season usually runs from November 1 to the following February. Bear cull season runs in the fall and has just ended.

NPC set to lay down law on cross-border corruption
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
07:43:50 UTC
16:43:50 KST

The National People's Congress has begun deliberating on a draft law on combating cross-border corruption, including a provision on promoting the building of a fair and equitable global anti-corruption governance system.
The draft was submitted for its second reading at an NPC Standing Committee session that runs through Friday.
It further elaborates on the legislative purpose and enriches the principles guiding efforts to combat cross-border corruption.
It also stipulates that such efforts must be conducted in strict accordance with the Constitution and laws, follow statutory procedures, and respect and protect human rights.
The draft law was first submitted for deliberation in late August. The formulation of the law is an important step by China to put in place a systematic and comprehensive foreign-related legal framework for anti-corruption, according to the NPC.
Structured into six chapters and 47 articles, the draft sets out the principles, scope and key positions underpinning China's efforts to combat cross-border corruption.
The revised draft also sets out provisions on the use of information technology by authorities in combating cross-border corruption.
It requires relevant authorities and their staff to keep confidential any state secrets, work-related confidential information, trade secrets, personal privacy and personal information obtained during supervision and investigations.
It also requires Chinese companies operating across borders to set up integrity and compliance departments or appoint dedicated staff, based on their size, business scope, and risk prevention and control. (Xinhua)

Trump threatened Iran with a &quot;hammer,&quot; while Tehran warned of a longer war
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
09:43:50 EET
