Trump threatened Iran with a "hammer," while Tehran warned of a longer war
Kyiv • UNN
Trump said that new strikes on Iran were possible, while Tehran threatened a prolonged conflict. At the same time, both sides allowed for a diplomatic solution.
US President Donald Trump threatened Iran with a "hammer," and Tehran responded. UNN reports this, citing AFP.
Details
Iran warned on Sunday, November 1, that any resumption of war with the United States could last longer than the previous round of hostilities after President Donald Trump said he still needed to "take care of" more targets.
Diplomatic efforts to end the war in the Middle East have been interrupted by repeated threats from the United States and Israel to resume bombing, against the backdrop of their holding important elections.
"A potential future war could last longer than the previous conflict, and the American president will not be able to dictate the timing or terms of its end," army spokesman Mohammad Akraminiya said, according to Iranian state television.
At the most intense stage of the war, which began on February 28 with US-Israeli strikes on Iran, Tehran responded with missile and drone attacks across the region. Armed groups linked to Iran joined the fighting in Lebanon and Yemen.
Akraminiya's remarks came after Trump suggested that the United States could quickly strike the rest of its targets in Iran.
"We still need to take care of, I would say, one or two sites, but we can do that in 10 minutes," Trump told reporters.
"You could probably look at Mount Pikaks, and that needs to be taken care of. We can do all of that very quickly," he added, referring to the suspected underground nuclear facility.
Trump repeated his threat on Sunday, November 1, saying at a campaign rally in Iowa ahead of the midterm elections that he might have to give Tehran a "hammer" at some unspecified time.
Separately, before the rally, Trump said, as reported by CBS News, that he believed the United States would soon end the war with Iran, "one way or another." "We achieved such a victory, and we will end this very soon, one way or another," Trump said. "Either they will make a deal, or we will simply end it. … The work we have done is incredible."
The warning came after US media reported that Trump spoke by phone on Saturday with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu about whether and when to intensify military operations against the Islamic Republic.
Netanyahu urged Trump to strike Iran after the U.S. elections – Axios01.11.26, 23:21 • 3100 views
Speaking to reporters on Sunday, Trump confirmed that he had discussed Iran with Netanyahu but did not go into detail.
As CNBC notes, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said that President Donald Trump would like to resolve the war with Iran "through diplomacy" and prefers not to use military force.
Speaking over the weekend, Rubio told reporters that "He [Trump] has not yet made a decision... the president is expressing to you incredible confidence that if we needed to do something militarily, we would have the ability to do it, and we really do have everything necessary to succeed. But we would prefer to do this peacefully."
Iran's senior military and political officials have warned against any new strikes.
Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps spokesman Hossein Mohebbi on Sunday, AFP notes, repeated a warning made a day earlier in a written statement by Iran's new Supreme Leader, Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei.
"There are no geographical limits in a conflict with America; a vast theater of military operations has been designated to inflict harm on the enemy," Mohebbi said, according to state television.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said: "We hope the other side will show rationality and choose diplomacy," adding that Iran "remains ready for both defense and diplomacy," according to the official IRNA news agency.
The warnings came after Iran's security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, said on Saturday, October 31, that he had received a letter from US Vice President J.D. Vance requesting the resumption of negotiations.
Rezaei noted what he called a positive change in the US "tone" but said he had not yet responded.
He said that Tehran had previously informed Washington that if its conditions were not met, "the Strait of Hormuz would not be reopened, nor would there be any negotiations."
These conditions include the unfreezing of Iranian assets abroad, the lifting of the months-long U.S. naval blockade of Iranian ports, the cancellation of longstanding sanctions, and an end to the war on all fronts.
Since the beginning of the war, Iran has claimed control over the Strait of Hormuz, a vital global energy hub, and has repeatedly attacked vessels attempting to cross it without its permission.
The United States has imposed a naval counter-blockade of Iranian ports.
Anwar Gargash, the diplomatic adviser to the Emirati president, said on Sunday that the United Arab Emirates hoped that an exchange of agreements would lead to a breakthrough, but was preparing for the worst.
"The region is not interested in going through another round... But I think that we are also, as we have shown before, prepared for the worst," he said at a conference in Manama.

====================================================================================================

‘I thought this was the end’: Israeli designer Hagar Alembik recalls Flydubai terror and her comeback
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
07:43:32 UTC
16:43:32 KST

Even during the terrifying moments when the Flydubai plane plunged and shook violently in the sky, Israeli fashion designer Hagar Alembik did not suddenly discover faith. She did not turn to God or cry out "Shema Yisrael," the Jewish declaration of faith, as many of her fellow passengers did. "It was sheer terror," she recalls. "I was certain this was the end, that this was what the end of life looked like. But I didn't turn to God because I don't have a God. I've been an atheist through and through since birth. Ever since we landed safely, people have been asking me whether I've recited Hagomel, the Jewish prayer of thanksgiving after surviving danger, and I ask them what that is."
So whom do you thank for landing at Ben Gurion Airport without a scratch?
"Maybe the universe, maybe the world. The whole attempted hijacking is beyond my comprehension, and I don't pretend to understand it. But one thing is certain. It's behind me, behind all of us. It's over."
That's it? You've already moved on?
"Yes. The incident is over, and life goes on. I've always said that to live, you have to die a little. It's a philosophical idea that's accompanied me for years, through good times and bad. I always look forward, with my eyes wide open. Now I'd be happy to sell fashion to Japan, which hosted us so beautifully, and to Saudi Arabia, which welcomed us with open arms."
According to reports, every passenger on the flight is expected to receive about $250,000 in compensation.
"I heard. I think someone wrote about it in the passengers' WhatsApp group. One of the women opened a group for us while we were waiting in Saudi Arabia. She called it 'Flydubai Victims,' a name that grated on me, and later, perhaps because of the reactions, it was changed to 'Flydubai Survivors.' I'm not comfortable with either name, and I also don't believe we're talking about such large sums."
Maybe you need to prove that you're suffering from post-traumatic stress.
"Why would I try to prove something that isn't true? I have absolutely no intention of making a project out of proving that I'm traumatized. That's not my direction at all. If everyone receives compensation, then obviously my daughter, my grandson and I, who were all on the flight, will receive it too. I have no moral objection to accepting the money. It's not reparations from Germany. But the bottom line is that it wasn't worth it. I wouldn't recommend it."
‘To live, you have to die a little’
Dressed in black as always, her figure slimmer than ever ("At least 30 kilograms [66 pounds] lighter. I don't weigh myself. Thanks to whoever invented weight-loss injections"), Alembik, 71, opens the door to her apartment in a leafy area behind Ichilov Hospital in Tel Aviv. Parking is virtually nonexistent, but for her, living here feels like coming home.
"From third grade, I grew up two houses away from this building," she says. "Two years ago, I bought this apartment, across from my mother's apartment, and we had such a wonderful time together. We ate together, watched television together, we loved Raviv Drucker and Noa Koler's television series Makom Sameach, and talked endlessly. Those were the closest 18 months of our lives. My mother was a very opinionated, sharp woman, and she wasn't always easy to deal with. But thanks to living almost together, we gained a good relationship toward the end, with tenderness and love."
Her mother, Noa Hatzofe, died four months ago at the age of 92 "and a half," Alembik emphasizes. "Mom started to feel that things weren't right anymore. She wasn't prepared to reach a point where she'd have to sit in a wheelchair and could no longer go to the theater and the movies she loved. So she said goodbye."
The bright smile on Alembik's face does not disappear as she remembers. "She was unbelievably lucid. She always insisted on pointing out that her name was spelled Noa without a vav in Hebrew, and she was terrified of missing the moment after which she would no longer be able to express her wishes. That was her greatest fear. Forty years ago, she donated her body to science, so she called the university to check whether the arrangement was still valid, whether they were still interested in her body. She made sure every loose end was tied up. My mother was quite a character, a woman of tremendous strength."
Are you like her?
"In terms of strength, yes," says the eldest daughter of Noa, whose name was spelled without the Hebrew letter vav, and sculptor Emmanuel Hatzofe, whose works are displayed throughout her apartment. "I have two brothers: Ohad Hatzofe, who is seven years younger than me, an ecologist with the Israel Nature and Parks Authority who works to protect the country's vulture population, and Yonatan, who's 20 years younger than me. Same father, same marriage. And when Yonatan became religious, my mother almost died from it. Literally, not metaphorically. She was a complete atheist. Well, I'm like her in that respect too."
When you were 20 and already married, your mother had another baby.
"That was quite something. I accepted him completely, even though I was surprised at first. Because of the age differences between us, Mom used to say she'd raised three only children."
How did you react when she decided to say goodbye to life?
"It wasn't new to us. Mom had always said she wasn't prepared to die without dignity. She received palliative care, everything was legal and properly handled, and after a few days she departed on another journey, without suffering. Because she'd donated her body to science, there was no funeral. That's what she wanted. Some people might say she wanted to leave this world while remaining completely in control of the situation. I see it as an act of compassion toward us."
Do you support that approach?
"Absolutely. I'd follow exactly the same path. Her death taught me a lesson about life."
Following her mother's death, Alembik told herself, "Come on, it's time to fulfill some dreams," and decided to travel to Japan. "I'd wanted to go there for years, but I kept putting it off. There was always something that seemed more important, a fabric exhibition here, a fashion exhibition there. When I finally told myself, 'That's it, now it's happening,' I didn't look for friends to join me. I wanted to experience Japan with Lee, my only daughter, and her only son, Nimrod, who's also my only grandson."
For a moment, her eyes cloud over. "Imagine what would have happened if we'd really been hijacked and never returned. That would have been the end of the Alembik family. There are no other Alembiks in Israel, and only a handful in the world. Our family could have been wiped out."
Alembik entered the fashion world, and eventually established the Alembika chain that bears her name, after spending time in Düsseldorf, Germany, where she had moved with her former husband, Moshe Alembik, who opened an advertising agency there. "When we were about to return to Israel, a local friend told me, 'Go study at Shenkar.' She'd seen me running from one clothing store to another. Luckily, I was accepted. I was the oldest student in my class. Everyone else had just finished their military service, while I already had a daughter in second grade who would finish school and come to another day of classes, at Shenkar. It was a pleasure for both of us."
She and Moshe divorced after 18 years, partly because of her success. "We separated because I believed in a better future, and the financial position I'd reached meant I no longer had to be afraid. Last week, he immigrated to Israel from Berlin and returned to Tel Aviv. According to him, the streets had become much more fascist, and he felt he could no longer live there."
So will your ex-husband move into the empty apartment across from you?
"Absolutely not. Besides, I've already found a kind of 'replacement' for my mother. I'm joking, of course. After she died, we adopted Tali, an elderly white dog, from SOS Animals. It was Lee's idea. She found me someone to take care of."
In the mid-1980s, Alembik was considered a trailblazer. "I was the first designer to graduate from Shenkar and build a retail chain with my own two hands, operating 15 stores. Who else was around at the time? Only Dorin Frankfurt and Raziella Gershon. I remember standing in line at the cinema and hearing a woman ask her friend, 'Have you been to Hagara's new place yet?' That's when I realized the brand had caught on. I had 15 good years, very good years. 
Regular customers, and even women who didn't know me personally, named their daughters Hagar or Hagara after me. I bought a penthouse at Gan Ha'ir in Tel Aviv and filled the rooftop with plants. Life was smiling on me in a big way. But I worked alone, without any help, and I made poor management decisions until I reached the point where I lost everything."
The collapse came after she brought an investor into the business as a partner to steer the sinking ship. In an earlier interview, she told me: "He sprinkled fairy dust over me. At a certain point, I realized that my baby, the retail chain I'd built with my own ten fingers, had become a hornet's nest, and I stopped going to the office."
‘I thought: This is what death looks like’
Her daughter, Lee Alembik, 50, followed in her mother's creative footsteps and established a successful career as a costume designer, working "in cinema, on Eretz Nehederet, Israel's popular television satire show, and on the wonderful films of Ronit and Shlomi Elkabetz. She met her partner, Yaron Ashkenazi, whom everyone calls Rocco, on the set of Gett. He was the lighting technician, and Ronit brought them together. She whispered to my daughter, 'I've noticed that Rocco has noticed you, so you should notice him.' That's how their romance began. They have a wonderful relationship, and Lee has Nimrod, my wonderful 11-year-old grandson."
Both women rejected the idea of an organized tour of Japan, "so Lee took on the mission. She researched, consulted people, met with them, read and put together a dream itinerary for us. It's no simple task to keep three generations engaged for three weeks. I boarded the plane like a piece of luggage, without knowing where we'd be going, without having read anything. I trusted her."
Why did you fly with Flydubai?
"Four months earlier, it was already impossible to get El Al tickets to Japan, so we started looking for alternative routes. Dubai was the last place on earth I wanted to visit, but the travel agent said there was a good connection. We flew premium, and it was a wonderful experience. Spacious seats, all the amenities, amazing service. On the return flight, we sat in the middle of the plane, row 17. Nimrod was by the window, Lee was between us, and I was on the aisle. On the plane that eventually brought us back to Israel, Nimrod refused to sit by the window. He wanted to sit in the middle, between his mother and grandmother. He's still struggling. He says he'll never get on a plane again. I imagine he'll get over it. In any case, I've already told Lee that I'm booking El Al tickets for the three of us for next year. Where to? Japan, of course."
Unlike her usual habit, when they boarded the terrifying return flight, Alembik did not look around to see who was sitting nearby. "I was in my own bubble. I didn't see who was behind me or in front of me, and the flight was normal until about an hour before landing. Maybe even less. I'd already started preparing for landing, organizing my belongings and folding up my newspaper, when suddenly, all at once, everything turned upside down. It's difficult for me to describe in words because it was both a physical and an out-of-body experience."
What do you mean?
"Suddenly I felt the plane plunging. There were terrible noises, and it was as though everything was spinning together. Objects weren't flying through the air, but I felt the plane making some kind of turn and plunging, then stabilizing slightly before plunging again. It was terrifying, and the entire plane was screaming. I assume we were too. There were screams like chickens being slaughtered. What I mainly remember is the three of us holding hands very, very tightly. An image from World War II flashed through my mind, a mother holding her child at the edge of a pit while a German gunman shoots them from behind. Lee says she saw the ground coming closer. I didn't, but I said to myself, 'Okay, Hagar, that's it, this is the end. What you've done, you've done. What you haven't done, you haven't done. You're here with your loved ones, and that's something too.'"
Those sound like words of farewell.
"Because I understood there was nothing we could do. If we perish, we perish. The physical sensation was terrible too. I felt as though something was exploding inside me, that my body simply couldn't withstand it anymore. Lee says it was the opposite for her, that she couldn't feel her body at all because she'd become disconnected from it."
What did you think was happening?
"I thought something had happened to the pilot. Lee thought the plane had been hit. I remember telling myself, 'This is what death looks like.' The plane kept circling for about another hour until it landed in Saudi Arabia. We were awake and aware that there was no pilot at the controls, and we couldn't understand how it would land at all. Then we started seeing men coming out of the cockpit covered in blood. One of them was absolutely drenched in blood, and someone shouted, 'We neutralized him!' Only then did we understand there had apparently been an attacker. Even before landing, the plane shook again for a moment and didn't fully stabilize, and one of the flight attendants said it was going to be a hard landing and instructed us to bend forward and put our hands over our heads. So there was an hour of sheer terror, with every worst-case scenario from the most frightening movies running through our minds. But a minute after we landed in Saudi Arabia, I calmed down."
How?
"We received an incredible welcome. They seated us in a spacious hall with comfortable reclining armchairs, somewhere between sitting and lying down, and served us coffee and food. In the morning, we received a light breakfast, and at lunchtime, chicken and rice. Doctors and psychologists were constantly walking among us, asking in English how they could help. In all the accounts I've seen in the media, nobody mentioned this royal treatment, and I don't understand why. I'm happy to be the first to thank them for such extraordinary hospitality. I felt they would have tried to bring down the stars from the sky just to make us happy. It was simply amazing. Israel should learn a lesson from the Saudis about how to welcome people."
After landing in Saudi Arabia, Alembik began trying to understand what had actually happened to them. "Once my breathing steadied, I started observing the passengers, making friends and approaching those who seemed to me to be our rescuers. Someone shouted, 'A round of applause for our saviors!' I asked them lots of questions. Only then did I understand that it had been the co-pilot."
The WhatsApp group created in Saudi Arabia helped the passengers exchange views about what to do next. "At around 5 p.m., someone wrote in the group, 'There's a plane that Dubai has sent.' Some passengers immediately protested. They weren't getting on it. They were afraid to fly with Flydubai and would board only an Israeli aircraft. My contribution to ending the ordeal was writing, 'There's a plane here, right now. Let's go home. This is our chance. Who knows what will happen later?' Someone wisely wrote that we could end up stuck in Saudi Arabia, and that Bibi [Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu] might want to exploit the situation for his own purposes, if that was a good enough reason to bring an Israeli plane there. I couldn't understand those who weren't rushing to board the plane waiting in Saudi Arabia. Who wants to remain at the center of a storm? You just want to go home."
The flight that was supposed to land in Israel at 9 a.m. finally arrived at around 9 p.m. "Rocco, Lee's partner, had already come to the airport at 7 p.m. to pick us up. Then, suddenly, the plane disappeared from the screen, and he couldn't understand what had happened. He completely fell apart. He thought that was it, that we were gone. When we finally came out, there was a line of journalists from all over the world standing in front of us, pushing microphones into our faces. What happened? What was it like? Without any compassion or attempt to offer help. I vaguely heard a woman asking me where the female power had been, because the whole incident had been built around male heroism. I don't remember what I answered her. It's possible I didn't answer at all. I couldn't believe that was what concerned her. I also couldn't believe they were keeping us there until Bibi arrived. It took him half an hour to get there. Of course I thought about all the people Bibi still hasn't come to see, even to this day."
Her gentle tone does nothing to soften the sting of her criticism. "Miri Regev told Ayala Hasson that she was prevented from responding to allegations made by Keren Turner, the former director general of the Transportation Ministry, because she's now involved in an election campaign. And what about you, Miri Regev? Aren't you worried about keeping your seat? Another broadcaster, a particularly repulsive one, said the plane was almost hijacked because the person responsible for approving foreign pilots has been sitting in his position for 20 years. Hasn't Bibi been stuck in his seat for 20 years? There are no words."
So how do you go on? What do you do now?
"Make lots of clothes. Even more clothes."
Twenty-one years ago, when detractors were taking pleasure in the fashion designer's spectacular downfall, Alembik learned an important lesson: Life goes on even when you move from a penthouse into a shoebox-sized apartment.
One person who stood by her and picked up the phone was Dr. Judy Fadlon, an anthropologist who had studied alongside her in an army teacher-training course.
"I left the course after six months because I was desperate to get married, and we lost touch. We arranged to meet for coffee, and she brought her husband, Gadi Fadlon, an accountant, along. The connection between Judy and me was immediate, and Gadi offered to help us with an attitude of 'Let the girls have fun and play.' Maybe he didn't believe how serious we were. Since then, Judy and I have been equal partners, and Gadi owns 50 percent of his wife's share. I called him from Saudi Arabia to tell him I wouldn't be coming to work that day. The two of us work at Alembika for 10 to 12 hours a day, and our partnership just keeps getting better. We work in harmony, with the joy of creating. We have 14 stores in Israel, and the 15th will open at Bilu Junction in December."
Without saying 'God willing.'
"Without."
How did Alembika survive three years of COVID and three years of war?
"We export all over the world. Our clothes carry a 'Made in Israel' label, and now there's a sense of discomfort coming from some countries. Not from the United States, thankfully, but from Europe, particularly England and Ireland. We haven't encountered anything significant, but the atmosphere is much less pleasant. This cruel war brings out a lot of evil in people, on both sides."
She serves me an overly generous slice of orange cake that one of her friends baked to celebrate her safe return to Israel and says that at her heaviest, she weighed 105 kilograms (231 pounds).
"Today I'm 73 kilograms (161 pounds), which is amazing, but I didn't lose it all at once. It happened in stages. About 15 years ago, I had gastric sleeve surgery and lost 10 kilograms. I weighed 95 kilograms, which was nice, but nowhere near enough to satisfy me. And like most women, I was an accordion. I'd lose weight and gain it back."
Did you want to lose weight for your appearance or for your health?
"Mainly for my health. A friend connected me with an amazing doctor, Dr. Maya Ish-Shalom, an endocrinologist, who opened the door to the world of injections for me. Four years ago, I started with Ozempic, and over time I switched to Mounjaro. And what can I say? Wonders of wonders. It's not just that I happily eat less because I'm full. The injections gave me complete freedom from constantly thinking about food. There's no more 'What should I buy for lunch?' I don't cook anymore either. I eat only when I'm hungry, and I don't need large quantities."
Have weight-loss injections reduced demand for larger clothing sizes?
"Absolutely. It started in the United States and spread across the world. Women are shrinking everywhere. That doesn't mean you can no longer find dresses in XXL. It's not black and white. Fashion houses continue producing clothes in all sizes, but the difference is noticeable in the quantities. In Israel, as elsewhere, the bestselling clothes are in sizes 2 and 4, corresponding to sizes 38 and 40. To me, this is a socioeconomic and cultural phenomenon. The women who've lost weight thanks to the injections are conscious of their health, they're connected to the here and now, and they can afford the expense. These are all things that tell you something about the profile of my customers."
At 71, aren't you thinking about retirement?
"Every single day, I give thanks for so many things. I'm grateful for my work, grateful that I find it interesting, grateful that I'm having fun and that it excites me. I'm also grateful for my family, for my loved ones, for everything that can't be taken for granted."
At a Friday night family dinner, she heard her grandson Nimrod say, "I was thinking that at some point we all have to die. Everyone dies eventually."
In response, she sent him a moving WhatsApp message. "My Nimrod, on our trip to Japan, I discovered a curious, intelligent and mature grandson. Not that I didn't know that before. I enjoyed being with you and sharing experiences with you so much. The ending was straight out of a movie, but the three of us were more together than ever. We went through an indescribable brush with death, and we were also born again. So come on, here's to life."
Has anything changed in you since the flight? You haven't discovered spirituality or God?
"Since we returned to Israel and came home, I've been sleeping very well. Lee less so. She's taking it harder than I am. God isn't part of my language. I'm living fine, I'm living peacefully, I'm living. I don't need to call on God for every problem."
Her collections are remarkably colorful, but even after losing nearly a third of her body weight, Alembik remains loyal to black. "When I was young, I dressed in colors all the time. I remember having pink clothes and loving the all-over look, pink shoes and a pink shirt. After I graduated from Shenkar, I started wearing black. That was also when I started gaining weight."
Does black make you look slimmer?
"No, it absorbs and conceals. Now, in Japan, I came across something I've never seen anywhere else in the world. In large, prestigious department stores, there are entire sections devoted exclusively to black clothing. I couldn't understand the thinking behind it. I'll ask ChatGPT."

UN staffer’s death in custody exposes Houthi ‘political extortion’ in Yemen
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
07:43:05 UTC
16:43:05 KST

UN staffer’s death in custody exposes Houthi ‘political extortion’ in Yemen
The United Nations and human rights experts demand an independent investigation after an arbitrarily detained staff member died in Houthi custody in Yemen.
The United Nations is demanding a thorough investigation into the death of a human rights employee while in Houthi detention in Yemen.
Mohammad el-Shami, who worked for the UN Human Rights Office, died more than a month ago but his family was only recently notified. He had been arbitrarily detained by the rebel group, which controls much of northern Yemen, since June 2024.
His death has highlighted the number of UN and NGO workers targeted by the Houthis, since they captured the capital Sanaa in September 2014.
UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Turk has urged the Houthi authorities in Sanaa to ensure a prompt, transparent and independent investigation into el-Shami’s death.
“This is a heartbreaking loss for the UN Human Rights Office and the wider United Nations. Mohammad’s family has not received any explanation of the cause or circumstances of his death – they deserve to know the truth,” said Turk.
“This requires disclosure of all relevant medical and detention records, preservation of evidence and independent scrutiny of any stated cause of death. There must be accountability for wrongdoing.”
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres also expressed his dismay and demanded the immediate release of all detained personnel.
“I am appalled & deeply saddened by the death of a @UN colleague, Mohammad el Shami, while in the custody of the Houthi de facto authorities in Yemen,” Guterres stated.
“I remain gravely concerned for the safety & wellbeing of the UN personnel, former UN staff & personnel from humanitarian & civil society organisations who remain detained. I reiterate my call for their immediate & unconditional release.”
The Houthis have repeatedly accused detained workers of being spies.
The Houthis accused more than 60 UN and NGO workers detained in 2024, when el-Shami was arrested, of being part of an “American-Israeli spy network”.
The group has routinely arrested civil rights activists, NGO workers and other civilians on espionage allegations.
As of February this year, 73 UN staff and dozens of other humanitarian workers were in detention, according to Amnesty International. El-Shami is the second UN staff member to die in Houthi custody, following the death of a World Food Programme employee in February 2025.
The Minister of Human Rights for Yemen’s internationally recognised government, Meshdal Mohammed, held the militia fully responsible for el-Shami’s abduction, forced disappearance and death.
“The continued abduction of [civil rights workers] for more than two years, culminating in the announcement of the death of one of them without enabling his family to visit him or know his condition, dictates a serious review of the way this file is handled,” he said.
Local human rights advocates highlight the severe difficulty of achieving accountability for deaths and other civil rights abuses by the Houthis.
Tawfik Alhamidi, President of SAM Organization for Rights and Liberties, outlined the systematic obstacles faced by NGO workers operating in Houthi-controlled territories in Yemen.
“The group is the one that controls prisons, medical records and witnesses, in addition to the fact that there is no judicial or human rights oversight over places of detention,” he told Al Jazeera.
“This delay by this group and the withholding of information may reflect a systematic pattern or behaviour by this group, at least in order perhaps to hide some features or make it difficult to conduct an examination.”
He said that the deaths of many Yemenis in Houthi custody have been put down to disease, sudden death or suicide.
The Houthi authorities remain fully accountable for any deaths in custody, regardless of the exact cause, Alhamidi added.
“Even if illness is proven, the question remains: Did the detainee also receive medical care, or is there negligence or is there deprivation?”

Belgium's PM meets with king to offer resignation to king after budget talks fail
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
07:40:54 UTC
16:40:54 KST

King Philippe said he regrets that no agreement had been reached and that the country cannot afford a prolonged political crisis.
Belgium’s Prime Minister Bart De Wever was at the royal palace on Monday morning to offer his government's resignation to King Philippe following failed overnight budget talks.
It comes after overnight negotiations with his core cabinet on the budget failed to reach an agreement.
De Wever left the palace after meeting with King Philippe for around 1.5 hours without addressing the press.
Following the meeting, the king announced he "is taking his decision under consideration and will consult the chairs of the various coalition parties from tomorrow.”
He added that he regrets that no agreement has been reached and that the country cannot afford a prolonged political crisis.
He calls on all parties involved “to put the general interest and a willingness to compromise first”. De Wever is set to meet with the king again on Friday.
According to Foreign Minister Maxime Prévot, there were “too many sticking points”. “If I were to list all the sticking points, it would take an eternity,” he told Belgian media.
The government must save €10 billion to stay within EU spending limits.
The budget deficit amounted to 5% last year, while a deficit of a maximum of 3% is permitted under European rules.
The Belgian national debt amounts to over €735 billion, more than 110% of Belgium's GDP, while 60% is permitted.
Due to the failure to reach an agreement, interest rates on government bonds have increased, and Belgium has to pay more to meet its debt obligations.
If the King accepts De Wever's resignation, new elections will be called.
Left-right divide
Belgium's coalition government is made up of De Wever's conservative N-VA, liberals MR, centrists Les Engagés, socialists Vooruit and Christian Democrats CD&V. The agreement between the so-called "Arizona" parties was reached after a striking 234 days of negotiations.
Sunday's budget talks showed that disagreements persisted between the N-VA and MR on one side of the coalition and Vooruit, CD&V and Les Engagés on the other. The centrist and socialist parties want €1 billion to €1.5 billion to come from taxing higher incomes, while the conservatives want to clamp down on spending.
Deputy Prime Minister David Clarinval blamed the socialist Vooruit for the failed talks as they insisted on their position for higher taxes.
Matti Vandemaele of opposition party Groen said “Prime Minister De Wever is failing to get his government on the same page, unless everyone follows his N-VA programme.”
“De Wever likes to present himself as the man of the big deals, but in practice he is mainly the prime minister of standstill. The fact that we risk falling back on provisional twelfths for the second year in a row is a complete humiliation for a sitting prime minister.”
This is not the first time the Arizona-coalition faced internal tension in the budget negotiations. Last year, De Wever also addressed the king following fruitless talks on how to save €10 billion.
In early November 2025, De Wever did not offer his resignation, but asked the king to extend the deadline, receiving 50 extra days to reach an agreement.

Securing 2028 Paralympic quota place a valuable achievement: Nasrin Shahi
TEHRAN - Iranian para-shooter Nasrin Shahi was less than impressed with Japan’s hosting of the fifth Asian Para Games, but was delighted to win a bronze medal and secure a quota place for the Los Angeles 2028 Paralympic Games.
Shahi finished third in the SH1 women’s 50m Pistol event with a score of 196.3 points, claiming the bronze medal. She competed in two events at the Games: the 10m Air Pistol and the 50m Pistol. In addition to her podium finish, she secured a place for herself at the Los Angeles Paralympics.
“This was my second appearance at the Asian Para Games, and I am satisfied with my performance. Due to flight restrictions, we had to take a very long route, and our journey to the host city took around 60 hours. Naturally, such a long and exhausting trip affects athletes’ preparation, but despite all the difficulties, we managed to achieve a good result,” Shahi said.
Shahi also voiced her disappointment with the organization of the Games in Nagoya, pointing out that, as had been the case at the previous edition in Hangzhou, China, the organizers had not provided an athletes’ village.
“The host country did not have an athletes’ village this time, and the teams were accommodated in different hotels,” she said. “The shooting team was based in Toyota City, around an hour and a half away from the competition venue. This had a significant impact on our planning, rest and concentration.”
She added that Japan’s hosting arrangements had fallen well short of expectations.
“The organization was much weaker than we had anticipated. Athletes faced problems with food and transportation. However, I should also say that the Japanese people are very kind, patient, hardworking and disciplined. Although there were delays, they eventually addressed the problems.”
Turning to the competitive standard, the Iranian shooter said the level of competition had been particularly high, with 113 athletes from 18 countries taking part.
“I competed in the 10m Air Pistol and the 50m Pistol events. Unfortunately, I missed out on a medal in the 10m Air Pistol, but I gave everything I had in the 50m event, which is much more challenging than the air pistol competition,” Shahi said.
Her efforts paid off with a bronze medal and, more importantly, a quota place for the Los Angeles 2028 Paralympic Games.
Shahi concluded by emphasizing the significance of securing the Paralympic quota, describing it as the most important achievement of her campaign at the Asian Para Games.

Chris Williamson, chief business economist at S&P Global Market Intelligence, said:
Another solid PMI reading extends the eurozone’s best growth spell for manufacturing for over four years. The sustained growth recorded since February paints an encouraging picture of resilience for the manufacturing sector, which has been buffeted by the headwinds of tariffs and conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine, and in particular the surge in costs and supply difficulties that these have caused.
Instead, increased defence spending, precautionary inventory building, diversification and changing trade patterns due to US tariffs have created growth opportunities for many producers.
However, he adds, growth is not broad-based – manufacturers in France and Italy have struggled, with the former suffering the “additional stress of domestic political uncertainty”.
In France, the index fell from a reading of 50.6 in September to 49.5 in October. Anything below 50 signals a decline. Williamson added:
Furthermore, with input cost inflation surging sharply higher again in October, climbing to one of the highest rates seen over the past four years thanks to higher energy prices and supply bottlenecks, the latest PMI data add to pressure on the [European Central Bank] to hike rates further in the coming months, providing another headwind to businesses.”

Good morning, and welcome to our rolling coverage of business, the financial markets, and the world economy.
Crypto scammers are now in “overdrive”, the founder of crypto exchange Binance has warned, as customers pull billions in funds from the platform as it recovers from a record hack.
The platform was hit by a $6.3bn theft on Thursday, which has since been described as the biggest heist in history. Experts identified North Korea as the probable culprit.
Binance initially froze withdrawals as it investigated the breach but on Sunday announced it had begun a phased reopening.
By Sunday afternoon, the platform had processed $4.6bn in withdrawals and $1bn in deposits, resulting in a net outflow of about $3.6bn – 2.1% of its $171bn in total assets under management. Some of you may have seen posts and screenshots circulating recently. Please be aware that these screenshots are fake and the information in them is false. For accurate and up-to-date information, always refer to our official channels and announcements.

….We’re seeing a similar shift in options trading on Derive.xyz. In the first 12 hours following the hack, put options accounted for 68% of Bitcoin options premiums traded, compared with 43% in the preceding five days.
Trading activity also remained elevated, with approximately $55 million in daily Bitcoin options volume since the hack, compared with $34 million the day prior.
Traders have been moving quickly to protect themselves against further losses, with downside protection taking a much larger share of options activity.
He added that the odds of Bitcoin hitting the $100,000 level by the end of the year were now just 3.5%.

Taiwan to receive 4 MK-48 training torpedoes by year-end
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
07:36:16 UTC
16:36:16 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan is set to receive all four MK-48 Mod 6 Advanced Technology heavyweight training torpedoes from the US by the end of this year.
The training torpedoes could be used during next year’s Han Kuang exercises, the Navy’s Hai Chiang exercises, and precision munitions firing drills, Liberty Times reported. Both the Narwhal and the Hai Lung submarines, which have extensive operational experience, could take part.
The Navy expects to complete acceptance procedures by the end of this year and begin underwater launch assessments for submarine crews next year. This will allow the Narwhal sub to test its critical wire-guidance technology and torpedo-tube functions.
Raytheon and Science Applications International Corporation manufactured the heavyweight torpedoes. Components for the dummy and live torpedoes, including the propulsion system, control section, and active and passive sonar systems, come from the same standardized production line, per Liberty Times. The only difference is that live torpedoes are fitted with warheads filled with high explosives. Meanwhile, exercise torpedoes use a mass-equivalent electronic instrument section made by Raytheon to record navigation data and maintain buoyancy balance.
The Navy is still awaiting delivery of 24 live MK-48 torpedoes it purchased from the US. They are scheduled to arrive in stages from 2027 to 2028. The Navy said a dedicated project team is closely monitoring progress in the US, adding that there is no need for concern about a potential capability gap in which Taiwan has submarines but no torpedoes.

Major metal and electrical union calls for thousands to strike
The trade union IG Metall, which represents workers in the metalworking, electrical, steel, automotive and industrial manufacturing sectors, has called on thousands of employees to walk out at more than 2,000 workplaces nationwide by the end of the week.
A number of companies are expected to be affected, including carmakers Opel and Rolls-Royce, consumer goods giant Procter & Gamble, e-mobility supplier Vitesco, Daimler Truck AG and precision engineering firm Paul Beier GmbH.
The union, Germany and Europe's largest, is calling for a 5% pay rise over a 12-month period, along with job and site security.
Employers have put forward an offer of a one-off payment next year and a pay rise of 1.3% in July 2028, citing Germany's economic woes and cost pressures on industry to justify not meeting the union's demand.
Riots on weekend raised questions of integration — education minister
Education Minister Karin Prien has said the violence that occurred in the aftermath of youth protests on Saturday evening was in part an indication that the integration of people of migrant background into German society could be improved.
Prien told broadcaster Deutschlandfunk said that the "for the most part peaceful demonstrations" had been followed by rioting by left-wing radicals "but also by others who probably come from migrant milieus."
She said that recognizing this fact was not about stirring up resentments, which she called "politically wrong," but about facing reality and getting a picture of why people resort to such means.
"And if they come from migrant milieus, we should be worried about it and look at the causes," said Prien, a member of Chancellor Friedrich Merz's conservative Christian Democrats (CDU).
She said one question was why integration succeeds less well in some groups than in others.
"And it's not about the question of a passport. It's about the question: Why have people not been integrated into our society and what can be done so it works better in future," she said.
Her comments came despite the fact that authorities in Frankfurt, which saw the worst of the violence, said that most of the people they arrested in connection with rioting over the weekend were German citizens.
Interior minister blames 'migrant anarchists'
Prien's remarks came after archconservative Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt of the Bavarian Christian Social Union (CSU) said the "peaceful demonstrations were hijacked toward the evening by violence-prone left-wing groups and migrant anarchists," without offering evidence for who was behind the violent turn in the demonstrations.
Dobrindt's comment was, however, called into question by Defense Minister Boris Pistorius of the center-left Social Democrats (SPD), the junior partner in Germany's federal coalition government.
"What are migrant groups, then? Are these people living in Germany in the third generation who are German nationals? Where do we stop differentiating here? I think this is going in the wrong direction," he said.
Pistorius said, however, that whoever had been responsible for the rioting had to be punished for it.
His intervention comes as the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) continues, without evidence, to blame migration for most of the country's problems, with Dobrindt seeming to adopt some of the populist party's anti-migrant rhetoric.

Germany's gas storage level well below target — AGSI
German natural gas storage facilities are currently only around 61.2% full, according to figures from a European platform that monitors storage levels. AGSI.
That falls well short of the 70% targeted by Sunday.
However, a spokeswoman for Economy Minister Katherina Reiche said there was no cause for concern.
"Germany's gas supply is secure for the coming winter, even with the current storage levels," she said.
"Based on the current assessment, we expect Germany to get through the winter in good shape. Security of supply depends not only on storage levels, but also on actual gas withdrawals, ongoing gas imports and additional precautionary measures," the spokeswoman said.
But Sebastian Heinermann,  Sebastian Heinermann, managing director of the Initiative Energien Speichern (Energy Storage Initiative), a mouthpiece for the sector, said the current storage levels were a "serious warning."
"Germany is entering the heating season with smaller safety reserves. This increases the vulnerability of the gas supply, particularly in the event of exceptionally low temperatures or additional disruptions to gas imports," Heinermann said.
The Economy Ministry has said the war in Iran, which has brought a partial blockage of the Strait of Hormuz, a vital transport route for global gas and oil, was one factor behind the current low storage level.
However, it says Germany now has more options to access additional gas than was the case in 2022, when the gas supply from Russia was cut off amid Moscow's launch of its invasion of Ukraine.
AI on the agenda at German-British talks on military cooperation
The German and British defense ministers are also expected to focus on artificial intelligence as a field for enhanced military cooperation at talks on Monday.
"By jointly testing, developing and, finally, introducing AI in our armed forces, we want to deepen our cooperation and keep pace with those who want to hurt us," UK Defense Minister Wes Streeting wrote in the daily Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung ahead of talks with his German counterpart, Boris Pistorius.
"Our opponents' readiness to harm us is not new. What is new is their abilities to do so. This demands an answer from all of us in Europe," he wrote.
Representatives from government and industry from both countries are to meet in the spring of next year to push ahead with the implementation of these plans, he wrote.
Two years ago, Germany and the United Kingdom agreed to cooperate more closely on military matters in the so-called Trinity House Agreement.
A year later, both countries announced that they would be focusing more on cyber defense as part of this cooperation.
Government to open AI-focused Digital Summit in Berlin
A two-day conference in Berlin that will look at ways of enhancing Germany's digital infrastructure, particularly in the field of artificial intelligence (AI), is to be opened by the minister for digital affairs, Karsten Wildberger, on Monday morning.
More than 1,000 guests, including digital ministers from Europe and Canada, are expected to attend the summit, which this year will focus largely on the uses and safety of AI and new developments in the field.
Chancellor Friedrich Merz is scheduled to hold a speech in the afternoon and to meet with a robot from the German company Neura Robotics.
The company develops robots that can see, hear and feel and are potentially utilizable in both industries and households.
The event is being held for the 19th time since its inception in 2006 as the National IT Summit. It did not take place in 2021, an election year in Germany.

Antonelli’s achievement is particularly remarkable given that he is only in his second Formula 1 season. He joined Mercedes in 2025, replacing seven-time world champion Lewis Hamilton, and secured his first Grand Prix victory in China in March 2026.
His rapid rise from Formula 1 newcomer to world champion marks one of the fastest breakthroughs in the sport’s history.
The historic achievement came amid a chaotic Mexico City Grand Prix marked by collisions, penalties and tensions between drivers.
Ferrari’s Charles Leclerc received a five-second penalty for gaining an advantage by leaving the track during an opening-lap battle with teammate Lewis Hamilton. Meanwhile, Max Verstappen overcame a one-place grid penalty following a practice collision with Liam Lawson to win the race.
Haas also faced an eventful weekend, with Esteban Ocon replaced by Japanese driver Ryo Hirakawa, who made his Formula 1 debut and finished 10th following post-race penalties imposed on other drivers, earning his first championship point.
Despite the drama, Antonelli emerged from Mexico City with the weekend’s biggest achievement - his maiden F1 World Championship title and a place in the sport’s history books.
Battle for second and third remains open
Although Antonelli has secured the drivers’ title with 380 points, the fight for second and third place remains wide open.

Following the Mexico City Grand Prix, Verstappen sits second with 261 points, just two ahead of Hamilton on 259. Mercedes driver George Russell follows with 250 points, while Ferrari’s Charles Leclerc remains in contention with 245.
With only 16 points separating second from fifth, the remaining four rounds could significantly change the final championship standings.
The battle resumes at the São Paulo Grand Prix in Brazil on November 6-8, followed by Las Vegas on November 19-21, Qatar on November 27-29 and the season finale in Abu Dhabi on December 4-6.
While Antonelli has already secured his place in Formula 1 history, the final positions behind the new world champion may not be settled until the last race of the season.

Polish Member of the European Parliament Michał Wawrykiewicz (EPP) of the Civic Coalition, which is Tusk's political party, just told Europe Today that the constitutional crisis first started in 2015 when Law and Justice rose to power. Un-SAFE? The UK recently declined to opt in to the EU's €150 billion Security Action for Europe (SAFE) defence loan programme, after the Commission offered a multi-billion euro entry fee. London said it was too expensive and wasn’t value for money, according to UK sources at the time.
British companies can still participate in EU-funded defence projects under third-country procurement rules, but their involvement is capped at 35% of a project's value.

The report also documents damaSudan’s Transitional Sovereignty Council’s Advisory Authority has published an evidentiary report entitled Launched from Ethiopia, presenting forensic, geospatial and documentary evidence accusing Ethiopia of direct involvement in the drone war against Sudan.
According to the report, armed drone operations targeting Sudanese territory are launched from inside Ethiopia, specifically from Bahir Dar airbase, the Asosa area and the border sector around Kurmuk and Geissan.
The report is based on data extracted from flight control systems recovered from drones shot down by Sudanese air defences, as well as drone wreckage, satellite images and incident records.
Among the key pieces of evidence presented is a flight control unit recovered from a long-range attack drone shot down in the Damazin area on 20 September 2026. The unit’s memory revealed a pre-programmed 12-point mission starting at coordinates 10.7220° north and 34.7662° east, near Geissan. Sudanese analysis places the starting point inside Ethiopian territory, 1.7 kilometres from the border.
READ: Egypt, US discuss Sudan crisis and efforts to end conflict
The report also documents wreckage from Bayraktar Akinci drones launched from Bahir Dar airbase, including serial numbers on components that could help trace their supply chain.
It records 70 attacks launched from Ethiopia between 15 February and 27 October 2026. These included 187 one-way attack drones and 82 munitions fired by strategic aircraft. October alone accounted for 28 incidents and 97 of the recorded one-way attack drones.
According to official figures compiled in the report, the attacks killed 484 civilians and 176 Sudanese soldiers, while injuring another 200 soldiers.
Among the most serious incidents was an attack on 9 October in the Wad Al-Mahi area of Blue Nile State, which killed 30 civilians, including 26 women and four children, and injured around 100 people. On 19 October, three young children were killed inside their home in Khartoum.

The EU must truly empower towns and regions to make decarbonisation a reality
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
07:30:34 UTC
16:30:34 KST

“Decarbonisation starts at local level” was the main takeaway from a conference held by the EESC’s Sectionfor Transport, Energy, Infrastructure and the Information Society (TEN). Towns and regions must be given the appropriate means to step up the EU’s energy transition and ensure energy security and local energy autonomy.
The European Economic and Social Committee (EESC) stresses that the EU can only achieve its climate neutralitygoals by enabling local actors to turn climate ambitions into action on the ground. At a conference held in Brussels on 27 October 2026, participants underlined that municipal and regional authorities have a key role in driving the energy transition.
On the one hand, cities are responsible for the majority of greenhouse gas emissions. On the other, localauthorities are responsible for implementing most climate adaptation measures. It is therefore essential that the EU empower local authorities if it wants to achieve its climate neutrality objectives and increase its strategic energy autonomy.
The event, entitled “Decarbonisationstarts locally – empowering cities and regions for Europe’s energy transition”, brought together people representing the European Commission,local authorities, trade unions, civil society and the clean energy sector, and put forward practical pathways towards an affordable and community-driven clean energy transition.
Highlighting that the energy transition would only be successful if people saw it as an opportunity to haveclean, more secure and affordable energy and not as an additional burden, Thomas Kattnig, president of the EESC’s Permanent Group on Energy, said: “The energy transition will not be decided just in Brussels, it will be decided in our towns and our regions.Cities and regions are the backbone of our energy transition. The green transition will only succeed if it is underpinned by the right regulatory framework, financing and high-quality jobs.”
Towns and regions are part of the solution
Cities are responsible for 71–76% of global greenhouse gas emissions. This means that they are part of thecause of the problem, but they can also be part of the solution. While the EU and national governments set strategic direction, local and regional authorities, together with their citizens, are responsible for implementing 90% of the EU’s climate adaptationpolicies on the ground.
The energy transition must be put in place in a way that is closer to households and businesses on the ground,focusing on both urban energy supply management and the shift to active energy consumers. Together, these actions reinforce security of supply, reduce energy prices and bolster local energy autonomy.
“Europe’s clean energy future starts in our communities, where local and regional leaders empower citizensto turn renewable energy into shared prosperity, lower bills and greater resilience,” added the European Commission’s Alejandro Ulzurrun de Asanza y Muñoz, responsible for Just Transition, Consumers, Energy Efficiency and Innovation.
Towards an affordable and community-driven clean energy transition
The conference made clear that it was possible to build local energy sovereignty through decentralised renewableenergy systems, smart grids, energy storage and innovative clean technologies.
Decentralised energy systems are becoming a cornerstone of resilient and sustainable cities. Local authoritiescan accelerate the deployment of locally managed renewable energy sources, including solar, wind and geothermal energy and heat pumps. Emerging solutions also have an important role to play. Biofuels, hydrogen and waste-to-value technologies, alongside smartgrids, energy storage and district energy systems, can strengthen local energy security, reduce emissions and bring energy production closer to consumers.
The top priority must be to make a community-driven, affordable clean transition a reality. To reach thisobjective, citizens need to be empowered as active participants in the energy transition through inclusive governance, community ownership and affordable clean energy solutions.
The clean energy transition can only succeed if citizens are active participants rather than passive consumers.Cities can foster social acceptance, strengthen community ownership of renewable energy projects and empower consumers through innovative governance and financing models. Local initiatives can make clean energy affordable, inclusive and beneficial for communities,reinforcing energy citizenship and ensuring that the transition brings about concrete social and economic value for local communities.
“The European Union cannot, on the one hand, draw up ambitious climate strategies in Brussels, while onthe other tying the hands of local authorities with complicated procedures and debt limits. If cities are to implement 70% of the EU’s climate mitigation measures, then the energy transformation must cease to be a financial burden for us and instead becomea catalyst for development,”- Hanna Zdanowska, Mayor of Łódź and member of the European Committee of the Regions.
“Possible pushback from citizens is something we have to address. How much land do we need for self-sufficiencyfor renewables? Roughly 90% of renewable energy capacity is located in rural areas. We only win local support by having local citizens participate and share the benefits,”- Davide Sabbadin, Policy Manager, European Environmental Bureau (EEB).
“Energy is an essential service for everybody. Nobody can live without heating, light or power. Energy cannotbe treated as a simple commodity or a financial asset designed to give stable returns to investors. The point is not how much we invest, but who will make the decisions, who will carry the risks and who will benefit,”- Pauline Dulongcourty, Policy Officer for utilities, European Federation of Public Service Unions (EPSU).

China mulls amendment to Tax Collection and Administration Law
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
15:30:17 CST
16:30:17 KST

BEIJING, Nov. 2 (Xinhua) -- China's top legislature on Monday began deliberating a draft amendment to the country's Tax Collection and Administration Law, seeking to further improve tax administration measures and enhance the efficiency of tax administration.
The draft amendment was submitted for its first reading at a session of the Standing Committee of the National People's Congress, which runs through Friday.
The proposed changes would adhere to the principle of coordinating legislation with reform by incorporating effective measures and practices developed through tax administration reforms in recent years into law, while leaving room for further reform.
The draft would adopt a problem-oriented approach by improving tax administration measures, closing institutional loopholes and maintaining order in tax administration, in response to new developments and challenges.
The revision also seeks to take a balanced approach by enhancing the efficiency of tax administration, regulating tax law enforcement, improving taxpayer services and strengthening the protection of taxpayers' lawful rights and interests.
The draft amendment consists of 100 articles in six chapters.
China's current Tax Collection and Administration Law was adopted in 1992 and underwent a major amendment in 2001, with partial amendments in 1995, 2013 and 2015. ■

Details: An orange alert An orange alert in Latvia refers to a high-level warning issued by authorities either for airspace threats (such as detected drones or aircraft) or for severe weather conditions (such as violent thunderstorms and heavy hail) was declared in the Krāslava and Ludza districts of Latvia after an unidentified drone violated the nation's airspace at 18:59 on Sunday.

China Focus: Chinese cities turn idle offices into affordable, convenient homes for young people
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
15:29:57 CST
16:29:57 KST

WUHAN, Nov. 2 (Xinhua) -- A shared study room, a gym and a youth activity hub line the ground floor of a building in the central Chinese city of Wuhan, where a bulletin board advertises camping trips and board-game nights.
Once a quiet office building struggling to attract tenants, the block has been transformed into a residential community for young people to live, work and socialize.
Located beside the Maying Road metro station, this youth community has 825 furnished apartments ranging from 28 to 69 square meters. The property is part of the city's efforts to turn vacant commercial buildings into government-subsidized housing, with support from China's relending program.
A 40-square-meter loft costs around 2,000 yuan (about 298 U.S. dollars) in monthly rent, while various activities for young people are held regularly in public spaces.
In recent years, many cities have struggled with excess office space while young people and new urban residents find it difficult to secure reasonably priced homes near workplaces and public transport. According to real estate services firm Cushman & Wakefield, the office vacancy rate in 13 major Chinese cities had exceeded 25 percent in 2025.
Meanwhile, roughly 70 percent of new urban residents and young people in large Chinese cities rely on rental housing, the Ministry of Housing and Urban-Rural Development has noted. Many face a trade-off between affordable rent and convenient locations.
To address this mismatch, China introduced measures in 2024 allowing local state-owned enterprises to purchase completed but unsold commercial properties at reasonable prices for conversion into government-subsidized housing, with financial support through a relending scheme.
Wuhan has a population of more than 13 million people and is home to numerous universities and technology companies, attracting approximately 300,000 college graduates each year who choose to stay for either work or entrepreneurship.
At a renovated building in the city's technology hub, Guanggu Square, developers designed shared study areas, fitness equipment and e-sports rooms, while smart delivery robots were introduced to bring meals directly to residents' doors.
"Renovation is not simply a matter of repainting walls. It involves a fundamental redesign of how a building is used," said Wu Shiya, an official with Wuhan's housing and urban renewal authority.
Liu Ying, a postgraduate law student at Huazhong University of Science and Technology, moved into a one-bedroom apartment in this area of Wuhan in August. She pays 2,100 yuan a month and can reach her university by electric scooter in less than 10 minutes.
"Safety was my biggest consideration," she said, noting the building's surveillance coverage and elevator access controls. She also makes frequent use of the shared study room.
Wuhan's housing and urban renewal authority said the city had acquired 21 commercial property projects for conversion, with a combined floor area of about 484,400 square meters.
These projects are expected to provide 10,034 affordable rental apartments. Of these, 14 projects, offering more than 5,300 apartments, are already operating, with an overall occupancy rate exceeding 90 percent.
Shenzhen, a major technology hub in southern China, meanwhile, also offers such converted affordable housing. In its Nanshan District, a former office tower has been converted into 744 apartments, more than 80 percent of which measure between 43 and 60 square meters in size.
Shared kitchens, a gym and an audiovisual room are among the facilities provided. The project recorded an occupancy rate of 95 percent in the first half of 2026, according to Yicai, a Chinese financial news outlet.
National figures point to a growing role for renovated properties in rental housing supply. According to China Real Estate Information Corp., a housing market research platform, conversion projects accounted for 33 percent of newly launched rental housing projects in the first half of 2026, up 7 percentage points year on year.
During the same period, 16 monitored cities added more than 103,625 rental units, including around 90,700 government-subsidized rental units, the Industry Council for China Rental Apartment, an industry think tank, has noted.
Xiao Wei, head of strategic consulting at real estate service company CBRE China, said the move could help property owners ease the burden of vacant assets while addressing demand for reasonably priced homes in urban areas.
"Government authorities can expand affordable housing supply and put underused assets to better use, property owners can improve their cash flow, and residents can gain access to housing with manageable rents and relatively good living conditions," Xiao said. ■

Draft law on China's state-owned assets submitted for second reading
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
15:29:54 CST
16:29:54 KST

BEIJING, Nov. 2 (Xinhua) -- A draft law on state-owned assets in China was submitted on Monday to the ongoing session of the Standing Committee of the National People's Congress for a second reading.
The draft law clarifies that the management and supervision of state-owned assets shall adhere to the principle of coordinating development and security, and improves relevant provisions on the paid use and rational allocation of state-owned natural resource assets.
The added provisions make clear that natural resource assets such as state-owned land, minerals and sea areas shall be subject to a paid-use system, and that the relevant use rights shall in principle be granted through competitive means.
The allocation of state-owned natural resource assets shall adhere to protection priority and rational utilization by strictly complying with requirements like territorial spatial planning, use regulation, and ecological and environmental protection.
The second-reading draft also improves relevant provisions to strengthen the management of state-owned asset returns.
The draft law was submitted late last year for its first deliberation. According to legal experts, this legislation is poised to improve the legal system for enhancing the efficiency of state-owned asset governance. ■

Russia has lost 1,592,770 troops in Ukraine since the beginning of its full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported on Nov. 2.
The number includes 2,500 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.
According to the report, Russia has also lost 12,452 tanks, 25,629 armored combat vehicles, 169,110 vehicles and fuel tanks, 51,801 artillery systems, 2,251 multiple-launch rocket systems, 1,731 air defense systems, 452 aircraft, 356 helicopters, 3,063 unmanned ground vehicles, 35 ships and boats, and two submarines.

Ukraine's General Staff has not revealed its own losses during the full-scale invasion, citing operational secrecy. Independent Western think-tank reports agree that the Russian casualties significantly surpass Ukraine's losses, with the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimating the ratio to be "roughly 2.5:1 or 2:1."
A January 2026 CSIS report said Ukraine has likely suffered between 500,000 and 600,000 casualties from February 2022 to December 2025, of which between 100,000 and 140,000 are thought to be killed in action.
While Ukrainian officials rarely disclose the figure, President Volodymyr Zelensky told France TV on Feb. 4 that at least 55,000 Ukrainian soldiers have been killed in action since the beginning of the full-scale war, in addition to significant numbers who are missing in action.
The intensity of Russian drone attacks and the fighting has made it extremely difficult for Ukraine to retrieve the bodies of fallen soldiers, which are needed for DNA confirmation.

Latvia's insolvent Valka stops cooperation programs with Estonia's Valga
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
07:25:00 UTC
16:25:00 KST

Latvia's insolvent Valka stops cooperation programs with Estonia's Valga
Cross-border cooperation projects between Estonia's Valga and Latvia's Valka have been suspended as the Latvian municipality is insolvent and must undergo a financial restructuring process.
In Latvia, the size of a local budget depends on the number of residents. There are 8,000 people registered as living in Valka municipality, but another thousand or so have registered as residents of Valga municipality in southern Estonia over the years because benefits are higher and the healthcare system is better.
Another 500 people commute to work in Estonia every day. However, their taxes do not reach Valka, and they are not included in its population register either, even though their families continue to live on the Latvian side and use services there.
"We have the same obligations imposed by the state as a municipality with, for example, a thousand more residents. The tasks do not change – children's rights must still be protected, municipal policing and the prevention of cyberattacks must still be ensured. All this costs a lot and means that we can allocate less and less money to sports, culture and community events. This is not right," said Vents Armands Krauklis, chairman of Valka municipality.
Latvia's State Audit Office has criticized Valka for spending more money than it could guarantee in the budget, and for disorder in the heating and water supply sectors.
For many years, Valka municipality has operated as a property management company, through which residents paid their utility bills. However, many failed to pay, debts were not collected. Calculations by the State Audit Office show the tariffs did not reflect actual costs either. At the end of last year, residents owed the municipality more than €1 million.
"In our assessment, the reason for Valka's financial difficulties is weak financial management and insufficient internal controls. More revenue was planned in the budget than could realistically be collected. Obligations to implement European Union projects were also undertaken too optimistically, even though there was no certainty that these expenditures could be made at all," said Ilze Badere, a member of the council of Latvia's State Audit Office.
There are currently €400,000 in unpaid bills.
The Pudrumäe recreation area connects the two countries and has been a joint development project. In the future, such projects with Valga will be put on hold. The Ministry of Finance will primarily focus on ensuring that Valka municipality fulfills the duties laid down in the constitution and other laws.
No one can say how long the process will last or if a long-term solution for the budget will be found.
"Valka does not directly owe Valga any money. At the same time, Valga municipal government has begun drafting the joint Valga-Valka strategy, which is a very important document for obtaining funding from the European Union, together with the Vidzeme Planning Region. It may be inevitable that Valka municipality will merge with a somewhat wealthier municipality in the region, be it Smiltene or Valmiera," said Valga municipal mayor Mart Kase.

South Africa’s splintering vote sets up multi-party battle for cities
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
08:22:32 CET
16:22:32 KST

By Bate Felix and Nellie Peyton
JOHANNESBURG, Nov 2 (Reuters) - The first time Mpho Moroka voted, in 2008, she backed the African National Congress. Almost two decades on, the unemployed 38-year-old from Soweto has switched sides to the rival Democratic Alliance ahead of local elections.
“I’m from the township. I saw the poverty, I saw the struggles and I saw that there is no change,” she told Reuters at a Democratic Alliance campaign rally. “So I said no more ANC.”
Moroka’s shift reflects a broader fragmentation of South Africa’s electorate that has made outright majorities increasingly difficult to secure.
Polls suggest the historically dominant ANC will remain the biggest single party overall, but suffer a haemorrhaging of support in the November 4 votes.
In the absence of clear victories, the party and its rivals will have to sit down to the fraught task of negotiating coalitions to govern South Africa’s major municipalities.
Their challenge — to get over their differences and form administrations stable enough to improve services, rebuild infrastructure and attract investment.
‘WE’VE BEEN LIED TO BY MANY PARTIES’
Louw Nel, senior political analyst at Oxford Economics Africa, said polling suggested support for the ANC could fall to as low as 31% to 34% — around half the more than 60% it secured in the 2011 local elections.
But the Democratic Alliance, the second-biggest party, was not capturing all of its deserters, Nel told Reuters.
Instead, he said, voters were dispersing among a number of parties including the left-leaning Economic Freedom Fighters and uMkhonto weSizwe, led by former president Jacob Zuma. Hundreds of parties are taking part in the votes.
Signs of disaffection extend beyond Johannesburg.
In Cape Town, unemployed first-time voter Abdul Tonta, 28, said he wanted change and jobs.
“Obviously we’ve been lied to a lot of times … by many parties in the past,” he said. “I’m at least voting because I want to see people like me and people like my brothers having jobs as well.”
‘COALITIONS HOLD YOU BACK’
While some welcomed the prospect of change, others warned of downsides to a future of city hall coalition deals and closed-door negotiations.
“One problem with coalitions under the current legislation is that they are left to parties to negotiate amongst themselves,” said Yunus Chamda, coordinator of the civil society group Joburg Crisis Alliance, formed in 2023 to deal with what he called “coalition chaos”.
Shifting political alliances and a revolving door of mayors have contributed to worsening services and financial decline in Johannesburg, including by giving small parties too much power and allowing politicians to evade accountability, Chamda said.
Johannesburg’s previous two mayors were from a party that had only three out of 270 seats in the city council. The city has seen seven mayors since 2021.
“It’s created this huge instability. And when you confront political parties, they are able to divert the attack to the fact that it’s a coalition,” Chamda said.
Analysts said one route to stable municipal governments in highly contested municipalities could be for the ANC and the DA, traditional rivals that joined forces in the national government after the 2024 election, to replicate that arrangement locally.
“The most important question in cities like Johannesburg, Tshwane and Ekurhuleni is whether they will produce a stable government,” Nel said.
Both parties would need to weigh the political cost of governing together across national, provincial and municipal levels. Neither is enthusiastic about the prospect.
“Coalitions make it difficult for us to fully implement our programme,” the ANC’s Johannesburg regional chairperson, Loyiso Masuku, said at a campaign stop last month.
The DA’s candidate for mayor of Johannesburg, Helen Zille, said partners often don’t respect the agreements that were signed.
“By definition, coalitions hold you back,” she said.
(Reporting by Bate Felix and Nellie Peyton; Additional reporting by Esa Alexander in Cape Town and Siyabonga Sishi in Johannesburg; Editing by Andrew Heavens)
