Factbox-Water, jobs and crime among key issues for South African voters
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
08:21:54 CET
16:21:54 KST

By Nilutpal Timsina
JOHANNESBURG, Nov 2 (Reuters) - South Africans vote in municipal elections on November 4, with basic services, unemployment and crime topping the agenda in the country’s biggest cities.
In Johannesburg, Cape Town, Pretoria and Durban, concerns range from unreliable water and electricity supplies to joblessness, public safety and a lack of affordable housing.
Here are some of the key issues shaping the vote in the major metros:
WATER, ELECTRICITY AND SERVICE DELIVERY
Water shortages and unreliable electricity supplies have become symbols of municipal failures that have angered voters and eroded support for the ruling African National Congress.
About a third of Johannesburg’s water supply is lost, with ageing infrastructure, burst pipes, leaks and illegal connections among the main causes, according to the annual report of the city’s water agency.
Tshwane, which includes the administrative capital Pretoria, faces similar challenges from ageing water and electricity networks and maintenance backlogs.
In eThekwini, which includes the port city of Durban, more than half of its water supply is lost before it reaches paying customers due to ageing infrastructure, leaks and illegal connections, the city’s oversight report says.
Cape Town has directed significant investment towards water, electricity and transport infrastructure as it seeks to keep pace with population growth, though long-term water-security risks remain a concern.
JOBS AND ECONOMIC OPPORTUNITY
Employment remains a key electoral issue, although labour-market conditions vary sharply between metros.
Johannesburg’s unemployment rate rose to 35.9% in the second quarter from 33.0% a year earlier, while Tshwane’s increased to 34.2% from 30.8%, according to Statistics South Africa.
Cape Town and eThekwini recorded the lowest unemployment rates among the major metros at 21.9% and 21.2%, respectively.
eThekwini overtook Cape Town as the metro with the lowest official unemployment rate, while employment in the municipality increased by about 90,000 over the past year to 1.29 million.
CRIME AND PUBLIC SAFETY
Crime remains a major voter concern across South Africa’s largest cities despite improvements in some categories.
Police statistics for the first quarter showed murders, carjackings and aggravated robberies declined in Tshwane from a year earlier.
In Johannesburg, murders and carjackings also fell, though violent crime remains high.
Cape Town recorded fewer murders than a year earlier, but gang violence continues to drive killings in parts of the city.
In eThekwini, carjackings and aggravated robberies declined, while murder and attempted murder remained elevated.
HOUSING, AFFORDABILITY AND URBAN PRESSURES
Rapid urbanization is placing pressure on affordable housing and municipal services in most municipalities.
Cape Town has attracted an influx of people and businesses, benefiting from a strong tourism recovery after the COVID pandemic, but rising property prices, short-term rentals and rental demand have taken their toll.
Tshwane faces increasing demand for housing and basic services, while in eThekwini, sanitation backlogs remain a challenge in some communities.
(Reporting by Nilutpal TimsinaEditing by Bate Felix and Andrew Heavens)

The presidential vote comes against the backdrop of a series of drone attacks in the past month on merchant ships off the Black Sea coast of Bulgaria, a NATO and European Union member state. The attacks have killed at least 24 seafarers, sparked international condemnation and stoked concerns about the growing reach of the war in Ukraine.
Both Iotova and Gyurov have condemned the attacks. Radev said the strikes’ outcome “benefits the Russian Federation”.
Iotova, a former member of the European Parliament, became Bulgaria’s acting president in January after Radev resigned to enter — and win — a parliamentary race on what many political analysts considered a Kremlin-friendly ticket.
Both he and Iotova have called for a diplomatic end to Russia’s war in Ukraine.
Gyurov, who served as caretaker prime minister this year, secured the support of pro-Western, reformist parties during his presidential campaign and he has long expressed support for Ukraine. He signed a security cooperation agreement with Kyiv during his time as premier.
In Bulgaria, parliament holds most decision-making powers.
(Reporting by Alex Lefkowitz; Writing by Antonis Pothitos and Edward McAllister; Editing by Clarence Fernandez and Gareth Jones)

PROFILE – Who is Iliana Yotova, Bulgaria’s first woman elected president?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
07:21:17 UTC
16:21:17 KST

Seyit Kurt
02 November 2026•Update: 02 November 2026
- Yotova has opposed further military aid to Ukraine and called for diplomacy to end the war
Iliana Yotova is poised to become Bulgaria’s first elected woman president, completing a political rise that has taken her from the European Parliament to the country’s highest office.
Yotova, who had been serving as president since Rumen Radev resigned in January, won Sunday’s runoff against former caretaker Prime Minister Andrey Gyurov, according to parallel counts.
A Trend parallel count based on 100% of polling stations put Yotova and her vice presidential candidate Kiril Valchev at 58.1%, compared with 38.9% for Gyurov and Georgi Kandev.
Her victory is another major milestone in a political career spanning European and Bulgarian institutions.
 
From European Parliament to vice presidency
Before entering Bulgaria’s presidential institution, Yotova served as a member of the European Parliament.
She later became Radev’s running mate and served as his vice president during both of his presidential terms.
Radev and Yotova were reelected in 2021, securing 63.9% of the vote in the second round.
Yotova’s political position changed significantly in January when Radev resigned as president to enter party politics.
Under Bulgaria’s constitutional rules, Yotova succeeded him as president.
Radev subsequently established Progressive Bulgaria, which secured 131 of the National Assembly’s 240 seats in April’s parliamentary election, giving it an outright majority.
The party backed Yotova in the presidential race.
 
How did she reach the presidency?
Yotova entered the Oct. 25 election as the incumbent but was seeking her first mandate directly from voters.
She and Valchev finished first in the opening round with 34.76% of the vote, narrowly ahead of Gyurov and Kandev on 31.95%.
Low turnout meant neither ticket could win outright, sending the two leading candidates into the Nov. 1 runoff.
The election came amid prolonged political instability in Bulgaria, which has held eight parliamentary elections since April 2021.
 
What are her political positions?
Foreign policy, particularly the Russia-Ukraine war, emerged as one of the main dividing lines in the campaign.
Yotova has opposed further Bulgarian military assistance to Ukraine, repeatedly arguing that the conflict has no military solution and calling for a “coalition for peace” focused on diplomacy.
Her position contrasted with Gyurov, who criticized reduced support for Ukraine and argued for closer coordination with NATO and EU partners.
Yotova has also emphasized Bulgaria maintaining greater room for independent decision-making in foreign policy while remaining part of a “strong Europe.”
After casting her ballot in the runoff, she said: “I voted for the president of peace.”
She said she wanted a Bulgaria that “makes its own decisions,” shapes its own future and builds national consensus through dialogue and functioning institutions.
As president earlier this year, Yotova also vetoed legislation restricting the number of polling stations available to Bulgarian citizens outside the EU, arguing that the changes risked limiting voting rights.
Her election now gives her a full mandate of her own after nearly a decade in Bulgaria’s presidential institution — first as vice president alongside Radev and, since January, as his successor.

Ayodhya temple donation embezzlement: SC disposes of pleas, allows petitioners to assist trial
NEW DELHI: Uttar Pradesh government on Monday informed the Supreme Court that a chargesheet has been filed in the alleged embezzlement of donations at the Shri Ram Janmabhoomi temple in Ayodhya, with the court permitting the petitioners to assist the local magistrate during the trial.A bench led by Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant disposed of the petitions concerning the alleged theft of temple donations and directed the judicial magistrate to proceed with the case in accordance with the law.The Supreme Court also clarified that it had not expressed any opinion on the merits of the allegations.
Solicitor General Tushar Mehta, appearing for the Uttar Pradesh government, informed the court that the alleged theft took place during the counting of donations at the temple. He said certain officials involved in counting the money would allegedly take the funds and either invest them elsewhere or deposit them into bank accounts.Taking note of the public interest involved in the matter, the court permitted the writ petitioners to assist the magistrate in the proceedings in the same manner as victims are allowed to assist criminal proceedings.The court clarified that its decision to allow the petitioners to participate in the trial should not be construed as an observation on the merits of the case.The proceedings will now continue before the local magistrate, who will examine the allegations in accordance with the law.

Iran warned on Sunday that any renewed war with the United States could last longer than the previous round of fighting, after President Donald Trump said he still had to "take care" of more targets.
Diplomatic efforts to end the Middle East war have been punctuated by repeated threats from the United States and Israel to resume bombardments as they hold crucial elections.
"A potential future war could last longer than previous conflict, and the American president would not be in a position to dictate the timing or the conditions of its conclusion," said army spokesperson Mohammad Akraminia, according to Iranian state television.
In the most intense phase of the war, which began on February 28 with US-Israeli strikes on Iran, Tehran retaliated with missile and drone attacks across the region.
Akraminia's remarks followed Trump's suggestion that the United States could swiftly strike its remaining targets in Iran.
"We still have to take care of, I would say one or two sites, but we can do that in 10 minutes," Trump told reporters.
"You probably could look at Pickaxe Mountain, and you have to take care of that. We can do that all very quickly," he added, referring to a suspected underground nuclear complex.
Trump reiterated his threat on Sunday, telling a campaign rally in Iowa ahead of midterm elections, that he may have to give Tehran "the hammer" at some unspecified time.
The warning came after US media reported that Trump had held a call with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Saturday over whether and when to ramp up combat operations against the Islamic republic.
Axios quoted one US and one Israeli official saying the two leaders discussed the state of negotiations with Iran, with Netanyahu pressing the president to strike the country immediately after Tuesday's US midterm elections and Trump eager to let negotiations play out.
The Israeli source described the call as "tough", while the US source said it was "direct", according to Axios.
Speaking to reporters on Sunday, Trump confirmed he had discussed Iran with Netanyahu, but would not elaborate.
'No geographical limitations'
Top military and political officials in Iran have warned against any new attack.
Spokesperson for Iran’s Revolutionary Guard Hossein Mohebbi on Sunday echoed a warning issued a day earlier in a written message by Iran's new supreme leader, Mojtaba Khamenei.
"In a conflict with America, there are no geographical limitations; a vast theatre has been defined for inflicting damage upon the enemy," Mohebbi said, according to state television.
Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said: "We hope the other side will exercise rationality and choose diplomacy," adding that Iran "remains prepared for both defence and diplomacy", according to the official IRNA news agency.
The warnings came as Iran's security chief Mohsen Rezaei disclosed on Saturday that he had received a letter from US Vice President JD Vance seeking to revive talks.
Rezaei noted what he described as a positive change in "tone" from the US side but said he had yet to respond.
He said Tehran had previously told Washington that unless its conditions were met, "neither would the Strait of Hormuz be reopened nor would there be any negotiations".
Those conditions include unfreezing Iranian assets abroad, ending the months-long US naval blockade of Iranian ports, lifting longstanding sanctions and ending the war on all fronts.
Since the war began, Iran has claimed control over the Strait of Hormuz, a vital global energy conduit, and repeatedly targeted vessels attempting to cross without its authorisation.
The United States has imposed a naval counter-blockade on Iranian ports.
'Braced for the worst'
Anwar Gargash, diplomatic adviser to the Emirati president, said on Sunday that the United Arab Emirates hoped the exchanges would yield a breakthrough, but was preparing for the worst.
"It is not the interest of the region to go through another round... But I think we're also, as we've shown before, braced for the worst," he told a conference in Manama.

Japan’s manufacturing purchasing managers’ index (PMI) fell to a seven-month low in October as output and new orders expanded at their weakest rates since March, according to a report by US-based financial services company S&P Global on Monday.
The October figure dropped to 53.3 from 54.1 in September, though it remained above the long-run average of 50.6.
"The Japanese manufacturing sector has been unable to sustain the rates of growth in output and new orders we saw earlier in the year, but we are still looking at a decent pace of expansion by historical standards at the start of the fourth quarter," said Phil Smith, economics associate director at S&P Global Market Intelligence.
Growth in total sales and export orders hit seven-month lows, despite support from global artificial intelligence (AI) and semiconductor demand, the report said.
Employment continued to expand rapidly, with job creation remaining among the fastest seen over the past decade as backlogs of work increased.
Input cost inflation accelerated for the first time in five months on higher oil, raw material and component prices, the report said.
Business confidence edged up to an eight-month high, supported by growing order books.

Carpet Diem and 1000 VASES unite craft works at Espace Commines
Curated by Francesco Pirrello, two international design exhibitions, Carpet Diem and 1000 VASES, converge at Espace Commines in Paris from October 23rd to 25th, 2026. The joint event pairs 32 textile pieces with 100 ceramic and glass objects, creating a unified material dialogue within the historic hall. Through a distinctive vertical scenography, the exhibitions explore contemporary interpretations of craft, form, and material boundaries.
32 TEXTILE WORKS DIALOGUE WITH 100 CERAMIC AND GLASS SCULPTURES
Conceived by Hervé Sauvage and Jean-Christophe Vaillant, the exhibition scenography utilizes a pronounced vertical arrangement to integrate the two disciplines within a singular volume. Rather than isolating objects into segregated typological zones, the layout elevates hanging woven surfaces, embroidered textiles, and sculptural fabrics directly above and adjacent to ceramic and glass vessels displayed on tiered plinths. Carpet Diem showcases diverse fiber manipulations, ranging from structural weaving to experimental surface finishes, while 1000 VASES presents sculptural explorations of the functional vase typology, using glassblowing, slip-casting, and ceramic glazing to bridge functional design and spatial sculpture.

The future of the Palestinian vote in Israel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
07:14:44 UTC
16:14:44 KST

The future of the Palestinian vote in Israel
The backlash against the high Palestinian turnout reveals much about the state of Israeli democracy and its future.
In the October 27 Israeli elections, 38 parties ran for office. Of these, only two supported peace, equality and an end to the occupation of Palestinian territories. Both were “Arab parties” – made up of Palestinian citizens of Israel.
These two parties earned a historic result, securing 19 seats in the Knesset, after some 80 percent of Palestinian citizens cast a vote.
This unprecedented turnout contributed to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s failure to secure a majority. His bloc won 53 seats, while the Jewish-led opposition won 48.
The electoral mobilisation of Palestinians was immediately spun as a threat and Palestinian communities now face intensified incitement by members of Netanyahu’s camp. The pro-Netanyahu camp has alleged that the election was “stolen” and is now calling for restrictions on the “Arab vote”.
Thus, Palestinian electoral success exposed an uncomfortable question for Israeli politics: what happens when citizens who are informally isolated on the political scene but whose vote is formally equal become powerful enough to determine who governs?
Palestinian citizens face a fundamental question: Can they truly determine the political outcome and if they can, does that make them equal citizens?
Formal inclusion, informal exclusion
Palestinian citizens of Israel have long faced a dilemma over voting. If they do not mobilise to vote, the risk is that the Jewish right would come to power is high. If they do vote, there is no guarantee that their participation would translate into policies that protect or benefit their communities.
In 1999, Arab turnout reached approximately 75 percent in the elections and Palestinian citizens overwhelmingly supported Ehud Barak of the Labour Party against Netanyahu. A year later, after Ariel Sharon’s visit to Al-Aqsa compound and the outbreak of the second Intifada, Israeli police killed 13 Palestinian citizens. Outrage and disillusionment contributed to an Arab boycott of the 2001 election, when turnout fell to about 19 percent. Sharon won.
Today, Palestinian electoral participation still retains its sway. Higher turnout among Palestinians means fewer seats for two main blocs – the pro- and anti-Netanyahu camps – which could tip the balance in the Knesset. This is what happened on October 27 .
But this potentially powerful position of the Palestinian parties has been diminished by the refusal of Jewish-led parties to work with them on government formation.
The logic of this exclusion was made clear in April 2021, when far-right politician Bezalel Smotrich rejected Netanyahu’s attempt to establish a government supported by one of the Palestinian parties, Ra’am. Smotrich argued that doing so would encourage greater Palestinian turnout which would allow the Palestinian community to enable the return of the left to power in Israel. Accepting Palestinian parties would therefore challenge the Jewish right’s political dominance.
Ra’am eventually joined the short-lived coalition government formed by Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid, without making any national demands, but its participation came at the cost of significant concessions on national issues. For the first time, Palestinian political leaders recognised Israel as a Jewish state and were even willing to set aside the national question in favour of addressing civil and socioeconomic issues.
Despite these concessions, the Bennett–Lapid government ultimately collapsed following the resignation of two coalition members who opposed sitting in a government alongside Palestinian representatives.
Netanyahu then realised that to prevent the formation of any future government of change, he needed to delegitimise the Palestinian parties and limit their political representation.
Following October 7, 2023, Palestinian citizens experienced a sharp contraction of political space. Students faced disciplinary proceedings over social-media posts; employees lost jobs; antiwar speech prompted police investigations and arrests.
The electoral process itself reflected this climate. Israel’s Central Elections Committee voted to disqualify both Palestinian electoral lists, along with lawmaker Ofer Cassif and Balad chairman Sami Abu Shehadeh. The Supreme Court eventually reversed the bans on the lists.
Meanwhile, attacking Palestinians, including Palestinian citizens of Israel, became a political staple. Ahead of this election, media outlet Arabic Post conducted an analysis of more than 10,000 election-related social-media items. It reported that 40 percent of posts by candidates from Netanyahu’s camp concerned Arabs or Palestinians, and that 94 percent of those were hostile.
More troubling were the police raids on the homes of Ra’am activists in the Negev, following suspicions of electoral bribery which led to the arrest of three men.
Police acknowledged searches without warrants and later reports questioned the strength of the evidence. All three men were released. But the ripple effect of those allegations helped shape a narrative of suspicion against the Palestinian community.
Attacks on the Palestinian vote
In this election, after years of repression and incitement, Palestinian citizens did not retreat. They organised, voted in unprecedented numbers and achieved a remarkable result. They took a gamble by taking their citizenship seriously and by asserting their right to full political equality and a meaningful say in shaping the country’s future.
However, the parties they voted for face isolation unless they fulfil the conditions set by the Jewish-led opposition: namely, recognising Israel as exclusively Jewish, labelling Hamas a “terrorist” organisation and accepting compulsory military or national service, from which Palestinian citizens are now exempt.
In other words, Palestinians can access the political power they should have only if they fully capitulate on the Palestinian question, embrace Zionism and accept their own status as unequal citizens.
In parallel, the Palestinian community also faces intensified incitement, particularly by the pro-Netanyahu camp. Politicians and public figures are throwing claims of electoral manipulation, insisting “the Arabs stole the election”.
Former Deputy Knesset Speaker Moshe Feiglin went as far as declaring that the Palestinian electoral mobilisation was the “October 7” of Israeli politics. Yair Netanyahu, the prime minister’s son, called Palestinian citizens of Israel “the greatest danger to the survival of the State of Israel—aside from the Iranian nuclear threat”.
Many Palestinian citizens now fear that political success could bring further intimidation, restrictions or violence rather than recognition.
Thus, the high voter turnout among Palestinian citizens has forced Israeli society and its political establishment to confront the inherent contradiction between Israel’s identity as a Jewish state and its claim to be a democracy.
This fundamental dilemma may ultimately be resolved in favour of Jewish political dominance, leading to legislation that further undermines Palestinian civil rights and expands the system of apartheid and Jewish supremacy.
It would not be surprising if a bill were introduced in the next Knesset aimed solely at restricting Palestinians’ voting rights. There are already calls on social media for such a move.
A July survey by Israel Democracy Institute found that only 46 percent of respondents in the right-wing Jewish camp supported Palestinian citizens’ right to vote.
In the current reality, following the genocide in Gaza, there is a growing sense among Jewish Israelis that there are no longer any limits to what they can do, pushing the state to act with virtually no restraint towards Palestinian citizens.
If Israeli society does not change direction, its pretence of democracy may soon no longer hold.

Water, jobs and crime among key issues for South African voters

Water, jobs and crime among key issues for South African voters
JOHANNESBURG, Nov 2 - South Africans vote in municipal elections on November 4, with basic services, unemployment and crime topping the agenda in the country's biggest cities.
In Johannesburg, Cape Town, Pretoria and Durban, concerns range from unreliable water and electricity supplies to joblessness, public safety and a lack of affordable housing.
Here are some of the key issues shaping the vote in the major metros:
WATER, ELECTRICITY AND SERVICE DELIVERY
Water shortages and unreliable electricity supplies have become symbols of municipal failures that have angered voters and eroded support for the ruling African National Congress.
About a third of Johannesburg's water supply is lost, with ageing infrastructure, burst pipes, leaks and illegal connections among the main causes, according to the annual report of the city's water agency.
Tshwane, which includes the administrative capital Pretoria, faces similar challenges from ageing water and electricity networks and maintenance backlogs.
In eThekwini, which includes the port city of Durban, more than half of its water supply is lost before it reaches paying customers due to ageing infrastructure, leaks and illegal connections, the city's oversight report says.
Cape Town has directed significant investment towards water, electricity and transport infrastructure as it seeks to keep pace with population growth, though long-term water-security risks remain a concern.
JOBS AND ECONOMIC OPPORTUNITY
Employment remains a key electoral issue, although labour-market conditions vary sharply between metros.
Johannesburg's unemployment rate rose to 35.9% in the second quarter from 33.0% a year earlier, while Tshwane's increased to 34.2% from 30.8%, according to Statistics South Africa.
Cape Town and eThekwini recorded the lowest unemployment rates among the major metros at 21.9% and 21.2%, respectively.
eThekwini overtook Cape Town as the metro with the lowest official unemployment rate, while employment in the municipality increased by about 90,000 over the past year to 1.29 million.
CRIME AND PUBLIC SAFETY
Crime remains a major voter concern across South Africa's largest cities despite improvements in some categories.
Police statistics for the first quarter showed murders, carjackings and aggravated robberies declined in Tshwane from a year earlier.
In Johannesburg, murders and carjackings also fell, though violent crime remains high.
Cape Town recorded fewer murders than a year earlier, but gang violence continues to drive killings in parts of the city.
In eThekwini, carjackings and aggravated robberies declined, while murder and attempted murder remained elevated.
HOUSING, AFFORDABILITY AND URBAN PRESSURES
Rapid urbanization is placing pressure on affordable housing and municipal services in most municipalities.
Cape Town has attracted an influx of people and businesses, benefiting from a strong tourism recovery after the COVID pandemic, but rising property prices, short-term rentals and rental demand have taken their toll.
Tshwane faces increasing demand for housing and basic services, while in eThekwini, sanitation backlogs remain a challenge in some communities. REUTERS

‘Traitors in every family’: Hungary to unmask communist-era informants and confront past
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
07:09:25 UTC
16:09:25 KST

Hungary’s new government will on Wednesday reveal the names of tens of thousands of state informants from the communist era in an attempt to confront the past and rebuild public trust.
From 1945 to 1989, Hungary’s communist state-security services relied on an extensive network of informants to monitor society and suppress dissent. Some were blackmailed or coerced into reporting on neighbours, friends, colleagues and even family members; others were recruited through promises of various advantages.
For decades, the extent of this network was hidden from public view. The “agent files”, held in the basement of the Historical Archives of the State Security services, remained largely inaccessible to the public, despite repeated calls and partial leaks.
During his campaign leading up to Hungary’s April parliamentary elections, Péter Magyar promised to make the state-security files public, a promise he seems intent on fulfilling now he is in power.
In September, his government passed a law paving the way for the files to be made public, a move more than two-thirds of the country supported according to polls. The release was initially scheduled for the anniversary of the 1956 anti-Soviet revolution but was pushed back to 4 November.
“A democratic society has the right to know its past,” Zoltán Tarr, the minister of social relations and culture, wrote on Facebook.
Previously, access to the reports on informants was restricted to researchers and relatives of victims. With the new, searchable online database, Hungary’s former state-service will become the most transparent in the former eastern bloc, researchers say.
“We are opening wide a door that was left ajar,” said István Papp, a historian and head of the academic department of the archives.
“As a historian, I agree with the release of the files. But on a personal level, I feel for those who will face their family’s history for the first time,” Papp said. Of the 50,000 to 60,000 people whose names appear in the files, historians estimate 10% are alive today.
For three decades, the former eastern bloc has been divided on how to publish agent files, and when. In East Germany, the Bundestag opened state security Stasi files in 1992. In the Czech Republic, they became open to the public in 2003. Most recently, Latvia published files on informants in 2018.
Miklós Kiss, a survivor of a Hungarian forced labour camp and president of an association for victims, would have preferred if Hungary had followed Germany’s example and released the files earlier. “If that would have happened, everything would be done and dusted by now.
“People will learn that there were traitors in every family, in every neighbourhood and street,” he added. “But what are we supposed to do with that now?”
Placed side by side, the documents would stretch for three miles, enough to trace the perimeter of London’s Hyde Park. Even so, the collection is small compared with that of the Polish or Romanian secret services, Papp said. In Hungary, many files were destroyed during the 1956 anti-Soviet uprising; others disappeared during the transition of 1989, a gradual, largely peaceful process that gave the authorities time to get rid of incriminating material.
Many of the records will be incomplete, as the agent’s motivation, or extent of reporting, will remain unknown. Of the 60,000 people mentioned in the files, the archives include detailed files, background checks and statements for only 9,000 people. These will be released in February, after personal information, including details of health, addictions and sexuality, as well as information about victims, has been redacted in accordance with privacy laws.
Alexander Faludy, a freelance journalist and Anglican priest, read the files on his family almost two decades ago. His grandfather, György Faludy, spent more than three years in a Hungarian labour camp on fabricated accusations, and later while in exile wrote his book, My Happy Days in Hell.
One report in the files, by a Hungarian woman living in London who befriended Faludy’s grandmother as she was dying of cancer, made him particularly angry. “But then, I looked at the details of the informant. There was a really ominous part in her file, with names of relatives living in Hungary, including details of her elderly parents. Suddenly, my anger evaporated. I just felt very sorry for her,” Faludy said.
“Exile was very painful for my family, but it also conferred certain moral luxuries. And that makes me hesitant in terms of passing judgment on people for what they did if they had to stay in Hungary,” he added.
The identities of secret-service agents have long fascinated Hungarians. Since the 2000s, several partial lists have emerged, naming politicians and prominent artists. Many of them denied involvement, but the allegations alone were enough to plunge governments into political crises.
To date, not many former agents have spoken publicly about their experiences, and the subject remains taboo.
In July, Szemlélek, an independent, religious online journal, published a call for former agents to come forward. Religious figures were a known target of the state services and they were often blackmailed into reporting on their congregation. According to some estimates, 7-10% of them cooperated with the state.
So far, no one has volunteered to tell their story. “I think many people feel that there isn’t really much to speak about,” the paper’s editor-in-chief, Szilárd Szőnyi, told the Guardian. “Or they think that their story is so complex that they cannot, do not want to, or are not ready to tell it.”
Domokos Szokolay, a historian, said he was hopeful that this time “the release won’t turn into a public shaming, but that people will understand that these are complex issues”. His father, Zoltán Szokolay, a poet and politician, was outed as an informant in an unofficial list published in 2005.
Szokolay has yet to read all the reports on his father, who died in 2020. By speaking openly about transgenerational trauma, he hopes to reassure others who discover their loved ones were agents that they are not alone, and to encourage them to start conversations about what they find.
“There are so many family secrets or traumas that we can already talk about: if someone’s parent is an alcoholic, or a gambling addict. But people worry that they will be judged based on the agent files,” he said. “I know confronting one’s family history can be scary or even painful. But learning about it is always better.”

Bangladesh garment factories disrupted as protests continue for third day
Workers in Bangladesh’s largest export sector are demanding a minimum wage increase amid rising inflation.
Hundreds of garment factories in Bangladesh are facing disruptions as worker protests over low pay and the rising cost of living rock the country’s industrial hubs.
There was a heavy police presence in the Mirpur industrial area of Dhaka on Monday and reports of protests taking place for the third day in the Savar, Ashulia and Gazipur areas, Al Jazeera’a Tanvir Chowdhury reported from the capital.
About 500 factories were temporarily shuttered after the protests began on Saturday. Thousands of workers have taken to the streets, facing tear gas and sound grenades from police.
In an attempt to quell the demonstrations, Bangladesh formed a new wage board on Sunday to review the minimum wage for garment workers. Prime Minister Tarique Rahman, meanwhile, held an emergency meeting with his ministers and advisers.
Workers are seeking a minimum monthly wage of 30,000 taka ($242), more than double the current wage of 12,500 taka ($101).
Bangladesh’s garment industry is worth about $38bn and is a key source of export earnings and employment.
But workers’ current wages are “not enough because of the rising cost of living”, Chowdhury said.
Workers “cannot handle the lifestyle with that kind of money, and they want a share” of the multibillion-dollar export industry, he added.
Slowing demand
The protests come as Bangladesh’s garment industry, which competes with Vietnam’s, Cambodia’s and India’s, faces a range of challenges.
Factory owners said the industry is struggling with higher costs, energy market uncertainty during the United States-Israel war on Iran and slowing demand in some export areas.
Still, Bangladesh has “among the lowest garment wages in the world”, said Babul Akhter, general secretary of the Bangladesh Garment and Industrial Workers Federation and a representative for workers on the wage board.
“If factory owners cannot pay workers properly, they should negotiate better prices with international buyers. They cannot build a business on the backs of underpaid workers,” Akhter added.
The president of the Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association, Mahmud Hasan Khan, said the government “has already taken a step by forming the wage board”.
“We expect workers to allow the review process to proceed,” he said.
If protests continue throughout Monday, Khan added, “we will have no option but to invoke the ‘no work, no pay’ provision.”

South Africa's splintering vote sets up multi-party battle for cities
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02

South Africa's splintering vote sets up multi-party battle for cities
JOHANNESBURG, Nov 2 - The first time Mpho Moroka voted, in 2008, she backed the African National Congress. Almost two decades on, the unemployed 38-year-old from Soweto has switched sides to the rival Democratic Alliance ahead of local elections.
"I'm from the township. I saw the poverty, I saw the struggles and I saw that there is no change," she told Reuters at a Democratic Alliance campaign rally. "So I said no more ANC."
Moroka's shift reflects a broader fragmentation of South Africa's electorate that has made outright majorities increasingly difficult to secure.
Polls suggest the historically dominant ANC will remain the biggest single party overall, but suffer a haemorrhaging of support in the November 4 votes.
In the absence of clear victories, the party and its rivals will have to sit down to the fraught task of negotiating coalitions to govern South Africa's major municipalities.
Their challenge — to get over their differences and form administrations stable enough to improve services, rebuild infrastructure and attract investment.
'WE'VE BEEN LIED TO BY MANY PARTIES'
Louw Nel, senior political analyst at Oxford Economics Africa, said polling suggested support for the ANC could fall to as low as 31% to 34% — around half the more than 60% it secured in the 2011 local elections.
But the Democratic Alliance, the second-biggest party, was not capturing all of its deserters, Nel told Reuters.
Instead, he said, voters were dispersing among a number of parties including the left-leaning Economic Freedom Fighters and uMkhonto weSizwe, led by former president Jacob Zuma. Hundreds of parties are taking part in the votes.
Signs of disaffection extend beyond Johannesburg.
In Cape Town, unemployed first-time voter Abdul Tonta, 28, said he wanted change and jobs.
"Obviously we've been lied to a lot of times ... by many parties in the past," he said. "I'm at least voting because I want to see people like me and people like my brothers having jobs as well."
'COALITIONS HOLD YOU BACK'
While some welcomed the prospect of change, others warned of downsides to a future of city hall coalition deals and closed-door negotiations.
"One problem with coalitions under the current legislation is that they are left to parties to negotiate amongst themselves," said Yunus Chamda, coordinator of the civil society group Joburg Crisis Alliance, formed in 2023 to deal with what he called "coalition chaos".
Shifting political alliances and a revolving door of mayors have contributed to worsening services and financial decline in Johannesburg, including by giving small parties too much power and allowing politicians to evade accountability, Chamda said.
Johannesburg's previous two mayors were from a party that had only three out of 270 seats in the city council. The city has seen seven mayors since 2021.
"It's created this huge instability. And when you confront political parties, they are able to divert the attack to the fact that it's a coalition," Chamda said.
Analysts said one route to stable municipal governments in highly contested municipalities could be for the ANC and the DA, traditional rivals that joined forces in the national government after the 2024 election, to replicate that arrangement locally.
"The most important question in cities like Johannesburg, Tshwane and Ekurhuleni is whether they will produce a stable government," Nel said.
Both parties would need to weigh the political cost of governing together across national, provincial and municipal levels. Neither is enthusiastic about the prospect.
"Coalitions make it difficult for us to fully implement our programme," the ANC's Johannesburg regional chairperson, Loyiso Masuku, said at a campaign stop last month.
The DA's candidate for mayor of Johannesburg, Helen Zille, said partners often don't respect the agreements that were signed.
"By definition, coalitions hold you back," she said. REUTERS

China’s record-breaking clean tech exports could cut CO2 emissions by 8,400 million tonnes - report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
07:02:18 UTC
16:02:18 KST

Clean tech is growing "much faster than anyone predicted just a few years ago” as gas prices continue to soar.
China is exporting a record amount of clean energy technology and equipment as the energy crisis from the Iran war drives surging demand for renewables. This will help reduce global emissions, according to a report released on 29 October.
Once installed or deployed, these 2026 exports will likely avert emissions of about 450 million tonnes of carbon dioxide per year, roughly equal to Brazil’s annual emissions, says the analysis by the Finland-based Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA).
It's a small sign of progress as global efforts to curb climate change fall short. In November, Türkiye will host annual UN climate talks where electrification is expected to be a leading topic.
"This is a pivot point for the outlook of global energy and global emissions," says Lauri Myllyvirta, with CREA. “We’re seeing growth in clean energy that is much, much faster than anyone predicted just a few years ago.”
Record-breaking year for Chinese exports
China is by far the largest global supplier of renewable energy equipment, from solar panels and wind turbines to electric vehicles and batteries. Most of what it makes is sold domestically, but a sizeable share is exported.
In the first nine months of 2026, CREA tracked a 61 per cent increase in exports of electric vehicles, a 45 per cent jump in shipments of wind turbines, a 39 per cent spike in battery exports and 22 per cent growth in overseas sales of solar equipment, compared to the same period last year.
Southeast Asia was a major destination. China's clean energy exports to the region jumped nearly 160 per cent from last year to this September, according to Ember, an independent global energy think tank.
The value of China's electric vehicle exports hit $72.8 billion (€65bn) in the first nine months of this year, up from $39.7 billion (€35.5bn) last year, according to the research firm Atlas Public Policy.
Chinese clean tech dents emissions
If these export trends continue for the rest of 2026, about 8,400 million tonnes of carbon dioxide will be averted over the lifetime of all the clean tech China exported this year, CREA estimates.
That's about 24 per cent of annual global emissions, more than the United States' and India's emissions combined.
The analysis by CREA is based on export data, the electricity systems in destination countries and Chinese emissions during manufacturing. Independent experts said the estimate was in line with the scale of China's exports, but were unable to validate the data.
Despite President Donald Trump's higher tariffs, Chinese clean tech exports to the US rose 13 per cent in January-September compared to a year earlier.
“The demand is much stronger than I expected,” Myllyvirta says. “That’s certainly noteworthy.”
China is both the world's biggest provider of clean tech equipment and the largest global source of carbon emissions.
Muyi Yang, a senior policy analyst at Ember, likens China's energy transition to replacing the engine of a ship while it's still at sea.
Interest in renewables likely to persist, experts say
The drastic war-related disruptions to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, usually the source for a fifth of the world’s oil and gas, hit import-dependent Asian countries first and hardest.
Renewed interest in clean energy options is likely to persist even after the war, says Yu Sun Chin, with the research group Zero Carbon Analytics.
Consumers in Southeast Asia are paying more for their electricity and fuel and opting for renewable alternatives such as rooftop solar.
Laos, Thailand and Vietnam have offered various incentives for installing solar and purchasing electric vehicles to help reduce dependence on imported fossil fuels.
The Philippines implemented similar policies and became the second-largest destination for Chinese solar exports in the first quarter of 2026. Indonesia has pledged to install 100 gigawatts of solar power by 2029.
“The surge in clean energy policies in Southeast Asia shows there is a paradigm shift happening,” Chin says. “Considering Southeast Asia is one of the most vulnerable regions to climate impacts, every emission cut matters in limiting a rise in global temperatures.”

Domestic violence survivor living ‘in terror’ after attacker released without tag
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
07:00:35 UTC
16:00:35 KST

A domestic violence survivor who was punched, threatened with a knife and had her front door kicked in by her former partner is “living in terror” because he has still not been fitted with a tracking tag, weeks after his release from prison.
Michelle, 38, who now lives in a static caravan with her four children, said relatives were sleeping on her floor in case the man tried to attack again. He had been recalled to prison on several occasions before for breaching his probation conditions.
“The police and probation know that he is a threat to me and has breached the terms of his probation before. It is as if they are waiting for something really bad to happen to me or my children before they help,” she said.
Michelle is among hundreds of domestic violence survivors demanding to know why tags are not being fitted on offenders as they leave prison. Instead, the private-sector firm Serco is being contracted to fit them after they have been released.
“They should be tagged as soon as they come out,” Michelle said. “Who knows where violent people are going to go and what they are going to do? Tags should be fitted in prison before they walk out the door.”
Nearly half of offenders are not tagged “promptly” on release, and in one in 10 cases a device is fitted up to five months later, according to a report released on Thursday by the chief inspectors for probation and prisons.
The prison officers’ union, POA, has written to the justice secretary, Alex Norris, suggesting members should be trained to fit tags in prison.
Michelle said she was first punched in the face by her former partner, a crack cocaine user and the father of her three-year-old boy, in early 2024. She called the police, and he was arrested and bailed.
The following day, he returned to her then five-bedroom, privately rented home, kicked in the door and threatened her with a knife, she said. “My 16-year-old son had to intervene to drag him off me after he held me down by my hair and waved a knife around. My ex-partner was convinced I had another man in my bedroom,” she said.
He was convicted of two counts of assault by beating and one count of affray, and sentenced to 38 months in November 2024. On release in February 2025, he was ordered to stay away from Michelle’s home and the town where she lives.
He breached the terms of his probation in July 2025 and April and August this year: photos he and his friends uploaded showed him at parties and pubs in towns from which he was barred.
Michelle reported two of these breaches, resulting in the man being recalled to prison for 56 days on both occasions. On 15 October, he was released, with Michelle’s police liaison officer reassuring her that a GPS tag would be fitted to keep track of his movements.
But no tag has been fitted, leaving Michelle “living in terror” that he could attack her home, her now 18-year-old son, or attempt to abduct the three-year-old.
Michelle said she was forced to leave her five-bedroom rented house and move into a caravan, following council advice.
“The police know that he has breached the terms of his probation before, they know that he is violent. It is really unfair that he can be released straight into the local area and his movements are not monitored. We have had to completely change our lives. I hardly let my children out and I am worried that he could attack at night,” she said.
Vikki Slade, the Liberal Democrat MP for Mid Dorset and North Poole, raised Michelle’s case in parliament on Monday, demanding to know why domestic violence survivors with children were not being given more protection. “The fact that we are still releasing people without a tag from prisons is utterly crazy,” she said.
The watchdog’s report released this week disclosed that Serco, the tagging contractor, had been deemed to have met its performance targets by attempting to fit the devices, rather than actually fitting them and ensuring they worked.
It said that one of the main reasons for tags not being fitted was that the offender was not at an agreed address when contractors arrived. This accounted for a third of the 5,000 criminals in the community without tags.
In a letter to Norris this month, Mark Fairhurst, the national chair of the POA, proposed that the government train prison officers to fit and activate electronic tags before prisoners are freed.
“Given the documented performance issues, the importance of public protection and the availability of an experienced public sector workforce, there is a compelling case for a formal assessment of insourcing,” he wrote.
The Ministry of Justice said: “We inherited a justice system in crisis after a decade of underinvestment but are taking the tough decisions needed to fix it. This includes the biggest ever expansion of electronic monitoring and tagging more offenders before they leave the prison gates.”
A Serco spokesperson said the firm attempted to fit an electronic monitoring device to every person required to wear one. “Where it is not possible to fit a device, or where the person breaches the conditions of their release, the individual is reported to the relevant authorities, who are responsible for considering and taking any further action,” they said.

What to look for if you’re buying a smart lock in the UK
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
07:00:34 UTC
16:00:34 KST

As the nights draw in, thoughts turn to home security. A growing number of British homeowners are choosing to upgrade their front doors with tech-enabled “keyless” smart locks, which allow them to be opened by phone, fob, fingerprint or a number pad.
But you need to make sure you have the right lock for the door – and that your insurance isn’t invalidated by installing it.
What are they?
They allow you to get into your home without a key, instead using a code, a phone, a fingerprint, a voice assistant such as Siri or facial recognition to give you entry.
Some can be operated remotely via wifi so that if a tradesman calls to do work, you can let them in wherever you are. Many offer a combination of several options.
In South Korea, and some Scandinavian countries, they are becoming the norm, says Steffan George of the Master Locksmiths Association (MLA), a UK trade body. In the UK they are more common on offices, but interest is increasing.
The types vary in complexity. Some have the smart feature and a handle in one unit that fully replaces an existing door handle. Others are made up of a small unit which can be fitted on an existing lock, sitting on top of it, opening the door when activated. This type essentially turns a traditional lock into a smart one.
And there is a third type where the existing mechanical lock cylinder is swapped for an electronic one, which opens the lock once activated. Some allow for a physical key to be used in an emergency.
How much do they cost?
They range from less than £100 to well over £1,000. Shane Hales, of HalesLocks in Sidcup, Kent, puts the starting price for a good quality version at between £200 and £250 for the unit. Getting a professional to fit them will add to the cost.
Look out for the Kitemark on the faceplate to ensure that it meets security requirements set by theBritish Standards Institution.
Sold Secure, an agency which judges the performance of locks, has a certification called SS504. To qualify, locks are tested for physical security, technical performance and cybersecurity.
Hales highlights the Black X (about £200) and the Ultion Nuki (£339) as two well-regarded units.
George says that a smart lock is unlikely to last as long as a traditional one, which “will last 20 years easily with just a little bit of lubrication”. Hales adds that, in his experience, smart locks will last for five to six years before they need to be replaced.
Will it work on my front door?
In the UK front doors are made from a variety of materials, including UPVC, timber, and a composite of different types. Checking the lock works with whatever type of door you have is vital. Many US imports will be unsuitable for British doors because of differences in the locking cylinders.
Lots of lockmakers have guides on their websites so you can check whether their product would work for your home. For example, Yale has a “smart lock compatibility checker” which uses a visual guide on what your lock looks like to recommend options.
You can email in pictures of your existing fitting and door to some installers and manufacturers, and they will advise what is suitable.
How are they installed?
Retrofit smart locks are usually installed on the inside of the door and work with the existing cylinder – the barrel in which you insert the key. They have a motorised unit inside which connects to the lock and turns it open.
To install one yourself, you will need basic tools. Most people will also want to choose a lock that has been designed to be easy to install, with no modifications needed to the door itself.
Things get more complicated when wiring, drilling or carpentry is needed to get the lock to fit properly, or if the door you have is UPVC, composite or non-standard.
Checkatrade, the tradespeople’s recommendation site, says installation costs vary; it puts the labour at between £63 for a basic keypad lock and £210 for a Z-wave-enabled lock, a communication system similar to Bluetooth and wifi.
Will this affect insurance?
If you are considering getting a smart lock, it is important to run it by your home insurer to be sure that what you buy adheres to its standards.
The Association of British Insurers (ABI) says you should check the terms of your policy before making any changes. “Some home insurers have specific requirements for the type of lock you use to protect your home, and your provider will be able to advise you,” says its general insurance policy adviser, Charlie Inwood.
Your insurer may also require that the lock is put in by a professional.
Hales says people should always get professional advice. “There is no one size that fits all doors. For that lock to be compliant, it needs to fit properly, and if it’s not fitted properly, then you know you could leave yourself open to problems.”

Nine big oil firms on track to share more than £95bn profit two quarters in a row
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
07:00:34 UTC
16:00:34 KST

The world’s biggest oil companies are on track to amass profits of more than $95bn (£71bn) in the third quarter as the war in the Middle East drives up the price of fossil fuels.
The windfall war profits have sparked calls for oil corporations such as Saudi Aramco and BP to pay for environmental damage and help the world transition towards renewable energy.
Analysis by the investment broker AJ Bell has found that nine of the biggest listed oil producers are on course to make more than $95bn in the three months to the end of September. The windfall came seven months after the US-Israel war on Iran caused a surge in global oil prices to highs above $126 a barrel, and followed a second quarter in which the same businesses made $96bn in profit.
The companies have used the biggest disruption of fossil fuel supplies in the market’s history to bolster their profits, with campaigners warning that millions of households are left to pay the price in higher bills and climate chaos.
Saudi Arabia’s state-owned Aramco is expected to top the profits chart for the third quarter. Analysts anticipate the $1.7tn company to report a 7% increase in its quarterly net income to $30bn, even though it was targeted by Iran-backed Houthi forces.
Aramco’s fossil fuel production has made it responsible for more carbon emissions than any company in history, according to the database Carbon Majors, followed by Chevron and ExxonMobil, with Shell and BP also in the top 10.
The London-listed BP published its results for the July to September period last week, reporting quarterly profits of $8.46bn – its biggest since 2008.
The industry’s profits have been driven higher by refining divisions, which have capitalised on higher prices and made up for a supply shortfall after the Iran war in hit shipments through the strait of Hormuz.
The big oil companies “are raking in enormous profits while millions of people struggle to afford their energy bills and the planet burns”, said Mike Childs, of the campaign group Friends of the Earth. “Instead of investing in cheap, homegrown renewables that would drive down bills, strengthen energy security and create new jobs, the fossil fuel industry is fighting for permission to extract even more oil and gas. This would further lock us into a polluting energy system that is driving climate breakdown and exposing communities to extreme heat, flooding and storms.”
Childs added: “We need an energy system that works for people, not one that rewards polluters and leaves the public footing the bill. Ministers must act now to decisively accelerate the transition to renewables, make our homes more energy efficient and end our reliance on volatile fossil fuel markets. And those polluters making billions from the current system must be forced to contribute more to build the cleaner, cheaper energy system we urgently need.”
Robin Wells, the director of the climate activism organisation Fossil Free London, questioned why the UK government continued to subsidise an industry that was making billions in profit each quarter.
“The oil lobby is pushing hard right now for more drilling, even adopting the tactics of grassroots campaigners by holding banners in Parliament Square,” he said. “As they rake in billions they want billions more in tax breaks to develop Rosebank – an oilfield that won’t lower our energy bills by a single penny, because the oil will be exported and sold for the profit of a select few shareholders.”
The UK energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, is weighing up whether to allow drilling in the Rosebank oilfield in the North Sea after approving a licence for the less controversial Jackdaw gasfield in October.
Experts estimate Rosebank could emit 1m additional tonnes of carbon dioxide a year by 2042, against an overall projected UK target of 90m tonnes.
A decision to approve the oilfield would be met with dismay from climate campaigners and some Labour backbenchers who view it as a step away from prioritising net zero.
Shell and Saudi Aramco declined to comment. A spokesperson for BP pointed to comments from its chief executive, Meg O’Neill, at an industry event this year, in which she highlighted the company’s role in responding to the global energy crisis, ensuring supply of diesel and jet fuel.
A spokesperson for Eni said: “[Its profits are a result] of an effective operational and financial management model that first of all enables the company to develop new hydrocarbon resources to meet global demand, which continues to structurally rely on oil and gas to ensure energy security and affordable energy for households and the industries.”
They added that Eni had expanded its energy transition business, including renewables.
Equinor, TotalEnergies, Chevron, ExxonMobil and ConocoPhillips were contacted for comment.

‘Unable to tell morning from afternoon, I felt my sense of time opening up’: a (mostly dark) winter break in magical Swedish Lapland
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
07:00:33 UTC
16:00:33 KST

Looking over the edge of the snow-smoothed canyon down to dark rushing water, we thought we saw a moose or a reindeer, but it could have been a rock. The light was fading fast so it was hard to tell. It was time to turn back; we didn’t want to get lost in the wood, or fall into the river. By the time we’d retraced our steps to Abisko, the blue world had turned to black and dust-like snowflakes whirled around the little village. Back in our hotel room after our expedition, I looked at my phone – it was only 2pm!
Travelling to the Arctic Circle in winter had always been a dream, but when I realised the sun wouldn’t get above the horizon on my holiday, it made me twitchy. I usually pack my limited annual leave as tightly as I pack my working life. I was already using up three days’ holiday travelling by train from London to Abisko. How would I make the most of my time there with barely any daylight?
My partner and I chose to stop in this small village in Swedish Lapland almost by chance, when we researched the most northerly stops on the train line between Stockholm and Narvik. Abisko looked on the map like a tiny enclave surrounded by lakes and mountains. Reading more about it, we found that it was home to the Abisko blue hole – a unique microclimate where the geography creates frequent clear skies, making it one of the most reliable places on Earth to see the aurora borealis.
After a blur of cities and sleeper trains, we arrived at Abisko Ostra, a tiny station comprising just one low platform and a glass shelter over the exit door, at 11am. We jumped down from the high step of the carriage into soft, deep snow, our feet creating the only imprints on the length of the walkway. White mist hung all around us, and the couple of buildings we could see were fading into the sky. Apart from the icy train tracks cutting a sharp black detail, everything in the landscape appeared icing soft.
We walked along an empty road that curved up to the Abisko Mountain Lodge, one of a handful of accommodation options we had found online. Our room wasn’t quite ready, so we spent a while in the hotel’s warm, firelit bar watching people change into their outdoor gear then disappear into the cold. Knowing that darkness would soon set in, I was itching to get outside as well – while we could still see our surroundings.
By the time we were salopetted up, thick clouds had made the white world grey, but it was still everything my Christmas-film-loving inner child had imagined. The path we followed was lined with low lights glowing yellow against the white landscape, guiding us among houses with bright windows illuminating the dusk. We followed our phone map towards a viewpoint by a river. It was only half an hour’s walk, but in the deep snow it seemed much longer, and felt like walking through a thick white cloud.
We had expected to spend the day exploring. Instead, we’d somehow finished our outing before the afternoon had properly begun. Feeling the luxury of time stretching out, we made tea in our room and read for a while, but we still had plenty of time before dinner, so we went for a few rounds in the sauna.
In the restaurant later, we heard an excited murmur among the diners. The aurora! We rushed out, wearing the clothes we’d been eating dinner in, and watched the green glow, our feet growing more and more numb. But the night was still young, so we got back into our cold-weather gear and walked up a path to higher ground where a family were making snow angels while watching nature’s light show. Their enthusiasm added to our excitement, and we found ourselves not wanting to look away from the dancing sky in case it got better or brighter. Our initial walk to the canyon felt like days ago but we’d only arrived 12 hours earlier.
The next day, after a long and leisurely breakfast of pickled herring, gherkins and lots of delicious rye bread, we hiked a few hours along the bank of Lake Torneträsk. The snow on the path was compact enough for us to explore in our hiking boots, but we saw a few adventurous groups snowshoeing through the wilderness. We followed a narrow path through bare silver birches weighed down with bulbous drifts, until we found a picnic spot near a frozen waterfall, where we enjoyed some provisions we’d squirreled away from the generous breakfast.
I did a double-take as I looked back at the way we had come. The sunrise-like colour seemed to be glowing in exactly the same way as when we’d set off, hours before. Unable to tell if it was morning or afternoon, I felt my sense of time opening up. The sun remained below the horizon, but its colourful glow hung in the sky for hours. The pinks and oranges slowly brightened, lingered, then imperceptibly began to fade. The ideas of dawn, midday and evening began to fade, too.
From the waterfall, we walked up to a high viewpoint and ate flapjacks as we watched the hidden sun cast a last ray of deep orange towards the horizon. We warmed up with hot chocolate in the Abisko Turiststation hotel, drying snow-damp clothes on a radiator before heading back into the cold. The stars were out by then – in the mid-afternoon. We took the long path back to the village and headed through the misty gloom towards the red neon sign and strip-light interior of the supermarket to stock up on snacks for the next day’s train journey.
The supermarket was designed for people likely to get snowed in, with lots of produce for sale in bulk, but we found delicious jars of pickled herring, cloudberry jam and more of the region’s dense rye bread to tide us over, along with a squeezy tube of cheese spread from the surprisingly varied range that covered almost a whole aisle. Back at our hotel, we had another sauna, then dinner, before a beer in the cosy hotel bar. Then we headed outside again. It had been dark for hours, but it was still only early evening.
We were due to take a cable car up to Abisko Sky Station, a mountain viewpoint 900 metres (nearly 3,000ft) above sea level, but high winds meant the 20-minute cable car journey was too dangerous, so our evening’s plans changed shape. Our guide took us to an outcrop above Lake Torneträsk, where we got another spectacular show of the aurora, complete with shooting stars, courtesy of the Geminids. I have no idea how long we stood there, admiring the sky. I’d stopped trying to fit the holiday into my idea of what should be done when.
Later, we warmed up with reindeer soup in a building shaped like a traditional Sámi lávvu, a conical structure with a central fire for warmth and light. Our guide told us some of the myths and legends surrounding the aurora: that the lights were ancestors dancing, or a fox spirit running through the sky with snow attached to its tail. He also showed us the best forecasting apps to use, like the Aurora Buddy and My Aurora, and what all the bars on the various graphs meant. The northern lights lit the darkest part of our walk home.
I came to Abisko worrying that darkness would take something away from my trip, but instead it removed the boundaries that normally suggest what I should be doing when. When the distinction between night and day dissolved, there unexpectedly seemed to be more holiday in front of me. It felt like a surprisingly liberating way to travel.

Inference refers to the process of running trained AI models to respond to user requests, which involves processing units of data known as tokens. As AI adoption accelerates, the volume of token calls, which refers to AI usage through public cloud service providers, provides an indication of growing demand for AI services.

The Hebron Governorate said the military aggression had also damaged infrastructure and the local economy, while disrupting education across the affected areas.
With Israeli forces now withdrawn, Palestinian authorities say they are working to facilitate the safe return of displaced families and monitor conditions across the city.

Gas supplies from Azerbaijan accounted for 3.6%.

Saab announces Combat Boat 90 CX

Saab announces Combat Boat 90 CX
Saab is introducing the new Combat Boat 90 Capability X (CB90 CX), representing a new dimension of capability with three optionally crewed configurations: intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance (ISR), anti-ship warfare, and short-range air defence (SHORAD). Together, these capabilities address the evolving threats of modern naval reality, enabling a more distributed, flexible, and resilient naval force.
When maritime threats become increasingly complex, navies need platforms that can detect threats earlier, share information faster and deliver effects from dispersed positions. CB90 CX expands the role of combat boats beyond troop transport, enabling them to contribute directly to surveillance, surface strike, and air defence missions.
Larger than the popular existing vessel trusted in-service around the world, the new CB90 CX features increased payload capacity and comprehensively updated onboard systems, across a wider range of sea states. Designed for optionally crewed operations using Saab’s Autonomous Ocean Core, CB90 CX retains the well-regarded characteristics of its troop-carrying predecessors while enabling the integration of a broader range of capabilities.
“The future of naval operations is not just about having more platforms; it is about distributing greater combat capability across the force. As operational realities change, so does CB90. CB90 CX reflects this evolution, moving beyond troop transport to connecting sensors and weapons and delivering combat capability directly from the boat, whether crewed or uncrewed,” says Anders Hellman, head of Saab's business unit Docksta.
The three initial configurations have distinct operational roles. The ISR configuration focuses on multi-domain situational awareness and uses Saab's Giraffe 1X radar. The anti-ship warfare configuration provides over-the-horizon strike capability against surface vessels, while the SHORAD configuration uses an anti-aircraft autocannon for air defence at a time when Uncrewed Air Systems proliferate. By operating together, they provide navies with complementary capabilities that enhance their combined operational effectiveness or as part of a wider joint forces mix.
CB90 CX is currently under production for Sweden as the launch customer and will co-exist alongside the existing smaller CB90 NG. CB90 serves in nine navies and operates across the world from Europe, the Middle East, Africa, Asia Pacific, and the Americas.

Why are laundromats becoming more popular in Tallinn?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
06:53:00 UTC
15:53:00 KST

Why are laundromats becoming more popular in Tallinn?
In Estonia, it is generally not customary to wash one's dirty laundry in public, but suddenly a whole string of self-service laundromats has appeared in Tallinn. Although there are hardly any homes without a washing machine, ERR investigated why people no longer want to do their own laundry at home.
The first self-service laundromats opened 60 years ago, when many people still had their water supply outside and wastewater indoors. The Riga washing machine, which constantly gave electric shocks, was an unattainable dream for many housewives.
Laundromats died out several decades ago, when automatic washing machines went from being luxury goods to everyday household appliances. However, recently, new self-service laundromats have sprung up in the capital like mushrooms after rain.
Is the trend connected to the changing size of apartments, ETV's evening news show "Aktuaalne kaamera" asked?
Ingmar Saksing, a member of the management board of LVM Real Estate, told the show: "There is some truth to that, apartments are indeed getting smaller and smaller. But just because an apartment is getting smaller does not mean that dirty laundry cannot be washed at home. We have reached a point where people have little time. They increasingly dislike mowing the lawn themselves, robots do it; robots also clean many people's homes, and doing the laundry has remained a tedious chore."
Saksing said there are few homes without a washing machine. If there is not enough room for one in the bathroom, it is hidden under the sink or built into the kitchen furniture.
Even if a corner can still be found for a washing machine in the bathroom, problems can arise when it comes to drying clothes – where do you put a drying rack in such a small apartment? Clotheslines between apartment buildings have been replaced by parking spaces, and attics have become penthouse apartments.
"If you do not have a balcony, you do not want to turn your home into a laundry drying room. That's the reason," Saksing said.
Aljona, who lives in Mustamäe, has both a washing machine and a dryer at home, but still prefers to visit the laundromat.
"It's more convenient here because it takes less time. Washing bed linen at home takes two to two and a half hours, but here it's done in half an hour. You load the machine, go shopping, and when you come back, everything is already done," Aljona told the show.
Drying takes 15 minutes, while at home the machine would rumble away for an hour and a half. Laundry can be washed so quickly because the machines do not waste time heating water.
However, if you add the time spent going to the laundromat, the question arises whether washing one's dirty laundry in public actually saves any time at all.
"Since there are more machines here, and they are bigger, you can put more laundry in, so you could say it gets washed faster. I sometimes come here to do the laundry myself. You could say I'm buying my wife time," said Mairo Matsi, a member of the management board of laundromat chain Laundrix.
Kristiina Lõhkivi, a representative of the company Laundromat, said the main customers of self-service laundromats are single men, who struggle to understand which cyle to pick, and mothers.
"These are our main customers, who have more laundry, large items, such as blankets and pillows, which you otherwise could not fit into a machine at home, but which fit into ours very easily," Lõhkivi said.
She said domestic washing machines are considerably less efficient than industrial models, unless you have bought a machine costing several thousand euros.
"If you have a machine that costs €4,000, then the only thing we can offer you is saving time," she said.
The most popular time to visit the laundromat is at weekends or later in the evening, from 10 pm to midnight. A quarter of customers bring wet laundry to dry.

Bulgaria elects Iliana Iotova, ally of PM Radev, as its first female president
SOFIA, Nov 2 - Bulgaria has elected Iliana Iotova as its first female president, official results showed on Monday, providing a political boost for Prime Minister Rumen Radev who had backed her for the largely ceremonial role.
Iotova, 61, won 57.6% of the votes cast in Sunday's run-off contest, while her rival, former caretaker prime minister Andrey Gyurov, 50, won 39.5%.
The presidential vote comes against the backdrop of a series of drone attacks in the past month on merchant ships off the Black Sea coast of Bulgaria, a NATO and European Union member state. The attacks have killed at least 24 seafarers, sparked international condemnation and stoked concerns about the growing reach of the war in Ukraine.
Both Iotova and Gyurov have condemned the attacks. Radev said the strikes' outcome "benefits the Russian Federation".
Iotova, a former member of the European Parliament, became Bulgaria's acting president in January after Radev resigned to enter — and win — a parliamentary race on what many political analysts considered a Kremlin-friendly ticket.
Both he and Iotova have called for a diplomatic end to Russia's war in Ukraine.
Gyurov, who served as caretaker prime minister this year, secured the support of pro-Western, reformist parties during his presidential campaign and he has long expressed support for Ukraine. He signed a security cooperation agreement with Kyiv during his time as premier.
In Bulgaria, parliament holds most decision-making powers. REUTERS

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Ocean Affairs Council said Saturday that it held a seaborne and underwater drone competition for colleges and universities at Kaohsiung's Hsinta Harbor.

OAC Administrative Deputy Minister Wu Hsin-hsou (吳欣修) said drones are becoming increasingly important in ocean observation, underwater surveys, and maritime security.

The second team's “Ocean Guard 1” is designed for ocean governance and coastal missions. The lightweight ship can navigate autonomously and swap equipment such as water quality sensors and sonar to track pollution, as well as use oil-absorbent mats to clean up oil spills.
The “Sea Sentinel” is fitted with weather radar and a multi-laser echosounder for sea weather observation. Its team built an AI platform to collect real-time sea wind, wave, and ocean current data to predict weather, making it suitable for observation and maritime safety.
