What the US midterms could mean for Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
06:44:23 UTC
15:44:23 KST

What the US midterms could mean for Ukraine
U.S. President Donald Trump delivers remarks during a campaign rally at Crossroads Arena in Corinth, Mississippi, U.S. on Oct. 26, 2026. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)
For months, Ukraine has faced mounting pressure from U.S. President Donald Trump, as he seeks to secure political gains ahead of the November midterm elections.
With both chambers of Congress at stake on Nov. 3, the key question is how heavily Republicans will lose — and whether the scale of any setback will be enough to shift Washington's foreign policy.
The vote comes at a low point in U.S.-Ukraine relations.
Trump drew fire from U.S. lawmakers, Kyiv, and European capitals for allowing Russian diesel into the U.S. and easing sanctions on Russia, running counter to the West's long-standing strategy for ending the war in Ukraine.
And while Moscow avoids pressure, Kyiv is pressed to end its strikes against Russian refineries while grappling with disruptions in intelligence support and Patriot air defense shipments.
A Democratic victory might give Ukraine a sympathetic Congress and offer greater scrutiny over Trump's foreign policy pivots. However, experts who spoke with the Kyiv Independent say that the U.S. president would ultimately keep firm control over his country's foreign policy.
read also
Pushing Ukraine aid past Trump
This week, U.S. voters will elect all 435 members of the House of Representatives, where Democrats are widely expected to win a majority for the first time since 2020.
The Democratic Party faces steeper — but not insurmountable — odds in the Senate, where only about one-third of the 100 seats are up for a vote, with a mere seven considered toss-ups.
Even if the Democratic Party ends up with 51 Senate seats needed for a majority, they would still need the Republican Party to overcome a filibuster, a U.S. policy where 60 votes are needed in the Senate to pass crucial legislation.
For Kyiv, that is not the end of the road, however.
U.S. senators have shown they can build a bipartisan majority around support for Ukraine, most recently in August, when they passed the Lindsey Graham Act — spearheaded by the late Republican Senator Lindsey Graham — with 86 votes.
But this bipartisan consensus cannot be taken for granted when it comes to Republican lawmakers challenging Trump.
"In today's highly polarized political environment, most lawmakers hesitate to oppose a president of their own party, even when they disagree with his policy choices," James M. Lindsay, a U.S. foreign policy expert at the Council on Foreign Relations, told the Kyiv Independent.
Should Democrats muster enough support to push through a bill on assistance for Ukraine or tougher sanctions against Russia, Trump wields powerful veto rights.
Only a two-thirds supermajority in both chambers can override it, and that number is something Democrats are unlikely to whip up.
"Congress has a poor track record in overturning presidential vetoes, especially in foreign affairs," Lindsay notes.
Still, a Congressional majority would hold some leverage.
Lawmakers could include measures supporting Ukraine in "must-pass" legislation, such as defense appropriations bills or the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA).
Congress would then "dare Trump to veto it," said Daniel Hamilton, a U.S. foreign policy expert at the Brookings Institution. "He is unlikely to do so, since the overall bill funds the Defense Department."
But even when the bill leaves the desk with a presidential signature, there comes another obstacle — the chance of Trump simply ignoring it afterward.
read also
When the president sidelines Congress
It has happened before.
A sweeping Russia sanctions bill, championed by the late Senator Graham, was passed with great fanfare and signed into law by the president in September.
Yet, Trump has not toughened up on Russia since — quite the opposite.
On Oct. 16, the president issued a broad waiver of Graham's sanctions, days after his Treasury lifted restrictions on Russian diesel purchases.
This was not the first time the administration had sidestepped Congress on Ukraine matters either.
Earlier this year, the Pentagon delayed $400 million in military assistance under the Ukraine Security Assistance Initiative (USAI) for months, even though Congress had already authorized it.
This illustrates the limits of Congress's power: passing a law does not guarantee that the executive will carry it out as lawmakers intended.
Ironically, Congress was quite capable of disrupting the White House's Ukraine course during the Biden administration.
The Republican-led House famously blocked a massive aid bill from late 2023 until 2024, leading to a critical ammunition "hunger" among Ukrainian forces.
But this dynamic would not translate to a clash between Trump and a Democratic-led House. For the Ukraine policy he is pursuing, Trump does not need congressional consent, Lindsay said.
"Some presidential powers, such as when to negotiate, whom to negotiate with, and what to negotiate over, are beyond Congress's power to direct, restrain, or regulate."
It was Trump who — to the chagrin of many pro-Ukraine lawmakers — publicly humiliated President Volodymyr Zelensky in the Oval Office in February 2025 and who pulled Russia out of diplomatic isolation by hosting Russian President Vladimir Putin in Alaska a few months later.
"A Democratic House or Congress may bristle at President Donald Trump's diplomacy with Russia, but it cannot compel him to change it," Lindsay said.
Beyond legislation
A Democratic victory would not upend Trump's policy, but could boost Ukraine's voice on Capitol Hill.
If House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries replaces Mike Johnson as speaker, Republican skeptics could no longer keep pro-Ukraine legislation off the floor, as they did with Biden's aid bill.
Majorities in one or both chambers would also give Democrats leadership of committees and allow them to subpoena executive officials.
According to Hamilton, Democrats may use this power to investigate SpaceX founder Elon Musk, U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, or Trump's peace envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner.
Musk is allegedly responsible for the temporary throttling of Starlink services in Ukraine, Hegseth is said to be delaying shipments of Patriot missiles, and the U.S. peace envoys have faced scrutiny for at times pushing peace deals favorable to Moscow.
A House majority would also allow Democrats to impeach executive officials, including, for the third time, Trump. This would not guarantee a conviction and removal — a supermajority of senators is needed for that.
Lawmakers who spoke to the Kyiv Independent see the midterm election as a chance to set the legislative agenda on Ukraine and to scrutinize Trump's policies more closely.
"We will use every legislative and oversight tool available to hold this administration accountable and ensure Ukraine receives the security assistance it needs to defend itself," said Mike Levin, a Democratic representative for California's 49th congressional district.
Backchannel deals with the Kremlin, and any disruptions to intelligence sharing or Ukraine's Starlink terminals would face "rigorous oversight" if Democrats win House committee gavels, he told the Kyiv Independent.
Gregory Meeks, a Democratic representative and ranking member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, pledged to work with lawmakers from both parties to push through legislation to "compel the Trump administration to deliver to Ukraine the security, economic, and intelligence support it needs to defend its people from Putin's brutal and illegal invasion."
In his statement for the Kyiv Independent, Meeks further committed to "fixing" the Graham Act, "including by denying President Trump the ability to unilaterally import Russian energy and undermine U.S. national security interests."
Nevertheless, Ukraine is unlikely to be front and center in Democrats' focus after the midterms.
The party's 100-day post-victory plan focuses on issues most pressing for U.S. voters, such as the cost of living and restraining Trump's war against Iran, which has driven up inflation and fuel prices.
Ukraine is far from the top of the agenda.
And even with his back against the wall in the legislature, the president will still have a bite on the international scene.
"Historically, most presidents in this situation have turned to foreign policy, and so Trump is likely to be even more outrageous in some of his initiatives than before, perhaps including working with Putin and (Chinese President) Xi (Jinping) at the expense of Ukraine and Europe," Hamilton said.
"A Democratic Congress would do what it could to block that; how such battles unfold will depend on the specific issues."
Lindsay also argues that Trump appears unconcerned about how unpopular his foreign policy maneuvers are, be it the Russian diesel deal or the sanctions waiver.
And since he cannot run for another term, he has even less incentive to temper his policy, the expert added.
"Those are not decisions of a president who is following the political winds."

Note from the author:
Hi, this is Martin, the author of this article.
After Russia launched its full-scale invasion, the U.S. has been Ukraine's first and foremost ally. American weapons, intelligence, and sanctions have helped Ukraine hold the line.

Le Pen condemns Poland's Constitutional Tribunal crisis, Sikorski tells her not to interfere
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
06:44:01 UTC
15:44:01 KST

The dispute over the composition of Poland's top court has fuelled an open confrontation with President Karol Nawrocki, who attempted to enter the building on Friday night.
The leader of France's far-right National Rally (RN) party has weighed in on Poland's deepening Constitutional Tribunal crisis, saying it is cause for "profound concern."
"The contested suspension of the Tribunal's president, and the intervention of security forces around this institution, appear to resemble a forcible takeover of a constitutional body," Le Pen wrote in a post on X.
"The indifference of the European Union and the silence of the media in the face of the Polish crisis are raising legitimate questions: one cannot claim to defend democracy and the rule of law while remaining silent when the constitutional balance of a member state is gravely threatened."
The dispute over the composition of Poland's top court has fuelled an open confrontation with President Karol Nawrocki, who attempted to enter the Tribunal building amid a deadlock over the appointment of new judges on Friday night.
Police surrounded the building as the confrontation unfolded live on television, drawing attention to the crisis beyond Poland and into the wider European political debate.
The opposition has accused Donald Tusk's government of attempting a coup, while the government says it is pushing ahead with long-needed reforms to restore the rule of law after years of Law and Justice (PiS) party interference in the judiciary.
Sikorski responds
Poland's foreign minister commented on Le Pen's post, writing "Ms Le Pen, as a friend and ally of France, Poland does not interfere in your politics. We ask you to respect us by not interfering in ours."
The European Commission said on Saturday it was closely monitoring the crisis.
A spokesperson told Euronews on Saturday: "It is for the Polish authorities to ensure that the Constitutional Tribunal can operate in accordance with the Polish constitution and with respect for the relevant case law of the Court of Justice of the European Union."
"The appointment of eight new members of the Constitutional Tribunal falls within the constitutional powers of the Sejm, the Polish parliament," the spokesperson added.
Dispute over control of the judiciary
Tusk said his government had tried to resolve the crisis, but its proposals were blocked by PiS and the president, further deepening the dispute.
He said the parliamentary majority then waited for the terms of judges appointed under the previous PiS-led government to expire in an effort to avoid a confrontation.
“We waited calmly for new judges to be chosen, until the terms of their predecessors appointed by PiS expired. The Sejm made its choice, the judges took the oath, but the president did not deign to receive that oath,” Tusk said.
The Sejm, Poland’s lower house of parliament, elected the new judges, who took their oaths of office. Nawrocki did not formally receive the oaths, while Tribunal President Bogdan Święczkowski refused to allow the new judges to take up their duties.
Tusk described the newly elected judges as legally appointed and said they had been attacked. He also criticised politicians and activists linked to PiS and the far-right Confederation party over their conduct during the confrontation.
He compared the dispute to a thief stealing an elderly woman’s handbag and then accusing others of violence when they try to recover it.
“In certain matters there can be no compromise,” he said, adding that lawlessness could not be negotiated away.
Physical force, aggression and party interests must not determine who is right in a state governed by the rule of law, he added.
Tusk also said no politician, including the president, had the right to enter a court or tribunal, issue instructions to judges or intimidate them. He was referring to Nawrocki’s visit to the Tribunal building after turning his plane around while travelling to Senegal.
Tusk warns against playing into Russia’s hands
Tusk warned that pro-Russian groups could exploit the political conflict.
He pointed to Russian bots operating online which, in his assessment, were supporting opponents of Poland’s current constitutional order.
He said the Constitutional Tribunal would operate in accordance with the constitution and independently of the executive.
As head of government, Tusk pledged to provide the institution with the security and conditions needed to carry out its duties.
“And I intend to fulfil this task,” he said.
However, the speech offered no concrete agreement with Nawrocki or detailed plan to resolve the dispute.

Your next mobile game could come from Roblox
Roblox plans to let creators release games as standalone apps outside its platform. The first selected titles are expected in the first half of 2027, Qazinform News Agency reports.
The company outlined its Roblox Everywhere initiative in its October 29 shareholder letter. Developers would publish games built on Roblox through app stores of their choice.
Those games would retain access to Roblox’s payment, communication, social and safety features. The company expects the first phase to launch during the first half of 2027.
Roblox also outlined a separate initiative called Universal Player. It aims to use artificial intelligence to bring existing console, PC and mobile games onto Roblox. The company wants those games to support multiplayer play across devices.
Both initiatives form part of Roblox’s ambition to capture 10% of the global gaming market.
“Over the past month, more than 80% of the top 100 games on Roblox (ranked by hours engaged) used AI tools to accelerate creation, and the number of daily asset uploads to the Roblox cloud tripled month-over-month,” the company said.
Its Build tool allows users to create games through text prompts. More than 500,000 users have tried it, publishing over 70,000 games. The tool launched in alpha testing in New Zealand, Singapore, Serbia and Thailand.
Roblox is also seeking to expand its adult audience. At the end of September, adults represented 29% of daily users who completed age checks. That share rose from 27% at the end of June.
The platform averaged 138 million daily active users during the third quarter. Users spent nearly 34 billion hours on Roblox.
Quarterly revenue rose 16% year over year to $1.6 billion. Bookings, generated mainly through virtual currency sales, fell 12% to $1.7 billion. The company attributed that decline to unusually strong growth in 2025.
Roblox reported a quarterly net loss of $230 million.

Kazakhstan's processed agricultural exports surge 35% to $3 billion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
06:40:56 UTC
15:40:56 KST

Kazakhstan's processed agricultural exports surge 35% to $3 billion
Kazakhstan's exports of processed agricultural products reached $3.04 billion in the first eight months of 2026, up 35.1% from the same period last year, Qazinform News Agency reports.
Processed products accounted for 54.1% of Kazakhstan's total agricultural export value, highlighting the country's growing focus on higher-value-added goods.
Grain processing remains a key driver of this growth, with grain and flour exports reaching a record 16 million tons in grain equivalent during the 2025/2026 marketing year.
From January to August 2026, Kazakhstan exported 1.38 million tons of wheat and wheat-rye flour, up 23% year-on-year, while export revenue rose by 36% to approximately $400 million.
The vegetable oil sector also saw strong growth, with exports of sunflower, safflower, and cottonseed oils rising by 49% to $673 million. Meanwhile, the value of rapeseed and mustard oil exports more than doubled to $90 million.
Other agricultural exports also recorded significant increases. Feed flour exports rose by 61% in value to $578 million, with shipments reaching 2.5 million tons. Beef export revenue climbed by 78% to $164 million, while volumes grew by 13% to 29,000 tons. Exports of oilseed processing byproducts, including oilcakes and meals, increased by 42% to $113 million.
To sustain this growth, the Ministry of Agriculture is providing support through preferential loans, investment subsidies, and tax incentives. Between 2024 and 2026, approximately 230 billion tenge was allocated to finance working capital for agricultural processing enterprises.
Kazakhstan is also stepping up efforts to develop advanced grain processing. The country currently has three specialized facilities with a combined annual capacity of 510,000 tons of raw materials. Over the past five years, production of starch-based products has more than doubled, while bioethanol output has reached 21,200 tons.
To further expand the industry, six major investment projects worth approximately $4 billion are underway, with a combined annual processing capacity of 5.8 million tons of raw materials. These projects are expected to boost domestic production of starch, gluten, amino acids, and bioethanol.
Progress is already being made on several facilities. The Kazkrakhmal plant, with an annual capacity to process 150,000 tons of corn, began operations in Turkistan region this year, while the first phase of Fufeng Group's production complex was completed in Zhambyl region. The Qostanai Grain Industry and Tiryaki Agro projects are also moving forward, with two more facilities planned for Akmola region.
To meet growing demand for raw materials, Kazakhstan has expanded its corn cultivation area by 60% to 106,000 hectares.
These investments, along with government support measures, are expected to increase exports of finished and advanced processed agricultural products, reduce reliance on raw material exports, and strengthen Kazakhstan's position in international markets.
Earlier, it was reported that the North Kazakhstan region received its first shipment of pedigree cattle from Australia, with 305 Aberdeen Angus animals arriving via a special cargo flight.

Türkiye’s exports of “critical technology” products, comprising medium-high and high-technology goods, reached $86.4 billion in the January-September period.
Türkiye has increased exports across a range of technology-intensive industries, including aerospace products, weapons and ammunition, motor vehicles, medical products, computers and electrical equipment, according to data from the Turkish Statistical Institute (TÜİK).
Exports of medium-high and high-technology products rose from $53.1 billion in 2013 to $60.1 billion in 2017. The figure increased to $77.4 billion in 2021, $88.7 billion in 2022, $97.3 billion in 2023, $101.1 billion in 2024 and $111.9 billion last year.

The largest contribution came from the manufacture of computers and electronic and optical products, which generated $3 billion in exports. This was followed by aerospace manufacturing at $2.5 billion and pharmaceutical, medical, chemical and botanical products at $1.9 billion.
Exports of medium-high technology products increased 7.1 percent year-on-year to $79 billion during the same period. Motor vehicle manufacturing led the category with $29.2 billion in exports. Chemical products followed at $15.7 billion, electrical equipment at $15.1 billion and machinery and equipment not elsewhere classified at $14.1 billion.
Other contributors included weapons and ammunition manufacturing with $3.4 billion in exports, medical and dental instruments at $818 million and other transport equipment, excluding shipbuilding and aerospace-related machinery, at $664 million.

Volkswagen may weigh Türkiye assembly plan for China-built models

2026-11-02

A view of the Volkswagen plant in Zwickau, Germany, Thursday, July 9, 2026. (dpa via AP, File)
Volkswagen is evaluating plans to assemble vehicles in Türkiye through a partnership with Turkish distributor Doğuş Otomotiv, reviving discussions of local production years after the German automaker abandoned an earlier manufacturing project in the country.
The two companies signed a letter of intent, with attention now focused on how production would be structured and which models could be included. The announcement coincides with a period in which Volkswagen is reshaping its global manufacturing network amid financial pressures, while uncertainty remains over whether Türkiye will be included in the European Union’s “Made in Europe” framework.
A Volkswagen spokesperson told German automotive publication Automobil Produktion that the company is considering supplying semi-knocked-down (SKD) vehicles from production facilities outside Europe for the Turkish market through cooperation with Doğuş Otomotiv. Meanwhile, German publication Automobilwoche reported that vehicle parts produced by Volkswagen’s Chinese partner FAW could be shipped to Türkiye and assembled locally using the completely knocked-down (CKD) method.
Industry assessments suggest that models developed and produced in China are the most likely candidates for Turkish assembly, particularly as Volkswagen expands exports from China to markets in Asia and the Middle East. In this context, the strongest contenders are the Magotan sedan, marketed as the Passat in China and the Sagitar, the Chinese version of the Jetta.
Volkswagen began exporting the FAW-produced Magotan and Sagitar models to the Middle East in September 2025. Both vehicles had previously enjoyed strong sales in Türkiye before being withdrawn from European markets.
The strategy aligns with Volkswagen’s broader China plans. In January 2026, the company said it would use China’s lower manufacturing costs to increase exports to Southeast Asia, the Middle East and South America, while excluding Europe from the initiative. The approach was reinforced in late October with the launch of its “In China, Beyond China” strategy, aimed at turning China into a global development and export hub.
Volkswagen could adopt a model similar to its semi-assembly operation in Uzbekistan for Türkiye. However, the long-term objective should be broader manufacturing involving local suppliers, advanced technologies and export-oriented production rather than a facility limited to assembling imported components.
If Türkiye is eventually included within the EU’s “Made in Europe” framework, a Turkish facility could become part of Volkswagen’s wider European production network. In that case, manufacturing could extend beyond the Magotan and Sagitar models to include additional Volkswagen Group vehicles produced in China for export markets.

As Europe’s right advances, Germany’s AfD rethinks its anti-euro roots
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
07:36:39 CET
15:36:39 KST

By Miranda Murray
BERLIN, Nov 2 (Reuters) - The far-right Alternative for Germany, founded more than a decade ago in opposition to the EU’s handling of the euro crisis, is recalibrating its vision for Europe as it and its right-wing allies abroad gain influence.
After a historic victory in a regional election in Saxony-Anhalt in September, Germany’s most popular party in nationwide surveys now appears closer than ever to entering government at national level before the end of the decade.
The prospect is prompting debate over how to balance an anti-establishment identity with the need to appear as a credible partner to potential allies at home and abroad.
Founded in 2013 amid anger over bailouts for heavily indebted fellow members of the euro zone, the AfD began life as a movement opposed to the common currency.
While it later expanded its criticism to the European Union itself, it gained traction above all with its opposition to immigration - a line that opponents, and the domestic intelligence agency, say strays perilously close to the supremacism and xenophobia that scarred Germany’s recent past.
FAR-RIGHT IDEOLOGY GAINS GROUND ACROSS EUROPE
The AfD rejects allegations of extremism, and many members now argue that increasing acceptance of more radical right-wing views and the growing sway of like-minded parties elsewhere in Europe make reforming the bloc from within more productive than abandoning it altogether.
“Never since the end of the Second World War have the prospects for reforming the EU in line with our vision been better,” said AfD national lawmaker Sebastian Muenzenmaier.
But the aim of quitting the euro - dear to many of the AfD’s founders and early supporters - has proved harder to address.
Younger members such as Jean-Pascal Hohm, 29-year-old head of the party’s youth wing, Generation Deutschland, argue that hardline positions on Europe could complicate the AfD’s most realistic route to federal power: eventual cooperation with Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s conservative Christian Democrats (CDU), who currently rule out any alliance.
Last month, AfD co-leader Alice Weidel presented a strategy paper at the European Parliament in Strasbourg on a “New Deal for Europe” alongside allies in the Europe of Sovereign Nations (ESN) grouping.
The paper shifts the emphasis away from quitting the euro zone and the EU, focusing instead on renegotiating treaties to establish a looser union.
It proposes an “opt-out” mechanism for members who reject common policies on defence spending or immigration, for example, as well as stricter enforcement of budget rules - leaving open the possibility of retaining the euro.
Should reform efforts fail, the paper suggests the issue of Germany’s future European direction would be decided by referendum.
AFD HOPES FOR ‘EUROPE OF FATHERLANDS’
Weidel told journalists that the AfD and ESN stood for “a European union, a Europe of fatherlands” but declined to say whether she still wanted Germany to leave the euro zone or the EU.
By setting aside its opposition, the AfD would be following a path already trodden by far-right parties that have had success elsewhere in the euro zone.
France’s National Rally long campaigned to abandon the euro but gradually dropped that demand under Marine Le Pen as it sought to broaden its appeal, and is now favourite to win next year’s presidential election.
In Italy, Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni’s Brothers of Italy has reined in its eurosceptic rhetoric since taking office, opting to pursue its objectives from within the EU.
Closer to home, Austria’s far-right Freedom Party (FPOe), which has close ties to the AfD, renounced most of its anti-European positions on its way towards a share of power in national ruling coalitions.
“Austria serves as a blueprint for the AfD,” said Wolfgang Schroeder, a political science professor at Kassel University.
“In that sense, it’s probably just a matter of time before they drop these positions,” Schroeder said, adding that he did not think this would trigger significant resistance.
EXPORT-BASED GERMAN ECONOMY BENEFITS FROM EU MEMBERSHIP
In any case, Germany’s economy is so intertwined with the global market and driven by exports that leaving the EU or the euro would be a disaster, he said.
“An autarky movement such as the one Hitler developed in 1933 is virtually impossible under these conditions, unless one is willing to risk the collapse of the entire national economy.”
Hohm’s younger AfD colleagues make a similar argument, saying Europe’s changing political realities, as well as growing competition from China and a less reliable United States, make the case for more, not less, cooperation in the bloc.
“If we were to basically cancel the common currency and everyone goes their own way again, that is completely utopian and that would also do us massive damage,” Hohm said.
“Young Europeans, regardless of nationality, more often see themselves as Europeans and are less willing to continue fighting the conflicts of their grandparents.”
But in the party as a whole, the issue is far from settled.
Hohm submitted a resolution at a congress in August that read: “Generation Deutschland is committed to the European idea … Europe is more than an economic area, more than a monetary union and more than the European Union.”
Yet although the resolution was phrased to emphasise the EU’s role in reinforcing shared history and heritage, rather than economic cooperation, it was withdrawn after failing to gain sufficient support.
“The euro issue turned out to be more controversial than we had expected,” he said.
(Reporting by Miranda Murray; Editing by Kevin Liffey)

It requires relevant authorities and their staff to keep confidential any state secrets, work-related confidential information, trade secrets, personal privacy and personal information obtained during supervision and investigations.
It also requires Chinese companies operating across borders to set up integrity and compliance departments or appoint dedicated staff, based on their size, business scope and risk prevention and control. ■

After a grueling three-day search-and-rescue operation, authorities recovered the body of German hiker Friederike Elisabeth Newrzella from a rocky ravine off Türkiye’s famed Lycian Way in the southern province of Antalya, escalating calls for strict security measures along the trail.

He further recommended closing the Lycian Way for one month annually to conduct routine maintenance, refresh faded markers and mitigate environmental hazards such as landslides and rockfalls.
Çevik also called for establishing a centralized management structure in which public institutions, local governments, security forces and non-governmental organizations will work in coordination.

Heather plants in Latmos sustain bees and biodiversity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
06:32:05 UTC
15:32:05 KST

İHA Photo
Heather plants growing naturally in the Latmos (Beşparmak) Mountains, which stretch across the Aegean provinces of Aydın and Muğla, play an important role in maintaining the ecosystem and supporting traditional livelihoods, according to local conservationists.
Bahattin Sürücü, head of the Association for the Protection of Ecosystems and Nature Lovers (EKODOSD), said areas covered with heather were not barren or unproductive land, but important habitats supporting a wide range of wildlife and human activities, including beekeeping and livestock farming.
Known locally as funda, püren and broom shrubs, the plants add pink and purple hues to the landscape among Latmos’ natural stone pine forests. Heather species that bloom particularly in autumn provide honeybees with an important source of nectar and pollen when fewer other plants are flowering.
Honey produced mainly from heather nectar is known for its dark color and distinctive, strong aroma, making the plants an important part of the region’s beekeeping activities.
EKODOSD scientific adviser Professor Ali Çelik said the genus Erica, belonging to the Ericaceae family, comprises more than 700 species worldwide, mainly found in South Africa, the Mediterranean and Western Europe. Five taxa grow naturally in Türkiye, one of which is endemic to the country.
Çelik said autumn-flowering species were particularly valuable because they helped honeybee colonies maintain their food supply when other sources became scarce, contributing to their health and survival through winter.
He warned that climate change and the destruction of natural habitats could disrupt ecological balances, reduce food sources for bees and negatively affect colony health as well as the quantity and quality of honey production.
Sürücü also highlighted the region’s long history of beekeeping, noting that honey production and trade were important to the economy of ancient Caria. Historical records indicate that honey was sent to Egypt from ancient settlements including Heracleia under Latmos, Pidasa and Theangela.
Bee shelters, locally known as “kovanlık,” can still be found on massive rocks throughout the mountains, reflecting the area’s beekeeping traditions dating back thousands of years.
He said heather-covered maquis areas also serve as grazing grounds for goats and provide habitats for wildlife, linking beekeeping, livestock farming, biodiversity and traditional local livelihoods.
Warning that olive groves, stone pine forests, natural vegetation and cultural heritage sites in Latmos are facing increasing pressure, Sürücü said the destruction of heather habitats would affect not only plant life but also bee food sources, grazing areas and traditional production practices.
He called for the region’s natural, archaeological, geological and cultural assets to be protected together under a comprehensive conservation framework.

Austria investigates suspected Ukrainian spies – media
Austria has launched an espionage investigation after two Ukrainian military intelligence operatives were detained in Vienna, the Austrian newspaper Kurier reported on Saturday.
The report comes after former Ukrainian Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko, who fled to Austria in September, alleged that a team had been sent to kill him on orders from Ukraine’s presidential office.
According to Kurier, the head of the Artan Group, a special operations unit within Ukraine’s military intelligence agency (HUR), was spotted at the Park Hyatt hotel in Vienna. The man, identified as Viktor T., reportedly told Austrian security officials that he was on vacation. The unit was originally established to carry out operations in Russia but has also been accused of involvement in plots to assassinate “Ukrainian defectors,” the newspaper said.
Kravchenko and Ukrainian media identified the Artan commander as Viktor Torkotyuk, known by his callsign Titan.
On October 5, Austrian police reportedly arrested two operatives under Torkotyuk’s command who were carrying surveillance equipment. Investigators initially believed that one of the men had rented a car in Vienna together with Yaroslav Bondarenko, a cameraman working with Ukrainska Pravda investigative journalist Mikhail Tkach. Subsequent findings, however, indicated that Bondarenko had been mistaken for someone else.
Tkach and Bondarenko were detained on October 8 and released the following day. Tkach said he had been trying to locate Kravchenko as part of a journalistic investigation and denied any wrongdoing.
The Vienna Public Prosecutor’s Office said the journalists had been detained because investigators suspected they were conducting surveillance at a location also monitored by the two men already in custody. Prosecutors later said the suspicion against the journalists could not be substantiated.
Kravchenko fled Ukraine after the country’s Western-backed anti-corruption agencies, NABU and SAPO, launched an investigation into allegations that his subordinates had protected fraudulent call centers. He accused anti-corruption investigators of abusing their powers and claimed the case was politically motivated. Both agencies rejected his allegations.
The former prosecutor general has also drawn parallels with a bombing in Monaco earlier this year that targeted Ukrainian businessman Vadim Yermolayev. The explosion injured Yermolayev, his teenage son and his partner.
Two men linked to Ukrainian intelligence, active-duty HUR officer Vladislav Reut and former Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) officer Vitaly Zhikovich, were subsequently arrested over the killing of Anastasia Berezovskaya, who was filmed planting the bomb in Monaco and later found shot dead in Ukraine.
In an October interview with the BBC, Zhikovich claimed that senior HUR officials had authorized the Monaco operation.
Moscow has long accused Kiev of carrying out terrorist attacks abroad. Following the Monaco bombing, Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova argued that Western governments “could no longer control the monster they had created.”

An Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo has killed more than 5,000 people, government data released on Oct. 30 showed, as health officials urged stronger surveillance to contain its spread.
More than 10,000 people have been infected since the outbreak was declared in May.
It is the country’s largest Ebola outbreak and the second-largest worldwide, after the 2014-2016 epidemic in West Africa.
Jean Kaseya, director-general of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention, has called for stronger monitoring at borders and health facilities.
“No country is safe unless we strengthen surveillance,” he told RFI in an Oct. 22 interview.
Cases linked to the outbreak have been reported in Uganda, Kenya and Nigeria.
A woman diagnosed in Nigeria was medically evacuated to Geneva on Oct. 26. A doctor diagnosed in France in June after returning from the DRC later recovered, with no secondary cases reported.
The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control assessed the likelihood of infection for people living in the European Union and European Economic Area as very low in its Oct. 29 update.
Cambridge University virologist Charlotte Houldcroft said Ebola’s incubation period could last up to 21 days, allowing infected travelers to arrive in another country before developing symptoms.
People do not transmit Ebola before symptoms appear, according to the World Health Organization.
It spreads mainly through direct contact with the blood or other bodily fluids of infected people who are ill or have died, or with contaminated materials.
The outbreak is caused by Bundibugyo virus, for which there is no approved vaccine.
Early supportive care can improve survival, while isolation, contact tracing and infection control remain essential to containing transmission.
Diagnostic limitations delayed recognition of the outbreak. WHO representative Anne Ancia said in May that initial tests in Bunia targeted the Zaire Ebola virus and returned negative results, leading doctors to suspect malaria and salmonella infections.
A vaccine trial began in Bunia on Oct. 23 to assess protection against Bundibugyo.
The first vaccine being tested is Ervebo, which is already licensed against the Zaire Ebola virus.

Shadowy Indian election ‘consultants’ add US midterms to global footprint
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
06:28:01 UTC
15:28:01 KST

Shadowy Indian election ‘consultants’ add US midterms to global footprint
India’s political consultancies grow by covertly managing the world’s biggest elections. Now, they are exporting the dirty tricks to manipulate global elections, like the US midterms.
New Delhi, India — In an unfurnished flat in a nondescript Ahmedabad neighbourhood in western India, a 22-year-old digital content creator worked through the nights, designing posters and editing videos for a presidential campaign thousands of kilometres away — William Ruto’s 2022 bid for the presidency in Kenya.
Rajan Kumar’s content was not shared by Ruto’s official campaign. Instead, the 50 social media posts he created for $7 a day were shared on shadow social media accounts that conceal their identity to make coordinated messaging appear independent while backing Ruto’s campaign.
For content, Kumar said he would trim opposing leaders’ speeches or interviews to twist their statements, or create posters with false claims amplifying Ruto’s prospects and popularity ahead of the election.
“If there’s a woman politician, we simply link her to someone to damage her reputation. It’s one of the easiest ways to discredit,” Kumar told Al Jazeera, adding that “all controversial content” is diverted to shadow pages for “extensive distribution”.
Ruto won the 2022 election and became Kenya’s fifth president.
Four years later, as the United States heads into its midterm elections on Tuesday, researchers have found that Indian social media bots and accounts have been shadow-posting videos backing specific campaigns. The New York Times first reported such posts supporting US Democratic politician Haley Stevens ahead of the August 4 Senate primary in Michigan, which she lost to Abdul El-Sayed, the party’s candidate for the midterm election.
But the US is only the latest theatre of electoral war where politicians are banking on Indian social media mercenaries-for-hire, who have fought shadow election campaigns in several countries in South America and Africa.
Nearly a dozen political consultants in India, who spoke with Al Jazeera for this report, say there are no limits, guardrails, or red lines in such shadow campaigns.
“We are manipulating elections; there is no other way to say it,” said Tushar Giri, a political consultant in New Delhi. “The concept of electoral democracy is so overrated. There is no free will for voters. Everything is manipulated.”
‘Hidden sources of power’
Political consultancies advise politicians and election campaigns on how to win public support and elections. Such specialised private companies selling political persuasion as a service emerged in the US in the 1930s.
With the boom in social media, dirty tricks have spread to online platforms to manipulate and attract voters, especially by running targeted advertising campaigns on Meta and Google platforms to reach millions of voters. Previous reports have found that Russia used similar tactics to influence voters in the US, for instance.
Strategies for dissemination of content deemed too controversial for official accounts during election campaigns vary, ranging from political consultancies taking over a party’s established shadow pages on Meta or Google to making new ones from scratch, rebranding existing pages to suit a campaign’s needs, or opting for pages for hire.
An Al Jazeera investigation in the run-up to India’s 2024 national election revealed a sprawling network of such shadowy pages on Meta and Google products like Facebook, Instagram and YouTube on sale — skirting the platforms’ policies against such misuse of targeted advertisements to influence voters.
Antibot4Navalny, an anonymous group of disinformation researchers that investigates and exposes coordinated online influence operations, particularly those linked to Russia, told Al Jazeera that it found at least 28 such accounts on X (formerly Twitter) sharing videos supporting Stevens’s campaign in the Democratic primary in Michigan, garnering more than seven million views.
At least 15 of the identified accounts were posting from India, a review by Al Jazeera has found.
Researchers at Clemson University’s Media Forensic Hub have also identified similar tactics being used by for-hire Indian accounts and pages to support Stevens’s campaign against El-Sayed.
Amogh Dhar Sharma, author of Backstage of Democracy — a book on Indian political consultancies’ workings, said politicians like to keep voters’ focus ahead of elections “on things that happen in the public eye”.
“But sometimes the real power is being wielded, completely hidden from the public eye,” Sharma told Al Jazeera, referring to political consultancies. “The way it creates certain, hidden sources of power in a democracy is one of the biggest ethical concerns.”
‘Be careful, hide footprints’
In India, such political consultancies now make up the backbone of any election campaign, and their work serves as marketing material to lure politicians in other countries.
“We have a proven track record of delivering desired results in a complicated electoral democracy like India, which now attracts foreign campaigns too,” said Giri, the New Delhi-based consultant.
Rules set by Meta, Facebook’s parent firm, disallow users from any “attempt to or successfully sell, buy, or exchange” accounts, or from operating under false or stolen identities. In general, both Meta and Google’s policies require political advertisers to verify their identities and disclose who paid for election advertisements, though specific rules vary from country to country.
But Indian consultants tell Al Jazeera that these community standards are routinely violated.
“These platforms have long pages of such rules, but when you read between the lines, there are several loopholes one can exploit,” said Giri. Premium virtual private networks (VPNs) are the go-to tools for such consultancies when they face restrictions in one geography. Sometimes, changing an account’s country of origin simply does the job, enabling a person sitting in a foreign country to run targeted political advertisements.
Giri recalled meeting representatives of a presidential campaign in Suriname last year, although negotiations ultimately fell through. Sharma, the author, told Al Jazeera that he found Indian consultancies working in Australia and Germany as well during his research. Consultants told Al Jazeera that they have similarly worked on campaigns in India’s neighbouring countries, including Nepal and Sri Lanka.
Kumar, who worked for Ruto’s campaign for the Kenyan presidency in 2022, said he was paid about $7 a day under a monthly contract and was asked to deliver up to 100 creatives on some days, coordinated via groups on Telegram.
He said he never worked directly with any of Ruto’s representatives, and that content creators like him are never informed of the identities of all the individuals involved in the supply chain that leads up to senior officials in a campaign.
“One always needs to be careful and hide footprints nonetheless,” he said. Chats are deleted, and SIM cards are destroyed frequently.
The risks are real.
Two Indian political consultants, Zulfiqar Ahmad Khan and Mohamed Zaid Sami Kidwai, who were working for Ruto’s campaign, went missing in Nairobi in July 2022 ahead of the election. They were found dead in October, allegedly abducted by an elite police unit in Kenya. After winning, Ruto disbanded that unit. Fifteen officers were accused of murder, but in August 2026, Kenya’s High Court terminated those charges after the prosecution requested that the murder investigation be discontinued.
The shadowy nature of the work that consultants like Kumar do extends to payments, several political consultants explained.
“Black money is a pillar of political consultation,” one consultant told Al Jazeera, requesting anonymity, fearing for their safety. “We have companies abroad that hire a person on paper for random work to make payments, but it is just a front to funnel money.”
Several consultancies rely on hawala networks — an informal, trust-based money-transfer system that allows people to send funds across borders through brokers, bypassing conventional banking channels.
At least three consultants identified export-focused businesses in Old Delhi’s sprawling Chandni Chowk market in the national capital territory as one such hub. A consultant who spoke with Al Jazeera for this report on condition of anonymity recalled a dramatic business deal two years ago.
The consultant carried an Indian banknote bearing a specific serial number, which served as a code to identify and collect the payment. “I saw people use 10-rupee notes to collect millions in cash,” they told Al Jazeera. “It was like I’m in a movie.” They refused to disclose the country or campaign that paid for this particular transaction.
‘What are the limits?’
Giri, the consultant, told Al Jazeera that in the last couple of years, India has turned into “a big wholesale market to run these shadow political campaigns”.
“It is like you buy toys from China; similarly, you can manipulate elections anywhere in the world at the cheapest cost in India,” he said.
Author Sharma had a similar analogy to explain the nature of India’s political consultancies.
“This is perhaps an extension of the global outsourcing industry that has been central to India’s economic growth,” Sharma argued. “Just as India became a hub for business-process outsourcing in the 2000s”, the country is now seeing the rise of political consultancies that campaigns can hire to outsource their less transparent operations.
Sharma added that the physical distance of those behind these shadowy social media promotions and the campaigns they work for gives everyone involved “plausible deniability” if operations are revealed.
Giri, the consultant, argued that what makes consultants successful is how far they are willing to go to help a campaign.
“What are the limits? If one agency can execute filthy tricks to manipulate a voter — and think beyond the political party’s own imagination — they are rewarded accordingly,” he said. “The dirtier you can get, the more money and opportunities there are.”

Hebron governor says Israeli forces withdraw from city after 10-day siege
Hebron Mayor Youssef al-Jaabari says families forced from their homes can return and students can go to school.
The governor of Hebron says Israeli forces have withdrawn from the city in the southern occupied West Bank after a 10-day siege, allowing displaced families to return home.
“Palestinian security forces have taken full control of the area following the Israeli withdrawal,” Governor Khaled Dudin announced on Monday.
“Relevant authorities and Palestinian security forces are monitoring developments on the ground and working to provide the necessary conditions for residents to return safely,” he said.
The Israeli military imposed a siege on Hebron on October 23 after a shooting attack near the city allegedly by two Palestinians that killed two Israeli soldiers and wounded three others. Israeli forces later killed the two suspects.
Hebron Mayor Youssef al-Jaabari told Al Jazeera the municipality was officially informed of the withdrawal at 6am (04:00 GMT).
“For the first time in 10 days, schoolchildren are going to their schools; university students are now on their way to their universities,” he said, adding that five universities had been closed during the siege.
“There was a complete closure, no entry or exit from the city, and all aspects of life, whether economic, educational, health, or even those related to municipal work, had completely stopped.”
Al Jazeera’s Mohamad Atrash, reporting from Hebron, said vehicles carrying displaced families began arriving minutes after the withdrawal, with residents congratulating one another on returning safely.
In one residential building used as a military post, Atrash found damaged furniture, ransacked rooms and food left behind by soldiers.
Residents of the building told Al Jazeera they had been forced out of their homes at 2am, with Israeli troops giving them five minutes to gather any medicine, phones or personal documents.
Families had been told the displacement would last one to three days, Atrash said. Instead, it stretched to 10, and some returning residents said money and personal belongings had been taken from their homes.
The Palestinian Civil Defence urged residents not to touch suspicious objects or enter damaged buildings before they had been inspected, the official Palestinian news agency Wafa reported.
Atrash said Israel’s military initially said the Hebron operation would target the homes of the two suspects in the killing of Israeli soldiers, but later widened the scope of the operation to the entire governorate, home to about 800,000 people, closing its checkpoints and seizing homes in al-Jalda and Ein Deir Bahha as military posts. Some 537 families were forced out at night and had to take shelter with relatives elsewhere in the city.
More than 3,300 Palestinians were displaced or otherwise affected, according to the Hebron governorate.
The Hebron municipality said on Sunday that Israeli forces had demolished 15 homes and structures and that 327 shops had closed, with direct economic losses exceeding 12 million shekels ($3.8m) a day, Wafa reported.
“Everything damaged we will rebuild,” Mayor al-Jaabari said, as municipal crews headed to al-Jalda, Ein Deir Bahha and Shubat al-Malh to assess damage.
About 80,000 students in the city were unable to attend school, according to Wafa. Atrash said some 262,000 students across the governorate missed nine days of classes.
Hebron, the occupied West Bank’s main economic centre, contains 220 of the Palestinian territory’s 940 Israeli military checkpoints and gates, Atrash said, adding that the closures disrupted 4,000 factories.
Mohamed Helles, an expert on Israeli affairs, said the operation was launched days before Israel’s general elections last month and was partly “an attempt to harvest electoral points at the ballot box” for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his right-wing allies.
Netanyahu’s electoral bloc secured the most seats but failed to win a majority in the vote, leaving Israel without a clear path to a new government.

Could government spending cuts help fight inflation? Here are the facts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
06:22:27 UTC
15:22:27 KST

Could government spending cuts help fight inflation? Here are the facts
The Reserve Bank is tipped to increase interest rates tomorrow because of an ongoing concern that inflation is not under control. It would be the fifth hike of the year, and the 18th in five years.
The consequences are familiar: rates are a "blunt instrument", painful for all borrowers.
But is there an alternative? In the past week, much commentary has focused on whether government spending cuts could be a "precise instrument", taking pressure off inflation in a targeted way and alleviating the pain of high rates.
The government has flagged at least some fresh savings. So where could cuts come from, and could they influence inflation?
How inflation happens
In simple terms, inflation happens when an economy is operating above capacity. When the demand to spend is more than what an economy can supply, the extra demand pushes prices up.
The cause can come from anywhere. The Reserve Bank thinks the resurgence of inflation in the past year has been driven by the Middle East war, an AI investment boom, and the fact Australia was already above capacity before those things.
Whatever its origins, economists worry about inflation becoming entrenched in an economy. RBA governor Michele Bullock explains it this way:
"High inflation hurts all Australians, especially the most vulnerable. Every household has seen how the price of everything has gone up in recent years. Pay packets don't go as far as they used to …
"It's critical that we stop [this] from becoming embedded in price-setting decisions across the economy or the problem will only become worse."
How interest rates work
Policies to fight inflation can seek either to expand supply or suppress demand. While supply policies are important, demand suppression works quicker and is the main frontline response.
The aim is not to address the causes of inflation or to lower specific prices. For example, policymakers can do little about high fuel prices. Instead, they aim to take pressure off elsewhere as a counterweight.
The Reserve Bank has one main lever: higher interest rates. High rates suppress demand in multiple ways. Existing borrowers — people and businesses — pay more on their loans, leaving less money to spend elsewhere. New borrowing is discouraged.
Saving is encouraged, because the returns are higher. And Australian dollars become more expensive, pushing down overseas demand for our exports.
How government spending can help or hinder
The government's main lever is its budget. Every year, the government raises and spends hundreds of billions of dollars. Taxing more or spending less can directly reduce demand.
This can be a precise instrument because the government can choose exactly what programs it cuts, or exactly where it raises taxes.
In theory, it means the government can fight inflation with regard for "fairness" in a way that the Reserve Bank cannot, because it can decide who should bear the brunt of the pain. But inflicting pain with higher taxes or spending cuts is politically fraught.
And in fact, governments are often pulled in the other direction. When prices are high, voters expect relief in the form of tax cuts or subsidies. Governments often oblige, even though this can push up inflation by expanding demand rather than suppressing it.
The cost of 'cost-of-living relief'
The Albanese government has made a virtue of offering this sort of cost-of-living relief, and despite its criticisms, the Coalition has advocated for relief too. Treasurer Jim Chalmers argues this is justified, because the government has multiple roles:
"We have to balance the inflationary pressures in our economy with the fiscal pressures in our budget and try to do the best that we can for people … We think we've struck [the balance] relatively effectively."
How much has the Albanese government spent?
There are several ways to assess how the government has struck that balance. One is to look at the overall level of spending. On that measure, spending under the Albanese government is abnormally high, remaining at levels comparable to the pandemic.
But many of the drivers of this spending are long-term factors that are hard to control. Of the fastest-growing spending categories, only child care has been substantially expanded by the Albanese government. Another, the NDIS, has been curbed.
Another way to approach the question is to look at how the budget has changed under Labor. Taking the combined effect of all the government's budget updates, the budget balance has improved in most years, meaning lower deficits and even two surpluses.
But that graph includes factors that the government cannot take responsibility for. In fact, even inflation itself has helped: inflation means people pay more income tax, improving the budget.
Stripping out these external factors shows a different picture, with the budget balance worse off in each year thanks to government decisions.
This is often described as the "truest" picture of the government's responsibility. But even this is imperfect, because the government argues that many of these "decisions" are unavoidable and would be made by all governments, like the indexation of some payments and the listing of new PBS medicines.
Going line by line
Each of these measures tells us something about the contribution of the government to inflation, but not everything. Doing that requires evaluating each government decision line by line.
Here are just a handful of the largest decisions highlighted in budget papers. This non-exhaustive list shows one of the reasons government ministers have defended their spending decisions. The items are central to the government's political narrative, including its changes to bulk-billing, cheaper child care and tax cuts.
In theory, the government could have taken pressure off inflation if it had decided against any of these new spending policies. But as well as any political consequences, the result would also be less money for the recipients of these policies.
Some of the government's political opponents have pointed to individual policies that could be cut. For example, the Coalition has named the Cheaper Home Batteries Program and the EV discount, among others. Independent MP Allegra Spender has named fuel tax credits, an existing subsidy that costs more than $10 billion a year.
Cutting some of these spending programs could mean fewer rate hikes. Economist Chris Richardson estimates that $7 billion to $10 billion of spending cuts per year is equivalent to one rate hike (note: the figures in the table are over four years, not per year).
But the challenge for the government, and for other political parties, is deciding whether the pain of those spending cuts is preferable to the pain on borrowers from a rate hike. Either way, the intent is the same: to suppress demand.

US pushes to restore Russian gas sales to Europe via Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
06:15:09 UTC
15:15:09 KST

The U.S. is backing a quick resumption of Russian natural gas sales to Europe via pipelines running through Ukraine as part of negotiations aimed at securing an energy ceasefire ahead of the coming winter, the Wall Street Journal reported, citing U.S., European and Ukrainian officials.
The idea, broached by U.S. envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff during trips to Moscow and Kiev in September, would involve selling Russian gas via a U.S. intermediary to circumvent European sanctions—and could create a lucrative opportunity for American investors, people who attended the discussions said.
The plan was put on the back burner last month after Ukraine unilaterally stopped striking Russian refineries under pressure from President Trump, the WSJ reported.
Kiev, however, resumed its air campaign on Oct. 30, launching three attacks on three major Russian refineries in the past three days, which has brought new urgency to the pursuit of a more comprehensive energy ceasefire ahead of three-way peace negotiations that are planned between the U.S., Russia and Ukraine for mid-November in Abu Dhabi, according to the Journal.
In the view of U.S. negotiators, a Russian comeback to the European natural-gas market would create a powerful incentive for President Vladimir Putin to agree to an energy ceasefire, said the WSJ.
Using the Soviet-era pipeline network that runs to Europe via Ukraine from the Urengoi gas fields in Siberia would also provide Kiev with badly needed revenue from transit fees, it said.

Hebron Governor Khaled Dudin announced Monday the withdrawal of Israeli forces from the entire city of Hebron in the southern occupied West Bank.

The Israeli army launched the operation in Hebron on Oct. 23 following a shooting attack by two Palestinians that killed two Israeli soldiers and wounded three others. Israeli forces later killed the two attackers.

The operation also involved forced displacement, demolitions of homes, other structures and commercial properties, and damage to infrastructure.
More than 3,300 Palestinians were displaced or otherwise affected, particularly in Al-Jalda and Ein Deir Baha, while 15 homes and other structures were demolished, according to the Hebron Governorate.
The governorate said the operation also caused damage to the local economy and infrastructure and disrupted education.

South Korea to double spending on AI and chips in 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
06:12:40 UTC
15:12:40 KST

South Korean President Lee Jae Myung delivers a budget speech for 2027 at the National Assembly in Seoul, South Korea, Monday, Nov. 2, 2026. (AP Photo)
South Korea will double spending on AI and semiconductors in 2027 to a record high, the president said on Nov. 2, pledging to use the technology to turn the military into a "smart, elite force."
President Lee Jae Myung in his annual budget speech to parliament said 21.3 trillion won ($16 billion) would be allocated to chipmaking and artificial intelligence, spanning data centers to robotics.
"We will make bold investments in AI and future growth engines to boost our economy's growth potential," he said, adding that the figure was "nearly double this year's amount."
On the defence budget, the government wants to see an increase of around eight percent from this year to 73.3 trillion won, aiming to secure nuclear-powered submarines and KF-21 fighter jets.
Lee said Seoul aims to "rapidly transform our military into a smart, elite force by establishing integrated manned and unmanned systems based on AI, robots and drones."
North Korea has recently tested a slew of weapons, including a new precision-guided torpedo system and an intermediate-range hypersonic missile, both of which it said used AI technology.
And last year, Seoul announced an agreement with Washington to build nuclear-powered submarines, with Pyongyang slamming the submarine programme as a "dangerous attempt at confrontation."
Overall, the 2027 budget plan totals 821 trillion won, a 12.8 percent increase on-year, making it the largest budget proposal on record.
Lee now needs parliament to pass the budget proposal, which is likely given his party's majority.
The country is a tech powerhouse, home to Samsung Electronics and SK hynix, two of the world's three biggest makers of memory chips -- components in huge demand thanks to the AI boom.
Lee said the government will invest 4.7 trillion won to support "frontier AI development projects, with the aim of achieving world-leading performance for our own AI model, a national strategic asset."
In June, Lee announced a public-private partnership centred on "three mega-projects" -- aiming to expand chip production hubs nationwide, establish robotics research and development centres, and build gigawatt-scale AI data centres.
The government at the time unveiled plans for nearly $1.2 trillion in investment, equivalent to more than two-thirds of South Korea's GDP.
Samsung and SK hynix also in June announced plans to invest more than 4,755 trillion won ($3.5 trillion) in South Korea, marking a record level of corporate investment in the country.
South Korean chipmakers have seen profits and share prices skyrocket as frenzied demand for AI infrastructure squeezes the global supply of memory chips.
The boom has also spurred chip engineers and other workers to seek higher payouts in tense negotiations at companies including Samsung and SK hynix.
In September, Seoul announced plans for a 162.3 trillion won "Future Fund" next year, aimed at channelling record tax revenues from the country's chip boom into long-term growth.
Lee said on Nov. 2 that the government would also invest 2.1 trillion won in electricity, water supply and industrial complex infrastructure, as semiconductor plants require a stable power supply around the clock, 365 days a year.
