Midterms 2026: Georgians on the front lines of the people’s war against data centres
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
06:11:55 UTC
15:11:55 KST

Midterms 2026: Georgians on the front lines of the people’s war against data centres
Artificial intelligence emerged as a major issue on the 2026 US midterm campaign trail, with opposition to data centres drawing supporters across partisan divides united over ecological worries, increased utility bills and business interests outweighing citizen concerns. Georgia, the top US market for data centre construction, has been on the front line of the struggle.
Quilliam Barber surveyed his backyard on a beautiful fall morning – the towering trees shading the southern sun, early autumn leaves dotting the green lawn, a tuneful bird working the quiet of this rural Georgia district to its advantage – and let out a heavy, forlorn sigh.
“I feel terrible. It's right there,” said the 67-year-old retired truck driver, gesturing towards the sprawling open land behind his backyard. “It’s right up under my arm, you know. And I can do nothing about it.”
The Barbers’ property abuts a massive, 800-acre tract earmarked for a hyperscale data centre in Georgia’s Coweta County in the Middle Chattahoochee River Basin, part of the wider Apalachicola Basin in southeastern USA.
His new neighbour, the Project Sail data centre, made headlines in early 2025, when the eye-popping scale of the plan came to light. The $17 billion venture, estimated to require roughly 900 megawatts of electricity and 9 million gallons of water, includes 13 buildings, each covering 378,000 square feet, taking the total land area to more than 4.9 million square feet, according to county filings.
Standing next to her husband, Wilhemina Barber knows that with such a mega project coming up next door, things are about to change – dramatically. “It’s very quiet and peaceful out here. We love it, I love it, he loves it. We’ve got a pretty clear feeling it's going to play an important role if they do put it right in our back door," she said.
Around two miles down the road, Ron Bockrath, picked up a poster from a pile on his kitchen buffet table. “Protect Coweta: No Data Center Here” read the yard sign in bold red.
Bockrath’s opposition to the data centre has kept him busy over the past few months. From organising collectives and filing lawsuits, to collecting petition signatures, his efforts are part of a multi-pronged community campaign to stop the Sail project.
Across the US, in cities and counties rich or poor, rural, urban or semi-urban, citizens are raging against the machine. Artificial Intelligence (AI), and the mega centres required to power it, emerged as one of the major campaign issues ahead of the November 3 midterm elections, popping up in debates and town hall gatherings, leaving many candidates scrambling to articulate a cogent position and their constituents dissatisfied. The public sentiment has been at odds with US President Donald Trump’s promotion of AI as “Superior Intelligence” (SI).
Community-led initiatives have targeted AI-driven surveillance systems, including cameras misused by law enforcement officials.
Read more'Get the Flock out': Americans respond to AI-driven surveillance cameras
The backlash has at times been spearheaded by software engineers and geeks capable of hacking systems to identify guardrail weaknesses, and the gap between spin and reality. But with data centres, the mega infrastructure required to power AI, the pushback has been sweeping, drawing together Democrat and Republican supporters in a rare display of bipartisanship in a bitterly divided country.
That’s because they represent a confluence of concerns: from rising electricity bills, to environmental hazards affecting local communities and impacting global warming, to a public dissatisfaction over millionaires, billionaires, tech mandarins and financiers profiting from the new technology amid a cost-of-living crisis.
Georgia, a state that defined itself as a symbol of the “New South” after the American civil war, has kept up with the times. A technological boom, centred around Atlanta – “The capital of the New South” – has seen the area overtake Northern Virginia as the country’s top market for data centre construction.
It has left Georgians on the front lines of pitched, local battles in the people’s war against data centres.
A revamp from ‘rural conservation' to industrial district
At the entrance to the Bockrath property in Newnan, Western Coweta County, another yard sign proclaims the mission that has occupied the 83-year-old retired research scientist for months.
“NO Industrial Zoning. NO Data Center,” reads the sign, referring to a rezoning of this rural area into an industrial zone.
In April, county commissioners in this traditionally Republican stronghold approved a zone code revamp from “rural conservation district” to industrial area by a narrow 3-2 vote.
Bockrath attended the meeting in a room packed with county residents, activists and journalists – and was dismayed by the proceedings.
“People were supposed to be allowed to speak – for or against. That's good if you've got a population that's somewhat equally divided, then it makes sense to give equal time to both sides. However, in this case, the local population, not just the Western Coweta County, but the entire county, wanted nothing to do with these data centers and the way they were being forced upon us. But they gave equal time to each side to speak,” he explained.
Project Sail is just one of at least five planned data centres in the county. Residents and collectives opposed to the various projects come together for countywide decision meetings. They also keep an eye on community initiatives across Coweta County, located around 50 miles southeast of Atlanta and home to around 146,158 people.
“Twenty minutes was allowed for opposition, which isn't really very long, considering the magnitude of this project. That may be legally okay, but morally, it’s not okay. I got there almost two hours before the meeting. The 20 minutes were up before I was allowed to speak. They’re supposed to give great credence to people living in the area, but they were not allowed to express their opinion,” he said.
The 2-3 vote was hailed by the commissioners who approved the rezoning. “This is a no-brainer for the county,” Commissioner Alphonso Smith told the Atlanta Journal-Constitution. “I will stake my political career on it.”
A representative of the project’s developer, Prologis, a Fortune 500 company, said the rezoning would be transformative for the area and would generate tax revenues, the local newspaper reported. “The question isn’t if this site will be developed. It’s just how,” JC Witt, Prologis senior vice president of data centre investments told the commission meeting.
‘Miles of backup traffic’ for a signature drive
The rezoning vote sparked multiple initiatives aimed at reversing the decision.
Bockrath, along with some of his neighbours, including the Barbers, promptly filed two lawsuits in a Coweta County court, challenging the rezoning. The cases, filed in May, are currently making their way through the legal system.
Meanwhile a grassroots collective, Citizens for Rural Coweta, launched a campaign for a “home rule petition”, which under Georgia's Constitution allows residents to petition the county's court to amend or repeal resolutions. In counties with more than 50,000 residents, signatures from at least 10% of registered voters are required.
The signature drive saw Bockrath hit the road, knocking on doors to inform neighbours about the initiative. Local businesses across the county opened their doors for petition signings. Every week, venues and schedules were posted on the group’s social media accounts, followed by weekly updates.
The response was overwhelming, said Bockrath. “There were miles, literally miles of backup traffic to come in and sign these things,” he recounted with a smile.
To display this content from Instagram, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
Finally, on Friday, October 16, Citizens for Rural Coweta volunteers submitted boxes with more than 14,800 signatures to a county court. The 10% mark had been reached. Under Georgia's Constitution, the probate judge has 60 days after a petition is filed to determine whether it’s valid. If it is, the judge must call an election to be held between 60 and 90 days after the filing.
‘We need to speak the truth’
Community-led campaigns against data centres are taking up time and considerable mobilisation effort from citizens across the US.
Bockrath admits it can be discouraging at times but he believes he has no choice. “Somebody has to do it,” he maintained. “We can't just give up. I don't think we want to see our country, or the world for that matter, get that messed up.”
Volunteers have been drawn to the movement for a variety of reasons and causes, from the hyperlocal to global. For Bockrath, the motivation is primarily scientific.
The retired researcher is concerned about the massive amounts of water required to cool systems in mega data centres. In Georgia’s Fayette County, for instance, many households face low water pressure complications, while some Newton County residents have been unable to drink the murky, brown water trickling out of their taps.
Energy consumption and the impact on global warming is an issue that particularly worries Bockrath. “If you keep using more of our electricity, generating more heat, climate change is going to accelerate,” he said urgently before launching into a mini-lecture on global temperature percentages and melting polar ice caps.
Underlying all these issues, Bockrath notes, is the spinning of truth. “In studying science, one of the things you learn is that you don't need to necessarily agree with your advisor, or chairman. What you're trying to do is find the truth,” he explained. “I'm not sure if that's the case always in things like marketing, in sales. There, I think, the idea is to sell your product or your idea, truth may not be as important. But I think it is. And I think we need to speak the truth.”
Finding ‘another place to go’
Georgia’s data centre boom has been driven in large part by tax breaks and low electricity rates granted to many projects under outgoing Republican Governor Brian Kemp, who has held the state’s top post since 2019.
But while companies get cheap rates, the cost of electricity for households has been rising exponentially. New data centres are driving up utility bills in at least 13 states, according to the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis. A Bloomberg analysis last year found residents living near data centres were paying as much as 267% more a month for energy than five years ago.
The increase in utility bills is also adding to the cost-of-living crisis fueled by rising gas prices due to the Iran war. Coweta residents such as Bockrath are not persuaded by the arguments made by developers, and accepted by some commissioners, that data centres bring in tax revenues.
“At the state level, we've got Governor Kemp, who's been very, very pro-business. I think he's been so pro-business that he's forgetting about the citizens,” he said. “You can bring in tax revenue from a data center, but if the citizens are being made to bear that cost in terms of their electrical bills, how is that helping them? It's not. It's hurting them.”
It’s also hurting across ideological lines, making the resistance to AI, and data centres in particular, a rare bipartisan issue as the US prepares to vote in the midterms.
While Coweta County, like most rural areas outside Atlanta, has long been a Republican stronghold, Bockrath notes that volunteers never discuss their partisan inclinations. The octogenarian grandfather describes himself as an independent, voting "both ways" in the past, depending on candidate platforms and performance. Although he declines to divulge how he plans to vote on November 3, Bockrath expresses disappointment with Republicans who have failed to challenge some of Trump's policies. "The Republicans didn't say, hey, that's not right, which they should have," is all he's willing to say.
The anti-data centre movement, he explains, straddles partisan divides. Taking the example of the recent signature drive, Bockrath guesses that there had to be a mix of supporters of both parties. “To pick up almost 15,000 registered voters to sign a petition here, many of them had to have been Republican. Also, a number of them, I'm sure, are Democrat. It's not that much of a political issue. It shouldn't be. This is a humanity issue,” he said.
For Barber, it’s also a matter of being forced to lose his past and links to the land.
“I might have to relocate if I can. I feel terrible. I love this area. I grew up in this area. I raised my family here. I had kids, my grandkids, they all played, we played, in the woods out there,” he said. “But if they made me an offer, then yes, I would relocate.”
His wife listens silently, her eyes fixed on the grass. “I'd be sad. I'd be very sad because it's just like starting all over again,” she revealed. “But if push comes to shove, we've discussed it, if they offer us a price and if it's something that we can live with, we'll take it and we'll find another place to go.”

Professor Snyder and ‘Trump’s Big Lie’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
06:11:00 UTC
15:11:00 KST

In his recent article reprinted in Kyiv Post “Trump’s Big Lie About Ukraine,” Professor Timothy Snyder has done a superb job exposing US President Donald Trump’s false narrative about Ukraine’s contributions to the US, Europe, and world peace.
According to Trump, the US has “done a lot” for Ukraine, but Ukraine has “done nothing” for the US. In other statements, Trump intimated that Ukraine has been a free-loader in receiving “billions” from the US but has given “nothing back”.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
So, here are some estimates of how much the US has saved and how much Russian military power Ukraine has destroyed in exchange for the “billions” it has received.
Let’s first agree on how many billions the US has actually provided “directly” to Ukraine. According to a recent New York Post article, direct aid to Ukraine during former US President Joe Biden’s administration totaled $130 billion. Although Congress approved $164 billion in Ukraine-related funding, that included associated US activities, indirect costs, and payments to third parties, not direct aid to Ukraine. A reasonable starting point for calculating US investment in Ukraine’s defense is $150 billion.
Trump’s comments indicate that he may have forgotten why Biden gave Ukraine $150 billion. He should review Russian President Vladimir Putin’s oft-repeated insistence on restoring Russian geopolitical influence and control over territory once governed from Moscow.
Trump May Consider Major Iran Strike if Republicans Lose Midterms
The 2022 US National Security Strategy (NSS) identifies Russia as an existential threat, and states that Russia’s invasion of Ukraine demonstrates its willingness to use military force to redraw borders and undermine European security. Had Putin defeated Ukraine, he would have greatly increased Russia’s military power and been emboldened to move against NATO and embroil US forces in NATO’s confrontation with Russian troops. It was only a matter of time.
However, Ukraine defied all expectations and, for almost five years, has held Putin’s forces in check and frustrated Putin’s ambition. NATO’s European members acknowledge they were entirely unprepared to face the threat. They have only begun developing their own military-industrial base and increasing their forces. But they will need at least five more years to become independent of the US.
As long as Europe and the US continue providing Ukraine what it needs to defend itself, Ukraine will hold Russia back. Putin will not open a “second” (NATO) front while facing a powerful, undefeated Ukraine to its south. But, if Ukraine is defeated, and Russia absorbs Ukraine’s human and material resources into its military, then only US deterrence stands between Russia and Europe.
The cost of a Russian victory
The conservative American Enterprise Institute, in assuming that the US would honor its NATO commitment to deter Russia, estimated that the long-term cost to the US would likely be far higher than the cost of supporting Ukraine. Without Ukraine, Russian forces would be poised on the borders of a half dozen NATO countries, capable of immense mischief, and undeterred by either a solely European NATO or a Ukrainian “second front.”
The Institute estimates that “a world in which Russia prevails would be more dangerous and more expensive for America, requiring an estimated increase of $808 billion in US defense spending over five years.” A separate RAND perspective did not offer cost estimates, but concurred that a Russian victory would impose additional “colossal” costs on the US and its allies.
What would it then cost the US to participate with other NATO countries in stopping a much strengthened and emboldened Russia? No publicly available information can be found, but Ukraine’s experience can serve as a model, and artificial intelligence (AI) may have to do the heavy lifting.
AI was tasked with the following: “What would it cost the US if American Forces had to fight a conventional NATO-Russia war and absorb casualties and equipment losses on the scale of Ukraine?” We included assumptions such as three levels of US participation in the conflict, the types and costs of equipment, the current versus original value of equipment, potential casualty numbers, duration of hostilities, and, most importantly, comparison with America’s wars of this century.
The one factor that made the greatest difference but was most elusive was the probable casualty count and type because the US has the highest veteran life-care cost in the world, but no experience with new-generation warfare.
AI’s “reasonable and central” estimate of the costs the US would bear if Ukraine had been defeated and it participated 50% in the fighting to stop Putin’s move into Europe is $2-3 trillion. This may seem high to some and low to others, but it’s not unreasonable compared with the estimated cost of the Afghanistan war ($2.3 trillion), the Iraq war ($1-2 trillion), and even “peaceful” 5-year deterrence ($0.8 trillion). According to Brown University’s analysis of the 20 years of US Middle East wars, the total cost of those wars would be about $8 trillion.
The damage done to Russia’s military
One final factor we must not overlook is the military loss that Ukraine has inflicted on Russia. Notwithstanding Putin’s bravado in threatening one country or another with extinction, or declaring (as he has done recently) that he is “ready for war in Europe”, the simple reality is that Ukraine has inflicted such damage on Russia’s military capability that it is much weaker than it was before the war.
The Center for Strategic and International Security (CSIS) estimates that as of July, Putin’s military force has sustained 1,400,000 casualties, of which 450,000 have been killed. In addition, the CSIS estimates that Russia has lost one third to one half of its pre-invasion major combat equipment and has been forced to draw heavily from Cold War stockpiles to sustain the war.
It would take a long time to rebuild Russia’s conventional forces to a level that Putin, known to be a cautious man, would consider ready to launch a “war on Europe.” This should also be credited to Ukraine as a deterrent… and one that is still growing.
For those whose minds are open and eyes can see beyond their personal interests, it should be obvious that for every $1.00 that the US has provided Ukraine, Ukraine has “given back”, with its blood and suffering, and in addition to the invaluable boons and blessings listed by Professor Snyder, an estimated $20.00 saving of the costs the US is likely to incur if it were to honor its obligations to deter Russian attacks or in supporting our NATO allies in defeating those attacks.
As a side note, it bears remembering that Ukraine had “done a lot” for the US in destroying Russia’s ICBM force targeting hundreds of US cities, but the US had “done nothing” in return except default on its commitments. Had the US honored the terms of the Budapest Memorandum guaranteeing Ukraine’s sovereignty, Putin would not have invaded.
Ukraine would not need the “billions” that President Trump is bemoaning. And the five years of bloodshed and destruction need not have occurred. So, Mr. President, which came first... the chicken or the egg?
The views expressed in this opinion article are the author’s and not necessarily those of Kyiv Post.

South Korea launches emergency measures to keep $17.5B Czech nuclear project on track

15:10:38 KST

Faisal Mahmud
02 November 2026•Update: 02 November 2026
South Korea on Monday announced an emergency management system to prevent delays to its $17.5 billion nuclear power plant project in the Czech Republic after contract negotiations with a domestic construction consortium collapsed, Yonhap News Agency reported.
The Ministry of Trade, Industry and Resources said the government would devise measures to keep the Dukovany project on schedule and prevent similar contractual setbacks.
The move follows a decision by Korea Hydro & Nuclear Power Co. (KHNP) last week to terminate negotiations with a consortium comprising Daewoo Engineering & Construction and Doosan Enerbility after the parties failed to agree on key contract terms.
The ministry was scheduled to hold its first emergency meeting Monday to discuss follow-up measures.
KHNP, South Korea's state-run nuclear power operator, will launch a new tender to select a construction contractor, aiming to sign an agreement by July 2027.
Construction is scheduled to begin in November 2027.
"The minister and vice minister will personally review key project issues every week and take necessary measures for the time being," Industry Minister Kim Jung-kwan said.
The 25 trillion won ($17.5 billion) project involves building two 1,000-megawatt APR1000 nuclear reactors at Dukovany.
A KHNP-led South Korean consortium secured the project last year and subsequently entered negotiations with the Daewoo-Doosan consortium designated to undertake construction.

Binance resumes withdrawals after billions stolen in hack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
06:10:00 UTC
15:10:00 KST

Binance said it had seen withdrawals of around $4.7 billion (€4.21bn) on Sunday, after more than $6 billion (€5.38bn) in virtual assets were stolen from the cryptocurrency exchange in a major hack for which the FBI said North Korea was responsible.
Binance is the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange by daily trading volume. News of the hacking attack, which is thought to be the biggest-ever crypto heist, caused the prices of most major cryptocurrencies to fall sharply on Friday.
The company has offered reassurances that it will cover the losses from the attack, saying it has used company funds to buy tokens to replenish 90% of what was stolen.
Binance suspended user withdrawals after the attack but said they would resume in phases, the first of which began on Sunday.
Between 0600 GMT (0700 CET) and 1530 GMT (1630 CET), the platform said it had processed $4.65 billion (€4.17bn) in withdrawals and $1.01 billion (€905m) in deposits.
The net outflow of $3.64 billion (€3.26bn) amounted to about 2.1% of the total assets managed by the company.
The US Federal Bureau of Investigation accused North Korea of being behind the hack in a statement on Saturday, confirming earlier suspicions from private investigators and analysts that a Pyongyang-affiliated group called TraderTraitor was responsible.
TraderTraitor is the same group blamed for a $1.5 billion (€1.34bn) theft from the Bybit platform in February last year.
"The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) is releasing information advising the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (North Korea) was responsible for the theft of more than $6 billion (€5.38bn) in virtual assets from cryptocurrency exchange Binance, on or about October 29, 2026," the statement said.
The FBI added that it had observed "TraderTraitor actors" converting stolen assets into Ethereum and expected those assets to be laundered further through decentralised finance platforms and instant swap services.
It said it was urging private sector entities "to block transactions with or derived from addresses TraderTraitor actors are using to launder these stolen assets."
US President Donald Trump cast doubt on North Korea's involvement in the hack.
"I'm not concerned. We're learning about it. We don't know if it's North Korea," Trump told reporters at his residence in Florida late on Saturday.
The president often reflects with pride on the summits he held with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un during his first term.
'Commitment' to cover losses
Binance said on Saturday that it had set aside more than $6.34 billion (€5.68bn) in company funds to cover losses resulting from the hack.
"Our commitment remains the same: Binance will fully cover the financial impact of the funds stolen in this incident," the company said on X.
It said it had used company funds to buy tokens to replenish 90% of the stolen assets, while the remaining 10% of tokens were "less liquid, which means they may take longer to source in the required amounts."
The attack on Binance came as many observers expressed concerns that the ever-expanding capabilities of artificial intelligence models could compromise cryptography and IT security protocols.
Bitcoin plunged nearly 5% following news of the hack, while Ethereum dropped nearly 6% and BNB, Binance's native cryptocurrency, tumbled nearly 10%.
The sheer scale of the hack has put a spotlight on North Korea's capacity to find illicit means of acquiring funds, despite facing extensive international sanctions over its nuclear and missile programmes.
TraderTraitor is believed to be part of the Lazarus Group, which gained notoriety in 2014 when it was accused of hacking into Sony Pictures in retaliation for "The Interview", a film that mocked North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.

As Europe’s right advances, Germany’s AfD rethinks its anti-euro roots
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
06:07:05 UTC
15:07:05 KST

As Europe’s right advances, Germany’s AfD rethinks its anti-euro roots
- Germany’s AfD is softening its old anti-euro stance as it grows stronger at home and with right-wing allies across Europe.
- Alice Weidel’s new plan calls for a looser EU, treaty changes, and possible opt-outs, while leaving open euro membership and a referendum if talks fail.
- Party members are split, but many now say leaving the EU or euro would hurt Germany’s export-led economy and weaken chances of working with the CDU.
AI generated
BERLIN – The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), founded more than a decade ago in opposition to the European Union’s handling of the euro crisis, is recalibrating its vision for Europe as it and its right-wing allies abroad gain influence.
After a historic victory in a regional election in Saxony-Anhalt in September, Germany’s most popular party in nationwide surveys now appears closer than ever to entering government at the national level before the end of the decade.
The prospect is prompting debate over how to balance an anti-establishment identity with the need to appear as a credible partner to potential allies at home and abroad.
Founded in 2013 amid anger over bailouts for heavily indebted fellow members of the euro zone, the AfD began life as a movement opposed to the common currency.
While it later expanded its criticism to the EU itself, it gained traction above all with its opposition to immigration – a line that opponents and the domestic intelligence agency say strays perilously close to the supremacism and xenophobia that scarred Germany’s recent past.
The AfD rejects allegations of extremism, and many members now argue that increasing acceptance of more radical right-wing views and the growing sway of like-minded parties elsewhere in Europe make reforming the bloc from within more productive than abandoning it altogether.
“Never since the end of the Second World War have the prospects for reforming the EU in line with our vision been better,” said AfD national lawmaker Sebastian Muenzenmaier.
But the aim of quitting the euro – dear to many of the AfD’s founders and early supporters – has proved harder to address.
Younger members such as Jean-Pascal Hohm, the 29-year-old head of the party’s youth wing, Generation Deutschland, argue that hardline positions on Europe could complicate the AfD’s most realistic route to federal power: eventual cooperation with Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s conservative Christian Democratic Union of Germany, which currently rules out any alliance.
In October, AfD co-leader Alice Weidel presented a strategy paper on a New Deal For Europe at the European Parliament in Strasbourg alongside allies in the Europe of Sovereign Nations (ESN) grouping.
The paper shifts the emphasis away from quitting the euro zone and the EU, focusing instead on renegotiating treaties to establish a looser union.
It proposes an “opt-out” mechanism for members who reject common policies on defence spending or immigration, for example, as well as stricter enforcement of budget rules – leaving open the possibility of retaining the euro.
Should reform efforts fail, the paper suggests the issue of Germany’s future European direction would be decided by referendum.
AfD hopes for ‘Europe of fatherlands’
Weidel told journalists that the AfD and ESN stood for “a European union, a Europe of fatherlands”, but declined to say whether she still wanted Germany to leave the euro zone or the EU.
By setting aside its opposition, the AfD would be following a path already trodden by far-right parties that have had success elsewhere in the euro zone.
France’s National Rally long campaigned to abandon the euro but gradually dropped that demand under Marine Le Pen as it sought to broaden its appeal, and is now the favourite to win the 2027 presidential election.
In Italy, Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni’s Brothers of Italy has reined in its eurosceptic rhetoric since taking office, opting to pursue its objectives from within the EU.
Austria’s far-right Freedom Party, which has close ties to the AfD, renounced most of its anti-European positions on its way towards a share of power in national ruling coalitions.
“Austria serves as a blueprint for the AfD,” said Wolfgang Schroeder, a political science professor at Kassel University.
“In that sense, it’s probably just a matter of time before they drop these positions,” he said, adding that he did not think this would trigger significant resistance.
Export-based German economy benefits from EU membership
In any case, Germany’s economy is so intertwined with the global market and driven by exports that leaving the EU or the euro would be a disaster, Schroeder said.
“An autarky movement such as the one Hitler developed in 1933 is virtually impossible under these conditions, unless one is willing to risk the collapse of the entire national economy.”
Hohm’s younger AfD colleagues make a similar argument, saying Europe’s changing political realities, as well as growing competition from China and a less reliable US, make the case for more, not less, cooperation in the bloc.
“If we were to basically cancel the common currency and everyone goes their own way again, that is completely utopian, and that would also do us massive damage,” Hohm said.
“Young Europeans, regardless of nationality, more often see themselves as Europeans and are less willing to continue fighting the conflicts of their grandparents.”
But in the party as a whole, the issue is far from settled.
Hohm submitted a resolution at a congress in August that read: “Generation Deutschland is committed to the European idea... Europe is more than an economic area, more than a monetary union and more than the European Union.”
Although the resolution was phrased to emphasise the EU’s role in reinforcing shared history and heritage, rather than economic cooperation, it was withdrawn after failing to gain sufficient support. “The euro issue turned out to be more controversial than we had expected,” he said. REUTERS

Still Life in Israel with Jessica Steinberg: Keith and Aviva Siegel on how they kept calm in Gaza
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
06:05:47 UTC
15:05:47 KST

How Europeans can become ‘better grid citizens’ – without cutting their electricity use
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
06:02:56 UTC
15:02:56 KST

Green technology is allowing more Europeans to take control of their energy bills and help the continent’s outdated grid.
European gas prices have hit highs last seen during the peak of the 2022 energy crisis, as the war on Iran continues to expose the volatility of fossil fuels.
It means energy prices are likely to remain high well into next year, as Europe scrambles to top-up its dwindling gas reserves ahead of the cold winter months.
Back in June, the European Commission urged households to use less energy at peak times to reduce bills and take pressure off the continent’s already-strained grid. It comes as the artificial intelligence (AI) boom sees power-hungry data centres pop up across the continent.
It may feel like there is little the average European can do to shield themselves against the current turbulence. However, one expert says every single household has the potential to play an active role in balancing Europe’s energy supply and demand.
How Europeans can be ‘better grid citizens’
“Consumers are becoming increasingly important participants in the energy ecosystem,” Niklas Persson, CEO of grid integration at Hitachi Energy tells Euronews Earth.
“A ‘better grid citizen’ is not simply someone who uses less electricity. It is someone who uses electricity more intelligently.”
Smart EV charging, flexible heating systems, and rooftop and plug-in solar can all help reduce strain on the grid during peak periods, lowering energy bills at the same time. However, accessing these technologies often requires thousands of euros upfront – pricing out millions of Europeans.
But many households can still participate in demand-response programmes through the use of technologies like smart meters – allowing them to access cheaper electricity at certain times of the day.
Uptake of these devices vary across Europe, with high rates in countries like Denmark and Sweden. In Germany, where the devices have been enmeshed in a huge culture war, only 5.9 per cent of electricity connections have a smart meter, an increase of just 1.5 per cent in the past six months.
Households with solar power and battery storage can also sell renewable energy back to the grid when it is most needed, typically in the evenings when people come back from work or school, further lowering their bills.
In the future, Persson hopes that millions of Europeans will play an active role in balancing supply and demand, helping to integrate more renewable energy while potentially lowering their own energy costs.
This could not only help tighten the purse strings for cash-strapped Europeans but also prevent clean energy from being wasted.
According to energy think tank Ember, smart charging EVs alone would have the potential to absorb around three per cent of peak hourly wind and (utility) solar generation in Spain.
“This would be significant to the system considering that in May 2026, an estimated 10 per cent of monthly power generated by Spanish wind and solar farms was curtailed,” Ember states.
Europe’s outdated grid stalls progress
“However, individuals can only play that role if the right infrastructure is in place,” Persson points out.
“Governments, utilities and technology providers must work together to create simple incentives and user-friendly solutions that make flexibility easy and rewarding.”
Europe’s outdated energy grid – which was originally built around coal, and later gas – is crying out for greater investment. According to an Ember report from April this year, bottlenecks triggered by the grid are putting more than 120 GW of anticipated renewables at risk.
For context, a power plant with a capacity of 1 GW could power approximately 876,000 households for one year, if they consume the average of 10,000 kWh of electricity per year.
Persson argues that the transition towards a more sustainable, affordable and secure energy system therefore can’t be achieved by utilities alone. It will be a “partnership” between grid operators, technology providers, businesses and consumers.
“The good news is that the technology already exists and the relevant solutions are being deployed to address these challenges,” he says.
“We need to upgrade existing transmission corridors, accelerate permitting for new grid projects, more widely deploy advanced power electronics and digital technologies, and strengthen connections between countries to allow power to flow where it is needed most.”
Inside Europe’s race to electrification
As economies become more electrified, the importance of the grid grows stronger.
Türkiye, who will co-host the upcoming UN climate summit COP31 in November, has made electrification one of its main priorities – aiming to raise the global share of energy demand from electricity to 35 per cent, up from around 20 per cent, by 2035.
Experts argue that the pledge could allow governments to count expanded gas-fired generation as progress towards electrification targets – a move they say will “seriously undermine climate goals”.
Persson says that electrification is one of the most effective tools to decarbonise the global economy, but “not all electrification delivers the same climate benefit”.
“To maximise emissions reductions, increased electricity demand must be matched with increased deployment of clean generation and the grid infrastructure needed to connect it,” he adds.
“If governments want electrification to deliver its full environmental and economic value, they must accelerate investment in grid infrastructure with the same urgency as investment in power generation.”
Persson argues that the grid– should be treated as critical national infrastructure, deserving the same level of attention as highways, railways and airports.
“Without sufficient investment in transmission and distribution networks, it becomes much harder to integrate clean energy, attract industrial investment, or strengthen energy security,” he explains.
“The energy transition will ultimately be won or lost on infrastructure. Renewable generation is essential, but grids are what enable that energy to reach consumers; If electrification is the backbone of decarbonisation, then the grid is the backbone of electrification.”

The design throughput capacity of the railway is up to 50 million metric tons of coal per year.
In 2025, 35.1 million metric tons of coal were mined at the Elga deposit, and by the end of 2026, the mining volume will exceed 40 million metric tons.

Crimes committed by young people rise 10% during school holidays
The number of offenses committed by schoolchildren increases by a tenth during school holidays, data from the police show. Police took action to stop young people disturbing the peace in Pirita last week.
Late on Friday evening, police went to speak to young people who frequently gather in Pirita in the Merivälja areas.
Those who ERR encountered appeared to be between 10 and 15 years old. Some were even younger. According to locals, loud bangs can be heard in the area in the evenings.
Those ERR managed to speak to said they did not set off fireworks themselves. It is difficult for the police to establish exactly who is using firecrackers and disturbing public order.
"We have not made this a focus either, because young people are seeking attention this way, so that the police will respond and they can create more content for their TikTok world," said Mari-Liis Mölder, a senior superintendent at the Police and Border Guard Board (PPA).
Proceedings are initiated against those who are caught. Pirita district councillor Kaido Saarniit said the problem is not that young people gather in groups, but that they disturb other people.
"These bangs can be heard not only in the Merivälja neighborhood, but even further away. It depends on what is being used to make the bang," he said.
The district will continue to have security patrols in the Pirita and Merivälja areas until the end of the year.
The police said Estonia is not experiencing the kind of threat seen in France, Italy and elsewhere, where gatherings of young people have led to serious consequences.

Harry Potter set-jetting by train: Five magical rail journeys in the UK
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
06:00:35 UTC
15:00:35 KST

From Platform 9¾ at King’s Cross station in London to the Scottish viaduct crossed by the Hogwarts Express, these real-life locations bring the wizarding world to life. With the first film marking its 25th anniversary this November, here’s where to go for a spellbinding UK getaway by train.
It’s almost impossible to believe, but 25 years ago in November, the first Harry Potter film, “Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone”, was released.
Alongside all the magic and mayhem, there was another icon on the screen: The Hogwarts Express train, portrayed in the film by the GWR 4900 Class No. 5972 Olton Hall steam locomotive.
Harry Potter and his wizarding chums walked through a wall at King’s Cross station in London and boarded a train into another world and made history.
While the magic we saw onscreen was very much fictional, the journey the Hogwarts students made – and many of the locations they spent time in – were not.
Now, Rail Europe has picked five places across the UK which travellers can visit to experience what is arguably the best part of the Harry Potter universe – the backdrops.
Here’s where to go to get your fix of magic this spooky season.
Platform 9¾, London, England
No Harry Potter-inspired trip would be complete without a stop at Platform 9¾ at London King’s Cross station, where fans can pose with the famous luggage trolley disappearing into the wall.
It’s a fitting place to kick off a magical rail adventure, with trains heading north from King’s Cross towards destinations including Durham and Yorkshire, also featured in this list.
Warner Bros. Studio Tour London, Hertfordshire, England
For even more wizarding magic, head to Warner Bros. Studio Tour just outside London for "Hogwarts in the Snow", running from 14 November 2026 to 17 January 2027. The original sets are transformed for Christmas, with snow-covered scenes and festive decorations bringing the films to life.
To get there, take a train from London Euston to Watford Junction, then hop on the Studio Tour shuttle. Just remember that entry to the attraction needs to be booked separately.
Glenfinnan, Scotland
Few images from the Harry Potter films are more iconic than the Hogwarts Express making its way over a sweeping stone viaduct, surrounded by Highland mountains.
If you want to see it for yourself, you’re in luck – the Glenfinnan Viaduct, which appears in the films, exists in real life.
You don’t even need to hop aboard a heritage train to experience it, as regular ScotRail trains between Fort William and Mallaig follow the same scenic route and offer the stunning view.
Oxford, England
Oxford’s winding lanes, ancient colleges and grand halls wouldn’t look out of place at Hogwarts, and many of them stood in for the school in the film series.
The Bodleian Library’s Divinity School doubled as the hospital wing, while Duke Humfrey’s Library and the staircase at Christ Church also featured in the movies.
Between filming locations, there are bookshops, cafés and centuries of history to explore. With fast trains from London taking around 45 minutes, Oxford is an easy day trip for Harry Potter fans.
Durham, England
Durham’s striking cathedral is one of the most recognisable real-life locations for Harry Potter fans, with its Norman architecture and stone cloisters helping bring Hogwarts to life in the early films.
The cloisters feature in scenes from Harry Potter and the Philosopher’s Stone, including where Harry releases Hedwig, while the cathedral’s Chapter House was used as Professor McGonagall’s classroom.
Beyond the film connections, there’s a dramatic hilltop setting, riverside walks and narrow streets to explore.
With direct trains from London King’s Cross taking around three hours, you can swap the capital for cathedral views, winding lanes and a little Hogwarts nostalgia in a single trip.
Goathland, North Yorkshire, England
Goathland station in North Yorkshire will be familiar to Harry Potter fans as Hogsmeade station in the first film.
The old-fashioned platforms are part of the North Yorkshire Moors Railway, a heritage line that winds through rolling moorland.
Whitby and Grosmont are useful gateways for exploring the area, although the final leg to Goathland needs planning separately.
Heritage trains run seasonally, so check the timetable before setting off.

Disco cauliflower and bhajis: Maray’s cauliflower recipes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
06:00:35 UTC
15:00:35 KST

Cauliflower is a culinary gem. Often overlooked, it possesses a remarkable ability to absorb complex seasonings and textures while maintaining a satisfying bite. It’s also perfect for braising, frying or roasting, and provides a canvas for bold, herbaceous and spicy flavour profiles that elevate an ostensibly simple brassica into a true centrepiece.
Disco cauliflower with chermoula, tahini and harissa
The quantities for the green sauce will make more than you need to dress the cauliflower, but it keeps very well in a jar or sealed container in the fridge for up to a week and is delicious on all sorts, so it’s well worth making extra.
Prep 10 min
  
Cook 50 min
  
Serves 2
3 tbsp sea salt
  
2 tsp ground turmeric
  
1 large cauliflower (about 1.2kg), leaves trimmed, then cut in half from top to root (900g net)
  
3 tbsp vegetable oil
 
For the tahini sauce
  
3 tbsp tahini paste
  
1 tbsp lemon juice
 
For the green sauce
  
100g fresh coriander
 , including stalks
  
100g fresh parsley, including stalks, plus a little extra to finish
 
2 garlic cloves, peeled and roughly chopped
  
2 medium red chillies
 , stalks removed and roughly chopped
  
50g lemon juice
  
10g 
 fine table salt
  
180ml rapeseed oil
  
For the honey dressing
  
2 tbsp harissa paste
  
1 tsp honey
  
1 tsp white-wine vinegar
  
To finish
  
100g natural yoghurt
 
  
Pomegranate seeds
  and flaked almonds
 
1 tsp paprika
 
Bring a large pan of water to a boil, then stir in two tablespoons of the salt and a teaspoon of the turmeric. Drop in the cauliflower halves, simmer for about 10 minutes, until just tender, then drain and leave in the colander for 10 minutes to steam-dry and to drain off all the excess water.
Heat the oven to 220C (200C fan)/425F/gas 7. In a small bowl, mix the vegetable oil with the remaining salt and turmeric, then rub this all over the cauliflower. Put the blanched cauliflower halves cut side down on an oven tray and roast for 20-25 minutes, turning once halfway, until charred at the edges.
While the cauliflower is roasting, prepare the three sauce toppings. In a small bowl, mix the tahini and lemon juice with a tablespoon of water and set aside.
For the green sauce, put the coriander and parsley in a food processor, blitz for a few seconds, then add the garlic, chilli, lemon and salt, and blitz again briefly, so the mix still has some texture. Slowly work in the rapeseed oil, until nicely emulsified.
Finally, in another small bowl, loosen the harissa with the honey and wine vinegar.
When the cauliflower is ready, transfer it to a large platter. Spoon the yoghurt evenly over the top, followed by drizzles of the tahini, green and harissa sauces. Scatter generously with pomegranate seeds, flaked almonds and chopped parsley, finish with a dusting of paprika and serve hot.
Maray bhajis
Prep 20 min
 
Cook 15 min
  
Serves 4-6
Salt
  
1 tsp ground turmeric
  
1 small cauliflower (about 500g), leaves trimmed
  
500g white onion
 , peeled and finely sliced
 
Rapeseed oil
 
125g frozen garden peas
  
65g desiccated coconut
  
20g black onion seeds
 
20g white sesame seeds
  
1 tsp chilli flakes
  
2 tsp garam masala
  
60g cornflour
  
65g gram flour
 
  
1 tsp lemon juice
  
50
 ml sparkling water
Bring a large pan of water to a boil, then stir in two tablespoons of salt and the turmeric. Drop in the whole cauliflower and simmer for about eight minutes, until the cauliflower is cooked but retains a little bite. Drain, leave to cool, then grate the cooked cauliflower on the large holes of a box grater to shred it.
Meanwhile, in a pan on a medium heat, saute the sliced onions in two tablespoons of rapeseed oil for six or seven minutes, until just soft. In a large bowl, mix the grated cauliflower, sauteed onions, peas, coconut, seeds, spices, flours, lemon juice and a teaspoon and a half of salt, then slowly whisk in the sparkling water until you have a loose batter that is thick enough to retain its shape when frying. The mixture should feel light, not dense.
Pour enough rapeseed oil into a heavy-bottomed pan to come 2½cm up the sides and put on a. medium-high heat. When it’s up to frying temperature, check the seasoning of the bhaji mix by frying a small blob of the batter until golden brown and crisp, then taste and adjust the bhaji mix as required. Working in batches, scoop large dessertspoonfuls of the bhaji mixture into the hot oil and fry for two minutes on each side, until golden brown and crisp. Drain on kitchen paper and keep warm in a low oven while you repeat with the remaining batter. Season with more salt to taste, and serve hot with some of the chutney below.
Kara chutney
A vibrant, tangy and fresh condiment that’s a great accompaniment to the bhajis.
Prep 10 min
  
Cook 25 min
  
Serves Makes 1 big jar
125g banana shallots, peeled and thinly sliced
 
1 tsp cumin seeds
  
25ml rapeseed oil
  
25g red lentils
  
3 garlic cloves
 , peeled and finely chopped
  
10g grated fresh ginger
  
30g desiccated coconut, toasted in a dry frying pan until golden
  
10g salt (about 1⅔ tsp)
  
25g sugar
  
35ml white-wine vinegar
  
10g tomato puree
  
100g plum tomatoes, cut into chunky dice
To finish
 
50ml rapeseed oil
  
1 tsp mustard seeds
  
10 fresh curry leaves, or 2 tbsp dried curry leaves, but fresh are by far best
 
1 pinch chilli flakes, or to taste
Over a medium heat, fry the shallots and cumin seeds in the rapeseed oil for 10-15 minutes, until golden, then stir in the lentils, garlic and ginger, and fry, stirring, for another minute. Add 25g of the toasted coconut (save the rest to garnish) and the remaining chutney ingredients, then pour in 75ml water and bring to a simmer. Leave to cook gently, stirring occasionally, for 15-20 minutes, until the lentils are completely soft and the mix has reduced and thickened. Tip the chutney into a blender and blitz to a smooth puree.
To finish the chutney, heat the rapeseed oil in a small saucepan, then add the mustard seeds and curry leaves, and cook for about 20 seconds, until they start to pop. Take off the heat, tip the seeds, leaves and oil into the pureed chutney, then fold in thoroughly.
Spread the chutney on a platter, top with the cooked bhajis above, scatter over the reserved toasted coconut and some chilli flakes, and serve.

Starwatch: Catch the striking trifecta of Venus, the moon and Spica at break of dawn
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
06:00:34 UTC
15:00:34 KST

Early risers have a beautiful sight to look forward to this week as brilliant Venus joins the waning crescent moon and the star Spica in the morning sky.
The chart shows the view looking east-south-east from London at 0600 GMT on 7 November. Venus will be the easiest object to identify, shining brilliantly. Next to it will be Spica, the brightest star in the constellation of Virgo, the virgin, situated about 250 light years from Earth.
The tiny sliver of the waning moon completes the tableau. On this morning, the moon will be just two days away from new, with only 4% of its Earth-facing disc illuminated. It may also be possible to see the faint outline of its unlit portion, illuminated by sunlight reflected from Earth. This phenomenon is known as earthshine.
The three objects will form a striking grouping low above the horizon, so you will need a clear view towards the east-south-east to appreciate the spectacle. At 0600 GMT, the sky will still be relatively dark, although the approaching sunrise will gradually wash out the fainter stars.
The grouping will also be visible from the southern hemisphere, where Venus, the moon and Spica will appear higher in the eastern sky before sunrise.

Millions in UK brace to remortgage on worse deals as rate rise looms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
06:00:34 UTC
15:00:34 KST

More than 2.3m UK households face a sharp rise in mortgage payments as they come off fixed-rate deals in 2027, with the Bank of England expected to begin raising interest rates this week.
The Bank’s nine-member monetary policy committee (MPC) is widely expected to increase the base rate from 3.75% to 4% on 5 November after UK inflation rose further to 3.5% in September.
It could be the first of four quarter-point rises over the next 12 months, according to financial market expectations, which would exacerbate the financial pressure on households grappling with higher energy and food bills.
Thousands of borrowers are due to come off fixed contracts in the final months of this year, with 700,000 having been forecast to switch over to new rates between July and December.
A further 2.3m households will reach the end of their fixed rates next year, according to data collected by UK Finance, a banking industry body.
There has been no change in the Bank of England base rate since December last year, but volatility in the bond markets – triggered in part by energy prices and inflation fears linked to the war in the Middle East – has driven up the swap rates that affect the pricing of fixed-rate mortgages.
An increase in the Bank of England rate could drive those rates, and wider household costs, even higher.
Data released last week showed that mortgage approvals in the UK fell to a near three-year low in September as potential buyers were deterred by the jump in borrowing costs.
Alongside last week’s budget, the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) warned that household disposable incomes would fall by 0.6% next year after taking account of inflation. The downgrade compares with the 0.6% increase in disposable incomes the watchdog had forecast in March – an outlook the OBR’s David Miles described as “a pretty grim picture”.
That income squeeze is also being driven by the energy price shock, which the OBR said would push consumer inflation to 3.5% this year, significantly higher than the 2% forecast in March.
Ofgem’s energy price cap, which determines household bills, is expected to rise by more than £400 in January, according to the latest forecast from EDF.
John Healey, the chancellor, made a £100 payout to 20m households the centrepiece of his budget, saying he wanted to “take the pressure off in the coldest months and see people through to the spring”.
His cost of living package – which also included cancelling fuel duty rises planned by Rachel Reeves and extending a VAT cut on electricity bills – was paid for by tax rises on banks, savers and landlords.
The Bank of England has taken a wait-and-see approach to rising inflation since the start of the Iran war, in contrast to other central banks, including the US Federal Reserve, Bank of Japan and European Central Bank, which have already raised borrowing costs this year.
Andrew Bailey, the governor of the Bank of England, has made clear that the MPC is watching closely to see if rising prices are being passed through into higher wages for workers – evidence of the so-called “second-round effects” that can lead to inflation becoming embedded.
Before the war in the Middle East, the Bank had been expected to cut interest rates several times this year, with inflation expected to drift back down towards its 2% target.
But an extended period of historically high oil prices, affected by the closure of the strait of Hormuz choking off supplies, has instead fed through into high and rising inflation.
The Bank will publish updated forecasts for economic growth and inflation alongside its interest rate decision this week.
The UK economy beat expectations to be the joint fastest-growing in the G7 in the first half of 2026, which the Office for National Statistics said was partly driven by AI-related sectors.
But official forecasts for next year have been cut sharply amid fears that the higher cost of energy will eventually start to weigh on economic growth.
Although money market pricing suggests the Bank will raise interest rates four times by next July, many City economists suggest two rate rises are more likely.

Israel has ‘historic’ opportunity to change direction, says leader of Arab coalition

2026-11-02

The leader of Israel’s main Palestinian coalition, which holds the balance of power after Tuesday’s elections, has said the country is facing a historic opportunity to change direction.
Yousef Jabareen, the head of the Joint List, said he was ready to join forces with the “Change” bloc to oust Benjamin Netanyahu and his far-right coalition, and to wrest control of the Knesset.
Turnout among Arab Israelis (Palestinians with Israeli citizenship, 20% of the population) more than doubled to about 80%, transforming the political landscape. Palestinians in the occupied West Bank and Gaza had no vote.
Jabareen said the first demand of the roughly 840,000 Palestinian Israeli voters was to get rid of the Netanyahu government, and in particular its most extreme members, Itamar Ben-Gvir, the national security minister, and Bezalel Smotrich, the finance minister.
“This has been an awful four years … in all areas of life: in terms of house demolition, criminal gangs within the Arab community without any [intervention] from the police; not allocating the needed resources for our municipalities, for our education, for our youth in general; racism in all areas of life – physical attacks against Arabs, the brutality of the police,” Jabareen told the Guardian in one of his first interviews since the election. “So this has been really a very dangerous period.”
He said the next few days would be critical. Israel’s president, Isaac Herzog, is due to summon political leaders as early as Wednesday to canvass their recommendations on who should be given the first chance to form the next government, with no single grouping commanding a clear claim on power.
Netanyahu’s coalition lost its majority, dropping from 68 to 53 seats in the 120-seat Knesset. The Change bloc of Zionist parties led by the retired general Gadi Eisenkot has 48 seats, leaving the Arab-Israeli parties as potential kingmakers with a record 19 seats. The Joint List has 11, while the more conservative, Islamist Ra’am has eight.
Eisenkot and his partners have pledged not to form a unity government with Netanyahu, but Eisenkot has also put conditions on any potential coalition with Arab parties: they have to recognise that Israel is a Jewish state, accept conscription, and denounce Hamas as a terrorist organisation.
Ra’am and its leader, Mansour Abbas, have signalled it is ready to join an Eisenkot coalition. The Joint List has no intention of joining such a government, but Jabareen said the coalition was ready to keep it afloat from the outside with tactical voting in the Knesset.
“The conditions that [Eisenkot] speaks of are more relevant for parties who would be in the coalition. We are not planning to be in the coalition … for very clear reasons,” Jabareen said at his family home in the northern city of Umm al-Fahm. “As long as the occupation of our people in the West Bank continues, we cannot be part of a government.
“However, in order to use our political power to get rid of the extreme Netanyahu government, we said that we will consider the possibility of supporting from outside. This is an opportunity to change policies, to change attitudes, including towards the Arab community and towards the Palestinian people.
“This is really a historic moment and I hope that there will be partners within the opposition to go ahead with that. We are thinking that this could be the start of a change.”
Jabareen, 54, a former law professor and the leader of the socialist Hadash party, has yet to talk to Eisenkot since Tuesday’s elections, but he confirmed that informal discussions among opposition parties were under way.
Forming a new government was unlikely to be straightforward. The party leaders in the Change bloc have to agree on a candidate for prime minister. They would also have to accept partnership with Arab parties, either in coalition or from outside. The rightwing opposition leader, Avigdor Lieberman, is said to be the most resistant. Joint List officials said it was unclear whether partnership with Palestinians really crossed Lieberman’s red lines, or whether he was just holding out for a top cabinet position.
Even before a new government could be formed, Jabareen argued, the 67 opponents of Netanyahu in the new Knesset could use their clear majority to wrest control of legislative power. “That would start by changing the speaker of the Knesset,” he said, adding that the opposition could also take control of the committee that oversees the legislative agenda.
“That could be very crucially important … even before we reach conclusions on the issue of a coalition and a new government,” he said, adding that one of the priorities of the new Knesset should be to repeal laws passed by the outgoing majority that infringed the independence of Israel’s judiciary.
To allow an opposition coalition to oust Netanyahu and function as a minority government, Jabareen made clear it would also have to address deep-seated inequality in Israeli society.
“We have suffered from systemic discrimination for years, so if Eisenkot speaks of change, I believe that the change should come also for our community. We need to be treated equally,” he said. “We also ask for a political horizon. We would like to see the war stopped and the resumption of negotiation with the Palestinian leadership. We would like to see a start of a change.”
The Joint List leader said he was concerned over what Netanyahu might do to keep his grip on power. The prime minister has already made allegations, without evidence, that the Arab parties had used Qatari funds illegally in the election campaign, which Jabareen dismissed as a bid to “delegitimise the political power of the Arab community” and “a dangerous incitement”.
One of Jabareen’s concerns was that the Israeli leader would join Donald Trump in the resumption of war on Iran as a pretext for putting off political transition.
“This is really a critical period,” he said. “There should be a clear voice from the opposition to go against any attempt by him to initiate war … or dictate a new military agenda in Israel.”

====================================================================================================

These midterms could effectively end the Trump era – but neither side is yet ready for what comes next | Nesrine Malik
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
06:00:32 UTC
15:00:32 KST

The stats and polling all suggest one thing: the Republicans are set for a hammering in the midterms. Donald Trump has the lowest approval rating of any US president going into a midterm election since Harry Truman. And it’s still dropping. The Democrats are projected to win by a margin of 11 percentage points, the largest swing by any party in almost 20 years. It is possible that the Democrats flip the Senate and secure a large majority in Congress. Those majorities would make a material difference, perhaps finally establishing oversight of the policies Trump has brought in during his second term: immigration enforcement, trade disputes, gutting the federal workforce, the Iran war, to say nothing of his own family’s corruption. The tide seems to be turning, and one question is on everyone’s mind: is the Trump era really ending?
“Nobody wants to jinx it,” wrote David Wallace-Wells of the New York Times, but: “All the signs we have suggest that, historic or not, these midterms are likely to mark the end of a political era.” What that gives way to is a much more complicated picture in which the US will be delivered from Trump himself, but remains a country riven and undermined by what he has unleashed. By the time he is gone, Trump will have been president for eight years, and a toxic force for more than 12. That is a long time even for a normal politician. Under one who shatters norms and forces himself into the centre of everything, Trump’s effect is as if he were president for decades.
He has already enacted policy that is nearly irreversible, things that can only be overturned with a huge amount of work and legislative wrangling and improbable bipartisan consensus. USAID is gone. Probably also gone are government departments effectively eliminated or incapacitated by Doge, the “department of government efficiency”. There are entire global tariff regimes and the executive and budgetary empowerments of ICE to deal with. And most difficult to unspool is a war with Iran that, despite its promised, imminent end, is looking to be an open-ended conflict. Even if the midterms augur a win for the Democrats in 2028, the country they will inherit will have been permanently shaped by Trump.
And that is still a big if. Trump is a singular figure who cohered an otherwise inchoate and disparate coalition, from white evangelical Christians to working-class Latinos to Silicon Valley billionaires. Maga is a movement that is bound up with Trump, and feels increasingly weakened by his incumbency. Like Brexit and other insurgent movements, the galvanising anti-establishment power is lost when you are the establishment and have been for quite a long time. Looking for new people to blame, new grievances to exploit, becomes less an exercise in rebellion, more in whining and negativity. But whoever comes after Trump as a candidate, even if it is the black hole of charisma that is JD Vance, may still find some success using the same general pitch. That combination of combativeness and fractiousness might still read as authentic and subversive to the base. It may even seem comparatively sharp and legible against the opaque generic blah-ness of the Democratic establishment.
And that Democratic establishment itself is reason to worry. It is a ways to go yet, but the Democrats themselves seem unable to go either back or forward decisively. The party’s old guard is spent, either gerontocratic or gerontocracy-adjacent. In the latter camp is Kamala Harris, whose last campaign summons not the hope of a fresh candidate in 2026, but an apparatchik who offers only continuity without gravitas. In the former, there is a cohort who now only project entitlement and the out-of-touch, glassy-eyed bloat of so many years of capital acquisition - Nancy Pelosi, Chuck Schumer, Hillary Clinton.
Only Barack Obama still enjoys some sprightly relevance, and has used it to back Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, a candidate who is making that break with the past in a journey that Obama has cast as a passing of the baton. “He’ll finish the job we started,” Obama has said.
But even as El-Sayed is on the verge of making history as the first Muslim senator in a state that is pivotal to the presidential race, he is either drawing lukewarm, reluctant endorsements from other senior Democrats or he is openly attacked, primarily on his position towards Israel, which he believes has committed genocide in Gaza and should be defunded. Only a few days out from the election, Democratic congresswoman Haley Stevens, who El-Sayed narrowly beat last August to clinch the candidacy, has been taking big swipes at El-Sayed and his comments on Israel, and demanding he disavow election ads not even run by him, but by a leftwing group that backed him. The result is an unseemly scuffle that resulted first in El-Sayed saying he did not want Stevens appearing with him at a party unity event held on Sunday, and culminated later that day with an extraordinarily disgraceful development: Stevens endorsed El Sayed’s Republican opponent, Mike Rogers.
Divesting from Israel has become a flashpoint that appears to be less about political and ideological positions than the emergence of a new orientation in the party that breaks from an old guard overtaken by rapid changes of attitude. This was encapsulated by a quote from David Kramer, a Democrat who chaired Stevens’s primary campaign: “There’s a lot of talk about it being a big tent party, but sometimes we worry the tent is maybe devolving into a circus and we’re going to be pushed out.” Kramer is also voting for Rogers for the Senate. And there you have it. Some Democrats would rather lose than win on the left’s terms and be pushed out.
All of this suggests a future in which Trump is no longer on the scene, but there is still enough residual momentum among Trump’s acolytes, and disarray within the Democratic party, to render a midterm surge a temporary setback for Trumpism, not the restoration of the old order or the beginnings of a new one.
We have been here before. In fact, it’s worse than that, we have been here before in vastly better circumstances for the Democrats. Trump’s loss in 2020 happened in a context where there was a strong and familiar Democratic candidate in Joe Biden, a pandemic that research found hit Trump’s support, and no big live crisis in the Middle East roiling domestic politics. The midterms may spell the end of a certain Trump era, but what follows may probably be a case of long-Trump: a Republican party still unable to plot a path without him, and a Democratic party still unable to locate what it stands for outside of opposing him.
- Nesrine Malik is a Guardian columnist

The black list: Which countries does Lithuania advise its citizens to avoid traveling to?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
06:00:00 UTC
15:00:00 KST

Lithuania is seeking consular access to two citizens detained in Iran, but providing assistance is proving particularly difficult. The case has drawn attention to the Foreign Ministry’s travel warnings and the challenges diplomats face when Lithuanian citizens encounter trouble in countries where Lithuania has no diplomatic representation.
The Foreign Ministry confirmed that the two women, whom Vilnius police had been searching for since October 11, were detained in Iran in mid-October. The ministry is trying to arrange consular assistance but has said the process is complicated.
Iran is marked in black on the ministry’s travel advisory map, meaning Lithuanian citizens are urged to leave the country immediately.
Five levels of travel warnings
The Foreign Ministry divides countries into five categories, marked in green, yellow, orange, red and black, depending on the level of risk and the recommended precautions.
- Green: No specific travel warnings apply. Countries in this category include Canada, Finland, Norway, Germany and Poland.
- Yellow: Travelers are advised to take precautions. This category includes the United States, Iceland, Sweden, the United Kingdom, Turkey and Kazakhstan.
- Orange: Travelers are advised to assess whether their trip is necessary. Mexico, Egypt, China and Jordan are among the countries in this category.
- Red: Travel is not recommended. Countries in this category include Venezuela, Pakistan, Iraq and Algeria.
- Black: Travelers are urged to leave immediately. The list includes Russia, Belarus, Ukraine, Mali, Burkina Faso, Eritrea, Myanmar, Afghanistan, North Korea and Iran.
The Foreign Ministry publishes its full travel advisory map on its website, where travellers can check recommendations for individual destinations before departure.
Lithuania seeks help from other countries
Remigijus Motuzas, a diplomat who chairs the Lithuanian parliament’s Foreign Affairs Committee, told LRT.lt that assisting citizens detained abroad can be difficult, particularly when Lithuania lacks diplomatic representation in the country concerned.
He said consular assistance has two main priorities: establishing contact with the local authorities to determine why a citizen has been detained, and reaching the detainee to assess their situation and ensure their rights are respected.
“The other, even more important, task is to contact the detained citizen to establish the conditions in which they are being held, whether their rights have been violated under international conventions, whether they are receiving medical care if they have health conditions, and whether they are being tortured, among other things,” Motuzas said.
Assistance can also include support for the detainees’ relatives and help obtaining legal representation, he added.
The detention of the two Lithuanian women has prompted questions about their decision to travel to Iran despite the government’s strong warning against visiting the country.
Motuzas said, however, that the state remains responsible for helping citizens who find themselves in danger abroad, regardless of whether they followed official travel advice.
“We say that people are responsible for their own decisions when travel is not recommended. But, on the other hand, it is a diplomat’s duty not to abandon someone in distress,” he said. “Assistance is provided regardless of the circumstances in which a person arrived.”
EU partners can help when Lithuania has no embassy
When a Lithuanian citizen is detained in a country where Lithuania has no diplomatic mission, the government seeks assistance from other European Union member states that may be able to intervene.
“That is also the case with Iran at the moment,” Motuzas said.
Lithuanian authorities are seeking to arrange a consular visit to the two detained women to establish their health and detention conditions and determine whether they have access to legal assistance and other necessary services.
