Pharma giants pay millions to Russian distributor entangled in corruption allegations to win cancer drug business
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
05:59:21 UTC
14:59:21 KST

CANCER CALCULUS
Pharma giants pay millions to Russian distributor entangled in corruption allegations to win cancer drug business
Confidential whistleblower reports allege that Western companies offer huge bonuses to Russian middlemen, inflating prices for lifesaving treatments at the expense of patients.
In selling its blockbuster anticancer drug Keytruda to the Russian government, the pharmaceutical giant Merck turned to a hospital supplier with friends in high places: Alexey Repik, a now-sanctioned oligarch close to Russian President Vladimir Putin and fluent in the ways of Russia and Western business.
A native of Moscow, trained as an economist, Repik started R-Pharm in 2001 after selling his car and borrowing $15,000 from his mother. Serving as an intermediary for pharmaceutical firms bidding on massive government contracts for medicine, the firm took off.
In 2009, the year New Jersey-based Merck forged a strategic alliance with R-Pharm, the Russian company was expanding and soon teamed up with other Western firms and formed new lines of business.
Repik amassed billions of dollars, a mansion in San Francisco and a precious collection of modern art and Japanese prints. He enjoyed high-stakes poker events at luxury casino hotels in the West, joining high-roller pros and gaining a reputation as a somewhat aggressive and unorthodox player. And he attracted scrutiny. Some in the media questioned whether insider connections to government officials helped him win contracts. Repik brushed off the question. “In the classical sense, no,” he said in a 2015 interview. “Officials and shadow leaders have never stood behind us.”
R-Pharm also faced scrutiny from Russia’s Federal Antimonopoly Service, which investigated whether the firm coordinated bidding with other medicine distributors and in separate cases engaged in anticompetitive conduct designed to maintain high drug prices and influence winners.
Yet R-Pharm kept growing, deepening its relationship with Merck by sharing manufacturing know-how and producing medicines jointly. Along the way, Repik became a political heavyweight. He met one-on-one with Putin, was invited to mingle with the super elite at the World Economic Forum and attended Donald Trump’s first presidential inauguration festivities in 2017. The oligarch bragged on Facebook that he was able to “check the handshake strength” of the president-elect. And news investigations later found that an offshore company linked to Repik owned a Bombardier business jet apparently used by one of Putin’s daughters.
Merck wasn’t the only major Western drugmaker to partner with a politically connected Russian distributor entangled in corruption allegations. Nor was it the only one to operate in a system in which improper payments, conflicts of interest, bid rigging and inflated medicine prices were recurring public concerns.
Now confidential whistleblower reports obtained by the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists say that four pharmaceutical giants paid tens of millions of dollars to proxies to supply lifesaving drugs to Russian government entities as part of a corrupt system that helped keep prices high and limit access for cancer patients and others with serious ailments.
The probe into the role of intermediaries in Russia’s cancer medicine infrastructure, by ICIJ, Proekt and the Swiss media outlet Republik, is part of ICIJ’s Cancer Calculus project. The series explores strategies that pharmaceutical firms use to maintain multibillion-dollar monopolies and to keep cancer drug prices high — at the expense of patients and depleted healthcare resources around the world.
The new whistleblower reports say that between 2020 and 2023, the drug companies provided “excessive” bonuses to R-Pharm and other intermediaries in Russia, even as those middlemen participated in dubious bidding practices or faced scrutiny for alleged bid rigging or anticompetitive conduct.
These whistleblower reports, made in 2024 and 2025, allege that Merck (known as MSD outside of the U.S. and Canada), Eli Lilly, Novartis and AstraZeneca paid the large sales bonuses, or rebates, to a network of Russian distributors and sub-distributors. The distributors or firms they controlled, in turn, paid government healthcare officials and hospital administrators in return for awarding public contracts and boosting prescriptions of high-priced medicines without real competition, the whistleblower disclosures say.
The Western companies paid bonuses of between 15% and 35%, the disclosures claim, including bonuses based on the volume of a drug bought or other types of incentives. The distributors allegedly used the bonuses to fund kickbacks to officials who approved purchases of drugs such as Merck’s anticancer medicine Keytruda, Eli Lilly’s Cyramza, Novartis’s Kisqali and AstraZeneca’s Tagrisso.
The whistleblower reports are part of a trove of hundreds of pages of documents, including company emails, bidding records and letters to the drugmakers’ audit committees, submitted to the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission and alleging violations under the U.S. Foreign Corrupt Practices Act. The FCPA prohibits bribery of officials to secure or retain business and requires publicly traded companies to maintain accurate and transparent accounting. The disclosures also said the information would be provided to the Justice Department’s FCPA unit.
The whistleblower cited in each report is a longtime pharmaceutical industry employee who asked to remain anonymous for fear of reprisal. The SEC and DOJ declined to comment.
A Novartis spokeswoman said in a statement that the company conducted a thorough investigation into the FCPA allegations but wouldn’t comment on what it found or whether company officials had spoken to the SEC about the matter. AstraZeneca declined to comment. Merck and Lilly did not respond to requests for comment.
To corroborate some of the whistleblower’s claims, ICIJ reviewed Russia’s public procurement database, as well as procurement records shared by Proekt, for records relating to several bids that the whistleblower reports allege had been rigged. ICIJ also verified the accuracy of facts asserted in the reports, including the name of the drug, the companies involved, dates of the bid solicitations and bid amounts. ICIJ corroborated some of the whistleblower’s claims by reviewing facts asserted in the statements alleging a “fake auction” for a drug bid solicitation.
Granting bonuses is a common business practice in the pharmaceutical sector and sometimes takes a non-cash form, specifically by reducing the outstanding amount that distributors pay for products. Under one bonus arrangement, a drugmaker may send a drug to a distributor in return for a promissory note. The distributor then sells the medicine to a hospital at a government bidding auction. The drugmaker effectively pays a bonus by issuing a credit note that reduces the amount the distributor owes.
Russian distributors told ICIJ they complied with all laws and adhered to strict ethical business standards.
R-Pharm said that its use of bonuses was legitimate and that it was not aware of any investigation into improper payments. “We deny any involvement of R-Pharm and/or its officers and/or affiliates in any instances of improper payments to public officials in Russia or any other country in the world in exchange for non-competitive medicine contracts,” Vasily Ignatiev, R-Pharm’s general director, wrote to ICIJ.
But the whistleblower disclosures claim that the only reason Western companies would provide such large bonuses is because their Russian management teams knew the distributors needed large margins to fund alleged kickbacks for medicines.
The whistleblower reports do not contain evidence of direct payments from intermediaries to government officials, but they do offer an array of red flags that indicate the intermediaries had encountered legal trouble, that the system they were navigating was rife with corruption and that the bonuses the pharmaceutical firms were paying may have been beyond industry norms.
The whistleblower’s claims also raise questions about whether bonuses can improperly influence medical decisions, including whether patients receive the right medicines, whether public funds are used effectively and whether artificially high costs prevent access to treatment for those who need it.
The whistleblower disclosures claim that there was no business justification for such large bonuses and that the Western firms’ conduct “is the very definition of being willfully blind.”
‘Exceptionally large’ bonuses
While problems in Russia’s drug procurement system are publicly known, reforms have been hard to come by because so many distributors and others in the supply chain benefit from it. Meanwhile, many patients can’t access medicines because of limited supply or high prices, and taxpayers must finance a system that experts say is built on bribery instead of one that funds lifesaving medicines.
Under the FCPA, using a third-party distributor doesn’t shield a manufacturer from liability for improper payments. A manufacturer may face liability if it knows or deliberately ignores warning signs that a distributor is using its margins to fund improper payments. Because companies can be held liable for the actions of their distributors, federal regulators expect firms to conduct a thorough due diligence process, including checks into the distributor’s business history, ownership structures and links to government officials.
The whistleblower disclosures say it is unclear whether the companies’ audit and compliance units were “aware of the distributor corruption scheme and have chosen to ignore the scheme to maintain their jobs or have been poorly trained at identifying and preventing systematic FCPA violations.” Letters addressed to the firms’ audit committees, which are part of the whistleblower reports, urge corporate investigators to conduct reviews of the distributor schemes.
The letters to the audit committees mention six key distributors used by the pharma giants that had documented red flags, including alleged shell company transactions, bid-rigging cases, faked auction schemes and high-profile bribery or antitrust investigations. Proekt’s investigation found the bonuses cited in the whistleblower reports were broadly consistent with amounts quoted in a confidential industry survey conducted by the Russian audit firm Kept. That survey found the average bonus paid to government distributors in Russia in 2022 was 30%, seven times as high as bonuses paid to retail distributors selling medicine to pharmacies, according to Proekt. But in a written statement, Kept said it was unfair to compare bonuses in the retail and public sectors. In particular, Kept said the retail market, unlike the government one, involves others in the distribution chain including pharmacy chains and e-commerce players, “which results in additional costs for pharmaceutical companies.”
“Based on this, it is necessary to consider the entire spectrum of relationships among participants in the pharmaceutical market,” a Kept spokesperson said.
Kept added: “Bonus mechanisms regulate exclusively commercial relationships between distributors and pharmaceutical companies and have no bearing on the effectiveness of government procurement.”
Retail distributors supply both prescription and over-the-counter medicines often bought directly by consumers. Government distributors are typically different companies that cover medicines including high-priced cancer drugs under patent, paid for by Russian government agencies. These medicines tend to be purchased through government auctions for public hospitals and public health agencies. The Russian government did not respond to ICIJ’s requests for comment. In his statement, R-Pharm’s Ignatiev described the system as transparent and “based on open competitive bidding procedures.”
Proekt’s investigation found that bonuses to Russian distributors participating in government auctions were “exceptionally large” compared to several countries where they rarely exceeded 10%.
Researchers and investigators have found that pharmaceutical distributors and other intermediaries can raise the price of prescription medicines. At a 2015 industry compliance conference in Washington, Andrew Ceresney, then-director of the SEC’s Division of Enforcement, said distributors were in a position to “use their margin or spread to create a slush fund of cash that will be used to pay bribes to foreign officials.”
‘There is no competition’
Distributors have been at the center of bribery probes before. In Kazakhstan, the SEC alleged that distributors for the French pharmaceutical giant Sanofi generated funds to bribe Kazakh officials to win contracts and boost sales of the company’s prescription drugs. The SEC issued a cease-and-desist order alleging that Sanofi and distributors typically created a 20% to 30% “discount” to increase distributors’ profit margins, designating some of that money for bribes, and then having the distributor kick back funds to Sanofi employees. Distributors tracked the financial accounting on internal spreadsheets where the kickbacks were masked under the code word “marzipans.” Sanofi paid $25.2 million to settle the allegations in 2018 without admitting or denying wrongdoing.
In Brazil, the SEC found that a subsidiary of Indianapolis-based Eli Lilly allegedly gave a distributor a 17% and 19% discount for drug sales to the government. The SEC described these discounts as “unusually large.” The U.S. investigation showed the distributor used about 6% of the purchase price to pay bribes to Brazilian government officials. Lilly reached a civil settlement with the SEC and agreed in 2012 to pay more than $29 million without admitting or denying the allegations. “Lilly requires our employees to act with integrity with all external parties and in accordance with all applicable laws and regulations,” Anne Nobles, Lilly’s chief ethics and compliance officer, said in a statement at the time. “Since ours is a business based on trust, we strive to conduct ourselves in an ethical way that is beyond reproach.”
ICIJ reviewed a page from a 2022 Eli Lilly business plan that indicated, without specifying any country, that the company budgeted a bonus of 34% for Cyramza, a costly infusion drug approved to treat various advanced cancers. The whistleblower disclosure in the Lilly case cited nine Cyramza contracts valued at more than $5 million that the Moscow City Department of Health awarded in 2021 to the distributor Pharmstandard. An ICIJ review of Russian procurement data shows that Pharmstandard was the only bidder for most of those contracts. Lilly had provided Pharmstandard a 29% volume bonus for achieving its annual sales target and a 5% bonus for paying on time, according to the whistleblower’s disclosure. “As a result, Lilly received about $3.4 million from these Cyramza tenders,” or bid solicitations, the report said, adding that the distributor’s primary task was to deliver the vials of medicine to the Moscow Health Department’s warehouse in a small truck equipped with a cooler and thermometers.
Neither Lilly nor Pharmstandard responded to requests for comment. Bidding systems are supposed to secure the lowest possible price for the government. And in many countries, a drug’s official list price is considerably higher than the net price ultimately paid by insurers and government programs. But in Russia, the whistleblower reports allege, distributors often obtained single-participant or noncompetitive awards for medicine. As a result, the price of cancer and other high-cost medicines could end up even higher than the list price. For example, between 2019 and 2023, Tagrisso, a medication used to treat adults with non-small cell lung cancer, had a list price of about $3,000-$3,500 for a box of 30 tablets. Yet the whistleblower’s written report about Tagrisso’s manufacturer, U.K.-based AstraZeneca, said so many batches were awarded without competition that a pack of 30 tablets of Tagrisso was sold at slightly above the list price from 2020 to 2023. “The reason for this is that there is no competition,” the whistleblower wrote to AstraZeneca’s audit committee chairman in 2024. Single bidders won in the majority of the Tagrisso bid solicitations.
Indeed, Russian procurement data reviewed by ICIJ shows single-participant bidding in about 95% of Tagrisso bids from 2020 to 2023.
An AstraZeneca spokesperson declined to comment.
The confidential whistleblower reports also describe how distributors allegedly channeled work through sub-distributors — some allegedly shell companies — that provided an extra layer of plausible deniability to mask allegedly improper payments. Proekt says it found at least 100 shell and “front companies” in different regions that entered bids for medicines supplied by Pharmstandard and R-Pharm.
In his statement, R-Pharm’s Ignatiev said the company “participates in procurement procedures independently and does not appoint distributors and/or sub-distributors.”
A review of Russian procurement data by Proekt and ICIJ confirms some details of the whistleblower’s account of cases relating to Kisqali, the best-selling breast cancer therapy made by Swiss giant Novartis. In one case, two distributors submitted the same bid, allowing the first company that entered the auction to win the contract — what the whistleblower’s report called a clear example of bid rigging.
A Novartis representative told ICIJ: “Novartis takes all allegations of misconduct or irregular business practices by its third-party partners very seriously. Regarding the topic in question, Novartis conducted a thorough investigation into the specific activities.”
The whistleblower reports about Novartis and AstraZeneca urged the companies’ audit committees to review why the firms used the distributor Pharmimex to obtain government contracts for oncology and rare drugs.
Pharmimex and affiliates often supplied not only Novartis’ Kisqali but also AstraZeneca’s Koselugo on a noncompetitive basis, according to the whistleblower.
Procurement data reviewed by ICIJ shows most government contracts for Koselugo, used to treat children with a rare type of tumor, were awarded after single-participant bids from 2022 to 2024. During that period, Pharmimex won $114.3 million worth of Koselugo contracts out of a total of nearly $129 million with virtually no competition. Such deals can drive up the prices of lifesaving drugs, generating substantial profits that potentially can be used to corruptly influence officials awarding the contracts.
In 2019, Pharmimex came under scrutiny when Russian regulators accused Penza Regional Oncology Dispensary, a state-funded cancer center, of engaging in anticompetitive conduct to favor Pharmimex.
Russia’s anti-monopoly agency found that the Penza dispensary had given Pharmimex advance information about planned medicine purchases, tender requirements and delivery conditions, creating potentially preferential treatment for the distributor in the bidding process. The agency discontinued the antitrust proceedings against Pharmimex itself.
Russia’s anti-monopoly agency found that Penza violated competition law because its dispensary gave Pharmimex preferential treatment in procurement. Penza didn’t respond to requests for comment. Pharmimex compliance director Maxim Tkachenko did not respond to specific questions but said the company conducts business “in full compliance with applicable law and standards of business ethics.”
Ignatiev, the R-Pharm director, said the auction system “virtually eliminates the risks of unfair competition, collusion, and bias on the part of the contracting authority during the bidding.”
The whistleblower’s complaints against AstraZeneca and Eli Lilly say the firms used the distributor Pharmstandard, which had attracted scrutiny in a 2011 bid-rigging probe. Inspectors at Russia’s Federal Antimonopoly Service found Pharmstandard and another company coordinated the sale of the cystic fibrosis drug Pulmozyme before a tender auction. Their conduct allegedly resulted in keeping the drug price high. Pharmstandard was fined $6.4 million in 2012.
Deepening relationships with the West
Proekt found that a large number of Russian elites — from Putin’s family to his security detail, ministers and key government bureaucrats — have taken jobs in the pharmaceutical industry, a revolving door between regulators and the firms they regulate. And some of the politically connected Russian executives have ties to Western pharmaceutical companies, notably Alexey Repik, now 47.
As a young entrepreneur, Repik gained a reputation for street smarts after promptly growing sales tenfold at his first distribution company. Repik declined to answer ICIJ’s questions, saying in a brief email that he was on a business trip to Japan and Thailand. He previously told HSE University, his alma mater, that he used his knowledge of English and familiarity with the rules of Western business conduct to approach foreign pharmaceutical companies. “I went to foreign pharmaceutical companies — which I just found in the … telephone directory and called — and offered them the opportunity to work with us like they learned in economics school,” he said.
In 2009, the same year Merck began working with R-Pharm, the Federal Antimonopoly Service opened cases against Repik’s firm and other distributors. The regulatory agency suspected that R-Pharm and other suppliers coordinated their bids to maintain high prices but closed the collusion case because of insufficient evidence.
It would be among eight cases that regulators opened over the years into alleged antitrust violations by R-Pharm; Ignatiev said most of the cases were dropped for lack of evidence.
Repik’s relationships with Western drug companies deepened. R-Pharm teamed up with drug giants to localize production of their medicines or develop and sell drugs under a license in Russia, including Lilly’s insulin treatments for diabetes and Merck’s hepatitis C antiviral narlaprevir. While winning a large number of government contracts in Russia, R-Pharm opened offices in San Diego and Boston to develop relationships with U.S. scientific, academic and venture-capital communities.
In Russia, Repik’s influence grew after he became chairman of Delovaya Rossiya, a top business lobby. By 2017, Repik had business ties with Silicon Valley and, according to Proekt, owned a mansion in a posh San Francisco neighborhood with views of the Golden Gate Bridge. Repik shared photos on social media at Trump’s first inauguration, showing his proximity to figures including Eric Trump, incoming Vice President Mike Pence and incoming White House chief of staff Reince Priebus. Months later, Repik debuted on the Forbes billionaires list with a reported net worth of about $2.1 billion.
Russian regulators’ scrutiny of R-Pharm became more serious in 2018 when they inspected a large pharmaceutical office. They found flash drives bearing the electronic signatures of several companies, all under the control of R-Pharm employees. It raised suspicions that R-Pharm was using nominally independent firms to create the appearance of competitive bidding, including contracts reserved for small businesses.
In its report, Proekt writes: “Several small companies — including Sanalek, Plexpharm, Pharmakhan, Spacepharm, Unilek, Medgazpharm and Vitalek — submitted bids from the same IP addresses belonging to R-Pharm, sometimes only minutes apart. … Their auction bids sometimes differed by as little as half a percentage point.”
Shortly after that 2018 revelation, Repik denied any allegation of collusion and said there were no grounds for opening a cartel case. He acknowledged knowing about the photos of the seized flash drives but said they didn’t demonstrate wrongdoing.
The regulators didn’t find evidence of collusion or preferential treatment. But in a separate case, they fined R-Pharm $1.4 million for allegedly participating in an anticompetitive arrangement that helped maintain artificially high prices on medicines bought with public money.
A ‘monopoly’ on Keytruda
In 2021, as Keytruda was on its way to becoming the world’s top-selling medicine, the Russian Ministry of Health listed it at about $2,100 a vial, or $4,200 for two vials, a single dose. R-Pharm, according to the whistleblower report, was capturing much of the state hospital business through noncompetitive awards.
Keytruda public procurement records reviewed by ICIJ show that R-Pharm dominated the public market from 2020 to 2022, winning 2,400 out of nearly 5,000 Keytruda bids (about $360 million worth of contracts out of a total $870 million). A closer look at the data shows that 96% of all bids were with a single participating company.
But Ignatiev stressed that the firm had a license to be Merck’s local production partner for Keytruda, which was under patent with no competing drug in Russia at the time. “If such local partner holds a license from the patent holder granting it the right to carry out the final stages of production and release quality control, the primary source of supply of that drug can be none other than this local partner,” Ignatiev wrote in reply to ICIJ’s questions.
The whistleblower report said that R-Pharm allegedly funneled some contracts to affiliates “to make it appear on paper that other companies are also winning some of the Keytruda business, even though R- Pharm is controlling everything and has a monopoly on supplying Keytruda to the Russian government.”
Ignatiev noted that Keytruda’s prices in Russia were lower than in many countries, including the U.S. and China. Still, R-Pharm reported revenue of nearly $2.5 billion in 2021, with Keytruda as 25% of its top 10 product revenue mix, according to an investors presentation. And the drug soon became a Russian and global blockbuster, leading public procurement of oncology medicines.
Meanwhile, Repik’s influence grew as he gained direct access to Putin. He had a private working meeting with the president in the Kremlin in December 2021 and again the following year.
But Repik’s Western ties unraveled after Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022. The U.K., Canada, Australia and Ukraine sanctioned Repik because of his ties to Putin. The oligarch left the company he built as Merck and other Western giants scaled back operations in Russia. Ramping up a campaign to get drugmakers to produce medicines within Russia, Putin began dismantling protections for foreign patent holders, particularly those from “unfriendly countries.”
The push led to Russia’s first generic version of Keytruda, Pembroria, manufactured by Biocad and priced at about $1,300 for a single 100 milligram vial. An even cheaper copycat produced by R-Pharm, Arfleyda, hit the market shortly thereafter. Its maximum price: about $1,000 a vial, nearly half the price of Merck’s Keytruda. Merck had lost most of its Keytruda business in Russia.
The whistleblower report included internal Merck emails indicating that the company received the report in July 2024 and that Merck retained the law firm Jones Day to advise it on the allegations. “Merck has engaged us to represent the company in this matter,” Jones Day partner Jordan Matthews wrote in an email that was included in the whistleblower’s report to the SEC.
Matthews did not respond to requests for comment, nor did Merck. The report also said the whistleblower’s claims were submitted to the SEC in November 2024 and would be sent to the Justice Department’s FCPA Unit.
The Trump administration cut back on FCPA enforcement in 2025. The SEC effectively disbanded its FCPA unit, and the U.S. shifted Justice Department prosecutors away from corporate bribery investigations toward cases targeting drug cartels.

ISW Russian Offensive Campaign Assessment, November 1, 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

14:57:37 KST

Key Takeaways from the ISW:
- Russian forces lost ground on the battlefield in October 2026 for the second month in a row.
- Russian forces suffered their highest monthly losses of the war thus far in October 2026, paying a growing price for their territorial losses.
- Russian forces have managed to make marginal advances in the Dobropillya direction by committing substantial resources and personnel, but the seizure of Dobropillya would not enable sweeping Russian advances in Donetsk Oblast.
- The Russian military command does not appear to have modified plans even for the forces defeated by Ukraine’s Operation Vivaldi in the Lyman direction.
- Ukraine’s Operation Vivaldi has had cascading effects on Russian offensives against the Fortress Belt directly from the east.
- Russian forces have not yet completed the seizure of Kostyantynivka over a year after first infiltrating into the town.
- Russian forces continue to commit personnel and mechanized elements in the Hulyaipole direction and western Zaporizhia Oblast and are making limited and mostly local advances.
- Russian forces continue limited offensive efforts to expand their claimed “buffer zone” along the international border in northern Sumy and Kharkiv oblasts but have achieved only localized tactical gains.
- Russian forces are largely deprioritizing offensive operations in the Kupyansk and Borova directions following the recent successful Ukrainian operations Vivaldi and Veles.
- Ukraine and Turkey are advancing joint cooperation to support a limited ceasefire in the Black Sea and secure the maritime security of global grain exports, as sea transport has become increasingly dangerous amid ongoing long-range strikes.
- Likely Russian drones violated Moldovan and Romanian airspace on the evening of October 31, as Russia continues to normalize its increasingly frequent and intense violations of European airspace.
- Ukrainian forces continued their long-range strike campaign against Russian oil infrastructure overnight on October 31 to November 1. Russia launched 433 drones (including 64 jet-powered ones) against Ukraine overnight.

====================================================================================================

‘We wanted to end the humiliation’: Why Arab Israelis turned out in historic numbers to vote
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
05:57:14 UTC
14:57:14 KST

We sat beneath an old ficus tree and asked Jaber Abu Assa which of the piles of shattered concrete and protruding steel rods had once been his home. All around us lay the rubble of what was once the unrecognized Bedouin village of Wadi al-Khalil, just a few dozen yards east of Highway 60, near the Tel Shoket interchange.
Until May 8, 2024, 70 houses stood here, home to 70 families comprising about 400 Israeli Bedouins from the Negev. All that remains of what was once a living community are mounds of beams, broken concrete blocks, drywall and shattered ceramic tiles. Lives reduced to rubble.
How many of us heard about the destruction of this community, the demolition of 70 homes in a single day? It began at 8 a.m. and ended shortly before 5 p.m. Ten bulldozers were deployed for the operation, protected by 2,000 police officers.
We searched online for the news headlines from that day. They reported on the progress of the Israeli military operation in Rafah, negotiations over a hostage deal and ceasefire and a confrontation between Israel and the Biden administration over military aid. Not a word about the demolition of 70 homes in Wadi al-Khalil, just a few minutes’ drive from the little square of chocolate served with coffee at the nearest Aroma café.
“The disagreement wasn’t about leaving this place, but about where we would go,” Abu Assa says. “They want to expand Highway 6 through this land, and the state said it would give us an alternative site in the Al-Muthali neighborhood of Tel Sheva. We said fine. But after we agreed, the state went back on its word and said that instead of Tel Sheva, we would move to land in Umm Batin.
“That land is the subject of a dispute between families, and we said we didn’t want to move into an area of conflict. We didn’t want to get into a dispute with anyone. I’m telling you all this because there had been a dialogue and various ideas were being discussed, until Ben-Gvir intervened. He said enough talking and gave the order to demolish our homes. Just demolish them.
“We got one day’s notice. What can you take from your home in a single day? There were some terrible scenes here. Children, elderly people, entire families were left homeless. Some people put up tents next to the ruins of their homes, and a day or two later inspectors came and demolished the tents too. They gave us no alternative. They threw us out onto the street, literally.
“The state demolished 6,000 homes in the Bedouin communities of the Negev, and Ben-Gvir made TikTok videos about it. ‘I’m in charge, I’m the boss, me, me, me.’
“People had been waiting a long time for this week’s election. We understood that the people really running this terrible government weren’t Likud, but Ben-Gvir and Smotrich, who demolish people’s homes and enjoy doing it. They turn it into a campaign.
“We waited for the election so we could replace a government that didn’t want to talk to us, that only wanted to humiliate us and trample on us, to ignore us as though we didn’t exist. With one hand, they legalized illegal outposts in the territories, outposts that sprang up overnight like thieves in the night, and with the other hand, they crushed us. They didn’t see us as human beings with basic rights.
“We were literally counting the days until the election. You should have seen the lines at the polling stations here in the Negev. People stood in line for an hour, sometimes longer, just to vote.”
The blood toll paid by Arab society under the far-right government has been unbearable. During Itamar Ben-Gvir’s four years as the minister responsible for the Israel Police, 913 Arab citizens were murdered.
That is a number worth reading several times to grasp the magnitude of the crisis facing this community. The fear and insecurity are so pervasive that people are afraid to leave their homes after dark. In far too many communities, the sound of bursts of gunfire is now met with indifference.
In any properly functioning country, a commission of inquiry would be established to investigate how things reached such a level of lawlessness, a reality in which criminal gangs control entire communities.
Arab Israelis certainly turned out in droves, and they had every reason in the world to do so. While the bloc seeking to replace Netanyahu failed to secure a majority over his political camp, voter turnout in Arab society approached 80%, with Arab parties winning 19 Knesset seats as of this writing.
Issawi Frej, a former Knesset member and minister from the Meretz party who lives in Kafr Qasim, says Arab voters needed no encouragement to go to the polls.
“It’s like a soccer team preparing for a decisive match, with the tension building as the game gets closer,” he explains. “When the moment finally comes and the referee blows the opening whistle, the players charge onto the field fired up. That’s what happened with us. We exploded onto the field.
“The desire and willingness to vote were extraordinary. People asked me every day, ‘So, when is the election?’ There was no need for any campaign. Believe me, the parties barely campaigned.
“Look what happened in Umm al-Fahm. In the previous election, turnout there was 41%. This time it jumped to 75.7%.
“What people had in mind was a video from a wedding in the city where police showed up and forced 300 guests to lie on the ground, including the bride and groom. Enough was enough. That alone was sufficient to get people to the polls.
“Or take Kafr Qasim, for example. Here, election day was sluggish until noon. There were no lines and not much enthusiasm. But then Ben-Gvir showed up at the entrance to the city and made a video declaring, ‘I’m the boss here. I’m the tough guy.’
“The young people saw it on TikTok and went crazy. Listen to me carefully: That video spread like wildfire on TikTok. And just as quickly as it spread, people here rushed to the polls after seeing it.
“Kafr Qasim ended election day with a historic turnout of 86%. In Majd al-Krum, turnout reached 83%. At three polling stations there, it reached 100%.
“You know why? It was all ‘thanks’ to the hilltop youth who tried to establish a settlement right on the village’s doorstep.”
Is this Judaism?
We were sitting at a café at the Tel Shoket junction when several young men approached us and asked what would happen next.
One of them said, “The right won’t accept the results in our communities. You’ll see. They’ll accuse us of all kinds of lies.”
And indeed, a few hours later, Likud issued a special statement accusing the Arab parties of “stealing the election through serious criminal offenses.”
Raed Abu Al-Qiyan, a social activist from Hura and a member of the Negev Arab Steering Committee, says people went to the polls because their lives were at stake.
“To live, to live with dignity, like human beings,” he says. “Nobody needed to be encouraged.
“You have to understand, throughout our lives, we always had an open door in the government, including under Netanyahu’s previous governments. We didn’t get the budgets we should have, and there wasn’t enough investment in our communities, but there was always someone who listened to us, heard what we had to say and tried to help.
“Under this Ben-Gvir government, every door was closed to us. What more motivation did I need to vote in a situation like that? Ben-Gvir was our motivation.
“You want to find out why we turned out? Go to his TikTok. Look into it there. He celebrated the demolition of our homes at the expense of the suffering of people left without a roof over their heads.
“And I’ll tell you something else. We have thousands of teachers, doctors, nurses, people with doctorates and professors in academia. We live among Jews. I myself am an environmentalist. I’m not a kid anymore. I’m 49.
“We went to vote to save you from yourselves, too. The Judaism of Ben-Gvir and Smotrich is not the Judaism I know. Their Judaism does not respect other people, does not respect those who are different. They have no compassion for the suffering of others.”
We sat there for half an hour, and at every table around us, people were discussing the election results. Everyone said this had been the largest protest vote in the history of Arab society in Israel.
Social activist Abu Latif Ezzedine from Rahat argued that the massive turnout was a clear and unequivocal statement by Arab citizens that they want to be significant players in the political system.
“We wanted to say that we are Israeli citizens no less than you are, with the understanding that this is the only way to influence our lives and help ourselves,” he says.
“Voting in elections strengthens my sense of belonging. It’s knowing that there is one place where I have exactly the same right as you do as a Jewish Israeli: to put my ballot in an envelope and drop it into the ballot box.
“I’m not bothered by all the accusations. Let those making false claims about irregularities say whatever they want.
“Nine residents of our city have been murdered since the beginning of the year. That alone was a strong enough reason for us to turn out in large numbers, vote and make our voices heard.”
Not even a kind word
Visit an Arab city or village in the Negev, the Triangle region in central Israel or the Galilee sometime. The disparity immediately hits you.
It is visible everywhere, in every aspect of public space: the potholed roads, the missing streetlights, the bare traffic circles because there is no budget for plants and landscaping. These are things that we Jews take for granted.
This week, Arab citizens wanted a say in how their lives in this country would unfold.
Ignoring their massive turnout would have devastating consequences. Everyone we spoke to said so.
“If we end up going to another election, Arab society will have suffered a huge defeat,” Ezzedine says.
“People had hope that they could make a difference, bring about change and bring down the government. Another election would seriously undermine their motivation to vote again.
“People will say, ‘We tried to make a difference, and nobody counted us. Why should we bother voting again?’
“Think about how deeply hurtful it is to us as human beings to realize that we are not seen as partners.
“Bibi’s right-wing bloc talks about a Jewish majority. The bloc seeking change talks about a Zionist majority. But nobody talks about an Israeli majority.
“After all, I’m not Jewish and I’m not a Zionist. I’m simply Israeli. Count us among the Israelis. With us, there is a majority in the Knesset. The arithmetic is so simple.”
Frej, from Kafr Qasim, says that less than 24 hours after the polls closed, a profound sense of frustration was already taking hold in Arab society.
“We came out to vote with our children and our elderly to bring down this terrible government, and we haven’t heard a single thank-you from Eisenkot for our participation. Not one word of thanks for going out to vote to make this place better, more sane. Not even one small kind word.
“That is not leadership.
“Listen to me carefully. Another election would be a huge victory for Netanyahu, but more than that, it would be a knockout blow to the liberal-democratic camp for many years to come.
“It would destroy the hope for change for generations. Generations, I’m telling you.
“We are at a defining moment in Israeli history, and the bloc seeking change must not miss it. It would be a tragedy for Israel and for the entire region.”
Abu Assa also sounds pessimistic.
As we sifted through the pile of broken concrete blocks that had once been his home, he told us that the residents had scattered among Bedouin communities in the area. Some rented rooms, while others found shelter with relatives in Segev Shalom, Umm Batin and Lakiya.
They receive no money from the state.
“With our votes, we wanted to send a message that this extremism in the way we are treated is unacceptable to us,” he concludes.
“People are no longer willing to suffer. If people see that their votes are disregarded, what are they supposed to understand? You tell me. What will we conclude if our votes have no meaning at all?
“People will reach a point of despair. That’s what will happen.
“Look how they demolished our home and gave us no alternative, no solution. It’s an unforgivable crime.
“People went to vote so they would be seen, so their votes would bring change. If they realize it doesn’t help, things could turn violent.
“Look how they left us with nothing,” he says, pointing to the mound of rubble that had once been his home and his children’s home.
“They left us abandoned like dogs.”

Air defenses down 154 out of 193 drones used by Russia to attack Ukraine since evening
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
05:56:49 UTC
14:56:49 KST

Air defenses down 154 out of 193 drones used by Russia to attack Ukraine since evening
According to Ukrinform, the Ukrainian Air Force Command reported this on Telegram.
On the night of November 1-2 (from 18:00 on November 1), Russia attacked Ukraine with 193 strike UAVs, including Shahed-type drones (75 of them jet-powered), Gerberas and Parodiya decoy drones. They were launched from Oryol, Kursk and Bryansk in Russia, temporarily occupied Donetsk, and Hvardiiske in the temporarily occupied Autonomous Republic of Crimea.
The air attack was repelled by aircraft, anti-aircraft missile units, electronic warfare and unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups of Ukraine's Defense Forces.
According to preliminary data, as of 08:00, air defenses had shot down or suppressed 154 enemy UAVs, including Shahed-type drones (58 of them jet-powered), Gerberas and drones of other types.
More than six attack drones are still in Ukrainian airspace.
Hits by enemy weapons were recorded at 26 locations, while debris from downed drones fell at nine locations.

Russians strike transport company in Kirovohrad Oblast, causing large-scale fire – photos
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher

Russians strike transport company in Kirovohrad Oblast, causing large-scale fire – photos
A large-scale fire has broken out at a transport company in the Kropyvnytskyi district of Kirovohrad Oblast as a result of a Russian strike on the evening of 1 November. As of the morning of 2 November, the fire had been extinguished.
Source: Andrii Raikovych, Head of Kirovohrad Oblast Military Administration; State Emergency Service (SES) of Ukraine
Quote from Raikovych: "A transport company was hit as a result of the evening enemy attack in the Kropyvnytskyi district."
Details: The SES added that the fire has already been extinguished.
Quote from the SES: "The SES unit was working under the constant threat of further attacks. As of now, the fire has been extinguished. Fortunately, there were no fatalities or injuries."

Taiwanese students rank 3rd worldwide in academic performance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
05:52:02 UTC
14:52:02 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwanese students ranked third worldwide in an overall comparison of 15-year-olds' academic performance based on the latest international education assessment.
Taiwan scored an average of 531.3 points across mathematics, science, and reading in the 2025 Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA), according to a ranking published Saturday by Visual Capitalist. China's participating regions of Beijing, Shanghai, Jiangsu, and Zhejiang topped the list with 578.7 points, followed by Singapore with 552.7.
Taiwan placed fourth in mathematics with 546 points, behind China (612), Singapore (563), and Macao (549). It also ranked fourth in science with 540 points, trailing China (597), Singapore (560), and Macao (541).
In reading, Taiwan scored 508 points, placing third behind Singapore (535) and China's participating regions (527). Japan ranked fourth with 503 points, while South Korea and Macao tied for fifth with 501 points each.
The ranking is based on the OECD's PISA 2025 results, released in September, covering mathematics, science, and reading. Visual Capitalist calculated the overall standings by taking the equally weighted average of each education system's scores in the three subjects.
Macao ranked fourth overall with 530.3 points, followed by Japan in fifth place with 522 points. South Korea ranked sixth with 516.3, followed by Estonia with 511.3, Hong Kong with 499.3, the UK with 497.7, and New Zealand with 495.3. Canada placed 11th with 495 points, while the US ranked 16th with 485.
The OECD assessment involved more than 760,000 students across 91 countries and economies, representing approximately 33 million 15-year-olds. The tests assess students' knowledge and their ability to apply what they have learned in real-world situations.
The OECD identified Taiwan, Estonia, Japan, Korea, Singapore, and the UK among the education systems that ranked in the top 10 across all three subjects. Average scores across OECD member countries were 482 in science, 463 in mathematics, and 461 in reading.
Compared with 2022, Taiwan's science score rose by two points, while mathematics fell by one point and reading by seven points, although none of the changes were statistically significant. The OECD said global academic performance had largely stagnated or continued to decline in many education systems following the unprecedented drop recorded in 2022.
Taiwan also ranked fifth in computational problem-solving, scoring 551 points, behind Macao (572), Singapore (563), China's participating regions (560), and Japan (557). The assessment measures students' ability to use block-based programming and computer modeling, conduct experiments, analyze data, and build or debug digital creations.
The OECD's country note for Taiwan found that 87% of Taiwanese students achieved at least Level 2 proficiency in science, compared with the OECD average of 74%. Meanwhile, 20% reached the top two proficiency levels (Levels 5 and 6), nearly three times the OECD average of 7%, demonstrating their ability to apply scientific knowledge to unfamiliar situations.
In reading, Taiwan was one of only three education systems where the proportion of girls among top performers exceeded that of boys by more than five percentage points, alongside New Zealand and Singapore. Taiwan also saw its science gender gap widen between 2022 and 2025, with girls' average scores rising by 10 points while boys' scores fell by four points.

Taiwan expands free flu and COVID-19 vaccinations to those aged 50-64
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
05:51:38 UTC
14:51:38 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Publicly funded flu and COVID-19 vaccinations for adults aged 50 to 64 without high-risk chronic conditions have begun, with recipients eligible to receive health coins.
The government has expanded its vaccination program, which began in October alongside the launch of the health coin incentive scheme. Health authorities report vaccination rates in the first phase increased 11% to 35% compared with the same period last year, with pneumococcal vaccination rates rising 2.4 to 3.5 times, per CNA.
The Centers for Disease Control urged eligible residents to get their influenza shots as soon as possible to ensure adequate protection before flu activity reaches its seasonal peak.
Health authorities have procured both single-dose and multidose formulations of Moderna's COVID-19 vaccine. The single-dose formulation, intended for people aged 12 and older, has been upgraded to a newer-generation vaccine containing one-fifth the antigen dose of its predecessor.
Real-world data indicate that post-vaccination discomfort has been reduced by approximately half, while clinical studies show a stronger immune response than the previous-generation vaccine, the CDC said.
The health coin program awards people over 18 years old 450 coins for a flu vaccination and 900 for a COVID-19 vaccination, allowing people who receive both to collect 1,350 coins. The coins can be redeemed for health-related products beginning Dec. 1, per a CDC press release.
The CDC also urged the public to maintain good hygiene, including frequent handwashing, wearing masks when appropriate, and staying home when sick.
People experiencing warning signs such as shortness of breath, difficulty breathing, bluish skin discoloration, bloody sputum, chest pain, altered consciousness, or low blood pressure should seek immediate medical attention. Doctors can assess whether antiviral treatment is appropriate.

“Trust isn’t earned by what you say in good times. It’s earned by what you do in hard times,” he added.
Meanwhile, Binance said a new Proof of Reserves snapshot had been taken at 00:00 UTC on October 31, with zero-knowledge proof calculations underway. The updated report was expected to be published on November 2.

Binance also maintained that market conditions remained stable.

Tivoli extends Christmas season into January 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
05:46:35 UTC
14:46:35 KST

The Danish government hopes to allow wolf hunting as early as 2027. Researchers will now determine how large the country’s wolf population needs to be to remain viable.
Denmark is taking another step towards allowing wolves to be hunted, after EU rules protecting the species were relaxed last year.
The government has commissioned work to determine how many wolves Denmark needs to maintain a stable and viable population in the long term.
At the same time, authorities want to introduce more precise monitoring using DNA to identify individual wolves.
Nature and Animal Welfare Minister Christian Rabjerg Madsen of the Social Democrats said the scientific work could pave the way for hunting as early as 2027.
“We need a population model in place. It is a step towards being able to regulate – that is, hunt wolves in Denmark,” he said.
The Agency for Green Land Transformation and Water Environment (SGAV) will put the development of the population model out to public tender. A separate tender will cover individual monitoring of wolves.
At least 49 adult wolves
Denmark does not currently have an exact count of its wolf population.
In spring 2026, researchers from the Natural History Museum Aarhus and Aarhus University estimated that there were at least 49 adult wolves in Denmark.
The government now wants a more precise assessment based on DNA, making it possible to identify individual animals.
“We need a scientific count of the wolves, and we need a model for a minimum population,” Rabjerg Madsen said.
Once that work has been completed, the government hopes it will provide the scientific basis for introducing regulated hunting.
EU rules on wolves were relaxed in 2025
Wolves remain protected under EU law, but their protection status was changed in 2025.
The species was moved from Annex IV to Annex V of the EU Habitats Directive, changing its status from “strictly protected” to “protected”.
The change gives EU countries greater flexibility to manage their wolf populations, including through hunting.
However, it does not mean Denmark can simply introduce unrestricted wolf hunting.
Any hunting or population management must be compatible with maintaining the wolf at what EU rules call a “favourable conservation status”.
Determining that status involves more than simply counting wolves. Authorities must also consider factors including the population’s geographical range, habitat and long-term prospects.
The population model being commissioned by the Danish authorities is expected to be ready during 2027.
Minister hopes for hunting in 2027
Rabjerg Madsen said his ambition is to allow wolf hunting that same year.
“It is my ambition that we can have wolf hunting in 2027, because that is when we will start getting the numbers,” he said.
“My expectation is that they will show that we have a viable wolf population and that we therefore can have hunting of the wolf.”
Asked whether he was anticipating the researchers’ conclusion before the calculations had been made, the minister said the outcome would have to remain within the scientific and international rules governing Denmark.
“I have been very careful to say that it is my assessment and hope that we have a viable wolf population, so that we can have wolf hunting within the scientific boundaries we are committed to by international rules,” he said.
Individual wolves can already be killed under certain circumstances in Denmark. This can include wolves that repeatedly attack livestock protected by approved wolf-proof fencing or animals that display an abnormal lack of fear of humans.

UN peacekeeping mission in Western Sahara ends after 35 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
05:46:31 UTC
14:46:31 KST

The United Nations is withdrawing its peacekeeping mission from Western Sahara after the Security Council failed to agree on renewing its mandate, ending a 35-year presence in the disputed territory.
UN Secretary-General António Guterres announced Sunday that the mission, known as Minurso, had entered a “winding-down phase” beginning November 1, Reuters reported.
Equipment will now be returned to countries that contributed personnel to the operation.
Minurso was established in 1991 following a UN-brokered ceasefire between Morocco and the Polisario Front, an independence movement backed by Algeria.
Morocco claims sovereignty over Western Sahara, while Polisario has sought independence since Spain withdrew from the territory in 1976.
Morocco welcomed the mission’s closure, but Polisario expressed concern.
The decision follows disagreements within the Security Council over the territory’s future.
Last year, the council adopted a U.S.-drafted resolution describing Morocco’s proposal for autonomy under Moroccan sovereignty as the “most achievable” solution to the conflict.
Russia abstained from that vote but vetoed a new U.S.-backed resolution this year that would have strengthened support for Morocco’s proposal while reducing the peacekeeping force.
A subsequent Russian proposal also failed to secure approval, leaving Minurso’s mandate to expire.
According to UN figures from June, 41 countries contributed military or police personnel to the mission, with Egypt, Ghana and Pakistan among the largest contributors.
Minurso was responsible for monitoring the ceasefire and organizing a referendum on Western Sahara’s future.
However, the referendum never took place because the parties could not agree on who would be eligible to vote.

====================================================================================================

Judge tosses Trump attempt to block Alaska vote results if Republican loses
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
05:46:18 UTC
14:46:18 KST

(Reuters) -- A federal judge on Sunday threw out a lawsuit by President Donald Trump's administration seeking to block Alaska from certifying a loss by Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Tuesday's midterm elections if votes for a rival who shares his name could have changed the outcome.
The ruling by U.S. District Judge Sharon Gleason in Anchorage was the latest blow to Trump's efforts to assert a greater federal role in elections, which under the U.S. Constitution are administered by the states.
Democratic former U.S. Rep. Mary Peltola is challenging Sullivan in the race, whose outcome could prove critical for determining whether Trump's fellow Republicans can retain control of the Senate in the midterms. Democrats need a net gain of at least four seats in November's midterm elections to gain control of the Senate.
Alaska's ballot features the names of the incumbent senator, Daniel S. Sullivan, and Peltola, as well as a retired teacher whose name is Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., and another long-shot candidate.
Peltola has denied involvement in any effort to recruit Daniel J. Sullivan, who lives in a remote fishing village, to enter the race, saying at a rally that she is "not interested in tricking voters." The retired teacher has denied in interviews with U.S. news outlets that his aim is to cause confusion, but has said he would prefer Peltola winning over the incumbent senator.
In her decision, Gleason wrote that the administration's proposal to segregate ballots would violate the right of voters in Alaska to a secret ballot, and dismissed the case on the basis that the federal government lacked the necessary legal standing to bring it.
"The United States provides no workable plan as to how it proposes to segregate ballots cast for Daniel J. Sullivan on Election Day and then conduct a court-ordered unspecified 'investigation' of those ballots in a manner that would preserve voter secrecy," Gleason wrote, referring to the Trump administration's lawsuit.
The Justice Department said in a court filing it intends to appeal the ruling. In a statement, it said the judge's order dismissing the lawsuit was on procedural grounds. Alaskan voters deserve a fair election, not to be misled "in an attempt to rig outcomes," the Justice Department said.
Alaska's elections division welcomed the ruling, saying it rejected a last-minute administration effort to intervene in the election and allows the state to focus on administering a fair vote while protecting ballot secrecy.
The American Civil Liberties Union, which intervened in the lawsuit in support of Alaska, said the judge rebuffed a Justice Department effort to "throw out Alaska's election results before a single ballot was counted."
"This administration keeps trying to tilt the midterms, and today (Sunday) it lost again," the ACLU said.
The administration has taken an increasingly aggressive approach to election oversight, pressing states for voter-registration data and arguing that stricter measures are needed to ensure public confidence in the vote. Critics, including Democratic and some Republican election officials, view the moves as federal overreach.
The lawsuit filed by the Justice Department on Oct. 22 challenged the candidacy of the retired teacher. According to the lawsuit, he is running "with the intention of misleading supporters of Senator Sullivan into voting for him." The administration said that certifying the election could violate the federal government's duty to protect the integrity of elections.
The suit sought to temporarily bar Alaska election officials from certifying a Peltola victory in the event that assigning all of Daniel J. Sullivan's votes to the incumbent would have changed the results. The lawsuit said that, in such a scenario, Gleason should investigate whether voters who selected Daniel J. Sullivan had instead intended to support the incumbent.
The New York Times reported on Oct. 28 that Peltola campaign staff members had worked with a Democratic operative from Ohio to find another Dan Sullivan to run to peel votes from the Republican senator. Reuters has not verified the report.
It is not clear what, if any, laws may have been broken. Both parties have engaged in "ballot stacking" by propping up lesser-known candidates to siphon votes from their opponents.
Trump, who has told reporters he ordered the Justice Department to file the lawsuit, has called for Peltola to be criminally prosecuted. The Justice Department has brought criminal charges against a number of Trump's adversaries.
Peltola's campaign had called the lawsuit meritless.

Copenhagen kiosk inspections uncover violations at 21 of 22 businesses

14:46:17 KST

The Danish government hopes to allow wolf hunting as early as 2027. Researchers will now determine how large the country’s wolf population needs to be to remain viable.
Denmark is taking another step towards allowing wolves to be hunted, after EU rules protecting the species were relaxed last year.
The government has commissioned work to determine how many wolves Denmark needs to maintain a stable and viable population in the long term.
At the same time, authorities want to introduce more precise monitoring using DNA to identify individual wolves.
Nature and Animal Welfare Minister Christian Rabjerg Madsen of the Social Democrats said the scientific work could pave the way for hunting as early as 2027.
“We need a population model in place. It is a step towards being able to regulate – that is, hunt wolves in Denmark,” he said.
The Agency for Green Land Transformation and Water Environment (SGAV) will put the development of the population model out to public tender. A separate tender will cover individual monitoring of wolves.
At least 49 adult wolves
Denmark does not currently have an exact count of its wolf population.
In spring 2026, researchers from the Natural History Museum Aarhus and Aarhus University estimated that there were at least 49 adult wolves in Denmark.
The government now wants a more precise assessment based on DNA, making it possible to identify individual animals.
“We need a scientific count of the wolves, and we need a model for a minimum population,” Rabjerg Madsen said.
Once that work has been completed, the government hopes it will provide the scientific basis for introducing regulated hunting.
EU rules on wolves were relaxed in 2025
Wolves remain protected under EU law, but their protection status was changed in 2025.
The species was moved from Annex IV to Annex V of the EU Habitats Directive, changing its status from “strictly protected” to “protected”.
The change gives EU countries greater flexibility to manage their wolf populations, including through hunting.
However, it does not mean Denmark can simply introduce unrestricted wolf hunting.
Any hunting or population management must be compatible with maintaining the wolf at what EU rules call a “favourable conservation status”.
Determining that status involves more than simply counting wolves. Authorities must also consider factors including the population’s geographical range, habitat and long-term prospects.
The population model being commissioned by the Danish authorities is expected to be ready during 2027.
Minister hopes for hunting in 2027
Rabjerg Madsen said his ambition is to allow wolf hunting that same year.
“It is my ambition that we can have wolf hunting in 2027, because that is when we will start getting the numbers,” he said.
“My expectation is that they will show that we have a viable wolf population and that we therefore can have hunting of the wolf.”
Asked whether he was anticipating the researchers’ conclusion before the calculations had been made, the minister said the outcome would have to remain within the scientific and international rules governing Denmark.
“I have been very careful to say that it is my assessment and hope that we have a viable wolf population, so that we can have wolf hunting within the scientific boundaries we are committed to by international rules,” he said.
Individual wolves can already be killed under certain circumstances in Denmark. This can include wolves that repeatedly attack livestock protected by approved wolf-proof fencing or animals that display an abnormal lack of fear of humans.
Sources: Ritzau, European Commission and Agency for Green Land Transformation and Water Environment (SGAV)

How Surface Materials Shape Contemporary Interiors
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
05:45:00 UTC
14:45:00 KST

Whether in residential interiors, workplaces, hospitality environments, or public spaces, the relationship between aesthetic intentions and technical performance can redefine how surfaces are used and how they perform. A material selected for its specific color, texture, or finish must remain visually coherent when applied to furniture fronts, cabinetry, countertops, and other interior elements. Yet how can architects and designers create visually distinctive and tactilely engaging interiors while preserving their original design intentions across different applications?
The choice of surface materials influences the user experience in ways that extend beyond the visual appearance of a space. Each material has its own characteristics and proportions, allowing it to establish specific relationships with other architectural elements. Material compatibility, specification reliability, and maintenance requirements must also be considered to develop a cohesive design language across a range of applications. Given the frequency and nature of use, each surface material must meet specific functional requirements while retaining its original appearance and remaining consistent with the design principles that define the project.
Rather than treating each surface as an independent design decision, EGGER has developed its PerfectSense portfolio as an integrated solution that combines lacquered finishes, coordinated materials, and specification support. The system enables architects and designers to establish a unified material language while maintaining flexibility across different applications.
Exploring the Relationship Between Visual Depth and Tactile Experience
Material perception extends beyond what the eye can recognize. The interaction between light, texture, reflectivity, and touch contributes to the atmosphere of an interior space, influencing how surfaces convey depth, warmth, and material character. In this context, matte finishes have become an architectural resource that offers a restrained visual expression while allowing variations in texture and color to define spatial relationships.
Within the Decorative Collection 26+, EGGER's PerfectSense Premium Ambiance textures introduce an approach that combines velvety matte surfaces with decor-specific partial gloss effects. Its synchronized visual and tactile textures allow different areas of the surface to reflect light according to the underlying pattern, reinforcing the perception of material depth. For example, the F128 PA Black Ambiance Granite and the F129 PA Beige Ambiance Granite decors integrate glossy areas within predominantly matte surfaces, creating subtle contrasts that become visible as lighting conditions and viewing angles change. The coordination between printed pattern and surface texture also introduces a tactile dimension, encouraging a more sensory experience of the material.
Meanwhile, the F199 PA Black Ambiance Marble decor explores a different expression through a super-matte black surface complemented by golden veining. The finish, recognized with an iF Design Award in 2026 in the Product Design category, demonstrates how decorative surfaces can reinterpret natural materials while introducing specific visual and functional characteristics. These variations provide architects with opportunities to develop interiors through contrasts in reflectivity, material appearance, and tactile perception. Instead of relying solely on color differences, surfaces can contribute to spatial definition through subtle changes in light and texture.
From Material Selection to a Consistent Architectural Language
While individual finishes establish a project's material identity, maintaining that identity across different architectural components presents another challenge. A surface specified for cabinetry may require a different substrate or technical configuration when used for countertops, furniture bodies, or edging. EGGER's Decor Match system coordinates decorative finishes across different product formats. Depending on the selected design, architects can specify lacquered MDF boards, particleboards, laminates, worktops, and matching ABS edging, supporting continuity between vertical and horizontal applications. The EGGER Decorative Collection 26+ includes 25 solid-color decors, eight of which are new additions, available in coordinated PM PerfectSense Premium Matt solutions for lacquered MDF boards, laminates, and ABS edging, alongside TM PerfectSense Matt particleboard options.
Material coordination allows designers to select products according to their intended function without necessarily changing the established visual language. Cabinet fronts, furniture bodies, and horizontal surfaces can therefore respond to different technical requirements while contributing to a coherent interior composition. Beyond aesthetics, consistency also depends on predictability throughout the design and construction process. Industrial manufacturing supports reproducible surface quality, while access to samples, technical information, and supporting services helps architects evaluate finishes before finalizing specifications. Long-term decor availability further contributes to planning reliability, particularly for larger developments or projects implemented in successive phases.
Equally important is the relationship between appearance and everyday performance. The anti-fingerprint properties of PerfectSense matte lacquered surfaces help reduce visible marks and cleaning requirements, making them suitable for frequently touched elements and regularly occupied environments. Their easy-care characteristics connect refined surface aesthetics with practical maintenance considerations.
The value of a coordinated material portfolio lies in its ability to connect creative decisions with their physical implementation. From individual rooms to larger interior projects, EGGER's PerfectSense portfolio illustrates how a consistent surface system can support architectural expression while reducing uncertainty between concept and execution. Its combination of coordinated decors, application-specific products, and accessible specification resources offers a framework for developing interiors in which visual identity, functionality, and material consistency remain closely aligned. Exploring the available decors, requesting physical samples, and reviewing technical documentation can become essential steps in establishing a material strategy that remains consistent from initial selection to everyday use.

Australians urged to take care with raw seafood as 60 pct consume it

14:41:58 KST

CANBERRA, Nov. 2 (Xinhua) -- About 60 percent of Australians consume raw fish or seafood, with 17 percent eating it at least weekly, prompting food safety experts to warn of the risks of foodborne illnesses and parasites.
Ahead of Australian Food Safety Week, running from Nov. 7 to 14, the Food Safety Information Council released research on Monday showing that raw seafood consumption is widespread, including in dishes such as sushi, sashimi and ceviche, which can pose food safety risks, including from parasites.
Council Scientific Director Julian Cox said raw fish could carry parasites and harmful bacteria, while traditional additions such as vinegar, lemon juice or salt would not reliably kill the infectious stages of parasites, destroy toxins or kill pathogens.
The research found that 18 percent of respondents prepared raw fish dishes using purchased fish, while 5 percent used fish they had caught themselves. Another 4 percent bought pre-made raw fish dishes through social media vendors, who may be unregulated.
Cox warned that pregnant women, the elderly and those with weaker immune systems should avoid raw fish dishes, cold cooked prawns and cold-smoked fish because of the potential risk of Listeria infection, which can be fatal.
He advised consumers preparing raw fish to source it from reputable suppliers and ensure it had been appropriately handled and frozen to control parasites. Recreationally caught fish should be cooked thoroughly.
The online survey was conducted among 1,239 Australians aged 18 and over from Aug. 26 to 31. ■

====================================================================================================

Explainer: How AI muddies the waters ahead of U.S. midterm elections?
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
13:41:58 CST
14:41:58 KST

WASHINGTON, Nov. 2 (Xinhua) -- AI-driven disinformation is flooding voters' feeds as the United States heads toward its Nov. 3 midterm elections.
"AI is making its way into the 2026 midterms in a big way this year," said the Wesleyan Media Project, which tracks AI-generated political advertising.
Earlier in October, the project said it had identified 220 such advertisements worth more than 137 million U.S. dollars -- a staggering increase from 50,000 dollars during the 2024 election cycle, and an "almost certainly" low estimate given the difficulty in detecting the use of AI.
With much of this content carrying no disclosure that AI had been used, analysts warned that it could mislead voters and undermine the integrity of elections.
AI ADS AND LIES
Some AI-generated advertisements have been particularly provocative, such as one showing a Republican candidate for governor embracing Hillary Clinton, cheek to cheek and hand in hand, beneath the slogan "Clinton Lover. Trump Hater."
Others have gone even further. One depicted Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed laughing at cards that read "Death to America" and "Celebrate 9/11." Another showed James Fishback, a Republican primary candidate for Florida governor, hosting a party with Iranian leaders who used scimitars to attack the Star of David, a recognized symbol of Jewish identity and the religion of Judaism.
"You can run an information operation now with quality that was impossible in 2016 for super, super cheap," said Frances Haugen, a former Facebook data engineer turned whistleblower and advocate for transparency and accountability in big tech.
Those seeking to spread disinformation can get around content moderation rules "because you can just keep tweaking the post a little bit each time you create them, and some of them are going to get through," she said.
Meanwhile, a survey by the American Association of Political Consultants Foundation found that though only 1 percent of respondents considered AI their most credible source of election information, one in five voters plans to use AI to look into a race on their ballot.
Twice that proportion has already received election details through an AI search summary, according to the survey.
A cottage industry has quickly emerged, advising candidates on how to shape what AI says about them.
The left-wing advocacy group Run for Something has launched CampSight, a platform that tracks what large language models say about issues or candidates and recommends ways to shape those narratives. On the right, the Center for Campaign Innovation (CCI) has published research on how AI models respond to questions about candidates and which sources they cite most frequently.
"We're campaigning for the AI vote now," Eric Wilson, executive director of the CCI, told The Atlantic, an American magazine and multi-platform publisher.
LOBBYING AGAINST REGULATION
The AI giants, however, are pouring millions of dollars into lobbying to block unfavorable legislation and shape the political landscape ahead of the midterm elections.
The Wall Street Journal reported last year that Silicon Valley was channeling more than 100 million dollars into a network of political-action committees (PACs) and advocacy groups to fend off stringent AI regulation and defend the industry's interests in the midterm elections.
Among the biggest efforts is Leading the Future, a super PAC backed by OpenAI President Greg Brockman and venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz.
The group reportedly spent 8 million dollars seeking to unseat Democratic New York State Assemblymember Alex Bores in a congressional primary, targeting him over his sponsorship of the RAISE Act, an AI safety bill signed into law last December.
It came amid Washington's continued efforts to stop or limit state-level AI legislation.
In 2025, a group of Republican senators proposed a moratorium on state AI laws as part of budget reconciliation, following a last-minute lobbying push by tech groups eager to roll back rules they saw as barriers to unfettered innovation.
Though the Senate rejected that proposal, related preemption efforts continued to emerge in other forms.
In December, U.S. President Donald Trump issued an executive order establishing an AI litigation task force to challenge state laws deemed more than "minimally burdensome" and directing the Commerce Department to consider withholding federal broadband funds from states with "onerous" AI regulations.
DISINFORMED VOTERS
Analysts warned that undisclosed AI advertisements can manufacture alternate facts, making it harder for voters to distinguish reality from falsehoods.
Susan Hyde, a professor of Political Science at UC Berkeley, said the deeper concern is whether voters could make informed decisions when they could no longer trust the information they receive.
"Classical theorists of democracy focus on the necessity for citizens to be informed about their choices in order to make an educated choice about who to vote for," Hyde said. "The other thing that's interesting is the ease with which politicians can use propaganda-style communication and lie to their supporters directly."
Similarly, the Brennan Center for Justice said transparency and human oversight are lagging behind AI's rapid development, adding that its research offers a glimpse of how deepfakes, readily enabled by chatbots, could become "potent tools for electoral cheaters."
It found that chatbots like ChatGPT, Gemini and Grok failed to decline requests to generate images playing on familiar election conspiracies, such as election workers stuffing ballot boxes or large numbers of non-U.S. citizens voting.
"We can't have a robust debate or fair electoral decisions if we cannot trust the information by which we vote and with which elections are run," the center said. "Policymakers need to act quickly to find ways to curb the bots' tendency to create or ignore election disinformation." ■
