Bangladesh garment factories reopen, fresh clashes keep industry on edge
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
06:41:47 CET
14:41:47 KST

By Ruma Paul
DHAKA, Nov 2 (Reuters) - Bangladesh’s garment factories reopened on Monday, but fresh clashes between police and workers demanding higher wages broke out in Dhaka and nearby industrial hubs, keeping manufacturers on edge after Sunday’s widespread closures.
More unrest erupted across Dhaka and key industrial areas on Monday, police said, adding that they used tear gas to disperse garment workers trying to block roads in the capital after protesters hurled bricks and stones.
The ready-made garment sector accounts for more than 80% of Bangladesh’s export earnings. It employs about 4 million workers and accounts for about 10% of the country’s economic output.
The latest unrest disrupted operations in key manufacturing hubs and raised concerns over export shipments and buyer confidence in Bangladesh, the world’s second-largest apparel exporter after China and a major supplier to global brands such as H&M, Zara, Walmart and Primark, as workers demanded a minimum monthly wage of 30,000 taka ($243), up from 12,500 taka.
The government formed a six-member minimum wage board on Sunday to review the demand, which reflects mounting pressure from living costs and persistent inflation.
VIOLENCE CONTINUES
In Ashulia and Gazipur, on the outskirts of the capital, workers tried to block major highways. Police fired tear gas and water cannon in Ashulia, and authorities deployed Border Guard Bangladesh personnel in Gazipur.
The clashes follow Sunday’s protests and factory closures, with workers continuing to demand higher wages and the resolution of employment grievances.
“Bangladesh has among the lowest garment wages in the world,” said Babul Akhter, general secretary of the Bangladesh Garment and Industrial Workers Federation and a workers’ representative on the wage board.
“If factory owners cannot pay workers properly, they should negotiate better prices with international buyers. They cannot build a business on the backs of underpaid workers.”
‘NO WORK, NO PAY’ PROVISION
Factory owners said the industry faces higher costs, energy market uncertainty linked to conflict in the Middle East and slowing demand in key export markets.
The Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association said demonstrations in multiple cities disrupted operations at 529 factories on Sunday and affected nearly 1 million workers.
BGMEA President Mahmud Hasan Khan said workers should let the government’s wage board carry out its review.
“If protests break out later in the day and we are forced to shut factories, we will have no option but to invoke the ‘no work, no pay’ provision,” he said.
Home Affairs Minister Salahuddin Ahmed warned of firm action against those orchestrating the violence after a meeting with garment industry leaders.
“Those acting against workers’ interests under the guise of labour protests and attempting to destabilise the country will be dealt with firmly,” he said.
Selim Raihan, an economics professor at the University of Dhaka, said that workers’ demands were understandable given high inflation and that there could be further unrest.
On the other hand, he said a substantial wage increase could raise production costs, squeeze exporters’ profit margins and weaken Bangladesh’s price competitiveness.
“A phased wage adjustment, improved productivity and fairer pricing from international buyers are essential to balancing workers’ welfare with industrial sustainability,” he said.
($1 = 123.30 taka)
(Reporting by Ruma Paul; Editing by Hugh Lawson)

Trump looks for a scapegoat as Iran war drags on, questions Hegseth and Caine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
05:31:21 UTC
14:31:21 KST

U.S. President Donald Trump is considering resuming military strikes against Iran immediately after Tuesday's congressional midterm elections, while privately questioning the performance of two of his most senior defense advisers as he searches for someone to blame for the prolonged war and its political consequences. The Atlantic reported Sunday that Trump has begun asking allies about Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Gen. Dan Caine, chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, who have played central roles in directing the campaign against Iran.
Trump also threatened Iran with further military action during a campaign rally in Iowa on Sunday night. The president said he had held back from further attacks because he wanted to avoid additional casualties. "I want to try and save all those lives if I can," he told supporters, warning that at some point the United States would have to "give them the hammer."
According to The Atlantic, whose reporting was based partly on conversations with two outside advisers close to Trump and administration officials, the president is increasingly frustrated that the war has continued for more than eight months despite assurances from his advisers that it would be short, decisive and over well before the midterm elections. With Republicans facing the possibility of losing control of the House of Representatives and potentially the Senate, Trump has come to believe that the conflict with Iran is at least partly responsible for his political difficulties.
Much of the criticism has focused on Hegseth, whom some people close to the president accuse of presenting an excessively optimistic assessment of the war to maintain Trump's approval. "Hegseth is good at telling the president what he wants to hear," one outside adviser told The Atlantic. Sources close to Trump suggested that the defense secretary has failed to fully convey the difficulties facing U.S. forces. The Pentagon strongly rejected those allegations. 
Spokesperson Sean Parnell said Hegseth consistently provides the president and senior White House officials with a complete picture of military operations and dismissed suggestions otherwise as false. The White House also defended both officials, with spokesperson Anna Kelly saying Trump and his team retain full confidence in Hegseth and Caine and that both are working to carry out the president's objectives.
Against this backdrop of growing tensions within the defense establishment, Hegseth and Caine visited the White House last week to present Trump and Vice President JD Vance with a range of military options intended to create the conditions for the president to declare victory. Adm. Brad Cooper, commander of U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM), which oversees American military operations in the Middle East, also visited the White House last week. According to current and former U.S. defense officials who spoke to The Atlantic, the options include a limited strike lasting several hours, a military operation lasting several days or a broader campaign extending over several weeks. Trump could also maintain the American naval blockade in the Strait of Hormuz while continuing to threaten renewed strikes, or decide against any further escalation.
Supporters of renewed military action believe the economic pressure on Tehran is beginning to work and that additional strikes could force the Iranian government back to the negotiating table. One proposal involves an extended campaign against Iranian air defenses and infrastructure, similar to the initial phase of the war before U.S. attacks shifted toward Iranian forces operating around the Strait of Hormuz. According to the report, Washington would be expected to argue that infrastructure targeted in such an operation serves both military and civilian purposes. Such attacks, however, could endanger civilians and potentially violate international humanitarian law. Another proposal calls for a campaign lasting several days against Iran's nuclear program.
Officials within the Trump administration expect Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to support renewed attacks, given his backing for the war and his belief that continued confrontation with Iran could help him retain political power. The Atlantic noted, however, that Netanyahu's political future remains uncertain following Israel's elections last week. Even a large-scale offensive would not necessarily force Tehran to surrender. The Iranian government could survive another round of strikes and portray its continued survival as a victory. According to the magazine, the limited American strikes carried out since the extended military campaign that began in late February have failed to secure Iranian concessions. Instead, they have hardened Tehran's position and prompted retaliatory attacks against American assets and U.S. allies in the region. A renewed campaign would also further deplete American munitions stockpiles.
Michael Cohen, a researcher at the Washington-based Stimson Center, warned that another unsuccessful round of attacks could expose the limitations of American military power. If Tehran continues to reject Washington's demands despite additional strikes, he argued, the administration would have to confront the question of whether to continue escalating the conflict, even after demonstrating that military pressure alone had failed to achieve its objectives.
Alongside the military preparations, diplomatic efforts to bring Iran back to negotiations are continuing. According to The Atlantic, Vance sent a letter last Sunday to Mohsen Rezaei, a senior Iranian security official, proposing the resumption of direct talks between Washington and Tehran. The vice president emphasized that Iran's nuclear program would have to be addressed from the beginning of any negotiations, but did not specify what concessions or incentives the United States might offer in return.
International mediators who delivered the letter sought to arrange a meeting later this week, around the time Trump is expected to decide whether to resume military operations. However, the prospect of renewed negotiations has also generated skepticism within the administration, after previous attempts to use military pressure to secure an agreement failed to produce the desired results.
The military proposals also offer no clear solution to the threats posed by Iran's regional allies and proxy groups, particularly the Houthis in Yemen, who have recently attacked targets in Saudi Arabia. Eliminating the threat from Iranian-backed groups was among the objectives Trump outlined at the beginning of the war. The economic consequences are another source of concern, as renewed American strikes could drive oil prices higher and place additional pressure on the U.S. economy and Washington's allies. One administration official told The Atlantic that Trump's recent shift in his approach toward Ukraine was partly motivated by a desire to allow more Russian energy supplies to reach international markets, potentially limiting the impact of renewed fighting in the Middle East on global energy prices.
The plans have also drawn criticism in Congress. Democratic Sen. Chris Murphy, who was briefed on some of the military options, described them last week as "insane." He warned that the proposals could trigger devastating escalation and seriously undermine the United States' commitment to the rule of law.
Three polygraph tests and a firing: Turmoil at the Pentagon
As Trump considers his next steps against Iran, tensions within the Pentagon are intensifying following a series of dismissals of senior military officers ordered by Hegseth. Last week, the defense secretary unexpectedly fired Army Lt. Gen. Brett Sylvia, one of the most senior officers on the Joint Staff and its director of planning. 
According to officials working with Hegseth, Sylvia failed polygraph examinations conducted as part of an investigation into leaks to the media. The defense secretary had ordered him to undergo at least three such tests following reports that disclosed details of White House discussions and ammunition shortages resulting from the war in Iran. Sylvia has not publicly responded to the allegations, and The Atlantic said it was unable to reach him for comment.
Hegseth believes the Joint Staff, which reports to Caine, has a serious problem with unauthorized disclosures. According to the report, Caine did not strongly challenge that assessment, although he appeared to have been unaware of some of the circumstances surrounding Sylvia's dismissal. Initially, Caine's office issued a statement thanking Sylvia for 32 years of military service. After receiving further information from the defense secretary's team, the office released a revised statement acknowledging that the original announcement had not accurately reflected the full circumstances of his departure.
According to The Atlantic, Hegseth has sought to strengthen his standing with Trump by portraying himself as someone determined to protect the president against damaging leaks. Some Pentagon officials suspect Sylvia's dismissal was intended to weaken the influence of the Joint Staff at precisely the moment Trump is reassessing the performance of his advisers and the outcome of the war. Hegseth has already dismissed or forced the departure of more than two dozen generals and admirals. The latest removal has fueled unease within the Pentagon, where senior officers are questioning who might be next and what message the defense secretary is attempting to send.
The report describes Trump's frustration as having intensified in recent weeks, particularly as his political messaging has failed to improve the Republicans' standing ahead of the midterms. Within the White House, concerns have grown that the party could lose its House majority and perhaps control of the Senate as well. Having previously declared victory in the war against Iran, Trump is now trying to understand why promises of a swift and decisive outcome have not materialized. The Atlantic portrays the president as looking for someone to hold responsible, with particular attention falling on those who assured him at the outset that the conflict would be quickly resolved.
Nevertheless, Republican losses in Tuesday's elections would not necessarily reduce the likelihood of renewed attacks. The magazine pointed to the 2006 U.S. midterm elections, when Republicans lost control of both chambers of Congress amid widespread public dissatisfaction with the Iraq war. President George W. Bush subsequently blamed Defense Secretary Donald Rumsfeld for the defeat and forced him from office. Yet just two months later, Bush ordered a major increase in American troop levels in Iraq, escalating the military campaign rather than bringing it to an end.
As of the report's publication, Trump had not ordered the resumption of strikes against Iran. According to people close to him, even if he decides to launch another offensive, he may keep that decision secret until the last possible moment. The central question now facing the president is whether the advisers who once promised him a quick victory can offer a new strategy capable of delivering a different outcome.

Country diary: As winter approaches, all eyes here are on heating oil prices | Nicola Chester
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
05:30:31 UTC
14:30:31 KST

Beyond the reach of the gas mains, there is tension about the coming winter. Many rural homes have an open fire or wood burner, but most rely on kerosene oil for hot water and heating. Since the US-Iran war began, its cost has more than doubled. Currently, 1,000 litres (lasting 10-12 weeks) is £1,219. A year ago, it was £549. Seasoned wood is in demand.
We watch the oil price rise, with none of the consumer protections afforded to gas customers. If the price per litre drops, as during the June ceasefire, the village WhatsApp group lights up.
Some residents still have a back boiler system: a water tank tucked behind a fireplace that heats and circulates hot water to taps and through radiators. It is possible, if you have access to firewood, to heat your home for nothing. Until recently we supplemented our oil heating with wood we could take from the estate, until that “right” was rescinded by the gamekeeper we fell out with. But this isn’t the first time a villager has had a run-in about collecting wood.
In between rain showers we head out, past the gamekeeper’s old residence, to where the estate woodsman’s cottage once was, on the way to the former Wadsmere Common (now an unfenced field, grazed by pheasants). We step over branches felled by storms Austen and Boelo. It’s mostly ash; the best for burning.
Beside the pile of stones where the cottage stood, a tree creaks like a garden gate swinging open. “Granny” Bulpitt, as she was known, was the last occupant. Her father-in-law was the estate bailiff, and after the common and down were enclosed in 1840, he informed on villagers who persisted in collecting firewood.
To the estate owners, King’s College, Cambridge, “their” wood was lucrative commerce. Plunged into fuel poverty, the villagers took the estate to court and won, their plight taken up by the Times. But in retaliation, the estate evicted five tenant families into a severe January snowstorm, and pulled down their houses.
“Granny” Bulpitt’s associations were not forgotten. When she died in 1903, the college let the house fall to ruin. No one lives on Granny’s Lane now, except her rumoured ghost. Winter fuel is forever a contentious issue.

Why a new war on Iran could backfire on Israeli regime
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
05:30:30 UTC
14:30:30 KST

The experience of the recent war with Iran has shown that resorting to the military option against Tehran, contrary to the calculations of its architects, is not only not a guarantee for achieving political and security objectives, but can also bring heavy costs and unpredictable consequences for its initiators. Now, under conditions in which some political and military circles of the Zionist regime speak of the possibility of a new round of confrontation with Iran, the media and military figures of this regime are warning about the consequences of such a decision.
The Hebrew-language newspaper Haaretz, in a report, has emphasized that the start of a new round of conflict with Iran could be a strategic error; an error whose consequences will not be limited to Iran's borders and the occupied territories and may even involve the countries of the Persian Gulf region in a widespread crisis. This assessment shows that concern about the expansion of the scope of confrontation with Iran has become one of the serious topics in Israel's media and political circles.
In this regard, Itzhak Brik, a retired general of the Zionist regime's army, in a note in the Ma'ariv newspaper, has warned about the possibility of Donald Trump, the American president, and Benjamin Netanyahu, the prime minister of the Zionist regime, moving toward a new military action against Iran. According to Brik, if American and Israeli decision-makers move toward such an action under the influence of political calculations and domestic developments, its consequences will go far beyond a bilateral confrontation.
This retired general believes that renewed confrontation with Iran can spread the fire of crisis across the region, intensify the Zionist regime's internal problems, and place this regime in a situation from which exit will be very difficult. The importance of this warning increases when we know that Brik speaks from within Israel's military structure, and his assessment is based on an understanding of this regime's military capacities, operational limitations, and vulnerabilities.
The Costs of a Miscalculation
One of the most important lessons of the recent war with Iran is the change in Israel's and America's security calculations regarding the costs of military action against Tehran. In the past, part of the decision-making circles in Tel Aviv imagined that weapons superiority and the possession of American military support could provide the possibility of imposing will on Iran. However, practical experience showed that entering a military confrontation with Iran does not mean beginning a path whose end can be easily determined.
Iran, possessing diverse military capacities, extensive strategic geography, and the ability to use various instruments of power, has the possibility of raising the costs of action against it to a level beyond the opposing side's initial calculations. For this reason, any decision to start a new round of confrontation must be made by taking into account a set of military, security, and economic consequences; consequences whose control may slip out of the hands of the initiators of the crisis.
Under such circumstances, the issue is not only the extent of possible damage to Israel's military targets. The expansion of the scope of conflict can also affect vital infrastructure, economic centers, energy facilities, and important transportation routes in the region. The countries of the Persian Gulf region, due to their geographical position and their role in the global energy market, are vulnerable to the consequences of a widespread crisis. Any disruption in the security of this region can transfer its economic effects to global markets, energy prices, and international trade.
From this perspective, Haaretz's warning about the possibility of the crisis expanding to the Persian Gulf countries is not merely a limited security concern, but expresses the economic and geopolitical dimensions of a possible confrontation with Iran. In other words, the decision for renewed war with Tehran can impose costs on various actors that do not necessarily have a clear place in Tel Aviv's and Washington's initial calculations.
Israel's Internal Crisis; A Determining Variable
Another important point in Brik's warning is the emphasis on the effect of a possible confrontation with Iran on the internal situation of the Zionist regime. This regime faces a set of political, social, and security challenges, and any widespread military crisis can increase pressure on its political and economic structure.
Under such conditions, decision-making about entering a new confrontation may be influenced by the political considerations of Israel's leaders rather than being based on a realistic assessment of security interests and costs. Netanyahu also faces numerous pressures and challenges in the domestic political atmosphere, and this issue highlights the necessity of separating the Zionist regime's strategic interests from its government's short-term political considerations. On the other hand, America's entry into such an equation will not be cost-free either. Washington must strike a balance between supporting Israel, maintaining the security of its forces and facilities in the region, and preventing the expansion of the crisis in the Persian Gulf. The wider the scope of the confrontation becomes, the more America's political and military costs will also increase. Therefore, support for a new military action does not necessarily mean the ability to control all its consequences.
Why Is Renewed Confrontation with Iran Not Strategic?
The set of these developments shows that the main issue for Tel Aviv and Washington is not merely the possibility of starting a new military action; rather, the fundamental question is the ability to achieve the desired result and control its consequences. Starting a military operation may be technically possible, but this by no means guarantees that the desired political and security objectives will be realized.
The experience of the past eight months has also shown that Iran possesses the necessary capacity to respond and impose costs on the opposing side. This experience has made the calculations related to confrontation with Tehran more complex and has shown that Iran cannot be considered an actor that, in the face of military pressure, will suffice merely with limited and predictable reactions.
In fact, one of the most important factors of Iran's deterrence is the ability to link military capacities with geopolitical position and to influence the region's security equations. This very issue causes any military action against Iran to probably be accompanied by a set of chain consequences whose containment will not be easy for America and the Zionist regime.
Ultimately, the warnings published in Haaretz and Ma'ariv should be seen as a sign of the existence of serious concern in part of Israel's media and military circles about the costs of renewed confrontation with Iran. These warnings indicate that even within the Zionist regime, this reality has been taken into consideration that military superiority alone is not a guarantee of political and strategic victory.
For Tel Aviv and Washington, the issue is no longer merely choosing between military action and non-action; rather, it is choosing between accepting the new realities of the region and entering a crisis whose dimensions and costs may be far beyond initial predictions. From this perspective, the start of a new round of confrontation with Iran is not a display of power, but can be the beginning of a strategic error with widespread consequences for the entire region.

Herzog & de Meuron and EHDD to Transform a Mid-Century Warehouse into the Eames Institute of Infinite Curiosity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
05:30:00 UTC
14:30:00 KST

The Eames Institute of Infinite Curiosity has unveiled the masterplan for its forthcoming archives in Marin County, California. The project, designed by Swiss architects Herzog & de Meuron and Bay Area-based EHDD, transforms a mid-century modern warehouse into a cultural destination, with art installation space, flexible galleries, learning and gathering spaces, a theater, and dining offerings. The large-scale adaptive reuse project is accompanied by a transformation of the gardens and grounds of the surrounding 88.5-acre site, led by Field Operations. While the Institute's Eames Archives will form one part of the museum, its exhibitions and programming are intended to extend far beyond the work of Charles and Ray Eames, bringing together different disciplines, creative processes, and ideas.
In August 2025, the Eames Institute acquired the roadside campus in Novato, California, on the 60th anniversary of its completion. The industrial building, known for its folded, origami-like white hyperbolic paraboloid concrete roof, was designed in the 1960s by Polish-born American architect Jan Lubicz-Nycz for the office of modernist architect John Savage Bolles. It was commissioned by the McGraw-Hill publishing company as a textbook publishing, warehouse, and distribution facility. The company left the facility in 1991, and the building later served as headquarters and warehouse for Birkenstock USA. Today, the project to transform the complex into a new multidisciplinary museum by 2030 is in the first phase of the review, permitting, and approval process with the City of Novato.
With an emphasis on showing process and ideas, the Institute is collecting works ranging from industrial design and painting to monumental works of art and public sculpture, to be housed in the converted warehouse. Herzog & de Meuron's project preserves the hyperbolic paraboloid roof while integrating new building systems. The former industrial building will open to the landscape with new recessed glass facades and porches along its north and south sides. The new spaces respond to the geometry of the existing structure, with a material palette of color-stained plywood, plaster, and aluminum windows that complements the preserved concrete structure. Visitors are expected to arrive through a new exterior room carved into an existing landscape berm, the Arrival Court, where the building can be seen against an infinity-edge fountain in the foreground.
The 185,000-square-foot interior is organized as a series of interconnected experiences, starting with a wood-clad space housing admissions, the museum shop, lockers, restrooms, and elevators. A grand staircase connects to a 120-foot polished stainless steel bridge that appears to float across the warehouse, offering views into the central Great Hall and the exhibitions below. The Great Hall will be 400 feet long by 120 feet wide and will host art installations and galas. Six interconnected galleries; making and collection spaces, including wood and ceramics workshops; storage, library and resting rooms; and a 275-seat theater for performing arts, film screenings, speaker series and live concerts form the rest of the cultural spaces. The complex also includes a café, a bistro, and a fine-dining restaurant with views over the surrounding landscape.
As an extension of the museum experience, Field Operations is redesigning the exterior of the complex, drawing on Marin County's oak savannas, coastal prairies, woodlands and meadows. The firm has selected native and climate-adapted plantings to create varied landscapes connected by a network of trails. According to the architects, the landscape project builds on the original approach of landscape architect Tito Patri, whose design used layered berms to integrate the buildings into their surroundings and buffer the campus from the highway, with new and existing berms framing public gardens and gathering spaces. Field Operations also cites as a reference the Eameses' Powers of Ten, a nine-minute short documentary written and directed by the couple, which explores the relative scale of the universe.
New exterior features include native stormwater gardens and wet meadows throughout the campus to capture and filter rainwater; interactive landscape features and custom furnishings designed by Field Operations; children's play spaces drawing on the firm's work on the Bay Area's Tunnel Tops Park; a tree-filled upper court that turns a former employee parking area into a gathering space next to the museum's café, bistro and restaurant; a redesigned parking and arrival area; and large gardens to the north and south of the warehouse in place of former truck turnarounds and loading docks. An adjacent 45,000-square-foot former office building will be restored as a pavilion for retreats, lectures, seminars, and other gatherings, with meeting spaces and a large multipurpose room overlooking the warehouse roof. Behind the pavilion, a Japanese-inspired garden will incorporate historic concrete relief murals by artist Gurdon Woods, carved into the existing retaining walls.
 We have an extraordinary opportunity to rethink what a museum can be in the 21st century — not simply a place that preserves the past, but one that actively helps shape what comes next. Our goal is to create a place that makes people more curious, more connected, and more capable of imagining what comes next. By bringing art, design, making, and learning together under one roof, we aim to create a place where new ideas and unexpected connections can take shape. — John Cary, Founding President & CEO of the Eames Institute.
The Eames Institute of Infinite Curiosity was launched in 2022 as a nonprofit organization that aims to advance the design processes and problem-solving approaches of designers such as the Eames couple, equipping a new generation of creatives with tools for addressing contemporary challenges. The Institute extends the designers' approach across Northern California, adding to the material legacy of Case Study House No. 8, commonly known as the Eames House. The house was recently restored after smoke damage from the Palisades Fire in early 2025, with comprehensive cleaning and restoration work. As part of the reopening, the adjacent Eames Studio is open to the public for the first time.

According to local authorities and law enforcement officials, 3 people were killed and at least 30 more were injured, including children, UNN reports.
Details
In the Sumy region, Russians carried out 43 strikes on 15 settlements over the past day. In the Hlukhiv community, a 70-year-old woman was killed when a drone hit a car. Overall, 8 casualties were reported in the region, three of whom sought medical assistance after the October 30 attack.
In the Vinnytsia region, a Russian drone attacked the Koziatyn community. A 13-year-old girl and a woman were killed, while 6 people were injured, including 4 children. A dormitory housing internally displaced people from the Donetsk region was damaged.
Consequences of attacks in other regions
Kharkiv region. On the evening of November 1, Russians attacked the village of Vasyshcheve, likely with a Geran-3 jet-powered drone. 11 people were injured, including a 3-year-old girl. The roof of a five-story building caught fire, and private houses were damaged.
Zaporizhzhia region. As a result of Russian attacks on Zaporizhzhia and the Zaporizhzhia district, 4 people were injured. Over the course of the day, the enemy carried out numerous strikes on settlements in the region, including 21 airstrikes.
Odesa region. Russian forces attacked Odesa at night. 4 people were injured, and infrastructure facilities, 2 residential buildings and a garage were damaged.
Poltava region. In the Hradyzk community, 4 houses and cars were damaged and one person was injured as a result of a drone falling. In the Lokhvytsia community, drone debris damaged a residential building; preliminary reports indicate there were no casualties.
Rescuers, medics and law enforcement officers are working at the sites of the strikes. Information about the consequences of the attacks is being уточined.

Trump Invites Haley Stevens to Join GOP as Democrats Condemn Her ‘Betrayal’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
05:15:35 UTC
14:15:35 KST

President Donald Trump invited outgoing congresswoman Haley Stevens, a longtime Michigan Democrat, to join the Republican Party after she surprisingly endorsed her state’s GOP nominee for the U.S. Senate, Mike Rogers, in a last-minute move her partymates have called a “betrayal.”
“I don’t know Haley, I’ve never met Haley,” Trump said at a rally in Iowa on Sunday, the final weekend before the Nov. 3 midterm elections. “But Haley said what few people are willing to say. I think I’d probably—I’d love her to join the Republican Party actually.”
Stevens ran for the U.S. Senate seat herself but lost the Democratic primary to progressive Abdul El-Sayed in August. While she initially congratulated and offered her support to El-Sayed for the general election, the two have been at odds, primarily over concerns about antisemitism, which Stevens has accused El-Sayed, who is Muslim, of not denouncing strongly enough.
On Friday, Stevens demanded that El-Sayed denounce a controversial ad that blamed Michigan’s cost-of-living issues on U.S. aid to Israel. El-Sayed, whose campaign was not behind the ad though it supported his candidacy, responded with a statement that the focus of his campaign is on the “challenges Michiganders are facing” and defeating Rogers, while Stevens “seems intent on relitigating a primary that ended three months ago.” He told reporters that he did not agree with the ad’s contents but did not want to “play the condemn game” about an unaffiliated ad.
Stevens was supposed to appear with El-Sayed at a planned Democratic campaign event on Sunday, but Rep. Debbie Dingell (D, Mich.) said in an interview that before the event, she disinvited Stevens on account of her strained relationship with El-Sayed. “There’s nothing to be gained by the two of them being in the same place,” Dingell said Saturday.
On Sunday, Stevens appeared instead at an event at Perfecting Church in Detroit with Rogers. “Our Democratic nominee for Senate, Abdul, said I was no longer welcome in his campaign and that I should stay away,” Stevens said in a video posted on social media later that morning. “And he’s right. And that’s why I am endorsing Mike Rogers for the United States Senate today.”
On CNN on Sunday night, Stevens attempted to explain her move, saying it was because of El-Sayed’s “anger and lack of kindness.” She cited his past associations with controversial political influencer Hasan Piker and Piker’s uncle Cenk Uygur, whose Rebellion PAC was behind the recent anti-Israel ad. She insisted that she is “trying to help” the Democratic Party by turning on El-Sayed, whom she compared to Graham Platner, the former scandal-plagued Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate from Maine who withdrew from that race in July.
Stevens said she remains a “really proud Democrat” who “absolutely” wants Democrats to win control of the Senate, but her shock announcement of an endorsement for the GOP candidate just days before Election Day could upend a tight race that may decide the fate of the upper chamber.
Democrats denounce, Republicans pounce
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer slammed what he called Stevens’ “despicable betrayal,” posting on social media that Senate Democrats were “united” in their support for El-Sayed.
Other Democrats have also shared their dismay and disappointment.
House Speaker Emerita and veteran California Democrat Rep. Nancy Pelosi said on social media that Stevens “has chosen to dangerously betray Michigan families’ healthcare, freedoms and future with her horrific endorsement of Mike Rogers.”
Elissa Slotkin, Michigan’s Democratic Senator elected in 2024 and a former House colleague of Stevens from the same 2018 blue wave that saw a record number of women elected to Congress, posted on social media: “Anyone who makes an election this important about themselves, and not Michiganders and our democracy, should think hard about whether they are serving the greater good.”
Ex-Rep. Susan Wild (D, Pa.), also elected in 2018 and formerly a roommate with Stevens in Washington, said in an emotional post about the Rogers endorsement that “the fallout for Haley won’t just be in Dem politics; she will be a pariah among her friends in the Democratic caucus in Congress.”
Ex-Rep. Andy Levin, a Michigan Democrat who was elected alongside Stevens in 2018 but after redistricting lost to her in a 2022 primary, posted that Haley’s endorsement of Rogers was “unconscionable, beyond the pale.”
Stevens’ chief of staff and multiple other staffers resigned on Sunday. “I speak on behalf of our team in wholeheartedly supporting Abdul El-Sayed for Senate,” Justin German, Stevens’ former chief of staff of eight years wrote in a statement. “This election is too important to sow division or stand on the sidelines.”
Stevens’ communications director Logan Basch, appears to have also left his post: his email sent back an auto-reply to TIME that read, “Hello, as of November 1st I am no longer with the Office of Congresswoman Haley Stevens.”
The Michigan Democratic Party also appeared to have distanced from Stevens, with state party chair Curtis Hertel posting on social media Sunday: “Congresswoman Stevens is not a current member of the Michigan Democratic Party, nor will she be in the future.”
Republicans immediately jumped on the opportunity, which could offer a late boost amid an election year where retaining the majority in either chamber of Congress has looked unlikely. Rogers touted Stevens’ endorsement on social media, adding that she “showed courage and bravery in putting Michigan first” and that he’s “grateful for her support.”
House Speaker Mike Johnson told reporters Sunday as he flanked Trump upon his arrival in Iowa that he sent Stevens a note commending “how courageous she was, how much we appreciate that she’s standing for truth.”
For his part, El-Sayed, who leads Rogers in public opinion polling, has appeared unfazed by Stevens’ actions, telling reporters: “At the end of the day, I actually don’t think about Haley Stevens.”
—Rebecca Schneid contributed reporting.

According to the Ukrainian Navy, successful combat operations resulted in the following estimated Russian losses in October: approximately 373 personnel killed or wounded; six aircraft; 123 vehicles; ten multiple launch rocket systems; seven artillery systems; one cruise missile; 8,218 FPV drones; 17 operational-tactical unmanned aerial vehicles; 690 attack drones; three ammunition depots; and 190 Shahed-136/131 drones.
The Russian army also lost seven watercraft, three naval mines, two air defense systems, one armored combat vehicle and one unmanned surface vessel (USV) as a result of Ukrainian Navy operations.

Bank RBK and KHC: A partnership for integrated residential development
Kazakhstan Housing Company JSC (KHC), a subsidiary of Baiterek National Investment Holding JSC, and Bank RBK JSC have signed a cooperation agreement to develop a conditional financing mechanism for integrated residential development projects, Qazinform News Agency correspondent reports.
The partnership will expand domestic developers’ access to bank loans on preferential terms and create additional opportunities to implement large-scale housing projects, including the comprehensive development of urban areas.
Under the agreement, KHC will place funds with Bank RBK in the form of conditional deposits, which the bank will use to provide targeted loans to developers. With funding from KHC, the bank will finance integrated residential development projects that meet established requirements at a preferential annual interest rate of 12.6%.
The mechanism aims to reduce borrowing costs, ease the financial burden on developers, and improve the economic efficiency of construction projects.
Priority will be given to integrated residential development projects that involve building not just individual apartment blocks, but entire residential neighborhoods with the necessary social, commercial and engineering infrastructure. This approach will help create modern urban environments that provide comfortable conditions for living, working and recreation.
The implementation of integrated residential development projects involves coordinated planning of housing, transport links and pedestrian access, public spaces, landscaping and site improvements. Particular attention is paid to ensuring that projects comply with established requirements and standards for integrated residential development, which aim to improve housing quality and promote the efficient development of urban areas.
For developers, the conditional financing mechanism provides additional opportunities to secure affordable loans for capital-intensive projects. For second-tier banks, cooperation with KHC offers a way to expand their involvement in financing the construction sector through targeted funding.
Overall, the mechanism is expected to stimulate investment, support the construction industry, and increase the supply of quality housing on the market.
Kazakhstan Housing Company JSC is a subsidiary of Baiterek National Investment Holding JSC that finances and supports housing construction.
Established in 2000 as the Kazakhstan Mortgage Company, KHC was renamed in 2021 and became the single operator for housing construction following its merger with Baiterek Development JSC and the Housing Construction Guarantee Fund JSC.
KHC offers a wide range of instruments, including guarantees for shared housing construction, financing for integrated residential development projects, the purchase of housing through the redemption of bonds issued by local executive bodies (akimats), and the development of mortgage and rental housing programs, among others.
Bank RBK is currently one of Kazakhstan’s most financially stable and fastest-growing banks. It ranks 5th among the country’s largest commercial banks by corporate loan portfolio, 7th by assets and 10th by equity.
The bank actively serves its customers through 13 branches across Kazakhstan, including in the country’s largest economic centers. Thanks to its extensive branch network, Bank RBK serves approximately 33,000 corporate clients and nearly 1 million retail customers.

====================================================================================================

Counsellors and psychotherapists call for UK statutory regulation in ‘watershed moment’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
05:01:31 UTC
14:01:31 KST

Ministers should introduce statutory regulation for counsellors and psychotherapists to protect the public from abuse, according to a report that has been hailed as a “watershed moment” for the profession.
Unlike most other healthcare roles, including doctors, midwives and osteopaths, “psychotherapist” and “counsellor” are not protected titles nor statutorily regulated professions in the UK.
This means that anyone can call themselves a therapist without a qualification, and can continue to practise even after an episode of misconduct, under a system that is poorly understood by the public.
For the first time, the professional bodies that represent counsellors and psychotherapists, and which run the current voluntary accreditation scheme, are calling for statutory regulation to boost confidence in the profession and protect the public from the growing number of cases of abuse and malpractice.
The report, the culmination of an independent review launched in October 2025 by the Commission for the Future of Counselling and Psychotherapy, argues that counsellors and psychotherapists are an untapped resource that could fill a mental health treatment gap estimated at about 1.8 million people on waiting lists. Practitioners told the commission they had extra capacity, which the report estimated could cumulatively provide more than 370,000 hours of additional therapy appointments every week.
The commission co-chair Phil Hope, a former Labour minister for care services, said: “For me, the report became a bit of a watershed moment for the profession, a real landmark of the opportunity there is for the government, and all its departments really, to unlock that potential.”
Ella Janneh, who successfully sued her therapist in the high court for rape and sexual assault in 2024, and has campaigned for regulation with the support of the law firm Leigh Day, welcomed the “collective call for regulation”. She said it had taken “years and a lot of honest and difficult conversations between victims, other campaigners and conscientious professionals”.
“Statutory regulation would lock abusive and unethical people out of the system. The current lack of centralised regulation allows for repeat offenders to continue practising with no oversight. That is reason enough to bring in regulation,” Janneh said.
The report cites her “powerful testimony” as an illustration of the “devastating, ongoing impact” the absence of statutory regulation can have, since her therapist is still able to practise despite the outcome of her civil case.
“One of the main reasons why the lack of government regulation has skated under the radar of public awareness,” said Janneh, “is that most people assume it’s already in place. They only realise it’s not when something’s gone wrong … Currently your Friday night kebab is subject to stronger regulation than a therapist who sits in rooms alone with vulnerable people.”
The report’s co-chair Andrea Sutcliffe, the former chief executive of the Nursing and Midwifery Council and an expert on regulation, said: “We’ve been on a journey around regulation with counselling and psychotherapy over many, many, many years, and the coalition government set its face against statutory regulation in 2011.
“We heard some really powerful testimony about the risk and the fact that people have been harmed. What the government asks for is a compelling case for statutory regulation because it costs and [it’s not] an easy thing to do … but as independent co-chairs, we feel that a compelling case exists.”
Regulation was especially important for counselling and psychotherapy because they were complex interventions requiring years of training to practise, Sutcliffe said. Therapy takes place in a one-on-one setting; most practitioners are independent, meaning there is no employer oversight; and their patients are typically vulnerable people.
“People are in difficult, vulnerable situations, why would we expect them to be experts in working out who they should go to and who is safe? That’s not what we do for choosing a brain surgeon or a cardiologist. We expect those things,” she said, adding that the lack of regulation contributed to misconceptions and mistrust, which prevented people from seeking help.
Regulation would also be helpful in setting standards for education, training and development, Sutcliffe said. The report noted that this would also improve diversity in the profession, which is much needed.
The report further argues that the evidence base for counselling and psychotherapy should be improved, and notes that its lack is resulting in “insufficient and unsustainable public commissioning and investment”. Hope said commissioners in the NHS and local government often had “legitimate concerns, is this a qualified psychotherapist or not?”
A more coordinated, professionalised industry could better inform the government’s approach to regulation and guardrails around the growing use of AI for mental health support. “[Psychotherapists are] seriously concerned at the risk that people may be accessing services that are totally unregulated. And therefore, the profession needs, I think, to up its game a bit and move up the pace here because this is happening,” said Hope.
The commission hopes the report’s call will be taken up by policymakers. The Labour MP Sojan Joseph, the chair of the all-party-parliamentary group on mental health and a former nurse, said he supported the case for statutory regulation and would raise the issue in parliament.
Jon Levett, the UK Council for Psychotherapy’s chief executive officer, said he would welcome statutory regulation that “protects the public, sets clear standards and preserves people’s choice of therapy”, though he argued that “any new system must be developed with practitioners and people with lived experience”.
Dr Lisa Morrison, the British Association for Counselling and Psychotherapy’s chief regulation and standards officer, agreed that collaboration was key to ensure regulation “places public protection, public benefit and public confidence at its heart, while avoiding barriers to access, diversity and established practice”.

"I'm speechless. I’m trying to process what has just happened," said Antonelli after finishing the race.
His parents and sister were there to embrace him when he stepped out of the car.

UK making up China policy ‘as it goes along’, MPs warn
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
05:00:33 UTC
14:00:33 KST

The UK is making up policy on China “as it goes along” and risks having its strategy dictated by Washington or Beijing, a parliamentary report has concluded.
An investigation by the Commons business, innovation, science and trade select committee said Labour’s failure to formulate a coherent strategy since 2024 “combined the worst of both worlds” for the UK in relation to China.
Liam Byrne, Labour MP and chair of the committee said the UK’s policy on China meant it was also endangering its business with the EU with the risk of being “cut off” from big manufacuring contracts.
The government could neither deliver commercial opportunities to British businesses nor control the “increasing exposure to unquantified, managed risk” in relations with China, it found.
The report said: “In 2024, the new government promised a strategic, long-term, consistent UK approach to China. It has not delivered on this.
“Britain must shape its own relationship with China or risk having that relationship shaped for us in Washington or Beijing.”
The UK’s relationship with China has been marked by a lack of engagement in the last 10 years, with Keir Starmer making the first official visit in January since Theresa May in 2018.
That trip was billed as an effort to end the “diplomatic ice age”, but since 2018 China has benefited from an export boom that is now fuelling fears about deindustrialisation, adding to deep-seated existing concerns about cyber espionage and national security.
The MPs acknowledged the advantages of trading with Beijing in their report, noting that British businesses have profitable operations in China and “are ambitious to grow” and learn from the country’s “world-leading” innovations.
At the same time, consumers benefit from low-cost imports when household incomes are squeezed, with electric vehicles being a case in point.
However, Byrne sharply criticised the government’s piecemeal approach.
“Britain’s businesses cannot plan for the future when the government keeps making up its China policy as it goes along.
“Ministers promised clarity and consistency. Instead, we have opportunities missed, risks unmanaged and decisions left until the 11th hour.”
The committee cited the decision in March to block the Chinese firm Ming Yang from building a £1.5bn wind energy plant in Scotland after years of negotiation because of unspecified security risks.
Scotland’s first minister, John Swinney, has called on Andy Burnham to reconsider Starmer’s decision.
That decision, along with the emergency takeover of British Steel from its Chinese owners, “has been characterised by reactivity, inconsistency and opacity”, the report said.
Work on a new strategy, the committee said, should be combined with official preparations for new trade remedies to counter unfair competition, including potential tariffs on EVs, something Downing Street has not ruled out.
The report calls for “clear new rules of the game” and recommends the designation of a “red zone” for industries that would be off-limits for Chinese investment and a “green zone”, where trade should be encouraged.
Byrne said a China strategy was an urgent concern as “Europe is changing fast” and “proposing new trade protections as it gets bolder with Beijing and warier of Washington”.
The new laws “may trap Britain outside EU trade walls, cutting us off from our largest market”.
Byrne said the government “should be prepared to consider dynamic alignment” with the EU include tariffs on EVs “as the price of securing British firms a place in the EU’s Made in Europe project” and to help guard against China dominance.
The UK is already under pressure to align with the EU on tariffs on EVs, but the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, has said he will make a decision in the best interests of the UK.
The EU has already imposed tariffs on Chinese EVs, capped the number of hybrid cars that can be imported from China and is now considering a Franco-German proposal for a “kill switch” to block imports if China weaponises trade – as it did last year with curbs on exports of rare-earth minerals and chips. “The UK’s partners are moving further and faster,” the report noted.
China is now on track to surpass last year’s record $1.19tn trade surplus with the rest of the world.
Its latest five-year plan, covering 2026 to 2030, gives a glimpse of where China is going next in prioritising the strategic expansion of high-value green exports such as EVs, batteries, wind turbines, hydrogen and solar panels.
A government spokesperson said it did not accept the committee’s verdict. “We recognise the committee’s work on this report, but we disagree with its conclusion.”
They added that the government’s approach was “consistent” - it cooperated where it could and challenged where it must.
“Our trade strategy makes clear that we will capitalise on every opportunity to grow our economy while never compromising on our national security, and our increased discussions with China allows us to directly raise concerns where they arise,” the spokesperson said.

====================================================================================================

‘They have schedules to follow’: how fast ferries can threaten endangered whales in the Mediterranean
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
05:00:32 UTC
14:00:32 KST

Marine biologist Alice Barbarioli waits with her camera trained on the horizon. A few minutes earlier, the hydrophone beneath the Pelagos research vessel detected codas – the sequence of clicks sperm whales use to communicate.
The sperm whale reveals its head and dorsal fin as those onboard the vessel in the Pelagos sanctuary, a conservation area established to protect marine mammals in the north-western Mediterranean, rush to take photos and note the rhythm of its breathing. After a few minutes, the animal arches its back, and begins to head back into the depths of the sea. They wait to catch a glimpse of its tail.
Barbarioli, the lead researcher of the citizen-science expedition, organised by the Tethys Research Institute, immediately notices an injury on its left fluke: “Given how precise the mark is, it’s probably the result of a [vessel] collision,” she says.
Collisions have long been recognised as a leading human-induced cause of death for the Mediterranean’s endangered sperm and fin whales. Now, a Guardian investigation using data from the maritime intelligence firm Veson Nautical, has found that large passenger and cargo vessels operated by four companies – the Grimaldi Group, Corsica Ferries, Baleària and Moby Lines – have frequently travelled through a protected habitat that includes the Pelagos sanctuary at 15 knots (17mph) or above – speeds that almost always kill cetaceans in cases of a collision. Strikes are unlikely to kill when a vessel is travelling below 10 knots.
Slowing vessels is the most effective mitigation strategy when rerouteing isn’t possible, according to conservation NGO Oceancare.
The sea between Valencia and Genoa, which includes the Pelagos sanctuary, is a key cetacean habitat, home to about two-thirds of the Mediterranean’s fin whales and more than a fifth of its sperm whales. In July 2023, the International Maritime Organization (IMO) created the north-western Mediterranean Sea particularly sensitive sea area (PSSA). In a voluntary speed recommendation (VSR), it advised vessels weighing 300 gross tonnes and above to sail at 10 to 13 knots in the area to reduce the risk of fatal collisions.
Despite the IMO’s recommendation, the Guardian, using additional data from Global Fishing Watch, found that ships with IMO identification numbers spent more than 280,000 hours travelling at 15 knots and above through the PSSA in 2025. The data also showed that ships spent more than 6,000 hours travelling above 25 knots. It builds on previous analysis that found the voluntary recommendations were largely ineffective.
In 2022 and 2025, ferries owned by the Grimaldi Group, including Cruise Roma – at more than 250 metres, the world’s longest cruise ferry – dominated the top-20 list of vessels spending the most time at 15 knots or above in the habitat.
Speeding remained concentrated among a few operators in the PSSA in 2025, with just seven vessels – four Baleària fast ferries and three Grimaldi cruise ferries – responsible for 70% of the hours spent above 25 knot. Seven Grimaldi cruise ferries amounted to about 8% of all hours recorded for all vessels at 15 knots or above in 2025.
The Guardian spoke to six captains – five current and one former – who have sailed in the PSSA since its designation. The seafarers, still or previously at the helm of ships owned by Grimaldi Group and Moby Lines, say their companies have not introduced measures to encourage slow steaming after the IMO’s VSR.
“As long as it’s only a recommendation, nobody will reduce speed,” says one Grimaldi captain. “It would mean overhauling the whole commercial system. The ferries in the area travel at 25 [knots], especially the ones carrying tourists. They have schedules to follow.”
Grimaldi and Moby Lines were contacted for comment but did not respond.
Thomas Folegot, the CEO of maritime tech company Quiet-Oceans, says that while slow-moving container vessels could stand to slightly cut speeds in the PSSA, it was far more challenging for ferries: “For their business, it’s a killer. [Passengers] will fly to Corsica.”
Quiet-Oceans and Oceancare’s analysis found that 80% of the journeys by merchant ships in the PSSA in 2023 were at speeds above 10 knots.
Simone Panigada, president of the Tethys Research Institute and chair of a scientific committee dedicated to the conservation of cetaceans, says it is time to “move, progressively, from voluntary to mandatory” rules on reducing collision risk.
“A binding framework would create more level conditions for all operators, encouraging compliance among shipping companies and ensuring the adoption of these measures doesn’t rest solely on individual corporate decisions,” he says.
The International Whaling Commission (IWC) told the Guardian it has recorded six incidents since July 2023 in the PSSA: five near-miss events and one collision. It believes most strikes go unrecorded.
While the annual time spent travelling through the PSSA above the key threshold of 15 knots remained high in 2025, it represented an 11% reduction compared with 2022. The time above 25 knots also fell by about a third between 2022 and 2025.
These overall declines are probably caused by factors including altered shipping routes, says Olivia Watkins, associate director at Veson Nautical, who adds: “The PSSA recommendation is unlikely to be a significant cause of the year-on-year decline in the data results.”
Wei-Jun Mun, director of public policy at the World Shipping Council, says the industry is committed to PSSA’s protective measures, while noting slower navigation involved “commercial trade-offs and operational concerns”, including having to add ships to a service for schedule reliability.
A spokesperson for Corsica Ferries says the company supports Mediterranean marine megafauna research and ship-strike mitigation through measures including continuous monitoring, crew training and the development of whale alert tools. Researchers from programmes including conservation project Life Conceptu Maris monitor wildlife using its ships, it says.
The company says it instructs captains to navigate with particular caution through the PSSA, and to lower speeds to 10 to 13 knots, “while seeking to avoid possible negative impacts of reduced speeds”, including on manoeuvrability. It says its captains have reported a reduced capacity to avoid cetaceans that appear suddenly when navigating at reduced speeds.
A spokesperson for Baleària says it is “committed to the conservation of marine biodiversity” and actively working to mitigate the risk of collisions, including through crew training and the use of real-time monitoring systems to allow captains to adjust speed and course where necessary. Baleària says none of its fast ferries had recorded a collision with cetaceans.
Baleària adds that it participates in marine conservation programmes, including the Life Conceptu Maris and Life Intemares initiatives.

====================================================================================================

Radical-right youth groups are at the root of Europe’s populist surge | Cas Mudde and Duncan McDonnell
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
05:00:31 UTC
14:00:31 KST

The leaders of the most successful populist radical right parties in western Europe have one thing in common that is often overlooked. Italy’s Matteo Salvini, Jordan Bardella from France, Jimmie Åkesson from the Sweden Democrats, and Tom Van Grieken from Belgium’s Vlaams Belang all led the youth wing of the parties they now run. These movements shaped the politicians they are today, and they are now shaping Europe’s political future.
As Italy’s prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, another former radical right youth-wing leader, put it: “Even more than my growth as a politician, I owe my growth as a person and as an Italian to my youth-wing activism. There is no more formative training ground than this.” And yet, until recently, we knew little about these incubation chambers of populist radical right parties.
In researching our new book, Youth Wings of the Populist Radical Right, we looked at 10 such organisations from across Europe. From the youth wing of Austria’s Freedom party to that of France’s National Rally, we found they help to recruit, train and promote the radical right’s grassroots members, their representatives and leaders of the future. They also perform important functions for their parties in the present, encouraging young people to vote for them, providing a key source of labour during election campaigns, running party branches and influencing policy.
In particular, we found that youth-wing leaders and their rank and file members are helping to achieve three key goals for the radical right as their parties expand in the 2020s: internationalisation, professionalisation and normalisation.
First, these youth wings go even further than their older equivalent organisations in building new transnational alliances. Away from the spotlight, there has been a proliferation of international far-right workshops and conferences, such as the Transatlantic Patriot Summit, held each year in Budapest since 2022. These and similar events have brought together youth leaders from Europe, India, Israel, Latin America and the US, to talk about common aims and establish ties that will last through their careers. Many of the youth leaders we spoke to talked openly about how these international ties will benefit them “when we are the ones in government”.
Second, they are heavily involved in political training at international, national and local levels. Once derided as a bunch of amateurs (and with good reason, in some cases), the populist radical right now invests considerably in professionalisation. The young people who join are taught not only about policies and history, but also rhetoric and media communications. They are being trained as future politicians, and the likes of Åkesson, Bardella, Meloni and Salvini are proof of concept.
Third, the recruitment of university-educated young people – who look and sound very different from the stereotypical media image of the angry far-right youth – feeds into the growing normalisation of the populist radical right. Producing more articulate, professional and presentable leaders can help their parties be seen by voters as legitimate political actors. And the more distance they can put between themselves and previous generations of uncouth leaders, such as Jean-Marie Le Pen in France or Umberto Bossi in Italy, the more they can attract young people like themselves.
But this smartening up of the radical right’s public image does not reflect a softening of the message. The young leaders we spoke to will not lead their parties down a path to moderation. They may have found ways to smooth down their movements’ rough edges, but the ideology is still an exclusionary, nationalist one. In other words, the regeneration of the radical right through its youth wings makes it an even more significant challenge to liberal democracy.
How can mainstream parties respond to this challenge? One way would be to stop focusing on the radical right as the root of their problems, and to look at themselves and their own youth wings.
Recent research into youth-wing membership has found that centre-left and centre-right youth groups are dominated by men, people from political families and careerists. If mainstream parties are to regain ground with young people, this needs to change.
Governing parties could also do far more to address the problems that young people are facing in the 21st century. For most of the postwar period, younger generations in western Europe grew up with the implicit promise that they would have better life prospects than their parents. That promise has been broken. In fact, with the rise of insecure employment, compounded by the housing crisis, a significant minority of young Europeans are still living with their parents into their late 20s and early 30s. It is no surprise that many have little faith in the capacity of mainstream parties to change their lives.
By contrast, the young populist radical-right activists we interviewed talked about how their parties spoke to them in clear terms about the issues that concerned them, and offered them solutions. Mainstream parties should be doing the same.
- Cas Mudde is the Stanley Wade Shelton UGAF professor of international affairs at the University of Georgia, and author of The Far Right Today; Duncan McDonnell is professor of politics at the Jeff Bleich Centre in Flinders University in Adelaide, Australia.
- Youth Wings of the Populist Radical Right, co-authored by Duncan McDonnell, Sofia Ammassari, Ann-Cathrine Jungar, Anders Ravik Jupskås, and Cas Mudde, is published by Oxford University Press

Michigan Senate race: Will Haley Stevens spoil the party for Democratic candidate El-Sayed?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
05:00:00 UTC
14:00:00 KST

Field Notes from Detroit
Michigan Senate race: Will Haley Stevens spoil the party for Democratic candidate El-Sayed?
Marina Lopes and Lila Barron
DETROIT – Reporters were waiting outside the Detroit church where Democrat Haley Stevens was due to appear on the morning of Nov 1 with Abdul El-Sayed, the progressive physician who had defeated her in the primary, in a show of Democratic unity.
Led by Representative James E. Clyburn of South Carolina, one of the country’s most influential black Democrats, the event was intended to signal an end to a bitter feud and rally black voters, a crucial constituency that had backed Stevens.
But Stevens never arrived. Instead, to the surprise of her own staff, she was sitting in a church pew miles away beside Mike Rogers, the Republican her party had spent millions trying to defeat.
This year’s October surprise arrived on Nov 1, when Stevens endorsed Rogers’ campaign in a Michigan Senate race that could determine control of Congress.
When Abby Ronson, a Rogers spokesperson, posted a photograph of the pair on social media platform X, we – like other news media outlets – jumped into our van and raced across Detroit’s broad boulevards, quiet on a fall Sunday. We drove past shuttered shops and factories to Perfecting Church, a black Pentecostal church outside Detroit.
By the time we arrived, television crews were already gathering around a makeshift microphone stand. As Stevens emerged through the church’s double doors, flanked by Rogers and his wife, reporters’ phones buzzed with a statement she had posted on X endorsing Rogers.
As reporters shouted questions and camera flashes lit up her face, Stevens stepped up to address the media.
“I am endorsing Mike Rogers for the United States Senate,” she told reporters.
“This is a very close election, we all know that. But Abdul made very clear that I was not welcome in his campaign, that he didn’t need me there, didn’t want me there. At some point, you’ve got to look at who’s standing for country.”
Protesters standing with the media shouted “traitor”.
The endorsement followed a week of public feuding between Stevens, a centrist, and El-Sayed over his stance on US support for Israel. It also marked a striking reversal for a lawmaker who had recently urged voters to reject Rogers.
“Mike Rogers will be another rubber stamp for Donald Trump’s dangerous agenda. We can’t afford to give MAGA another Senate seat in November,” she posted on X in August.
Republicans across the country celebrated a twist they hope will translate into votes on Nov 3. Speaking at a campaign rally in Iowa, President Donald Trump called Stevens’ decision “brave” and said: “I’d love her to join the Republican Party.”
Michigan Senate race splits Democrats over Israel
Democrats condemned the endorsement as a betrayal. More than half of Stevens’ staff quit in the hours after her announcement.
Her chief of staff, Justin German, said in a statement: “We are shocked and heartbroken by Congresswoman Stevens’ decision to support Mike Rogers.”
The rupture exposed divisions over Israel that have roiled the Democratic Party, even as it gains wider support among voters. The American Israel Public Affairs Committee poured tens of millions of dollars into supporting Stevens.
El-Sayed, who would become the country’s first Muslim senator if elected, has described the war in Gaza as “a genocide”.
For several voters interviewed on Nov 1, however, the political drama did little to change their calculations.
Kennedi Young, a 20-year-old university student, described the joint appearance as a “nice tactic to try to appeal to black voters”, but doubted it would sway her friends and family.
“I don’t feel like (Rogers and Stevens) came for the service,” she told The Straits Times.
Adrienne Bronaugh, 70, attended the service with Rogers and Stevens but had already voted for El-Sayed. She said she “doesn’t trust Rogers” and was more concerned about the cost of tariffs on Canada.
Tariffs imposed since Trump returned to office have disproportionately affected Michigan, a state bordering Canada that relies on imports to fuel its manufacturing industry. The Canadian flag flutters just across the river from downtown Detroit.
Trump’s tariffs on Canadian imports include 25% on vehicles and auto parts, and 50% on steel, aluminium and copper, with exemptions for some products. Introduced in 2025, the tariffs have remained widely unpopular. Some 60% of Americans disapprove of the tariff increases, according to a February poll.
America is “making a mess with our neighbours across the border”, Bronaugh said. “The tariffs are impacting all of us... We’re paying more for everything.”

Lacaton & Vassal wins Le Prix Charlotte Perriand 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
05:00:00 UTC
14:00:00 KST

Lacaton & Vassal wins Le Prix Charlotte Perriand 2027
The Créateurs Design Association & Awards has named Pritzker Prize-winning French studio Lacaton & Vassal Architectes the recipient of the Le Prix Charlotte Perriand 2027.
Lacaton & Vassal Architectes, which is led by architects Anne Lacaton and Jean-Philippe Vassal and known for its social housing designs, was recognised for contributing to contemporary architecture by transforming and improving existing buildings.
The Créateurs Design Associates (CDA) said the studio’s work improves “living conditions while preserving resources and architectural heritage”.
The duo said it was “very happy” to receive the award.
“Charlotte Perriand’s tireless pursuit of comfort, well-being, and the pleasure of the inhabitant and of everyday life, her modernity, and her political commitment to exposing poor housing conditions and to transmission and education remain profoundly relevant today and are a source of inspiration,” Anne Lacaton and Jean-Philippe Vassal said.
“Her manifest spirit of openness and freedom touches us deeply. We are very happy to receive this distinction.”
The architects founded their studio in 1989 and have since worked on high-profile projects such as the transformation of the Palais de Tokyo in Paris, the Nantes School of Architecture and the Cité du Grand Parc housing transformation in Bordeaux.
The latter, which was completed with Frédéric Druot and Christophe Hutin, won the European Union’s Mies van der Rohe Award in 2019.
Lacaton & Vassal Architectes’ other social housing projects include the renovation of the 1960s Tour Bois-le-Prêtre tower block in Paris, also in collaboration with Frédéric Druot, which was completed in 2011.
It also converted and extended a former shipbuilding workshop to create the FRAC Nord-Pas de Calais contemporary art gallery in Dunkirk.
The Le Prix Charlotte Perriand was established in collaboration with the family of the late architect and recognises practitioners whose contributions have advanced architecture and design.
“In awarding Le Prix Charlotte Perriand to Lacaton & Vassal, the CDA members recognise the care and imagination with which they approach the places people call home. Their work shows how much can be gained by understanding what is already there,” Créateurs Design Association co-founder Meredith Xavier said.
The award will be given to Lacaton & Vassal Architectes in a ceremony on 16 January 2027, at the Shangri-La Paris. Architect Kengo Kuma will also be honoured at the event as the winner of the Andrée Putman Lifetime Achievement Award 2027.
Lacaton & Vassal Architectes has previously won the Pritzker Architecture Prize in 2021, as well as the 2023 Soane Medal for architecture.
Last year, Lacaton won the 2025 Jane Drew Prize for women in architecture.
Photography by Philippe Ruault

Kimi Antonelli becomes youngest F1 champion as Max Verstappen wins race
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
04:54:49 UTC
13:54:49 KST

Mercedes driver Kimi Antonelli made history and become the youngest Formula 1 world champion. The 20-year-old driver finished third in the Mexico City Grand Prix race behind Max Verstappen and Lewis Hamilton.
Kimi Antonelli became Formula One's youngest world champion as he drove his Mercedes to a 16th podium finish at the Mexico Grand Prix on Sunday.
The 20-year-old Italian driver finished in third place behind Red Bull's Max Verstappen and Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton.
“I’m still trying to realise and understand what just happened, when you work so hard and then you finally achieve it is truly special,” Antonelli said.
The Italian driver was joined by his parents and younger sister. "All the emotions come, to be able to witness this moment with my family is a moment I will always remember".
Antonelli is the first Italian to win the world champion title since Alberto Ascari in 1953. At just 20 years old, he became the youngest-ever world champion, breaking Sebastian Vettel's previous record, set when he won the title aged 23 in 2010.
"It’s been an incredible season, and to share this podium with Max and Lewis is truly incredible. And looking forward to some more battles in the future," Antonelli said.
The Mercedes driver secured the title despite a difficult start to the race weekend, as Antonelli fell ill ahead of the race weekend and was forced to miss Thursday’s media day.
Verstappen claims sixth victory at Mexico City GP
Meanwhile, four-time world champion Max Verstappen claimed his sixth victory at the Mexico City Grand Prix.
“The ‘Max-ico’ Grand Prix will be a great name to call it,” Verstappen said. “To be honest I love the city and the fans, but I have no idea why I have won it six years, it just happened. It always comes together for me here".
Lewis Hamilton, who had secured pole position on Saturday, lost his position while battling for the lead with his teammate Charles Leclerc on the fourth lap.
"I think we had the pace to win today, but it wasn't meant to be and we'll take it offline and figure out what we can do in the background," said a visibly irritated Hamilton.
"We have to hold some serious talks behind the scenes."
Leclerc finished fourth while McLaren's outgoing world champion Lando Norris came in fifth position. Antonelli's teammate, George Russell, finished sixth.
After this weekend's race, F1 will travel to Brazil before heading to Las Vegas. The final races of the season are scheduled to take place in Qatar and Abu Dhabi, although it remains unclear whether both will go ahead as planned amid ongoing regional instability.

China's draft law calls for fair, equitable global anti-corruption governance system
