BEIJING, Nov. 2 (Xinhua) -- China's top legislature began deliberating a draft law on combating cross-border corruption, which includes a provision on promoting the building of a fair and equitable global anti-corruption governance system.
The draft was submitted for its second reading at a session of the Standing Committee of the National People's Congress, which runs through Friday.
The draft further elaborates on the legislative purpose and enriches the principles guiding efforts to combat cross-border corruption.
It also stipulates that such efforts must be conducted in strict accordance with the Constitution and laws, follow statutory procedures, and respect and protect human rights.
The draft law was first submitted for deliberation in late August. The formulation of the law is an important step by China to put in place a systematic and comprehensive foreign-related legal framework for anti-corruption, according to the top legislature.
Structured into six chapters and 47 articles, the draft sets out the principles, scope and key positions underpinning China's efforts to combat cross-border corruption. ■

Interview: Tajikistan-China cooperation under BRI, SCO boosts regional development, says expert
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
12:52:19 CST
13:52:19 KST

DUSHANBE, Nov. 2 (Xinhua) -- Closer cooperation between Tajikistan and China under the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) and the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) will unlock greater potential for regional development, said Guzel Maitdinova, director of the Center for Geopolitical Studies at the Russian-Tajik (Slavonic) University.
"Tajikistan-China relations are taking on increasingly greater strategic significance," Maitdinova told Xinhua in a recent interview, citing China's growing economic cooperation with Central Asia and Tajikistan's efforts to diversify its economy.
The two countries established diplomatic relations in 1992, and elevated their ties to a comprehensive strategic cooperative partnership in the new era in 2024, opening up new prospects for bilateral cooperation, said the expert.
Tajik President Emomali Rahmon's state visit to China in May 2026 set another milestone in bilateral relations, Maitdinova said. During the visit, the two sides signed a series of cooperation documents, including the Treaty on Permanent Good-Neighborliness, Friendship and Cooperation, and the Joint Statement on Deepening the Comprehensive Strategic Cooperative Partnership in the New Era.
Maitdinova highlighted the importance of aligning Tajikistan's National Development Strategy for the period up to 2030 with the China-proposed BRI. Tajikistan, a landlocked country with mountainous terrain, is keen to develop transport corridors, while China can help strengthen cross-border economic connectivity, improve transport links and foster more resilient trade and production networks across Eurasia, she said.
Energy and water resources are another strategically important area in bilateral cooperation, Maitdinova noted. Tajikistan has considerable hydropower potential, but tapping it requires modernizing energy infrastructure, expanding grid capacity and securing long-term financing.
Chinese technology and investment can support the development of hydropower, renewable energy and digital management systems, she said.
Maitdinova also underscored the importance of bilateral cooperation on security, as both countries have a shared interest in closer coordination between law enforcement agencies to combat the "three evil forces" of terrorism, separatism and extremism.
This year marks the 25th anniversary of the founding of the SCO. "As one of the organization's founding members, China has helped broaden its economic, technological and institutional agenda and strengthen cooperation on security," Maitdinova said.
The SCO and the BRI play different but complementary roles, she said. The SCO provides a political and institutional platform for coordinating the interests of member states, while the BRI promotes cooperation through infrastructure projects, investment and trade links. "Together, they create opportunities to develop cross-border transport corridors, energy networks, digital infrastructure and production chains," Maitdinova said.
"Overall, Tajikistan-China relations are characterized by a high level of political trust, expanding economic cooperation and a transition toward a more comprehensive model of strategic partnership," she said. ■

Ukraine's territorial integrity is in Türkiye's long-term interests – expert
Sinan Demirtürk, a Turkish scholar, lecturer at Gazi University in Ankara and head of the Turkish Foundation for Political and Strategic Research (TÜRPAV), made this statement on CNN Türk while commenting on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky's visit to Istanbul, Ukrinform reports.
"Türkiye also has a historical memory. In other words, when it comes to preserving Ukraine's territorial integrity and possible peace talks between Russia and Ukraine, Türkiye understands that Ukraine's stability and territorial integrity will directly affect its policy in the Black Sea region and towards the Turkic world in the long term," Demirtürk said.
According to the expert, meaningful peace talks are unlikely in the short term but could take place in the medium term.
He believes that Russia achieving its desired outcome, including legitimizing the occupation of Ukrainian territories or bringing about a change in the country's leadership by replacing President Zelensky, would not be in Ankara's interests.
"Given the history of Turkish-Russian relations, we can see the problems facing Türkiye's foreign policy and its borders when Crimea is lost and Russians are present in Ukraine. Therefore, as a participant in this process, Türkiye is steering it towards a balanced compromise," the scholar said.
Demirtürk also linked the significance of Zelensky's visit to the fact that it took place immediately after the summit of leaders of the Organization of Turkic States.
"The fact that such an important visit was scheduled immediately after the summit of leaders of the Organization of Turkic States further underscores Türkiye's role in ensuring international peace, security in the Black Sea and building a lasting and sustainable peace that would make it possible to preserve Ukraine's territorial integrity," he said.
According to the expert, while maintaining contacts with the United States and Russia, Türkiye is also demonstrating that it remains a neighbor and partner that does not leave Ukraine to fend for itself.
On October 31, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky met with Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan in Istanbul. Much of their talks focused on finding ways to unblock the Black Sea. The leaders also discussed the possibility of holding peace talks in Türkiye.

Deeper China-Oman ties strategic for both sides, Xi says
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
05:46:15 CET
13:46:15 KST

BEIJING/DUBAI, Nov 2 (Reuters) - The Middle East and Gulf region should not become a battleground for great-power rivalry and China is willing to work with Arab nations to achieve lasting peace, Chinese President Xi Jinping told Oman’s sultan on Monday.
China has traditionally played a low-key diplomatic role in the Middle East, but has stepped up efforts to try to help end tensions amid the US-Israeli war on Iran, which has snarled the Strait of Hormuz and driven up global energy and shipping costs.
Xi told Omani Sultan Haitham bin Tariq al-Said that the world is undergoing profound changes.
“The Middle East Gulf region should not become an arena for great-power rivalry and geopolitical conflict. Peace and stability in the region require joint nurturing and protection by all parties,” Xi said, according to China’s Foreign Ministry.
China has consistently been committed to stopping the war, and hopes to contribute “wisdom and solutions to resolving the region’s security dilemmas,” he added.
China is willing to strengthen communication and coordination with Arab countries, including the Gulf Cooperation Council states, to work together toward restoring peace and achieving lasting stability and security, Xi said.
In a 20-point joint statement, both sides said they agree that normal and safe navigation should resume in the Strait of Hormuz. The countries also called for the US and Iran to pursue peaceful options, return to the agreement struck in June aimed at ending the conflict and restart dialogue.
China’s Foreign Ministry said later on Monday that Zhai Jun, its special envoy to the Middle East, would visit Iran, Oman and Saudi Arabia this month.
FIRST CHINA TRIP
Haitham arrived in Beijing on Sunday for a two-day visit, the first by an Omani head of state since the countries established ties in 1978.
Haitham told Xi his government had deep appreciation for China’s positions on key issues concerning the region, Omani state media reported.
“We believe that development and stability are inextricably linked,” he said.
“The prosperity of nations requires an environment defined by security, peace, respect for state sovereignty, and adherence to international law — an environment where disputes are resolved through peaceful means.”
He also said Oman was open to entering into a preferential bilateral trade and investment agreement with China.
“We are confident that such an agreement would open new avenues for trade and investment, facilitate and enhance commercial and investment exchanges between our two nations,” Haitham said.
China is Oman’s largest trade partner, with tourism and business links boosted by direct flights between Beijing and Muscat since November last year.
Oman, which exports crude oil and energy products to China, has also been looking to further develop its renewable energy supply chains and digital commerce.
Their joint statement said the countries have agreed to deepen practical cooperation in the oil and natural gas sector, as well as expand cooperation in new energy fields such as solar photovoltaics, wind power, power transmission and transformation, and energy storage.
The Omani leader, who was welcomed on the tarmac in Beijing by People’s Bank of China Governor Pan Gongsheng, also emphasised cooperation between investment and financial institutions.

Former Israeli general warns of 'irreversible collapse' amid international isolation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
04:42:12 UTC
13:42:12 KST

Retired Israeli Major General Itzhak Brik has warned that Israel is facing an irreversible breakdown across its military, economy and state institutions, arguing that the country has lost international legitimacy and allies and cannot withstand prolonged isolation.
In an opinion article published on Sunday by the Israeli daily Maariv, Brik described the situation as a comprehensive collapse rather than a political crisis.
He called the results of last Tuesday’s parliamentary election “the official death certificate of the State of Israel as we knew it”, accusing television commentators of focusing on seat counts and coalition negotiations while overlooking what he described as far deeper national problems.
He compared their coverage to an orchestra playing aboard the Titanic as it sank.
Brik warns of military and economic deterioration
Brik, a former commander of military colleges and former ombudsman for soldiers’ complaints at the Defence Ministry, said Israel had become an international pariah.
“We have lost legitimacy and allies,” he wrote, warning that the country could not endure complete isolation for long.
He described the ground forces as suffering from structural weaknesses and declining morale, arguing that they lacked the capacity to defend Israel against simultaneous threats from inside and outside its borders.
An exhausted military, he warned, would struggle to repel large-scale incursions or protect civilians in a wider regional conflict.
Brik also put Israel’s national debt at 1.4 trillion shekels ($445 billion), saying prolonged warfare had placed an increasing burden on the economy. He alleged that sanctions, restrictions on arms supplies and growing financial isolation were adding to the pressure.
He dismissed Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s proposal to use cryptocurrencies to counter possible European sanctions as “naive and absurd”, warning that further economic deterioration could put Israelis’ savings at risk.
‘Silent civil war’ and institutional decline
Turning to domestic tensions, Brik said Israeli society was experiencing a “silent civil war”, rather than mere political polarisation.
He claimed that doctors, scientists, technology entrepreneurs and other highly skilled professionals were leaving the country, taking with them expertise built up over decades.
Brik also accused Israel’s political leadership of undermining the rule of law and public institutions, alleging that political loyalty and appointments were being prioritised over competence and integrity.
Election leaves political blocs short of majority
The warning came after the October 27 parliamentary election left Netanyahu’s bloc with 53 seats in the 120-member Knesset.
The opposition bloc led by Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot secured 48 seats, while Arab parties won 19.
Neither of the two main blocs reached the 61 seats required for a parliamentary majority, leaving the political landscape uncertain as coalition negotiations loom.

Write-In Ralph: South Carolina Republicans challenge Trump’s Senate pick
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
04:31:02 UTC
13:31:02 KST

Write-In Ralph: South Carolina Republicans challenge Trump’s Senate pick
As Trump supports Senator Darline Graham, one conservative group is rallying around someone else.
Charleston, South Carolina – Avery Milton thought he was a die-hard supporter of US President Donald Trump. The 28-year-old South Carolina native had voted for Trump in the past three elections and believed in his promise to put America first. But ahead of the midterm elections, the president has left him feeling betrayed.
“He stabbed us in the back during his second term,” Milton told Al Jazeera.
Milton’s disillusionment is not isolated. He said many people close to him share this frustration, particularly younger conservatives around his age who are starting families and entering the workforce. Trump launching a war on Iran, after campaigning on a promise to avoid new wars, was a particular breaking point.
Now, Milton is helping lead a grassroots effort to write in Republican Congressman Ralph Norman for the US Senate, rather than support the party nominee, Senator Darline Graham, who has Trump’s endorsement.
A write-in candidate is someone whose name does not appear on the ballot but can still be chosen by voters who write it in themselves. The option is often used to indicate dissatisfaction with the official candidates, but rarely leads to a victory. One of those rare victories happened in 2010, when Senator Lisa Murkowski of Alaska won after launching a write-in campaign, having lost her Republican primary that year.
In the 2022 South Carolina Senate race, write-in votes accounted for just 0.1 percent of all votes cast.
Despite the president’s endorsement, Graham has struggled to unite conservatives behind her, potentially giving Democratic challenger Annie Andrews an opening in a state that has not elected a Democrat to the US Senate since 1998.
Darline’s unlikely path to Republican Senate candidate
After the sudden death of Republican US Senator Lindsey Graham on July 11, his younger sister, Darline, was appointed to serve out the remainder of his term.
Her appointment followed a tradition of family members succeeding deceased lawmakers, most commonly their spouses. But she made history as the first sibling appointed to fill a Senate vacancy.
Graham initially described the role as an opportunity to finish her brother’s work during the remaining months of his term. But days later, Trump urged her to run for a full six-year term, posting “RUN, DARLINE, RUN!” on Truth Social and promising his “complete and total endorsement” if she entered the race. Three days later, Graham announced on Fox News that she would run.
For some Republicans, the transition from temporary appointment to a full-term campaign happened too quickly. Milton said he felt the appointment had effectively “installed” a candidate.
Graham went on to defeat Republican Ralph Norman in the state’s August primary elections.
Norman, who represents South Carolina’s fifth congressional district, has repeatedly declined to campaign alongside Graham since losing the primary. He has made clear that his support for Graham is limited.
“You have to earn the vote. She hasn’t done that,” he told The Wall Street Journal. “The campaign has been about trying to prop up a candidate.”
The tensions have been particularly pronounced in Upstate South Carolina, where Norman has considerable support. Milton said Graham has done little to reach voters there during the campaign, aside from private dinners and appearances alongside Trump.
“She [Graham] never tried to reach out to everyday people here Upstate. And that spoke volumes about how this South Carolina GOP establishment feels about the grassroots conservatives. They just really don’t care,” Milton said.
Frustrated by what he saw as a failure to represent grassroots conservatives, Milton helped launch the Write-In Ralph movement, building a website and giving the campaign a public platform.
Milton said he and other supporters wanted a senator who would think independently, rather than simply fall in line with party leadership.
“We don’t necessarily want somebody that’s a rubber stamp for everything,” he said, adding that he wanted someone willing to “think of all the sides of an issue and policy”.
South Carolina’s independents
A sizeable group of South Carolina voters does not identify with either major party.
While the state does not register voters by party, a New York Times/Siena poll conducted in October suggested that 30 percent of likely voters identified as independents. Among those voters, Democratic Senate candidate Andrews led Graham by 20 percentage points.
The findings point to a potential blind spot for Republicans seeking to consolidate support around Trump’s Make America Great Again (MAGA) coalition.
John Connolly, a 77-year-old retiree who lives in South Carolina’s Lowcountry, is one example of a voter whose political allegiances have shifted over time. He sees Graham’s appointment as part of a political culture that rewards loyalty over experience.
“I see her as nothing more than a puppet,” he told Al Jazeera. “To nod her head yes whenever she’s told to.”
Leila Ali, a regional campaign adviser who has spent more than a decade working with grassroots organisations across the US South, said political strategists often underestimate the diversity of the Southern electorate.
“The biggest thing that people get wrong is that they think the Southern vote is this monolith,” she told Al Jazeera.
Ali pointed to South Carolina’s early voting figures as evidence of that engagement. Nearly 950,000 early votes have been cast in the state, according to the state’s Election Commission, setting a new record for early voting in a midterm election.
An increasingly close Senate race
The stakes of this race have become increasingly apparent as the November 3 election approaches.
Despite Trump winning South Carolina by nearly 18 percentage points in 2024, he has made two trips to South Carolina in three months to campaign for Graham – an extraordinary show of presidential attention.
And polling suggests the race is far more competitive than Republicans might have expected. The October New York Times/Siena College poll had Graham and Democratic challenger Annie Andrews tied at 48 percent among likely voters.
For Democrats, this division offers a rare opening in a deep-red state where the party has struggled to compete.
Even with the race tightening, Republicans like Milton are willing to risk a Democratic victory by writing in Ralph Norman on their ballot. And if Graham loses, Milton says the blame should not fall on the write-in effort.
“They’re going to try to point the finger on this Write-in Ralph movement,” he said. “But I just want to make something very clear: that would assume that our votes would have gone to Darline anyway, and that’s just not the case.”

Foster + Partners and MANICA Unveil Design for New Stadium to Replace Milan's San Siro
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
04:30:00 UTC
13:30:00 KST

AC Milan and FC Internazionale Milano (Inter) have unveiled the design for Generali Stadium, a 71,500-seat venue planned to become the shared home of the two football clubs in Milan, Italy. Designed by Foster + Partners and MANICA, the new stadium will be built alongside the existing San Siro as part of a 281,000-square-meter redevelopment of the surrounding area. The project follows years of discussions over the future of the historic venue, which the clubs acquired in 2025 with the intention of replacing it. Construction is expected to begin in 2028, with the stadium scheduled to host its first match during the 2031/32 season, subject to planning approvals.
The design draws on Milan's architectural and engineering heritage, with a concrete X-frame structure extending from the stadium's colonnades across the facade to support the roof. Diamond-shaped entrances lead into panoramic concourses, while a double-curved roof establishes the building's overall profile. Measuring approximately 244 by 270 meters, the roof incorporates a spoke-wheel structural system and 27,500 square meters of photovoltaic panels. The design also includes naturally ventilated spaces, rainwater harvesting, greywater recycling, and high-efficiency LED lighting. The stadium is planned as an all-electric facility, with the project targeting LEED Gold certification and carbon-neutral operation.
Inside, two seating tiers form a continuous 360-degree bowl, with the arrangement intended to provide clear sightlines and bring spectators closer to the pitch. At either end, two steeply inclined seating sections, each accommodating approximately 11,700 supporters, reinterpret the Curvas, the traditional gathering areas for the clubs' most active fan groups. With a total capacity of 71,500, the facility will include 8,088 hospitality seats, 3,698 premium general admission seats, and 394 wheelchair positions. In addition to football, the stadium is designed to accommodate concerts, rugby, and American football events.
The proposal marks the latest development in a process that began in 2019, when the two clubs first announced plans to replace San Siro. Opened in 1926 as AC Milan's home ground, the stadium became a shared venue in 1947, when Inter moved in. Also known as Stadio Giuseppe Meazza, it has undergone several expansions and renovations, most notably ahead of the 1990 FIFA World Cup, and has hosted domestic and international football matches, as well as major concerts. Previous redevelopment discussions included proposals to renovate the existing structure, while a new stadium scheme by Populous was selected by the clubs in 2021. These plans did not proceed, and the debate over the venue's future continued amid discussions concerning its architectural significance and heritage protection.
In September 2025, the Milan City Council approved the sale of the stadium and surrounding land to the two clubs, which subsequently acquired the property for €197 million. The new development is intended to extend beyond the stadium itself, introducing public spaces, landscaped areas, retail, and leisure facilities designed to remain active throughout the year. The clubs estimate the new stadium's construction cost at approximately €1.2 billion and have also secured a naming-rights agreement with Italian insurance company Generali, reportedly valued at €650 million through 2052. However, the decision to replace San Siro continues to face opposition from some supporters and heritage advocates. During the design unveiling on October 29, 2026, a group of Inter fans protested against the plans, displaying a banner calling for the preservation of the existing stadium. San Siro is expected to remain in operation until the new venue opens, after which most of its structure is planned for demolition.
Other stadium developments continue to shape the international sports architecture landscape. Recent announcements include Heatherwick Studio and MANICA Architecture's design for a 62,000-seat stadium in Birmingham, planned as the centrepiece of the city's forthcoming Sports Quarter, and the masterplan by BDP, Cox Architecture, and Collage Design for a 350-acre sports district in Ahmedabad, India, organized around the 132,000-seat Narendra Modi Stadium.

'2.5 lakh shops shut, Rs 10,000 crore loss': Delhi traders blame INDIA bloc rally for business disruption

Delhi traders claim Rs 10,000 crore loss as 2.5 lakh shops shut during INDIA bloc rally.
NEW DELHI: Around 2.5 lakh shops across 20 to 25 major markets in Delhi remained closed on Sunday, with traders claiming losses of Rs 10,000-11,000 crore due to disruptions caused by the INDIA bloc rally at Ramlila Maidan during the peak Diwali shopping season.Chamber of Trade & Industry (CTI) chairman Brijesh Goyal said nearly 80% of the approximately three lakh shops in markets surrounding the rally venue remained shut amid concerns over traffic restrictions, congestion and the expected arrival of large crowds.The disruption also affected the movement of customers, suppliers and dealers from towns surrounding the national capital. According to Goyal, around three lakh to four lakh people who regularly travel to Delhi for business did not arrive, while approximately 5,000 vehicles, including tempos and trucks, could not transport goods to markets in Old Delhi and Central Delhi.“Due to the rally held at Ramlila Maidan today, about 20 to 25 major markets in the vicinity were affected. These historic markets house approximately 3,00,000 shops. Based on data we received this evening from various WhatsApp groups—comprising traders from different markets under the CTA (Confederation of All India Traders)—about 80% of these shops—roughly 2,50,000 out of 3,00,000—remained closed today,” he said.
Goyal added that loading and unloading operations were disrupted, affecting wholesale and retail businesses during one of the busiest periods of the year.“The movement of goods—loading and unloading—was completely disrupted. During the peak Diwali season, these markets with individual turnovers collectively generate business worth approximately 10,000 to 12,000 crore rupees. Even where shops remained open, sales were virtually non-existent; there were simply no customers,” he said.Putting the estimated losses at Rs 10,000-11,000 crore, Goyal questioned who would compensate traders for the business disruption.“The question now arises: who will compensate for this loss, or who will make up for it—will the organisers do so?” he said.He said the timing of the rally had compounded the impact, as traders were preparing for the festive rush ahead of Dhanteras, scheduled four days later. Businesses in the affected markets depend heavily on the movement of customers and goods during this period.
Traders had warned of business losses ahead of rally
Ahead of the gathering, traders across several major commercial hubs in Delhi had opposed holding the rally at Ramlila Maidan during the peak Diwali shopping season. They warned that traffic congestion and restrictions could disrupt wholesale markets and affect the livelihoods of thousands of daily-wage workers.The Automotive Parts Merchant Association (APMA), based at Kashmere Gate, said the rally's location could affect commercial activity across a three-kilometre radius, covering several major trading hubs in the capital.APMA president Vinay Narang said traders were not opposed to democratic protests but objected to the timing and choice of venue."We are not aligned with any political party, nor are we against democratic protests. But the timing and the venue are completely wrong. Ramlila Maidan is located in the middle of Asia’s largest commercial zone—with major markets like Chandni Chowk, Sadar Bazaar, Daryaganj, Mori Gate, and Kashmere Gate within a three-kilometre radius," Narang said.
Rahul's video appeal for participants to shop from local traders
Amid concerns raised by traders' associations, Congress leader Rahul Gandhi had appealed to people travelling to Delhi for the rally to support local businesses by shopping from their stores during the festive season.In a video message posted on X on Saturday, Gandhi urged participants to combine their participation in the protest with shopping from small businesses.“Tomorrow, lakhs of people are coming to Delhi for the Ramlila March. It is the festive season. The time of Diwali, Chhath, and Bhai Dooj has arrived. I want those lakhs of people coming to Delhi from outside to support the traders here,” Gandhi said.“Protest, march, hold rallies, and along with that, do a little shopping too - it will benefit the traders,” he added.The leader of opposition in the Lok Sabha also accused the BJP of spreading rumours about the rally's potential economic impact.“I know the rally will not harm the traders. The BJP is scared, that's why it's spreading rumours,” he said, adding, “But let's do both. Tomorrow there will be a march, there will be a rally, and lakhs of people will buy goods from the small shops of our traders.”
INDIA bloc holds rally against SIR, alleged electoral irregularities
The INDIA bloc held the rally at Ramlila Maidan on Sunday to protest against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, alleging irregularities in the exercise.Several Opposition leaders attended the gathering, including Lok Sabha leader of opposition Rahul Gandhi, Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge, former West Bengal chief minister Mamata Banerjee and Samajwadi Party chief Akhilesh Yadav. Protesters also raised slogans such as "Vote chor, gaddi chhod", demanding accountability over alleged electoral irregularities.

Countdown until US midterm elections are over feels like waiting for war with Iran - editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
04:18:32 UTC
13:18:32 KST

Wednesday, 3 p.m. Dentist.
Thursday, 4 p.m. Pick up the children.
Friday, 11 a.m. Resume war with Iran.
Don’t forget to put it in your calendar.
It is a ridiculous way to discuss a war, particularly one whose consequences could be felt across the Middle East. Yet it is becoming difficult to escape the impression that renewed fighting with the Islamic Republic has been penciled into the diary, awaiting only a convenient date.
First came Israel’s election. Now Americans go to the polls on Tuesday for their midterms. Once those votes are counted, the thinking goes, Washington and Jerusalem can return to the unfinished business of Iran.
The headlines this weekend have done little to dispel that impression. On Saturday, President Donald Trump said the United States had largely destroyed Iran’s nuclear capabilities but still had “one or two sites” to deal with, including the underground facility known as Pickaxe Mountain. “We can do that in 10 minutes,” he told reporters.
Ten minutes. Barely enough time for a coffee, apparently, and sufficient to settle what remains of the Iranian nuclear question.
Electoral timetable feels like a countdown
Trump also spoke with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Saturday, amid reports of American preparations for renewed strikes. The Post reported that US military aircraft have delivered equipment to the region, while Washington and Israel continue coordinating their plans.
None of this means a strike has been ordered. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Saturday that Trump “hasn’t made a decision” and still prefers a diplomatic solution. Trump himself said negotiations were progressing, although he questioned Tehran’s reliability. The distinction matters: military planning can be intended to strengthen diplomacy as much as to prepare for its failure.
Nevertheless, the electoral timetable is hard to ignore. Trump explicitly ruled out attacking Iran before November 3.
Reports have also described an Israeli operation contemplated for October that did not proceed amid American opposition. Whether these accounts capture every consideration behind the decisions is another matter. But the public message has been unmistakable: there are dates on which war is apparently less convenient than others.
Of course, governments must weigh domestic political circumstances before committing their countries to military action.
Democracies cannot operate in a vacuum, and leaders have an obligation to consider the public they represent. There is, however, something deeply uncomfortable about the suggestion that an Iranian nuclear facility can remain an intolerable danger on Monday but become a suitable target only after Tuesday’s ballots have been cast.
Countdown seems to downplay importance of the decision
Iran’s threat is not imaginary. Its nuclear ambitions, ballistic missiles, support for armed proxies, and repeated threats against Israel have given successive Israeli governments ample reason for concern. Tehran’s leaders have also made clear that further attacks would invite retaliation, potentially against American allies and civilian infrastructure throughout the region. Israelis know well that even successful operations can carry a heavy price at home.
That is precisely why the conversation should be more serious than the current countdown suggests. What, exactly, would another campaign achieve? Is the objective to destroy the remaining nuclear infrastructure, prevent Iran from rebuilding its missile arsenal, force a credible agreement, or create conditions in which Iranians themselves can finally determine their country’s future?
These objectives overlap, but they are not interchangeable. A 10-minute strike might destroy a facility. It cannot, by itself, resolve the political and strategic problem posed by the Islamic Republic. Nor should anyone assume that Tehran will respond according to the timetable Washington prefers.
Civilians deserve to know impacts of what leaders are preparing
For the Iranian people, who have endured repression, economic hardship, and the regime’s brutality, this is considerably more than a discussion about American polling dates. For Israelis, too, the stakes are measured in lives, not campaign cycles.
Israel must retain the freedom to act against genuine threats, and the United States must not allow Tehran to use negotiations indefinitely as cover for rebuilding its capabilities. But decisions of such consequence require clear objectives, sober judgment, and an honest explanation of the risks.
The public deserves to know whether leaders are preparing a limited operation, a prolonged confrontation, or another round whose ending nobody can confidently predict.
The calendar may tell us when the elections are over. It cannot tell us when war is necessary, still less when it will end.

Taiwan orchid breeders target premium overseas markets
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
04:09:57 UTC
13:09:57 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan's flower industry generates approximately NT$18 billion (US$551 million) in annual production value, with moth orchids (Phalaenopsis) accounting for more than 90% of flower exports.
Taiwan Orchid Breeders Association Chair Chou Po-yi (周伯倚) told reporters at a flower promotion event that the US and Japan remain major markets, per CNA.
He added that Taiwanese-bred mutant moth orchids are highly sought after. One variety features distinctive markings resembling eyes and can command prices up to 10 times higher than conventional moth orchids in certain markets, Chou said.
He expressed confidence in orchid exports, citing the industry's strong virus-testing capabilities and cultivation expertise. Although domestic growers face price competition from other countries, some overseas buyers who previously switched suppliers have returned after recognizing the quality of Taiwan's orchids, he said.
Chou said the US remains Taiwan's largest market, but developing additional destinations is also important. Growers should develop varieties suited to different markets rather than relying solely on government promotion efforts, he added.
For example, Middle Eastern consumers prefer darker-colored moth orchids, prompting Taiwanese growers to cultivate varieties with deeper hues, including nearly black flowers, per CNA.
Orchid production is concentrated in central and southern Taiwan, with growers relying on tissue culture, greenhouse technology, and specialized breeding to maintain quality and increase value.

Taiwan showcases its health-based approach to chemsex at Asia-Pacific symposium
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
04:09:39 UTC
13:09:39 KST

KAOHSIUNG (Taiwan News) — As US cuts to HIV funding ripple across Asia and programs that help prevent infections among people who engage in chemsex lose funding, Taiwan has been largely spared because it finances care through national health insurance, prompting policymakers across the region to look to its example.
Chemsex, the use of drugs before or during sex to enhance sexual experiences, is raising the risk of HIV and other sexually transmitted infections across the region, UN agencies warn. The Asia-Pacific Chemsex Symposium, held in Kaohsiung last week, seeks to promote an evidence-based approach to the emerging crisis of drug deaths.
Globally, harm reduction, or efforts to help people use drugs more safely, has been severely underfunded. In 2022, only 6% of the funding needs of low- and middle-income countries were met. Recent cuts, including those to UN-affiliated programs, have deepened the gap.
In Thailand, Nattaya Phanuphak, executive director of the Institute of HIV Research and Innovation in Bangkok, said her organization had cut 20% of its staff and struggled to expand care for people who use drugs. In another example, research in Thailand exploring the experiences of young people who engage in chemsex was suspended prematurely.
Taiwan’s situation is different because the work is financed domestically. Through the National Health Insurance system, harm reduction is built into state-funded hospitals, sexual health clinics, and LGBTQ+ centers.
A health problem
In Asia, some of the world’s strictest drug laws are in force. The conversation about chemsex rarely gets past fear and moral judgment, and the people affected are often considered criminals rather than patients.
The Asia-Pacific Chemsex Symposium, founded in 2019, is one of the few regional gatherings to treat the practice as a public health issue, said Stephane Wen-Wei Ku, who leads the Taiwan HIV Education and Research Association (HEART).
“Sex and drugs are taboo across Asia,” he said. “But in Taiwan, we realized the importance of this issue, and civic groups and the government have been working to raise awareness.”
Like most Asian countries, Taiwan criminalizes the use, production, and possession of illicit drugs. Methamphetamine, the most common substance associated with chemsex, is a Category 2 narcotic under the Narcotics Hazard Prevention Act.
Even so, Phanuphak said Taiwan has moved ahead of its neighbors in treating chemsex as a health matter, with the infrastructure and sustainable financing in place to support harm reduction. She hopes the symposium, which moves to Thailand next year, will “create an effect” that eventually changes policy across the region.
What Taiwan did
One of Taiwan’s main programs to address the risks of drug use during sex is the distribution of pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP), a prescription medication that the Taiwan CDC called an “internationally recognized complementary strateg[y] for HIV control.”
Studies show that, when taken consistently, PrEP cuts the risk of HIV infection from sex by about 99% among people who do not inject drugs and by at least 74% among those who do.
Lo Yi-chun, the CDC’s director-general, told the conference the program was launched following a sharp rise in HIV infections among men who have sex with men in the 2010s. After a medical exam, physicians can prescribe PrEP to eligible HIV-negative individuals.
In 2022, eligibility expanded to include chemsex users, sex workers, and people under 35 at high risk, he added.
The results are measurable. New HIV cases among the group fell from 2,175 in 2017 to 754 in 2025, a drop of about 65%. Lo credited the PrEP program, along with Taiwan’s marriage equality movement, which he said rallied the CDC and community groups around the goal of HIV prevention.
Matteo Cassolato, an adviser to the Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria, sees growing recognition of chemsex across the region but says responses rarely match the need. He called it “inspiring” to see the Taiwanese government attuned to its people’s needs.
For Phanuphak, that makes Taiwan a lesson worth exporting. “The example of Taiwan must be taught outside of Taiwan, on a larger scale,” she said.

Egypt signs $1 billion World Bank financing agreement for second phase of reform program
Egypt has signed a $1 billion financing agreement with the World Bank to implement the second phase of its Development Policy Financing (DPF) program, aimed at supporting structural reforms, strengthening economic resilience and improving the country's business environment, Qazinform News Agency cites WAM.
The agreement was signed by Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty, who also serves as Egypt's governor at the World Bank, and Alwaleed Alatabani, the World Bank's Division Director for Egypt.
Titled “Building Resilience, Creating Opportunities and Enhancing Wealth for Egypt's Prosperity and Stability,” the program seeks to enhance the competitiveness of the Egyptian economy, strengthen its capacity to withstand external economic shocks and accelerate the country's transition towards a green economy.
The second phase focuses on a range of structural reforms, particularly those related to the governance of state-owned enterprises. Key priorities include removing barriers to private-sector investment and business growth, promoting fair competition, improving domestic revenue mobilization and reducing government borrowing costs.
The financing agreement forms part of the Egyptian government's broader efforts to secure development funding from international and regional financial institutions to support economic stability and resilience.
It is also intended to advance Egypt's economic competitiveness, encourage sustainable and green development, and establish a more favorable investment climate capable of attracting private-sector investment and generating employment opportunities.

Feature: Australian exhibitors eye long-term partnerships at China's import expo
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
12:05:14 CST
13:05:14 KST

MELBOURNE, Nov. 2 (Xinhua) -- "It's progressing very well," Sam Zhang said of the partnership Australian dairy producer Bulla formed with Chinese grocery platform Dingdong Fresh at last year's China International Import Expo (CIIE).
Zhang, who oversees international business at Bulla, told Xinhua that the company's products were doing well on the platform.
The ninth CIIE will run from Nov. 5 to 10 in Shanghai. Bulla is preparing to return with new ice cream products, while probiotics company Biome Australia is getting ready for its debut. Both companies hope to use the expo to gain a better understanding of Chinese consumers and build long-term business partnerships.
Zhang said Bulla has participated in the expo every year since 2019. Opportunities to connect with consumers and buyers, showcase its brand and explore business partnerships have kept the company coming back.
The 2024 and 2025 editions were particularly memorable. Bulla reached agreements with Chinese customers at both the 2024 and 2025 expos, including a direct-sourcing agreement with Dingdong Fresh in 2025. Chinese pizza restaurant chain BigPizza is the company's largest customer in China, Zhang said.
Bulla had limited brand recognition in China when it first attended the expo. It has since expanded its business network in the retail and food service sectors. Zhang said the expo has helped the company connect with consumers and business partners while keeping pace with changing market demands.
Bulla's exports to China exceeded 10 million Australian dollars (about 7 million U.S. dollars) in the financial year ended June 30, 2026, Zhang said.
Zhang said growing health awareness among Chinese consumers has prompted Bulla to adjust its packaging and product information. The company has also worked with Sam's Club, a membership-based warehouse retailer in China, for several years, developing products tailored to the retailer each year.
This year, Bulla plans to showcase ice cream products for food service businesses, as well as new ice cream cones, with samples available for visitors to try.
Over the years, Zhang has seen more international brands and a wider range of products at the expo, which offer Chinese consumers more choices. He described the growing competition as "the nature of doing business."
"We're ready for it," he said.
As Bulla prepares to return to China, Biome is getting ready for its first appearance. During an interview in Melbourne, Rebecca Edwards, the company's director of education, showed some of the probiotic products it plans to exhibit, including those for babies and children as well as for daily use.
Biome already operates in Canada, New Zealand, Britain and Ireland. Having followed the Chinese market for some time, the company is now preparing to enter its first Asian market, Edwards said.
"China feels like the natural next step," she said.
Edwards sees growing interest among Chinese consumers in probiotic products designed for specific health needs. At the expo, Biome hopes to hear directly from consumers about their health concerns and meet people familiar with China's health products market and cross-border e-commerce sector to explore potential partnerships.
Preparations for entering China are already underway. Biome has signed a heads of agreement with cross-border e-commerce company H&S Global and is working toward a formal distribution agreement, which it hopes to sign by the end of this year, Edwards said. The company plans to develop its business in China through cross-border e-commerce.
"We see a lot of potential in China," she said.
Rhys Roberts, national president and chair of the Australia China Business Council, said in written responses that the CIIE offers Australian exporters a practical way to meet importers, distributors and retailers from across China in a single week, rather than traveling to a dozen cities.
"What matters most to our members is what happens after the expo. Conversations that start on the show floor become distribution agreements, repeat orders and long-term partnerships, and that is where the real value lies," he said.
Predictability is particularly important to businesses, he said. Clear rules, consistent customs and regulatory processes, and reliable market access give them confidence to commit to a market for the long term.
"Every step that makes it easier to do business in China is welcomed by Australian companies."
On the outlook for Australia-China business ties, Roberts said: "The mood I hear from our members is practical optimism."
Businesses that succeed in China, in his view, are those that invest in relationships, understand consumers and take a long-term view. ■

Faisal Mahmud
02 November 2026•Update: 02 November 2026
Japan launched a new national agency Monday to strengthen disaster preparedness and coordinate responses to major earthquakes, floods and volcanic eruptions, Kyodo News Agency reported.
The Tokyo-based National Disaster Management Agency, headed by Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, will establish regional hubs to improve coordination with local governments and prepare for potentially devastating earthquakes along the Nankai Trough, Japan Trench and Chishima Trench as well as beneath metropolitan Tokyo.
Locations for the regional hubs will be selected by the summer of 2027, with operations scheduled to begin by July 2028.
Reconstruction Minister Goshi Hosono will concurrently serve as disaster management minister, said Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara.
The agency, the first established directly under Cabinet supervision since the Digital Agency in September 2021, will support municipalities facing budget constraints and shortages of disaster management specialists.
The disaster management minister will have the authority to recommend improvements to other government bodies.
Priorities include improving evacuation shelters, reducing disaster-related deaths and ensuring that essential supplies reach displaced residents.
The agency will also oversee reconstruction in earthquake-hit regions while addressing increasingly severe flooding linked to heavy rainfall across Japan.

US midterms: What to know about independent voters and candidates
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
03:53:42 UTC
12:53:42 KST

US midterms: What to know about independent voters and candidates
Despite a record number of independents, third-party candidates and voters struggle to penetrate the two-party political system.
As Americans head to the polls on Tuesday in the much-anticipated midterms, the record number of voters identifying as independent could prove decisive for control of the US Congress and state legislatures.
Nearly half of US voters – as many as 117 million adults – now identify as politically independent, with the two major parties, Democrats and Republicans, jockeying for their votes.
At the same time, independent or third-party candidates win few federal or state seats. The Democratic and Republican parties have dominated US politics, from state legislatures to the US Congress and the presidency, for generations.
“The whole [electoral] system is built to frustrate the independence of voters,” says Rick Bennett, the former Republican Party chair in Maine, where he is running to become only the third independent governor in the state’s history.
Bennett’s candidacy runs headlong into one of the most stubborn contradictions in US politics: While millions of eligible voters reject Republican and Democratic labels, far fewer will cast their ballots for independent candidates.
“For decades, candidates outside the Democratic and Republican parties have struggled to achieve [a high] level of support,” political scientist AJ Simmons said. “[But] 2026 is shaping up to be one of the strongest election cycles for independent candidates in recent memory.”
Who are independents and how will they vote?
According to the Pew Research Center’s annual National Public Opinion Reference Survey, 44 percent of US adults identify as politically independent. This is in contrast to 29 percent who identify as Democrat and 28 percent as Republican.
But there is a caveat: Most self-described independents still gravitate towards one of the major parties. Independents who express absolutely no partisan leaning make up only about 7-10 percent of the total electorate.
These “true” independents are sought after by candidates because they are persuadable, the core of the coveted so-called swing vote in a deeply divided and partisan electorate and political system.
In the 2026 midterm elections, 52 percent of likely independent voters are supporting Democrats, while 39 percent back Republicans, polling firm Marist suggests.
Frustration with President Donald Trump is permeating the midterm electoral landscape, with independent respondents more than three times as likely to say their vote is mainly against the president, and 28 percent saying they are voting for “change”.
Why does the US have a two-party system?
The US does not legally restrict elections to two parties, and many local officials are not party-affiliated.
But for more powerful federal and statewide seats like Tuesday’s House of Representatives and Senate races, the winner-take-all electoral system and single-member congressional districts work against outsiders and can discourage voters from backing them.
Even substantial support for a minor party is rarely concentrated enough in one district to win a congressional seat.
Voters, too, can unknowingly reinforce the system.
Polling trends and data further suggest that voters who identify as or prefer an independent will often instead back a Republican or Democrat they see as more politically viable. Voters are also reluctant to support “spoilers”, who may peel away votes from one of the two major-party candidates.
Why do third parties struggle to win US elections?
Bernard Tamas, a political scientist at Valdosta State University who studies third parties, said that although laws are often blamed for keeping third-party candidates off the ballot, “there is very little evidence that legal barriers are undermining these candidates”.
The real barrier, he says, is money.
A total of $14.8bn was spent on federal elections during the 2024 presidential cycle, and the 2026 midterms are projected to surpass that, reaching up to $11.6bn in political advertisement spending alone.
The Democratic National Committee (DNC), which heads the Democratic Party, raised nearly $252.3m during the 2026 midterm campaign cycle while the Republican National Committee (RNC) took in about $341m.
Unlike other democracies, the US “offers virtually no public support” or funding to political parties and does not set limits on campaign spending”, Tamas said. Independent candidates “raise very little money” and are less well known by voters.
Why don’t more Americans vote independent?
Lesley Shedd, a Republican strategist, told Al Jazeera that the surge in voters identifying as independents obscures their support for one of the two major parties.
“When somebody says they are independent, they really are a Republican or Democrat but they maybe don’t agree with the party on absolutely every issue,” Shedd said. “Or they [just] don’t want to feel as though they are part of the culture of the swamp of [Washington] DC.”
The real test for independent candidates is persuading Americans to vote for them, not just a “protest vote” against the system. And voters are reluctant to cast a “wasted” ballot, Simmons said, given the most competitive candidates are Democrats or Republicans.
There are efforts to support independent candidates. The Independent Leadership Council, launched in July by former Democrat-turned-independent Senator Joe Manchin, provides donors and campaign resources for independent congressional candidates. The project has raised more than $10m.
But the longer-term test, analysts maintain, is whether independent candidates can be viable across multiple races and election cycles.
Will third-party candidates influence the 2026 midterms?
There is currently one independent in the US House and two in the US Senate. None holds a state governor seat.
Bennett, the independent Maine candidate, is one of just 11 independent or third-party candidates vying for gubernatorial or US Senate seats whom Simmons expects to surpass the 5 percent vote threshold often used to gauge electoral viability.
Additionally, Simmons sees several ways independent congressional hopefuls could throw the midterm map into disarray, mainly in two key states: Nebraska and Montana.
He identified Nebraska’s independent Senate candidate Dan Osborn, a 51-year-old Navy veteran, as the “most likely alternative candidate to win” across the country, given the race has been deemed a toss-up by RealClearPolling, an election analysis website.
The Nebraska Democratic Party chose not to field a replacement nominee after its candidate withdrew, leaving Osborn as the principal challenger to Republican Pete Ricketts.
In Montana, Simmons sees another opening for an independent, though the race is complicated by the possibility of an unpredictable “spoiler” effect.
Seth Bodnar, a former University of Montana president and Army veteran, is running against Republican Kurt Alme for the US Senate seat. He is being backed by the Independent Leadership Council, which is also supporting California Congressman Kevin Kiley, who left the Republican Party to seek re-election as an independent.
Democratic US Senate candidate Alani Bankhead could siphon off support from the same centre-left and anti-Republican pool of voters that Bodnar draws from, risking a three-way vote and potentially leaving the Republican to collect the spoils.
“Montana is the second most likely,” Simmons said, adding that “if that were to happen, the Republican Party would be having an extraordinarily bad night”.
In Idaho and South Dakota, independent candidates are not forecast to win, but they are expected to make Republicans pay for treating those seats as safe, diverting money, campaign time and attention to races Republicans may have otherwise taken for granted.
The greatest impact of independents may be the pressure they have historically brought to bear on the major parties to “implement a new policy or govern more effectively”, Simmons said.

Prime minister to discuss British backpacker rule tightening
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
03:39:46 UTC
12:39:46 KST

PM Anthony Albanese to discuss British backpacker rule changes with Burnham
In short:
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese is expected to discuss changing the rules for British backpackers with his UK counterpart Andy Burnham.
Under a free trade deal, UK citizens are exempt from regional work requirements for Working Holiday Maker visas.
What's next?
The National Farmers' Federation has welcomed the discussions, but said the regional worker shortage issue was far broader.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese will discuss tightening the rules for British backpacker visas when he meets with UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham in the Caribbean this week.
Currently, the UK free trade deal allows British backpackers to stay in Australia for up to three years without requiring specific work to be undertaken.
However, other Working Holiday Maker visa holders must work in regional and rural areas if they wish to extend their visas beyond a year.
That arrangement has seen a sharp rise in UK backpackers, from about 47,000 in 2024 to nearly 80,000 last financial year, according to Home Affairs data.
But with the government under political pressure to lower its net overseas migration numbers, Mr Albanese is set to seek a change to the rules for UK citizens when he meets Mr Burnham at the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM) in Antigua and Barbuda.
The discussions mark a departure from Mr Albanese's previous position, when he told the ABC in August that there would be no changes to the deal that exempts British backpackers from regional work rules.
Mr Albanese flagged last week that he would be bringing up the issue with Mr Burnham.
"Those UK backpackers are arriving in very large numbers … and they are staying at Bondi Beach or Coogee or around particularly the capital cities and working in hospitality there," Mr Albanese said.
"That's placing enormous pressure because it's distorting the labour market in these areas as well.
"That's just one of the areas in which we'll put forward changes. That requires discussions, and I'll be meeting with Prime Minister Andy Burnham."
Backpacker back-and-forth
The Coalition and One Nation have repeatedly advocated for backpacking visas to survive migration cuts, saying they are a vital resource in their regional electorates.
The National Farmers' Federation (NFF) has also stressed the backpacking workforce is essential for the agriculture sector.
In August, Home Affairs quietly slowed the processing of working holiday visas, sparking concerns about workforce shortages in the regions.
In September, the NFF made an emergency deal with the government to fast-track urgent visa requests for backpacker workers in harvest and fruit-picking.
Under changes proposed by Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke at the National Press Club in September, a ballot and cap system would be introduced.
Loading...
For backpackers hoping to stay on for a second year, places would be capped at 45,000 and they would need to undertake 88 days of regional work to enter the ballot.
Third-year spots would be capped at 5,000 places with a six-month regional work requirement.
NFF head Michael Guerin welcomed the prime minister's discussions, but said the issue of worker shortages in the agriculture sector was broader than the UK deal, pointing to a slowing of visa processing and a proposed cap and ballot system for backpackers.
"[It's] a step in the right direction, but not dealing with the fundamental underlying issue,"
he said.
"We have a crisis point in Australia, based on the inability to get a hold of the workforce we need to guarantee that food security we've taken for granted for generations.
"One in seven of our workers to harvest our food, keep our supermarket shelves filled, come from overseas."
Opposition leader Angus Taylor said Mr Albanese's "outsourcing" of the issue to his UK counterpart was "desperate", despite highlighting that the Coalition's position was to encourage more backpackers to go regional.
"This is a desperate prime minister who's not only lost control of the economy, he's lost control of our borders," Mr Taylor said.
"We want them doing rural and regional work. That's a centrepiece of our policy.
"But what Labor's proposing is a ballot for who gets to stay; it's a raffle. I mean, seriously, pick the people who are going to contribute in the places where we need them."
Nationals leader Matt Canavan said the Coalition had a "completely elegant solution" and would put a fee in place for any backpacker wanting to stay in Australia for a second or third year working in a capital city.
"We would impose a fee on that, and that fee would help encourage people to get back to the regional work," he said.

Arab League demands international inquiry into torture of Gaza detainees in Israeli prison
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
03:27:20 UTC
12:27:20 KST

The Arab League has demanded an independent international investigation into the torture and systematic abuse of Palestinian detainees from Gaza held at Israel's Ramla Prison, insisting on accountability for those responsible.
In an official statement, the pan-Arab organisation condemned recurring assaults against prisoners in the facility’s Rakevet wing, reporting that the violence has left detainees with severe injuries and burns.
The league described the practices as flagrant breaches of international humanitarian law, including the Geneva Conventions and the Convention against Torture, declaring that they constitute crimes against humanity requiring legal accountability.
The league called for an immediate halt to all mistreatment and urged Israeli authorities to grant unrestricted access to the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) and independent international monitors to document conditions and provide necessary medical care.
It further demanded the unconditional release of sick and wounded detainees and an immediate end to arbitrary detention.
Systematic weekend raids
The diplomatic appeal follows an October 27 report by the Palestinian Prisoners' Media Office documenting recurring violence against Gaza detainees inside the Rakevet wing.
According to the report, assaults take place regularly on Fridays and Saturdays, involving beatings with batons, tear gas, pepper spray, rubber bullets, and stun grenades.
The monitor also reported that prison guards enter cells with police dogs and forcibly transfer detainees to rooms without surveillance cameras to conduct assaults out of sight.
The office warned that the ongoing violence poses an acute risk to prisoners' lives, particularly those suffering from pre-existing injuries and chronic illnesses.
The Arab League urged the wider international community, the United Nations Human Rights Council, and the UN General Assembly to intervene decisively to protect Palestinian prisoners and dismantle the culture of impunity.
Ramla Prison, situated in central Israel, is administered directly by the Israel Prison Service.

The tournament features four teams: South Korea’s Sangmu Phoenix, Japan’s Tochigi Golden Braves, National Taiwan Sport University, and the Hsinchu City Baseball Team.
Tickets for Monday and Tuesday’s games are free. Spectators should enter through Gates 10, 11, or 12 and follow the seating instructions on their tickets and directions from on-site staff.
The renovation included rebuilding the field’s foundation, improving drainage, reinforcing parts of the underground parking structure, and replacing natural grass with artificial turf. The city government said the improvement project took 266 calendar days, per a city government press release.
Construction teams also removed unsuitable material from the outfield soil and installed new drainage layers to improve water permeability and ground stability. The new artificial turf is designed to reduce heat absorption. An automatic irrigation system was also installed to cool the playing surface when needed.
The latest improvement project passed final inspection on Sept. 14. The city government said it would continue monitoring the stadium’s structural safety, drainage, artificial turf, and related facilities. Future operations and maintenance are to be handled through an operations-transfer arrangement, per CNA.
The city has also implemented traffic controls around the stadium. The underground parking facility is designated for motorcycles during the tournament. If it is full, riders are advised to use the temporary parking area on Guangzhou Street. Motorists are advised to park at Shulintou Parking Lot or Crystal Mall Parking Lot.

It pledged to continue monitoring maritime activity and take necessary measures to defend Taiwan’s sovereignty and ensure maritime security.

Over 70 pct of Australians say country more divided than 12 months ago: survey
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
11:17:40 CST
12:17:40 KST

CANBERRA, Nov. 2 (Xinhua) -- A survey found that almost three-quarters of Australians believe the country is more divided than it was a year ago.
According to the survey, conducted by independent think tank McKinnon, 41.9 percent of Australians strongly agree the country is more divided than 12 months ago, and another 32.5 percent said they somewhat agree.
The proportion of respondents who said they were either very or somewhat satisfied with the way Australia is heading declined from 28.8 percent in 2025 to 26.1 percent in 2026, while the proportion of those who said they are very dissatisfied rose by 7.2 percentage points.
The survey, which was conducted in June and July, polled over 4,000 people on their views about the Australian political system, leaders and institutions.
It found that 30.5 percent of respondents said they have a high degree of trust in federal politicians, down from 35.9 percent in 2025, while the proportion who said they have a high degree of trust in political parties fell from 31.2 percent to 24.4 percent.
"Australians have considerably more confidence in the institutions of democracy than they do in the politics conducted within them," John Thwaites, McKinnon's interim executive chair and former deputy premier of the state of Victoria, said.
"One of the findings I found most striking is the divide by education. Satisfaction with democracy is 59 percent among Australians with a university degree or higher. Among Australians whose highest qualification is high school or below, it is just 39.7 percent."
Asked if they feel understood and represented by Australia's federal politicians, 34.6 percent of respondents said they strongly disagree compared to 27.0 percent in 2025.
The proportion of respondents who said they have a low degree of trust in the federal government increased from 46.3 percent in 2025 to 52.8 percent in 2026. ■

====================================================================================================

Canavan's seat switch might backfire, but does he have a better option?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
03:16:55 UTC
12:16:55 KST

analysis
Matt Canavan's lower house switch might backfire, but does he have a better option?
Is it a high-risk, high-reward gamble? Or is it the move of a man backed into a corner?
Matt Canavan's decision to make a tilt for the lower house seat of Capricornia at the next federal election is a signal of his eagerness to take up the Coalition's fight against Pauline Hanson's One Nation.
It also puts him at the front of the queue of potential casualties, should that battle go pear-shaped for the opposition.
While Capricornia is the seat that Canavan lives in, and is therefore the natural one for him to stand in, it also appears to be highly vulnerable.
At the 2025 election, One Nation recorded its third-highest primary vote in Capricornia, and nationally it is an outlier for the party.
One Nation polled 15.5 per cent of the primary vote in the seat in 2025, more than double its national result of 6.4 per cent.
With One Nation support nationally now roughly quadruple that result, you would expect its support in Capricornia to be well north of 30 per cent, perhaps even higher than 40 per cent.
It's why the seat is routinely on the list of likely One Nation gains if an election were held today.
At the state level, this is also a One Nation hotspot: The seat of Mirani, which One Nation won in 2017 and 2020 (before disendorsing its sitting MP ahead of the 2024 election), sits entirely within Capricornia.
So does Keppel, which One Nation's now-party director James Ashby stood for in the 2024 Queensland election, polling a quarter of the vote.
The mining sector makes up a large part of Capricornia's economy, including the major mining centres of Collinsville, Moranbah and Clermont, and Canavan has long sought to brand himself as a supporter of the coal mining industry.
The outgoing member, Michelle Landry, has held the seat since 2013, but with the area's industrial past, it has a long history of Labor members before that.
The Nationals have previously been able to see off threats around the country, in recent times largely from independents, partly because their incumbents were well known in their communities.
With Landry retiring, it is smart for the Nationals to run a high-profile and known candidate in her place (presuming Canavan wins preselection).
And despite the Nationals' current struggles in the polls, all is not lost for the party. To win in these parts, One Nation needs to be far enough ahead of the Nationals on primary votes to stay ahead after preferences are distributed. Labor and Greens preferences (however many there are in 2028) are likely to break the Nationals' way.
The other pathway for One Nation is to beat the LNP down into third place and benefit from the preferences of excluded Nationals.
After much chatter, Hanson and party director Ashby (who has been a state election candidate in the area) have ruled out going for the seat.
Either way, the incumbents need to keep their primary votes high to hang on, and if anyone can keep their party's support afloat in a seat like Capricornia, it's Canavan.
It still all adds up to a gamble for the leader of the Nationals, but one he seems willing to make.
"I want to be on the front lines with my troops as well … [and] I'm happy to sacrifice potentially my own political future to do that," Canavan told ABC Radio Capricornia today.
"I just have to be there in the trenches with them."
Capricornia is near the top of a long list of problems
Capricornia may become one of the highest-profile contests between the conservative parties when the next federal election rolls around, but the big problem for the Nationals is that it is far from the only seat under threat.
If you run your finger down the list of One Nation's best seats in 2025, you'll see most of the Nationals party room.
Among the top 20, there are four Labor seats, five Liberal party room members, and 11 Nationals, most of whom are in Queensland.
If the party can't abate the threat posed by One Nation, it faces electoral annihilation.
And the damage wouldn't be limited to the lower house.
Canavan is up for re-election in 2028, and he holds the second LNP seat in Queensland, behind Liberal colleague James McGrath.
Polls of federal voting intention in Queensland have, more often than not, put One Nation ahead of the LNP in recent months.
If the figures in Newspoll's most recent quarterly aggregate of voting intention bore out at the next election, Queensland would most likely elect two Labor senators, two from One Nation, one from the Greens, and just one LNP senator.
It means that unless something changes, the Nationals leader is currently at risk of losing his seat.
Running for Capricornia may be a gamble, but what does he have to lose?
Canavan's odds of staying in parliament would have probably been better (but maybe only a bit better) had he chosen to run for the Senate for another term.
While he takes on a bit more personal risk by making this chamber switch, it may actually be his best opportunity to revive the Nationals' fortunes.
If he goes down with the ship, he'll at least be able to say he tried.

AFoCO approves $1.08mln project to strengthen forest restoration and fire resilience in Mongolia

Unknown Publisher

AFoCO approves $1.08mln project to strengthen forest restoration and fire resilience in Mongolia
The project, titled “Establishment of a Climate-Resilient Forest Restoration and Fire Resilience Hub with Carbon Market Readiness in Mongolia,” was approved during the 15th Session of the AFoCO Assembly held in Seoul, South Korea.
The initiative will focus on rehabilitating degraded and fire-damaged forests, establishing tree nurseries and a dedicated training center, and enhancing the country's capacity to prevent and respond to forest fires. It will also support the development of systems for forest carbon accounting and monitoring.
The project is expected to contribute to Mongolia's national “Billion Trees” movement by connecting large-scale tree-planting efforts with long-term forest restoration, sustainable management and protection initiatives.
A Mongolian delegation led by the director general of the National Forest Agency attended the Assembly, where it presented the country's forestry priorities and potential areas for international cooperation. The delegation also expressed its support for the implementation of the newly approved project.
Earlier, Qazinform reported a wildfire scorched more than 500,000 hectares in eastern Mongolia.

Scientists find a way to send smells online
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
03:13:35 UTC
12:13:35 KST

Scientists find a way to send smells online
Called Scentronic, the system combines AI with gas sensors and a small device that releases controlled amounts of scented liquid.
The system uses 6 sensors to detect and classify odors. AI algorithms then identify the source from 5 tested categories: beer, cake, coffee, orange and red wine. The results are transmitted over the internet to a device that releases the corresponding scent.
The researchers developed several designs, including wristbands, necklaces and handheld devices. They also built a cup that combines smell and taste stimulation. In a demonstration, selecting virtual beer or coffee in a mixed reality environment triggered the cup to release the corresponding aroma and taste cues.
Tests involving 14 participants showed 72.86% accuracy in identifying five odors. Participants distinguished combinations of two scents with 71.43% accuracy. Their accuracy in ranking 5 levels of alcohol scent intensity was 58.57%.
The technology could eventually support remote smell tests, allowing clinicians to assess patients’ ability to detect odors and monitor changes in their sense of smell. It could also help make virtual reality, online shopping and digital communication more immersive.
However, Scentronic cannot yet reproduce smells with complete accuracy. It identifies an odor category and recreates it using prepared scent options rather than copying the exact chemical makeup of the original smell. The researchers say the system needs more sensors and scent channels to recognize and reproduce a wider range of odors.
Earlier, Qazinform News Agency reported that smelling coffee might ease anxiety and fatigue.
