North Korea touts BBQ restaurant boom, but sceptics dismiss it as propaganda
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
02:16:24 CET
10:16:24 KST

By Maggie Grether and Soohyun Jung
SEOUL, Nov 2 (Reuters) - North Korea is projecting a new culinary obsession: multi-story barbecue restaurants with waterside terraces, marble tabletops inlaid with grills, and menus featuring beef, pork, and ostrich.
Since September, state media has announced over a dozen new ”bulgogi” restaurants nationwide, a Korean word that usually refers to grilled meat in North Korea.
Dismissed by some as government propaganda, the proliferation is striking in a country that has long struggled to feed its people. The UN food body said in its latest report on the country that more than two out of every five North Koreans were undernourished.
Analysts say the openings reflect a push by leader Kim Jong Un to portray a growing prosperity across the country although sceptics wonder how accessible or busy the restaurants will be.
One new restaurant in Sinuiju, a city on the Chinese border, is three stories tall. In northern Kanggye, patrons can drink draft beer alongside a fish tank, while in the west coast city of Nampo, an opening ceremony included fireworks. Other restaurants tout unusually large floor plans that can seat hundreds.
Meat is an important symbol for the regime and recalls the promise of the late Kim Il Sung, a former leader and grandfather of Kim Jong Un, to give his people “white rice with meat soup”, said Benjamin Katzeff Silberstein, head of Korean Studies at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem.
The openings mirror the spread of other leisure initiatives like waterparks, coffee bars, and high-end malls. While Kim has not yet been pictured at these openings, they are usually attended by high-level local officials.
“I think it’s a way of showing all these nice things … they’re coming to people outside of Pyongyang, too,” Silberstein said.
The restaurants may be further evidence that some North Koreans, especially in trade and construction, are benefiting from growing ties with Russia, said Hazel Smith, professorial research associate in Korean Studies at University of London’s School of Oriental and African Studies.
But “this is not a sign that you’ve got a thriving economy—it’s a sign that some people at the moment are able to get by and afford to go out and have a meal now and then,” she said.
North Korea’s economy grew 3.5% in 2025, a third straight year above 3%, South Korea’s central bank said in July.
FOOD STRUGGLES
During the 1990s famine, the state’s food distribution system collapsed and hundreds of thousands of people died, pushing North Koreans toward private markets to survive.
Semi-private markets and support from China and Russia have since brought more stability, analysts say. Meat imports from China more than quadrupled between 2023 and 2025 to nearly $39 million, according to UN Comtrade data.
Joung Eun-lee, director of the North Korean Research Division at the South Korean government-funded Korea Institute for National Unification, says the rising imports show domestic production can not meet demand.
The state media coverage of restaurant openings serves as a “powerful form of propaganda,” she said.
Kim has urged cadres to improve domestic livestock production, but food supply is believed to remain precarious. The UN World Food Programme estimated that 10.7 million people, more than 40% of the North Korean population, were undernourished in 2022.
Lee Ae-Ran, who defected from North Korea in 1997, said beef was very hard to obtain because cows were reserved as working animals on farms. She remembers eating once at a Pyongyang duck bulgogi restaurant where patrons had to pay in foreign currency.
Lee now runs a North Korean restaurant in Seoul. She said the openings likely serve as propaganda projecting prosperity. “In North Korea, high-end restaurants are only for special classes of people,” she said.
(Reporting by Maggie Grether and Soohyun Jung; Editing by Brenda Goh and Neil Fullick)

By Andrew Goudsward and Nathan Layne
ANCHORAGE, Alaska/DETROIT, Nov 1 (Reuters) - A prominent Michigan Democrat endorsed Republican Mike Rogers on Sunday, giving President Donald Trump’s Republicans an unexpected boost in a critical US Senate race two days before midterm elections that will decide control of Congress.
US Representative Haley Stevens, who lost the Michigan Democrats’ Senate primary to Abdul El-Sayed in a bitterly contested race, publicly backed Rogers and appeared with him at a Detroit church, threatening to worsen divisions in a state viewed as crucial to Democratic hopes of retaking the US Senate.
“I don’t belong in Abdul’s campaign,” Stevens said in a video posted to social media.
Hours later at a political rally in Iowa, Trump invited Stevens to join the Republican Party. He told reporters beforehand that he would reach out to her to thank her for the endorsement, which he called “a smart thing to do because El-Sayed would destroy our country.”
Thirty-five Senate seats and all 435 House of Representatives seats are on the ballot on Tuesday. Republicans hold narrow majorities in both chambers. Polls show Democrats are favored to win a majority of the House and are locked in a tight battle for control of the Senate, where the outcome likely will rest with a handful of states, including Michigan and Alaska.
If Democrats take control of the House or Senate, they could block Trump’s legislative agenda for his final two years in office and launch investigations of an administration that has so far faced largely compliant Republican majorities. The White House has been preparing to implement portions of Trump’s agenda without the aid of Congress.
MICHIGAN RIFT
Stevens’ endorsement of Rogers came on the day she was scheduled to appear with El-Sayed in a show of party unity. But the planned event unraveled after Stevens called on El-Sayed to condemn an outside group’s ad that she said blames Israel for high grocery prices.
“We can’t stand with hate,” Stevens told reporters on Sunday, standing alongside Rogers after the church service.
El-Sayed’s campaign recently asked Stevens to skip his events through Election Day so as “not to distract from the central issues of the campaign,” a person familiar with the matter said.
Republicans sought to capitalize on Stevens’ move. ”This is courage in politics in America today,” Rogers said. “When you see a party, and at least a sliver of the party, veering off into the virulent hate that they have been spewing toward a group of people, it gets dangerous.”
Later on Sunday at the Iowa rally, Trump repeated false claims that El-Sayed is a “jihadist” - attacks that fit a broader pattern of inflammatory rhetoric from Trump and other Republicans targeting Arab Americans and Muslims.
El-Sayed, who has been subjected to a campaign of racist and Islamophobic attacks, has rejected such accusations and called questions about his loyalty to the United States “shameful.”
He declined to directly address Stevens’ endorsement on Sunday, saying he was focused on other issues.
The move appeared to have little effect on some early voters in Michigan, where El-Sayed has a nearly 4-point lead over Rogers, according to the RealClearPolling estimate.
“Haley Stevens is a traitor,” said Pamela Johnson, 72, after casting her ballot for El-Sayed in Warren, a Detroit suburb.
David Kolar, a 32-year-old elementary teacher, said Stevens’ endorsement “seemed like a last-second distraction.” He said he voted for El-Sayed because of his support for universal government-funded healthcare.
A number of Stevens’ congressional staff resigned over the endorsement, according to reports from CNN and the Hill.
Stevens’ longtime chief of staff, Justin German, could not immediately be reached to verify the reports, which quoted a statement from him saying, “as of this morning, many members of our team have resigned, including myself.” The statement described him as “shocked and heartbroken” by Stevens’ endorsement.
ALASKA INTERVENTION FALTERS
Also on Sunday, the Trump administration’s attempt to intervene in Alaska’s Senate race faltered when a federal judge dismissed the US Justice Department’s lawsuit seeking to block certification of the results if Republican incumbent Senator Dan S. Sullivan narrowly loses.
The Justice Department argued voters may be confused by the presence of a challenger named Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. on the same ballot.
The issue has roiled the campaign over the last several days after the New York Times reported that Democrat Mary Peltola’s campaign was involved in recruiting Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. into the race as a spoiler.
The senator said on Sunday he would accept the results of Tuesday’s election even as the Trump administration presses a criminal investigation into the issue. But Alaska Governor Mike Dunleavy, a Republican, has suggested he may not certify a victory by Peltola, and the incumbent Sullivan declined to say whether he would support efforts to refuse certification.
He joined his party colleagues in accusing the other Sullivan of trying to confuse voters with his similar name.
“They got the decoy guy on the ballot,” the senator told CNN’s “State of the Union” program. “I’m sure I’m going to lose a lot of votes to that trickery. So what I say to Alaskans is, ‘Don’t let them get away with the tricks.’”
Peltola has denied involvement, and Sullivan Jr. has denied coordinating with Peltola’s campaign.

KYIV, Nov 2 (Reuters) - Ukraine and Russia said their emergency alert apps had been hacked overnight, sending false warnings to citizens about impending air raids, chemical and nuclear attacks.
The warnings coincided with the expiry of a six-day local ceasefire brokered by US first lady Melania Trump in a small area of southern Ukraine — the longest such pause in fighting since Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022.
Ukraine’s public air raid app started to send false alerts just before 11 p.m. (2100 GMT) on Sunday for the capital Kyiv and other areas warning of radiation and chemical attacks and also the risk of street combat in some areas.
One of the fake alarms said Russia had launched a hypersonic Oreshnik missile — which is capable of carrying a nuclear warhead — and that a nuclear alert had been declared across Ukraine.
Ukraine’s air force said shortly afterwards on the Telegram messaging app that the alert system appeared to have been hacked by Russia, noting that the alerts were broadcast in the Russian language. The Ukrainian language is compulsory for all official communications in Ukraine.
“The air alert app appears to have been subjected to enemy influence,” the air force statement said. “There is no radiation threat! Stay calm and follow our updates on our channel!”
KYIV RESIDENTS UNFAZED BY FALSE ALERTS
All-clear messages were sent shortly afterwards for each of the alerts and Ukraine’s Ministry for Digital Transformation said the emergency app had been temporarily suspended, but other means of alerting the public were functioning, as were air raid sirens.
On the streets of Kyiv, residents played down the impact of the hack.
Artem Pyndyk, 37, a businessman, said he was briefly surprised to see the messages but then realised what had happened.
“This did not trigger the kind of reaction in society that they expected,” said Pyndyk, adding that family members and friends he had checked in with had also not panicked.
“You can laugh about it but, on the other hand, they gained a certain level of access and were able to hack the programme,” he added.
Oksana Vostrykova, 48, also shrugged off the incident.
“I am calm about it, I kind of immediately understand that it might be a false message,” the pizzeria employee said. “You worry more not for yourself but for your children who are nearby.”
RUSSIAN MINISTRY SAYS ITS APP WAS ALSO HIT BY A CYBERATTACK
Russian state news agency TASS quoted the Ministry of Emergency Situations in Moscow as saying early on Monday its mobile app had also been hit by a cyberattack that resulted in the spread of false information to the public.
Atesh, a pro-Ukrainian hacking group, posted a screenshot of the alert message on its Telegram channel early on Monday, with a message saying: “The Ministry of Emergency Situations app has been hacked!”
However, the ministry played down the impact, saying it was not one of its main public warning system channels, but just what it called a supplementary source of information.
A fake message posted by the hackers, seen by Reuters, did not attempt to mimic an official communication and was laced with colloquialisms, profanities and derogatory language about Russia, calling its regions “swamps”.
The fake message told Russians that nuclear warheads had been launched against all Russian regions and advised people to stock up on three weeks of food and take shelter in their cellars.
The Russian ministry said in a statement on Telegram that its experts were working to restore the app to normal operation.
“We ask the public to remain calm and to trust only official sources of information — the Russian Ministry of Emergency Situations’ website and the department’s official social media accounts,” it said.

Father Rody Noura, the community's priest, said he was shocked by the unusual incident but stressed that he suspects no one and forgives those responsible.
The vandalism was discovered Sunday at around 5:45 p.m., when a woman from the community arrived at the building in the northern part of the city to prepare for prayers. "This is a place that belongs to the Nahariya municipality, and we as a community use part of it," Noura said. "We have various activities during the week, and on Sundays we sometimes hold prayers there. A woman from the community came to open the place and begin preparations, and she saw all the destruction. I arrived 15 or 20 minutes later and saw everything. All our religious images and symbols were broken and destroyed on the floor."
According to Noura, the incident was unprecedented for the community, which includes former SLA members who came to Israel from Lebanon more than two decades ago. "Nothing like this has ever happened to us," he said. "The Lebanese, the SLA members, have been in Nahariya for 26 years, and nothing like this has ever happened. The place has never been targeted before."
Among the religious items kept at the building, Noura mentioned symbols depicting the Virgin Mary and St. Charbel, a figure particularly revered by Maronite Christians in Lebanon. However, he said he did not know for certain where the items originated or whether they had been brought from Lebanon or purchased in Israel. Some, he said, had belonged to the community for many years, even before he began serving as its priest.
Despite the damage and the desecration of symbols sacred to the community, Noura sought to convey a message of forgiveness. "I don't suspect anyone," he said. "Whoever did this is certainly someone who is angry about something, someone who is hurting. He lacks love. He lacks someone to stand by him, someone to forgive him. We certainly forgive him, even though I don't know who he is, who they are or who did it."
Noura emphasized that his words were not intended to justify the act. "This is unacceptable and certainly immoral. But I am sure that something good will come out of this evil, both for the person who did it and for us," he said.
According to Noura, there are no security cameras inside the building, but nearby facilities, including a sports hall and a school, may have cameras. At this stage, it remains unclear who was behind the vandalism or what motivated the act.
Israel Police said officers from the Nahariya station had opened an investigation following a complaint about damage to the municipal building used as a Christian place of worship. "As part of the investigation, investigators are carrying out a range of investigative measures. All lines of inquiry are being examined," police said.
"Israel Police takes seriously any attack on holy sites or freedom of worship and will act decisively, using all means at its disposal to identify those responsible and bring them to justice," the statement added.

====================================================================================================

The growing divides shaping Australians' trust in democracy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
01:04:43 UTC
10:04:43 KST

in brief
- Geography, age, gender and education increasingly affect people's attitude towards democracy and politics, new research indicates.
- The key trends in this year's McKinnon Index could impact politics and policy, one expert says.
Those born overseas trust the government more and are more satisfied with its services, but a survey suggests more Australians are losing faith in politicians and parties.
Geography, age, gender and education increasingly affect people's attitudes towards democracy and politics, and could shape how they vote in upcoming elections, according to the McKinnon Index.
The 2026 survey of 4,000 Australians indicates trust in federal politicians has fallen from 35.9 per cent to 30.5 per cent in a year, while trust in state and territory politicians has dropped six percentage points to 32.7 per cent.
Falls in faith come amid a divisive time in Australian politics, where debates over freedom of speech, immigration and antisemitism have coincided with rising distrust.
At the same time, young people's attitudes towards violence is shifting, with more men believing violence can sometimes be justified to advance a cause they care about.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Associate professor Josh Roose from the Alfred Deakin Institute for Citizenship and Globalisation at Deakin University told SBS News that the survey data should be considered "tentatively", but does line up with broader social patterns.
The survey has only been run for the last two years. But other studies like the Australian Election Study indicate satisfaction with democracy increased between the 2019 and 2025 federal elections.
The key trends in this year's index could affect politics and policy. So how have people's attitudes shifted in the last 12 months?
Background and geography
People living outside major cities remain less satisfied with democracy, less trusting of government and less content with public services.
Just 40.3 per cent of those in outer regional and remote areas are satisfied with democracy, compared with 52.9 per cent of major-city residents.
Support for democracy is also weaker outside metropolitan areas. Only 68.5 per cent of people in outer regional areas believe democracy is preferable to other forms of government, compared with 77.1 per cent in both inner regional areas and major cities.
Roose said that Australians are more likely to trust and be satisfied with the government if they have benefited from funding and programs, which could explain why urban areas scored higher.
"There's been a stripping of public services and infrastructure from regional Australia for decades where political parties tend to prioritise areas of high growth, in particular in urban Australia," he said.
The gap is also evident in perceptions of political influence. Just 38.6 per cent of people in outer regional and remote areas feel they have a say in politics, compared with 50.6 per cent in major cities.
By contrast, people born overseas report greater trust in government and higher satisfaction with public services.
Roose said that people born in Australia would be more aware of declining services or access over time compared with newer arrivals who may see Australia's support systems as superior to their home countries.
"There's a different understanding. People have different starting points for when they're engaging with that system and what they're likely to view it as," he said.
Young men's attitude to violence, speech shift
Young Australians remain much less supportive of democracy than older generations, and this year young men widened the gap further.
Support for democracy among men aged 18 to 24 fell 10.3 percentage points to 56.1 per cent points in 2026.
Among young men, belief that people can freely express political opinions fell 22.8 percentage points to 49.8 per cent.
Social media and time spent online play an "enormous role", Roose said.
"There's also been a concerted effort online by not only platform providers, but also potentially other states to undermine confidence in democracy, particularly amongst younger users," he added.
Attitudes towards violence have also taken a turn, with men of all age groups believing violence for a cause can be justified, at a higher rate than women.
The biggest jump was an 8.2 per cent increase in men aged 18-24, with 27.5 per cent saying extreme measures such as violence can sometimes be justified to advance a cause.
However, women in this age group are more satisfied with democracy than they were last year, and less accepting of violence.
Education levels a key factor in democracy satisfaction
Educational attainment appears to be a more significant fault line than income for democratic confidence and political participation, raising questions about whether Australia's democratic institutions serve all sections of the community equally.
Just 39.7 per cent of Australians whose education ended at high school are satisfied with democracy, compared with 59 per cent of university graduates.
"There's been a professionalisation of the political class over a period of time where there are very few people with real-world experience entering politics," Roose said.
"There's a quite binary view of the professional politician as someone who's not like them, someone who doesn't represent their interests, someone who doesn't really care about them."
The divide is even more pronounced when it comes to confidence in elections.
Almost three-quarters of university graduates express confidence in election outcomes, compared with fewer than half of those with a high school education or less.

4 Americans among 69 people killed in train crash in Spain, officials say
Four United States citizens were among the at least 69 people who were killed when a high-speed train slammed into the rear of another train in central Spain last week, officials said Sunday.
The Center for Integrated Data, the legal body in Spain in charge of identifying victims of events with a high death toll, said on Sunday night that the casualties in the country's second deadly rail collision this year also included one citizen each from Canada, Japan, Argentina, Mexico, Tunisia and the Czech Republic. Two citizens of Australia and a citizen of Japan remain missing, the Agence France-Presse and local media reported.
The center, which had already announced the deaths of a French and Portuguese citizen as well as 54 Spaniards, said that all but three of the victims had been identified.
"As the contacted families have expressed their wish to travel to Spain to carry out in-person identification, we are awaiting their arrival in the country," the statement said, AFP reported.
The crash occurred on the morning of Oct. 28 in Urda, in the province of Toledo, when the high-speed train slammed into the rear of another train that had stopped, derailing two cars. Officials said 58 people were injured.
The two trains, with more than 540 people on board, were heading in the same direction from Madrid to Seville.
Transport Minister Óscar Puente has blamed a traffic controller's poor judgment for much of what went wrong. However, railway unions have pushed back, citing deteriorating working conditions. They say too few controllers are handling growing workloads, making it increasingly difficult to ensure the safety of millions of passengers.
The independent investigators said their initial findings indicated that the state-owned RENFE train was moving at between 100 and 125 mph when it struck the privately owned IRYO train.
It was the second major crash on the Madrid-Seville line this year. In January, more than two hours farther south along the route, a train derailed and struck another traveling in the opposite direction, killing 46 people. That crash remains under investigation.
Spain's high-speed rail network, the world's second-largest after China's, has long been regarded as a success of state industrial policy. Until this year, it had recorded no fatal crashes since entering service more than three decades ago.

Halloween shootings leave at least 24 dead and 94 wounded in the US
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
00:50:00 UTC
09:50:00 KST

Halloween shootings leave at least 24 dead and 94 wounded in the US
Bernard Mokam, Jesus Jimenez and Georgia Gee
- Halloween violence across the US left at least 24 dead and 94 wounded, with shootings reported from California to Delaware at clubs, stores, stadiums and campuses.
- Dallas saw three shootings in Deep Ellum within 75 minutes, killing at least four and injuring 15, while police said the cases were not clearly connected.
- Other attacks hit Detroit, Jacksonville and college areas, showing the danger for young people and the difficulty of stopping gun violence on Halloween.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – Three shootings early on Nov 1 left at least four people dead and 15 injured in the Deep Ellum neighbourhood of Dallas, Texas, US officials confirmed.
The hail of Texas gunfire was part of a wave of violence on Halloween that left at least 24 dead and 94 wounded across the country, according to police statements.
The shootings stretched from California to Delaware. They unfolded at nightclubs, costume stores, outside stadiums and near college campuses.
The violence came as the nation celebrated Halloween, a holiday that mixes costume-clad revellers with alcohol consumption and drug use.
Those ingredients, coupled with access to firearms, can lead to violence, experts say.
It is unknown whether the weekend’s violence was outsized for recent holiday weekends, but previous studies have shown spikes in violence on Halloween.
For instance, Oct 31 ranks as the third-most violent day of the year, following only July 4 and Jan 1, according to an analysis of Federal Bureau of Investigation incident data for Boston from 2005 to 2009 by James Alan Fox, a criminologist at Northeastern University.
For minors, Oct 31 is the most dangerous day of the year, he said. “They are out in the evening, interacting with strangers,” Fox said in an interview on Nov 1.
In Detroit, a five-year-old still in her Halloween costume was struck in the chest by a bullet as she played in the back room of her house after a night of trick-or-treating, Arnold Williams, deputy chief of the Detroit Police Department, said at a news briefing.
“She had to tell her mom, ‘I think I’ve been shot,’” he said. The five-year-old is in stable condition.
In Jacksonville, Florida, 13 people were shot, and two died in two unrelated shootings.
While waiting in line for a Halloween party, a 17-year-old girl was killed by a stray bullet at around 1.40am local time on Nov 1. Two others injured in that incident had also been “unintended targets”, according to the Jacksonville Police Department.
At another location in Jacksonville, 10 people were shot at around 3.45am on Nov 1 as a house party of more than 100 people spilt into the street.
A 20-year-old man was killed, and a 15-year-old girl was injured but is in stable condition. One victim remains in critical condition.
A shooting also occurred at a nightclub in Jackson, Mississippi, leaving two dead and four injured.
At a costume store in Northern California, a gunman killed a pregnant mother of four and injured six others, including two teenagers who were in critical condition on Oct 31.
In Oklahoma City, officers responded to a disturbance at a trailer park during a Halloween party.
One person was shot multiple times in the leg and is expected to survive. Two people at the scene were fatally struck by a vehicle, but the circumstances were unclear, according to the Oklahoma City Police Department.
More than two dozen people were shot near college campuses or at university events.
One person was killed, and eight were injured outside Legion Field in Birmingham, Alabama, where Alabama A&M played Alabama State earlier in the day, in a rivalry matchup known as the Magic City Classic.
About 970km north, in Bloomington, Illinois, officers assisted eight gunshot victims near the Illinois Wesleyan University campus.
A 19-year-old woman was pronounced dead at the scene. Seven others were transported to area hospitals, and one of them remains in critical condition, according to the Bloomington Police Department.
As officers responded in Illinois, the police in Bloomington, Indiana, about 320km south-east, heard gunfire erupt from a large crowd near the campus of Indiana University, which was celebrating homecoming in addition to Halloween.
“Multiple individuals were located in the downtown area with wounds believed to have been caused by the shooting,” the Bloomington Police Department said in a statement.
Seven people were transported to area hospitals. Officers detained a male subject who fled the area with an exposed firearm, but they said they did not know if he had discharged the weapon.
Even as the data points to the risk of violence on Halloween, preventing it is difficult, experts on gun violence say.
“The police can’t be inside every bar. They can’t be in every parking lot,” said Alexis Piquero, a criminologist at the University of Miami and former director of the Bureau of Justice Statistics in the Justice Department during the Biden administration.
In Dallas, at least four people were killed, and 15 others were injured in the three shootings in the Deep Ellum neighbourhood, which occurred within a 75-minute period.
There was no indication that the shootings were connected, and the number of casualties could continue to rise, the authorities said.
“We knew it was Saturday night. We knew it was Halloween, so we were staffed properly,” Daniel Comeaux, the Dallas police chief, said at a news briefing on Nov 1.
Images and videos circulating on social media showed people running for safety in the streets of Deep Ellum, which is home to several bars, restaurants and concert venues.
Recently, the neighbourhood has been plagued by safety concerns over a wave of crime. At least seven bars and restaurants, including some long-time establishments, have closed in Deep Ellum in 2026.
By the morning of Nov 1, the streets were largely empty and littered with trash after the police cordoned off parts of the neighbourhood.
“This is completely unacceptable,” Comeaux said. NYTIMES

Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Culture and Information nominated Kaseinov in recognition of his professional achievements and longstanding work in international cultural affairs aimed at strengthening spiritual and humanitarian ties among Turkic states.
The Alisher Navoi International Prize was established in 2021 on the initiative of the President of Uzbekistan. It was first awarded posthumously in 2022 to Kyrgyz writer Chingiz Aitmatov. In 2025, the award went to Turkish scientist and Nobel laureate Aziz Sancar.

Ebola fatality rate tops 50% after hundreds of deaths added to Congo toll
- Congo’s Ebola outbreak has passed a 50% death rate, with 10,414 confirmed infections and 5,372 deaths, the National Institute of Public Health said on Oct 31.
- Health officials added 314 earlier deaths in Ituri after reviewing records in 97% of affected zones, which pushed the fatality ratio from 48.6% to 51.6%.
- The outbreak has spread to eight provinces and 67 health zones, and the US will tighten travel rules from Nov 3 for people who have been in Congo.
AI generated
KINSHASA – The death rate among confirmed Ebola cases in the Democratic Republic of Congo has climbed above 50% after the health authorities added hundreds of previously unallocated fatalities to the official toll.
The outbreak has caused 10,414 confirmed infections and 5,372 deaths, giving it a reported case-fatality ratio of 51.6%, the National Institute of Public Health said in its most recent report released on Oct 31.
A review of records across 97% of affected health zones in Ituri, the epidemic’s epicentre, resulted in 314 earlier Ebola deaths being added to the province’s cumulative toll, health officials said.
The adjustment pushed the reported fatality ratio up from 48.6% two days earlier, even as the number of confirmed infections rose by just 140.
The revision comes as the health authorities continue to report dozens of new infections a day from an epidemic that has spread to eight provinces and 67 health zones.
It is the largest Ebola outbreak in Congo’s history and the largest globally after the 2013-2016 epidemic in West Africa.
The outbreak has also spilled beyond the country, though transmission elsewhere remains limited.
Nigeria said on Oct 31 that two suspected cases in Adamawa state tested negative after two rounds of testing, leaving the country with one confirmed infection.
The US said on Nov 1 it will further tighten travel restrictions in response to the outbreak.
Beginning late on Nov 3, anyone boarding an international flight to the US must attest that they have not been in the Democratic Republic of Congo during the previous 21 days, according to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
Travellers who have been in the country during that period generally will not be allowed to board US-bound commercial flights. BLOOMBERG

SYDNEY, Nov. 2 (Xinhua) -- Australian house prices fell for the seventh consecutive month in October as the downturn reached the fastest pace in 40 years, according to new data.
Property data firm Cotality said on Monday that the national median house price fell by 1.2 percent in October, taking the downturn into a seventh consecutive month.
It said that the national price has declined by 6.7 percent from its March peak, wiping 63,400 Australian dollars (about 44,565 U.S. dollars) in value off the median Australian dwelling.
Cotality said that the pace of decline in national home values is now tracking at the fastest pace over the last 40 years.
The monthly fall was driven by a 1.4 percent decline in the median capital city house price, accelerating from a 1.2 percent fall in September.
Brisbane overtook Sydney as the capital with the fastest pace of decline, recording a 2.0 percent drop in median house prices in October.
On a quarterly basis, Cotality said median prices across all capitals declined by 4.5 percent.
Tim Lawless, Cotality's research director, attributed the downturn to an array of headwinds, including interest rate hikes, persistently low confidence, cost-of-living pressures and a move by the federal government to wind back tax concessions for property investors.
The Reserve Bank of Australia's Monetary Policy Board at the end of September voted to raise the cash rate target by 0.25 percentage points for the fourth time in 2026 to a 15-year high of 4.6 percent.
The board will meet again to consider the key interest rate over Monday and Tuesday, with all four major banks predicting a fifth rise to an 18-year high of 4.85 percent. ■

Disturbing recordings in the plane’s cockpit shortly before the crash, retained by LiveATC.net, captured the pilot talking about “manageable” ice issues, before later saying the plane was rapidly losing altitude.
Shortly after, the panicked crew said, “We’re going to crash into the ground”.
The plane was a Learjet 60 – a popular business jet – heading from Austin, Texas, to the Bahamas. Austin-Bergstrom International airport confirmed that the plane was a private jet, but not who was on board.
Videos of the incident circulating online appear to show the jet striking the ground at high speed and on a sharp angle, followed by a huge explosion.
Footage of the aftermath appears to show flames flickering around debris and chunks of pavement, with people milling around the area.
The plane looked to have fallen just metres from homes and cars, but Florida Governor Ron DeSantis told reporters that there appeared to be no casualties on the ground.
Speaking from the scene, DeSantis described the crash as “cataclysmic” and said the plane “looked like a missile going down, and left a big crater on the side of the road”.

2015 notice of assessing officer issued on reasons duly recorded and is valid: SC

The head of Israel’s elections commission has said the results of the country’s general election would still stand even if claims of foreign interference were substantiated.
“Our position is that even if the suspicions are substantiated, this would not undermine the integrity of the electoral process or the election results as a whole,” Central Elections Committee head Noam Sohlberg said in a video on Sunday, in which he appeared with the head of the Shin Bet, Israel’s internal security agency, and the attorney general.
Prime Minister Benyamin Netanyahu’s Likud party had questioned the results after saying, without providing evidence, that Arab-led parties, which made significant gains in Tuesday’s elections, “stole” the vote and accepted funding from Qatar to do it.
Qatar has rejected the allegations, calling it a disinformation campaign.
Also on Sunday, Israeli police released two out of three political activists arrested before Tuesday’s polls opened. They were carrying envelopes of cash, allegedly to bribe voters, police said.
One was released on unspecified conditions, while another was ordered to remain on house arrest.
Police said the suspects were connected to the Arab-led Ra’am party, which won eight seats.
Its leader, Mansour Abbas, denounced the arrests as undemocratic and “an attempt to influence the election results”.
‘Orchestrated and organised campaign’
Main opposition leader Eisenkot on Sunday accused Netanyahu of launching an “orchestrated and organised campaign to delegitimise the results”.
Eisenkot has previously ruled out forming a coalition with Arab parties, but a deadlock in Tuesday’s elections means siding with the parties could help him form a government.
Netanyahu’s bloc won 53 seats in Tuesday’s elections, while the opposition bloc, led by Gadi Eisenkot, won 48, meaning neither side can form a government in Israel’s 120-seat parliament alone.
Israel’s three Arab-led parties, including the Ra’am party, won a record 19 seats.
A coalition of Arab parties with Eisenkot would provide a comfortable majority of 67 in parliament. However, for many in Israel, the idea of siding with Arab parties is politically unpalatable.
The results are due to be officially certified this week, after which President Isaac Herzog must nominate a candidate to form a new government.

Oleshky ceasefire expires, Ukraine evacuates civilians from parts of Kherson region
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
01:21:00 CET
09:21:00 KST

Nov 1 (Reuters) - Ukraine’s military said it evacuated 167 people from threatened areas of southern Kherson region on Sunday as a temporary local ceasefire expired — two days after buses carried residents out of the Russian-held town of Oleshky.
A six-day local ceasefire in Oleshky and the surrounding area was reached after mediation efforts by US first lady Melania Trump and with the involvement of Pope Leo.
The ceasefire expired at midnight Moscow time (2100 GMT). There was no immediate indication of any resumption of hostilities on either side.
It was the longest local pause in fighting since Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022.
Ukraine’s Ombudsman for Human Rights Dmytro Lubinets, writing on Telegram, said both sides had “upheld the obligations they undertook throughout the duration of this period.”
Lubinets said he and Yana Lantratova, Russia’s commissioner for human rights, were “exploring possibilities to continue similar humanitarian efforts. It is important to maintain this interaction mechanism so that we can keep helping people and saving lives.”
Earlier, Ukraine’s General Staff issued a statement saying that its units, in cooperation with local authorities, “evacuated 167 civilians to safer points in the Kherson region.”
It said the evacuees included 22 children and 21 people with limited mobility requiring special assistance.
The governor of Kherson region, Oleksandr Prokudin, urged residents to be vigilant as the expiry of the ceasefire neared.
“I also strongly urge you not to visit the so-called ‘red zones’ – areas and settlements near the Dnipro,” Prokudin wrote on Telegram. “The intensity of Russian strikes there remains high, and the threat to life is extremely high.”
In Moscow, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov, quoted by Russian news agencies, said Russia had a positive view of how the operation was conducted in Oleshky, as well as of the coordination between the two countries’ human rights commissioners.
The pope said he hoped cooperation between Russia and Ukraine in implementing a ceasefire in Oleshky would pave the way for broader peace efforts.
Melania Trump, writing on X, said the ceasefire “has provided residents with the freedom to move, access to food, clean water, medicine, plus a renewed sense of dignity without the constant threat of attack”.
CIRCUITOUS JOURNEY
On Saturday, starved and exhausted residents of Oleshky crossed into Ukraine after a circuitous journey from the area, just a few kilometres from the front line.
They first travelled by bus via Crimea, annexed by Russia from Ukraine in 2014, to the Russian town of Anapa, before flying to Belarus from where they continued to Ukraine.
Those wishing to leave Oleshky - some for Russia, some for Ukraine - were taken initially to Crimea in 25 buses and nine ambulances, Lantratova said, before splitting into separate convoys.
It was not known how many chose to stay in Russian-held Oleshky, which lies on the Dnipro River opposite the region’s Ukrainian-held main town of Kherson.
The ceasefire, in place since Tuesday, allowed for the roads to be demined and food, medicines and other supplies brought into the town.
Russian forces took control of the town immediately after the February 2022 invasion of Ukraine, but Ukrainian troops recaptured much of the region, including the town of Kherson, later that year.
Military action continued in other parts of Ukraine on Sunday.
Regional governors and emergency services reported one death in a strike in the Sumy region on the Russian border, a frequent target, and at least one in the central region of Vinnytsia.

In the Moscow region, 3 cases of monkeypox have already been detected in a month

In the Moscow region, 3 cases of monkeypox have already been detected in a month
Kyiv • UNN
A 38-year-old man with confirmed mpox was hospitalized in Domodedovo. This is the third case in the region in a month and the eighth in two years.
A third case of monkeypox infection in the past month has been recorded in the Moscow region. A 38-year-old man with a laboratory-confirmed diagnosis was hospitalized in Domodedovo. The Moscow Times reports this, citing local medical workers, writes UNN.
Details
The patient went to the hospital with characteristic symptoms of the disease: elevated temperature, skin rashes, and swollen lymph nodes. Doctors assess his condition as satisfactory.
According to the medical facility, this is already the third case of monkeypox in the past month and the eighth in two years. Russian epidemiologists are determining the source of the infection and checking people who had contact with the patient.
New cases of infection are being recorded in Russia
On October 8, Domodedovo Hospital completed the treatment of a 27-year-old man who claimed that he had contracted monkeypox inside Russia and had not traveled abroad.
In mid-October, five people who had contact with another infected person were also hospitalized. However, the disease was not confirmed in them.
In addition, on October 16, monkeypox infection was confirmed in five patients in St. Petersburg. Doctors assessed their condition as mild or moderate.
How monkeypox is transmitted
Monkeypox, or mpox, is a viral disease that can be transmitted through close physical contact with an infected person, as well as through contaminated objects.
The main symptoms include fever, headache and muscle pain, swollen lymph nodes, and characteristic skin rashes.
The incubation period usually lasts from 1 to 2 weeks.

France launches attempted murder investigation after petrol bomb thrown at police
- Published
Prosecutors in France have launched an attempted murder investigation after petrol bombs were thrown at police during unrest, French media reported.
An image of a police officer with his leg on fire during a clash with protesters in Paris on Saturday has prompted outrage and follows weeks of street protests in France that have also seen demonstrators injured.
The officer, who suffered burns to his ankle and minor injures to his hand, told French newspaper Le Figaro it was a "particularly sophisticated" incendiary device.
Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said throwing a molotov cocktail at a police line was "what I call a murder attempt", adding officers were working to find the perpetrators.
Hundreds of thousands of people demonstrated across France in largely peaceful protests on Saturday, the latest in a series of youth-led protests that began in late September demanding action on the high cost of living and poor public services, especially schools.
Following previous clashes and looting, thousands of police officers were deployed across the country over the weekend, and officers fired tear gas at demonstrators in some cities.
There were more than 770 arrests on Saturday, roughly half as many as the previous week's protests, the French interior ministry said.
But police said no one had been arrested for the attack caught on camera that set a police officer on fire, AFP reported.
The officer - part of the National Gendarmerie, a national law enforcement force that is technically part of the military but under the control of the interior ministry - said his unit "suddenly found ourselves facing several hundred hostile, well equipped adversaries".
Speaking to French newspaper Le Figaro, he said police were yet to identify the liquid used but that the incendiary device "had a far greater burning capacity than a standard Molotov cocktail".
"We faced hostile individuals who are not protesters," he said. "These adversaries are there with the intent to harm those who represent the state."
Fourteen other officers sustained wounds ranging from minor to serious, he said, adding some were struck by paving stones. The unit was supposed to be on leave but had been urgently recalled to police the weekend protests, he said.
French protest organisers, the Gilets Jaunes, or Yellow Vests, have said dozens of protesters have been seriously injured during recent demonstrations across the country, with many hurt by "grenades".
France suspended the use of one type of stun grenade while policing student protests in early October after a 15-year-old's hand was blown off, but French newspaper Le Monde has reported that police have continued to use a different model in subsequent protests.
Protests also took place in Germany and Italy over the weekend, as mainly youth-led protests continue across parts of Europe, with varying demands but broadly linked to a focus on cost-of-living issues and public services.

How a blue wave could test Trump in his final two years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
00:07:00 UTC
09:07:00 KST

How a blue wave could test Trump in his final two years
- Democrats could gain from a possible “wave election” on Nov 3, which may weaken Trump’s control of Congress and force more oversight, compromise and scrutiny.
- The House looks easier for Democrats to win than the Senate. They need three seats for the House, but four for the Senate, where the filibuster and 60-vote rule matter.
- If Democrats win one or both chambers, they could block Trump’s bills, launch investigations and slow nominees. Trump can still act through executive orders and vetoes.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – In his second term, US President Donald Trump has so far benefited from his Republican Party holding majorities in both houses of Congress, as he did in the top half of his first turn in the White House.
When one party controls both the presidency and Congress, ambitious legislation can become law, as evidenced by the tax-cut measures enacted under Trump in 2017 and 2025.
And with party faithful running congressional committees, a presidential administration is insulated, to some extent, from tough scrutiny from such bodies.
Now, public disapproval of Trump’s job performance threatens to bring the one-party Republican government to a crashing halt in the Nov 3 congressional elections.
A “wave election” that breaks in favour of the Democrats would, in Trump’s final two years in the White House, expose his administration to greater oversight and force it to accept compromise if it wants to enact legislation.
At the same time, there’s a lot a president can do without Congress.
Trump already has tested the bounds of a president’s power by issuing expansive executive orders, including some that have been struck down by the courts, and waging war against Iran without congressional authorisation.
What’s a wave election?
There’s no precise definition, but the term is used to describe when a political party makes major gains in the House of Representatives, the Senate or both.
Generally speaking, congressional wave elections have occurred at the midpoint of a president’s four-year term – when the president isn’t on the ballot – and have usually benefited the party that doesn’t occupy the White House, which right now is the Democratic Party.
In a wave election, the closest races can tend to break all in the same direction.
How many seats are being contested in 2026?
All 435 House of Representatives seats and 35 of the 100 Senate seats. Republicans hold a 218 to 214 edge in the House.
(There is also one independent, Representative Kevin Kiley of California, who aligns himself with Republicans for his committee assignments.)
There are two vacant seats in the House.
In the Senate, Republicans have a 53-to-47 advantage.
All 35 races are for full six-year terms except for special elections in Florida and Ohio to serve out terms that will expire at the end of 2028.
Can Democrats win control?
The Democrats are better positioned to win control of the House than the Senate.
Democrats need a net gain of just three seats for a majority in the House and have over-performed in special elections held since Trump returned to the presidency in January 2025.
The Senate poses a steeper challenge.
Democrats need a net gain of four seats for a 51-seat outright majority because Vice-President J.D. Vance could break any 50-50 split in favour of Republicans.
Democrats would likely have to retain all or almost all of their 13 current seats that are being contested, including in the politically competitive states of Michigan, Georgia and New Hampshire.
Of the 22 states with Republican-held seats on the ballot, all but Maine and North Carolina favoured Trump by more than 10 percentage points in the 2024 election.
Democrats would need to flip at least two of those double-digit Trump states.
That looked unlikely at the start of the campaign cycle but is more realistic now.
Strong candidate recruitment and an anti-Trump political environment have made Democrats highly competitive in a raft of traditionally Republican-leaning states such as Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Ohio and Texas.
Why do waves happen?
One theory is that anger energises citizens, so those opposed to the President and his policies are more motivated to turn out at the polls than those happy with the status quo.
The backlash can be severe: Since the end of World War II, the president’s party on average has suffered a net loss of about 25 House seats and 3.5 Senate seats in midterm elections.
What are polls and prediction markets saying?
Polls suggest that most of the public is deeply dissatisfied with the direction of the country and with the President.
Trump’s approval rating – 37% in a New York Times average of daily polls as at Oct 30 – is one of the lowest of any president since World War II and comparable to Republican George W. Bush’s 38% approval rating in a Gallup Poll on Election Day 2006, when Democrats won majorities in both the House and Senate for the final two years of Bush’s presidency.
The less popular the president, the more seats his party tends to lose.
Polls show Democrats leading Republicans in voter enthusiasm and in a generic congressional ballot question that asks voters which party they support in the upcoming election.
Prediction markets Polymarket and Kalshi point to a Democratic sweep, giving the party better than 90% odds of winning control of the House and about a two-thirds chance of securing a Senate majority.
What would Democratic victories in Congress mean for legislation?
Even if control of only one chamber flips, Trump’s ability to get Congress to pass legislation opposed by Democrats would be thwarted.
A Bill must be approved by both the House and Senate before it is sent to the president’s desk to be signed into law or vetoed.
So a united Democratic majority in either chamber would be able to block any Bill.
For those same reasons, control of just one chamber wouldn’t enable the Democrats to pass legislation on their own.
Their ability to do so would be limited even if they take both the House and Senate.
That’s because for most legislation, Senate approval requires a supermajority, which the Democrats are unlikely to achieve in this election.
In the Senate, members enjoy a privilege known as the filibuster, which is the prerogative to demand never-ending debate to thwart legislation.
It takes 60 votes in the 100-seat Senate to end a filibuster – and thus 60 votes to pass most legislation.
With control of both houses of Congress, the Democrats could get around the filibuster using a process called budget reconciliation that’s permitted for Bills relating to spending, taxes and the federal debt limit, which is a cap established by Congress on US government borrowing.
First, the House and Senate must agree to a budget resolution, which sets overall spending and revenue targets.
Then, Bills advanced in the name of “reconciling” tax and spending practices with that budget resolution need only a simple majority vote to win approval in the Senate.
It’s this process that Republicans, then in full control of Congress, used to pass tax cuts in 2017 in Trump’s first term and again in 2025 in his second.
Of course, Trump can veto any Bill passed by Congress.
To overcome a presidential veto requires a two-thirds supermajority in both the House and Senate, improbable goals for Democrats in this election.
At the same time, were Trump to veto Bills with significant popular support, for example, Bills aimed at addressing issues of affordability that were top of mind for voters going into the election, he would risk further tanking his approval rating.
Options for such Bills would include a reversal of the 2025 tax law’s spending reductions to Medicaid, a government health insurance programme primarily for the poor, and a revival of enhanced subsidies to help people pay for health insurance.
Given a willingness to compromise, significant legislation can become law even when one party has the White House and the other controls one or both chambers of Congress.
Examples include a Social Security rescue package in 1983, a major tax overhaul in 1986, and sweeping changes to the welfare system in 1996.
Would Democratic victories in Congress mean new investigations into Trump?
Trump and his administration would likely face new or re-energised investigations by congressional committees that would switch to Democratic control.
Potential targets for probes include the Trump family’s stock trading and cryptocurrency ventures, private companies’ funding of Trump’s White House ballroom project, the administration’s immigration enforcement policies, and its handling of files related to the late sex offender and financier Jeffrey Epstein.
However, the power of congressional investigations has important limits.
Congressional committees can issue subpoenas to try to compel private citizens, businesses or government officials to produce documents or testify, and committees can cite those who refuse for criminal contempt of Congress, which is punishable by a fine and imprisonment for up to 12 months.
But while Congress can refer officials to the Justice Department for criminal prosecution, it cannot bring charges itself.
The Justice Department, which is part of the executive branch, has discretion over whether to act on a referral and holds the exclusive power to bring federal criminal charges.
Is Trump’s impeachment a possibility?
A Congress run by Democrats could pursue a third impeachment of Trump, but it is not a focus of the Democrats’ messaging.
The impeachment process starts in the House.
If the House approves articles of impeachment against the president with a simple majority, the president is impeached, though not yet removed from office.
The Senate then holds a trial. If the Senate votes to convict by a two-thirds majority, the president is removed from office.
Trump was impeached twice in the second half of his first term, after Democrats won control of the House in the 2018 midterms.
In December 2019, the House impeached him on charges of abuse of power and obstruction of Congress.
The House alleged that the President conditioned military aid to Ukraine on its government opening investigations into the President’s political rival Joe Biden and Biden’s son Hunter.
The House impeached Trump a second time in January 2021, charging him with inciting an insurrection in connection with the Jan 6 attack on the US Capitol, which delayed the certification of Biden’s victory over Trump in the 2020 presidential election.
Neither impeachment led to a Senate conviction.
If Democrats pursue another impeachment, they’re unlikely to successfully remove Trump from office because of the Senate’s requirement of a two-thirds majority vote to secure a conviction.
Even if Democrats make significant gains in the chamber, it’s highly improbable they will reach that threshold.
In any case, party leaders have downplayed an impeachment scenario during the 2026 election campaign and urged their candidates to run on a platform of lowering everyday living costs and easing economic burdens for working families.
How would Trump’s ability to make appointments be affected?
A Democratic-run Senate could stall or block Trump’s judicial and executive nominees.
Among the presidential appointees that require Senate confirmation are Cabinet members, Supreme Court and federal judges, ambassadors and the heads of government agencies and commissions.
Republican control of the Senate enabled Trump to win confirmation – just barely – of a number of controversial figures, including Pete Hegseth as defence secretary, Robert F. Kennedy Jr. as health and human services secretary, and Kash Patel as Federal Bureau of Investigation director.
There’s been less turnover among officials in his second administration than in his first, but Trump would have considerably less leeway filling vacancies if he needs Senate Democrats to okay his picks.
What can Trump do without Congress?
The president can enact significant policy changes without Congress through executive action.
Trump has ordered military strikes on Iran, imposed and removed tariffs, fired large swaths of the federal workforce, withdrawn the US from the World Health Organization and the 2015 international climate treaty the Paris Agreement, and seized and extracted long-time Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro to the US – all without legislative action from Congress.
Ches McDowell, managing partner of Checkmate Government Relations and a lobbyist with close ties to the Trump administration, said Trump will remain the centre of power in Washington regardless of the outcome of the midterms.
“We’ve been telling clients, the administration is still going to be the primary body to get anything done, no matter if the Democrats take the House and the Senate,” McDowell said at a Bloomberg Government executive dinner roundtable on Oct 21.
Are Republicans worried about losing their majorities?
Yes, though party leaders rarely convey worry publicly because they don’t want to dispirit their voters and donors.
Speaker of the House Mike Johnson, a Republican, has repeatedly said his party will “defy history” and keep control of the chamber.
Senator Tim Scott, who leads the Senate Republicans’ campaign organisation, told reporters on Sept 30 that “we will hold the Senate majority, without question,” though he said there are a “record number” of toss-up Senate races and acknowledged tight races in traditionally Republican-leaning states such as Kansas and Nebraska.
Trump, in a rare acknowledgement of his weak standing with voters, said on Sept 30 that he’s “done a very bad job of explaining how good the country is doing”.
Senator Thom Tillis, a North Carolina Republican who’s not seeking re-election, said in his book released on Oct 6 that he expected a “bloodbath” for his party on Nov 3.
Republican super political action committees (PACs) are spending much more to defend their own states and districts, many of which strongly favoured Trump in the 2024 election, than they are on contesting Democratic-held seats.
In early October, the leading super-PAC defending the Senate Republican majority pulled out of North Carolina, where Democrats are likely to win a seat from Republicans, and instead shifted resources to races in Republican-leaning Kansas, Mississippi and South Carolina.
Do Republicans have any advantages?
Yes. In recent months, seven states – Alabama, Florida, Louisiana, North Carolina, Ohio, Tennessee and Texas – have adopted a more Republican-skewing electoral district map.
Some acted after the US Supreme Court in April 2026 curtailed the use of the Voting Rights Act to draw predominantly black and Hispanic districts.
However, a Democratic “wave” could significantly limit the gains Republicans had expected to make through redistricting. Also, Democrats retaliated against Republican-led redistricting across the country with a partisan map of their own in California, and they’re likely to wrest one seat in Utah from Republican control under a new court-approved map.
Another Republican advantage: The party’s PAC generally are more cash-flush than their Democratic counterparts.
The pro-Trump MAGA Inc super-PAC had more than US$415 million (S$531 million) in the bank as at early September, and the Republican National Committee had a cash advantage of more than US$100 million over the Democratic National Committee.
However, super-PACs pay higher advertising rates than federal candidates, and a favourable political environment can neutralise the opposition’s cash advantage. BLOOMBERG

Ukraine: Russia’s increased attacks on energy and heating infrastructure ‘creating a deadly situation for civilians’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
00:01:00 UTC
09:01:00 KST

- Civilian death toll increased significantly in recent months
- Unlawful renewed attacks on infrastructure ahead of winter
Russia’s increased targeted attacks on energy and heating infrastructure risks creating a new humanitarian catastrophe for civilians ahead of winter, Amnesty International warned today.
The civilian death toll during Russia’s full-scale illegal invasion has increased significantly in recent months, with October 2026 expected to be one of the deadliest periods for civilians in years.
Based on prior Russian military attacks in the approach to previous winters, there is overwhelming evidence that the deliberate targeting of energy and heating infrastructure intended to cause civilian suffering will result in immense harm. The International Criminal Court (ICC) has indicted Russia’s Lieutenant General Sergei Ivanovich Kobylash and Admiral Viktor Nikolayevich Sokolov on charges of war crimes for allegedly directing attacks on Ukrainian electrical infrastructure.
This is an illegal campaign, carried out with flagrant disregard for the rules of war, and appears to be designed to create unliveable conditions for Ukrainian civilians.
Scott Edwards, Director of Amnesty International’s Crisis Response Programme
“The Russian Federation is once again implementing a large-scale campaign against Ukrainian energy and heating infrastructure ahead of a freezing winter, including attacks far from the front lines of conflict,” said Scott Edwards, Director of Amnesty International’s Crisis Response Programme.
“These attacks on essential infrastructure are creating a deadly situation for civilians, who directly suffer the consequences. This is an illegal campaign, carried out with flagrant disregard for the rules of war, and appears to be designed to create unliveable conditions for Ukrainian civilians.
“Whatever the motives behind the Kremlin’s plan to make life unbearable for civilians, it is criminal and cannot be tolerated. World leaders seeking to end this conflict must immediately use their leverage to minimize any potential harm to civilians, before another intentional humanitarian catastrophe begins with the arrival of winter.”
On 26 October, the International Commission of Inquiry on Ukraine reported that Russia had committed war crimes and crimes against humanity in Ukraine by intentionally attacking energy infrastructure, leaving millions of people without electricity and heat in freezing temperatures.
Amnesty International has previously documented how Russia’s widespread attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure may constitute war crimes and highlighted their life-threatening consequences for the civilian population.
Civilian casualties and widespread power cuts
The UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine found that at least 328 civilians were killed and 2,105 injured in September 2026 as a result of Russian attacks, an 85% increase over September 2025. Casualties were recorded in 22 of 24 regions in Ukraine. The Mission also described the first half of October 2026 as one of the deadliest periods for civilians in years.
On 13 and 14 October, strikes reportedly hit multiple energy installations, including Kyiv’s three principal power stations, temporarily leaving approximately 600,000 people without electricity. On 17 October, further Russian attacks reportedly killed at least eight people, injured 60 and interrupted electricity supplies to more than one million people across nine regions.
Both the Russian Ministry of Defence and President Vladimir Putin have made public statements announcing intentional attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure. Prior attacks on energy and heating infrastructure in Ukraine caused widespread and widely reported civilian suffering that is known to Russian military and strategic planners.
During the winter of 2025–2026, the Russian Armed Forces carried out at least 423 attacks on electricity infrastructure and 74 strikes on heating facilities, according to UN monitoring. These attacks caused rolling outages affecting millions of people and interrupted heating for hundreds of thousands as temperatures fell below -20°C. The resulting loss of electricity, water and heating disrupted healthcare and education, and also disproportionately harmed older people, persons with disabilities, women and families with children.
Under international humanitarian law, electricity and heating installations are civilian objects unless and for such time as they meet the strict definition of a military objective. Even where an installation constitutes a military objective, attacking forces must comply with the principles of distinction, proportionality and precaution. Intentionally directing attacks against civilian objects, launching indiscriminate attacks, or carrying out attacks expected to cause excessive civilian harm in relation to the concrete and direct military advantage anticipated can constitute war crimes.
Ensuring accountability for such crimes requires strong and independent international justice mechanisms capable of investigating and prosecuting those responsible, including the most senior officials.
Meanwhile, the US administration is currently engaged in a campaign to dismantle the work of the ICC. Amnesty International has called for all relevant states to take appropriate measures to resist this attack and actively protect the Court and the broader international justice system. President Vladimir Putin is wanted on charges of war crimes by the ICC, and Amnesty International has called for President Putin to be arrested and surrendered to the ICC by any parties in a position to do so.
Calls to Russian authorities
Amnesty International is calling on Russian forces to end their systematic attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure. The Russian authorities must also immediately end other violations of international humanitarian law, including attacks on other civilian infrastructure in Ukraine, such as residential buildings, hospitals, and schools, and end its campaign of targeting non-combatants.
All parties to the conflict must respect the principles of distinction, proportionality and precaution and protect civilians and civilian objects. States supporting accountability mechanisms must provide the expertise and resources needed to effectively investigate allegations of violations, secure evidence, and identify suspected perpetrators, including commanders and senior officials who may bear responsibility. All states must urgently act to protect the functioning of the ICC and should execute arrest warrants when and where they can.
