Bibi and the Blockchain: When a Prime Minister Plans for Sanctions Evasion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
00:00:00 UTC
09:00:00 KST

Bibi and the Blockchain: When a Prime Minister Plans for Sanctions Evasion
Benjamin Netanyahu’s interest in cryptocurrency reveals both the continuing power of financial sanctions and the current limits of technological attempts to circumvent them.
Thanks to the widely reported efforts of the Russian Federation, it is no longer fantasy that cryptocurrency and blockchain-based payment systems can help sanctioned actors move money, circumvent restrictions and sustain particular commercial relationships. But importantly, while crypto might facilitate payments, its use cannot replicate the broader economic benefits of access to the international financial system. Governments considering crypto as protection against financial isolation risk confusing the ability to transfer value with the ability to participate in the global economy.
While Russia’s experience provides the principal case study of both the possibilities and limitations of alternative financial arrangements, the recent Israeli debate, in the days before the 27 October election, provides a particularly revealing illustration of how these considerations are spreading. Appearing on Israel’s Channel 10 TV station, Netanyahu said he was preparing for the possibility that sanctions would be applied against Israel. This is not speculation. In September, the UK and other Western governments announced their intention to apply sanctions and trade measures against certain elements of the Israeli economy in response to, in the words of UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband, the unlawful occupation of the Palestinian Territories, specifically against ‘those who finance or facilitate illegal settlements’.
In particular, he noted that ‘There could be sanctions, and sanctions on banks, so you need to set up a bypass economy’ using currencies – including cryptocurrency – that can bypass sanctions, revealing in conclusion that ‘we are also working on that’.
His comments were met with criticism by the Bank of Israel that suggested he would do better to focus on policies that did not require such measures, noting that ‘The right course for Israel’s economy is to preserve our economic relations with our main trading partners, and to focus on preventing sanctions and their negative impact on the economy.’ An open letter signed by more than 100 economists also poured scorn on Netanyahu’s actions, saying that he is ‘knowingly leading the State of Israel toward boycott and international economic isolation, and all he has to offer the Israeli economy is a puzzling solution, one accepted in criminal organisations, that will not help in the slightest’.
While tactical advantage might be secured, running an entire economy – particularly as developed as Israel’s – through the so-called ‘cryptoverse’ remains out of reach
His political opponent, Gadi Eisenkot, likewise ridiculed the plan as ‘madness’, calling it the ‘BibiCoin policy’ and predicting it would encourage Israeli companies to move abroad and threaten national security.
Regardless of the merit of the idea, it is striking in itself that a sophisticated, internationally integrated economy such as Israel is contemplating alternative financial arrangements in anticipation of possible sanctions. The fact that its leadership apparently regards sanctions as a credible economic threat will not have escaped notice in those countries – including the UK – that have threatened sanctions in response to the further expansion of Israel’s illegal settlements. Sanctions may not change Israel’s behaviour towards settlements in the occupied territories, but the threat of application certainly has the potential to cause disruption.
Zooming out from the specifics of Israel, Netanyahu’s comments pose an important question: have crypto and the blockchain matured sufficiently to allow a country to pre-emptively crypto-proof itself against sanctions? The attraction is alluring, particularly when a government anticipates looming financial isolation. If conventional banking relationships are likely to be interrupted, why not build an alternative system that cannot be so easily disrupted?
The experience of other sanctioned countries such as Russia, Iran and other actors that have already explored alternative financial systems is that while tactical advantage might be secured, running an entire economy – particularly as developed as Israel’s – through the so-called ‘cryptoverse’ remains out of reach, even for such a technically sophisticated country. Accessing sufficient crypto liquidity, identifying the necessary range of trading partners who will deal in crypto, and rewiring an economy to accommodate such a move are all immense (and mostly insurmountable) challenges.
Bibi’s vision rests on a fundamental misunderstanding of what makes financial sanctions powerful for a globally integrated economy: the ability to move money is not the same as the ability to participate in the international economy.
What Do Sanctions Actually Do?
This might seem like an obvious question, but much of the rhetoric on sanctions – particularly from political leaders – is misguided and aspirational, and it is thus important to ensure expectations are correctly set.
Sanctions do not switch off the target’s economy. Consider the extent to which – and the way in which – Russia’s economy has continued to function. But sanctions do force an economy to reshape and rewire, adding friction and cost, and forcing the country’s leadership to make choices. Thus, while banks are required to stop processing payments, the core power of sanctions stems from their ability to restrict access to the complex network of global institutions, services, markets and commercial relationships that allow a developed economy like Israel to function.
The plumbing of the international commerce that enables an economy and its exporters and importers to function includes correspondent banking, trade finance, credit, insurance, investment, reserve management and the engagement of trusted finance and trade counterparties. Sanctions create legal, regulatory, reputational and commercial risks that affect all these relationships – and secondary sanctions and the prospect of losing access to major markets amplify these risks and the resulting effects.
In short, running a nation’s economy depends on far more than merely enabling payments settlement.
So, What Could Cryptocurrency Actually Do?
It would be wrong to dismiss the use of cryptocurrency outright. Russia has very effectively developed crypto-based payment systems that allow it to pay for the procurement of the critical high-priority list items it needs to wage its illegal war of aggression in Ukraine. It is thus important to recognise these advantages to understand both the appeal (even if misplaced) and the limitations of the greater adoption of crypto in the face of sanctions.
Let us start with the legitimate appeal. Crypto can enable cross-border value transfers without relying on traditional correspondent banking arrangements; stablecoins, such as USDT from Tether, can provide a relatively convenient means of transferring dollar-denominated value; and peer-to-peer transactions, decentralised systems and intermediaries operating in permissive jurisdictions can make sanctions enforcement more difficult. All of these features will seem alluring to a political leader faced with the impact of major financial restrictions stemming from broadly arrayed sanctions.
Russia’s development and use of alternative financial systems, most famously the A7 payment platform, which has been openly backed by Vladimir Putin, demonstrates that such mechanisms are not merely theoretical. In short, crypto can support specific transactions, intermediary networks and sanctions-circumvention operations.
But can crypto support the operation of an entire economy, particularly one as large (the 25th largest in the world), networked, and exposed to the West, as Israel’s?
Three fundamental – and existential – challenges exist. First, liquidity, scale and reliable conversion will present material constraints. There simply is not enough capacity in the cryptoverse to accommodate any but the smallest economies. Second, stablecoins introduce meaningful risk dependencies (just look at the 29 October Binance hack) that the traditional financial system has spent decades addressing. And third, crypto might provide an alternative payment mechanism for an individual transaction, but providing an alternative market for a country’s exports is another question entirely, which would require a rewiring of counterparty nations’ payment systems to accommodate such a transformation.
Circumvention is Not Substitution
As widely studied and reported, Russia provides the most instructive contemporary example of the distinction between circumventing particular restrictions and replacing the entire basis on which a country interacts with the international financial system.
Since triggering wide-ranging financial sanctions and economic restrictions on itself as a result of the Kremlin’s 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Russia has made considerable strategic investment in developing alternative payments infrastructure, including bilateral settlement arrangements (with Iran) and broader mechanisms designed to reduce dependence on Western financial institutions and markets.
Cryptoassets have become elements of this effort – but not uniquely. Russia has also relied on third countries for trade circumvention, opaque corporate structures and ledger systems for offshore payments, and a range of other obfuscation and evasion tactics.
The breadth and complexity of this range of arrangements demonstrate the need for adaptability and the extent to which sanctions evasion requires an array of tools.
Governments considering the adoption of crypto as insurance against sanctions should recognise what they are proposing
The result? Russia has maintained substantial international trade despite sanctions, but the mechanisms it has needed to use are often more costly, less efficient, more time-consuming and more risky than those it used previously. Is that what Israel wants?
The Sovereign Crypto Illusion
Thus far, the focus has been on what the government of a country targeted by sanctions can do – what it can almost certainly not do is compel the rest of the world to sign up to the same mission. For example, is a foreign supplier going to have confidence that it will receive the same trusted value via a new blockchain-based ‘currency’; and are third-country facilitators of such a scheme (for example banks converting stablecoins into local currency) going to be willing to run the risk that they too may become subject to sanction as a result? Financial sovereignty is inextricably linked to the willingness of other economic actors to trust, accept and use the proposed system.
Will Bibi’s Blockchain Bypass Work?
So, can Bibi use the blockchain to set up a bypass economy? In short, no. Could certain payments be moved from the traditional banking system onto the blockchain? Yes – this is what Russia has done to pay for many of the critical components it needs for its military. But that does not isolate those payments or those that facilitate them from further sanction and disruption. The only way to do that is to follow the advice of the Israeli central bank and ‘focus on preventing sanctions and their negative impact on the economy’.
More broadly, governments considering the adoption of crypto as insurance against sanctions should recognise what they are proposing. Crypto may offer a means of moving money when conventional routes are closed, but it cannot guarantee that anyone will want to receive that money, provide credit, insure a shipment or invest in the economy. Building an alternative payments system is not the same as building an alternative means of engaging with the international economy.

Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
02:00:00 EET
09:00:00 KST

The United Kingdom could pay compensation for the slave trade through investments in education and healthcare
Kyiv • UNN
Andy Burnham is open to investments in healthcare, education and development instead of direct reparations. The opposition fears new financial claims.
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham is ready to consider financial support for countries in Africa and the Caribbean as a form of compensation for the historical role of the British state in the transatlantic slave trade. The focus would primarily be on investment in healthcare, education and economic development. The Telegraph reports, according to UNN.
Details
Burnham plans to discuss the issue at the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting in Antigua. He also allows for an official apology on behalf of the British state for its involvement in the slave trade.
At the same time, the prime minister ruled out the possibility of direct one-off reparations, explaining that the current government cannot be held responsible for crimes committed several centuries ago.
What compensation is London considering
According to the publication, future agreements could provide for the financing of healthcare and education projects with funds from British taxpayers or private investors.
Barbados Prime Minister Mia Mottley welcomed London's readiness to negotiate and said she expected investment in healthcare, education and development partnerships.
Representatives of Jamaica, Saint Lucia and Ghana also supported the launch of a dialogue. At the same time, they stressed that an official apology should not replace the issue of compensation for historical harm.
No additional payments are planned for the current financial year. However, in the following years, the parties may agree on new development programmes.
Opposition warns of possible lawsuits
Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch criticised the initiative, saying that an official apology could trigger new financial demands against the United Kingdom.
Former Attorney General Michael Ellis also suggested that such a move could strengthen the position of countries seeking reparations through international legal mechanisms.
Meanwhile, Burnham proposed launching a structured dialogue with states affected by the slave trade and considering the possibility of restructuring their debts.

IDF again promises drop in reserve duty days in 2027, but security concerns remain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
23:58:03 UTC
08:58:03 KST

As the academic year begins, the IDF has assessed the expected scope of reserve duty over the coming year as part of a plan to provide benefits and academic accommodations for student reservists. Under the plan, the number of reserve duty days in 2027 is expected to fall by 30% to 40% compared with 2026, depending on security developments and the military's ability to scale back operations. The IDF has already reported a roughly 30% reduction in training exercises and operational deployments planned for December, January and February.
A key consideration in developing the plan was ensuring that reservists would not lose eligibility for benefits simply because they serve fewer days next year. Eligibility thresholds have therefore been adjusted so that those who serve fewer reserve duty days in 2027 than in 2026 can still receive benefits under the established criteria. The military and academic institutions also agreed that degrees earned by reservists who make use of academic accommodations will carry the same standing as any other degree, without distinction or any reduction in academic recognition.
However, promises to reduce annual reserve duty are nothing new. Since the war began, the government and senior defense officials have repeatedly announced plans to cap and significantly reduce the number of reserve duty days required of each reservist, aiming to ease the financial and personal burden of prolonged military service.
Despite efforts to formalize these limits through draft government decisions and legislation, the measures were never finalized or fully implemented. In practice, prolonged operational demands took precedence over the promises. These included the 12-day war against Iran during Operation Rising Lion in June 2025, the continued deployment of forces along the Yellow Line in the Gaza Strip and, later, Operation Roaring Lion against Iran, which lasted more than 40 days.
These operations were compounded by the ground offensive and seizure of territory in southern Lebanon, which began simultaneously in March this year and required a far larger and more sustained deployment of combat troops than originally planned. The IDF continues to maintain a security buffer zone in the area of the Yellow Line in southern Lebanon, with troop levels varying according to operational needs.
This security reality has left the same reservists carrying a heavy burden through open-ended emergency call-up orders, known as Tzav 8. As a result, many reservists have continued to receive lengthy mobilization orders that significantly exceeded the service limits they had previously been promised, deepening exhaustion and further eroding trust.

Japan establishes National Disaster Management Agency
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
23:55:55 UTC
08:55:55 KST

Japan establishes National Disaster Management Agency
Japan launched the National Disaster Management Agency on Monday to strengthen its preparedness for possible huge natural disasters, such as a temblor in the Tokyo metropolitan area and an eruption of Mount Fuji, JIJI PRESS reports.
The agency, set to serve as the government's command center to respond to natural disasters, is headed by the prime minister. Postdisaster reconstruction minister Goshi Hosono is set to be the first disaster management minister tasked with overseeing the agency.
The agency was reorganized from the Cabinet Office's disaster management division, which had been expanded in terms of personnel and budgets so that the government can better deal with possible huge disasters, also including megaquakes in the Nankai Trough off the Pacific coast of central to southwestern Japan.
The agency will cover preparation for disasters, assistance to people hit by disasters and restoration and reconstruction projects in affected areas.
The disaster management minister will have the authority to issue recommendations to other government organizations, which must respect such recommendations. The government aims to work as one on disaster management so it can respond effectively to huge quakes or other disasters.
Earlier, it was reported that Japan is moving forward with plans to establish a backup capital for Tokyo.

Eisenkot says Netanyahu’s bid to discredit Israeli election results has ‘failed’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
23:55:03 UTC
08:55:03 KST

Mohammed Al Ragawi and Rania Abushamala
02 November 2026•Update: 02 November 2026
Israel’s Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot said Sunday that efforts by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his Likud party to discredit the results of last week’s parliamentary elections and steer the country toward another election had “failed.”
In a post on the US social media platform X, Eisenkot described the attempt as “despicable and malicious.”
“The despicable and malicious attempt to disown the election results, challenge the public’s will, smear an entire community and drag Israel into new elections has failed,” Eisenkot wrote.
“Only someone who realizes he has lost would be prepared to wage such a crude delegitimization campaign, even at the cost of further damaging public trust in state institutions,” he added.
Eisenkot said the results of the elections for the 26th Knesset were “firm and clear,” welcoming remarks by Central Elections Committee Chairman Justice Noam Sohlberg affirming the integrity of the vote.
“Ignore the background noise and the political maneuvers that change every hour. The people are sovereign, and they have spoken: The government of failure has no majority and has lost the election,” he said.
Netanyahu and Likud have alleged Qatari interference through funding intended to increase turnout among Arab voters and influence the results.
Likud claimed to possess recordings and other materials documenting bribes, including cash and fuel vouchers offered in exchange for votes, describing the alleged activity as “election theft.”
The party has not publicly presented evidence establishing Qatari interference or widespread electoral fraud.
Qatar rejected the accusations Thursday, calling them a “new disinformation campaign” aimed at drawing it into Israel’s internal political disputes.
United Arab List leader Mansour Abbas also denied allegations of attempts to unlawfully influence the election through foreign funding.
Earlier Sunday, Sohlberg said that voting had proceeded properly and that the results reflected the electorate’s will.
Israel’s Yedioth Ahronoth daily quoted him as saying that claims that the available material and evidence could cast doubt on the election results as a whole were “incorrect.”
He said potential irregularities and suspicions were being examined, stressing that even if substantiated, they would not undermine the overall integrity of the election or its results.
Sohlberg spoke in the presence of Shin Bet chief David Zini and Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara.
With all votes counted, Netanyahu’s bloc secured 53 seats in the 120-member Knesset compared with 48 for the opposition camp led by Eisenkot and 19 for Arab parties. Neither main bloc reached the 61 seats needed for a governing majority.
Final turnout stood at 77.9%, the highest since 1999, according to the elections committee.
The results leave Israel facing a political impasse, with the government’s formation dependent on agreements between blocs and opposition parties divided over the possibility of relying on Arab parties’ support.
The official results are due to be submitted to President Isaac Herzog on Wednesday, ahead of consultations with parties represented in the Knesset on whom to task with forming a government.

Michael Mann, the director of the cult film "Heat," accidentally shot himself at a shooting range in Los Angeles
Kyiv • UNN
83-year-old Michael Mann suffered a superficial injury from an accidental shot while his gun was in its holster. After treatment, the director was discharged from the hospital.
American director Michael Mann, known for the crime thriller "Heat," suffered a gunshot wound as a result of an accidental discharge at a shooting range in Los Angeles. The 83-year-old filmmaker was hospitalized but was released and allowed to return home after receiving medical treatment. NBC News reports, UNN writes.
Details
The incident occurred on Saturday, October 31, when Mann was practicing target shooting. According to the director’s representative, the firearm accidentally discharged while it was in its holster.
The director suffered a superficial wound as a result of the discharge. He was taken to a hospital in stable condition and was released after examination and treatment.
What is known about the incident
The Los Angeles Police Department confirmed that officers arrived at the shooting range after receiving reports of gunshots. Following an investigation, they determined that the incident was accidental.
Mann’s representative noted that the director has been engaged in target shooting for decades.
Michael Mann is known for his crime dramas, including the 1981 film "Thief," the 1986 film "Manhunter," and the 1995 film "Heat," starring Al Pacino and Robert De Niro.
The director pays particular attention to the realism of scenes involving firearms. In particular, during the filming of "Heat," the actors used blank cartridges to convey the authentic sound of gunfire.
Mann is currently working on a sequel to the cult thriller—the film "Heat 2," based on a novel he co-wrote with Meg Gardiner.

BELGRADE, November 2. /TASS/. The Republic Electoral Commission (REC) of Serbia has released the final results from 100% of polling stations in the country’s snap parliamentary elections, confirming a victory for the Student List movement with 53.01% of the vote.

What Ukraine can use to replace the scarce Patriot missiles as early as this winter: experts name possible options
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
01:50:05 EET
08:50:05 KST

What Ukraine can use to replace the scarce Patriot missiles as early as this winter: experts name possible options
Kyiv • UNN
The delivery of 500 PAC-3 MSE missiles could take years due to the 24-month production timeline. For the winter, European stocks and Japan are being considered.
Ukraine may receive additional interceptor missiles for Patriot systems from European partners or Japan to strengthen protection against Russian ballistic missiles this winter. At the same time, it would be unwise to count on the rapid delivery of 500 PAC-3 MSE missiles, the sale of which has been approved by the United States. Defense Express reports this, according to UNN.
Details
The U.S. Department of State has approved the sale to Ukraine of 500 PAC-3 MSE missiles, along with spare parts and equipment, worth approximately $2.1 billion. The funding will be provided by Canada, Germany, and Norway במסגרת the JUMPSTART program, as well as through funds associated with an EU loan.
However, the main contractor for the deal is manufacturer Lockheed Martin, and the full production cycle for one missile takes approximately 24 months. Therefore, the delivery of all 500 interceptors could take several years, even if Ukraine's order is given priority.
Where Ukraine could obtain missiles this winter
According to Defense Express, one of the most realistic short-term options is the transfer of PAC-3 MSE missiles from the stocks of European allies, particularly Poland and Germany.
These countries have already transferred such interceptors to Ukraine. However, the number would likely be measured in dozens of missiles rather than hundreds. In addition, the partners need guarantees that their own stocks will be replenished quickly.
Another potential source is Japan—the only country that has localized PAC-3 MSE production. Japanese officials had previously indicated that the transfer of surface-to-air missiles to Ukraine was possible, but there have been no specific decisions regarding this particular modification yet.
Will new air defense systems help?
In the long term, French-Italian SAMP/T NG systems equipped with Ground Fire 300 radars could become an alternative to Patriot.
Ukraine expects to receive four such systems starting in 2027. Therefore, it is currently not possible to count on them as a solution for the winter of 2026–2027.
Another promising area is the European FREYJA antiballistic system project, whose first tests are scheduled for early 2027.
Defense Express emphasizes that even 500 new PAC-3 MSE missiles would not solve the shortage problem for long. With an estimated need of approximately 150 interceptors per month, such a stockpile would last only slightly more than three months.

WASHINGTON, Nov. 1 (Xinhua) -- A plane carrying nine people crashed in a residential neighborhood in Florida on Sunday, killing all those on board, U.S. Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy said.
At 12:50 p.m. Eastern Time, a Learjet 60 crashed in a neighborhood near Cresthaven, FLorida, Duffy said in a post on X. "All nine people on board were killed."
The aircraft departed from Austin, Texas and was bound for the Bahamas, he added, calling the crash a "horrific tragedy."
The Federal Aviation Administration is sending a team to the scene to support the National Transportation Safety Board investigation, Duffy said.
It was unclear if anyone was hurt on the ground.
Minutes before the crash, the pilot of the plane reported ice accumulating on the aircraft and moderate turbulence, according to a recording of air traffic control radio calls captured by LiveATC.net.
Moments later the plane declared an emergency and plunged about 8.2 km in one minute.
There were scattered storms in the area at the time of the crash, and the plane passed through a stronger storm cell a few minutes before it began descending, local media reported.
Video of the crash showed the aircraft nose-diving from the sky and erupting into a giant flame ball near a major roadway, creating a crater. ■

Haredi groom arrested days after wedding for evading draft, sentenced to 20 days in military prison
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
23:45:52 UTC
08:45:52 KST

Haredi (ultra-Orthodox) yeshiva student Yaari Lieberman, who married just days earlier, was arrested by IDF Military Police in front of his wife on Sunday while the couple was on their way to a family celebration marking their wedding.
Lieberman was transferred to a military prison and sentenced to 20 days in jail by a military court, sparking outrage among senior haredi political figures who demanded his immediate release.
The incident is expected to trigger violent demonstrations in the coming days.
The arrest took place as the newlyweds got off a bus on their way to a Sheva Brachot celebration, one of the festive meals traditionally held in honor of Jewish couples during the week following their wedding.
According to reports, the Military Police officers who arrived at the scene were in civilian clothes and not wearing identification badges.
The officers reportedly tracked Lieberman through his cellphone's location. It was also alleged that the officers did not identify themselves as Military Police to his wife, leaving her fearing that her husband had been kidnapped.
Lieberman was taken from the scene and transferred to a military prison.
Goldknopf blames Netanyahu for arrest of yeshiva student
Agudat Yisrael chairman MK Yitzhak Goldknopf strongly condemned the arrest, accusing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of responsibility for the situation facing yeshiva students.
"The arrest of a young groom in front of his bride in the midst of the Sheva Brachot festival is a new low in the hunt against Torah scholars," Goldknopf said.
"The obsessive pursuit of yeshiva students, whose only sin is Torah study, has crossed every line of humanity and sensitivity. This shameful arrest is a disgrace to the Jewish state. I demand the groom's immediate release."
Goldknopf also directed his criticism at Netanyahu, accusing him of failing to fulfill his commitment to advance legislation regulating the status of yeshiva students.
"Prime Minister Netanyahu has not been able to keep his promise to pass a law that will regulate the status of yeshiva students, and the result is the disgraceful arrests we are witnessing. The responsibility for this situation lies on his shoulders," he said.
United Torah Judaism chairman MK Yaakov Asher also appealed to the defense minister on Sunday, demanding that he intervene to secure Lieberman's immediate release.
"This is not a totalitarian state and not a police state. Arresting a son-in-law in the midst of his happy days is an opaqueness that knows no bounds. I demanded that the Defense Minister act for his immediate release and return him to his family and his happiness," Asher said.
Shas chairman MK Yinon Azoulay also moved to sign an urgent petition calling on the defense minister to secure the immediate release of the newlywed yeshiva student.
Previous arrest attempt thwarted by protesters
Sunday's arrest was not the first attempt by Military Police to detain Lieberman.
On October 6, Military Police arrived at his parents' home in Modi'in in an attempt to arrest him. However, they encountered resistance from protesters who gathered outside the residence.
Crowds assembled near the house and demonstrated against the attempted arrest. After approximately two hours, the protesters reportedly succeeded in preventing Lieberman from being taken into custody.
Fears of escalation as haredi opposition to IDF draft intensifies
Lieberman's arrest is expected to lead to violent demonstrations in the coming days, amid growing opposition within the haredi community to the arrest of yeshiva students as part of the enforcement of the mandatory IDF draft.
The incident comes amid the ongoing controversy surrounding the military draft of ultra-Orthodox men and the absence of legislation regulating the military service status of yeshiva students.
While the defense establishment continues to enforce mandatory conscription requirements, representatives of the haredi parties are demanding legislation that would regulate the status of yeshiva students and prevent further arrests.

Scientists reconstructed the face of a person who lived 315,000 years ago: what one of the earliest Homo sapiens looked like
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
01:42:57 EET
08:42:57 KST

Scientists reconstructed the face of a person who lived 315,000 years ago: what one of the earliest Homo sapiens looked like
Kyiv • UNN
The digital reconstruction was created from remains found at Jebel Irhoud in Morocco. It combines data from several individuals and is not an exact portrait.
Scientists have created a digital reconstruction of the face of a person who lived approximately 315,000 years ago in what is now Morocco. To do so, they used fossilized remains found at the Jebel Irhoud archaeological site. LRT reports this, citing ScienceAlert, writes UNN.
Details
The reconstruction makes it possible to imagine the appearance of some of the earliest known representatives of Homo sapiens. The reconstructed face has distinctive features and a massive jaw.
According to 3D designer Cicero Moraes, such a person might hardly stand out in a modern crowd. However, upon closer examination, their unusual facial features would be noticeable.
How scientists reconstructed the face of a person from the distant past
The first skull at Jebel Irhoud was discovered back in the early 1960s. Further excavations led to the discovery of other human remains and stone tools.
These finds changed perceptions of the origins of Homo sapiens, pushing the known history of our species approximately 100,000 years further into the past.
Since the researchers did not have a complete skull, they created a digital model from several fossils. The skull "Irhoud 1" served as the basis, while the missing parts, including the lower jaw and teeth, were reconstructed using other remains.
After that, the specialists used a computed tomography scan of a modern adult to model the facial soft tissues on the ancient skull.
The scientists presented two versions of the reconstruction: a black-and-white version without hair and a color version with hair, a beard, and skin tone.
At the same time, the researchers emphasize that the image is not an exact portrait of a specific person. It was created based on the remains of several individuals, while the actual skin and hair color and the characteristics of the soft tissues remain unknown.

Ukrainian forces evacuate civilians around Kherson Oblast during Oleshky ceasefire
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
23:38:34 UTC
08:38:34 KST

Ukrainian forces evacuated 167 civilians from around the Kherson Oblast amid the Oleshky humanitarian ceasefire, Ukraine's General Staff announced on Nov. 1.
"During the ceasefire regime," the General Staff said, "the Ukrainian Defense Forces used the opportunities created by the security situation to evacuate residents of the right bank of the Kherson region."
From Oct. 27 to 11 p.m. local time on Nov. 1, Russian and Ukrainian forces observed a ceasefire around the city of Oleshky in the southern Kherson Oblast. Occupied by Russian forces since the early days of the full-scale invasion, 2,000 residents of Oleshky faced starvation and humanitarian crises as Russian forces blockaded aid to the city.
On Oct. 31, evacuated residents of Oleshky began returning to Ukrainian-controlled territory as the humanitarian ceasefire held.
Throughout the war, the Kherson Oblast has remained one of the most beleaguered and hazardous regions of Ukraine, with constant threats trapping citizens even in Ukrainian-held territories.
"Those who were able to leave were those who had not previously had the opportunity to leave the dangerous areas," said the General Staff about the additional residents evacuated from the oblast in the new operation.
Units from Ukraine's "South" task force cooperated with local authorities to evacuate Kherson Oblast residents trapped on the right bank of the Dnipro River to safer areas in the region. 22 children and 21 people with limited mobility were among the evacuated, the General Staff said.
The "South" task force units "strictly" adhered to the ceasefire agreement during the operation while helping conduct the evacuation through mined roads and areas littered with destroyed military equipment and civilian vehicles.
"Despite these risks, the main priority remains the preservation of the lives of the civilian population and the provision of assistance to those who are unable to leave dangerous areas on their own," the General Staff said. "Each person saved is the result of joint work and coordinated interaction of all those involved in the humanitarian mission."

Israel elections chief says inquiry into irregularities will not undermine result
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
23:31:00 UTC
08:31:00 KST

Israel elections chief says inquiry into irregularities will not undermine result
- Israel’s election chief said an inquiry into alleged foreign funding will not change the result. He said the vote was proper and that “suspicions remain suspicions”.
- The Shin Bet is checking claims that Raam got money from Qatar. Raam and Qatar deny this, while Netanyahu’s Likud says “a dark cloud hangs over the election results”.
- The Oct 27 vote gave no bloc a majority. Arab parties won 19 seats, and a court also released one suspect in a separate vote-buying case linked to Raam.
AI generated
JERUSALEM – The head of Israel’s Central Elections Committee said on Nov 1 that an ongoing investigation into alleged foreign funding in the country’s recent vote would not call into question its result, noting that so far “suspicions remain suspicions”.
The Shin Bet security agency launched the inquiry last week, at the elections chief’s request, to determine whether the Arab Israeli party Raam received money from Qatar – an accusation both the Gulf state and the party deny.
In the days since, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his Likud party have relentlessly accused Arab groupings of having “stolen” the vote, in which they notched unprecedented gains and made themselves potentially instrumental to the formation of an opposition-led government.
Elections committee head and Supreme Court Justice Noam Sohlberg, flanked by the head of the Shin Bet and Israel’s attorney-general, assured Israelis in a video message on Nov 1 that “your choice at the ballot box will be respected” and that the elections “were conducted properly”.
“If any irregularities exist, they are currently under review,” he said, adding that as yet, “suspicions remain suspicions”.
“We will examine them thoroughly and get to the very bottom of the matter in order to establish the full truth,” he continued.
“Our position is that even if the suspicions are ultimately confirmed, this would not call into question the integrity of the electoral process or the overall results of the elections.”
Likud said on Nov 1 that it was “puzzling” that Sohlberg could acknowledge the gravity of the allegations, while also insisting they would not affect the vote.
“Until the investigation is concluded, a dark cloud hangs over the election results in Israel,” it said.
Netanyahu’s main rival Gadi Eisenkot, who has accused the premier of attempting to delegitimise the results, welcomed Sohlberg’s statement.
“The vile and malicious attempt to deny the election results, to undermine the will of the public, to smear an entire community, and to drag Israel into additional elections has failed,” he said on X.
‘Ridiculous and dangerous’
The hard-fought vote on Oct 27 did not deliver an outright parliamentary majority to any bloc, with Netanyahu and his allies winning 53 seats and Eisenkot’s camp securing 48 – both well short of the 61 needed to form a government.
The results did, however, cement the rise of the Arab groupings Raam and the Joint List, with the two winning a combined 19 seats.
Eisenkot, who ran a campaign casting Netanyahu as unfit to lead, is weighing whether to accept the Arab parties’ support in forming a government to unseat the premier – something many of his voters have urged him to do, despite some of his coalition allies’ opposition.
Netanyahu’s claims of malfeasance by Arab parties began on election day itself, following a campaign in which he cast them as a threat to the country.
That strategy played a hand in driving unprecedented turnout among Israel’s Arab minority – descendants of Palestinians who stayed after the country’s creation in 1948 and who account for about 20% of the population.
Raam chief Mansour Abbas has denied the allegations of foreign funding, welcomed an investigation and said his party has “no connection whatsoever to the affair”.
Qatar called the accusations “ridiculous and dangerous”.
Noting on Nov 1 that the review of the allegations would continue in “utmost seriousness”, Sohlberg insisted that “these remarks must in no way cast doubt on the vote of the Arab community”.
“The citizens who went to the polls exercised their democratic right,” he said.
Suspect released
An Israeli court, meanwhile, released a suspect arrested on election day over a separate case of suspected vote-buying for Raam, while extending the police custody of another and placing a third under house arrest, police said on Nov 1.
The police had previously said that three people were arrested with envelopes and cash on suspicion of trying to buy votes for Raam, which denied any involvement with the case.
The Times of Israel quoted Judge Eran Tzabari as saying he had ordered house arrest for the one suspect because of the “serious suspicions” he faced, though the case against him had not become stronger, and had “even weakened”, since his arrest.
The outlet reported that the judge had also criticised police for not bringing new evidence to support the extended detention of the suspect who was ordered to be released.
Netanyahu had publicised the arrests in a video on election day, saying they showed why his supporters needed to “go to the polling station and vote Likud”. AFP

Trump has torn down part of the White House to build a ballroom, put his image on money and official buildings, disrupted the global economy with sweeping economic tariffs, and threatened to invade or annex allies like Canada and Greenland.
A big Democratic win would kick start the post-Trump era and could even begin the race to replace him in 2028.
Winning the House would put Democrats in charge of the federal budget and powerful committees set to probe allegations of mass corruption, Trump’s links to infamous sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, and other explosive topics.
The outcome of the contest for the Senate remains in doubt.
Only a third of the Senate’s 100 seats are being contested in these midterms and few of the races were seen as favourable to Democrats.
However, with surprisingly strong challenges mounted in deeply Republican states like Texas and Kansas, pollsters now say the odds of a Democratic flip are at minimum even.
A Democratic Senate would be able to shut down Trump’s lifetime appointments to courts – especially the Supreme Court.
Will Trump accept results?
The midterms have seen about US$11 billion spent on advertising, with large chunks coming from individual mega-donors.
Elon Musk, a close Trump ally who led the so-called DOGE effort in dismantling entire government departments, has given a staggering nearly half-billion dollars to help get Republicans elected.
The campaigns have also been marked by blistering language and insults, led by Trump who falsely accused leading Democratic candidates of being everything from vegans to jihadists.
And hanging over everything is concern that Republicans will refuse to accept a loss, leading to a constitutional crisis similar to Trump’s attempt to overturn his 2020 presidential election defeat.
A federal judge on Nov 1 tossed out an extremely unusual attempt by Trump’s administration to hold up a potential victory by a Democratic candidate for Senate in Alaska.
The lawsuit contended that if Democrat Mary Peltola beats the Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan, the result should not be certified because there is a third, minor candidate also called Dan Sullivan, allegedly recruited by Democrats to siphon off votes. AFP

Why governors’ races are important in the 2026 US midterms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
23:24:56 UTC
08:24:56 KST

Why governors’ races are important in the 2026 US midterms
Historic turnover in this election will allow dozens of states to vote on significant changes in leadership.
Much of the attention ahead of Tuesday’s midterm elections has fallen on the battle for control of the United States Congress.
But key state-level races are also unfolding, with far-reaching consequences for the country’s future.
This year, 36 US states will vote for their next governor, the most powerful elected official in state government.
An unusually high proportion of those races centre on open seats, with no incumbent governor on the ballot seeking re-election.
In 19 of the races, the current officeholder is either term-limited, like California Democrat Gavin Newsom, or voluntarily opted to not run again, like Iowa Republican Kim Reynolds.
This historic turnover creates the potential for several states to take on significant changes in leadership.
Here’s why these races matter:
A state’s chief executive
Governors serve as the chief executives of their states, overseeing government departments and agencies responsible for delivering public services.
Their powers vary by state. In general, governors propose budgets, appoint senior state officials, direct state agencies about how to enforce existing law, and issue executive orders.
They can also choose to sign into law bills passed by their state’s legislature — or veto them.
One of their most visible areas of influence is reproductive rights. Since the US Supreme Court ruled in 2022 that there is no constitutional right to abortion access, state governments have played a central role in determining whether the procedure is legal.
Each state can now regulate abortion within its boundaries, and some 13 state legislatures have passed complete or near-total abortion bans.
But the Guttmacher Institute, a US-based reproductive rights organisation, noted that about a dozen governors have issued executive orders to “mitigate” the harm done by such bans.
“By issuing executive orders, governors could quickly declare immediate protections for providers and patients,” the organisation said. “This was particularly helpful in states such as North Carolina, where the governor is supportive of abortion rights — but the legislature is not.”
Governors can also influence how US elections are administered.
In some states, governors appoint the officials responsible for overseeing elections, while in others, those officials are elected independently. Governors may also sign or veto legislation changing voting rules, giving them significant influence over election administration.
Challenging the US government
Governors also help shape how states respond to the federal government.
They may challenge federal policies in court or negotiate with Washington over funding and programme requirements.
State governments also play a major role in implementing federally funded programmes, making cooperation between governors and the White House important.
One example came after former US President Barack Obama’s landmark healthcare policy, the Affordable Care Act, passed the US Congress in 2010.
In the aftermath of its passage, many governors were in a position to decide whether their states adopted the Affordable Care Act’s expansion to Medicaid, an insurance programme for low-income households.
Some governors, like Steve Beshear of Kentucky and Earl Ray Tomblin of West Virginia, issued executive orders in 2013 to adopt Medicaid expansion without their legislatures’ approval.
Others, like Florida’s then-Governor Rick Scott, opposed Medicaid expansion and directed their state legislatures not to adopt it. Scott, who now serves as a US senator for the state, later dropped his opposition, but the Republican-led Florida legislature did not take up a bill to agree to the expansion.
Future presidential candidates
As their state’s chief executives, governors have a unique platform to showcase their political talents.
Many use the governor’s mansion to catapult to the nation’s highest office, the presidency.
At least 17 former US presidents – including Jimmy Carter, Ronald Reagan, Bill Clinton and George W Bush – were governors before they occupied the White House.
But some governors find their presidential ambitions thwarted by backlash to their state-level policies.
The Eagleton Institute of Politics estimates that only 53 percent of the presidential nominees who were previously governors were ultimately victorious in their races.
During the 2016 presidential election cycle, for instance, the governor of New Jersey at the time, Chris Christie, hoped to secure the Republican Party’s nomination.
He dropped out of the race in February of that year, however, amid criticism of several actions undertaken during his governorship.
His administration in New Jersey was still reeling from a scandal known as “Bridgegate”, which concerned accusations that a major roadway was closed to punish the mayor of a nearby city.
And some Republicans denounced the way Christie had greeted Obama, a Democrat, when he visited New Jersey during Hurricane Sandy in October 2012.
Setting the stage for 2028
This year’s midterm races are expected to set the stage for the presidential election in 2028.
Several outgoing governors are among the likely hopefuls. Newsom, who has served as California’s governor since 2019, is prevented from running for a third term this year.
Instead, he is widely speculated to be a frontrunner for the Democratic nomination in 2028, having established himself as a vocal critic of Republican President Donald Trump.
Several other potential Democratic contenders are also locked in re-election campaigns this midterm cycle that could serve as previews for future presidential bids. They include Wes Moore of Maryland and Josh Shapiro of Pennsylvania.

Details

We did it, thank you very much
After the race, the young champion was met by his parents, sister, and the Mercedes team.
The previous record belonged to Sebastian Vettel, who became world champion in 2010 at the age of 23 years and 134 days, racing for Red Bull.

UN warns of security risks in Western Sahara as peacekeeping mission ends
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
23:19:51 UTC
08:19:51 KST

UN warns of security risks in Western Sahara as peacekeeping mission ends
The mission, known as MINURSO, has been in place in the disputed region since a ceasefire in 1991.
United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres has warned of potential escalation of hostilities in the disputed Western Sahara region after the expiry of a 35-year-long peacekeeping mission.
“The Secretary-General said he remains concerned about the security situation throughout the territory and the risk of hostilities escalating,” his spokesperson, Stephane Dujarric, said in a statement on Sunday.
Guterres also confirmed the end of the peacekeeping mission on Sunday, after the UN Security Council (UNSC) failed to renew its mandate on Friday.
He urged all concerned “to exercise maximum restraint and to refrain from actions that could further increase tensions or undermine regional stability”.
November 1 marked the start of the “liquidation phase” of the peacekeeping mission, with assets transported back to troop-contributing countries, Guterres said.
The UN established the Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara (MINURSO) in 1991 to monitor a ceasefire and prepare a referendum on the territory’s future.
Morocco has considered Western Sahara its territory since 1975, when Spain withdrew from the desert region in northwest Africa, roughly the size of Britain.
The Polisario Front, an Algeria-backed movement acting on behalf of the Indigenous Sahrawi people, seeks to establish an independent state called the Sahrawi Republic.
At the UNSC on Friday, the US proposed a resolution to support the principle of self-determination in the Western Sahara. Washington’s draft would have extended the mission for a year, removed “referendum” from its name and made Morocco’s autonomy proposal the only basis for further talks.
Russia vetoed the resolution, despite support from 11 of the 15 UNSC members, including fellow permanent members France and the United Kingdom.
The council then defeated a competing Russian resolution, leaving the mission to expire without a new mandate.
“While MINURSO’s peacekeeping operations have concluded, the United Nations stands ready to continue supporting efforts to advance dialogue and pursue a peaceful resolution of the conflict,” Guterres said on Sunday.
‘Deep regret’
Morocco’s royal palace said the fact the mission was not renewed was a “significant development” in withdrawing the Western Sahara issue from the UNSC’s consideration.
On Saturday, Algeria’s Foreign Ministry, however, expressed “deep regret” over the non-renewal, blaming the “excessive bias” of the US towards Morocco’s position.
The Polisario Front said in a statement that it was “concerned at the deadlock in the Security Council meeting”.
Speaking after Friday’s vote, US Ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz said it was truly unfortunate that in 2026, the veto was used to “preserve the letter R [in the Mission’s name] for referendum”.
He added Washington’s proposal “would have moved the 50-year conflict forward” and that the status quo is unacceptable.
Russia’s UN ambassador, Vassily Nebenzia, said at the same meeting that Moscow opposed the draft because it favoured one side.
“We stress the fact that the Security Council cannot automatically predetermine matters relating to sovereignty,” he said.

The Russian &quot;Filin&quot; missile, which has begun to be used against Ukraine, has significant limitations: what is known about its threat
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
01:16:03 EET
08:16:03 KST

The Russian "Filin" missile, which has begun to be used against Ukraine, has significant limitations: what is known about its threat
Kyiv • UNN
Russia has been using the "Filin" against Ukraine on a limited basis since the summer of 2026. The missile is dangerous because it flies at extremely low altitudes, but its specifications are contradictory.
The Russian Filin cruise missile, which the occupiers began using on a limited basis against Ukraine in the summer of 2026, has significant technical limitations. In particular, it cannot simultaneously provide the stated range of 1,200 km and a maximum speed of 800 km/h. Defense Express reports this, citing its own calculations and data from the Main Intelligence Directorate of Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense, UNN writes.
Details
According to Ukrainian intelligence, the missile was developed by the Russian company NPO Molniya. It is 3.5 m long, has a wingspan of 3 m, and its warhead weighs either 50 or 100 kg, depending on the modification.
The Filin is launched from a ground-based installation using a solid-fuel booster. The missile can fly at extremely low altitudes or climb to 6 km.
What makes the missile dangerous and what are its limitations
The Filin’s ability to fly at extremely low altitudes poses a potential threat, as this may complicate its timely detection by air defense systems.
At the same time, the characteristics stated by Russia raise doubts among analysts. According to Defense Express’s calculations, the missile’s most efficient flight speed is approximately 420 km/h.
The Filin is equipped with a compact Reynolds R500 turbojet engine, whose maximum thrust near the ground is approximately 50 kgf and decreases to about 32.5 kgf at an altitude of 5 km.
Experts believe that the stated speed of 800 km/h and range of 1,200 km can be achieved only under different flight conditions and warhead configurations.
Thus, maximum speed does not mean that the missile is capable of maintaining it throughout its entire route. The actual range depends on the flight altitude, the warhead’s weight, and the amount of fuel.

Wildberger told public broadcaster ARD that it involved “a notification from Apple that certain devices may have been compromised by so-called spyware.”
The Federal Office for Information Security (BSI) reacted quickly and informed all those affected in writing, according to Wildberger.
According to the letter, as reported by ARD, iPhones have been receiving threat notifications from Apple since Oct. 29 stating that an attack involving so-called “Mercenary” spyware had been detected.

Apple describes its threat notifications as highly reliable warnings that a person has been specifically targeted. The notification does not indicate whether the attack was successful.
The BSI recommended that those affected “assume, as a precaution, that the device may have been compromised.”
Wildberger did not provide any further information on specific details. At the same time, he expressed concern about the reports.
Spyware is software that secretly collects or monitors a user's information or activities without their knowledge or informed consent, often transmitting that information to third parties. It can be installed without the user's knowledge or consent, sometimes by exploiting software vulnerabilities or through deceptive installation methods.
According to the BSI, attackers could use this to access messages—including those on encrypted messaging apps—as well as calls, contacts, calendars and location data and activate the microphone and camera.

The Kremlin referred questions about Kyiv's allegations to the Russian Defense Ministry, with spokesman Dmitry Peskov suggesting Ukrainian troops had also used the cease-fire to regroup, calling it "standard practice."
British broadcaster Sky News reported that a Ukrainian unit had granted its team exclusive access to its drone reconnaissance command center in southern Ukraine, providing a real-time view of their long-range drone footage.
The footage showed Russian troops deploying heavy military equipment and delivering supplies during the cease-fire in Russian-occupied territory in and around Oleshky, Sky News reported.
"Before, they wouldn't even dream of traveling along the road, day or night, in bad weather or under any other conditions. Now they have the opportunity to do so," a Ukrainian military officer told the British broadcaster.
Moscow resumed attacks on Ukraine's Kherson region following the end of the local cease-fire, Kyiv said on November 2.
Russian forces struck central Kherson with a drone, hitting a medical facility, said regional military administration head Yaroslav Shanko.
Signs Of Cyberwar?
Meanwhile, there were signs of a potential cyberwar heating up between the two countries, although details remained scarce.
Ukraine's air force on November 1 said it suspected the country's air raid alert system had been hacked but that systems had been restored to normal.
"The Air Alarm application appears to have been subjected to hostile interference," Ukraine's Air Force said in a statement on November 1. "Stay calm and follow our updates on our channel."
Separately, Russia's Emergency Situations Ministry early on November 2 said a cyberattack on its online app caused false information to be spread to the public.
"Attention! The mobile application of the Emergencies Ministry of Russia has been subjected to a massive cyberattack, enabling attackers to send false information to the public," the ministry wrote on Telegram.
There was no indication if the two incidents were linked, but Russian websites in recent days have reported multiple cyberattacks.
With reporting by RFE/RL senior correspondent Alex Raufoglu in Washington, Reuters, Fox, and AFP

Haley Stevens endorses Republican candidate in Michigan race
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
22:58:55 UTC
07:58:55 KST

Breadcrumb
Haley Stevens endorses Republican candidate in Michigan race
A staunchly pro-Israel Democratic congresswoman in Michigan has endorsed the Republican candidate in the state's closely contested US Senate race, turning against progressive Muslim candidate Abdul El-Sayed, who defeated her in the Democratic primary despite millions of dollars in pro-Israel backing.
Haley Stevens announced her support for Republican Mike Rogers on Sunday, breaking party ranks just two days before the midterm elections and deepening divisions among Democrats over US support for Israel.
Stevens, an outspoken supporter of Israel who once declared that the country "visits me in my dreams", had spent weeks avoiding a public endorsement of El-Sayed following her defeat in August.
During a Hanukkah celebration in Detroit, Stevens pledged her unwavering support for Israel, declaring: "I will continue fighting for the people of Israel in the United States Congress."
"Israel visits me in my dreams. I see Israel's future," she added.
Pro-Israel lobbying groups reportedly spent more than $67 million backing Stevens against El-Sayed in the Democratic primary, but failed to prevent the progressive candidate from securing the nomination.
Her decision to endorse a Republican comes as Democrats fight to retain Michigan's Senate seat, currently held by Gary Peters, who is retiring in January.
Stevens turns against El-Sayed
Despite initially pledging to support El-Sayed after losing the primary, Stevens repeatedly refused to publicly endorse him in television appearances, citing disagreements over his opposition to Israel.
El-Sayed has called for an end to Israeli apartheid and genocide in Gaza, demanding that Washington halt military assistance to Israel and redirect American taxpayer money towards domestic needs.
Tensions escalated after Stevens demanded that El-Sayed publicly disavow an advertisement produced by an outside group targeting her and apologise.
El-Sayed rejected the demand, pointing out that his campaign had already condemned the advertisement and made clear that it had no connection to his team.
On Saturday, El-Sayed announced that Stevens was no longer welcome at a campaign event scheduled for Sunday at a church, despite having previously been invited alongside other Democrats.
Stevens subsequently appeared alongside Rogers at a campaign rally before announcing her endorsement of the Republican candidate in a video.
"As you have seen, our Democratic candidate for the Senate, Abdul El-Sayed, has stated that I am not welcome in his campaign and asked me to stay away, and he is right," Stevens said.
"That is why I am announcing today my support for Mike Rogers for the United States Senate."
She later told reporters that she remained a Democrat and would continue voting for other Democratic candidates.
"This is a very close election, we all know that, but Abdul made very clear that I was not welcome in his campaign," she said.
Democrats accuse Stevens of betrayal
Stevens' decision to campaign alongside a Trump-backed Republican triggered a fierce backlash from Michigan Democrats, who accused her of undermining the party at a critical moment.
Michigan Democratic Party chair Curtis Hertel condemned what he described as attempts by Stevens and other bad-faith actors to divide Democrats ahead of Tuesday's vote.
"Mike Rogers is Donald Trump's handpicked candidate for the US Senate," Hertel said, accusing Rogers of advancing Trump's agenda while prioritising his own political interests.
Hertel said Michigan Democrats stood firmly behind El-Sayed, arguing that Stevens had abandoned the very causes she claimed to champion by supporting a Republican who had failed Michigan's working-class communities, sought a nationwide abortion ban and pledged loyalty to Trump.
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer described Stevens' endorsement as a "despicable betrayal", while the chair of Michigan Democrats' Black Caucus called her a "sellout".
Trump, meanwhile, welcomed Stevens' decision, praising her "bravery" on Truth Social.
"Haley said what few people are willing to say," Trump wrote.
El-Sayed dismisses pro-Israel rival's move
El-Sayed refused to be drawn into the controversy, dismissing questions about Stevens' endorsement and insisting that his attention remained on the issues affecting Michigan residents.
"At the end of the day, I actually don't think about Haley Stevens. I think about the 9,999,998 people who are not those two," he said, referring to Stevens and Rogers.
"Because you know what, I am just less interested in the politics of it all than I am in the policy of it all."
If elected, El-Sayed would become the first Muslim member of the US Senate.
The progressive candidate has also faced repeated Islamophobic attacks from Trump, who has called him a "jihadist" and falsely claimed he wants to impose Islamic law on the United States.
Michigan's Senate race is a closely watched contest in Tuesday's midterm elections, with Democrats seeking to retain the seat as they attempt to regain control of Congress.

Egypt's Grand Egyptian Museum launches immersive "Eternal Sun" light experience
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
06:58:37 CST
07:58:37 KST

An immersive light and sound experience titled "Eternal Sun" is staged at the Grand Egyptian Museum in Giza, Egypt, Nov. 1, 2026. Egypt's Grand Egyptian Museum (GEM) launched an immersive light-and-sound experience on Sunday, offering visitors a new way to explore the country's ancient civilization through modern visual and audio technology. (Xinhua/Ahmed Gomaa)
CAIRO, Nov. 1 (Xinhua) -- Egypt's Grand Egyptian Museum (GEM) launched an immersive light-and-sound experience on Sunday, offering visitors a new way to explore the country's ancient civilization through modern visual and audio technology.
The launch coincides with the first anniversary of the museum's official opening.
Titled "Eternal Sun," the 35-minute show takes visitors on an audiovisual journey through ancient Egyptian history, drawing inspiration from natural cycles such as sunrise and sunset, the Nile's annual flooding and harvest seasons, which shaped ancient Egyptians' relationship with their natural environment.
With architectural projection mapping, dynamic lighting, live music, and storytelling in Arabic and English, the project transforms the museum's Grand Hall into an immersive stage.
Ahmed Ghoneim, CEO of the GEM, described the show as part of the museum's efforts to present archaeological, cultural and historical content through innovative approaches.
He added that the show would run for six months, until April 30, 2027.
Since its opening, the museum has welcomed over 5 million visitors from around the world, Ghoneim said. ■

Ukraine says public air raid alert app sent false alerts after being hacked
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
22:56:59 UTC
07:56:59 KST

Ukraine and Russia say emergency alert apps were hit by hacks
KYIV, Nov 2 - Ukraine and Russia said their emergency alert apps had been hacked overnight, sending false warnings to citizens about impending air raids, chemical and nuclear attacks.
The warnings coincided with the expiry of a six-day local ceasefire brokered by US first lady Melania Trump in a small area of southern Ukraine — the longest such pause in fighting since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022.
Ukraine's public air raid app started to send false alerts just before 11 p.m. (2100 GMT) on Sunday for the capital Kyiv and other areas warning of radiation and chemical attacks and also the risk of street combat in some areas.
One of the fake alarms said Russia had launched a hypersonic Oreshnik missile — which is capable of carrying a nuclear warhead — and that a nuclear alert had been declared across Ukraine.
Ukraine's air force said shortly afterwards on the Telegram messaging app that the alert system appeared to have been hacked by Russia, noting that the alerts were broadcast in the Russian language. The Ukrainian language is compulsory for all official communications in Ukraine.
"The air alert app appears to have been subjected to enemy influence," the air force statement said. "There is no radiation threat! Stay calm and follow our updates on our channel!"
KYIV RESIDENTS UNFAZED BY FALSE ALERTS
All-clear messages were sent shortly afterwards for each of the alerts and Ukraine's Ministry for Digital Transformation said the emergency app had been temporarily suspended, but other means of alerting the public were functioning, as were air raid sirens.
On the streets of Kyiv, residents played down the impact of the hack.
Artem Pyndyk, 37, a businessman, said he was briefly surprised to see the messages but then realised what had happened.
"This did not trigger the kind of reaction in society that they expected," said Pyndyk, adding that family members and friends he had checked in with had also not panicked.
"You can laugh about it but, on the other hand, they gained a certain level of access and were able to hack the programme," he added.
Oksana Vostrykova, 48, also shrugged off the incident.
"I am calm about it, I kind of immediately understand that it might be a false message," the pizzeria employee said. "You worry more not for yourself but for your children who are nearby."
RUSSIAN MINISTRY SAYS ITS APP WAS ALSO HIT BY A CYBERATTACK
Russian state news agency TASS quoted the Ministry of Emergency Situations in Moscow as saying early on Monday its mobile app had also been hit by a cyberattack that resulted in the spread of false information to the public.
Atesh, a pro-Ukrainian hacking group, posted a screenshot of the alert message on its Telegram channel early on Monday, with a message saying: "The Ministry of Emergency Situations app has been hacked!"
However, the ministry played down the impact, saying it was not one of its main public warning system channels, but just what it called a supplementary source of information.
A fake message posted by the hackers, seen by Reuters, did not attempt to mimic an official communication and was laced with colloquialisms, profanities and derogatory language about Russia, calling its regions "swamps".
The fake message told Russians that nuclear warheads had been launched against all Russian regions and advised people to stock up on three weeks of food and take shelter in their cellars.
The Russian ministry said in a statement on Telegram that its experts were working to restore the app to normal operation.
"We ask the public to remain calm and to trust only official sources of information — the Russian Ministry of Emergency Situations’ website and the department’s official social media accounts," it said. REUTERS

Myanmar Remains on FATF Blacklist Due to Money Laundering Concerns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
22:55:00 UTC
07:55:00 KST

The world’s top financial crime watchdog will keep Myanmar on its blacklist due to its failure to make enough progress in combating money laundering and terrorist financing.
In a statement issued on Friday, the Paris-based Financial Action Task Force (FATF) said that it had called for the continued “application of enhanced due diligence” on Myanmar by its members, in part due to ongoing cyber scam activities in the country.
FATF, a Paris-based intergovernmental body established in 1989, describes itself as a “global money laundering and terrorist financing watchdog,” which helps to coordinate international efforts “to prevent organized crime, corruption, and terrorism.” In October 2022, it added Myanmar to its category of “high risk jurisdictions subject to a call for action,” commonly known as its blacklist, due to “strategic deficiencies” first identified in 2018. The only other countries currently on FATF’s blacklist are Iran and North Korea, whose designations were also reconfirmed on Friday.
The FATF blacklisting places Myanmar banks and financial entities outside the mainstream of the international financial system, and forces firms dealing with Myanmar citizens or companies to fulfill onerous reporting requirements.
The FATF said on Friday that as part of “enhanced due diligence,” financial institutions should “increase the degree and nature of monitoring” of business relationships involving Myanmar, “in order to determine whether those transactions or activities appear unusual or suspicious.”
In its statement, FATF issued a June assessment in which it found that “fraud and cyber scam activities in Myanmar remain extensive and present significant illicit finance risks.” While acknowledging that Myanmar’s new military-backed government has taken some steps to combat these operations, “the FATF reiterates its call on Myanmar to take appropriate action to address the illicit finance risks associated with fraud and cyber scam threats.” It said that it would “continue to work with Myanmar in this regard.” If no further progress is made by February 2027, the FATF added that it “will consider countermeasures,” including greater oversight and potential banking restrictions.
However, the FATF added that when applying enhanced due diligence, “countries should ensure that flows of funds for humanitarian assistance, legitimate [non-profit] activity and remittances are neither disrupted nor discouraged.”
The FATF announcement was unsurprising, given the extent to which online scamming and associated money laundering have grown in Myanmar since the 2021 coup, particularly in outlying regions of the country, and the largely cosmetic nature of the efforts to combat them. The post-coup conflict has also led to a spike in the production and trafficking of illicit drugs, particularly methamphetamines, in eastern Myanmar that shows no sign of abating.
However, the FATF statement was preceded shortly by a Reuters report claiming that Japan’s government was lobbying for FATF to remove Myanmar from the blacklist in hopes of encouraging business in the country. In particular, Tokyo hoped that the watchdog would “drop requirements that its members apply enhanced screening to financial transactions with Myanmar to avoid money laundering and terrorist financing.” The report cited one anonymous source as saying that “at least one other major Asian country was pushing for Myanmar’s removal.”
While the efforts to remove Myanmar from the blacklist were not successful, Japan’s push was just the latest sign of a growing regional willingness to re-engage with Myanmar since direct military rule was replaced by a quasi-civilian administration in April.
Since then, coup leader-turned-president Min Aung Hlaing has been on a diplomatic offensive aimed at shoring up relationships with key partners and securing full reintegration into the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN). The United States has also held direct talks with Myanmar officials on several occasions in the past few months, in some instances with support from the Japanese government.
