Pro-Israel Democrat Haley Stevens endorses Republican Rogers in Michigan US Senate race
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
22:52:13 UTC
07:52:13 KST

Michigan pro-Israel Democratic congresswoman Haley Stevens endorsed Republican Mike Rogers over her own party’s nominee, Abdul El-Sayed, for US Senate on Sunday, telling reporters, “We can’t stand with hate.”
The surprise move two days before Election Day further exacerbated the growing fracture between Zionist Jewish communities and the Democratic Party, as El-Sayed’s critical rhetoric on Israel has alienated many Jewish voters in a state that could decide control of the chamber.
Jewish Democrat leaders were among the voices attacking Stevens, who ran against El-Sayed in the Democratic primary for the seat, following her announcement. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer called it “a despicable betrayal.”
President Donald Trump, on his social network Truth Social, celebrated Stevens’ endorsement as “bravery.”
The endorsement capped a whirlwind week for Stevens, whose Jewish fiancée, Democratic megadonor Jason Turkish, announced days earlier he would also be supporting Rogers. Until Sunday, Stevens had publicly claimed to be in El-Sayed’s camp and had been scheduled to attend a get-out-the-vote Detroit church event Sunday with him and Black Democratic leaders.
El-Sayed refuses to condemn ad blaming Israel for grocery prices sparking conflict
But on Friday, she publicly urged El-Sayed to repudiate an outside PAC ad that had blamed Israel for the rising price of groceries as a condition of appearing with his campaign. When El-Sayed refused, instead calling out the pro-Israel lobby AIPAC’s spending heavily in favor of Stevens in the primary, cracks between their camps spilled out into the open.
By Sunday, it was an earlier antisemitism-related grievance Stevens referenced in rescinding her endorsement of the Democratic candidate. She named El-Sayed’s spring campaign appearances with anti-Israel streamer Hasan Piker on college campuses as a key reason why she was switching her endorsement.
“I don’t belong in Abdul’s campaign. I do not stand with Hasan Piker, who gets trafficked on our college campuses,” the congresswoman said in a video message announcing her Rogers endorsement, saying that “education is on the ballot.”
Appearing later in a brief press conference with Rogers, she again referenced the streamer: “We can’t stand with hate. We can’t stand with Hasan Piker.”
Rogers, standing next to Stevens, invoked darker messaging when referencing the PAC ad.
“Blaming a certain group of people for your problems, that sounds like 1933,” he said. “And it has consequences for those communities. Jewish Democrats are calling me, afraid for their children to stay in the state of Michigan.”
Piker, on social media, called Stevens “a self interested striver who’s weirdly obsessed with Israel and has been paid handsomely for this strange obsession.” El-Sayed has distanced himself multiple times from Piker since they campaigned together in the primary, including this week after Piker compared a heavily Jewish Michigan suburb to “a KKK neighborhood.”
A Jewish Telegraphic Agency request for comment to the Stevens-Turkish camp was not immediately returned. Stevens, who represents a heavily Jewish district in suburban Detroit, told The New York Times this weekend that she was considering converting to Judaism for their wedding.
El-Sayed, in his own press conference Sunday, dismissed Stevens’ move and preemptively warned reporters not to ask him about it. “At the end of the day I actually don’t think about Haley Stevens,” he said.
He did, however, push back on the idea that a Rogers endorsement was standing against hate.
“If you are somebody who believes that we should stand up to hate, and you have watched this last campaign, I think we probably would not want to support Mike Rogers and Donald Trump and JD Vance,” he said. The GOP’s messaging against El-Sayed has been criticized for leaning heavily into stoking fears about Islam.
Stevens' staff push back against endorsement
Stevens insisted she was “still a very proud Democrat.” Yet many of her staff, including her chief of staff, resigned en masse following her move Sunday. Arik Wolk, Stevens’ former campaign spokesperson, wrote on X that her endorsement was “ridiculous and pathetic.”
Some Jewish Democrats also heavily criticized Stevens on Sunday, saying she was hurting the party and the country. “Anyone who makes an election this important about themselves, and not Michiganders and our democracy, should think hard about whether they are serving the greater good,” moderate Michigan Sen. Elissa Slotkin, who is Jewish and who has hit the campaign trail with El-Sayed, wrote on X.
J Street, the liberal pro-Israel lobby that did not endorse El-Sayed, said Stevens was “weaponizing real fears about rising antisemitism to further her own grievances.”
The Jewish Democratic Council of America, an organizing body for Jewish interests in the Democratic Party, had pointedly not endorsed El-Sayed during the campaign. Yet following Stevens’ announcement, its CEO Halie Soifer wrote, “A vote for any Republican in 2026 is a vote for Donald Trump.”

Houthis repeat threats against Saudi oil giant, aviation

- The conflict has intensified since July, with attacks killing 24 in Saudi Arabia and an airport strike in Riyadh killing at least 13.
- The war has displaced more than 300,000 people in western Yemen, while the UN says more than 1,600 have been killed since fighting restarted.
AI generated
SANAA – Houthi media, citing an anonymous military official, on Nov 1 repeated threats against Saudi oil giant Aramco and aviation in the kingdom.
Yemen’s Houthis, fighting a Saudi-led coalition backing the internationally recognised government, are allies of Iran, which on Nov 1 warned the US and Israel not to renew strikes on the Islamic republic after they had threatened a return to war.
“Aramco facilities are within range of the Yemeni Armed Forces, and investments in them are a venture fraught with losses,” the Houthis’ Saba news agency quoted the military official as saying.
The official also warned international airlines against using Saudi airspace “except for the airspaces of Mecca and Medina”.
The Houthis have targeted oil facilities and airports in the kingdom since Yemen’s once-dormant war reignited in July, killing 24 people in Saudi Arabia in October.
An Oct 10 strike on Riyadh’s international airport became the deadliest on Saudi soil in years when it killed at least 13 people.
On Nov 1, the coalition said it had intercepted a missile and a drone both launched by the Houthis “towards the southern region”.
Meanwhile, fighting in Yemen has displaced more than 300,000 people in the western part of the impoverished country.
Most of them forced from their homes in the last two months, the displaced “urgently need shelter, food, clean water and health care”, the International Organization for Migration said in a statement on Nov 1.
The United Nations says more than 1,600 people have been killed since fighting in Yemen reignited.
Saba on Nov 1 said that Saudi Arabia had “targeted the Faculty of Medicine at Hodeidah University with two raids”, and two Hodeidah residents told AFP they heard an explosion in the area.
The coalition, for its part, said on Nov 1 it had conducted “a precision operation to neutralise vital resources” used by the Houthis, and published video footage that it said showed attacks on the Hodeideh and Dhamar governorates.
A fragile 2022 truce fell apart in July after the Houthis allowed an Iranian plane to land in Yemen’s capital Sanaa in defiance of Saudi control over Yemeni airspace, setting off a spate of attacks. AFP

Kimi Antonelli becomes youngest F1 world champion with 3rd-place finish in Mexico
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
22:49:52 UTC
07:49:52 KST

Halis Sunnetci
02 November 2026•Update: 02 November 2026
Mercedes driver Kimi Antonelli became the youngest world champion in Formula 1 history on Sunday, securing the 2026 drivers' title with a third-place finish at the Mexico City Grand Prix.
The 20-year-old Italian, who replaced seven-time world champion Lewis Hamilton at Mercedes in 2025, claimed his maiden championship in only his second Formula 1 season, with four rounds remaining.
Antonelli broke Sebastian Vettel's record as the youngest Formula 1 world champion and became the first Italian to win the drivers' title since Alberto Ascari in 1953.
Red Bull's Max Verstappen won the 71-lap race at the Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez, while Ferrari's Hamilton finished second ahead of Antonelli.
Antonelli entered the race with a commanding championship advantage, needing only a ninth-place finish or better to secure the title regardless of his rivals' results.
Starting fourth on the grid, the Italian maintained his position after a chaotic opening lap in which Ferrari's Charles Leclerc took the lead following an off-track battle with teammate Hamilton.
Antonelli briefly led the race as the frontrunners made their pit stops, extending his opening stint until lap 44 before switching from soft to medium tires.
The Mercedes driver rejoined in fourth place before a crash involving Cadillac's Valtteri Bottas brought out the safety car and subsequently a red flag.
After the race restarted on lap 47, Hamilton overtook Leclerc, while Antonelli held off Lando Norris.
On lap 48, Antonelli made a decisive move on Leclerc at Turn 1, overtaking the Ferrari driver to take third place and put himself on course for the world title.
Antonelli maintained his position through another safety car period triggered by Arvid Lindblad's crash on lap 59, keeping his title hopes firmly on course.
With Verstappen and Hamilton battling ahead, Antonelli controlled his pace in the closing laps and crossed the finish line third to become the 2026 world champion.
"We did it! And I wouldn't be here without Mercedes and without my family. I'm speechless, I'm trying to process what's just happened," Antonelli said after the race.
"It's been an incredible season, and to share this podium with Max and Lewis is incredible. I look forward to more battles in the future.
"This weekend, I did feel a little more tense. I'm just so happy I got it done," he added.
Verstappen finished 0.799 seconds ahead of Hamilton to claim victory, while newly crowned world champion Antonelli completed the podium, 4.006 seconds behind the winner.
Charles Leclerc finished fourth, followed by Lando Norris, George Russell, Oscar Piastri, Franco Colapinto, Liam Lawson and Pierre Gasly.

A bitter Democratic primary in Michigan has returned to haunt the party just days before Americans vote in the midterm elections, after Congresswoman Haley Stevens stunned her party by endorsing Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers over the man who defeated her for the Democratic nomination.
Abdul El-Sayed has received support from senior Democratic figures in the final stretch of his campaign, as party leaders seek to contain the fallout from Stevens' extraordinary break with her own side.
Former vice president Kamala Harris, former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi and Michigan Congresswoman Debbie Dingell, among others, have backed El-Sayed and publicly condemned Stevens' decision, turning an already fiercely contested Senate race into a test of Democratic unity.
The political rupture came on Sunday, barely two days before the election, when Stevens released a video announcing her support for Rogers while insisting she remained a Democrat.
“I’m just letting you know where I am,” she said.
For Michigan Democrats, the explanation offered little comfort.
Within little more than an hour, state party chairman Curtis Hertel announced that Stevens would no longer have a place in the organisation.
“Congresswoman Stevens is not a current member of the Michigan Democratic Party, nor will she be in the future,” Hertel wrote on X.
The swift response underscored the stakes for Democrats, who see Michigan as central to their hopes of winning control of the US Senate.
The race is considered competitive, with polling suggesting El-Sayed faces a tougher contest than some other Democratic candidates running statewide.
A defeat in Michigan could complicate the party's already difficult path to a Senate majority.
Democrats respond
Harris has sought to reinforce El-Sayed's campaign in the closing days, recording a telephone message urging Michigan voters to support him.
“Abdul El-Sayed is as Michigan as it gets,” Harris says in the robocall.
“Abdul is for the people. I’m Kamala Harris, and I endorse Dr Abdul El Sayed for United States Senate.”
Pelosi delivered a considerably sharper response to Stevens, accusing her Democratic colleague of abandoning the interests of Michigan voters.
“Haley Stevens has chosen to dangerously betray Michigan families’ healthcare, freedoms and future with her horrific endorsement of Mike Rogers,” Pelosi wrote on X.
“@AbdulElSayed must win — because Michigan and our country deserve better. -NP.”
Dingell, another influential Michigan Democrat, expressed astonishment at Stevens' decision, saying she had received assurances only hours earlier that such an endorsement would not happen.
“I was stunned since she had told me she wasn’t doing that last night at midnight,” Dingell told CNN on Sunday.
Asked whether Stevens still had a political future within the Democratic Party, Dingell offered a pointed assessment.
“Unfortunately, she seriously hurt herself,” she said.
El-Sayed shrugs off political storm
Speaking to reporters outside a Detroit church during Sunday's early-voting drive, El-Sayed dismissed the controversy and sought to shift attention back to the economic pressures facing Michigan families.
“None of this matters,” he said, referring to the dispute with Stevens.
The former public health official, who could become the first Muslim elected to the US Senate, has made affordability and healthcare central to his campaign.
His rival, Rogers, is a former Republican congressman.
The two are competing to replace retiring Democratic Senator Gary Peters, in a state whose political and demographic divisions have made it a crucial battleground for both parties.
Israel dispute reopens old wounds
Behind the public rupture lies a disagreement that has shadowed Michigan's Democratic campaign for months.
Stevens is a staunch supporter of Israel, while El-Sayed has been sharply critical of Tel Aviv.
The dispute intensified last week over an advertisement produced by an independent progressive group linking American support for Israel to rising grocery prices.
Stevens demanded that El-Sayed condemn the advertisement, arguing that its message was unacceptable.
El-Sayed said his campaign had not produced the advertisement, while accusing Stevens of reopening arguments settled during the August primary.
Their differences ultimately derailed plans for a joint appearance at a Detroit church on Sunday, which Democratic organisers had hoped would demonstrate unity.
Instead, Stevens appeared alongside Rogers at another church, offering the Republican a politically valuable endorsement in the final hours of the campaign.
Rogers said he was “honoured” by her support.
The consequences extended into Stevens' own office, with her longtime chief of staff resigning and other departures expected, according to reports.
A party racing against the clock
For Democratic strategists, the concern is not simply that Stevens has endorsed a Republican.
More than 1.8 million Michigan voters had already cast ballots by Friday, according to the Associated Press, meaning much of the electorate had made its choice before the latest dispute erupted.
Yet with voting continuing until Tuesday, the question remains whether Democrats can prevent their internal disagreements from affecting the final result.

Matt Canavan to run in Capricornia as One Nation's James Ashby rules out bid
In short:
Nationals leader Matt Canavan has announced he will nominate for preselection in the Queensland seat of Capricornia.
The seat will be vacated by retiring LNP member Michelle Landry before the next election.
One Nation's party director James Ashby was considering a tilt but has now ruled out running for the seat.
Nationals leader Matt Canavan says he wants to run for the seat of Capricornia at the next election.
Senator Canavan confirmed today he would seek preselection for the Central Queensland seat that will be vacated by outgoing Nationals chief whip Michelle Landry, as revealed by the ABC.
Officially announcing his nomination alongside Ms Landry on the banks of the Fitzroy River in Queensland, Senator Canavan acknowledged the political risk of switching from the Senate to the lower house.
"My political career may die, but I'm not going to die wondering,"
Senator Canavan said.
After the announcement, One Nation's party director James Ashby ruled out running for the Central Queensland electorate, despite previously considering a tilt at the lower house seat.
Senator Pauline Hanson also said she would not run in Capricornia.
Senator Canavan said he needed to "step up" and take a risk by running for the House of Representatives during a "volatile" climate.
"It falls to me," he said after Ms Landry's resignation, adding he "desperately wanted" a change of government.
"I'm happy to sacrifice potentially my own political future to do that," he said.
"I want to be on the front lines with my troops as well. I'm the leader of the Nationals.
"I just have to be there in the trenches with them."
Ashby rules out run
In a statement confirming he would not join the race in Capricornia, Mr Ashby, a close political ally of Senator Hanson and her former chief of staff, said he knew "a number of very worthy contenders" and he would be encouraging them to put up their hands.
"I'll play a role in the campaign here in Capricornia, but my position as national director is one that I take serious; therefore I won't be nominating at pre-selection," Mr Ashby said.
"Capricornia is a seat One Nation can win, so I intend to throw the resources and people behind a strong campaign."
He said the electorate had been "enormously betrayed" by the Coalition in government and in opposition, saying that the mining, agriculture and tourism sectors were suffering.
"Matt Canavan and his colleagues have never shouldered any of the responsibility," he said.
"Until he and the Nationals admit they've been a part of the problem, voters across Capricornia will continue shifting their support to One Nation."
Coalition backs Canavan switch
Senator Canavan, who lives in Yeppoon in the electorate, became the leader of the Nationals in March, replacing David Littleproud, who stepped down.
He currently holds the number two spot on the Liberal National Party of Queensland (LNP) Senate ticket, behind Liberal James McGrath.
A successful move from the Senate to the lower house would shore up the likelihood of Senator Canavan becoming deputy prime minister in a Coalition government, and assure those in the Nationals who hold the view that their leader should sit in the House of Representatives with the other major party leaders.
Opposition Leader Angus Taylor, when asked if a One Nation surge in popular support was pushing Senator Canavan out of the upper house, declined to comment on the minor party but backed Senator Canavan's bid.
"He's a valued colleague and I'd love to see him in the lower house," Mr Taylor said.
Nationals deputy Bridget McKenzie was asked on ABC Radio National Breakfast if the move was a risk for her Senate colleague.
"In this current political environment there is always a risk running for lower house seats," she said.
"I think Matt's got a great proposition. He has delivered for that community alongside Michelle Landry for a long period of time."
She said One Nation had "made a big song and dance … of wanting to get the PM out of the lodge" and she urged the party to target Labor seats instead of Coalition-held electorates.
Election a 'referendum on net zero'
Senator Canavan said he had been mulling the decision for a while after Ms Landry approached him a few months ago to signal she was considering leaving politics.
He stressed he was nominating for preselection in the seat, which the LNP holds with a 5.8 per cent margin, and was not yet the candidate.
"We're a grassroots party, and whether I'm leader or whatever, I've got to go and present before the Capricornia branch of the LNP and seek their support," he said.
He said the next election would be a "referendum on net zero" and that government needed to "unleash our nation's energy resources again", including coal, oil, gas and uranium.
"We should be building nuclear power stations," he said.
"The way to get cost of living down is to do everything, to build everything, to increase the supply of electricity."
Last year, the Nationals went ahead of their Coalition partners in abandoning their commitment to reach net zero emissions by 2050, with the Liberals under then-leader Sussan Ley following.

In Russia’s Nizhny Novgorod region, gasoline sales have been limited to 40 liters following a strike on an oil refinery
Kyiv • UNN
Following the attack on the NORSI oil refinery, no more than 40 liters of gasoline are being sold per vehicle, while fuel sales in canisters have been banned. Queues have formed at gas stations.
In Russia's Nizhny Novgorod region, restrictions were imposed on gasoline sales after Ukrainian drones attacked the Lukoil-Nizhegorodnefteproekt oil refinery. Drivers were allowed to purchase no more than 40 liters per vehicle, while the sale of fuel in canisters was banned. The Moscow Times reports this, UNN writes.
Details
At the same time, no restrictions were imposed on the sale of diesel fuel. Local authorities are also tightening controls over the "odd-even" system, under which the right to refuel on a particular day depends on the first digit of a vehicle's license plate.
In addition, fuel sales to drivers from other regions will be restricted at gas stations near the regional borders. Police and the Russian National Guard will once again take turns at the gas stations, while the removal of fuel from regional storage facilities will be temporarily prohibited. An exception will be made for Russia's Ministry of Defense and emergency services.
Queues formed at gas stations after the strike on the refinery.
On the night of November 1, Ukrainian drones attacked the NORSI oil refinery in the Kstovo district. Governor Gleb Nikitin reported significant damage to the industrial facility.
A large-scale fire broke out at the refinery after the attack. Ukrainian monitoring channels reported fires at the AVT-5 and AVT-6 units. The city of Kstovo was shrouded in smoke, and local residents complained of the smell of burning.
Amid fears of a fuel shortage, queues formed at gas stations in Nizhny Novgorod, Kstovo, and Balakhna. Authorities urged residents not to stockpile gasoline and to refuel only when necessary.
NORSI is one of Russia's largest oil refineries. Its capacity is approximately 17 million tons of oil per year. In terms of refining volume, the facility ranks fourth in the country, and in gasoline production, second.
Damage to municipal infrastructure and possible disruptions to electricity, hot water, and heating supplies were also reported in the region after the attack.

“The main problem with elections in Bulgaria is the widespread apathy. I imagine that if people were deprived of their right to vote, more of them would take an interest in the presidential candidates and turn out at the polling stations.” This is what our compatriot Petya Konstantinova, who lives in Prague, wrote to the Radio Bulgaria editorial team. She cast her ballot early this morning together with her entire family.
She notes that many Bulgarians travelled to the Czech capital especially to vote on Sunday, as once again polling stations in the country had been opened only in Prague, with none elsewhere in the Czech Republic.
“Bulgaria’s political ‘elite’, however, is content with this situation and has even been fuelling mass apathy over the past 20 years. There are not enough active people to change the status quo,” the young Bulgarian continues.
“Otherwise, we Bulgarians in the Czech Republic look to the future with hope and go out to vote, but I would not dare say that I see any great optimism among the people around me. I have the feeling that they have, rather, lost faith that any change is possible. Bulgarians here tend to be more active in the afternoon, so we shall see what happens. My personal impression, however, is that there are more people voting this Sunday than in the first round.”
PHOTO Private archive
Schools in the Czech Republic are currently on their autumn break, which is why Petya’s family travelled back from Croatia to cast their ballots in Prague.
“I can feel the fatigue after the journey, but voting is important,” she says, explaining:
“Because voting is a way of making your position known. Ultimately, everything depends on the choices we make. If we do not exercise that choice, we leave things in the hands of others. Everyone has a voice and everyone should be able to exercise it freely. It is a civic duty, and by making your position known, you have the right to hold those you elect accountable for the trust you have placed in them.
“What strikes me, although it comes as no surprise, is the deep divide between people. I feel that it is becoming increasingly pronounced in Bulgaria. An almost aggressive battle between two camps is being waged, both on social media and in our discussions with one another. But are we not all part of one Bulgaria? Does it not belong to all of us? We all want a better future for our country. I do not think things should be allowed to escalate to such an extent. I simply do not understand it. Dialogue is constructive. Everything else is largely unproductive.
I would very much like people to calm down, because their reactions are, in fact, those of unsettled and frightened people. Politics often plays on people's fears, and this was particularly evident during the current election campaign. Those who do not vote have lost hope and faith; they no longer believe that anything can change. And yet there is always light at the end of the tunnel. It is up to us!”

Ukrainian air force says public air raid alert app has been hacked
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
23:38:28 CET
07:38:28 KST

KYIV, Nov 2 (Reuters) - Ukraine and Russia said their emergency alert apps had been hacked overnight, sending false warnings to citizens about impending air raids, chemical and nuclear attacks.
The warnings coincided with the expiry of a six-day local ceasefire brokered by US first lady Melania Trump in a small area of southern Ukraine — the longest such pause in fighting since Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022.
Ukraine’s public air raid app started to send false alerts just before 11 p.m. (2100 GMT) on Sunday for the capital Kyiv and other areas warning of radiation and chemical attacks and also the risk of street combat in some areas.
One of the fake alarms said Russia had launched a hypersonic Oreshnik missile — which is capable of carrying a nuclear warhead — and that a nuclear alert had been declared across Ukraine.
Ukraine’s air force said shortly afterwards on the Telegram messaging app that the alert system appeared to have been hacked by Russia, noting that the alerts were broadcast in the Russian language. The Ukrainian language is compulsory for all official communications in Ukraine.
“The air alert app appears to have been subjected to enemy influence,” the air force statement said. “There is no radiation threat! Stay calm and follow our updates on our channel!”
KYIV RESIDENTS UNFAZED BY FALSE ALERTS
All-clear messages were sent shortly afterwards for each of the alerts and Ukraine’s Ministry for Digital Transformation said the emergency app had been temporarily suspended, but other means of alerting the public were functioning, as were air raid sirens.
On the streets of Kyiv, residents played down the impact of the hack.
Artem Pyndyk, 37, a businessman, said he was briefly surprised to see the messages but then realised what had happened.
“This did not trigger the kind of reaction in society that they expected,” said Pyndyk, adding that family members and friends he had checked in with had also not panicked.
“You can laugh about it but, on the other hand, they gained a certain level of access and were able to hack the programme,” he added.
Oksana Vostrykova, 48, also shrugged off the incident.
“I am calm about it, I kind of immediately understand that it might be a false message,” the pizzeria employee said. “You worry more not for yourself but for your children who are nearby.”
RUSSIAN MINISTRY SAYS ITS APP WAS ALSO HIT BY A CYBERATTACK
Russian state news agency TASS quoted the Ministry of Emergency Situations in Moscow as saying early on Monday its mobile app had also been hit by a cyberattack that resulted in the spread of false information to the public.
Atesh, a pro-Ukrainian hacking group, posted a screenshot of the alert message on its Telegram channel early on Monday, with a message saying: “The Ministry of Emergency Situations app has been hacked!”
However, the ministry played down the impact, saying it was not one of its main public warning system channels, but just what it called a supplementary source of information.
A fake message posted by the hackers, seen by Reuters, did not attempt to mimic an official communication and was laced with colloquialisms, profanities and derogatory language about Russia, calling its regions “swamps”.
The fake message told Russians that nuclear warheads had been launched against all Russian regions and advised people to stock up on three weeks of food and take shelter in their cellars.
The Russian ministry said in a statement on Telegram that its experts were working to restore the app to normal operation.
“We ask the public to remain calm and to trust only official sources of information — the Russian Ministry of Emergency Situations’ website and the department’s official social media accounts,” it said.
(Reporting by Ron Popeski, Bogdan Kochubey, Jekaterīna Golubkova, Vladyslav Smilianets and Lina Golovnya; Editing by Daniel Flynn and Gareth Jones)

Zelensky says Ukraine will stop hitting Russia’s refineries if US provides missiles
WASHINGTON - Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Nov 1 that his country would stop hitting Russian oil refineries – a key demand of US President Donald Trump – if Washington provided Kyiv with powerful Patriot interceptor missiles.
Trump, battling inflation at home driven in large part by soaring energy prices fuelled by his war on Iran and the Russia-Ukraine conflict, has demanded the European foes stop attacking each other’s energy sites.
Speaking to US broadcaster Fox News on Nov 1, Zelensky said he had had “different and several” conversations with Trump and his team about the issue.
“We asked that we can’t not respond after Russia’s attack on our energy, after Russia is killing our people, attacks on our electricity, gas, refineries, on everything,” he told Fox News host Trey Yingst.
“We said that if you want us not to attack Russia’s refineries, they have not to attack our energy system. Another alternative, give us Patriot missiles, we will find money, not just aid.”
Zelensky said if Washington provided the missile systems for one month, Kyiv would cease attacks on Russian refineries for the same period.
Patriot missiles are among the most important weapons Ukraine has to intercept Russian drones and missiles.
Asked if he was concerned that this would be seen as trying to “leverage” Trump, Zelensky answered in the negative.
“I don’t have any concerns when I share the truth between partners,” he said.
The Trump administration on Oct 30 green-lit the sale of 500 Patriot missiles to Ukraine, the State Department said, but the Ukrainian president warned deliveries could take years.
Ukrainian authorities have been warning for weeks that their supplies of the interceptor missiles were dwindling.
Last week, Zelensky suggested that US and European allies could give his country missiles from their stockpiles, which would later be replenished by the new purchase authorized on Oct 30.
The longest truce of the Ukraine war, limited to the eastern Kherson region, ended on Nov 1 after Russia refused the offer of an extension, Ukrainian officials said.
US-mediated talks between Russia and Ukraine are set to resume this month, having been effectively frozen since the United States and Israel launched joint strikes on Iran in February. AFP

Kherson braces for return of war as localised Russia-Ukraine truce ends
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
22:15:14 UTC
07:15:14 KST

Kherson braces for return of war as localised Russia-Ukraine truce ends
Moscow and Kyiv continue strikes elsewhere, but no reported violations in Kherson region during the six-day ceasefire.
The longest multi-day truce between Russia and Ukraine, limited to Ukraine’s eastern Kherson region, has come to an end with no violations reported by either side, but also no sign of an extension.
The truce, which ended on Sunday night, allowed hundreds of besieged residents of the Russian-occupied Ukrainian town of Oleshky to be evacuated in a rare joint operation between Kyiv and Moscow.
Russian strikes elsewhere in Ukraine on Sunday left hundreds of thousands of households without power, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said. In Russia, meanwhile, authorities reported major damage to an industrial site following Ukrainian drone attacks on the Nizhny Novgorod region.
The six-day localised ceasefire in the front-line Oleshky and the surrounding area was reached after mediation efforts by United States First Lady Melania Trump and with the involvement of Pope Leo XIV.
After the truce expired at 10:59pm on Sunday Ukrainian time (20:59 GMT), the first lady wrote on X that the ceasefire was “a success, delivering critical aid to the region and enabling the evacuation of nearly 800 people”.
“On behalf of America, I commend Russia and Ukraine for their leadership and cooperation surrounding the Oleshky ceasefire,” she said. “I hope Oleshky serves as a foundation for lasting peace between both nations.”
Earlier on Sunday, Pope Leo wrote on X, saying: “I hope that the cooperation between the parties, which made this necessary humanitarian act possible, will strengthen the desire for dialogue and lead to new concrete peace initiatives.”
On Sunday, Ukraine’s military said it evacuated 167 more people from threatened areas of the southern Kherson region, including 22 children and 21 people with limited mobility requiring special assistance.
“Units of civil-military cooperation of the ‘South’ group of forces, in cooperation with representatives of local authorities, evacuated 167 civilians to safer points in the Kherson region,” Ukraine’s General Staff wrote on Telegram.
An estimated 2,000 civilians were in Oleshky when the temporary truce took hold. They were offered the choice to evacuate to Kyiv-controlled territory of Ukraine or territory occupied by Russia, or to remain in the town with replenished food and medical supplies.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov, quoted by Russian news agencies, said Moscow had a positive view of how the operation was conducted, as well as of the coordination between the two countries’ human rights commissioners.
A Ukrainian official, however, told the AFP news agency that Russia reportedly refused an offer to extend the ceasefire after Kyiv’s Foreign Ministry proposed it.
Since Russia launched a full-scale invasion of its neighbour in February 2022, Moscow’s forces have occupied most of the eastern Ukrainian regions of Donetsk and Luhansk, as well as the majority of territory in Ukraine’s southern Kherson and Zaporizhia regions.
Residents urged to remain vigilant
Kherson Governor Oleksandr Prokudin urged residents to be vigilant as the expiry of the ceasefire neared on Sunday.
“I also strongly urge you not to visit the so-called ‘red zones’ – areas and settlements near the Dnipro [River],” Prokudin wrote on Telegram. “The intensity of Russian strikes there remains high, and the threat to life is extremely high.”
Residents in Kherson city, one of the remaining areas of the region still controlled by Ukraine, remained calm, despite knowing the quiet of the localised ceasefire would soon end.
“Don’t be afraid, keep holding on,” Oleksandr Knyha, head of the Mykola Kulish Kherson Regional Academic Music and Drama Theatre, told the audience as he opened a concert.
Knyha is from Oleshky and used to commute from there to Kherson for work. He has not given up hope of returning home.
“That’s also what keeps me here,” he told the Associated Press news agency.
Fighting elsewhere
Elsewhere, Moscow and Kyiv have continued air strikes, with Zelenskyy saying on Sunday that Russia continues to target Ukraine’s energy systems before winter. Attacks on power infrastructure in four Ukrainian regions overnight cut electricity to hundreds of thousands of households, he said.
A Russian attack also killed three people, including a 13-year-old girl, in the Ukrainian region of Vinnytsia, when a drone hit the grounds of a vocational school, Ukraine’s State Emergency Service said. Four others were wounded.
Russian drone attacks targeting Ukraine’s Kyiv region for a second consecutive day wounded a woman and damaged homes, energy infrastructure and a retail establishment, regional authorities said.
In its daily report on Sunday, Ukraine’s Air Force said that Moscow’s forces attacked Ukraine with 433 drones overnight, of which 371 were destroyed or suppressed.
Meanwhile, more than 100 Ukrainian drones were shot down over the skies of Russia’s Nizhny Novgorod region east of Moscow, Governor Gleb Nikitin said on Sunday.
The attack sparked a blaze at the Kstovo oil refinery, Russian media outlets reported, sharing images of black plumes of smoke over the horizon.
Zelenskyy said Kyiv also struck a factory for missile components and air defence facilities in Russia’s southern Rostov region.
“We are justly defending ourselves against Russian aggression and doing everything to reduce Russia’s capability to continue it,” Zelenskyy said.

Iotova also argued that military aid would not help end the conflict. “If we pour even more money into Ukraine and deliver new, more sophisticated weapons, this will only lead to further destruction and many deaths on both sides,” she said during a televised debate last week, according to Euronews.
Gyurov, meanwhile, has backed closer security cooperation with Kiev and argued that Russia must end its military offensive before peace negotiations can advance. He accused Moscow of threatening European security while ruling out sending Bulgarian troops to Ukraine.
The elections took place after multiple cargo vessels were struck by drones off Bulgaria’s Black Sea coast and several aerial drones entered Bulgarian airspace, incidents Radev described as “absolutely unacceptable.”
Bulgaria summoned a Russian envoy last month following attacks on two commercial ships, one of which sank. Sofia also summoned a Ukrainian envoy in August after a drone exploded near the Trans-Balkan gas pipeline, a major energy route linking Russia and the Balkans through Ukraine, Romania and Bulgaria. The Bulgarian military said the UAV was likely a Ukrainian-made Maya decoy drone.

OPEC+ to maintain oil output for 3rd consecutive month in December

VIENNA, Nov. 1 (Xinhua) -- The Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) and its allies, known as OPEC+, will keep their oil output levels unchanged for the third consecutive month in December, OPEC said in a statement on Sunday.
Seven OPEC+ countries, including Saudi Arabia, Russia, Iraq, Kuwait, Kazakhstan, Algeria and Oman, announced the decision after a virtual meeting to review global market conditions and the outlook.
"The seven participating countries decided to maintain September 2026 required production for December 2026," the statement noted.
Under the agreement, the seven countries will maintain their combined required production level at approximately 31.01 million bpd in December. Saudi Arabia's required production level will remain at 10.48 million bpd, followed by Russia at 9.95 million bpd and Iraq at 4.43 million bpd.
They had been raising oil output on a monthly basis from April to September this year. They paused the increases in October and kept November's output unchanged.
OPEC said the seven countries will hold their next meeting on Nov. 29 to review market conditions. ■

SOFIA, Nov. 1 (Xinhua) -- Bulgaria's incumbent President Iliana Iotova wins Sunday's presidential runoff, according to exit polls announced on Bulgarian National TV.
According to pollster Alpha Research, Iotova would secure 52.5 percent of the vote while former caretaker Prime Minister Andrey Gurov would have 43.4 percent. The remaining 4.1 percent preferred the option "I don't support anyone."
Meanwhile, Myara Sociology Agency anticipated 51.1 percent for Iotova, 44.6 percent for Gurov, and 4.3 percent for "I don't support anyone."
The official results are due no later than Wednesday. Under the Bulgarian Constitution, the candidate receiving the most votes wins.
Bulgaria's president is elected directly by voters for five years. Nearly 6.6 million voters were expected to cast their ballots in the runoff.
Iotova, whose term will expire at the end of January 2027, is running with Kiril Valchev as her vice-presidential candidate, and Gurov, an adjunct professor of finance at the American University in Bulgaria, is seeking the presidency with Georgi Kandev as his running mate.
Iotova, 62, was elected vice president twice, in 2016 and 2021, serving alongside then President Rumen Radev. In accordance with the country's Constitution, she succeeded Radev as head of state after he resigned in January this year. Before that, she served on the National Council of the Bulgarian Socialist Party from 2000 to 2016, as well as in the Bulgarian National Assembly and the European Parliament. ■

CAIRO, Nov. 1 (Xinhua) -- Egypt signed a financing agreement worth 1 billion U.S. dollars with the World Bank on Sunday under the second phase of a development policy financing program to support the country's economic reforms, the Egyptian cabinet said.
The agreement was signed by Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty, who also serves as Egypt's governor at the World Bank, and Alwaleed Alatabani, the bank's division director for Egypt, Yemen and Djibouti, at a ceremony attended by Egyptian Prime Minister Mostafa Madbouly in the New Administrative Capital, east of Cairo.

These measures would "support the state's efforts to transition to a green economy and enhance its ability to address the impacts of climate change," the cabinet said.
The World Bank Group's board of directors approved the 1-billion-dollar financing in May 2026, in line with its 2023-2027 strategic partnership framework with Egypt, according to the cabinet. ■

Writing on the X platform, Duffy added: "Please join me in praying for the families and loved ones of those we lost".
The crash site is situated near Military Trail, between Cresthaven Boulevard and 10th Avenue North, located a few miles (kilometres) from US President Donald Trump's Mar-a-Lago estate.
Federal investigation
Video footage recorded by motorists inside their cars captured the moment the aircraft plunged steeply from the sky.
It was not immediately clear whether anyone on the ground suffered injuries.
Jim Reynolds, a spokesperson for Austin-Bergstrom International Airport, confirmed the aircraft was privately operated, though passenger details were not immediately released.
"This is definitely a tragedy," Reynolds said.
"Aircraft Incident," Palm Beach County Fire Rescue announced on X, warning the public to "avoid the area. This will be an extended incident."
The Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office closed all northbound and southbound lanes along Military Trail between Cresthaven Boulevard and 10th Avenue North until further notice to secure the area and allow emergency services to operate.
The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB), the independent federal agency tasked with probing civil transportation accidents across the United States, will lead the investigation alongside the FAA.
Authorities have not yet established what caused the aircraft to lose control and plunge.

While You Were Sleeping: 5 stories you might have missed, Nov 2, 2026
Longest truce of Ukraine war ends in Kherson
The longest truce of the Ukraine war, limited to the eastern Kherson region, ended on Nov 1 after Russia refused the offer of an extension, Ukrainian officials said.
The rare pause in fighting, brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump and which began early on Oct 27, enabled a humanitarian mission to the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky as the war grinds through its fifth year.
Neither side reported violations after the truce began, in what one Ukrainian lawmaker described as the “biggest de-escalation since 2022”.
Crew from NASA’s simulated Mars mission emerges after 378 days in isolation
The four members of a crew who took part in a simulated mission to Mars have emerged after 378 days in isolation at the US space agency’s Johnson Space Center in Houston, an endeavour designed to help prepare for a possible future excursion by NASA astronauts to Earth’s planetary neighbour.
“It’s been a hell of a year – analogue astronauts living in captivity of our own free will,” Ellen Ellis, the medical officer on the Crew Health and Performance Exploration Analog, or CHAPEA, mission, said in remarks at Johnson Space Center after emerging with her three crewmates on Oct 31.
The four entered the 1,700-square-foot (158sq m) 3D-printed habitat on Oct 19, 2025, and performed tasks such as growing crops in simulated Martian soil and interfacing with NASA officials with delays recreating those inherent in interplanetary communications.
Mbappe strikes after China controversy as Real Madrid beat Santander
Kylian Mbappe moved on from a tumultuous week by scoring a penalty to help Real Madrid win 3-0 at Racing Santander on Nov 1.
The French forward narrowly lost out on the Ballon d’Or to Bayern Munich’s Harry Kane on Oct 26 and then had to apologise after a social media storm following a video in which he joked about former Chinese leader Mao Zedong.
Real Madrid’s match, along with other Spanish fixtures this weekend, was not broadcast by Chinese state television because of the fallout.
Republicans risk losing South Asian voters over anti-Indian rhetoric
Dharminder Dargan used to be an enthusiastic Republican voter. The Indian American engineer, who lives near Houston, knocked on doors for GOP candidates, planted their signs in his yard and backed Donald Trump. But not this year.
Dargan, who has been a US citizen and voter for 15 years, said anti-South Asian rhetoric from some Republicans – and what he sees as the party’s silence in response to recent violence, including an attempted mass shooting at a Hindu temple – has pushed him away.
“The wind is changing, and I’m very disappointed in the GOP,” said Dargan, who’s in his late 50s.
Serbians mark railway disaster that led to rise of victorious student movement
Tens of thousands of people gathered at a Serbian railway station on Nov 1 to mark the anniversary of a deadly roof collapse that gave rise to the protest movement that toppled long-time Serbian president Aleksandar Vucic in an election a week ago.
Crowds converged from across the city of Novi Sad on the main train station, where the concrete awning crashed down shortly before noon on Nov 1, 2024, killing 16 people.
Mourners observed 16 minutes of silence before laying wreaths, flowers and candles near the site.

how ecoLogicStudio uses living organisms to build better spaces for living
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
21:45:07 UTC
06:45:07 KST

how ecoLogicStudio uses living organisms to build better spaces for living
architecture need not exclude microbes: these projects use algae, fungi and bacteria as active parts of healthier living environments.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
Exploring the forest of ecologicstudio
In 2025, a forest emerged in the Triennale Design Museum in Milan. It was DeepForest³, a project by the London-based design studio ecoLogicStudio, co-founded by Claudia Pasquero and Marco Poletto. It was presented as part of the exhibition We the Bacteria: Notes Toward Biotic Architecture, curated by Beatriz Colomina and Mark Wigley, who authored the book of the same title. While the installation looked as though a few saplings had risen from the shiny museum floors, what was on display was, in fact, a hypothesis about how domestic space could be transformed by processes inherent to nature, with Poletto describing it as a system constructed with a ‘fully functional and tangible biotechnological living system, grounded in the metabolic cycles of algae and fungi.’
Seeing the deep green cyanobacteria and the lichen growing from a cork bench felt like following a fungi-covered path back through the London-based studio’s projects. Since its inception in 2005 , the duo has proposed a built world that leverages the powers of nature – algae air-purifying mechanisms, waste-digesting mushrooms, and insulation that grows itself – to develop a style of architecture that grows with the environment instead of against it.
The Urban Algae Folly
Nearly ten years earlier, at EXPO Milano 2015 Future Food District, a pavilion of triangular panels glowing with a flow of green algae was erected in the event’s central square. Called The Urban Algae Folly, the canopy provided shade through the growth of Spirulina, a type of microalgae that is highly nutritious for people while also being an effective CO₂-capturing organism. Here, ecoLogicStudio created a symbiosis between the sun, the algae, and humans. On sunny days, more algae grows in the membrane of the canopy. When a person stands under it to take advantage of its shade, the CO₂ they release continues to feed the system. The project is born from the idea that architecture should work with microbial life rather than attempt to exclude it. Here, algae become active collaborators in shaping the environment, turning a pavilion into a living, carbon-consuming system.
EXPO Milan 2015 – Urban Algae Folly
The AirBubble in Nyon
In Nyon, Switzerland, the studio developed what they call ‘the world’s first biotechnological healthcare garden that combines air-purifying algae cultures with medicinal plants.’ Here, an outdoor space, a kind of circular, tent-like structure made of semi-transparent fabric, provides a respite for its inhabitants. Inside, the circumference is lined with ‘36 large bioreactors in borosilicate glass which contain 350 litres of living green Chlorella algae cultures that can filter a flow of polluted air of 150 litres/minute.’ The project challenges the assumption that healthy spaces must be sterile. Instead, it positions living organisms as essential infrastructure, using algae and plants to create an environment where ecological and human health are interconnected.
CryoflorE at MUDAC’s Solar Biennale
In collaboration with the Synthetic Landscape Lab at the University of Innsbruck, the studio also produced CryoflorE: a model for cyber gardening the city, which expanded this thinking beyond a singular structure and into the urban realm. As part of the MUDAC’s 2025 Solar Biennial, Soleil·s, the project takes the form of a near-hexagonal model resembling a miniature cityscape of high-rises filled with cyanobacteria.
Here, they ‘capture and channel electrons generated through photosynthesis into electrical currents flowing along the copper wires embedded in the streetscape.’ Using the energy-producing and CO₂-capturing potential of cyanobacteria, the studio takes initial steps towards developing a simulation of a city powered by bio-solar energy networks.
Constructing DeepForest³
In creating DeepForest³, Pasquero remarked, ‘We are now more and more aware that our own nature is cyborgian and collective, and that our own identities extend far beyond the limits of our bodies. We are microbial ecosystems, we are algorithmic networks. It is a necessary consequence that our home becomes an extension of these ecosystems and networks. Our home is our microbiome.’
The installation itself, on the sun-filled upper floor of the Milan design museum, looks like an abstraction of a forest. There are no leaves, dirt, or moss. Instead, there is a careful arrangement of what look like birch trunks, stripped of their twigs and standing upright on a textured floor. These are what ecoLogicStudio calls ‘biodegraders, built from 3D-printed bark-like shells made of algae biopolymers, [which] host living mycelium networks.’ They get their nutrition from coffee grounds and develop a layer of sinewy material that acts as a kind of insulation.
Between these structures are a series of glass containers holding ‘photosynthesizers, 50 liters of living cyanobacteria, actively capture CO₂ from the gallery environment,’ which serve as living, breathing filters. Lastly, there are ‘carbon storers,’ which digest waste material and give life to living lichen. Among these elements are the tubes, seams, and cords that make this environment possible. In this installation, ecoLogicStudio proposes not a traditional space for living, but a space that lives, grows, digests, and filters. It draws on the logic of the forest to propose an alternative way of living, in which human technologies take a back seat to organic processes.
Colomina, Wigley, and We the Bacteria
DeepForest³ serves as a case study for the ideas presented in We the Bacteria. Written by Colomina and Wigley and published by Lars Müller Publishers, the book acts as a sequel to their previous book, Are We Human? In We the Bacteria, the authors examine the sterility of contemporary architecture – its impulse to kill bacteria and what we interpret as germs and grime – and reposition this hostility as a threat to both human and planetary health. Within the text, they write, ‘this book is covered in microbes,’ offering preliminary evidence of how pervasive single-celled organisms are. The authors use evidence of disease in industrialized, developed spaces to encourage a return to the microbial, advocating forms of design that embrace environments in which bacteria can thrive.
We the Algae, Fungi, and Carbon as Well
Although We the Bacteria centers on the microbial world, it offers an equally useful framework for understanding ecoLogicStudio’s wider practice. Across these projects, algae, fungi, and carbon become active agents in architecture, challenging the separation between the built environment and the living world.
Together, these projects suggest that architecture can do more than accommodate human needs; it can actively support the organisms and ecological processes with which we share the planet. When done intentionally and carefully, these decisions can result in net-positive outcomes for human life as well. In these spaces, bacteria, fungi, and other organisms are not contaminants to be eliminated or resources to be exploited, but participants in the environments we inhabit. The home and the building become parts of a wider living system, proposing a form of mutualism in which human well-being is inseparable from the health of the more-than-human world. Rather than building against the environment, ecoLogicStudio proposes an architecture that works with it, using the capacities of living organisms to rethink how we construct our homes, buildings, and cities.
project info:
studio: ecoLogicStudio
projects: DeepForest³ (2025), The AirBubble in Nyon (2024), The Urban Algae Folly (2015), CryoflorE (2025)
This article is part of designboom’s POSTHUMAN UTOPIAS chapter, exploring what happens when humans are no longer the measure of all things. These stories rethink our relationship with the planet through interspecies architecture, living materials, regenerative landscapes and emerging technologies – learn more here! The chapter is presented in partnership with INDX|GLOBAL – a global cultural platform placing architecture, design, and creative intelligence in conversation with the world.

Trump, Netanyahu discuss Iran as Tehran reports tanker explosions in Strait of Hormuz
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
21:43:27 UTC
06:43:27 KST

U.S. President Donald Trump said Sunday that he had a "very good" conversation with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Saturday, with Iran among the topics discussed, as diplomatic efforts continued to avert renewed large-scale fighting between Washington and Tehran.
"Just had a very good talk with him," Trump said, confirming that the two leaders discussed Iran. He provided no further details about the conversation.
The call came as Iran signaled its willingness to pursue diplomacy while warning that it remained prepared for renewed military confrontation. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said consultations with mediators were continuing and that the prospects for an agreement depended on Washington's response to Tehran's demands. 
In an interview shared on his Telegram channel, Araghchi expressed hope that the United States would choose "diplomacy over other paths." He said Iran was prepared for both defense and negotiations, depending on Washington's "rationality."
Araghchi said Saturday that Iranian negotiators were in Qatar for discussions on a proposal that could reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days if the United States met several Iranian conditions. He emphasized that no direct negotiations were taking place between Tehran and Washington.
The proposed arrangement would allow shipping through the strategic waterway to resume after Washington fulfilled agreed measures. The strait is a critical route for global oil shipments, and restrictions imposed by Iran have disrupted maritime traffic amid the confrontation with the United States and Israel. 
Iran says two oil tankers exploded after striking mines
Meanwhile, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps navy said Sunday that two oil tankers had exploded after striking mines while traveling through what it described as an "unauthorized route" in the Strait of Hormuz, according to Iranian state media.
The claims could not be independently verified.
Iran has imposed restrictions on vessels attempting to navigate the strait and has attacked ships it accuses of violating those restrictions. Tehran has sought to strengthen its control over the strategic waterway and use maritime pressure as leverage against Washington. 
The reported explosions underscored the continuing risks to commercial shipping even as diplomatic efforts sought to restore access to the waterway.
Iran designates British military forces terrorist organizations
In a separate development, Iran designated Britain's Royal Navy and Royal Air Force as terrorist organizations and declared the country's MI6 foreign intelligence service a hostile entity, according to Iran's state-run IRNA news agency.
Iran's Foreign Ministry accused Britain of supporting U.S.-Israeli attacks on Iranian territory by providing military bases and logistical assistance.
The designation could expose individuals accused of cooperating with MI6 to prosecution under Iranian law and further heighten tensions between Tehran and London. 
The developments highlight the competing diplomatic and military pressures shaping the regional confrontation. While Tehran has indicated that negotiations could lead to the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, reported attacks on commercial vessels and its move against British forces illustrate the potential for further escalation.
No agreement to reopen the strait has been announced, and the outcome of the indirect U.S.-Iran talks remains uncertain.

A private business jet carrying nine people crashed into a residential neighborhood near Cresthaven, Florida, on Sunday, killing all those on board.
The Learjet 60 departed Austin-Bergstrom International Airport in Texas and was bound for North Eleuthera Airport in the Bahamas before coming down at approximately 12.50 pm local time (1850GMT), said the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA).

The Palm Beach Sheriff's Office closed all northbound and southbound lanes along Military Trail between Cresthaven Boulevard and 10th Avenue North until further notice to secure the area and allow emergency personnel to operate.
The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB), an independent US federal agency charged with investigating civil transportation accidents and significant incidents across the country, will lead the inquiry alongside the FAA.
Authorities have not established what caused the aircraft to go down.

Introspect on need to improve judiciary responsiveness: CJI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
21:30:55 UTC
06:30:55 KST

CJI Surya Kant calls for more transparent and predictable case listings, stressing that timely court intervention can make the difference between justice and injustice.
NEW DELHI: Flagging the importance of timely intervention by courts in crucial matters, CJI Surya Kant said the difference between justice and injustice was not in the final judgement but in whether the court intervened when "intervention was most needed".He underlined the need for the judiciary, particularly constitutional courts, to introspect to further improve their working and to make listing of cases "more transparent and predictable".Speaking at the platinum jubilee celebration of Kerala HC, CJI Kant said constitutional justice in India did not begin and end in New Delhi and its strength lay in the robust network of 25 HCs spread across the country, each entrusted with the duty of protecting rights and upholding the rule of law.He said HCs were better placed to deal with citizens' problems as they were closely connected with the everyday realities of people."It is in this context that I wish to emphasise the extraordinary constitutional significance of Article 226. Its breadth is one of the greatest strengths of our judicial architecture. While Article 32 guarantees access to SC for enforcement of fundamental rights, Article 226 empowers HCs to issue appropriate writs and directions not only for fundamental rights but also for other legal rights.
This wide constitutional canvas allows HCs to fashion meaningful remedies across diverse legal, statutory, administrative and contractual disputes. Equally important is their power to grant timely interim protection," the CJI said.
He said there has been a growing tendency of litigants to approach SC requesting directions for urgent listing or early hearing of matters pending before HCs and asked whether the present process could be improved, including listing of cases."SC has consistently respected the institutional autonomy of HCs, including their authority to regulate their own rosters. That position is rooted in respect for the constitutional status of these institutions. Yet, the frequency of such requests invites us to consider whether there is room to improve the responsiveness of our processes. We must ask ourselves: Can urgent matters be identified more effectively? Can listing procedures be made more transparent and predictable? Can technology assist in prioritising cases where delay may cause irreversible prejudice?..." he said."These are not questions of institutional criticism but of collective responsibility," the CJI added.

US court dismisses Trump administration lawsuit seeking to halt Alaska Senate certification
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
21:24:16 UTC
06:24:16 KST

A US federal court in Alaska has dismissed a lawsuit by the US Justice Department seeking to delay the certification of Alaska's Senate race over alleged voter confusion between two similarly named candidates, tossing out an extraordinary intervention ordered by the Trump administration.
The federal government sought a preliminary injunction to prevent Alaska from certifying election returns should Republican incumbent Senator Dan S. Sullivan lose to Democratic candidate Mary Peltola, arguing that votes drawn away by a minor third-party candidate, Daniel J. Sullivan, could alter the outcome.
The lawsuit alleged Peltola recruited a "decoy" to confuse voters intending to back the incumbent, a charge Peltola has denied.
Chief US District Judge Sharon L. Gleason rejected the request, ruling that sending federal law enforcement officers to interrogate voters about their intent would directly breach the right to a secret ballot.
Secret ballot protections
"Requiring the segregation of ballots cast by voters for Daniel J. Sullivan so that these voters can be further investigated by law enforcement is not a remedy that this Court can or should order as it clearly violates Alaskans’ right to a secret ballot," Gleason wrote in her decision.
Gleason held that the requested relief is unworkable because ballots cast by Alaskan voters are already commingled.
The ruling warned that such an intervention "would likely result in voter confusion and consequent incentive to remain away from the polls," adding that altering election rules on the eve of Tuesday's vote directly violates established judicial doctrine.
The legal manoeuvre sparked widespread alarm over potential efforts to contest midterm election outcomes as Democrats attempt to flip seats to capture the Senate majority.
Following the ruling, the Justice Department labelled the dismissal "procedural" and confirmed plans to appeal, writing on X that "Alaskan voters deserve a fair election, not to be misled in an attempt to rig outcomes."
Meanwhile, President Donald Trump took to his Truth Social platform to claim "the Fake Daniel J Sullivan Jr" had vanished, denouncing Democratic lawyers and activists as "criminals" abusing the legal process.

PM Narendra Modi cites World Bank data showing India's extreme poverty rate fell 90% to 2.6% between 2011 and 2023, with nearly 50 crore people lifted out of extreme poverty.
NEW DELHI: India has recorded one of the fastest poverty declines in the world, with the extreme poverty rate in the country "collapsing" by 90% between 2011 and 2023 to a low of 2.6%, Prime Minister Narendra Modi said on Saturday, while asserting that elimination of poverty is a commitment for his govt."A historic fall in poverty. A generational rise in opportunity... Gareebi hatao was never a slogan for us. It is our commitment. From more than 1 in 4 Indians to roughly 1 in 38 (in extreme poverty)," the PM posted on Instagram Saturday, citing the World Bank's latest numbers. He highlighted that nearly 50 crore people had moved out of poverty during these 12 years.
Besides, Modi added, employment had grown by 13.4 crore between 2017 and 2023, which was nearly twice the increase in India's working age population. "Inequality has fallen sharply. India's Gini index has dropped by over 20% from 29 in 2011 to 23 in 2023," the Prime Minister said in the Instagram post. The Gini index reflects how equitable is the distribution of income or wealth across a population, with a lower number indicating greater equality.
World Bank's latest Poverty and Equity brief, released last week, said that poverty rate in India, defined at $4.2 a day, will decline to 12.1% in 2028 from 57.7% in 2011, having fallen to 16.1% in 2023.
Meanwhile, extreme poverty, defined as spending $3 a day, declined from 27.1% in 2011 to 2.6% in 2023."This progress was mainly driven by strong consumption growth; rising employment, especially among women; and expanded social transfers, including food subsidies. As poverty declined, it became increasingly concentrated among households with lower education, fewer assets, limited access to stable employment and higher dependency ratios. Wage disparities, however, remain pronounced, as median earnings among the top 10% of workers were about 13 times those of the bottom 10% in 2023," the World Bank had said.

Superannuation watchdog warns widespread complaints signal industry 'failures'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
21:19:56 UTC
06:19:56 KST

IN BRIEF
- The watchdog found 25 per cent of super funds weren't analysing customer complaints data to identify systemic issues.
- Experts warn it's a concerning sign of customer and complaints culture, and risk culture across the industry.
Superannuation funds are ignoring warning signs as complaints about the way they treat customers mount, the corporate watchdog says.
The Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC) has found superannuation funds wanting in handling members' complaints at a critical time for the $3.4 trillion industry.
As millions of Australians transition from accumulating super balances to withdrawing their retirement income, issues such as timely payment of death benefits have been piling up.
Commissioner Simone Constant said super funds should treat complaints as the "canary in the coal mine", but were often ignoring the warning signs.
"Superannuation is too important for there to be failures now, in terms of member services and complaints," she told the Australian Associated Press.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
The death benefit failures were an example of how better complaints-handling could have saved members and their families from harm, the regulator found in a report released on Monday.
The regulator has been cracking down on the industry after finding widespread delays in trustees paying out deceased customers' remaining super balances and insurance payments to family members.
In some cases, loved ones waited years to receive money they were owed.
The regulator reviewed all 45 superannuation trustees and found a quarter were not regularly analysing their complaints data to identify systemic issues, Constant said.
That comes despite a 43 per cent year-on-year increase in superannuation complaints to the Australian Financial Complaints Authority (AFCA).
Constant said the issue was industry-wide, declining to single out any particular funds for poor complaints handling.
"We see some funds detecting zero or practically zero systemic issues from complaints, despite AFCA identifying complaints [that could be systemic] at twice the rate of the industry," she said.
While complaints growth flattened for a period after the death benefits issues were identified, the regulator has seen it rising again.
That raised real concerns about customer culture, complaints culture, and risk culture across the industry, Constant said.
"When we see several of the funds attributing well more than half of the root causes to the customers, essentially blaming the customer, we're really concerned about whether the industry has used the time, used the processes, and used their complaints data to understand what's really going on with their members in terms of these important services," she said.
The Association of Superannuation Funds of Australia said the industry heard loud and clear that trustees needed to do better.
"There are clear areas for improvement here, and the sector will use the information ASIC has collected and its recommendations to act quickly to better use complaints to improve how we look after members," the association's chief executive Mary Delahunty said.
"Members reasonably expect super funds to listen to them, and this should be uniform across the industry."

China's Pei breaks world records to claim gold at weightlifting worlds
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
05:19:30 CST
06:19:30 KST

Pei Xinyi of China competes during the women's 61kg snatch event at the 2026 IWF World Championships in Ningbo, east China's Zhejiang Province, Nov. 1, 2026. (Xinhua/Jiang Han)
NINGBO, Nov. 1 (Xinhua) -- China's Pei Xinyi broke world records and completed all six lifts successfully to win the women's 61-kilogram title at the IWF World Championships on Sunday, leading a Chinese one-two finish at the first qualifying event for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.
Pei, 21, lifted 112kg in the snatch and 142kg in the clean and jerk for a combined 254kg, sweeping all three gold medals. Compatriot Yang Liuyue took overall silver with 249kg, while DPR Korea's Pak Jin Hae claimed bronze with 243kg.
The snatch developed into a three-way contest involving Pei, Yang and Colombia's Karen Mosquera, who twice improved her personal best before finishing with 111kg.
Pei responded with 112kg on her final attempt, equaling the world record held by Yang to take gold. Yang finished third with 110kg after failing at 113kg, while Mosquera claimed silver. Pak missed twice at 109kg and finished outside the snatch medals.
Pei then took control in the clean and jerk, opening at 135kg before lifting 140kg on her second attempt to break the previous world record of 139kg, set by Pak at the Asian Games last month.
That lift also raised the world record for the total to 252kg. Pei improved both marks again on her final attempt, lifting 142kg for a combined 254kg to complete four world-record performances in the session.
Yang lifted 139kg to equal the previous clean-and-jerk world record but failed at 145kg on her final attempt, settling for silver in the discipline. Pak recovered from an opening failure at 135kg to lift 138kg and take bronze.
"I used to be timid and hold myself back, but not anymore," Pei said. "Being steady just means I can go for it on every lift."
Pei, a native of Zhejiang Province, credited the home crowd for helping her deliver under pressure.
"My family all came and cheered so loudly. With everyone behind me, there was nothing to fear," she said.
Yang, the Asian Games champion, said she needed to improve her composure after missing her final attempt.
"I wasn't relaxed enough mentally and my technique wasn't quite right. I'll keep working hard," she said, adding that building confidence would be her next priority.
The championships continue Monday with the men's 85kg competition, featuring China's Chen Shunnan and Lei Jiangqing. ■
