Pauline Hanson rules herself of running for Capricornia
Pauline Hanson has ruled herself out of running for the federal seat of Capricornia after Nationals leader Matt Canavan put his hand up.
Incumbent Nationals MP Michelle Landry last month announced she would retire at the next election, opening the door for Canavan to move from the Senate to the House of Representatives.
One Nation party director James Ashby hasn't ruled out contesting the central Queensland seat which includes the towns of Rockhampton and Yeppoon.

"Am I running in Capricornia? No I'm not running in Capricornia, so I'll give you a direct answer to that one. What Matt Canavan does is Matt Canavan's choice to do what he wants to do, but it's not my choice to run in Capricornia," Hanson says.
Asked whether Ashby would run for the lower house seat, Hanson wouldn't rule it out.
"Well, we're still over a year out from the election, a year and a half, so I'm not making any decisions for him."
Aerial firefighting fleet will help with evacuations, fodder drops, minister says
Emergency Management Minister Kristy McBain has stepped up in Western Sydney to announce a bolstering of the national firefighting fleet.
In May's federal budget, Labor announced $150 million over the next three years to support the National Aerial Firefighting Centre (NAFC).
The NAFC contracts nearly 170 aircraft each year to support states and territories in responding to bushfire emergencies.
McBain says the aircraft will be pre-positioned across the country ahead of the high-risk weather season.
"The important part about our aerial capability now is not only does it deal with fires, but it also deals with evacuations," McBain says.
"It deals with resupply when isolated communities are cut off, deals with animal welfare like emergency fodder drops when it is needed.
"So we've made sure that this fleet is fit for every event that may, you know, impact Australians lives over this next high risk weather season."
Falling trust in politicians
Trust in federal and state politicians is falling, according to research by McKinnon.
The survey of more than 4,000 people showed 30.5 per cent of respondents trusted federal politicians, with low trust more pronounced among people living in regional areas and those with lower levels of education.
Dishonesty, broken promises and being out of touch were among the key reasons respondents said they had little trust in politicians.
Concerns about declining social cohesion were also reflected in the survey results, with 74 per cent believing Australia was more divided than a year earlier.
About 29 per cent said they did not feel they could freely express their political opinions and ideas.
That feeling was even more strongly held among young men, with about 50 per cent believing they could freely express their political views, down from 73 per cent the previous year.
Minister won't give timeline on Woodside Browse basin project decision
The environment minister hasn't given a timeframe for when he'd approve or reject a Woodside proposal to develop the Browse gas basin off WA's coast.
Earlier this year, the ABC reported that the environment department was expected to deliver its final recommendation report to the minister in mid-to-late 2026.
The project would produce enough gas every year to power 800,000 homes, but any spill could cause an environmental disaster for nearby Scott Reef, a habitat for endangered pygmy blue whales and a nesting site for green turtles.
Murray Watt says the national Environmental Protection Authority needs to assess the level of impact the project would have on the environment.
"Under the former Coalition government, a decision was made at the time that that project was likely to have significant impact on a number of matters of national environmental significance, particularly things like threatened species like pygmy blue whales, green turtles, the Commonwealth Marine Environment," Watt says.
"That's what triggered this all off. That decision that the project was likely to have those significant impacts."
Watt calls on other states to adopt gun buyback
Environment Minister Murray Watt has urged other states to jump on board with the national gun buyback scheme.
The scheme has kicked off in New South Wales today, with the state to split the cost 50-50 with the Commonwealth.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese announced the buyback in the aftermath of the Bondi Beach terrorist attack.
Speaking to ABC Radio National Breakfast, Watt says the federal government doesn't want to "leave holes" in the system.
"In the immediate aftermath of that terrible Bondi incident, we saw the national cabinet meeting where all premiers and all chief ministers signed up to these reforms," Watt says.
"It is disappointing that many of them have, for the moment at least, walked away from those reforms. The more states and territories we can have participating in the gun buyback, the safer Australians would be.
"We don't want to leave holes in the system where guns can find their way around certain states and find a backdoor into states that are being part of a buyback."
McKenzie warns One Nation not to campaign against Nationals
Bridget McKenzie has urged One Nation not to campaign against her party at the next election, as her leader puts his hand up for a lower house seat.
As widely expected, Nationals Leader Matt Canavan will contest the Queensland seat of Capricornia at the next federal election, if he's pre-selected by the party.
But One Nation's party director James Ashby has left the door open to running in the seat, setting up a potential contest between the two.
Speaking to ABC Radio National Breakfast, McKenzie says One Nation should focus on targeting Labor.
"One Nation has made a big song and dance of wanting to fire the liar, wanting to get the prime minister out of The Lodge," McKenzie says.
"There's only one way to remove Albanese as prime minister, and that is to win more seats than the Labor Party in the House of Representatives.
"If One Nation wants to come after the National Party or the Liberal Party, that is one less effort going into getting rid of the Labor Party. I'm interested in getting a bad government out of The Lodge, and I hope that One Nation will join us in that effort."
McKenzie says NSW gun buyback scheme is 'morally wrong'
Nationals senator Bridget McKenzie has urged firearm owners in NSW and the ACT not to rush to hand in their firearms.
A gun buyback scheme for some registered firearms, supported by the federal government, begins in New South Wales today.
It splits the cost of the buyback equally between the commonwealth and New South Wales governments.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese announced the buyback after the Bondi Beach terrorist attack.
But McKenzie, who has opposed the buyback, has told gun owners via ABC Radio National Breakfast not to hand in their firearms.
She says she's not worried if there are more firearms in Australia now than before the Port Arthur massacre if they are lawfully registered.
"I think my advice to law-abiding firearm owners across New South Wales would be 'don't rush to hand your firearms in'. This goes for 12 months and I think we're all hoping the government changes in March in New South Wales and these draconian laws will be no more," McKenzie says.
"It's unjust because you're literally taking people's private property and not paying them due compensation and it's morally wrong."

Minns says everyone should look to cut spending
Chris Minns says he accepts states and territories have a role in reducing spending to help lower inflationary pressures on the economy.
The NSW premier has previously taken aim at the government over its spending after the Reserve Bank's decision to hike interest rates.
Speaking to ABC Radio National Breakfast, he says he thinks everyone has a responsibility in reducing spending and, according to media reports, the federal government is also looking to cut spending.
"I think everybody needs to do their bit. That includes me and the opposition parties in New South Wales in the immediate run-up to elections. That's when you're at most risk of government spending money that they don't have," Minns says.
"As it relates to the federal government, I understand from media reports that they're likely to do just that and I think everybody's got a responsibility to do what they can to take pressure off the Reserve Bank."
Minns says gun buyback is urgently needed
NSW Premier Chris Minns says the gun buyback scheme is urgent and needed because gun thefts have increased in his state.
Following the Bondi Beach massacre, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese announced a national government buyback scheme.
The plan was to split the cost of the buyback 50-50 between the Commonwealth and state and territories, but some jurisdictions have resisted.
NSW and the ACT are the only state and territory to have signed up.
Speaking to ABC Radio National Breakfast, Minns said that, while he'd like the scheme to go national, he's happy to go at it alone.
"The truth of the matter is we have more guns in circulation in Australia than before Port Arthur in 1996. This is an urgent and needed reform and I think it will make us safer, not just from mass shootings but also organised crime," Minns says.
"It's also a leading source of suicide … and that is having access to a handgun in a house. So less guns in our streets means safer streets."
Commonwealth-NSW gun buyback scheme begins today
A joint Commonwealth-New South Wales gun buyback scheme starts today, allowing people to surrender firearms in exchange for money.
NSW and the ACT are the only states and territories to sign up to the scheme, which splits the cost of the buyback 50-50 with the federal government.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese announced the scheme after the Bondi Beach terror attack.
NSW Premier Chris Minns told ABC News Breakfast the buyback was only for registered eligible guns and people would have to make an appointment to surrender firearms.
"It's not cheap but we believe it's worthwhile and hugely important in terms of driving down crime and making our community safer," Minns said.
Plibersek defends tax changes against new housing data
Tanya Plibersek has again defended the federal government's budget tax changes, after new data was released showing the value of homes has dropped.
Cotality data says national house prices have fallen for a seventh consecutive month, with the speed of the decline in home values tracking at the fastest pace seen over the past 40 years.
Its latest national Home Value Index (HVI) was down 1.2 per cent in October and is now 6.7 per cent below its March peak, equivalent to a decline of about $63,400 in the value of the median Australian dwelling.
But speaking to Channel Seven alongside One Nation MP Barnaby Joyce, the social services minister says she thinks the changes have made housing more affordable.
"The fact that the growth in house prices is moderated, I think that means that housing will be affordable for my kids and my grandkids one day," Plibersek says.
Plibersek has also been asked about polling showing Treasurer Jim Chalmers has an approval rating of minus 16.
The social services minister has thrown her support behind Chalmers, saying the treasurer is getting the "tough stuff" done.
"The treasurer is at the forefront of that and there's been no reforming treasurer in Australian history that hasn't copped it when they've made big changes and we all support Jim, we all make decisions together," she says.
Key Event
PM to seek change to UK free trade agreement at CHOGM
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese will seek a tightening of rules for British backpackers coming to Australia when he meets his UK counterpart this week at the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM) in Antigua.
In what will be his first official bilateral discussion with UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham, Albanese will seek to reverse part of the Morrison-era UK free trade agreement (FTA) that exempts British backpackers from regional and rural work.
The number of British backpacker visas has doubled to almost 80,000 per year since the 2021 decision.
The government has already imposed a lottery system to stem the flow of working holiday-makers and issued a go-slow on processing UK backpacker visas to reduce net overseas migration.
While the FTA is already law, it's understood regional work rules could be reimposed on British working holiday-makers with the consent of the UK government.

Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal to resume work in several weeks — justice minister
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
20:03:22 UTC
05:03:22 KST

MOSCOW, November 1. /TASS/. Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal may resume its work within several weeks, Justice Minister Waldemar Zurek said.
"It's only a matter of a few weeks before we have our first court hearings and the first cases are heard on the merits," he told the TVP Info television channel. According to the minister, priority will be given to claims from citizens that have been neglected for years.
A political crisis erupted in Poland following Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s decision to appoint Marcin Bereka, a former minister in his government, as a judge of the Constitutional Tribunal. Protests have been held regularly outside the court building in recent weeks. On October 30, Zurek filed a motion to suspend Bogdan Swieczkowski, acting president of the Constitutional Court, from his duties and to strip him of his immunity. Additional police forces were deployed to guard the court building. Overnight to October 31, protesters gathered outside the courthouse and attempted to break through the fence. Four people were detained.
Due to the escalating crisis, President Karol Nawrocki cut short his trip to Senegal and returned to Warsaw. A number of opposition politicians described the situation as an attempted coup.
This crisis is a continuation of a long-standing conflict over the Constitutional Tribunal that began back in 2015. Back then, the Law and Justice Party (which Nawrocki is a supporter of) began appointing its own judges to positions that were already filled, paralyzing the court and triggering a years-long dispute with Brussels. After coming to power in 2023, the Tusk government promised to restore the supremacy of law, but its efforts were met with resistance from Nawrocki. He refused to swear in several judges elected by parliament. At the same time, Swieczkowski barred these judges from taking up their posts.

🎙️Home values slide as RBA decision looms
Australia's housing downturn is getting faster.
Home values have now fallen for seven straight months, with capital city prices declining at the fastest pace of any housing downturn in four decades.
But falling prices don't automatically mean housing is becoming more affordable. Borrowing capacity is shrinking, rents are still rising, and the equity picture looks very different depending on where and when you bought.

Key Event
Residential approvals to stay 'solid' despite rate hikes: UBS
The October rebound in residential approvals shows home building remains solid, despite the challenges from RBA rate hikes and falling dwelling prices, according to the UBS economic team.
Residential building approvals rebounded 5.1% in September to 215-thousand new permits being issued.
"Overall, residential approvals over recent months remain relatively high, averaging around 212k; still near the highest level since 2021," UBS economist George Tharanou said.
"Residential approvals are tracking at-or above our forecast for dwelling commencements in 2026 of (around) 200k; but some approvals may be delayed or abandoned, given more recent weakness in dwelling prices.
"The actual supply of housing completions remains slow, though has improved somewhat.
"Hence, amid the backlog of work yet to be done, housing activity will likely keep rising over coming quarters; despite the negatives of RBA rate hikes and falling dwelling prices," Mr Tharanou said.
The ABS data also pointed to the extremely "lumpy" nature of non-residential building approvals amid the AI-related data centre boom.
Having slumped 45.5% in August, non-residential building approvals jumped 45.9% in September.
"Overall, the trend implies nominal non-residential building investment should rise over coming quarters. This is driven by the AI-related boom in data centres," Mr Tharanou said.
ANZ's analysis was a bit bleaker citing falling house prices and another likely RBA rate hike as a further dampener on sentiment in the market.
"So far, there has been a clear pullback in investor activity in the housing market, with the pace of private sector credit growth for investors slowing sharply" ANZ' Madeline Dunk and Adam Boyton wrote.
"And while building approvals are holding up, we expect the series to start trending lower."
Key Event
Chinese factory activity still expanding despite slowing export orders
China's factory activity expanded at a marginally slower pace in October as export order growth eased, according to the RatingDog/S&P manufacturing Purchasing Managers' Index (PMI).
The PMI edged down marginally to 52.0 points in October from 52.1 in September but still remained about the 50 level that separates expansion from contraction, supported by output rising at its fastest rate in six months.
The private survey differed from the official NBS PMI released over the weekend, which showed factory activity unexpectedly falling.
The official survey tends to have a heavier weighting towards larger state-owned enterprises while the private survey has a stronger representation of small- to medium-sized enterprises.
RatingDog's new orders index edged down to 53.3 from 53.4 in September.
Output expanded for the 11th successive month and total new orders rose for the 17th successive month
"New export orders rose for the fourth month in a row, with anecdotal evidence pointing to greater volumes of new work from clients in Asia, Europe and Africa," RatingDog founder Yao Yu said.
He said the pace of expansion eased to a three-month low and was modest, with growth slowing among consumer and intermediate goods makers while accelerating for investment goods firms.
"On the price front, output charges fell for a second time in three months, as intense competition compelled firms to lower charges to support sales, with easing input costs also enabling discounting."
Output prices fell after rising in September, as intense competition forced firms to cut prices to support sales, while easing input costs also allowed for discounting. Export prices declined for the first time since November 2025.

CBA rejigs forecasts
NAB is not the only big bank rejigging its forecast ahead of the RBA Q3 Statement on Monetary Policy update tomorrow.
CBA has joined NAB in taking a knife to its GDP forecast, cutting it to just 1% by mid-2027. Previously, it had pencilled in 1.8%.
"We expect the weakness to last longer than previously anticipated, with growth only recovering to its trend of 2.9% by H2 2028," CBA's head of Australian economics Belinda Allen said.
Other key CBA changes include:
- Unemployment rate rising to 5.1% compared to previous forecast of 4.8%
- Trimmed mean inflation at or above 3.5% until at least the middle of 2027
- Wage growth (measured by the WPI) to slow to 3.3% in Q4, 2026,3.0% in Q4 2027 and 2.9% at Q4 2028
"Households will bear the brunt of the needed slowdown in economic activity, with household spending making the largest contribution to the downgrade in our forecast," Ms Allen said.
"Spending is expected to slow from 1.8%/yr in Q2 26 to a low of 0.7% in mid 2027 and remain subdued for all of 2027.
"We expect per capita household consumption growth to contract and quarterly outcomes to be soft.
"The decline in household spending will be driven by weaker income growth, which we have downgraded in light of a higher cash rate, inflation and weaker labour market."
NAB tips sharp rise in unemployment rate, slower economic growth
Ahead of the RBA Monetary Policy Board meeting tomorrow (and an updated set of forecasts in the Statement on Monetary Policy or SoMP), the National Australia Bank (NAB) has made an "interim update" to its key macroeconomic forecasts.

"The overall narrative continues to be an outlook for below-trend GDP growth over 2027 and 2028."
The bank has also confirmed its forecast of a fifth RBA rate hike ahead of tomorrow's monetary policy decision.
Spence added that, "… given the apparent reassessment of capacity pressures in the economy, we expect they will remain hawkish and far from declaring the job done on inflation despite some signs of ongoing cooling in the economy and labour market".
Spence, alarmingly, also sees the unemployment rate reaching 5.4%.
We have also revised up our unemployment rate profile, now expecting the unemployment rate to reach 5.4% by end 2027. The adjustment continues to reflect slower labour demand growth being outpaced by population growth.

Key Event
Manufacturing contraction continues
Activity in Australia's factories has contracted for the second consecutive month, according to S&P Global's latest Purchasing Managers' Index (PMI) survey.
S&P Global noted a sharper fall in new orders drove another solid decline in output.
"In turn, goods producers scaled back both their purchasing activity and employment and also cut back on their inventory holdings as demand deteriorated," S&P Global said.
While the decline to 49.6 points represents only a marginal decline in activity — 50 points is the break-even point between expansion and contraction — the October PMI reading was the joint lowest since December 2024.
S&P Global economist Jingyi Pan said the survey showed manufacturers faced a "double whammy" at the start of the fourth quarter, with supply constraints piling on top of worsening demand.
"Subdued market conditions, higher interest rates and elevated prices contributed to the sharpest drop in new orders in almost two years, while shipment delays and port congestions were causes for one of the steepest extensions of delivery times since the post-COVID-19 pandemic period," she said.
"It was positive, however, to see business confidence recovering slightly from the September low amid hopes for improvements in the coming months. That said, the level of overall business optimism remained subdued by historical standards."
Key Event
NT data centre scraps start date on EPA concerns
The developer of one of Australia's biggest planned data centres has scrapped its target start date after a regulator said it needed longer than usual to set environmental parameters, a setback to the country's ambitions to be a fast-track destination for AI investment.
Startup Energy North, which says it has finance lined up for a sprawling gas and solar-powered data centre on a cattle ranch 100 kilometres south of Daly Waters (680km south of Darwin), had given a "first power" date of June 28, 2028, in regulatory filings four months ago.
But after the Northern Territory environment regulator said in an October 7 ruling it was suspending its seven-week deadline to decide what hurdles the project must clear, the developer told Reuters it had scrubbed its timeline.
"The June 2028 date in our referral was an indicative schedule at the time of lodgement, and we're no longer working to it," said Energy North vice-president of project development Daniel Hunter in an email.
The project is the biggest in Australia to put back its timing and shows how data centre ambitions face hurdles even in the isolated north, which has sought to differentiate itself from cities in the contest for the $7 trillion McKinsey forecasts will be invested in "AI factories" globally by 2030.
The Territory is counting on luring projects with its vast supply of uninhabited land and sunshine — 260,000 residents in an area twice the size of Texas, with as much sun as the Sahara — and a huge just-opened shale gas reserve for backup power.
But stopping the clock on Energy North, the Territory's regulator said it would seek advice from the federal government, which is "developing policy expectations for data centres and AI infrastructure developers", and gave no new timeframe.
Mr Hunter said the project was unfazed and would confirm timing once the regulator sets out terms for an environmental impact statement, required to identify and address potential adverse effects. He declined to say who is lined up to finance the project.

Binance hit by customer withdrawals after returning to trade
First, it was the thieves, then the customers moved in to shrink the assets of the world's biggest crypto exchange Binance.
Having just resumed trading after hackers made off with $US6.3 billion in what's being called the biggest bank heist in history, customers moved with the speed of the hackers themselves to shovel another $US3.6 billion ($5.1 billion) out the door.
That (legal) withdrawal represents more than 2% of Binance's assets.
However, that may be understating things. Crypto analytics platform DefiLlama said on its dashboard that outflows were higher, at $US4.4 billion ($6.3 billion).
Binance said withdrawals were stabilising after an initial spike and deposit volumes had remained "substantial". The exchange said it had now covered 95% of the $6.3 billion of stolen assets.
As Reuters reports, the heist, which analysts believe may be the biggest financial robbery ever, adds to a string of recent crypto thefts.
Withdrawal levels are an early test of whether customers still trust the exchange with their money after the attack.
Attackers stole $US2.9 billion ($4.1 billion) worth of cryptocurrency across nearly 150 incidents last year, according to researchers at TRM Labs.
With Reuters
Big tech's really bad month
A trillion here, a trillion there — and pretty soon you're talking serious money.
Indeed, more than $US2.6 trillion ($3.7 trillion) was wiped off the market value of the big tech stocks last month.
The Nasdaq shed about 6% as the AI trade ran into turbulence, with hyperscalers Meta Platforms, Alphabet and Amazon raising spending forecasts further as they race to expand AI infrastructure.
Alphabet suffered its biggest one-day percentage drop on record on Thursday after disappointing results in the core business of search advertising and a massive acceleration in cash burn.
Meta's plans for a record $US97.5 billion fund raise heightened concerns about shareholder dilution and whether mounting AI spending could force other Big Tech companies to increasingly tap capital markets.
Independent global investment strategist Gerard Minack says the investment bear case for AI is simple.
"The profits on selling AI services will generate a lousy return on the invested capital," Mr Minack wrote in a note to clients last week.
"History shows big investment booms end in a bust.
"Less dramatically, it also shows that companies that grow assets fast almost always underperform.
"There are no signs that AI providers will build the barriers to entry required to generate super-normal profits.
"Timing when the boom busts is fraught but AI stocks are no longer outperforming the market.
"History is unequivocal: big capex booms never end well for the original investors," Mr Minack said.
With Reuters

Its cash profit, excluding one-off items, came in at $7.0 billion, slightly above the consensus figure of $6.96 billion calculated by analysts.

Key Event
Wall Street tumbles on mounting AI fears, ASX on edge
Wall Street closed the week, maybe not in a blind panic, but there was certainly a disquieting dumping of stocks as investors fled to the exits and the weekend.
All three key indices fell sharply, the tech-centric Nasdaq fell the hardest and is down almost 8% from its record high of just three weeks ago.
- S&P 500: 1.8%
- Dow: -1.1%
- Nasdaq: 2.9%
The dump saw the global MSCI down 1.5% for the day, while the pan-continental Eurostoxx 600 fell a comparatively modest 0.4%.
The tech-lite ASX is unlikely to be as affected by anxieties over cash-burning AI investments as Wall Street was on Friday.
When trading closed on Saturday morning (AEDT) ASX 200 futures were flat, or to be precise 4 points (0.04%) lower.
The tech rout was sparked by disappointing quarterly results from Intel and Amazon released late on Thursday.
While Amazon pared losses as the session progressed, Intel shares cratered, down almost 30%.
Chip stocks veered sharply lower, with Nvidia down more than 4%.
The broader chips index shed 7.2%, slumping to a monthly loss of more than 15%. Server makers Dell and HP dropped 10.8% and 9.6%, respectively.
"It's fair to say that this week, not just today, has been very much about the future of AI and what that's going to look like, whether there will be a positive return on investment and if so, how quickly," Wealthspire adviser Oliver Pursche told Reuters.
"Companies that are performing and meeting the very lofty expectations that have been set are doing well," Mr Pursche said.
"Those that are falling short and seem to be missing the mark or not executing as expected are getting punished."
On the subject of being punished, cryptocurrency related firms all got walloped on the news that hackers nicked a lazy $US6.3 billion ($9 billion) worth of various stable coins, such as Bitcoin and Ethereum, while no-one was looking at the world's biggest crypto exchange Binance.
Listed crypto firms Coinbase, Strategy and Robin Hood all fell between 7 and 11%. All said they were safe, but they would say that.
Putting aside the Binance contretemps, it's worth noting that hackers have made off with about $US3 billion in crypto in around 150 incidents.
US Treasuries were one of the beneficiaries of the tech rout as investors decided they were a safer bet at the moment, which is saying something.
The benchmark 10-year yield closed the month with its biggest monthly drop in nearly three years.
Gold, once also considered a safe haven, didn't benefit from the conniptions — indeed, it slumped (-3.5%) to a one-year low, along with other precious metals. Silver shed 6.5% and palladium shed 3.0%.
"The sky is falling," independent metals trader Tai Wong told Reuters with a dramatic flourish.
"Metals will not be able to escape the gravity well of a nasty stock correction. Earnings have been the foundation of the AI rally and now that pillar is showing some cracks."
Oil seems to be blithely ignoring Mr Wong's "gravity well". The key benchmarks both gained more than 2% on Friday.
- Brent crude futures: +2.4% to $US117.64/barrel
- WTI crude futures: +2.1% to $US113.43/barrel
For the month, Brent finished almost 14% higher, while WTI rose even more, up 15%.
On Friday, a tanker in the Strait of Hormuz was hit by explosive devices, believed to be limpet mines attached by a small boat, according to UKMTO, the British maritime security service.
It is believed to be the first successful use of limpet mines since the war began in February. Probably not the last either.

Bulgaria Elects First Woman President as Yotova Defeats Gyurov in Runoff
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
20:01:00 UTC
05:01:00 KST

Iliana Yotova has won Bulgaria’s presidential runoff against Andrey Gyurov by a wide margin, according to parallel vote counts reported by polling agencies, while record-low voter turnout has raised questions about the political weight of her mandate.
Further reading: Presidential Candidate Iliana Yotova: The Status Quo
All polling agencies reported a clear lead for the ticket of Iliana Yotova and Kiril Valchev over the pairing of Andrey Gyurov and Georgi Kandev.
A 100% parallel count by Market Links put Yotova at 57.4%, against 39.6% for Gyurov, with turnout at 29.1%. Alpha Research initially reported 57.1% for Yotova and 39.3% for her opponent in its own 100% parallel count. Its later figures showed Yotova and Valchev with 57.4%, compared with 39.6% for Gyurov and Kandev.
Trend's 100% parallel count gave Yotova 58.1%, a lead of 19.2 percentage points over the opposing ticket, which received 38.9%. Myara's initial 100% count put the incumbent president at 58.1%, against 38.6% for Gyurov. Its later figures showed Yotova and Valchev with 58.2%, while Gyurov and Kandev remained at 38.6%. The agency also reported that 3.2% of voters had selected the "I do not support anyone" option and estimated turnout at 27.2% as of 8:00 PM.
Gallup's 75% parallel count showed Yotova and Valchev leading with 56.1%, compared with 39.9% for Gyurov and Kandev, a gap of more than 16 percentage points.
Alpha Research's later figures also put the share of voters selecting "I do not support anyone" at 3%. The agency estimated turnout at 29.1% as of 8:00 PM and said 1,920,000 people had voted.
Turnout had reached 19.33% by 4:00 PM. Polling agencies expected the final figure to remain just below 30%. The limited participation was described not simply as a temporary consequence of weather conditions or election organization, but as evidence of persistent public alienation from the political system.
The historical figures for previous presidential elections underline the scale of the decline. Zhelyu Zhelev received 2,738,420 votes in 1992, while Petar Stoyanov secured 2,502,517 in 1996. Georgi Parvanov won 2,043,443 votes in 2001 and 2,050,488 when he was reelected in 2006. Rosen Plevneliev received 1,698,136 votes in 2011, while Rumen Radev secured 2,063,032 in 2016 and 1,539,650 in 2021.
Even the lowest vote total among those presidential winners was considerably higher than the support expected for the new president under the current turnout conditions. Yotova is expected to have won with approximately 1 million to 1.1 million votes, substantially fewer than Zhelev and his successors received when they were elected.
The difference does not affect the election's legal validity, but it raises questions about the political weight of the mandate. The president is the constitutional head of state for all Bulgarian citizens, not only those who voted in the runoff. When most eligible voters stay away from the polls, the claim to represent a unifying national figure faces the challenge of limited public legitimacy. The institution's influence will depend not only on the powers attached to the office but also on the new president's capacity to rebuild lasting public confidence beyond her core supporters.
Prime Minister Rumen Radev made a brief statement after the election, saying: "We have known each other for 10 years and I know that Iliana Yotova will be a worthy president."
Representatives of Progressive Bulgaria defended the legitimacy of Yotova's victory. Petar Vitanov, a member of her initiative committee, thanked those who had voted and said he expected Bulgaria to become more stable and calm.
* "Every vote matters. We succeeded in mobilizing the public, and voter turnout in the second round was about 10 percentage points higher. I believe there are ample grounds to affirm that the president has been elected with full legitimacy,"* Vitanov said. He argued that the presidential election should not be compared with parliamentary votes.
Aleksandrina Pendachanska, co-chair of Gyurov's initiative committee, said both Gyurov and Georgi Kandev had promising political prospects.
* "We cannot speak of any decline or loss of votes. They are only just beginning to expand their base of support. Gyurov will receive significant support from abroad,"* she said.
Asen Vassilev, leader of We Continue the Change, said support for Gyurov had almost doubled compared with the first round. He also argued that votes from GERB and the DPS had not determined the outcome for either candidate.
* "One-third of DPS voters turned out to vote; half of their votes went to Andrey Gyurov, and the other half to Iliana Yotova,"* Vassilev said. He called the presidential election result a "red card" for the Progressive Bulgaria government.
Interior Minister Ivan Demerdzhiev said the Ministry of Interior had stopped attempts to buy votes and manipulate the election outcome.
* "Despite numerous reports and indications of attempts to achieve a specific outcome through vote-buying, the professional and preventive work of the police demonstrated that we can curb this phenomenon. We succeeded,"* he said.
Demerdzhiev also pointed to the involvement of certain mayors, some of whom are currently facing pretrial proceedings. He said police had blocked schemes used in previous elections from affecting the vote.
* "We can confidently state that the results recorded in the official election documents were in no way influenced by these corrupt practices,"* the interior minister said.
Vassilev said the preliminary results, if confirmed, would represent almost twice as many votes for Gyurov as he received in the first round. He attributed the outcome in part to the campaign's failure to generate sufficient voter mobilization.
* "What was lacking in this campaign was sufficient mobilization. It became clear that the number of GERB supporters who turned out to vote in the first round was the same as the number who voted in the second,"* Vassilev said.
He called on the public to wait for the final results, adding that although the margin between the candidates could become narrower, he did not expect the outcome to be reversed.
Vassilev also stressed that We Continue the Change (PP) was following an independent economic and political course. Recent opinion polls, he said, showed the party as the country's second-largest political force even without the support of Democratic Bulgaria. He described GERB's backing for Gyurov as "pro forma."
The PP leader also expressed hope that the budget decisions of the Progressive Bulgaria government would not repeat the approach of the Zhelyazkov cabinet, warning that the consequences would be the same.
Progressive Bulgaria's first response to the preliminary results came from Petar Vitanov, chair of the party's parliamentary group. He thanked voters who had gone to the polls despite bad weather and what he called a "vicious, mud-slinging campaign" filled with smear tactics that had driven many people away from the election.
* "After tomorrow, Bulgaria will be more stable and calmer,"* Vitanov said.
He described the trend in the initial exit poll figures, which showed Yotova in the lead, as consistent with public expectations. MP Dimitar Zdravkov also said the results followed a logical pattern.
Vitanov said turnout had increased by almost one-third, calling the rise unprecedented. He noted that participation in a presidential runoff had been higher only twice in Bulgaria's democratic history and said turnout this time was nearly 10 percentage points higher. He maintained that the campaign had succeeded in mobilizing voters and that there were solid grounds to consider the president-elect's mandate fully legitimate.
Kiril Valchev, Yotova's running mate, was the first to arrive at the campaign headquarters in the National Palace of Culture (NDK). Asked whether Bulgaria would have a woman president, he replied: "I am certain of it," BTA reported.
Yotova also arrived at the campaign headquarters.

Golden Triangle's North East drug trade thrives on barter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
20:00:52 UTC
05:00:52 KST

Cash doesn't cross Myanmar border, payments made in kind: ED
NEW DELHI: International illicit drug syndicates operating out of the Golden Triangle of Myanmar, Thailand and Laos have turned to age-old barter trade, under which drugs like heroin and methamphetamine are smuggled into India through the porous borders of Northeastern states and payments are made in kind through supplies of petrol, diesel, flour, edible oil, groceries, medicines, footwear and clothing from their Indian network.Drug lords across border ensure transactions are made without any money actually crossing border, according to an investigation report compiled by the ED after week-long searches at 38 locations across the Northeast last week.
Myanmar has already replaced Afghanistan as world's largest illicit opium-producing region. With precursor chemicals moved from India to Myanmar, where drug manufacturing units are located, finished heroin, brown sugar and synthetic drug methamphetamine tablets are produced and carried across the Tiau river at Zokhawthar, the border crossing opposite Khawmawi in Myanmar. Consignments are staged at Champhai, from where they travel down the Champhai-Aizawl road and NH-06A to Aizawl, Vairengte and then to Assam and the rest of India, the ED report said.ED has traced intermediaries who procured and supplied goods to syndicates in Myanmar. Over 1,400 mule bank accounts, mostly belonging to traders who procured these goods and supplied them to the network, have been frozen. Transactions involving goods worth over Rs 270 crore have been identified so far and six persons arrested.
These transactions were handled by illicit money exchangers, or hawala networks, in Champhai, including Rs 125 crore in cash received from Assam, Nagaland, WB, Tripura & Delhi, ED said.Significantly, drug money reaching hawala accounts in Aizawl and Champhai came substantially from Delhi, Kolkata and Mumbai, ED added. Illegal money is converted into ordinary, commercially marketable goods, which are sent to border towns of Mizoram and onward to Myanmar.
"The banking system is thus used only for Indian leg of the transaction, where the payment looks like an ordinary trade payment backed by a GST invoice. The cross-border leg moves as goods and leaves no money trail. In effect, fuel, flour and groceries have become currency in which Myanmar-based drug suppliers are paid," ED said.The probe is in progress to identify consignees in border towns, those who move goods across border, Myanmar-based recipients, petrol pumps, shops and suppliers paid in the same manner, and money exchangers directing the accounts. ED is also tracing and attaching further proceeds of crime as it works to dismantle the financial networks sustaining narcotics trafficking.

'Annoying' Alcaraz denies de Minaur Vienna Open title in final
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
19:47:48 UTC
04:47:48 KST

In short:
Carlos Alcaraz has defeated Alex de Minaur in straight sets in the final of the Vienna Open.
De Minaur came into the match on good form having downed world No.1 Alexander Zverev in the semifinal, but was beaten 6-1, 6-4.
Alcaraz has dropped just two sets to de Minaur in seven career meetings with the Australian.
Alex de Minaur served up some brilliant tennis, but it still wasn't enough for him to break his dispiriting duck against his "annoying" and virtuoso nemesis Carlos Alcaraz in the Vienna Open final.
In their seventh meeting, Australia's No.1 did his utmost to earn a first-ever win over the great young Spaniard in Sunday's championship match, but despite dragging him into some breathtaking rallies, he invariably came off worse as Alcaraz scorched to a 6-1, 6-4 victory.
"It's great to have you back on tour," de Minaur told the Spaniard afterwards in the Wiener Stadthalle, but couldn't resist adding with a smile: "I will say one thing though: it is very annoying to play against you!"
"But you're one of the good ones, one of the great guys on tour … As for myself, it's been a great week too."
Indeed, de Minaur could find plenty of consolation after a tournament in which he knocked out the new world No.1 Alexander Zverev in the semis, earning his first victory over the German in an individual rather than team tournament, and played perhaps his best tennis of the season.
Now he will fly straight off to Paris for the Masters tournament there, the crucial last qualifying event for the ATP Finals, also knowing he's in the eighth and final spot to be part of the Turin end-of-season men's championship.
"I'm proud to be standing up here and still fighting," said de Minaur, who'll move back to No.8 in the world from No.10 after reaching his third final of the year.
"So I'm excited for what's left for this year, and hopefully I can continue pushing and have a longer year."
Still, though, de Minaur couldn't cope with the brilliance of 23-year-old Alcaraz, who lifted his fourth title of the season and the 28th of his career, sweeping to victory without dropping a set all week.
After the wrist trouble that ripped a hole in his season, he really is looking back to something like the world-beater who lifted the Australian Open crown at the start of 2026.
Alcaraz, who has dropped only two sets to de Minaur in their seven contests, never looked back again after a scintillating start when he caught the Aussie cold by breaking in the first game, before uncorking a champagne cross-court backhand winner to earn a second break en route to a 4-0 lead.
Happy just to eke out a single game in the opener, de Minaur was stubbornly competitive in the second, producing three sensational points when at break point and 3-4 down just to stay in the fight.
But serving to stay in the match at 4-5, the seven-time grand slam champ went into overdrive, and after applying the pressure to grab match point, played a fittingly wonderful final rally, delivering a drop shot, a lob and then a killing forehand, his 14th of the match, which clipped the baseline to seal the deal.
"He's really fast, you have to earn every point. You might have a winner against everybody — except him," said Alcaraz, acknowledging his opponent's excellence.

Israel election chief: Irregularities inquiry won’t alter result
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
19:42:31 UTC
04:42:31 KST

Breadcrumb
Israel elections chief says inquiry into irregularities will not undermine result
The head of Israel's Central Elections Committee said on Sunday that an ongoing investigation into alleged foreign funding in the country's recent vote would not call into question its result, noting that so far "suspicions remain suspicions".
The Shin Bet security agency launched the inquiry last week, at the elections chief's request, to determine whether the Arab Israeli party Raam received money from Qatar -- an accusation both the Gulf state and the party deny.
In the days since, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his Likud party have relentlessly accused Arab groupings of having "stolen" the vote, in which they notched unprecedented gains and made themselves potentially instrumental to the formation of an opposition-led government.
Elections committee head and Supreme Court Justice Noam Sohlberg, flanked by the head of the Shin Bet and Israel's attorney general, assured Israelis in a video message on Sunday that "your choice at the ballot box will be respected".
"The elections to the 26th Knesset were conducted properly. If any irregularities exist, they are currently under review," he said.
He added that the investigation was ongoing, and that "suspicions remain suspicions".
"We will examine them thoroughly and get to the very bottom of the matter in order to establish the full truth," he continued.
"Our position is that even if the suspicions are ultimately confirmed, this would not call into question the integrity of the electoral process or the overall results of the elections."
'Ridiculous and dangerous'
Ever since the probe was announced, the committee has sought to allay concerns over it, with the body's acting director insisting the same day that any suggestion of widespread issues was "entirely groundless".
Netanyahu's claims of malfeasance by Arab parties began on election day itself, following a campaign in which he cast them as a threat to the country.
That strategy played a role in driving unprecedented turnout among Palestinian citizens of Israel.
Raam chief Mansour Abbas has denied the allegations of foreign funding, saying his party had "no connection whatsoever to the affair" and welcoming an investigation.
Qatar called the accusations "ridiculous and dangerous".
Netanyahu's main challenger, Gadi Eisenkot, who is weighing whether to accept the support of Arab parties in forming a government, has accused the premier of "seeking to delegitimise the results of the election".
Noting on Sunday that the review of the allegations would continue in "utmost seriousness", Sohlberg insisted that "these remarks must in no way cast doubt on the vote of the Arab community".
"The citizens who went to the polls exercised their democratic right. High voter turnout is a positive thing, both within Arab society and in all communities in Israel."

Creditor has "taken control" of forever cruise, message to residents shows
Residents of Villa Vie Odyssey — which remains stuck in Cambodia — have been informed the cruise ship is now under control of its lender, according to a message sent to residents and obtained by CBS News.
The ship will soon be moved from Cambodia to Singapore, where it could eventually be auctioned off, according to multiple sources familiar with the matter. Company leadership, however, said they're optimistic they can get the ship back — if they find an operational partner.
"This is a 30- to 90-day process, and, during that process, we have time to get a restructure done," Mike Petterson, the company's founder and executive chairman, told CBS News.
Passengers had only the weekend to remove all of their belongings from the ship before it became inaccessible to them, as the lender took over the operational costs of the ship.
"They have now the responsibility to pay the crew, fuel and the operations of the vessel and safekeeping of the vessel," Petterson said, stressing that they're exploring options to keep the ship going. "They would be willing to work with a funded plan — they're not out of negotiations — it's not like you get your car repossessed and you can't get it back."
Some passengers expressed frustration with the company's optimistic tone and worried it gave some residents a sense of "false hope."
"The lender has taken possession of the ship, but that does not mean the Odyssey's future has been decided," the message to residents read, in part. "No sale has been scheduled. We believe there is time to bring forward a viable plan and are working to do that."
An effort by a group of residents to buy the ship from the company also failed, after a lender denied them funding, according to sources who spoke with CBS News. The effort had received pledges from 169 residents who were willing to put more money into the project.
Internal communications reviewed by CBS News showed the ship was in financial distress for at least three months prior to Cambodia. Now, additional documents show that the company had a sense of urgency in getting more residents to provide even more funds.
During a meeting that took place in early August, the company wrote in an internal PowerPoint presentation: "A significant new line of inquiry is the need to distinguish actual inability to contribute from unwillingness to contribute further."
Joel Greiff from Naples, Florida spent $350,000 on a cabin on board, but he spent just 26 days on the ship after moving into it in October. Greiff told CBS News he paid an initial deposit in August 2025 and paid the remainder in May 2026.
In late July, Greiff said he received a message from the company about its financial woes. At the time, the company was asking residents for more money to keep the ship afloat.
"I sell my RV on August 3rd and I'm like — oh," Grief said. "This is gonna fail. Every sign is there."
Since being kicked off the ship, he has found a place to live in Kompat, Cambodia.
"I went and found a place to stay for $200 a month. Beautiful place," he said. "It's right on the river. It's what I wanted and what I needed."
Greiff said he has come to terms with the fact that he may never see the money he invested in the ship again.
"I do not feel ill will, I just feel that they don't know how to run a business whatsoever," he said. "They might want to contemplate never running a business again."
It is still unclear what will happen to the Odyssey next, but, prior to becoming stranded in Cambodia, Residential Cruise Holdings, the parent company of Villa Vie, was in the process of acquiring at least one additional cruise ship and working on two residential cruise projects.
"I don't have any update on that," said Petterson. "Our focus is 100% on the Odyssey. Villa Vie was entirely capitalized by the residents themselves. There is no stakeholder outside of the residents."
A Chapter 11 bankruptcy for Villa Vie would cost the ship about $3 million for the first 60 days of the process, according to the message sent to residents.
"The plan we are pursuing is to support those operations through DIP financing and resident maintenance collections," the message read. "The debt and legal issues are serious, but they do not erase the value of the ship, the resident community or the opportunity to build a stronger operating model. A structured transition with new capital and experienced operators can address the challenges and create a path forward."
Petterson said the company is entirely owned by employees and residents, "so, when there is a financial need, residents are by definition the shareholders of the company and are naturally asked as shareholders to contribute."

From an LGBTQ+ rally to Trunk or Treat, Becerra and Hilton barnstorm California hoping to be next governor

From an LGBTQ+ rally to Trunk or Treat, Becerra and Hilton barnstorm California hoping to be next governor
- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- In the final days before Tuesday’s election, Xavier Becerra and Steve Hilton crisscrossed California, trading barbs at rallies and Halloween events in a largely one-sided governor’s race.
- Polls give Democrat Becerra a commanding lead; he has made the contest a referendum on President Trump, seeking to mobilize Democrats and boost House candidates.
- Hilton has cast himself as an underdog, blaming Democratic rule for high prices and homelessness while promising sweeping tax cuts and lower gas prices; voters also voiced concerns about housing and living costs.
Donning a creepy mask of Democratic rival Xavier Becerra, Republican gubernatorial candidate Steve Hilton dashed around a children’s Halloween event dishing out candy and warnings about potential liberal tax policies.
“Vote for Becerra, and your parents will have to pay every mile they drive. Isn’t that great?” Hilton sarcastically said at a Trunk or Treat gathering Saturday in Highland Park. “These children are very pricey because if their parents vote for Becerra, they will be taxed every mile they drive. Yay! Yay! Mileage tax! Mileage tax! Mileage tax!”
Becerra was not spooked when he heard of Hilton’s get-up and put-down.
“I suspect, if he takes off that mask, you’ll see Donald Trump right underneath,” Becerra, a former congressman, state attorney general and member of President Biden’s Cabinet, said at a campaign event in Sacramento on Saturday. “That’s who he really is. Either that or he’s a clown.”
As Tuesday’s election barrels toward them, Becerra and Hilton traded barbs and barnstormed California in a relatively sedate race to succeed Democrat Gavin Newsom, who is wrapping up his final term as governor and considering a run for president. Recent polls show Becerra leading Hilton by a wide margin, which is unsurprising in a state where Democratic voters vastly outnumber Republicans and GOP candidates last won a statewide election two decades ago.
Former Vice President Kamala Harris and Newsom — two potential 2028 presidential candidates — campaigned for Becerra on Sunday evening in Hollywood.
Harris, who has been campaigning for candidates across the country and seemed optimistic about Democrats’ prospects in the midterm election, told voters to use their frustration and ire about Trump’s attacks on the vulnerable and bungling of the economy as motivation to take action.
“The momentum is on our side ... because people are done with the brutality,” Harris said. “They’re done with living in fear. They’re done with not being able to pay for gas or groceries. They’re done with an administration that cuts Medicaid.
“The last year and a half, we’ve [spent] plenty of time throwing things at the TV, saying things ... that we don’t say where we pray,” Harris said. “That phase is over, because we’re now in the phase where we can do something about it, where we can turn anger into action, where we can show the world who we are and what we care about.”
Becerra has spent the final days of the campaign stumping for Democrats in competitive congressional races in the Central Valley and Southern California.
On Sunday, Becerra sought to boost support for Reps. Dave Min (D-Irvine) and Derek Tran (D-Orange) alongside Newsom.
“I’m so grateful to our current and future governor for being here, passing the baton,” Min said at a rally in Irvine, where he and Becerra referred to Newsom as a future president. “We are living in a historic moment, one that everyone’s going to look back [at and] ask, ‘What did we do at this moment when America was in crisis, when our democracy was in crisis?’”
Newsom said Californians could have lamented Trump’s attempts to gerrymander districts in GOP-led states to boost his party’s ability to keep control of Congress, but that Californians responded by redrawing the state’s congressional boundaries last year.
“Donald Trump does not believe in the rule of law. He believes in the rule of Don,” Newsom said.
Democratic leaders are capitalizing on anti-Trump sentiment to juice the state’s liberal electorate and win House seats that were redrawn to favor their party, including a Sacramento-area seat held by Republican-turned-independent Rep. Kevin Kiley of Rocklin.
“We’re not just gonna take back these seats in California. We’re gonna take back the House and the Senate,” Becerra told costumed, cheering volunteers during a quick Saturday stop in support of Richard Pan, the Democrat challenging Kiley, who Becerra said wants to “destroy democracy.”
The Republican president is a big motivator for Democrats this year. California’s high cost of living was among the top concerns of California voters this election, but that was recently eclipsed by fears about Trump’s policies and their desire for a governor to fight back against his administration.
“Everything the Trump administration has done so far is something I disagree with,” 19-year-old Arthur Galvan said after Becerra spoke at Pan’s campaign headquarters. But the UC Davis sophomore said his top priorities are education and one day being able to afford a home, even in Lincoln, the semi-rural and fast-growing town he grew up in.
LA Times/Berkeley poll on California governor’s race, October 2026
“Compared to the rest of the state, housing over there is slightly cheaper. But even still, that’s not attainable,” Galvan said. “I don’t think that there’s many easy ways to go about this but it’s something that we have to look into.”
Asked about his support for a proposed mileage tax — which would require drivers to pay a fee based on the total number of miles driven in a period of time — Becerra said he is considering all options to maintain road funding as more Californians adopt electric vehicles and stop paying the gas tax.
“We need to pay for our roads and our bridges and our highways. We need to pay for mass transit. You can’t do it if you don’t have the money,” he said. “I’m not gonna say exactly how it will be, because that’s work we have to do with the Legislature, and with every community having a chance to speak up.”
Hilton, a former Fox News commentator and political advisor to British Prime Minister David Cameron, has embraced his underdog status. The quick-witted Republican has pinballed from California’s deeply red northern territories to Democratic strongholds in San Francisco and L.A., generating enough heat to remain in the spotlight but not enough to catch fire. He tailgated with Chargers and Rams fans at SoFi Stadium on Sunday, and spoke with survivors of the devastating 2025 wildfire in the Pacific Palisades.
Hilton blamed the disaster on the state’s Democratic leadership, which he described as a combination of incompetence, ideology and corruption.
“This is not a blue state. It is not a red state. It’s the Golden State,” Hilton said. “We are going to fight with everything we’ve got in the two days left to make sure that this Golden State that we love so much is truly golden again.”
He has promised to lower gas prices to $3 per gallon, and on Thursday held a $3-a-gallon fill-up event in the San Joaquin Valley. Hilton also vowed to eliminate state taxes on workers’ first $150,000 of income, scuttle the behind-schedule, over-budget high-speed rail project and abolish the DMV.
Though endorsed by Trump, Hilton has framed his campaign around the many ills facing California — including the lack of affordable housing, a persistent and worsening homelessness crisis, entrenched budget deficits and high gas prices — all of which he blames on years of Democratic rule.
At the Halloween event Saturday, Hilton asked Italia Sandoval’s 3-year-old daughter Milania if she would prefer candy or a potential mileage tax. The toddler, understandably confused, opted for candy. Her mother, 31, jumped in, saying that such a levy would mean less story time, field trips and park and library visits for her family’s home-schooled children and further hamper their dreams of one day buying a home.
“Taxes are killing Californians. I want to buy my own home. Can’t afford it,” said the Huntington Park resident, a registered Republican who become politically engaged after studying theater at Cal State L.A.
Federal judges have repeatedly rejected the Trump administration’s efforts to wrest control over state voting processes and intimidate state and local elections officials.
The daughter of a Mexican immigrant said her husband proposed moving to Idaho because of the cost of living in California, but she balked because their families live here. So they found other methods of cutting their budget.
“I shop at Goodwills, yard sales, Facebook Marketplace, you name it,” Sandoval said. “I even sadly say I pick up clothes off the side of the street sometimes. ... It’s taught me to be resourceful in this state. But it’s like, come on.”
Aided by his Halloween mask and cardboard cutouts portraying Becerra as a hand puppet controlled by Newsom, Hilton has turned his opponent into a symbol of California’s high cost of living and “killjoy” rules. During a Friday night rally in Sacramento, the Republican candidate lamented local bans on gas appliances and a statewide prohibition on flavored tobacco products.
“It’s ridiculous. They don’t mind the fentanyl, they give out free drugs to hopeless addicts, but you try getting flavored Zyn in California — no way. That is insane,” he said, drawing cheers mostly from younger audience members. Lawmakers approved the ban in 2020 and voters upheld it two years later.
Though Becerra is considered unbeatable in blue California in the race, many Hilton fans are clinging to hope that the Republican candidate will overcome the odds.
“We need help. I bought a hybrid and still am like, the gas, it’s killing me,” said Marina Gabel, adding that the paycheck from her school district job is “crumbs.” The Roseville Republican wore a shirt to Hilton’s Sacramento rally that described Newsom as a “California Horror Story” in a nod to the long-running FX anthology series.
Hope and despair simmers among California Republicans as election day approaches.
In the final days of his campaign Becerra seized on voter anxiety about Trump’s policies, heightened by the administration’s recent efforts to wrest control over state voting processes.
Becerra forcefully argued that Tuesday’s election is a referendum on the president, and accused Hilton of being beholden to a White House that has attacked immigrants, launched an unnecessary war against Iran and created economic havoc by imposing tariffs and other unhinged policies.
“We see that wolf in that sheep’s clothing. We see right through you, Donald Trump,” Becerra said Friday at a social club in San Francisco’s Castro district, one of the nation’s most iconic LGBTQ+ communities. “In California, we say no más ... that’s why this election is so important, because we gotta prove that California does not take a knee to Donald Trump.”

Israeli opposition seeks Knesset control as election chief dismisses irregularities probe impact
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
19:28:32 UTC
04:28:32 KST

The head of Israel's Central Elections Committee has said that an ongoing investigation into alleged foreign funding in the country's recent vote would not call into question its result, as the opposition seeks Knesset control and legislation targeting incumbent Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
Committee chief Noam Sohlberg said on Sunday that so far "suspicions remain suspicions".
"We will examine them thoroughly and get to the very bottom of the matter to establish the full truth," Sohlberg said in a video message.
"Our position is that even if the suspicions are ultimately confirmed, this would not call into question the integrity of the electoral process or the overall results of the elections."
Preliminary results from Tuesday's parliamentary elections gave Netanyahu's bloc 53 seats in the 120-member Knesset, against 48 for the opposition and 19 for Arab parties.
Neither bloc has so far secured the minimum 61 seats needed to form a government.
Opposition eyes Knesset control
Meanwhile, opposition leaders are planning a four-way meeting at the home of Yesh Atid leader Yair Lapid to develop a joint plan to translate the election results into political power inside the Knesset, Walla news website reported, citing unnamed sources.
Lapid will be joined by Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot, Avigdor Lieberman of Yisrael Beiteinu and Yair Golan of the Democrats.
The meeting will take place ahead of consultations scheduled to begin on November 4 at the residence of President Isaac Herzog, who will determine who receives the first mandate to try to form a government.
Opposition sources told Walla that Eisenkot has decided to accept the mandate. He has repeatedly ruled out joining a government with Netanyahu, even under a power-sharing arrangement in which they would rotate as prime minister.
Shifting balance of power
Another key date for opposition leaders is November 10, when newly elected Knesset members are scheduled to take the oath of office, according to Walla.
The opposition plans to replace Knesset Speaker Amir Ohana, a member of Netanyahu's Likud party, a move that could give it control over parliamentary business and allow it to try to pass legislation during the six weeks before the deadline for forming a government.
The opposition leaders are expected to discuss a consensus candidate for the post, with Eisenkot, Lapid and Oded Forer of Yisrael Beiteinu among the names being considered.
They see replacing the speaker as an important first step towards shifting the political balance of power while government formation talks continue, Walla said.
But carrying out the plan will require opposition leaders to agree on a candidate and secure enough votes to elect their candidate.
Legislation targeting Netanyahu
The opposition seeks to pass a bill that would bar anyone facing a criminal indictment from forming a government, even before a conviction.
Such a bill would affect Netanyahu, 76, who is on trial on corruption charges, including bribery, fraud and breach of trust. He could face prison if convicted.
He has led a coalition of far-right parties since late 2022, widely described as the most right-wing government in Israel's history.
The opposition also wants to advance a bill to establish an official commission of inquiry into the events of October 7, 2023, Walla said.
Israel’s Gaza genocide has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians, leaving the entire enclave in ruins.
Netanyahu has also been sought by the International Criminal Court since 2024 on accusations of war crimes and crimes against humanity related to the war in Gaza.

Sydney housing market has reached a new low. But are homes affordable?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
19:23:16 UTC
04:23:16 KST

IN BRIEF
- The national home price slump has dropped 6.7 per cent since the March peak, according to new data.
- Experts warn buyers seeking affordability may have to wait for prices to fall further, or for interest rate cuts.
Sydney home prices are lower than they were five years ago but Australia's housing downturn has a way to go to return to affordable values.
National median dwelling values fell another 1.2 per cent in October, extending the home price slump to 6.7 per cent since the March peak, data provider Cotality reported on Monday.
In a market already constrained by elevated affordability and serviceability pressures, rising interest rates and higher taxes have further weighed on housing demand.
In Sydney, the market that led the downturn, prices fell 1.6 per cent in the month.
At $1,178,959, the median Sydney dwelling is more than 10 per cent cheaper than the February peak and has dropped below where it was five years ago.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
But the mid-sized capitals of Perth and Brisbane are falling even faster.
"We saw such an enormous accumulation of value in those mid-sized capitals over the past five years," Cotality head of research Gerard Burg said.
"It means when you see these sizeable declines in those markets, they have a lot they can give up, with a lot of homeowners not feeling too much direct pain."
Brisbane's median value plunged two per cent in October but was still 46 per cent more expensive than five years earlier.
In Perth, where prices were growing at an annual rate of about 25 per cent a few months ago, values fell 1.7 per cent.
In Melbourne, it was a very different story, Burg said.
The Victorian capital has underperformed the rest of the country for five years but is now giving up value more slowly than the other mainland capitals.
Melbourne's affordability advantage was starting to attract residents on net, a reversal from the exodus to cities like Perth and Brisbane during the COVID-19 pandemic, Burg said.
Still, Melbourne-based Ray White real estate agent Dexter Prack says the declines are the biggest he has witnessed in his 28-year career.
"Some properties, they've gone back to 2017, 2018 prices, which is scary," he told the Australian Associated Press.
In the prestige Mornington Peninsula market, Prack said some properties were going on the market at a 25 per cent discount.
By exiting a falling market, some investors would have taken a sizeable haircut. But for owner-occupier vendors buying in a falling market, Prack said there were plenty of opportunities.
However, prospective buyers would have to wait for prices to fall further, or for the Reserve Bank to start cutting interest rates, to see affordability really improve.
Nationally, the median dwelling value is worth approximately $63,400 less than in March.
Four interest rate rises have eroded a median household's borrowing capacity by about $71,000 since February, Burg said.
The Reserve Bank is widely tipped to hike rates again on Tuesday.
With most economists not forecasting a cut until late 2027, Burg expects values to keep falling until then.

Ukraine evacuates civilians from parts of Kherson region as expiry of Oleshky ceasefire nears
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
19:11:58 UTC
04:11:58 KST

Oleshky ceasefire expires, Ukraine evacuates civilians from parts of Kherson region
Nov 1 - Ukraine's military said it evacuated 167 people from threatened areas of southern Kherson region on Sunday as a temporary local ceasefire expired — two days after buses carried residents out of the Russian-held town of Oleshky.
A six-day local ceasefire in Oleshky and the surrounding area was reached after mediation efforts by US first lady Melania Trump and with the involvement of Pope Leo.
The ceasefire expired at midnight Moscow time (2100 GMT). There was no immediate indication of any resumption of hostilities on either side.
It was the longest local pause in fighting since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022.
Ukraine's Ombudsman for Human Rights Dmytro Lubinets, writing on Telegram, said both sides had "upheld the obligations they undertook throughout the duration of this period."
Lubinets said he and Yana Lantratova, Russia's commissioner for human rights, were "exploring possibilities to continue similar humanitarian efforts. It is important to maintain this interaction mechanism so that we can keep helping people and saving lives."
Earlier, Ukraine's General Staff issued a statement saying that its units, in cooperation with local authorities, "evacuated 167 civilians to safer points in the Kherson region."
It said the evacuees included 22 children and 21 people with limited mobility requiring special assistance.
The governor of Kherson region, Oleksandr Prokudin, urged residents to be vigilant as the expiry of the ceasefire neared.
"I also strongly urge you not to visit the so-called 'red zones' – areas and settlements near the Dnipro," Prokudin wrote on Telegram. "The intensity of Russian strikes there remains high, and the threat to life is extremely high."
In Moscow, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov, quoted by Russian news agencies, said Russia had a positive view of how the operation was conducted in Oleshky, as well as of the coordination between the two countries' human rights commissioners.
The pope said he hoped cooperation between Russia and Ukraine in implementing a ceasefire in Oleshky would pave the way for broader peace efforts.
Melania Trump, writing on X, said the ceasefire "has provided residents with the freedom to move, access to food, clean water, medicine, plus a renewed sense of dignity without the constant threat of attack".
CIRCUITOUS JOURNEY
On Saturday, starved and exhausted residents of Oleshky crossed into Ukraine after a circuitous journey from the area, just a few kilometres from the front line.
They first travelled by bus via Crimea, annexed by Russia from Ukraine in 2014, to the Russian town of Anapa, before flying to Belarus from where they continued to Ukraine.
Those wishing to leave Oleshky - some for Russia, some for Ukraine - were taken initially to Crimea in 25 buses and nine ambulances, Lantratova said, before splitting into separate convoys.
In total, nearly 800 people were evacuated, Melania Trump said on X, adding: "I hope Oleshky serves as a foundation for lasting peace between both nations."
It was not known how many chose to stay in Russian-held Oleshky, which lies on the Dnipro River opposite the region's Ukrainian-held main town of Kherson.
The ceasefire, in place since Tuesday, allowed for the roads to be demined and food, medicines and other supplies brought into the town.
Russian forces took control of the town immediately after the February 2022 invasion of Ukraine, but Ukrainian troops recaptured much of the region, including the town of Kherson, later that year.
Military action continued in other parts of Ukraine on Sunday.
Regional governors and emergency services reported one death in a strike in the Sumy region on the Russian border, a frequent target, and at least one in the central region of Vinnytsia. REUTERS

Sen. Chris Murphy, a Connecticut Democrat, was hospitalized Saturday after suffering a stroke at his son's hockey game, his office announced on Sunday.
Murphy is "awake and alert," according to a statement from his chief of staff, Allison Herwitt.
"Yesterday afternoon, Senator Murphy started experiencing numbness in his arm while at his son's hockey game. He was taken to a local hospital, where it was discovered he had experienced a stroke. He was transferred to Johns Hopkins for further monitoring and is responding well to treatment," Herwitt said.
Johns Hopkins Hospital's main campus is in Baltimore, though it has other locations in and around Washington.
"The doctors are encouraged by his progress," Herwitt said. "We are optimistic he will make a full recovery."

He was due in New Hampshire on Sunday to campaign with Democratic Senate candidate Rep. Chris Pappas.
He's seen as a potential 2028 presidential candidate and is a prolific Democratic fundraiser.
Murphy, 53, spent six years in the House before running for the Senate. He rose to national prominence as an advocate for stricter gun control laws in the wake of the Sandy Hook shooting, which occurred in his home state. He's been a vocal critic of President Donald Trump and has opposed the war in Iran and the White House's deportation policies.
He's one of multiple sitting senators to suffer a stroke in recent years.
Democratic Sens. Ben Ray Luján of New Mexico and Chris Van Hollen of Maryland each had a stroke in 2022. And Sen. John Fetterman, D-Penn., who was then running for office, suffered a stroke just days before his state's Senate Democratic primary.
"Thinking of my great friend & colleague, Chris Murphy. I know how fiercely he fights & I'm certain I'll be welcoming him back to the Senate soon," Sen. Richard Blumenthal, a fellow Connecticut Democrat, posted to X on Sunday.

Zelenskyy ready to meet Trump and Putin in Türkiye: "The war must end"
