Qeshm launches multimedia documentation project to preserve island’s intangible heritage
TEHRAN - Qeshm Island has launched a multimedia documentation project to record and preserve its indigenous knowledge, oral history and intangible cultural heritage, with the aim of passing the island’s traditional knowledge and cultural practices on to future generations.
Seyyed Mehdi Mousavi-Ojagh, deputy for cultural, social and tourism affairs of the Qeshm Free Zone Organization, said the initiative involves conducting multimedia interviews with local cultural figures and tradition bearers to document their knowledge, experiences and accounts of the island’s cultural heritage.
According to the official, the project focuses on several aspects of Qeshm’s traditional culture, including indigenous maritime knowledge, local stories and narratives, traditional knowledge related to water heritage, and other elements of the island’s oral history.
He stressed that much of a community’s intangible heritage is preserved in the memories, skills and personal experiences of local people, warning that valuable knowledge could disappear permanently if it is not documented before its bearers pass away.
The initiative seeks to prevent the loss of indigenous knowledge and facilitate the transmission of previous generations’ experiences and cultural practices to younger people, ensuring their continued recognition as part of Qeshm’s historical and cultural identity.
Mousavi-Ojagh also identified community-based cultural tourism as one of the expected benefits of the project, saying that documenting local narratives, skills and traditional knowledge could help introduce the island’s cultural attractions more comprehensively and encourage tourism rooted in local identity and authenticity.
Located in the Persian Gulf, Qeshm is Iran’s largest island and is known for its distinctive combination of natural, geological and cultural heritage. Its cultural traditions include traditional wooden boatbuilding, known as Lenj construction, Bandari embroidery and mat weaving, as well as distinctive local customs and oral traditions.
The island is also home to the Hara mangrove forests and the Qeshm Island UNESCO Global Geopark, which encompasses 26 geological sites and was the first geopark of its kind in West Asia.
The documentation project is intended to turn the knowledge and experiences of older generations into a lasting cultural resource, supporting heritage preservation, education and the development of cultural tourism, the official underlined.

====================================================================================================

Sasanian-era rock carvings of human hands discovered in Marvdasht
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
13:09:59 UTC
22:09:59 KST

Sasanian-era rock carvings of human hands discovered in Marvdasht
TEHRAN - Archaeologists have identified previously undocumented Sasanian-era rock carvings depicting human hands without accompanying figures in the historic Marvdasht Plain in Fars province, southern Iran.
The unusual engravings, found alongside a Sasanian-era prayer inscription in Middle Persian (Pahlavi), may shed light on ancient practices of prayer, oath-taking and religious rituals.
Archaeologist and historian Abolhassan Atabaki announced the discovery during ongoing archaeological surveys and documentation in the Marvdasht Plain, Ana news agency reported on Sunday.
He said the newly identified carvings depict human hands together with parts of the forearms, engraved directly onto rock surfaces without any accompanying human figures. Their artistic style and visual characteristics suggest that they date to the Sasanian period (224–651 CE).
Atabaki noted that although hands frequently appear in Sasanian rock reliefs as symbols of respect and homage, their independent depiction also has precedents in seals and seal impressions from the period.
Examples held in collections at the British Museum, Bandar Abbas, Takht-e Soleyman, Tell Abu Shaaf in Iraq and the University of California, Berkeley, demonstrate that Sasanian artists sometimes depicted hands independently of other parts of the human body.
Studies of Sasanian art suggest that the hand motif was associated with concepts such as greeting, goodwill and benevolence. In some instances, researchers have also proposed connections with covenants, the deity Mithra and religious ceremonies.
One notable example is a seal impression discovered at Takht-e Soleyman, which depicts a hand accompanied by a Pahlavi inscription reading abestan o yazdan, meaning “seeking the assistance of the deities.”
In that regard, Najmeh Ebrahimi, a historian, said the available evidence suggests that the independent depiction of hands may have served as a symbolic means of expressing prayer, oaths, covenants and wishes for good fortune.
She explained that because the hand plays a central role in carrying out such acts, depicting it independently could have conveyed the intended meaning without the need to portray the entire human figure.
Ebrahimi said the Marvdasht carvings may likewise have had a devotional purpose, possibly representing prayers or appeals for divine assistance.
She added that this interpretation is reinforced by the discovery of a Sasanian-era prayer inscription beside one of the hand carvings.
The depiction of part of the forearm, ending in a straight edge, together with the distinctive positioning of the fingers, gives the newly documented carvings particular archaeological and artistic significance.
Researchers say further examination and documentation will be needed to establish more precisely the meaning and function of the unusual motifs.

Eight Palestinians, including a child, were killed and other people in Israeli attacks across Gaza amid Israel’s daily violations of last year’s ceasefire, medics said.
Medics at Nasser Hospital in Khan Younis, southern Gaza, told Anadolu that five Palestinians were killed in an air strike in Al Mawasi, west of the city.
Later, Gaza’s interior ministry said the five people killed in the strike were identified as police officers.
Locals said that the strike hit near schools for children, causing panic among them.
Deliberate attacks
Since the start of Israel’s genocide in Gaza, it has repeatedly targeted police personnel and infrastructure in Gaza, in what Palestinian authorities say is weakening public order institutions and undermining civilian infrastructure.
In the months following the October 2025 ceasefire, the attacks have continued with a series of strikes hitting police vehicles, checkpoints and patrol units.
Palestinian authorities in the enclave have said Israel has killed nearly 3000 police officers since the start of the genocide in October 2023, and the attacks on police are part of a broader pattern that has persisted despite the truce
The Palestinian resistance group Hamas has accused Israel of targeting police officers trying to maintain public security and stability in Gaza.
Hamas says the attacks represent a continuation of the Israeli brutal crimes against Palestinians in Gaza and an attempt to create chaos by targeting civilian police forces.
Another attack
In a separate attack, a medical source at al-Shifa Hospital in Gaza City said three Palestinians, including a child, were killed in an Israeli air strike on al-Thawra Street.
The source added that six other Palestinians sustained injuries of varying severity.
Local sources said that an Israeli drone targeted a gathering of civilians on al-Thawra Street.
The ongoing ceasefire violations have killed 1,580 Palestinians and wounded 5,711 people since October 10, 2025, according to figures from Gaza's health ministry.
Since October 2023, Israeli genocide in Gaza has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians and wounded over 175,000 people, figures from the ministry showed. 
Israeli genocide has also destroyed around 90 percent of Gaza’s civilian infrastructure.

U.S. Marine Corps attack helicopters set for major upgrade
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
13:02:58 UTC
22:02:58 KST

- The U.S. Marine Corps is refining the SPINE upgrade for AH-1Z and UH-1Y helicopters using data from two test aircraft at Patuxent River.
- PMA-276 and Bell are preparing the Amarillo plant to begin modifying operational fleet helicopters in fiscal 2027.
The U.S. Marine Corps’ H-1 program office is using flight test data from the first two upgraded AH-1Z Viper and UH-1Y Venom helicopters to lock down the SPINE configuration, with modification of the first fleet aircraft set to begin in fiscal 2027. Naval Air Systems Command’s Light/Attack Helicopter Program Office, PMA-276, said test points flown so far are feeding into the final aircraft configuration and the technical drawing package for Phase 3.0, the stage that moves the upgrade from test aircraft to operational helicopters.
SPINE, short for Structural and Power Improvements for NextGen Effects, strengthens the airframes to carry heavier loads and adds electrical generating capacity so the helicopters can take on new weapons and mission systems. The Marine Corps lists SPINE among its H-1 lethality priorities in its 2026 Aviation Plan. The program office did not say how many test points remain, when the configuration will be frozen or how much additional power the upgrade provides.
Developmental testing continues at Naval Air Station Patuxent River, Maryland, with Air Test and Evaluation Squadron 21, Bell Textron and PMA-276 working as an integrated test team. Bell finished the two test aircraft, one AH-1Z and one UH-1Y, in March 2026 after 19 months of structural and electrical work at its Amarillo Assembly Center in Texas. The effort was known as the Structural Improvement and Electrical Power Upgrade, or SIEPU, until early 2026.
PMA-276 and Bell are now preparing the Amarillo plant to take in operational helicopters. The work includes buying parts, setting up manufacturing and production lines, readying support equipment and specialized tooling, planning how aircraft will be moved to and from Texas, and aligning SPINE with other H-1 modifications so the work can be done in the same visits. The two organizations are also choosing which aircraft go first and scheduling inductions to keep squadrons supplied with helicopters and to keep the fleet’s configuration consistent.
“H-1 modernization is critical to maintaining a capable and ready force for aviation-delivered fires in support of Marine Air-Ground Task Force crisis response,” said Lt. Col. Benjamin Carlton, capabilities and combat relevance pillar lead for PMA-276. “SPINE will provide greater flexibility for utility mission kits and a digital weapons bus capable of integrating advanced lethality systems, including AIM-9X and other digital weapons.”
The contracts for that first batch are already in place. In July, the U.S. Navy awarded Bell $33.6 million for SPINE Phase III hardware, including A-kits, D-kits, power generation components and drivetrain assemblies. Bell described the award as a base contract with three option years covering up to 49 aircraft, 28 AH-1Zs and 21 UH-1Ys, with work in Amarillo starting in mid-2027 and first deliveries in 2028. In October, the U.S. Navy exercised a $114.7 million option for 15 A-kits, four mission kits and nine aircraft installations, all due by June 2028.
Fiscal 2027 began on Oct. 1, 2026, and runs through September 2027, so the first inductions would fall inside the window Bell gave for the start of work in Amarillo.
A digital weapons bus is a data connection between the aircraft’s mission computers and its stores stations. It lets the helicopter exchange data with smart weapons before launch, which analog connections cannot do, and new weapons can be added largely through software. That matters for a fleet that is no longer being built: U.S. production of the UH-1Y ended in 2020 and of the AH-1Z in 2022, and the Marine Corps operates about 189 Vipers and 160 Venoms. The two types share about 85% of their components, so one set of SPINE changes covers both.
The Marine Corps is already testing missions that will draw on that capacity. On May 13, during an exercise at Twentynine Palms, California, Marine Light Attack Helicopter Squadron 169 used UH-1Ys as airborne control nodes for Neros Archer first-person-view drones, launching one from a helicopter in flight and taking over another launched from the ground.
“Government and Bell SPINE teams are continuing developmental testing while preparing for Phase 3.0 modifications in FY27,” Carlton added. “The team has prioritized critical test points before the first installations and maintained close coordination throughout engineering reviews. By addressing critical test requirements early and incorporating refinements as the program progresses, the team is delivering enhanced capability to the fleet sooner.”
Bell and PMA-276 are also working to keep a common technical baseline for the upgraded aircraft, combining Bell’s role as original equipment manufacturer with PMA-276’s program management, so the modified airframes and mission systems can be supported for the rest of their service lives.

Genes may explain about a third of earnings differences, according to a study of 44,500 U.S. twin pairs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
13:00:52 UTC
22:00:52 KST

A massive analysis of census and tax records indicates that inherited genetic factors account for nearly one-third of the variation in earnings among steadily employed Americans in their late 20s and 30s. At the same time, the research suggests that standard twin studies may overstate the genetic component of career success, partly because same-sex twins are unusually likely to end up working at the same company. The findings were published in PNAS.
Why do children from certain families consistently earn higher paychecks in adulthood than children from other families? Social scientists examine this question using a statistical concept called heritability, which measures the proportion of differences in a trait across a population that can be traced to inherited genetic variation rather than environmental conditions.
To estimate heritability without directly sequencing DNA, researchers have traditionally relied on the classical twin design. This method compares identical twins, who develop from a single fertilized egg and share 100 percent of their genes, with fraternal twins, who develop from two separate eggs and share about 50 percent of their genes, just like ordinary brothers and sisters.
Because both types of twins grow up in the same household, researchers attribute any extra similarity between identical twins to their shared DNA. This rests on what is known as the equal-environments assumption, which holds that identical and fraternal twins share their home environment to the same degree.
Sorting out genetic inheritance from family upbringing has proven challenging in economics. For instance, a 2008 study of American brothers and sisters found that siblings’ adult earnings are moderately correlated, indicating that family background accounts for a sizable share of economic inequality. But ordinary sibling comparisons cannot separate shared DNA from parental wealth and parenting styles.
Twins offer a way to separate those channels. A 2012 review of genetics and economics indicated that long-term income appears roughly as heritable as personality traits or many medical conditions. The review’s authors also warned that separating true genetic effects from social influences remains difficult.
Complicating matters further, a person’s paycheck is not determined solely by the individual skills, education, or personality they bring to the labor market. Labor economists separate wages into two main parts. The first is a portable worker component, which reflects an individual’s earning capacity across different jobs. The second is an employer pay premium, the extra pay or discount a specific company gives to all of its staff.
In a 2013 study of West German workers, study co-author David Card and colleagues found that growing differences between workers and in company pay premiums, along with the increasing sorting of high-earning workers into high-paying companies, accounted for much of the rise in wage inequality. Whether access to these high-paying companies reflects inherited traits, personal connections, or simple luck has remained an open question.
Because population registries rarely record whether twins are identical or fraternal, previous twin studies of income have typically relied on small survey samples. To investigate how genetics and social interactions shape both individual earning power and workplace pay premiums on a national scale, Card and Jesse Rothstein of the University of California, Berkeley, along with Moises Yi of the US Census Bureau, analyzed administrative records covering the full population of young adult twins in the United States.
Unlike physical traits such as height, career outcomes depend heavily on social choices, including where a person wants to work and who else works there. The authors reasoned that if twins influence each other’s job choices or prefer working together at the same workplace, standard twin comparisons could mistake that social coordination for genetic inheritance.
The researchers linked household records from the 2000 United States Census to quarterly wage records from state unemployment insurance tax filings. These records cover formal wage and salary jobs, and the team used data from 2018 through the first quarter of 2023. They omitted the last three quarters of 2020 to avoid labor market disruptions caused by the COVID-19 pandemic.
The sample tracked biological children of household heads who were between 9 and 17 years old in 2000 (born between 1983 and 1990). Twins were defined as children in the same household born within two days of each other, and non-twin siblings as children born at least nine months apart. The employment analysis encompassed 87,000 twin pairs (60,000 same-sex and 27,000 opposite-sex) and 2,168,000 non-twin sibling pairs (1,072,000 same-sex and 1,096,000 opposite-sex).
For the detailed wage analysis, the authors focused on pairs in which both siblings maintained stable full-time work. This meant having at least eight quarters in which they earned more than $3,800 from one employer (roughly full-time minimum-wage pay), excluding the first and last quarters of each job spell. That restriction yielded 44,500 twin pairs (31,500 same-sex and 13,000 opposite-sex) and 1,007,000 non-twin sibling pairs (507,000 same-sex and 500,000 opposite-sex).
Because census files do not record whether twins are identical or fraternal, the researchers relied on biological sex. All opposite-sex twins are fraternal, whereas same-sex twins are a mix of fraternal and identical twins. Identical twins made up an estimated 58.7 percent of same-sex pairs in the sample.
Families may also treat sons and daughters differently. To filter out that possibility, the team used a statistical technique called difference-in-differences. They subtracted the similarity gap between same-sex and opposite-sex regular siblings from the similarity gap between same-sex and opposite-sex twins.
The team analyzed average quarterly earnings using a logarithmic scale, a standard economic measure that captures proportional differences in pay. They also used a statistical wage decomposition model to split each worker’s pay into two parts: their portable individual earning capacity and the average pay premium of the companies they worked for. The model controlled for work experience and calendar time.
That employer pay premium was further broken down into three pieces. These were a geographic location premium (the average employer pay premium among companies in the local commuting zone), an industry premium (the average employer pay premium among companies in that industry), and a remaining workplace-specific pay premium.
Across the full wage sample, same-sex twins showed a correlation in average earnings of 0.543 (on a scale where 0 indicates no relationship and 1 indicates that one twin’s earnings perfectly predict the other’s). By comparison, the correlation was 0.317 for opposite-sex twins, 0.386 for same-sex non-twin siblings, and 0.265 for opposite-sex non-twin siblings.
The researchers also examined non-twin siblings separated by age gaps of one to three years, excluding pairs born less than a year apart to avoid adoption or recording errors. Earnings similarity barely faded as the age difference grew, and the gap between same-sex and opposite-sex siblings remained steady. This pattern supported the assumption that shared family and gender influences do not change drastically for siblings born close together.
Based on their extended twin model, the researchers initially estimated that inherited genetic factors accounted for 36 percent of the variance in overall earnings. Genetic factors also accounted for an estimated 23 percent of the variance in having any employment and 32 percent of the variance in the number of quarters employed.
When the researchers separated earnings into individual and workplace components, portable individual earning power had an estimated heritability of 40 percent. The employer pay premium had an estimated heritability of 21 percent.
Within the workplace component, the industry pay premium had a heritability estimate of 26 percent and the remaining workplace-specific premium had an estimate of 20 percent. The geographic location premium (18 percent) was not statistically significant, because most siblings remained in the region where they grew up.
Finding heritability in employer pay premiums even within regions and industries made it look on the surface as though genetic factors affected not just workers’ skills, but also their access to high-paying companies. Because the 21 percent estimate was roughly twice as large as what skill-based hiring alone would produce, the authors examined whether twins were ending up at the same establishments.
The employment records showed that 11.4 percent of same-sex twin pairs worked at the exact same establishment at some point between 2018 and 2023 (not necessarily at the same time). That was double the rate for same-sex non-twin siblings (5.7 percent), triple the rate for opposite-sex twins (3.8 percent), and more than five times the rate for opposite-sex non-twin siblings (2.2 percent).
The researchers then re-estimated their model after removing all twin and sibling pairs who ever worked at the same establishment. The estimated heritability of the employer pay premium dropped by two-thirds, from 21 percent to 7 percent, and was no longer statistically significant. The heritability of the industry premium fell from 26 percent to 12 percent, and that of the workplace-specific premium fell from 20 percent to essentially zero.
The remaining link between genetics and employer pay premiums fit what would be expected from high-paying companies hiring high-skilled workers alone. Excluding coworkers also lowered the estimated heritability of portable individual earning power from 40 percent to 35 percent. The estimated heritability of overall earnings fell from 36 percent to 31 percent (a relative decline of about 15 percent), and the authors regard these lower figures as their best estimates.
Even with that downward adjustment, the finding that genetics account for roughly a third of individual earning differences aligns with a recent German study, which found that higher cognitive ability at age 23 predicted higher socioeconomic status at age 27 largely due to shared genetic factors. That study looked at educational attainment and occupational prestige in young adulthood rather than wages, but both point to a substantial genetic influence on socioeconomic outcomes.
“The results show that estimated heritability is clearly present, as one would totally expect, but the effect depends a lot on whether the twins work at the same firms,” said Felix Bittmann, a postdoctoral researcher at the Leibniz Institute for Educational Trajectories and the University of Bamberg who was not involved in the research. “It’s an interesting aspect that deserves more attention. Clearly, the paper shows that even well-done genetically informed studies cannot partial out ‘pure’ genetic effects as social interactions will always be present and can influence the findings strongly.”
“While this study is done with twins, its implications extend a lot further: in the social sciences, it is an important question to understand how success is determined (nature vs. nurture),” Bittmann noted. “Twin designs are usually an elegant way to attempt to account for both factors, which classical research designs (surveys) cannot capture at all, as genetic transmission pathways are usually not measured; often, even proxies are lacking (like IQ tests for both children and parents).”
Sociologists often try to separate what they call primary and secondary effects: how family background shapes a child’s academic performance, and how families make choices about continuing education. Those two pathways are harder to separate when genetic inheritance goes unmeasured.
“Especially in sociology, when primary and secondary effects are to be separated, genetic pathways are usually ignored, which is a biasing factor,” Bittmann said. “This research can help to estimate how large such a bias could probably be.”
“The research design is clever, as they exploit a huge US database with official statistics,” Bittmann told PsyPost. “These databases do not contain information about twins, so this information is lacking, but they can reconstruct it from birth dates, which is a good idea. While they need to make some assumptions and correct for the aspect that same-sex twins can be identical or not …, they can account for this statistically; I think this part is fine.”
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind. A heritability estimate of 31 percent describes variation across a population. It does not mean that 31 percent of any one person’s paycheck comes from their genes, or that an individual’s earnings are biologically fixed at birth.
Even when genetic differences influence earnings, they can operate through indirect or social pathways, such as how parents’ genetic traits shape the home environment they create for their children. In addition, the wage analysis only included sibling pairs in which both people held stable, full-time wage and salary jobs. That leaves out self-employed workers, federal employees, and adults with minimal attachment to the labor market.
Model assumptions can also pull the heritability estimates in opposite directions. The baseline model assumes parents pair up randomly with respect to genes related to earnings. If spouses instead tend to share genetic traits tied to education and earning potential (known as assortative mating), regular siblings and fraternal twins would share more than half of those relevant genes. The authors calculate this could make the estimates about 16 percent higher than reported (for example, roughly 36 percent rather than 31 percent).
On the other hand, even after removing siblings who worked at the same company, the remaining estimates for portable earning power may still be inflated by unmeasured social interactions. Twins might, for instance, influence each other’s education choices or decide to attend the same college.
The authors suggest this kind of sibling influence could be one contributor to the “missing heritability” problem in genetics. Studies that directly analyze DNA using polygenic scores (scores that add up the small effects of many genetic variants) estimate lower heritability for social outcomes like education and income than twin studies do.
“I’d say the paper confirms known aspects with a larger and better sample size and is generally trustworthy,” Bittmann said. “When it comes to disentangling nature vs. nurture, the paper contributes but can, of course, not give a definite answer. Maybe other researchers can use the same research plan on other databases from other countries to add more insight and external validity.”
The study, “Heritability and social interaction in labor market outcomes: Evidence from the population of twins in the United States,” was authored by David Card, Jesse Rothstein, and Moises Yi.

No paneer, no honey, no milky chai? The real challenge of going vegan in India
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
12:56:26 UTC
21:56:26 KST

World Vegan Day is observed annually on November 1.
For many Indians, the day begins with a cup of milky chai, followed by breakfast cooked in ghee. Lunch may come with a bowl of curd and paneer on the menu, while a Sunday meal is often incomplete without chicken curry.These familiar food habits are so deeply woven into everyday life that giving up all animal-derived products can seem like a difficult choice.But for people who turn vegan, the change goes beyond replacing meat with vegetables. It means rethinking everyday ingredients, from milk and butter to honey, as well as choices involving clothing, cosmetics and other products.“There are alternatives for practically everything. You can make curd at home using plant milk, use tofu instead of paneer, and use different nut and soy milks,” says Sarahana, who has been vegan since 2018.On World Vegan Day, observed on November 1, the question is not just why people choose veganism, but what it takes to follow the lifestyle.
Dal, rice, roti, rajma, chole, idli, dosa, poha, upma and vegetable dishes can all be part of a vegan diet.
What is veganism?
According to The Vegan Society, veganism is a way of living that seeks to exclude, as far as possible and practicable, all forms of animal exploitation and cruelty.
While a vegan diet avoids meat, fish, eggs, dairy and honey, the lifestyle also extends to products made from animals, those tested on animals and activities that use animals for entertainment.
For some, the decision is rooted in animal welfare; for others, environmental concerns or health considerations play a role.But the experiences of vegans show that the transition is as much about changing everyday habits as it is about changing one's perspective.India has a long tradition of vegetarian food, but veganism goes a step further by excluding all animal-derived products, including milk, curd, ghee, paneer and honey.According to estimates compiled by World Population Review, around 9% of India's population followed a vegan diet in 2021, amounting to an estimated 121.5 million people. The country also has a substantial vegetarian population, reflecting its diverse food traditions.However, the figure should be treated as an estimate rather than a definitive count, as veganism surveys often rely on self-reported responses and vary in methodologies.
Rice with tofu and cucumber. (Photo credit: Utkarsh)
What does a vegan Indian kitchen look like?
A vegan diet does not necessarily mean giving up familiar Indian food or relying on expensive, imported alternatives. Dal, rice, roti, rajma, chole, idli, dosa, poha, upma and vegetable dishes can all be part of a vegan diet, provided they are prepared without animal-derived ingredients.Utkarsh Garg, a representative of People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals (PETA), says their meals are a mix of familiar Indian dishes and plant-based alternatives.“Breakfast is usually a protein smoothie bowl or soaked oats, although I’m definitely not above a plate of poha, chhole-kulche or one enormous aloo paratha when the mood strikes!”“Lunch and dinner usually include things like tofu, soybeans, dals, rajma and plenty of vegetables. My current obsession is tempeh. I seem to be finding increasingly creative excuses to put it into everything I eat.”“As for living without milk, paneer, curd or ghee, I genuinely don’t find it difficult anymore. There are so many vegan alternatives available now, and many things are surprisingly easy and inexpensive to make at home as well.” Utkarsh said.Sarahana says she relies largely on everyday Indian food rather than packaged substitutes.“As for food, my everyday diet is actually quite simple and Indian. Dal, rice, roti, vegetables, chickpeas, rajma, seasonal produce and different legumes. There are so many naturally plant-based foods available in India. You don’t need expensive imported alternatives or packaged vegan products to survive without dairy.“There are alternatives for practically everything. You can make curd at home using plant milk, use tofu instead of paneer, and use different nut and soy milks. Ghee is essentially clarified butter, and personally, I don’t feel the need to replace it.”The distinction is important. A vegan diet does not require a direct substitute for every non-vegan food. It can instead be built around naturally plant-based ingredients that are already widely used in Indian kitchens.
Breakfast is usually a protein smoothie bowl or soaked oats. (Photo credit: Utkarsh)
Why are people choosing veganism?
For Utkarsh, the decision began in childhood. Watching a chicken being slaughtered made them connect the food on their plate with the animal it came from. He turned vegetarian that day and later went vegan.“For me, veganism has always been about animals. I’ve loved animals for as long as I can remember. While most kids my age were watching Cartoon Network or Pogo, I was glued to National Geographic, completely fascinated by dogs, cats, cows, snakes, and pretty much every animal I came across,” Utkarsh said.As he learnt more about animal exploitation, vegetarianism no longer felt enough. “My love for animals naturally led me to veganism. I’ve been vegan for four years now, and honestly, it is one of the best decisions I have ever made. More than changing what I eat or wear, it has changed the way I look at the world and my place in it.”
Yellow Thai Curry. (Photo credit: Sarahana)
For Sarahana, the turning point came in 2018, when she watched a video of a pregnant cow being slaughtered after she was no longer productive for the dairy industry.“My decision came from questioning something very basic: why do we, as human beings, consider ourselves superior to other animals? Why do we love some animals, consider some family, see some as entertainment, and others as food?” she said.While studying gender, Sarahana began drawing parallels between the exploitation of women's bodies and that of female animals in the dairy industry.“How can I study feminism, gender and the exploitation of female bodies and not extend that understanding beyond human beings? How can I talk about patriarchy and exploitation while continuing to pay an industry that repeatedly impregnates female animals, takes away their babies and exploits their reproductive systems?” she said.Coming from a Dalit community, Sarahana also views veganism through the lens of social justice, questioning how societies decide whose lives are valued.“We love cats and dogs, welcome them into our homes and call them family, but we look at chickens, goats and buffaloes and see food. We have created categories of animals that deserve affection and animals that can be exploited,” she added.
The figure should be treated as an estimate rather than a definitive count, as veganism surveys often rely on self-reported responses.
The price of going vegan
One common perception is that veganism is an expensive lifestyle, largely because plant-based milk, meat substitutes and other packaged alternatives can cost more than conventional products. However, both Utkarsh and Sarahana say that a vegan diet need not depend on these products.Utkarsh points out that many Indian staples are naturally plant-based. “India is one of the easiest places in which to eat vegan, because so much of the food we already know and love either naturally contains no animal-derived ingredients or can be veganised with ridiculously small changes.“Think about dal, rajma, chole, idli, dosa, poha, upma, roti, sabzis, rice dishes and countless regional foods. Veganism doesn’t have to mean buying an expensive imported mock meat or drinking a fancy packaged plant milk every morning. Those products are great if you enjoy them, but they aren’t what veganism depends on.”
Vegan food item. (Photo credit: Utkarsh)
Sarahana agrees that the bigger challenge is often social rather than financial.“I don’t think being vegan in India is inherently expensive. Our traditional food already has so many affordable plant-based options. What can become expensive is the packaged vegan alternatives, not the basic diet itself. The bigger challenge is social conditioning. At family gatherings, weddings or even casual conversations, you constantly have to explain why you don’t consume something that everyone else considers normal.”Both say their families initially had questions and reservations. Utkarsh says their family is now supportive and has started incorporating more vegan foods and products into their lives. Sarahana, meanwhile, says she continues to face comments that she has been “brainwashed”.
Is a vegan diet actually healthier?
Veganism is often associated with better health, but a plant-based diet is not automatically a balanced one. Its nutritional value depends on the foods included and whether essential nutrients are adequately supplied.Dt Gausiya Aziz, consultant and head of nutrition and dietetics at SPARSH Hospital, Yelahanka, says a well-planned vegan diet can support cardiovascular and metabolic health.“Research suggests that plant-based dietary patterns rich in fibre, antioxidants and unsaturated fats can help lower LDL cholesterol, improve blood pressure and support healthy weight management. They may also reduce the risk of developing type 2 diabetes,” she says.However, claims that veganism automatically prevents cancer, reverses chronic diseases or guarantees a longer life are exaggerated, she cautions. Health outcomes depend on overall diet quality, lifestyle and individual medical conditions.
White sauce (made with soy milk) pasta with nutritional yeast (Photo credit: Sarahana)
A key concern is meeting nutritional requirements. Vitamin B12, iron, calcium, vitamin D, iodine, zinc, omega-3 fatty acids and protein need particular attention.Vitamin B12 is especially important because reliable natural plant-based sources are limited. Fortified foods or supplements may therefore be necessary.Aziz recommends a varied diet containing whole grains, legumes, vegetables, fruits, nuts and seeds, along with appropriate supplementation and regular nutritional assessment.Utkarsh says he pay close attention to their nutritional needs and take vitamin B12 supplements.“I am also quite particular about my nutrition. I take my B12 regularly and pay attention to vitamin D and other essential nutrients. B12 supplementation is important for vegans, and these supplements are accessible at pharmacies,” he said.The PETA representative added that he has noticed less bloating since turning vegan and feel healthier, but stresses that dietary planning matters.“Of course, I think any diet needs to be properly planned rather than treated as automatically healthy simply because it carries a particular label. For me, veganism has actually made me more conscious of what I eat and what my body needs.”Aziz also warns that highly processed vegan foods are not necessarily healthy. Packaged snacks, meat substitutes and desserts can contain high amounts of sodium, refined carbohydrates, added sugars and saturated fats. She advises prioritising minimally processed foods and checking nutritional labels.“Children, pregnant women and older adults have specific nutritional requirements that demand careful consideration before adopting a vegan diet. During childhood, adequate energy, protein, calcium, iron, vitamin B12 and vitamin D are essential for growth and development. Pregnant women must additionally ensure sufficient folate, iodine, choline and omega-3 fatty acids to support maternal health and fetal development. Older adults should prioritise protein intake, calcium and vitamin D to preserve muscle strength and bone health. Vitamin B12 supplementation is particularly important across these groups,” Aziz added.Nutritionist Aziz also recommends consulting a qualified dietitian or healthcare professional before making significant dietary changes.
Vegan Pizza with Oat Milk Coffee
Is veganism about health, animals or the planet?
Animal welfare is not the only reason people choose veganism. Environmental concerns are also part of the conversation.Aziz says vegan diets generally have a lower environmental footprint than diets containing substantial amounts of animal products, particularly red meat and dairy.Plant-based food production typically requires less agricultural land and generates fewer greenhouse gas emissions than livestock farming. It can also reduce pressure on biodiversity and freshwater resources.However, the environmental impact varies with farming methods, transportation, processing and food waste. Choosing locally available, seasonal and minimally processed plant foods can help reduce the footprint further.For Utkarsh, the values behind veganism are also connected to ideas of compassion and non-violence.“We grow up hearing about ahimsa and vasudhaiva kutumbakam, the idea that the world is one family. To me, animals shouldn’t be excluded from that circle of compassion simply because they belong to another species,” he said.
Utkarsh says lunch and dinner usually include things like tofu, soybeans, and plenty of vegetables.
What should you know before going vegan?
Going vegan involves more than changing what is on the plate. It can mean checking product labels, asking about ingredients when eating out and finding alternatives to everyday items.Some medications and personal-care products may also contain animal-derived ingredients, making it important to check rather than assume that a product is vegan.For someone considering the transition, Utkarsh suggests starting by understanding where everyday products come from.“For anyone considering going vegan because they care about animals, I would say: start by looking. Look honestly at where our milk, meat, eggs, leather, wool, silk, cosmetics and entertainment come from.”“Once I did that, veganism stopped feeling like something I was ‘giving up’. It started feeling like the most natural extension of something I had believed all along.”Sarahana says the idea is to extend compassion beyond the animals people traditionally consider companions or pets.She also points to the growing number of Indian businesses offering vegan alternatives. For her, such businesses are helping make animal-free choices more accessible.
For those thinking of making the switch, the practical starting point may be simple: understand what a vegan diet excludes, plan for essential nutrients and explore the plant-based foods already available in the kitchen.World Vegan Day was established in 1994 by Louise Wallis, then president of The Vegan Society, to mark the 50th anniversary of the organisation's founding in November 1944.The day is now observed annually on November 1 to raise awareness about veganism and its ethical, environmental and health-related aspects.
Kanchan Yadav is a writer at The Times of India, where she covers business, politics, international affairs and social issues. Her reporting also focuses on policy, governance and economic developments, with a close lens on how decisions in corridors of power affect everyday lives and community well-being.

U.S. Army’s HADES spy plane prototype makes first flight
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
12:55:46 UTC
21:55:46 KST

- The U.S. Army’s HADES Prototype 1, a modified Bombardier Global 6500 jet, made its first flight on Sept. 11, the service announced Oct. 30.
- The aircraft now enters developmental flight testing of its multi-domain sensing and signals intelligence systems ahead of operational demonstrations.
The U.S. Army’s first HADES prototype, a Bombardier Global 6500 business jet modified by Sierra Nevada Corporation for long-range signals intelligence and deep sensing, made its first flight on Sept. 11, the service announced on Oct. 30, seven weeks after the event.
The flight followed a flight readiness review and moves the High Accuracy Detection and Exploitation System into mission system integration and a developmental flight test program. The Army said those tests will check the aircraft’s multi-domain sensing and signals intelligence equipment ahead of operational demonstrations. It did not say where the aircraft flew, how long the flight lasted or what mission equipment was installed.
“The first flight of HADES Prototype 1 transitions our vision for deep sensing from concept to reality,” said Lt. Col. (P) James Hickey, project manager for the Fixed Wing Project Office. “This achievement reflects the dedication, technical precision, and shared mission focus of our military, civilian, and industry partners working to deliver transformational capabilities to the Army and joint force.”
The Fixed Wing Project Office ran the flight with SNC, the program’s lead systems integrator, and with the Project Director Sensors–Aerial Intelligence, part of the Army’s Portfolio Acquisition Executive for Command and Control/Counter-Command and Control. Before the flight, engineers, test pilots and mission system architects completed the structural modifications, installed mission system hardware and finished preliminary airworthiness checks. HADES is government-owned and contractor-operated, and SNC told Defense Daily in January that its own pilots and technicians would fly the tests alongside the Army.
Bombardier delivered the first Global 6500 for the program to the Army in Wichita, Kansas, in November 2024, and the Army passed it to SNC’s facility in Hagerstown, Maryland, for conversion. The Army had picked SNC as lead systems integrator in August 2024 under a 12-year contract worth $93.5 million at award, with a ceiling of $991.3 million, beating a team of L3Harris, Leidos and MAG Aerospace. L3Harris protested the decision, which stopped work until the Government Accountability Office denied the protest on Dec. 23, 2024. SNC received the second Army-owned jet in September 2025, and at the end of 2025 it bought a fourth Global 6500 with its own money to become the first non-prototype aircraft in the fleet.
The Army plans to field HADES in stages. In April 2026, Army officials said the program would deliver three prototypes, with the second adding an advanced radar and the third described as “combat credible”, and that the first aircraft would reach units later this year. The service also wants to pair HADES with launched effects, small unmanned systems released from the aircraft. In 2025, the Army said it would buy about half as many of the jets as it had previously planned, and it has not published a final fleet size.
When it announced the 2024 award, the Army said SNC would integrate communications intelligence, electronic intelligence, synthetic aperture radar and moving target indicator sensors on the Global 6500. A Pentagon budget reprogramming document approved in early 2025 confirmed that Raytheon’s Advanced Synthetic Aperture Radar System-2B, developed for the U.S. Air Force’s U-2, is part of the HADES sensor suite. The Oct. 30 release mentions only multi-domain sensing and signals intelligence for the current test phase.
HADES grows out of a string of contractor-owned bridging aircraft the Army has flown since 2020. Leidos built ARTEMIS on a Bombardier Challenger 650 and ARES on a Global 6500, and ARES deployed to the Indo-Pacific in 2022. Under the follow-on ATHENA effort, a MAG Aerospace and L3Harris team modified Global 6500s for radar collection, while SNC converted two jets to its RAPCON-X signals intelligence configuration, which became the basis for HADES. SNC says the HADES aircraft will be the first Army-owned large-cabin business jets used for aerial intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance.
The jets are meant to replace the Army’s legacy turboprop intelligence aircraft. The Army says the Global 6500 airframe offers greater speed, range, payload and operating altitude than those platforms, which lets HADES collect from farther away and spend more time on station in large-scale operations.
“Deep sensing is critical to maintaining decision advantage in the future fight,” Hickey said. “HADES will help commanders see farther, understand faster, and act with greater precision across the multi-domain battlefield.”

U.S. Marine Corps wants new cargo drones that fly 100 pounds 40 miles out
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
12:50:44 UTC
21:50:44 KST

- The U.S. Navy will host a cargo drone demonstration in Huntsville from Jan. 25 to Feb. 5, 2027, for the U.S. Marine Corps’ TRUAS Increment II.
- Entrants must carry 100 pounds 40 nautical miles and back without refueling, using heavy fuel or hybrid power.
The U.S. Navy is inviting companies to bring cargo drones to Huntsville, Alabama, from Jan. 25 to Feb. 5, 2027, to compete for the U.S. Marine Corps’ second-generation Tactical Resupply Unmanned Aircraft System, or TRUAS Increment II, which must carry 100 pounds (45 kg) to a point 40 nautical miles (74 km) away and fly back without refueling. Applications to take part in the demonstration are due Nov. 30, 2026.
The Navy’s new Direct Reporting Portfolio Manager for Robotic and Autonomous Systems posted the notice on Oct. 30 through its Air Warfare program office at Naval Air Station Patuxent River, Maryland. Companies that perform well in Huntsville may receive an other transaction prototype agreement under 10 U.S.C. § 4022, and a successfully completed prototype can lead to a follow-on production agreement without further competition. The government may award no agreements, one or several, and the notice gives no dollar value or planned quantity.
Each selected company must show ground setup, flight preparation and refueling, then fly up to five autonomous sorties. On the first required flight, the drone carries a 100-pound load 40 nautical miles, releases it, flies 40 nautical miles back empty and lands at its launch point. On the second, it carries at least 150 pounds (68 kg) out 10 nautical miles (18.5 km) and returns empty, again without refueling. The aircraft must cruise at no less than 50 knots (93 km/h), stay below 1,000 feet (305 m) above ground, launch and recover without a catapult, net or arresting cable, and carry a transponder with at least Mode 3/C capability. Up to three more flights may be allowed to show other features.
Applicants must meet two threshold requirements just to be considered: the payload-and-range performance above and a powerplant that runs on heavy fuel such as JP-5, JP-8 or diesel, or on a hybrid fuel-battery system. The Navy also states a preference for aircraft with a maximum gross takeoff weight of up to 350 pounds (159 kg).
The Marine Corps’ current TRUAS is the TRV-150C, a battery-electric aircraft with eight rotors on four arms, designed by Malloy Aeronautics and sold in the United States by Survice Engineering. The Navy bought the first 21 in April 2023 for $8.4 million and declared initial operational capability on Oct. 27, 2023, with the 3rd Littoral Logistics Battalion at Marine Corps Base Hawaii. The Marine Corps later ordered 31 more TRV-150Cs in a $9.8 million contract modification. The Marine Corps rates the TRV-150C at about 9 miles (14 km) with a full 150-pound load. Increment II asks for the same load carried 18.5 km out and back, plus a 100-pound load over a round trip of 80 nautical miles (148 km).
Heavy-fuel engines would let the new aircraft draw from the same JP-8 or diesel supply that Marine vehicles and generators already use, instead of depending on charged battery packs in the field. The notice does not explain why the program chose that requirement.
Marine units have been using the TRV-150C for two years to work out how drone resupply fits into logistics formations. In October 2025, Marines pushed the TRUAS through field tests aimed at giving company and platoon commanders their own way to resupply small units in hard-to-reach places. In 2024, Marine officials said they planned to issue three to six TRUAS drones to every logistics battalion by 2028. The U.S. Army has also evaluated the TRV-150 at Fort Stewart, Georgia, in February 2026. The notice describes Increment II as an organic aerial distribution capability for small-unit logistics across the last tactical mile, in Expeditionary Advanced Base Operations and Distributed Operations.
The requirements tables attached to the notice go well beyond the demonstration flights. A single operator must be able to control up to four aircraft at once, and the system must accept natural-language voice commands such as changing heading or altitude. The complete system has to fit in one ruggedized container no larger than 4 by 3 by 2 feet and weighing no more than 150 pounds, be ready to launch within 20 minutes, and reach a mean time between failures of at least 30 flight hours, with 90 as the objective. By default, the aircraft must not launch without mission approval from the Marine Corps’ Multifunction Air Operations Center, though a designated supervisor can override that rule when no airspace control authority is available. It must also navigate without GPS, use encrypted radios that meet FIPS 140-3 Level 2, and keep its electrical components sealed to an IP-56 rating.
“Operating the TRUAS UCC shall be comparable in terms of ease and intuitiveness to common smartphone tasks, such as ordering food delivery or ride-sharing services,” the requirements table states.
Participation is limited to U.S.-based, U.S.-owned companies using U.S. manufacturing and repair facilities, or to firms that can show strict compliance with 10 U.S.C. § 4881 and the American Security Drone Act, which restrict the government’s purchase and use of foreign-made drones. Companies pay their own costs, must sign a cooperative research and development agreement before flying and must join the Naval Aviation Systems Consortium to be eligible for an award. There is no fee to apply.
The program has changed owners since Increment I, which was run by the Navy and Marine Corps Small Tactical Unmanned Aircraft Systems program office, PMA-263. Acting Secretary of the Navy Hung Cao established the Direct Reporting Portfolio Manager for Robotic and Autonomous Systems on Aug. 5, 2026, to bring requirements and acquisition of unmanned systems for the Navy and Marine Corps under a single office.
On request, the Navy may also share flight performance data with the Army-run Drones.mil Marketplace, an online storefront where U.S. units and allies can buy vetted drones. The Army said in October that the marketplace had generated more than $800 million in sales in its first four months.

Common pesticide linked to 2.5 times the risk of Parkinson’s disease
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
12:33:13 UTC
21:33:13 KST

Common pesticide linked to 2.5 times the risk of Parkinson’s disease
- Date:
- November 1, 2026
- Source:
- University of California - Los Angeles Health Sciences
- Summary:
- A UCLA study found that long-term exposure to a common pesticide was linked to more than 2.5 times the risk of Parkinson's disease. Scientists also uncovered how the chemical damages brain cells and identified a promising way to protect them.
- Share:
A pesticide used for decades in agriculture may be linked to a much greater risk of Parkinson's disease, and scientists have uncovered a possible explanation for how it damages the brain.
Researchers at UCLA Health found that people with long-term residential exposure to chlorpyrifos, a widely used pesticide, had more than 2.5 times the risk of developing Parkinson's disease compared with those who were not exposed. Laboratory experiments also revealed how the chemical can interfere with the brain's ability to remove damaged proteins, leading to the loss of nerve cells essential for controlling movement.
The study, published in Molecular Neurodegeneration, goes beyond identifying a connection between pesticide exposure and Parkinson's. By examining what happens inside affected brain cells, the researchers uncovered a biological mechanism that could eventually provide new ways to protect the brain from damage.
A Common Pesticide With a Troubling Link to Parkinson's
Parkinson's disease affects nearly one million Americans. The progressive neurological condition gradually damages brain cells involved in movement, often causing tremors, muscle stiffness, slowed movement, and difficulties with coordination.
One of the defining features of Parkinson's is the loss of neurons that produce dopamine. This chemical messenger allows nerve cells to communicate and helps the brain coordinate smooth, controlled movements. As dopamine levels decline, the brain becomes less capable of regulating those movements.
Although inherited genetic factors can influence who develops Parkinson's, researchers have increasingly focused on environmental exposures that may also contribute to the disease. Pesticides are of particular interest because some chemicals used to kill insects or other agricultural pests can also interfere with biological processes in the nervous system.
Chlorpyrifos has been used extensively in agriculture for decades. Its residential use was banned in the United States in 2001, and agricultural applications faced additional restrictions in 2021. However, the pesticide remains in use on many crops in the United States and continues to be widely applied in other countries.
Because exposure may have occurred years before symptoms appeared, understanding the potential long-term effects of chlorpyrifos is particularly important. Identifying specific chemicals associated with Parkinson's could help researchers develop prevention strategies and determine whether previously exposed individuals might benefit from additional neurological monitoring.
Researchers Find More Than Double the Parkinson's Risk
To investigate the connection, UCLA scientists examined information from 829 people diagnosed with Parkinson's disease and 824 people without the condition. All participants were enrolled in the university's long-running Parkinson's Environment and Genes study, which investigates how environmental exposures and inherited factors influence Parkinson's risk.
The researchers combined California's detailed pesticide application records with participants' residential and workplace address histories. This allowed them to estimate how much chlorpyrifos individuals may have encountered over time based on where they lived and worked.
The results revealed a striking association. People with prolonged residential exposure to chlorpyrifos had more than 2.5 times the risk of Parkinson's disease compared with those who had no such exposure.
Although this population analysis could not establish that the pesticide directly caused Parkinson's, the researchers took an additional step to investigate whether chlorpyrifos could produce the kinds of brain damage seen in people with the disease.
How the Pesticide Damages Brain Cells
The team exposed mice to chlorpyrifos in aerosol form for 11 weeks. The inhalation approach was designed to resemble a common way people may encounter pesticides in the environment.
The exposed mice developed movement difficulties and lost neurons responsible for producing dopamine. This was particularly significant because the degeneration of these same nerve cells is a central feature of Parkinson's disease.
The researchers also detected inflammation in the animals' brains, along with abnormal accumulations of a protein called alpha-synuclein.
Under normal conditions, alpha-synuclein is found in nerve cells and plays a role in their functioning. However, the protein can accumulate in abnormal clumps that are closely associated with Parkinson's disease. These deposits are a major focus of research into why certain brain cells gradually deteriorate.
Together, the findings showed that chlorpyrifos exposure could reproduce several important characteristics of Parkinson's in laboratory animals, strengthening the biological evidence behind the human population findings.
Scientists Uncover a Breakdown in the Brain's Cleanup System
The researchers then turned to zebrafish to investigate exactly how chlorpyrifos harms neurons. These small fish are frequently used in neuroscience research because they allow scientists to study biological processes involved in nerve cell development and survival.
Their experiments pointed to a disruption in autophagy, a natural cellular maintenance process that helps remove damaged proteins and other unwanted material.
Autophagy functions much like an internal recycling system. Cells use it to break down worn-out or defective components so that potentially harmful material does not accumulate. This process is especially important for neurons, many of which must remain functional throughout a person's lifetime.
When chlorpyrifos interfered with this cleanup system, damaged material accumulated inside neurons, contributing to their deterioration.
The researchers also made an encouraging discovery. When they restored the cellular cleanup process or removed synuclein protein in their experiments, the neurons were protected from damage.
This finding suggests that the pesticide's harmful effects may depend partly on a biological pathway that researchers could potentially target with future treatments.
A Potential New Strategy for Protecting Against Parkinson's
The discovery raises the possibility of developing therapies that strengthen the brain's cellular cleanup mechanisms and help protect vulnerable neurons. Such treatments might eventually prove useful for people exposed to chlorpyrifos or other pesticides that disrupt similar processes.
However, the protective effects have so far been demonstrated in laboratory models. Additional research will be needed to determine whether enhancing autophagy can prevent or reduce pesticide-related brain damage in humans.
Scientists also want to investigate whether other commonly used pesticides interfere with the same cellular mechanisms. Although chlorpyrifos use has declined in the United States, many people were exposed before restrictions were introduced, and related agricultural chemicals remain widely used.
The findings could also help identify people with a history of substantial pesticide exposure who may benefit from closer neurological monitoring. Earlier recognition of possible changes in brain function could become increasingly important as researchers work toward treatments that slow or prevent Parkinson's progression.
Dr. Jeff Bronstein, professor of Neurology at UCLA Health and the study's senior author, emphasized the importance of identifying a particular chemical rather than treating all pesticides as a single category.
"This study establishes chlorpyrifos as a specific environmental risk factor for Parkinson's disease, not just pesticides as a general class," said Dr. Jeff Bronstein.
"By showing the biological mechanism in animal models, we've demonstrated that this association is likely causal. The discovery that autophagy dysfunction drives the neurotoxicity also points us toward potential therapeutic strategies to protect vulnerable brain cells."

Deliveryman chases his poetic dream
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
20:32:32 CST
21:32:32 KST

Wang Jibing and his wife arrange goods at their family-run small store in Kunshan City, east China's Jiangsu Province, Oct. 8, 2026. Born in 1969 in east China's Jiangsu Province, Wang Jibing dropped out of school during junior high. To make a living, he worked as a construction worker, a sand dredger, a street vendor and a scrap collector. Yet, he never lost his appetite for reading, often lingering at secondhand book stalls and sifting through discarded newspapers. Life was hard, yet his love for literature never faded. "Literature is a candy in my life." He said. "I've never found that writing is mentally challenging. Passion is all that drives me."
In 2019, hearing that delivering food could pay well, Wang decided to give it a shot. At 50, he became the oldest courier at his station. On his way to deliver takeout food, while waiting for red lights and for the food to be served, he composed verses. When inspiration struck, he used his mobile phone to jot down moments of his experience on streets and the sentiment.
This year, Wang's poetry collection "Low Flight" won him the Lu Xun Literature Prize, making him the first takeout rider-turned-laureate. In plainspoken language, Wang captured the rhythms, challenges and moments of warmth that mark the lives of delivery riders: slippery roads during storms, brief exchanges between couriers and customers, and solitary journeys beneath streetlights late at night.
Since receiving the honor, he has received many work invitations. Even so, whenever he has free time, he still puts on his delivery uniform and rides through the streets of Kunshan.
"Delivering food keeps me grounded. It is where my power lies. To find fresh emotion and creative inspiration, I must stay immersed with real life." He said. (Xinhua/Ji Chunpeng)

Australia expands subsidized access to medicines for cystic fibrosis, cancer, thyroid disease
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
20:32:26 CST
21:32:26 KST

CANBERRA, Nov. 1 (Xinhua) -- The Australian government has expanded access to subsidized medicines for patients with cystic fibrosis, blood cancer and thyroid eye disease under the country's Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme (PBS), Health Minister Mark Butler said on Sunday.
Under the changes taking effect on Nov. 1, children aged six to 11 with cystic fibrosis who weigh less than 30 kg will be eligible for a granule form of Trikafta, a medicine targeting the underlying cause of the genetic condition.
The new formulation is designed to help children who have difficulty swallowing tablets. About 3,300 Australians are expected to benefit from the expanded listing each year, according to a government statement.
Without PBS subsidies, the treatment could cost patients more than 20,300 Australian dollars (about 14,200 U.S. dollars) per prescription.
The government has also added Tepezza to the PBS as a treatment for active, moderate-to-severe thyroid eye disease, with around 310 Australians expected to benefit annually.
Meanwhile, subsidized access to Adcetris has been expanded to provide a new first-line treatment option for patients with advanced CD30-positive classical Hodgkin lymphoma, a type of blood cancer, benefiting an estimated 370 Australians each year.
The PBS listing for Repatha, a medicine used to treat high cholesterol, has also been amended to allow eligible patients to obtain larger quantities under the government's 60-day prescription initiative.
Under the PBS, eligible patients will pay a maximum of 25 Australian dollars per prescription, or 7.70 Australian dollars for concession card holders.
The government said it has approved additional funding for 511 new and amended PBS listings since July 2022. ■

Australia introduces upfront fees for protection visa reviews
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
20:32:26 CST
21:32:26 KST

CANBERRA, Nov. 1 (Xinhua) -- People seeking reviews of most protection visa decisions in Australia are now required to pay an upfront application fee of 1,863.50 Australian dollars (about 1,300 U.S. dollars), the country's Administrative Review Tribunal (ART) announced on Sunday.
The new requirement, which took effect on Nov. 1 following amendments to Australia's Migration Regulations 1994, applies to applications for reviews of decisions to refuse or cancel protection visas, as well as certain decisions to withdraw protection findings.
Under the new rules, applicants must pay the fee when lodging a review application, rather than after the review process.
The tribunal said non-citizens held in immigration detention and applicants whose cases can be combined with another application for which a fee has already been paid are exempt from the requirement.
Applicants who successfully challenge a protection decision, or whose applications are found to be invalid, will receive a full refund.
However, those who withdraw their applications after Nov. 1 will be eligible for refunds only in very limited circumstances.
The tribunal said people who started online applications before Nov. 1 but failed to submit them before the new rules took effect must restart the application process and pay the upfront fee.
Applications lodged before Nov. 1 will generally remain subject to the previous payment arrangements, under which unsuccessful applicants are required to pay a fee after their reviews are completed. ■

Shang Chunsong wins Beijing Parkour World Cup gold, overall title
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
20:32:21 CST
21:32:21 KST

Gold medalist Shang Chunsong (C) of China, silver medalist Nagai Nene (L) of Japan and bronze medalist Isa Smits of the Netherlands pose on the podium during the awarding ceremony of the women's freestyle competition at the Parkour World Cup Beijing 2026 at Shougang Park in Beijing, capital of China, Nov. 1, 2026. (Xinhua/Zhang Chenlin)
BEIJING, Nov. 1 (Xinhua) -- China's Shang Chunsong won the women's freestyle gold medal at the 2026 Beijing Parkour World Cup on Sunday, securing the overall World Cup title in the season's final event.
The 30-year-old former artistic gymnast, who claimed bronze at the 2016 Rio Olympics, added to a successful season that included freestyle gold medals at the World Games in Chengdu, the World Championships in Kitakyushu and the World Cup in Montpellier.
Shang entered the Beijing event ranked second in the overall World Cup standings, level on points with Japan's Nene Nagai and the Netherlands' Noa Man, who had won the women's speed title.
The overall World Cup title is awarded to the athlete with the highest points total after the season's events, with rankings determined by each competitor's two best results.
Man failed to qualify for the freestyle final after competing in three speed runs on Saturday, while Shang topped the women's freestyle qualification standings by more than six points.
In Sunday's final, Shang impressed the home crowd with a series of difficult tricks across bars and walls, earning 26.8 points to claim both the event gold and the overall title.
Her teammates rushed onto the course to celebrate, lifting her into the air after her victory was confirmed.
"I'm very proud to win this gold at home. It has a special meaning for me and my team," Shang said. "I could have done better on my landing, but I'll work on that later. Right now, I just want to celebrate with my friends."
Nagai finished second with 22.3 points, while the Netherlands' Isa Smits edged China's Zhou Jie by 0.1 points to take bronze.
In the men's speed competition, Montpellier World Cup winner Siebe Van de Spijker claimed gold in 22.46 seconds, also securing the overall World Cup speed title.
Ukraine's Bohdan Kolmakov took silver, while Italy's Luca Demarchi finished third.
The Beijing competition, held from October 30 to November 1, was the third and final stop of the 2026 Parkour World Cup series. ■

Chinese Ambassador to Tanzania Chen Mingjian speaks at a farewell ceremony for Tanzanian exhibitors attending the ninth China International Import Expo (CIIE), in Dar es Salaam, Tanzania, Oct. 31, 2026. Tanzania is sending 36 enterprises and government institutions to the ninth CIIE, scheduled for Nov. 5 to 10 in Shanghai, as the country seeks to boost exports and expand access to the Chinese market. (Xinhua/Emmanuel Herman)
DAR ES SALAAM, Nov. 1 (Xinhua) -- Tanzania is sending 36 enterprises and government institutions to the ninth China International Import Expo (CIIE), scheduled for Nov. 5 to 10 in Shanghai, as the country seeks to boost exports and expand access to the Chinese market.
The delegation was introduced at a farewell ceremony organized by the Chinese Embassy in Tanzania in Dar es Salaam on Saturday, where some participating exhibitors displayed their products, including coffee, tea and honey.
Deputy Minister for Industry and Trade Dennis Londo said the expo offered Tanzanian businesses an important opportunity to showcase their products, establish partnerships and attract investors from China and other international markets.
He urged exhibitors to actively engage with potential buyers, understand Chinese market requirements and explore opportunities to increase exports of agricultural and value-added products.
Director of Trade Promotion at the Tanzania Trade Development Authority (TanTrade) Jonathan Nkwabi said that 36 enterprises from the public and private sectors had been mobilized for the country's participation, demonstrating a coordinated effort to promote Tanzanian products internationally.
Chinese Ambassador to Tanzania Chen Mingjian said China's zero-tariff policy for African countries maintaining diplomatic relations with China was creating new opportunities for Tanzanian exporters.
She said China's imports from Tanzania reached 290 million U.S. dollars in the first half of 2026, up 12 percent year on year, adding that the first consignment of Tanzanian honey had entered the Chinese market through a dedicated green channel for African agricultural products.
Chen said 15 categories of Tanzanian agricultural products had been granted access to the Chinese market, while 469 Tanzanian enterprises had registered to export agricultural and food products to China.
She encouraged Tanzanian businesses attending the expo to use the platform to establish commercial partnerships and bring more high-quality local products to Chinese consumers.
Cathy Wang, managing director of the East Africa Commercial and Logistics Center, said Tanzania's participation grew from six enterprises in 2021 to 36 enterprises and institutions this year, reflecting growing interest among local businesses in the Chinese market.
She said her organization was working with TanTrade to help exhibitors meet Chinese import standards and navigate export procedures, customs clearance and logistics. ■

India's External affairs minister S Jaishankar has discussed the protection of civilian shipping with Russia, Ukraine, and European nations
External affairs minister S Jaishankar on Sunday said India has held discussions with Russia, Ukraine and European countries on protecting civilian shipping, restoring grain exports through the Black Sea and preventing attacks on energy infrastructure amid the ongoing Russia-Ukraine war.According to news agency ANI, Speaking on the sidelines of the G20 foreign ministers' meeting in Atlanta, Jaishankar said India was engaging with the parties on three key aspects of the conflict, including the safety of civilian vessels and seafarers, the restoration of grain shipments from Russia and Ukraine, and preventing attacks on energy infrastructure. He said India was trying to bring the concerned parties together to address these issues."One, not to attack civilian shipping and seafarers," he said, outlining the first of the three areas discussed with Russia, Ukraine and Europe.
On the second issue, Jaishankar stressed the need to restore grain shipments from both Russia and Ukraine, warning that exports through the Black Sea had declined sharply amid the conflict."The second, to find a way by which the grain exports from both Russia and Ukraine, these are two major exporters of grain for the global markets, can be restored, because that flow has cut down very sharply in the Black Sea," he said.
Jaishankar further highlighted the complexities involved in ensuring the safety of energy infrastructure, saying different parties had different interpretations of what should be covered under such an understanding."And the third is with regard to energy. Non-attack on energy is probably the most complicated piece because it means different things to the different players. There is energy infrastructure itself. To some, it would mean a refinery; to some, it would mean grids. There would be issues relating to ships carrying fuel," he said.He added that India is attempting to bring the concerned parties together to find common ground on these issues, particularly on the protection of energy infrastructure and fuel shipments.
The concerns raised by Jaishankar extend beyond the immediate conflict, given the Black Sea's importance to global trade. Any disruption to commercial shipping can affect the movement of essential commodities, raise freight and insurance costs and put pressure on international supply chains.Similarly, attacks on refineries, electricity grids and fuel-carrying vessels can disrupt energy supplies and push up global prices. Together, the safety of maritime routes, grain exports and energy infrastructure remains critical to maintaining stability in global food and energy markets.
