Iran among 30 countries with rare blood preservation technology
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
12:24:26 UTC
21:24:26 KST

Iran among 30 countries with rare blood preservation technology
TEHRAN - Iran is among only 30 countries worldwide with the technology to preserve rare blood types for 10 to 30 years through glycerol-based cryopreservation, and is the only country in the region with this capability, according to the head of the Iran Blood Transfusion Organization (IBTO).
Rare blood types refer to blood groups that have a very low prevalence in society and are classified into three categories: rare, very rare, and extremely rare. A rare blood type is defined as one occurring in only 1 out of every 1,000 or one million people, Ahmad Qarah-Baghian, IBTO’s chief executive, told Mehr News Agency.
Once a rare blood type is identified, the IBTO collects required samples and freezes them for long-term storage. According to published scientific articles, rare blood type storage spans from 10 to 30 years. Based on some documentation, blood frozen for 20 years still remains usable.
People with rare blood types are identified in different ways, and they are invited to donate blood. Like others, these individuals can donate blood four times a year if they meet the requirements, he added.
According to Mehdi Karbadizadeh, an official with the IBTO, a total of 350 rare blood units are frozen and stored in the rare blood bank. Some 1,500 individuals with rare blood types are identified in the country. However, not all of them are eligible to donate blood.
‘Iran the only Islamic country in Eastern Mediterranean with rare blood program’
Iran is the only Islamic nation in the Eastern Mediterranean region that has a rare blood program, an official with the Iranian Blood Transfusion Organization (IBTO) has said.
In the Iranian year 1389 (2010-2011), the country joined the International Rare Blood Association, which currently has 30 member states, IRNA quoted Mehdi Karbasizadeh as saying.
The official went on to say that Iran, China, and Japan are the only member states of the association in Asia that have rare blood management programs.
One out of 5,000 to 10,000 individuals in Iran has a rare blood type. The frequency of rare blood types in each country depends on its population and the blood type. Bombay blood type is among the rarest blood groups known in the country, the official added.
There are currently fewer than 10 of the rarest blood types and 30 rare blood types in the country. About 150 out of 376 solidified units of blood stored at a rare blood bank are the rarest, Karbasizadeh said.
Presently, 262 individuals with a really rare blood type are identified in the country, but not all of them can donate blood.
The official urged those with (really) rare blood types to donate blood at least once a year, saying that blood units solidified at minus 65 to 85 degrees centigrade can be stored for 10 years.
In 2025, Jaffar Hussain, the former World Health Organization (WHO) Representative to Iran, highlighted Iran’s capacity to serve as a model for other nations in the realm of blood transfusion and rare blood management.
Addressing National Rare Blood Day on January 22, the official praised the country’s steadfast commitment to equitable health care access, ensuring that no one is left behind, regardless of their blood type.
National Rare Blood Day is a day dedicated to celebrating the lives saved, challenges overcome, and unwavering commitment to ensuring every individual, regardless of their blood type, has a fighting chance at life.
The official commended the country’s unwavering dedication to tackling the unique challenges surrounding rare blood, emphasizing the critical importance of collaboration, innovation, and unwavering determination in this global endeavour, the WHO website announced in a press release on January 27.
Hussain painted a vivid picture of the struggles faced by those with rare blood types, individuals who often find themselves in desperate need, their lives hanging in the balance as they search for that elusive, compatible match.
He paid tribute to these unsung heroes, recognizing their generosity and unwavering commitment to the well-being of others. “Blood donors,” he declared, “represent the epitome of human solidarity, offering a lifeline to those in need without expecting anything in return.”
WHO, Hussain emphasized, believes that universal health coverage must encompass access to safe blood and blood products. He lauded IBTO’s leadership in blood safety and transfusion services, highlighting their remarkable achievement of a 100 percent voluntary, non-remunerated blood donation system, a testament to the principles of universal health coverage in action.
In closing, the official extended his deepest gratitude to the IBTO for their unwavering dedication to advancing blood transfusion services and ensuring equitable access to rare blood. He thanked the blood donors, whose selflessness serves as an inspiration to all.
The event concluded with a renewed commitment to innovation, partnership and universal health coverage, leaving attendees with a sense of determination to continue the fight for rare blood access, ensuring that every drop counts, every donation matters and every life is valued.
In July 1979, the IBTO was established to organize blood transfusion activities, promote blood donation, and supply safe blood and its products free of charge for patients suffering from diseases like hemophilia, thalassemia, and leukemia.
Iran is the only Islamic country that is a member of the International Society of Blood Transfusion’s rare blood donor working party (ISBT WP).
Thanks to a rich culture of selflessness, the country maintains a six-month blood reserve ensuring preparedness for crises.
Blood reserves and their products are considered strategic and vital resources for the country, and voluntary donations help to meet the needs of the country, particularly during crisis.

Some 90 earthquakes hit Iran in a week

Some 90 earthquakes hit Iran in a week
TEHRAN – A total of 89 earthquakes have been recorded across the country in a week from October 24 to 30, according to the seismological networks of the Institute of Geophysics of the University of Tehran.
Statistically, 79 earthquakes with magnitudes smaller than 3, and 10 earthquakes with a magnitude between 3 and 4 have occurred in the country, irsc reported.
Of the total quakes, one had a magnitude of 3.9 on the Richter scale which occurred on October 28 in Bushehr province.
Among the provinces of the country, Khorasan Razavi experienced the highest number of earthquakes with 14, followed by Yazd with 9, Semnan with 9, and Khuzestan with 7 earthquakes.
During the same period, four earthquakes hit Tehran. No earthquakes were recorded in Alborz, Ilam, Zanjan, Sistan-Baluchestan, Qom, Qazvin, Kordestan, Markazi, and Hamedan provinces.
A total of 2,380 earthquakes with a magnitude of more than 2.5 on the Richter scale were recorded across the country over the past calendar year (March 2025–March 2026), according to the Seismological networks of the Institute of Geophysics of the University of Tehran, Mehr news agency reported.
Out of recorded earthquakes, 910 had a magnitude greater than 3, 130 had a magnitude greater than 4, and 15 had a magnitude greater than 5 on the Richter scale.
The Iranian plateau is located in a very seismically active region of the world and is known not only for its major catastrophic earthquakes but also for the disasters relating to natural hazards, especially earthquakes.
About 2 percent of the earthquakes in the world occur in Iran, but more than 6 percent of the victims of the world’s earthquakes during the 20th century are reported from Iranian earthquakes.

Number commercial trucks going into Gaza falls by over 50%
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
12:11:19 UTC
21:11:19 KST

Breadcrumb
Number of commercial trucks into Gaza falls by over 50% in October amid Israeli restrictions
The number of commercial trucks entering the Gaza Strip fell by 53.5% in October compared to September, marking a sharp decline that reduced the flow of goods into local markets.
This coincided with a drop in food supplies and consumer goods, continued shortages, and rising prices following the closure of the crossing to commercial traffic for more than a week.
Statistics released by the Crossings and Borders Authority showed that 1,758 commercial trucks entered the Gaza Strip in October, compared with 3,781 in September—a decrease of 2,023 trucks. The total number of incoming trucks, including commercial shipments, aid and fuel, also fell from 5,265 to 3,836, a decline of 27.1%, or 1,429 trucks.
By contrast, the number of aid trucks increased from 1,244 in September to 1,815 in October, a rise of 45.9%. Fuel trucks also increased from 240 to 263, representing a 9.6% increase. However, these increases did not offset the sharp decline in commercial traffic, which is a key source of goods and product variety in local markets.
Decline in food supplies
By category of goods, the number of trucks carrying food supplies and groceries fell from 3,450 in September to 2,337 in October, a decrease of 1,113 trucks, or 32.3%.
The number of trucks carrying consumer goods and household items also declined from 1,273 to 799, a drop of 37.2%. Meanwhile, trucks carrying medical and healthcare equipment and supplies fell from 104 to 76, a decrease of 26.9%.
Trucks carrying shelter and relief supplies increased from 139 to 330.
Trucks carrying animal feed and seeds fell from 45 to 27, a decline of 40%. Those carrying corrugated zinc sheets decreased from five to four, while October's statistics recorded no trucks specifically designated for transporting water, compared with nine in September.
These figures reflect a widening gap in the flow of commercial goods into the Gaza Strip, despite the increase in aid trucks. The impact of this decline is not limited to the volume of incoming goods; it also affects the variety of products available and traders' ability to meet consumer needs.
Rising prices
These developments come as local markets continue to experience shortages of a number of essential and consumer goods, alongside rising prices and declining purchasing power among residents as a result of the war, damage to economic activity, and the loss of income sources.
Reduced commercial imports mean smaller quantities of goods are available to consumers and limit traders' ability to replenish depleted stocks. This adds to pressure on markets, particularly given the heavy reliance on imported goods and the decline in local production.
The effects of the closure of the Kerem Shalom crossing—the only crossing connecting Gaza to the outside world for commercial traffic—continue to weigh on the market. Shortages of supplies are continuing to affect the availability and prices of goods, as residents face increasingly difficult living conditions.
The comparison between September and October highlights the scale of the decline in commercial activity: commercial trucks fell by more than half, while the total number of incoming trucks decreased by more than a quarter. This underscores the challenges facing local markets and the need to resume a regular flow of commercial goods to address shortages and ease price pressures and the growing cost-of-living burden.

Your teenage mental health may say something about your vote at 40, study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
12:00:51 UTC
21:00:51 KST

A person’s mental health trajectory starting in adolescence predicts their political preferences nearly three decades later. Researchers found that early experiences with anxiety or behavioral issues are associated with distinct voting patterns and lower political trust in midlife. The research was published in the journal Political Psychology.
Political scientists and psychologists often study how adverse life events shape civic participation. Many studies evaluate how factors like poverty, discrimination, or dropping out of high school change adult voting habits. The specific role of mental health development over a person’s life has received less attention in political science.
Researchers wanted to understand if persistent psychological challenges correspond with specific political profiles. Sam Fluit, a psychology researcher at the University of Oslo, led a team to investigate this relationship. They focused on two broad categories of mental health conditions that often begin in youth.
The first category is internalizing problems, which refer to inward-facing symptoms. These typically include feelings of depression, general anxiety, and a sense of hopelessness about the future.
The second category involves externalizing problems, which describe outward-facing maladaptive actions. In adolescence, this might look like vandalism, skipping school, or getting into physical fights. In adulthood, externalizing behaviors often transition into issues like substance abuse, driving under the influence, or aggression in the workplace.
The researchers analyzed data from a large study of 2,215 individuals in Norway. The participants were tracked across five different time points over 28 years. The study began in the early 1990s when the subjects were around 15 years old and concluded in 2020 when they were in their early forties. At each stage, the participants reported the frequency and severity of their mental health symptoms.
During the final survey in midlife, the participants answered questions about twelve different political preferences. These included their voting history, their level of trust in government, their trust in other people, and their general interest in politics.
The survey also measured specific ideological attitudes. Participants placed themselves on the left-to-right political spectrum and answered questions about their views on social equality. They also reported their perceptions of immigrants and their support for conservative policies, such as stricter punishments for criminals.
To understand the data, the team grouped participants based on how their mental health symptoms changed over time. For internalizing problems, they identified three distinct life paths. Most people maintained a low, stable level of symptoms. A second group started with elevated symptoms in adolescence that decreased over time, while a third, smaller group experienced elevated symptoms that actually increased as they grew older.
For externalizing problems, the researchers categorized the participants into two paths. The vast majority of the sample had elevated outward-facing behavioral issues in their youth that eventually declined. A smaller group exhibited elevated externalizing problems that remained steady from adolescence into adulthood.
The researchers then examined how these distinct mental health paths corresponded to adult political outcomes. They discovered that elevated levels of either internalizing or externalizing problems were associated with lower voter turnout. Among the internalizing groups, those whose elevated adolescent symptoms later decreased were less likely to have voted in the last national election than those with low, stable symptoms. Among the externalizing groups, those with persistently elevated problems were less likely to have voted than those whose problems declined.
Both categories of mental health challenges were also linked to lower political and social trust in midlife. Participants in the elevated internalizing groups and the stable externalizing group reported less faith in political institutions. They were also less likely to agree that other people could be trusted in general.
When looking at specific political leanings, the two types of mental health problems diverged. Participants who had elevated internalizing problems in adolescence tended to develop a more left-wing political profile by midlife, regardless of whether their symptoms later increased or decreased. They were less likely to vote for mainstream center-right parties. Those whose internalizing symptoms decreased over time were especially likely to vote for far-left political parties.
The researchers proposed that people dealing with depression and anxiety might be drawn to egalitarian political platforms. Left-leaning ideologies often focus on systemic inequalities, which might resonate with individuals seeking political environments that prioritize social inclusion and community support.
On the other hand, individuals with persistently high externalizing problems demonstrated a more right-wing political profile. This group was more likely to oppose social equality and express support for conservative policies. They also reported higher levels of perceived threat from immigrants.
When casting their ballots, people in this stable externalizing group were twice as likely to vote for populist-right parties. They were half as likely to vote for center-left parties compared to their peers. Externalizing problems are often characterized by antagonism and a general opposition to others. The authors suggested this adversarial worldview might translate into support for populist politicians who use exclusionary rhetoric or position themselves against the established political system.
Because the study relies on observational survey data, the results do not prove that mental health conditions directly alter a person’s political ideology. The relationship might work in multiple directions, with political beliefs and emotional well-being influencing each other over time in a reinforcing loop.
The researchers could only measure political attitudes at the final survey in midlife. This limitation meant they could not track how those specific views shifted simultaneously with mental health changes during adolescence. The externalizing behavior assessments also had to change as the participants aged, since teenagers and adults break rules in different ways.
The data also comes from a single country with a strong social welfare system and a multi-party political landscape. The extensive social safety net in Norway might buffer some of the political disillusionment that can accompany chronic health problems. Different associations might emerge in nations with fewer social protections or in countries dominated by a two-party electoral system.
Future research could explore these dynamics in other populations and track political attitudes from an earlier age. Measuring specific mechanisms, such as how educational attainment or economic hardship link mental health to political choices, might help explain how early psychological experiences translate into adult voting behavior.
The study, “The mental health–politics nexus: How mental health trajectories from adolescence to midlife shape political attitudes and voting patterns,” was authored by Sam Fluit, Kinga Bierwiaczonek, Jonas R. Kunst, and Tilmann von Soest.

Top Trump Officials Are Hitting the Campaign Trail Ahead of the Midterms. Are They Allowed To?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
12:00:04 UTC
21:00:04 KST

Top Trump Administration officials have taken to the campaign trail to boost Republican candidates ahead of the pivotal midterm elections as the party battles to retain control of Congress.
Last month alone, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Federal Communications Commission Chair Brendan Carr, and Interior Secretary Doug Burgum appeared alongside President Donald Trump to support Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in his tight reelection fight against Democrat Mary Peltola at a rally in Wasilla, Alaska, on Oct. 13. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth appeared in Wisconsin alongside GOP Rep. Derrick Van Orden on Oct. 20 to speak to manufacturing workers during a Pentagon tour highlighting U.S. defense production. Last Monday, Vice President JD Vance and Burgum spoke at a rally in Topeka, Kansas. And on Tuesday, Secretary of State Marco Rubio briefly joined Trump on stage, at the President’s urging, during a rally in Corpus Christi, Texas.
Cabinet members and other leading Trump officials have been wading into the midterms in these and other ways for months. In August, for instance, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy endorsed Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers in Michigan.
Legal experts and advocacy groups contend that in making such moves, members of the Administration have violated a decades-old law: the Hatch Act, passed by Congress in 1939, which places restrictions on certain political activities for federal executive branch employees.
The Administration has argued that the officials have participated in political events in a strictly personal capacity, which is permitted under the Hatch Act, and that their actions have been cleared by lawyers and ethics officials.
But several top Trump aides—including at least nine of his 15 Cabinet secretaries—have been hit with formal complaints that their actions have violated the law.
“The number of Hatch Act violation complaints is extreme and abnormal for election time, especially for complaints against senior officials,” Kedric Payne, the head of ethics at the Campaign Legal Center, a legal non-profit that has filed a complaint against the Trump Administration for using taxpayer money to fund political ads, tells TIME.
“We are seeing with the Trump Administration why the Hatch Act is so important,” Payne says, “because when it is not enforced quickly, it can be abused.”
Here’s what to know about the Hatch Act, and the accusations that Trump officials have violated it.
What is the Hatch Act?
The Hatch Act is an 87-year-old federal law that prohibits certain government employees from using their “official authority or influence for the purpose of interfering with or affecting the result of an election,” among other limits it imposes on officials’ political activity. It states that such interference applies to “an activity directed toward the success or failure of a political party” or candidate.
The law was established to ensure that “federal programs are administered in a nonpartisan fashion, to protect federal employees from political coercion in the workplace, and to ensure that federal employees are advanced based on merit and not based on political affiliation,” according to the Office of Special Counsel (OSC), which enforces it.
Many of the Hatch Act complaints against Trump officials on the campaign trail have centered around one specific aspect of the law that says federal employees cannot use or identify with their official title while engaging in political activity. In a handful of such complaints against members of the Administration, legal and press advocacy groups have pointed out that they were introduced at rallies by their Cabinet positions.
“Political activity must be conducted purely in your personal capacity, without using your official title, without implying endorsement of the United States government. In your personal time at your own personal expense,” Richard Painter, the former chief White House ethics lawyer under George W. Bush and a professor at the University of Minnesota law school, tells TIME.
The Trump Administration has pushed back on the accusations, saying that its members were acting in a personal capacity at the times in question.
How Trump Administration officials have been accused of violating the Hatch Act on the campaign trail
A number of complaints have been filed against the Trump Administration for violating the Hatch Act in recent months.
Two advocacy non-profits, The Democracy Defenders Fund and Reporters Without Borders, filed a complaint in October over the rally in Alaska that featured Trump, Lutnick, Burgum, and Carr. The groups claimed that Carr “impermissibly mixed his official work into his personal remarks” and requested that the OSC open an investigation into each Trump official’s conduct at the rally.
In September, the two advocacy groups also filed a complaint against Duffy for his appearance in Michigan and his endorsement of Rogers.
Chief Counsel at the Democracy Defenders Fund said in a statement that Duffy’s conduct “crossed the legal and ethical line” and more broadly stated that it was “part of a broader pattern of this administration playing fast and loose with the law.”
Spokespeople for the Interior and Transportation departments have denied wrongdoing on the part of their respective leaders to media outlets. The FCC and Commerce Department did not immediately respond to TIME’s request for comment.
These complaints are among many more that have been filed over Administration officials’ participation in campaign activities.
“We haven't seen since the first Trump Administration this number of complaints against officials, and I've lost track, but I do think it's well over 20 complaints just in recent weeks,” Payne says.
In addition to complaints over officials’ appearances at campaign rallies, others have similarly alleged that Trump officials used their official titles in efforts to influence the midterms through social media and television network appearances.
CREW, a nonprofit government watchdog organization, has made several such claims. In one complaint from earlier this month, it argued that White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller violated the Hatch Act during an interview on Fox News in which he spoke against specific Democratic candidates running for office and urged voters to support a “pro-American Trump agenda.” The group has also filed complaints against Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. and Federal Bureau of Investigation Director Kash Patel for comments made while speaking to Fox.
“These accusations are baseless and amount to a manufactured political attack," the Department of Health and Human Services said in a statement. "Secretary Kennedy takes his ethical obligations seriously, follows federal ethics laws, and consults HHS career ethics officials to ensure his activities comply with the standards governing public service.”
The Department of Department of Justice, which houses the FBI, did not immediately respond to TIME’s request for comment regarding the accusations against Patel.
When asked about the various Hatch Act complaints against Administration officials, White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis tells TIME that “it has long been established that senior administration officials are allowed to discuss current events, policies, and the candidates involved with those policies in order to advance the agenda of the administration.”
Complaints allege further Hatch Act violations
Top Trump officials have additionally been accused of violating the Hatch Act through other means than direct statements and appearances in support of—or opposition to—midterm candidates that complaints allege may also affect the outcome of upcoming elections.
Payne and his colleagues filed a complaint accusing several Administration officials of using taxpayer money for political ads which the complaint describes as “touting partisan and political rhetoric” to influence the outcome of the midterms. The complaint cites three ads: one that promotes Trump’s actions in Iran, another that decries socialism, and a third that features Trump speaking at Mount Rushmore. The Campaign Legal Center in its complaint quotes parameters set by the OSC that say the Hatch Act is designed “to prevent the use of federal power and taxpayer resources to shape electoral outcomes and to preserve public confidence in the nonpartisan administration of the law.”
“Voters deserve to know that elected officials are campaigning using their own money and not taxpayer dollars,” Payne says. “Clearly these advertisements that were paid for by U.S. taxpayer dollars were intended to promote the Republican Party and influence the upcoming election.”
The complaint specifically requests an investigation into Trump officials including Office of Management and Budget Director Russell Vought, Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles, and White House Appointments Secretary Natalie Harp for their involvement in putting together the ads.
“There’s a statute that prohibits use of government funds for publicity or propaganda, unless expressly permitted by Congress,” Painter says. “Those ads that Trump was paying for with taxpayer dollars that said ‘paid for by the White House,’ that was propaganda. That violated that statute.”
Trump has defended the ads by saying he was “only promoting the country,” rather than specific candidates. “That’s an ad for the spirit of our country,” he said when asked about the ads in the Oval Office in September.
A Hatch Act complaint was also filed against the Administration by the Democracy Defenders Fund over the raid federal agents conducted at Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar’s home in Minnesota in October. The raid was reportedly part of an ongoing Department of Justice investigation into potential immigration fraud. Omar has denied all wrongdoing.
“The timing of this outrageous action against a long-time target of Trump’s evinces illegal political intent,” Norm Eisen, the co-founder of Democracy Defenders Fund, said in a statement. “Staging a public raid on the home of a sitting member of Congress weeks before a consequential election is an abuse of power.”
Trump has maintained that he has “nothing to do” with the investigation, but has continued to levy public attacks against Omar, including calling her “crooked.”
The flurry of recent complaints against the Trump Administration are far from the first instances in which the President and his aides have come under fire for alleged Hatch Act violations.
An OSC report from 2021, for instance, found that in 2020, at least 13 senior Trump Administration officials violated the Hatch Act.
What is the penalty for a Hatch Act violation?
Following an investigation by the OSC, disciplinary measures for Hatch Act violations are determined by the Merit Systems Protection Board (MSPB), an independent judicial agency within the Executive branch. For Cabinet or senior officials, OSC refers its findings to the President, who determines disciplinary action.
“The potential of those consequences happening under this President are small because it is up to the President usually to hold members of the administration accountable when they violate the Hatch Act,” Payne says, noting that in some cases, officials may be required to only issue a public apology for their violation, or face no consequence at all.
Federal officials who have previously been found to have violated the Hatch Act under Trump largely have not faced repercussions because the President either declined to punish them or because the OSC reported the violations after Trump and the officials in question left office.
After one OSC report from 2018 found Kellyanne Conway, a former counselor to Trump, had violated the Hatch Act, for example, Trump declined to fire her, telling Fox & Friends at the time that “it looks to me like they’re trying to take away her right of free speech and that’s just not fair.”
The OSC itself has meanwhile acknowledged that it was reporting other violations at a point when disciplinary action could not be taken. “Though discipline is no longer possible once subjects leave government service, OSC is issuing this report to fully document the violations, highlight the enforcement challenges that OSC confronted in investigating the violations, and to deter similar violations in the future,” one OSC report from 2021 reads.
Federal employees can face several civil penalties if they are found to have violated the Hatch Act, however, including a fine, a suspension, or a letter of reprimand. For a criminal violation, up to three years in prison may be imposed as a penalty if an official is found to have “intimidate[ed], threaten[ed], command[ed], or coerce[ed] … any employee of the Federal Government … to engage in, or not to engage in, any political activity.”
“If President Trump or anyone overreaches the point of trying to coerce someone in the government to engage in partisan conduct, that's a violation of the criminal provision of the act, but all the rest of it's civil,” Painter explains.

COP17: Nations chart ‘Yerevan Pathway’ to speed up action for nature
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

COP17: Nations chart ‘Yerevan Pathway’ to speed up action for nature
At the halfway mark to 2030, countries meeting in Armenia have agreed a roadmap to accelerate action for nature, after a global review found the world off track to meet its biodiversity targets.
Agreement was formalised through the Yerevan Pathway as the UN Biodiversity Conference (COP17) closed in the Armenian capital on Saturday.
It sets out priorities for the four years left to deliver the 23 targets of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework.
Mixed message
“We cannot protect nature while continuing to finance its destruction,” said Astrid Schomaker, Executive Secretary of the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD).
The pathway calls on countries to tackle subsidies that harm nature and to increase financial, scientific and technical support for developing countries.
It also calls for national budgets and economic decisions to be aligned with the framework, and for stronger monitoring and reporting.
“Over these two weeks we have demonstrated that differences can be bridged, commitments can become decisions and cooperation can deliver,” said COP17 President Hambardzum Matevosyan.
Progress made
Parties adopted nearly 50 decisions, covering areas including protected areas and forests, wildlife management, invasive alien species, marine and coastal biodiversity, and synthetic biology.
After intensive negotiations, they also agreed the Sevan Guidelines.
These set the rules of operation for a new permanent body strengthening the role of Indigenous Peoples and local communities in shaping global biodiversity policy.
Funding boost
Nearly $2 billion in new biodiversity funding was announced. This included $560 million under the Global Environment Facility’s latest replenishment and $500 million through the Species Recovery Alliance.
Another $330 million is going to the Value Nature Fund, which aims to mobilise private capital for nature.
Other initiatives included a new biodiversity bond and investment incubator launched by the Asian Development Bank, and new indicators to improve biodiversity monitoring and accountability.
Spirit of compromise
“In Yerevan, we saw environmental multilateralism prevail once again,” said Inger Andersen, Executive Director of the UN Environment Programme (UNEP).
“Countries came together, found the spirit of compromise and allowed us to agree important decisions that will support real progress for people and for planet.”
The next conference, COP18, will be held in Ecuador, with two years remaining to achieve the targets.
“Ultimately, the test is not what governments agreed in Yerevan, but what they change when they return home,” said Ms. Schomaker.

Western Sahara: UN ‘stands ready’ to keep supporting peace efforts as MINURSO mission ends
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

Western Sahara: UN ‘stands ready’ to keep supporting peace efforts as MINURSO mission ends
The UN remains committed to supporting a just, lasting and mutually acceptable political solution in Western Sahara that provides for the self-determination of its people, Secretary-General António Guterres said on Sunday, as the UN peacekeeping mission there began to wind down.
The departure of the UN Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara (MINURSO) “does not abrogate” the people’s “inalienable right to self-determination”, his statement said, delivered by his Spokesperson.
It called on all parties “to respect and promote the rights of the people of Western Sahara.”
The mission’s mandate expired at midnight on Saturday, after the Security Council failed on Friday to agree on its future.
A draft resolution from the United States was vetoed by Russia, while a rival Russian text failed to win the nine votes needed for adoption.
Although MINURSO’s operations have now ended, the UN will keep working towards a peaceful resolution through the Secretary-General’s Personal Envoy, Staffan de Mistura.
Orderly withdrawal
Mr. Guterres recognized the “central role” MINURSO has played since 1991 in helping to monitor the ceasefire and in creating conditions for the pursuit of a political solution.
He expressed his “deepest gratitude” to the mission’s personnel, including the Special Representative for Western Sahara, Alexander Ivanko. Mr. Ivanko led the mission through a “particularly challenging period" after hostilities resumed in 2020.
The UN chief also paid tribute to the 20 MINURSO personnel who lost their lives during the mission’s 35 years in the territory.
When its mandate ended, the mission was headquartered in Laayoune, with nine team sites – four west of the berm and five east of it – and a liaison office in Tindouf.
It had about 200 civilian staff, military observers and staff officers from over 35 countries, and a dedicated mine action capability.
Sunday marks the start of a liquidation period. A smaller team reporting to the UN Department of Operational Support will oversee the disposal of UN equipment.
Mr. Guterres called for the full cooperation of the parties so the process can be completed in an orderly way as soon as possible.
‘Maximum restraint’
The Secretary-General said he remains concerned about the security situation throughout the territory and the risk of hostilities escalating.
He urged all concerned “to exercise maximum restraint and to refrain from actions that could further increase tensions or undermine regional stability.”
Divided council
The US delegate in the council on Friday said his country’s draft would have supported the principle of self-determination and “moved the 50-year conflict forward”, calling the status quo unacceptable.
Explaining the veto, the Russian delegate said the text would have imposed one-sided solutions, describing his vote as “a life-saving veto, so to speak”.
Russia’s alternative, a one-year extension of the mandate to 31 October 2027, failed to attract enough support from the 15 nation body.
MINURSO was established under Council resolution 690 (1991), in line with UN-Organization of African Unity settlement proposals accepted in 1988 by Morocco and the Frente POLISARIO.
These provided for a referendum in which the people of Western Sahara would choose between independence and integration with Morocco. While the referendum never took place, MINURSO continued to carry out the tasks entrusted to it by the council.
In 2007, Morocco put forward an Autonomy Proposal as a basis for negotiations. It envisages the territory as self-governing under Moroccan sovereignty.
In closing, the statement said that while MINURSO’s peacekeeping operations had concluded, “the United Nations stands ready to continue supporting efforts to advance dialogue and pursue a peaceful resolution of the conflict.”

Breaking the silence in Mexico’s barracks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

Breaking the silence in Mexico’s barracks
In Mexico’s armed forces, an order from a superior is meant to be obeyed without question. For many women in uniform, investigative journalist Zorayda Gallegos found, that can include an order to step into an officer’s bedroom.
“If an officer says, ‘Come into my bedroom,’ she must go in, otherwise she would be disobeying an order from her superior,” she told UN News.
Her investigation into sexual violence inside the military has won her the 2026 Breach/Valdez Award for Journalism and Human Rights. It has also made her a target, in one of the most dangerous countries in the world to be a reporter.
Her story, told ahead of the International Day to End Impunity for Crimes Against Journalists on Monday, shows both why a free press matters and how much it can cost.
An X-ray of impunity
Her report, Sexual violence in the barracks: an X-ray of impunity, tracked more than 520 women who reported sexual offences over a 12-year period.
Only three per cent of those cases ended in a conviction. The other 97 per cent led to no effective sanctions.
This is not an isolated problem, Ms. Gallegos says, but a structural one. It reaches beyond the barracks into military schools and hospitals.
She also documented how high-ranking officials cover up abuse, and how gender inequality and institutional obstacles discourage victims from filing complaints at all.
Taught to follow orders
For Ms. Gallegos, part of the problem starts with military training itself, which she describes as “a very hierarchical, top-down system where women are always taught to follow orders from their superiors”.
That leaves female soldiers vulnerable to the very officers they answer to.
Deep-rooted sexism makes things worse, she maintains, shaping who gets which jobs and who gets promoted. Female soldiers are often assigned tasks associated with “caregiving and nursing, even though they are qualified for higher-ranking positions,” she explains.
Forgive, forget, carry on
Women who do get their cases to court risk being victimised all over again. Some judicial rulings, she found, contain sexist remarks or lack any gender perspective.
Inside the institution, she says, the psychological support offered to complainants is geared towards getting them to forgive their aggressors, forget what happened and carry on with their military careers.
The men accused, meanwhile, are often given recommendations rather than punishments – “that’s the maximum”, Ms. Gallegos alleges.
To break the cycle of silence and impunity, she believes more women are needed in senior military leadership and decision-making roles, and in the judiciary and prosecution services.
Uncomfortable truths
Exposing all this has come at a personal cost. Ms. Gallegos has faced intimidating remarks, veiled threats and pressure because of her work.
She still defends the right to publish information in the public interest, and to report independently and impartially.
In Mexico, that takes courage. The UN Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) regularly highlights the country as one of the deadliest in the world for the press, even though it is not officially at war.
Collusion between organized crime and local authorities is a serious threat to reporters, and its effects are felt at every level of the justice system. Journalists investigating politics or crime face threats, kidnapping, enforced disappearance and murder, and many are forced to flee abroad.
Deadly profession
According to UNESCO which tallies threats to media workers worldwide, 154 journalists have been murdered in Mexico in the past 20 years.
The agency has confirmed that eight journalists have been murdered in Mexico so far in 2026.
Press freedom groups including Article 19 and Reporters Without Borders (RSF) put the toll at nine, after the killing of Hamurabi Huesca Manzano in Oaxaca on 9 October.
The award Ms. Gallegos won carries the names of two of those killed. Miroslava Breach and Javier Valdez were assassinated because of their work.
“They always stood for brave journalism, rooted in their communities and committed to telling uncomfortable truths. Until it cost them their lives. That should never have happened,” she said.

"Rahul Gandhi is speaking and empty chairs. Congress couldn't even fill full Ramlila Maidan of capacity 50,000. Super Flop rally," Patra said
NEW DELHI: BJP on Sunday mocked the INDIA bloc's rally at Delhi's Ramlila Maidan, calling it a "super flop" event and claiming that around 40% of the ground was empty. BJP MP Sambit Patra took a swipe at Congress leader Rahul Gandhi and other opposition leaders, questioning their claims of a massive turnout and asking where the 10 lakh people they had expected to gather were."Rahul Gandhi is speaking and empty chairs. Congress couldn't even fill full Ramlila Maidan of capacity 50,000. Super Flop rally," Patra said, sharing a video of the gathering.Speaking to reporters, Patra said the BJP had been watching the rally since morning and listening to Gandhi's address, but felt it had ultimately been a "complete waste of time".
"Where were the 10 lakh people? Show us. No one becomes a leader or Prime Minister through such tricks. PM doesn't just mean Prime Minister. P stands for Paseena (sweat) and M stands for Mehnat (hard work). A Prime Minister is made through sweat and hard work. Despite bringing together so many parties and flags, they could not manage to gather 10 lakh people," he said.
Accusing the opposition of using camera angles to create an impression of a larger gathering, Patra dismissed the visuals as "trick photography". He also took a swipe at Gandhi, saying, "Rahul ji, Hindustan is not your abujan’s property.
Hindustan belongs to Hindustanis. Here, even a chaiwala can become the Prime Minister, and that is what bothers you."The INDIA bloc rally was organised to protest alleged electoral irregularities and raise the issue of 'vote chori'. Addressing the gathering, Rahul said that Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar would be removed from office and face jail for "treason" in the future.
He also warned Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Union home minister Amit Shah that they would face legal action over alleged vote theft."Amit Shah ji said Narendra Modi is not going anywhere. I am telling you the opposite: Narendra Modi cannot go anywhere; even if he wants to go, we will not let him," Gandhi said, adding that the opposition would stand against the two leaders after Gyanesh Kumar.

Scientists shrink Archimedes’ screw to the size of a single molecule
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
11:55:46 UTC
20:55:46 KST

Scientists shrink Archimedes’ screw to the size of a single molecule
- Date:
- November 1, 2026
- Source:
- University of Augsburg
- Summary:
- Scientists have built a groundbreaking molecular motor that spins in either direction using electricity, inspired by a machine invented more than 2,000 years ago. Even more remarkably, its rotation can boost electrical conductivity by up to 100 times, potentially transforming the future of molecular electronics.
- Share:
Scientists have developed a remarkable new molecular motor that spins when electricity passes through it. Inspired by an ancient invention, the tiny machine can even reverse its direction when the electrical voltage is switched. The achievement marks an important step toward creating working machines at the smallest possible scale.
Molecular machines are widely seen as a promising next frontier in miniaturization. Nature already provides examples inside living cells, where molecular motors use energy to produce movement. Researchers have spent decades trying to recreate these remarkable biological systems artificially, and progress in this field was recognized with the 2016 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
An Ancient Invention Inspires a Molecular Motor
Scientists first developed molecular motors powered directly by electricity in 2011. However, those earlier designs operated on surfaces and relied on the tip of a scanning tunneling microscope to drive their movement.
The new motor takes a different approach, borrowing its basic design from the Archimedes screw, one of the oldest machines in recorded history. Traditionally used to move water uphill, this simple device relies on a rotating spiral to transport material.
Researchers adapted that principle to the molecular scale. Instead of moving water, their design allows electrons to travel through a spiral-shaped molecule, causing it to rotate as electrical current passes through.
A Tiny Molecular Screw Suspended Between Gold Tips
The motor's central component is a specially designed spiral molecule created by the research group of Prof. Michael Pittelkow at the University of Copenhagen. Measuring only a few millionths of a millimeter, the molecule can attach to gold surfaces through sulfur atoms.
At the Weizmann Institute of Science in Israel, researchers led by Prof. Oren Tal and Dr. Anil Kumar Singh positioned individual molecules between two gold tips sharpened to atomic dimensions. By carefully changing the separation between these electrodes, the team could stretch or compress the molecular screw.
When the scientists applied an electrical voltage, measurements revealed that the molecule began rotating. Even more importantly, they could reverse its direction simply by changing the voltage's polarity.
This represents the first demonstration of a molecular motor that is driven by electrical current, firmly connected to two metal electrodes, and capable of rotating in a controllable direction.
How Electricity Makes a Single Molecule Spin
The driving force comes directly from electrons traveling through the spiral molecule. As they move, they transfer angular momentum to the molecular structure, producing rotation in much the same way that moving air turns a wind turbine.
The spiral's shape determines how it responds to this flow, similar to the difference between screws with right- or left-handed threads. Once the applied voltage exceeds a certain threshold, the movement becomes continuous rotation.
But the experiments revealed another intriguing effect. The rotating molecule conducted electricity much more efficiently than it did when stationary, raising an important question about what was happening inside the tiny machine.
Scientists Discover a Surprising 100-Fold Electrical Effect
To investigate this unexpected behavior, Prof. Dr. Fabian Pauly and his PhD students Léon Martin and Yuta Ito, working at the Chair of Theoretical Physics I at the University of Augsburg, used quantum mechanical simulations on the LiCCA supercomputer.
Their calculations revealed a close relationship between the molecule's rotation and its ability to carry electrical current. Conductivity changes dramatically depending on the angle of the molecule, increasing by as much as two orders of magnitude, or 100 times, during rotation.
The reason turned out to be particularly surprising. Some of the molecular positions that allow electricity to pass most easily are also positions that the molecule naturally avoids when it is not moving. Rotation makes those highly conductive arrangements accessible.
"The surprising thing is that it is precisely the positions that the molecule avoids when at rest that conduct electricity best. It is only the rotation that makes these positions accessible," explains Léon Martin.
The finding demonstrates that molecular motion does more than simply consume electrical energy. The movement itself can strongly influence how electricity flows through the machine.
International Collaboration Solves the Mystery
The researchers then worked with theoretical physicists Per Hedegård of the Niels Bohr Institute in Copenhagen and Jing-Tao Lü of Huazhong University of Science and Technology in Wuhan.
Using the simulation results, the scientists developed a simplified theoretical model that successfully recreated both the rotation observed in the experiments and the accompanying increase in electrical current.
This combination of experimental measurements and theoretical calculations was essential to understanding the mechanism. Although researchers could measure the current passing through the molecule, they needed simulations to determine what was happening at such an extraordinarily small scale.
"In the experiment, you only see the current. Our calculations allow us to glimpse what is happening inside the nanocontact. It was only through close collaboration between experiment and theory across several countries that the mystery of the current increase could be solved," says Yuta Ito, a PhD student originally from Japan.
A New Frontier for Molecular Electronics
The achievement could eventually contribute to the development of molecular electronic components and technologies involving spintronics, which uses properties of electrons beyond their electrical charge. It may also offer possibilities for microfluidic systems, which manipulate extremely small quantities of fluids.
Beyond these potential applications, the motor provides scientists with a new way to investigate physical processes at the atomic scale. Its ability to convert electricity into controlled rotation, while allowing that rotation to influence electrical current, introduces a new principle for designing extraordinarily small machines.
"We have shown that an electric current can be used to generate a directed rotation and that this rotation, in turn, controls the current. This is a new operating principle for machines at the very limits of miniaturization," explains Pauly.
The work at the University of Augsburg received funding from the German Research Foundation (DFG) through Collaborative Research Center (SFB) 1585 (project number 492723217). The computational research was conducted using the University of Augsburg's LiCCA supercomputer (DFG project number 499211671).
Additional support for the collaborating institutions came from the European Research Council (ERC, Horizon 2020, Grant 864008), the Israel Science Foundation (2129/23), the Minerva Foundation, the Villum Foundation, the Novo Nordisk Foundation, the Independent Research Fund Denmark (DFF), the National Key Research and Development Program of China, and the National Natural Science Foundation of China.

Russians enter team from occupied Luhansk in Russian Ice Hockey Federation competition
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01

Russians enter team from occupied Luhansk in Russian Ice Hockey Federation competition
Russia has entered an ice hockey team from occupied Luhansk in a competition as part of its continued attempts to integrate Ukraine's occupied territories into its own sports system.
Source: chess grandmaster Peter Heine Nielsen on X (Twitter)
Details: The Diesel team from occupied Luhansk has been entered in the Interregional Competitions of the Southern and North Caucasus Federal Districts.
All the children listed in the team's roster were born in 2014 and 2015: an entire generation of Ukrainian children have been taken from their homeland.
The competition is held under the auspices of the Russian Ice Hockey Federation, which recently secured the Russian national team's return to international competitions through the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS).
This is far from the first attempt by Russia to integrate temporarily occupied territories into its own sports system. Earlier this year, CAS ordered the Russian Chess Federation to withdraw from Ukrainian territories under occupation, but the ruling was ignored.
Later, the International Chess Federation temporarily suspended the Russian Chess Federation over its failure to comply with the CAS ruling.
